stops.caption: You've come up about nine hundred feet, and the reward is the whole city at once.
stops.transcriptText:
You've come up about nine hundred feet, and the reward is the whole city at once. From up here, near the geographic center of San Francisco, you can see almost all of it — the grid of streets running out to the bay, the downtown towers, the two bridges, and on a clear day the hills of the East Bay beyond. This is one of the highest points in the city, and the single best place to understand how San Francisco is actually put together.

Because that's the thing to look at from here — not just the pretty bits, but the pattern. Look at the streets. They run in a dead-straight grid, block after block after block, marching right over the tops of hills and down the other side as if the hills weren't there. San Francisco was laid out on paper by people who loved a clean grid and didn't much care what the land underneath was doing. So you get streets that climb at impossible angles, intersections perched on slopes, that whole vertical rollercoaster the city is famous for. From the ground it feels like chaos. From up here you can see it's the opposite — it's a stubbornly rational plan, slammed down on top of stubbornly irrational terrain, and neither one gave an inch.

Watch the weather, too. If there's fog, this is a great seat for it. The fog comes off the cold Pacific to the west and spills over the hills in slow motion, and Twin Peaks sits right in its path. You can stand up here in bright sun and watch a gray river of cloud pour silently across the neighborhoods below.

One practical note: it's almost always windier and colder up here than down in the city, sometimes dramatically so, so whatever you're wearing, you probably want one more layer. But it's worth it. Most viewpoints just give you a nice picture. This one gives you the logic of the place — the grid against the hills, the fog against the sun — the argument San Francisco has been having with its own landscape since the day it was drawn. Take a minute. Find your hotel. Trace your day. It's all down there.

tours.title: California Academy of Sciences
tours.shortDescription: Renzo Piano's natural-history museum in Golden Gate Park — crowned by a rolling, planted "living roof" of native green hills.
tours.longDescription: Renzo Piano's 2008 building puts an aquarium, planetarium, rainforest, and natural-history museum under one roof — and tops it with a 2.5-acre living roof of rolling green hummocks planted with native species, one of the most-copied pieces of architecture in the city.

stops.title: California Academy of Sciences
stops.caption: Step back far enough to see the roof, because the roof is the whole idea.
stops.transcriptText:
Step back far enough to see the roof, because the roof is the whole idea. It rolls and humps in a series of low green hills, planted edge to edge with living plants, with round skylights set into it like bubbles. That is a living roof — about two and a half acres of native California plants growing on top of the building — and it tells you exactly what kind of museum this is: one that would rather be part of nature than just describe it.

This is the California Academy of Sciences, and the trick of it is what's packed underneath that roof. Most cities make you choose. You go to the aquarium, or the planetarium, or the natural history museum, or the rainforest, on four different days. Here they're all in one building, under one roof. There's a full aquarium below your feet, a planetarium dome you can sit back and watch the universe in, a natural history collection, and — the showstopper — a four-story rainforest sealed inside a giant glass sphere, warm and humid and full of free-flying butterflies and birds, that you climb on a spiral ramp.

The institution itself is old — founded in 1853, which makes it one of the oldest scientific bodies in the West — but this building is new. It was rebuilt in 2008 by the architect Renzo Piano, and that roof isn't just for looks. The hills are shaped to draw warm air up and out through those round skylights, cooling the building without much air conditioning, and the plants soak up rainwater that would otherwise run off. The roof is doing real work.

There's a nice honesty to it, when you think about what a science museum is for. This one doesn't lecture you about the environment from behind glass and then guzzle power doing it. It tries, in its own structure, to behave the way it's telling you to behave — a building that grows a meadow on its head, cools itself with hot air, drinks the rain, and keeps a rainforest breathing inside a bubble. Go in. Look up through the glass sphere at the canopy, then go down and watch the same water in the tanks below. It's the rare museum that's also an argument.

tours.title: Sutro Baths & Lands End
tours.shortDescription: The roofless concrete ruins of the world's largest indoor swimming complex, at the wild cliff edge of Lands End.
tours.longDescription: Adolph Sutro's 1896 Baths enclosed seven saltwater pools under three acres of glass — the largest indoor swimming complex on earth — until it closed and burned in 1966. Its skeletal ruins now sit half-returned to the sea at Lands End, one of the most dramatic walks in the city.

stops.title: Sutro Baths & Lands End
stops.caption: Down below you, at the edge of the surf, are the ruins.
stops.transcriptText:
Down below you, at the edge of the surf, are the ruins. Roofless concrete walls, a grid of rectangular pools now filled with green tidewater and gulls, the bones of something enormous half-returned to the sea. People wander through them today as if they were ancient. They're a little over a century old, and what stood here was one of the most ambitious public pleasures any American city ever built.

This was the Sutro Baths. In 1896 a man named Adolph Sutro — a self-made mining millionaire who would go on to be mayor — opened on this spot a glass-and-iron palace the size of a stadium, filled with swimming pools. Not one or two. Seven of them, most fed straight from the ocean by the tides, ranging from cold seawater to heated, under a vast greenhouse roof. The place could hold something like ten thousand people at once. And Sutro's whole point was that it should be for everyone — cheap enough that an ordinary working family, not just the rich, could come spend a day swimming at the edge of the Pacific.

It never quite paid for itself, the public's tastes changed, and in 1966, as it was being demolished for redevelopment, the whole structure burned. What's left is what you see: the concrete footprint, slowly losing its argument with the ocean.

Just up the bluff is the Cliff House, the big pale building that for generations was the restaurant out at the end of the world. It's been closed since 2020 and its future is uncertain, so don't count on a meal — but the setting is still extraordinary. And the real treasure is the trail from here: the Lands End path, winding along the cliffs through cypress trees, with the Golden Gate Bridge swinging into view and the wrecks of old ships sometimes showing at low tide.

It's a melancholy, beautiful corner, and worth the wind. Stand at the railing over the ruins and picture it full — the glass roof, the steam, ten thousand people laughing in the surf, a rich man's gift to everyone who couldn't afford the sea. Then look at the tide working through the empty pools. Few places hold the whole arc of a grand idea — the dream, the crowds, the slow return to water — as plainly as this one does.

tours.title: Golden Gate Bridge
tours.shortDescription: The bridge almost everyone said couldn't be built — and the International Orange icon that defines the city.
tours.longDescription: Opened in 1937 across a deep, fierce strait that engineers called impossible, the Golden Gate Bridge was for decades the longest suspension span in the world. Its Art Deco towers, painted the warm International Orange that glows in the fog, made it the most recognizable bridge on earth.

stops.title: Golden Gate Bridge
stops.caption: Here it is — the one you came for.
stops.transcriptText:
Here it is — the one you came for. And the first thing worth knowing about the Golden Gate Bridge is that almost everyone said it couldn't be built. The strait it crosses is deep, the current is ferocious, the water is freezing, and the fog and wind come howling in off the open Pacific. For years the conventional wisdom was that no bridge could stand here. They built it anyway, and it opened in 1937.

Look at the towers first. They rise about seven hundred and forty-six feet above the water, and the main span between them stretches a little over four thousand two hundred feet — for nearly thirty years after it opened, the longest suspension span in the world. Everything hangs from those two great cables sweeping between the towers; the whole roadway is essentially dangling from steel rope.

Now the color, because the color was a fight. It's a specific shade called International Orange, and it was not the plan. The Navy wanted the bridge painted in black and yellow stripes so ships could see it. Others pushed for ordinary gray. But the consulting architect, Irving Morrow, noticed that the steel was arriving coated in a burnt-orange primer, and argued hard that this was the color — warm, glowing against the cool blues and grays of the water and sky, and oddly easy to see in fog. He won. The most famous color in American engineering started as a rust-proof undercoat that one man refused to paint over.

One more thing, looking toward the south end. Tucked underneath the bridge down there is Fort Point, a brick fortress from the Civil War era. The bridge's engineers could have simply demolished it. Instead, the chief engineer, Joseph Strauss, threw a special steel arch over the top of it so the old fort could stay. So the bridge actually bends around a building older than itself.

So stand here for a while and take it in. The fog may be pouring through the cables, or the whole thing may be glowing clear in the sun — both are the real bridge. And know that nearly everything you're admiring was an argument someone had to win: that it could be built at all, that it should be orange, that the old fort beneath it was worth bending steel to save. It's not just beautiful. It's a stack of stubborn good decisions, six hundred feet tall.

tours.title: Palace of Fine Arts
tours.shortDescription: Bernard Maybeck's romantic faux-Roman rotunda and colonnade beside a Marina lagoon — the last survivor of the 1915 world's fair.
tours.longDescription: Bernard Maybeck designed the Palace of Fine Arts for the 1915 Panama-Pacific International Exposition as a deliberately melancholy "Roman ruin" — a domed rotunda and curving colonnade reflected in a lagoon. Built to be temporary, it was so loved the city rebuilt it permanently in the 1960s.

stops.title: Palace of Fine Arts
stops.caption: It looks like a Roman ruin that somehow drifted up against a San Francisco lagoon — a great domed rotunda the color of old sand, a sweeping colonnade, all of it weathered and romantic and clearly very old.
stops.transcriptText:
It looks like a Roman ruin that somehow drifted up against a San Francisco lagoon — a great domed rotunda the color of old sand, a sweeping colonnade, all of it weathered and romantic and clearly very old. Here's the joke: it was built to look that way on purpose, and it isn't old at all.

This is the Palace of Fine Arts, and it went up in 1915 for the Panama-Pacific International Exposition — a world's fair San Francisco threw partly to celebrate the opening of the Panama Canal, and partly to announce to the world that the city had fully recovered from the 1906 earthquake. The fair was a temporary fantasy city of palaces along the waterfront, and this was its most beloved building. The architect, Bernard Maybeck, didn't want it to feel triumphant. He wanted it to feel a little sad — the beautiful melancholy of a classical ruin, the sense of something grand slowly decaying. So he designed a brand-new building to look like a magnificent wreck.

Look closely at the colonnade and you'll catch the detail that gives the game away. On top of the columns are large urns, and around them, women carved with their backs turned outward, leaning over as if weeping into the planters. Maybeck meant them as a meditation on the sadness of life without art. A fake ruin, built to mourn.

And here's the lovely twist. The whole fair was meant to be torn down when it ended, and almost all of it was. But San Franciscans loved this melancholy ruin so much they couldn't bear to lose it. It was patched and propped up for decades, and finally, in the 1960s, completely rebuilt in permanent materials so it would last. A building designed to look like it was crumbling refused to actually crumble, because the city wouldn't let it.

So walk the colonnade, sit by the lagoon with the swans and the wedding photographers, and enjoy the strangeness of it. You're standing in a deliberate illusion — a hundred-year-old monument to the idea of ruins, made to look ancient, built to be temporary, and saved out of pure affection. It's the most sincere fake in San Francisco, and one of the most beautiful spots in the city to do nothing at all.

tours.title: Fisherman's Wharf
tours.shortDescription: The old working waterfront at the north edge of the city — a fishing port since the Gold Rush, now equal parts crab stands, sea air, and tourist bustle.
tours.longDescription: Fisherman's Wharf grew from the Italian fishing families who worked these waters from the 1850s on, and a small commercial fleet still ties up here. Behind the crab-wheel sign and the souvenir crowds, Pier 45, the lateen-rigged boats, and the smell of cracked Dungeness keep the old port alive.

stops.title: Fisherman's Wharf
stops.caption: Stand at the foot of Taylor Street, where the sidewalk runs out and the harbor begins.
stops.transcriptText:
Stand at the foot of Taylor Street, where the sidewalk runs out and the harbor begins. Most people come to Fisherman's Wharf for the things behind you — the t-shirt racks, the wax museum, the sourdough shaped like a crab, the guy who's been hiding behind a bush startling tourists since the Reagan administration. Turn the other way.

In front of you is a working harbor. Not a reproduction of one. A real one, still going, though smaller every year.

Look at the boats first. The squat wooden ones with the high curved bows are Monterey hulls — "Monterey clippers" — the design Italian fishermen brought to this coast more than a century ago, built to take a beating from the Pacific and still come home loaded. Many of the boats in front of you go out before dawn. The catch that built this place, and still defines it, is Dungeness crab — the season opens in November, and when it's running, the docks here smell like salt and diesel and the cold, sweet funk of fresh shellfish.

The fleet that fishes out of here was founded by Genoese and Sicilian families, and before them by Chinese fishermen who were pushed out by law in the late 1800s. The Italian names on the old restaurants — Alioto, Tarantino, Sabella — were fishing families first and restaurant families second. They sold their catch off the back of the boat, then opened a stand, then a dining room. The trap, in other words, grew out of the trade.

Here's the thing worth standing here for. Everyone calls Fisherman's Wharf a tourist trap, and they're not wrong. But underneath the souvenir city is the actual reason it exists, still happening, just out of frame: a few dozen real boats, a real catch, a real fleet hanging on against rising costs and shrinking waters. The spectacle didn't replace the fishery. It grew on top of it, like a barnacle — and now it's the thing keeping the barnacle's host alive.

So before you buy the crab, walk down to Fish Alley, behind the restaurants on Jefferson Street, where the boats actually unload. That's the Wharf the postcards forgot — and it's the only part that was ever really here.

tours.title: Hyde Street Pier
tours.shortDescription: A pier of historic ships at the foot of Hyde Street — a floating museum of the vessels that built the Pacific coast.
tours.longDescription: Hyde Street Pier, the heart of San Francisco Maritime National Historical Park, berths a fleet of preserved working ships: the square-rigger Balclutha, the side-wheel ferry Eureka, the schooner C.A. Thayer. Before the bridges, boats like these were how the West Coast moved its people and its cargo.

stops.title: Hyde Street Pier
stops.caption: You're standing on Hyde Street Pier, and the first thing to understand is that this isn't a museum about ships.
stops.transcriptText:
You're standing on Hyde Street Pier, and the first thing to understand is that this isn't a museum about ships. It's a parking lot for them — a working pier turned into a place to keep the actual vessels that built this coast floating, where they belong.

Look at the big one with three masts and the black-and-white hull. That's the Balclutha, launched in Scotland in 1886, and she's no replica or stage set. She rounded Cape Horn — the brutal passage at the bottom of South America — seventeen times, hauling grain, coal, and lumber back when that journey was simply how cargo crossed the world. Walk her deck later and you're standing where sailors stood through storms that sank plenty of ships just like her.

Now find the wide, blunt-faced boat that looks like a floating building. That's the Eureka, and in her day she was the largest passenger ferry in the world. Before the bridges, this is how you crossed the bay — you and your car packed onto a boat like this, chugging from San Francisco to Sausalito or Oakland, thousands of people and over a hundred cars at a time, all day, every day.

Which gets at the thing this pier is quietly telling you.

For most of San Francisco's history, the bay wasn't an obstacle. It was the highway — the fastest, and sometimes the only, way to move people and freight around the region. The ships tied up here were the trucks, the ferries, and the freighters of their age, and the water was thick with them. Then, in 1936 and 1937, the Bay Bridge and the Golden Gate opened within months of each other, and within a few short years the whole system of ferries and sailing freight was simply over. The Eureka isn't just an old boat. She's the thing the bridges replaced.

So the next time you drive across the Golden Gate, picture this: a few decades earlier, you'd have made the same crossing the slow way, standing at the rail of a boat like the Eureka, watching the fog come in. These ships didn't retire because they failed. They retired because we built something faster overhead — and somebody had the sense to keep a few of them tied up right here, so we could remember what the bay used to be.

tours.title: City Lights & Kerouac Alley
tours.shortDescription: The North Beach bookstore that published Ginsberg's "Howl" and stood trial for it — birthplace of the Beat movement, beside the alley named for Kerouac.
tours.longDescription: Lawrence Ferlinghetti's City Lights opened in 1953 as the first all-paperback bookstore in the country and became the publisher of Allen Ginsberg's "Howl" — the obscenity trial that followed, and its acquittal, was a landmark for free speech. The painted alley alongside honors Jack Kerouac and the Beat writers who made this corner their own.

stops.title: City Lights & Kerouac Alley
stops.caption: There's a small bookstore on the triangular corner ahead of you, where Columbus cuts across the grid, and it looks like exactly what it is: three crammed floors of paperbacks, a poetry room up top, hand-lettered signs telling you to sit down and read.
stops.transcriptText:
There's a small bookstore on the triangular corner ahead of you, where Columbus cuts across the grid, and it looks like exactly what it is: three crammed floors of paperbacks, a poetry room up top, hand-lettered signs telling you to sit down and read. What it doesn't look like is a place that changed American law. It did.

City Lights opened in 1953, founded by the poet Lawrence Ferlinghetti and a partner named Peter Martin, as the country's first all-paperback bookstore — a genuinely radical idea back when paperbacks were treated as cheap and disposable. That alone would have earned it a footnote. But in 1956, City Lights published a thin book of poems by a young writer named Allen Ginsberg, and the book was called Howl.

It was raw, furious, and sexually frank, and the authorities came for it. In 1957 the store's manager was arrested and Ferlinghetti was charged with selling an obscene book. The trial that followed wasn't really about one poem. It was about whether the government got to decide what Americans were allowed to read.

Ferlinghetti won. The judge ruled that a work with — in the court's phrase — redeeming social importance could not be banned as obscene, no matter how much it offended. That single ruling cracked the door open for nearly everything that came after it: the books that could finally be printed, sold, and argued about in the open.

And that's the reframe worth standing here for. People treat this corner as a shrine to the Beat poets — and it is one; Ginsberg, Kerouac, and the whole restless crowd drank across the alley at Vesuvio and argued here for years. But the monument isn't the poetry. The monument is the verdict. City Lights matters less as a clubhouse than as the place that went to court for the right to sell a difficult book, and won.

Step into the alley on the north side of the store. It's named for Jack Kerouac, and the pavement is set with quotes pressed into the stone. Then go inside, climb to the poetry room, and pull something off the shelf. You're allowed to stand there and read the whole thing — the signs say so, and a courtroom once said so too.

tours.title: Washington Square
tours.shortDescription: North Beach's village green, framed by the white twin spires of Saints Peter and Paul Church — the heart of San Francisco's Little Italy.
tours.longDescription: Washington Square is the social center of North Beach: morning tai chi on the lawn, Italian cafés around the edges, and the soaring marble-white facade of Saints Peter and Paul Church — "the Italian Cathedral of the West" — closing the north side. (Not to be confused with New York's Washington Square.)

stops.title: Washington Square
stops.caption: Find a bench in the open green and look across at the church with the two white spires.
stops.transcriptText:
Find a bench in the open green and look across at the church with the two white spires. This is Washington Square, one of the oldest parks in the city, and almost nothing here is quite what its name promises.

Start with the statue near the center. In a square named for Washington, you'd reasonably expect George Washington. It's Benjamin Franklin. He's stood here since the 1870s, put up by a dentist and temperance crusader who — fittingly — plumbed the base to dispense free drinking water. The square kept Washington's name and got somebody else's monument: the first of several small switches you're surrounded by.

Now the church. Saints Peter and Paul, finished in 1924, the twin-spired heart of what was once a densely Italian North Beach. They called it the Italian Cathedral of the West, and it anchored a neighborhood of Genoese and Sicilian families — often the same families who fished the wharf a few blocks downhill.

Here's the detail people come looking for. In 1954, Joe DiMaggio and Marilyn Monroe stood on the steps of this church and were photographed by what felt like every newspaper on earth. It became one of the most famous wedding-day images of the century — except they weren't married here. DiMaggio had been divorced, so the church wouldn't perform the ceremony; they'd married that morning at City Hall, and came here only for the pictures. Another substitution. The image everyone remembers is of a wedding that never happened on these steps.

And that's the quiet truth of this square — a place of stand-ins and overlaps, layered rather than fixed. The Italian neighborhood that built the church has largely moved on, out to the avenues, while Chinatown presses in from the south.

So on a given morning you'll see the result: rows of people, many of them Chinese, moving slowly through tai chi on the grass of a square named for Washington, in front of an Italian church, watched over by a statue of Franklin. Stay a few minutes and watch the green fill up. Nothing here matches its label, and somehow it all fits together anyway — which is about as San Francisco as a single block gets.

tours.title: Waverly Place
tours.shortDescription: Chinatown's "Street of the Painted Balconies" — a two-block lane stacked with brilliantly colored temple and association balconies.
tours.longDescription: Waverly Place runs just two blocks through the heart of Chinatown, lined with the ornate painted balconies of family associations and temples — among them Tin How, one of the oldest Chinese temples in the United States, perched on an upper floor. It's the neighborhood's most atmospheric lane, and a fixture of its literature.

stops.title: Waverly Place
stops.caption: You're on Waverly Place, a two-block lane running parallel to Grant, and the trick to this street is simple: don't look at the shops.
stops.transcriptText:
You're on Waverly Place, a two-block lane running parallel to Grant, and the trick to this street is simple: don't look at the shops. Look up.

They call this the Street of Painted Balconies, and once you raise your eyes you'll see why. The upper floors are banded in color — deep reds, golds, greens, jade blues — tier on tier of carved and painted balconies climbing three and four stories over your head. It's the most beautiful street in Chinatown, and almost all of its beauty is above eye level, which is the whole point.

Here's why it's up there. When Chinatown rebuilt after the 1906 fire, the neighborhood was hemmed in — boxed by hostile city politics, denied room to spread out. So it grew the only direction left: up. The ground floors went to shops and restaurants, the rent-payers. But the soul of the community — the family associations, the social clubs, and above all the temples — climbed to the top floors, where the air was cleaner and the spirits, by tradition, belong closer to the sky.

Find number one-twenty-five. On its top floor sits the Tin How Temple, founded in 1852, generally called the oldest Chinese temple in the United States. It's dedicated to Tin How — the goddess who protects sailors and travelers — which makes sense for a community that crossed an ocean to get here. To reach it you climb several narrow flights past the association offices, and you emerge into a small, red, incense-thick room hung with hundreds of gold lanterns, suspended right over the street you were just standing on.

And that's the thing worth carrying with you down the block. The Chinatown most visitors photograph is the ground-floor one — the lanterns and souvenirs along Grant. But the real one was built upward, deliberately, a vertical neighborhood stacked floor by floor because that was the only room it was allowed. The temples on the top floors aren't hidden by accident. They're up there on purpose — and the only way to find them is to stop, on a lane like this one, and look up.

tours.title: Ross Alley
tours.shortDescription: Chinatown's oldest alley — a narrow brick lane home to the Golden Gate Fortune Cookie Factory, where the cookies are still folded by hand.
tours.longDescription: Ross Alley is said to be the oldest alley in Chinatown, once lined with gambling halls and now best known for the tiny Golden Gate Fortune Cookie Factory, where workers fold warm cookies by hand on small rotating griddles. The crooked, film-friendly lane has stood in for old Chinatown in more than one movie.

stops.title: Ross Alley
stops.caption: Step into Ross Alley and the noise of Grant Avenue drops away.
stops.transcriptText:
Step into Ross Alley and the noise of Grant Avenue drops away. It's narrow, a single block, brick on both sides — one of the oldest alleys in the city, and for a long stretch of its life one of the most notorious, lined with gambling dens and worse. Today it's quiet, photogenic, a favorite of film crews. But halfway down you'll find a small open doorway, and the smell coming out of it — warm, sweet, vanilla — is the reason most people come.

This is the Golden Gate Fortune Cookie Factory, and inside, women sit at small rotating griddles folding fortune cookies by hand, one at a time, the way it's been done here for decades. Watch for a minute. A flat, hot disc comes off the iron, a paper slip goes in, and three quick folds turn it into the shape you know. It's mesmerizing, and it's a good place to buy a warm bag straight off the griddle.

Now, the cookie itself — here's the part worth knowing. The fortune cookie is one of the most "Chinese" things in the American imagination, and it isn't Chinese at all. You won't find it in China; people there often find it baffling. Its real roots trace to Japan — a grilled cracker with a paper fortune tucked inside — brought to California by Japanese immigrants around the turn of the last century, including, by the most common account, the family that ran the Japanese Tea Garden across town in Golden Gate Park.

San Francisco claims it invented the fortune cookie. So does Los Angeles, loudly, and the two cities have genuinely feuded over it — there was even a mock trial. The honest answer is that nobody can fully prove it, so treat the claim as exactly that: a claim, and a very San Francisco one.

Which is the real story of this little cookie. The thing the whole world reads as ancient Chinese wisdom is actually an immigrant invention — Japanese in origin, Chinese-American by adoption, born somewhere in California — that became a cliché before anyone thought to ask where it came from. Crack one open before you leave. The fortune won't be true. The history behind the cookie is the better one anyway.

tours.title: Transamerica Pyramid
tours.shortDescription: The 853-foot tapering spire that became the city's signature skyline silhouette — controversial when built, beloved ever since.
tours.longDescription: William Pereira's 1972 Transamerica Pyramid was attacked as a gimmick when it rose over the Financial District, but its tapering form — designed to throw less shadow and let more light to the streets — became the defining shape of the San Francisco skyline, on the site of the old Montgomery Block.

stops.title: Transamerica Pyramid
stops.caption: Stand back far enough to take in the whole shape — the white spire narrowing to a point above the Financial District.
stops.transcriptText:
Stand back far enough to take in the whole shape — the white spire narrowing to a point above the Financial District. You know this building even if you've never been to San Francisco. It's on the postcards, the souvenir mugs, the logo of half the local businesses in town. The Transamerica Pyramid is the city's signature, its most recognizable silhouette. And when it was proposed, people despised it.

Go back to 1969. San Francisco was a city of flat-topped towers and bay windows, and the architect William Pereira handed it a four-sided pyramid, eight hundred and fifty-three feet of it, tapering to a hollow spire. Critics called it an insult to the skyline. There were protests. The nicknames were unprintable. A building that's now beloved arrived as something close to a civic scandal.

It opened in 1972 and held the title of the city's tallest for more than forty years. The shape, it turned out, was practical — the taper lets more light reach the streets below than a boxy tower would, and as it narrows the upper floors get smaller, ending in that pointed crown that's purely there to be looked at. There's nothing functional in the top spire at all. It exists to give the building its profile.

Now walk to the base, on the Washington Street side, into Redwood Park. Here's the surprise the skyline doesn't tell you: at the foot of this tower is a small grove of coast redwoods, transplanted from the Santa Cruz Mountains, growing in the middle of the Financial District. A 2024 renovation reopened the grove and the lobby to the public, so you can sit under real redwoods with the glass canyons of downtown rising all around you.

And that's the quiet lesson of this place. The most distinctive thing on the San Francisco skyline is the one the city fought hardest to keep out. People wanted it gone; now they can't imagine the view without it. Tastes change, and the buildings we're sure we hate have a way of becoming the ones we put on the postcard — a useful thing to remember the next time something new goes up and everyone tells you it ruins everything.

tours.title: Union Square
tours.shortDescription: Downtown's central plaza, crowned by the Dewey Monument column — the city's premier shopping district and civic gathering place.
tours.longDescription: Union Square took its name from pro-Union rallies held here on the eve of the Civil War. The granite column at its center, topped by a bronze Victory, commemorates Admiral Dewey's 1898 victory at Manila Bay. Today the plaza anchors the city's flagship shopping district and its holiday crowds. (Distinct from New York's Union Square.)

stops.title: Union Square
stops.caption: You're standing in Union Square, the city's front room — a single block of open granite ringed by department stores and hotels, the place San Francisco does its shopping, its protesting, its ice-skating at Christmas, and a fair amount of its people-watching.
stops.transcriptText:
You're standing in Union Square, the city's front room — a single block of open granite ringed by department stores and hotels, the place San Francisco does its shopping, its protesting, its ice-skating at Christmas, and a fair amount of its people-watching. Most people pass through it on the way to a store. Give it five minutes and it pays you back.

Start with the name, because it isn't about labor unions or the shape of the streets. In the eighteen-sixties, on the eve of the Civil War, this was the spot where San Franciscans held mass rallies in support of the Union — for keeping the country together. The name stuck, a small political fossil sitting in the middle of the luxury district.

Now look at the tall column in the center, with the bronze figure on top. That's the Dewey Monument, raised in 1903 to mark Admiral Dewey's naval victory at Manila Bay. It came through the 1906 earthquake standing, while much of the city around it fell. But the better story is the figure herself — Victory, holding a wreath and a trident. The sculptor needed a model, and he chose a tall young working-class woman named Alma de Bretteville, who posed for the goddess for a few dollars.

Here's where it turns into a fairy tale. That same Alma later married Adolph Spreckels, heir to a sugar fortune, became one of the richest women in the city, and spent decades giving the money away — she's the reason the Legion of Honor museum out at Lands End exists. So the goddess of Victory on this column isn't an abstraction. She's a real San Francisco woman, modeled before she was wealthy, watching over the shopping district she'd one day help shape.

That's the trick of Union Square. It looks like pure commerce — flagship stores, glossy windows, somebody always handing out samples. But the granite under your feet remembers Civil War rallies, the column remembers a war most people have forgotten, and the woman on top climbed from a few-dollar modeling job to one of the great fortunes in the city. Stay on a bench a while. The square is busier with history than it lets on.

tours.title: Nob Hill
tours.shortDescription: The hilltop where the railroad barons built their mansions — almost all lost in 1906, leaving the brownstone Flood Mansion as the lone survivor.
tours.longDescription: Nob Hill was the address of the "Big Four" railroad magnates, whose ostentatious mansions crowned the city until the 1906 fire swept them away. Only James Flood's brownstone survived — now the Pacific-Union Club — alongside the grand hotels, the Fairmont among them, that rose from the ashes on the same proud height.

stops.title: Nob Hill
stops.caption: You've made it to the top of Nob Hill — and notice it actually is a climb, which is the whole reason this place exists.
stops.transcriptText:
You've made it to the top of Nob Hill — and notice it actually is a climb, which is the whole reason this place exists. In the eighteen-seventies, when cable cars finally made these slopes livable, the men who'd just gotten very rich building the transcontinental railroad raced to the top and put their mansions where everyone below could see them. The hill's name is a clipped version of "nabob" — an old word for someone newly, conspicuously wealthy. Locals had a sharper version: Snob Hill.

The kings of the hill were the so-called Big Four — Crocker, Huntington, Hopkins, Stanford — railroad barons whose wooden palaces sprawled across these blocks in a competition of pure ostentation. And then, in 1906, the earthquake and the fire that followed erased nearly all of it. The wooden mansions burned to their foundations in an afternoon.

Look across to the brownstone building that's now the Pacific-Union Club. That one survived — it was the Flood mansion, built of Connecticut stone instead of wood, and its walls were about the only thing on the hilltop the fire couldn't take. It's the last of the barons' houses left standing.

Here's what's interesting about what came next. The families didn't rebuild their private palaces. The empty lots became hotels — the Fairmont, the Mark Hopkins, the Huntington — and Grace Cathedral rose on land the Crocker family gave away. The fire turned a hill of private wealth into a hill of public luxury. Where you once needed to be a railroad baron to get past the gate, you can now ride a cable car up, walk into the Mark Hopkins, and take the elevator to the Top of the Mark — a sky-high bar where, during the Second World War, sailors shipping out to the Pacific drank a last round and their wives watched the convoys sail under the Golden Gate. They called one window Weepers' Corner.

So stand here a moment and read the hill correctly. It was built as a monument to keeping people out, then rebuilt, by accident of disaster, as a place that lets people in. Ride the cable car down when you're done. It's the same machine that made the climb worth it in the first place.

tours.title: SFMOMA
tours.shortDescription: The San Francisco Museum of Modern Art — Mario Botta's striped brick-and-skylight landmark, doubled in size by Snøhetta's rippling white addition.
tours.longDescription: SFMOMA opened its Mario Botta building in 1995, a banded brick mass split by a great cylindrical oculus — the first museum on the West Coast devoted to 20th-century art. Snøhetta's 2016 expansion folded a rippling ten-story white wall around it, making it one of the largest modern-art museums in the country.

stops.title: SFMOMA
stops.caption: You're on Third Street, looking at two buildings pretending to be one.
stops.transcriptText:
You're on Third Street, looking at two buildings pretending to be one. The older part, down at street level, is a stout brick block with a wide black-and-white striped cylinder rising out of its center like an eye turned up at the sky — that's the original San Francisco Museum of Modern Art, designed by Mario Botta and opened in 1995. Then, behind and above it, a great rippling white wall billows upward like a sheet caught in the wind. That's the part that doubled the place.

The white addition opened in 2016, designed by the Norwegian firm Snøhetta, and its wavy skin is meant to echo both fog and bay water — though most people just find it strange and beautiful and slightly hard to photograph. Behind it, the museum roughly tripled its gallery space, turning a respectable city museum into one of the largest spaces for modern and contemporary art in the country.

But the detail worth walking around for is on the third-floor outdoor terrace, where you'll find a living wall — a vertical garden of tens of thousands of plants, nearly all of them native to this region, one of the largest public living walls in the United States. It's a piece of the building that grows, breathes, and changes with the seasons, hung right there among the sculpture.

Here's the part I like best, and it's free. When the museum expanded, it pushed art down to the ground floor and out toward the street, so a good stretch of it costs nothing to see. You can walk in off the sidewalk and stand in front of a towering Richard Serra sculpture — sheets of rust-colored steel curving over your head, taller than you'll expect — without ever buying a ticket. The art comes out to meet the city instead of hiding behind the admissions desk.

And that's the quiet argument this whole building makes. A modern art museum can feel like a locked white box, intimidating by design. This one did the opposite — it grew a wall that's alive, set sculpture at street level for anyone walking by, and made the threshold low on purpose. Go in for the free floors at least. The hardest part of a museum like this is usually deciding to walk through the door, and here they've made that part easy.

tours.title: Dolores Park
tours.shortDescription: The Mission's sunny hillside gathering spot — palm-lined lawns, a downtown skyline view, and the city's most social patch of grass.
tours.longDescription: Mission Dolores Park sits in one of the sunniest microclimates in San Francisco, and on a warm weekend the terraced lawns fill with the whole city: picnics, music, dogs, vendors. From the upper slope the view runs across the Mission rooftops to the downtown towers.

stops.title: Dolores Park
stops.caption: Find a spot on the slope facing northeast, looking downhill toward the city.
stops.transcriptText:
Find a spot on the slope facing northeast, looking downhill toward the city. On a sunny weekend this is the most San Francisco scene there is: a green hillside packed shoulder to shoulder, music drifting from a dozen directions, the downtown skyline framed by palm trees, and the whole sloping lawn tipped toward the view like a giant set of bleachers. This is Dolores Park — the city's communal backyard.

It works because of the tilt. The land rises as it runs west, which turns the whole park into natural seating angled at the skyline. People sort themselves across it almost by neighborhood: families and dogs lower down, the sunny southwest corner long known as a gathering spot for the city's queer community, everybody arranged on the grass like a crowd that showed up early for a show that never quite starts.

But the ground under all this leisure has a heavier past, and it's worth knowing. For decades these two blocks were Jewish cemeteries — until the city, running out of room, relocated nearly all its dead to the south early in the twentieth century. And in 1906, when the earthquake and fire drove tens of thousands from their homes, this hillside became a refugee camp, rows of army tents covering the slope where the picnic blankets are now.

That's the quiet thing to hold while you sit here. San Francisco has a habit of turning solemn ground into a place to lie in the sun — of letting a hillside that once held graves and then held the homeless become, a century later, the city's favorite spot to do absolutely nothing on a Saturday. It isn't disrespect. It's more like the city's deepest reflex: take what was hard, and make it a place to gather.

So stay a while. Watch the skyline catch the late light, listen to the overlapping music, let the slope do its job. You're sitting in the city's living room, on ground that has been a graveyard and a disaster camp and is now, simply, where San Francisco comes to be together. Few places carry their history this lightly — or this well.

tours.title: Balmy & Clarion Alleys
tours.shortDescription: Two Mission District lanes wall-to-wall with murals — the dense heart of the city's street-art and Chicano-mural tradition.
tours.longDescription: Balmy Alley has been a canvas since the 1970s, when Mission artists began painting its fences and garage doors with murals of Central American solidarity and Latino life — the densest concentration in the city. Clarion Alley, a few blocks north, carries that tradition forward with constantly changing political street art.

stops.title: Balmy & Clarion Alleys
stops.caption: You're in the Mission, in front of a wall that's talking.
stops.transcriptText:
You're in the Mission, in front of a wall that's talking. Whichever alley you've started in — Balmy, down off Twenty-fourth Street, or Clarion, over near Valencia — the rule is the same: every surface is painted, top to bottom, fence to garage door, and none of it is decoration. These are two of the most concentrated mural alleys in the country, and they're the loud, painted heart of a neighborhood that has used its walls to talk for fifty years.

Start with Balmy Alley, the older of the two. The murals here began in the nineteen-seventies and eighties, and many of the earliest were explicitly political — made by Latino artists in solidarity with people living through the wars and upheavals of Central America, the Mission being home to families who'd fled exactly those places. Walk it slowly. Among the bright, dense imagery you'll find grief, protest, memory, and celebration, often on the same wall.

Then there's Clarion Alley, started in 1992 by a collective of artists, and it runs hotter and rougher — more punk, more queer, more openly furious. Its defining feature is that it never holds still. Murals here are painted over, replaced, and renewed constantly, so the alley you see today is not the one from two years ago, and won't be the one two years from now.

And that's the reframe worth carrying out of here. We tend to treat murals as monuments — finished, fixed, protected behind a velvet rope of respect. These aren't that. They're a conversation, an argument the neighborhood keeps having with itself and with the wider world: about immigration, displacement, police, gentrification, identity, joy. A wall says something; the times change; someone paints a reply. The art being temporary isn't a flaw. It's the entire point.

Take your time, and read it as the living thing it is. The Mission has been pushed and pulled for decades — newcomers and rising rents pressing against a deep Latino community that built this place. These alleys are where that whole struggle gets said out loud, in color, where everyone can see it. Come back in a year and some of it will be gone, replaced by something newer and just as urgent. That's not the art failing to last. That's the neighborhood still speaking.

tours.title: Castro Theatre
tours.shortDescription: The 1922 movie palace at the heart of the Castro — a Spanish-Colonial landmark famous for its Wurlitzer organ and its neon blade sign.
tours.longDescription: Timothy Pflueger designed the Castro Theatre in 1922, a lavish Spanish-Colonial movie palace with a cast-plaster ceiling and a mighty Wurlitzer that still rises before screenings. Its neon marquee presides over the Castro, and for decades it has been the spiritual home of the city's film festivals and sing-along revivals.

stops.title: Castro Theatre
stops.caption: Stand across the street so you can see the whole front — the great neon blade sign spelling out CASTRO down the side of the building, the marquee below it, the Spanish-cathedral facade rising behind.
stops.transcriptText:
Stand across the street so you can see the whole front — the great neon blade sign spelling out CASTRO down the side of the building, the marquee below it, the Spanish-cathedral facade rising behind. This is the Castro Theatre, opened in 1922, one of the last great movie palaces left standing in America and, for generations, the beating heart of queer San Francisco.

Step inside later and look up — the ceiling is the showpiece, a vast plaster fantasy cast to look like the inside of a tent, dripping with ornament, anchored by a chandelier. The architect was Timothy Pflueger, a local who gave the city some of its most theatrical interiors. For decades, before the lights went down, an organist rose on a lift playing the mighty house organ, the whole crowd singing along, and the film didn't start until the organ sank back into the floor. This wasn't just a theater. It was a congregation.

Which is exactly why what happened next mattered so much. By the twenty-twenties the building was failing — water damage, old wiring, no real climate control — and a concert company took over with a forty-one-million-dollar plan to save it. The work reopened the Castro in early 2026, and it is genuinely restored: the ceiling glows, the neon blazes, a new organ, billed as the largest of its kind, sits where the old one did.

But the rescue came with a fight, and you should know about it. To make the place pay for itself, the new operators pulled out the fixed, sloped rows of cinema seats and replaced them with movable tiers, so the room can hold concerts and standing crowds as well as films. Many in the Castro fought hard against it — they didn't want their movie palace, their queer cultural sanctuary, turned into a flexible event space, and they pushed for nonprofit hands instead. The other side argued, just as sincerely, that a theater that can't pay its bills doesn't survive at all, and a changed Castro beats a shuttered one.

Both sides love this building. That's what makes it hard. So stand here and hold the real question it poses: when a beloved place is dying, do you save it by keeping it exactly as it was — or by letting it change enough to live? There's no clean answer. There's just this theater, lit up again, and a neighborhood still arguing about what it costs to keep something alive.

tours.title: Harvey Milk & the Castro
tours.shortDescription: The plaza and storefront where Harvey Milk ran his camera shop and his campaigns — ground zero of the gay-rights movement, under the giant rainbow flag.
tours.longDescription: From his Castro Camera shop at 575 Castro, Harvey Milk built the campaign that made him one of the first openly gay elected officials in the country, before his 1978 assassination. The neighborhood remains the symbolic capital of LGBTQ life, marked by the giant rainbow flag flying over Harvey Milk Plaza.

stops.title: Harvey Milk & the Castro
stops.caption: Look up at the rainbow flag flying over the plaza at Castro and Market.
stops.transcriptText:
Look up at the rainbow flag flying over the plaza at Castro and Market. It's enormous, deliberately so, and it marks this corner as the symbolic capital of gay America. The flag itself was designed here, in this neighborhood, in 1978 — and the reason this corner became a capital at all comes down largely to one man who ran a camera shop a few blocks up the street.

Walk up Castro to number five-seventy-five. Today it's a storefront with a plaque, but in the nineteen-seventies it was Castro Camera, and behind the counter was Harvey Milk. He hadn't planned to be a politician. He came to San Francisco, opened a shop, and watched gay people pour into this neighborhood from all over the country — drawn here because here, finally, they could live openly. Milk turned his store into an unofficial community center and himself into its loudest advocate, and people started calling him the Mayor of Castro Street long before he held any office.

In 1977 he won a seat on the Board of Supervisors, becoming one of the first openly gay people elected to public office anywhere in the country. He served barely eleven months. In November of 1978 he was assassinated inside City Hall, together with Mayor George Moscone — a loss this neighborhood has never really stopped feeling, and one it marks every year with a candlelight march down Market Street.

But here's what Milk understood, and why this corner matters more than his short time in office would suggest. His whole strategy was visibility. He believed the single most powerful political act a gay person could perform was simply to be known — to come out, to families, to coworkers, to neighbors — because it's harder to fear or legislate against people you actually love. He pushed people to do it relentlessly, and he led by example, living his life completely in the open at a time when that took real courage.

That's the idea this giant flag is really flying for. Not a man — though he's worth remembering — but a conviction: that being seen, plainly and without apology, changes the world more than almost anything else. Stand under it a moment. The whole neighborhood below you is what happens when a lot of people decide to stop hiding.

tours.title: de Young Museum
tours.shortDescription: Golden Gate Park's fine-arts museum — Herzog & de Meuron's perforated-copper building, topped by the twisting Hamon observation tower.
tours.longDescription: Rebuilt after the 1989 earthquake, the de Young reopened in 2005 as a Herzog & de Meuron design clad in dimpled, perforated copper meant to weather green over time, with a torqued nine-story Hamon Tower offering a free view across the park. It holds the city's collection of American, Oceanic, and African art.

stops.title: de Young Museum
stops.caption: Stand in front of the de Young, in the heart of Golden Gate Park, and the first thing to make peace with is the color.
stops.transcriptText:
Stand in front of the de Young, in the heart of Golden Gate Park, and the first thing to make peace with is the color. The whole building is sheathed in copper — dimpled, perforated, and embossed all over its surface — and when it opened in 2005 a lot of people thought it looked like a battleship that had wandered into the trees. Give it time. The architects, the Swiss firm Herzog and de Meuron, knew exactly what they were doing, and they were playing a long game.

Look closely at that copper skin. It's punched and textured to mimic the pattern of light falling through a forest canopy — leaves, dapples, shadow. And copper does one thing reliably over time: it weathers. The architects designed this building to corrode on purpose, so that as the decades pass the bright metal turns a soft, mottled green and the whole museum slowly dissolves, visually, into the surrounding park. It's a building engineered to disappear.

The museum holds American art, and art from across the Pacific, Africa, and the Americas — well worth a few hours. But there's one part you can enjoy for nothing, and it's the reason a lot of locals come. At one end the building twists upward into the Hamon Tower, and the observation floor at the top is free. No ticket, no gallery admission. You ride up, step out, and get a glassed-in, three-hundred-sixty-degree view over the whole park, the avenues, and out to the ocean.

That free tower is the generous heart of the place. A museum could easily charge for the best view in the park; this one decided the view belonged to everybody, members and passersby alike, and just gave it away.

So take the elevator up first, before you decide anything else. Get the lay of the land — the green canopy you're standing in, the city beyond it, the Pacific at the edge. Then come back down and look at that copper one more time, and picture it fifty years from now, gone soft and green, the building finally keeping its promise to vanish into the trees it was always trying to become.

tours.title: Chinatown: The City That Refused to Move
tours.shortDescription: A walk through the oldest Chinatown in North America — where the curved roofs and dragon lamps are a century-old act of self-defense.
tours.longDescription: After the 1906 earthquake leveled the neighborhood, powerful interests tried to push San Francisco's Chinese residents to the city's edge and seize this downtown-adjacent land. The community fought back with architecture — rebuilding on the same ground, deliberately more theatrical and "Chinese" than before, to make Chinatown an attraction too valuable to bulldoze. This five-stop walk runs from the Dragon Gate up Grant Avenue through the painted lanes of Waverly Place and Ross Alley to Portsmouth Square, the neighborhood's living room and the spot where the American flag was first raised over the city.

stops.title: Welcome to Chinatown
stops.caption: Before you take a step, here's the idea that makes this walk worth doing.
stops.transcriptText:
Before you take a step, here's the idea that makes this walk worth doing. You're about to walk through the oldest Chinatown in North America — and almost everything you'll find charming about it, the curved roofs, the dragon lamps, the color, was a deliberate act of self-defense.

Here's why. In 1906, the earthquake and the fire that followed leveled this neighborhood completely, and a lot of powerful people in San Francisco saw an opportunity: clear the Chinese residents out, push them to the edge of the city, and take this valuable downtown-adjacent land for themselves. The community fought back — and they fought back, in part, with architecture. Merchants and their architects rebuilt Chinatown on the same ground, but flashier, more theatrical, more "Chinese" than it had ever actually looked, on purpose. The bet was simple: make it a place the whole city wants to visit, an attraction too valuable to bulldoze, and you make it permanent. It worked. What looks like decoration is really a survival strategy a century old.

So as we walk, look past the souvenir shops and read the neighborhood as what it is: a city within the city that refused to be moved.

The good news for your feet: this is one of the flattest, tightest walks in San Francisco. Four stops, a handful of blocks, no real hills until the very end. We'll start at the grand front door, work our way up Grant and into the back alleys where the real life is, and finish in the square where the whole city was born.

Let's begin at the Dragon Gate, at the corner of Grant Avenue and Bush Street, the southern entrance to Chinatown. Make your way there, and meet me at the gate.

stops.title: Dragon Gate
stops.caption: You should be standing in front of the Dragon Gate, looking north up Grant Avenue into Chinatown.
stops.transcriptText:
You should be standing in front of the Dragon Gate, looking north up Grant Avenue into Chinatown. Three openings, a green tiled roof curling up at the corners, and a pair of stone lions standing guard. This is the front door, and it's worth a second look before you walk through it.

Start with the gate itself. It's younger than you'd think — it went up in 1970, a gift from Taiwan, modeled on the ceremonial gateways you'd find at the entrance to a Chinese village. Read the inscription up top if you like; it's a line attributed to Sun Yat-sen, the founder of modern China, and the gist is that everything under heaven is for the good of all. Grand words for a tourist arch — but they suit a neighborhood that has always been about more than it looks.

Now look up the street. Grant Avenue is the oldest street in San Francisco — this was the main road of the original Yerba Buena settlement, back before the city had a name. The Chinatown strung along it, the lanterns between the buildings, the pagoda cornices, the dragon-wrapped lamp posts, almost all of it dates from after 1906. Remember the idea from the start of the walk: this look was chosen. Before the fire, Chinatown was mostly plain brick. The version you're walking into was rebuilt to be seen.

One small thing to carry with you. The dragon lamp posts down Grant were installed in the 1920s, and they were genuinely bold for their moment — a Chinese-American neighborhood insisting, in public, in the middle of an era of brutal exclusion laws, that it belonged here and intended to stay.

When you're ready, walk a few blocks up Grant and turn right onto Waverly Place — a narrow side street that's about to ask you to look up.

stops.title: Waverly Place
stops.caption: You're on Waverly Place now, a two-block lane running between Grant and Stockton.
stops.transcriptText:
You're on Waverly Place now, a two-block lane running between Grant and Stockton. It's narrow, it's quieter than Grant, and people call it the Street of Painted Balconies. Tilt your head back and you'll see why — the upper floors are stacked with balconies painted in bright reds, greens, and golds.

Here's the thing to understand about this street, and really about all of Chinatown: the life you're looking for isn't at street level. Down here it's shops. The real heart of the community went up. When this neighborhood was packed into a few square blocks by law and by prejudice, with nowhere to expand outward, it expanded the only direction it could — vertically. Family associations, clubs, and temples took the upper floors, and they're still up there.

Look at number one hundred and twenty-five Waverly. On the top floor sits the Tin How Temple, founded in 1852, said to be the oldest Chinese temple in the United States. It's dedicated to Tin How, the goddess who protects sailors and travelers — fitting, for a community that crossed an ocean to get here. You climb several flights of a narrow stairway to reach it, and you come out into a small, dim room thick with incense smoke and hung with hundreds of red lanterns. If it's open to visitors when you're here, it's worth the climb.

That's the lesson of Waverly: the postcard is at street level, but the neighborhood's soul is one, two, three floors up, where it's been quietly keeping faith for more than a hundred and seventy years.

From the far end of Waverly, head over to Ross Alley — the next lane along, and the oldest alley in Chinatown, where we'll find something the whole world thinks it knows about Chinese food.

stops.title: Ross Alley & the Fortune Cookie Factory
stops.caption: You're in Ross Alley now, a narrow, slightly crooked lane that's the oldest alley in Chinatown.
stops.transcriptText:
You're in Ross Alley now, a narrow, slightly crooked lane that's the oldest alley in Chinatown. It's barely wide enough for the light to reach the ground, which is exactly why filmmakers love it — it's stood in for old Chinatown in more movies than its residents would probably like. But you didn't come down here for the scenery. You came for the smell: sweet, warm, vanilla, drifting out of a doorway on your right.

That's the Golden Gate Fortune Cookie Factory, and it's tiny — a couple of women at small round griddles, folding cookies by hand, the way it's been done for decades. Step in if there's room. You'll watch a flat, hot disc of batter get a paper fortune laid across it and folded into that familiar shape in about two seconds, faster than you can follow.

Now here's the twist, and it's a good one. The fortune cookie — the single most "Chinese" thing in the whole American imagination — almost certainly isn't Chinese at all. The best evidence traces it back to Japanese rice crackers, and to Japanese-American families in California who were serving a version of it around the early 1900s. San Francisco and Los Angeles both claim to have invented it, and in 1983 the two cities staged a mock trial to settle the argument; San Francisco "won," which tells you about as much as a mock trial should.

So the cookie in your hand is really an immigrant story folded into a snack — invented by one community, adopted by another, sold to everyone, and claimed by a city. Very San Francisco.

Eat the cookie. Then we'll walk the last short stretch over to Portsmouth Square — the spot where this whole city began.

stops.title: Portsmouth Square
stops.caption: And here we are at the end of the walk, at Portsmouth Square — except, right now, you're standing at the edge of a construction site.
stops.transcriptText:
And here we are at the end of the walk, at Portsmouth Square — except, right now, you're standing at the edge of a construction site. Fences, hoarding, the hum of machinery. The square closed in June 2026 for a two-year rebuild and won't reopen until 2028, so I'm going to ask you to do something a little strange: stand here at the fence, on Kearny or up at the Clay Street corner, and picture it.

Because of everywhere we've walked today, this is the most important ground. This is where San Francisco began. It was the central plaza of a small settlement called Yerba Buena, and in 1846 a U.S. Navy captain came ashore and raised the American flag right here, the first time it flew over the town. The place was renamed San Francisco the next year. California's first public school opened on the southwest corner in 1848. The whole city radiated outward from this one square.

And then it became something else — the heart of Chinatown. Chinatown's living room, people call it. For generations this was where elders played mahjong and Chinese chess in the sun, where kids ran the play structure, where the neighborhood gathered to celebrate and, when it had to, to protest. It's the civic center of the city within the city we've been walking through.

That's what the rebuild is protecting, not replacing. They're pulling down the ugly 1960s footbridge over Kearny to open the views back up, adding a stage, a new clubhouse, canopies built to carry lanterns at Lunar New Year. The old monuments are in storage, waiting to come home. So picture the square full again — because it will be. You've just walked the oldest Chinatown in North America, a neighborhood that was told to move and refused, and you're ending where the city itself first stood up. It's still here. It's just catching its breath.

tours.title: Golden Gate Park: The Music Concourse
tours.shortDescription: A walk through the cultural heart of Golden Gate Park — John McLaren's forest-on-sand, from the Conservatory of Flowers to Stow Lake.
tours.longDescription: Golden Gate Park was built on bare, shifting sand dunes — a thousand acres that gardener John McLaren spent half a century coaxing into one of the great urban parks in the world. This six-stop walk circles the Music Concourse at its cultural core: the glittering white Conservatory of Flowers, the copper-clad de Young Museum and Renzo Piano's living-roofed California Academy of Sciences facing each other across the concourse, the serene Japanese Tea Garden, and finally Stow Lake, where you can climb Strawberry Hill for a view back over the forest McLaren made.

stops.title: Welcome to Golden Gate Park
stops.caption: Here's something almost nobody believes when they first hear it: every tree around you was planted on purpose, on bare sand.
stops.transcriptText:
Here's something almost nobody believes when they first hear it: every tree around you was planted on purpose, on bare sand. Before this was a park, this was dunes — windswept, shifting, treeless dunes running out to the ocean, land everyone agreed was worthless. The whole green world you're about to walk through is artificial, in the best sense of the word. Someone willed it into being.

That someone was mostly a Scottish gardener named John McLaren, who ran this park for over fifty years and is said to have planted something like two million trees. He took a few square miles of sand and grew a forest on it — and then he filled that forest with things for everyone. Not a private estate, not a rich man's garden: a public park, free, open, democratic, with museums and gardens and lakes that anybody could walk into.

This walk takes you through the cultural heart of that idea, the cluster around the Music Concourse — the sunken, tree-lined bowl that's been the park's living room since a World's Fair came through in 1894. Five stops: a Victorian glass greenhouse, two great museums facing each other across the Concourse, a Japanese garden with a complicated and beautiful history, and finally a lake that started life as a reservoir.

For your feet, this is one of the gentlest walks in the city — flat, paved, about a mile and a half end to end, with the stops bunched close together in the middle. Take your time; the park rewards it.

We'll start at the east end, at the oldest thing in the whole park. Head for the Conservatory of Flowers, the big white glass greenhouse on the rise off John F. Kennedy Drive, and meet me on the lawn out front.

stops.title: Conservatory of Flowers
stops.caption: You're standing in front of the Conservatory of Flowers — and you're looking at the oldest building in Golden Gate Park, older than the park's museums, older than most of its trees.
stops.transcriptText:
You're standing in front of the Conservatory of Flowers — and you're looking at the oldest building in Golden Gate Park, older than the park's museums, older than most of its trees. It's a Victorian greenhouse, all white-painted wood and glass, a long central dome with two wings, sitting up on its little rise like a wedding cake.

It opened in 1879, and it has the kind of origin story this park specializes in. The whole thing started as a prefabricated kit — milled wood and thousands of panes of glass — ordered by an eccentric millionaire named James Lick, who died before he ever put it together. It sat in crates until a group of wealthy San Franciscans bought it and gave it to the new park. The design was modeled on the great Palm House at Kew Gardens in London, which is why, if you've been to Kew, this might feel like a smaller cousin a long way from home.

Step inside if you have time — it's warm, wet, and dense with tropical plants, including high-altitude orchids and water lilies with pads big enough to worry you. But here's the thing to hold onto: this building has nearly been lost more than once. It survived the 1906 earthquake, but a windstorm in 1995 shattered nearly half its glass and almost finished it off. The city raised twenty-five million dollars and spent the better part of a decade rebuilding it pane by pane.

So this delicate-looking glass box is actually one of the toughest survivors in the park — a Victorian greenhouse that refuses to break for good.

When you're ready, follow John F. Kennedy Drive west, about a ten-minute walk, toward the Music Concourse. The first museum you'll come to, with the strange twisting copper tower, is the de Young — meet me out front.

stops.title: de Young Museum
stops.caption: You're at the de Young Museum now, on the north side of the Music Concourse.
stops.transcriptText:
You're at the de Young Museum now, on the north side of the Music Concourse. You can't miss it — it's the building wrapped in copper, with that nine-story tower twisting up out of one end. It's the city's main art museum, and the building itself is the first thing worth reading.

Look closely at the skin. The whole exterior is copper, perforated and embossed with a dimpled pattern, and it was designed to do something most buildings try to avoid: corrode. The architects, the Swiss firm Herzog and de Meuron, wanted the copper to oxidize over time, to streak and darken and slowly turn green, so the building would settle into the green of the park and half-disappear into it. It's a museum engineered to age, on purpose.

The de Young is here at all because the old building on this spot was wrecked in the 1989 earthquake and had to come down. This copper replacement opened in 2005.

Now, the gift, and it's a generous one. That twisting tower has an observation floor at the top, with windows on all sides and one of the best free views in San Francisco — the park below, the city beyond, the ocean to the west. You don't need a museum ticket to ride up. A lot of people never realize that.

So before you move on, consider going up: a free, quiet, glass-walled room above the treetops, in a building designed to vanish into them.

When you're done, turn and look across the Concourse. The low building with the wavy roofline and the dome poking out of it is the California Academy of Sciences — that's our next stop, straight across the bowl.

stops.title: California Academy of Sciences
stops.caption: You're at the California Academy of Sciences, directly across the Music Concourse from the de Young.
stops.transcriptText:
You're at the California Academy of Sciences, directly across the Music Concourse from the de Young. From the front it looks low and modern and fairly calm — but the whole trick of this building is on top, where you can't quite see it from here.

The roof is alive. It's a two-and-a-half-acre living roof, planted with native California wildflowers and grasses, rolling in seven green hills that echo the hills of San Francisco itself. It insulates the building, soaks up rainwater, and gives native bugs and birds a home seventy feet up. The architect, Renzo Piano, basically lifted a piece of the California landscape and draped it over a museum.

And what's under that roof is the real wonder: this is four institutions in one. A natural history museum, an aquarium, a planetarium, and a four-story indoor rainforest under a glass dome, all beneath a single roof. You can stand in a rainforest, ride down to a coral reef, and walk out under a model of the universe, without ever stepping outside. There's even an albino alligator, which the city has a strange amount of affection for.

That's the idea this whole park keeps repeating, in one building: the natural world, gathered up and handed to the public, free to wander into. A roof that's a meadow, over a museum that's a planet.

From the Academy, walk a short way west, just past the de Young, and you'll reach the entrance to the Japanese Tea Garden — the next stop, and the oldest of its kind in the country.

stops.title: Japanese Tea Garden
stops.caption: You're at the gate of the Japanese Tea Garden — five acres of winding paths, ponds, stone lanterns, and clipped pines, tucked right beside the Music Concourse.
stops.transcriptText:
You're at the gate of the Japanese Tea Garden — five acres of winding paths, ponds, stone lanterns, and clipped pines, tucked right beside the Music Concourse. It's the oldest public Japanese garden in the United States, and like a lot of this part of the park, it's a leftover from that 1894 World's Fair, which set up its whole midway right here where you're standing.

Walk in and a few things will find you. There's a drum bridge, an arc so steep you climb it more than cross it, built to make a perfect circle with its own reflection in the water. There's a five-tiered pagoda, and a great bronze Buddha, and a tea house that still serves tea the way it has for generations. Take it slowly — the garden is designed to slow you down, that's the entire point.

But the garden's heart is a family. After the fair, a Japanese gardener named Makoto Hagiwara took over the site and spent the rest of his life turning a fairground exhibit into a real garden, importing plants, birds, and stone from Japan, raising his family in a home right here on the grounds. The Hagiwaras tended this place for nearly fifty years.

And then, in 1942, they were forced out. Like a hundred and twenty thousand other Japanese Americans during the war, the Hagiwara family was sent to an internment camp, and they were never allowed to return to the garden they had built. For a time the city even stripped the name, calling it the Oriental Tea Garden, before it was set right. It's a quiet place with a hard history, and the garden marks it honestly, which is the right thing to do.

One small, sweeter footnote, and it connects to something the rest of this city likes to claim: the modern fortune cookie was very likely first served right here, by the Hagiwara family, before it ever became a Chinatown staple. The thing San Francisco files under "Chinese" was, once again, a Japanese invention — and this exact garden is where it started.

When you're ready, leave the way you came and head west a few minutes to Stow Lake — now also called Blue Heron Lake — where this walk comes to rest on the water.

stops.title: Stow Lake & Strawberry Hill
stops.caption: And here's where the walk comes to rest: Stow Lake — though if you look at a new sign, you'll see it now goes by Blue Heron Lake.
stops.transcriptText:
And here's where the walk comes to rest: Stow Lake — though if you look at a new sign, you'll see it now goes by Blue Heron Lake. We'll come back to that name in a moment. Stand anywhere on the path that rings the water and take in the shape of the place: a doughnut of lake wrapped all the way around a single wooded island.

That island is Strawberry Hill, and it's the highest point in the entire park. The whole scene looks utterly natural, like it's always been here — and it's completely man-made. Remember the dunes from the start of the walk? This lake was dug out of that sand in 1893, partly as a reservoir to water the rest of the park, partly as a place for people to drift around in rowboats on a Sunday. You can still rent a boat at the boathouse and do exactly that.

Look across to the island and you'll spot two gifts. One is Huntington Falls, a hundred-and-ten-foot waterfall tumbling down Strawberry Hill — also entirely artificial, funded by a railroad baron and engineered to look wild. The other is the Golden Gate Pavilion, a bright Chinese pagoda given to San Francisco by its sister city, Taipei, as a gesture of friendship.

Now, that name. The lake was named for a nineteenth-century politician named William Stow, and when the city took a harder look at his record — he was openly, aggressively antisemitic — it decided, recently, to rename the water Blue Heron Lake. You'll hear both names for a while yet. It's a small, honest example of a city deciding what it wants its public places to stand for.

And that's the park, in miniature: a forest, a lake, a waterfall, all conjured out of bare sand and handed to everyone, and still being argued over and cared for more than a century on. Find a bench. Watch the boats. You've reached the calm center of the thing McLaren built.

tours.title: The Mission: Where the City Began
tours.shortDescription: A walk through the Mission — from the 1791 adobe where San Francisco started to the muraled alleys where its art keeps starting.
tours.longDescription: The Mission is where San Francisco began, around the 1776 founding of Mission San Francisco de Asis, and where it keeps reinventing itself. This five-stop walk runs from the thick-walled adobe of Mission Dolores — the oldest building in the city — down to sunny Dolores Park, then into the Mission's living tradition of street art: Clarion Alley's ever-changing political murals and Balmy Alley, painted since the 1970s with the densest concentration of Latino and Central American murals in the city. Oldest building to youngest art, in about a mile.

stops.title: Welcome to the Mission
stops.caption: THE MISSION — Walk Intro  Here's something most people get wrong about San Francisco: it didn't start at the water.
stops.transcriptText:
THE MISSION — Walk Intro

Here's something most people get wrong about San Francisco: it didn't start at the water.

It started here, in the Mission — a flat, sunny valley a few miles inland that the fog usually forgets, which is exactly why the Spanish picked it in 1776, and why everyone from earthquake refugees to artists has wanted to be here ever since. This is the warmest, sunniest neighborhood in the city, and on a good afternoon it shows.

This walk is an easy one. It's mostly flat, it's short — a little over a mile, end to end — and it runs from the oldest building in San Francisco to some of the youngest art in it.
