We'll start at the mission that gave the city both its birthplace and its name, climb a gentle slope to a park with one of the best free views in town, then drop into two alleys where the neighborhood paints exactly what it thinks, right on the walls.

That's the thread to hold onto. This is the place where San Francisco began, and it's still beginning — still arguing, still changing, still announcing itself. The mission tells you where the city came from; the murals tell you who lives here now, and what they're not willing to lose.

A note before we go. The Mission is, today, the heart of San Francisco's Latino community — a culture that's been here for generations and has had to fight, more than once, to stay. You'll see that fight on the walls toward the end of this walk, so it's worth arriving ready to read it.

Our first stop is the mission itself. Make your way to the corner of Sixteenth and Dolores Streets, where a low, pale adobe church sits beside a much grander one. The small, plain one is the one we want. I'll meet you there.

stops.title: Mission Dolores
stops.caption: THE MISSION — Stop 1: Mission Dolores  You're standing in front of the oldest building in San Francisco — and it's easy to walk right past it, because it's small.
stops.transcriptText:
THE MISSION — Stop 1: Mission Dolores

You're standing in front of the oldest building in San Francisco — and it's easy to walk right past it, because it's small.

That's almost the point. Look at the little pale church, not the big ornate one beside it. The grand one is the basilica, and it's just over a hundred years old. The modest one — thick white walls, four squat columns, a red-tiled roof — is Mission San Francisco de Asís, finished in 1791. While nearly everything around it burned or fell in the earthquake and fire of 1906, this building simply stood there, the way it had stood for over a century, and the way it's stood ever since.

It survived because of how it was made. The walls are adobe — sun-dried mud brick — and they're roughly four feet thick. The roof beams are redwood, lashed together with rawhide by the Ohlone people, the Native Californians who were here long before the Spanish, and who built this place with their hands. Step inside if it's open, and look up: the ceiling is painted in patterns the Ohlone designed, using colors made from vegetable dyes. It's their work, on their land, in a building meant to replace the world they already had.

That's the harder truth underneath this pretty white chapel. The mission was the beginning of San Francisco, and it was the end of something, too. Out back there's a small cemetery — a camposanto — and thousands of Ohlone are buried in this ground, many of them lost to diseases that arrived with the missionaries. The garden is quiet and kept with care, and it asks you to remember them.

One more thing, and it's where the name comes from. The mission's formal name honors Saint Francis — San Francisco — and that's the name the whole city took. But there was a creek nearby the Spanish called the Laguna de los Dolores, the lagoon of sorrows, and that nickname stuck — first to the mission, then to the street, then to the park we're walking to next.

Here's the detail to carry with you. The mission was founded in 1776 — the same summer that, on the far side of the continent, a group of colonists was declaring the United States independent. San Francisco and the country are almost exactly the same age, and they both began in that one remarkable year.

When you're ready, walk up Dolores Street, away from the church, three blocks to the green slope of Dolores Park. It's a gentle uphill, lined with palm trees, and the view at the top earns the climb.

stops.title: Dolores Park
stops.caption: THE MISSION — Stop 2: Dolores Park  You've reached the part of this walk where the whole neighborhood lies down in the sun.
stops.transcriptText:
THE MISSION — Stop 2: Dolores Park

You've reached the part of this walk where the whole neighborhood lies down in the sun.

This is Dolores Park, and the first thing to do is climb to the top corner — the southwest corner, up to your right as you came in, the high ground near Twentieth and Church. Turn around when you get there. The park drops away below you like a green grandstand, and past it, framed by palm trees, is the downtown skyline. It's one of the best free views in San Francisco, and on a sunny weekend half the city is up here sharing it, sprawled on blankets, watching the same thing you are.

It wasn't always this gentle. For decades this land held two Jewish cemeteries, until the city moved the graves out and turned the hill into a park in 1905. A year later, the earthquake hit. When the fire that followed drove tens of thousands of people from their homes, they came here — Dolores Park became one of the city's great refugee camps, a slope covered in tents and cooking fires and families who had lost everything overnight. The same view you're enjoying was, for a while, the last thing a lot of people had left.

That's the quiet history under the picnic blankets, and it tells you something about what this park is for. San Francisco doesn't have many backyards — it's a dense city of apartments and stairs and small rooms — so it shares one. Old families and brand-new arrivals, the comfortable and the barely-hanging-on, everybody ends up on this same hill, and nobody really owns the best spot. You just have to get there early.

Take a minute up here. Let the city show off a little.

When you're ready, head back down and out the bottom of the park, and make your way a few blocks northeast toward Valencia Street and a narrow lane called Clarion Alley. The view you just had is the postcard San Francisco; Clarion Alley is the city talking back.

stops.title: Clarion Alley
stops.caption: THE MISSION — Stop 3: Clarion Alley  Turn into Clarion Alley and the temperature of the art changes.
stops.transcriptText:
THE MISSION — Stop 3: Clarion Alley

Turn into Clarion Alley and the temperature of the art changes.

This is a single block, running between Valencia and Mission Streets, and nearly every inch of it — both walls, the fences, the garage doors, the backs of buildings — is painted. It's been this way since 1992, when a handful of local artists started the Clarion Alley Mural Project, and the rule from the beginning was simple: the work would be free to make, free to see, and open to anyone in the community who had something to say.

So look closely, because these murals are not here to be pretty. They're here to argue. You'll find pieces about evictions and rising rents, about police and prisons, about queer and trans rights, about the people being pushed out of this exact neighborhood as the money moves in. The art is loud, direct, sometimes raw — and that's the point. Clarion Alley is the Mission's op-ed page, published right on the brick.

It also doesn't sit still. Unlike a museum, where a painting might hang for a century, the work here gets painted over and replaced as new artists and new fights come along, which means whatever you're looking at right now is really a snapshot — a record of what this neighborhood is angry about, hopeful about, fighting for, this particular season. Come back in a year and the conversation will have moved on.

Step back out onto Valencia for a second and you'll feel the whole reason this alley exists. Out there: the new restaurants, the boutiques, the polished version of the Mission that money built. In here: the neighborhood that was here first, still holding its ground, one wall at a time.

Take your time reading these. They reward it.

When you're done, we're headed to the alley that started it all. Make your way south and east, down toward Twenty-fourth Street, to a smaller, older lane called Balmy Alley — the place where the Mission's painted walls began, and where the story underneath them gets deeper.

stops.title: Balmy Alley & 24th Street
stops.caption: THE MISSION — Stop 4: Balmy Alley & 24th Street  This is where the Mission's painted walls began.
stops.transcriptText:
THE MISSION — Stop 4: Balmy Alley & 24th Street

This is where the Mission's painted walls began.

Balmy Alley is narrower and quieter than Clarion, a single block off Twenty-fourth Street, and the murals here go back further than almost anywhere in the city. Artists started painting these walls in the early 1970s, but the alley became what it is today in 1984, when a group of local muralists called PLACA covered it with work protesting the wars and the suffering then tearing through Central America — places many people in this neighborhood had come from, or still had family in. The murals weren't decoration, and they weren't tourism. They were a community on one side of the world refusing to look away from another.

Decades later, the walls are still working. Some honor that original Central American story; others celebrate Mexican and indigenous heritage, or mourn neighbors lost, or — like Clarion — push back against the displacement pressing in on the Mission right now. The tradition gets repainted here, carefully, by people who treat these walls as something closer to a community altar than a gallery.

Walk back out to Twenty-fourth Street and look around. This stretch has an official name now — the Calle Veinticuatro Latino Cultural District, recognized by the city in 2014 — a designation meant to protect the murals, the businesses, and the culture of a neighborhood that has spent decades being told, in one way or another, to leave. The taquerias, the bakeries, the produce stands, the music coming out of open doors: this is a living culture, not a preserved one.

So think about where this walk started. A few blocks from here, two and a half centuries ago, the Spanish built a small adobe church, called the place San Francisco, and began the city — which was also the end of the Ohlone world that came before. And here, at the other end of the same neighborhood, another community paints its own survival onto the walls, year after year, so that no one can pretend it isn't here.

That's the Mission. It's where San Francisco was born, and it's still, every single day, insisting on who it is. You picked a good place to stand and pay attention. Stay a while — get something to eat, read a few more walls. The neighborhood's glad to have you, as long as you're really looking.

tours.title: North Beach & the Climb to Coit
tours.shortDescription: A walk through bohemian, Italian North Beach and up Telegraph Hill's hidden garden stairways to Coit Tower.
tours.longDescription: North Beach is San Francisco's Little Italy and the old capital of the Beats — espresso bars, Italian delis, and the bookstore where the Beat Generation found its voice. This five-stop walk starts at City Lights and Kerouac Alley, crosses Washington Square in the shadow of Saints Peter and Paul, then climbs the leafy, half-hidden Filbert and Greenwich Steps up Telegraph Hill to Coit Tower, where the Depression-era murals and a wide view of the bay reward the climb.

stops.title: Welcome to North Beach
stops.caption: NORTH BEACH & THE CLIMB TO COIT — Walk Intro  First, a correction: there is no beach in North Beach.
stops.transcriptText:
NORTH BEACH & THE CLIMB TO COIT — Walk Intro

First, a correction: there is no beach in North Beach.

There used to be — a real one, on the bay — but the city filled it in more than a century ago, and the name stuck to dry land the way names do. What's here instead is something better: the closest thing San Francisco has to a European village, an Italian neighborhood layered over a bohemian one, wrapped around the base of a steep green hill with a tower on top.

This walk has a shape to it, and it's worth knowing before you start. We begin at the bottom, in the flat heart of North Beach, where the Beat poets ran a bookstore that went to court for the right to publish, and where the Italian San Francisco of cafés and a twin-spired church still holds on. Then we climb — and I mean climb — up the side of Telegraph Hill, past hidden garden staircases where a flock of wild parrots actually lives, to Coit Tower at the summit and one of the great views in the city.

Here's the honest part. The climb to the top is a real one — steep streets, then steep stairs — and it's the whole point of the walk, the slow rise from the bohemian village to the lookout above it. If your knees would rather not, you have an easy out: the number thirty-nine bus runs from Washington Square right up to Coit Tower, so you can ride up and walk down instead. No shame in it. The parrots don't care how you arrive.

Our first stop is at the bottom, where it all starts. Find the corner of Columbus Avenue and Broadway, and look for a wedge-shaped bookstore with its name running down the side: City Lights. I'll meet you out front.

stops.title: City Lights & Kerouac Alley
stops.caption: NORTH BEACH — Stop 1: City Lights & Kerouac Alley  You're standing in front of the bookstore that went to court — and won.
stops.transcriptText:
NORTH BEACH — Stop 1: City Lights & Kerouac Alley

You're standing in front of the bookstore that went to court — and won.

This is City Lights, opened in 1953 by the poet Lawrence Ferlinghetti and a partner, and it was the first bookstore in America to sell nothing but paperbacks. That sounds ordinary now. At the time it was close to radical — paperbacks were considered cheap, throwaway things, and a serious bookshop selling only those, staying open late, and letting people sit and read without buying a thing, was a genuinely new idea about what a bookstore could be.

Then it became something bigger. In 1956, City Lights published a slim book of poetry by Allen Ginsberg called Howl. The poem was raw, furious, and frank about sex and drugs in a way that got Ferlinghetti arrested the next year for selling obscene material. The trial that followed, in 1957, became a landmark: the judge ruled that the poem was not obscene because it carried real social value, and that decision helped clear the way for publishing serious work that earlier could have been banned outright. A bookstore on this corner, in other words, helped widen what Americans were legally allowed to read.

Now look to the side of the building, at the narrow lane running alongside it. That's Jack Kerouac Alley, named for the author of On the Road, who drank and argued just across the way at Vesuvio, the bar still standing on the far side. Lines from Kerouac and other writers are set right into the pavement under your feet, so down here it's worth looking at the ground as much as the walls.

This little corner — a bookstore, an alley, a bar — is where the Beats turned San Francisco into the capital of the American counterculture, a full decade before the hippies took over the Haight. It started with cheap paperbacks and one furious poem.

When you're ready, walk up Columbus Avenue a few blocks to the open green of Washington Square, the living room of Italian North Beach, where two white spires are waiting.

stops.title: Washington Square
stops.caption: NORTH BEACH — Stop 2: Washington Square & Saints Peter and Paul  This is Washington Square, and it's the closest thing North Beach has to a town square — the neighborhood's shared front yard.
stops.transcriptText:
NORTH BEACH — Stop 2: Washington Square & Saints Peter and Paul

This is Washington Square, and it's the closest thing North Beach has to a town square — the neighborhood's shared front yard.

Come in the morning and you'll find people doing tai chi on the grass; come in the afternoon and it's sunbathers, dog walkers, and old men arguing in Italian. But here's the first surprise: the statue in the middle isn't George Washington. It's Benjamin Franklin, donated in the 1870s by a wealthy dentist and temperance crusader who wanted to give San Franciscans something to drink other than alcohol — which is why the base once ran with fountains of free water. A Washington Square with a Franklin standing in it, and the city never bothered to fix the mismatch.

Now look up at the church. Those two white spires belong to Saints Peter and Paul, finished in 1924 and long known as the Italian Cathedral of the West — the spiritual center of North Beach back when this was a dense neighborhood of Italian fishermen and immigrants. The most famous of those Italian sons was the baseball player Joe DiMaggio, who grew up just a few blocks from here. When he married the movie star Marilyn Monroe in 1954, the couple came straight to these steps to be photographed afterward, and you'll still see wedding parties doing exactly the same thing today — which is part of how the place picked up its reputation as a marriage church.

Stand here a moment and take the measure of it. Down at the bottom, the Beats; up the hill ahead, the parrots and the tower; and right here in the middle, the ordinary Italian village that both of those stories grew up around. This is the everyday heart of the whole thing.

When you're ready, we start climbing. Head east, toward the green hill rising in front of you, and find the base of the Filbert Steps, where the sidewalk gives up and turns into a garden staircase. This is where the walk gets wild — in every sense of the word.

stops.title: Filbert & Greenwich Steps
stops.caption: NORTH BEACH — Stop 3: The Filbert & Greenwich Steps  The sidewalk just ended and turned into a staircase.
stops.transcriptText:
NORTH BEACH — Stop 3: The Filbert & Greenwich Steps

The sidewalk just ended and turned into a staircase. You're now climbing the Filbert Steps, and this is one of the strangest, loveliest corners of San Francisco.

Telegraph Hill is steep — too steep, in places, for ordinary streets — so on its eastern face the roads simply give up and become wooden staircases threading up through gardens. As you climb, notice the cottages tucked along the steps, some of them small wooden houses from the 1860s and 70s. They survived the great fire of 1906 for a blunt reason: this hillside was too steep and too awkward for the flames, and for the crews dynamiting buildings to make firebreaks, so a pocket of the old wooden city lived on right here while grander neighborhoods burned to the ground.

The gardens you're walking through aren't an accident either. For decades much of this slope was a neglected dumping ground, until a woman named Grace Marchant moved in around 1949 and spent the next thirty years clearing the trash and planting by hand, turning the hillside into the lush public garden that still carries her name. You're climbing through one person's stubbornness, basically.

And then there's the sound. Listen — and look up. Telegraph Hill is home to a flock of wild parrots, bright green with flashes of red, descended from escaped and released pet birds that found each other, bred, and never left. They're loud, they're fast, and they became famous enough to end up in a documentary. If a squadron of green birds tears overhead screaming, you've just met the locals.

One more thing, about the name. There's no telegraph up there now, but in the 1850s the hilltop held a signal station with a wooden semaphore that told the city below which kind of ship was sailing in through the Golden Gate. The hill was San Francisco's early-warning system, back when a ship full of news or gold could change everything.

Catch your breath here — the view is already good, and it's about to get better.

Keep climbing. The steps deliver you almost to the foot of Coit Tower, the great pale column at the summit, which is our last stop.

stops.title: Coit Tower
stops.caption: NORTH BEACH — Stop 4: Coit Tower  You made it.
stops.transcriptText:
NORTH BEACH — Stop 4: Coit Tower

You made it. This is Coit Tower — two hundred and ten feet of pale concrete at the top of Telegraph Hill, and one of the most misunderstood landmarks in the city.

Here's the misunderstanding. The money for the tower came from Lillie Hitchcock Coit, a wealthy and famously eccentric San Franciscan who, as a girl, had adored the city's volunteer firefighters — she chased their engines, became a mascot of one of the companies, and signed her name with a little number five, for her beloved Engine Company Number Five, for the rest of her life. So when she left a fortune to beautify the city and this tower went up in 1933, everyone decided it must be built to look like the nozzle of a fire hose, in her honor. It's a wonderful story. It also isn't true — the architects always insisted the shape was simply a clean fluted column, and any resemblance is in the eye of the beholder. But the story is so good the city has never let go of it.

Step inside before you go up, because the ground floor is the real treasure, and it's free. The walls are covered in murals painted in 1934 by dozens of artists put to work by a Depression-era government program. They show California labor — people in the fields, on the docks, in the factories — in a bold, social-realist style, and a few of the details were political enough to cause a small scandal when they were first unveiled. They're some of the finest public murals in the country, and most visitors march straight past them to the elevator.

So go up too, if you like — there's a small fee, and the view from the top is the whole bay at once, both bridges included. But take a second down here first.

Think about what you just climbed through. A bookstore that fought for free speech, an Italian square with the wrong man on its statue, a staircase full of parrots and one woman's garden, and now a tower paid for by a firefighter-obsessed heiress and decorated by out-of-work painters. Not one piece of this was built by the people who usually get monuments. North Beach is a neighborhood that made its own landmarks, on its own terms, all the way up the hill — and you just climbed the whole story. Enjoy the view. You earned it.

tours.title: 21_21 Design Sight | 21_21 DESIGN SIGHT
tours.shortDescription: Two folded steel sheets pressed gently into a garden — Japan's first design museum announces itself by refusing to announce itself.
tours.longDescription:
Look at the roofline and you'll see two steel panels, each fifty-four metres long, folded once and set down on the grass like a piece of origami. The form reads as a building that doesn't quite want to be seen — and that's the point. Eighty per cent of it lies underground, with a sloped concrete entrance drawing you down into subterranean galleries lit by a sunken courtyard cut into the earth.

Tadao Ando designed it with the fashion designer Issey Miyake, who had been arguing for a dedicated design museum since the eighties and finally tabled a formal proposal in 2003. The roof draws directly on Miyake's "A Piece of Cloth" idea: a single uncut sheet, folded once, becomes something three-dimensional. Ando translated that into two folded sheets of steel, finished with the longest double-glazed panels in Japan.

There's something telling here. A country celebrated for its design finally builds itself a museum for it — and the two people responsible buried it underground.

stops.title: 21_21 Design Sight | 21_21 DESIGN SIGHT
stops.caption: Look at the roofline — two steel panels, each fifty-four metres long, folded once and pressed gently into the earth.
stops.transcriptText:
ATLAS AUDIO TOUR — 21_21 DESIGN SIGHT, TOKYO

Location: 9-7-6 Akasaka, Minato-ku, Tokyo (within Midtown Garden, Tokyo Midtown, Roppongi)
Approximate duration: 2:15 (≈345 words)

---

Look at the roofline. Two steel panels, each fifty-four metres long, folded once and pressed gently into the earth — as if the building doesn't want to be seen.

The structure sits in Midtown Garden at the edge of the park area of Tokyo Midtown, Roppongi, a low-lying form that reads from a distance as a piece of origami that has simply been set down on the grass. The two steel-plate roofs slope from roughly knee height at their peaks down to ground level, and eighty per cent of the building lies underground beneath them. The entrance is a sloped concrete hall that draws you down into the subterranean galleries, where a sunken courtyard cut into the earth provides natural light. The space you couldn't imagine from outside opens up considerably once you're beneath the surface.

The building was designed by Tadao Ando and conceived with the fashion designer Issey Miyake, who had been advocating for a dedicated design museum in Japan since the nineteen eighties and finally published a formal proposal in two thousand and three. The roof form was drawn directly from Miyake's design philosophy — his concept of "A Piece of Cloth," the idea that a single uncut sheet of fabric, folded once, becomes something three-dimensional and wearable. Ando translated that into architecture: two sheets of steel, folded once, become a building. The sheets themselves required the longest double-glazed glass panels in Japan to complete the envelope.

I find the building's relationship to the ground rather telling. This is Japan's first dedicated design museum — a country whose design output has been internationally celebrated for decades — and when it finally arrived, the two people responsible for it buried it. Built on a former military site where zoning required minimal surface disruption, the choice to go underground became an architectural statement: Japan's design museum announces itself by refusing to announce itself.

The Suntory Museum of Art and the National Art Center Tokyo are both within a ten-minute walk — the three institutions together make Roppongi one of the densest concentrations of serious museum space in the city, if you have the afternoon for it.

---

tours.title: Asahi Beer Hall | アサヒビールホール
tours.shortDescription: Philippe Starck's golden flame crowns a black beer-glass of a building on the Sumida — beloved, derided, and known locally as the golden turd.
tours.longDescription:
On the east bank of the Sumida, directly across from Asakusa, sits a low black building clad in polished granite, its walls curving gently outward toward the top to suggest the profile of a beer glass. This is the Asahi Beer Hall, or Super Dry Hall, completed in 1989. Atop it perches the Flamme d'Or — "Golden Flame" — designed by Philippe Starck to represent, the brewery insists, the burning heart of Asahi beer. It is forty-four metres long, weighs three hundred and sixty tonnes, was built by shipbuilders using submarine techniques, and is entirely empty inside.

Tokyo opinion on the flame is decided, if not flattering. Residents call it kin no unko, the golden turd, and the building the unko biru, the poo building. Starck has not objected.

Both buildings were commissioned for Asahi's 1989 centennial, the year the brewery reclaimed its original riverside site. The taller amber tower beside it, crowned in white "froth," houses the headquarters — together one of the more gloriously literal corporate gestures in recent Tokyo.

stops.title: Asahi Beer Hall | アサヒビールホール
stops.caption: Stand on the Azumabashi Bridge or the riverbank facing the building — a low black beer-glass profile beneath its golden flame.
stops.transcriptText:
ASAHI BEER HALL — FLAMME D'OR
Atlas Audio Tour

The object on the roof is forty-four metres long, weighs three hundred and sixty tonnes, and was built by shipbuilders using submarine construction techniques. It is empty inside.

The building beneath it is the Asahi Beer Hall, also known as the Super Dry Hall, completed in 1989 on the east bank of the Sumida River directly across from Asakusa. You should be standing on the Azumabashi Bridge, or nearby on the riverbank, facing the building: a low black structure clad in polished granite, its walls curving gently outward toward the top to suggest the profile of a beer glass. The golden object on its roof is the Flamme d'Or — French for "Golden Flame" — designed by Philippe Starck and representing, according to Asahi Breweries, "the burning heart of Asahi beer."

Local opinion on the Flamme d'Or is divided, but not very. Tokyo residents have nicknamed it kin no unko — the golden turd — and the building itself is correspondingly known as the unko biru, the poo building. Starck has not publicly objected.

Both buildings were commissioned for Asahi's centennial in 1989, the same year the brewery reclaimed its original site on the Sumida River, which had housed the Azumabashi Brewery from 1903 until its closure in 1985. The taller building to the left — amber-tinted mirrored glass with a white crown representing froth — is the Asahi headquarters tower; the black building is the event and restaurant hall. Together they form one of the more unusually literal corporate architecture programmes in recent Tokyo history: a beer glass, a full pint, and a flame of golden passion, on the banks of the river.

The Asahi Sky Room on the twenty-second floor of the headquarters tower is open to the public and offers a panoramic view of the Sumida, Asakusa, and Tokyo Skytree — a worthwhile detour on a clear day.

tours.title: Asahi Sky Room | アサヒスカイルーム
tours.shortDescription: The Skytree deck costs three thousand yen; this one costs a beer — Tokyo spread out beyond the bay windows of a lager-shaped tower.
tours.longDescription:
The observation deck at Tokyo Skytree will set you back around three thousand yen. The Asahi Sky Room costs a beer. It sits on the twenty-second floor of the Asahi Beer Tower — the amber building shaped, quite deliberately, like a well-poured glass of lager, white panelling at the top standing in for the foam. There's no admission fee: you order at the counter, take a window seat, and let the rest unfold.

And what unfolds is Tokyo. The Sumida River runs directly below, Senso-ji's pagoda sits to the northwest, bridges string across the water, and the Skytree rises six hundred and thirty-four metres to the north. On a clear day Mount Fuji appears over the western horizon. The neighbouring Flamme d'Or — flame, beer head, or something more irreverent, take your pick — and both buildings were designed by Philippe Starck in 1989.

It's a retro café lounge: Super Dry on tap, no rival brands, no time limit. The beer costs a touch more than an izakaya. The view costs nothing at all.

stops.title: Asahi Sky Room | アサヒスカイルーム
stops.caption: Take a window seat on the 22nd floor — the Sumida below, Senso-ji's pagoda northwest, the Skytree to the north.
stops.transcriptText:
ASAHI SKY ROOM — AZUMABASHI, SUMIDA
Atlas Audio Tour

The observation deck at Tokyo Skytree costs around three thousand yen. This one costs a beer.

On the twenty-second floor of the Asahi Beer Tower — the tall amber-coloured building you're entering, designed to look like a glass of well-poured lager, with white panelling at the top to suggest the foam — the Asahi Sky Room sits inside the company's working headquarters. There is no admission fee. You order at the counter, you take a window seat, and the rest is Tokyo spread out in front of you: the Sumida River directly below, Senso-ji Temple's pagoda to the northwest, the bridges strung across the river, and the Skytree standing six hundred and thirty-four metres above everything else to the north. On a clear day, Mount Fuji appears above the western horizon.

A word on navigation, because it confuses people: the building you want is the taller golden one, not the shorter black building next to it with the large golden sculpture on the roof. Enter from the south side, take the lift to the twenty-first floor, then the escalator up to twenty-two. The Flamme d'Or on the neighbouring building — the sculpture variously described as a flame, a beer head, or something rather more irreverent — was also designed by the French designer Philippe Starck, who was responsible for both buildings. He came up with a beer glass and a flame in the same commission in 1989 and apparently had no objections to either interpretation.

The Sky Room itself is a retro café lounge: counter seating along bay windows, Asahi Super Dry on tap, no competing brands on the menu, and no time limit on the seats. The beer is slightly more expensive than in an izakaya. The view is considerably better.

If you're timing a visit, the sunset hour — when the Skytree begins its nightly illumination against a darkening sky while the river below catches the last of the light — is worth the extra twenty minutes of waiting for a window seat.

tours.title: Asakura Museum of Sculpture | 朝倉彫塑館
tours.shortDescription: The Yanaka studio a sculptor spent forty years building for himself, where a clay-and-bronze workshop wraps a hidden carp-pond garden.
tours.longDescription:
On a side street in Yanaka, half-turned away from the world between a sembei shop and a temple wall, stands the studio Fumio Asakura spent the better part of forty years building for himself. He moved here in 1908 after graduating from the Tokyo School of Fine Arts and rebuilt the premises over the following decades, completing the present pair of buildings in 1935: a concrete western-style studio wing with north-facing skylights, joined by a single internal door to a Japanese residence of tatami rooms and sliding screens.

The studio was at once his workplace, his school, and eventually the museum he asked his family to open after his death. Over four hundred of his works were requisitioned and melted down for the war effort, yet he kept working until he died at eighty-one.

What matters most is the conjunction of studio and garden, both designed by Asakura to be experienced together. Students tended the rooftop garden — Tokyo's oldest — on the principle that gardening sharpened the senses. The former orchid greenhouse now holds his sculptures of cats; he once owned ten.

stops.title: Asakura Museum of Sculpture | 朝倉彫塑館
stops.caption: On a Yanaka side street, find the skylit concrete building half-turned away between a sembei shop and a temple wall.
stops.transcriptText:
ATLAS AUDIO TOUR — ASAKURA MUSEUM OF SCULPTURE (朝倉彫塑館), TOKYO

Location: 7-18-10 Yanaka, Taito-ku, Tokyo (3–5 minutes from Nippori Station west exit, JR Yamanote Line and Keisei Line)
Hours: 9:30am–4:30pm; closed Mondays and Thursdays (if a public holiday, opens that day and closes the following day)
Admission: ¥500 adults. Remove shoes on entry.
Approximate duration: 2:10 (≈330 words)

---

On a side street in Yanaka, between a sembei shop and a temple wall, a concrete building with skylights sits half-turned away from the street — the studio a sculptor spent the better part of forty years building for himself.

The building is at 7-18-10 Yanaka, three minutes from Nippori Station: two connected structures designed by Fumio Asakura and completed in nineteen thirty-five, a ferroconcrete western-style studio wing with high ceilings and north-facing skylights joined by a single internal door to a Japanese residential wing of tatami rooms and sliding screens. Asakura moved to Yanaka in nineteen oh eight after graduating from the Tokyo School of Fine Arts, set up his studio, and gradually designed and rebuilt the entire premises over the following decades. The studio served simultaneously as his workplace, his school — the Asakura School of Plastic Arts ran here from nineteen twenty to nineteen forty-four — and eventually as the museum he requested his family open after his death. Over four hundred of his works were requisitioned and melted down for the war effort. He continued working until he died at eighty-one.

The building is registered as a national tangible cultural property, and the grounds — which include a courtyard Japanese garden enclosed on all four sides by the two wings, with a carp pond and stepping stones — were designated a National Place of Scenic Beauty in two thousand and eight. The roof garden above the studio is the oldest extant roof garden in Tokyo; Asakura required his students to work in it, growing vegetables, on the principle that gardening would sharpen their senses and bring them closer to the physical world they were trying to represent in clay and bronze. The third-floor Orchid Room, which was Asakura's greenhouse for his orchid collection, now houses his sculptures of cats. He owned ten at one point.

I find the conjunction of the studio and the garden rather the most important thing about Asakura's vision. He designed both, and they were always meant to be experienced together.

Yanaka Cemetery is directly adjacent to the east — one of Tokyo's most atmospheric old burial grounds, worth a quiet walk after the museum, particularly in cherry blossom season.

---

tours.title: Asakusa Underground Street | 浅草地下街
tours.shortDescription: Japan's oldest surviving underground arcade, opened in 1955 and barely touched since — bare pipes, neon, and a seven-hundred-yen barber.
tours.longDescription:
It is 1955. Tokyo is rebuilding, Asakusa is still the entertainment heart of the city, and someone decides the district needs a shopping corridor beneath its main street. They build one, and it lasts. This is the Asakusa Underground Street, the oldest surviving underground arcade in Japan — two older ones are gone, this one is not.

Running about fifty metres beneath Kaminarimon-dori, it connects the Ginza Line station to the Tobu terminus and looks much as it did when it opened: pipes along the ceiling, water pooling on the floor for reasons no one quite explains, signboards untouched since the Showa era. Roughly twenty shops cling on — a barber charging seven hundred yen, a fortune teller, a yakisoba stall, a long-standing Thai restaurant, a sundry shop on permanent discount.

Above, tourists stream toward Sensoji. Down here the regulars are local: office workers on lunch, old men who come for the barber and stay for the beer.

stops.title: Asakusa Underground Street | 浅草地下街
stops.caption: You've descended beneath Kaminarimon-dori — pipes overhead, neon signs, and twenty Showa-era shops along the tunnel.
stops.transcriptText:
ASAKUSA UNDERGROUND STREET — 浅草地下街
Atlas Audio Tour

It's 1955. Tokyo is ten years out of the war, rebuilding at pace, and Asakusa is still the entertainment heart of the city — its theatres and markets drawing crowds from across the capital. Someone decides that what this busy district needs is an underground shopping corridor beneath its main commercial street. They build one. It lasts.

The tunnel you've descended into is the Asakusa Underground Street, opened in 1955 and the oldest surviving underground shopping arcade in Japan. Two of the arcades that opened earlier are gone; this one is not. It stretches about fifty metres beneath Kaminarimon-dori, connecting the Tokyo Metro Ginza Line station to the Tobu Railway terminus, and it looks much as it did the decade it was built: bare pipes running along the ceiling, water pooling on the floor for reasons nobody quite explains, neon signs and signboards that appear not to have been updated since the Showa era.

The corridor holds around twenty shops. The barber charges seven hundred yen for a haircut. There is a DVD shop, a fortune teller, a yakisoba stall serving one plate of noodles for three hundred and fifty yen, a Thai restaurant of long standing, and a sundry goods shop with permanent discounts of between fifty and ninety percent. Many of these businesses have been here for decades, run by the same families that opened them when the arcade was new.

Above you, the streets of Asakusa are busy with tourists heading toward Sensoji Temple. Down here, the main customers are local — office workers on lunch, old men who come for the barber and stay for the beer, people who simply prefer this to the street.

Exit to the east and you emerge at the base of Shin-Nakamise arcade; exit west, and you are back on Kaminarimon-dori with the main gate to Sensoji fifty metres ahead.

tours.title: Daikanyama T-Site | 代官山 T-SITE
tours.shortDescription: A bookshop conceived as a library in a forest, where the owner's logo hides in the perforated facades, the bridges, and even the floor plans.
tours.longDescription:
The whole complex is built around a single letter. The Ts of the Tsutaya logo are cut into the white perforated facade screens, and the building plans themselves are T-shaped — the branding runs all the way into the floor without ever once appearing on a sign. London-born, Tokyo-based Klein Dytham retained the site's mature trees as the governing condition of the design, then arranged three two-storey pavilions along a Magazine Street, linked above by bridges clad in polished stainless steel.

They won the commission in the final round of a 77-architect invited competition, beating Kengo Kuma among others, and built it in eleven months despite the disruption of the Tohoku earthquake.

The concept was a library in a forest. Sections cover art, architecture, cooking, travel, cars and design, each with an expert concierge — in travel, one who can book your flight. It was designed for premium-age customers, the over-fifties whom algorithms never quite captured. It's a rather well-argued case that physical retail survives by offering what online shopping can't.

stops.title: Daikanyama T-Site | 代官山 T-SITE
stops.caption: Look at the facade: the white perforated screens are cut into the Ts of the Tsutaya logo — and so are the floor plans.
stops.transcriptText:
ATLAS AUDIO TOUR — DAIKANYAMA T-SITE (代官山 T-SITE), TOKYO

Location: 17-5 Sarugakucho, Shibuya-ku, Tokyo (5 minutes from Daikanyama Station, Tokyu Toyoko Line)
Hours: Open until 2am most nights
Approximate duration: 2:10 (≈330 words)

---

The building in front of you is covered in the letter T. They are the logo of the company that owns it, rendered into architecture so subtly that most people take a few seconds to notice.

The complex occupies a corner site in Daikanyama, set back from the main street among the mature trees that the architects — London-born Klein Dytham, based in Tokyo since the late nineteen eighties — retained as the primary condition of their design. Three two-storey pavilions are connected by a Magazine Street running the length of the site, with two bridges clad in polished stainless steel battens linking the buildings above it. The facade panels are white perforated screens whose cut-out shapes are the Ts of the Tsutaya logo. The building plans themselves, if you could see them from above, are also T-shaped — the branding goes all the way into the floor plans and is never once put on a sign. Klein Dytham won the commission in the final round of a 77-architect invited competition, beating Kengo Kuma, among others, and built the whole project in eleven months despite the disruption of the Tohoku earthquake and tsunami.

The concept was a library in a forest, and the programming followed from that: sections covering art, architecture, cooking, travel, cars, and design, each with a concierge — over fifty years old, expert in their subject — who can advise on stock, recommend titles, or in the travel section, book a flight. The store was designed specifically for what Tsutaya called premium-age customers: the over-fifties, the demographic that digital commerce had not captured because it values the quality of a considered recommendation over the speed of an algorithm. The Anjin lounge above the magazine section — named for William Adams, the English navigator who became Japan's first Western samurai in the early Edo period — is open until two in the morning.

I find the whole thing rather a well-argued case that physical retail survives not by competing with online shopping but by offering something algorithms can't.

The Hillside Terrace complex immediately next door was designed by Pritzker Prize-winner Fumihiko Maki between nineteen sixty-nine and nineteen ninety-eight — worth a slow walk through the courtyard sequence that sits behind T-SITE's east wall.

---

tours.title: Dior Azabudai Hills | ディオール 麻布台ヒルズ
tours.shortDescription: Kengo Kuma's carbon-fibre facade for Dior — thousands of fine threads that move with the air, behaving less like a building than like fabric.
tours.longDescription:
Look at what the building is wearing. That shimmering, layered surface is carbon fibre — thousands of ultra-fine threads stretched across multiple planes, so that as the light changes or a breeze passes through, the whole facade moves. It behaves less like a building material and more like cloth.

The boutique sits in Garden Plaza, the lower-rise retail section of Azabudai Hills, the mixed-use complex that opened in November 2023 and is anchored by the 325-metre Mori JP Tower, the tallest building in Japan. Kengo Kuma, whose instinct is to make hard materials behave softly, applied his usual question here: what does the material do when light moves through it? The carbon fibre answers by shifting between opacity and shimmer as you change your angle.

The interior follows through — artisanal metalwork, handmade Japanese washi paper, and Nishijin brocade, the thousand-year-old Kyoto silk-weaving technique. Two craft traditions from opposite ends of the map, sharing one space. Kuma wanted a building that breathes with the city; what he made is a building that gets dressed.

stops.title: Dior Azabudai Hills | ディオール 麻布台ヒルズ
stops.caption: Stand with the Central Green behind you for a clear view of the full elevation, the tower above and to your left.
stops.transcriptText:
DIOR AZABUDAI HILLS — GARDEN PLAZA
Atlas Audio Tour

Look at what the building is wearing. That shimmering, layered surface you're standing in front of — neither solid nor transparent, shifting with any movement of the air — is carbon fibre. Thousands of ultra-fine threads stretched across multiple planes, so that as the light changes, or a breeze comes through, or rain hits the strands, the whole facade moves. It behaves less like a building material and more like fabric.

The Dior boutique sits within Garden Plaza, the lower-rise retail section of Azabudai Hills — the vast mixed-use complex that opened here in November 2023, anchored by the Mori JP Tower, which at three hundred and twenty-five metres is the tallest building in Japan. The Garden Plaza buildings step down from that tower in a series of undulating forms studded with greenery. The Dior store occupies one of those lower volumes, and its facade — designed by architect Kengo Kuma — faces the Central Green. Stand with the green space behind you and you have a clear view of the full elevation. The tower will be visible above and to your left.

Kengo Kuma is a Japanese architect whose defining instinct is to make hard materials behave softly — stone that reads like water, steel that suggests wood. Here he was asked to collaborate with a French couture house, and the logic he reached for was the same one he applies to every material: what does it do when light moves through it? The carbon fibre responds to the answer by shifting between opacity and shimmer as you change your angle. Kuma described what he was after as a building that breathes with the city. What he actually made is a building that gets dressed.

The interior follows through: artisanal metalwork on the wall panels, handmade Japanese washi paper, and decorative elements using Nishijin brocade — the Kyoto silk-weaving technique that has been producing some of the most technically complex textiles in the world for over a thousand years. Two craft traditions from opposite ends of the map, sharing the same space.

The Central Green behind you also offers the most unobstructed view of the tower from within the complex — and the teamLab Borderless digital art museum is in the basement of Garden Plaza, directly below where you're standing.

tours.title: Edo-Tokyo Open Air Architectural Museum | 江戸東京たてもの園
tours.shortDescription: Thirty rescued buildings reassembled in a park — Edo farmhouses to a 1930s photo studio, and the bathhouse that inspired Spirited Away.
tours.longDescription:
There's a moment as you cross into the East Zone when modern Tokyo simply stops — the noise goes, the road signs go, and a bathhouse that has stood since 1929 sits at the end of the street. The museum occupies seven hectares of Koganei Park, a forty-minute journey west of Shinjuku, and exists to answer a hard problem: Tokyo loses buildings at an extraordinary rate to fire, earthquake and redevelopment, and by the time anyone thinks to preserve one, the site is usually gone.

The answer was to dismantle thirty significant structures across the city and rebuild them here, across three zones — farmhouses and a 1942 modernist house Kunio Maekawa built for himself in the West, a 1940 ceremonial pavilion in the Centre, and a downtown street of early-twentieth-century shopfronts in the East.

Hayao Miyazaki visited that East Zone repeatedly while making Spirited Away; the bathhouse here, Kodakara-yu, was the direct model for the film's. The resemblance is no coincidence.

stops.title: Edo-Tokyo Open Air Architectural Museum | 江戸東京たてもの園
stops.caption: Cross into the East Zone — the downtown street, with the bathhouse at the far end and a tram parked in the lane.
stops.transcriptText:
ATLAS AUDIO TOUR — EDO-TOKYO OPEN AIR ARCHITECTURAL MUSEUM (江戸東京たてもの園), TOKYO

Location: Within Koganei Park, 3-7-1 Sakura-cho, Koganei City, Tokyo (bus from Musashi-Koganei Station, JR Chuo Line, north exit; approximately 40 minutes from Shinjuku)
Hours: 9:30am–5:30pm (summer); 9:30am–4:30pm (winter); closed Mondays
Admission: ¥400 adults
Approximate duration: 2:20 (≈355 words)

---

There's a moment as you cross from the entrance plaza into the East Zone when modern Tokyo stops. The noise goes. The road signs go. The bathhouse at the end of the street has been standing here — or standing somewhere that became here — since nineteen twenty-nine.

The museum occupies seven hectares of Koganei Park, a forty-minute train journey west of Shinjuku, in the western suburbs where Studio Ghibli is also based. Opened in nineteen ninety-three, it was built to answer a specific problem: Tokyo loses buildings at an extraordinary rate to fire, earthquake, redevelopment, and simple disuse, and by the time people thought to preserve something, the original site was usually gone. The solution was to dismantle significant structures across the city and reassemble them here — thirty buildings in total, from Edo-period farmhouses to a nineteen thirties Art Deco photo studio, from a mausoleum from sixteen fifty-two to a working public bathhouse with separate men's and women's sections still tiled as they were.

The park is divided into three zones. The West Zone has farm homes and residential buildings, including the modernist house that architect Kunio Maekawa built for himself in nineteen forty-two — a concrete and timber structure that looks as though it arrived from a different century entirely, which in this neighbourhood it rather did. The Centre Zone holds the former Kōka-den, a ceremonial pavilion built in nineteen forty to mark the supposed two-thousand-six-hundredth anniversary of the imperial dynasty, relocated here a year later. The East Zone is the downtown reproduction: a commercial street of early-twentieth-century shopfronts, the public bathhouse, a soy sauce shop, an izakaya from the eighteen fifties, a tram car parked at the end of the lane.

Well, Hayao Miyazaki visited the East Zone repeatedly while creating Spirited Away, and the Studio Ghibli diary records that the bathhouse here — called Kodakara-yu, the Children's Bathhouse — was the direct inspiration for the bathhouse at the centre of the film. He designed the museum's own mascot as a form of acknowledgement. The resemblance between the commercial street and the uncanny empty town at the start of the film is not a coincidence.

Allow at least two hours. The buildings are entered, not observed — you take off your shoes at each threshold, walk through the rooms, and find the tram at the far end of the East Zone sitting in a patch of afternoon light as if it had simply pulled in.

---

tours.title: Tsukiji Outer Market | 築地場外市場
tours.shortDescription: The retail heart of Tokyo's old fish market — narrow lanes, standing sushi counters, and tamagoyaki, all the better since the auction floors left.
tours.longDescription:
At its peak this market moved over two thousand tonnes of seafood a day. The wholesale floors that did that work decamped to Toyosu in 2018, and what remains is the part that was always the better visit. The outer market fills a few dense blocks between Ginza and the Sumida — a tight grid of around four hundred and fifty shops, sushi counters, street stalls and knife dealers, open from five in the morning until early afternoon.

The name Tsukiji means "constructed land": the whole district was reclaimed from Tokyo Bay during the Edo period, and the fish market only arrived in 1935, after the previous one was destroyed in the 1923 Great Kanto earthquake.

When the inner auction market left, the famous queueing restaurants went with it. What stayed are the retail vendors, the tamagoyaki shops, the professional knife dealers, and the standing counters where you eat elbow-to-elbow with the people who work here. The fish still arrives each morning from Toyosu — so the quality came here, not away. The old auction site, fittingly, is becoming a baseball stadium.

stops.title: Tsukiji Outer Market | 築地場外市場
stops.caption: Wander the tight grid of lanes between Ginza and the Sumida — make for a standing sushi counter, not the photo-menu restaurants.
stops.transcriptText:
ATLAS AUDIO TOUR — TSUKIJI OUTER MARKET (築地場外市場), TOKYO

Location: Between Shin-Ohashi-dori and the Sumida River, Chuo-ku, Tokyo (1 minute from Tsukiji Station, Tokyo Metro Hibiya Line, exits 1 and 2; or Tsukijishijo Station, Toei Oedo Line, exit A1)
Hours: Approximately 5am–2pm, closed Sundays and some Wednesdays
Approximate duration: 2:05 (≈315 words)

---

At its peak, this market handled over two thousand tonnes of seafood a day. The wholesale floors that did that work moved out in twenty eighteen. What's left is the part that was always better to visit anyway.

The outer market occupies a few dense blocks between Ginza and the Sumida River in Chuo-ku — a tight grid of narrow lanes packed with around four hundred and fifty shops, sushi counters, street food stalls, and knife shops that open from around five in the morning and close by early afternoon. The name Tsukiji means "constructed land" — the entire district was reclaimed from Tokyo Bay during the Edo period, and the fish market itself only arrived here in nineteen thirty-five, after the previous market was destroyed in the nineteen twenty-three Great Kanto earthquake.

The wholesale inner market — the auction floors where professional buyers bid on giant tuna at dawn — relocated to a modern facility in Toyosu in October twenty eighteen. The famous long-queue sushi restaurants went with it. What didn't move was everything you're standing in now: the retail vendors, the tamagoyaki shops that supply sushi restaurants across Tokyo, the professional knife dealers, and the standing sushi counters where you eat elbow-to-elbow with the people who work here. The fish arrives from Toyosu each morning, which is actually where the inner market's quality went, rather than away from it.

The site where the inner wholesale market stood — visible as open ground or construction just east of here — is being redeveloped into a baseball stadium for the Yomiuri Giants, which is a rather Tokyo way of marking the end of an era.

Arrive before nine to beat the tour groups. Order at a standing sushi counter and skip the restaurants with photographs on the menu posted outside — the better spots tend not to need them. The knives in the specialist shops here are the real thing, made for professional kitchens, and worth a look even if you're not buying.

---

tours.title: Fuji Television Building | フジテレビ本社ビル
tours.shortDescription: Kenzo Tange wanted to rebuild Tokyo across its bay in 1960; thirty-six years later he returned to build twin towers cradling a titanium sphere.
tours.longDescription:
In 1960, Kenzo Tange — Japan's most celebrated architect — proposed extending Tokyo out across its own bay, a vast megastructure of towers and corridors on reclaimed water. Tokyo declined. Thirty-six years later he came back to that same bay, now the artificial island of Odaiba, and built this: the Fuji Television headquarters, a pair of titanium-clad towers linked by three sky corridors, with a thirty-two-metre titanium sphere, the Hachitama, slung between them around a hundred metres up.

The building reaches one hundred and twenty-three metres — the maximum permitted on site, with the sphere accounting for the extra forty-five centimetres at the top. The sphere weighs one thousand three hundred and fifty tonnes, its centre of gravity off its core, and was raised by hydraulic jacks over nine and a half hours as Tange and some thirteen hundred onlookers watched.

Completed in 1996, it was the last major project Tange personally led before his death in 2005. The first Japanese architect to win the Pritzker, in 1987, he trained Isozaki, Maki, and Kurokawa besides.

stops.title: Fuji Television Building | フジテレビ本社ビル
stops.caption: From Odaiba, look up at the twin towers — the titanium Hachitama sphere slung between them, around a hundred metres up.
stops.transcriptText:
FUJI TELEVISION HEADQUARTERS — ODAIBA
Atlas Audio Tour

It's 1960. Kenzo Tange, Japan's most celebrated architect, presents a plan to extend Tokyo across its own bay — a vast megastructure of towers, elevated corridors, and capsule platforms, built on reclaimed land, spreading the city out over the water. Tokyo declines. The plan is famous, the land stays empty, and Tange goes on to build other things.

Thirty-six years later, he comes back to that same bay — and this is what he builds on it.

You're standing in Odaiba, the artificial island that now occupies the very water Tange wanted to restructure, looking at the Fuji Television headquarters: a pair of towers in titanium-clad concrete, connected by three enclosed sky corridors, with a thirty-two-metre titanium sphere — the Hachitama — suspended between them at a height of roughly a hundred metres. The building is one hundred and twenty-three metres tall, which is the maximum height permitted on site. The extra zero point four five metres at the top is the sphere.

The sphere weighs one thousand three hundred and fifty tonnes and its centre of gravity is not at its core, which made installation considerably more complicated than it sounds. It was built on the seventh-floor rooftop garden during construction, supported on three beams, and then raised by hydraulic jacks over the course of nine and a half hours — at five metres per hour, with Tange and around thirteen hundred spectators watching from the ground. It now houses an observation room with two-hundred-and-seventy-degree views of Tokyo Bay and, on clear days, Mount Fuji.

The building was completed in 1996 and is the last major project Tange personally led before his death in 2005. He was the first Japanese architect to win the Pritzker Prize — the profession's closest equivalent to a Nobel — receiving it in 1987, nine years before this building opened. The students he trained at Tokyo University included Arata Isozaki, Fumihiko Maki, and Kisho Kurokawa, who between them account for a substantial portion of late-twentieth-century Japanese architecture.

The Hachitama observation room is open to the public on most days except Monday, with an entry fee on the upper floors. The Yurikamome monorail, which runs directly past the building and offers some of the best elevated views of it, runs from Shimbashi.

tours.title: Ghibli Museum | 三鷹の森ジブリ美術館
tours.shortDescription: Hayao Miyazaki designed this Mitaka museum with storyboards rather than plans — no maps, no route, just "let's get lost together."
tours.longDescription:
There are no maps inside, the signs are in Japanese only, and the museum's own slogan is "let's get lost together." All of it was deliberate. The Ghibli Museum opened on the first of October 2001, on the western edge of Inokashira Park in Mitaka, where Hayao Miyazaki has long lived. He designed it as he designs his films — not with architectural plans but with storyboards, drawing each space in sequence as if it were a scene.

The result refuses to behave like a museum. There is no prescribed route, no chronological narrative. Instead there is a spiral staircase that leads somewhere unexpected, stained-glass windows lit by natural light, a rooftop garden where a five-metre robot soldier from Castle in the Sky stands among the trees, a theatre showing exclusive short films, and a basement zoetrope that makes Totoro appear to run in midair.

The architecture nods to the Italian hill town of Calcata, north of Rome — a medieval village of narrow lanes opening onto unexpected sky. Miyazaki wanted exactly that feeling: round a corner, find something you weren't expecting.

stops.title: Ghibli Museum | 三鷹の森ジブリ美術館
stops.caption: Step inside without a map and look for the spiral staircase, the stained glass, and the rooftop robot among the trees.
stops.transcriptText:
GHIBLI MUSEUM — 三鷹の森ジブリ美術館
Atlas Audio Tour

There are no maps inside. The signs within the building are in Japanese only. The museum's own slogan is "let's get lost together." This was all deliberate.

The Ghibli Museum opened on the first of October 2001, on the western edge of Inokashira Park in Mitaka — the suburb where Hayao Miyazaki, the studio's co-founder and the museum's designer, has long lived. He designed the building as he designs his films: not with architectural plans but with storyboards, drawing each space in sequence, as if it were a scene. The result is a building that does not operate like a museum in the conventional sense. There is no prescribed route. No roped-off exhibits. No chronological narrative that the visitor follows from entrance to exit.

What there is: a spiral staircase that leads somewhere unexpected; stained glass windows featuring characters from the films, back-lit by natural light; a rooftop garden where a five-metre robot soldier from Castle in the Sky stands guard among the trees; a small theatre showing exclusive short films that are not available anywhere else; and on the basement floor, a zoetrope — a spinning drum whose strobed illumination makes still clay figures of Totoro and his companions appear to run and bounce in midair, demonstrating in one image exactly how animation works.

The architecture was influenced by the hill towns of Italy — specifically Calcata, north of Rome, a medieval village built on volcanic rock with narrow lanes leading to views of unexpected sky. Miyazaki wanted the museum to feel like that: a place where you round a corner and find something you were not expecting to find.

Tickets must be booked well in advance through the Lawson ticketing system — same-day entry is not possible. Access is by bus from Mitaka Station or on foot through the park.

tours.title: Gōtoku-ji | 豪徳寺
tours.shortDescription: A quiet Setagaya temple where ten thousand white beckoning cats raise a paw — each one an offering left after a wish.
tours.longDescription:
The lucky cats here hold nothing: no gold coin in their paws, only the idea that they can invite opportunity. What you do with it is your own affair. The temple sits at the end of a quiet residential street in Setagaya, about fifteen minutes from Shinjuku, and the Shofuku-den Hall is ringed with shelves stacked with hundreds — by some counts ten thousand — small white ceramic maneki-neko, all facing outward, right paws raised. Every figure was left by a visitor, brought after a wish was made or granted.

The legend dates to 1633, when Ii Naotaka, lord of Hikone, was beckoned inside by a white cat at the gate just as a thunderstorm broke. He credited the cat with his survival and made Gotokuji the Ii clan's temple. It remains their burial ground — Naotaka's grave, and that of Ii Naosuke, the shogunate's chief minister assassinated at the Sakurada Gate in 1860, both lie here among their porcelain successors.

The sheer scale of the collection is quietly overwhelming, which is not what one expects in suburban Tokyo.

stops.title: Gōtoku-ji | 豪徳寺
stops.caption: Through the main gate and past the incense holder, look left to the Shofuku-den Hall and its shelves of beckoning cats.
stops.transcriptText:
ATLAS AUDIO TOUR — GŌTOKU-JI TEMPLE (大谿山 豪徳寺), TOKYO

Location: 2-24-7 Gotokuji, Setagaya-ku, Tokyo (5 minutes from Miyanosaka Station, Tokyu Setagaya Line; 10 minutes from Gotokuji Station, Odakyu Line)
Approximate duration: 2:10 (≈330 words)

---

The lucky cats in front of you are holding nothing. No gold coin in their paws, no token of wealth. The idea is that they can invite opportunity — what you do with it is entirely your own affair.

The temple sits at the end of a quiet residential street in Setagaya, a low-key part of western Tokyo that takes about fifteen minutes to reach from Shinjuku. Through the main gate and past the incense holder, the Shofuku-den Hall stands to the left, its surrounding shelves stacked with hundreds — by some estimates ten thousand — small white ceramic maneki-neko, all facing outward with right paws raised. Every figurine was left here by a visitor, brought as an offering after a wish was made, or after one was granted. The figures at Gotokuji raise the right paw, which is associated with the invitation of wealth and business prosperity rather than people. They carry no koban — no gold coin — because they were never meant to deliver luck ready-made.

The legend behind the temple dates to sixteen thirty-three, when Ii Naotaka, feudal lord of the Hikone province, was returning from a falconry expedition when a white cat at the temple gate beckoned him inside. A thunderstorm broke as he sheltered there, and Naotaka attributed his survival to the cat's invitation. He subsequently made Gotokuji the ancestral temple of the Ii clan, and it remains their burial ground: the graves of Naotaka and, in the far corner of the cemetery, Ii Naosuke — the chief minister of the Edo shogunate, assassinated at the Sakurada Gate in eighteen sixty — are both here, surrounded on all sides by their porcelain successors.

I find the scale of the cat collection rather quietly overwhelming, which is not an experience I expected to have in a temple in suburban Tokyo.

The Tokyu Setagaya Line runs a maneki-neko decorated tram on this route — if you take the tram rather than the Odakyu Line to get here, you arrive having already been welcomed. The cemetery in the far grounds is accessible and worth a few quiet minutes, regardless of whether you can read the gravestones.

---

tours.title: Hachiko Statue | 忠犬ハチ公像
tours.shortDescription: The bronze dog who waited nine years, ten months and fifteen days for a man who would never come home again.
tours.longDescription:
In November 1923 a fifty-day-old puppy was wrapped in a rice sack for a twenty-hour train journey to Tokyo. Born near Ōdate in Akita Prefecture, he was named from the character hachi, meaning eight, because when he stood his front legs formed that exact shape. The original statue was raised on this spot in 1934 — while Hachikō was still alive — then melted down in the war; the one before you was recast in 1948 by the original sculptor's son.

The story is brief and devastating. Adopted in 1924 by Professor Hidesaburō Ueno, Hachikō met him at this station each evening. On 21 May 1925 Ueno died at work and never came home. The dog didn't know, and kept returning at the train's due time every day until his own death in 1935.

Taught to schoolchildren as a lesson in loyalty, the story even moved Helen Keller, who in 1937 asked for an Akita of her own.

stops.title: Hachiko Statue | 忠犬ハチ公像
stops.caption: The bronze dog before you is Hachikō, and the station exit directly behind you carries his name.
stops.transcriptText:
It's November 1923. A puppy is wrapped in a rice sack to keep warm for a twenty-hour train journey south to Tokyo. He is fifty days old, born near the city of Ōdate in Akita Prefecture, and his name comes from the character 八 — hachi, meaning eight — because when he stands, his front legs form that exact shape.

The bronze dog in front of you is Hachikō, and the exit directly behind you is named after him. The original statue was erected here in April 1934 — while Hachikō was still alive — by sculptor Teru Andō, after a national newspaper story turned a quietly devoted animal into a symbol recognised across Japan. That original statue was melted down during the Second World War for metal. The one you're looking at now was cast in 1948 by Takeshi Andō, the original sculptor's son.

The story, briefly: Hachikō was adopted in 1924 by Professor Hidesaburō Ueno, an agricultural scientist at Tokyo Imperial University who lived near Shibuya. Ueno walked to this station every morning; Hachikō would return each evening to meet him. On May 21st, 1925, Ueno died of a cerebral haemorrhage at work and never came home. Hachikō didn't know this, and kept coming. For nine years, ten months, and fifteen days, the dog returned to this spot, every day, at the time the train was due, until his own death on March 8th, 1935.

Hachikō's story is taught to Japanese schoolchildren as a lesson in loyalty. In 1937, Helen Keller visited the statue and asked to be given an Akita of her own.

Hachikō's grave is in Aoyama Cemetery, a short bus ride east, where his ashes were buried beside Professor Ueno's. His preserved body is on display at the National Museum of Nature and Science in Ueno Park. The two statues are reunited only there: Hachikō leaping up, Ueno bending to meet him — the moment that never happened in life.

tours.title: Heiwa Doburoku Kabutocho Brewery | 平和どぶろく兜町醸造所
tours.shortDescription: Beside the Tokyo Stock Exchange, a tiny brewery makes doburoku — the oldest, unfiltered form of rice fermentation, the ancestor of sake.
tours.longDescription:
There's a curious thing about this corner of Kabutocho: it sits next to the Tokyo Stock Exchange, in Japan's historic financial district, and what it makes in a small room behind the counter is the oldest form of rice fermentation in the country.

The brewery opened in June 2022 on the ground floor of the timber-hybrid KITOKI building, run by Heiwa Shuzo, a Wakayama brewery known for the sake brand KID and the plum wine Tsuraume. There's history in the address — Kabutocho and Nihonbashi were the Edo-period landing point where sake barrels arrived by boat from Kansai, and the brewery came here partly in acknowledgement of that.

The product is doburoku: unfiltered, unpressed rice fermentation, the ancestral form of sake before straining was introduced. Under Japanese tax law it can't legally be called sake, because sake must be filtered — a fine distinction, but a meaningful one. The brewer works behind the counter, tuning the flavours to what the regulars tell him, so the menu rotates from plain and hops-infused to azuki bean, mikan, rosemary and basil. Each is brewed on site and served fresh.
