tours.title: Hōrin-ji Temple | 法輪寺
tours.shortDescription: A small Waseda temple where the head priest floats seasonal flowers in the water basins himself — and posts when he's refreshed them.
tours.longDescription:
You'll likely hear it before you see it: wind chimes above the gate, and coloured umbrellas strung across the ceiling of the covered stair. The stone steps climb through the Sanmon gate to Hōrin-ji, a Nichiren Buddhist temple that has occupied this Waseda side street since 1662, having been founded in 1606 before Edo Castle's moats forced two relocations. The grounds are small and beautifully kept, with the main hall ahead and several stone water basins set around the compound.

Those basins are what the temple is known for now: the hana-chōzu, or flower water basins, filled with seasonal blooms — dahlias in February, cherry blossom in April, hydrangea in June, cosmos in October. The head priest arranges every one himself, sources the flowers, and updates the temple's social media when they're refreshed.

The temple also issues monthly goshuin as intricate paper-cut designs mirroring the current bloom — and people plan their visits around which month's design they want to collect.

stops.title: Hōrin-ji Temple | 法輪寺
stops.caption: Climb the stair beneath the umbrellas and through the Sanmon gate; the flower-filled basins are set around the compound.
stops.transcriptText:
HŌRIN-JI TEMPLE — WASEDA, SHINJUKU
Atlas Audio Tour

Before you reach the gate, you'll probably hear it: the thin, bright sound of wind chimes from the entrance above, and below them, the coloured umbrellas strung across the ceiling of the covered stair.

The stone steps in front of you lead up through the Sanmon gate to the grounds of Hōrin-ji, a Nichiren Buddhist temple that has occupied this particular Waseda side street since 1662 — though the temple itself was founded in 1606, before Edo Castle's outer moats forced it to relocate twice. The grounds are small and kept with great care: once through the gate, you'll find the main hall directly ahead, and several stone water basins — the chōzuya — arranged across the compound, each one filled with seasonal flowers floating on the surface.

This is what the temple is best known for now: the hana-chōzu, or flower water basins. Flowers follow the bloom calendar through the year — dahlias in February, cherry blossom in April, hydrangea in June, cosmos in October — and the arrangements are changed regularly. The detail worth knowing is that the head priest arranges every one of them himself. He sources the flowers, sets the displays, and updates the temple's social media to tell visitors when the basins have been refreshed. A fourth-century Buddhist practice and an Instagram notification, coexisting without apparent awkwardness.

The temple also issues monthly goshuin — the ink stamps that serve as records of a temple visit — in the form of intricate paper-cut designs that mirror the current flower in the basins. Each one is a different colour and pattern, and people plan visits specifically around which month's design they want to collect.

Waseda University is a five-minute walk east from here, and the neighbourhood has a number of older temples and shrines within easy reach. The Ana Hachimangu Shrine, a short walk away, is worth adding to the route.

tours.title: Imperial Palace | 皇居
tours.shortDescription: An address with five centuries of history and almost no original fabric — moats, watchtower and bridges where Japan's emperor still lives.
tours.longDescription:
In 1657 the main keep of Edo Castle — then the tallest tower in Japan, perhaps the largest fortress on earth — burned to the ground in a fire that killed around a hundred thousand people. The shogunate judged it too expensive to rebuild, and that, more or less, is why the site looks as it does today.

From the lawn of Kokyo Gaien, the wide grey-green moat lies ahead, the stone walls of Edo Castle rising behind. Two bridges cross in sequence: the double-arched stone Meganebashi, nicknamed the Eyeglass Bridge for the shape its arches make in the water, and behind it the iron Nijubashi. Above them stands the Fushimi-yagura watchtower, a mid-seventeenth-century keep that survived fire and war — the oldest structure on the site.

The palace buildings themselves date only from 1968, concrete beneath traditional rooflines, rebuilt after the 1945 bombing destroyed the Meiji palace of 1888. Little here predates the twentieth century, yet it remains the residence of Emperor Naruhito, the hundred-and-twenty-sixth emperor, who has lived here since 2019.

stops.title: Imperial Palace | 皇居
stops.caption: Face the palace from the open lawn of Kokyo Gaien — moat ahead, the two bridges in sequence, the Fushimi-yagura above.
stops.transcriptText:
IMPERIAL PALACE — KOKYO GAIEN PLAZA
Atlas Audio Tour

It's 1657. The main keep of Edo Castle — at that point the tallest tower in Japan, possibly the largest fortress on earth — burns to the ground in a fire that kills around a hundred thousand people across the city. The shogunate decides it's too expensive to rebuild. And that, more or less, is why what you're looking at today looks the way it does.

Face the palace from the open lawn of Kokyo Gaien, the broad public garden to the south. The moat is directly ahead, grey-green and wide, with the stone walls of the original Edo Castle rising behind it. Two bridges cross the water in sequence: the graceful double-arched stone bridge in the foreground — nicknamed Meganebashi, the Eyeglass Bridge, for the shape its arches make in the water below — and behind it, the iron Nijubashi, the Double Bridge, its name a reference to the wooden two-storey structure it replaced in 1888. Above both of them, framed against the walls, is the Fushimi-yagura watchtower: a mid-seventeenth-century keep that survived the fires and the war and is now the oldest standing structure on the entire site.

That detail is worth pausing on. The current palace buildings date from 1968 — concrete under their traditional rooflines, rebuilt after Allied bombing in 1945 destroyed the Meiji-era palace that had itself only stood since 1888. The moat walls are older, and some of the stonework dates back to the castle's Tokugawa construction, but as a piece of living architecture, almost nothing here predates the twentieth century. What you're standing in front of is, in a sense, an address with five hundred years of history and very little original fabric left — and yet it remains the residence of the hundred-and-twenty-sixth emperor of Japan, Emperor Naruhito, who has lived here since 2019.

The East Gardens, entered through the Otemon Gate to the north, are open to the public without a reservation on most days, and they contain the stone foundations of the keep that never came back — a flat-topped platform rising from the lawn, all that physically remains of what was once the highest point in the city. It's worth finding.

tours.title: Inokashira Park | 井の頭恩賜公園
tours.shortDescription: A pond that watered Edo for two centuries — source of the Kanda River, named the "wellhead" by a shogun for exactly what it did.
tours.longDescription:
The pond is the reason this place exists. Not the cherry trees or the swan boats, but the water — Inokashira Pond, source of the Kanda River, which runs twenty kilometres east to meet the Sumida near Ryogoku. During the Edo period that river was the city's main drinking supply, the Kanda Aqueduct drawing on these springs to slake a city of over a million for more than two centuries.

The first Tokugawa shogun, Ieyasu, is said to have brewed his tea from the spring called Ochanomizu here. The third, Iemitsu, gave the pond its name: Inokashira, the "wellhead." He named it for what it did. The original springs have weakened and are now topped up by a pump from 150 metres down, but the river still begins here, still ending at the Sumida.

The park opened in 1917 as a gift from Emperor Taisho — the first of its kind in Japan. The Benzaiten shrine in the western arm dates to the Heian period; her domain is water, music, and the arts, and legend warns that couples who row here may stir her jealousy. Draw your own conclusions.

stops.title: Inokashira Park | 井の頭恩賜公園
stops.caption: Stand at the pond's edge — this is Inokashira, source of the Kanda River and once the drinking water of Edo.
stops.transcriptText:
INOKASHIRA PARK — KICHIJOJI / MITAKA
Atlas Audio Tour

The pond in front of you is the reason this place exists. Not the cherry trees, not the swan boats, not the museum on the far side — the pond, and specifically what comes out of it.

Inokashira Pond is the source of the Kanda River, which flows twenty kilometres east through central Tokyo before joining the Sumida near Ryogoku. During the Edo period, that river was the city's primary drinking water supply — the Kanda Aqueduct drew from these springs here to provide water to one of the largest cities on earth, over a million people, for more than two centuries. The first Tokugawa shogun, Ieyasu, is said to have prepared his tea from the spring known as Ochanomizu — "tea water spring" — that rises in the western end of the park. The third shogun, Iemitsu, gave the pond its current name: Inokashira, which means "wellhead." The source. The head of the well. He named it for what it did.

The original springs that fed the pond have largely weakened over time and are now supplemented by a pump drawing from 150 metres underground. The pond itself is still here, still long and narrow, still lined with cherry trees that make this one of Tokyo's most-visited hanami spots in spring. And the Kanda River still begins here, still running east, still ending at the Sumida.

The park opened in 1917 as a gift from Emperor Taisho to the people of Tokyo — the first park of its kind in Japan, and the reason it is formally called Inokashira Onshi Kōen: the Imperial Grant Park. Before that it had been an imperial forest, sealed to the public. Before that it had been the water supply for a city. The Benzaiten shrine tucked into the western arm of the pond dates to the Heian period and was restored by the third Tokugawa shogun. Her domain is water, music, and the arts; local legend holds that couples who row on the pond may incur her jealousy. Draw your own conclusions.

Utagawa Hiroshige included the pond in his series One Hundred Famous Views of Edo. The Ghibli Museum occupies the southwest edge of the park, about a fifteen-minute walk from here, and requires tickets booked well in advance.

tours.title: Kayanoya Ginza | 東京銀座 茅乃舎
tours.shortDescription: A Fukuoka soy-sauce brewery made famous by a sachet of dried fish, reborn as a Kengo Kuma flagship in the heart of Ginza.
tours.longDescription:
There's a curious thing about this shop: it began as a soy-sauce brewery in a Fukuoka village in 1893, and the thing that made it famous was a sachet of dried fish. The Ginza flagship opened in November 2025, designed by Kengo Kuma, whose wooden signatures run throughout — soy-sauce tubs suspended in the ceiling, shelving drawn from the brand's old warehouse aesthetic. The first floor carries the full dashi range alongside more than twenty individually sold dried ingredients, each sourced from a specific region, plus five regional kits bundling the characteristic flavours of Tokyo, Nagoya, Noto, Kyoto and Hakata.

The real origin lies in a countryside restaurant the Kubara Honke company opened in Hisayama in 2005, under a thatched roof said to be the largest in western Japan. Customers kept asking how to make the same broth at home. The answer was the additive-free Kayanoya dashi packet — bonito, charcoal-grilled flying fish, sardine and true kelp — which built the brand into thirty-three stores.

The Ginza shop is the furthest thing from that farmhouse, which is rather the point.

There's a curious thing about this shop — it started as a soy sauce brewery in a village in Fukuoka in eighteen ninety-three, and the thing that made it famous was a sachet of dried fish.

The Ginza flagship opened in November twenty twenty-five, designed by Kengo Kuma, whose trademark wooden elements appear throughout the interior — suspended soy sauce tubs in the ceiling, shelving drawn from Kayanoya's traditional warehouse aesthetic. The first floor carries the brand's full dashi range alongside over twenty types of individually sold dried ingredients: bonito flakes, kelp, charcoal-grilled flying fish, sardines, each one sourced from a specific region. There are also five regional dried ingredient kits — Tokyo, Nagoya, Noto, Kyoto, Hakata — that bundle the characteristic dashi ingredients of each area together, with recipes.

The brand's actual origin is in a countryside restaurant in Hisayama, Fukuoka, that the Kubara Honke company opened in two thousand and five: seasonal food, local ingredients, a thatched roof said to be the largest in western Japan. Customers kept asking how they could make the same broth at home. The answer was the Kayanoya Dashi packet — dried bonito, charcoal-grilled flying fish, sardine, and true kelp, blended and bagged, additive-free — which is actually the product that built the brand into thirty-three stores across Japan.

The Ginza shop is rather the furthest thing from that Fukuoka farmhouse, which is perhaps the point: the same dashi, in the centre of one of the most expensive retail streets on earth, designed by one of Japan's most celebrated architects.

Take the dashi packet home. Make miso soup. The instructions are on the back and the result is worth the trouble.

tours.title: Kioi Seido | 紀尾井清堂
tours.shortDescription: A glass-wrapped concrete cube whose architect was told to build it first and decide what it was for later.
tours.longDescription:
The client told the architect to design the building however he wished, then decide later what it was for. The result stands at Kioicho in Chiyoda, between the Akasaka Palace grounds and the Imperial Palace moats: a fifteen-metre concrete cube raised on four pilotis, wrapped entirely in glass, five storeys up and one below. Completed in December 2021, it was designed by Hiroshi Naito for the RINRI Institute of Ethics, whose chairman said the function would be worked out once the building existed. Its listed use is, officially, "unknown."

Naito answered with a modern Pantheon — taking the Roman original, a building still compelling precisely because its purpose stays unclear, as his model. The exterior is sealed and opaque above the ground floor, the glass giving back reflections rather than views. The lower floors are dark and dense, rough concrete and earthen tones nodding to the prehistoric Jomon period, while a central skylight lets daylight fall from above like a temple lantern.

The only specific instruction, beyond the absence of a brief, was that Naito think about the Jomon period — a precise demand, in its way.

---

The client told the architect to design the building however he wished, then decide later what it was for. The building in front of you is the result of that conversation.

Kioi Seidō stands at 3 Kioicho in Chiyoda, between the grounds of the Akasaka Palace and the moats of the Imperial Palace — a fifteen-metre concrete cube raised on four pilotis, wrapped entirely in glass, five storeys above ground and one below. Completed in December twenty twenty-one, it was designed by Hiroshi Naito for the RINRI Institute of Ethics, a private organisation with a longstanding interest in moral education. The institute's chairman told Naito that the function would be worked out after the building existed. The official listed use of the building is "unknown."

Naito's response was to build a modern Pantheon. He engaged with the Pantheon in Rome as a model — a building whose original purpose remains unclear after two thousand years, yet which has remained continuously compelling for exactly that reason. The exterior is sealed, opaque above the ground floor, the glass walls giving back reflections rather than views inside. The lower floors are dark, grounded, materially dense — rough concrete and earthen tones referencing the Jōmon period, Japan's prehistoric era of knotted rope pottery and abstract clay figurines. Above, a central skylight opens the upper space to diffuse daylight that falls through the building from above rather than entering from the sides, in the manner of a temple lantern or a burial mound with a smoke hole.

The client's only specific instruction, beyond the absence of a programme, was that Naito think about the Jōmon period. I find that rather a precise brief, in its way: design something that connects the oldest possible layer of Japanese culture to the present, without knowing what you'll do with it once it's finished.

The Akasaka Palace grounds — the State Guest House, a Meiji-era classical building used for state visits — are directly adjacent to the north, and worth a slow walk round the perimeter even if the interior is closed.

tours.title: Kyū Asakura House | 旧朝倉家住宅
tours.shortDescription: A 1919 Taisho-era house on a Daikanyama hillside that survived both the Great Kanto Earthquake and the firebombing of Tokyo.
tours.longDescription:
In 1919 Torajiro Asakura — former timber merchant, adopted son of a rice dynasty, chairman of the Tokyo Metropolitan Assembly — built himself a house on a Daikanyama hillside. It is a very good house, and unlike almost everything else standing in Tokyo that year, it is still here. A two-storey wooden building with a tiled roof, characteristically Taisho in its balance of traditional planning and restrained modernity.

Inside, the rooms split by function: reception rooms for political visitors on one side, family rooms on the other. The cedar Suginoma rooms look out onto a stroll garden that follows the slope of the cliff behind — stone lanterns, moss, stepping stones, azaleas in spring and maples in autumn.

The house came through the 1923 Great Kanto Earthquake and the 1945 firebombing, sheltered by its hillside. Almost all of Tokyo's Taisho residential fabric was lost in those two catastrophes; this is one of the few survivors. It owes its life partly to architect Fumihiko Maki, who argued for keeping it. Designated an Important Cultural Property in 2004.

stops.title: Kyū Asakura House | 旧朝倉家住宅
stops.caption: Through the gate, the main house sits back on a slight rise — remove your shoes at the entrance before you go in.
stops.transcriptText:
KYU ASAKURA HOUSE — DAIKANYAMA, SHIBUYA
Atlas Audio Tour

It's 1919. Torajiro Asakura — former timber merchant, adopted son of a rice dynasty, chairman of the Tokyo Metropolitan Assembly — is at the peak of his influence, and he builds himself a house on a hillside in what is now Daikanyama. It is a good house. A very good house. And unlike almost everything else that stood in Tokyo in 1919, it is still here.

Through the gate in front of you, the main structure sits back from the street on a slight rise — a two-storey wooden building with a tiled roof, characteristically Taisho in its balance of traditional Japanese planning and restrained modernity. Remove your shoes at the entrance. Inside, the rooms are arranged around the logic of the house's dual function: reception rooms on one side for Asakura's political visitors, family rooms on the other. The cedar rooms — the Suginoma — on the western side were where he received private guests. They look directly out onto the garden, which follows the natural slope of the cliff-line behind the house in a stroll design: stone lanterns, moss, stepping stones, the azaleas coming in spring and the maples in autumn.

The house survived the 1923 Great Kanto Earthquake — the storehouse was damaged and later repaired — and the wartime firebombing of 1945 left it unscathed, sheltered by the hillside and its relative distance from the urban centre. Tokyo has been catastrophically rebuilt twice in a single century, and almost all of the residential fabric of the Taisho era was lost in those two events. The Kyu Asakura House is one of the few to have come through both.

It owes its continued existence in part to Fumihiko Maki, the architect commissioned in the 1960s and 70s to build the Hillside Terrace shopping complex on what had been part of the original Asakura estate. Maki — who would later win the Pritzker Prize — looked at this building and argued, successfully, that it was worth keeping. The house was designated a national Important Cultural Property in 2004 and opened to the public the same year.

Worth noting before you go in: when the house was built in 1919, Mount Fuji was visible from the second floor. The city has since taken care of that. But the cedar rooms, the garden, and the moss are as they were.

tours.title: Louis Vuitton Ginza Namiki | ルイ・ヴィトン 銀座並木通り店
tours.shortDescription: Jun Aoki's rippling glass tower in Ginza, built to look like water — on ground that was once the floor of Tokyo Bay.
tours.longDescription:
The ground beneath your feet was once Tokyo Bay, and the building in front of you was designed to look like water. There is a logic to this.

Seven storeys of curved, rippling glass rise from a double-height transparent ground floor that wraps the corner of Namiki-dori. The facade is two layers of glass, the outer panes shaped into three-dimensional curves and coated with dichroic film that shifts colour as you pass: silver in flat light, then blue, green and violet. Higher up, the surrounding towers distort into wavy apparitions, and after dark the upper floors seem to dematerialise.

The architect Jun Aoki described it as a pillar of water, citing two sources — Heihachiro Fukuda's 1932 painting Sazanami, or Ripples, in ultramarine on platinum foil, and Debussy's Reflets dans l'eau. If painters and composers could make something from the playfulness of water, he reasoned, so could an architect. Inside, Peter Marino's sculpted oak staircase unfurls upward like a ribbon. Ginza was a waterfront district in the Edo period, reclaimed over centuries; this building reaches back to the water that was here before the land.

The ground beneath your feet was once Tokyo Bay. The building in front of you was designed to look like water. There is a logic to this.

The building occupies a corner on Namiki-dori in Ginza — seven storeys of curved, rippling glass rising from a double-height transparent ground floor that wraps round the corner. The facade is two layers of glass, the outer panes shaped into three-dimensional curves and coated with dichroic film that shifts through colour as you move past it: silver in flat light, blue and green and violet as the angle changes, and at the higher floors the surrounding tower reflections distort into wavy apparitions, the glass dissolving the city grid above the street. After dark, the bright activity at the base fades upward and the upper floors appear to dematerialise.

I find the building's relationship to its own site the most interesting thing about it. Ginza was a waterfront district during the Edo period; the bay was reclaimed over centuries to produce the grid of streets you're standing in. The previous Louis Vuitton building on this corner was designed to evoke Meiji-era brick — this one reaches further back, to the water that was here before the land.

tours.title: Matcha & Espresso Miyano-yu | 宮乃湯
tours.shortDescription: A 1951 bathhouse turned café in Nezu, where you order beneath the old boiler chimney and your table number rides a wooden locker key.
tours.longDescription:
A public bathhouse opened on this Nezu backstreet in 1951 and served it for fifty-seven years, until the last customers came in 2008 and the water was turned off. Find the broad grey chimney still standing beside the entrance — in a working sento that stack was the boiler signature, visible streets away, the signal that the baths were open. The café is up a short flight of steps beside it, its counter built from the bathhouse's original shoe lockers, your table number written on one of the wooden key blocks that once sealed them.

The building's owner considered turning it into flats, then chose instead to preserve the sento's community function — the local bathhouse being the old shitamachi neighbourhood's meeting place and reason to leave the house. Opened in 2021 and managed by Emi Osato, the café takes that argument seriously.

Duck under the low beam and the former men's bathing room opens out: high arched ceiling, original tiles, planting, and two Tadanori Yokoo paintings on the back wall.

stops.transcriptText:
MATCHA & ESPRESSO MIYANO-YU — NEZU
Atlas Audio Tour

A public bathhouse opened here in 1951, in the slow recovery after the war, and it served this Nezu backstreet for fifty-seven years until the last customers came in 2008 and the water was turned off for good.

Find the chimney — the broad, grey stack that you can see from the street, still standing beside the entrance. In a functioning sento, that chimney was the boiler signature, visible from several streets away, the signal that the baths were open. The entrance to the café is right beside it, up a short flight of steps and through a sliding door. The counter you'll find inside is built from the bathhouse's original shoe lockers, and when you order, your table number is written on one of the wooden key blocks that used to seal them — an object that has had roughly the same function in this building across two entirely different businesses.

The developer who owns the former bathhouse building considered converting it into flats, and then decided not to. The conversion into Miyano-yu café — which opened in 2021, managed by Emi Osato — was undertaken specifically to preserve the community function of the sento rather than its architecture alone. In Japan's postwar shitamachi neighbourhoods, the local bathhouse was the communication node: a daily meeting place, a shared space, a reason to leave the house. The café takes that argument seriously. Pass through the narrow corridor beyond the counter, ducking slightly under the low beam, and the former men's bathing room opens out — high arched ceiling, large windows, the room planted with greenery, the original tiles still on the walls. On the back wall, two paintings by Tadanori Yokoo, made in collaboration with the Tokyo Bath Association.

The matcha is sourced from Shizuoka, in the Oceania-style espresso tradition, and the coffee is house-roasted on site — you can see the roaster in what used to be the changing room, behind a seating area for four.

Nezu Shrine is a ten-minute walk, and the neighbourhood's main shopping street runs parallel to this one heading towards Yanaka. Both are worth the detour once you've finished your drink.

tours.title: Maison Hermès Le Forum | 銀座メゾンエルメス フォーラム
tours.shortDescription: Renzo Piano's Ginza "magic lantern" — thirteen thousand bespoke glass blocks that glow like a paper lantern and sway with the earth.
tours.longDescription:
The building before you is made of glass, yet you cannot see through it — which is the most interesting thing about it. Fronting Harumi-dori with a frontage of just eleven metres, the Maison Hermès runs fifty-six metres back along the side street and rises fifteen storeys, clad top to bottom in thirteen thousand bespoke glass blocks, each forty-five centimetres square. Made by a glassworks in Florence, they are translucent rather than transparent — closer to a Japanese shoji screen than a shop window — and curved at the corners so the whole skin reads as a single membrane.

Renzo Piano, who designed it in 2001, called it a magic lantern, after the chōchin paper lanterns of traditional houses. By day the facade is silvered and sparkling; by night it glows warmly from within. In a street of neon, the restraint carries weight.

Less visible is the engineering. The glass is hung from the steel frame on arms, with flexible seals between every block, so the facade can shift up to four millimetres in an earthquake — moving with the city's geology rather than against it.

stops.title: Maison Hermès Le Forum | 銀座メゾンエルメス フォーラム
stops.caption: Stand on Harumi-dori and read the glass skin as one continuous membrane — silvered by day, glowing from within by night.
stops.transcriptText:
MAISON HERMÈS LE FORUM — GINZA
Atlas Audio Tour

The building in front of you is made of glass, but you can't see through it. That's the first thing to notice — and, if you ask me, the most interesting.

Harumi-dori runs north–south through the heart of Ginza, and the Maison Hermès sits along it with a frontage of only eleven metres, which is very little given what's behind: the building runs fifty-six metres back along the side street, rising fifteen storeys and clad from top to bottom in thirteen thousand bespoke glass blocks, each one forty-five centimetres square. They were made specifically for this project by a glassworks in Florence, pressed and textured so that they are translucent rather than transparent — closer in effect to a Japanese shoji screen than to a conventional shop window. At the building's corners, the blocks are curved, softening the edges so that the whole skin reads as a single continuous membrane rather than a box.

Renzo Piano, who designed the building in 2001, described his intention as a magic lantern — a reference to the chōchin, the paper lanterns that hang from the doorways of traditional Japanese houses. By day the facade is silvered and sparkling; by night the building glows from within, and the light it gives off is warm rather than harsh. In a street of neon, that restraint carries considerable weight.

What's less visible from the pavement is the engineering. The glass skin is not structural — it's hung from the building's steel frame on a series of arms, with flexible seals between every block, so that in the event of an earthquake the facade can shift by up to four millimetres in any direction, absorbing the shock rather than resisting it. The building doesn't fight the city's geology. It moves with it.

Le Forum, the free gallery on the eighth and ninth floors, is reached not through the main store entrance but via a separate door on the side street — look for it between the buildings. The space is flooded with natural light through the glass blocks, and it hosts site-specific installations from Japanese and international artists roughly three times a year. The entrance to Le Studio, a small cinema on the tenth floor showing free films at weekends, is through the same door.

tours.title: Meiji Jingu | 明治神宮
tours.shortDescription: A forest planted in 1915 to last a century, designed to silence the city the moment you step through the twelve-metre cypress torii.
tours.longDescription:
In 1915, a group of forestry scientists stood on a barren field in what would become central Tokyo and decided what kind of forest Japan would have in a hundred years. They specified one hundred and twenty thousand trees from three hundred and sixty-five species, planted by a hundred and ten thousand volunteers, calculated to grow into a self-sustaining canopy needing no maintenance. It is now doing exactly that — and the way the city's noise cuts off the moment you pass the gate was no accident. It was designed.

The great south torii behind you stands twelve metres tall, cut from a fifteen-hundred-year-old cypress found on a Taiwanese mountain. The inner shrine buildings, destroyed in wartime air raids, were rebuilt in 1958. Emperor Meiji himself rests in Kyoto; this is a symbolic memorial to his reign, which carried Japan from feudal isolation into a modern industrial state.

Before the inner shrine you'll pass two rows of barrels — sake offered by breweries across Japan, and opposite them wine from Burgundy, a nod to Meiji's documented fondness for it. A rather precise summary of what his reign meant.

stops.title: Meiji Jingu | 明治神宮
stops.caption: Stand on the gravel approach inside the south torii — a twelve-metre cypress gate behind you, the forest path ahead.
stops.transcriptText:
ATLAS AUDIO TOUR — MEIJI JINGŪ (明治神宮), TOKYO

Location: 1-1 Yoyogikamizonocho, Shibuya-ku, Tokyo (2 minutes from Harajuku Station, JR Yamanote Line, Omotesando exit)
Approximate duration: 2:20 (≈360 words)

---

It's nineteen fifteen, and a group of forestry scientists is standing on a barren field in the middle of what will become central Tokyo. They are deciding what kind of forest Japan will have in a hundred years.

You're on the gravel approach inside the main south torii, the path running through the forest toward the inner shrine — a twelve-metre wooden gate behind you, made from a fifteen-hundred-year-old cypress found on a mountain in Taiwan, third in a series of torii that have stood here since nineteen twenty. The sound you left behind at the gate was the city: trains, crowds, the daily machinery of Harajuku. That cut-off effect was not an accident. It was designed. The scientists who planned this forest in nineteen fifteen specified one hundred and twenty thousand trees from three hundred and sixty-five species, planted by a hundred and ten thousand volunteers across Japan, calculated to grow into a self-sustaining canopy requiring no maintenance — a forest that would generate its own shade, its own soil, its own ecosystem. They planned it to regenerate naturally for a century. It is now doing exactly that.

The shrine buildings in the inner precinct were destroyed in wartime air raids and rebuilt in nineteen fifty-eight, so the structures you'll see ahead are about sixty years old. Emperor Meiji himself is not buried here — his body rests in Kyoto; this is a symbolic memorial, built after his death in nineteen twelve to enshrine his spirit and honour the Meiji period's transformation of Japan from feudal isolation into a modern industrial state. Before the inner shrine, you'll pass two rows of objects worth actually looking at: sake barrels donated by breweries from across Japan — a traditional Shinto offering — and directly opposite them, wine barrels from Burgundy in France. Emperor Meiji had a well-documented fondness for wine; his government actively encouraged the adoption of Western culture alongside the preservation of Japanese tradition. Both rows are rather a precise summary of what his reign meant.

The inner shrine compound is free to enter; leave the main path and walk the perimeter of the inner garden if you have time — the iris beds bloom in mid-June, and the well in the garden, Kiyomasa's Well, is said to be a power spot and is roughly four hundred years old.

---

tours.title: MoN Takanawa — The Museum of Narratives | MoN高輪
tours.shortDescription: A Kengo Kuma museum on the ground of Japan's first railway, named to mean both "gate" and "question" — asking what culture will be in a century.
tours.longDescription:
In 1872 Japan's first railway ran through this exact ground — the first train between Shimbashi and Yokohama. The building standing here now, MoN Takanawa, opened in March 2026 and has been asked to carry the next hundred years of Japanese culture. Designed by Kengo Kuma across six floors above ground and three below, it brings layered timber and natural materials into dialogue with the dense city, reaching toward its landscape rather than asserting itself against it.

Inside are three halls — a 1,500-square-metre exhibition space, a thousand-seat LED theatre, and a smaller room for performances — alongside a hundred-mat tatami hall and terraces built for foot baths, moon viewing and cherry blossoms. The benches are timber upcycled from JR East's railway forests; some furniture had a previous life at Expo 2025 Osaka.

The name carries a deliberate double meaning: MoN can mean gate or question. On a site that has been a point of departure for a hundred and fifty years, the museum asks what Japanese culture will be in a hundred years' time — gate and question, both at once.

It's eighteen seventy-two, and Japan's first railway is running through this exact ground — steam, coal smoke, the first train between Shimbashi and Yokohama. The building standing here now opened in March twenty twenty-six, and it has been asked to carry the next hundred years of Japanese culture.

The building is MoN Takanawa, designed by Kengo Kuma, six floors above ground and three below, part of the Takanawa Gateway City development that has emerged around the station behind you. Kuma's exterior brings layered timber and natural materials into dialogue with the surrounding urban density — characteristic of his approach, the building reaches toward its landscape rather than asserting itself against it. Inside, the spaces are called Box fifteen hundred, a fifteen-hundred-square-metre exhibition hall designed for large installations; Box one thousand, a full-stage LED theatre seating over a thousand; and Box three hundred, a smaller space for performances and screenings. There is also a hundred-mat tatami hall and outdoor terraces designed for ashiyu — foot baths — as well as moon viewing and cherry blossom viewing in season. The benches in the public areas are made from timber upcycled from JR East's railway forests, and some of the furniture was previously used at Expo twenty twenty-five Osaka before being given a second life here.

The name carries a deliberate double meaning in Japanese. MoN can mean 門 — gate — or 問 — question. The building sits on the site of Japan's first railway, historically the gateway that connected Tokyo to the rest of the country. The museum's stated purpose is to ask what Japanese culture will be in a hundred years' time. Gate and question, both at once, on a site that has been a point of departure for a hundred and fifty years.

I find that rather well-considered, if you'll allow me the understatement.

The museum runs its programmes in six-month seasons, each built around a single theme — the opening season runs until September twenty twenty-six. The terraces are accessible without a ticket and are worth the detour at dusk.

tours.title: Nakajima Tea House | 中島の御茶屋
tours.shortDescription: Cross the long cypress bridge to a tatami pavilion on a tidal pond — where a shogun's retreat became the stage for imperial statecraft.
tours.longDescription:
The water you crossed is not a park pond but a tidal inlet, linked to Tokyo Bay by floodgates, rising and falling with the ocean as it always has. When the sixth Tokugawa shogun, Ienobu, built the first pavilion on this island in 1707, the view from the veranda was open bay; the Shiodome skyscrapers behind you are recent, the tide is not.

You are on the small central island of the Incoming Tide Pond, reached by a hundred-and-eighteen-metre cypress bridge. Take off your shoes and step onto tatami, with windows opening on three sides. The menu is deliberately short — matcha, or matcha with a seasonal wagashi sweet that changes each month. The present building dates from 1983, rebuilt from records after wartime firebombing levelled most of the gardens.

The garden's diplomatic history runs deep: in 1879 Emperor Meiji received former US President Ulysses Grant here before some eight hundred guests, a staged signal that Japan stood as an equal. What a shogun built as a retreat, an emperor used for statecraft — and you can now watch the tide come in for five hundred yen.

stops.transcriptText:
NAKAJIMA TEA HOUSE — HAMARIKYU GARDENS
Atlas Audio Tour

The water you just crossed to get here is not a park pond. It is a tidal inlet, connected to Tokyo Bay by floodgates, rising and falling with the actual ocean as it always has. When the sixth Tokugawa shogun, Ienobu, built the first tea pavilion on this island in 1707, the view from its veranda was open bay. The skyscrapers of Shiodome behind you now are recent. The tide is not.

You're on the small central island of the Shioiri-no-ike — the Incoming Tide Pond — reached by the one-hundred-and-eighteen-metre cypress bridge from the western bank. The Nakajima Tea House is the low, dark-tiled building directly ahead; the veranda runs around the water-facing side. Take off your shoes at the entrance. Inside, the floor is tatami, the tables are low, and the windows open onto the pond on three sides. The menu is deliberately short: matcha, or matcha with a wagashi sweet. The sweet changes monthly — each one handcrafted to reflect the flowers and motifs of that particular season.

The current structure dates from 1983, rebuilt from historical records after the original was destroyed in the wartime firebombing that levelled most of these gardens. It is the only one of the four teahouses in Hamarikyu that currently serves visitors; the others are restored but not open as cafés. Before the war, the garden itself had a longer diplomatic history than most formal rooms in central Tokyo. In 1879, Emperor Meiji received former US President Ulysses Grant here at the Nakajima Tea House — an audience attended by some eight hundred guests, the meeting a carefully staged signal that Japan was a nation of equal standing on the world stage.

What the shogun built as a private retreat, the emperor used for statecraft, and what the emperor used for statecraft is now a place where you can sit on a tatami mat for five hundred yen and watch the tide come in.

The garden itself — designated both a Special Historic Site and a Special Place of Scenic Beauty, the highest dual classification under Japanese cultural property law — is worth walking in full before you leave. The three-hundred-year-old black pine near the main entrance is the most impressive single object in it.

tours.title: Nanago-Dori Park Toilets | 七号通り公園 公衆トイレ

tours.longDescription:
This is a public toilet, and it won a gold iF Design Award, one of the three most prestigious design prizes in the world. The sphere sits in Nanago Dori Park in Hatagaya — a white hemispherical shell floating slightly above the ground on a narrow base, with an air vent running round the gap. It was designed by Kazoo Sato of TBWA Hakuhodo and opened in August 2021.

It's part of the Tokyo Toilet Project, a Nippon Foundation initiative that commissioned seventeen public toilets across Shibuya from sixteen notable designers, among them Tadao Ando, Kengo Kuma and Shigeru Ban. This is the Hi Toilet, built around contactless use: door, flush, taps and music all answer to voice command in Japanese or English, with foot pedals as backup. No handles to touch anywhere inside.

The broader project draws on omotenashi — hospitality as unnoticed care — and the belief that the smallest public architecture can carry as much cultural weight as any other. It's the sharpest argument I know for taking public infrastructure seriously as a design problem.

Location: Nanago Dori Park, Hatagaya 2-53-5, Shibuya, Tokyo
Approximate duration: 2:05 (≈315 words)

---

This is a public toilet. It won a gold iF Design Award, one of the three most prestigious design prizes in the world.

The sphere sits in Nanago Dori Park in Hatagaya, Shibuya — a white hemispherical shell floating slightly above the ground on a narrow base, with a visible air vent running round the gap between the building and the earth. The structure was designed by Kazoo Sato, chief creative officer at TBWA Hakuhodo, and opened in August twenty twenty-one as part of the Tokyo Toilet Project, a Nippon Foundation initiative that commissioned seventeen public toilets across Shibuya from sixteen of Japan's most notable architects and designers, including Tadao Ando, Kengo Kuma, and Shigeru Ban.

The toilet is called the Hi Toilet, and its central concept is contactless use. The door, flush, taps, and ambient music are all operated by voice command — in Japanese or English — with foot pedals as a backup. There are no handles to touch anywhere inside. The idea, developed from user behaviour research, was to create the cleanest possible environment by removing physical contact with the building's surfaces entirely.

The broader project was inspired by the concept of omotenashi — Japanese hospitality as a form of unnoticed care, offered without expectation. The project's originator believed that the smallest form of public architecture could carry as much cultural weight as any other. Wim Wenders made a film about the toilet cleaners who look after these seventeen buildings; the lead actor won Best Actor at Cannes in twenty twenty-three for his performance.

Actually, the project is rather the sharpest argument I know for taking public infrastructure seriously as a design problem. Seventeen toilets. Seventeen different answers to the same brief.

The nearest other Tokyo Toilet installations are a short walk in either direction along the Keio Line — there are five in the immediate area, including a glowing lantern toilet in Nishihara Itchome Park that's worth finding after dark.

---

tours.title: Nezu Museum | 根津美術館
tours.shortDescription: A railway baron's collection of pre-modern art, reached down a bamboo corridor that makes you slow down before you've even arrived.
tours.longDescription:
The approach does something rare in this part of Aoyama. Bamboo closes in on both sides, the low roof appears ahead, and Omotesando — three minutes behind you — stops being audible. Kengo Kuma designed this entrance corridor as a decompression chamber between the commercial district and the museum. The building sits low and long under a wide black-tiled roof that nods to traditional teahouses, its cypress columns and glass walls dissolving the line between interior and garden.

Through those windows lies seventeen thousand square metres of grounds — four teahouses, stone lanterns, ponds and maples — giving no hint that it occupies one of Tokyo's most expensive postcodes.

The collection was assembled by Nezu Kaichiro, a railway industrialist and president of Tobu Railway, who made his fortune from modern infrastructure and spent much of it on the art of earlier centuries: over seven thousand pieces, seven of them National Treasures. The centrepiece is Ogata Korin's early eighteenth-century byobu Irises, shown each April and May to coincide with the garden's own irises. A man who built a career on speed was given a museum that works by making you slow down — rather a well-considered memorial.

The approach does something you don't often feel in this part of Aoyama. The bamboo closes in on both sides, the roof of the building appears ahead at a low angle, and Omotesando — three minutes' walk behind you — has entirely stopped being audible.

The entrance path is a long corridor formed by a dense bamboo thicket on one side and the building's plain wall on the other, designed by Kengo Kuma to function as a decompression chamber between the commercial district and the museum inside. The building itself sits low and long under a wide black-tiled roof that references the architecture of traditional Japanese teahouses, with cypress columns and glass walls that dissolve the boundary between interior and garden. Through those windows, the garden is already visible from the moment you enter: seventeen thousand square metres of landscaped grounds, four teahouses, stone lanterns and pagodas, a path through ponds and maples that gives no indication it is sitting inside one of the most expensive postcodes in Tokyo.

The collection was assembled by Nezu Kaichirō, a railway industrialist and president of Tobu Railway who made his fortune from the infrastructure of modern Japan, and spent a significant part of it buying the art of the centuries before. Over seven thousand pieces — folding screens, ceramics, lacquerware, Buddhist painting, ancient bronze — with seven National Treasures among them. The centrepiece is the byōbu Irises, painted by Ogata Kōrin in the early eighteenth century and displayed for a few weeks each April and May to coincide with the irises planted in the garden outside. Kaichirō evacuated the collection from this site before the nineteen forty-five bombing raids destroyed the estate buildings, and his son opened the museum in the rebuilt premises after the war.

I always think the approach says the most important thing about this place. Nezu Kaichirō built a career on speed — railways, networks, the acceleration of Meiji-era Japan. Kengo Kuma built him a museum that works by making you slow down before you've even arrived. That's rather a well-considered memorial.

The NEZUCAFÉ inside the garden has floor-to-ceiling windows on three sides and is included in the admission fee — worth the stop after the galleries, particularly in late autumn when the maple colours are at their peak.

tours.title: Nishi-Sando Public Toilets | 西参道公衆トイレ
tours.shortDescription: The seventeenth and final Tokyo Toilet — a Sou Fujimoto vessel in a project of Pritzker winners, made famous by a Wim Wenders film.
tours.longDescription:
This is the last of seventeen. The Nishi-Sando toilet opened on 24 March 2023, completing a project begun nearly three years earlier, built through a pandemic, largely ignored by the tourists it was meant to welcome — and then made famous by a German film director.

The Tokyo Toilet Project was conceived by Koji Yanai, son of Uniqlo's founder, and funded by the Nippon Foundation with Shibuya City. The brief was pointed: take seventeen public toilets people avoided and have world-class designers make them places people might actually want to use. Pritzker winners signed on — Tadao Andō, Toyo Ito, Fumihiko Maki, Shigeru Ban — alongside Marc Newson, NIGO, and, for this last one, Sou Fujimoto. His design treats the toilet as a vessel, public infrastructure as a kind of fountain.

Then Wim Wenders made Perfect Days, following a man who cleans several of these toilets with quiet attentiveness. Kōji Yakusho won Best Actor at Cannes, the toilets became destinations, and the project had, by any measure, worked.

tours.title: Onibus Coffee Nakameguro | オニバスコーヒー 中目黒三丁目店
tours.shortDescription: A specialty roaster named for the public bus, in a converted porridge shop wedged between a playground and the rattling Toyoko Line tracks.
tours.longDescription:
The name comes first. Onibus is Portuguese for public bus, and for founder Atsushi Sakao that was no accident: he wanted a coffee shop that works the way a bus does — something the neighbourhood boards each morning, part of the daily route rather than a destination.

The building sits on a narrow strip between a children's playground and the elevated Toyoko Line, where trains pass every couple of minutes. Small and two-storey, it was once an okayu rice-porridge restaurant before Sakao converted it in 2016 into the main roastery and café for one of Tokyo's most respected specialty roasters. Trained as an architect, he discovered café culture backpacking in Australia and came home with a different plan, building the first Onibus in Okusawa with his carpenter father.

Inside, the side wall is tiled with handmade ceramics from Tokoname, one of Japan's oldest pottery towns; the back carries a seed-to-cup mural by the local artist Chalk Boy; the cups come from Yumiko Iihoshi Porcelain, based a few stations down the same line.

ONIBUS COFFEE — NAKAMEGURO 3-CHOME
Atlas Audio Tour

The name is the first thing worth knowing. Onibus is the Portuguese word for public bus — and for founder Atsushi Sakao, that wasn't an accident. He wanted a coffee shop that functions the way a bus does: something the neighbourhood boards every morning, that connects people to each other, that isn't a destination so much as part of the daily route.

The building is on a narrow strip between a children's playground to your left and the elevated Toyoko Line tracks to your right. Trains pass every couple of minutes — you'll either have noticed already or you're about to. The building itself is small and two-storey, former premises of an okayu restaurant, a rice porridge place, before Sakao converted it in 2016 into the main roastery and café for what had by then become one of Tokyo's most respected specialty roasters.

Sakao's backstory is worth a moment. He trained as an architect — and then, in his mid-twenties, went backpacking through Australia. He encountered the café culture there, the light-roasted single-origin coffees, the easy relationship between baristas and regulars, and came back to Tokyo with a different plan entirely. He built the first Onibus in Okusawa partly with his father, who was a carpenter. The Nakameguro shop is the expansion that let the business grow without losing the grain of that original instinct.

Inside, the side wall is tiled with handmade ceramics from Tokoname, one of Japan's oldest pottery towns. The back wall carries a mural by a local artist called Chalk Boy, tracing the coffee process from seed to cup. The cups themselves are made by Yumiko Iihoshi Porcelain, a ceramicist based a few stations away on this very train line.

If the café is open, go upstairs — the A-framed wooden room has windows that look directly out onto the tracks, close enough that you understand why the trains feel like part of the experience rather than an intrusion on it.

tours.title: Oedo Antique Market | 大江戸骨董市
tours.shortDescription: Two hundred and fifty licensed dealers of Edo lacquerware and vintage English china, laid out beneath Rafael Viñoly's elliptical glass hall.
tours.longDescription:
Behind the trestle tables, Rafael Viñoly's elliptical glass hall soars above the plaza — and beneath it, two hundred and fifty dealers lay out Edo-period lacquerware beside vintage English tableware. The market fills the long outdoor corridor of the Tokyo International Forum at Yurakucho, a minute from the Ginza flagships and ten from Tokyo Station.

Oedo launched in September 2003 to mark the four-hundredth anniversary of the Edo shogunate, with a specific brief: not a flea market, but a professional antique event with licensed dealers who could account for what they sold. It runs twice a month and draws around fifteen thousand visitors an event, making it Japan's largest outdoor antique market. The organiser calls it "a jungle," and that's fair — an eighteenth-century English clock three tables from Meiji-era sake cups, a ukiyo-e display sharing a run with European jewellery.

The setting is the most interesting thing about it. This is no heritage precinct but a professional fair in the plaza of a major convention building — which says something about how a city that rebuilds itself every generation treats the things its previous generations made.

Approximate duration: 2:00 (≈305 words)

Look at the building behind the trestle tables. Rafael Viñoly's elliptical glass hall soars above the plaza and the two hundred and fifty dealers of Edo-period lacquerware and vintage English tableware arranged beneath it.

The market occupies the long outdoor corridor of the Tokyo International Forum, directly accessible from Yurakucho Station — one of the most commercially saturated postcodes in Tokyo, a minute's walk from the Ginza luxury flagships and ten minutes from Tokyo Station. Oedo launched in September two thousand and three to mark the four-hundredth anniversary of the founding of the Edo shogunate, and the organizers had a specific brief: not a flea market, not a craft fair, but a professional outdoor antique event with licensed dealers who could account for what they were selling. It runs twice a month and draws around fifteen thousand visitors per event, making it Japan's largest outdoor antique market by both measure.

The market is described by its own organiser as "a jungle," and that's accurate in the best sense — two hundred and fifty stalls running the full length of the plaza, with no division between Japanese and Western stock. An eighteenth-century English clock sits three tables down from a collection of Meiji-era sake cups. A ukiyo-e print display shares a run of tables with vintage European jewellery. The stock covers everything from Edo-period ceramics and kimono to Shōwa-era toys and contemporary studio crafts. Arrive before ten for the best selection; many serious collectors and dealers are there at opening.

I find the setting rather the most interesting thing about Oedo. This is not a heritage neighbourhood or a weekend market in a temple precinct. It's a professional antique fair in the plaza of one of Tokyo's major convention buildings — which says something about how a city that rebuilds itself every generation treats the things its previous generations made.

The indoor spaces of the Forum are open on market days — the glass hall is worth a walk through on your way in or out, and the cafés inside are considerably less crowded than the ones on the plaza edge.

tours.title: Omoide Yokocho | 新宿西口 思い出横丁
tours.shortDescription: A two-minute maze of eighty smoky stalls beside the Shinjuku tracks, grilling the same offal and yakitori it has served since 1945.
tours.longDescription:
The smoke reaches you first — charcoal, caramelised soy, sizzling fat — with the JR trains rumbling overhead every few minutes. On the west side of Shinjuku Station, a gap between buildings marked by red lanterns opens into two parallel alleys, barely two metres across, the whole thing two minutes end to end. Around eighty stalls and tiny bars line the lanes, most with counter seats for six to ten and open kitchens grilling yakitori, offal, nikomi stew and sake right in front of you.

In 1945 the area around the station was firebombed rubble, and a black market grew in the wreckage, trading the offal nobody wanted because nobody controlled it. The makeshift stalls hardened into permanent structures; a 1999 fire destroyed much of the north side, rebuilt in the same cramped style — look for scorch marks on the older timbers.

The name changed after that fire. For decades it was Piss Alley, from the toilet-less postwar years; afterwards it became Memory Lane. That renaming is the most revealing thing here: in 1945 it sold food for a hungry city; now it sells the memory of it.

ATLAS AUDIO TOUR — OMOIDE YOKOCHO / MEMORY LANE (思い出横丁), TOKYO

Location: West exit of JR Shinjuku Station, beside the Yamanote Line tracks, Shinjuku-ku, Tokyo
Approximate duration: 2:10 (≈330 words)

---

The smoke reaches you first. Charcoal, caramelised soy sauce, sizzling fat — and underneath all of that, the JR trains rumbling past overhead every few minutes.

The entrance is on the west side of Shinjuku Station — a narrow gap between buildings marked by red lanterns, just wide enough for two people to pass. Two parallel alleys run north to south, connected by short cross-passages, the whole thing roughly two minutes end to end and sometimes barely two metres across. Around eighty stalls and small bars line either side, most with counter seating for six to ten people and open kitchens where the food is grilled directly in front of you. The fare is yakitori, offal, nikomi stew, beer, sake — the same dishes that have been served here in one form or another since the late nineteen forties.

In nineteen forty-five, Tokyo had been firebombed and the area around Shinjuku Station was rubble. A black market set up in the wreckage, selling whatever wasn't subject to rationing — pig and beef offal, primarily, because those were the cuts nobody wanted and therefore nobody controlled. The makeshift stalls gradually became permanent structures. In the nineteen sixties, part of the market was demolished to build the current station complex. In nineteen ninety-nine, a fire destroyed much of the north side. The shops were rebuilt in the same cramped style, and if you look carefully you'll still find scorch marks on some of the older timbers.

Well, the name changed after that fire. It was called Piss Alley for decades — a reference to the postwar years when there were no public toilets and patrons made do as best they could. After the rebuild, it became Memory Lane. The renaming is rather the most revealing thing about the place: what it sold in nineteen forty-five was food for a hungry city; what it sells now is the memory of that.

Golden Gai is a seven-minute walk east — two hundred tiny bars in a similar maze of postwar lanes, with a more literary and arts-bar atmosphere than the purely food-focused Omoide Yokocho, and worth the walk if you want to compare.

tours.title: Prada Aoyama | プラダ 青山店
tours.shortDescription: A six-storey crystal of bulging and dished glass that handed two-thirds of its plot back to the street.
tours.longDescription:
Most luxury flagships fill every square metre their site allows. This one gave two-thirds of its land back to the street. On a corner of Minami-Aoyama stands a six-storey, five-sided glass structure with a pointed top, completed in 2003 by Herzog and de Meuron, who compressed Prada's entire retail programme into just 369 square metres on a plot nearly three times that size. The open plaza is what was left. Notice the boundary wall, faced with living moss in a grid that echoes the building's geometry while doing what the glass cannot — it grows.

The facade is a rhomboid diagrid of steel, each diamond filled with flat, convex, or concave glass. The convex panels bulge outward, the concave draw inward, and walking along the side the whole surface seems to shift — not because anything moves, but because each panel is a different lens. The diagrid is the structure itself, carrying the load with two interior cores.

Most interesting is how it refuses the inside/outside divide: the street is always visible from the shop, the shop from the street. In a district where buildings turn their backs, this one stays in conversation with Aoyama.

Most luxury flagships occupy every square metre their site will allow. This one gave two-thirds of its land back to the street.

The building occupies the corner of the plot in Minami-Aoyama, a six-storey five-sided glass structure with a pointed top, completed in two thousand and three by Herzog and de Meuron. The open plaza in front of you — the area between the boundary wall and the building itself — is what was left after the architects compressed Prada's entire retail programme into a vertical footprint of just three hundred and sixty-nine square metres on a site nearly three times that size. You'll notice the boundary wall as you cross into the plaza: it is faced with living moss in small square blocks, set in a grid pattern that continues the building's geometric logic while doing something the glass tower itself cannot — it grows.

The facade is a rhomboid diagrid of steel, with each diamond of the grid filled by one of three types of glass: flat, convex, or concave. The convex panels bulge outward, as if pressing the interior toward the street; the concave panels draw inward, as if pulling passers-by toward the merchandise. Walk slowly along the side of the building and the surface appears to shift and move — not because anything moves, but because each panel is a different lens, and your position changes what each one shows you. The glass is not a decorative skin over a structure; it is the structure, with the diagrid actively carrying the building's load in conjunction with two interior vertical cores.

If you ask me, the most interesting thing the building does is refuse the usual inside/outside distinction of a luxury retail environment. The street is always visible from the shop; the shop is always visible from the street. In a district where almost every commercial building turns its back on its surroundings, this one is in permanent conversation with Aoyama.

The Nezu Museum is a five-minute walk east along the back of Omotesando — a traditional Japanese art collection housed in a Kengo Kuma building with a bamboo garden, and a different kind of answer to the same question of how a cultural institution sits in this neighbourhood.

tours.title: Reflection of Mineral | レフレクション・オブ・ミネラル
tours.shortDescription: A faceted white house in Nakano whose crystalline shape isn't a design flourish but the exact form Tokyo's sunlight codes carved out.
tours.longDescription:
There's a useful way to think about this building: the shape is not a design choice, it's a consequence. Completed in 2006 by Atelier Tekuto on a plot of just forty-four square metres, it sits where two narrow streets meet at an acute angle. Tokyo's building codes impose strict height limits at varying angles from neighbouring streets and properties, to keep sunlight reaching them. Applied to this irregular plot from every direction at once, those rules trimmed the volume down to a multi-faceted polyhedron — the maximum buildable space that satisfies every regulation.

The architects, Yasuhiro Yamashita and Yoichi Tanaka, likened it to cutting a gemstone: the legal constraints, like crystal geometry, decided where the surfaces would fall. That's the mineral. The reflection is the interior — transparent, translucent and opaque facets, mirrors, skylights and corner windows draw the eye along the longest diagonals, so eighty-six square metres across four levels read as far larger. As the light shifts through the day, the facets change character.

It is a private house: four levels for one household, on a corner barely large enough to park two cars.

stops.transcriptText:
REFLECTION OF MINERAL — ATELIER TEKUTO
Atlas Audio Tour

There's a useful way to think about this building: the shape is not a design choice, exactly. It is a consequence.

The white faceted structure at this corner in Nakano was completed in 2006 by the practice Atelier Tekuto, on a plot of land forty-four square metres in size — roughly the floor area of a generous living room. Two narrow streets meet here at an acute angle, which gave the plot its irregular outline. Tokyo's building codes impose strict height restrictions at varying angles from neighbouring properties and streets, to ensure that adjacent buildings and roads receive adequate sunlight. Those restrictions, applied to this irregular plot from multiple directions simultaneously, produced a shape: the volume was trimmed and trimmed until what remained was a multi-faceted polyhedron that satisfies every regulation while occupying the maximum buildable space.

The architects — Yasuhiro Yamashita and Yoichi Tanaka — described the process as analogous to cutting a gemstone. The legal constraints, like the crystallographic geometry that determines how a stone can be cut along its planes, determined where the surfaces would fall. What emerged is the mineral. The reflection is the interior logic: by shaping those same facets as transparent, translucent, and opaque surfaces, and by using mirrors, skylights, and corner windows that draw the eye along the longest diagonal sight lines, the eighty-six square metres of floor area distributed across four levels reads as considerably larger than it is. As the light shifts through the day, the facets change character.

The building is a private house. Four levels, including a basement, serve a single household on a corner where the allowed footprint is barely large enough to park two cars.

The street intersection itself gives the best view: step back to the point where both narrow streets are visible and the full faceted outline can be read in one glance.

tours.title: Reiyūkai Shakaden | 霊友会釈迦殿
tours.shortDescription: Nicknamed the Star Wars Temple, this black granite pyramid was completed two years before the film was released — and hides a reservoir below.
tours.longDescription:
The building in front of you is nicknamed the Star Wars Temple. It was completed two years before Star Wars was released. A massive black pyramidal structure of dark red and black granite, sheathed in electrochemically darkened stainless steel shingles, it carries a roof spanning fifty by a hundred metres and a hall holding three and a half thousand people. Architect Kenichi Iwasaki of Takenaka Corporation finished it in 1975. A cavernous recessed opening runs the full width of the lower facade — the gaping mouth that earns its other nickname, the trilobite. Inside, a giant Buddha carved from ancient camphor wood presides over the hall.

This is the headquarters of Reiyukai, a Buddhist lay movement founded in 1919 with no priests and no clergy, focused on ancestor veneration and the Lotus Sutra, now over five million members strong. Shakaden means the House of Shakyamuni. The movement drew much of its early momentum from the 1923 Great Kanto earthquake, which killed over a hundred thousand people. That history shows quietly in the building's deepest layer: beneath the temple sits a reservoir of some twelve thousand gallons of drinking water, held against another major quake. A building that looks like the future turns out to be a response to the past.

The building in front of you is nicknamed the Star Wars Temple. It was completed two years before Star Wars was released.

The complex occupies a side street in Azabudai, Minato-ku, hemmed between office towers and small houses — a massive black pyramidal structure of dark red and black granite, sheathed in electrochemically darkened stainless steel shingles, with a roof spanning fifty by a hundred metres and a main hall capable of holding three thousand five hundred people. Construction was completed in nineteen seventy-five by architect Kenichi Iwasaki of Takenaka Corporation. The entrance is a cavernous recessed opening that runs the full width of the lower facade — the gaping mouth that gives the building its other popular nickname, the trilobite. Inside, the scale is consistent with the exterior: a giant Buddha carved from ancient camphor wood presides over the main hall, and the granite surfaces and ornamented ceilings continue the building's refusal of any conventional religious register.

The Shakaden is the headquarters of Reiyūkai, a Buddhist lay movement — no priests, no clergy — founded in nineteen nineteen and focused on ancestor veneration and the Lotus Sutra. Membership today stands at over five million, predominantly in Japan. The name Shakaden means the House of Shakyamuni, another name for the historical Buddha. The movement took much of its early momentum from the nineteen twenty-three Great Kantō earthquake, which killed over a hundred thousand people in Tokyo and left the city in ruins. That origin shows up, quietly, in the building's infrastructure: beneath the temple sits a reservoir holding approximately twelve thousand gallons of drinking water, maintained for use by the city in the event of another major earthquake.

I find the reservoir rather the most revealing thing about the place. A building designed to look like it arrived from the future turns out to be, in its deepest practical layer, a response to something that happened in the past.

Entry is free, the building is open to visitors, and free Japanese lessons are offered inside — worth going in if only to understand the scale from the inside, which the exterior understates considerably.

tours.title: Ryōgoku Kokugikan | 両国国技館
tours.shortDescription: Sumo's spiritual home, where wrestlers in robes part the crowd and a shrine-like roof hangs over the sacred clay ring.
tours.longDescription:
On tournament days the wrestlers arrive at the south entrance, moving through the crowd in their robes and wooden sandals, and the crowd parts — it's worth knowing where to stand. The Ryōgoku Kokugikan opened in January 1985 on a Sumida site the Japan Sumo Association bought specifically to return sumo to its historical home, after three decades at a temporary hall in Kuramae. The Emperor attended that first tournament, the first time a reigning emperor had watched sumo on a new year's opening day.

The green roof is its signature from outside. Within, the hall is arranged around the dohyo — the raised clay ring — beneath a suspended roof that echoes the lines of Shinto shrines, marking the ring as the sacred space it is held to be.

Closest to the action are the masu-seki: low wooden boxes where four people sit shoeless on cushions at near-eye level with the wrestlers. Watching from there is unlike any other sports viewing in Japan.

stops.transcriptText:
RYOGOKU KOKUGIKAN — 両国国技館
Atlas Audio Tour

On tournament days, the wrestlers arrive at the south entrance. They come in their own time, moving through the crowd in their robes and wooden sandals, and the crowd parts. It is worth knowing where to stand.

The Ryogoku Kokugikan opened in January 1985 — on a site in the Sumida district that the Japan Sumo Association had purchased specifically to return sumo to its historical home in Ryogoku, after three decades at a temporary hall in Kuramae. Capacity is eleven thousand and ninety-eight. Three of sumo's six annual tournaments — in January, May, and September — are held here, each lasting fifteen days. The Emperor attended the very first tournament in 1985, the first time a reigning emperor had watched sumo performed on the opening day of a new year's tournament.

The building's green roof is its most distinctive feature from the outside. Inside, the hall is arranged around the dohyo — the raised clay ring at its centre — with a suspended roof hung above it that recalls the rooflines of Shinto shrines. The sumo ring is considered a sacred space, and the roof marks it as such, as it has in Japanese sumo halls for centuries.

The ground-floor seating closest to the ring is not conventional seating. Those are masu-seki boxes: low wooden partitions on the floor, where four people sit on cushions with their shoes off, in the Japanese style, with a small table between them. The experience of watching a match from masu-seki, at near-eye level with the wrestlers as they meet in the ring, is unlike any other sports viewing in Japan.

The Sumo Museum, on the ground floor of the building, is free to enter on weekdays outside tournament season — a useful introduction to the history and ritual of the sport if you are visiting between basho.

tours.title: SCAI The Bathhouse | スカイザバスハウス
tours.shortDescription: A 1787 neighbourhood bathhouse in old Yanaka, its tiles and chimney kept intact, now a white-cube gallery showing major contemporary art.
tours.longDescription:
Ceramic roof tiles, a tall chimney, a low eave: the building has the unmistakable shape of a neighbourhood bathhouse that has stood here since before Napoleon — because it is one. The address is 6-1-23 Yanaka, in old Taito, one of the few corners of Tokyo to escape wartime flattening and keep the feel of shitamachi, the low downtown where ordinary people lived. From 1787 until 1993 it was a working public bathhouse called Kashiwayu, before its conversion into SCAI The Bathhouse.

The exterior is exactly as it was — original tiles, the chimney, the entrance lockers still inside. Only when you pass through to the main space does the conversion reveal itself: a white cube eight metres high, lit through the same skylights that once filtered afternoon light onto the steam above the tubs.

Director Masami Shiraishi sees the continuity plainly — a bathhouse was where people gathered, talked, and learned the news; contemporary art, he believes, now does the same work. Since 1993 the gallery has shown Lee Ufan, Kohei Nawa, Mariko Mori, Anish Kapoor and Louise Bourgeois, among others.

SCAI THE BATHHOUSE — YANAKA
Atlas Audio Tour

Look at the building in front of you: ceramic roof tiles, a tall chimney, a low eave, the general shape of a neighbourhood bathhouse that has been here since before Napoleon. That's because it is one.

The address is 6-1-23 Yanaka, in the Taito district of old Tokyo — one of the few corners of the city that wasn't flattened in the Second World War and has kept something close to its prewar character. The gallery is a short walk from Ueno Park and around the corner from Yanaka's long shopping street, in a quarter that still has the feel of what the Japanese call shitamachi: the old downtown, the low town, the place where ordinary people lived. The building was a working public bathhouse, called Kashiwayu, from its construction in 1787 until 1993, when it was converted and opened as SCAI The Bathhouse — a contemporary art gallery that now represents some of the most significant artists working in Japan and internationally.

The exterior has been kept exactly as it was. The chimney is still there; the tiles are the original ones; the entrance hall inside still has its lockers. It's only when you pass through into the main gallery space that the conversion reveals itself — a white cube, eight metres high, naturally lit through skylights that run across the top of the room. Those are the same skylights that once filtered afternoon light down onto the steam above the bathtubs. Now they illuminate whatever the gallery is currently showing.

Director Masami Shiraishi has described the connection between the two uses of the building directly: a neighbourhood bathhouse, he has said, was a place where people could not only wash but gather, talk, and find out what was happening around them. The gallery, he believes, has the same purpose — contemporary art replacing hot water as the common medium. The artists SCAI has worked with since 1993 include Lee Ufan, Kohei Nawa, Mariko Mori, Anish Kapoor, and Louise Bourgeois, among others.

Admission is free, but the gallery closes between exhibitions, so it's worth checking the schedule before you come. The Yanaka cemetery and the long shopping street leading towards Nippori are both worth exploring once you've been inside.

tours.title: Sensō-ji | 浅草寺
tours.shortDescription: A temple of gates, halls and a five-storey pagoda, all rebuilt around a golden statue that no living person — not even the priests — has ever seen.
tours.longDescription:
The statue at the heart of this temple has been here for nearly fourteen hundred years, and nobody living has ever seen it. The Kaminarimon — Thunder Gate — stands before you, its four-metre, seven-hundred-kilogram red lantern flanked by Fujin and Raijin, gods of wind and thunder. This version was rebuilt in 1960, funded by Konosuke Matsushita, founder of Panasonic, grateful to Kannon for his success in business. Beyond it, the Nakamise street runs to the Hozomon Gate, where two giant straw sandals — four and a half metres tall — hang on the far side.

Everything in the main compound was built after 1945: the complex burned in the March firebombing, and the reconstructions ran through the decades that followed. The temple that has stood here since 628 is, in its physical form, about sixty years old.

The original Kannon — a golden statue pulled from the Sumida by two brothers in 628 — has never been shown. It is a hibutsu, a hidden Buddha, unseen even by its priests. All of this, visited by twenty million people a year, exists for the sake of something nobody looks at.
