stops.caption: Stand before the Kaminarimon — the four-metre red lantern overhead, Fujin and Raijin flanking the gate.
stops.transcriptText:
ATLAS AUDIO TOUR — SENSŌ-JI TEMPLE (浅草寺), TOKYO

Location: 2-3-1 Asakusa, Taito-ku, Tokyo (2 minutes from Asakusa Station, all lines)
Approximate duration: 2:25 (≈380 words)

---

The statue at the centre of this temple has been here for nearly fourteen hundred years. Nobody living has ever seen it.

The Kaminarimon — Thunder Gate — is directly in front of you, the four-metre red lantern hanging at its centre, weighing seven hundred kilograms, painted to suggest thunderclouds and lightning on one face and inscribed with the gate's official name, Fūraijinmon, on the reverse. Flanking the gate are statues of Fujin and Raijin, the gods of wind and thunder. This version of the gate was rebuilt in nineteen sixty, funded by Konosuke Matsushita, the founder of Panasonic, who was apparently grateful to Kannon for his success in business. Beyond the gate, Nakamise-dori, a two-hundred-and-fifty-metre shopping street, leads to the inner Hōzōmon Gate — and if you turn and look at the back of that second gate as you pass through, you'll find two giant straw sandals hanging from it. They are four and a half metres tall, weigh five hundred kilograms, and are replaced every ten years; eight hundred people spend eighteen months weaving each pair.

Everything you can see in the main compound — the main hall, Hōzōmon Gate, the five-storey pagoda — was built after nineteen forty-five. The entire complex was destroyed in the firebombing raids of March nineteen forty-five, and the reconstructions were completed piecemeal through the nineteen fifties, sixties, and seventies. The temple that has stood here since six hundred and twenty-eight is, in its physical form, about sixty years old. The ceiling of the main hall carries a dragon painted by Ryushi Kawabata, completed in nineteen sixty when the hall reopened.

Well, the original Kannon — the golden statue pulled from the Sumida River by two brothers in six hundred and twenty-eight, the object that caused all of this to be built around it — has never been placed on public display. It is a hibutsu, a hidden Buddha, sealed and not shown. The priests who serve the temple have not seen it either. The compound of gates and halls and a five-storey pagoda, rebuilt after a firebombing and visited by twenty million people a year, exists entirely for the sake of something that nobody looks at.

Arrive before eight in the morning to see the temple without the crowds, and without the Nakamise stalls open. The grounds are accessible around the clock, free of charge, and the main hall opens at six. The Asakusa Shrine sits directly to the east of the main hall — a Shinto shrine, technically separate, dedicated to the three men who founded the Buddhist temple, which is rather the kind of thing that only makes complete sense in Japan.

tours.title: Shibuya Antique Market | 渋谷アンティークマーケット
tours.shortDescription: Twice a month, a hundred vendors lay out Edo ceramics and vintage kimono in a corporate plaza above the Shibuya scramble.
tours.longDescription:
On the second and fourth Sunday of each month, a market sets up in the plaza of the Shibuya Garden Tower, a glass-and-steel office building about ten minutes uphill from the scramble crossing. Around a hundred vendors lay out their stock on open-air trestle tables: Edo-period ceramics, vintage kimono fabric reworked into new pieces, folk tools, European mid-century glassware, handmade jewellery, old woodblock prints, even cut flowers. Entry is free, and the sellers are mostly small collectors and craftspeople rather than trade dealers, so it runs far quieter than the district below.

The official name is Tokyo Romantic Market — a somewhat ambitious title for what is, in practice, a very pleasant Sunday morning in a corporate plaza. That is rather exactly the point. The tower behind you stands empty, the offices are closed, and the Shibuya that usually moves at speed has, for a few hours, slowed to the pace of someone deciding whether to buy a nineteenth-century sake cup.

tours.title: Shibuya Crossing | 渋谷スクランブル交差点
tours.shortDescription: The world's busiest pedestrian intersection, where up to three thousand people cross in every direction at once — then clear before the cars move.
tours.longDescription:
There is a moment, every couple of minutes, when everything stops — cars, trucks and vans in every direction at once — and the pavement fills with people waiting. That pause before the lights change is what makes this crossing what it is. You are at one of six approach corners feeding the busiest pedestrian intersection in the world, with up to three thousand people crossing in a single green cycle. All vehicles halt together, so pedestrians can cross to any corner, including diagonally, in the thirty seconds they have. No markings, no barriers — the flow organises itself.

The scramble system was actually invented in North America in the 1940s; Japan's first appeared in Kumamoto in 1968, Shibuya's in 1973, and there are now around three hundred nationwide. What made this one famous is the combination: its scale, its place at the exit of one of Tokyo's busiest stations, and the wall of giant video screens filling every surface. At night, screens blazing, it is why film directors keep choosing it.

The detail worth pausing on is the order of it — thousands converging from six directions, navigating without marshals, the junction clear again before the cars get their light.

---

There's a moment, every two minutes or so, when everything stops. The cars, the trucks, the vans — all of them, in every direction simultaneously — and the pavement fills with people waiting. That moment before the lights change is what makes this crossing what it is.

You're at the pavement edge of Shibuya Scramble Crossing, one of the six approach corners that feed into the junction — the busiest pedestrian intersection in the world, with up to three thousand people crossing in a single green-light cycle. The scramble system works by stopping all vehicles at once, which means pedestrians can cross to any corner, including diagonally, in the thirty seconds available. There are no lane markings, no barriers, no instruction beyond the light itself. The flow organises itself.

The scramble crossing system was actually invented in North America in the nineteen forties. Japan's first scramble appeared in Kumamoto in nineteen sixty-eight; Shibuya's followed in nineteen seventy-three. There are now around three hundred scramble crossings across Japan. What made this one famous is not the engineering but the combination: the crossing's scale, its position at the exit of one of Tokyo's busiest station complexes, and the surrounding wall of giant video screens and neon signage that fills every vertical surface. The whole effect at night, with the screens blazing and the people moving in every direction at once, is why film directors keep choosing to shoot here. Lost in Translation used it. So did Tokyo Drift, and dozens more.

The detail worth pausing on is how orderly it is. Thousands of people converging from six directions, navigating around each other without barriers or marshals, and the intersection is clear of pedestrians again before the vehicles are given the light. It is rather a precise summary of something particular to Tokyo.

The Hachiko statue is round the corner at the station exit — a bronze Akita dog honouring the dog who kept returning to this station every day for nine years after his owner died. It is one of the most visited statues in Japan and worth a look before or after crossing.

tours.title: Shibuya Nonbei Yokocho | 渋谷のんべい横丁

Three minutes' walk north of the busiest intersection on earth, wedged between the Yamanote Line embankment and a back street, sit two low wooden buildings barely a decade past condemned. The alley between them is so narrow two people passing must turn sideways, its entrance marked by a row of red paper lanterns. Turn your back on the glass towers of Shibuya Scramble Square and you stand, very precisely, above the Shibuya River, buried during the postwar reconstruction and still flowing beneath your feet.

Nonbei is Edo-period slang for a drunkard — or, more charitably, someone who genuinely loves a drink — and the alley earned the name honestly, growing from the black markets that clustered around the station in the early 1950s.

Roughly forty bars fill both buildings across two floors, most holding four to eight people, some so small the owner can pass your highball without leaving their stool. What's interesting is the scale of the whole thing: a social physics completely at odds with a neighbourhood built for thousands at a time. Some managers are now third generation.

The entrance to Nonbei Yokocho is just ahead of you, marked by a row of red paper lanterns strung above the gap between the buildings. The alley splits into two parallel corridors, each lined with tiny bar fronts, running the length of the buildings on two floors. You are, very precisely, above the Shibuya River, which was buried underground during the postwar reconstruction and still flows beneath your feet.

The word nonbei is Edo-period slang — it means a drunkard, or more charitably, someone who genuinely loves drinking — and the alley earned the name honestly. It grew from the postwar black markets that clustered around Shibuya Station in the early nineteen fifties, when informal stalls selling cheap food and drink occupied whatever space the war had left unburned. Walk the full length of the alley before you choose a bar — the ones near the entrance see more foot traffic; the quieter counters are further in and upstairs. tours.title: Shinjuku Golden-Gai | 新宿ゴールデン街
tours.shortDescription: Six wooden alleys of tiny bars grown from a postwar black market — once the intellectual underground of Shinjuku, saved from developers by night patrols.
tours.longDescription:
It's 1945. The war has just ended, the city is largely rubble, and a black market runs along the east side of Shinjuku Station. By 1949 the Occupation has cleared it out, but it doesn't vanish — it walks six hundred metres north to the patch of waste ground where you're standing. Six narrow alleys run east to west, linked by passages barely wide enough for two, lined with two-storey wooden buildings some no broader than a wardrobe. Across six and a half thousand square metres sit around two hundred and eighty bars, most seating five or six.

A red-light district until that was outlawed in 1958, it became a drinking district and, through the 1960s, a gathering place for writers, directors, actors and musicians — Yukio Mishima drank here, and literary debates ran until dawn.

The 1980s bubble brought developers, suspicious fires and pressure to sell. Bar owners and regulars organised night patrols against arson, and the land grab failed. Several bars have run since the 1960s; one or two since the late fifties.

stops.transcriptText:
SHINJUKU GOLDEN-GAI
Atlas Audio Tour

It's 1945. The war has just ended, the city is largely rubble, and a black market has set up along the east side of Shinjuku Station selling whatever anyone can get hold of — food, black-market cigarettes, basic necessities. By 1949 the Allied Occupation has cleared the market out, but the market doesn't disappear; it just walks six hundred metres north and sets up in the patch of waste ground where you're standing now.

Six narrow alleys run east to west in front of you, connected by passages barely wide enough for two people to pass each other. The buildings on both sides are two-storey wooden structures, some no wider than a large wardrobe. Golden-Gai covers about six and a half thousand square metres — roughly the footprint of a large hotel — and it contains around two hundred and eighty bars. The alleys are private roads, not public streets. Most bars seat five or six people. Some seat fewer.

Through the 1950s the district ran as a red-light district until that was outlawed in 1958. Then it became a drinking district, and in the 1960s it became something else as well: a gathering place for Tokyo's writers, film directors, actors, and musicians. Literary debates ran until dawn. The writer Yukio Mishima was among those known to drink here. The alleys began to carry a reputation as the intellectual underground of Shinjuku.

During the bubble economy of the 1980s, this reputation didn't protect Golden-Gai from developers. Land values in Shinjuku were extraordinary; the district was a small wooden obstacle in the path of enormous money. There were fires — suspicious ones — and pressure to sell. In response, bar owners and regulars organised night patrols, taking turns to stand guard and prevent arson. The land grab failed. Several bars here have been running since the 1960s; one or two since the late 1950s.

When you go in, expect a cover charge — typically five hundred to fifteen hundred yen per person — which is how a bar with six seats pays the rent. Hanazono Shrine, immediately to the east, is the useful landmark for finding your way back out.

tours.title: Shiseido Building | 東京銀座資生堂ビル
tours.shortDescription: Ricardo Bofill's deep terracotta-red tower interrupts Ginza's glass canyon — and hides Japan's oldest gallery five metres deep beneath the street.
tours.longDescription:
The first thing to say about the Shiseido Building is that it is red — a deep, warm, terracotta red that makes it instantly legible on a street otherwise competing in glass, steel and neon. Facing Chuo-dori at the Ginza 7-chome intersection, fifty-six metres tall, it was designed by the Spanish architect Ricardo Bofill and completed in 2001 on a very small, very expensive plot.

The stucco facade carries two stories. One holds that it nods to the red-brick buildings that lined Ginza in the Meiji era, before the district became a glass canyon; the other that it recalls the red sands and robes Bofill met crossing the Sahara. Bofill never quite settled the question. The interior staircase, meanwhile, recreates the atmosphere of Shiseido's original 1930s headquarters that once stood here.

What the facade hides lies underneath. Down the side staircase is the Shiseido Gallery — Japan's oldest gallery still operating, opened in 1919 by company founder Shinzo Fukuhara, an accomplished photographer. Free of charge, it has hosted over three thousand one hundred exhibitions beneath a five-metre ceiling, the tallest exhibition space in Ginza.

stops.title: Shiseido Building | 東京銀座資生堂ビル
stops.caption: Look up Chuo-dori for the deep terracotta-red tower, then take the side staircase down to the Shiseido Gallery beneath it.

This is the Shiseido Building, and the first thing to say about it is that it is red — a deep, warm, terracotta red that makes it immediately identifiable on a street that otherwise competes in glass, steel, and neon.

The building faces Chuo-dori at the Ginza 7-chome intersection, fifty-six metres tall, designed by the Spanish architect Ricardo Bofill and completed in 2001. Bofill — who spent his career working across three continents, building housing blocks in Paris and cultural centres in Barcelona — was commissioned directly by the Shiseido company's presidency and given a very small, very expensive plot. The red facade, which is stucco with a brick-red finish, has two explanations. One is that it references the red-brick buildings that lined Ginza's streets in the Meiji era, before the district reinvented itself as a glass canyon. The other — and some insist on this — is that it recalls the red sand dunes and robes Bofill encountered travelling through the Sahara. Both stories have been in circulation since the building opened, and Bofill himself has never quite settled the question. What's clear is the effect: the building interrupts Ginza's prevailing palette in a way that is quite deliberate, and has been recognisable from the top of the block ever since.

The interior staircase was designed to recreate the atmosphere of the Shiseido company's original 1930s headquarters that stood on this site — an act of corporate memory embedded in a new building. The upper floors hold restaurants, a café, and a bar; the company's flagship confectionery shop is at ground level.

What the facade doesn't show is what's underneath. Down the staircase on the building's side, or by lift from the main entrance, is the Shiseido Gallery — Japan's oldest art gallery still in operation. It opened in 1919, founded by Shinzo Fukuhara, the company's first president and an accomplished photographer, and has hosted over three thousand one hundred exhibitions since, free of charge. The basement ceiling is five metres high, making it the tallest exhibition space in Ginza. Shiseido's Hanatsubaki magazine, also free, is usually available at the entrance and worth picking up.

tours.title: St. Mary's Cathedral, Tokyo | 東京カテドラル聖マリア大聖堂
tours.shortDescription: Eight steel wings curving skyward into a cross of light — Kenzo Tange's 1964 cathedral, and the place his own funeral was held.
tours.longDescription:
Look at the wings — eight of them, each curving upward at a different angle, sheathed in stainless steel that shifts from silver to white to grey with the light. The cathedral stands in Sekiguchi, a rhomboid mass of swept concrete rising from dark stone, its bell tower set apart at sixty-one metres. Designed by Kenzo Tange and completed in 1964, it replaced a wooden Gothic cathedral destroyed in the 1945 air raids, with partial funding from the Archdiocese of Cologne — postwar reconciliation between German and Japanese Catholics.

The structure is eight hyperbolic parabolic shells that serve at once as walls and roof, rising from a rhombus plan to a cross of light at the apex. Vertical gaps draw daylight in as four slashes down the facades. Outside it is bright and sleek; inside, rough exposed concrete and that cross of light shifting through the day.

It divided opinion from the start — the Cardinal Archbishop was ambivalent, a historian called it one of Tange's weaker works. Tange disagreed. The Pope awarded him the Order of St. Gregory the Great in 1970, and in 2005 his funeral was held here. A definitive endorsement.

stops.title: St. Mary's Cathedral, Tokyo | 東京カテドラル聖マリア大聖堂
stops.caption: Take the cathedral head-on from the approach — eight steel wings curving upward, the bell tower set apart to the west.
stops.transcriptText:
ATLAS AUDIO TOUR — ST. MARY'S CATHEDRAL, TOKYO (東京カテドラル聖マリア大聖堂)

Location: 3-16-15 Sekiguchi, Bunkyo-ku, Tokyo (10 minutes from Edogawabashi Station, Tokyo Metro Yurakucho Line; bus to Sekiguchi stop)
Hours: Open daily; free entry
Approximate duration: 2:15 (≈345 words)

---

Look at the wings. Eight of them, each curving upward at a different angle, sheathed in stainless steel that shifts from silver to white to grey depending on where the light is and where you're standing.

The cathedral stands in the Sekiguchi district of Bunkyo, at the end of a short approach path that gives you the building head-on — a rhomboid mass of swept concrete and steel rising from a base of dark stone, with the bell tower standing apart to the west at sixty-one metres. Designed by Kenzo Tange and completed in nineteen sixty-four, it replaced a wooden Gothic cathedral on the same site that survived the nineteen twenty-three Kanto earthquake and was destroyed in the nineteen forty-five air raids. A competition to rebuild was launched in nineteen sixty to mark the centenary of the reintroduction of Catholicism to Japan, with partial funding provided by the Archdiocese of Cologne — an act of postwar reconciliation between German and Japanese Catholic communities.

The structure is eight hyperbolic parabolic concrete shells that function simultaneously as walls and roof, rising from a rhombus plan to form a cross of light at the top. Vertical gaps between the shells bring daylight into the interior as four vertical slashes that extend the cross downward along the facades. Inside, the material switches from polished stainless steel to rough exposed concrete: bright and sleek outside, dark and textured within. The cross of light at the apex is the only significant source of natural illumination, and it changes through the day as each wing reaches a different height.

Actually, the building divided opinion from the start. The Cardinal Archbishop was ambivalent, and the plans were reluctantly approved. After completion, at least one architectural historian described it as one of Tange's weaker works. Tange himself judged it more favourably: the Pope awarded him the Order of St. Gregory the Great for the design in nineteen seventy. And in March two thousand and five, Kenzo Tange's own funeral was held here — I find that rather a definitive endorsement.

Enter through the side door on the east face if the main doors are closed. The interior experience — the concrete curves, the cross of light from above, the organ installed in two thousand and four — is significantly different from what the exterior prepares you for, and worth the few minutes inside.

---

tours.title: Sumida Park | 隅田公園
tours.shortDescription: A riverside line of cherry trees descended from those an eighth shogun planted in 1717 so ordinary Edo could have somewhere to come in spring.
tours.longDescription:
In 1717 the eighth Tokugawa shogun ordered cherry trees planted along both banks of this river, so that the merchants, craftspeople and labourers of Edo would have somewhere to come in spring. The ruling class had private gardens for their hanami; this was a deliberate provision for everyone else. Face the river from the western bank: the Sumida flows south, Azumabashi bridge to your right, the Skytree above the rooftops to the north, and across the water the black beer-mug headquarters of Asahi with its golden rooftop flame. The kilometre of cherry trees on both banks are direct descendants of Yoshimune's.

The park itself is younger. After the Great Kanto Earthquake of 1923 destroyed the Mito Tokugawa estate on the eastern bank, Home Minister Goto Shinpei turned the ground into public parkland. Sumida Park opened in 1931 as Japan's first public riverside park, with Azumabashi rebuilt alongside; the X-shaped Sakurabashi came in 1985.

The middle bridge, Kototoibashi, named for a ninth-century poem, was the site of a catastrophic loss of life during the firebombing of March 1945.

stops.transcriptText:
SUMIDA PARK — ASAKUSA / MUKOJIMA
Atlas Audio Tour

In 1717, the eighth Tokugawa shogun ordered cherry trees planted along both banks of this river so that ordinary people — the merchants and craftspeople and labourers of Edo — would have somewhere to come in spring. The ruling class had private gardens for their hanami; this was a deliberate provision for everyone else.

Face the river from the western bank. The Sumida flows south in front of you, with the broad Azumabashi bridge to your right and the Skytree visible above the roofline to the north. Across the water on the eastern bank, the building that looks like a black beer mug with a large golden sculpture on its roof is the Asahi Beer headquarters — the sculpture is officially a flame representing passion for brewing; the Tokyo nickname for it is rather more irreverent and has to do with what flames sometimes resemble. The stretch of park running along both riverbanks, from Azumabashi north to Sakurabashi, is Sumida Park, and the one-kilometre line of cherry trees on both sides are direct descendants of the trees Yoshimune ordered in seventeen seventeen.

The park itself is younger. After the Great Kanto Earthquake of 1923 destroyed the private Mito Tokugawa clan estate that occupied the eastern bank, Home Minister Goto Shinpei directed its transformation into public parkland — part of his wider vision for a rebuilt Tokyo with wider streets, proper parks, and new bridges. Sumida Park opened in 1931 as the first public riverside park in Japan, and the bridge closest to you, Azumabashi, was rebuilt as part of the same reconstruction. The X-shaped pedestrian bridge to the north — Sakurabashi — came much later, in 1985, connecting the two halves of the park across the river.

The middle bridge, Kototoibashi, is named after a poem from the ninth century. It was the site of a catastrophic loss of life during the firebombing of March 1945, when people fleeing the flames converged on the bridge from both directions and could not escape.

The Sumidagawa Fireworks Festival, held every July, is one of the oldest fireworks festivals in Japan, dating to the Edo period. The park is one of the prime viewing positions. River cruises departing from Azumabashi run south to Hamarikyu Gardens and Odaiba, which connects several stops on this tour.

tours.title: SunnyHills Minami-Aoyama | サニーヒルズ南青山
tours.shortDescription: A cypress-lattice cloud built with no nails or glue using temple joinery — and a free pineapple cake waiting upstairs.
tours.longDescription:
Step inside if you can: the light comes through the wood the way it comes through trees. One block from Omotesando stands a three-storey building wrapped in a three-dimensional lattice of hinoki cypress slats, each sixty millimetres square, woven at thirty and sixty degrees into something between a bamboo basket and a cloud. Over five thousand metres of timber, no nails, no glue — the whole thing held by a traditional joinery technique called jigoku-gumi. Jigoku means hell: the joints, once locked, cannot be taken apart. The same method built shoji screens at Kyoto's Toji Mieido, some standing six hundred years.

Inside, the lattice scatters shifting light across cork floors, plants sprout from irregular stair treads, and it feels remarkably like standing under a forest canopy. Upstairs the staff bring a pineapple cake and Taiwanese tea, free and without obligation — the cake is the reason the building exists, this being the Tokyo flagship of a Taiwanese confectioner.

It was designed by Kengo Kuma in 2013, his aim to create a forest in the city. His method was a joinery system built for temples meant to last five centuries — applied to a shop whose cakes keep for three days.

stops.transcriptText:
ATLAS AUDIO TOUR — SUNNYHILLS MINAMI-AOYAMA (サニーヒルズ南青山), TOKYO

Location: 3-10-20 Minami-Aoyama, Minato-ku, Tokyo (5 minutes from Omotesando Station, exit A4)
Approximate duration: 2:10 (≈330 words)

---

Step inside if you can. The light in here comes through the wood the way it comes through trees.

The building is at 3-10-20 Minami-Aoyama, a side street one block from Omotesando — a three-storey structure wrapped entirely in a three-dimensional lattice of hinoki cypress slats, each one sixty millimetres square, woven together at thirty and sixty-degree angles into a form that reads from the outside as something between a bamboo basket and a cloud. Over five thousand metres of timber were used. There are no nails. There is no glue. The whole structure is held together by a traditional Japanese joinery technique called jigoku-gumi, and jigoku means hell — the joints, once assembled, are so tightly interlocked that the structure cannot be taken apart. The same technique was used to build shoji screens in Kyoto's Toji Mieido temple, some of which have been in place for over six hundred years.

Inside, the lattice filters the light into shifting patterns across cork tile floors, and the irregular stair treads between floors have small plants sprouting from them — the interior, actually, does feel remarkably like standing under a forest canopy. On the upper floor, the friendly staff will bring you a pineapple cake and a cup of Taiwanese tea. No charge, no obligation. The pineapple cake is the reason the building exists: SunnyHills is a Taiwanese confectionery brand, and this is their Tokyo flagship. Their Japan recipe uses French Échiré butter, Japanese flour, and Japanese eggs — rather a long way from a side street in Aoyama to a Taiwanese pineapple, going via Brittany.

The building was designed by Kengo Kuma in two thousand and thirteen. His stated aim was to create a forest in the city. The method he chose to do it was a joinery system designed for temples built to last five centuries — applied to a shop whose cakes have a three-day shelf life.

The Nezu Museum is a four-minute walk further down the street, also designed by Kengo Kuma — a traditional Japanese art collection with a bamboo garden, and the quietest place in this part of Aoyama.

---

tours.title: Toraya Akasaka | とらや 赤坂店
tours.shortDescription: Five hundred years of wagashi and eighteen generations of one family, still making the imperial household's confectionery beside the Akasaka Estate.
tours.longDescription:
Five hundred years of wagashi, eighteen generations of the same family, one purveyor that moved from the Kyoto imperial court in the fifteen-hundreds to this Akasaka street in 1964. The four-storey building stands beside the Akasaka Estate, whose greenery fills its ground-floor windows — not accidental. Toraya has supplied the imperial household since the reign of Emperor Goyozei in the late sixteenth century, and followed the capital to Tokyo in 1869.

The name means tiger store, after the tiger that travels a thousand li in a day and returns. The oldest document showing the company at work dates to 1600; a 1635 record lists twenty wagashi prepared for an empress. During wartime rationing they sold bread because sugar was unavailable, then returned to wagashi when peace came. They opened in Paris in 1980, before France's Japanese-food boom.

The one to buy is Yoru no Ume — Night Plum — a yōkan of azuki bean jelly that takes three days to make, the beans just visible on the cut surface like plum blossom at night. Through glass on the ground floor you can watch the day's fresh sweets being made each morning.

stops.title: Toraya Akasaka | とらや 赤坂店
stops.caption: Through the wide ground-floor windows, look to the greenery of the neighbouring Akasaka Estate — placed there by design.

ATLAS AUDIO TOUR — TORAYA AKASAKA MAIN STORE (とらや 赤坂店), TOKYO

Location: 4-9-22 Akasaka, Minato-ku, Tokyo (8 minutes from Akasaka-Mitsuke Station, exit B)
Hours: 8:30am–8pm weekdays; 8:30am–6pm weekends; café open from 9am
Approximate duration: 1:55 (≈290 words)

---

Five hundred years of wagashi. Eighteen generations of the same family. One address, moving from the Kyoto imperial court in the fifteen hundreds to this street in Akasaka in nineteen sixty-four.

The Toraya Akasaka building stands on a quiet street directly beside the Akasaka Estate — the imperial property whose greenery is visible through the building's wide ground-floor windows, which is not accidental. Toraya has been a purveyor to the imperial household since the reign of Emperor Goyozei in the late sixteenth century, and when the capital moved to Tokyo in eighteen sixty-nine, Toraya followed. The current building is four storeys, with a production workshop visible through glass on the ground floor where the day's fresh wagashi are made each morning, and a tea room upstairs where the menu changes with the season and the garden view changes with the light.

The name means tiger store — from the tiger's reputation for travelling a thousand li in a day and returning a thousand li. The oldest document in Toraya's archive showing the company in operation dates to sixteen hundred. A 1635 record lists twenty types of wagashi prepared for an empress on a palace visit. The company sold bread during wartime rationing in the nineteen forties because sugar was unavailable, then went back to wagashi when the war ended. It opened in Paris in nineteen eighty, before the Japanese restaurant boom in France, and the Rue Saint-Florentin store is still there.

Actually, the one to buy is Yoru no Ume — Night Plum. A yōkan of azuki bean jelly that takes three days to make, in which the individual beans are just visible on the cut surface, compared to plum blossoms at night. It is rather the kind of description that makes you want to stop and think about a piece of confectionery in a way you might not have expected.

The tea room on the upper floor serves seasonal wagashi with tea and has a clear view of the Akasaka Estate treetops — worth going up for the stillness as much as the menu, particularly in May when the fresh leaf colour is at its best.

---

tours.title: Taro Okamoto Memorial Museum | 岡本太郎記念館
tours.shortDescription: Taro Okamoto's home and studio, left exactly as it was — paint on the floor, half-finished canvases, and a deliberately wild garden.
tours.longDescription:
In 1946 Taro Okamoto returned to Tokyo from the war in China to find his family home in Aoyama bombed flat and his prewar work destroyed with it. He rebuilt on the same ground and started again. The building you approach today, down a short concrete path flanked by tropical vegetation with sculptures peering out between banana leaves and ferns, was designed in 1954 by Junzo Sakakura, a pupil of Le Corbusier, in concrete block with a convex, lens-shaped roof. Okamoto lived and worked here for forty-two years until his death in 1996, aged eighty-four.

The ground-floor studio is left exactly as it was — paint splattered across the floor, brushes on the table, half-finished canvases, a palette of dried pigment. From here he made the Tower of the Sun for Osaka's Expo 70 and murals for the Yoyogi Olympic Stadium; here he wrote his most famous line, art is an explosion.

The garden is the most revealing thing about the place. Next door the Nezu Museum is immaculate; Okamoto's is the deliberate opposite — wild, overgrown, slightly menacing, with sculpted faces emerging from the vegetation and grass growing from the eyes of one work, making no effort to be polite.

stops.caption: Approach through the tropical path and look for the sculptures peering out between the banana leaves and ferns.

ATLAS AUDIO TOUR — TARO OKAMOTO MEMORIAL MUSEUM (岡本太郎記念館), TOKYO

Location: 6-1-19 Minami-Aoyama, Minato-ku, Tokyo (7 minutes from Omotesando Station, exit B1)
Hours: 10am–6pm; closed Tuesdays
Admission: ¥650 adults
Approximate duration: 2:10 (≈330 words)

---

It's nineteen forty-six. Taro Okamoto has come back to Tokyo from the war in China. His family home in Aoyama has been bombed flat, and his prewar artwork has been destroyed with it. The first thing he does is rebuild on the same ground and start again.

The museum is at 6-1-19 Minami-Aoyama, on a bystreet between Kotto-dori and the Nezu Museum — a building you approach through a short concrete path flanked by dense tropical vegetation, sculptures peering out between banana leaves and ferns. The building itself was designed in nineteen fifty-four by Junzo Sakakura, a pupil of Le Corbusier, who built it at Okamoto's request with concrete block walls and a convex, lens-shaped roof that was celebrated as a striking piece of architecture when it was new. Okamoto lived and worked here for forty-two years until his death in nineteen ninety-six at the age of eighty-four.

The studio on the ground floor has been left exactly as it was: paint splattered across the floor, brushes on the table, half-finished canvases on the shelves, a palette with dried pigment. The salon alongside it has floor-length windows that look directly into the garden. The grass is wild, the sculptures are placed as if haphazardly, and in one of the works you can see grass growing out of the eyes. Okamoto made the Tower of the Sun for Osaka's Expo seventy from this studio. He made large-scale murals for the Yoyogi Olympic Stadium from this studio. His most famous phrase — art is an explosion — was written here.

I find the garden the most revealing thing about the place. The neighbouring Nezu Museum is immaculately maintained, one of the most refined spaces in this part of Aoyama. Okamoto's garden next door is rather the deliberate opposite: wild, overgrown, slightly menacing, with sculpted faces emerging from the vegetation and making no effort to be polite about it.

Go inside and take off your shoes before the studio entrance. The wax figure of Okamoto at the desk is either a very good likeness or exactly what you'd want to find sitting there, depending on how much you already know about him.

tours.title: Tennō-ji | 天王寺
tours.shortDescription: Yanaka's oldest temple, where granite foundations are all that remain of a pagoda that inspired a celebrated Meiji novel and burned twice.
tours.longDescription:
Look to the far corner of the cemetery: the granite foundations there are all that remains of a pagoda that inspired Japan's most celebrated novel about craftsmanship — and burned twice. Tennōji is the oldest temple in Yanaka, founded in 1274 as a Nichiren temple beside what is now Yanaka Cemetery. Most buildings are later reconstructions, lending the walled precinct a modest air, though the bronze Daibutsu in the courtyard has stood here since 1690.

Its history is one of repeated dispossession. In 1698, under Tokugawa pressure, it was forced to convert from the Nichiren to the Tendai sect. In 1872 the Meiji authorities seized its extensive grounds for a public cemetery and never returned them. During the Edo period it was one of only three temples permitted to hold lotteries — rights withdrawn in 1842.

The pagoda was built in 1644, burned in 1771, rebuilt in 1908, and burned again in 1957 in a double-suicide. Rohan Koda had already immortalised the original in his 1891 story The Five-Storied Pagoda. The stone foundations are worth standing at for a moment.

stops.transcriptText:
ATLAS AUDIO TOUR — TENNŌJI TEMPLE (天王寺), TOKYO

Location: 7-14-8 Yanaka, Taito-ku, Tokyo (3 minutes from Nippori Station west exit, JR Yamanote Line and Keisei Line; free entry)
Approximate duration: 2:10 (≈330 words)

---

Look toward the far corner of the cemetery. The granite foundations you can see are all that remains of a pagoda that inspired Japan's most celebrated novel about craftsmanship, and burned twice.

Tennōji stands at 7-14-8 Yanaka, directly adjacent to Yanaka Cemetery and three minutes from Nippori Station — the oldest temple in the district, founded in twelve seventy-four as a Nichiren Buddhist temple. The buildings you see now are mostly later reconstructions; the main hall and its low, walled precinct give the site a quieter, more modest presence than the scale of its history suggests. The bronze Buddha in the courtyard, known locally as Tennoji Daibutsu, was cast in sixteen ninety and has stood here through everything that followed.

The temple's history is one of repeated dispossession. In sixteen ninety-eight, under Tokugawa shogunate pressure, it was forced to convert from the Nichiren sect to the Tendai sect. In eighteen seventy-two, Meiji authorities confiscated the temple's extensive grounds and declared them a public cemetery — the largest in Tokyo at the time — and never returned the land. During the Edo period, Tennōji was one of only three temples in the city permitted to hold lotteries, drawing enormous crowds to the precinct; the lottery rights were withdrawn in eighteen forty-two.

The pagoda that once stood on the cemetery grounds was built in sixteen forty-four, burned in seventeen seventy-one, rebuilt in nineteen oh eight, and then burned again in nineteen fifty-seven when two people set fire to it as part of a double-suicide. Well, the novelist Rohan Koda had already immortalised the original structure in his eighteen ninety-one story The Five-Storied Pagoda, one of the most read works of Meiji-era literature — a story about the obsessive craftsman who refuses to abandon a pagoda in a typhoon. The stone foundations are what's left. They're rather worth standing at for a moment.

Yanaka Cemetery itself, which was once part of this temple's grounds, contains around seven thousand graves — among them Tokugawa Yoshinobu, the last shogun of the Edo period. The cherry-blossom avenue running through its centre is one of the most atmospheric walks in old Tokyo, particularly in late March.

---

tours.title: The Giant 3D Cat | 新宿東口の猫
tours.shortDescription: A lifelike calico cat peers over a Shinjuku rooftop every fifteen minutes — an anamorphic illusion that only resolves from one spot on the pavement.
tours.longDescription:
Look up and slightly to your left. Every fifteen minutes a cat appears on the curved LED screen atop the Cross Shinjuku building, above the East Exit plaza — one hundred and fifty-four square metres of 4K display spanning three floors, running from seven in the morning until one at night. Among the adverts and short films, the thing that stopped a hundred and ninety thousand daily commuters when it launched in July 2021 was a calico cat: lifelike, three-dimensional, peering over the building's edge with genuine feline curiosity.

The illusion is anamorphic. The curved screen and the precise viewing angle from this pavement conspire to produce the 3D effect; stand anywhere else and the cat flattens into an image on a curved wall. Stand here, and it seems truly to be sitting above you.

The origin is telling. The screen launched during a state of emergency, the Olympics summer of 2021, after months of restrictions. The makers chose a cat, they said, because the world had grown dark and people needed something to stop for. The cat has no official name; fans call it Neko-sama, Lord Cat.

Look up and slightly to your left. The cat appears every fifteen minutes. Stand here long enough and it will turn and look directly at you.

The curved LED screen sits on the roof of the Cross Shinjuku building, directly above the East Exit plaza — one hundred and fifty-four square metres of 4K display spanning three floors, running from seven in the morning until one at night. The screen runs advertisements and short films around the clock, but the thing that stopped one hundred and ninety thousand daily commuters in their tracks when it launched in July twenty twenty-one was a calico cat: lifelike, three-dimensional, apparently peering over the edge of the building with genuine feline curiosity.

The illusion is anamorphic — the curved shape of the screen and the specific viewing angle from this pavement are calculated to produce the 3D effect. From any other angle, it flattens. Stand elsewhere, the cat becomes a flat image on a curved wall. Stand here, and it appears to actually be sitting above you.

I find the origin of the cat rather telling. The screen launched during a state of emergency, Japan's Olympics summer of twenty twenty-one, when the city had been under restrictions for months. The company that made the cat said they chose it because the world had become dark, and people needed something to stop for. A hundred and ninety thousand people a day were passing this spot already. The cat just gave them a reason to look up.

The cat has no official name. Fans call it Neko-sama — Lord Cat. Official merchandise is sold inside the building if you feel that's appropriate.

This is the National Art Center, Tokyo. It is the largest art museum space in Japan. It owns no art.

The building faces south on Roppongi, the wave-like glass curtain wall running for a hundred and sixty metres along the street — twenty-one and a half metres high, made of over six hundred slender steel columns and undulating glass that shifts in appearance with the light and the angle of approach. Designed by Kisho Kurokawa and opened in January two thousand and seven, it was the last major building he completed before his death that October. The site was previously occupied by a military installation, then by the University of Tokyo's Institute of Industrial Science. Inside the lobby, two inverted concrete cones rise through the atrium, their wider tops housing a café and the Paul Bocuse restaurant above, the whole space open and unpartitioned in a way that most museum buildings are not.

The absence of a permanent collection was deliberate, not a funding compromise. Kurokawa described the building as an "artistic airport" — a space for temporary exhibitions, travelling shows, and work by Japanese artists' associations who could rent the galleries to display their members' work. In its first year, the centre hosted seventy-nine exhibitions, and its opening Monet show was the second most-visited art exhibition in the world that year. Fourteen thousand square metres of exhibition space across twelve galleries, none of them fixed to a single discipline or period.

Well, the concept is more radical than it first appears. A national art museum that insists on owning nothing is also insisting that what it offers — the space, the building, the infrastructure — has value independent of any collection. Kurokawa had spent his career designing buildings as systems rather than objects. This is rather the final version of that argument.

The Art Library on the third floor is free to use without purchasing an exhibition ticket, and contains one of the most comprehensive collections of exhibition catalogues in Japan — worth the visit on its own if you want to spend time with art books in an unexpectedly beautiful room.

tours.title: The National Museum of Western Art | 国立西洋美術館
tours.shortDescription: Le Corbusier's only East Asian building, raised in Ueno Park to house a war-impounded art collection France returned on one condition.
tours.longDescription:
After the war, Japan asked France to return an art collection. France agreed — on one condition: Japan had to build a museum, designed by a French architect, to put it in. The result stands in Ueno Park, a low horizontal building of exposed concrete raised on slim columns, with Rodin's The Thinker, The Gate of Hell and The Burgesses of Calais waiting in bronze on the forecourt. These came with the Matsukata Collection, assembled by industrialist Kōjirō Matsukata in Europe between 1920 and 1923, impounded by France in the Second World War, and returned in 1959 under that architectural condition.

The chosen architect was Le Corbusier — his only completed building in East Asia, now a UNESCO World Heritage Site. He designed it by his Modulor system of human proportions, lifting the galleries on pilotis and moving visitors up a promenade ramp, conceived as a spiral "Museum of Unlimited Growth." The 1979 annex came from Kunio Maekawa, one of his apprentices.

Matsukata was a friend of Claude Monet, and some of the Water Lilies inside came from that friendship — a collection scattered by war and returned by diplomacy.

stops.transcriptText:
ATLAS AUDIO TOUR — NATIONAL MUSEUM OF WESTERN ART (国立西洋美術館), TOKYO

Location: 7-7 Ueno-koen, Taito-ku, Tokyo (8 minutes from Ueno Station; Ueno Park main entrance on the left)
Hours: 9:30am–5pm (Fri/Sat until 8pm); closed Mondays
Approximate duration: 2:20 (≈355 words)

---

The Japanese government asked France to return an art collection after the war. France agreed — on one condition: Japan had to build a museum designed by a French architect to put it in.

The museum stands in Ueno Park on your left as you come through the main park gate from Ueno Station — a low, horizontal building of exposed concrete and geometric panels, raised on slim columns above the forecourt. Before you reach the entrance, you'll find three bronze figures already waiting: Rodin's The Thinker on a pedestal to the right, The Gate of Hell in the centre, and The Burgesses of Calais to the left. These are among the Rodin casts that came to Japan as part of the Matsukata Collection — assembled by industrialist Kōjirō Matsukata in Europe between nineteen twenty and nineteen twenty-three, impounded by the French government during the Second World War, and returned in nineteen fifty-nine under the condition that France's chosen architect design the building to receive them.

That architect was Le Corbusier — his only completed building in East Asia, and now a UNESCO World Heritage Site. Le Corbusier designed the building according to his Modulor system, a proportional framework based on human body measurements applied throughout the structure, from the ceiling heights down to the exterior panel dimensions. The main body of the galleries is lifted on pilotis, the signature concrete columns. Entry is at ground level through the double-height nineteenth-century hall, lit by a pyramidal skylight, and the painting galleries above are reached by a promenade ramp — Le Corbusier's preferred way of moving people through a building slowly. The design was based on his concept of a Museum of Unlimited Growth: a spiral that could expand outward without disrupting the internal sequence. The annex added in nineteen seventy-nine was designed by Kunio Maekawa, one of Le Corbusier's own Japanese apprentices, who supervised the original construction.

I find the Matsukata story rather more interesting than the building's biography usually lets on. Matsukata was a personal friend of Claude Monet — the Water Lilies inside the museum came partly from that friendship — and the collection he assembled, scattered by war, impounded by a foreign government, and finally returned as a condition of diplomacy, is now one of the best holdings of European art anywhere in Asia.

The permanent collection on the upper floors covers European painting from the fourteenth to the early twentieth century, with the emphasis on French Impressionism. The Monet room is the one to find first.

tours.title: The Sumida Hokusai Museum | すみだ北斎美術館
tours.shortDescription: A mirrored aluminium museum in the district where Hokusai was born — built to a master who thought he hadn't yet started.
tours.longDescription:
Katsushika Hokusai made around thirty thousand works over ninety years, yet said nothing before the age of seventy was worth looking at — and that at one hundred and ten he might finally achieve something. The museum stands in Kamezawa, Sumida Ward, in the district where he was born in 1760 and spent almost all of his life. Designed by Kazuyo Sejima of SANAA and opened in November 2016, it is five storeys of slightly mirrored aluminium, sliced by angular cut-outs so it reads differently from every approach — the reflecting surfaces meant to absorb the neighbourhood rather than stand apart from it.

The site has its own Hokusai connection: once the residence of a daimyo clan, where he is said to have painted a horse on a folding screen at their request. The fourth-floor permanent exhibition recreates his cramped studio, layered with papers and brushes, alongside high-quality replicas of his major series, including Thirty-six Views of Mount Fuji. The light-sensitive originals rotate through changing exhibitions on the third floor.

He wrote that line about his age at around seventy-five, in a postscript — by which point he had already produced the Great Wave, and still thought he hadn't started.

---

Katsushika Hokusai made around thirty thousand works over ninety years. He said that nothing he produced before the age of seventy was worth looking at — and that at one hundred and ten, if he lived that long, he might finally achieve something.

The museum stands in Kamezawa, Sumida Ward, a few minutes' walk east of Ryogoku Station, in the district where Hokusai was born in seventeen sixty and spent almost the whole of his ninety years. The building was designed by Kazuyo Sejima of SANAA and opened in November twenty sixteen — five storeys of aluminium panels with a slightly mirrored surface, angular cut-outs slicing into the mass from different directions so the building reads differently from every approach. The reflecting facades were intended to let the building absorb and echo its neighbourhood rather than standing apart from it, and the angular slits bring light into the interior and make the building feel permeable from the street, even from the outside.

The site has its own connection to Hokusai: it was the Edo-period residence of a daimyo clan, and Hokusai is said to have visited to paint a horse on a folding screen at the clan's request. The permanent exhibition on the fourth floor recreates Hokusai's studio — cramped, layered with papers, brushes, pigments, and a figure of Hokusai himself at work on the floor — alongside high-quality replicas of his major series, including Thirty-six Views of Mount Fuji and the Hundred Poems series. The originals are too light-sensitive to display continuously; they rotate through the temporary exhibitions on the third floor, which change throughout the year.

Well, the claim about his age is well-documented — he wrote it in a postscript to the Hundred Poems series at around seventy-five. What makes it rather remarkable is that by the time he wrote it, he had already produced the Great Wave. He still thought he hadn't started.

The Ryogoku Kokugikan sumo stadium is a ten-minute walk, and the Edo-Tokyo Museum is immediately adjacent — a good pairing with the Hokusai if you have the afternoon.

tours.title: Tiffany & Co. Ginza | ティファニー 銀座
tours.shortDescription: A sixty-six-metre Ginza flagship wrapped in curving Tiffany Blue glass, designed not to look like a building but like wisteria swaying in the wind.
tours.longDescription:
There's a curious thing about this building: it isn't trying to look like a building. It's trying to look like a plant. Rising sixty-six metres on a corner of Ginza's Chuo-dori, the Tiffany flagship is clad entirely in curving glass panels in Tiffany Blue — the house colour worn on the box since 1845. Architect Jun Aoki set himself the brief of a facade like a wisteria trellis swaying in the soft wind. "There is no nature in Ginza," he has said. "I wanted to add something that invokes nature rather than just another man-made object."

To manage it, a quarter of the facade is made of panels each given a unique three-dimensional shape, angled differently at every fixing point so light catches the surface afresh across the building's full height. The wisteria came from the Tiffany archives — a stained-glass study, and Louis Comfort Tiffany's White Wisteria table lamp of around 1904, now displayed inside.

It opened in July 2025 as Tiffany's largest flagship in Asia, fifty-three years after the house first reached Tokyo. Japan accounts for more Tiffany sales than any country outside the United States.

TIFFANY & CO. — GINZA FLAGSHIP
Atlas Audio Tour

There's a curious thing about the building in front of you: it isn't trying to look like a building. It's trying to look like a plant.

Along Chuo-dori, Ginza's main avenue, the Tiffany flagship rises sixty-six metres on a corner plot, its entire facade clad in curving glass panels in Tiffany Blue — the house colour that, since 1845, has appeared on the box you're handed when you buy something you clearly hope will go well. The building was designed by Jun Aoki, who has previously given Louis Vuitton a pearlescent facade and Loro Piana a quiet Ginza presence, and who was commissioned here to do something rather larger. His stated brief to himself was a facade like a wisteria trellis swaying in the soft wind. "There is no nature in Ginza," he has said. "It's all just buildings. I wanted to add something that invokes nature rather than something that is just another man-made object."

To achieve that, Aoki designed each curved glass panel individually — twenty-five per cent of the facade's surface is made up of panels with a unique three-dimensional shape each, angled differently at every fixing point so that light catches the surface at a different angle across the full height of the building. The source for the wisteria idea came from the Tiffany archives: a stained glass study featuring the flower, and beyond that, Louis Comfort Tiffany's White Wisteria table lamp of around 1904, which is on display inside the store. The challenge Aoki described was making something that looks artisan-made at industrial scale — and the difficulty only shows if you go looking for it.

The building opened in July 2025 as Tiffany's largest flagship in Asia, fifty-three years after the house first arrived in Tokyo in 1972. Japan accounts for more Tiffany sales than any country outside the United States, which goes some way to explaining the scale of the investment.

Inside, Japan's first Blue Box Café is on an upper floor, with a terrace and a floral installation by Azuma Makoto. The Kanazawa gold-leaf ceiling on the jewellery floor is the interior detail most worth finding.

tours.title: Todoroki Ravine | 等々力渓谷
tours.shortDescription: Descend the steps and the city vanishes — the only natural ravine in Tokyo's twenty-three wards, a kilometre of river, moss and birdsong.
tours.longDescription:
Go down the steps from the street and the temperature drops, the canopy closes overhead, and the sound of the city gives way to running water and birdsong. You are, technically, still inside Tokyo. This is Todoroki Keikoku Park in Setagaya Ward, the only natural ravine within all of Tokyo's twenty-three special wards. A kilometre of trail follows the Yazawa River through a valley some fifteen metres deep, cut over thousands of years through the edge of the Musashino Plateau, with zelkova, oak, bamboo and mountain cherry above moss, fern and more than thirty natural springs.

The red steel arch at the foot of the stairs is Gorufu-bashi, Golf Bridge, named for an eight-hectare golf course built above the ravine in the 1930s by the Tokyu Corporation, the same company that runs the train line here. The course is long gone; the ravine remained.

Todoroki means thunder or roar, said to come from the waterfall halfway along — Fudo-no-Taki — where water falls between two dragon statues into a stone basin. Buddhist monks have used the spot for ascetic practice for centuries, and seventy-one steps climb to Todoroki Fudoson Temple above. On the east bank, a sixth-century kofun burial mound survives in the hillside.

stops.transcriptText:
TODOROKI RAVINE PARK — SETAGAYA, TOKYO
Atlas Audio Tour

Go down the steps from the street and the temperature drops. The canopy closes overhead. The sound of the city disappears, replaced by running water and birdsong. You are, technically, still inside Tokyo.

The red steel bridge at the foot of the stairs is the entrance to Todoroki Ravine — officially Todoroki Keikoku Park, in Setagaya Ward, and the only natural ravine within all of Tokyo's twenty-three special wards. One kilometre of walking trail follows the Yazawa River downstream through a valley roughly fifteen metres deep, cut by the river over thousands of years as it worked through the edge of the Musashino Plateau. The trees here — zelkova, oak, bamboo, mountain cherry — form a dense canopy above a floor of moss and fern and more than thirty natural springs that keep the river clear and cool year-round.

The bridge you're standing by is called Gorufu-bashi — Golf Bridge. The name comes from an eight-hectare golf course built above the ravine in the nineteen thirties by the Tokyu Corporation, the company that also operates the train line that brought you here. The current bridge, the red arch, replaced a wooden one in 1961. The golf course is long gone; the ravine remained.

As you walk downstream, the valley earns its name. Todoroki means thunder or roar in Japanese, and the name is said to come from the sound of the waterfall roughly halfway along the trail — Fudo-no-Taki — where the water falls between two dragon statues into a stone basin below. Buddhist monks have used the spot for ascetic practice for centuries, and the waterfall feeds a small but considered devotion that continues today. Above it, seventy-one steps lead up to Todoroki Fudoson Temple, a calm and unpopular shrine in the best sense.

On the east bank, a kofun burial mound from the sixth century has been preserved in the hillside — a designated Tokyo cultural property, and as easy to walk past as it is to stop at.

At the far end of the trail, Setsugekka is a small traditional teahouse that serves oshiruko and kuzumochi. After a walk through a fifteen-metre-deep forest in the middle of a city of fourteen million people, it tends to feel exactly right.

The Uruguayan architect Rafael Viñoly won Japan's first international architectural competition for it in 1989, and it was completed in 1996. On a long, narrow site wedged between the rail lines of Tokyo and Yurakucho stations, he split the scheme in two: four theatre and conference halls of diminishing size, granite-clad and stacked above a public plaza, and, opposite, the Glass Hall.

The Glass Hall is two hundred and twenty-eight metres long and sixty high, carried over its full length by just two columns. Its roof is shaped like a ship's hull, engineered by Kunio Watanabe with steel trusses suspended from the perimeter; at night, light off those trusses turns it into a floating horizontal light source over the city.

The New York Times called it "a perfectly realized building" in 1997, and the AIA gave it its Twenty-Five Year Award in 2024.

stops.transcriptText:
TOKYO INTERNATIONAL FORUM — 東京国際フォーラム
Atlas Audio Tour

The Tokyo International Forum sits on the site of the old Tokyo City Hall, which moved to Nishi-Shinjuku in 1991, and what replaced it is one of the great civic spaces of the 1990s anywhere.

The building was designed by the Uruguayan architect Rafael Viñoly, who won Japan's first international architectural competition for the project in 1989. Construction was completed in 1996. The site is long and narrow — wedged between the rail lines of Tokyo Station to the north and Yurakucho Station to the south — and Viñoly divided it into two halves. On the western edge of the site, four theatre and conference halls of diminishing size float above a public plaza, clad in granite and aligned like stacked boxes. On the eastern edge, and directly in front of you now, is the Glass Hall.

The Glass Hall is two hundred and twenty-eight metres long, sixty metres high, and supported by just two columns over its full length. Its roof is shaped like the hull of a ship — a comparison Viñoly encouraged — and the structure was engineered by Kunio Watanabe using steel trusses suspended from the perimeter. At night, light reflecting off the surface of those trusses transforms the roof into what the architect described as a floating horizontal light source over the city.

The New York Times, reviewing the completed building in 1997, called it "a perfectly realized building" and ranked the Glass Hall among the world's great spaces. The American Institute of Architects gave it its Twenty-Five Year Award in 2024. In the interim, the building had been used for G7 summits, classical music festivals, fashion shows, anime conventions, and — after the 2011 earthquake — as emergency shelter for thousands of people stranded in central Tokyo.

Walk the length of the Glass Hall from end to end and look up at the trusses. The scale is clearest from the inside, moving.

tours.title: Tokyo Metropolitan Government Building | 東京都庁
tours.shortDescription: Kenzo Tange's twin-towered city hall — part Gothic cathedral, part integrated circuit — with free observation decks over Tokyo and, on clear days, Fuji.
tours.longDescription:
There is a curious thing about this building: it was destroyed on film eight months after it was finished, and the comparison has lingered. The complex fills three blocks of Nishi-Shinjuku — the forty-eight-storey, 243-metre Building No. One splitting into twin towers at the thirty-third floor, the lower Building No. Two, and the semicircular Assembly Building between them. Designed by Kenzo Tange, completed in 1990 and opened in 1991, it cost some hundred and fifty-seven billion yen — about a billion dollars — at the height of the bubble economy, to considerable public discomfort.

Tange meant it to read at once as a Gothic cathedral and an integrated circuit; a Christian, he modelled the split twin-tower silhouette directly on Notre-Dame de Paris, filtered through postmodern concrete. The commission was also civic strategy: Nishi-Shinjuku was once a red-light and Yakuza district, and the city hall anchored its turn into a financial and administrative centre.

Tange won the job twice over, having designed the previous city hall in Yūrakuchō in 1957. The two observation decks, on the forty-fifth floor of each tower at 202 metres, are free — rather more than the building's critics felt it deserved.

There's a curious thing about the building in front of you — it was destroyed on film eight months after it was finished, and the comparison has lingered ever since.

The complex occupies three city blocks in Nishi-Shinjuku: the main Building No. One to your left, forty-eight storeys and two hundred and forty-three metres, splitting into twin towers at the thirty-third floor; Building No. Two to the south at thirty-four storeys; and the semicircular Assembly Building between them. Designed by Kenzo Tange, completed in nineteen ninety and opened in nineteen ninety-one, it cost one hundred and fifty-seven billion yen — around a billion US dollars — at the height of Japan's bubble economy, a figure that generated significant public discomfort. The two free observation decks sit on the forty-fifth floor of each tower at two hundred and two metres, with views east over the full spread of Tokyo and, on clear days, Mount Fuji to the west.

The design was intended to read simultaneously as a Gothic cathedral and an integrated circuit — Tange was Christian, and the twin-tower silhouette split at the top is a direct reference to Notre-Dame de Paris, filtered through the language of postmodern concrete. The faceted granite surfaces and deep-set windows carry the vertical emphasis upward. The building also signalled something beyond its own programme: the district around it was formerly a red-light district and Yakuza territory, and Tange's commission was part of the city's deliberate effort to transform Nishi-Shinjuku into a financial and administrative centre. Twenty years later, that transformation is complete. The skyscrapers that now surround the metropolitan government building include some of the largest corporate headquarters in Japan.

Well, Tange received the same commission twice: he designed the previous Tokyo city hall in Yūrakuchō in nineteen fifty-seven, and won the new one here thirty years later. The Yūrakuchō building's site is now the Tokyo International Forum. The observation decks here are free, which is rather more than the building's original critics felt it deserved.

Take the lift to the North Observatory — the views across Shinjuku's skyscraper cluster to the east and the ridge of the Tanzawa Mountains to the west are best from that side, and in February and March the deck is occasionally open at night for the winter illumination of the plaza below.

tours.shortDescription: A 1938 building that asked how to look modern without ceasing to be Japan — a temple roof grafted onto a Western body, the Imperial Crown Style.
tours.longDescription:
Every nation eventually asks how to look modern without abandoning what makes it itself, and Japan spent the early twentieth century arguing about the answer. This building is what that argument looks like in concrete and clay tiles. Stand at the top of the approach and the Honkan faces you: a symmetrical, imposing facade, a neoclassical base of pale stone crowned by a double-tiered roof of dark ceramic tiles, like a temple. To the left, the Meiji-era Hyokeikan of 1909; to the right, the angular Toyokan of 1968.

Designed by Jin Watanabe and opened in 1938, the Honkan replaced an earlier structure by the British architect Josiah Conder, lost in the Great Kanto Earthquake of 1923. Its style has a name — teikan yoshiki, the Imperial Crown Style — grafting a Japanese temple roof onto a Western body. It opened before Emperor Hirohito.

Here is the interesting part: the building meant to project a modern imperial nation has outlasted that nation, and now holds the very things it was built to glorify — eighty-nine National Treasures among some hundred and twenty thousand objects, from ten-thousand-year-old Jomon pottery to Edo-period armour.

stops.title: Tokyo National Museum | 東京国立博物館
stops.caption: Stand at the top of the forecourt facing the Honkan — neoclassical stone below, a temple roof of dark tiles crowning it.
stops.transcriptText:
TOKYO NATIONAL MUSEUM — HONKAN ENTRANCE
Atlas Audio Tour

There's a question every nation asks at some point: how do you look modern without abandoning what makes you yourself? Japan spent much of the early twentieth century arguing about the answer, and this building — the one in front of you right now — is what that argument looks like in concrete and clay tiles.

The main entrance to the Tokyo National Museum faces south across a wide forecourt, so you should be at the top of the approach path, looking straight at the Honkan, the museum's central building. The facade is symmetrical, imposing, and deliberately hard to place in time — a broad neoclassical base of pale stone punctuated by columns, with a double-tiered roof of dark ceramic tiles sitting above it all like a temple crown. To your left stands the Hyokeikan, a white building with green domes that is pure Meiji-era Westernism, built in 1909. To your right, the angular Toyokan from 1968. The Honkan, in the middle, is doing something quite different from both.

The building was designed by Jin Watanabe and opened in 1938, replacing an earlier structure — designed by British architect Josiah Conder — destroyed in the Great Kanto Earthquake of 1923. Watanabe's design was chosen through a public competition, and the style has a name: teikan yoshiki, or Imperial Crown Style. The idea was to graft the silhouette of a Japanese temple roof onto a Western structural body — something that felt neither purely imported nor purely nostalgic. It cost seven million yen, took six years to complete, and was opened in the presence of Emperor Hirohito. The Honkan is now itself a National Important Cultural Property.

And here's the rather interesting part: the building meant to project the confidence of a modern imperial nation has outlasted that nation entirely, and now holds the very things it was built to glorify — eighty-nine National Treasures among some hundred and twenty thousand objects in all, ranging from Jomon pottery ten thousand years old to Edo-period samurai armour. This has been Japan's oldest museum since it first opened, in an earlier form, in 1872.

Before you go in, the garden behind the Honkan is worth finding — it opens in spring and autumn, with historic teahouses and a pond that feel entirely removed from the city outside the gates. Head straight inside and it's easy to walk past without ever knowing it's there.

tours.title: Urasando Public Toilets | 裏参道公衆トイレ
tours.shortDescription: Marc Newson's copper-roofed public toilet beneath the expressway, designed to oxidise green and grow quietly into its surroundings.
tours.longDescription:
Look at the roof: that warm reddish-brown copper is meant to change, oxidising over the years into the muted green-grey patina you see on old temple rooflines. The designer intended it — the building is supposed to grow into its surroundings. This is one of seventeen facilities commissioned for the Tokyo Toilet Project, a Nippon Foundation initiative running from 2020 to 2023 that invited sixteen designers to rebuild public toilets nobody wanted to go near.

This one is by Marc Newson, the Australian industrial designer known abroad for the original Apple Watch and the Lockheed Lounge chair, and it opened in January 2023. He called his method "product thinking" rather than architecture, treating the small, single-purpose building as he would an object. A stacked-stone wall and a copper Minoko roof nod to shrine and tearoom traditions, while the interior is a bright, seamless monochrome green.

Tucked under the Shuto Expressway, the spot is hardly picturesque, and Newson knew it — the design simply insists on its own quiet dignity beneath the overpass. Even the cleaners' khaki uniforms, designed by NIGO, frame the upkeep as something worth wearing well.

stops.title: Urasando Public Toilets | 裏参道公衆トイレ
stops.caption: Look up at the copper Minoko roof under the Shuto Expressway — the reddish-brown will slowly turn temple-green.
stops.transcriptText:
Look at the roof. That gentle curve, that particular warm brown — that's copper, and it's going to change. Over the next several years, the copper will oxidise and develop a verdigris patina, shifting from the current reddish-brown to the same muted green-grey you see on old temple rooflines across Japan. The designer intended this. The building is supposed to grow into its surroundings.

You are standing outside one of seventeen public toilets commissioned across the Shibuya district as part of the Tokyo Toilet Project — a Nippon Foundation initiative that began in 2020 and concluded in 2023, which invited sixteen internationally recognised designers to rebuild public facilities that, by most assessments, nobody wanted to go near. This particular toilet was designed by Marc Newson, an Australian industrial designer perhaps best known outside Japan for his work on the original Apple Watch and for the Lockheed Lounge chair. He opened here in January 2023.

Newson's approach was what he called product thinking rather than architecture — the building is small, the purpose is specific and clear, and he treated those constraints as he would treat the design of an object. The stacked stone wall wrapping the exterior and the copper Minoko roof are explicit references to traditional Japanese shrine and tearoom architecture; the interior is a bright, seamless monochromatic green — clean, slightly clinical, reassuring. The whole thing is tucked under the Shuto Expressway overhead, which means the location is not exactly picturesque, and Newson knew it: the design doesn't try to compete with the overpass, it simply insists on its own quiet dignity beneath it.

The cleaning staff across the entire Tokyo Toilet network arrive two or three times daily, wearing khaki uniforms designed by the fashion designer NIGO — a choice that was deliberate, intended to frame the maintenance work as something worth wearing well.

The Yoyogi entrance to Meiji Jingū is a short walk from here — through the tree-lined approach and into one of the largest and most carefully tended shrine forests in Tokyo. It's a useful counterpoint to the expressway overhead.

*~300 words / approx. 2:00*

tours.title: Waseda El Dorado | ドラードギャラリー
tours.shortDescription: Lily-pad balconies, a Medusa floor mosaic, and a giant hand that is secretly a chair — one architect's utopian "city of gold".
tours.longDescription:
Look at the balconies: shaped like lily pads, wrought-iron curves looping from the facade in a way no planning brief ever demanded. On Sodai-dori near Waseda University stands a residential and gallery complex completed in 1984 by Von Jour Caux — legal name Tanaka Toshiro. He left Waseda's architecture department for Chicago in 1962 meaning to study Mies van der Rohe, but spent his years there on painting, sculpture and craft at the School of the Art Institute, where he met his lifelong collaborator and wife. Back in Japan, he founded an art-complex movement granting every contributor complete creative freedom — pointedly unlike Gaudi, who controlled every detail himself.

The name combines three kanji — harmony, world, and the charm of virtue — and the building was conceived as a "city of gold," the utopian idea that art-saturated space could change those who live in it. The exterior mixes Art Nouveau, Japanese woodblock and Celtic motifs, ceramic figures and zigzagging iron banisters past stained glass. Inside, a Gorgoneion mosaic — a Medusa head to ward off evil — sits at the entrance, and a giant hand descends from a stained-glass ceiling. It is actually a chair.

The Japan Times called Von the Japanese Gaudi in 1992. He found it inaccurate: Gaudi was an autocrat; Von gives his collaborators the building.

stops.title: Waseda El Dorado | ドラードギャラリー
stops.caption: Look up at the lily-pad iron balconies from Sodai-dori, then step into the gallery for the Medusa mosaic and the hand.
stops.transcriptText:
ATLAS AUDIO TOUR — WASEDA EL DORADO (ドラード和世陀), TOKYO

Location: 517 Wasedatsurumakicho, Shinjuku-ku, Tokyo (5 minutes from Waseda Station, Tōzai Line; facing Sodai-dori Street)
Gallery hours: Ground floor gallery open to visitors; upper floors residential
Approximate duration: 2:10 (≈335 words)

---

Look at the balconies. They are shaped like lily pads — wrought-iron curves that loop and unfurl from the facade in a way that no planning brief has ever demanded and no conventional architect has ever proposed.

The building is at 517 Wasedatsurumakicho in Shinjuku-ku, on Sodai-dori Street near Waseda University — a multi-storey residential and gallery complex completed in nineteen eighty-four and designed by Von Jour Caux, whose legal name is Tanaka Toshirō. He graduated from Waseda University's architecture department in nineteen fifty-six, left for Chicago in nineteen sixty-two intending to study Mies van der Rohe at the Illinois Institute of Technology, and instead spent his years there studying painting, sculpture, and craft at the School of the Art Institute. He met his wife and life-long collaborator there. When he returned to Japan, he broke with architectural convention and founded the art complex movement with his wife and a group of artist friends, a collaborative practice whose philosophy was to give all contributors complete creative freedom — explicitly unlike Gaudí, who controlled every detail himself.

The name of the building combines three kanji: 和 (harmony), 世 (world) and 陀 (the charm of virtue). The building was conceived as a "city of gold" — a utopian idea that beautiful, art-saturated living space could change the people who lived inside it. The exterior mixes Art Nouveau, Japanese woodblock and Celtic motifs, ceramic figures with tattoo-style designs, and wrought-iron banisters zigzagging past stained-glass windows. Inside the entrance, the floor mosaic is the Gorgoneion — a stylised Medusa head, tongue extended, which in antiquity was believed to ward off evil. At the end of the interior corridor, a giant hand descends from a stained-glass ceiling. It is actually a chair.

The Japan Times called Von Jour Caux the Japanese Gaudí in nineteen ninety-two. He found the comparison rather inaccurate — Gaudí was an autocrat. Von gives his collaborators the building.

The ground-floor gallery is open to visitors. Go in, look up at the hand, and take your time with the corridor walls. The building is better understood from inside than from the street.

---
