The first thing you encounter is Monet's Water Lilies, laid flat on the bottom of a shallow reflecting pool, visible through a film of actual water. The effect is peculiar and unexpectedly right. Further down, Michelangelo's Last Judgement fills a wall fourteen metres high — nearly full-scale, composed of a hundred interlocking ceramic sections. It is not a reproduction so much as a translation; the same image, different matter, different context, different kind of permanence.

The other six works include Leonardo's Last Supper, Seurat's Sunday on the Grande Jatte, Renoir, Van Gogh, and two East Asian scrolls — a medieval Japanese animal caricature and a twelfth-century Chinese river scene. All at the same stubborn, outlasting ceramic permanence.

Entry is a hundred yen. The Kyoto Botanical Garden is immediately adjacent and included in the same afternoon without difficulty.

tours.title: Ginkaku-ji | 銀閣寺
tours.shortDescription: The Silver Pavilion has never had any silver on it. The name is, technically, false advertising — and why is more interesting than the silver would have been.
tours.longDescription:
Ginkaku-ji was begun in 1482 as a retirement villa for the shogun Ashikaga Yoshimasa, modelled deliberately on the Golden Pavilion his grandfather had built at the other end of the city. Yoshimasa meant to cover it in silver leaf to complete the pairing — gold answered by silver — but the Ōnin War delayed construction so badly that he died in 1490 with the silver never applied. What survives is the building exactly as he last saw it: bare dark timber, unfinished by intention but complete by every other measure, now regarded as one of the clearest expressions of wabi-sabi, the aesthetic that finds completeness in imperfection.

The garden holds two sand features: the Ginshadan, a raked expanse representing a sea, and Kōgetsudai, a truncated cone angled to catch and reflect moonlight across the garden.

A path behind the buildings climbs the hillside to a viewpoint over the whole temple and the city — a five-minute walk most visitors skip. The Philosopher's Path begins just outside the south gate and runs two kilometres along the canal toward Nanzen-ji, lined with cherry trees.

stops.title: Ginkaku-ji | 銀閣寺
stops.caption: The Silver Pavilion that never received its silver — bare dark timber left by the Ōnin War, now a touchstone of wabi-sabi.
stops.transcriptText:
The building called the Silver Pavilion has never had any silver on it. The name is, technically, false advertising — and the reason why is more interesting than the silver would have been.

The approach to the main gate is behind you, through the tall hedge corridor you've just walked. The pavilion itself stands at the edge of the upper pond, two storeys, dark unfinished timber, its reflection visible in still water on calm mornings.

Ginkaku-ji was begun in fourteen eighty-two as a retirement villa for the shogun Ashikaga Yoshimasa, modelled deliberately on the Golden Pavilion his grandfather had built at the other end of the city. Yoshimasa intended to cover his pavilion in silver leaf to complete that pairing — gold answered by silver — but the Ōnin War, a decade of civil conflict that burned much of Kyoto to the ground, delayed construction so badly that Yoshimasa died in fourteen ninety with the silver never applied. What survives is the building exactly as he last saw it: bare dark timber, unfinished by its original intention but complete by every other measure, and now regarded as one of the clearest expressions of wabi-sabi — the aesthetic that finds completeness in imperfection — in Japanese architecture.

The garden in front of the pavilion includes two sand features: the Ginshadan, a raked expanse of white sand representing a sea, and Kōgetsudai, a truncated cone believed to have served as a platform for moon viewing, its surface angled to catch and reflect moonlight across the garden.

A path behind the main buildings climbs the hillside to a viewpoint over the entire temple and the city beyond — a five-minute walk that most visitors, absorbed in the pavilion below, skip entirely.

The Philosopher's Path begins just outside the south gate and runs for two kilometres along the canal toward Nanzen-ji, lined with cherry trees planted in nineteen twenty-one by Hashimoto Kansetsu's wife. The Hakusasonsō garden and museum, Kansetsu's former home, is a short walk further along.

tours.title: Gion | 祇園
tours.shortDescription: A service town for a sacred place that gradually became more famous than the place it served.
tours.longDescription:
The district grew up around Yasaka Shrine — for centuries called Gion Shrine — whose stone torii stands at the east end of Shijō Street; the whole neighbourhood borrows its name. Pilgrims stopping before or after a shrine visit needed somewhere to eat, sleep and be entertained, and over several centuries the area became exactly that.

You're at or near the Hanamikoji intersection, the central spine of Gion Kōbu, the larger of the district's two geisha communities. The street runs south between dark wooden machiya whose cantilevered upper storeys and narrow frontages reflect an Edo-period tax on width — which is why old Kyoto buildings are tall and thin. Some are restaurants; some are ochaya, teahouses where geiko and maiko entertain by invitation only, and from outside the two are indistinguishable. Gion uses geiko — "a woman of art" — rather than geisha, and the distinction matters here. The Miyako Odori, staged each April since 1872, remains the most accessible way to see what the district actually produces.

At dusk the paper lanterns outside the ochaya are lit and the pace of the street changes. Walking slowly and quietly at that hour gives you a different Gion than the daytime one.

stops.title: Gion | 祇園
stops.caption: The Hanamikoji spine of Gion Kōbu — dark machiya teahouses where Kyoto's geiko still entertain by invitation only.
stops.transcriptText:
The district grew up around a shrine. Yasaka Shrine, whose large stone torii gate stands at the east end of Shijō Street, was for centuries called Gion Shrine — and the name of this entire neighbourhood is borrowed from it. Pilgrims and travellers stopping before or after shrine visits needed somewhere to eat, sleep, and be entertained, and so the district that now surrounds you developed over several centuries as exactly that: a service town for a sacred place, which gradually became more notable than the place it served.

You're standing at or near the Hanamikoji intersection — the central spine of Gion Kōbu, the larger of the two geisha districts that occupy this neighbourhood. The street runs south from Shijō-dōri between rows of dark wooden machiya townhouses, their facades preserving the cantilevered upper storeys and narrow frontages that were taxed by width in the Edo period, which is why old Kyoto buildings are typically tall and thin. Some of these buildings are restaurants. Some are ochaya — teahouses where geiko and maiko entertain private guests by invitation only. From the outside, the two are indistinguishable.

Gion uses the word geiko rather than geisha — "a woman of art" rather than "artist" — and the distinction matters here. Kyoto's five hanamachi, or flower districts, are the most formal geisha communities remaining in Japan, with training regimes, hierarchies, and standards of practice that have persisted through the twentieth century with relatively little compromise. The Miyako Odori, the public dance performance Gion Kōbu has staged each April since eighteen seventy-two, remains the most accessible point of entry for anyone who wants to see what the district actually produces.

At dusk, the paper lanterns outside the ochaya are lit, and the pace of the street changes. This is when the district functions as it was designed to — as a place for those with appointments, moving through with purpose. Walking slowly and quietly at this hour gives you a different Gion than the daytime one.

tours.title: Giōji Temple | 祇王寺
tours.shortDescription: In late November, when the maples turn, this may be the most quietly beautiful corner of Arashiyama. In May, deep in moss and bamboo, it runs it close.
tours.longDescription:
Giōji is a small thatched-roof temple at the northern edge of Arashiyama, set back from the tourist streets down a narrow lane most visitors miss. It takes its name from Giō, a shirabyōshi dancer and favourite of the twelfth-century warlord Taira no Kiyomori; when he abandoned her for a younger dancer, Hotoke-gozen, Giō retired here with her mother and sister, and eventually Hotoke followed them into seclusion, so moved by what she saw. The story is one of the more elegiac passages of the Tale of the Heike, and five wooden statues in the main hall represent all five women.

The garden is the reason to come. A deep carpet of moss — many species layered under the maples and bamboo — absorbs light in a way that makes the interior feel cooler and quieter than the air outside. The thatched roof holds rain long after it falls, and the sound of water dripping into the moss, at the right moment, completes the sense of having stepped somewhere held apart from the city.

The path north leads toward Adashino Nembutsuji, twenty minutes on, where thousands of small stone figures mark abandoned graves.

stops.title: Giōji Temple | 祇王寺
stops.caption: A small thatched temple down a lane most visitors miss — a layered moss garden tied to an elegiac tale from the Heike.
stops.transcriptText:
In late November, when the maples turn, this may be the most quietly beautiful corner of Arashiyama. In May, when the bamboo is at its deepest green and the moss is still thick from the spring rain, it runs it close.

Giōji is a small thatched-roof temple at the northern edge of the Arashiyama district, set back from the main tourist streets and reached via a narrow lane that most visitors to the area miss entirely. The temple takes its name from Giō, a shirabyōshi dancer who was a favourite of the powerful warlord Taira no Kiyomori in the twelfth century. When Kiyomori abandoned her for a younger dancer named Hotoke-gozen, Giō retired here with her mother, her sister, and eventually Hotoke herself, who was so moved by what she witnessed that she followed them into seclusion. The story is one of the more elegiac passages of the Tale of the Heike, the great chronicle of the Genpei War period, and the five wooden Buddhist statues in the main hall represent all five women.

The garden is the reason to come. A deep carpet of moss — multiple species layered over the ground under the maples and bamboo — absorbs light in a way that makes the interior of the garden feel cooler and quieter than the air outside it. The thatched roof of the main hall holds rain for a long time after it falls, and the sound of water dripping from it into the moss, if you are there at the right moment, adds to the general atmosphere of having stepped somewhere held apart from the city.

The path north from Giōji leads through the rural edge of Arashiyama toward Adashino Nembutsuji Temple, a twenty-minute walk further, where thousands of small stone figures mark the sites of abandoned graves.

tours.title: HARIO CAFE | ハリオカフェ
tours.shortDescription: HARIO translates as "King of Glass." For a certain coffee enthusiast, it's the maker of the standard dripper, the standard glass server — the vessel before the liquid.
tours.longDescription:
HARIO has made heat-resistant glass in Japan since 1921, and over the decades it became, for a particular kind of coffee enthusiast, the maker of the standard pour-over dripper, the standard glass server, the standard glass teapot — the name on the packaging so familiar it's easy to forget it refers to the vessel before anything about what's inside.

The café is HARIO's own retail and café space in Fushimi, south of the city centre and a short walk from Fushimi Inari Taisha. The room is clean and minimal in the way HARIO products are, the company's glassware visible throughout — used for brewing, displayed on shelves, available to buy. The point is to experience the equipment in use rather than on a shelf: coffee brewed in a V60 and served in a clear glass tastes as it would anywhere, but the process slows down and the physics of extraction becomes legible — you watch the bloom, and the colour, through the glass.

Fushimi is also a sake-brewing district, with breweries including Gekkeikan a short walk south along the old canal streets. An afternoon of coffee then sake is, depending on temperament, either a reasonable programme or an excellent one.

stops.title: HARIO CAFE | ハリオカフェ
stops.caption: The Fushimi café of HARIO — "King of Glass" since 1921 — where you drink pour-over from the glassware that made the company's name.
stops.transcriptText:
HARIO translates as "King of Glass" — 硝子の王様. The company has been making heat-resistant glass in Japan since 1921, and over the decades it has become, for a particular kind of coffee enthusiast, the maker of the standard pour-over dripper, the standard glass coffee server, the standard glass teapot. The name on the packaging is so familiar that it is easy to forget it refers to a company that makes the vessel before it refers to anything about the liquid inside.

The café in front of you is HARIO's own retail and café space in the Fushimi district of southern Kyoto, south of the city centre and a short walk from Fushimi Inari Taisha. The building is on a quiet street; the space inside is clean and minimal in the way that HARIO products are clean and minimal, with the company's glassware visible throughout — used for brewing, displayed on shelves, available to purchase.

The point, if you accept the invitation, is to experience the equipment in use rather than on a shop display. Coffee brewed in a HARIO V60 dripper and served in a HARIO glass tastes the same as it would in any other vessel, but the brewing process slows down in a way that makes the physics of extraction legible — you can watch the water bloom through the grounds and observe the resulting colour in a transparent cup rather than an opaque one.

The Fushimi district has a coherent identity as a sake-brewing area, with several major breweries — including Gekkeikan — accessible by a short walk along the old canal streets to the south. An afternoon that begins with coffee and ends with sake is, depending on your temperament, either a reasonable programme or an excellent one.

tours.title: Heisei Chishinkan Wing, Kyoto National Museum | 平成知新館
tours.shortDescription: Designed by the architect who extended MoMA in New York — the same approach here: transparency, restraint, the building as a container of light rather than a statement.
tours.longDescription:
The wing in front of you was designed by Yoshio Taniguchi, one of the defining museum architects of the late twentieth century and the man who extended the Museum of Modern Art in New York in 2004. His method is the same in both places: transparency, precision, restraint — the building a container of light rather than a rival to its contents.

The Kyoto National Museum was established in 1897; its original red-brick Beaux-Arts hall, still standing to the south, was designed by Tokuma Katayama, architect of the Nara and Tokyo national museums. In 2014 the Heisei Chishinkan — the "Hall of New Knowledge" — opened opposite it as the primary exhibition space. Taniguchi's wing is low, horizontal and almost entirely glass at ground level, linking the entrance plaza to the garden beyond.

Inside is art from ancient to medieval Japan: Buddhist sculpture, Heian painting, ceramics, swords, lacquerware, decorated screens. They tend to look better here than in the old brick building — Taniguchi filters daylight through glass and deflects it off surfaces to avoid direct illumination, which suits the subtlety of what the museum holds. Sanjūsangendō, with its thousand-and-one Kannon, is a four-minute walk south.

stops.title: Heisei Chishinkan Wing, Kyoto National Museum | 平成知新館
stops.caption: Yoshio Taniguchi's low glass wing at the Kyoto National Museum — daylight deflected off surfaces to suit ancient and medieval Japanese art.
stops.transcriptText:
The new wing in front of you was designed by the same architect who extended the Museum of Modern Art in New York in 2004 — Yoshio Taniguchi, one of the defining museum architects of the late twentieth century. His approach in both cases was the same: transparency, precision, restraint, the building as a container of light rather than a statement competing with its contents.

The Kyoto National Museum was established in 1897, and its original Meiji-era building — red brick Beaux-Arts, still standing to the south — was designed by Tokuma Katayama, the architect who also built the Nara and Tokyo national museums. For more than a century that Victorian edifice housed the full programme of exhibitions. Then in 2014, after years of planning, the Heisei Chishinkan — the "Hall of New Knowledge" — opened as the museum's primary exhibition space on the opposite side of the entrance plaza.

Taniguchi's wing is low, horizontal, and almost entirely glass at ground level, creating a visual connection between the entrance plaza and the garden beyond. The collection inside focuses on art and artefacts from ancient to medieval Japan: Buddhist sculpture, Heian-period paintings, ceramics from the great kiln traditions, swords, lacquerware, decorated screens. These things tend to look better in the Taniguchi wing than in the old brick building — his handling of natural light, which he filters through glass and deflects off surfaces to avoid direct illumination of sensitive works, suits the subtlety of what the museum contains.

Sanjūsangendō — the hall containing one thousand and one gilded wooden Kannon statues — is a four-minute walk south from the museum entrance and is open to visitors daily. If you are seeing one thing in this part of Kyoto, it is that.

tours.title: Ippodo Tea Kyoto | 一保堂茶舗 京都本店
tours.shortDescription: A tea merchant opened on Teramachi Street in 1717. Three hundred years later the shop is still here, its blends traced back to the same centuries-old logic.
tours.longDescription:
In 1717 a tea merchant opened on Teramachi Street, in the commercial district running south from the imperial palace, selling matcha, gyokuro and sencha to the temple estates, court families and tea-ceremony practitioners of the city. Three centuries on, the shop is still here, its teas chosen by blenders working from recipes whose logic traces back to those same traditions.

Ippodo's main Kyoto store is designed for buying tea, not lingering: long wooden counters, staff who know the stock in detail and will ask what you want the tea for before recommending anything. Matcha for drinking differs from matcha for cooking; gyokuro, the most shaded and sweetest of green teas, wants cooler water than sencha; the house blends are built to perform consistently across seasons as the harvest varies.

Through the back is the small Kaboku Tearoom, where tea is prepared by the correct method — a bowl of matcha whisked to order, or gyokuro steeped at fifty degrees for two and a half minutes — the price including being shown how to drink it. Nishiki Market is a short walk west if you want the contrast.

stops.title: Ippodo Tea Kyoto | 一保堂茶舗 京都本店
stops.caption: A tea merchant on Teramachi since 1717 — house blends built from centuries-old recipes, with a tearoom that shows you how to drink them.
stops.transcriptText:
It's 1717. A tea merchant opens a shop on Teramachi Street in Kyoto, in the commercial district running south from the imperial palace. He sells matcha, gyokuro, and sencha to the temple estates, the court families, and the tea ceremony practitioners of the city. Three hundred years later, the shop is still here, and the selection of teas is determined by blenders working from recipes that trace their logic back to those same centuries-old traditions.

The building you are standing in front of is Ippodo's main Kyoto store — one of the most venerated tea merchants in Japan, and the one that most serious students of Japanese tea culture eventually find their way to. The shop interior is designed for the purchase of tea, not for lingering: long wooden counters, staff who know the stock in detail and will ask what you want the tea for before recommending anything. Matcha for drinking is different from matcha for cooking; gyokuro, the most shaded and therefore the sweetest of green teas, requires water at a lower temperature than sencha; the house blends are constructed to perform consistently across seasons when the character of the harvest varies.

There is a small tea room — Kaboku Tearoom — through the back of the shop where you can order tea prepared according to the correct method: a bowl of matcha whisked to order, or a pot of gyokuro steeped at fifty degrees for two and a half minutes. The price of the tea includes the experience of being shown how to drink it.

The Nishiki Market is a short walk west, if a direct contrast to the quiet of this shop sounds useful.

tours.title: KYO AMAHARE | 居雨:KYO
tours.shortDescription: Kaiseki's reference points — seasonal produce, precise preparation, the composition of a dish — adapted for a contemporary room rather than a formal tatami hall.
tours.longDescription:
There's a particular kind of Kyoto restaurant that draws on kaiseki, the multi-course seasonal cuisine developed in the tea-ceremony tradition, but adapts the format for a contemporary setting. KYO AMAHARE is that kind of place — in Fushimi, close to the Fushimi Inari complex, in a part of the city that works as a neighbourhood rather than a tourist corridor. The street here is quieter than Higashiyama or the central shopping districts, with a pace that suits a long dinner rather than a quick passage between sights.

"Amahare" means the clearing of rain — the moment the weather lifts and the sky opens, used in Japanese for both the meteorological change and the relief that comes with it. The name frames the meal as a transition from the density of the day into something more expansive, which, when it works, is exactly what a good dinner in Kyoto does.

The menu changes with the seasons; reservations are required, and worth making well ahead for evening sittings in the spring and autumn high seasons.

stops.title: KYO AMAHARE | 居雨:KYO
stops.caption: A contemporary Fushimi restaurant working from kaiseki principles — its name, "the clearing of rain," framing dinner as a transition.
stops.transcriptText:
There's a particular kind of Kyoto restaurant that takes its culinary reference points from kaiseki — the multi-course seasonal cuisine developed in the tea ceremony tradition — but adapts the format for a contemporary setting rather than a formal tatami room. KYO AMAHARE is that kind of place: a restaurant in the Fushimi district that draws on the kaiseki emphasis on seasonal produce, precise preparation, and the visual composition of a dish, without requiring the full ceremonial apparatus of a traditional kaiseki encounter.

The building itself is in the southern stretch of Kyoto, close to the Fushimi Inari shrine complex, in a part of the city that functions as a neighbourhood rather than a tourist corridor. The street character here is quieter than Higashiyama or the central shopping districts — residential, with a pace that suits a long dinner rather than a rapid passage between attractions.

"Amahare" means the clearing of rain — the moment when the weather lifts and the sky opens, used in Japanese as a term for both meteorological change and the sense of relief that comes with it. The name positions the experience as a kind of transition from the density of the day into something more expansive, which is, when it works, exactly what a good dinner in Kyoto does.

The menu changes seasonally. Reservations are required and recommended well in advance for evening sittings, particularly during the spring and autumn high seasons.

The Gekkeikan Ōkura Sake Museum is a short walk south, in the old sake-brewing district along the Fushimi canal — a useful pre-dinner orientation to the district's deeper history, and open to visitors with tastings included in the admission fee.

tours.title: Kibune River Dining Hirobun | ひろ文
tours.shortDescription: The platform extends out over the river on wooden stilts, a few feet above cold, fast water — which is entirely the point.
tours.longDescription:
Kawadoko dining — eating on platforms built out over mountain streams — is a summer tradition in the Kibune valley precisely because nowhere else in Kyoto's reach offers this combination of cool air, moving water and food. The platform you're on sits a few feet above the narrow, fast, cold Kibune River.

Hirobun is one of the valley's most established kawadoko restaurants, known especially for nagashi-sōmen: thin wheat noodles floated down bamboo channels of running water, plucked out with chopsticks as they pass. It's more skill than it sounds, and more enjoyable than almost anything else you might do with noodles — the water genuinely cold, the flow calibrated to give you a reasonable window.

The valley sits in the mountains north of Kyoto, forty minutes from the centre and several degrees cooler; Kyoto's basin traps heat that makes July and August oppressive, and the valley's reputation as a retreat from it is centuries old. Kifune Shrine, the water-deity shrine that names the valley, is a short walk further up the lantern-lined steps.

stops.title: Kibune River Dining Hirobun | ひろ文
stops.caption: A kawadoko platform on stilts over the cold Kibune River, famous for nagashi-sōmen — noodles caught from running bamboo channels.
stops.transcriptText:
The platform you are seated on — or are about to step onto — extends out over the Kibune River on wooden stilts, a few feet above the water flowing beneath you. The river at this point is narrow, fast-moving, and cold even in summer, which is entirely the point: kawadoko dining, the practice of eating on platforms built over mountain streams, is a summer tradition in the Kibune valley specifically because no other place in Kyoto's reach offers this combination of cool air, moving water, and food.

Hirobun is one of the valley's most established kawadoko restaurants, and it is specifically known for nagashi-sōmen — a dish in which thin wheat noodles are floated down channels of running water cut from bamboo, and diners pluck them out with chopsticks as they pass. The exercise is more skill than it sounds, and more enjoyable than almost anything else you might do with noodles. The water is genuinely cold and the speed of the flow is calibrated to give you a reasonable window of interception.

The Kibune valley sits in the mountains north of Kyoto, a forty-minute journey from the centre of the city. In summer, the temperature here is several degrees cooler than the city below — Kyoto's basin traps heat in a way that makes July and August genuinely oppressive, and the valley's reputation as a retreat from that heat is well-earned and centuries old. The cedar and maple forest closes in on both sides of the narrow road from the valley floor.

Kifune Shrine, the ancient water deity shrine that gives the valley its name, is a short walk further up the road — the lantern-lined stone steps are worth the ascent.

tours.title: Kibune River Dining | 貴船 水源の森 天山
tours.shortDescription: Lean over the railing: clear water running over dark rocks in a constant shallow rush. The air rising off it is the only air conditioning this valley has ever needed.
tours.longDescription:
Kawadoko dining in Kibune dates to at least the Edo period, when the valley became a summer retreat for Kyoto's merchant and scholarly classes who found the city's July and August unliveable. Restaurants built platforms over the river to catch the cold water running down from the Kitayama mountains; the flow here is fast and shallow, shaded by the narrow valley walls and forest, and the air rising off it drops the temperature on the platforms by several degrees.

Tenzan sits at the lower end of the kawadoko district, where the valley floor widens and the river is a little more accessible. Its cooking, like most in Kibune, draws on kaiseki principles — seasonal, refined, course-structured — adapted to the outdoor setting: mountain vegetables and river fish in spring and early summer, preparations built around the cooling setting in late summer.

The kawadoko season runs May through September, after which the platforms come down and the valley turns to coloured maples and indoor dining. The road continues north to Kifune Shrine, about fifteen minutes on foot.

stops.title: Kibune River Dining | 貴船 水源の森 天山
stops.caption: Tenzan, at the lower end of Kibune's kawadoko district — kaiseki cooking on a platform cooled by the river running beneath it.
stops.transcriptText:
Lean over the railing and look at the river directly below the platform. The water is running over dark rocks in a constant shallow rush, clear enough to see the bottom. The temperature rising from it is the only air conditioning this valley has ever needed.

The kawadoko dining tradition in Kibune dates to at least the Edo period, when the valley became a summer retreat for Kyoto's merchant and scholarly classes who found the city's heat unliveable in July and August. Restaurants built platforms over the Kibune River to take advantage of the cold water running down from the Kitayama mountains — the flow here is fast and shallow, shaded by the narrow valley walls and the forest that covers them, and the cool air rising from the surface drops the ambient temperature on the platforms by several degrees relative to the road.

Tenzan sits at the lower end of the kawadoko district, where the valley floor widens slightly and the river is a little more accessible. The cuisine, as with most kawadoko establishments in Kibune, draws on kaiseki principles — seasonal, refined, course-structured — adapted to the outdoor setting and the season. In spring and early summer this means the valley's mountain vegetables and river fish; in late summer, preparations designed around the cooling quality of the setting itself.

The kawadoko season runs from May through September, after which the platforms are dismantled and the valley shifts to its quieter autumn and winter character — coloured maple leaves replacing the green canopy, and most of the restaurants operating indoors.

The valley road continues north from here to Kifune Shrine, approximately fifteen minutes on foot. A walk up and back makes a coherent half-day of the entire valley.

tours.title: Kinkaku-ji | 金閣寺
tours.shortDescription: The story most visitors carry to this building is the wrong one. Its permanence has always been a product of reconstruction, not unbroken survival.
tours.longDescription:
The Golden Pavilion that burned in 1950, set alight by a young monk, was not the original — it was already a reconstruction. What you're looking at was rebuilt in 1955 with gold leaf thicker than before, itself a faithful copy of a fifteenth-century structure built as a retirement villa for a fourteenth-century shogun. The permanence on which its reputation rests has always come from sustained reconstruction rather than unbroken survival.

Kinkaku-ji — formally Rokuon-ji — was first built in 1397 as the retirement villa of the shogun Ashikaga Yoshimitsu, who gathered an extraordinary art collection here around an existing lake and garden. When he died in 1408 the site became a Rinzai Zen temple by his wishes, and the pavilion he'd used as a reception hall was converted to a reliquary for Buddhist relics on its upper floor. The lake that mirrors it is Kyōkochi, the Mirror Pond.

The pavilion carries three distinct architectural styles, one per floor — aristocratic shinden below, the warrior's bukke in the middle, Zen at the top — and from across the pond you see all three at once, stacked.

stops.title: Kinkaku-ji | 金閣寺
stops.caption: The Golden Pavilion — a 1955 reconstruction of a copy — its three stacked architectural styles mirrored in Kyōkochi, the Mirror Pond.
stops.transcriptText:
The story most visitors carry to this building is the wrong one. The Golden Pavilion that burned in 1950, set alight by a young monk named Hayashi Yōken in an act of obsessive destruction, was not the original — it was already a reconstruction. And the building you are looking at now, rebuilt in 1955 with the top two floors covered in gold leaf thicker than the 1950 version, is itself a faithful copy of a fifteenth-century structure that was in turn built as a retirement villa for a shogun who lived in the fourteenth century. The permanence on which the Golden Pavilion's reputation rests has always been a product of sustained reconstruction rather than unbroken survival.

Kinkaku-ji — formally Rokuon-ji — was originally constructed in 1397 as the retirement villa of the shogun Ashikaga Yoshimitsu, who gathered an extraordinary art collection and built a complex of structures on this site around an existing lake and garden. When Yoshimitsu died in 1408, the site became a Rinzai Zen temple per his wishes, and the pavilion — which he had used as a personal reception hall — was converted to a reliquary housing Buddhist relics on its upper floor. The lake, which mirrors the building, is called Kyōkochi — the Mirror Pond.

The Pavilion has three distinct architectural styles, one on each floor: shinden aristocratic style at the bottom, the warrior's bukke style in the middle, and a Zen Buddhist style at the top. From across the pond you can see all three simultaneously, stacked.

Ryōan-ji Temple, home to the most famous dry-stone garden in Japan — fifteen rocks in raked white gravel, no two visible simultaneously from any seated position — is a twenty-minute walk west.

tours.title: Kyoto City KYOCERA Museum of Art | 京都市京セラ美術館
tours.shortDescription: The oldest municipal art museum in Japan still operating in its original building — a 1933 block wearing a curved Japanese roof "like a hat that belongs to a different outfit."
tours.longDescription:
The building opened in 1933 as the Kyoto City Art Museum, making it the oldest municipal art museum in Japan still working in its original structure. Built to mark the city's 1,100th anniversary, it was done in the Teikan or "Imperial Crown" style — a state-mandated blend of Western neo-classical structure with Japanese roof elements: grey stone walls, large windows, and a curved swept-eave roof sitting on the classical block like a hat from a different outfit.

A major renovation in 2020, designed by Yoshio Taniguchi, added the KYOCERA name after the company's donation; Taniguchi sank a new gallery underground and set a glass entrance lobby level with the forecourt, putting the 1933 exterior in dialogue with a contemporary interior without disturbing the historic facade. The collection ranges across Japanese modern and international contemporary art, with rotating exhibitions and a large international art fair each spring.

The wide forecourt connects the museum to Okazaki Park, with the Heian Shrine to the north and the National Museum of Modern Art to the south. On Sunday mornings a market takes over; other mornings it's simply a good place to stand and look at the roof.

stops.title: Kyoto City KYOCERA Museum of Art | 京都市京セラ美術館
stops.caption: Japan's oldest municipal art museum in its original 1933 Teikan-style building — its historic roof set against Taniguchi's 2020 glass lobby.
stops.transcriptText:
The building behind you opened in 1933 as the Kyoto City Art Museum — making it the oldest municipal art museum in Japan still operating in its original structure. It was built to mark the 1,100th anniversary of the establishment of the city, and the style that the architects chose was Teikan — "Imperial Crown" — a state-mandated blend of Western neo-classical structure with Japanese roof elements that was fashionable for civic buildings in the early Showa period: grey stone walls, large windows, and a distinctive curved roof with swept eaves that sits on top of the classical block like a hat that belongs to a different outfit.

In 2020, after a major renovation, the building was renamed for KYOCERA Corporation, which contributed a substantial donation to the restoration fund. The renovation was designed by Taniguchi Yoshio, who extended the museum by sinking a new gallery underground and adding a glass entrance lobby that sits level with the forecourt — creating a dialogue between the 1933 exterior and a contemporary interior without disturbing the historic facade.

The collection ranges across Japanese modern art and international contemporary, and the building hosts several rotating exhibitions and residencies each year, including the large-scale international contemporary art fair that brings the Okazaki cultural district to life each spring.

The forecourt in front of the building is a wide, flat plaza connecting the museum to the Okazaki Park, a public green space that contains the Heian Shrine to the north and the National Museum of Modern Art Kyoto to the south. On Sunday mornings a market takes over the area; on other mornings it is simply a good place to stand and look at the roof.

Nanzen-ji Temple and its famous aqueduct are a ten-minute walk northeast — the aqueduct is a Meiji-period red-brick structure running through the temple grounds that creates one of the more peculiar architectural juxtapositions in the city.

tours.title: Kyukyodo | 京都鳩居堂 本店
tours.shortDescription: A pharmacy opened on this street in 1663. Because the herbs of a pharmacy and the ingredients of fine incense were the same substances, it became known as much for fragrance as for remedies.
tours.longDescription:
The pharmacy opened on Teramachi — Temple Town — the street named for the temple grounds relocated here during Toyotomi Hideyoshi's late-sixteenth-century reorganisation of the city. The pharmacist supplied Chinese herbs and aromatic materials to the temples and those who served them; because the herbs of a pharmacy and the ingredients of incense were essentially the same, the shop became known as much for its fragrance as its remedies.

The building is Kyukyodo's Kyoto main store, successor to that pharmacy on very nearly the same site, now selling incense, washi paper, calligraphy brushes, ink and stationery. The family crest — two doves on a floral garland, from a twelfth-century military honour to the Kumagai family — gives the shop its name: Kyu, written with the character for dove, and kyodo, hall.

In 1877 the imperial household entrusted Kyukyodo with the complete secret formulas for the Heian court incenses, a tradition preserved for over nine hundred years; between 1891 and 1945 it was official stationer to the Imperial Household. Honno-ji, where Oda Nobunaga died in 1582, is through a gate a few metres north.

stops.title: Kyukyodo | 京都鳩居堂 本店
stops.caption: Successor to a 1663 Teramachi pharmacy — now selling incense, washi and brushes, and keeper of the Heian court's incense formulas since 1877.
stops.transcriptText:
A pharmacy opened on this street in 1663. The street was called Teramachi — Temple Town — because it ran alongside a row of temple grounds relocated here from various parts of the city during Toyotomi Hideyoshi's urban reorganisation of the late sixteenth century. The pharmacist supplied Chinese herbs and aromatic materials to the temples and the people who served them: incense, medicines, and the raw materials for both. And because the herbs of a pharmacy and the ingredients of fine incense were essentially the same substances, the shop gradually became known as much for its fragrance as for its remedies.

The building in front of you is Kyukyodo's Kyoto main store — the successor to that pharmacy, on very nearly the same site, now selling incense, washi paper, calligraphy brushes, ink, and stationery. The family crest — two doves facing each other on a floral garland — dates to a military honour awarded to the Kumagai family in the twelfth century, and gives the shop its name: Kyu, written with the character for dove, kyodo meaning hall.

In 1877, the imperial household formally entrusted Kyukyodo with the complete secret formulas for the Heian court incenses — a ceremonial fragrance tradition preserved for over nine hundred years by that point. Between 1891 and 1945 the shop served as official stationer to the Imperial Household. The incense sold here today is produced from the same tradition, and the paper goods carry a weight and consideration in their design that comes from three and a half centuries of supplying people for whom materials mattered.

Honno-ji Temple, where the warlord Oda Nobunaga died in 1582, is accessible through a gate a few metres north of the shop — the entrance is easy to miss, and the contrast between the temple grounds and the street you're standing on is rather striking.

tours.title: La Collina Ōmi-Hachiman | ラ コリーナ近江八幡
tours.shortDescription: From the approach road the main building reads as a low green hill — grass giving way to grass, its profile against the mountain behind almost exactly continuous.
tours.longDescription:
La Collina opened in January 2015 as the flagship of the Taneya Group, a sweets-maker rooted in this town since 1872. The main building was designed by the architect and architectural historian Terunobu Fujimori, who works with natural materials — earth, timber, living plants — and who set out to make a building that belonged to the landscape rather than sat on it. The grass roof is the literal answer, mimicking the contours of Mount Hachiman behind and growing pine trees straight out of it.

Inside, more than a hundred chestnut trees, personally selected by Fujimori from Nagano, serve as structural pillars in the adjacent Castella shop — the effect of standing inside a temporarily roofed grove. The wider site, nearly twelve hectares, holds rice paddies, orchards, a factory shaped like a cross-section of baumkuchen and an earthen staff tower; the rice fields are farmed with local organisations and managed as a firefly habitat.

The name means "hill" in Italian, coined by Fujimori and the Italian designer Michele De Lucchi on a walk through the grounds in 2012. Lake Biwa, Japan's largest, is visible from the upper approaches to the site.

stops.title: La Collina Ōmi-Hachiman | ラ コリーナ近江八幡
stops.caption: Terunobu Fujimori's grass-roofed building for the Taneya sweets group — a structure built to read as a continuation of the hill behind it.
stops.transcriptText:
From the approach road, the main building reads as a low green hill. Look for a moment before you decide it's a building: the profile against Mount Hachiman behind it is almost exactly continuous, grass giving way to grass, slope to slope.

La Collina opened in January 2015 as the flagship site of the Taneya Group, a sweets-maker with roots in this town going back to 1872. The main building was designed by the architect and architectural historian Terunobu Fujimori, who works primarily with natural materials — earth, timber, living plants — and who was born in the alpine forests of Nagano. The brief, as far as there was one, was that the building should belong to the landscape rather than sit on top of it. The grass roof is the literal answer to that brief. It mimics the contours of Mount Hachiman behind, incorporating pine trees as they grow.

Step inside and the connection to the ground continues. Over a hundred chestnut trees, personally selected by Fujimori from Nagano, serve as structural pillars in the adjacent Castella shop; the effect is of being inside a grove that has been temporarily roofed. The wider site — nearly twelve hectares — contains rice paddies, orchards, small farm buildings, a factory shaped like a cross-section of baumkuchen, and a staff entrance that resembles an earthen tower. The rice fields are cultivated in partnership with local agricultural organisations and managed as a firefly habitat.

The name means "hill" in Italian. Fujimori and the Italian designer Michele De Lucchi, who collaborated on the site's wider design, coined it during a walk through the grounds in 2012.

The baumkuchen at Club Harie — the Western sweets arm of Taneya, founded in 1951 — is baked here on-site and worth the queue. Lake Biwa, Japan's largest lake, is visible from the upper approaches to the site.

tours.title: Le Labo Cafe Kyoto Machiya | ル ラボ カフェ 京都町家
tours.shortDescription: A building standing since 1879 — sake brewery, then flower shop, then empty — read by its architect as "the senior partner" in its own restoration.
tours.longDescription:
The building has stood on Kiyamachi Street beside the Takase Canal since 1879: first a sake brewery run by one family across three generations, later a flower shop, then empty. In 2024, after a year of restoration by the Tokyo practice Schemata Architects, it reopened as Le Labo's Kyoto flagship — fragrance store, café and creative atelier in a preserved townhouse.

The architect, Jo Nagasaka, had earlier designed Blue Bottle's Kyoto café in a machiya nearby, but the brief here was more layered: a New York niche fragrance brand, born in Grasse and raised in Manhattan, working inside a building carrying a hundred and fifty years of Kyoto history in its beams. Nagasaka's approach was to read the building as the senior partner — floors, walls, framing and an original sink preserved, new elements introduced in the building's own language: reclaimed timber counters, copper plumbing, ceramic tile. Le Labo's signature distressed-steel lab booth was rebuilt here in Japanese reclaimed wood. Upstairs, two tatami rooms hold a fragrance organ of hundreds of essential oils and an open atelier for local craftspeople.

The café occupies the original rear garden — a private courtyard of stone, plants and restored statues — serving matcha, coffee and vegan pastries.

stops.title: Le Labo Cafe Kyoto Machiya | ル ラボ カフェ 京都町家
stops.caption: An 1879 machiya — sake brewery, then flower shop — restored by Jo Nagasaka as Le Labo's Kyoto flagship, the old building kept as senior partner.
stops.transcriptText:
The building in front of you has been standing since 1879. It began as a sake brewery, run by one family across three generations, then later served as a flower shop, then stood empty. In 2024, after a year of careful restoration by the Tokyo architectural practice Schemata Architects, it opened as Le Labo's Kyoto flagship — a fragrance store, café, and creative atelier in a preserved traditional townhouse on Kiyamachi Street beside the Takase Canal.

The architect was Jo Nagasaka, who had previously designed Blue Bottle Coffee's Kyoto café in a machiya a short distance east of here. His brief for Le Labo was similar but distinct: where the Blue Bottle project resolved a meeting of West Coast coffee culture with Kyoto architecture through the logic of equal relationships, the Le Labo project needed to resolve something older and more layered — a New York niche fragrance brand that describes itself as born in Grasse, France, and raised in Manhattan, working inside a building that carries a hundred and fifty years of Kyoto history in its beams and walls.

Nagasaka's approach was to read the building as the senior partner. Floors, walls, framing, and an original sink are preserved; new elements — reclaimed timber counters, copper plumbing, ceramic tile — are introduced in the building's own language rather than against it. The fragrance lab booth, normally built from Le Labo's signature distressed steel, was constructed here from Japanese reclaimed wood. The second floor holds two tatami rooms, one serving as a fragrance organ displaying hundreds of essential oils, the other as an open atelier for local craftspeople.

The café is in the original garden at the rear of the house — a private courtyard of stone, plants, and restored statues, reached through heavy wooden doors, serving matcha, coffee, and vegan pastries.

tours.title: d-matcha Kyoto | d:matcha Kyoto
tours.shortDescription: The village of Wazuka has grown tea for eight hundred years; most of its leaf disappears into blends. A small proportion goes, traceably, to d:matcha.
tours.longDescription:
Wazuka sits about forty kilometres south of Kyoto in the mountains of Minami Yamashiro, surrounded by terraced tea fields cultivated for over eight hundred years. Most of the leaf grown there goes into blended products under larger brand names; a small proportion goes to d:matcha, a family-run organic farm that has been reclaiming abandoned fields and converting them to single-origin, pesticide-free cultivation.

The farm runs guided tours into the fields themselves — through the shade structures raised in the weeks before harvest, into the processing facility, through the grinding, drying and sorting that turn picked leaf into powder. This Kyoto café and shop is the starting point for those tours and a place to taste the tea directly.

What d:matcha offers that most Kyoto matcha destinations do not is traceability: the village, the field, the farmer, the harvest all known and documentable — the opposite of the blending that governs most of the market — alongside organic certification. The café uses the Wazuka teas across everything from ceremonial matcha to hojicha lattes and desserts, and the retail shelves change with each harvest.

stops.title: d-matcha Kyoto | d:matcha Kyoto
stops.caption: The Kyoto café of a family-run organic tea farm in Wazuka — single-origin matcha you can trace to the field, and the start of its farm tours.
stops.transcriptText:
The village of Wazuka sits about forty kilometres south of Kyoto in the mountains of the Minami Yamashiro region, surrounded by terraced tea fields that have been cultivated for over eight hundred years. Most of the leaves grown there go into the blended products sold under larger brand names. A small proportion goes to d:matcha.

d:matcha is a family-run organic tea farm that has been reclaiming abandoned fields in Wazuka and converting them to single-origin, pesticide-free cultivation. The farm runs guided tea tours that take visitors into the fields themselves — through the shade structures used to block sunlight in the weeks before harvest, into the processing facility, and through the grinding, drying, and sorting that turns the picked leaf into the powder that reaches the cup. The Kyoto café and retail space that brings the farm to the city is the starting point for those tours, as well as a place to taste the tea directly.

What d:matcha offers that most Kyoto matcha destinations do not is traceability. The village, the field, the farmer, the harvest — all of it is known and documentable, which is the opposite of the commercial blending practices that govern most of the Japanese tea market. Organic certification is part of that same commitment: no chemical fertilisers, no pesticides, and a cultivation approach that maintains the soil for the next planting.

The café menu uses the Wazuka teas across a range of preparations — from straight ceremonial matcha to hojicha lattes and desserts — and the retail shelves stock teas that are available seasonally rather than year-round, which means the selection changes with each harvest.

Wazuka itself is around an hour from central Kyoto by train and bus — the farm's website carries the current tour schedule and booking information for anyone who wants to continue from the café to the fields.

tours.title: lisn Kyoto | リスン 京都
tours.shortDescription: In Japan there's an old expression for smelling incense — not "kagu," to smell, but "kiku," to listen. This shop takes its name from it.
tours.longDescription:
The idea behind "kiku" is that fragrance, like music, asks for a quality of attention — to be still, to receive, to let it arrive on its own terms. lisn, which takes its name from that expression, was created by Shoyeido, a Kyoto incense house making fragrance since 1705, as a contemporary retail project for people who were not already incense practitioners.

The Kyoto flagship sits on the ground floor of COCON Karasuma, a 2004 building by Hisao Kohyama who preserved an older structure's steel frame. The interior is curved and almost fluid, with plaster and glass walls that undulate as if depicting drifting smoke and a floor of square clay roof tiles. Around a central counter, roughly a hundred and fifty incense varieties are displayed by colour in small triangular boxes, each stick available singly from thirty yen up.

Every variety is named for its character rather than its ingredients — "Since," "Hit My Soul," "Mother's Chest" — and the staff, trained as incense concierges, will spend as long as needed helping you find the right scent. Shoyeido's main Kyoto shop is a short walk north on Karasuma.

stops.title: lisn Kyoto | リスン 京都
stops.caption: Shoyeido's contemporary incense shop in COCON Karasuma — named for "kiku," the old word for smelling incense that means "to listen."
stops.transcriptText:
In Japan, there is an old expression for smelling incense: not "kagu" — to smell — but "kiku" — to listen. The idea is that fragrance, like music, requires a quality of attention; it asks you to be still, to receive, to let it arrive on its own terms. The incense company that takes its name from that expression, lisn, was created by Shoyeido — a Kyoto incense house that has been making fragrance since 1705 — as a contemporary retail project for people who were not already incense practitioners.

The shop in front of you is the Kyoto flagship, located on the ground floor of COCON Karasuma — a commercial building on Karasuma Street designed in 2004 by Hisao Kohyama, who converted an old building while preserving its steel structure. The interior of lisn is curved, almost fluid in plan, with plaster and glass walls that undulate as if depicting the slow drift of smoke. The floor is laid in square clay roof tiles. Around a central counter, approximately a hundred and fifty incense varieties are displayed by colour in small triangular boxes, each stick available to purchase individually at prices from thirty yen upward.

Every variety in the lisn range is given a name that evokes its character rather than its ingredients — names like "Since," "Hit My Soul," "Mother's Chest" — and the selection process, if you approach it properly, becomes a form of that listening the brand describes. The staff are trained as incense concierges and will spend as long as needed helping you find the right scent.

Shoyeido's main Kyoto shop, one of the oldest incense makers in Japan, is a short walk north on Karasuma — a useful comparison if you want to understand how the tradition and its contemporary descendant relate to each other.

tours.title: Amanohashidate | 天橋立
tours.shortDescription: A three-and-a-half-kilometre pine-covered sandbar across Miyazu Bay — one of Japan's three great scenic views, and the fallen heavenly bridge of Shinto myth, best seen upside down through your own legs.
tours.longDescription:
A continuous corridor of some eight thousand salt-hardy Japanese black pines runs the full three and a half kilometres across Miyazu Bay, from Amanohashidate Station to the shrine on the far shore. Old and weathered, a few have grown into shapes distinctive enough to have earned their own names.

This is one of the Nihon Sankei, the three views grouped alongside Matsushima and Miyajima by the Confucian scholar Hayashi Gahō in a seventeenth-century text. The land itself is far older: Shinto mythology records the bar as the bridge the deity Izanagi descended from heaven, fallen while he slept into the bay below.

A packed dirt path runs its length — forty-five minutes on foot, fifteen by bicycle — past the Amanohashidate Shrine and the Isoshimizu spring, listed among Japan's finest waters since the Heian period. From the Kasamatsu viewpoint, seen upside down, the sandbar resolves into a single straight line.

stops.title: Amanohashidate | 天橋立
stops.caption: A pine-lined sandbar three and a half kilometres across Miyazu Bay — one of Japan's three great views, and Izanagi's fallen bridge from heaven.
stops.transcriptText:
Turn around, bend over, and look at the bay through your legs. From that position, the sandbar appears to float free of the water beneath it, rising into the sky like a bridge — which is precisely what the name means, and precisely what has been bringing people up to these viewpoints for over a thousand years.

The path begins at the southern end of the sandbar, a five-minute walk from Amanohashidate Station along the edge of the bay; you'll know you're in the right place when the trees begin — a continuous corridor of Japanese black pine extending the full three and a half kilometres across Miyazu Bay to the shrine on the far shore. The pines, roughly eight thousand of them, are salt-hardy and old, and some have grown into shapes distinctive enough to earn individual names.

This is one of Japan's three designated scenic views — Nihon Sankei — a designation that has been attached to Amanohashidate, Matsushima in Miyagi, and Miyajima in Hiroshima since a Confucian scholar named Hayashi Gahō first grouped them together in a seventeenth-century text. The sandbar itself is considerably older than any classification: Shinto mythology records it as the bridge the deity Izanagi descended from heaven, which fell while he slept and landed in Miyazu Bay as the landform you're looking at now.

Running lengthwise through the pines is a packed dirt path — forty-five minutes on foot, fifteen by bicycle — with white sand beaches along the eastern side in summer, and the Amanohashidate Shrine and a freshwater spring called Isoshimizu partway along, the spring having been listed among Japan's hundred finest waters since the Heian period.

The two hillside viewpoints — Amanohashidate View Land to the south and Kasamatsu Park across the bay to the north — give different perspectives on the sandbar's curve, and it's worth knowing that the matanozoki upside-down viewing tradition originated at Kasamatsu, where the bar appears as a single straight line from the northern angle.

tours.title: Gionmachi Minamigawa | 祇園町南側
tours.shortDescription: The south side of Gion — an Important Traditional Buildings Preservation District of ochaya and machiya, and the last functioning geisha district of what was once a far larger entertainment quarter.
tours.longDescription:
Gionmachi Minamigawa runs east from Shijo-dori toward the Shirakawa canal, one of the most intact historic streetscapes in Japan. Its wooden-latticed ochaya teahouses and machiya townhouses are protected as an Important Traditional Buildings Preservation District, so their facades cannot legally be substantially altered. Behind them, maiko and geiko are trained, apprenticed and employed.

The closed ochaya work by introduction only, guests brought by regular patrons who vouch for them. From the street one sees only the edges of an engagement — a geiko walking to an appointment, a maiko adjusting her obi at a gate. The stone-paved Ishibe Kōji, a private lane parallel to the east, quietens after the main thoroughfare.

In July the Gion Matsuri fills the street with floats maintained by neighbourhood associations for over a thousand years; the rest of the year it earns its own viewing, best in late-afternoon light.

stops.title: Gionmachi Minamigawa | 祇園町南側
stops.caption: The south side of Gion, running from Shijo-dori to the Shirakawa canal — a protected streetscape of ochaya and machiya, and Kyoto's last working geisha district.
stops.transcriptText:
In the late afternoon, the light falls along this street at an angle that makes the wooden lattice screens on the facade of every ochaya glow amber. At that hour, on a weekday, with the tourist numbers down and the evening not yet started, Hanamikoji is as close to what Gion looked like a hundred years ago as anything still standing in Japan.

Gionmachi Minamigawa — the south side of Gion — is one of the most intact preserved historic streetscapes in the country, running east from Shijo-dori toward the Shirakawa canal. The buildings lining it are traditional ochaya teahouses and machiya townhouses, designated as an Important Traditional Buildings Preservation District, which means that modifications to their exteriors are strictly regulated and that the character of the street cannot legally be substantially altered. Behind these facades, maiko and geiko are trained, apprenticed, and employed in the last functioning geisha district of what was once a much larger entertainment quarter spreading across this entire part of Kyoto.

The closed ochaya operate on an introduction-only basis — you cannot simply walk in. Guests are brought by regular patrons who vouch for them. What you can observe from the street is the beginning and end of engagements: a geiko emerging in full dress to walk to an appointment, a maiko pausing to adjust her obi before entering a gate. The stone-paved alleyway called Ishibe Kōji, running parallel a little to the east, is a private lane of small restaurants and tea houses that gets considerably quieter after the main thoroughfare.

The Gion Matsuri festival fills this street in July with processions of floats that have been maintained by local neighbourhood associations for over a thousand years. The rest of the year the street earns its own viewing.

tours.title: Hakusa Sonso Hashimoto Kansetsu Garden & Museum | 白沙村荘 橋本関雪記念館
tours.shortDescription: The garden and studio the nihonga painter Hashimoto Kansetsu shaped from rice paddy over thirty-two years — ten thousand square metres of pond, tea house, and gathered Buddhist stone, held below Mount Daimonji.
tours.longDescription:
Hashimoto Kansetsu lived and worked here, between this gate and the Higashiyama mountains, from 1916 until his death in 1945. On what had been rice paddy he built a central pond framing a view of Mount Daimonji, a painting studio lit by northern light off the water, a tea house, and a private Buddhist temple. Buddha statues and stone lanterns from the Heian, Kamakura, and Momoyama periods, gathered on his travels in China and Japan, sit throughout as found objects within a composed landscape.

Kansetsu painted in the nihonga tradition — mineral pigments on silk and paper — but his eye was formed equally by Chinese classical literature, the Impressionism he absorbed in Europe in 1921, and more than sixty trips to China. The museum shows his layered ink and colour work in rotation, alongside the East Asian antiques, screens, and ceramics he collected.

Designated a National Site of Scenic Beauty, it is one of the largest private artist residences in Japan, largely as he left it.

stops.title: Hakusa Sonso Hashimoto Kansetsu Garden & Museum | 白沙村荘 橋本関雪記念館
stops.caption: The garden and studio of nihonga painter Hashimoto Kansetsu, shaped from rice paddy over thirty-two years below Mount Daimonji, off the Philosopher's Path.
stops.transcriptText:
The cherry trees along the Philosopher's Path were planted by the person who built this garden. His name was Hashimoto Kansetsu, and he lived and worked here, between this gate and the Higashiyama mountains behind it, from nineteen sixteen until his death in nineteen forty-five.

The garden in front of you occupies approximately ten thousand square metres of land that was rice paddy when Kansetsu began buying and shaping it. Over thirty-two years he built a central pond with a view of Mount Daimonji, a large painting studio with northern light reflecting off the water, a tea house, a small private Buddhist temple, and several stone structures gathered during his travels in China and Japan — Buddha statues and stone lanterns from the Heian, Kamakura, and Momoyama periods, placed throughout the garden as found objects within a composed landscape. The garden holds the status of a designated National Site of Scenic Beauty. It is one of the largest private artist residences in Japan, and most of it survives as Kansetsu left it.

Kansetsu painted in the nihonga tradition — Japanese-style painting using mineral pigments on silk or paper — but his sensibility was formed equally by Chinese classical literature, Western Impressionism absorbed during a visit to Europe in nineteen twenty-one, and more than sixty trips to China, where he gathered materials, observed landscapes, and developed the layered, often melancholy ink and colour works the museum displays in rotating exhibitions. The secondary interest of the collection is his eye as a collector: the East Asian antiques, folding screens, and ceramics he accumulated during those journeys fill the museum rooms, and they constitute a serious collection in their own right.

Hōnen-in, the temple known for the moss-covered raked sand mounds flanking its thatched gate, is a five-minute walk south along the canal. This is one of the quieter stretches of the Philosopher's Path, and one of the better ones.

tours.title: Hosen-in | 宝泉院
tours.shortDescription: An Ohara temple whose ceiling is made from the blood-stained floorboards of Fushimi Castle, set above a framed garden built around a seven-hundred-year-old pine pruned into the shape of Mount Ōmi-Fuji.
tours.longDescription:
The boards overhead were once the floors of Fushimi Castle. After the twelve-day Siege of Fushimi in 1600, the garrison under Tokugawa Ieyasu's retainer Torii Mototada committed seppuku rather than surrender, and their blood soaked into the timber. Preserved and set into temple ceilings as a memorial, the stains are honoured by being walked over rather than trodden upon — one of several blood-ceiling temples in Kyoto.

Below, the tatami room frames a garden called Bankan-en, a view so beautiful it is hard to leave. Its central pine, roughly seven hundred years old, has been pruned across the centuries into the silhouette of Mount Ōmi-Fuji. In one corner of the veranda a bamboo pipe feeds a buried resonating chamber, the suikinkutsu, where dripping water rings underfoot.

Admission includes a bowl of matcha and a sweet, served at your place while you sit with all of it.

stops.title: Hosen-in | 宝泉院
stops.caption: An Ohara garden temple with a ceiling of Fushimi Castle's blood-stained floorboards, framing a seven-hundred-year-old pine and a hidden suikinkutsu water chamber.
stops.transcriptText:
Look up at the ceiling of the hall before you look at the garden.

The wooden boards above you were floorboards from Fushimi Castle, removed after the Siege of Fushimi in 1600 and installed as ceiling panels in several temples across Kyoto. At Fushimi Castle, when the forces of the warlord Ishida Mitsunari breached the defences after a twelve-day siege, the garrison — under Tokugawa Ieyasu's retainer Torii Mototada — committed seppuku rather than surrender. Their blood soaked into the wooden floors of the castle. The boards were preserved and placed in temple ceilings as a memorial, the custom being that a ceiling was sacred space and that the dead would be honoured by being walked over rather than trodden upon. This is one of several blood-ceiling temples in Kyoto, and the stains visible above you are those of men who died in a battle that determined the course of Japanese history.

Now look at the garden. The framed view from the tatami room — the garden visible through the space between the pillars, which act as a natural frame — is called Bankan-en, meaning a garden so beautiful it is hard to leave. The pine at the centre is approximately seven hundred years old and has been pruned over centuries into the shape of Mount Ōmi-Fuji. In the right corner of the veranda, a bamboo pipe leads to an underground resonating chamber called suikinkutsu: lean close and listen for the sound of water dripping into the buried vessel beneath your feet.

The admission fee includes a bowl of matcha and a small sweet, served at your place while you sit with all of this.

Sanzen-in, the great Ohara garden temple, is a fifteen-minute walk east from here and is the other essential stop in this valley.

tours.title: Ine no Funaya Houses | 伊根の舟屋
tours.shortDescription: A working fishing village of Edo-period boat-houses ringing a sheltered bay — more than two hundred funaya standing inches from the water, boats moored in their open ground floors, families living above.
tours.longDescription:
Ine sits on a narrow strip of land between mountain and bay, with almost no flat ground for a house, a boat shed and a yard in one place. The Edo-period solution was the funaya: a two-storey building set over the tidal zone, its ground floor open so a boat can be moored directly inside, its upper floor the family's living quarters, the forest slope behind left intact.

More than two hundred funaya stand in a continuous row around the bay's five kilometres of shoreline. The geometry that makes this possible is the small island of Aoshima at the bay's mouth, which deflects the worst of the Sea of Japan and keeps the water calm enough for tide-level boathouses. That same shelter once made Ine a port on the ancient trade route between China and the Kyoto court.

Since 2005 the village has been an Important Preservation District, and some funaya are now guesthouses — though this remains a working village, its garaged boats in daily use.

stops.title: Ine no Funaya Houses | 伊根の舟屋
stops.caption: A working village of Edo-period boat-houses ringing a sheltered bay, sheltered by Aoshima island — boats moored below, families living above.
stops.transcriptText:
The problem the people of Ine faced, in building a life on this narrow strip of land between the mountains and the bay, was that there was almost no flat ground — no room between the forest slope and the water's edge for a house, a boat shed, and a yard all in the same place. The solution arrived at during the Edo period was the funaya: a two-storey building set directly over the tidal zone, its ground floor open to the bay so a boat could be moored directly inside, its upper floor serving as the family's living quarters. The mountains behind were left intact.

The bay curves in front of you, and around its full perimeter — roughly five kilometres of shoreline — more than two hundred funaya stand in a continuous row, their facades inches from the water, the narrow lanes running between them and the foot of the hills. The arrangement looks almost theatrical from a distance, but this is a working fishing village, not a preserved museum site, and the boats moored in the ground-floor garages are in daily use.

The protected geometry of Ine Bay is what made this architecture possible: a small island called Aoshima sits at the bay's mouth and deflects the worst of the Sea of Japan's weather, keeping the water inside calm enough for low, tide-level boathouses to function without constant wave damage. That same sheltered quality made Ine a significant port on the ancient trade route between mainland China and the Kyoto court, a history that runs considerably deeper than the Edo-period buildings visible today.

Since two thousand and five, the village has been designated an Important Preservation District for Groups of Traditional Buildings, and some funaya have been converted into guesthouses — a visit of a single day never quite captures the scale of the thing as well as staying the night and seeing the bay at dawn.

Boat cruises leaving from the pier give a view of the funaya from the water that is difficult to appreciate from the narrow lane, and the fishermen who operate the smaller sea taxis are generally willing to explain as they go.

tours.title: Kawai Kanjiro's House | 河井寛次郎記念館
tours.shortDescription: The Kyoto townhouse and studio of potter Kawai Kanjirō, preserved as he left it — a founder of the Mingei movement who declined the country's highest honour on the principle that the work was its only measure.
tours.longDescription:
In 1964 the government offered Kawai Kanjirō the Order of Cultural Merit, the highest recognition for artists and scholars. He declined it, holding that a genuine craftsman had no business accepting official awards and that the work itself was the only measure that mattered.

He lived and worked here from 1937 until his death in 1966, and the house survives almost exactly as he left it: a substantial traditional townhouse of heavy beams and tatami, filled with his own ceramics and folk craft gathered from Japan, Korea, China, and Okinawa. Kawai was a central figure of the Mingei movement, founded with the critic Yanagi Sōetsu and the potter Hamada Shōji to recognise anonymous, functional handmade craft as art in its own right.

The nobori-gama climbing kiln he built and used stands intact in the garden. Throughout the house, his own designs sit undistinguished among the collected objects — an argument about who makes art, made without words.

stops.title: Kawai Kanjiro's House | 河井寛次郎記念館
stops.caption: The preserved Kyoto house, studio and climbing kiln of Mingei potter Kawai Kanjirō, who declined the Order of Cultural Merit in 1964.
stops.transcriptText:
In 1964, the Japanese government offered Kawai Kanjirō the Order of Cultural Merit — the country's highest recognition for artists and scholars. He declined it. His position was that a genuine craftsman had no business accepting official awards, and that the work itself was the only measure of what mattered. He was seventy-four. The refusal was consistent with the principles he had spent his life articulating.

The house and studio in front of you is where Kawai lived and worked from 1937 until his death in 1966. It is preserved almost exactly as he left it — a substantial traditional Kyoto townhouse with heavy wooden beams and tatami rooms filled with the objects of a long working life: his own ceramics alongside folk craft pieces he collected from across Japan, Korea, China, and the Okinawan islands. Kawai was one of the central figures of the Mingei movement, which he founded with the critic Yanagi Sōetsu and the potter Hamada Shōji — a campaign to recognise and preserve the tradition of anonymous, functional handmade craft as an art form in its own right, at a time when industrialisation was ending the conditions that had produced it.

The nobori-gama climbing kiln in the garden is the one he built and used throughout his career, still intact. The workshop beyond it contains his tools.

Walking through the house, the accumulation of objects — pots, wood carvings, old agricultural tools, pieces from weaving traditions, his own designs displayed without distinction from anything else — communicates a view about what art is and who makes it that is more persuasive than any essay on the subject.

The Kyoto National Museum is a fifteen-minute walk north, and contains several Mingei-related works in its folk craft collection.

tours.title: Keage Incline | 蹴上インクライン
tours.shortDescription: A 582-metre cable-hauled railway that carried canal boats over a 36-metre drop from 1891 — once the world's longest incline of its kind, now a cherry-lined walking path.
tours.longDescription:
The Keage Incline runs 582 metres downhill from the Keage Basin, where the Lake Biwa Canal enters Kyoto, to the Nanzenji Basin, dropping 36 metres. When it opened in 1891 it solved a break in the canal: the ground fell too steeply for boats to pass under their own power, so they were loaded onto wheeled trolleys and hauled up or lowered by cable, powered by the Keage hydroelectric station — the first public power station in Japan.

At its peak the system moved some 220,000 tonnes of cargo a year, then the longest incline railway of its kind in the world. Commercial shipping ceased in 1948 as railways made water transport uneconomical, and the incline has been a walking path since its 1977 restoration.

Ninety somei-yoshino cherry trees, planted after the restoration, line both sides; in early April the blossom canopy transforms the slope, though the engineering stays legible beneath. A restored cargo boat of sake barrels sits berthed at the upper end.

stops.title: Keage Incline | 蹴上インクライン
stops.caption: An 1891 cable-hauled railway that carried canal boats over a 36-metre drop between the Keage and Nanzenji basins, now a cherry-lined path.
stops.transcriptText:
The rails descend ahead of you at a steady angle, disappearing between the trees, and if you look along their length you'll see that they're not a decoration — the gauge is real, the sleepers are set at working intervals, and a restored cargo boat loaded with sake barrels sits berthed at the upper end, as if a delivery is still expected.

The tracks begin above the Keage Basin, at the upper end of the Lake Biwa Canal where it enters Kyoto from the east, and run five hundred and eighty-two metres downhill to the Nanzenji Basin, dropping thirty-six metres in elevation. When the incline opened in eighteen ninety-one, it solved a specific logistical problem: the canal that carried goods, water, and passengers between Lake Biwa in Shiga Prefecture and Kyoto had a break in continuity here — the ground dropped too steeply for boats to navigate under their own power, so they were loaded onto wheeled trolleys and hauled up or lowered down the slope by a cable system powered by the Keage hydroelectric station, the first public power station in Japan. At its peak, the system was moving around two hundred and twenty thousand tonnes of cargo annually, at the time the longest incline railway of its kind in the world.

Commercial shipping on the canal stopped in nineteen forty-eight as railways made water transport uneconomical, and the incline has been open as a walking path since its restoration in nineteen seventy-seven. The ninety cherry trees lining both sides — somei yoshino, planted after the restoration — are what most people come for in early April, when the blossom canopy over the tracks turns the whole slope into something rather different from a logistics heritage site, though the engineering remains just as legible underneath.

From the lower basin, a short walk through the grounds of Nanzenji Temple leads to the brick aqueduct known as the Suirokaku — part of the same canal system, carrying water across the temple precincts on a Roman-arch bridge completed two years before the incline opened.

tours.title: Kifune Shrine | 貴船神社
tours.shortDescription: A shrine to the water deity at the head of the Kibune valley, roughly thirteen hundred years old, where the imperial court once prayed for rain to come or to stop — and where fortunes read only when floated on water.
tours.longDescription:
Kifune Shrine sits at the head of the Kibune valley, reckoned by its priests to be about thirteen hundred years old, though the date of the first structure is not precisely known. The deity is Takaokami-no-kami, god of water, rain, and the flow of seasons. In dry years the imperial court prayed here for rain; in wet years, for the rain to stop. The shrine was the direct line of appeal in both directions.

That association is made legible in the mizuura mikuji, a paper fortune that appears blank until set on water, when characters written in wet-only ink emerge in your hands.

The approach from the valley road climbs between two rows of stone lanterns — roughly four hundred and fifty of them — converging at the main torii. Lit on festival evenings, the light on stone and surrounding cedar is genuinely particular. The main shrine stands at the top, with two sub-shrines further up the valley, linked by a forest path.

stops.title: Kifune Shrine | 貴船神社
stops.caption: A shrine to the water god at the head of the Kibune valley, its lantern-lined approach climbing to a main hall roughly thirteen centuries old.
