stops.transcriptText:
The paper fortune you can buy here only reveals its text when you float it on water. Hold it above the surface and it appears blank; set it on the water and the characters appear, written in an ink visible only when it is wet. The shrine is dedicated to a water deity, and the mizuura mikuji — the water fortune — is a piece of ritual theatre that makes the association between the deity and the element legible in your hands.

Kifune Shrine sits at the head of the Kibune valley, approximately a thousand three hundred years old by the reckoning of its priests, though the date of the first structure here is not precisely known. The deity enshrined is Takaokami-no-kami, the god of water, rain, and the flow of seasons — one of the deities who presides over agriculture, drought, and flood. In dry years, prayers for rain were offered here by the imperial court; in wet years, prayers for the rain to stop. The shrine was, in both directions, the direct line of appeal.

The approach path from the valley road is lined with stone lanterns on both sides, approximately four hundred and fifty of them, ascending the slope in two rows that converge at the main torii gate. On festival evenings they are lit, and the effect of lantern light on the stone and the surrounding cedar trees is, if you catch it at the right hour, genuinely particular.

The main shrine is at the top of the approach; two smaller sub-shrines extend further up the valley, connected by a walking path through the forest.

The valley below the shrine contains a string of kawadoko riverside restaurants, open in summer, where dining platforms are built over the fast-moving river.

tours.title: Kitano Tenman-gu | 北野天満宮
tours.shortDescription: The principal shrine to Sugawara no Michizane, deified as Tenjin the god of learning after his wrathful spirit was blamed for a wave of disasters — its plum gardens and monthly antique market both drawing crowds.
tours.longDescription:
By 947, Kyoto had endured years of lightning strikes, epidemic, and imperial deaths since the scholar-poet Sugawara no Michizane died in exile on Kyushu, stripped of his court positions by rivals. The court concluded his wrathful spirit was to blame, and resolved to deify him and build this shrine.

Kitano Tenman-gū is the most important of the several thousand shrines dedicated to Michizane, now revered as Tenjin, god of learning, scholarship, and calligraphy. Students come before examinations to leave votive plaques asking for success. The plum trees he had loved and written about in exile flower in February and early March, drawing some of the densest crowds of any plum garden in Japan.

On the twenty-fifth of each month, the Tenjin-ichi flea market fills the forecourt and surrounding streets with dealers in old textiles, ceramics, tools, and clothing until late afternoon.

stops.title: Kitano Tenman-gu | 北野天満宮
stops.caption: The foremost shrine to Sugawara no Michizane, deified as Tenjin the god of learning, with famed plum gardens and a monthly antique market on the twenty-fifth.
stops.transcriptText:
It's 947. A great scholar and poet named Sugawara no Michizane died in exile on the island of Kyushu eight years ago, having been stripped of his positions at court by political rivals — and since his death, Kyoto has been experiencing a sequence of disasters: lightning strikes, epidemic, the deaths of several members of the imperial family. The court decides that Michizane's spirit, now wrathful, is responsible for all of it. The solution is to deify him and build him a shrine.

This is Kitano Tenman-gū, the most important of the several thousand shrines across Japan dedicated to Sugawara no Michizane — now revered as Tenjin, the god of learning, scholarship, and calligraphy. Students visit before examinations to leave votive offerings and wooden plaques inscribed with requests for academic success. The plum trees — Michizane had loved plum blossoms specifically, and had composed poems about them in exile — flower in February and early March, and the shrine's plum garden is one of the most densely visited in Japan during that season.

On the twenty-fifth of every month, the shrine grounds host Tenjin-ichi, an antique and flea market that spreads across the entire forecourt and surrounding streets. On these days the population of the shrine is substantially different from a regular morning: dealers in old textiles, ceramics, tools, clothing, and anything that might plausibly be described as vintage occupy every available surface and the market runs until late afternoon.

The Tofu Cuisine restaurant within the shrine's precinct serves shōjin ryōri — Buddhist vegetarian cuisine — and is one of the better places in this part of the city to eat in the middle of a long day of temple-visiting.

tours.title: Kiyomizu-dera | 清水寺
tours.shortDescription: A cliffside temple whose nail-free wooden stage — 139 zelkova pillars, some fifteen metres tall — projects thirteen metres over the hillside toward central Kyoto, above a waterfall that has flowed since before the temple existed.
tours.longDescription:
Kiyomizu-dera, the Temple of Pure Water, was founded in 778 and takes its name from the Otowa waterfall below, which has flowed continuously from the base of the cliff since before the temple stood. The current main hall, with its celebrated stage, was built in 1633 under Tokugawa patronage and is a UNESCO World Heritage Site, among the most visited buildings in Japan.

The stage was assembled without a single nail — 139 zelkova pillars, some twelve to fifteen metres tall, locked together by interlocking joints in the kumiage technique to carry a platform extending thirteen metres beyond the cliff. It gave rise to the expression "to jump from the Kiyomizu stage," meaning a bold, irreversible risk; some 234 people are recorded attempting the leap between 1694 and 1864 before it was banned.

The Otowa waterfall splits into three streams — longevity, love and study — and custom holds that you drink from only one.

stops.title: Kiyomizu-dera | 清水寺
stops.caption: A cliffside temple founded in 778 whose nail-free zelkova stage juts thirteen metres over the hillside, above a waterfall said to grant three blessings.
stops.transcriptText:
The wooden stage projecting from the main hall was built without a single nail. One hundred and thirty-nine zelkova pillars, some of them twelve to fifteen metres tall, assembled entirely through interlocking joints — a technique of traditional Japanese carpentry called kumiage — support a platform that extends thirteen metres beyond the cliff face and provides a view across the cedar-covered hillside toward central Kyoto.

Kiyomizu-dera — the Temple of Pure Water — was founded in 778, its name derived from the Otowa waterfall below, which has been flowing continuously from the base of the cliff since before the temple existed. The current main hall, which includes the stage, was built in 1633 under the patronage of the Tokugawa shogunate. It is a UNESCO World Heritage Site and one of the most heavily visited buildings in Japan.

There is a Japanese expression: "to jump from the Kiyomizu stage" — which means to take a bold and irreversible risk. The idiom comes from an Edo-period belief that jumping from the stage and surviving would grant a wish. Around two hundred and thirty-four people are recorded to have attempted this between 1694 and 1864. Roughly eighty-five percent survived — the undergrowth at the base is dense — but the practice was eventually banned.

The Otowa waterfall at the base of the cliff is divided into three separate streams, each said to grant a different blessing: longevity, luck in love, and success in study. The custom is to drink from one only — drinking from all three is considered greedy.

The approach streets — Ninenzaka and Sannenzaka — are lined with shops and are genuine historic preservation zones, their stone-paved lanes and machiya townhouses protected and intact. The walk down from the temple through these streets is most of the reason to visit this part of Kyoto.

tours.title: Kochidani Amida-ji Temple | 古知谷 阿弥陀寺
tours.shortDescription: A quiet hill temple above Ohara, founded in 1609, holding in a cave behind its main hall the southernmost known self-mummified monk in Japan — and an eight-hundred-year-old maple that reddens the slope each November.
tours.longDescription:
Japan's mummified monks are almost all found in the cold northern mountains of Yamagata, where hard winters and low humidity allowed the extreme ascetic practice to preserve the body. The sokushinbutsu enshrined in a cave behind the main hall here, in the hills north of Kyoto, is considered the southernmost known example in the country.

Kōchidani Amida-ji was founded in 1609 by the priest Tanzei, who settled in this valley above Ohara after long travels and established a training hall for sutra chanting. In 1613, at sixty-three, he entered a stone cave and died there in an act of voluntary self-mummification; his preserved body remains in a sarcophagus, not open to view.

The approach climbs through forest, and the distance from Ohara keeps visitor numbers low. In November some three hundred maples turn on the slope, the oldest — a single tree estimated at eight hundred years and designated a natural monument — visible from the path well before the gate.

stops.title: Kochidani Amida-ji Temple | 古知谷 阿弥陀寺
stops.caption: A secluded 1609 temple above Ohara holding Japan's southernmost self-mummified monk, and an eight-hundred-year-old maple that fires the slope each November.
stops.transcriptText:
In most of Japan, the mummified monks are in the Tōhoku region — the cold northern mountains of Yamagata, where the extreme winters and low humidity allowed certain extreme practices of ascetic Buddhism to produce intact preservation. The mummified monk enshrined in a cave behind the main hall here, in the northern hills of Kyoto, is considered to be the southernmost known sokushinbutsu in Japan.

Kōchidani Amida-ji was founded in 1609 by a priest named Tanzei, who had travelled extensively before arriving at this valley above the Ohara district and deciding to settle. Tanzei established the temple as a training hall for sutra chanting, planted and tended the grounds, and in 1613 — four years after the temple opened — at the age of sixty-three, entered a stone cave and died there in an act of voluntary self-mummification, the ultimate expression of the Buddhist practice of sokushinbutsu. His preserved body remains in a sarcophagus in the cave, not open to public view but present in the structure of the site.

The approach path to the temple climbs through forest from the road below. The grounds are quiet in a way that more accessible temples rarely are — the distance from Ohara village, which requires either a long walk or a specific bus connection, keeps casual visitor numbers low. In November, approximately three hundred maple trees on the slope above and around the main hall turn, and the oldest among them — a single maple estimated at eight hundred years old, designated a natural monument by Kyoto City — produces a canopy of red and orange that is visible from the approach path well before you reach the gate.

The main Ohara temple complex, including Sanzen-in and Hōsen-in, is a forty-minute walk south through the forest path and valley road.

tours.title: Kōshō-ji Temple | 興聖寺
tours.shortDescription: The first Japanese monastery devoted to Sōtō Zen, founded in 1233 by Dōgen on the Uji River — reached by a maple avenue that turns famously red in November.
tours.longDescription:
Kōshō-ji was founded in 1233 by Dōgen Zenji, the monk who had returned from China with the teachings of Sōtō Zen and established here, on the banks of the Uji River, the first monastery in Japan devoted to that practice. It preceded his move north to Eiheiji, the great training monastery in Fukui he founded in 1244, which remains the school's headquarters.

Kōshō-ji was Dōgen's first attempt. The community he built trained in the disciplines he brought back from the Chinese monasteries: seated meditation, ritual, communal agricultural work, and the conviction that enlightenment was present in the act of practice itself. The main hall and hōjō garden are modest and well-proportioned, with a dry stone garden that reads quietly.

The approach is the drama: an avenue of Japanese maples running several hundred metres above the river, its canopy turning orange and deep red in mid-November. The stone bridge midway is where most photographs are taken. Byōdō-in lies a twenty-minute walk south.

stops.title: Kōshō-ji Temple | 興聖寺
stops.caption: The first Japanese monastery of Sōtō Zen, founded in 1233 by Dōgen on the Uji River, reached by a maple avenue that turns deep red in November.
stops.transcriptText:
The avenue leading to the main gate is lined on both sides by Japanese maples and extends for several hundred metres along the course of the Uji River above the road. In November — the peak is usually mid-month — the canopy above the path turns a sequence of orange, yellow, and deep red, the light coming through it at the angle that makes autumn maples in Kyoto look as if they are lit from within. The stone bridge over the stream midway along the avenue is where most of the photographs are taken.

Kōshō-ji was founded in 1233 by Dōgen Zenji, the monk who had returned from China with the teachings of Sōtō Zen and who established here, on the banks of the Uji River, the first monastery in Japan devoted to that practice. This was before his move north to what would become Eiheiji — the great training monastery in Fukui that Dōgen founded in 1244 and that remains the headquarters of the Sōtō school. Kōshō-ji was Dōgen's first attempt, and the community he built here trained in the disciplines that he had brought back from the Chinese monasteries: seated meditation, ritual, communal agricultural work, and the conviction that enlightenment was not a distant destination but present in the act of practice itself.

The main hall and the hōjō garden are modest and well-proportioned, with a dry stone garden that reads quietly after the drama of the avenue approach.

Byōdo-in — the Phoenix Hall, on the ten-yen coin — is a twenty-minute walk south along the river from here, and completing both in a single afternoon is a natural and unhurried way to spend the Uji valley.

tours.title: Kyoto International Conference Center (ICC Kyoto) | 国立京都国際会館
tours.shortDescription: Sachio Otani's 1966 conference centre, won in Japan's first national architecture competition — a Metabolist landmark of inclined trapezoidal geometry where, in 1997, the Kyoto Protocol was brokered in a corridor.
tours.longDescription:
In 1963, fresh from winning the 1964 Tokyo Olympics, Japan wanted a conference centre to answer the United Nations headquarters in New York. The country's first national architecture competition drew a hundred and ninety-five entries; the commission went to Sachio Otani, a former associate of Kenzo Tange only recently in his own practice.

Opened in 1966, the building sets every element — walls, columns, bridges, walkways — on a repeating trapezoidal grid inclined at twenty-two degrees, reading by turns as the Japanese character for "person" or for "enter." It is one of the last remaining examples of Metabolism in Japan, the movement that imagined buildings as living organisms of interchangeable parts.

Its largest moment came in 1997, hosting COP3. With talks stalled, the director moved them into the informal lobby spaces Otani had designed for exactly such gatherings, and the Kyoto Protocol was agreed in a corridor.

stops.title: Kyoto International Conference Center (ICC Kyoto) | 国立京都国際会館
stops.caption: Sachio Otani's 1966 Metabolist conference centre of inclined trapezoidal geometry, where the Kyoto Protocol was brokered in a corridor in 1997.
stops.transcriptText:
ICC KYOTO — KYOTO INTERNATIONAL CONFERENCE CENTER
Atlas Audio Tour

It's 1963. Japan has just won the right to host the 1964 Tokyo Olympics, and the government wants a building to match that ambition: a major international conference centre — nothing less than Japan's answer to the United Nations headquarters in New York. They hold the country's first national architecture competition, receive a hundred and ninety-five entries, and give the commission to Sachio Otani, a former associate of Kenzo Tange who has only recently set up his own practice.

The building in front of you is the result. Stand at the entrance and look back at the main facade: that geometry is not accidental. Every element — walls, columns, bridges, walkways — is built on a repeating trapezoidal grid, inclined at twenty-two degrees. The structure reads, depending on your angle, like a Japanese character for "person" or for "enter." Otani said both interpretations satisfied him equally.

Opened in 1966, this is one of the last remaining examples of Metabolism in Japan — the movement that imagined buildings as living organisms, made of interchangeable, expandable parts. Its main rival for that distinction, the Nakagin Capsule Tower in Tokyo, was demolished in 2022.

The building earned its largest moment in 1997, when it hosted COP3 — the United Nations Climate Change Conference. Negotiations between delegations had stalled; the deadline was approaching. Then the director of the conference moved discussions out of the formal meeting rooms and into the open lobby and waiting areas — the informal public spaces Otani had designed for exactly this kind of gathering. The Kyoto Protocol was agreed in a corridor. The document that set binding emissions targets for the first time in history was brokered in a building that its architect had designed specifically for conversations to happen in.

The Japanese garden on the lakeside, designed by Otani alongside the building, is accessible to visitors and offers a view of the whole structure from across Lake Takaragaike — the vantage point Otani used when he first visited the site and decided what kind of building this needed to be.

tours.title: Kyoto Wand | 京都湾処
tours.shortDescription: A 2022 machiya renovation named after wand, the term for a quiet river backwater — a corner cafe stripped back to timber by master carpenter Okimoto and returned to its Kyoto townhouse character.
tours.longDescription:
The Japanese term wand, written 湾処, describes a bay-shaped stretch of riverbank set apart from the main current, where the water flows slowly and nurtures its own small ecosystem. The architects chose the word deliberately, putting the concept into the building's name before they put it into the building.

KYOTOWAND is a machiya renovation completed in 2022, about five minutes from Kiyomizu Gojo Station. The townhouse had been altered so many times its original structure was almost unrecognisable, so the team worked with master carpenter Okimoto to dismantle it back to that structure, then repair, reinforce, and restore the traditional facade.

The result is a quiet corner cafe and rest space, one side onto a wider road, the other onto a cul-de-sac linking to the Kyoto Round Trail — a place to pause between arriving and leaving, in the slower current.

stops.title: Kyoto Wand | 京都湾処
stops.caption: A 2022 machiya renovation on a Kyoto corner lot, dismantled and rebuilt by master carpenter Okimoto into a quiet cafe named for a slow river backwater.
stops.transcriptText:
KYOTOWAND — 京都湾処
Atlas Audio Tour

There's a Japanese geographical term — wand, written 湾処 — for a specific kind of place: bay-shaped land on the bank of a river, separated from the main current, where the water flows gently and slowly, a little apart from everything, nurturing its own small ecosystem. The architects who named this building chose that word deliberately. The name is a description of what they wanted it to feel like.

The building in front of you is KYOTOWAND, a machiya renovation completed in 2022, about five minutes' walk from Kiyomizu Gojo Station. The machiya itself had been renovated several times over its lifetime, to the point where the original structure had become almost unrecognisable. For this project, the team worked with a master carpenter named Okimoto to dismantle the building back down to its existing structure, then repair and reinforce it while restoring the traditional Kyoto townhouse character of the facade.

The result is a quiet corner cafe and rest space on a corner lot — one side facing a wider road, one side onto a private cul-de-sac that connects eastward to the Kyoto Round Trail. The interior is stripped back to timber and exposed structure; the restored exterior brings the building back into relationship with the neighbouring machiya townscape it had drifted away from.

What the name points to is the intended function: a place that is neither origin nor destination, exactly — somewhere to pause between arriving and leaving, to sit for a while in the slower current. The architects put the concept in the building's name before they put it in the building itself.

The Kyoto Round Trail passes close to the east entrance. Kiyomizu-dera Temple, with the main pilgrimage approach, is a twenty-minute walk uphill from here.

tours.title: Nakamura Tokichi Byodo-in | 中村藤吉平等院店
tours.shortDescription: A tea house on the Uji River, set in a preserved former ryokan whose reception hall was named by Japan's first prime minister — matcha and gyokuro from the family's own cultivars, made edible as much as drinkable.
tours.longDescription:
The building on the Uji River bank was once the Kikuya Manpekiro, a celebrated ryokan whose main reception hall was named Geikakuro by Ito Hirobumi, Japan's first prime minister — a name it still carries outside. Nakamura Tokichi, founded in Uji in 1854, opened this branch in the old inn, a seven-minute walk from Byodoin Temple's Phoenix Hall. The interior is modernised, the old exterior preserved, and the riverside seats are among the better places in Uji to sit with tea.

Uji has produced green tea since the Kamakura period, when the Zen priest Eisai brought seeds from China and planted them here. Nakamura Tokichi grows matcha and gyokuro from its own cultivars — Kyo Midori and Uji Hikari — and the café turns them into dessert: a raw tea jelly served in a frozen bamboo tube with matcha ice cream and sweet red bean paste.

stops.title: Nakamura Tokichi Byodo-in | 中村藤吉平等院店
stops.caption: A tea house in a preserved Uji River ryokan near Byodoin, serving matcha and gyokuro from the Nakamura family's own cultivars.
stops.transcriptText:
The building on the Uji River bank was once a celebrated ryokan — the Kikuya Manpekiro — loved, according to its own records, by literary figures, artists, politicians, and business people. Japan's first prime minister, Ito Hirobumi, gave the main reception hall the name Geikakuro, the name it still carries on the building's exterior.

Nakamura Tokichi was founded in 1854 as a tea merchant in Uji, and this branch, opened in the original Kikuya Manpekiro building, sits on the Uji River approach to Byodoin Temple — the Phoenix Hall, on the ten-yen coin, a seven-minute walk from here. The interior has been modernised while the exterior of the old inn is preserved, and the building's position overlooking the river makes the riverside seats among the better places in Uji to sit with tea.

Uji has been producing green tea since the Kamakura period — the leaves introduced to Japan by the Zen priest Eisai, who brought seeds back from China and planted them here, establishing the cultivation methods still in use. Nakamura Tokichi's matcha and gyokuro are grown from varieties developed by the family's own research: Kyo Midori, a gyokuro cultivar, and Uji Hikari, which serves both tencha and gyokuro production. The desserts on the café menu — particularly the raw tea jelly, served in a frozen bamboo tube with matcha ice cream and sweet red bean paste — make these varieties edible rather than just drinkable.

Byodoin Temple and its museum, the Hoshokan, are a short walk south along the riverside path. The Nakamura Tokichi main store in Uji, a ten-minute walk north, houses a tearoom and stone-mill grinding experience.

tours.title: Ninenzaka | 二寧坂 (二年坂)
tours.shortDescription: A stone-paved Higashiyama lane of late-Edo machiya, its paving dating to 807 and its cables buried out of sight — a thousand-year pilgrimage route said to bring two years of misfortune to anyone who stumbles.
tours.longDescription:
A cautionary proverb holds that stumbling on these stones brings two years of misfortune. The paving dates to 807, which lends the warning a certain authority, and the stones are uneven enough to earn it.

The lane curves uphill for about a hundred and fifty metres — stone paving, wooden lattice facades, tiled roofs, and glimpses through gates into narrow inner gardens. It runs north from Sannenzaka through the preserved district of southern Higashiyama, linking the approach to Kiyomizudera with the lanes toward Kōdaiji and the Yasaka Pagoda, a route in constant use as pilgrimage and trade path for over a thousand years.

The houses are machiya in the strict sense — late Edo through Taishō, built tall rather than wide because frontage was taxed. The zone became one of Japan's first Important Preservation Districts in 1976. The painter Yumeji Takehisa lived nearby for about two years from 1917, marked by a small, easily missed stone.

stops.title: Ninenzaka | 二寧坂 (二年坂)
stops.caption: A preserved stone-paved Higashiyama lane of late-Edo machiya, dating to 807, on the thousand-year pilgrimage route between Kiyomizudera and Gion.
stops.transcriptText:
There is a tradition — most likely a cautionary proverb rather than actual prophecy — that stumbling on these stones brings two years of misfortune. The paving dates to 807, which gives the warning a certain authority, if only because the stones are uneven enough to earn it.

The lane curves ahead of you and slightly uphill, about a hundred and fifty metres from end to end: stone paving, wooden lattice facades, tiled roofs, and the occasional glimpse through gates into narrow inner gardens. Ninenzaka runs north from Sannenzaka as part of the preserved historic district of southern Higashiyama, connecting the approach to Kiyomizudera Temple with the lanes leading toward Kodaiji and the Yasaka Pagoda — a route that has been in constant use as a pilgrimage and trade path for more than a thousand years.

The houses along both sides are machiya in the strict sense — late Edo through Taisho period, with the cantilevered upper storeys and narrow frontages that were taxed by width, meaning buildings built tall rather than wide to minimise the levy. The entire zone was designated one of Japan's first Important Preservation Districts for Traditional Buildings in nineteen seventy-six, and the absence of overhead cables — relocated underground — is one of the few visible concessions to preservation effort rather than original character.

Yumeji Takehisa, the poet and painter of the Taisho era who helped define that period's aesthetic sensibility, spent about two years in the neighbourhood from nineteen seventeen, and a small stone marker records the approximate location of where he lived — easy to pass without noticing, which is perhaps fitting.

Ishibei Koji — the private stone-paved lane connecting Ninenzaka to Gion — begins a short walk further south and east, and is worth locating: narrower, quieter, and less photographed than the main slope, it's one of the more private corners of this part of the city.

tours.title: Nishiki Market | 錦市場
tours.shortDescription: Kyoto's Kitchen — a 400-metre covered arcade that has supplied the city with fish, pickles and produce for roughly four hundred years, made possible by cold, clean groundwater.
tours.longDescription:
Nishiki Market's covered arcade runs about 400 metres from Teramachi Street to Takakura Street, and has been Kyoto's central food supply for roughly four hundred years. Its nickname, Kyoto no Daidokoro — Kyoto's Kitchen — describes function: this was where households, temples and restaurants bought fish, vegetables, pickles, tofu and fresh produce.

Water is the reason it exists. The groundwater beneath this strip holds a steady fifteen to eighteen degrees Celsius year-round — stable, cold and clean. Called Nishiki no Mizu, it served as natural refrigeration, letting fresh fish from Lake Biwa and the coast survive the journey to market, each shop drawing on its own descendible well. The district was officially recognised as Kyoto's fish wholesale quarter in 1615.

Walking east to west, the stalls' specialisation shows: rare tsukemono pickles, live fish, yuba, fu, dried goods, and hand-crafted knives from Aritsugu, founded in 1560. Its roughly 130 shops are owned individually and change slowly. Standing to eat is accepted; walking while eating is not.

stops.title: Nishiki Market | 錦市場
stops.caption: A 400-metre covered arcade known as Kyoto's Kitchen, supplying the city's fish, pickles and produce for four centuries on cold, clean groundwater.
stops.transcriptText:
The covered arcade in front of you runs about four hundred metres from Teramachi Street in the east to Takakura Street in the west, and has been the central food supply point for Kyoto for roughly four hundred years. The market's nickname — Kyoto no Daidokoro, "Kyoto's Kitchen" — is a description of function rather than a compliment: this was where the city's households, temples, and restaurants came to buy fish, vegetables, pickles, tofu, and fresh produce, and where the city's water infrastructure made it possible.

That infrastructure is the reason the market exists at all. The groundwater beneath this particular strip of Kyoto maintains a temperature of between fifteen and eighteen degrees Celsius throughout the year — stable, cold, and clean. Called Nishiki no Mizu, "Nishiki Water," it served as natural refrigeration, allowing fresh fish from Lake Biwa and the coast to survive the journey from supplier to customer. Each shop had its own descendible well for the purpose. The market was officially recognised as Kyoto's fish wholesale district in 1615, though markets likely existed here in some form since the Heian period.

Walk from east to west and the specialisation of each stall becomes apparent: pickled vegetables of varieties found almost nowhere else — Kyoto's tsukemono tradition is specific and deep — alongside shops for live fish, yuba, fu, dried goods, and the hand-crafted knives from Aritsugu, founded in 1560. The market's approximately a hundred and thirty shops are owned individually and change slowly.

Eating while standing at a stall is accepted here. Eating while walking is not. The distinction is taken seriously and the sign at the entrance tells you so in several languages.

tours.title: Nittodo Kyoto Cafe | 日東堂 KYOTO COFFEE
tours.shortDescription: A converted two-storey machiya near Sannenzaka, part general store and part coffee stand, whose upstairs window frames the sixth-century Yasaka Pagoda almost as if it were a painting hung on the wall.
tours.longDescription:
This two-storey machiya, a traditional timber townhouse, has been converted into a shop and café. On the ground floor Nittodo works as a general store of life goods — ceramics, houseware, paper, small tools, stationery — made with attention to form as well as function. Behind the counter, KYOTO COFFEE serves a five-bean house blend of soft bitterness and a faint herbal note, made with milk from Kyoto's Clover Farm.

The second floor is the reason to linger: a low-ceilinged seating and occasional exhibition space where a window frames the Yasaka Pagoda — one of Kyoto's most recognisable structures, built in the sixth century and rebuilt repeatedly — at exactly the height and distance that makes the view feel like a painting already there when the building was converted.

It tends to be quieter upstairs than the busy lanes toward Sannenzaka below, particularly in the middle of the day.

stops.title: Nittodo Kyoto Cafe | 日東堂 KYOTO COFFEE
stops.caption: A converted machiya near Sannenzaka, general store and coffee stand, whose upstairs window frames the sixth-century Yasaka Pagoda like a painting.
stops.transcriptText:
The five-storey pagoda you can see from the upper floor of this building is the Yasaka Pagoda — one of the most recognisable structures in Kyoto, built in the sixth century, rebuilt repeatedly, and still standing in the narrow lane below. The view from the second-floor seating here, through a window that frames it almost perfectly, is not accidental.

The building in front of you is a two-storey machiya, a traditional timber townhouse that was converted and opened as a shop and café. On the ground floor, Nittodo operates as a general store selling life goods in the Japanese sense: ceramics, houseware, paper goods, small tools, stationery — things made with some attention to form as well as function. The coffee stand, KYOTO COFFEE, sits behind the counter on the same floor, serving a five-bean house blend with what the shop describes as soft bitterness and a faint herbal quality, made with milk from Kyoto's Clover Farm, a dairy holding a special certification for integrated production that most commercial dairies do not qualify for.

The second floor is the reason to linger. It functions as both a seating area and an occasional exhibition space, the ceiling low, the light warm, and the window to the Yasaka Pagoda positioned at exactly the height and distance that makes the view feel like a painting that was already there when the building was converted. It tends to be quieter up there than the street below, particularly in the middle of the day when the lanes approaching Sannenzaka are at their most busy.

Ishibei Kojii, the private stone-paved lane connecting the Sannenzaka area to the Gion district, begins a short walk downhill from here — one of the more peaceful corners of this heavily visited hillside, and easy to miss if you don't know to look for it.

tours.title: Noodle shop Rennosuke | 麺屋 練之助
tours.shortDescription: A small counter ramen shop in Fushimi working in Kyoto's lighter register — a soy-seasoned shoyu tare over house-made noodles, restraint offered as precision rather than timidity.
tours.longDescription:
The best ramen shops in Kyoto share a quality of restraint. The city's version of the dish leans lighter than the rich tonkotsu of Fukuoka or the dense miso of Sapporo — a clear or lightly opaque chicken or pork-bone stock, well-seasoned but not heavy, finished with a measure of tare adjusted for each bowl. At its best this restraint is not timidity but precision.

Rennosuke is a small shop in the Fushimi area of southern Kyoto, run from a narrow counter of a modest number of seats. Its broth draws on the shoyu tare tradition, a soy-seasoned stock that lets the quality of the base speak, and the noodles are made in-house to the density of this particular bowl.

The counter setup matters: a ticket machine at the entrance, a brief exchange about noodle firmness, the bowl assembled and placed in front of you — not theatre, simply how the thing is done.

stops.title: Noodle shop Rennosuke | 麺屋 練之助
stops.caption: A small counter ramen shop in Fushimi serving a soy-seasoned shoyu broth over house-made noodles, in Kyoto's characteristically restrained register.
stops.transcriptText:
There's a particular quality that the best ramen shops in Kyoto share: restraint. The city's version of the dish has historically leaned toward a lighter hand than the rich tonkotsu broths of Fukuoka or the dense miso bases of Sapporo — Kyoto ramen is typically a clear or lightly opaque chicken or pork bone stock, well-seasoned but not heavy, finished with a precise measure of tare that the cook adjusts individually for each bowl. At its best, this restraint is not timidity. It is precision.

Rennosuke is a small ramen shop in the Fushimi area of southern Kyoto, run from a narrow counter in a room that holds a modest number of seats. The approach to the broth here draws on the shoyu tare tradition — a soy-seasoned stock that allows the quality of the base to speak without masking it — and the noodles are made in-house, calibrated to the specific density of this particular bowl.

The counter setup is worth noting. Part of the experience of a ramen shop like this one is the proximity to the cook and the small ritual of the order — a ticket machine at the entrance, the brief exchange about noodle firmness, watching the bowl assembled and placed in front of you. This is not a form of theatre; it is simply how the thing is done, and doing it this way communicates something about the relationship between the person making the bowl and the person eating it.

Fushimi Inari Taisha and its ten-thousand-torii mountain path is a ten-minute walk from here — a reasonable way to justify appetite before arriving.

tours.title: Nunuka Life | ヌヌカ・ライフ
tours.shortDescription: A small, appointment-only ceramics shop in quiet Jōdo-ji near the Philosopher's Path — a curated collection of mostly contemporary Japanese work, chosen by point of view rather than market survey.
tours.longDescription:
Nunuka Life, in the Jōdo-ji neighbourhood of Sakyō Ward, functions less as a retail space than as a proposal — an argument in object form for a way of looking at things. It sits in the residential streets west of Ginkaku-ji, a short walk from the canal and the northern end of the Philosopher's Path. It is not large and keeps no conventional hours: opening days are posted on Instagram, and other visits are by appointment.

What you find, timed correctly, is a curated collection of ceramics — mostly Japanese, mostly contemporary, some historical — selected according to a point of view rather than a market survey. The makers tend to work in small quantities with care for material and form, and the shop acts as an editorial filter, showing the selection and letting the objects speak for themselves.

The surrounding neighbourhood, quieter than the Higashiyama slopes to the south, rewards slow, purposeful walking over any timed itinerary.

stops.title: Nunuka Life | ヌヌカ・ライフ
stops.caption: A small, appointment-only ceramics shop near the Philosopher's Path, showing mostly contemporary Japanese work chosen by a single editorial eye.
stops.transcriptText:
There's a particular kind of shop that functions less as a retail space than as a proposal — an argument in object form for a way of looking at things. Nunuka Life, in the Jōdo-ji neighbourhood of Sakyō Ward, is that kind of shop.

The address is in the residential streets west of Ginkaku-ji, a short walk from the canal and the northern end of the Philosopher's Path. The shop is not large, and it does not keep regular hours in the conventional sense — opening days are posted on Instagram, and visits on other days are by appointment. That arrangement is worth mentioning because it shapes the experience: this is not a destination you stumble into mid-morning. It requires a small amount of deliberate attention to find and access.

What you find, if you time it correctly, is a curated collection of ceramics — mostly Japanese, mostly contemporary, some historical, selected according to a point of view rather than a market survey. The makers whose work appears here tend to produce things in small quantities with considerable care for material and form, and Nunuka Life functions as a kind of editorial filter for that category: the owner picks, shows the selection in the space, and lets the objects speak for themselves without much apparatus around them.

The neighbourhood itself — Jōdo-ji, Sakyō Ward — is quieter and less visited than the Higashiyama slopes to the south, and the area around the Philosopher's Path canal has a density of small studios, galleries, and independently operated shops that rewards slow, purposeful walking more than a timed itinerary.

Ao Onigiri, the made-to-order rice ball counter, is on the same residential streets nearby — a reasonable pairing with a slow morning in this part of the city.

tours.title: Otagi Nenbutsuji | 愛宕念仏寺
tours.shortDescription: A hillside temple in far northwest Arashiyama where twelve hundred moss-covered stone rakan — each carved by an untrained amateur between 1981 and 1991 — sit laughing, drinking, and no two alike.
tours.longDescription:
The twelve hundred rakan covering this hillside were carved by amateurs — every one of them. Between 1981 and 1991, ordinary people arrived from across Japan with no experience of sculpture and carved their own stone disciple of the Buddha under the guidance of the priest and sculptor Kōchō Nishimura, each figure different, each reflecting the person who made it.

Nishimura had been appointed head of Otagi Nenbutsuji in 1955, a temple repeatedly destroyed over its history and most recently damaged by a typhoon in 1950. The original was founded in 766 by Empress Shōtoku elsewhere in Kyoto; reduced by flood, fire and war to three core structures, it was moved here in 1922. The Kamakura-period main hall is the oldest surviving element.

Walk through slowly. Some figures hold sake cups, one a cassette player, several are doubled over laughing — and the moss that now covers many has softened whatever edges the carving left.

stops.title: Otagi Nenbutsuji | 愛宕念仏寺
stops.caption: A northwest Arashiyama temple where twelve hundred moss-covered stone rakan, each carved by an untrained amateur from 1981 to 1991, sit laughing and drinking.
stops.transcriptText:
The figures surrounding you were carved by amateurs. Every one of them.

One thousand two hundred rakan — stone representations of the disciples of the historical Buddha — cover the hillside of this temple in the far northwest of Arashiyama, carved between 1981 and 1991 by people who came here with no prior experience of sculpture, under the guidance of a priest and sculptor named Kocho Nishimura. Nishimura had been appointed head of Otagi Nenbutsuji in 1955 — a temple that had suffered repeated destruction across its long history, most recently typhoon damage in 1950 — and his restoration project, when it finally took form, consisted of inviting ordinary people from across Japan to carve their own rakan under his instruction, each one different, each one reflecting the particular person who made it.

The original temple was founded in 766 by Empress Shotoku, in a different part of Kyoto entirely. Floods, fires, and civil war reduced it to its three core structures, which were moved here in 1922. The main hall, which dates to the Kamakura period, is the oldest surviving element. Everything else around it is recent — but recent in a particular way, made by hands that were learning as they worked.

Walk through slowly. Some figures hold sake cups. One carries what appears to be a cassette player. Several are doubled over laughing. No two expressions are the same, and the moss that now covers many of them has softened whatever edges the original carving left behind.

The Saga-Toriimoto preserved street, lined with traditional merchant buildings and tea houses, runs downhill from the temple gate toward the main Arashiyama district.

tours.title: POJ Studio | ポージェイ・スタジオ
tours.shortDescription: A Fushimi design studio, bookshop and exhibition space working across East Asian typography — named after Pe̍h-ōe-jī, a nineteenth-century romanisation of Taiwanese Hokkien.
tours.longDescription:
POJ Studio takes its name from Pe̍h-ōe-jī, a romanisation of Taiwanese Hokkien developed by Presbyterian missionaries in the nineteenth century to enable literacy in a spoken language that had no standard written form. The choice is deliberate, positioning the practice at the intersection of cultural preservation, typography, and the relationship between spoken and written identity.

Founded by Julius Hui and Tung-Yu Chen, the studio works across typeface design, book publishing and graphic design, focused on East Asian typographic systems — Chinese, Japanese, Korean and the space between them. Its editions and type releases have earned a following among designers who care about how Chinese characters are translated into digital and print type.

The space in the Fushimi district functions as studio, bookshop and occasional exhibition venue. The books and printed objects combine the studio's own work with pieces it considers important, selected by editorial judgment rather than commercial availability — many not findable outside specialist channels. The Fushimi Inari approach lies a short walk north.

stops.title: POJ Studio | ポージェイ・スタジオ
stops.caption: A Fushimi studio, bookshop and exhibition space working across East Asian typography, named after a nineteenth-century romanisation of Taiwanese Hokkien.
stops.transcriptText:
POJ Studio takes its name from a romanisation system for Taiwanese Hokkien — Pe̍h-ōe-jī, a transcription method developed by Presbyterian missionaries in Taiwan in the nineteenth century to enable literacy in a spoken language that had no standard written form. The choice of that name for a design studio in Kyoto is deliberate: it positions the practice at the intersection of cultural preservation, typography, and the relationship between spoken and written identity — which is precisely where much of their work sits.

The studio, founded by Julius Hui and Tung-Yu Chen, works across typeface design, book publishing, and graphic design with a focus on East Asian typographic systems — Chinese, Japanese, Korean, and the intersection between them. Their printed editions and type releases have earned a following among designers and typographers who care about the long, complex problem of how Chinese characters are translated into digital and print type systems.

The space in the Fushimi district functions as studio, bookshop, and occasional exhibition venue. The books and printed objects on the shelves here are a combination of their own publications and work they consider important from elsewhere — a selection made according to rigorous editorial judgment rather than commercial availability. Many items are not findable outside specialist channels.

If you have any interest in how type design navigates across languages, how editorial books are structured, or how a small studio sustains a very particular practice without compromising it, this is a useful place to spend time. The staff are willing to explain what they make and why.

The Fushimi Inari approach and the adjacent older streets of Fushimi are a short walk north — a neighbourhood worth moving through slowly on the way to or from the studio.

tours.title: Pharaoh | ファラオ
tours.shortDescription: Shin Takamatsu's 1984 corner block of concrete and steel — three chimneys, circular steel-framed windows, a facade the client asked to be built as armour against the noise and intrusion of the city.
tours.longDescription:
Pharaoh stands at a busy Kyoto intersection, completed in 1984 by Shin Takamatsu, a year after his ARK dental clinic in Fushimi-ku. The client had lived in a wooden house on the site for years and wanted it replaced with something that would shut the city out. Takamatsu answered with a corner block of concrete and steel: three chimneys rising above, circular steel-framed windows in the upper faces, and vertical and horizontal banding across the whole surface. "The entire architecture became a mask," he said.

The building houses a dental clinic and a residence, its exterior designed to respond to the city while the interior follows only the logic of the person within — two registers in one small structure.

Where ARK faced its railway line in direct dialogue, Pharaoh faces the street the way a sealed vault faces a crowd: heavy, repetitive, windows too high or small to see through. That indifference is the most unsettling thing about it.

stops.title: Pharaoh | ファラオ
stops.caption: Shin Takamatsu's 1984 corner block of concrete and steel, three chimneys and circular windows — a facade built as a mask against the city.
stops.transcriptText:
There's a curious thing about the building on this corner — the man who commissioned it asked for a facade that would defend him against the street.

Pharaoh stands at the intersection of two busy streets in Kyoto, completed in nineteen eighty-four by Shin Takamatsu, a year after ARK — his dental clinic in Fushimi-ku. The brief here was different. The client had lived in a wooden house on this site for many years and wanted it replaced with something that would shut the noise and intrusion of the city out. What Takamatsu built in response is a corner block of concrete and steel with three chimneys rising above it, circular steel-framed windows punctuating the upper faces, and vertical and horizontal concrete banding across the whole surface. Hermetic, closed, indifferent to what surrounds it. "The entire architecture became a mask," Takamatsu said. "The severe and extreme demands of the client permitted me to take unparalleled architectural risks."

The building houses a dental clinic and a residence. Takamatsu's own account of the project describes the exterior as designed to respond to the city while the interior follows only the logic of the person who lives there — two entirely separate registers in the same small structure. The scale is modest, the footprint compact; it sits in a city of wooden townhouses and temple compounds and does not attempt to negotiate with any of them.

Well, this is what separates Pharaoh from ARK: ARK was built in direct dialogue with its site — the locomotive facing the railway line. Pharaoh faces the street the way a sealed vault faces a crowd. Its surfaces are heavy and repetitive, the windows too high or too small to see through from pavement level. The building is rather less interested in you than you are in it, and that indifference is the most unsettling thing about it.

Nijo Castle is about fifteen minutes' walk north — the one building in this part of Kyoto that deployed defensive architecture for reasons similar to Pharaoh's, though with considerably more ceremony about it.

tours.title: Pontocho Alley | 先斗町
tours.shortDescription: A five-hundred-metre alley barely wide enough for two, built on reclaimed Kamo River sandbar in 1670 and grown into a geiko and maiko district of teahouses, some eighty restaurants, and white-plover lanterns.
tours.longDescription:
The alley runs five hundred metres due north, at its narrowest just wide enough for two people to pass. Wooden machiya facades line both sides, hung with paper lanterns bearing the district's white plover emblem, the sound of grilling drifting from interiors invisible from the street.

Pontocho began as a sandbar in the Kamo River; the embankment work that created the strip was finished in 1670. By the early eighteenth century it had become an entertainment district of teahouses and inns serving the Takase Canal boatmen, and gradually the geiko and maiko houses that define it now. Geisha were officially permitted here from 1859, and the Kamogawa Odori dance has been staged every May since 1872.

Around eighty restaurants form the visible surface today, but the ochaya teahouses still operate behind them, and in the early evening geiko and maiko move through the alley to their engagements.

stops.title: Pontocho Alley | 先斗町
stops.caption: A narrow five-hundred-metre alley on reclaimed Kamo River sandbar, a geiko and maiko district of teahouses and some eighty restaurants marked by white-plover lanterns.
stops.transcriptText:
The alley in front of you runs five hundred metres due north. It is, at its narrowest, just wide enough for two people to pass without turning sideways. On both sides: wooden machiya facades, paper lanterns bearing the white plover emblem of the district, and the sound of grilling from establishments whose interiors are invisible from the street.

Pontocho began as a sandbar in the Kamo River. The embankment work that created this strip of land was completed in 1670, and by the early eighteenth century it had become an entertainment district — teahouses, inns serving the boatmen who worked the Takase Canal, and gradually the geiko and maiko houses that give the district its present character. Official permission for geisha to operate here was granted in 1859. The Kamogawa Odori dance performance, first staged in 1872 as part of a Kyoto exhibition programme, has been performed here every May since.

The visible surface of Pontocho today is restaurants — around eighty of them, ranging from five-hundred-yen yakitori to kaiseki meals that cost considerably more and require the right introduction. But the ochaya teahouses are still operating behind the restaurant facades, and in the early evening, geiko and maiko move through the alley on their way to engagements. The white plover lanterns mark the authentic establishments; the alley's proportions, unchanged since the Edo period, make it impossible to miss the people who belong here from those who are passing through.

From May to September, the restaurants on the eastern side construct wooden platforms over the Kamo River, and that is probably the most pleasant way to spend an evening in this part of Kyoto.

Nishiki Market is a five-minute walk west. Gion, the larger geisha district, is directly across the river.

tours.title: Sannenzaka | 産寧坂 (三年坂)
tours.shortDescription: A short, much-photographed flagstone slope of wooden shopfronts and old ceramic roof tiles, linking the Kiyomizu-dera approach down to Gion — a Heian-era path preserved as a historic district.
tours.longDescription:
The stone steps of Sannenzaka are among the most photographed in Japan, for reasons not entirely obvious: no towering gate, no gilded pavilion, just a narrow flagstone path dropping through a preserved district of wooden shopfronts, stone walls and old ceramic roof tiles. The name means either "three-year slope" or "slope of safe delivery," and the path has been here since the Heian period.

It connects the Kiyomizu-dera approach to Gion and Ninenzaka below, and the whole stretch is a designated preservation district, its machiya facades regulated and maintained. The scale surprises: end to end is perhaps a three-minute walk. Its ceramics shops sell Kiyomizuyaki, the pottery tradition specific to this hillside, still fired by kilns in the area; the lacquerware and craft dealers on the side lanes carry work from workshops named in the city's production records for two hundred years.

Ishibei Koji, a private stone lane, runs east from the bottom toward Gion.

stops.title: Sannenzaka | 産寧坂 (三年坂)
stops.caption: A short, much-photographed Heian-era flagstone slope of preserved machiya and craft shops linking the Kiyomizu-dera approach down to Gion.
stops.transcriptText:
The stone steps descending in front of you are among the most photographed in Japan, and for reasons that are not entirely obvious. There is nothing spectacular here — no towering gate, no gilded pavilion — just a narrow flagstone path dropping through a preserved district of wooden shopfronts, stone walls, and old ceramic roof tiles, lined with shops selling Kyoto crafts, sweets, and ceramics.

Sannenzaka — the name means either "three-year slope" or "slope of safe delivery," depending on which etymology you follow — connects the Kiyomizudera approach to the Gion and Ninenzaka districts below. The entire stretch, along with Ninenzaka to the north and the streets running between them, is designated as a preservation district of historic buildings, which means that modifications to the facades are regulated and that the townhouses and machiya lining the path have been maintained in their original form. The path itself has been here since the Heian period.

What the photographs tend not to convey is the scale: this is a short walk, maybe three minutes end to end. What the photographs also tend not to convey is how the street functions. The ceramics shops on Sannenzaka sell Kiyomizuyaki — the pottery tradition specific to this hillside, developed over centuries by kilns that still operate in the area. The small lacquerware shops and craft dealers on the side lanes carry objects made by workshops whose names appear in the city's production records going back two hundred years.

Ishibei Koji — a stone-paved private lane connecting these streets to the Gion area — runs east from the bottom of Sannenzaka and is worth locating: it is one of the more private corners of this heavily visited hillside.

tours.title: Sanzen-in Temple | 三千院
tours.shortDescription: An eighth-century imperial temple in the Ohara valley, built around a thousand-year-old moss garden of layered green — its low hills studded with old maples and three small round-faced Jizō half-submerged among them.
tours.longDescription:
The lane to the gate climbs through the Ohara valley past stone walls and shops selling shibazuke, the purple-red pickle of red shiso and aubergine. Twenty kilometres north of central Kyoto, Ohara behaves like somewhere that made its peace with the distance long ago.

Sanzen-in was founded in the eighth century as a monzeki temple, headed by an imperial prince, and its Oujōjō-in garden has been cultivated for over a thousand years. It is a moss garden of considerable depth: low rounded hills of several layered species, studded with old maples and cedars, through which a narrow path descends. In rain, or just after, the green reaches a shade photographs cannot reliably convey.

About halfway through, three small stone Jizō carved in the Ohara style — small-bodied and round-faced — sit half submerged in the moss as if they had grown there. They are the temple's most recognisable image, though relatively recent; the garden around them is the older achievement.

stops.title: Sanzen-in Temple | 三千院
stops.caption: An eighth-century imperial temple in Ohara built around a thousand-year-old moss garden, its layered green studded with old maples and three small Jizō figures.
stops.transcriptText:
The path to the gate climbs through the Ohara valley on a narrow stone lane, past stone walls and small shops selling local pickles and shibazuke — the purple-red Kyoto pickle made from red shiso leaves and aubergine — and the atmosphere shifts noticeably from the city below. Ohara is twenty kilometres north of central Kyoto, and it behaves like somewhere that made its peace with the distance long ago.

Sanzen-in was founded in the eighth century as a monzeki temple — a temple headed by an imperial prince — and the garden at its centre has been cultivated for over a thousand years. The Oujojo-in garden is what you come for. It is a moss garden of considerable depth and quiet ambition: low, rounded moss hills studded with old maples and cedar trees, through which a narrow path descends. The moss itself is several species layered, and in rain or immediately after it, the density and colour of the surface reaches the shade of green that photographs cannot reliably convey.

Among the moss, about halfway through the garden, are three small stone figures of the Jizo bodhisattva — carved in a style associated with the craftsmen of Ohara, small-bodied and round-faced, half submerged in the moss as if they have been growing there as long as the trees. They have become the most recognisable image of this temple, though they are relatively recent; the garden around them is the older achievement.

Hosen-in, the temple known for its blood-stained ceiling from the Siege of Fushimi, is a fifteen-minute walk north through the valley — the two together make a complete afternoon in Ohara.

tours.title: Shirakawa Canal | 祇園白川
tours.shortDescription: A willow-hung canal along Shimbashi-dori, its banks lined with Edo-form machiya and ochaya — and once the source of the white sand raked across Kyoto's Zen rock gardens.
tours.longDescription:
For centuries the pale, fine gravel of Kyoto's Zen rock gardens was quarried from this river. Called Shirakawa-suna, the white river sand, it was collected from the upper reaches and spread across temple gardens across the city until extraction was restricted in the late 1950s — the river gave Kyoto's most contemplative spaces their particular colour.

The canal runs along the north side of Shimbashi-dori, a narrow stone-paved lane flanked by two-storey machiya and ochaya, their facades largely rebuilt after the great Gion fire of 1865 and kept in that Edo-period form since. Willows hang over the water and about forty cherry trees line the banks; the combination in early April is the most photographed scene in the district.

This stretch of Gion has been a centre of entertainment culture since the Heian period, developing into an officially sanctioned hanamachi where geiko and maiko still pass in the evenings. The small vermilion Tatsumi Daimyojin Shrine, dedicated to Benzaiten, stands beside the most photographed bridge.

stops.title: Shirakawa Canal | 祇園白川
stops.caption: A willow-hung Gion canal lined with Edo-form machiya and ochaya, once the source of the white sand raked across Kyoto's Zen rock gardens.
stops.transcriptText:
The gravel at the bottom of Kyoto's Zen rock gardens — the pale, fine-textured material that holds raked patterns so well — was for centuries quarried from this river. Called Shirakawa-suna, the white river sand, it was collected from the upper reaches of the Shirakawa and spread across temple gardens across the city, until restrictions on its extraction came into effect in the late 1950s and alternatives were sourced elsewhere. The river gave Kyoto's most contemplative spaces their particular colour and character.

The canal runs along the north side of Shimbashi-dori, which you're either standing on or approaching — a narrow stone-paved lane flanked by two-storey machiya townhouses and ochaya teahouses, the facades largely rebuilt after the great Gion fire of eighteen sixty-five and maintained in that Edo-period form since. Willow trees hang over the water, and about forty cherry trees line the banks — the combination in early April is the single most photographed scene in this district, though the canal earns its own quiet reputation in every other season, particularly in the early evening when the ochaya lanterns are lit.

This stretch of Gion, between the canal and Shijo-dori to the south, has been a centre of Kyoto's entertainment culture since the Heian period, developing through the Edo period as an officially sanctioned hanamachi — a flower district — where geiko and maiko still pass in the evenings on their way to engagements. The Tatsumi Daimyojin Shrine, a small vermilion shrine beside the most photographed of the canal's stone bridges, is one they visit frequently — dedicated to Benzaiten, the goddess of arts and water, which makes it a natural destination for practitioners of both.

The Shinbashi Preservation District — this street and its immediate surroundings — has been designated an Important Preservation District for Traditional Buildings; the late-evening walk, after the tourist footfall has subsided, gives the most accurate sense of how the street was designed to function.

tours.title: TOBI-EN | とび園
tours.shortDescription: A Uji tea business founded by a German resident, Tobias, working directly with local farmers — offering guided access to the shaded fields and hand-harvests behind the region's rounder, sweeter, first-harvest tea.
tours.longDescription:
The tea fields of Uji are recognisable before you understand them: long parallel rows of shrubs under taut shade covers of black fabric or bamboo reed, suspended to block direct sunlight in the final weeks before harvest. That shading is what makes Uji tea different — the plant produces more chlorophyll and L-theanine, the amino acid behind sweetness and umami, and fewer of the catechins that cause bitterness, giving a rounder, sweeter, more complex cup.

TOBI-EN takes its name from its founder, Tobias, joined with the character EN, meaning garden. It began as a way for a German resident of Uji to make genuinely good local tea available abroad, working directly with trusted farmers rather than through the distribution chains that dilute traceability. Guided tours reach fields accessible only with a knowledgeable guide, the shade structures, hand-harvest demonstrations, and the chain from leaf to powder.

The tea here is ichibancha — first harvest, specific cultivars and fields, bought in limited seasonal quantities.

stops.title: TOBI-EN | とび園
stops.caption: A Uji tea business founded by a German resident, offering guided access to the shaded fields and hand-harvests behind the region's first-harvest tea.
stops.transcriptText:
The tea fields of Uji are recognisable before you understand what you are looking at: long, low, parallel rows of densely planted shrubs under taut shade covers — black fabric or bamboo reed mat, suspended on frames above the growing tips to block direct sunlight in the final weeks before harvest. That shading is what makes Uji tea different. By blocking light, the plant produces more chlorophyll and L-theanine — the amino acid responsible for sweetness and umami — and less of the catechins that cause bitterness. The result is a tea that is rounder, sweeter, and more complex than the same plant grown in full sun.

TOBI-EN takes its name from its founder: Tobias — Tobi — combined with the Japanese character EN, meaning garden. The business began as a way for a German resident of Uji to make genuinely good local tea accessible to buyers outside Japan, working directly with trusted farmers in the city rather than through the multi-layered distribution chains that aggregate and dilute the traceability of most commercial Japanese tea. The guided tours offered through TOBI-EN take visitors into tea fields accessible only with a knowledgeable guide — into the shade structures, to the hand-harvest demonstrations, and through the tea processing chain from leaf to powder.

The tea available here represents the first harvest — ichibancha — from specific cultivars in specific fields, bought in limited quantities and available seasonally. This is the opposite of blended commodity tea, and the difference is measurable in the cup.

Byodoin Temple — the Phoenix Hall, on the ten-yen coin — is a short walk from the Uji riverside. The town of Uji itself, with its matcha shops, is worth a slower look than most visitors give it.

tours.title: Takase River | 高瀬川
tours.shortDescription: An eleven-kilometre canal dug between 1608 and 1611 at the expense of one merchant, Suminokura Ryoi, to give inland Kyoto a water route to Osaka — later the setting of Mori Ogai's story Takasebune.
tours.longDescription:
One man dug this canal at his own expense between 1608 and 1611, because Kyoto was an inland city with no reliable water route to Osaka. Suminokura Ryoi, a merchant who had made a fortune in the overseas trade with Vietnam, spent much of it on eleven kilometres of navigable waterway that transformed the city's economy for three hundred years.

The canal follows Kiyamachi Street, its water rarely more than thirty centimetres deep; the flat-bottomed takasebune boats built for that draft carried casks of Fushimi sake and timber. Nine funairi loading docks once punctuated the route at hundred-metre intervals, but only Ichi-no-Funairi survives intact, marked now by a replica cargo boat.

Mori Ogai set his 1916 story Takasebune here, in which a criminal bound for exile shows an inexplicable contentment — a meditation on desire and justice that became one of modern Japan's most anthologised works. The canal stopped carrying cargo in 1920.

stops.title: Takase River | 高瀬川
stops.caption: An eleven-kilometre canal dug 1608–1611 by merchant Suminokura Ryoi to link inland Kyoto to Osaka, later the setting of Mori Ogai's 1916 story Takasebune.
stops.transcriptText:
One man dug this canal, at his own expense, in the years between sixteen oh eight and sixteen eleven, because Kyoto was an inland city with no reliable water route to Osaka and no way to get building materials, sake, rice, and charcoal in and finished goods out efficiently. His name was Suminokura Ryoi — a Kyoto merchant who had made a fortune in the overseas trade with Vietnam and spent a substantial portion of it on civic infrastructure — and what he built was eleven kilometres of navigable waterway that transformed the economy of the city for three hundred years.

The canal follows Kiyamachi Street, running parallel to it on the right as you head south, and you're most likely standing somewhere along the stretch between Sanjo and Shijo where the street is best known today for its cafés and bars. The water is shallow — rarely more than thirty centimetres — and the flat-bottomed boats called takasebune that worked this route were built specifically for that draft, loaded with casks of Fushimi sake and timber, their boatmen calling out as they moved. Nine funairi — loading docks set at right angles to the canal — once punctuated this stretch at roughly hundred-metre intervals; only the first, Ichi-no-Funairi, survives intact, and a replica cargo boat is moored there to mark the site.

Mori Ogai, the Meiji-era novelist and army physician, used this canal as the setting for his nineteen sixteen short story Takasebune, in which a criminal being transported by boat to exile displays an inexplicable contentment — a meditation on desire, sufficiency, and justice that became one of the most anthologised stories in modern Japanese literature. The canal stopped carrying cargo in nineteen twenty, after the railways had made it redundant, but it has given Kiyamachi Street its particular character ever since.

Ichi-no-Funairi is a short walk north on the west bank, just south of Nijo-dori — the replica boat and the preserved dock are the most legible surviving evidence of what this waterway once was.

tours.title: Tetsugaku No Michi | 哲学の道
tours.shortDescription: A two-kilometre canal-side path beneath Higashiyama, its cherry trees first planted in 1921 — named for the Kyoto University philosophers said to have walked it while they thought.
tours.longDescription:
The canal beside the path carries water from Lake Biwa in Shiga Prefecture through Meiji-era mountain tunnels, built to supply Kyoto with water for industry, power and irrigation. This branch follows the Higashiyama foothills for roughly two kilometres, between Ginkaku-ji to the north and Nanzen-ji to the south.

The canal is the reason the cherry trees are here. The route was once an unmade track alongside an irrigation channel, until in 1921 the wife of the painter Hashimoto Kansetsu, who worked nearby at Hakusasonsō, planted the first three hundred cherry trees along it. The name came later, for two Kyoto University philosophers thought to have walked here in the 1910s and 1920s — Nishida Kitarō, working on what became the Kyoto School, and Hajime Tanabe. A stone bearing one of Nishida's poems is set into the western bank.

Several temples line the path, among them thatched-gated Hōnen-in and Eikan-dō Zenrin-ji, known for its autumn maples.

stops.title: Tetsugaku No Michi | 哲学の道
stops.caption: A two-kilometre canal-side path below Higashiyama, its 1921 cherry trees and its name owed to a painter's wife and two walking philosophers.
stops.transcriptText:
The canal beneath you brings water from Lake Biwa in Shiga Prefecture, through mountain tunnels built during the Meiji period to supply Kyoto with water for industry, power, and irrigation. This particular branch follows the contours of the Higashiyama foothills, and the path beside it runs for roughly two kilometres between Ginkaku-ji to the north and the neighbourhood of Nanzen-ji to the south.

The canal itself is the reason the cherry trees are here. The path was originally an unmade track alongside an irrigation channel, and it was only in nineteen twenty-one that the wife of painter Hashimoto Kansetsu — who was living and working at Hakusasonsō, a short walk east — planted the first three hundred cherry trees along its length. Those plantings, and the ones that followed, are why this stretch of canal looks the way it does in early April.

The path's name came later, and is associated with two philosophers who were teaching at Kyoto University and are thought to have walked this route regularly in the nineteen tens and nineteen twenties — Nishida Kitarō and Hajime Tanabe. Nishida in particular: he was working on what became known as the Kyoto School of philosophy, an attempt to synthesise Buddhist thought with Western philosophical traditions, and found that walking helped him think. A stone bearing one of his poems is set into the bank about halfway along, on the western side of the canal.

The path passes several temples along its length worth noting: Hōnen-in, with its thatched gate and raked sand mounds, accessible via a short lane off the east side; and Eikan-dō Zenrin-ji at the southern end, known for its autumn maples and its Amida statue, which turns its head over one shoulder to look back at those who follow.

tours.title: The Little Indigo Museum | ちいさな藍美術館
tours.shortDescription: An 1796 thatched headman's farmhouse deep in mountain Miyama, where the dyer Hiroyuki Shindo works natural indigo and shows a lifetime's collection of a single colour drawn from across the world.
tours.longDescription:
Getting here is the work: a thatched farmhouse in Miyama, a mountain village roughly two hours from central Kyoto, so those who arrive have come on purpose. The building dates to 1796, raised on higher ground for the Nakano family, who served for generations as village headman — a status marked by the seven pairs of chestnut chigi cross-beams at the gable peak, which ordinary Miyama farmhouses lacked.

In 1981 the Kyoto-born artist Hiroyuki Shindo bought the property and moved his family from the city, drawn by groundwater essential for the fermentation vats and by the rural abundance of wood ash. He studied indigo at the Kyoto City University of Arts in the late 1960s and has worked in natural indigo exclusively since.

The ground floor holds his working studio; the former thatch-storage attic above displays a rotating selection from some three hundred indigo objects — Indonesian ikat, Nigerian resist-dye, Edo work clothing, Chinese Miao costume — thousands of years of one colour.

stops.title: The Little Indigo Museum | ちいさな藍美術館
stops.caption: An 1796 thatched headman's house in mountain Miyama, home to dyer Hiroyuki Shindo's natural-indigo studio and a global collection of a single colour.
stops.transcriptText:
Getting here was the work. The thatched farmhouse in front of you is in Miyama, a village in the mountains of southern Kyoto Prefecture roughly two hours from central Kyoto by train and bus — which means the people who find themselves standing here did so on purpose.

The building dates to seventeen ninety-six, when it was constructed on raised ground for the Nakano family, who served as the village headman for generations. The seven pairs of chestnut cross-beams decorating the gable peak — called chigi — indicate the family's status; ordinary farmhouses in Miyama did not have them. In nineteen eighty-one, the Kyoto-born artist Hiroyuki Shindo bought the property and moved his family here from the city, drawn by the quality of the groundwater — essential for the fermentation vats used in natural indigo dyeing — and by the availability of wood ash, which the rural setting made possible in quantities that urban dyeing simply could not match.

Shindo studied indigo at the Kyoto City University of Arts in the late nineteen sixties and has worked in natural indigo exclusively since then. The ground floor of this building houses his workshop: the floor-set fermentation vats, tools, drying racks, and the evidence of an active practice rather than a preserved one. The second floor, occupying what was once the attic used for storing thatching grass, displays a rotating selection from Shindo's collection of around three hundred indigo objects gathered over a lifetime — Indonesian ikat, Nigerian resist-dyed cloth, Edo-period work clothing, Miao costumes from China, alongside his own work. The collection covers thousands of years of a single colour.

Kayabuki no Sato, the preserved thatched village surrounding this property, is worth a slow hour on its own — most of the surviving farmhouses are inhabited, and the scale of the place as a working village is unusual even by Japanese preservation standards.

tours.title: Tousuiro Kiyamachi Main Shop | 豆水楼 木屋町本店
tours.shortDescription: A tofu kaiseki restaurant in a preserved Taisho-era machiya off Kiyamachi-dori, built on Kyoto's exceptionally soft groundwater — its signature the barely-set oboro-dofu.
tours.longDescription:
Tousuiro — the name means "house of beans and water" — draws both ingredients and logic from one source: the exceptionally pure, soft groundwater beneath central Kyoto that has underpinned the city's tofu for as long as tofu has been made here. Tofu arrived from China via Nara, carried by Buddhist monks, and followed the imperial capital to Kyoto; the local water, consistent in temperature and unusually low in mineral content, gives a tofu of particular delicate texture.

The lantern marks the entrance down a narrow lane off Kiyamachi-dori. The building is a preserved machiya from the Taisho era — gate, tatami and wooden counter dating its setting to the early twentieth century, though the restaurant itself was founded in 1992.

The signature is oboro-dofu: freshly made, barely set, served cold on crushed ice, more liquid custard than block. Around it a multi-course kaiseki menu builds on yuba, namafu and seasonal vegetables. From May to September, riverside kawayuka seats extend over the Kamo River.

stops.title: Tousuiro Kiyamachi Main Shop | 豆水楼 木屋町本店
stops.caption: A tofu kaiseki restaurant in a preserved Taisho-era machiya off Kiyamachi-dori, built on Kyoto's soft groundwater, with kawayuka seating over the Kamo River.
stops.transcriptText:
Tousuiro — the name means "house of beans and water" — takes its ingredients and its logic from the same source: the exceptionally pure groundwater beneath central Kyoto, which has been the foundation of the city's tofu production for as long as tofu has been made here.

The lantern marks the entrance, down a narrow lane off Kiyamachi-dori, and the building behind it is a preserved machiya from the Taisho era — its gate, tatami floors, and wooden counter dating the restaurant's physical setting to the early decades of the twentieth century, though the restaurant itself was founded in nineteen ninety-two. Tofu culture arrived in Japan from China via Nara, carried by Buddhist monks for whom it provided both protein and a connection to monastic dietary practice, and when the imperial capital moved to Kyoto the monks followed and brought the tradition with them. Kyoto's water — underground springs at a consistent temperature year-round, unusually soft in mineral content — produces a tofu with a particular delicate texture that is specific to this place.

The signature preparation is oboro-dofu: freshly made, barely set, served cold in a lacquerware bowl on crushed ice — more liquid custard than firm block, made from one hundred percent domestic soybeans and water, and impossible to replicate with harder water elsewhere. Around it, a kaiseki menu built across multiple courses uses tofu and its derivatives — yuba (the fresh skin from heated soymilk), namafu (wheat gluten), and seasonal vegetables — to build a full meal in which every element is as carefully considered as the bean curd at its centre.
