From May through September, riverside seats extend over the Kamo River — the kawayuka tradition — making this one of Kyoto's more atmospheric places for summer dining.

The canal view is worth requesting when booking; the rooms that face the Takase River have the better of it, particularly in the evening when the lanterns on the lane outside are lit.

tours.title: Uji Kouchakan supported by Mlesna Tea | 宇治紅茶館 サポーテッド バイ ムレスナティー
tours.shortDescription: A black tea house on the Uji riverside — a deliberate choice in a matcha city — pouring Sri Lankan Mlesna teas blended for Japanese water, best known for a copper-griddled hotcake with a black-tea reduction sauce.
tours.longDescription:
Uji has produced shaded, ground matcha for over eight hundred years, and it appears in almost every café window along the approach to Byōdō-in. Uji Kouchakan is not that. It is a black tea house, which in a city so defined by green tea is a deliberate choice.

The shop sits on the Uji riverside, within walking distance of the Uji Bridge and the Phoenix Hall. The tea is Mlesna, a Sri Lankan brand founded in 1983 by tea taster Anselm Perera, whose company name reverses his own. It sources mainly from the Nuwara Eliya highlands, known for a light, bright, high-altitude character, and the blends here are made for Japanese water and palates — softer mineral content, different extraction than harder European water.

The café is known for its hotcake, a thick copper-plate griddled pancake with an original black-tea reduction sauce, served alongside a single-estate tea. On Wednesdays and Thursdays a Sri Lankan meal plate appears.

stops.title: Uji Kouchakan supported by Mlesna Tea | 宇治紅茶館 サポーテッド バイ ムレスナティー
stops.caption: A black tea house on the Uji riverside pouring Sri Lankan Mlesna blends, best known for a copper-griddled hotcake with black-tea reduction sauce.
stops.transcriptText:
Most visitors come to Uji for green tea — specifically for matcha, the shaded, ground variety that this city has been producing for over eight hundred years and that appears in some form in almost every café window along the approach to Byōdō-in. This is not that. Uji Kouchakan is a black tea house, which in a city so thoroughly defined by green tea constitutes a deliberate choice.

The shop is on the Uji riverside, in walking distance of the Uji Bridge and the approaches to the Phoenix Hall. Inside, the tea served is Mlesna — a Sri Lankan brand founded in nineteen eighty-three by a tea taster named Anselm Perera, whose company's name is his own name reversed. Mlesna sources primarily from the Nuwara Eliya growing region in the central highlands of Sri Lanka, known for a light, bright, high-altitude character that suits careful preparation, and the teas available here are blended specifically for Japanese water and Japanese palates — softer mineral content, different extraction behaviour than the harder water of most European brewing traditions.

The pairing that the café has become known for is the hotcake — a thick, copper-plate griddled pancake served with an original sauce made from black tea reduction alongside one of the single-estate teas. On Wednesdays and Thursdays a Sri Lankan meal plate is available, an unusual step outside either the Uji tea tradition or the standard Kyoto café register.

Byōdō-in's Phoenix Hall and its museum, the Hōshōkan, are a short walk along the riverside from here. The Ujigami Shrine, the oldest surviving Shinto shrine building in Japan, is across the river — the two form a complete afternoon in Uji for anyone with the time.

tours.title: Uji Station | 宇治駅
tours.shortDescription: The 1995 Keihan Uji Station by Hiroyuki Wakabayashi — an open, circular concrete vault with curving walls and wide light openings, likened to a stargate and awarded a Good Design prize in 1996.
tours.longDescription:
The concrete arch overhead does something a train station rarely bothers with: it asks to be looked at. This is Keihan Uji Station, redesigned in 1995 by Kyoto architect Hiroyuki Wakabayashi, who had earlier designed the body of the Rapi:t express between Osaka and Kansai International Airport. The terminus sits at the end of a short branch line; the original station opened here in 1913.

Wakabayashi's structure is open-concept and circular in plan, with concrete walls that curve overhead and large openings that admit changing angles of daylight. The effect is of spatial expansion — the station does not feel the size it is. One writer called it a stargate: a historic city announced not by a timber torii but by a concrete vault.

It won the Good Design Award in 1996 and was named among the best hundred stations in the Kinki region in 2000 — both unusual honours for an infrastructure building.

stops.title: Uji Station | 宇治駅
stops.caption: The 1995 Keihan Uji Station by Hiroyuki Wakabayashi — a circular concrete vault of curving walls and wide light openings, a Good Design Award winner in 1996.
stops.transcriptText:
UJI STATION (KEIHAN LINE) — UJI, KYOTO PREFECTURE
Atlas Audio Tour

Look up before you step inside. The concrete arch above you is doing something a train station does not usually bother to do: it is asking to be looked at.

This is Keihan Uji Station, and the building enclosing the platforms was redesigned in 1995 by a Kyoto architect named Hiroyuki Wakabayashi — who, in an earlier version of himself, had just finished designing the body of the Rapi:t express train between Osaka and Kansai International Airport. The station sits at the end of a short branch line and is the terminus for this stretch of the Keihan Railway. The original station opened here in 1913. What Wakabayashi built over it in 1995 is something considerably more difficult to categorise.

The structure is open-concept and circular in plan, with concrete walls that curve overhead and large wall openings that admit natural light in changing angles throughout the day. The effect is of spatial expansion — the station does not feel the size it is. One architectural writer described it as a stargate: the entrance to a historic city announced not by a timber torii but by a concrete vault. That description is either exactly right or rather over-serious, depending on your mood.

The station won the Good Design Award in 1996, in the category of architecture and environmental design. It was selected as one of the best hundred stations in the Kinki region in 2000. Both distinctions are a little unusual for an infrastructure building.

The platform is a five-minute walk from Byodoin Temple — the building depicted on the ten-yen coin, dating to 1053, and one of the oldest surviving examples of Heian-period architecture in Japan. The town of Uji is also the historical centre of Japanese matcha cultivation, which is worth knowing before you reach the main street and find yourself standing in front of twelve shops all selling variations on the same green powder.

tours.title: Unagiya Segawa | 鰻屋 瀬がわ
tours.shortDescription: An unagi restaurant in a renovated Kyoto townhouse off Shinmachi-dori, grilling live eel the Kansai way — split along the belly, no steaming, over charcoal — so the fish carries the dish rather than the sauce.
tours.longDescription:
The smell arrives before the building — binchotan charcoal and caramelising tare, the sweet-salt glaze applied and reapplied to freshwater eel as it grills. An alley off Shinmachi-dori leads through a wooden gate into a renovated Kyoto townhouse, where Segawa occupies private and semi-private rooms alongside counter seating.

Segawa uses the Kansai method: the eel is split along the belly rather than the back, skewered and grilled directly over high heat without the initial steaming of Tokyo-style preparation, so the skin crisps decisively and the flesh keeps its natural fat. Live eels are brought in and prepared in-house on the day, without artificial seasonings, so the flavour of the fish itself carries the dish.

The main formats are unaju — eel over rice in a lacquer box kept warm on a lava stone — and hitsumabushi, the Nagoya-style tub eaten across three courses: plain, then with spring onion and wasabi, then with dashi poured over as ochazuke.

stops.title: Unagiya Segawa | 鰻屋 瀬がわ
stops.caption: An unagi restaurant in a renovated townhouse off Shinmachi-dori, grilling live eel the Kansai way — belly-split, unsteamed, over charcoal.
stops.transcriptText:
The smell arrives before the building does — binchotan charcoal and caramelising tare, the sweet-salt glaze that is applied and reapplied to freshwater eel as it grills, producing the particular deep-brown crust that makes unagi as identifiable by scent as by sight.

The alley leads off Shinmachi-dori through an interior wooden gate into a renovated Kyoto townhouse, where the restaurant occupies private and semi-private rooms alongside open counter seating. Segawa uses the Kansai method of preparation: the eel is split along the belly rather than the back, skewered, and grilled directly over high heat without the initial steaming used in Tokyo-style preparation. The result is a skin that crisps more decisively, and flesh that retains the eel's natural fat and texture rather than softening it. Live eels are brought in and prepared in-house on the day of service, without artificial seasonings, so the flavour of the fish itself — its richness, the slight earthiness that separates fresh unagi from any substitute — carries the dish rather than the sauce alone.

The main formats are unaju — eel over rice in a lacquer box, kept warm by a lava stone — and hitsumabushi, the Nagoya-style serving in which a full eel is placed over rice in a small wooden tub and eaten across three progressively transformed courses: plain, then with condiments of spring onion and wasabi, then with dashi broth poured over the remainder and drunk as a kind of ochazuke. The third iteration of hitsumabushi, if you ask me, is the best argument for the format.

Eel populations in Japan have come under considerable pressure from overfishing, which is reflected in the price and the increasing care serious restaurants take with sourcing. It is worth noting that the higher price for domestically produced and carefully sourced eel is, here, the point.

tours.title: Uzumasa Kyoto Village | 太秦映画村
tours.shortDescription: A working open-air film set in western Kyoto — Japan's Hollywood, recreating an Edo townscape of merchant streets and samurai residences that has supplied period drama since the 1920s, with costumed actors and sword shows through the day.
tours.longDescription:
The street in front of you is a film set. The wooden shop facades, clay-roofed buildings and stone paths were all built to be filmed, and have been since the studio was established here in the 1920s. Uzumasa is Japan's Hollywood, the production centre for jidaigeki — period drama — for over a century.

Kyoto was chosen for the same reason it was the imperial capital for a thousand years: its historic fabric survived where Tokyo's and Osaka's did not, giving production companies the authentic Edo-period locations they needed. The Toei Uzumasa Eigamura is the open-air part of the complex, built to recreate an Edo townscape and opened to the public in 1975.

The experience is deliberately theatrical — costumed actors roam the streets, ninja shows and sword-fighting run through the day — and the merchant streets, samurai residences and teahouses are detailed enough to remain functional locations, appearing in hundreds of television dramas.

stops.title: Uzumasa Kyoto Village | 太秦映画村
stops.caption: A working open-air Edo-townscape film set in western Kyoto, Japan's Hollywood for period drama since the 1920s, opened to the public in 1975.
stops.transcriptText:
The street in front of you is a film set. The wooden shop facades, the clay-roofed buildings, the stone pathways — all of it was constructed to be filmed, and has been filmed continuously since the studio was established in this part of Kyoto in the 1920s. Uzumasa is Japan's Hollywood, and this district in the western part of the city has been the production centre for jidaigeki — period drama — for over a century.

Kyoto was chosen for this function for the same reason it was Japan's imperial capital for a thousand years: the city's historic fabric survived intact in ways that Tokyo and Osaka did not. Production companies working on period dramas needed authentic Edo-period locations, and here they found them. The Toei Uzumasa Eigamura — Kyoto Village — is the open-air portion of this studio complex, built specifically to recreate an Edo-period townscape for film and television and opened to the public in 1975.

The experience is deliberately theatrical. Actors in period costumes roam the streets; ninja shows and sword-fighting demonstrations are performed throughout the day; and the sets themselves — the narrow merchant streets, the samurai residences, the teahouses — are detailed enough to be functional as film locations and have been used as exactly that, appearing in hundreds of television dramas. Many of the jidaigeki series that have dominated Japanese Sunday evening television for decades have been shot on these streets.

The Koryuji Temple, home to Japan's oldest surviving wooden sculpture — the Miroku Bosatsu, carved in the seventh century — is a ten-minute walk east from the studio. The contrast in time periods is rather considerable.

tours.title: Waterway Pavilion | 水路閣
tours.shortDescription: A red-brick Roman-arcade aqueduct carrying the Lake Biwa Canal through Nanzenji's grounds since 1890 — designed by Tanaka Sakuro at twenty-two, still flowing today.
tours.longDescription:
When this aqueduct was proposed in 1888, the head abbot of Nanzenji objected: a Western-style red brick viaduct through the grounds of a thirteenth-century Zen temple was, in his view, no appropriate combination. He was overruled, and a hundred and thirty years later its arches — framing temple roofs, brick patinated with moss in the Higashiyama foothills — are among the most photographed structures in Kyoto.

The arcade rises nine metres high and runs ninety-three metres long, built of red brick and granite by the engineer Tanaka Sakuro, twenty-two years old and on his first major commission. It carries a branch of the Lake Biwa Canal, the Meiji-era waterway that brought freshwater across the mountains into Kyoto, and it still carries water today, feeding the city's agricultural and industrial supply as it has since 1890.

The canal was a civic rescue: after Kyoto lost capital status to Tokyo in 1869, it restored water, generated hydroelectric power at Keage, and enabled boat transport. You can walk along the top and follow the water still moving in the channel.

stops.title: Waterway Pavilion | 水路閣
stops.caption: A red-brick Roman-arcade aqueduct carrying the Lake Biwa Canal through Nanzenji's grounds since 1890, designed by Tanaka Sakuro at twenty-two.
stops.transcriptText:
When this aqueduct was proposed in eighteen eighty-eight, the head abbot of Nanzenji Temple objected: a Western-style red brick viaduct running through the grounds of a thirteenth-century Zen Buddhist temple was not, in his view, an appropriate combination. He was overruled, the aqueduct was built, and a hundred and thirty years later it has become one of the most photographed structures in Kyoto — its arches framing temple roofs, its brick patinated with age and moss, sitting in the cedar and maple of the Higashiyama foothills as if it had always been part of the composition.

The arches rise through the trees ahead of you — nine metres high, ninety-three metres long, built of red brick and granite in a Roman arcade form by the engineer Tanaka Sakuro, who was twenty-two years old when he designed it and was working on his first major commission. The aqueduct carries a branch of the Lake Biwa Canal, the Meiji-era waterway that brought freshwater from Japan's largest lake across the mountains into Kyoto — and it is still carrying water today, a trickle flowing continuously in the channel above the arches, supplying the city's agricultural and industrial water system as it has done since eighteen ninety.

The Lake Biwa Canal project was conceived as a civic rescue operation: Kyoto had lost its status as imperial capital to Tokyo in eighteen sixty-nine, and its economy was contracting. The canal restored water supply, generated hydroelectric power at the Keage station nearby, enabled boat transport, and eventually fed the Philosopher's Path canal and the Keage Incline — all parts of a single interconnected system of which this aqueduct is the most visible survivor.

You can walk along the top of the aqueduct, following the waterway as it continues north through the temple grounds — a short additional path that lets you see the water still moving in the channel, which is, if anything, more satisfying than viewing the arches from below.

tours.title: Wife & Husband | ワイフ・アンド・ハズバンド
tours.shortDescription: A coffee shop run by the married couple who named it — a converted oden stall near the Kitaoji Bridge that lends out baskets of house-roasted coffee for ninety-minute picnics on the Kamo riverbank.
tours.longDescription:
A real husband and wife run this coffee shop, and the name is also the explanation. Kyoichi and Ikumi Yoshida met, began roasting coffee together, and in 2015 converted an old oden stall near the Kitaoji Bridge into the space here — a coffee shop made by two people who happen to be married, which turns out to be a very specific kind of place.

The building is small: a wooden counter, a couple of tables, and a large collection of objects gathered over years of travel — antique furniture, baskets, chairs, hats, curiosities. Bicycles hang from the eaves. The baskets and stools at the front are not decoration but equipment for the shop's other offering, a riverside picnic service.

The Kamo River runs a short walk east, its long grassy bank used by Kyoto residents for picnics and evenings out. WIFE & HUSBAND will lend a basket — thermos of house-roasted coffee, ceramic cups, tablecloth, rusks — for a ninety-minute stretch on the grass.

stops.title: Wife & Husband | ワイフ・アンド・ハズバンド
stops.caption: A coffee shop run by the married couple who named it, a converted oden stall near Kitaoji Bridge lending picnic baskets for the Kamo riverbank.
stops.transcriptText:
A real-life husband and wife run this coffee shop. That is the name, and it is also the explanation: Kyoichi and Ikumi Yoshida met, began roasting coffee together, and in 2015 converted an old oden stall near the Kitaoji Bridge into the space in front of you. The name is both description and manifesto — a coffee shop made by two people who happen to be married, which turns out to be a very specific kind of place.

The building is small. It holds a wooden counter, a couple of tables, and a large collection of objects the owners have gathered over years of travel and looking: antique furniture, old baskets, chairs, hats, and miscellaneous things of interest whose purpose is not always immediately clear. Several bicycles hang from the eaves outside. These are not decorative: the baskets and stools hanging at the front serve as equipment for the shop's other offering, which is a riverside picnic service.

The Kamo River runs along the east side of Kitaoji Bridge, a short walk from here, and the riverbank is a long, flat grassy space that Kyoto residents use for picnics, cycling, and sitting in the evenings. WIFE & HUSBAND will lend you a basket containing a thermos of their house-roasted coffee, ceramic cups, a tablecloth, and rusks, for a ninety-minute stretch on the grass. This is the service the shop has become best known for, and it is one of the more pleasant ways to spend a slow morning in this part of the city.

The Kyoto Botanical Garden is a ten-minute walk south — Japan's oldest public botanical garden, established in 1924, and worth an hour of any afternoon.

tours.title: Yasaka Shrine | 八坂神社
tours.shortDescription: A shrine established in 656 at the foot of Higashiyama, dedicated to the storm god Susanoo and origin of the Gion Matsuri, begun in 869 to purify the capital during an epidemic.
tours.longDescription:
The vermilion west gate at the end of Shijō Street is not the main entrance — that faces south, toward Gion below. The west gate exists because Shijō Street does, and because this has been the point where the city meets the foothills, and where Gion meets the shrine that gave it its name, for over a thousand years.

Yasaka Shrine was established here in 656, at the base of the Higashiyama range. Its deity, Susanoo no Mikoto, the storm god associated with protection against pestilence, was pointedly relevant to a city periodically devastated by epidemic. The Gion Matsuri began in 869 as a purification ritual during one such outbreak and continues each July, its enormous yamaboko floats moving through the streets in one of Japan's largest processions.

Within the precinct, the honden and haiden are joined by a covered corridor in an arrangement called gion-zukuri, specific to this shrine, among stone paths lined with granite lanterns donated over the centuries.

stops.title: Yasaka Shrine | 八坂神社
stops.caption: A shrine founded in 656 to the storm god Susanoo, source of the Gion Matsuri begun in 869, its inner halls joined in the gion-zukuri style unique to it.
stops.transcriptText:
The west gate in front of you — the large vermilion structure at the end of Shijō Street — is not actually the main entrance. The main entrance to Yasaka Shrine faces south, toward the Gion district below. The west gate exists because Shijō Street exists, and because this has been the point where the city meets the foothills, and where Gion meets the shrine that gave it its name, for well over a thousand years.

Yasaka Shrine was established in this location in six fifty-six, on land at the base of the Higashiyama range that the city of Heian-kyō would later grow westward from. The deity enshrined — Susanoo no Mikoto, the Shinto god of storms, associated with protection against pestilence — was particularly relevant to a city that was periodically devastated by epidemic disease, and the shrine's most important annual event, the Gion Matsuri, began in eight sixty-nine as a ritual to purify the capital during one such epidemic. The festival continues each July, the procession of enormous decorated floats called yamaboko moving through the streets in one of the largest of its kind in Japan.

Within the main sanctuary precinct, behind the gate directly ahead, the honden and haiden — the inner and outer halls — are connected by a covered corridor in an arrangement called a gion-zukuri, specific to this shrine. The granite lanterns lining the stone paths inside are donated by merchants and townspeople across the centuries, and their density gives the precinct a particular quality in the early morning, before the day's visitors arrive.

Maruyama Park, Kyoto's most popular cherry blossom site, adjoins the shrine to the northeast — the two are effectively continuous at the boundary, and the weeping cherry at the park's centre is visible from the shrine grounds in spring.

tours.title: Yumekoubou | 夢工房
tours.shortDescription: A Gion gallery in a 150-year-old machiya, entered through a woven bamboo gate by Tanabe Chikuunsai IV — where Edo antiques, contemporary art and vintage furniture are arranged to converse across the centuries.
tours.longDescription:
The bamboo arch at the entrance stops you first: woven from natural bamboo into a rounded gate, installed in 2022 by the sculptor Tanabe Chikuunsai IV, it signals that the categories you arrived with may not apply. Behind it, on Nakano-chō in Gion's antiques quarter, stands a machiya over 150 years old, originally built as an inn and relocated here, its large pillars, exposed beams and mud walls largely preserved.

Yumekoubou opened in 2002, founded by two siblings trained at a family antique business in Shiga Prefecture. It began as a Japanese antiques shop and remains one in part, carrying Edo and Meiji ceramics, lacquerware, bronzes and screens. The founders later added contemporary art, then early-twentieth-century vintage furniture, on the principle that excellent work is excellent regardless of when it was made.

The result is a space where a centuries-old ceramic might sit beside a contemporary bamboo sculpture and a mid-century chair — the arrangement itself the point.

stops.title: Yumekoubou | 夢工房
stops.caption: A Gion gallery in a 150-year-old machiya, entered through a bamboo gate by Tanabe Chikuunsai IV, where antiques and contemporary art converse.
stops.transcriptText:
The bamboo arch at the entrance is the first thing that stops you. Woven from natural bamboo into a gently rounded gate — wide enough to pass through, low enough to make you notice — it was installed in twenty twenty-two by the sculptor Tanabe Chikuunsai IV, and it does something rather useful for a gallery: it signals, before you've seen a single object inside, that the categories you came in with might not apply here.

The building behind the gate, on Nakano-chō in the antiques quarter of Gion, is a machiya — a traditional townhouse with a history of over one hundred and fifty years, originally built as an inn and relocated to this site, with large original pillars, exposed beams, and mud walls that have been largely preserved. Yumekoubou opened here in two thousand and two, founded by two siblings who had trained at a family antique business in Shiga Prefecture, and the building's unhurried atmosphere makes immediate sense as the setting they chose — this is not a white-cube gallery, and the works inside are not displayed as if they need defending from the room.

The gallery began as a Japanese antiques shop, which it remains in part, carrying pieces from the Edo and Meiji periods: ceramics, lacquerware, bronzes, screens. Then, a few years into its history, the founders began adding contemporary art — not as a departure but as an extension of the same instinct, because, as they've put it, excellent work is excellent work regardless of when it was made. Vintage furniture from the early twentieth century arrived next, for the same reason. The result is a space where a centuries-old ceramic might sit beside a contemporary bamboo sculpture beside a mid-century chair, and the point of the arrangement is the conversation between them rather than any single object's category.

The bamboo gate outside is one of Tanabe Chikuunsai IV's ongoing explorations of bamboo as architectural form — a line of practice the Tanabe family has pursued across four generations since the Meiji period. The gallery handles works from all four generations, which makes this a good place to trace how a craft tradition holds and evolves across a century and a half.

tours.title: √2 Riverside Takao Kyoto | ルートツーリバーサイド 高雄
tours.shortDescription: A riverside dining room in the Takao valley, set on a traditional kawayuka platform above the Kiyotaki River — an old Japanese house serving soba, salads and coffee within earshot of the water.
tours.longDescription:
The mountains around Takao close in quickly once you leave the city, and this valley — where the Kiyotaki River cuts through cedar and maple about forty minutes northwest of central Kyoto — feels more remote than the transit time suggests. Autumn draws the crowds, the hillsides deep red and orange, but the cool river and dense shade reward a summer visit too.

A few steps down from the road, through a white noren curtain, the building opens onto a kawayuka — a riverside platform of tatami and retro glass-screen shoji overlooking the water from ground level, the river close enough to hear throughout.

√2 Riverside opened in October 2024 as the latest branch of the Kyoto ROOT2 group, whose other locations focus on organic salads and specialty coffee. Set in an old Japanese house, this branch extends the menu toward soba served with a generous seasonal arrangement of condiments — duck and spring onion, grated daikon, mitsuba, pickled ginger.

stops.title: √2 Riverside Takao Kyoto | ルートツーリバーサイド 高雄
stops.caption: A riverside dining room on a traditional kawayuka platform above the Kiyotaki River in the Takao valley, serving soba, salads and coffee since October 2024.
stops.transcriptText:
The mountains around Takao close in quickly once you leave the city — and this valley, where the Kiyotaki River cuts through cedar and maple forest about forty minutes northwest of central Kyoto, feels considerably more remote than the transit time suggests. Autumn is when this area is at its most visited, the hillsides running deep red and orange, but even in summer the cool river and dense shade make the journey worthwhile.

A few steps down from the road, through a white noren curtain, the building opens onto a kawayuka — a riverside platform of traditional Japanese dining, its tatami and retro glass-screen shoji overlooking the water from ground level. The river is close enough that you can hear it clearly, and on warmer days steps lead down to the bank itself.

√2 Riverside opened in October twenty twenty-four as the latest branch of the ROOT2 group, a Kyoto operator whose other locations focus on organic salads and specialty coffee. This branch, set in an old Japanese house of tatami floors and patterned glass, extends the menu toward soba noodles alongside the usual salads and lighter fare — a nod to the location's character as a destination rather than a neighbourhood stop. The soba here comes with a generous arrangement of condiments: duck and spring onion, grated daikon, mitsuba, pickled ginger, depending on the season, with the river audible throughout.

The wider Takao area has been a destination for Kyoto residents since the Heian period — the three mountain temples of Jingoji, Saimyoji, and Kozanji sit within walking distance, the last of which holds the twelve-and-thirteenth-century ink handscrolls known as Choju-Giga, widely considered among the earliest ancestors of manga, and listed as National Treasures.

The autumn foliage here typically peaks a week or two after the city centre — worth keeping in mind if you're timing a trip for colour.

tours.title: Ando Museum | アンドーミュージアム
tours.shortDescription: A century-old Honmura house, its timber shell preserved and a raw concrete interior slipped inside — Tadao Ando's museum to his own architecture.
tours.longDescription:
From the lane this looks like every other traditional house in Honmura — dark-stained timber, a low tiled roof, modest scale. The gap between what it appears to be and what it holds is entirely deliberate. When Ando rebuilt the 1913 house in 2013 he salvaged its original beams, columns, and tiles and reassembled them with traditional joinery, then built the interior wholly from the smooth pale concrete that is the signature of his career. Wood and concrete, past and present, warmth and austerity: those contrasts are the museum's explicit subject.

Inside, photographs, sketches, and models trace Ando's work across Naoshima and beyond — Benesse House, Chichu, the Church of the Light in Osaka, later commissions as far as Paris and Texas. The spaces are lit entirely by natural light from a skylight along the roof beam, and the sequence ends in an underground circular chamber barely three metres across, lit by a conical shaft from above.

The surrounding Honmura district is the hub of Naoshima's Art House Project, converting abandoned homes into installations since 1998.

stops.title: Ando Museum | アンドーミュージアム
stops.caption: A traditional Honmura house rebuilt by Tadao Ando in 2013 — salvaged timber outside, poured concrete within.
stops.transcriptText:
It's 1913, and a family in Honmura is building a house. They use local timber, traditional joinery, and tiled roofing in the style of every other house in this quarter of the village — because that is simply what houses look like here, and what they have looked like for centuries. A century later, Tadao Ando disassembled it, inserted a raw concrete structure inside the original shell, and opened it as a museum dedicated to his own architectural practice.

The building in front of you looks, from the outside, like every other traditional house on this lane — dark-stained timber, low-pitched tiled roof, modest scale. The gap between what it appears to be and what it contains is, of course, entirely deliberate. When Ando rebuilt the house in 2013, he salvaged the original beams, columns, and roof tiles and reassembled them using traditional joinery, while constructing the interior entirely from the smooth pale concrete that has become the signature material of his career. Wood and concrete, past and present, warmth and austerity — these contrasts are the explicit subject of the museum, and also of Ando's wider architectural philosophy.

Inside, photographs, sketches, and models trace Ando's projects across Naoshima and the wider world: the Benesse House Museum, the Chichu Art Museum, the Church of the Light in Osaka, and later commissions as far as Paris and Texas. The exhibition spaces are lit entirely by natural light channelled through a skylight running parallel to the roof beam, and the sequence concludes in an underground circular chamber, barely three metres across, lit by a conical shaft from above — a compressed version of the spatial drama Ando creates in his larger buildings.

The Honmura district around you is the hub of Naoshima's Art House Project, which has been transforming abandoned homes into art installations since 1998. James Turrell's Minamidera — a building that appears to be in total darkness but slowly reveals a blue twilight as your eyes adjust — is a short walk east along the same lane.

tours.title: Benesse House Museum | ベネッセハウス ミュージアム
tours.shortDescription: A museum you can sleep in — Tadao Ando's 1992 building half-buried in the headland, its galleries opening onto the Seto Inland Sea.
tours.longDescription:
When Benesse House opened in 1992 the idea behind it was that art should be part of how you live rather than a cultural obligation — which is why it is at once a museum and a hotel. On the promontory at the island's southern tip, Ando embedded more than half the structure into the hillside so it neither dominates the view nor competes with the sea and sky framed by every opening. The galleries flow between interior rooms and open terraces where works are placed to catch a particular light or angle of water.

The collection began with Soichiro Fukutake, the collector whose vision remade the island. Warhol hangs near Richard Long's mud paintings; George Segal's plaster figures occupy a stairwell; Hiroshi Sugimoto's seascapes vary in atmosphere in ways that only reveal themselves in front of them. Several works were made for this building and exist nowhere else.

Hotel guests have 24-hour access after closing — quieter, differently lit, and the better way to feel the building's bond with its hillside.

stops.title: Benesse House Museum | ベネッセハウス ミュージアム
stops.caption: Tadao Ando's 1992 museum-and-hotel, sunk into the headland above the Seto Inland Sea.
stops.transcriptText:
When the Benesse House Museum opened in 1992, the working idea behind it was that art should be experienced not as a cultural obligation but as part of how you live — which is why the building is simultaneously a museum and the hotel you might be sleeping in tonight.

On the promontory above the Seto Inland Sea, the building occupies the southernmost tip of the island, where Tadao Ando embedded more than half the structure into the hillside so that it would neither dominate the view nor compete with the sea and sky visible through every opening. The concrete is Ando's signature material — smooth, board-marked, precisely cast — and the galleries flow between internal rooms and open terraces where artworks are positioned to catch particular qualities of light or to draw the eye toward particular angles of the water.

The collection began with Soichiro Fukutake, the businessman and collector whose vision turned this island into what it is, and whose choices over three decades produced a body of work that moves between Western and Japanese contemporary art without obvious hierarchy. Warhol's silkscreens hang beside Richard Long's mud paintings; George Segal's plaster figures occupy a stairwell; Hiroshi Sugimoto's seascape photographs, each one technically identical in exposure time, vary in atmosphere to a degree that requires standing in front of them to understand. Several works were made specifically for this building and cannot be experienced elsewhere.

Hotel guests have 24-hour access to the museum after closing time, which is — if you can arrange it — the better way to see it: the galleries quieter, the light different, and the sense of the building's relationship to its hillside considerably easier to absorb without other people around. Advance booking is essential and sells out quickly during the Setouchi Triennale years.

tours.title: Benesse House Oval | ベネッセハウス オーバル
tours.shortDescription: Six rooms wrapped around a sky-open elliptical pool on a hilltop, reached only by cable car — Ando's place apart from the museum below.
tours.longDescription:
The cable car that brings you here is not merely transport; it is the transition the architecture requires. The Oval sits on a hilltop above the main Benesse House complex, joined to it only by a few minutes suspended over the tree canopy. This is the part meant for sleeping rather than looking at art, and Ando designed it as a place apart.

Six guest rooms wrap around an elliptical inner atrium holding a pool open to the sky — precise oval concrete walls, the water mirroring whatever weather is overhead. Each room opens from the atrium with floor-to-ceiling windows facing out over the Inland Sea. Moving between room and courtyard becomes a daily rhythm of compression and release that is, in its quiet way, the building's real subject. The artworks were chosen for their exact positions, not to decorate.

The view at night, from the window seat or looking up from the atrium, is the reason to stay rather than visit — and it cannot be had by arriving for the day.

stops.title: Benesse House Oval | ベネッセハウス オーバル
stops.caption: A hilltop annexe of six rooms around a sky-open oval pool, reached by cable car — by Tadao Ando.
stops.transcriptText:
The cable car that brought you here is not merely convenient transport — it is the transition the architecture requires. The Oval sits on a hilltop above the main Benesse House complex, connected to it only by that few minutes of suspended movement over the tree canopy, and that separation is deliberate: this is the part of the building meant for sleeping in rather than looking at art, and Tadao Ando designed it as a place apart from the museum below.

The cable car from Benesse House deposits you at the entrance to a building whose six guest rooms wrap around an elliptical inner atrium containing a pool, open to the sky. The geometry is Ando's — precise oval concrete walls, the water's surface acting as a mirror for whatever light and weather is overhead — and the rooms open from the atrium, each with floor-to-ceiling windows facing outward over the Seto Inland Sea. The ellipse contains the feeling of enclosure the atrium creates; the windows provide the expansion; and the transition between the two, when you move from your room into the interior courtyard, becomes a repeated daily experience of compression and release that is, in its modest way, the central subject of the whole building.

There are six rooms. Each has the same proportions, the same quality of concrete wall and minimal furniture, the same window seat above the sea. The artworks in the rooms were selected with the same intention as those in the museum below — not to decorate, but to be part of a specific space — and include photography and sculpture made or chosen for these exact positions.

The view at night, from the window seat or the atrium looking up at whatever the sky is doing over the Inland Sea, is the real reason to stay here rather than elsewhere on the island — and it cannot be replicated by arriving for the day.

tours.title: Benesse House Park | ベネッセハウス パーク
tours.shortDescription: Where the gallery leaks out into the landscape — lawns, clifftops, and paths scattered with sculpture above the sea.
tours.longDescription:
Naoshima can feel like a gallery that leaked out into the landscape, and the Park area of Benesse House is where that reading is most convincing. Art here doesn't wait inside rooms; it occupies lawns, clifftops, and the space between things. Richard Long's mud-painted stone circle, made on site; Niki de Saint Phalle's coloured figures; Karel Appel's frog and cat, here since 1990 and now weathered into the grass. The outdoor works are free to reach from the Tsutsuji-so bus stop, no ticket required, and the cliff path takes in several without demanding a decision about where to go next.

The Hiroshi Sugimoto Gallery: Time Corridors, opened in 2022, surveys Sugimoto's photography and sculpture — the seascapes, the Opticks polaroids — in a space he designed himself, with the Glass Tea House Mondrian on the terrace outside.

The cliff walk south to Kusama's polka-dotted Yellow Pumpkin at the pier takes about fifteen minutes and, in outdoor art per metre, is worth every one.

stops.title: Benesse House Park | ベネッセハウス パーク
stops.caption: Benesse's outdoor art park — sculpture across the lawns and clifftops, plus the Sugimoto gallery.
stops.transcriptText:
There's a way to look at Naoshima that makes it feel like a gallery that leaked out into the landscape — and the Park area of Benesse House is probably where that reading is most convincing. Art here doesn't wait inside rooms. It occupies lawns, clifftops, paths, and the space between things.

The lawns around you spread south and west toward the sea, and the outdoor works distributed across this terrain include sculpture, installation, and pieces that sit somewhere between the two — some monumental, some almost easy to walk past if you're not looking. Richard Long's mud-painted stone circle, made on site; Niki de Saint Phalle's large coloured figures; Karel Appel's frog and cat, which have been here since 1990 and have developed a relationship with the grass and weather around them that newer pieces are still working out. The outdoor works are free to access for anyone who arrives at the Tsutsuji-so bus stop, without a museum ticket, and the path along the cliff edge toward the southern pier takes in several of them without requiring a decision about where to go next.

The Hiroshi Sugimoto Gallery: Time Corridors, which opened in 2022 in the Park building, offers a comprehensive survey of Sugimoto's photography and sculpture across different periods — including his ongoing seascapes series and the polaroid Opticks works — in a space Sugimoto himself designed, with furniture by his New Material Research Laboratory. The Glass Tea House Mondrian, a Sugimoto work that has previously appeared in Venice and Paris before finding a permanent home here, is on the terrace outside.

The walk from the Park building south along the cliff path to the Yellow Pumpkin pier — Yayoi Kusama's iconic polka-dotted sculpture at the water's edge — takes about fifteen minutes and is, in terms of sheer outdoor art per metre, worth every one of them.

tours.title: Chichu Art Museum | 地中美術館
tours.shortDescription: A museum buried in a hillside, lit only by the sky — Monet, Turrell, and De Maria in rooms Ando designed around them.
tours.longDescription:
From ground level the entrance is just a concrete wall rising from a grassy hill: no facade, no signage at scale. Chichu means underground, and the building takes the word seriously — the whole structure is buried in a former salt-harvesting hillside, visible from above only as geometric cuts in the earth. The path from the ticket centre passes a garden of some 150 species drawn from Monet's garden at Giverny.

Inside there is no artificial light anywhere; each room changes with the hour, the season, and the weather over the skylights. Ando designed the spaces with the artists rather than after them. The Monet room holds five Water Lilies on white rounded walls, its floor laid in two-centimetre marble tiles to diffuse light upward. Walter De Maria's Time/Timeless/No Time sets a gilded granite sphere beneath an oculus. James Turrell's Open Sky is a roofless room in which the square of sky shifts across a sitting.

A sunset viewing programme for Open Sky runs most evenings — a separate experience, and the better of the two by most accounts.

stops.title: Chichu Art Museum | 地中美術館
stops.caption: An underground museum lit only by daylight, with Monet, Turrell, and De Maria — by Tadao Ando.
stops.transcriptText:
From ground level, the entrance is just a concrete wall rising out of a grassy hill — no facade, no signage at scale, almost nothing to indicate that a museum is here at all. Chichu means "underground," and the building takes the word seriously: the entire structure is buried in a hillside that was once used for salt harvesting, visible from above only as a pattern of geometric cuts and openings in the earth.

The path from the ticket centre follows a garden of roughly 150 plant species selected from Claude Monet's garden at Giverny — an introduction to one of the three artists inside, and to the museum's central argument about art and nature. Once inside, there is no artificial light anywhere, and the experience of each room changes continuously with the time of day, the season, and the weather passing across the skylights overhead. Ando designed the spaces in collaboration with the artists rather than after them, which means the architecture and the works are inseparable in a way that is unusual even by the standards of site-specific art.

The Monet room holds five large paintings from the Water Lilies series, its walls white and rounded, its floor laid in two-centimetre marble tiles to diffuse natural light upward — a room that Monet himself specified in his blueprints for the Grandes Décorations in Paris, and that Ando recreated here with those original specifications in mind. Walter De Maria's Time/Timeless/No Time places a gilded granite sphere in a stairwell beneath an oculus, the sphere's weight and the light's movement at deliberate tension with each other. James Turrell's Open Sky is a roofless room in which the square of sky above shifts, across a sitting, from one quality of light to another.

A sunset viewing programme for Turrell's Open Sky is available on most evenings — a separate experience from the daytime visit, and the better of the two according to most people who have done both.

tours.title: Lee Ufan Museum | 李禹煥美術館
tours.shortDescription: The world's first museum devoted to Lee Ufan — a semi-buried Ando building where stone rests against steel and the space between things carries the meaning.
tours.longDescription:
The first museum in the world dedicated to Lee Ufan opened here in 2010 — a surprising fact given his influence on post-war Japanese and Korean art. Born in Korea in 1936, Lee moved to Tokyo in 1956 to study philosophy and became the centre of Mono-ha, the movement that reduced the art object to minimal interventions — stone beside steel, rope beside glass — and asked the space between things to carry as much meaning as the things themselves.

A tall steel column stands in the gravel forecourt as you arrive: Lee's Porte vers l'infini (Gate to Infinity, 2019), a single vertical form as concise a statement of his philosophy as anything inside. The building, designed by Tadao Ando to follow the hillside, is semi-subterranean; a narrow passage opens into an atrium before descending to the galleries.

Inside, the work spans five decades — from the early Relatum pieces, where stone and steel simply rest together unfastened, to later canvases of a single deliberate brushstroke, the stroke and the silence around it weighted equally.

stops.title: Lee Ufan Museum | 李禹煥美術館
stops.caption: The first museum devoted to Lee Ufan — a semi-buried Tadao Ando building above the sea.
stops.transcriptText:
The first museum in the world dedicated to Lee Ufan's work opened here on Naoshima in 2010 — which is, given the scale of his influence on post-war Japanese and Korean contemporary art, a fact that invites a double take. Lee was born in Korea in 1936, moved to Tokyo in 1956 to study philosophy, and became the theoretical and artistic centre of Mono-ha — a movement of the late 1960s and 1970s that reduced the art object to minimal material interventions, placing stone next to steel, or rope next to glass, and asking the space between things to carry as much meaning as the things themselves.

A tall steel column stands in the open gravel forecourt as you arrive — Lee Ufan's Porte vers l'infini (Gate to Infinity, 2019), a single vertical form in a horizontal landscape, generating a tension between the weight of the ground and the openness of the sky that is as concise a statement of Lee's philosophy as anything inside the building. The building itself, designed by Tadao Ando to conform to the hillside's topography, is semi-subterranean, its entrance sequence moving through a narrow passageway that suddenly opens into an atrium before descending into the gallery rooms.

Inside, the works span five decades — from the early Relatum series of the 1970s, in which stone and steel plates simply rest against each other without fastening, to later paintings of single deliberate brushstrokes on large white canvas, in which the stroke and the silence around it carry equal weight. Everything in the museum is in conversation with Ando's concrete walls and the quality of light admitted through precisely positioned apertures, in keeping with Lee's description of his practice as "rather than making an object to be seen, offering a visual opportunity to encounter the world."

The walk between this museum and the Chichu Art Museum follows a hillside path with views over the Seto Inland Sea — a fitting transition between two buildings that both insist, in different registers, on the relationship between art, architecture, and landscape.

tours.title: Naoshima New Museum of Art | 直島新美術館
tours.shortDescription: Ando's tenth Naoshima building, opened 2025 — a black-plastered museum descending underground, devoted to Asian contemporary art.
tours.longDescription:
Tadao Ando's tenth building on Naoshima opened in spring 2025, thirty-seven years after his first work on the island — ten commissions from one client over four decades, a relationship with few parallels in contemporary architecture. The hilltop entrance looks north over the water toward Teshima, and the ground-floor cafe extends that panorama across an open terrace.

Then the building goes down: three floors, two of them subterranean, reached by a staircase descending through a skylit atrium whose walls close in before releasing into a cavernous lower gallery. The exterior breaks from Ando's earlier white concrete — black plaster evoking the charred-cedar yakisugi of island houses, with pebble walls echoing Honmura's stone fencing.

The collection is defined by a decision: this is the museum for Asian contemporary art, a complement to the Western-leaning holdings of Benesse House and Chichu. The inaugural shows include Cai Guo-Qiang's Head On — ninety-nine wolves leaping through a two-storey gallery — alongside artists from the Philippines, Indonesia, Japan, and Korea.

stops.title: Naoshima New Museum of Art | 直島新美術館
stops.caption: Tadao Ando's tenth Naoshima building (2025) — black-plastered, descending underground, for Asian contemporary art.
stops.transcriptText:
Tadao Ando's tenth building on Naoshima opened in spring 2025 — thirty-seven years after his first work on the island, a summer camp in 1989. Ten commissions from a single client over four decades, on one small island in the Seto Inland Sea, is a relationship without many parallels in contemporary architecture.

The hilltop site gives the entrance terrace an immediate view north over the water toward Teshima island, and the café on the ground floor extends that panorama across an open terrace — a deliberate contrast to the enclosed underground galleries below. The building goes down: three floors, two of them subterranean, connected by a staircase that descends through a skylit atrium whose walls close in as you go lower, then release into a cavernous lower gallery at the bottom. The exterior, distinctly different from the white concrete of Ando's earlier Naoshima buildings, uses black plaster evoking the yakisugi — charred cedar — technique used on traditional island houses, with pebble walls that echo the stone fencing of the Honmura district nearby.

The collection here is defined by a decision: this is the museum for Asian contemporary art, a complement to the Western-dominated holdings of the Benesse House Museum and Chichu. The inaugural exhibitions include Cai Guo-Qiang's Head On — ninety-nine wolves in formation, leaping through a two-storey gallery — alongside works by artists from the Philippines, Indonesia, Japan, and Korea. The shift reflects Soichiro Fukutake's stated conviction that Japanese cultural identity needs to be understood as part of Asia, not apart from it, and the programming is intended to evolve rather than settle.

The Honmura district below the hill, reached on foot via a staircase path, has been the base of the Art House Project since 1998 — old houses converted into art installations, still embedded in the village where people actually live.

tours.title: Naoshima Pavilion | 直島パヴィリオン
tours.shortDescription: A white mesh polyhedron at the harbour's edge, designed by Sou Fujimoto in 2017 to be the twenty-ninth island of Naoshima.
tours.longDescription:
What you see from the ferry dock — a white, irregular polyhedron somewhere between a geodesic dome and a crumpled sheet of paper — was designed by Sou Fujimoto in 2017 with a deliberately odd ambition: to be the twenty-ninth island of Naoshima. His idea was that the town is made of twenty-eight islands, and that this would add one more; not a building in the conventional sense but a spatial condition.

Built from white-painted stainless steel in a framework where no two faces share an angle, it stands seven metres tall and open enough that wind passes through while the mesh diffuses light into shifting shadow. You can walk inside and climb across the irregular interior, which Fujimoto shaped for sitting, resting, and looking out — a space neither indoor nor outdoor, neither sculpture nor architecture, and more comfortable than that sounds. At night, internal lighting turns the mesh luminous against the dark water — a lantern rather than a stone.

A three-minute walk leads to the I Love Yu bathhouse and Kusama's Red Pumpkin.

stops.title: Naoshima Pavilion | 直島パヴィリオン
stops.caption: Sou Fujimoto's 2017 white mesh pavilion at the harbour — conceived as Naoshima's twenty-ninth island.
stops.transcriptText:
What you can see from the ferry dock — the white, irregular polyhedron resting at the water's edge, somewhere between a geodesic dome and a crumpled piece of paper — was designed by architect Sou Fujimoto in 2017 with a deliberately odd ambition: to be the twenty-ninth island of Naoshima.

The white mesh structure near the harbour entrance is built from white-painted stainless steel in a framework that is irregular rather than geometrically predictable — no two faces the same angle, the whole thing seven metres tall and open enough that wind passes through freely while the mesh diffuses light and creates shifting patterns of shadow inside. Fujimoto's concept, as he described it, was that Naoshima is a town of twenty-eight islands, and that this structure would add one more — not a building in the conventional sense, but a spatial condition: enclosed enough to feel like somewhere, open enough to remain part of the sea and sky around it.

You can walk inside and climb across the irregular interior topography, which Fujimoto designed to offer different levels and angles for sitting, resting, and looking out. The effect is of a space that is neither indoor nor outdoor, neither sculpture nor architecture, in a way that turns out to be more comfortable than the description suggests. At night, internal lighting makes the mesh luminous against the dark water, and the structure becomes a different object entirely — a lantern rather than a stone, warm against the harbour rather than white in the daylight.

A three-minute walk from here along the harbour leads to the I Love Yu bathhouse — Shinro Ohtake's functioning art sento — and Yayoi Kusama's Red Pumpkin, two works that offer a very different register of public art from the quiet minimalism of Fujimoto's pavilion, but belong to the same island-wide conversation.

tours.title: Naoshima Public Bath "I♥湯" | 直島銭湯「I♥湯」
tours.shortDescription: A functioning public bath that is also an artwork — Shinro Ohtake's riotous collage sento near Miyanoura Port, where the name is a pun on hot water.
tours.longDescription:
This is a working public bath — admission six hundred and sixty yen, towels for sale, soap and shampoo provided — and you are meant to use it, not merely photograph it. The building is the work of artist Shinro Ohtake, who in 2009 converted a former structure near Miyanoura Port into an official sento that is, in every visual detail, an artwork.

The exterior reads as a riot of collage: fragments of other buildings grafted on, tiles, pipes, signage, a vintage Coca-Cola machine, architectural elements from many periods welded into a surface that is aggressively energetic yet coherent. Ohtake has always worked this way — accumulation as composition, chaos as a deliberate strategy. Inside, a large ceramic elephant presides over the wall dividing the men's and women's baths; the ceiling is painted, the mosaic walls shift between figure and abstraction — and yet the baths work perfectly and the water is hot.

Yu means hot water. The name is a pun, and also a statement of intent: this is art you can get into.

stops.title: Naoshima Public Bath "I♥湯" | 直島銭湯「I♥湯」
stops.caption: Shinro Ohtake's 2009 art-sento near Miyanoura Port — a functioning bath built as a riot of collage.
stops.transcriptText:
This is a functioning public bath. The admission fee is six hundred and sixty yen, towels are available to purchase, soap and shampoo are provided, and you are expected to use it — not merely to photograph it.

The building you're facing is the work of artist Shinro Ohtake, who in 2009 converted a former building near Miyanoura Port into what is officially a sento — a Japanese communal bathhouse — but is also, in every visual and sensory detail, an artwork. The exterior reads as a riot of collage: entire fragments of other structures have been grafted onto the original building, with tiles, pipes, signage, a vintage Coca-Cola machine, and architectural elements from various periods welded into a surface that is aggressively energetic without being incoherent. Ohtake's aesthetic across his career has consistently worked this way — accumulation as composition, chaos as a deliberate structural strategy rather than an absence of one.

Inside, the division between men's and women's sections is presided over by a large ceramic elephant sculpture that peers from the dividing wall across both baths. The ceiling above the bathing area is painted by Ohtake, the mosaic walls carry imagery that shifts between the figural and the abstract, and the space is alive with pattern and colour in a way that is entirely unlike a conventional sento — and yet the baths themselves work perfectly, the water is hot, and on a full day of walking between museums in all weathers, the logic of ending here rather than at a café becomes increasingly clear.

Yu, in Japanese, means hot water. The name is a pun, and it is also a statement of intent: this is art you can get into.

tours.title: Porte vers l'infini (Gate to Infinity) | 李禹煥「無限門」
tours.shortDescription: A single tapered steel column in an open gravel forecourt — Lee Ufan's 2019 work, less an object to study than a way of seeing the world around it.
tours.longDescription:
A single column stands in the open gravel in front of you: steel, roughly the height of a lamp post, tapered toward the top, its surface carrying the marks of its making rather than concealing them. No plinth, no frame, no explanation. The title Lee Ufan gave it when he installed it here in 2019 translates as Gate to Infinity.

It stands in the forecourt of the Lee Ufan Museum, where visitors arrive before entering — something to pass near rather than to study, changing its relationship to the sea and the hillside depending on where you stand. Lee's practice has been consistent for five decades: rather than making objects that absorb attention, he creates conditions in which the world around the object becomes visible. The column does not try to be more present than the sky behind it.

The relationship between vertical column and horizontal gravel, manufactured steel and organic hillside, single mark and surrounding silence — that is the argument the work makes, and it takes a minute of standing still to land.

stops.title: Porte vers l'infini (Gate to Infinity) | 李禹煥「無限門」
stops.caption: Lee Ufan's 2019 tapered steel column in the museum forecourt — a gate to infinity against sea and sky.
stops.transcriptText:
A single column stands in the open gravel in front of you — steel, roughly the height of a lamp post, tapered toward the top, its surface carrying the marks of fabrication rather than concealing them. No plinth, no frame, no explanation mounted beside it. The title, given by Lee Ufan when he installed it here in 2019, translates as Gate to Infinity.

The column stands in the open gravel forecourt of the Lee Ufan Museum, placed where visitors arrive before entering the building itself, so that it functions as both an introduction and a preparation — something to pass near rather than to study, something that changes its relationship to the sea and the hillside behind it depending on where you're standing. Lee's practice has been consistent across five decades: rather than making objects that absorb attention entirely, he prefers to create conditions in which the world around the object becomes visible. The column doesn't try to be more present than the sky behind it. In his description of his own work, Lee has said that he aims to offer not an object to be seen but a visual opportunity to encounter the world — and this work is perhaps the most direct expression of that intention anywhere on the island.

The relationship between the vertical column and the horizontal gravel plain, between the manufactured steel and the organic hillside, between the single mark and the surrounding silence, is the argument the work is making — and it takes a minute or two of standing still for it to fully land.

The Lee Ufan Museum entrance is directly behind this work, and the progression from outdoor column to indoor gallery is worth treating as a continuous sequence rather than two separate visits — the contrast between sky and concrete ceiling, open and enclosed, is part of what the museum is about.

tours.title: Red Pumpkin | 「赤かぼちゃ」草間彌生
tours.shortDescription: Yayoi Kusama's polka-dotted red pumpkin at Miyanoura Port — big enough to walk inside, where the sculpture becomes an environment.
tours.longDescription:
Kusama's red pumpkin at Miyanoura Port: the polka dots, the scale, the colour against the sea. There is no shortage of photographs — which is precisely why it is worth knowing what it does that they don't capture. The sculpture at the end of the pier is large enough to walk inside, through one of the oval openings cut into its base.

The interior is dark and indirectly lit, its walls and ceiling covered in the same black dots as the exterior — but from inside, looking up and out, the relationship inverts. What was an object becomes an environment, the dots around you and the sea visible in slices through the apertures, and Kusama's lifelong repetition — the same mark at every scale, dissolving the boundary between self and world — suddenly makes sense in a way it doesn't from twenty metres away.

Kusama placed the Yellow Pumpkin at the southern pier in 1994 and this red one followed in 2006 — a greeting and a departure for the island. The yellow original, damaged by Typhoon Lupit in 2021, was replaced in 2022; the red, set back from the exposed pier, survived.

stops.title: Red Pumpkin | 「赤かぼちゃ」草間彌生
stops.caption: Yayoi Kusama's 2006 red pumpkin at Miyanoura Port — walk inside and the sculpture becomes an environment.
stops.transcriptText:
Yayoi Kusama's red pumpkin at Miyanoura Port. The polka dots. The scale. The colour against the sea. There is no shortage of photographs of this — which is precisely why it's worth also knowing what it does that the photographs don't capture.

The red sculpture at the end of the pier is large enough to walk inside, through one of the oval openings cut into its base. The interior is dark, lit indirectly, its ceiling and walls covered in the same black polka dot pattern that covers the exterior — but from inside, looking up and out through the openings, the spatial relationship inverts. What was a sculptural object from outside becomes an environment from inside, the dots around you and the sea visible in slices through the apertures, and the logic of Kusama's repetition — the same mark applied at every scale across a lifetime's work as a way of dissolving the boundaries between self and world — suddenly makes sense in a way it doesn't from twenty metres away.

Kusama installed the Yellow Pumpkin at the southern pier in 1994, and this red version followed in 2006 — the two forming a kind of greeting and departure for the island, one on the western pier where ferries arrive and one on the southern edge where the Benesse House complex begins. The yellow original was irreparably damaged by Typhoon Lupit in 2021 and replaced by a new version in 2022; the red pumpkin, being inland from the exposed pier, survived.

The walk from the Red Pumpkin to the Naoshima Pavilion and the I Love Yu bathhouse covers the central cluster of the port area in about fifteen minutes — a reasonable orientation circuit if you've just arrived on the island.

tours.title: The Naoshima Plan 2019 "The Water" | ナオシマ プラン 2019「水」
tours.shortDescription: An old Honmura house opened up by Hiroshi Sambuichi around a shallow pool of real groundwater — the artwork is the movement of water, wind, and light.
tours.longDescription:
What architect Hiroshi Sambuichi was attending to here was the way groundwater moves through Honmura's soil, the way seasonal wind passes between the houses, and the way a traditional north-south room layout aligns those forces into a natural ventilation the village understood without ever naming.

The old house on this quiet lane has been transformed since 2019 as part of the Benesse Art Site's expansion of the Art House Project, which has been embedding contemporary work into abandoned homes here since 1998. Sambuichi takes the house's original structure as his subject: he exposes the traditional layout, strips back the surfaces, and introduces a shallow pool that runs through the interior and out toward a pier, fed by the groundwater directly beneath.

The water is real and it moves. Wind through the opened axis creates ripples; light shifts across the surface with the hour and season. The relationship between the water's weight, the lightness of the structure, and the movement of air is the artwork — not any object placed within it. Sambuichi calls his architecture a study of moving materials, and a few minutes here make that feel earned rather than poetic.

stops.title: The Naoshima Plan 2019 "The Water" | ナオシマ プラン 2019「水」
stops.caption: Hiroshi Sambuichi's Honmura house (2019) built around a moving pool of real groundwater.
stops.transcriptText:
Here's what architect Hiroshi Sambuichi was paying attention to when he worked on this building: the way groundwater moves through the soil of Honmura, the way seasonal wind passes between houses in this part of the village, and the way a traditional north-south room layout aligns those forces into a kind of natural ventilation that the people who built this district understood intuitively and never had to name.

The old house on this quiet Honmura lane has been transformed since 2019 as part of the Benesse Art Site's expansion of the Art House Project — which since 1998 has been converting abandoned homes in this village into permanent art installations, embedding contemporary work into the fabric of where people actually live. Sambuichi's contribution to the project takes the house's original structure as its subject: he exposes the traditional layout, strips back the surfaces, and introduces a shallow pool that extends through the interior and outward toward a pier, fed by the rich groundwater directly beneath the building.

The water in the pool is real groundwater, and it moves. Wind passing through the opened north-south axis of the house creates ripples; light shifts across the surface depending on time and season; the relationship between the weight of the water, the lightness of the structure overhead, and the movement of air through the space is the artwork, rather than any object placed within it. Sambuichi describes his architecture as a study of "moving materials" — water, wind, light — and the experience of standing in this space for a few minutes makes that description feel earned rather than poetic.

The surrounding Honmura lanes are dense with Art House Project sites — Ando Museum, Minamidera, Kadoya, and others — and this one sits quietly among them, easy to walk past if you're not looking for it, which is, after all, in keeping with the building's entire approach.

tours.title: Valley Gallery | ヴァレーギャラリー
tours.shortDescription: Ando's ninth Naoshima building, where the approach path is the art — hundreds of Kusama's mirrored steel spheres spilling across a valley lake.
tours.longDescription:
Before you reach the building, the path offers you the artwork — and it is better than anything else on the approach to any gallery on this island. The path to Valley Gallery winds uphill through the valley between the Lee Ufan and Benesse House museums, and along it, across a small lake and up the hillside, are hundreds of polished stainless-steel spheres: Yayoi Kusama's Narcissus Garden, first made in 1966 and permanently installed here since 2022.

Each sphere is about the size of a football, mirror-bright, reflecting a distorted sky and trees and whoever stands near. When wind crosses the water the spheres on its surface click together in a low rhythmic sound unlike anything you expect in an art context. Walking through hundreds of your own distorted reflections, surrounded by that sound, is hard to prepare for.

The gallery at the top — Tadao Ando's ninth Naoshima commission, opened 2022 — is a semi-open concrete structure with a slit roof channelling daylight in. Inside, an indoor Narcissus Garden sits alongside Tsuyoshi Ozawa's Slag Buddhas: eighty-eight figures made from industrial waste reclaimed from Teshima.

stops.title: Valley Gallery | ヴァレーギャラリー
stops.caption: Tadao Ando's 2022 gallery reached through Kusama's Narcissus Garden — hundreds of mirrored spheres across a valley.
stops.transcriptText:
Before you reach the building, the path offers you the artwork — and the artwork is better than anything else on the approach to any gallery on this island, which is saying something.

The path that leads to Valley Gallery winds uphill through the valley between the Lee Ufan Museum and the Benesse House Museum, and along it, spilling across a small lake and up the surrounding hillside, are hundreds of polished stainless steel spheres: Yayoi Kusama's Narcissus Garden, first made in 1966 and now permanently installed here since 2022. Each sphere is roughly the diameter of a football, mirror-bright, reflecting a distorted version of the sky and the trees and whatever is standing near it. When the wind moves across the water, the spheres on the lake's surface click together, producing a collective sound that is low, rhythmic, and unlike anything you are likely to have heard in an art context before. The experience of walking through hundreds of your own distorted reflections, surrounded by that sound, in a wooded valley above the Seto Inland Sea, is difficult to prepare for.

The gallery building at the top, Tadao Ando's ninth commission on Naoshima, opened in 2022 — a semi-open concrete structure with angular walls and a slit roof that channels natural light into the interior. Inside, Kusama's work continues: an indoor component of Narcissus Garden alongside Tsuyoshi Ozawa's Slag Buddha statues, made from industrial waste reclaimed from Teshima island, eighty-eight Buddhas in a form that carries both the island's contamination history and its Buddhist pilgrimage tradition. Entry to Valley Gallery is included in the Benesse House Museum ticket.

The outdoor path between Valley Gallery and Chichu Art Museum continues west through the hillside, and the transition between them — Kusama's reflected multiplicity giving way to Ando's precise geometry — rewards the walk.

tours.title: Art House Project | 家プロジェクト
tours.shortDescription: Seven ordinary houses in the village of Honmura — a corner house, a ruined shrine, a former temple, a dentist's surgery — each hiding a contemporary artwork behind an unremarkable facade. The art lives in the gap between what they seem and what they hold.
tours.longDescription:
Since 1998 the Benesse Art Site has been taking empty houses in Honmura, an ordinary residential quarter of Naoshima, and handing them to artists — Tatsuo Miyajima, Hiroshi Sugimoto, James Turrell, Rei Naito, Yoshihiro Suda, Hiroshi Senju, Shinro Ohtake — to transform from the inside out. Seven sites now make up the Art House Project, scattered through the lanes with almost no signage to mark them, so that the work begins in the gap between what each building appears to be and what you find once you step through the door.

This walk takes them roughly in order, beginning at Kadoya, the corner house where it all started, and ending at Haisha, a former dentist's surgery turned into an exuberant collage. Collect a ticket and a map from the Honmura Lounge & Archive first — the houses are genuinely easy to walk past. Kinza admits one person at a time by advance booking; Minamidera runs timed entry every fifteen minutes. The circuit is only a few minutes' walking; how long you spend inside each is another matter entirely.

stops.title: Kadoya | 家プロジェクト「角屋」
stops.caption: A 200-year-old corner house holding Tatsuo Miyajima's 'Sea of Time '98' — 125 LED counters, each set to the pace of a different Naoshima resident.
stops.transcriptText:
This building is roughly 200 years old, and from the outside it has been carefully restored to look exactly like what it originally was — stucco walls, smoked cedar boards, traditional roof tiles, the corner position that gave it its nickname, Kadoya: "corner house."

At the far end of this lane, behind that facade, is the installation that launched the entire Art House Project in 1998, and it uses the darkened interior of the main room in a way that only becomes clear once you've removed your shoes and entered.

The work is called Sea of Time '98, by Tatsuo Miyajima, and it fills the floor of a shallow pool with 125 LED digital counters, each displaying numbers from one to nine and counting at a different speed, chosen by an individual Naoshima resident during a community meeting in February 1998. One hundred and twenty-five people — ranging in age from five to ninety-five — each set a counter to their preferred pace, so what you're looking at when you stand over the darkened water is not a random pattern but a record of 125 different relationships to time, encoded in blinking light. When visitors enter and the water ripples, the reflections flicker — but the speeds don't change. Each counter continues at the rate its resident chose.

Miyajima also has two smaller works in the house: Naoshima's Counter Window, a window whose glass surface has been replaced by three large liquid-crystal numerals that let light through their shapes, and Changing Landscape, a 19th-century scroll painting reworked so that the landscape beneath is visible only through the silhouettes of digital numbers.

The most precise thing about this project is the gap it doesn't try to fill: each counter runs from one to nine and skips zero, because Miyajima's practice treats zero — completion, cessation, nothingness — as the one number that falls outside the ongoing flow of time. From here, head uphill to the right toward Go'o Shrine.

stops.title: Go'o Shrine | 家プロジェクト｢護王神社｣
stops.caption: A working Shinto shrine with Hiroshi Sugimoto's 'Appropriate Proportion' — a glass staircase linking the hall above to a stone chamber below.
stops.transcriptText:
This is, and has always been, a Shinto shrine — one that fell into disuse during the second half of the twentieth century as Honmura's population declined, and was selected for the Art House Project because it was already a ruin, already asking for a kind of attention.

The stepped path rises to your right, leading up through the trees to the main worship hall of Go'o Shrine, and the first thing that registers as unusual is the staircase descending from it: a flight of steps made from solid optical glass, each tread transparent, the whole run catching and refracting whatever light passes through from above.

The work is by Hiroshi Sugimoto, titled Appropriate Proportion, and the glass staircase is its visible heart, connecting the surface of the shrine to an underground stone chamber directly below. The chamber was modelled on ancient kofun burial mounds — the large earthwork tombs of Japan's Kofun period, which predate the formal introduction of Buddhism to the archipelago — and Sugimoto's intervention draws a line between the Shinto world above ground and something considerably older below it. On rainy days, water infiltrates through the hillside and gathers at the base of the glass stairs, so the staircase appears to descend into its own reflection.

The underground chamber is accessible separately, via a narrow side entrance cut into the hillside — ask the attendant, who will provide a torch. The space inside is dark stone and silence, and the glass stairs are visible from below as a column of diffused light.

Sugimoto's broader practice has always been concerned with the relationship between perception and time — the same set of interests that produced his Time Exposed seascape photographs on the cliffs at Benesse House. Both works ask what it means to look at light, and what light was before anyone was looking. From here, head back down and along the main street toward Minamidera.

stops.title: Minamidera | 家プロジェクト「南寺」
stops.caption: A windowless Tadao Ando building housing James Turrell's 'Backside of the Moon' — total darkness your eyes slowly learn to read.
stops.transcriptText:
The long, dark wooden building with no windows is not a traditional Honmura house — it was built from scratch by Tadao Ando on the site of a temple that no longer stands, designed to house a single artwork by James Turrell. It is intended to look unremarkable from the street, and succeeds.
