Entry here is in groups of ten or fifteen, every fifteen minutes, so if you're waiting outside you're doing the right thing. What happens inside is not possible to explain without reducing it to something smaller than it is, but the broad shape of the experience is this: you are led into a room of complete darkness, guided by a staff member with your left hand on the wall, and seated on a bench. The darkness is thorough — not dim, not adjustable, but actual darkness, in which nothing is visible including the people beside you. After several minutes sitting quietly, a glow becomes perceptible, soft and blue-grey, at the far wall. The natural instinct is to walk toward it, which you may do when the attendant invites you.

The work is titled Backside of the Moon, and what makes it matter is the physics of what has happened: the light in the room has not changed. Nothing in the space has been adjusted or switched on. Your eyes have simply adapted, as human eyes do in darkness, revealing something that was always present but imperceptible. Turrell's installation uses no projectors, no electricity in the visible sense — only the biology of your own visual system, performing its ordinary function under unusual conditions, and suddenly becoming strange and legible to you for the first time.

The people leaving Minamidera squinting into the daylight have just had the same experience. The Ando Museum — Tadao Ando's own retrospective, installed in a 100-year-old machiya nearby — is a short walk east. Kinza and Gokaisho are just ahead on this street.

stops.title: Kinza | 家プロジェクトきんざ
stops.caption: The most restrictive of the seven — Rei Naito's installation, one visitor at a time, fifteen minutes, by advance booking only.
stops.transcriptText:
Kinza is the most restrictive of the seven Art Houses, and that restriction is part of the work.

The small house just beside Gokaisho can be visited only Thursday through Sunday, with advance reservation required, and it admits a single visitor at a time for a maximum of fifteen minutes. The name is another Honmura yago — a household nickname used when families shared surnames on the island — and the building itself, which is around 200 years old, was renovated by the artist Rei Naito over three years with an unusual degree of care for what was already there: she preserved the original carpentry structure as intact as possible, doing much of the renovation work by hand, and her installation emerged from the specific character of the space rather than being imposed on it.

The work inside plays with light, silence, and what it feels like to be entirely alone in a small old room, and the decision to allow only one person at a time is the argument as well as the rule: Kinza is making a case for the singular experience of art, against the group-move-and-cluster logic of most gallery visiting, and the fifteen-minute limit is a gift rather than a constraint — long enough to actually settle, short enough that settling feels precise and deliberate.

What you find inside is not something that translates well into description, partly because Naito's practice generally resists paraphrase and partly because the book has been deliberate about not circulating images of the installation. Part of the experience is arriving without knowing exactly what you'll encounter. The booking can be made through Honmura Lounge and Archive, and it is worth the effort of arranging well in advance.

Continue on to Gokaisho, which is immediately next door.

stops.title: Gokaisho | 家プロジェクト「碁会所」
stops.caption: A former go-players' club where Yoshihiro Suda's carved wooden camellias sit among the real thing.
stops.transcriptText:
Gokaisho means "go-meeting-place" — this was the building where Honmura residents gathered to play go, the ancient board game, and it has a different character from the former homes around it: slightly more public, slightly more communal in its proportions.

Through the gate ahead, two rooms open off a central courtyard, and Yoshihiro Suda has installed a work in each that operates by the same principle while arriving at it from different directions. In the first room, wooden camellia flowers — carved with the precision Suda is known for, painted to match real flowers in colour and texture — are scattered across the floor in positions that echo, without replicating, the camellia tree growing in the courtyard just outside the window. Real flowers, carved flowers, the tree visible beyond, the light falling across both: the work is in the question of whether you can tell them apart, and what happens to your looking once you start trying.

In the second room, a single stick of real bamboo stands alongside a carved wooden imitation of the same stick, and the match is close enough that without the context of the first room you might not immediately know which is which. Suda is a sculptor whose practice consistently does this: places natural and handmade objects in proximity and asks what the difference amounts to — whether craft can equal nature, or whether the attempt reveals a gap that nothing can close.

The curious part is that the work requires almost nothing from you except sustained attention, and offers almost nothing except the pressure of that attention, which turns out to be quite a lot.

From Gokaisho, walk north to Ishibashi, where the house belonged to a salt merchant's family, and the art is waterfall paintings on the sliding doors.

stops.title: Ishibashi | 家プロジェクト「石橋」
stops.caption: A salt merchant's home hung with Hiroshi Senju's waterfall paintings on the sliding fusuma doors.
stops.transcriptText:
The Ishibashi family were salt merchants — one of the most prosperous families in Honmura during the Meiji period, when salt production was a lucrative trade along the shores of Kagawa Prefecture, before the postwar government centralised and relocated the industry and the old coastal operations ceased.

This building, more spacious than most in Honmura, was the family home until 2001, and the renovation for the Art House Project was carried out with particular care to preserve its character: the smooth wooden floors, the tatami rooms, the sliding doors and creaking corridors are all as they would have been when the Ishibashis lived here, as much as the work allows.

The artworks are by Hiroshi Senju, and they take the form of large-scale paintings on the house's fusuma — the traditional sliding door panels — and in the adjacent storehouse. Senju's practice draws on the nihonga tradition of Japanese painting, using mineral pigments and a technique developed over centuries, and his dominant subject here is water: specifically, waterfalls, rendered in the misty, monochromatic grey-black tones that characterise his work. The painting The Garden of Ku can be seen from the courtyard, its images framed by the architectural opening of the house itself, so that the painted water and the visible garden exist in deliberate dialogue. In the storehouse, The Falls occupies a long wall and can be taken in more frontally.

Removing your shoes before entering is required here, as it was at Kadoya — a gesture that every traditional Japanese domestic space demands, and that has the effect of slowing the pace slightly, which is exactly what Senju's paintings reward.

The final Art House, Haisha, is south from here — the former dentist's surgery, and the loudest thing on this walk by a considerable distance.

stops.title: Haisha | 家プロジェクト「はいしゃ」
stops.caption: A former dentist's surgery turned by Shinro Ohtake into an overwhelming collage — a donated Statue of Liberty included.
stops.transcriptText:
Haisha means "dentist," and yes — there are dental motifs if you know to look for them, scattered into the surface of Shinro Ohtake's installation like small private jokes embedded in an otherwise overwhelming field of material.

What you're looking at from the lane is a building that has been substantially transformed on the outside as well as in, with found objects and fragments incorporated into its surface in a way that signals, even before you remove your shoes and enter, that the interior will not be quiet or restrained. The contrast with Ishibashi, or with Kinza, or with Gokaisho's precise carved camellias, is complete and is presumably intentional: Ohtake, an artist whose practice has always worked through accumulation, collision, and the aesthetic of the found and repurposed, was given a former dentist's surgery and turned it into what might charitably be described as an archive of everything.

Materials from abandoned Naoshima houses, structural elements from shipyards in Uwajima where Ohtake lives and works, a Statue of Liberty donated by a Niigata pachinko parlour — all of this and considerably more is layered into the two main spaces. One room is dark, its walls slick and deep-coloured against a spongy textured floor, reaching into a visual density that makes the eyes search for a way through. The other opens up through the second storey into natural light, painted in rich blue tones that make it feel like a different building entirely, or a different artist.

And that tension between the cramped and the expansive, the dark and the lit, the dental and the maritime and the American-kitsch, is what the work is about: the collision of incompatible things, held together by a building that absorbed all of it without collapsing.

From here, the Art House Project ends. The Ando Museum is a short walk south — a different kind of intelligence applied to a similar question about what a traditional house can hold.

tours.title: Benesse House Museum Outdoor Works | ベネッセハウスミュージアム屋外作品
tours.shortDescription: Twenty sculptures scattered across the lawns, clifftops, pier, and shore below Benesse House — from Kusama's yellow pumpkin to a functioning bath, a kinetic steel work that moves with the wind, and a photograph left out to decay. The sea is part of nearly every one.
tours.longDescription:
It started, in 1989, with a frog and a cat — Karel Appel's two animal sculptures set on what was then a children's camping ground above the Seto Inland Sea. Twenty works have accumulated here since, free to walk during daylight and needing the outdoors to make sense.

Yayoi Kusama's Pumpkin sits at the pier's end; Niki de Saint Phalle's exuberant menagerie is strewn across the lawn; Hiroshi Sugimoto contributes a mirrored glass tea house and a slowly-decaying seascape on the cliff; Shinro Ohtake's salvaged shipyard fragments anchor the collection to the island's industrial past; Cai Guo-Qiang offers a fire-heated communal bath; and the walk closes among the mirror-sphere fields of Narcissus Garden and Slag Buddha 88. This route takes all twenty in the order you meet them on foot from the pier — about a kilometre and a half, with some climb, ninety minutes to two hours at a relaxed pace.

stops.title: Pumpkin | 南瓜
stops.caption: Yayoi Kusama's yellow polka-dot pumpkin at the end of the pier — the image of the whole island (a 2022 replacement after a typhoon swept the original to sea).
stops.transcriptText:
The pier extends ahead of you into the Seto Inland Sea, and at its end, at the very edge where the land runs out, sits a yellow pumpkin two metres tall and covered in black polka dots. That is, if you're here to think about it, a slightly absurd thing to find at the tip of a Japanese island — and that slight absurdity is precisely the point.

Yayoi Kusama created this work for a 1994 outdoor exhibition here called "Out of Bounds," an event that used the natural landscape around Benesse House as its venue. The pumpkin was meant to be temporary, and then it stayed, and then it became the image of the whole island. The scale of that transformation — from seasonal sculpture to global cultural symbol — is something that still seems to surprise the people who run this place.

Here's the curious part of its history: in August 2021 a typhoon hit the island unexpectedly, the pumpkin was swept off the pier and into the sea within seconds, and footage of it floating away circulated around the world within hours. It was recovered, but the original was too damaged to reinstall — so what you're looking at now is a 2022 replacement, made in consultation with the artist.

Walk back along the pier toward the lawn and head up toward the cluster of colourful figures on the grass. Karel Appel's Frog and Cat is directly ahead — the work that started everything.

stops.title: Frog and Cat | かえると猫
stops.caption: Karel Appel's two bright animals on the lawn — the first work installed here, in 1990, that started everything.
stops.transcriptText:
The large, bright, slightly ungainly animal figures on the lawn are by Karel Appel, a Dutch painter and sculptor who worked in a style related to CoBrA — the loose post-war movement of artists from Copenhagen, Brussels, and Amsterdam who pushed back against rational, geometric abstraction in favour of something rawer, more intuitive, and frankly more fun.

Frog and Cat was the very first permanent outdoor artwork installed at Benesse Art Site Naoshima, placed here in 1990 when this was still a camping ground rather than a museum campus. Every subsequent work — the Kusama pumpkin, the Niki de Saint Phalle animals you're about to reach, the Sugimoto photographs on the cliff, all twenty pieces in the collection — came after this. Appel's two creatures, standing here on the grass above the sea, were the proof of concept.

There's something rather appropriate about beginning a serious art collection with a frog and a cat — unpretentious, approachable, slightly cartoonish — as if to say that art on this island will not be asking you to approach it reverently. From here, continue along the lawn toward the cluster of de Saint Phalle sculptures. You'll encounter the Camel first.

stops.title: Camel | らくだ
stops.caption: One of Niki de Saint Phalle's five bold, cheerful animal sculptures scattered across the lawn (1991).
stops.transcriptText:
The camel on the grass ahead is one of five works by Niki de Saint Phalle installed across the Benesse House lawns in 1991, alongside Appel's Frog and Cat from the year before — and the two artists sit in comfortable company, both committed to bold colour, animal subjects, and a refusal to take the sculptural tradition too seriously.

Niki de Saint Phalle was a French-American artist best known for her Nanas — monumental female figures in primary colours that became widely public sculptures across Europe in the 1970s and 80s — and for the Tarot Garden in Tuscany, an entire sculpture park she spent decades building as a personal project. Her animals here carry the same spirit: large, joyful, uninhibited, and designed to be encountered outdoors. They look more lively against the sea than they would against a gallery wall.

Continue along the path and you'll find the Cat and the other pieces nearby. They're scattered rather than arranged in a formal sequence, so take your time moving between them.

stops.title: Cat | 猫
stops.caption: Another de Saint Phalle animal on the grass — the works are spread out to be inhabited, not arranged in sequence.
stops.transcriptText:
Another de Saint Phalle on the grass — this time the Cat, painted in the same vivid, unambiguous palette as the Camel, with the same quality of being simultaneously monumental in scale and cheerful in mood.

What's worth pausing on here is the distribution of these works: they're not arranged along a formal path or presented as a sequence to be walked in order. They sit on the lawn the way animals might actually inhabit a landscape — spread out, at various distances, each commanding its own bit of grass. It's a curatorial choice that resists the formal procession of a gallery corridor, and the effect is that you're never quite done looking — there's always another one at the edge of your field of vision.

La Conversation is just ahead, where two figures face each other, followed by the Elephant further along the slope.

stops.title: La Conversation | 会話
stops.caption: A de Saint Phalle sculpture with two seats set facing each other — it doesn't depict a conversation, it hosts one.
stops.transcriptText:
There are two places to sit inside this sculpture. Take one of them.

On the grass between you and the slope, a sinuous, brightly painted form rises and curves back on itself — de Saint Phalle's serpentine lines in the bold, enamel-like colour she used throughout her career, somewhere between mosaic and painted ceramic. It reads, from a distance, as an abstract creature coiling on the lawn, but come closer and the functional detail becomes clear: seats have been set into opposing sides of the form, facing each other across the work's body, so that two people can sit within the sculpture itself.

That detail — the seats — changes what the work is asking you to do, and changes what the title means. La Conversation is French simply for "The Conversation," and de Saint Phalle, who worked extensively with public sculpture designed to be inhabited rather than merely observed, was not being metaphorical. The sculpture doesn't depict a conversation; it hosts one. Two people, sitting on opposite sides of a curved form that holds them at close quarters, facing each other with the sea and the grass visible behind whichever person they're not looking at — that is, structurally, what a conversation actually is: two positions in deliberate opposition, held together by something in between.

De Saint Phalle made this piece in 1991, the same year as the Camel, the Cat, and the Elephant nearby, all of which share her characteristic exuberance and refusal of solemnity. But La Conversation is the only one in this cluster that invites the viewer to sit inside it — which makes it, quietly, the most participatory work on the whole Benesse House lawn.

If you came here with someone, sit across from each other and see whether the sculpture changes the conversation. If you came alone, one of the seats belongs to nobody in particular, and the view from inside the work is rather good. Continue from here along the slope toward the Elephant, the largest of de Saint Phalle's five works on this site.

stops.title: Elephant | 象
stops.caption: The largest of de Saint Phalle's five works here, anchoring the group against the sea horizon.
stops.transcriptText:
The Elephant is the largest of de Saint Phalle's five works here, and in scale and presence it anchors the group — a reminder that these aren't decorative pieces scattered casually across a hotel garden, but monumental sculptures that hold their own against the landscape and the sea horizon behind them.

De Saint Phalle has always drawn on a tradition of art that belongs in public space, accessible to anyone who encounters it rather than to a specific collecting class — and there's something fitting about that instinct finding a home here, on an island where the outdoor works are free to access and available to anyone who walks the coast path. The museum entrance ticket is not required for the outdoor collection during daylight hours.

Le Banc is a short distance away — de Saint Phalle's fifth and final piece on this site, and one you can actually sit on if you'd like.

stops.title: Le Banc | 腰掛
stops.caption: De Saint Phalle's 'The Bench' (1989) — a functional sculpture you're invited to sit on, facing the Inland Sea.
stops.transcriptText:
Le Banc — The Bench — is the fifth de Saint Phalle work on these grounds and the one that holds a slightly different position: it was made in 1989, two years before the other four, and it is, true to its name, a bench, designed to be used as well as observed. Sit on it if you like.

De Saint Phalle made many functional sculptures over her career — chairs, tables, garden structures — and Le Banc carries the same exuberant colour and form as everything else she made, which means that sitting on it in front of the Seto Inland Sea is a fairly specific kind of experience. It's an invitation, in a way, to stop treating the outdoor collection as a walk to be completed and start treating it as a place to spend time.

From here, the path continues toward the Cylinder Bisected by Plane by Dan Graham — though note that this work is temporarily unavailable at time of writing, so check the current site map before heading that way. Anthony Caro's Final Call is reliably on display just ahead of the Park building entrance.

stops.title: Cylinder Bisected by Plane | 平面によって二分された円柱
stops.caption: Dan Graham's two-way-mirrored steel-and-glass pavilion (1995) — perception shifts with where you stand. (May be temporarily off view.)
stops.transcriptText:
Dan Graham's Cylinder Bisected by Plane is a two-way mirrored steel and glass structure — a cylinder cut through by a curved planar wall, both surfaces reflective — that, when it's on display, creates a situation where what you see changes completely depending on where you stand relative to it and to the light. Graham's practice across decades has been concerned precisely with this: the way perception depends on position, how the same object reads differently from different vantage points, and how architecture can make that visible.

The work at Benesse House was made in 1995 and is characteristic of Graham's "pavilion" works, many of which have been installed in landscapes and urban settings internationally. When available, it sits against the sea view in a way that layers the reflected landscape over the direct view — producing the slightly vertiginous sensation Graham clearly enjoys inducing.

Anthony Caro's Final Call is ahead, at the entrance to the Park building.

stops.title: Glass Tea House "Mondrian" | 硝子の茶室『聞鳥庵』
stops.caption: Hiroshi Sugimoto's mirrored-glass tea house above a pond — a working chashitsu that doubles in its own reflection.
stops.transcriptText:
The mirrored glass cube above the pond is the Glass Tea House, titled "Mondrian" — and it is, inside, a functioning tea house, with a tatami mat floor and all the proportional principles of a traditional Japanese chashitsu, translated into optical glass that reflects the sky and the surrounding landscape from every surface.

Hiroshi Sugimoto designed this work in 2014, and it had previous lives in Venice and Paris before finding a permanent site here in the Benesse House Park grounds. The name "Mondrian" refers to the grid-like effect of the glass pane divisions rather than to any formal connection to the Dutch painter — though the geometry of the reflections, fractured and layered, does produce something that sits between the structural and the optical in a way that earns the reference.

The pond below the tea house matters: the reflection of the cube in still water produces a doubling of the structure, so that it appears simultaneously grounded and floating. Whether or not a tea ceremony is taking place inside, the whole construction — glass cube, water reflection, surrounding trees — functions as a composed view rather than a single object. Take a moment to find the angle where the reflection completes it.

Continue up the slope toward Anthony Caro's Final Call.

stops.title: Final Call | ファイナル・コール
stops.caption: Anthony Caro's rusted-steel abstract work at the Park building entrance — raw engineering against de Saint Phalle's colour.
stops.transcriptText:
The three-dimensional work at the side of the Park building entrance, constructed from rusted steel, is Final Call by Anthony Caro — a British sculptor who, along with Henry Moore and Barbara Hepworth, helped define what large-scale abstract sculpture in Britain looked like in the second half of the twentieth century.

Caro's approach here differs markedly from the de Saint Phalle works you've just passed: where those are exuberant, figurative, and brightly painted, Final Call is raw steel, abstract, and built with an engineering sensibility — the individual elements visible, the construction process evident in the finished object. That contrast, spread across the lawns and paths of the same complex, is itself part of what makes the outdoor collection worth spending time in rather than walking past.

The title, Final Call, suggests urgency or closure, though Caro rarely gave his titles explanatory force — they were associations rather than keys.

From here the path climbs. Three Squares Vertical Diagonal by George Rickey is at the top of the slope, and it moves.

stops.title: Three Squares Vertical Diagonal | 三枚の正方形
stops.caption: George Rickey's kinetic steel blades at the top of the slope, turning with the wind — never the same twice.
stops.transcriptText:
At the top of the slope, the three large steel blades pivoting slowly on their axis are Three Squares Vertical Diagonal by George Rickey — an American sculptor who made movement the explicit subject of his practice, calibrating the weight and balance of metal elements so that they respond to the slightest air movement without motors or mechanisms.

Watch it for a minute. The blades turn — sometimes simultaneously, sometimes at different rates, sometimes catching the light on one face while another goes flat — and the sculpture is genuinely never the same twice. What looks, in a photograph, like a static geometric abstraction becomes something entirely different outdoors, because outdoors there is always wind, and wind has a clock that no human arrangement can predict.

There's something rather fitting about a kinetic sculpture sitting at the top of this hillside, with the Seto Inland Sea laid out below and the mountains of Shikoku visible on clear days. The work doesn't impose on the view; it joins it.

Rickey has three works at Benesse Art Site in total. From here, continue downhill toward the cliff path and the works closer to the water. Kazuo Katase's Drink a Cup of Tea is the next stop.

stops.title: Drink a Cup of Tea | 茶のめ
stops.caption: Kazuo Katase's teacup-shaped work holding real water, placed to greet visitors arriving from the sea.
stops.transcriptText:
The teacup-shaped structure ahead, large enough to walk around, contains real water — and it was made in response to a specific phrase from Zen teaching: "Eat it and drink a cup of tea," which is associated with an expression of seeking truth through the most ordinary of acts. Kazuo Katase positioned this work on the coastal path to welcome visitors arriving by ferry from the sea, so that the first significant work they encounter is not grand or monumental but quietly ceremonial: a cup of tea, at the edge of the water.

The outer surface is built from rusted steel wire, giving it a texture that softens and complicates the simple geometry of the cup form — it reads as both precise and weathered, which is consistent with the work's wider interest in the ordinary as a vehicle for the profound.

From here the path continues to Walter De Maria's Seen/Unseen Known/Unknown, a large granite sphere and gold-foiled element set within a concrete space — the work that De Maria later developed, at greater scale, into the Time/Timeless/No Time installation at the Chichu Art Museum.

stops.title: Seen/Unseen Known/Unknown | 見えて:見えず 知って:知れず
stops.caption: Walter De Maria's granite sphere and gold element in a concrete space — the outdoor precursor to his Chichu chamber.
stops.transcriptText:
Set within a concrete-surrounded space on the coastal path, Seen/Unseen Known/Unknown places a large granite sphere and a gold-foiled element in deliberate dialogue with the daylight overhead — the shadows the sphere casts shift across the floor as the sun moves, and the gold surface changes quality with the light's angle, so that the work is measurably different at different times of day.

Walter De Maria made this in 2000, and it's a significant precursor to understanding his installation at the Chichu Art Museum, where the same interests in weight, light, and the measurement of time were developed into the monumental Time/Timeless/No Time — a gilded granite sphere in a circular concrete chamber designed around the work's effect on its space. Seen/Unseen Known/Unknown is the earlier, outdoor version of that thinking, available without a museum ticket and viewable in full daylight.

The title's four terms — seen, unseen, known, unknown — are a fair summary of what De Maria was consistently investigating: what perception actually constitutes, how much of what we call seeing is construction, and where knowledge ends and experience begins.

Continue along the coastal path toward the Shipyard Works by Shinro Ohtake.

stops.title: Shipyard Works: Stern with Hole | シップヤード・ワークス 船尾と穴
stops.caption: Shinro Ohtake's boat-stern fragment on the shore (1990) — one of three works built from Naoshima's old shipyard.
stops.transcriptText:
The fragment of a boat on the shore ahead — the stern section, a hole cut through its hull — is one of three Shipyard Works by Shinro Ohtake, all made in 1990 using actual boat parts found in or near Naoshima's old shipyard. Ohtake is an artist whose practice has always worked through accumulation and collision — layering industrial objects, fragments, found materials, and personal imagery into constructions that read as simultaneously archaeological and newly made.

The site-specificity of these works matters: Naoshima's south coast was industrial before it was artistic, and the island still operates an active copper refinery at its northern end. Placing boat fragments on the shore here is not merely a formal choice — it anchors the outdoor collection to the island's actual working history, which the art-tourism narrative sometimes obscures.

The Cut Bow is close by along the coast, the third Shipyard Work.

stops.title: Shipyard Works: Cut Bow | シップヤード・ワークス 切断された船首
stops.caption: The cleanly-sliced bow of a boat, dressed with found objects — Ohtake's counterpart to Stern with Hole.
stops.transcriptText:
The bow of a boat, sliced cleanly across, adorned with found objects and materials — this is Cut Bow, the counterpart to Stern with Hole, placed at a different point along the same shoreline.

Together these two pieces ask a simple but persistent question: at what point does a repurposed industrial object become a sculpture? Ohtake has not transformed these boat parts into something unrecognisable — they're clearly what they are, clearly where they came from. The transformation is one of context and intention: placed on the coast, in deliberate relationship to each other and to the sea they once worked, they shift from debris to proposition.

What's easy to overlook, standing here, is that Ohtake also made the I Love Yu bathhouse near Miyanoura Port — a completely different register, riot-of-colour and collage, yet driven by the same instinct for accumulation and reuse. The Shipyard Works are his quieter argument.

Continue west along the coast to Cai Guo-Qiang's Cultural Melting Bath.

stops.title: Cultural Melting Bath | 文化大混浴
stops.caption: Cai Guo-Qiang's fire-heated Japanese communal bath, sited by feng shui — bathing as cultural encounter.
stops.transcriptText:
The large traditional Japanese wooden bath — a goemon-buro, the kind heated from below by fire — positioned on the Naoshima coastline is Cultural Melting Bath: Project for Naoshima, made by Cai Guo-Qiang in 1998. Its placement was chosen using principles of feng shui, positioned where the artist judged the site's energy flow to be most dynamic.

Cai's concept was communal bathing as cultural encounter — a goemon-buro is traditionally a shared family bath, and the title implies that a cultural identity dissolves in shared water the way it might dissolve in any genuine meeting. The work is available to hotel guests of Benesse House for bathing on Sunday mornings, when the bath is filled with herbal water; at other times it functions as a sculptural presence on the coast.

That said, even when no bathing is possible, the work's logic is legible from outside: a traditional Japanese form, placed in an unusually considered location, as a proposition about what it means to be genuinely open to other ways of being.

Continue west and slightly uphill toward Hiroshi Sugimoto's Time Exposed photographs on the cliff.

stops.title: Time Exposed: Caribbean Sea, Yucatan | タイム・エクスポーズド
stops.caption: Hiroshi Sugimoto's long-exposure Caribbean seascape mounted on the cliff, left to weather — time recording time.
stops.transcriptText:
On the clifftop where the land runs out above the Seto Inland Sea, a large-format photograph is mounted facing the water — and what it shows is another sea, the Caribbean off the Yucatan coast, photographed in 1990 with a long exposure that renders the water and sky as a single continuous grey tone, the horizon precisely centred.

This is from Hiroshi Sugimoto's Time Exposed series, which he photographed across more than a decade: always the same composition, always a different body of water, always exposed long enough for the surface movement to average out into stillness. The gift detail here, and the reason the series is called Time Exposed rather than simply Seascapes, is that Sugimoto was photographing the light as it existed at a specific moment in time — the same light, reflected off the same water, that human eyes have received for as long as there have been human eyes to receive it.

The photograph mounted outdoors here, exposed to the salt air, the UV, and the Pacific weather, is intentionally deteriorating. That is part of the work: Sugimoto showing what time does to a record of time.

From here, the path descends toward the Valley Gallery area, where Narcissus Garden and Slag Buddha 88 are waiting.

stops.title: Narcissus Garden | ナルシスの庭
stops.caption: Yayoi Kusama's ~1,700 mirror spheres across the pond and hillside — they click together in the wind.
stops.transcriptText:
Spread across the water of the pond and the hillside around it are roughly 1,700 polished stainless steel spheres — each one about the size of a football, mirror-bright, reflecting whatever is nearest to it in a distorted, convex version. Hundreds of your own reflections face you as you approach.

This is Narcissus Garden, first made by Yayoi Kusama in 1966 for the Venice Biennale, where she sold the spheres individually from a gondola outside the main venues, undercutting the art market's gravity with the price of a souvenir. The work at Benesse House is a 2022 reinstallation of the piece, expanded to occupy the Valley Gallery landscape — which means it has been here in this form for only a few years, though the logic of the work is nearly sixty years old.

When the wind moves across the water, the spheres click together, producing a low collective sound unlike anything else in a gallery setting. It's worth standing still for a moment and listening as well as looking — the work has a dimension that photographs, understandably, never capture.

Tsuyoshi Ozawa's Slag Buddha 88 is immediately nearby, by the pond's edge.

stops.title: Slag Buddha 88 | スラグブッダ 88
stops.caption: Tsuyoshi Ozawa's 88 Buddhas moulded from Teshima's remediated industrial waste — a monument to endurance.
stops.transcriptText:
The eighty-eight small Buddha figures by the pond's edge were made by Tsuyoshi Ozawa from industrial slag — the residual material left over from smelting processes — collected specifically from the illegal dumping of industrial waste on the neighbouring island of Teshima that was discovered and remediated beginning in the 1990s. Teshima had been used as an illegal dumping site for decades, with hundreds of thousands of tonnes of industrial and medical waste buried in its soil; the cleanup took until 2012, and the Teshima Art Museum that opened in 2010 was part of the island's wider reimagination.

There's something worth knowing about the number eighty-eight: in Japan, the great Shikoku pilgrimage visits eighty-eight temples tracing the path of the Buddhist monk Kukai, and the number carries a specific spiritual weight in this region, where the pilgrimage is still actively walked. Ozawa's eighty-eight Buddhas, moulded from the contaminated earth of a nearby island, are a monument to both remediation and persistence — the mess left by industry recast, literally, into a figure of endurance.

The final stop on this walk, Kimiyo Mishima's Another Rebirth, is to the north, near the Beach building.

stops.title: Another Rebirth 2005-N | もうひとつの再生 2005-N
stops.caption: Kimiyo Mishima's ceramic work near the Beach building — the northernmost stop, on rebirth and material.
stops.transcriptText:
The walk ends here, at the northernmost of the outdoor works, near the Beach building — with Kimiyo Mishima's Another Rebirth 2005-N, a ceramic work that carries the concept of regeneration embedded in its very material.

Mishima has worked since the 1970s with ceramic — a medium that requires heat to transform, that is made from earth and fixed by fire — and her practice has consistently engaged with the relationship between natural materials and human intervention. The suffix 2005-N indicates this specific version of an ongoing series: N for Naoshima, site-specific in the same way that a number of works on this walk have been, shaped by and for this particular coastal landscape.

Step back for a moment and consider the whole circuit. Twenty works, over thirty years of accumulation, across lawns and clifftops and shore and hillside — beginning with Appel's cheerful frog and cat, ending with Mishima's ceramic meditation on rebirth. The collection isn't themed in the way that museum exhibitions usually are; it's more like a gradual revelation of what the island thinks art can be when walls are removed from the equation. The sea has been visible from every stop. That is, in the end, the most consistent thing about this outdoor museum.

tours.title: Notre-Dame de Paris
tours.shortDescription: The Gothic cathedral at the heart of Paris and the nation — eight centuries of faith, revolution and fire.
tours.longDescription: Begun in 1163 on the Île de la Cité, Notre-Dame de Paris is the great Gothic cathedral around which the city — and the idea of France — organised itself; distances in the country are still measured from its forecourt. Its flying buttresses, rose windows and twin west towers set the template for the Gothic across Europe. Gutted by fire in April 2019, it was painstakingly restored and reopened in December 2024.

stops.title: Notre-Dame de Paris
stops.caption: The Gothic cathedral at the heart of Paris and the nation — eight centuries of faith, revolution and fire.
stops.transcriptText:
In April 2019, much of the world watched this building burn on live television. The spire fell. The roof — eight hundred years of oak — went up like a bonfire. For one night it looked as though Notre-Dame might not survive at all.

It did. And that's the strange thing you're standing in front of: a cathedral that is at once more than eight hundred years old and only a few months old.

You're on the wide square facing the west front — the two great towers, the round rose window between them, the three deep carved doorways below. Before you walk up, look down. Set into the ground near the centre of the square is a small brass marker: Point Zéro. Every road distance in France is measured from that exact spot — when a sign says Paris is so many kilometres away, this is the dot it means. You're standing on the centre of the country.

Now the building. It was begun in 1163 and took the better part of a century to finish — one of the first cathedrals anywhere to use flying buttresses, those stone arms bracing the walls from outside, which let the builders go higher and thinner and fill the gaps with glass. The three great rose windows are the result, and here is the gift: when the fire tore through in 2019, the rose windows survived. The thing everyone feared losing is the thing that lived.

The roof was another story. The medieval framing was known as "the forest" — around thirteen hundred oak trees, each beam shaped by hand. It burned completely. So they grew it back: felled new oaks, cut them with medieval tools, and rebuilt the forest exactly as it had been, along with the spire, reopened at the end of 2024.

That's the reframe to carry inside with you. People call Notre-Dame ancient, and it is — but it has been half-destroyed and remade more than once: in the Revolution, in the nineteenth century, and again in our own time. What you're looking at isn't a thing that survived unchanged. It's a thing that keeps being saved. Take your time on the square before you go in.

tours.title: Sainte-Chapelle
tours.shortDescription: A royal reliquary chapel that is really a cage of stained glass — fifteen towering windows of medieval light.
tours.longDescription: Built by Louis IX in the 1240s inside the royal palace to house the Crown of Thorns, Sainte-Chapelle is the purest expression of the High Gothic: the upper chapel's walls dissolve into fifteen 15-metre windows carrying more than a thousand scenes of stained glass. The structure is a container for something precious, and the effect on a bright day is of standing inside a jewel.

stops.title: Sainte-Chapelle
stops.caption: A royal reliquary chapel that is really a cage of stained glass — fifteen towering windows of medieval light.
stops.transcriptText:
Here's a question to hold as you go in: what does a building look like when its entire purpose is to be a container for something precious?

You're at Sainte-Chapelle, tucked inside a courtyard of the old royal palace on the Île de la Cité — these days ringed by the city's law courts, which is why you came through security to reach it. There are two chapels stacked one on top of the other. The lower one, where you start, is low and dim, and was for the palace servants. Don't linger. Take the narrow spiral stair up.

Because the upper chapel is one of the great rooms in Europe, and walking into it does something to people. The walls are essentially gone. In their place: fifteen windows, each more than fifteen metres tall, almost the whole surface of the room turned to stained glass — over a thousand small scenes, glowing, with barely any stone visible between them. On a bright day it feels less like a room than like standing inside a lantern.

Now the gift, and it explains everything. This was built in the twelve hundreds by King Louis the Ninth to house a single object: the Crown of Thorns, the relic he believed Christ had worn, which he had bought from the emperor in Constantinople. And here's the detail nobody forgets — he paid more than three times as much for the relic as he spent building this entire chapel to keep it in. The container cost a fraction of what went inside it.

That's the reframe. Sainte-Chapelle isn't a church that happens to have beautiful windows. It's a reliquary — one of those jewelled gold boxes made to hold a holy object — except scaled up to the size of a building, with the gems swapped for coloured light. You're not standing in a chapel admiring the decoration. You're standing inside the jewellery box. Find a seat, look up, and let it work on you.

tours.title: Conciergerie
tours.shortDescription: The oldest surviving piece of the medieval royal palace — later the Revolution's antechamber to the guillotine.
tours.longDescription: A long pale riverfront of round towers on the Île de la Cité, the Conciergerie is the remnant of the Capetian kings' palace and holds one of the largest surviving medieval halls in Europe. During the Terror it became a prison and revolutionary tribunal; Marie-Antoinette was held here before her execution. Power, justice and death share one address.

stops.title: Conciergerie
stops.caption: The oldest surviving piece of the medieval royal palace — later the Revolution's antechamber to the guillotine.
stops.transcriptText:
For a thousand years, this riverbank has been the address of power in Paris — and this building is the oldest piece of it left.

You're looking at the Conciergerie from across the water, or from the embankment beneath it: a long pale wall on the Île de la Cité, with round towers and pointed, cone-shaped roofs rising over the Seine. It doesn't look like much from the outside. Inside is one of the largest medieval halls anywhere in Europe.

This was the royal palace — the seat of the kings of France for some four hundred years, before they moved on to the Louvre and beyond. When they left, the building stayed in the business of the state: it became a courthouse and a prison. Step inside and you'll find the Hall of the Men-at-Arms, a vast vaulted Gothic space the size of a cathedral nave, built to feed and house the royal staff — thousands of them.

But that's not what most people come for, and it's the gift, though a heavy one. During the French Revolution, in the worst stretch known as the Terror, this prison became the last stop before the guillotine. The revolutionary court sat upstairs; the cells were down here; and over a few months, something like twenty-six hundred people passed through on their way to execution. The most famous was the queen, Marie-Antoinette, held here through the autumn of 1793. The cell where she spent her final weeks is now a small, quiet chapel.

Here's the reframe to stand with. The palace of kings became the place a queen was sent to die. The same walls, the same riverbank, the same idea — that this is the spot where France decides things — carried straight through from monarchy to revolution without missing a beat. Power kept its address; it only changed who held the key. Today, fittingly, the buildings alongside are still the nation's law courts.

This is a sombre place — treat it gently. When you step back out onto the embankment, the river and the islands are still there, beautiful and indifferent, which is its own kind of relief.

tours.title: Île Saint-Louis
tours.shortDescription: A whole island of Paris built at once around 1640 and left almost untouched ever since.
tours.longDescription: The smaller, quieter island in the Seine behind Notre-Dame, the Île Saint-Louis was laid out as a single speculative development around 1640 — uniform pale stone, tall shuttered windows, even rooflines street after street. It has the rare coherence of a place made all at once and never redeveloped, best felt walking the Rue Saint-Louis-en-l'Île or the stone quays.

stops.title: Île Saint-Louis
stops.caption: A whole island of Paris built at once around 1640 and left almost untouched ever since.
stops.transcriptText:
Most of Paris was torn up and rebuilt at some point. This little island is the rare patch that got it right the first time, around the year sixteen forty, and was simply left alone ever after.

You're on the Île Saint-Louis — the smaller, quieter of the two islands in the Seine, just behind Notre-Dame. The best way to feel it is to walk down the single street that runs the length of the island, the Rue Saint-Louis-en-l'Île, or along the stone quays at the water's edge. Notice how even it all is: the same pale stone, the same tall shuttered windows, the same rooflines, street after street.

That evenness is the gift, and it's no accident. For most of its history this was two muddy, empty islets, used for grazing cattle and stacking firewood. Then, in the early sixteen hundreds, a developer struck a deal with the king, joined the islets into one, threw a couple of bridges across, laid out a grid of streets, and built the whole thing as a single project — rows of elegant private mansions for people with money. It was, more or less, a luxury property development, four hundred years ago.

And it worked so well that almost nothing has happened since. There's no Métro station on the island. No grand monument, no department store, no through-traffic to speak of. Even the ice cream is part of the legend: Berthillon, made here since the nineteen fifties, draws a crowd that is often the busiest thing on the island.

Here's the reframe. When Baron Haussmann drove his great boulevards through Paris in the eighteen hundreds, flattening medieval neighbourhoods by the thousand, he largely left this island alone — because it was already finished, already elegant, already complete. The reward for getting it right early was never being torn down and done over. You're walking through the seventeenth century, still lived in. Slow down to its pace. That's the whole point of the place.

tours.title: Louvre
tours.shortDescription: The world's most-visited museum — and, in the building itself, eight centuries of French power made visible.
tours.longDescription: A medieval fortress that became a royal palace and then the greatest public museum on earth, the Louvre wraps its collections in the architecture of the French monarchy. I. M. Pei's glass pyramid, dropped into the Cour Napoléon in 1989 and furiously resisted at the time, is now the building's signature — the argument that old and new can share one courtyard.

stops.title: Louvre
stops.caption: The world's most-visited museum — and, in the building itself, eight centuries of French power made visible.
stops.transcriptText:
You could spend an entire day inside this building, see one of the great art collections on earth, and still have missed the biggest exhibit — which is the building itself.

You're standing in the main courtyard, the Cour Napoléon, ringed on three sides by the long ornate wings of a Renaissance palace, with a glass pyramid rising out of the paving in front of you. Start with the pyramid, because it's the argument.

When it opened in 1989 — glass and steel, designed by the architect I.M. Pei, dropped right into the middle of a centuries-old royal palace — much of Paris hated it. It was called a scar, a joke, a giant diamond in the wrong setting. Today it's as much a symbol of the city as the building behind it. The same thing happens here again and again: this year's outrage becomes next year's icon.

Now wind the building back. The Louvre began, eight hundred years ago, as a fortress — a defensive castle with a moat, guarding the edge of medieval Paris. You can still visit the stone foundations of it, down in the basement; the museum kept its own buried past. Over the centuries the fortress became a palace, expanded by king after king, until Louis the Fourteenth tired of it, moved the whole court out to Versailles in the sixteen eighties, and left this enormous place half-empty.

So what do you do with an abandoned royal palace? After the Revolution, France had an answer: you give it to the public. The Louvre opened as a museum in 1793 — the king's private treasures, now everyone's.

That's the gift to carry inside. The Mona Lisa is in there, and the Venus de Milo, and the crowds around them are enormous. But the real story is the one you're standing in: a war fortress that became a king's palace that became the most-visited museum in the world. Pei's glass pyramid is simply the seam — the visible joint where a palace finally admitted it belonged to everyone.

tours.title: Musée de l'Orangerie
tours.shortDescription: Two plain oval rooms built to hold Monet's Water Lilies — paintings that surround you rather than hang before you.
tours.longDescription: At the Tuileries' edge, the Orangerie was reshaped to Monet's own wishes to display his late Water Lilies: eight vast panels wrapping two oval rooms, unframed and nearly continuous, lit from above. The design makes the paintings an environment rather than objects. Below sits the Walter-Guillaume collection of Cézanne, Renoir, Matisse and Picasso.

stops.title: Musée de l'Orangerie
stops.caption: Two plain oval rooms built to hold Monet's Water Lilies — paintings that surround you rather than hang before you.
stops.transcriptText:
Most paintings hang on a wall and you look at them. These ones surround you, and the difference is the whole point.

You're in the Musée de l'Orangerie, at the edge of the Tuileries garden, in the first of two plain oval rooms. On the curved walls around you, with no frames and almost no gaps, are eight enormous panels of water, lilies, willows and sky — Claude Monet's Water Lilies, painted from the pond in his garden at Giverny. There's nothing else in the room. That's deliberate.

Here's the gift: Monet didn't simply paint these and hand them over. He designed the rooms. The oval shape, the soft natural light from above, the way the panels wrap all the way round with no beginning and no end — he planned every part of it, so that walking in would feel like stepping into the pond itself, surrounded on all sides by water and light. A century before anyone used the phrase "immersive experience," an old man built one out of paint.

And he was old, and nearly blind. Monet worked on these vast canvases through his seventies and eighties, his eyesight failing to cataracts, the colours turning muddy in his own vision even as he laid them down. He offered them to France as a gift — a memorial of peace, made in the shadow of the First World War. They were installed here in 1927, a few months after he died, so he never saw them finished in their rooms.

That's the reframe. People file in expecting some nice paintings of flowers, and instead they go quiet, and they sit, and they stay far longer than they meant to — because it isn't a picture of a pond. It's a room built to put you inside one, the last great work of a man who could barely see, asking only that you sit in the middle and look. There's a bench. Use it. And downstairs is a whole second collection — Cézanne, Renoir, Picasso — if you want more after the quiet.

tours.title: Jardin des Tuileries
tours.shortDescription: The grand formal garden that opens the straight-line 'spine of Paris' running west to the Arc de Triomphe.
tours.longDescription: Laid out for Catherine de' Medici and reshaped by André Le Nôtre in the 1660s, the Tuileries is the oldest and grandest public garden in Paris — gravel avenues, clipped trees and round ponds on a strict axis. Stand on its central path and the line runs on through the Concorde obelisk, up the Champs-Élysées, and dead-centre into the Arc de Triomphe: the deliberate spine of the city.

stops.title: Jardin des Tuileries
stops.caption: The grand formal garden that opens the straight-line 'spine of Paris' running west to the Arc de Triomphe.
stops.transcriptText:
This is the oldest and grandest public garden in Paris, and it's built as a straight line — one you can follow with your eye for kilometres.

You're at the Louvre end of the Jardin des Tuileries. Stand on the central path and look away from the museum, west, down the long gravel avenue with its clipped trees and round ponds. Keep your eye going: that line runs out through the gateway, across the great square beyond, all the way up the Champs-Élysées, and dead-centre into the Arc de Triomphe on the horizon. It's no accident. You're looking down the spine of Paris.

The man who drew that line was André Le Nôtre, the royal gardener, around the sixteen sixties. He took an older garden and reshaped it into the strict, symmetrical, geometric style we now think of as the formal French garden — everything balanced, everything ordered, the sightlines running clean to the horizon. Then he took the same idea and scaled it up into the gardens of Versailles. This was the prototype.

Here's the gift, and it's an absence. For three hundred years there was a palace here — the Tuileries Palace — closing off the end nearest the Louvre. In 1871, during the upheaval of the Paris Commune, it was burned, and later cleared away entirely. That's why the Louvre now opens straight onto the garden with nothing in between: you're standing where a royal palace used to be, looking at the empty space it left behind.

That's the reframe. This garden was designed as a corridor of power — a dead-straight line from the king's palace out to the edge of the world, meant to make anyone standing in it feel the reach of the crown. The palace is gone, the king is gone, and the grand axis they built is now where Parisians drag a green metal chair to the edge of a pond and fall asleep in the sun. The line outlived everything it was meant to glorify.

tours.title: Place Vendôme
tours.shortDescription: An elegant octagonal square built around Louis XIV's ambitions — now the address of the world's great jewellers.
tours.longDescription: Laid out around 1700 in uniform pale façades, Place Vendôme centres on a column raised by Napoleon and cast, it was said, from cannon captured at Austerlitz — toppled during the 1871 Commune and re-erected. A monument to conquest ringed by Cartier, Chanel and the Ritz, the square is Paris turning war into luxury with perfect composure.

stops.title: Place Vendôme
stops.caption: An elegant octagonal square built around Louis XIV's ambitions — now the address of the world's great jewellers.
stops.transcriptText:
A monument to war, ringed by the most expensive shops on earth. Paris has a real talent for turning conquest into luxury, and this square is the purest example of it.

You're in Place Vendôme, an elegant eight-sided square of pale, even façades, laid out for Louis the Fourteenth around the year seventeen hundred. Look at the column in the middle — that's where the story is.

Napoleon put it there, in 1810, to mark his great victory at the Battle of Austerlitz. It's modelled on a famous Roman column, and here's the gift: the bronze that sheaths it, all the way up, was cast from melted-down enemy cannon — guns captured from the Austrian and Russian armies he had just beaten. He took the weapons of the defeated and turned them into a monument to himself, with his own statue on top.

The column has had a violent life of its own. In 1871, during the Paris Commune, a crowd pulled the whole thing down — toppled it into the street as a symbol of empire and war they wanted gone. The painter Gustave Courbet was blamed for encouraging it, and when the column was later raised again, he was handed the bill for the cost — a sum so vast it ruined him, and he fled the country.

Now look around the edges of the square at what shares the address with all that martial glory: Cartier, Boucheron, Van Cleef — the great jewellers — and the Ritz hotel, where Coco Chanel lived for decades. The most warlike monument in the city stands at the dead centre of its diamond trade. That's the reframe: in Paris, even a pillar of melted cannon ends up surrounded by jewellery. Glory, then money. It tends to go in that order here.

tours.title: Palais-Royal
tours.shortDescription: The calmest courtyard in central Paris — once its loudest room, where the Revolution was talked into being.
tours.longDescription: Built for Cardinal Richelieu and later opened to cafés, shops and pamphleteers, the Palais-Royal's arcaded garden was the political hothouse where crowds gathered on the eve of 1789. Today its inner court holds Daniel Buren's field of black-and-white striped columns — a 1980s modern intervention the city first denounced and then embraced, exactly as it did the Louvre pyramid.

stops.title: Palais-Royal
stops.caption: The calmest courtyard in central Paris — once its loudest room, where the Revolution was talked into being.
stops.transcriptText:
The calmest courtyard in central Paris was once its loudest room — the place where, more or less, the French Revolution was talked into happening.

You're at the Palais-Royal, just across from the Louvre. Walk into the inner courtyard and you'll meet the surprise first: a grid of black-and-white striped columns, of varying heights, set into the stone like a field of candy-striped stumps. People sit on them, children leap between them, visitors photograph their feet on them. When the artist Daniel Buren installed them in the nineteen eighties, the city was furious — another modern outrage dropped into a historic setting, just like the Louvre pyramid. And just like the pyramid, the city came round.

Walk on through into the garden behind — arcades on all four sides, lime trees, fountains, one of the quietest green spaces in the middle of the city. Which is the gift, because it's so hard to believe what this place used to be.

In the seventeen eighties, the owner lined these arcades with cafés, bookshops, gambling rooms and theatres. And because this was private royal property, the king's police were not allowed inside — which made it the one place in Paris where you could say anything at all. Radicals, pamphleteers and gossips packed it day and night. In July 1789, a young man named Camille Desmoulins climbed onto a café table here and called the crowd to arms — and two days later, the Bastille fell.

That's the reframe to stand with in all this quiet. This peaceful garden, where people now read on benches in the shade, was the free-speech engine of a revolution — a shopping arcade that helped bring down a monarchy. The stripes that once scandalised the city are simply part of the calm now. Give it long enough, and Paris absorbs almost anything.

tours.title: Arc de Triomphe
tours.shortDescription: Napoleon's giant triumphal arch at the hub of twelve avenues, guarding the Unknown Soldier's eternal flame.
tours.longDescription: Ordered by Napoleon in 1806 after Austerlitz and finished in 1836, the Arc de Triomphe is a Roman triumphal arch scaled beyond anything Rome attempted — nearly 50 metres tall — carved with reliefs including Rude's roaring 'Departure of the Volunteers'. Beneath it lies France's Unknown Soldier and, since 1923, an eternal flame rekindled every evening. Twelve avenues spin out from its roundabout.

stops.title: Arc de Triomphe
stops.caption: Napoleon's giant triumphal arch at the hub of twelve avenues, guarding the Unknown Soldier's eternal flame.
stops.transcriptText:
Stand on the wide stone terrace at the base of the arch, with the twelve avenues spinning out around you and the long straight pull of the Champs-Élysées falling away to one side. If you can hear traffic coming from every direction at once, you're in the right place — this is the centre of a roundabout that twelve roads feed into, which is why you reached the arch through a tunnel under the road, not across it.

Look up first. Napoleon ordered this arch built in 1806, the year after his great victory at Austerlitz, as a monument to his armies — a Roman triumphal arch scaled up to a size Rome never attempted, nearly fifty metres tall. He wanted his soldiers to march home through it.

They never did. The arch took thirty years to finish, and Napoleon was dead fifteen years before the last stone went in — exiled, defeated, buried on a rock in the South Atlantic. The only time he ever passed beneath it was in 1840, when France brought his body home and the funeral procession carried his coffin through the arch on its way to the tomb. The emperor's triumphal arch received him exactly once, as a corpse.

Walk in under the vault and look at the walls. They're carved with the names of victories and the generals who won them — hundreds of names, a stone index of the empire's wars. On the outer face, toward the avenue, a group of figures surges forward behind a winged woman with her mouth open in a shout: that's the relief everyone calls La Marseillaise, the volunteers of 1792 marching off to war.

And then, on the ground, at the centre of all that carved glory, there's a plain slab and a low flame. That's the grave of the Unknown Soldier — one unidentified French body from the First World War, buried here just after it ended, to stand for all the missing. Every evening at half past six, someone relights the flame.

So the grandest monument to one named man's ambition ended up keeping watch over the most deliberately nameless grave in France. Stay until the flame is rekindled if you can — it has burned without going out since 1923, longer than almost anyone now standing around it has been alive.

tours.title: Champs-Élysées
tours.shortDescription: The 'most famous avenue in the world' — nearly two kilometres of straight ceremonial rise from obelisk to arch.
tours.longDescription: Named for the Elysian Fields of Greek myth, the Champs-Élysées began as Le Nôtre's tree-lined extension of the Tuileries view in the 1660s and grew into the ceremonial spine of the nation, host to Bastille Day parades and the Tour de France finish. Running dead-straight from the Concorde obelisk up to the Arc de Triomphe, it is as much stage-set as street.

stops.title: Champs-Élysées
stops.caption: The 'most famous avenue in the world' — nearly two kilometres of straight ceremonial rise from obelisk to arch.
stops.transcriptText:
You're standing on the most famous avenue in the world, which is a strange thing for a road to be, so it's worth asking what you're actually looking at. Face uphill, toward the arch on the horizon — that long, dead-straight rise ahead of you is the Champs-Élysées, almost two kilometres of it, running from the obelisk down at one end up to the arch at the other.

Start with the name. Champs-Élysées means the Elysian Fields — in Greek myth, the paradise where the souls of heroes go after death, the fields of the blessed. It's a grand thing to call a street. And for a long time it wasn't a street at all: this was marshy ground and market gardens outside the city, until the royal gardener André Le Nôtre extended the avenue out from the Tuileries in the 1660s, planting a long straight promenade of trees so the view from the palace would run on forever.

That's the thing to hold onto here — the Champs-Élysées was designed as a view before it was ever a destination. It's the middle stretch of a single line the French call the historic axis, running from the Louvre through the gardens and straight out to the arch and beyond. You're not standing on a road so much as inside a sightline.

Now look at what fills it. The lower half, nearer the obelisk, is still mostly green — gardens and trees with a couple of grand glass-roofed halls tucked among them. The upper half, where you probably are, is the famous part: wide walkways, café terraces, flagship stores selling cars and clothes and perfume to people from everywhere on earth.

So you've got an avenue named for paradise that began as a swamp, was built as a view for a king, and is now lined with shops selling luxury to the world. Every layer is still here if you look for it.

It earns its fame twice a year, when the whole width of it clears: once in July, when the cyclists of the Tour de France come sprinting up to the finish, and once on the national day, when the military parade comes down the other way. The rest of the time it's just a very long, very busy walk uphill — toward a paradise that turns out, when you reach it, to be a roundabout.

tours.title: Place de la Concorde
tours.shortDescription: The largest square in Paris — a royal plaza that became the Revolution's killing ground, now crowned by an obelisk.
tours.longDescription: Opened in the 1750s as Place Louis XV, renamed Place de la Révolution when the guillotine stood here and Louis XVI, Marie-Antoinette and over a thousand others were executed, it was finally named Concorde — concord — as an act of healing. The 3,300-year-old Luxor obelisk, a gift from Egypt, now rises where the scaffold stood, flanked by fountains and long views down every axis of the city.

stops.title: Place de la Concorde
stops.caption: The largest square in Paris — a royal plaza that became the Revolution's killing ground, now crowned by an obelisk.
stops.transcriptText:
You're standing in the largest square in Paris, and one of the most beautiful — open on every side, with fountains, long views down to the river and the gardens and the avenue, and a gold-tipped Egyptian column at the centre. Find that tall stone needle in the middle; it's your anchor for this one.

The square has had three names, and the order of them tells the whole story. It opened in the 1750s as Place Louis the Fifteenth, laid out around a statue of the king on horseback — a royal square, named for a living monarch. During the Revolution the statue came down, the square was renamed Place de la Révolution, and for a few years in the 1790s it became the main stage of the Terror: the guillotine stood here, roughly where the column now rises, and more than a thousand people were executed on this ground, the king and queen among them.

When the killing was over, the square was given its third and final name — Place de la Concorde. Concorde means harmony, agreement, reconciliation. It was chosen deliberately, to close the wound: a name meant to make people forget what had happened on the stones under their feet.

Now look at what stands on the exact spot. Not a French king, not a Revolutionary hero — a three-thousand-year-old Egyptian obelisk from the temple at Luxor, given to France in the 1830s and raised here in 1836. It is the single most neutral object you could possibly put in this place. It belongs to no side in any French quarrel; it predates the whole argument by millennia.

And that, almost certainly, is the point. Faced with the one patch of ground in Paris that nobody could agree how to mark, the city imported something so old and so foreign that it carried no French meaning at all — and set it down precisely where the guillotine had stood.

So the prettiest square in the city is also its quietest act of forgetting. Stand by the obelisk a moment. The fountains, the gold, the open sky — all of it arranged, very deliberately, over a place the city decided it would rather not remember.

tours.title: Grand Palais
tours.shortDescription: A Beaux-Arts stone shell wrapped around the largest glass-and-iron hall in Paris — built for one summer, kept for good.
tours.longDescription: Raised for the 1900 Exposition Universelle as a temporary showpiece, the Grand Palais hides beneath its masonry a single vast nave roofed entirely in glass and steel, with bronze chariots galloping along its corners. Meant to come down, it never did — and after a long restoration reopened as one of the city's great exhibition halls, an engineering flourish the age couldn't bear to lose.

stops.title: Grand Palais
stops.caption: A Beaux-Arts stone shell wrapped around the largest glass-and-iron hall in Paris — built for one summer, kept for good.
stops.transcriptText:
Stand back far enough to see the roof, because the roof is the whole point. You're looking at the Grand Palais — a long stone building on the outside, but under that masonry a single vast hall roofed entirely in glass and iron, a great curved canopy held up on a web of pale steel, with bronze chariots driven by winged figures galloping along the rooflines at the corners. Find the glass; that's what you came for.

Here's the thing worth knowing. The Grand Palais was never meant to last. It was thrown up for the World's Fair of 1900 — the Exposition Universelle, the same kind of event the Eiffel Tower had been built for eleven years earlier — as a temporary showpiece, a hall to display the art and industry of the age for one summer and then, in theory, come down.

It didn't come down. Like the tower a short distance away, the temporary thing turned out to be too good, too useful and too loved to remove, so it stayed, and became one of the great exhibition halls of Europe. The glass roof is among the largest of its kind on the continent, and on a bright day the whole interior fills with daylight in a way no electric hall ever quite matches.

And there's a neat twist to what's going on inside it now. The Pompidou Centre, the big modern-art museum across the river in the Marais, closed in 2025 for years of renovation, and a good part of its displaced programme has moved in here. So the building made to be temporary, the one that refused to leave, has become the temporary home for a museum that had to.

There's something very Parisian in that — a hall built for a single summer in 1900, still standing a hundred and twenty-odd years later, quietly taking in the homeless masterpieces of a younger museum until that one sorts itself out. If you can get in under that glass, for a show or an event, look up: the roof is the real exhibit, and always was.

tours.title: Pont Alexandre III & Petit Palais
tours.shortDescription: The most extravagant bridge in Paris — every gilded cherub on it a diplomatic toast to a Franco-Russian alliance.
tours.longDescription: Built for the 1900 Exposition and named for Tsar Alexander III, the Pont Alexandre III celebrates the 1890s Franco-Russian alliance in gold: four tall columns topped by gilded winged figures, a deck crusted with nymphs, cherubs and sea-creatures. Its low single steel arch was engineered not to block the view of the Invalides. Beside it the Petit Palais holds the city's fine-arts museum, free to enter.

stops.title: Pont Alexandre III & Petit Palais
stops.caption: The most extravagant bridge in Paris — every gilded cherub on it a diplomatic toast to a Franco-Russian alliance.
stops.transcriptText:
You're on what's generally agreed to be the most extravagant bridge in Paris, so take a second to look at it rather than across it. At each of the four corners stands a tall stone column topped with a gilded winged figure catching the light; the whole deck is crusted with cherubs, nymphs, sea-creatures and garlands in bronze and gold; and lamps on curling iron stems run the length of it. Walk to the middle and look back at one of the gold figures on its column.

Now, the question this bridge quietly answers: why is it quite this much? The answer is politics. The Pont Alexandre III is named for a Russian tsar, Alexander the Third, and it was built to celebrate a brand-new alliance between France and Russia in the 1890s. The foundation stone was laid by the tsar's son, Nicholas the Second, and every gilded flourish on it is, in effect, a diplomatic toast — a friendship between two nations cast in metal and laid across the river. The most romantic bridge in Paris is a piece of statecraft.

It's also a piece of clever engineering. Look at how flat it is — it crosses the whole river in one low, shallow arch of steel, with almost no hump in the middle. That was deliberate. The bridge sits on a straight line between the gold dome of the Invalides on one bank and the great glass halls on the other, and it was built low on purpose so it wouldn't block that view. All that decoration sits on top of a very disciplined idea.

And look across to the smaller of the two glass-roofed palaces on the far bank — the Petit Palais. It went up for the same World's Fair, in 1900, as the bridge and its bigger neighbour; today it's the city's own fine-art museum, and unlike almost everything else around here, walking in to see the collection costs nothing.

So this corner of Paris is essentially one very good year — 1900 — frozen in iron and gold: a bridge built to flatter a tsar, two palaces built to show off to the world, all of it arranged around a single straight view. Lean on the rail a while. Few cities ever spent quite this lavishly on a river crossing, and fewer still left it standing.

tours.title: Place des Vosges
tours.shortDescription: The oldest planned square in Paris — matching red-brick pavilions around a quiet garden in the Marais.
tours.longDescription: Completed in 1612 as Place Royale, the Place des Vosges is the prototype of the European residential square: thirty-six symmetrical pavilions of red brick and pale stone over arcades, framing a formal garden. Victor Hugo lived at number 6, now a museum. Uniform, calm and enclosed, it set the pattern that London and other cities would follow.

stops.title: Place des Vosges
stops.caption: The oldest planned square in Paris — matching red-brick pavilions around a quiet garden in the Marais.
stops.transcriptText:
Walk into the middle of the square and turn slowly all the way around, because the whole point of this place is that every side looks the same. Thirty-six houses of warm red brick and pale stone, identical pitched roofs, a continuous covered arcade running around all four sides at ground level — and a quiet garden of clipped trees and fountains in the centre, where you're standing. Pick a bench.

Here's what you're looking at: the first of its kind. Before this, Paris had no planned squares — it grew as a medieval tangle of streets. Then King Henri the Fourth decided, around 1605, to impose a single unified design on one open space: every facade matched, built to one plan, around a central garden. It was called the Place Royale, and it worked so well that it became the template — every grand square laid out in Paris and across Europe in the two centuries that followed owes something to this one. You're standing in the original.

Look at the two taller pavilions facing each other across the garden, one on the north side and one on the south — those were the King's and the Queen's, slightly grander than the rest, marking the axis.

Now, the name. It isn't "Royale" anymore — it's Place des Vosges, and the reason is wonderfully unromantic. In 1800 the new revolutionary government renamed it to honour the Vosges, a region in eastern France — specifically because the Vosges had been the first department in the country to pay its taxes in full. The most beautiful square in Paris is named, in effect, after the most punctual taxpayers in France.

One corner holds another draw: at number six, the house where Victor Hugo lived for sixteen years and worked on Les Misérables. It's a museum now, and it's free.

So: the square that invented the square, renamed for an accountant's gold star. Sit a while under the arcades. It has looked almost exactly like this for four hundred years — which, in a city that keeps tearing itself down and starting again, is its own quiet miracle.

tours.title: Centre Pompidou
tours.shortDescription: The building turned inside out — pipes and escalators on the outside so the galleries inside could be free.
tours.longDescription: Renzo Piano and Richard Rogers's 1977 Centre Pompidou scandalised Paris by hanging its structure, ducts and escalators on the exterior in primary colours, freeing vast open floors inside for the national collection of modern art. Loved and loathed in equal measure, it made the machinery of a building its architecture — and gave the city a rooftop view worth the climb.

stops.title: Centre Pompidou
stops.caption: The building turned inside out — pipes and escalators on the outside so the galleries inside could be free.
stops.transcriptText:
Stand back on the sloping open square in front of the building and just take in the facade, because there's nothing else in Paris that looks remotely like it. You're looking at a giant glass-and-steel box with all its insides on the outside: pipes, ducts, struts, and a glass tube of escalators climbing diagonally across the front — all of it painted in bright colours. That's the Centre Pompidou, and right now that facade is the whole show. The building closed in 2025 for a long renovation and won't reopen until the end of the decade, so we're here for the idea, not the art.

And the idea is genuinely radical. When two young, almost unknown architects — Renzo Piano and Richard Rogers — won the competition to design it in the early 1970s, they did something nobody had dared at this scale: they turned the building inside out. Every pipe, every duct, every stairway and structural beam was pushed onto the exterior, so that the inside could be left completely open — vast clear floors with nothing in the way, free to be rearranged however an exhibition needed.

Now look at the colours, because they aren't decoration — they're a code. Blue is for air, green for water, yellow for electricity, and the bright red is for movement: the escalators and the lifts that carry people. Once you know that, you can read the building like a diagram of its own organs.
