When it opened in 1977, plenty of Parisians hated it — they said it looked like an oil refinery dropped into the medieval Marais. Half a century later it's one of the most loved buildings in the city, and the open plaza in front, sloping down toward the entrance, has become exactly the kind of public gathering place its architects hoped for.

There's a small irony in the timing. A building designed to be endlessly flexible, easy to adapt and change — and here it is, shut for years for a top-to-bottom overhaul. Even the most adaptable buildings, it turns out, eventually have to close for repairs.

tours.title: Musée Picasso
tours.shortDescription: The world's greatest Picasso collection, housed in a grand 17th-century Marais mansion built on a salt fortune.
tours.longDescription: The Hôtel Salé, a lavish 1650s Marais mansion whose nickname recalls the salt-tax fortune that paid for it, holds the national Picasso collection — thousands of works the artist kept, given to the French state in lieu of inheritance tax after his death. The pairing of Baroque mansion and restless modern master is the point: one century's grandeur housing another's revolution.

stops.title: Musée Picasso
stops.caption: The world's greatest Picasso collection, housed in a grand 17th-century Marais mansion built on a salt fortune.
stops.transcriptText:
You're in front of the Hôtel Salé, one of the grandest private mansions in the Marais — a great seventeenth-century townhouse with a deep courtyard, carved stonework, and a sweeping staircase inside. It holds the largest public collection of Picasso's work anywhere in the world. Before you go in, two stories about how all this came to be — and both of them, oddly, are about tax.

Start with the house. It was built around 1660 for a man who had grown rich collecting the salt tax — the deeply unpopular levy on salt that the French crown imposed for centuries. The nickname stuck: locals called it the Hôtel Salé, the "salted mansion," a little dig at the source of the money. So the building itself is a monument to a tax.

Now the collection. When Picasso died in 1973 he left an enormous body of work — thousands of paintings, sculptures and drawings, the pieces he'd kept for himself across a seventy-year career. His heirs faced a vast inheritance-tax bill. And French law allowed something unusual: instead of paying in cash, they could pay the state in artworks of equivalent value. So they did — and the French nation acquired, as a tax payment, one of the greatest concentrations of Picasso anywhere on earth. The museum opened here in 1985 to house it.

So look at what you have. A mansion built by a salt-tax collector, now holding a collection assembled entirely from a tax paid in art. The whole place exists because of money owed to the government — twice over, three centuries apart.

There's something fitting in that. Picasso spent his life turning ordinary things — a bicycle seat, a sheet of newspaper, a scrap of metal — into art the state would one day chase. And in the end, his own art became the currency that settled the bill. Go in and find the bull's head made from a bicycle: handlebars and a seat, nothing more, and unmistakably a bull.

tours.title: Hôtel de Ville
tours.shortDescription: Paris's city hall for seven centuries — a lavish Renaissance-revival rebuild of the palace the Commune burned.
tours.longDescription: The seat of Paris's municipal government since 1357, the Hôtel de Ville faces a square that was for centuries the city's place of execution and, later, of revolution. The building the Commune burned in 1871 was rebuilt in exuberant Renaissance-revival style, its façade crowded with statues of French worthies. The square before it is now a civic stage — skating in winter, screens for great events.

stops.title: Hôtel de Ville
stops.caption: Paris's city hall for seven centuries — a lavish Renaissance-revival rebuild of the palace the Commune burned.
stops.transcriptText:
Stand in the open square facing the main facade — a long, ornate building bristling with statues, turrets and a high central pavilion, looking every bit the grand Renaissance palace. Here's the catch: almost none of what you're looking at is as old as it appears. This is the Hôtel de Ville, the seat of Paris's city government, and it has stood on this exact spot for more than seven centuries — but the building in front of you is essentially a careful copy of itself.

The original Renaissance city hall stood here for three hundred years. Then, in 1871, in the violent final days of the Paris Commune — the radical uprising that briefly seized the city — it was deliberately set alight as the rebels retreated, and it burned to the ground. When the city rebuilt it, between the 1870s and the 1890s, it chose not to modernise but to recreate: a near-replica of the lost Renaissance facade, only larger and more elaborate. What you see is a nineteenth-century reconstruction wearing a sixteenth-century face.

Now look at the open ground you're standing on, because it has a hard past and a strange legacy. For centuries this was the Place de Grève, the city's main square for public executions. But the word grève — which simply meant the sloping, gravelly riverbank here — gave the French language something unexpected. Out-of-work labourers used to gather on this open ground waiting to be hired, and to this day the French phrase for being on strike, en grève, comes straight from the name of this square.

So you're standing on the spot where, for hundreds of years, the city punished people, hired people, and governed people — all in the same place.

One more. In August 1944, when Paris was liberated, it was from a window of this building that General de Gaulle addressed the freed city. The square that had seen so much of Paris's hardest history was also where it celebrated its freedom.

tours.title: Musée Carnavalet
tours.shortDescription: The museum of the history of Paris itself, in two joined Marais mansions — and free to enter.
tours.longDescription: Spread through two grand Marais hôtels particuliers, the Carnavalet tells the story of Paris from prehistory to now — Revolutionary relics, shop signs, whole reconstructed interiors, Proust's cork-lined bedroom. It is the city examining itself, room by room, and admission to the permanent collection is free.

stops.title: Musée Carnavalet
stops.caption: The museum of the history of Paris itself, in two joined Marais mansions — and free to enter.
stops.transcriptText:
You're outside the Musée Carnavalet, spread across two linked mansions in the heart of the Marais, and it may be the most generous museum in Paris — because it's devoted entirely to the story of the city you're standing in, and it costs nothing to enter.

Start with the building, because its name is a small joke history played. The main mansion was once owned by a Breton noblewoman whose surname Parisians found unpronounceable, so they mangled it — and the mangled version, Carnavalet, stuck so hard it became the building's name, and then the museum's. A garbled name is the most Parisian thing imaginable: the city heard something foreign and simply reshaped it to suit itself.

Inside is the city's autobiography, told through the things it couldn't bear to throw away. Old painted shop signs that once hung over streets long since rebuilt. Carved panels rescued from demolished ballrooms. Relics of the Revolution. A model of the city as it looked centuries ago. And, reconstructed room by room, the actual cork-lined bedroom where Marcel Proust wrote much of his great novel, sealing himself off from noise and daylight to chase his own memories.

That's really the thread of the whole place. This isn't a museum of masterpieces brought in from elsewhere — it's a hoard of the city's own discarded pieces, the fragments Paris saved as it endlessly rebuilt itself. Every shop sign and staircase and bedroom here is something the city outgrew but couldn't quite let go of.

So if you want to understand how Paris became Paris — how the medieval town became the Revolutionary capital became the modern city — this is the place, assembled out of its own leftovers. And the city, fittingly, lets you in for free. Walk through it slowly. You're reading the autobiography of the ground beneath your feet.

tours.title: Panthéon
tours.shortDescription: A church that became the shrine of the Republic's great — and the place Foucault proved the Earth turns.
tours.longDescription: Begun as a church to Sainte-Geneviève and completed just as the Revolution arrived, the Panthéon was reassigned as a mausoleum for the nation's heroes: Voltaire, Rousseau, Hugo, the Curies, more. Its vast Neoclassical dome crowns the Left Bank hill, and from it in 1851 Foucault hung his pendulum to demonstrate the rotation of the Earth — a copy still swings there.

stops.title: Panthéon
stops.caption: A church that became the shrine of the Republic's great — and the place Foucault proved the Earth turns.
stops.transcriptText:
Stand back in the open square to take in the front, because it's pretending to be something it isn't. A row of huge Greek-style columns, a triangular pediment, an enormous dome behind — it looks like an ancient temple, but it's barely two and a half centuries old, and it has spent that whole time unable to decide what it's for.

It began as a church. King Louis the Fifteenth, gravely ill, vowed that if he recovered he would build a magnificent church to Saint Geneviève, the patron saint of Paris. He recovered; the church went up. But it was finished in the late 1700s, just as the Revolution arrived — and the Revolution had no use for a church. So it was converted into a secular temple to honour the nation's great citizens, and carved across the front went the words: To the great men, the grateful homeland. Then it became a church again. Then a temple again. In its first century it flipped back and forth between God and country something like five times.

It settled, finally, as a temple to the great. Down in the crypt lie Voltaire and Rousseau, the writers Hugo and Zola, the scientists Marie and Pierre Curie — Marie the first woman laid here for her own achievements. Above them, under the dome, hangs the real gift of the place.

In 1851 a scientist named Léon Foucault hung a long pendulum from the centre of the dome and set it swinging. Over hours, the direction of its swing slowly turned — not because the pendulum changed, but because the Earth was rotating beneath it. It was the first time anyone had directly, visibly shown that the planet spins, without looking at the sky. People came and watched the floor of the world turn under their feet.

So this is a building that set out to honour God, kept changing its mind, and ended up honouring people — and proving, with a weight on a wire, that the Earth itself moves. A pendulum still swings there today. Stand under it a while and watch the world rotate.

tours.title: Musée de Cluny
tours.shortDescription: The national museum of the Middle Ages, built over Roman baths — home to 'The Lady and the Unicorn'.
tours.longDescription: The Musée de Cluny occupies a late-medieval abbots' mansion grafted onto the surviving vaults of Gallo-Roman baths — two ancient layers of Paris in one building. Its treasure is the six-panel tapestry cycle 'The Lady and the Unicorn', a serene meditation on the senses. Recently reopened after renovation, it is the country's great museum of medieval life.

stops.title: Musée de Cluny
stops.caption: The national museum of the Middle Ages, built over Roman baths — home to 'The Lady and the Unicorn'.
stops.transcriptText:
You're at the Musée de Cluny, the museum of the Middle Ages, and before you even go in, look at the building, because it's two completely different eras stacked on top of each other. The lower portion — those thick stone walls and rounded arches — is Roman: the remains of a vast public bath-house built here nearly two thousand years ago, when this was the Roman town of Lutetia. On top of it sits an elegant late-medieval mansion, raised fifteen hundred years later for a powerful abbot. The museum of the medieval world is housed, literally, in the medieval world built on top of the Roman one.

Inside, you can still walk into the great cold room of the Roman baths — a soaring stone chamber, the best-preserved Roman interior in Paris. But most people come for what hangs upstairs.

In a darkened circular room hang six tapestries known as The Lady and the Unicorn, woven around 1500 and among the most beautiful things to survive from the medieval world. Five of them illustrate the five senses — touch, taste, smell, hearing, sight — each shown as a graceful scene with a noblewoman, a lion and a unicorn. The sixth is the mystery. It shows the lady before a tent bearing the words "To my only desire," and no one has ever fully agreed what it means: a sixth sense, the heart, free will, the giving up of desire. The greatest medieval artwork in France ends on a question nobody can answer.

One more thing to find, near the entrance. A row of large stone heads, battered and noseless — the original heads of the Kings of Judah, hacked off the front of Notre-Dame during the Revolution by a crowd who mistook them for French kings. They were thought lost forever. Then, in 1977, they turned up by accident, buried in the basement of a Paris bank.

So you've got Rome under your feet, a riddle on the wall, and the lost faces of Notre-Dame found under a bank. Few museums pack so much time into one building.

tours.title: Latin Quarter & Shakespeare and Company
tours.shortDescription: The English-language bookshop across from Notre-Dame that has sheltered writers and readers for generations.
tours.longDescription: In the medieval streets of the Latin Quarter, Shakespeare and Company carries the name of Sylvia Beach's legendary interwar shop that first published Joyce's 'Ulysses'. George Whitman's postwar successor, facing Notre-Dame across the Seine, still lets travelling writers — 'Tumbleweeds' — sleep among the shelves in exchange for a little work and a page of reading. It is a working monument to the city's literary life.

stops.title: Latin Quarter & Shakespeare and Company
stops.caption: The English-language bookshop across from Notre-Dame that has sheltered writers and readers for generations.
stops.transcriptText:
You're in the Latin Quarter, the oldest student district in Paris, and the first thing to know is why it's called that — because the answer is hiding in plain sight. For centuries, from the Middle Ages onward, this was the home of the university, and the students and scholars here all spoke and argued and studied in one shared language: Latin. Not because they were Roman, but because Latin was the common tongue of learning across all of Europe — a German, an Italian and an Englishman could all understand one another in it. The quarter is named for a language that nobody has spoken on these streets in two hundred years.

These are some of the oldest, narrowest streets in the city — a tangle of medieval lanes that the great nineteenth-century rebuilding of Paris mostly spared. Wander them and you're walking the same crooked paths students walked seven hundred years ago.

Now find the bookshop facing the river, across from Notre-Dame: Shakespeare and Company, green-fronted, books spilling from every shelf. It's famous — and it's also, in a sense, a loving tribute act. The original Shakespeare and Company was run by an American, Sylvia Beach, in the 1920s; it was the heart of the expatriate writers' scene, and it was she who first published James Joyce's Ulysses when no one else would touch it. That shop closed during the war and never reopened. The one you're looking at was opened later by a different American, George Whitman, who borrowed the name in homage.

He ran it as something more than a shop. Aspiring writers were allowed to sleep among the books — in beds tucked between the shelves — in exchange for a little work and a promise to read. Thousands have, over the years.

So the whole quarter runs on homage: named for a dead language, kept alive by a bookshop that took a dead shop's name. It's a place that honours the past by impersonating it — and somehow stays completely alive doing so.

tours.title: Jardin des Plantes
tours.shortDescription: The royal medicinal garden that became France's national botanical garden, natural-history museum and old menagerie.
tours.longDescription: Founded in 1626 as the king's garden of medicinal plants, the Jardin des Plantes grew into the centre of French natural science: formal flowerbeds, hothouses, one of the world's oldest zoos, and the Muséum national d'Histoire naturelle with its soaring Grande Galerie de l'Évolution. It is where Enlightenment Paris went to classify the living world.

stops.title: Jardin des Plantes
stops.caption: The royal medicinal garden that became France's national botanical garden, natural-history museum and old menagerie.
stops.transcriptText:
You're at the edge of the Jardin des Plantes — the Garden of Plants — which sounds like a pleasant city park and is, in fact, one of the most important pieces of ground in the history of French science. It began, four centuries ago, as something very specific: a medicine garden.

In 1626 the king's physicians laid it out to grow medicinal herbs and teach their properties — a working pharmacy in plant form, the royal garden of healing herbs. But over the next two centuries it grew into something far larger. The greatest French naturalists worked here — the people who first tried to classify all living things, to puzzle out how life was organised and whether species might change over time. The arguments that shaped modern biology in France happened on these paths and in the buildings around you. A garden planted to grow remedies became the place where people worked out the order of life itself.

Walk in and, among the formal flowerbeds, you'll find a small zoo — the menagerie. It's one of the oldest in the world, and its origins are pure Revolution. When the monarchy fell, the exotic animals of the royal court at Versailles, along with creatures seized from travelling fairs, had nowhere to go — so in the 1790s they were brought here, and the menagerie was born from the wreckage of the old regime.

It has seen hard times. During the harsh siege of Paris in the winter of 1870, when the city was cut off and starving, some of its animals were lost to the kitchens — a grim chapter the garden doesn't hide.

Today there's also a grand glass-roofed gallery telling the story of evolution and the staggering variety of animal life. But the garden itself is the real exhibit: four hundred years of curiosity, laid out in neat rows, still growing. Find a bench among the old trees and sit in the middle of it.

tours.title: Musée d'Orsay
tours.shortDescription: A Belle Époque railway station reborn as the world's great museum of Impressionism.
tours.longDescription: Built as the Gare d'Orsay for the 1900 Exposition and saved from demolition in the 1970s, this vaulted Beaux-Arts station now holds the national collection of art from 1848 to 1914 — the supreme gathering of Monet, Renoir, Degas, Van Gogh, Cézanne. The great station clock still tells the time above the galleries, and the old train shed makes the perfect naves for painting.

stops.title: Musée d'Orsay
stops.caption: A Belle Époque railway station reborn as the world's great museum of Impressionism.
stops.transcriptText:
You're looking at the Musée d'Orsay, and the first thing to understand is that it was never meant to be a museum at all — it was built to be a railway station. Stand back and you can still read it: the great arched roof, the vast hall meant for platforms, and high on the facade two enormous round clocks that once told travellers when their trains were leaving.

It went up for the World's Fair of 1900 — the grandest, most central station in Paris, right on the river facing the Louvre. But it had a fatal flaw: its platforms were too short for the longer trains that came later, and within forty years it was effectively useless as a station. For decades it sat half-abandoned, nearly torn down more than once. Then someone had the idea to turn the empty hall into a museum — and it opened, reborn, in 1986.

And here's the lovely fit. The art they filled it with is the art of roughly the same moment the station was built: the second half of the eighteen hundreds, the age of the Impressionists. Monet, Manet, Degas, Renoir, Van Gogh, Cézanne — the painters who walked away from grand historical scenes and started painting the modern world instead: train stations, riverbanks, dancers, ordinary afternoons. They painted the railway age, and now they hang inside a monument to it.

So the building and its contents are the same era talking to each other. The painters captured the new world of steam and leisure; the station was a piece of that new world; and when the trains outgrew it, it became the perfect frame for the pictures.

Don't leave without going up to one of those giant clocks. From behind, the clock face is translucent — you can stand inside the mechanism and look out through the great glass dial at the rooftops of Paris, the city framed inside the very instrument that once governed the timetables. It's the best view in the building, and almost nobody rushes to find it.

tours.title: Jardin du Luxembourg
tours.shortDescription: The Left Bank's beloved garden — sailboats on the basin, green chairs, and a palace now home to the Senate.
tours.longDescription: Created by Marie de' Medici in the 1610s around a palace built to recall her native Florence, the Luxembourg is the Left Bank's living room: gravel terraces, statues of French queens, toy sailboats on the octagonal basin, and rows of movable green chairs. The Palais du Luxembourg now houses the French Senate; the garden belongs to everyone.

stops.title: Jardin du Luxembourg
stops.caption: The Left Bank's beloved garden — sailboats on the basin, green chairs, and a palace now home to the Senate.
stops.transcriptText:
You're in the Jardin du Luxembourg, the most beloved garden on the Left Bank, and the surprising thing about it is that it was built out of one woman's homesickness.

Look toward the large palace at the north end — that's the Luxembourg Palace, home today to the French Senate. It was built in the early sixteen hundreds for Marie de Médicis, the Italian-born queen of France. She was from Florence, and after her husband died she was lonely in Paris, missing the city of her childhood. So she had a palace and gardens built deliberately to recall the Florentine ones she'd grown up among — a piece of Tuscany rebuilt on the far bank of the Seine. The garden you're standing in began as a cure for one queen's longing for home.

Now look at how people use it, because it has a quiet genius. There are almost no fixed benches. Instead, scattered everywhere, are hundreds of those green metal chairs — loose, movable, yours to drag wherever you like. Want sun, shade, the edge of the pond, a spot near friends? Move your chair. It sounds small, but it's why the garden feels less like a park you pass through and more like a vast shared living room you arrange to suit yourself.

Find the big octagonal pond in the centre. On weekends, children push old wooden sailboats out across it with long sticks, the same simple pleasure their great-grandparents had here. Off to one side, half-hidden, is the Medici Fountain — a shaded, romantic grotto Marie built to remember Italy, the most Florentine corner of the whole place.

So this is a homesick queen's Florence, opened up and handed to the city — a private cure for loneliness that became everyone's favourite room. Grab a chair, drag it somewhere that suits you, and stay a while. That's exactly what it's for.

tours.title: Saint-Germain-des-Prés
tours.shortDescription: The oldest church in Paris, at the heart of the postwar quarter of philosophers, jazz and café intellectuals.
tours.longDescription: Its Romanesque bell tower is the oldest in Paris, marking an abbey that dates to the 6th century and was once the most powerful in the city. Around it grew the Saint-Germain-des-Prés of the 20th century — Sartre and de Beauvoir at the Café de Flore and Les Deux Magots, jazz in the cellars, publishing houses on every corner. Faith and philosophy share the same crossroads.

stops.title: Saint-Germain-des-Prés
stops.caption: The oldest church in Paris, at the heart of the postwar quarter of philosophers, jazz and café intellectuals.
stops.transcriptText:
You're standing in front of Saint-Germain-des-Prés — and that stout stone tower ahead of you is, quite possibly, the oldest thing still standing in Paris. There's been an abbey on this spot since the sixth century, and the tower itself goes back about a thousand years, to a time when this was open country outside the city walls — des Prés means "of the meadows." For centuries this was one of the most powerful monasteries in France.

Step inside if it's open; it's plain and ancient and worth a moment. But the strange twist of this place is what happened just outside its doors, much more recently.

In the years after the Second World War, the cafés on the corner here — two in particular, the Café de Flore and Les Deux Magots, almost next door to each other — became the headquarters of French intellectual life. The philosophers Jean-Paul Sartre and Simone de Beauvoir worked at these tables for hours, day after day; the writer Albert Camus was part of the same circle. They sat and wrote and argued over coffee, and out of that café world came existentialism, the philosophy that defined a generation. Down the side streets, jazz clubs filled the cellars. For a couple of decades, this small corner was the centre of the thinking world.

So look at what shares this one intersection: a thousand-year-old abbey church, and the café tables where twentieth-century philosophers reinvented what it meant to be free. The sacred and the secular, faith and philosophy, separated by a few metres of street.

The cafés are still here, still serving — though now you pay handsomely for a coffee at the same tables, and you're more likely to share the room with tourists than philosophers. Sit anyway. The view of that ancient tower, from a café table where modern philosophy was hammered out, is a very Parisian kind of layered.

tours.title: Saint-Sulpice
tours.shortDescription: A vast Left Bank church of mismatched towers, Delacroix murals and a brass meridian line across its floor.
tours.longDescription: The second-largest church in Paris after Notre-Dame, Saint-Sulpice took over a century to build and shows it — its two west towers never matched. Inside are Delacroix's late murals of 'Jacob Wrestling the Angel', one of the world's great organs, and a brass gnomon line that tracks the sun across the floor, a piece of astronomy embedded in a church.

stops.title: Saint-Sulpice
stops.caption: A vast Left Bank church of mismatched towers, Delacroix murals and a brass meridian line across its floor.
stops.transcriptText:
You're in front of Saint-Sulpice, one of the largest churches in Paris — nearly the size of Notre-Dame. Look up at the two towers on the front and you'll notice they don't match: one is plainer, one more ornate. They were built by different architects, decades apart, and the second was never brought into line with the first. The church simply gave up and left them mismatched.

Inside, though, are two genuinely surprising things. The first is set into the floor. Walk toward the north side and you'll find a thin brass strip running across the stone, leading to a tall white marble obelisk. This is a gnomon — an astronomical instrument. A small hole high in a south-facing window lets a single ray of sunlight in, and at noon it falls onto this brass line; where it lands marks the date. The priests built it for a practical reason: to fix the date of Easter each year, which shifts with the sun and the moon. A scientific instrument, built into the floor of a church, to keep the religious calendar honest.

You may have heard of this brass line for the wrong reason. A hugely popular novel claimed it marked an ancient secret meridian tied to a grand conspiracy — none of which is true, and the parish grew annoyed enough to post a notice inside saying so. It's a sun-clock, nothing more, and that's plenty.

The second treasure is in a chapel just inside the door on the right: a set of murals by Eugène Delacroix, among the last great works he ever painted. One shows Jacob wrestling the angel — two figures locked together in a struggle, set against real trees. He worked on them at the very end of his life, and you can feel it; they have the urgency of a painter racing the clock.

So: a machine for tracking the sun set into the floor, and a dying master's final paintings on the wall. Two kinds of light, really — one let in through a pinhole, one mixed on a palette. Stand in the quiet and find them both.

tours.title: Eiffel Tower
tours.shortDescription: The iron tower Paris meant to tear down after twenty years — now the definitive symbol of the city.
tours.longDescription: Built by Gustave Eiffel's engineers for the 1889 Exposition marking the Revolution's centenary, the 300-metre tower was the tallest structure on earth and was fiercely denounced by the city's artists as a monstrous iron chimney. Meant to stand for twenty years, it was saved by its usefulness as a radio mast — and became, against every intention, the emblem of Paris itself.

stops.title: Eiffel Tower
stops.caption: The iron tower Paris meant to tear down after twenty years — now the definitive symbol of the city.
stops.transcriptText:
You're at the foot of the Eiffel Tower, looking up through the iron at the most recognisable structure on earth — so here's the thing almost nobody believes: it was supposed to be temporary, and plenty of Parisians wanted it gone.

It was built for the World's Fair of 1889, to mark a hundred years since the Revolution. Gustave Eiffel's company won the right to put up the tallest structure in the world — three hundred metres of iron, far taller than anything ever made — and the permit ran for twenty years. After that, it was to be taken down and sold for scrap.

And the cultured classes of Paris hated it. A group of the city's most famous artists and writers signed a furious public protest while it was still going up, calling it a monstrous iron eyesore that would disgrace the city. There's a story that the novelist Guy de Maupassant ate lunch in the tower's restaurant every day — because it was the one place in Paris from which he couldn't see the tower itself.

So why is it still here? Not because the city fell in love with it; that came later. It survived because it turned out to be useful. As the twenty-year deadline approached, the tower had become the perfect mount for the brand-new technology of wireless telegraphy — a giant antenna the military didn't want to lose. Radio saved the Eiffel Tower. Sentiment had nothing to do with it; a transmitter on top did.

For forty years it stayed the tallest structure in the world, until New York's skyscrapers finally passed it. It's repainted by hand every few years, and on a hot day it grows — the iron expands and the whole tower stands a little taller in summer than in winter.

So look up again. The symbol of Paris, of France, of romance itself, is a temporary structure that the tastemakers despised and a radio aerial rescued. It only became beloved once it was safe — which may be the most human thing about it.

tours.title: Trocadéro
tours.shortDescription: The great terrace that frames the classic head-on view of the Eiffel Tower across the Seine.
tours.longDescription: The Palais de Chaillot, built for the 1937 Exposition in curving Modern-Classical stone, opens onto a wide terrace and cascading gardens that deliver the postcard view of the Eiffel Tower straight across the river. Home to several museums, the terrace is the city's grandest belvedere — and a stage for gatherings and protests as often as photographs.

stops.title: Trocadéro
stops.caption: The great terrace that frames the classic head-on view of the Eiffel Tower across the Seine.
stops.transcriptText:
You're standing on the Trocadéro terrace, and you came here for one reason: this is the spot. Look across the river and there it is — the Eiffel Tower, head to foot, perfectly framed, the single best place in the whole city to see it whole. This wide stone terrace, with its two great curving wings of a building sweeping away on either side, was practically designed to make you turn your back on it and face the tower.

Which is the quietly funny thing about Trocadéro: it's a grand building, the Palais de Chaillot, raised for a World's Fair in the nineteen thirties — and in most people's minds it doesn't exist as a building at all. It exists as a viewpoint. People arrive, photograph the tower, and leave, having never once looked at the thing they were standing on. It's a monument defined entirely by what it looks at.

But it has had its own moments. On this terrace, in 1948, the nations of the world gathered and adopted the Universal Declaration of Human Rights — the founding statement that all people are born free and equal in dignity and rights. There's an inscription here marking it. So the place tourists treat as a photo backdrop is also where one of the most important documents of the modern age was proclaimed to the world.

Take your photograph — everyone does, and the view earns it. But then turn around for a second and look at the building behind you, and the wide plaza under your feet. Just so you can say you actually saw the place, and not only the view across the river.

tours.title: Champ de Mars
tours.shortDescription: The long green field at the foot of the Eiffel Tower — a former army parade ground turned public lawn.
tours.longDescription: Once the drill field of the military school at its far end, the Champ de Mars staged revolutionary festivals and early Expositions before becoming the great open lawn beneath the Eiffel Tower. Today it is where Paris and the world sit on the grass to look up at the tower — a parade ground turned into the city's front garden.

stops.title: Champ de Mars
stops.caption: The long green field at the foot of the Eiffel Tower — a former army parade ground turned public lawn.
stops.transcriptText:
You're on the Champ de Mars, the long green lawn that runs from the foot of the Eiffel Tower to the elegant old buildings at the far end. Today it's the most relaxed place in Paris — people sprawl on the grass with wine and bread, the tower rising over them. But the name gives away a very different past: Champ de Mars means the Field of Mars, the Roman god of war.

It was a parade ground. Those grand buildings at the far end are the old military academy, and for centuries this lawn was where soldiers drilled and marched — and among the cadets who once trained here was a young officer named Napoleon Bonaparte. The picnic blanket you might be sitting on is spread over a former field of war.

It saw the Revolution up close, too. In 1790, on the first anniversary of the fall of the Bastille, a vast crowd — hundreds of thousands of people — gathered here for an enormous festival of national unity, one of the great hopeful moments of the early Revolution. But the very next year the same ground saw bloodshed, when troops fired on a crowd of protesters gathered here. The Field of Mars lived up to its name.

Now it's grass and tourists and the tower's evening sparkle. There's something to that — that a ground named for war, drilled by armies and marked by the Revolution, has ended up as the gentlest lawn in the city, where the only thing anyone points at the sky is a phone camera. Find a clear patch, lie back, and look straight up at the iron.

tours.title: Les Invalides & Napoleon's Tomb
tours.shortDescription: Louis XIV's veterans' hospital, its gold dome now the tomb of Napoleon.
tours.longDescription: Built by Louis XIV as a home for wounded and aged soldiers, Les Invalides remains a military complex and museum, its Baroque Dôme church one of the high points of French classical architecture. Beneath the gilded dome, in an open crypt of red porphyry, lies Napoleon — moved here in 1840, nested in six coffins, at the centre of the army he led.

stops.title: Les Invalides & Napoleon's Tomb
stops.caption: Louis XIV's veterans' hospital, its gold dome now the tomb of Napoleon.
stops.transcriptText:
You're looking at Les Invalides, and the gold dome rising over it is one of the brightest things in the Paris skyline — covered in real gold leaf, it catches the sun from kilometres away. But the gold is the smaller story here. Look at the long, severe buildings spread out beneath it, because that's where this place begins.

Les Invalides was built in the sixteen seventies by Louis the Fourteenth, the Sun King, for a genuinely humane reason: to house and care for soldiers who had been wounded or grown old in his wars. Before this, broken-down veterans often ended up begging in the streets. This was, in effect, one of the first great veterans' homes and hospitals — a place for the men the wars had used up. Parts of it still serve old soldiers today, alongside a vast military museum.

Now, the dome. The golden church beneath it holds the most famous resident of all: Napoleon. After he died in exile on a remote South Atlantic island, France eventually brought his body home, in 1840, in a solemn procession that passed through the Arc de Triomphe and across the city to here. And then they buried him in extraordinary fashion.

Go in and look down into the open circular crypt at the great reddish-brown stone tomb in the centre. Inside that single massive sarcophagus the emperor's body rests not in one coffin but in six, nested one inside another like a set of Russian dolls — tin, mahogany, two of lead, ebony, and oak. A man who spent his life pushing outward, conquering Europe, sealed at the end inside six layers of box beneath a dome of gold.

There's a hard irony in standing here. The gold dome was raised to shelter the soldiers war had wounded; and at its very centre now lies the general who, more than almost anyone, sent men to be wounded. A home for the broken, watched over by the man who broke so many. Stand at the rail and look down at the tomb a while before you go.

tours.title: Musée Rodin
tours.shortDescription: The sculptor's works set in the mansion and rose garden where he worked — 'The Thinker' among the trees.
tours.longDescription: Rodin gave his work to the French state on condition it be shown in the Hôtel Biron, the elegant 18th-century mansion where he had his studio. The result is a museum as much garden as gallery: 'The Thinker', 'The Gates of Hell' and 'The Burghers of Calais' stand among clipped hedges and roses, sculpture in the open air where the sculptor placed it.

stops.title: Musée Rodin
stops.caption: The sculptor's works set in the mansion and rose garden where he worked — 'The Thinker' among the trees.
stops.transcriptText:
You're at the Musée Rodin, and it might be the most pleasant museum in Paris, because a good half of it is outdoors. This was the Hôtel Biron, a graceful eighteenth-century mansion with large gardens, and in his final years the sculptor Auguste Rodin lived and worked here. He struck a deal with the French state: he would give the nation all of his works, on the condition that the mansion become a museum devoted to them. He died in 1917; the museum opened two years later, and it has been here ever since.

Go into the garden first — that's the point of this place. Set among the roses and clipped hedges and gravel paths are Rodin's great bronzes, out in the open air, weathering and catching the light exactly as, in his view, sculpture was meant to. There's something right about meeting them under the sky rather than in a white room.

Find The Thinker. You know the figure — seated, hunched forward, chin on hand, lost in thought. But here's what most people don't know: he wasn't conceived as a standalone everyman. He began as a small figure meant to sit at the very top of an enormous sculpted doorway Rodin laboured over for decades, called The Gates of Hell, based on Dante's Inferno. And the thinker at the top was Dante himself — the poet, looking down over the damned souls writhing in the gates below, contemplating the whole of human suffering. Only later was he enlarged and set on his own pedestal, where he quietly became a symbol of thought itself.

So the most famous statue of a man thinking is really a poet staring down into Hell. Once you've seen the Gates here in the garden — and you can — you'll never quite see The Thinker the innocent way again.

Take your time among the bronzes. Few museums let you wander the masterpieces with birdsong and open sky around them. This one does, and that's the gift.

tours.title: Musée du Quai Branly – Jacques Chirac
tours.shortDescription: Jean Nouvel's museum of the arts of Africa, Asia, Oceania and the Americas, wrapped in a living green wall.
tours.longDescription: Opened in 2006 near the Eiffel Tower, Jean Nouvel's building dissolves into its garden behind a famous vertical wall of living plants, its galleries a dim, winding path meant to evoke a journey. Inside are the national collections of non-European art — masks, textiles, sculpture from Africa, Asia, Oceania and the Americas — presented as art rather than ethnography, though not without debate.

stops.title: Musée du Quai Branly – Jacques Chirac
stops.caption: Jean Nouvel's museum of the arts of Africa, Asia, Oceania and the Americas, wrapped in a living green wall.
stops.transcriptText:
You're outside the Musée du quai Branly, and even before you go in, the building is doing something unusual — it's trying to disappear into a garden. Look at the wall facing the street: a large part of the facade is alive, a vertical garden of thousands of plants growing straight up the side of the building, a green wall climbing several storeys. The architect, Jean Nouvel, wanted the museum to feel less like a stone monument and more like something half-swallowed by nature, glimpsed through trees.

Inside is a different kind of departure. Where the Louvre and the Orsay tell the story of European art, the quai Branly is devoted to almost everything else — the arts and cultures of Africa, Asia, Oceania and the Americas. Masks, sculptures, textiles, instruments and sacred objects from across the non-Western world, shown not as curiosities but as great art in their own right. When it opened in 2006, that was a central part of its purpose: to put these works on the same footing as anything hanging in the grand European galleries.

It also carries a question it doesn't hide from, and neither will we. Many objects in museums like this one left their original homes long ago, in the age of empire, and how they came to be in Paris — bought, gifted, or taken — is a live and sometimes painful debate. In recent years France has begun returning some pieces to the countries they came from. The museum sits squarely in the middle of one of the real open questions of our time: who should hold the cultural treasures of the world, and where do they truly belong?

You don't have to settle that to be moved by what's inside. Go in, look closely, and let the objects speak for themselves. Then come back out and look at the green wall one more time — a museum slowly being reclaimed by the living world, which feels, somehow, like the right note for everything it holds.

tours.title: Palais Garnier
tours.shortDescription: The most opulent opera house ever built — grand staircase, gilded foyers and the myth of the Phantom below.
tours.longDescription: Charles Garnier's opera house, opened in 1875, is the definition of Second Empire splendour: a marble grand staircase built for the spectacle of arrival, gold-and-red auditorium under a ceiling later painted by Chagall, mirrored foyers like a palace. A real underground lake beneath the building inspired 'The Phantom of the Opera'. It remains a working stage for ballet and opera.

stops.title: Palais Garnier
stops.caption: The most opulent opera house ever built — grand staircase, gilded foyers and the myth of the Phantom below.
stops.transcriptText:
You're in front of the Palais Garnier, the great opera house, and from the outside it already looks like it's showing off — gold, marble, columns, statues, a riot of ornament. That's no accident. When the architect Charles Garnier built it in the eighteen seventies, the building wasn't really designed around the opera. It was designed around the audience.

Step inside, if you can, and you'll see it at once. The grand staircase is enormous, a sweep of marble built so that society could descend it — so that ladies in gowns and gentlemen in tails could see and, more to the point, be seen. The foyers glitter like the halls of a palace. For the wealthy of nineteenth-century Paris, a night at the opera was theatre in both directions: there was a performance on the stage, and there was the performance of the audience itself, dressed and arranged across that staircase. The real show, half the time, was the crowd.

Now, the part you've probably heard of. This building is the setting of The Phantom of the Opera — and the eeriest details of that story are real. There genuinely is water beneath the opera house: a large underground reservoir, built because the ground was so wet during construction that the engineers couldn't drain it, so they enclosed it instead. And in 1896, during a performance, one of the great counterweights of the chandelier broke loose and crashed down into the audience, killing a woman. A writer named Gaston Leroux took the underground water and the falling chandelier and spun them into a novel about a phantom haunting the cellars. The legend grew straight out of the facts.

Look up at the ceiling inside, too, if you get the chance — the colourful painting overhead was added in the nineteen sixties by Marc Chagall, a dreamlike modern ceiling floating above all that old gold.

So: an opera house built mostly so the audience could perform to itself, with a real lake in the basement and a real falling chandelier in its past. The fiction barely had to invent a thing.

tours.title: Galeries Lafayette
tours.shortDescription: The Belle Époque department store crowned by a spectacular stained-glass and steel dome.
tours.longDescription: Opened in 1912, the flagship Galeries Lafayette is as much monument as shop: its great hall rises through galleried balconies to a soaring neo-Byzantine dome of stained glass and steel, a cathedral of consumption from the golden age of the department store. The rooftop terrace offers one of the best free views over the opera district and the city.

stops.title: Galeries Lafayette
stops.caption: The Belle Époque department store crowned by a spectacular stained-glass and steel dome.
stops.transcriptText:
You're inside Galeries Lafayette — and if you've just walked in off the street expecting a department store, stop and look straight up, because you're standing under one of the most beautiful ceilings in Paris. High overhead is an enormous dome of coloured glass and gilded ironwork, glowing like the rose window of a cathedral, with tiers of balconied shopfronts rising all around you toward the light. It's breathtaking — and it's selling handbags.

That's the whole idea, and it was a radical one when this dome went up in 1912. The department store was still a fairly new invention then — the notion of gathering every kind of merchandise under one roof and making the act of shopping itself a glamorous experience. And the people who built these places understood something: if you want buying to feel important, even sacred, you build it like a temple. So they gave it a dome worthy of a church, a soaring central hall, light pouring down from above — all to make purchasing a scarf feel like a visit to somewhere grand. A cathedral of commerce, quite deliberately.

It worked. Crowds came as much for the spectacle as the goods, and the great glass dome became one of the sights of the city in its own right — which is why you'll see plenty of people here, like you, just looking up, not shopping at all.

Before you go, there's a reward most people miss. Head for the rooftop — it's free, and open to anyone. From up there you get a wide, sweeping view across the rooftops of Paris: the opera house just below, and the Eiffel Tower off in the distance. One of the best free views in the city, sitting on top of a shop.

So look up at the dome, then go up to the roof. The store would love to sell you something in between — but it won't insist.

tours.title: La Madeleine
tours.shortDescription: A church that looks exactly like a Greek temple — Napoleon first meant it as a monument to his army.
tours.longDescription: Ringed by 52 Corinthian columns and no visible cross, La Madeleine reads as a Roman temple because that is what Napoleon commissioned — a Temple of Glory to his Grande Armée. Only after his fall was it completed as a church. Inside, a single top-lit nave and Rude's sculpture make it one of the strangest and grandest Neoclassical churches in Paris.

stops.title: La Madeleine
stops.caption: A church that looks exactly like a Greek temple — Napoleon first meant it as a monument to his army.
stops.transcriptText:
You're in front of La Madeleine, and your first question is probably the right one: is this even a church? It doesn't look like one. No spire, no cross on the front, no visible dome — just a huge rectangular box wrapped on every side by fifty-two towering columns, looking for all the world like a Greek or Roman temple lifted out of the ancient world and set down in the middle of Paris. And yet it is a church, a working Catholic one. The disguise is the whole story.

It had a famously confused life. Building started, stopped, and started again over the better part of a century, and during that time nobody could agree what it should be. It began as a church. Then Napoleon halted the work and declared it would instead be a Temple of Glory dedicated to his armies — a monument to soldiers, not to God. Plans were even floated, at various points, to turn it into the city's first grand railway station, or a bank, or a library. Only after Napoleon's fall was it finally finished — as a church again, but keeping the pagan-temple shell it had been given along the way.

So what you're looking at is a building that spent decades unsure whether it honoured a god, an emperor's army, or a train timetable — and ended up a Christian church that looks defiantly like a temple to no god in particular.

Climb the steps and look back the way you came. The Madeleine sits at the head of a straight line that runs across the river to the national parliament — two matching temple-fronts staring at each other across the city, a deliberate piece of grand planning. And inside, behind that severe exterior, it's surprisingly rich and dim and gold; the composer Frédéric Chopin's funeral was held here, with Mozart's Requiem filling the space.

A temple on the outside, a church within, and very nearly a railway station. Only in Paris.

tours.title: Sacré-Cœur
tours.shortDescription: The white domed basilica crowning Montmartre — penance, pilgrimage and the best free view in Paris.
tours.longDescription: Rising on the highest point of the city, the Basilica of the Sacré-Cœur was begun in the 1870s as a national act of penance after the trauma of war and the Commune, and its travertine stone whitens with age and rain. Byzantine in style and deliberately unlike Gothic Paris, it draws pilgrims and crowds to its steps for the sweeping view south over the whole city.

stops.title: Sacré-Cœur
stops.caption: The white domed basilica crowning Montmartre — penance, pilgrimage and the best free view in Paris.
stops.transcriptText:
You're at the foot of Sacré-Cœur, the great white domed church crowning the hill of Montmartre, the highest natural point in Paris. It looks ancient and timeless up there against the sky — and it's actually one of the youngest major monuments in the city. Building only began in the eighteen seventies, and it wasn't finished until just before the First World War.

And the reason it was built is heavier than its sugar-white domes suggest. In 1870 France suffered a catastrophic defeat in a war with Prussia, and in the bitter aftermath Paris tore itself apart in a brief, bloody civil uprising. Out of that double wound — a humiliating defeat abroad and Parisians turning on Parisians at home — came a movement to raise a great church as an act of national penance: an offering to ask forgiveness, to atone for what its backers saw as the nation's sins. Sacré-Cœur is, in its origins, a monument of guilt and mourning, built on the very hill where some of that internal conflict had begun.

That history still makes it quietly contested. To some it's a place of peace and pilgrimage; to others it has always been a victor's monument planted over a wound. Both readings live here together, and it's worth carrying both as you climb the steps.

Now, the thing everyone notices and few can explain: why is it so impossibly white, when every other old stone building in Paris is grey? It's a trick of the stone. The basilica is built from a special pale stone that reacts with rainwater and releases a white, chalky substance as it weathers. So instead of darkening with grime over the years like ordinary stone, Sacré-Cœur effectively washes itself whiter every time it rains. The dirtier the air, the harder it scrubs.

Turn around before you go in. From these steps all of Paris spreads out below you, flat and grey and endless, with the white church glowing at your back. The view is free, and it's one of the great ones.

tours.title: Place du Tertre
tours.shortDescription: The little square at the top of Montmartre where painters still set up their easels among the crowds.
tours.longDescription: A few steps from Sacré-Cœur, the Place du Tertre is the last stronghold of the Montmartre of Picasso, Utrillo and Toulouse-Lautrec, when the hill was a cheap village of artists and windmills. Portraitists and landscape painters still work its cramped, café-ringed square — touristy now, but a direct thread back to the neighbourhood that helped invent modern art.

stops.title: Place du Tertre
stops.caption: The little square at the top of Montmartre where painters still set up their easels among the crowds.
stops.transcriptText:
You're in Place du Tertre, a small square at the top of Montmartre, and right now it's probably packed — easels everywhere, artists offering to paint your portrait or snip your silhouette, crowds threading between the café tables. It can feel like a tourist trap, and in a sense it is. But stand still a moment, because the ground under all of this is the real thing.

A little over a century ago, Montmartre wasn't part of the busy city at all. It was a half-rural village on a hill, covered in windmills and vineyards, with cheap rooms and cheaper wine — which is exactly why poor young artists flocked to it. In the years around 1900, some of the most important painters of the modern age lived and worked within a few streets of where you're standing: names that now fill the world's great museums learned their craft up here, when Montmartre was scruffy and affordable and crackling with new ideas. Down the hill, in a ramshackle warren of artists' studios, Picasso painted the picture that cracked European art wide open.

Then fame did what fame does. The artists became famous, the rents climbed, the village was swallowed by the city, and the real bohemia scattered. What's left in this square is, in a way, a performance of that vanished world — painters working for tourists where geniuses once worked for themselves.

But don't be too cynical about it. They really were here; this really was the place. And if you want proof that it was once countryside, walk a couple of streets over and find it: a small working vineyard still grows on the hillside, rows of vines in the middle of the city, the last green ghost of the rural village Montmartre used to be.

So enjoy the square for what it is, then go find the vineyard for what it was. Both are true at once.

tours.title: Moulin Rouge
tours.shortDescription: The red windmill at the foot of Montmartre — birthplace of the cancan and the modern cabaret.
tours.longDescription: Opened in 1889, the Moulin Rouge and its red windmill made Montmartre the capital of Belle Époque nightlife, birthplace of the frenzied cancan and the subject of Toulouse-Lautrec's posters. It still runs its feathered, sequined revue every night beneath the sails, a survivor of the Pigalle of a century ago trading squarely on its own legend.

stops.title: Moulin Rouge
stops.caption: The red windmill at the foot of Montmartre — birthplace of the cancan and the modern cabaret.
stops.transcriptText:
You're in front of the Moulin Rouge, and the first thing your eye goes to is the red windmill turning on the roof. Here's the thing: it's a fake — a decorative one, built purely for show. But it's a fake with a point, because it's remembering something real.

Montmartre, this whole hill, was once covered in windmills — dozens of real working ones, grinding grain and pressing the grapes from the vineyards that used to blanket the slopes. As the city swallowed the village, the windmills came down one by one. So when this dance hall opened in 1889 — the same year the Eiffel Tower went up across the city — it put a bright red windmill on its roof as a wink to the rural Montmartre that was already disappearing. A monument to the working windmills, in the shape of a glamorous fake one.

And inside, it invented a legend. The Moulin Rouge was the birthplace of the modern cancan — that explosive, high-kicking, swirling-skirts dance that scandalised and thrilled Paris in equal measure. It was loud, athletic, a little outrageous, and utterly new, and it turned this place into the most famous cabaret in the world. The painter Toulouse-Lautrec, himself a fixture here, put its dancers and its dazzle into posters that are now as famous as the club itself.

More than a century on, it's still running, still putting on the spectacle, though the streets around it have slid from bohemian to frankly seedy in places. Look past that to the windmill.

Because that's the quiet story here: the most famous nightspot on earth wears a counterfeit windmill to honour the real ones it helped replace. Glamour built right on top of a vanished rural world — which is Montmartre in a single rooftop.

tours.title: Place des Abbesses & the Wall of Love
tours.shortDescription: A leafy Montmartre square with a rare Art Nouveau Métro entrance and a wall that says 'I love you' 300 times.
tours.longDescription: Reached by one of the last original Guimard Art Nouveau Métro canopies, the Place des Abbesses is the heart of village Montmartre. In the little Square Jehan Rictus beside it, the Wall of Love — 'Le Mur des je t'aime' — spells out 'I love you' in over 300 languages across 40 square metres of dark enamel tiles, a quiet modern pilgrimage.

stops.title: Place des Abbesses & the Wall of Love
stops.caption: A leafy Montmartre square with a rare Art Nouveau Métro entrance and a wall that says 'I love you' 300 times.
stops.transcriptText:
You're in Place des Abbesses, and if the rest of Montmartre felt like a crowded postcard, this is where it turns back into a village. Quieter streets, local cafés, a leafy square — this is the Montmartre that Parisians actually live in.

Start with the entrance to the Métro station here, because it's a small treasure. It's one of the original Art Nouveau station entrances designed by Hector Guimard around 1900 — green cast iron curling like plant stems, with a delicate glass canopy overhead shaped like a dragonfly's wing. Most of these were torn out over the decades; only a couple of the fully glass-roofed ones survive in the whole city, and this is one of them. Parisians once mocked them as ugly; now they're protected treasures and a symbol of the era. Down below, by the way, is the deepest station in Paris — a long spiral down into the hill.

Now find the small park just off the square, and in it, a wall: the Wall of Love. It's a panel of dark blue tiles covered in two words — "I love you" — handwritten more than three hundred times, in around two hundred and fifty different languages and dialects, from the everyday to the nearly extinct. A calligrapher and a musician collected the phrase from speakers all over the world and laid them out together on this single wall. Find your own language somewhere in the grid; almost everyone can.

There's something fitting about it sitting up here. Montmartre has spent more than a century being the city's romantic imagination — the hill of artists and lovers and late nights. A wall that says "I love you" in nearly every tongue on earth belongs exactly here.

So linger in this square a while. This is the village the tour groups miss, and it's the best of the hill.

tours.title: Père Lachaise Cemetery
tours.shortDescription: The great garden cemetery of Paris — a hillside city of the dead holding Chopin, Wilde, Piaf and Jim Morrison.
tours.longDescription: Opened in 1804 on a wooded hill in the east, Père Lachaise was the first of the grand garden cemeteries and remains the most visited in the world: cobbled avenues of tombs under old trees, drawing pilgrims to Chopin, Oscar Wilde, Édith Piaf, Jim Morrison and the Communards' Wall. It is at once a necropolis, an open-air sculpture park and a strange, beautiful garden.

stops.title: Père Lachaise Cemetery
stops.caption: The great garden cemetery of Paris — a hillside city of the dead holding Chopin, Wilde, Piaf and Jim Morrison.
stops.transcriptText:
You're at the gates of Père Lachaise, the most famous cemetery in the world — and one of the strangest success stories in Paris. It's laid out like a small city: cobbled lanes, street signs, tombs like little houses lining the avenues, all of it spilling across a green hillside. People come from everywhere to wander it. But when it opened, in 1804, almost nobody wanted to be buried here.

The problem was location. Back then this was well outside the city, and Parisians thought it too remote, too unfashionable, to be caught dead in — literally. The plots weren't selling. So the authorities did something brilliant and slightly absurd: they ran a marketing campaign using celebrities. They dug up the remains of several beloved famous figures — a revered playwright, a famous poet, and a pair of legendary medieval lovers whose tragic romance everyone knew — and reburied them here with great ceremony. The message was clear: if it's good enough for them, it's good enough for you.

It worked spectacularly. Suddenly a plot in Père Lachaise was the fashionable place to spend eternity, and it has been ever since. Over the years it filled with the famous. The composer Frédéric Chopin lies here; so does the American rock singer Jim Morrison, whose grave still draws quiet crowds; the Irish writer Oscar Wilde, whose tomb was kissed so often, in lipstick, that it had to be shielded behind glass; and Édith Piaf, the beloved singer of the Paris streets. People arrive with maps to find them, the way you'd tour a city's landmarks.

So as you walk in, remember what you're seeing: not only a graveyard, but a place that became desirable through sheer clever salesmanship — a cemetery that sold itself with stars and never stopped. Take a lane at random and let yourself get a little lost. That's the only way to do it, and the quiet up here, above the city, is its own reward.

tours.title: Place de la Bastille
tours.shortDescription: The square where the Revolution began — the prison is gone, its outline traced in the paving.
tours.longDescription: Nothing remains of the fortress-prison stormed on 14 July 1789 except its ghost — the Bastille was demolished within a year and its footprint is marked in the paving. At the centre rises the July Column, commemorating a later revolution, that of 1830. Still the natural gathering point for protest and celebration, the square is where Paris comes to make history out loud.

stops.title: Place de la Bastille
stops.caption: The square where the Revolution began — the prison is gone, its outline traced in the paving.
stops.transcriptText:
You're in Place de la Bastille, standing on the most famous spot in the history of the French Revolution — and there is almost nothing here to see. That's the point, and it's worth understanding.

On the fourteenth of July, 1789, a Paris crowd stormed the Bastille, a great medieval fortress-prison that stood right here. It was the spark of the Revolution, the day France still celebrates as its national holiday. You'd expect the building to be preserved, revered, queued around the block. But it isn't here at all. Within months of being stormed, the Bastille was completely demolished — pulled down stone by stone by the revolutionaries themselves, who wanted every trace of the hated royal prison gone. The stones were carted off; some were even carved into little souvenir models of the fortress and sold. The most famous building of the Revolution was erased by the Revolution.

All that marks where it stood is a line of paler stones set into the pavement, tracing the old foundations. Look down, and you can walk the outline of the vanished fortress. The birthplace of modern France is, fittingly, an absence — a shape in the ground where a building used to be.

Now look up at the tall bronze column in the centre of the square, with the gilded winged figure leaping from the top. Here's the twist most people get wrong: that column has nothing to do with 1789. It commemorates a completely different revolution — an uprising in 1830, decades later, that toppled another king. So the monument that does stand in Place de la Bastille honours a different revolution entirely, while the one everyone comes here for left no monument at all.

It's a strange, very French lesson in memory. Stand in the middle, find the outline in the stones, and picture the fortress that isn't there.

tours.title: Canal Saint-Martin
tours.shortDescription: A 19th-century working canal turned into the city's most relaxed waterside — iron footbridges, locks and plane trees.
tours.longDescription: Cut in the 1820s to bring clean water and freight into Paris, the Canal Saint-Martin lost its industry and gained a second life: tree-shaded quays, arched iron footbridges and a chain of locks that still lift the barges. Long stretches run underground; where it surfaces it has become the unhurried, faintly bohemian heart of the eastern city, best enjoyed sitting on the bank.

stops.title: Canal Saint-Martin
stops.caption: A 19th-century working canal turned into the city's most relaxed waterside — iron footbridges, locks and plane trees.
stops.transcriptText:
You're beside the Canal Saint-Martin, one of the most relaxed and fashionable corners of Paris today — young crowds picnicking on the stone banks, arched iron footbridges crossing the water, leafy trees leaning over the locks. It feels effortlessly cool. But it began as something completely unglamorous: a piece of plumbing.

The canal was dug in the early eighteen hundreds, under Napoleon, to solve a basic and urgent problem — Paris didn't have enough clean water, and disease spread easily through the crowded city. This waterway was built to carry fresh water in, and later to move goods: grain, building stone and timber, hauled through on barges. It was infrastructure, plain and useful, lined with warehouses and working docks. Not romantic in the slightest.

It nearly didn't survive. By the middle of the twentieth century the canal was seen as obsolete and in the way, and there were serious plans to pave the whole thing over and run a road along the top. Parts of it were in fact covered. It came surprisingly close to vanishing under traffic altogether — and then the plans stalled, the canal hung on, and slowly the neighbourhood around it became one of the most sought-after in the city.

So watch the water for a few minutes, and you might catch the best free show here: a boat passing through one of the locks. The gates close, the water level slowly rises or drops several metres to lift or lower the boat to the next stretch, and then the far gates swing open and it glides on. It's a two-hundred-year-old machine, still working exactly as it was designed to.

That's the charm of the place, once you know it: the coolest spot in Paris is a humble water pipe that was almost buried under a road, saved by delay and good luck, now living its best life. Find a spot on the bank and join in.

tours.title: Catacombs of Paris
tours.shortDescription: The underground ossuary where the bones of six million Parisians are stacked in tunnels beneath the streets.
tours.longDescription: When the city's overflowing cemeteries became a health crisis in the 18th century, Paris moved its dead into the disused limestone quarries beneath it, arranging the remains of some six million people into walls of skulls and long bones along the tunnels. A small, sombre stretch is open to visitors — a quiet, unforgettable descent into the literal foundations of the city.

stops.title: Catacombs of Paris
stops.caption: The underground ossuary where the bones of six million Parisians are stacked in tunnels beneath the streets.
stops.transcriptText:
You're at the entrance to the Catacombs, and what waits below is one of the most extraordinary and sobering places in Paris: the carefully arranged bones of some six million people, stretching through tunnels deep beneath the streets. To understand how they came to be here, you have to know two things about the ground under this city.

First, Paris is partly built from itself. For centuries the limestone that makes up so many of the city's buildings was quarried from directly beneath it, leaving a vast honeycomb of tunnels and empty galleries underground. The stone went up to make the city; the holes stayed below.

Second, by the late seventeen hundreds the city's old cemeteries were catastrophically full — overcrowded for generations, to the point that they had become a genuine danger to public health. The authorities needed somewhere to move the dead of centuries past. And there, conveniently, were the empty quarries. So over many years, working at night, the bones of millions were lifted from the overflowing graveyards and carried down into the old tunnels.

What makes it unforgettable is what was done with them. The bones weren't simply piled in heaps. They were stacked and arranged into neat, deliberate walls — long rows of skulls and limb bones set in patterns, lining the passages, turning a mass grave into something solemn and almost architectural. Above the doorway into the main ossuary, a carved inscription warns those who enter that this is the empire of the dead.

It's quiet down there, and cool, and it asks something of you. This isn't really a spectacle; it's a confrontation — the whole population of a city, anonymous and equal at last, quietly holding up the streets you walked in on. Go down respectfully. Six million people are a great many to stand among.

tours.title: Tour Montparnasse
tours.shortDescription: The lone 1970s skyscraper Parisians love to hate — and the source of the best skyline view, because you can't see it from up there.
tours.longDescription: The single black 210-metre tower that broke the Paris skyline in 1973 was so unpopular that the city banned high-rises in the centre soon after. Its saving grace is the observation deck: the finest panorama in Paris, precisely because it is the one viewpoint from which the tower itself is invisible, leaving the Eiffel Tower and the whole low city spread out below.

stops.title: Tour Montparnasse
stops.caption: The lone 1970s skyscraper Parisians love to hate — and the source of the best skyline view, because you can't see it from up there.
stops.transcriptText:
You're looking up at the Tour Montparnasse — a single, stark, dark skyscraper rising more than two hundred metres straight out of a city of low, pale, uniform rooftops. It looks completely out of place, and that is the most important thing about it, because Parisians have never quite forgiven it.

When it went up in the early nineteen seventies, it was meant to signal a modern, vertical future for the city. Instead, the reaction was horror. The lone black tower looming over the tender old skyline was so widely disliked that, just a couple of years after it was finished, the city effectively banned any more skyscrapers in the historic centre. So the Tour Montparnasse stands almost alone — not because no one else wanted to build tall, but because this one building made the very idea unthinkable. It's a monument to its own mistake.

But here's the joke, and it's a good one. Go up to the observation deck at the top, and you get what may be the finest panoramic view in all of Paris — the whole city laid out beneath you, the Eiffel Tower standing proud in the middle distance, the river curling through it all. And the reason it's the best view in the city is gloriously simple: it's the one high place in Paris from which you cannot see the Tour Montparnasse — because you're standing on it.

That's the line every Parisian will tell you with a perfectly straight face: the best view in Paris is from the top of the Tour Montparnasse, because it's the only spot in the city where the Tour Montparnasse doesn't spoil it.

So let the unloved building do you a favour. Ride to the top, turn toward the Eiffel Tower, and enjoy the one view of Paris that the tower beneath your feet can't ruin.

tours.title: The Measure of the World
tours.shortDescription: A Greenwich walk from the riverside up to the Prime Meridian — how Britain solved longitude and the world came to measure time and place from this hill.
tours.longDescription: This is the walk to the centre of the world's map. It runs from the Thames at Greenwich — past the tea-clipper Cutty Sark, Christopher Wren's baroque Old Royal Naval College, Inigo Jones's revolutionary Queen's House, and the free National Maritime Museum — then climbs through the oldest of London's royal parks to the Royal Observatory at the top. There, set into the courtyard, is the Prime Meridian: zero degrees longitude, the line the entire world agreed to measure itself from. About a mile and a half, flat along the river and then one good push up the hill.

stops.title: The Prime Meridian — Introduction
stops.caption: Zero degrees longitude runs through this hill in south-east London — the whole world measures east and west from here.
stops.transcriptText:
Pull out your phone, open a map, and look at the numbers — your longitude. Zero degrees runs through here. Not through Paris, not through Rome, not through Washington. Through this hill in south-east London. The entire world measures east and west from the spot we're going to finish on today.

You're in Greenwich, on the south bank of the Thames, downriver from the centre — far enough out that it still feels like its own town. You've probably come in by boat, or on the little driverless train. Start down by the river, where a great sailing ship sits in dry dock; you can't miss the masts.

Here's the thread. For centuries, the deadliest problem in the world wasn't war or plague — it was getting lost at sea. A ship could find how far north or south it was easily enough, but east or west — its longitude — was guesswork, and the guessing killed people by the thousand. The answer, it turned out, was time: know precisely what o'clock it is back home, compare it to the sun where you are, and you can work out where you are on the globe. So a king built an observatory on this hill to crack the problem. They cracked it. Britain got the oceans. And as a side effect, the world ended up agreeing to measure both time and place from right here.

So this walk runs uphill, in every sense. We start at the water with the age of sail, move through the grand naval buildings the empire built with its sea-power, and climb through the park to the observatory at the top — and the line itself, where you can stand with one foot in each half of the planet.

It's an easy walk: flat along the river, then one good push up through the park. About a mile and a half, all in one piece. Start at the ship. That's the Cutty Sark.

stops.title: Cutty Sark
stops.caption: The last of the great tea clippers, up on stilts in dry dock — built for pure speed.
stops.transcriptText:
The Cutty Sark. She's up on stilts in a dry dock, lifted clear of the ground, so the first thing to do is walk underneath her — under the actual hull, which almost no one ever gets to see on a ship. Look up at the shape of it: long, lean, and sharp as a blade. That shape was the whole point.

She was built in 1869 as a tea clipper — one of the last and fastest of a breed designed to do a single thing: race the new season's tea from China to London quicker than anyone else, because the first cargo home fetched the best price. Speed was money. The Cutty Sark could run over three hundred miles in a day, which for a sailing ship was blistering.

Now, the gift — her name. Go round to the front and find the figurehead: a woman, bare-armed, reaching forward. She's Nannie, a witch from a Robert Burns poem, caught grabbing the tail of a fleeing horse. In the poem she's wearing only a short little shirt — a "cutty sark" in old Scots. So this hard-driving cargo ship is named, cheekily, after a witch's nightie. Sailors had a sense of humour.

Here's the quiet irony of her, though. She was one of the finest sailing ships ever built — and she was already obsolete the day she launched. The Suez Canal opened that same year, steamers could take the short cut east, and within a generation sail was finished for serious cargo. She's a masterpiece of a technology that was already dying. The most beautiful possible answer to a question the world had just stopped asking.

She caught fire during restoration in 2007, badly, and what you're looking at is the careful rebuilding that followed. From here, turn and walk along the river towards the grand domed buildings just ahead — the Old Royal Naval College.

stops.title: Old Royal Naval College
stops.caption: Christopher Wren's baroque masterpiece — two domed blocks facing across a lawn to the river.
stops.transcriptText:
The Old Royal Naval College. Two huge stone blocks, each capped with a dome, facing each other across a long open lawn that runs down to the river. It's the grandest baroque set-piece in Britain, and the man behind it was Christopher Wren — the same architect who rebuilt St Paul's and half the City after the Great Fire.

But here's the thing it was built for, and it's not what you'd guess. This wasn't a palace or a parliament. It was a charity — a home for old, injured and worn-out sailors of the Royal Navy. The country that sent men to sea built them this to retire into. Pensioners shuffled around these royal courtyards in their three-cornered hats. Grandeur, for the discarded.

Step into the Painted Hall — it's just off the courtyard, and you should, even for five minutes. This was their dining room, and the ceiling and walls are covered, every inch, in a vast swirling scene that took the artist James Thornhill nineteen years to paint.
