People call it Britain's Sistine Chapel, and for once the comparison isn't silly: old sailors ate their dinners under one of the great painted ceilings of Europe. When Nelson was killed at Trafalgar — the man on the column you may have stood beneath in Trafalgar Square — his body was brought here, to lie in state under that ceiling.

Now the gift, and you can see it from the lawn. The two blocks don't join. There's a wide gap straight up the middle, and through it you can see a smaller white building beyond, with the hill rising behind. That gap is deliberate. Queen Mary insisted the river view from that white house must not be blocked, so Wren split his whole building in two and built the view a corridor. The grandest pile in Greenwich was made to bow to a sightline.

Walk up the lawn now, through the gap, towards that white house. That's where we're going.

stops.title: Queen's House
stops.caption: A plain white cube that changed English architecture — Inigo Jones's first classical building.
stops.transcriptText:
The Queen's House. A plain white cube, calm and symmetrical, sitting quietly between the wings of the maritime museum. It looks ordinary to a modern eye — which is exactly why it's one of the most important buildings in the country, and you have to do a little time-travel to see why.

When this went up, around 1616, everything in England was still built the Tudor way — red brick, gables, towers, lovely but a bit higgledy. Then the architect Inigo Jones came back from Italy, having studied the clean, mathematical buildings of the Renaissance, and dropped this white classical box into the middle of red-brick England. It was startling — a piece of the future landed in a field. It's reckoned the first truly classical building in the country.

And if the name Inigo Jones rings a bell, it should: he's the man who built the Banqueting House on Whitehall, the white hall with the Rubens ceiling. These two buildings are the ones that brought Italy to Britain — and nearly every grand white-columned building you've ever seen in this country traces back to them.

The gift is inside, and it's free to enter. Find the Tulip Stairs — a spiral that curls up through the house with nothing beneath holding it, each step seeming to float on the one below. It was the first self-supporting spiral staircase in Britain, and it still looks like a magic trick.

It was built for queens — begun for one, finished for another — which is where the name comes from. Inside now hangs the famous Armada Portrait of Elizabeth the First, her hand resting on a globe: England, looking out at the sea, deciding the sea was hers.

Step across to the long building beside it — the National Maritime Museum.

stops.title: National Maritime Museum
stops.caption: The world's largest maritime museum, free to enter — the sea, mapped and remembered.
stops.transcriptText:
The National Maritime Museum — the largest museum in the world devoted to the sea, and entry is free. You could spend hours; I'm going to point you at one object.

Everything Greenwich is about — the ships, the navigation, the empire built on sea-power — runs through this collection: charts, instruments, figureheads, the lot. But find the gallery with Nelson in it, and look for a small, plain naval coat in a glass case.

It's the coat Horatio Nelson was wearing at the Battle of Trafalgar, in 1805, when a French sniper's musket ball hit him. Look closely at the left shoulder and you'll see it — the actual bullet hole, the one that killed the most famous sailor in British history. We've already met Nelson twice today: on his column, if you came in from Trafalgar Square, and lying in state in the Painted Hall back down the hill. Here he is a third time, reduced to a single coat with a hole in it.

That's the gift of this whole museum, really. All the grandeur outside — the domes, the painted ceilings, the talk of empire and oceans — and then this: a piece of wool with a tear in the shoulder. The glory and the cost, two rooms apart.

When you've seen it, come back out and look up the hill. At the top, with a statue beside it and almost certainly a crowd, is the Royal Observatory. That's our climb, and our ending. Head into the park and start up.

stops.title: Greenwich Park
stops.caption: The oldest enclosed royal park in London — one good climb to the top of the hill.
stops.transcriptText:
Take your time on this hill — it's the only real climb of the day, and there's a bench or two if you want them. You're walking up through Greenwich Park, the oldest enclosed royal park in London, fenced off as a royal hunting ground nearly six hundred years ago. There were deer here for centuries.

Near the top you'll pass a statue of a soldier looking out over the view — that's General Wolfe, who won Quebec for Britain and is buried down in the town below. He's been given the best seat in Greenwich.

And here it is — the view. Stop at the top and turn back the way you came. Below you, the whole story of the walk is laid out at once: the two domes of the Naval College; the little white Queen's House framed dead-centre in the gap between them — that preserved sightline, seen now from the other end; the silver bend of the Thames; and rising straight behind it all, the glass towers of Canary Wharf. Four hundred years of the city in a single frame — a royal house, a naval palace, a working river, and the money that came after.

Get your breath. Then turn around. Behind you is the reason the whole world knows the name Greenwich — the Royal Observatory.

stops.title: Royal Observatory
stops.caption: The top of the hill and the centre of the world's map: the Prime Meridian, zero degrees longitude.
stops.transcriptText:
The Royal Observatory. This is it — the top of the hill, the end of the walk, and the centre of the world's map. Stand in the courtyard, find the metal strip set into the ground with a queue of people photographing their feet, and you've found the Prime Meridian: zero degrees longitude. One foot either side, and you're standing in both halves of the planet at once.

Remember the problem from the bottom of the hill — ships getting fatally lost because they couldn't tell how far east or west they were. King Charles the Second built this observatory in 1675 to solve it: map the stars precisely enough, the thinking went, and sailors could find their longitude from the sky. In the end the cleaner answer was a clock. A clockmaker named John Harrison spent his life building timepieces accurate enough to keep perfect home-time on a pitching, salt-soaked ship — and his strange, beautiful machines are inside, still ticking. Solve the time, and you solve the position. Greenwich became the place the world set its clock by.

Look up at the building behind you and you'll see a red ball on a pole. At one o'clock every day, it drops — and it has, since 1833, so ships down on the river could set their chronometers by it at the exact instant. The world's first public time signal, and it still falls daily.

Here's the thing to stand here and feel, though. There's nothing under your feet. No natural line runs through this hill. In 1884 the nations of the world simply met, voted, and agreed to measure all time and all longitude from this one spot — an arbitrary line on an English hilltop that became the truth because everyone chose to believe it together. Every time zone on earth is counted from here. Greenwich Mean Time. The zero of the whole map.

So that's the walk. You started at the river with a ship that got lost less often than the others, and you've climbed to the line the entire world agreed to measure itself from. Stand on it a moment, one foot in each hemisphere, and look back down the hill at everything that line paid for. Not a bad place to end.

tours.title: Le Marais
tours.shortDescription: A walk through the largest surviving piece of old Paris — the marsh that became the aristocrats' address, then a slum, and now the city's living room.
tours.longDescription: Le Marais — literally 'the marsh' — is the best-preserved stretch of pre-Revolutionary Paris, spared the boulevards Haussmann drove through the rest of the city. This flat, dense walk threads it together: from the grand Hôtel de Ville and the inside-out Centre Pompidou, through the aristocratic mansions that now hold the Musée Picasso and the Musée Carnavalet, to the perfect symmetry of the Place des Vosges, Paris's oldest planned square. Along the way the Marais tells its whole story — royal quarter, Jewish quarter, faded slum, and today one of the city's most alive neighbourhoods.

stops.title: Le Marais — Introduction
stops.caption: The name means the marsh — and that's exactly what this was.
stops.transcriptText:
The name means the marsh — and that's exactly what this was. Wet, low ground on the edge of the river, drained by monks in the Middle Ages, useless for anything grand until, in the 1600s, the kings and nobles decided this was where they wanted to live. They built mansions here, dozens of them, and for a while the Marais was the most fashionable address in Paris.

Then fashion moved on, as it does. The aristocrats drifted off to newer quarters and to Versailles, and the Marais came down in the world — its grand houses carved up into workshops and crowded tenements, a dense, poor, working quarter, and for a long stretch the heart of the city's Jewish community along with many others who'd found their way to cheap rooms in old streets. By the twentieth century, the city looked at the Marais and mostly saw a slum to clear.

Here's the twist that makes this walk worth taking. When Baron Haussmann tore up most of Paris in the 1800s and replaced it with wide straight boulevards, he largely left the Marais alone — too poor, too tangled, not worth the trouble. So the very neglect that brought it low also saved it. This is the largest surviving piece of old Paris: narrow medieval streets and Renaissance mansions that exist precisely because nobody thought them worth knocking down. In the end the city changed its mind, protected the whole quarter, and the Marais came back — not as an aristocrats' enclave this time, but as everyone's. The galleries, the boutiques, the cafés, the crowds: this is the city's living room now.

The good news for your feet: it's flat, and it's dense, with everything packed close together. We start at the city's grand front door on the river — the Hôtel de Ville.

stops.title: Hôtel de Ville
stops.caption: You're standing in front of the Hôtel de Ville — the city hall of Paris, and one of the grandest buildings you'll see all day: a long ornate facade bristling with statues and turrets, facing a wide open square by the river.
stops.transcriptText:
You're standing in front of the Hôtel de Ville — the city hall of Paris, and one of the grandest buildings you'll see all day: a long ornate facade bristling with statues and turrets, facing a wide open square by the river. It looks like it has stood here, untouched, for five hundred years. It hasn't.

This has been the seat of the city's government since the 1300s, when the merchants who effectively ran Paris first set up here. But the building you're looking at is younger than it pretends to be. The grand Renaissance city hall that stood on this spot was burned to the ground in 1871, in the violent collapse of the Commune, when much of central Paris went up in flames. Rather than build something new and modern, the city rebuilt its city hall almost exactly as it had been — a careful, slightly grander copy of what the fire had taken. So this is a nineteenth-century replica wearing a sixteenth-century face, and most people walking past never notice.

Now the square in front of it, because there's a word hiding in it. For centuries this was the Place de Grève — grève meaning the strip of sandy ground along the river. It was where men without work came to stand and wait, hoping to be hired for the day. Out of that grew a phrase the whole world now borrows: to be en grève, "on the strand," came to mean to stop work, to strike. Every strike, everywhere, quietly carries the name of this square.

It's also, it should be said, a square with a darker past — for a long time the city's public punishments were carried out here, in front of crowds. That's part of its history too.

When you're ready, head north, a few streets back from the river, toward a low modern building wrapped in coloured pipes that could not look more out of place. That's the Centre Pompidou.

stops.title: Centre Pompidou
stops.caption: And here it is — the building that looks like it's still under construction, or has been turned completely inside out.
stops.transcriptText:
And here it is — the building that looks like it's still under construction, or has been turned completely inside out. The Centre Pompidou. After streets of old stone, it's a deliberate shock: a great glass-and-steel box with all its skeleton and plumbing on the outside.

That's the whole idea, and it was radical when it opened in 1977. Two young architects won the competition with a building that wore its insides on its outside — every pipe, duct, beam, even the escalators, bolted onto the exterior, so that the entire interior could be left open and empty, free to be rearranged for any kind of art. And they colour-coded the outside like a diagram, so you can read the building from the street. The blue pipes carry air, the green ones water, the yellow ones electricity, and the red ones are for movement — the escalators that run up the outside, carrying people through it. Stand back and the whole facade explains itself.

It was hated at first — Parisians thought someone had abandoned a refinery in the middle of their old city — and then, slowly, loved, until it became one of the most visited buildings in the country.

One honest note. Right now you can admire it only from out here. The Pompidou closed in 2025 for a deep, years-long renovation and isn't due to reopen until around 2030; its modern-art collection has been scattered to other museums in the meantime, with a good part of it on show over at the Grand Palais. So today this is an architecture stop — the radical idea, read off the facade — rather than a visit inside.

From here we walk east, deeper into the old Marais and its narrow streets, to a grand mansion that now holds the work of one man. The Musée Picasso.

stops.title: Musée Picasso
stops.caption: This is the Hôtel Salé, and it's now the Musée Picasso — and the story of how those two things came together is really a story about taxes, twice over.
stops.transcriptText:
This is the Hôtel Salé, and it's now the Musée Picasso — and the story of how those two things came together is really a story about taxes, twice over.

Start with the mansion. It was built in the 1650s for a man who'd grown rich collecting the tax on salt — which in those days was a big, hated tax, since everyone needed salt and the crown squeezed it hard. The house he built with the proceeds was so showy that locals nicknamed it the Hôtel Salé — the "salted mansion," a dig at exactly where the money had come from. So before any Picasso ever hung here, the building itself was already a monument to tax.

Now the art. When Picasso died, his heirs faced an enormous bill in French inheritance tax. France has a clever law that lets you settle a tax debt by handing over works of art instead of cash — and so, rather than money, the state took Picassos. A flood of them: paintings, sculptures, sketches, the artist's own private collection. That windfall is the core of this museum, which holds the largest public collection of his work anywhere. The whole place exists because of a death and a tax bill.

If you go in, hunt for a small bronze called the Bull's Head. Look at it once and it's a bull; look again and it's exactly what Picasso built it from — a bicycle seat for the face, the handlebars for the horns, joined together and cast in bronze. He liked the thought that one day someone might find it, not knowing, melt it down, and turn it back into a bicycle.

From here it's a short walk south through the lanes to the grandest open space in the quarter — a perfect square of matching rose-brick houses around a garden. The Place des Vosges.

stops.title: Place des Vosges
stops.caption: Step out of the lanes and into the Place des Vosges, and let it open up around you: a large garden square, framed on all four sides by identical houses of rose-coloured brick and pale stone, with covered arcades running along the ground all the way around.
stops.transcriptText:
Step out of the lanes and into the Place des Vosges, and let it open up around you: a large garden square, framed on all four sides by identical houses of rose-coloured brick and pale stone, with covered arcades running along the ground all the way around. It's calm, symmetrical and complete in a way nothing else in the Marais is — and that's because it's the original. This is the oldest planned square in Paris, and arguably the model for the elegant city square anywhere.

It was laid out under Henri IV and inaugurated in 1612 as the Place Royale — royal by name and by intent, a piece of perfect order dropped into the medieval muddle, where the nobility could parade and duel and show themselves off. Every matching house, every arch, was built to a single design. The idea of a square as one unified composition — rather than just a gap where streets happen to meet — more or less starts here, and you can trace its descendants in grand squares right across Europe.

The name changed later, and it's the third tax story of this walk. After the Revolution, the new Republic needed money, and it renamed this square to honour the Vosges — the region of France that was first to pay its share of a new tax. A perfect aristocratic square, renamed as a gold star for prompt taxpayers.

One door is worth knowing: number six, in the corner, was Victor Hugo's home for sixteen years — the years he was writing toward Les Misérables. It's now a small museum, and it's free; you can stand in the rooms where he worked.

Our last stop is just around the corner, a couple of minutes away — the place where this whole quarter keeps its memories. The Musée Carnavalet.

stops.title: Musée Carnavalet
stops.caption: Here's our last stop, and the right one to end on: the Musée Carnavalet, the museum of the history of Paris itself, set inside two old Marais mansions joined together.
stops.transcriptText:
Here's our last stop, and the right one to end on: the Musée Carnavalet, the museum of the history of Paris itself, set inside two old Marais mansions joined together. Before anything else — it's free, always has been, one of the great no-cost pleasures of the city.

Even the name is a little Paris story. It comes from a long-ago owner with a Breton surname that French tongues couldn't be bothered with, so over the years they mangled it into "Carnavalet." The wrong name simply stuck, the way so much in this city did, and now it's the right one.

What's inside is the reason it belongs at the end of this walk. This isn't a museum of masterpieces; it's the city's attic. Paris has spent centuries saving bits of itself in here — carved shop signs from streets that no longer exist, whole panelled rooms rescued from mansions before they were demolished, keys and paintings and revolutionary relics, even the actual cork-lined bedroom where the writer Marcel Proust sealed himself away to work. Walk through it and you're walking through the physical leftovers of the city you've spent all afternoon in.

Which closes the loop on the Marais. You've spent this walk in the one quarter that survived — the old Paris that escaped the wrecking ball by being overlooked, then was loved back to life. And here at the end is the building where the city deliberately keeps the pieces of everything it didn't manage to save anywhere else. The marsh that became the address, that became the slum, that became the living room — remembering itself, for free, in a borrowed mansion with a mangled name. Take your time in here. It's the whole city, in one house.

tours.title: Montmartre
tours.shortDescription: A climb over the Montmartre hill — from the Art Nouveau métro at Abbesses up to Sacré-Cœur and the painters' square, then down to the Moulin Rouge.
tours.longDescription: Montmartre is the village on the hill that Paris never quite absorbed — and the place where modern art and Belle Époque nightlife were both more or less invented. This short, steep walk goes from the Place des Abbesses and its rare Guimard Art Nouveau métro entrance, past the Wall of Love, up to the white basilica of Sacré-Cœur and the crowded painters' square of the Place du Tertre, then back down the hill to the red windmill of the Moulin Rouge. Along the way it weighs the real village against the souvenir of itself.

stops.title: Montmartre — Introduction
stops.caption: Most of Paris is flat.
stops.transcriptText:
Most of Paris is flat. This corner isn't.

Montmartre is a hill — a steep one, the highest ground in the city — and for most of its history it wasn't even part of Paris. It was a separate village up here above the smoke, with windmills turning on top and gypsum mines hollowing out the rock below, close enough to the city to see it but far enough to feel like another world. Paris only swallowed it in 1860. And the name carries something older and darker: the mount of the martyr, after a bishop who, the legend says, was beheaded on this hill and then stood up and walked off carrying his own head.

This walk is about what happened next — when, around the year 1900, the cheap rents and the village quiet drew the artists up here, and Montmartre became, for a few decades, the most famous bohemia on earth. Painters, poets, dancers, drinkers. That moment is long over, but the hill has been performing it ever since, and the walk moves through both versions at once: the real village that still survives in the side streets, and the souvenir of itself that the crowds come to see.

A warning about the walk. It's short — you stay on and around one hill — but it is genuinely steep, with staircases instead of streets in places. Take it slowly. If your legs object, there's a little funicular that carries you up the worst of the climb to the church at the top.

We'll start partway up, in a square that's still the real Montmartre, climb to the white church on the summit and the painters' square behind it, and come down the far side to a red windmill at the bottom. Begin at the Place des Abbesses, at the green Métro entrance that looks like something grown rather than built.

stops.title: Place des Abbesses
stops.caption: You're at the Place des Abbesses, and the first thing to look at is the thing you probably just came up through: the Métro entrance.
stops.transcriptText:
You're at the Place des Abbesses, and the first thing to look at is the thing you probably just came up through: the Métro entrance. That curving green cast-iron canopy, with the word Métropolitain in those strange melting letters and a glass roof like a dragonfly's wing, is the real thing — designed by Hector Guimard around the turn of the twentieth century, when the Métro was new and Paris wanted its entrances to look like the future. Most of his canopies were ripped out over the years. This is one of only two of the fully glass-roofed ones left in the entire city, so you're looking at a genuine survivor.

There's a reason you arrived a little breathless, too. Abbesses is the deepest station in the Paris Métro — about thirty-six metres down, the depth of a ten-storey building, because the hill above it is solid rock. The spiral staircase is famous, and famously punishing; most people take the easier way up and regret nothing.

The square's name reaches further back. Abbesses means the abbesses — the women who ran a powerful abbey that once crowned this hill, centuries before any painter showed up. The convent is long gone, but the name stuck to the square.

Stand here a moment and notice what this place is not. No tour groups, no easels, no crush of people — just a café-lined square, someone buying bread, a carousel turning. This is the Montmartre that's still simply a neighbourhood, the village underneath the souvenir. Hold onto that feeling, because once we climb, it gets harder to find.

Just off the square is a small walled garden, and set into it is a wall covered in three words. Head there next — it's the Wall of Love.

stops.title: The Wall of Love
stops.caption: Here it is — a small garden tucked off the square, and along one side a low wall of dark blue enamelled tiles.
stops.transcriptText:
Here it is — a small garden tucked off the square, and along one side a low wall of dark blue enamelled tiles. Step close and you'll see it's covered in the same three words, over and over, in hundreds of different hands and alphabets: I love you. Written here around three hundred times, in roughly two hundred and fifty languages.

It's not ancient — it went up in the year 2000 — and the story behind it is simple and a little obsessive. A musician named Frédéric Baron spent years going around with notebooks, asking people to write "I love you" in their own language, collecting the phrase from strangers, from embassies, from anyone he could find. An artist, Claire Kito, arranged the whole collection onto this wall of lava stone, built to last.

Look for the scattered red shapes among the writing. They're the pieces of a broken heart — the idea being that all these separated fragments of love, in all these languages, add up to one whole.

It's a small thing next to the basilica you're about to climb to. But that's rather the point of Montmartre: the grand gesture up at the top, and the human-sized one down here in the village.

From the garden, turn uphill. You'll see the white domes of Sacré-Cœur floating above the rooftops — and a lot of steps between you and them. That's where we're going.

stops.title: Sacré-Cœur
stops.caption: You've climbed it, and you're standing under Sacré-Cœur — the great white basilica with its cluster of round pale domes, the building you can see from half of Paris.
stops.transcriptText:
You've climbed it, and you're standing under Sacré-Cœur — the great white basilica with its cluster of round pale domes, the building you can see from half of Paris. Catch your breath on the steps and turn around first, because the view is the reward: the whole city spread out below you, flat and grey-gold to the horizon, with the hill you're on as the highest natural point in Paris. People have been coming up here to look down at the city for about as long as there's been a city to look at.

Now the church itself, and two things worth knowing. The first is the colour. It never seems to get dirty, and that's not luck — it's built of a stone that bleaches itself. When it rains, the stone reacts with the water and releases a white mineral, so the building effectively washes itself paler with every shower. While the rest of Paris darkened with soot over the past century, Sacré-Cœur kept turning whiter.

The second thing is why it's here, and it's heavier than the bright domes suggest. It was begun in 1875, in the aftermath of a disastrous war and a brutal civil uprising — the Commune — that had begun, and been crushed, partly on this very hill. The church was raised as a kind of national penance: an act of atonement for what France had done and suffered. To some, that made it a monument of healing and faith; to others, then and now, it looked like the winners building a giant church on the grave of the losers. Both readings have followed it ever since.

So it's a more complicated building than the postcard lets on — beautiful, contested, and permanently, deliberately white.

When you're ready, walk around to the back of the basilica, into the small square just behind it. After the crowds on these steps it'll feel tighter and older, packed with easels and painters. That's the Place du Tertre.

stops.title: Place du Tertre
stops.caption: This is the Place du Tertre, and it's the strangest stop on the walk — because it manages to be the most authentic and the most fake place on the hill at the same time.
stops.transcriptText:
This is the Place du Tertre, and it's the strangest stop on the walk — because it manages to be the most authentic and the most fake place on the hill at the same time. This little square was the real heart of Montmartre when it was a village: the market square, the centre of everything. And around the year 1900, when the artists moved in, this was their neighbourhood square too.

The real thing happened just steps from here. In a ramshackle building nearby that everyone called the Bateau-Lavoir — the laundry-boat, because that's what it looked like — a young Spaniard named Picasso painted some of the pictures that broke art open, including, around 1907, the one that detonated modern painting. That genuinely happened, right here, on this hill.

But that was well over a century ago, and what fills the square now is the memory of it, sold by the metre. The painters you see crowded under umbrellas, offering to sketch your portrait in ten minutes, are working a kind of permanent costume drama — Montmartre playing the role of itself. It's easy to be sniffy about it. Try not to be; it's also the genuine descendant of something that was once entirely real.

Want the proof that this was a true village and not a stage set? Just down the slope on the far side there's a working vineyard — an actual one, still making wine each year, a last green survivor of the orchards and fields that covered this hill before the city climbed up to meet it.

From here, the walk goes downhill — a long descent off the front of the hill toward the bright lights at the bottom. Head down, and aim for a red windmill. That's the Moulin Rouge.

stops.title: Moulin Rouge
stops.caption: You've come down off the hill, and here at the bottom, on a busy boulevard, is the red windmill — the Moulin Rouge.
stops.transcriptText:
You've come down off the hill, and here at the bottom, on a busy boulevard, is the red windmill — the Moulin Rouge. Its sails turn in red neon now, but stop and think about that windmill for a second, because it's a clue to everything you just walked through.

It's fake. It always was — a decorative red windmill bolted to a cabaret roof when the place opened in 1889, the same year the Eiffel Tower went up across the city. But it's a fake of something that was once completely real. This whole hill was once covered in working windmills, dozens of them, grinding grain and pressing grapes back when Montmartre was farmland. By the time the cabaret opened, nearly all of them were gone — so the Moulin Rouge bolted a pretend one onto its roof, a bit of rustic nostalgia for a countryside the city had just paved over. Two of the genuine old windmills still stand a few streets away, if you want to find the real thing later.

What opened underneath that fake windmill, though, was brand new. The Moulin Rouge took a rowdy, high-kicking dance and turned it into a spectacle — the cancan as the world now knows it, fast and loud and deliberately scandalous. And a short, sharp-eyed painter named Toulouse-Lautrec sat in the audience night after night and put it all on paper, in posters so good they became the image of Paris nightlife forever.

So here's where the walk leaves you, and it's a fitting place. You started at the quiet top of the hill, in the real village under the souvenir, climbed past a white church built out of guilt, through a square performing its own past — and you've come down to a red windmill that was never a windmill, spinning over a dance floor, at the foot of the hill where the city finally caught up with the village. Montmartre, top to bottom: the real thing and the show of it, all on one slope. Stay for the lights coming on. They're worth it.

tours.title: The Triumphal Way
tours.shortDescription: Paris's Axe historique — the dead-straight 4 km sightline from the Louvre through the Tuileries, Concorde and Champs-Élysées to the Arc de Triomphe, with a coda out to La Défense.
tours.longDescription: One of the most deliberate pieces of urban design on earth: a single straight line, laid down over three centuries, along which Paris arranged its power. This walk follows the Axe historique from the Louvre's glass pyramid, down the Tuileries and across the Place de la Concorde, up the Champs-Élysées to Napoleon's Arc de Triomphe — and then, as a Métro coda, out to the hollow cube of the Grande Arche at La Défense, where the modern city answered the old axis in glass and steel. Power, drawn as a line.

stops.title: The Triumphal Way — Introduction
stops.caption: Stand in the right spot in Paris and the whole city seems to line up.
stops.transcriptText:
Stand in the right spot in Paris and the whole city seems to line up.

This walk follows that line. It's called the Axe historique — the historic axis — and it runs dead straight for kilometres, from the courtyard of the Louvre, through a royal garden, across the square where the guillotine once stood, up the most famous avenue in the world, to the great arch on the hill. Five monuments, one sightline, laid down over more than three hundred years by kings, emperors and republics who each wanted their stamp on the same straight road.

It is, in the most literal sense, power drawn as a line. Every regime that ruled France added to it, pushed it further west, and tried to make the whole city point at whatever it most wanted to be.

A word on the walk itself. This is the long one — about four kilometres from the Louvre to the Arc de Triomphe, more or less flat, almost perfectly straight, and busy the whole way. You can do it comfortably in an afternoon, but it's a real walk, so wear the right shoes. At the end, if you've still got the legs, the line keeps going past the Arc to a giant modern arch out in the business district — we'll point you to it, but that last stretch is a short ride on the Métro, not a walk.

One thing to carry with you. The line looks ruler-straight, but it isn't quite: the Louvre sits at a slight angle to the rest of it, a few degrees off, and that small kink gets echoed deliberately at the far modern end. Keep it in mind. The axis has a secret bend in it.

Start in the great courtyard of the Louvre, at the glass pyramid. Put the pyramid behind you and look west, the way the line runs.

stops.title: Louvre
stops.caption: You're in the Cour Napoléon, the great courtyard of the Louvre, standing at the glass pyramid.
stops.transcriptText:
You're in the Cour Napoléon, the great courtyard of the Louvre, standing at the glass pyramid. Before you start down the line, it's worth knowing what you're starting from — because the building wrapped around you on three sides has been almost everything a building can be.

It began as a fortress. In the 1190s a king threw up a defensive castle here to guard the western edge of Paris, and its foundations are still down there — you can walk around the base of the medieval keep in the basement, beneath the museum. Over the centuries the fortress became a palace, growing wing by wing into the largest royal residence in Europe, until Louis the Fourteenth grew bored of the city, decamped to Versailles in 1682, and left this enormous place half-empty.

Then the Revolution did something pointed with it. In 1793 the palace the kings had abandoned was reopened as a public museum — the nation's art, hung in the nation's house, free for the citizens who'd just got rid of the king. That's still what it is, and it's now the most-visited museum on earth.

The pyramid is the newest layer: glass and steel, dropped into the centre of all that old stone in 1989, and hated at first for exactly that contrast. It's since become as much a symbol of Paris as anything standing behind it.

Now turn your back to the pyramid and face west. Through the smaller arch ahead — the pink one, the Arc du Carrousel — a straight line opens up: a path through gardens, a distant obelisk, and, far off, a faint arch on a hill. That's the whole walk, visible in a single glance. The line technically begins right here.

Walk toward that little pink arch and through it into the gardens beyond. That's the Tuileries.

stops.title: Jardin des Tuileries
stops.caption: You've come through the pink arch into the Tuileries — a long formal garden of gravel paths, clipped trees and round ponds, running straight ahead toward the obelisk in the distance.
stops.transcriptText:
You've come through the pink arch into the Tuileries — a long formal garden of gravel paths, clipped trees and round ponds, running straight ahead toward the obelisk in the distance. Keep that obelisk in your sights; you're walking the line now, and this garden is where it was first drawn.

The man who drew it was André Le Nôtre, in the 1660s — the same gardener who laid out Versailles. He took an older royal garden here and straightened it into this: a central avenue, dead level, pulling the eye west to a vanishing point. That was a new idea about what a garden was for. Not a place to wander and get lost, but a line of sight — a way of standing at the palace and watching your power run, uninterrupted, all the way to the horizon. Everything west of here, right up to the arch on the hill, is Le Nôtre's idea, extended by everyone who came after.

There's something missing, though, and the gap is the point. For centuries a palace closed off this end of the garden — the Tuileries Palace, where kings and emperors actually lived. It burned during the violent end of the Commune in 1871, and what was left was pulled down. That's why the Louvre behind you now looks out over open sky instead of meeting another building: the home this garden was made for is simply gone, and most people walking here never know it stood.

These days the garden belongs to everyone. The green metal chairs scattered round the ponds are free; drag one to the water, point it west, and you're sitting in a king's private view that nobody owns any more.

Carry on toward the obelisk. The garden ends at a wide, busy square wrapped around it — the Place de la Concorde.

stops.title: Place de la Concorde
stops.caption: The garden opens out, and suddenly you're on the edge of a vast, traffic-ringed square with a single tall stone needle at its centre.
stops.transcriptText:
The garden opens out, and suddenly you're on the edge of a vast, traffic-ringed square with a single tall stone needle at its centre. This is the Place de la Concorde, the midpoint of the whole line — and the most loaded ground you'll cross all day.

Start with the needle, because it's the easy part. It's an Egyptian obelisk, around three thousand three hundred years old, that once stood at the temple of Luxor and was given to France in the 1830s. It was raised on this spot in 1836, and much later, in 1998, capped with a thin pyramid of gold. It is, by some distance, the oldest thing you'll see all walk — and it was put here, very deliberately, to fill a space the city wanted to stop thinking about.

Because this square has worn three names. It opened as the Place Louis the Fifteenth, with a statue of that king at its centre. The Revolution tore the statue down, renamed it the Place of the Revolution, and for a couple of years made it the central stage of the Terror: this is where the guillotine stood, where the king and queen were executed, and where well over a thousand people lost their lives in a matter of months. And then, when it was over, the city renamed it a third time — Concorde, meaning agreement, reconciliation — and eventually planted a neutral, ancient, foreign monument exactly where the blade had been. Not a memorial. The opposite of a memorial: a way of changing the subject.

It's worth standing here a moment with that in mind — that the calmest, grandest square in Paris is calm by design, built to let the city forget what happened on it. Whether that's wisdom or evasion, people still argue.

When you're ready, turn west again and face the long, rising avenue lined with trees. That's the Champs-Élysées.

stops.title: Champs-Élysées
stops.caption: Now you're at the foot of the Champs-Élysées, looking up a wide avenue that rises gently for almost two kilometres to the arch at the top.
stops.transcriptText:
Now you're at the foot of the Champs-Élysées, looking up a wide avenue that rises gently for almost two kilometres to the arch at the top. This is the stretch everyone has heard of — and the name is grander than you might guess. Champs-Élysées means the Elysian Fields: in Greek myth, the paradise where heroes went after death. Somebody named a Paris street after heaven.

What's strange is how little there was here when the name was coined. The lower end, where you're standing, was once marshy open ground and market gardens, well outside the city. Le Nôtre — the same man who drew the garden behind you — simply extended his sightline straight through it in the 1660s, planting a double row of trees to carry the view onward toward the horizon. So the Champs-Élysées was a line on a plan, a direction, long before it was a place. It was a view before it was an address.

You'll feel the avenue change as you climb. The lower half is still mostly that original idea — trees, gardens, room to breathe. Then it crosses a roundabout and becomes the famous part: the broad upper avenue of glass-fronted shops, café terraces, car showrooms and flagship stores, packed shoulder to shoulder with people from everywhere on earth. The city still calls it the most beautiful avenue in the world. Up close it's also, frankly, a very expensive shopping street — and both of those things are true at once.

Keep climbing, and keep your eye on the arch. It's been growing in front of you the whole way, and it only really gives up its scale when you're nearly under it.

At the top, the avenue ends at a vast roundabout with the arch marooned in the middle. That's the Arc de Triomphe.

stops.title: Arc de Triomphe
stops.caption: You've reached the top: the Arc de Triomphe, standing alone in the middle of a roundabout where twelve avenues meet like the spokes of a star.
stops.transcriptText:
You've reached the top: the Arc de Triomphe, standing alone in the middle of a roundabout where twelve avenues meet like the spokes of a star. Don't try to cross to it through the traffic — there's an underpass. But before you go to it, stop and turn around, because this is the best view on the walk. From up here the whole line you've climbed runs back east — avenue, square, obelisk, garden, the distant Louvre — every monument you've passed, strung on one thread. You can see the entire afternoon in a single look.

Now the arch. Napoleon ordered it built in 1806, at the height of his power, to honour his armies after a great victory. It was meant to be the ultimate triumphal gesture — soldiers marching home beneath it. But it was enormous and slow, and it wasn't finished in his lifetime. Napoleon fell, was exiled, and died on a distant island in 1821, with his arch still half-built. It was finally completed in 1836, fifteen years after his death — and the only time he ever passed beneath it was in 1840, as a coffin, when his remains were brought back to Paris and carried under the arch he never saw standing.

And there's a quieter thing underneath it now. After the First World War, an unknown soldier — one unidentified body, standing in for all the missing dead — was buried beneath the arch, and a flame was lit over the grave. It has been relit, by hand, every single evening since. So the monument built to glorify one man's victories now keeps watch, in the end, over a single nameless soldier. The grandest arch in Paris finishes on the most modest possible note.

That's the end of the walk on foot. But the line doesn't stop here. Look west, past the arch, and on a clear day you'll see another arch far off on the horizon — a vast, square one. To reach it you'll want the Métro. That's La Défense, and the Grande Arche.

stops.title: Grande Arche, La Défense
stops.caption: You've come up out of the Métro at La Défense, and the thing in front of you doesn't look like the rest of the walk at all.
stops.transcriptText:
You've come up out of the Métro at La Défense, and the thing in front of you doesn't look like the rest of the walk at all. No carved stone, no emperors — just glass towers, open plazas, and one enormous, impossibly clean white cube, hollow in the middle, big enough to see sky straight through. This is the Grande Arche, and it's where the line you've been following finally runs out — on purpose.

First, where you are. La Défense is Paris's business district, a forest of towers built from the 1960s onward and kept deliberately outside the historic centre, so the old city could stay low while the offices went high out here. The name is older than the towers: it comes from a statue that once marked where Parisians defended the city in the war of 1870.

Now the cube. It went up in 1989, for the two-hundredth anniversary of the Revolution, designed by a Danish architect as a near-perfect hollow cube — so large that the whole of Notre-Dame, spire and all, could sit inside the opening. And here's where it talks back to everything behind it. The old arch on the hill is a solid block of stone, raised to glorify an army. This one is open — a window, not a wall — and it was dedicated not to a victory but to human brotherhood. A triumphal arch you can see straight through.

Remember the secret bend, back at the start? The Grande Arche is turned a few degrees off the axis — the very same angle as the Louvre, all those kilometres east. The architects did it on purpose, a quiet nod from the newest end of the line to the oldest. And notice what they didn't do: they didn't close the line off. Stand in the opening and look west, and the axis simply carries on, out past the cube, toward nothing in particular — left open, handed to whatever comes next.

Which is the right way for this walk to end. You started in a king's courtyard, on a line drawn to make a city point at power, and you finish here, at an open square cube that points at no one and lets the line run on. From a palace to a window. That's most of the story of Paris, in one straight road.

tours.title: Paris Islands
tours.shortDescription: A walk across the two Seine islands where Paris began — the Île de la Cité, from the Pont Neuf to Notre-Dame, then over to the quiet Île Saint-Louis.
tours.longDescription: Paris started on the water. This flat, ~1.4 km walk crosses the two islands in the Seine at the city's heart: the Île de la Cité, where a Celtic tribe first settled and where the medieval city kept its cathedral, palace and prison — the Pont Neuf, the Conciergerie, the stained-glass jewel-box of Sainte-Chapelle, and Notre-Dame itself — then over the little bridge to the Île Saint-Louis, a serene 17th-century island-village left almost untouched. It's the oldest ground in Paris, and the best short introduction to how the city grew.

stops.title: Paris Islands — Introduction
stops.caption: Before there was a Paris, there was an island.
stops.transcriptText:
Before there was a Paris, there was an island.

Two thousand years ago, a tribe called the Parisii settled a teardrop of land in the middle of the Seine — defensible, easy to cross to either bank, impossible to ignore. The Romans took it and called the place Lutetia. Everything you think of as Paris — the boulevards, the towers, the twenty arrondissements spiralling outward — grew from this one island and the river around it.

This walk stays where the city started. It's short: a little under a kilometre and a half end to end, flat the whole way, along and across two islands that sit in the river one behind the other. You can do it in an afternoon with time to spare.

We'll begin at the western tip of the Île de la Cité, on the oldest bridge in Paris — which is, confusingly, the one called the New Bridge. From there we walk east along the island: past a medieval palace that became a prison, into a chapel built to hold a crown of thorns, and out to the cathedral that nearly burned down and came back. Then we cross one last short bridge to the Île Saint-Louis — the quiet island, the one where Paris stops performing and just lives.

The old coat of arms of the city is a ship riding the water, with a motto underneath: tossed by the waves, but never sunk. Stand on these islands long enough and you understand why. The river has flooded them, fire has taken parts of them, revolutions have emptied their palaces — and they're still here, still in the middle of everything.

Start at the Pont Neuf. Find the western point of the island, where the bridge crosses and a king sits on a bronze horse, looking downstream.

stops.title: Pont Neuf
stops.caption: You're standing on the Pont Neuf, the bridge that crosses the western tip of the island in two unequal spans.
stops.transcriptText:
You're standing on the Pont Neuf, the bridge that crosses the western tip of the island in two unequal spans. Walk out to the middle, to the point where the two halves meet and a king sits on a bronze horse. That's your spot.

First, the name. Pont Neuf means New Bridge — and it's the oldest one in Paris, finished in 1607. The joke writes itself, but stay with why the name stuck: when it opened, it genuinely was new, in a way the city had never seen. Every other bridge in Paris was lined with houses, shops stacked along both sides, so you crossed the river through a kind of tunnel and never saw the water. This one was built bare. No houses — just the span, the open sky, and, for the first time in the city, raised walkways set aside for people on foot, so you could cross without being run down by a cart.

So Parisians did something they'd never done on a bridge before: they lingered. They strolled out to the middle, watched the river, bought a song or a tooth-pulling from the hawkers who set up along it. The Pont Neuf didn't just cross the Seine — it invented the bridge as a place to be, rather than a thing to get over.

The king on the horse is Henri IV, who finished it. Look closely and you're looking at a replacement: the original statue was melted down for cannon during the Revolution, and this one was cast in 1818 to put him back where he belonged.

Now look past him, off the downstream point of the island, where the land narrows to nothing like the bow of a ship. There's a small park down at water level there — the Square du Vert-Galant. That shape, that prow, is the reason the old seal of Paris is a ship riding the current. You're standing at the front of it.

From here, turn and walk back onto the island, keeping the river on your left. A few minutes along the northern side brings you to a row of pale round towers rising straight out of the embankment — the Conciergerie. That's next.

stops.title: Conciergerie
stops.caption: The towers are the Conciergerie.
stops.transcriptText:
The towers are the Conciergerie. Stand on the walkway above the river so you can see them straight on — four of them, pale and round and capped with dark cones, rising right out of the embankment, and on the corner a square tower with a clock set into it.

That clock is the first public clock the city ever had, hung here in the 1370s so ordinary Parisians could tell the time without listening for church bells. But the clock is the gentle part of the story.

For around four hundred years, this was the centre of France — not a museum, not a courthouse, but the palace where the kings actually lived, the seat of royal power on the island where the city was born. When the kings finally moved out to grander places, they left the machinery of the state behind: courts, offices, and a prison in the lower floors of the old palace.

Then came the Revolution, and the prison became something the building's architects could never have imagined. In the 1790s the Conciergerie was the last address of the condemned — the place where prisoners waited, sometimes for a single night, before the cart came to carry them to the guillotine. Thousands passed through these rooms on that one-way trip. The most famous was the queen, Marie-Antoinette, held here through the autumn of 1793 in a small guarded cell, tried in the building, and taken out to her execution in October. Later, under the kings who returned to power, a chapel was built on the spot where her cell had stood.

So hold the whole arc of it in your head, standing here: the same walls that were once the proudest expression of French royalty became the place where French royalty was, quite deliberately, taken apart. Power and the end of power, in one building, on one island.

There's a single room left from the palace at its medieval height, and you don't have to imagine it — it's just inside, and it leads us to the next stop. Step into the complex behind these towers, among the law courts, and look for the slender spire rising above them. That's the Sainte-Chapelle.

stops.title: Sainte-Chapelle
stops.caption: You found it — that slender spire rising out of the cluster of law-court buildings.
stops.transcriptText:
You found it — that slender spire rising out of the cluster of law-court buildings. From the outside the Sainte-Chapelle barely shows itself; it's hemmed in now by the courts that grew up around it. Don't judge it from here. Go in, climb to the upper level, and look up.

What you'll be standing in is, in effect, the inside of a jewel. Fifteen windows, each about fifteen metres tall, run almost floor to ceiling all the way around, so the stone seems to vanish and the whole upper chapel becomes a cage of coloured glass — well over a thousand scenes from the Bible, glowing whenever the sun is behind them. On a bright afternoon the light comes through red and blue and lands on the floor in pools.

Here's why it exists. In the 1240s the king — Louis the Ninth, later made a saint — got hold of the most precious object in the Christian world: the Crown of Thorns, the one from the Passion, bought from the emperor in Constantinople, who was short of money. And here's the detail that tells you everything: the relics cost the king far more than this building did. Several times more. The Sainte-Chapelle isn't a church that happens to hold a relic — it's a reliquary you can walk inside, a glass case built around a crown, sized to the thing it was made to protect.

Think about what that means. A king took a sum that could have paid for fortresses or armies, spent it on a ring of thorns, and then wrapped it in the most beautiful room he could commission — not to hide it behind walls, but to flood it with light. That's not decoration. That's a thirteenth-century argument about what's worth the most, made in stone and glass.

The crown itself isn't here any more. It was moved long ago to the great cathedral at the other end of the island — and it was carried out of that cathedral by hand, in the dark, the night the building caught fire a few years back. That's where we're going next. Leave the law courts, keep walking east, and aim for the two square towers you'll start to see rising over the rooftops. Notre-Dame.

stops.title: Notre-Dame de Paris
stops.caption: Two towers, flat-topped and square, with a long row of carved figures across the front and a great round window in the centre.
stops.transcriptText:
Two towers, flat-topped and square, with a long row of carved figures across the front and a great round window in the centre. You're on the parvis — the wide open square in front of Notre-Dame. Find a spot where you can take in the whole west front, and let the crowd flow around you.

Before you look up, look down. Somewhere near the centre of the square, set into the ground, there's a small bronze marker — a star, with an inscription. That's Point Zéro: the exact spot from which every road distance in France is measured. When a sign out in the country tells you Paris is so many kilometres away, this is the point it means. The whole country is measured outward from the front step of this cathedral, on the island where the city began. The centre of France is, officially, right under your feet.

Now the cathedral. They began building it in 1163 and kept at it for the better part of a century — those towers, the rose window, the carved kings across the front. For more than eight hundred years it stood here, the heart of the city, until one evening a few years ago when the world watched it burn. The fire took the spire and tore through the roof — and that roof had a name. They called it the forest: a lattice of oak beams, hundreds of trees felled in the Middle Ages, each one shaped by hand, holding the lead roof above the stone.

And then France did something that wasn't guaranteed. It put the cathedral back. The forest was rebuilt the medieval way, with fresh oak and old tools, the spire went up again, and the stone was scrubbed of centuries of soot in the process. In December 2024 the doors reopened, and what you walk into now is brighter than anything in living memory — a building going on nine hundred years old that came back from the edge of being lost, and somehow looks new.

You've now walked the length of the older island, from its western point to here. One short bridge remains, just behind the cathedral, and it leads to the other island — the quiet one. Cross it, and the noise drops away. That's the Île Saint-Louis.

stops.title: Île Saint-Louis
stops.caption: You've crossed the Pont Saint-Louis, and you can probably feel the difference already.
stops.transcriptText:
You've crossed the Pont Saint-Louis, and you can probably feel the difference already. The crowds thin, the noise from the cathedral fades behind you, and you're on a single straight street running the length of a much smaller island. This is the Île Saint-Louis, and it's the quietest famous place in Paris.

Here's what makes it strange. Almost everywhere else in the city grew in layers, century on century. This island didn't. For most of its life it was muddy pasture — two little islets where cows were grazed — until, in the early 1600s, someone had the idea to join them together, throw a grid of streets across the result, and sell the plots. The whole island went up more or less at once, in one style, over a few decades, and then it essentially stopped. The tall pale houses lining this street are the originals.

So while the rest of Paris was torn up and rebuilt — most dramatically in the 1800s, when Baron Haussmann drove his wide boulevards through the medieval city — the Île Saint-Louis was left almost completely alone. No grand avenue cuts across it. To this day there's no Métro station on the island; you arrive on foot, over a bridge, the way you just did.

And the thing this island is most famous for, after centuries of being a discreet address for people who could afford the quiet, is ice cream. A shop called Berthillon has been making it here since 1954, and on a warm afternoon you'll see the evidence in every direction — people walking the bridges with a cone, in no hurry at all.

Which is the right note to end on. You started this walk at the prow of the island where Paris was born, among kings and relics and a cathedral that came back from the dead — and you finish it here, on the small island that chose, very deliberately, to be nothing grander than a good place to live. Find a spot on the stone edge above the water, sit down, and watch the river go by. It's been doing that since before there was a city. Tossed by the waves, never sunk.

tours.title: The Left Bank
tours.shortDescription: A downhill walk through the Latin Quarter — Paris's quarter of the mind — from the Panthéon past Shakespeare and Company and the Luxembourg gardens to the river and the Musée d'Orsay.
tours.longDescription: The Left Bank is where Paris goes to think: the Latin Quarter, named for the language its medieval students spoke, still wrapped around the Sorbonne. This ~2 km, mostly-downhill walk runs from the domed Panthéon — the Republic's shrine to its great minds — down through the old sloping streets to the English-language bookshop Shakespeare and Company, across to the Luxembourg gardens and the vast church of Saint-Sulpice, into the café-and-jazz heart of Saint-Germain-des-Prés, and finally to the river and the Impressionist galleries of the Musée d'Orsay. Philosophy, books, gardens and painting, in one line to the Seine.

stops.title: The Left Bank — Introduction
stops.caption: For roughly eight hundred years, this corner of Paris has been where the city goes to think.
stops.transcriptText:
For roughly eight hundred years, this corner of Paris has been where the city goes to think.

You're starting on the Left Bank — the south side of the river — in the part of town the maps call the fifth and sixth arrondissements and everyone else calls the Latin Quarter. The name isn't decoration. For centuries the students here studied, argued, and swore in Latin, the shared language of the medieval university, and the nickname stuck long after the language faded from daily use. The university in question is the Sorbonne, which has been teaching on these slopes since the Middle Ages, and the streets around it have been thick with students, booksellers and arguments ever since.

So this walk has a single subject: the life of the mind. Where the rest of Paris was built around power, money, or worship, this quarter grew up around ideas — around reading, teaching, writing, and the long habit of disagreeing in public.

The good news for your legs is that it's downhill. We begin at the highest point, the Panthéon, on the hill named for Sainte-Geneviève, and the route runs gently down from there — through the old university streets, past a famous bookshop, into a garden a queen built to cure her homesickness, by way of two old churches, and finally to the river, where the walk ends inside a museum that used to be a railway station. A little over two kilometres, easy going, mostly down.

One thread to carry the whole way: almost everything we'll stop at was built for one purpose and ended up serving another. The quarter has a habit of changing its mind — which, for a place dedicated to thinking, feels about right.

When you're ready, climb to the top of the hill and stand in front of the Panthéon — the enormous domed building that looks like it can't decide whether it's a church or a monument. As it happens, that's exactly the question, and it's where we start.

stops.title: Panthéon
stops.caption: You're at the top of the hill now, in front of the Panthéon — that vast, grey, domed building with a long row of columns across the front, looking for all the w
stops.transcriptText:
You're at the top of the hill now, in front of the Panthéon — that vast, grey, domed building with a long row of columns across the front, looking for all the world like a Roman temple that wandered into Paris and sat down.

Stand back far enough to take in the whole front and read the inscription across the top: it says, in French, that the grateful nation honours its great men. Hold on to that word — honours — because this building has spent its whole life arguing about who, exactly, deserves it.

It started as a church. A king, Louis the Fifteenth, fell ill, swore that if he recovered he'd build a magnificent church to Sainte-Geneviève, the patron saint of Paris — and he recovered, and he built it. But the work took decades, and by the time it was done the Revolution had arrived, and a building meant for a saint suddenly looked like the perfect home for the nation's heroes instead. So they turned it into a temple to the great dead. Then a later government turned it back into a church. Then back to a temple. Back and forth it went, something like five times, depending on who held power and what they believed.

What finally settled the argument is downstairs. Below your feet, in the crypt, lie the people France chose to keep: the writers Voltaire and Rousseau and Victor Hugo, the novelist Émile Zola, and — placed here in 1995, the first woman admitted for her own achievements rather than her husband's — the scientist Marie Curie.

And then there's the pendulum. Hanging from the centre of the dome is a long wire with a heavy weight swinging slowly at the end. In 1851 a physicist named Foucault hung one here to prove something nobody could otherwise see: that the Earth turns. The pendulum keeps swinging in a single fixed direction while the floor — and the building, and the city — rotate slowly beneath it. People came to watch the planet move.

Which is the whole quarter in one room. A building that couldn't decide whether to worship God or genius, that finally chose its dead by merit, with a piece of pure human reasoning swinging where the altar would have been.

When you've looked your fill, head back out and down the hill, north toward the river, into the tangle of old streets below. We're walking into the Latin Quarter itself — and a famous bookshop — next.

stops.title: The Latin Quarter & Shakespeare and Company
stops.caption: You've come down off the hill into a maze of narrow, sloping streets — some of the oldest in Paris, laid out long before anyone thought to straighten them.
stops.transcriptText:
You've come down off the hill into a maze of narrow, sloping streets — some of the oldest in Paris, laid out long before anyone thought to straighten them. You're near the river now, and if you've stopped where I think you have, you're in front of a green shopfront with books stacked in the windows and, more often than not, a small crowd gathered at the door. The sign reads Shakespeare and Company.

First, the streets themselves. This is the heart of the Latin Quarter, and the name is a fossil. For centuries the students of the university spoke and studied in Latin — the common tongue that let a scholar from anywhere in Europe argue with a scholar from anywhere else — and the quarter took its name from the language ringing through it. The students are still here; the Latin is long gone. The place is named for something nobody says anymore.

Which brings us to the bookshop, because it works exactly the same way. This shop — English-language, famous, photographed half to death — was opened in 1951 by an American named George Whitman. But the name over the door isn't original to it. He borrowed it, in 1964, from another shop entirely.

The first Shakespeare and Company belonged to a woman named Sylvia Beach, who ran it a few streets from here in the years between the wars. It was the clubhouse of the expatriate writers — and in 1922, when no respectable publisher would touch it, Beach herself published James Joyce's novel Ulysses. Her shop closed during the Second World War and never reopened.

So the shop in front of you is, in a sense, a tribute act: a homage, under a borrowed name, to a place that no longer exists.

And that's the quarter's whole trick. It honours the past by impersonating it — a neighbourhood named for a dead language, anchored by a bookshop named for a vanished shop, both of them thoroughly alive on the strength of the thing they're remembering.

When you're ready, walk west a few minutes to the tall iron gates of a garden — the Jardin du Luxembourg. A homesick queen built it, and we'll go in next.

stops.title: Jardin du Luxembourg
stops.caption: Through the gates and onto the gravel, and the whole garden opens out in front of you — wide paths, clipped trees, a big octagonal pond, and beyond it a grand pale palace.
stops.transcriptText:
Through the gates and onto the gravel, and the whole garden opens out in front of you — wide paths, clipped trees, a big octagonal pond, and beyond it a grand pale palace. Before anything else, find a chair. There are hundreds of them, dark green metal, scattered loose across the grounds, and the rule is wonderfully simple: drag one wherever you like and sit. We'll talk for a moment.

The palace at the far end was not built for the public. It went up in the early 1600s for Marie de Médicis — an Italian, from the great Florentine family, who had married a French king, been widowed, and found herself stranded in a grey northern city she never warmed to. So she built herself a piece of home: a palace modelled on the one she'd grown up around in Florence, heavy Tuscan stonework and all, an attempt to import a little Italy to the banks of the Seine. Today it houses the French Senate, which makes the garden you're sitting in, technically, the Senate's front lawn.

Off to one side, tucked under the trees, she added the thing she missed most — a long, shaded, dripping grotto of a fountain, Italian to its bones. It's called the Medici Fountain, it's the most un-Parisian corner of Paris, and it's the corner that feels most like the woman who ordered it.

Here's the turn, though. A homesick queen's private consolation has become, four centuries on, the most generous public room in the city — a place where students cram for exams, retirees doze in the sun, children sail toy boats on the pond, and you arrange your own chair exactly where the light is best. The mind needs somewhere to rest as much as somewhere to work, and the quarter put one right in its middle.

When you've had your sit, leave by the western side and walk a couple of minutes to a very large church with two mismatched towers — Saint-Sulpice. There's a machine hidden in its floor.

stops.title: Saint-Sulpice
stops.caption: Into the square, past the big lion-footed fountain, and up to the front of the church — Saint-Sulpice.
stops.transcriptText:
Into the square, past the big lion-footed fountain, and up to the front of the church — Saint-Sulpice. Look up at the two towers and you'll see they don't match: one is finished and ornate, the other plainer and slightly shorter, as if the builders ran out of money or patience. They more or less did. Step inside; it's vast, cool and usually quiet.

Now look down at the floor. Running across the church near the front, on your right, is a thin brass strip set into the stone, and at one end of it stands a white marble obelisk. This is a gnomon — an astronomical instrument hidden inside a church. There's a small opening high in a window opposite; at midday, sunlight falls through it and lands somewhere along that brass line, and exactly where it lands depends on the time of year. Built in the 1700s, its real job was severely practical: to fix the date of the spring equinox, and from there the date of Easter, which drifts around the calendar every year. A sun-machine, installed to keep the church's own calendar honest.

You may have heard a different story. A wildly successful novel, a couple of decades ago — you'll know the one — recast this brass line as an ancient pagan meridian thick with secret meaning. It made such an impression that the parish eventually put up a notice, in plain language, explaining that the line is a piece of eighteenth-century astronomy and nothing occult whatsoever. A church, defending science against a thriller.

Before you go, step into the first chapel on your right. The murals there are by Eugène Delacroix, and they were among the last things he ever painted — fierce, dark, restless work from the very end of a great career.

It's a fitting stop for this quarter: a building that set a scientific experiment into its floor, kept faith and reason under one roof, and then had to stand up for the reasoning when a good story tried to carry it off.

From the front of the church, head north a few minutes toward the oldest church in Paris — and the cafés that ended up more famous than it. Saint-Germain-des-Prés is next.

stops.title: Saint-Germain-des-Prés
stops.caption: You're in a small, busy square now, with a stout, square stone tower rising over it — older and plainer than almost anything around it.
stops.transcriptText:
You're in a small, busy square now, with a stout, square stone tower rising over it — older and plainer than almost anything around it. That's the church of Saint-Germain-des-Prés, and it is the oldest church in Paris. There has been an abbey on this spot since the year 558; the tower you're looking at went up around the year 1000, which makes it one of the oldest standing things in the whole city. For most of its life this was a powerful monastery out beyond the old city walls — the name means Saint Germain of the Fields.

Now turn to the two corners across the way, because this is where the story gets quietly funny. On one side sits the Café de Flore; a few steps along, Les Deux Magots. Two perfectly ordinary-looking cafés — and in the middle of the twentieth century they became the most famous thinking-spots in Europe.

This was the headquarters of the existentialists. The philosopher Jean-Paul Sartre and the writer Simone de Beauvoir more or less worked here, at the tables, for hours, day after day, and Albert Camus and half of literary Paris drifted through. There's a practical reason alongside the romantic one: the cafés were heated and their rooms were not, so the warm café became the office, the salon and the stage all at once.

Which is the through-line of this whole walk, sitting on a single corner. A thousand-year-old church, founded by monks who came here to think and pray in silence, quietly out-famoused by two coffee houses where a later set of thinkers did much the same job out loud. Same corner, same impulse, a millennium apart.

We're nearly at the river now. Walk north to the Seine, and a short way along the bank you'll find a huge old railway station with an enormous glass clock set into its wall. That's the Musée d'Orsay, and it's where we finish.

stops.title: Musée d'Orsay
stops.caption: Last stop.
stops.transcriptText:
Last stop. Stand in the great main hall and look up: a long, vaulted ceiling of glass and pale iron arching the length of the building, daylight pouring down through it. It doesn't look like a museum, and that's because it wasn't built as one. This was a railway station.

It's called the Gare d'Orsay, and it was put up in a hurry for the World's Fair of 1900 — a grand, modern terminus right in the centre of the city, all that glass and iron showing off how confident Paris felt about the new century. The trouble was that trains kept getting longer, and by the late 1930s the platforms here were simply too short for them. The station slid into odd, part-time uses, fell half-derelict, and came close to being torn down. Then, in 1986, it reopened as something else entirely: a museum.

And look at what they chose to fill it with. The collection here covers roughly the half-century before the First World War — the Impressionists and the painters who came just after: Monet, Renoir, Cézanne, Van Gogh and their whole restless generation. Which means the art on these walls was made at almost exactly the moment this building was going up. The station and the paintings are the same age.

Now find the great clock. High in the wall at the upper end of the hall is an enormous glass clock face, and you can stand right behind it and look out through the numbers at the city beyond — Paris framed inside a timepiece, which is about as on-the-nose as this place is willing to get.

And it's the right place to end. We started at the top of the hill, in a building that couldn't decide what it worshipped; we've come down through a quarter that names itself after a dead language, keeps a borrowed bookshop, and argues with novelists about its own floor. We finish inside a railway station that was nearly demolished and became, instead, a kind of mirror — the era looking back at itself, hung on the walls of its own train shed.

That's the Left Bank: the part of Paris that goes there to think, and that can't quite stop thinking about itself. Stay a while behind the clock. The view doesn't get old.

tours.title: Berczy Park
tours.shortDescription: A cast-iron fountain crowned with twenty-seven dogs — and one aloof cat — in the shadow of the city's oldest church spire.
tours.longDescription: A small triangular green behind the Gooderham flatiron, built around a tiered fountain swarming with dogs all gazing up at a single golden bone. The 2017 design nearly got rejected as too silly — approved only once a lone cat and two birds gave it a story. Two blocks north rises St. James Cathedral, whose 93-metre spire, the tallest church spire in Canada, once greeted every newcomer stepping off the train.

stops.title: Berczy Park
stops.caption: Stand by the dog fountain and count the pack, then look north up Church Street to the stone spire of St. James Cathedral.
stops.transcriptText:
Within a single block, this neighbourhood keeps both its most solemn thing and its most ridiculous one. And somehow they belong together.

Start in Berczy Park, the small triangular green space tucked right behind the flatiron building. Its centrepiece is a tall, tiered cast-iron fountain covered in dogs — a whole pack of them, every one gazing up at a single golden bone balanced at the very top.

Count the dogs first.

There are twenty-seven of them, all fixed on that bone. Look a little harder and you'll find a cat who refuses to join in — perched off to the side, staring instead at two birds on a nearby lamppost. That cat is the punchline of the whole design. When the fountain was first proposed, around 2017, the city nearly turned it down — a fountain of dogs seemed far too silly for serious public art — and only approved it once the cat and the birds were added to give it a story. Even the park's name is contested: people argued over it for years, until the city officially settled on "bear-ski." Think of a bear on skis, and you've got it.

Now look north, a couple of blocks up Church Street, to a tall stone spire rising over the rooftops. That's the Cathedral Church of St. James. Its congregation is the oldest in the city — it goes back to 1797, when this was still the town of York. The spire climbs to about ninety-three metres, the tallest church spire in the country, and for decades it was simply the tallest thing in Toronto: the first landmark newcomers saw as they stepped off the train at the old station. The main church opened in 1853; the spire and its ring of bells took another twenty years to finish.

One block, two ideas of what a place is for. A spire built to make you feel small and reverent, and a fountain built to make you laugh — and yet both of them are exactly the same thing underneath: somewhere people gather and look up together. Sit by the dogs a while, glance north at the spire, and notice the city left room for the sacred and the ridiculous within a two-minute walk.

tours.title: Distillery District
tours.shortDescription: Once the largest distillery in the British Empire — saved from demolition because, for a while, it was too old to run and too handsome to knock down.
tours.longDescription: A pedestrian lane of dark Victorian brick — the Boiler House, the Cooperage — where Gooderham and Worts distilled millions of gallons of whisky and once paid a startling share of the whole country's taxes. Production stopped in 1990; the too-solid, too-old buildings became the busiest film set in Canada, then reopened in 2003 as a chains-free quarter of shops and studios, often called the best-preserved Victorian industrial architecture in North America.

stops.title: Distillery District
stops.caption: Stand at the foot of Trinity Street and look up the cobblestone lane lined with red-brick warehouses — no cars, just brick.
stops.transcriptText:
This was once the largest distillery in the British Empire. And the reason it's still standing is that, for a while, nobody wanted it.
