It was built as the head office of the Gooderham distilling family — hold onto that name, because we'll end this walk at the distillery that made their fortune — and the rounded prow gave the executives on the top floor the best possible view down the street toward their empire.

Now turn and look at the building's flat back wall, the one facing the park. Someone has painted the entire thing as a giant optical illusion — a trompe-l'oeil of windows and a great sail-like facade peeling away from the brick. It's one of the most photographed walls in the city, and it exists for the simple reason that a blank Victorian back wall was too good a canvas to waste.

And the park you're standing in, Berczy Park, has a secret of its own: that central fountain is covered in cast-iron dogs — dozens of them, every one a different breed, all gazing up at a single golden bone on top. Look closely and you'll find exactly one cat, pointedly ignoring the whole affair. It's the least serious monument in Old Town, and locals adore it.

When you're ready, walk north up Church Street, a block or two uphill, toward the tall Gothic spire you can probably already see. That's St. James Cathedral.

stops.title: St. James Cathedral
stops.caption: Walk north up Church Street toward the tall Gothic spire — the tallest in the old city.
stops.transcriptText:
This is the Cathedral Church of St. James, and that spire is the tallest in the old city — for a long time the tallest structure in Toronto, full stop, and still one of the tallest church spires in the country. In a town this age, the church steeple was the skyline, the thing you steered by from the lake.

There's been a church on this corner since the 1790s, though the earlier ones kept burning down; the building you're looking at went up in the 1850s, its great spire finished a couple of decades later, in the confident Gothic style a young colonial city used when it wanted to look permanent. Step inside if the doors are open — it's quieter than you'd expect for a downtown corner, tall stained glass and a hush the traffic outside never quite reaches.

The thing to notice is where it sits. This was, for the early town, the centre of everything — the church, the market, and the seat of government all within a few minutes of each other, which is more or less the walk you're on right now. Old Town isn't a scatter of separate landmarks; it's the actual core of the original city, still arranged the way it always was.

Head back down toward Front Street and turn east. Two blocks along, at the corner of Front and Jarvis, you'll come to a long grey building with arched windows — and, across the street, a striking new one in glass and orange steel. That's the St. Lawrence Market.

stops.title: St. Lawrence Market
stops.caption: At Front and Jarvis, find the long grey South Market (once City Hall) and the glass-and-orange-steel North Market across the street.
stops.transcriptText:
Two buildings, one market, two hundred years of history. Start with the long grey South building, the one with the arched central hall — a market has stood on this spot since 1803, which makes it older than almost anything else you've seen today. But here's the part people miss: this building was once City Hall. The upstairs held the council chamber and the mayor's office; the basement held the city jail. For a stretch of the nineteenth century, Toronto bought its vegetables directly beneath the room where it governed itself, and not far from the cells. Commerce, democracy, and punishment, all under one roof.

Inside today it's a food market, six days a week — and if you try one thing, make it a peameal bacon sandwich, a Toronto institution this market is credited with making famous.

Now look across the street at the new building in glass and orange steel. That's the rebuilt North Market, reopened after years of the Saturday farmers' market camping under a tent while it went up — and it was designed by the same British architect behind the famous inside-out Pompidou Centre in Paris, which is why it wears its structure on the outside like that. It also quietly took in the courts that moved out of Old City Hall, so the market's old sideline in civic business isn't entirely gone.

For the last stop, we leave the old core behind. Walk southeast, about fifteen minutes, toward the lake and Parliament Street, to a cluster of Victorian brick buildings and cobblestone lanes closed to cars. That's the Distillery District.

stops.title: Distillery District
stops.caption: Southeast toward Parliament Street: a cluster of Victorian brick buildings and cobblestone lanes closed to cars.
stops.transcriptText:
You've arrived at the end of the walk, and at the other end of a story we started an hour ago. Remember the Flatiron — the wedge built as the head office of the Gooderham family? This is where their money came from. Gooderham and Worts began distilling here in 1832, and by the late nineteenth century this was one of the largest distilleries in the world: a small city of brick buildings turning Ontario grain into whisky by the barrel.

Look around at what that left behind — dozens of Victorian industrial buildings, widely called the best-preserved collection of their kind in North America, all in the warm red brick and cobblestone the era ran on. And the reason it survived, when so much of industrial Toronto was flattened, is almost aggressively simple: after the distillery closed, instead of tearing it down, the whole district was handed over to people on foot. No cars, at all. Cobblestone lanes, galleries, cafes, and studios in the old still-houses and warehouses.

It's a neat closing argument for the whole walk. Toronto spent a long time as a city that knocked down its own past without much sentiment — and Old Town is the counter-example, the founding core that got kept: the rail cathedral, the market that governed a town, the church that marked its centre, and the industrial engine that paid for it, all still here, still legible, block by block.

So take your time here at the end. Get a coffee, walk the lanes, look up at the brick. You've just walked the length of the city Toronto used to be — from the grandest door it ever built to the works that made it rich — and it's all still standing, which, for this city, is rather the whole point.

tours.title: Museum Mile: How Toronto Remade Its Institutions
tours.shortDescription: Toronto's knowledge quarter around Queen's Park — two museums, the old university, the legislature, and a great gallery — bookended by rupture (the ROM's glass Crystal) and homecoming (Gehry's AGO).
tours.longDescription: The gentlest walk of the set: five stops, north to south, through the leafy museum-and-university cluster around Queen's Park. Every stop is an institution that remade itself — from the Royal Ontario Museum, where a famous outsider drove a glass Crystal through the heritage wall, past the shoebox-shaped Bata Shoe Museum and the quietly reinvented University of Toronto, to Queen's Park (twice reborn from fire), and finally Frank Gehry's Art Gallery of Ontario, the local boy's gentle homecoming in wood and glass. Rupture at one end, homecoming at the other.

stops.title: Museum Mile — Introduction
stops.caption: Start up at Bloor Street and Avenue Road and look up at the ROM's glass Crystal before you begin.
stops.transcriptText:
If the last walk was about money and power, this one is about knowledge — and it runs in a rough line north to south, from a museum full of dinosaurs to a gallery remade by one of the most famous architects who ever lived.

You're starting up at Bloor Street, in the cluster of museums and university buildings that Toronto has quietly packed into a few leafy blocks around Queen's Park. Five stops: two museums, the provincial legislature, the old university at the heart of it all, and a great art gallery to finish. It's the gentlest walk of the set — flat, shaded, mostly through a university campus that most of the city forgets is even here.

Here's the thread to carry. Almost every building on this walk is an old institution that decided, at some point, to remake itself — and the two that bookend the route show the opposite ways a city can do that. It opens with a museum that had a giant glass crystal smashed into its side by a famous outsider, a building half of Toronto openly hated. It ends with a gallery that a local boy — who first fell in love with art and buildings inside its walls as a child — came home, decades later, to rebuild gently, from the inside, in wood and glass, and that almost everyone adores.

Rupture at one end, homecoming at the other. Start with the rupture.

Look up at the Crystal. This is the Royal Ontario Museum.

stops.title: Royal Ontario Museum — the Crystal
stops.caption: Stand at Bloor and Avenue Road and look at the jagged glass-and-aluminum Crystal bursting from the old stone museum.
stops.transcriptText:
Stand back on the corner of Bloor Street and Avenue Road and look at what's happened to this building. A stately old stone museum — and bursting out of its side, tilting over the sidewalk at angles that look almost dangerous, a huge jagged form of glass and brushed aluminum, like a shard of ice driven into the old stone. That's the Michael Lee-Chin Crystal, and it is probably the most argued-about building in the country.

The museum behind it is a century old — the Royal Ontario Museum opened in 1914, Canada's largest, with something like eighteen million objects: dinosaurs, meteorites, mummies, and one of the world's great collections of fossils. For most of that century it looked exactly like what it was, a dignified temple of learning. Then, in 2007, came the Crystal.

The architect was Daniel Libeskind, and the story goes that he sketched the first version on a paper napkin at a wedding held inside the museum — five interlocking crystal forms, inspired, he said, by the gem collection downstairs. When it opened, a great many Torontonians hated it, loudly and at length; one American critic called it the worst building of its decade. Others defended it just as fiercely, and both camps are still going.

Here's the thing to notice, and it's the key to the whole walk. By the time the Crystal went up, museums all over the world had figured out that a wild building could put them on the map overnight — and the ROM wanted in. So it let a famous outsider drive a shard through its heritage wall and dare the city to look away. Nobody has managed to look away yet.

Whatever you make of it, remember the gesture — the loud, deliberate rupture — because the last stop on this walk does the exact opposite.

For now, walk west along Bloor Street, just a couple of minutes, to a building shaped like a shoebox. That's the Bata Shoe Museum.

stops.title: Bata Shoe Museum
stops.caption: Walk west to Bloor and St. George; find the low limestone building shaped like a shoebox with its lid set slightly askew.
stops.transcriptText:
You've walked a couple of blocks west, to the corner of Bloor and St. George, and here's a very different kind of museum building. Look at its shape: a low box of pale limestone with the roofline tilted, just slightly, as though a lid had been set down on top and not quite pushed flush. That's deliberate. The whole building is designed to look like a shoebox with the lid a little askew.

This is the Bata Shoe Museum, and the joke of its architecture is also its subject. It holds the largest collection of footwear in the world — something like twelve thousand pieces, spanning four and a half thousand years, from ancient sandals to the shoes of the famous. It grew out of one woman's private collection: Sonja Bata, of the global shoe-making family, who spent decades gathering shoes as a way of reading whole cultures through what they put on their feet.

The architect, Raymond Moriyama, was one of the finest this country produced, and rather than build a temple, he built a container — even the limestone was chosen because it has the warm, soft look of leather. Where the ROM up the street shouts for your attention, this one makes a quiet, witty little bow: a museum disguised as the most ordinary object in your closet.

From here, cross the street and head south, down into the tree-lined heart of the University of Toronto, toward the wide green circle at its centre. That's King's College Circle.

stops.title: University of Toronto — King's College Circle
stops.caption: Cross south into King's College Circle, the big oval of lawn at the historic heart of the university.
stops.transcriptText:
You've come into King's College Circle, a big oval of lawn ringed by old stone buildings, and the first thing to notice is how quiet it is — you're in the geographic centre of downtown, and you can hear birds. This is the historic heart of the University of Toronto, almost two hundred years old, and in a very Toronto way it spends most of its time hiding in plain sight behind the office towers.

Nearly everything on this walk grew out of this campus. The university leased the land the provincial legislature now sits on; it ran the ROM in its early years; the whole strip of learning you're walking is, in a sense, the university's overflow. And it has a long habit of remaking itself: University College, the grand building on the west side, burned nearly to the ground in a fire in 1890 and was rebuilt.

It just did it again, underground. The lawn near you was recently torn up, the cars sent below ground, and in their place the university drilled hundreds of wells straight down into the bedrock — some two hundred and fifty metres deep, half the height of the CN Tower — to build the largest urban geothermal field in the country, quietly heating the century-old buildings around you.

No shard of glass, no famous name on it — the oldest institution here reinvented itself by digging down and going silent. Beneath it all runs a buried creek the campus is slowly bringing back to the surface, a nod to the older meeting place this land has always been.

Now walk east, out of the circle and across to the pink stone palace at the foot of University Avenue. That's Queen's Park, the Ontario Legislature.

stops.title: Queen's Park — Ontario Legislature
stops.caption: At the foot of University Avenue, look up at the long pink-sandstone legislature closing off the avenue.
stops.transcriptText:
You're standing at the foot of University Avenue, looking up at a long, heavy palace of pink sandstone — turrets, round arches, deep-set windows. This is Queen's Park, home of the Ontario Legislature, and it closes off the top of the avenue like a full stop at the end of a very grand sentence.

It opened in 1893, built from pink stone quarried west of the city and carved, block by block, right here on the lawn. The style is all rounded arches and rough stone, and at the time plenty of locals grumbled that it looked too American. But the building you see isn't quite the one that opened. On a September afternoon in 1909, a spark from a workman's fire-pot on the roof set the west wing alight; staff formed a human chain at the doors of the legislative chamber and saved it, but the wing and the library behind it — a hundred thousand books — were lost.

The man brought in to rebuild the west wing was E.J. Lennox, the same architect who left his fingerprints all over Victorian Toronto, including the old courthouse downtown. He rebuilt it a little taller and lined the inside in pale Italian marble — so today, if you climb the grand staircase within, the east wing is dark Victorian oak and the west wing is bright stone, a fire-line running right through the middle of the building.

Like the university behind you, this place burned and rose again — and it's about to be remade one more time: the whole building is due for a deep restoration, with the legislators to be moved, temporarily, somewhere the province has been oddly quiet about naming.

For the last stop, walk back down the length of University Avenue and turn west onto Dundas Street, to a gallery wrapped in glass and wood. That's the Art Gallery of Ontario.

stops.title: Art Gallery of Ontario
stops.caption: Down University Avenue and west on Dundas to McCaul: step under the long curving wall of glass and warm wood.
stops.transcriptText:
You've come down University Avenue and west along Dundas to the corner of McCaul, and running above you is a long, curving wall of glass and warm wood — like the upturned hull of a wooden boat stretched the length of a city block. Step under it. This is the Art Gallery of Ontario, and it's where the walk's argument lands.

The gallery grew, more than a century ago, out of a single donated house behind it — the Grange — and has expanded many times since. But the version you're standing in was shaped, in 2008, by Frank Gehry: one of the most famous architects who ever lived, the man behind the wildest, shiniest buildings of his era. This one is different from all of them, for one reason — Frank Gehry was born in Toronto. As a boy he came to this very gallery, and later said it was here he first felt the pull between art and building. This was his first work in his own country: a homecoming.

So instead of a titanium spectacle, he did something quieter. That wooden gallery over the street is the Galleria Italia — glass and Douglas fir, close to two hundred metres of it — and inside, a sculptural staircase spirals up and bursts through the roof. Critics who braced for Gehry to shout called it, instead, his most relaxed and graceful building: restraint, from the least restrained architect alive.

Frank Gehry died in late 2025, at ninety-six, which leaves this building as a kind of farewell — the local boy's last gift to the city that first showed him what a building could do. And it's the right place to end. The walk began at the ROM with a rupture: a stranger driving a glass shard through an old wall and daring you to look. It ends here with a homecoming: someone remaking the place he loved from the inside, in wood, so gently you could almost miss it. Two ways to keep an old city alive — and Toronto, being Toronto, kept them both, a few blocks apart.

Stay a while, and walk back and forth beneath the wood. It's the warmest ceiling in the city.

tours.title: Downtown Spine: Money, Power, and Two City Halls
tours.shortDescription: The money-and-power line north from the lake — the CN Tower, the bank towers and the hidden city beneath them, and the two city halls staring each other down across Bay Street.
tours.longDescription: A near-straight walk north from the waterfront through downtown's spine, tied by one Toronto habit: it would rather repurpose a building than lose it. From the CN Tower (an antenna that became the skyline), past a 19th-century bank now sheltering the Stanley Cup under Brookfield Place's ribbed canopy, into Mies van der Rohe's black TD Centre and the underground PATH, out to Nathan Phillips Square's space-age City Hall — and finally Old City Hall, saved from demolition, glaring across Bay Street at its replacement. An easy 20-minute line, mostly flat, with a warm underground twin in winter.

stops.title: Downtown Spine — Introduction
stops.caption: Stand at the foot of the CN Tower and look straight up, then north along the line of the walk.
stops.transcriptText:
Stand for a second at the foot of the CN Tower and look straight up — then look around. Almost everything on this walk is within sight of where you are now, more or less in a line running north, from the lake toward the old heart of downtown.

This is the money-and-power walk. It starts at the tower a railway built, runs through the black towers of the banks and the hidden city underneath them, and ends at a place where Toronto keeps both of its city halls — the one it built in 1899, and the one it built to replace it — standing across the street from each other, staring.

That's the thread to hold onto. Toronto has never been especially good at tearing things down. Some cities clear the past away and build clean; this one tends to keep the old version around, give it a new job, and let it sit next to whatever came after. You'll see it in a bank that became a shrine, and you'll see it most of all at the end, where the two city halls face off across Bay Street like an argument nobody won.

The route is an easy one: a fairly straight line north, mostly flat, maybe twenty minutes of walking if you don't stop — which you will. And in winter, most of the middle stretch has a warm underground twin you can duck into.

Start where the whole skyline starts. Look up at the CN Tower.

stops.title: CN Tower
stops.caption: Stand at the base of the CN Tower and follow the tapering concrete shaft up to the pod and antenna.
stops.transcriptText:
You're standing at the base of the tallest free-standing structure in the Western Hemisphere, which is a strange thing to build on purpose, and stranger still to build almost by accident.

Look up. It's five hundred and fifty-three metres to the top, and for thirty-two years — from the mid-1970s until 2007, when a tower in Dubai finally passed it — this was the tallest free-standing structure anywhere on earth. It held that title longer than most records survive, and it lost it quietly, the way this city tends to lose things: without much fuss.

Here's the part that usually gets left out. The CN Tower wasn't built to be a landmark. It was built to be an antenna. By the 1970s the downtown office towers had grown tall enough to block television and radio signals, and the railway — Canadian National, the CN in the name — happened to own a vast stretch of emptied-out rail land right here, so it poured the tallest broadcast mast it could into concrete. A fix for bad reception. The fact that it became the thing every postcard and every establishing shot reaches for whenever a film wants you to know you're in Toronto — that was never really the plan.

The railway sold it years ago, and nobody could bring themselves to change the name, so the CN quietly stopped standing for Canadian National and started standing for, more or less, nothing in particular. It's just the tower now.

For this walk, think of it as the starting gun. We begin at the highest, most vertical thing in the city — and from here on, everything comes back down to earth, and some of it goes underground.

So bring your eyes down to street level and walk east along Front Street, toward the corner of Yonge, where a very old bank is quietly keeping the Stanley Cup. That's the Hockey Hall of Fame.

stops.title: Hockey Hall of Fame (Brookfield Place)
stops.caption: At Front and Yonge, step into Brookfield Place and look up at the white glass-and-steel canopy over the old stone bank.
stops.transcriptText:
You've come up to the corner of Front and Yonge, and if you step inside Brookfield Place, look up before you look at anything else. There's a soaring white canopy of glass and curved steel overhead — like the ribcage of some enormous animal, or the nave of a cathedral that decided to skip the stone.

That canopy is new. What it's sheltering is not. Tucked underneath it, kept whole, is a small, richly carved stone building that used to be a bank — the Bank of Montreal, built in the 1880s, back when a bank wanted to look like a Greek temple so you'd trust it with your savings. Columns, a domed and gilded banking hall, the works. When the developers put up the glass towers around here, they didn't knock the old bank down. They built the entire complex around it, like a pearl forming around a bit of grit.

And then they filled it with the Stanley Cup.

That's the Hockey Hall of Fame, and its grandest room — the old banking hall, all gold leaf and stained glass — is now where people line up to stand beside the holiest object in the national game. A temple to money, quietly converted into a temple to hockey.

Hold onto that move, because you'll keep seeing it on this walk: this is a city that would rather repurpose a building than lose it. Give the old thing a new job, and keep it standing.

From here, turn north and walk up toward King Street, into the shadow of the black towers. That's the Financial District — and the TD Centre.

stops.title: Financial District — TD Centre & the PATH
stops.caption: At King and Bay, stand under the plain black towers of the Mies van der Rohe TD Centre — the PATH runs beneath your feet.
stops.transcriptText:
Now you're at King and Bay, the actual crossroads of Canadian money, standing under a cluster of plain black towers that look, at first glance, like the most anonymous buildings on the walk. Give them a second.

These are the towers of the TD Centre, and they were the last great work of Mies van der Rohe — the German-born architect whose entire philosophy fit into three words: less is more. No ornament, no flourish, nothing carved into the stone, because there's barely any stone at all — just black steel, bronze-tinted glass, and proportions so exact it took a genius to make them look like nothing in particular. When they went up in the 1960s, they swept away the older downtown that stood here and announced the modern city. This is the future side of the walk — the part that didn't keep the old thing.

But look down. Beneath your feet, and beneath most of the blocks around you, runs the PATH: a whole second downtown, underground. Roughly thirty kilometres of climate-controlled tunnels and shopping concourses, linking the towers so that office workers can cross the core in January without ever reaching for a coat. For years it was billed as the largest underground shopping complex in the world — a title it eventually lost, on length, to Montreal's rival network, which is a fact the city has decided not to dwell on.

So even here, on the future side, the old instinct sneaks back in: the city quietly built a second version of itself and tucked it underneath the first.

Keep heading north up Bay Street toward Queen, until the towers open onto a wide public square with a low, curved concrete city hall at the back of it. That's Nathan Phillips Square.

stops.title: Nathan Phillips Square (New City Hall)
stops.caption: Walk north up Bay to the open square: the curved concrete City Hall and the 3-D TORONTO sign at its back.
stops.transcriptText:
You've walked out of the canyon of towers into open air: a big public square, a reflecting pool that turns into a skating rink when it freezes, a run of concrete arches, and that unmistakable three-dimensional sign spelling out the city's name, which half the people here are busy photographing themselves in front of. This is Nathan Phillips Square, and the thing at the back of it is the city hall Toronto built when it wanted to feel modern.

Look at it properly. Two curved towers, one taller than the other, cupped around a low round chamber in the middle — the council chamber, which from above looks a little like an eye held between two parentheses. It's the opposite of everything else on this walk: no columns, no stone temple, nothing pretending to be older than it is. A Finnish architect named Viljo Revell won an international competition to design it, beating out hundreds of entries from around the world, and when it opened in 1965 it was the city announcing, in poured concrete, that it meant to be a serious modern place.

Off to one side of the square is the Spirit Garden, a memorial to the survivors of Canada's residential schools — a quieter, more recent addition to a space that is meant, above all, to belong to everyone.

Because that's what this square really is. The money on this walk has mostly been private, locked inside towers and vaults, but this ground is public: the city's living room, its skating rink, its protest site, its backdrop.

Now, one last thing — and it's the whole point of the walk.

Turn around, and look across Bay Street. That old sandstone building with the great clock tower, glaring back at this one? That's Old City Hall.

stops.title: Old City Hall
stops.caption: Across Bay Street, take in the rose-sandstone pile and clock tower of Old City Hall, glaring back at the new.
stops.transcriptText:
Cross Bay Street, or simply stand where you are and take it in from the square: a huge Romanesque pile of rose and brown stone, arched and turreted, with a clock tower rising more than a hundred metres over the street and pointing straight down the length of Bay like it owns the view. Which, for a long time, it did.

This is Old City Hall, finished in 1899, and when it opened it was one of the largest civic buildings on the continent — the work of an architect named E.J. Lennox, who, after years of fighting the councillors over the building's ballooning cost, took a small revenge in stone: he had his own name carved into the band of stonework running under the eaves, letter by letter, because the city had refused him a plaque. Look closely under the roofline and it's still up there — the architect signing his own building out of spite.

Here's why it's the end of the walk. When the space-age city hall behind you opened in the 1960s, this one was meant to come down. There were real plans to demolish it and drop a shopping centre on the site, keeping perhaps the clock tower as a keepsake. It was saved by a stubborn band of citizens who refused to let it go, and for the next half a century it served as the city's main courthouse.

Now even the courts have moved out — some of them, fittingly, into the rebuilt St. Lawrence Market North a few blocks east — and the building sits empty: a national historic site with no settled job, while the city argues gently about what it ought to become — a museum, perhaps, or a library, or a hall for weddings — and nobody's quite decided.

So here they stand. The hall the city built to replace this one, and this one, which the city could never quite bring itself to lose — facing each other across a single street, old stone and new concrete, an argument nobody ever really won. That standoff might be the most Toronto thing in the whole downtown: a city that refuses to choose between its past and its future, and makes them share a corner instead, and look each other in the eye.

Stay a moment, and let them.

tours.title: Immigrant West: The City That Grew by Addition
tours.shortDescription: The 'immigrant west' — the part of Toronto that grew by addition, not replacement: the AGO around a 200-year-old house, Chinatown, Kensington Market, Graffiti Alley, and the ever-westward cool of Queen West.
tours.longDescription: A flat, dense, walkable hour through the part of Toronto that grew by addition rather than replacement — wave after wave adding a layer without scraping off the last. From the Art Gallery of Ontario (accreted around the 1817 Grange), west to Chinatown on Spadina (cleared in one place, regrown two blocks over), up into the layered stalls of Kensington Market, down to the ever-repainted murals of Graffiti Alley, and out along Queen West, where 'cool' keeps migrating one block further. Five versions of a single stubborn habit: never quite finished.

stops.title: Immigrant West — Introduction
stops.caption: Stand on Dundas Street West at McCaul in front of the AGO, downtown at your back and the immigrant west ahead.
stops.transcriptText:
Most of downtown Toronto was built the way you'd expect a city to build itself: clear the old thing, put up the new one, and repeat until the skyline looks modern. The stretch you're about to walk did almost the opposite.

You should be standing on Dundas Street West at the corner of McCaul, with the long, low galleries of the Art Gallery of Ontario in front of you and the office towers of downtown at your back. Everything ahead — west, and a little north — is what the city loosely calls the immigrant west: Chinatown along Spadina, the tangle of Kensington Market, a painted lane below Queen, and the long mile of Queen Street West beyond it.

Here's the thread to hold onto for the next hour. This is the part of Toronto that grew by addition rather than replacement. Wave after wave of newcomers arrived and added a layer without scraping off the one before, so the neighbourhoods out here read less like finished places and more like something still being assembled, layer over layer, in public.

The good news for your feet: it's flat, dense, and genuinely walkable, maybe forty-five minutes of actual walking, with one short stretch back south in the middle. If you tire, the Queen and Spadina streetcars cover most of it.

We'll go from the gallery west to Chinatown on Spadina, up into Kensington Market, back down to the lane they call Graffiti Alley, and out onto Queen West to finish.

Start where the habit is easiest to see, with a museum that grew exactly the way the neighbourhoods around it did. Turn to the Art Gallery of Ontario.

stops.title: Art Gallery of Ontario — the Grange
stops.caption: In front of the AGO's glass-and-wood front, find the old brick Grange house (1817) folded within the galleries.
stops.transcriptText:
You're standing in front of the Art Gallery of Ontario, its entrance set back from Dundas behind a long glass-and-wood front. Most people come for what's inside. For this walk, the interesting thing is how the building got here.

Walk your eye to the older brick house tucked behind and within the complex. That's the Grange, built in 1817, and it's the oldest surviving brick house in Toronto. It was left to the gallery in 1909, and here's the part worth carrying with you: the entire museum grew outward from that one house. Expansion after expansion wrapped around it over more than a century, and rather than tear the old house down, the gallery kept it, folded inside the galleries like a seed still sitting in the fruit.

The collection was assembled the same way, layer by layer. The gallery holds the most complete collection of the Group of Seven anywhere on earth, the largest collection of Henry Moore's sculpture in the world — Moore chose to send it here himself — and a major gift of Canadian and European art from the Thomson family. There's a dedicated centre where Indigenous and Canadian works are hung to speak to each other. None of it replaced what came before; it was all added to it.

Which makes this gallery a small model of the walk ahead. It didn't reinvent itself by clearing the ground. It accreted, around one stubborn old house, keeping every layer.

When you leave, head west along Dundas for two blocks, until the signage turns to Chinese and the street opens out at Spadina. That's Chinatown.

stops.title: Chinatown (Spadina)
stops.caption: At Dundas and Spadina, streetcars running down the middle and Chinese signage in every direction.
stops.transcriptText:
You've reached the corner of Dundas and Spadina — Spadina, when it's the avenue, said spa-dye-na — one of the widest streets downtown, streetcars running down the centre, Chinese signage in every direction.

This is Chinatown, but it's worth knowing it isn't the first one. Toronto's original Chinatown sat east of here, in the old immigrant district called the Ward, near where City Hall stands today. In the late 1950s and through the 1960s, roughly two-thirds of it was expropriated and cleared to build New City Hall and the square in front of it — the same square you may have crossed earlier on this trip.

The community did something quietly remarkable: it moved west, to Spadina and Dundas, and rebuilt. And when the city floated plans to clear that too, a restaurateur named Jean Lumb organised the Save Chinatown Committee and fought it to a standstill. Lumb went on to become the first Chinese-Canadian woman appointed to the Order of Canada, in part for that work.

So the reframe here is almost the whole walk in one story. A neighbourhood was erased in one place and simply re-grew two blocks over — subtraction answered, stubbornly, with addition. It's still changing today, as it always has; newer arrivals, rising rents, the usual pressures of a downtown that everyone wants a piece of. Chinatown has never once stopped being remade.

From here, walk north up Spadina and duck west into the narrow streets — Augusta, Baldwin, Kensington Avenue. That's Kensington Market.

stops.title: Kensington Market
stops.caption: Duck west off Spadina into the narrow streets — Augusta, Baldwin, Kensington Avenue — as the awnings drop low.
stops.transcriptText:
You've turned off Spadina into Kensington Market, and you can feel the scale change immediately: the streets narrow, the awnings drop low, and the shops spill their produce and racks and crates straight onto the sidewalk.

Read the market as layers and it opens right up. It began in the early 1900s as a Jewish market — pushcarts and front-room shops — and two synagogues from that era still stand in the streets around you. Then came the Portuguese, then Caribbean, then Vietnamese and Latin American and East African arrivals, each adding a layer of food and shopfronts and language without erasing the one underneath. The fishmonger, the taqueria, the vintage rack, and the cheese shop end up sharing the same half-block, and somehow it works.

Two things have kept it that way. First, the streets themselves: they were laid out for handcarts and foot traffic, with almost no parking, which makes the market structurally hostile to chain stores and towers — they simply can't fit. Second, people fought for it. In the 1960s a planning proposal called for flattening the small houses and putting up apartment blocks, and the neighbourhood organised and killed it. It was later named a National Historic Site in 2006, and then, in 2025, a Heritage Conservation District — with the city's own plan naming the market's sense of anarchy, inclusivity, and experimentation as the very thing worth protecting.

There's a lovely contradiction in that: rules written to protect a place whose whole character is that it resists being tidied.

Kensington is the purest version of everything on this walk — a neighbourhood made entirely by addition, layer over layer, and never once declared finished.

When you've had your fill, make your way back down to Spadina and south toward Queen. Just below Queen, between Spadina and Portland, is a lane that took this same habit and made it literal. They call it Graffiti Alley.

stops.title: Graffiti Alley (Rush Lane)
stops.caption: Down to Rush Lane just south of Queen, between Spadina and Portland — three blocks of ever-repainted murals.
stops.transcriptText:
You've come down to the lane officially named Rush Lane, running parallel to Queen just south of it. If the subway works around Queen and Spadina have the usual way in blocked off, you'll have come at it from the side, off Richmond — the city has been digging a new line through here, and the access shifts with the construction.

Now look at the walls. Three blocks, about a kilometre, of near-continuous murals, floor to roofline, and the key thing to understand is that almost none of it is permanent. The lane is repainted constantly, new work going up over old, so the wall in front of you didn't look like this a year ago and won't a year from now. One long mural crams the whole city onto a single wall — the tower, the streetcars, the raccoons that treat this place as theirs.

Here's the twist that makes the lane worth the detour. It isn't a legal wall. It's tolerated. For years the city ticketed graffiti here as vandalism, and then, in 2011, it reversed course, designated the lane an area of municipal significance, and set up a program to fund murals outright. The thing the city once fined, it now protects and pays for — a sanctioned wall of the unsanctioned.

Which is the walk's habit again, only now you can watch it happen in paint: layer over layer, nothing finished, the newest arrival painted right on top of the last.

Climb back up to the daylight of Queen Street West and turn west. The last stop is that same habit stretched thin over a couple of kilometres.

stops.title: Queen Street West
stops.caption: Up on Queen Street West, the streetcar rattling past boutiques, cafés and record shops running west.
stops.transcriptText:
You're up on Queen Street West now, the streetcar rattling past — the Queen car, one of the longest streetcar routes in North America — with boutiques and cafés and record shops running west as far as you can see.

Queen West runs on one simple, ruthless pattern: cool migrates. A stretch gets discovered, gets interesting, gets expensive, and the genuinely interesting stuff moves one block further west to where the rent is still cheap — and then that block gets discovered, and it happens again. This street has been doing it for decades, block after block, which is how a former garment district ended up being named, at one point, the second-coolest neighbourhood in the world by a fashion magazine — a ranking Toronto accepted with its usual faint embarrassment.

And yet it hasn't fully smoothed out. There's a grittiness gentrification keeps failing to scrub off: the live-music dive bars, the stacked vintage shops, the independent bookstore near Trinity Bellwoods holding its ground. The next layer arrives, but the last one doesn't entirely leave.

Which is the whole walk, in the end. Step back and look at what you've crossed: a museum that grew around a two-hundred-year-old house, a Chinatown that regrew after it was cleared, a market built of stacked newcomers, a lane repainted over and over, and now a street where cool keeps adding the next block west. Five versions of a single stubborn habit.

Most of downtown gets torn down and rebuilt. Out here, the city just keeps getting added to, and you've spent the last hour walking the proof.

So stay on the corner a moment before you go. Watch the streetcar, watch the street. Whatever it is right now, it isn't finished — and out here, that has always been the point.

tours.title: Amorepacific Museum of Art | 아모레퍼시픽미술관
tours.shortDescription: David Chipperfield's single clear volume in Yongsan — three voids cut for daylight, a free museum, and a moon-jar restraint that doubles as brand positioning.
tours.longDescription:
The Amorepacific headquarters in Yongsan was designed by British architect David Chipperfield and completed in 2017, the museum opening in 2018. He gave it a single clear volume — not a tower, not a cluster of forms, but one simply proportioned rectangular block, with three large voids cut through to draw daylight and nature inside. Amorepacific's own writers compare it to the white moon jar, the Joseon porcelain that finds richness through restraint. Whether Chipperfield intended it or not, the comparison holds.

The museum draws on a collection begun by founding chairman Suh Sungwhan, who started acquiring Korean art in the 1940s — celadon, lacquerwork, calligraphy — shown alongside international contemporary work by the likes of Barbara Kruger and Lee Bul. On the ground floor, the apLAP library holds more than ten thousand exhibition catalogues, free to browse.

stops.title: Amorepacific Museum of Art | 아모레퍼시픽미술관
stops.caption: Stand outside the headquarters and take in the single rectangular block, with its three voids cut for daylight.
stops.transcriptText:
The building you are standing outside is one of the most considered pieces of corporate architecture in Seoul, and the museum inside it is free to enter — which is either a very generous public gesture or an extremely effective piece of brand positioning, and in practice is probably both.

The Amorepacific headquarters in Yongsan was designed by the British architect David Chipperfield and completed in 2017, with the museum opening in 2018. Chipperfield gave the building a single clear volume — not a tower, not a complex of forms, but one large, simply proportioned rectangular block — with three large rectangular voids cut through it to bring daylight and nature into the interior. Amorepacific's own writers have drawn a comparison to the white moon jar, the Joseon-period porcelain form that achieves richness through restraint rather than decoration. Whether Chipperfield had the moon jar in mind or not, the comparison holds.

The museum on the basement and ground floors holds exhibitions drawn from a collection that began with the personal acquisitions of the company's founding chairman, Suh Sungwhan, who started collecting Korean art in the 1940s. The collection spans Korean historical art — celadon, lacquerwork, calligraphy — alongside international contemporary work, and the exhibitions are mounted with the same uncluttered attention to space that characterises the building above them. Past shows have included Barbara Kruger, Mary Corse, Rafael Lozano-Hemmer, and Lee Bul.

The apLAP library on the ground floor — formally the Amorepacific Library of Art Project — holds more than ten thousand exhibition catalogues from galleries and museums worldwide, available to browse freely. If the current exhibition doesn't capture you, the library probably will.

tours.title: Audeum Audio Museum | 오디움
tours.shortDescription: Kengo Kuma's aluminium-wrapped 'architectural instrument' in Seocho — the world's first museum of audio, 150 years of sound, and the machines that ended the silent era.
tours.longDescription:
The world's first museum devoted entirely to audio equipment opened in Seocho in 2024. The facade — twenty thousand overlapping aluminium tubes that shift through the day like sunlight in a bamboo forest — is the work of Kengo Kuma, architect of the Japan National Stadium and the V&A Dundee. Kuma called it not a conventional museum but an architectural instrument, the building itself part of the experience.

Inside, seven floors span a hundred and fifty years: from phonograph cylinders and hand-cranked gramophones to the Western Electric systems that played The Jazz Singer in 1927 — the machines that ended the silent era, here in working condition. Founder Michael Chung, creator of Silbatone Acoustics, built the collection as a tribute to his late father. Entry is free by reservation; tours run about two hours.

stops.title: Audeum Audio Museum | 오디움
stops.caption: Stand before the facade and watch the twenty thousand aluminium tubes shift in the light.
stops.transcriptText:
The world's first museum dedicated entirely to audio equipment opened here in Seocho in 2024, which raises an obvious question: why did it take this long, and why did it open in Seoul?

The building in front of you — its facade wrapped in twenty thousand overlapping aluminium tubes that shift in light and shadow through the day, evoking the effect of sunlight accumulating in a bamboo forest — was designed by Kengo Kuma, the Japanese architect whose other work includes the Japan National Stadium for the Tokyo Olympics and the V&A Dundee. Kuma described Audeum not as a conventional museum building but as an architectural instrument — something that the materials and light of the structure itself contribute to the experience inside.

That experience spans seven floors and a hundred and fifty years of audio history: from the earliest phonograph cylinders and hand-cranked gramophones to the Western Electric 12-A and 13-A cinema sound systems of the 1920s, the very equipment that played the first talkie feature — The Jazz Singer in 1927 — in theatres across America. These are the machines that ended the silent era. They are here, in working condition, in a suburb of Seoul.

The museum was founded by Michael Chung, the creator of the Korean audio equipment company Silbatone Acoustics, as a tribute to his late father, and its founding collection is among the most significant concentrations of historic high-fidelity audio equipment anywhere in the world. Entry is free, by reservation, and guided tours run approximately two hours.

The reason it opened in Seoul, specifically, answers itself when you step outside and remember that South Korea is now one of the world's most significant music export economies. The question wasn't why here. It was why not much sooner.

tours.title: BAHR Seoul | 바흐르 서울
tours.shortDescription: A small bar-and-coffee concept tucked into Seochon's Joseon-era lanes — German name, easy to walk past, harder to leave, a short step from the old presidential residence.
tours.longDescription:
Seochon spreads west from Gyeongbokgung Palace along narrow lanes that, until the early 2000s, were largely unchanged since the Joseon period — the same courtyard-facing hanok, the same modest street facades hiding private interiors. Over the past decade it has become one of Seoul's most carefully curated pockets, drawing independent shops and small cultural spaces that take neighbourhood character seriously.

BAHR sits in this tradition: a small bar and coffee concept in the residential lanes near Cheong Wa Dae, the former presidential residence opened to the public in 2022. The name carries a German resonance, and the space has that particular Seochon quality — easy to walk past unknowing, easy to linger in once found. Nearby, Tongin Market still trades on tokens rather than cash, and the Suseongdong Valley threads quietly beneath Inwangsan.

stops.title: BAHR Seoul | 바흐르 서울
stops.caption: Find the modest street facade in the residential lanes — a short walk from Cheong Wa Dae.
stops.transcriptText:
The Seochon neighbourhood spreads west from Gyeongbokgung Palace along a grid of narrow lanes that, until the early 2000s, were largely unchanged since the Joseon period — the same proportions, the same courtyard-facing hanok, the same principle of the private interior hidden behind a modest street facade. Over the past decade the district has become one of the most carefully curated pockets of Seoul, drawing the kind of independent shops, cafés, and small cultural spaces that take neighbourhood character seriously rather than using it as a backdrop.

The address you are standing outside is in this tradition — a small bar and coffee concept tucked into the residential lanes a short walk from Cheong Wa Dae, the former presidential residence that opened to the public in 2022. The name BAHR carries a German resonance, and the space itself holds that particular Seochon quality of being genuinely easy to walk past without knowing it is there, and equally easy to linger in once you find it.

The neighbourhood around you is worth some time in itself. Tongin Market, a few minutes south, is one of the last traditional covered markets in the inner city, operating on the old practice of buying food with tokens rather than cash. The Suseongdong Valley, a short walk northwest, is a stream valley pressed between residential streets and the flank of Inwangsan Mountain, one of the more quietly useful pieces of urban nature in central Seoul.

tours.title: Bar Cham | 바 참
tours.shortDescription: A Seochon hanok built entirely of oak — 참 means oak tree — where Korean spirits get the cocktail-bar treatment, sixth on Asia's 50 Best in 2025.
tours.longDescription:
Every surface here is oak, which gives the name away: 참 in Korean means oak tree — 참나무 — and the material runs through the whole room as both design and argument. Bar Cham occupies a hanok on Jahamun-ro in Seochon, near Gyeongbokgung, and works on the principle that Korean spirits — soju, makgeolli, regional fruit distillates — deserve the same precise attention the best cocktail bars give to Western techniques.

Owner and head bartender Lim Byung-jin builds each drink around a specific Korean place: a cocktail named Hamyang uses ghee-washed rice spirit from South Gyeongsang, with Korean apple brandy, Islay whisky, lemon and ginger; another draws on the gins of Namyangju. That specificity is the editorial distinction, and it earned Bar Cham sixth place on Asia's 50 Best Bars in 2025. Book ahead — the space is genuinely small.

stops.title: Bar Cham | 바 참
stops.caption: Step into the oak-lined room and notice every chair, table and surface cut from the same wood.
stops.transcriptText:
Every chair, every table, every surface in this bar is made from oak. That detail gives the name away: 참 in Korean means oak tree — 참나무 — and the material runs through everything here as both a design decision and an argument about what a bar should feel like.

Bar Cham is inside a hanok on Jahamun-ro in Seochon, down a narrow lane a short walk from Gyeongbokgung Palace, and it operates on the principle that Korean spirits — soju, makgeolli, regional fruit distillates — deserve the same intellectual attention and precise execution that the best cocktail bars worldwide give to Western spirits and techniques. Owner and head bartender Lim Byung-jin has built his menu around specific Korean places and ingredients: a cocktail named Hamyang uses ghee butter-washed rice spirit from the Hamyang region of South Gyeongsang Province, combined with Korean apple brandy, Islay whisky, lemon, and ginger. Another is built around the gins of Namyangju, a city in Gyeonggi Province, alongside Italian citrus liqueur and quince shrub. Each drink tells you where in Korea it comes from.

That specificity is the editorial distinction, and it has been recognised accordingly: Bar Cham ranked sixth on Asia's 50 Best Bars list in 2025, one of the most consistently cited bar rankings in the region.

Book in advance — the space is genuinely small, accommodating only a few groups at a time, and the experience is better when the bar isn't at capacity. The oak is more noticeable when you can hear the quiet.

tours.title: Blue Bottle Studio Seoul | 블루보틀 삼청 한옥
tours.shortDescription: Six seats, ninety minutes, reservation only — a Samcheong hanok reshaped around a brass dripper, coffee treated with the seriousness of a wine bar.
tours.longDescription:
Six seats at the counter, ninety minutes a sitting, reservation required — the constraint is the point. This hanok on Samcheong-ro, in the lanes between Gyeongbokgung and Bukchon, was reshaped in collaboration with Korean architect Yang Tae-oh: the tiled roof kept, the old wooden gate opening onto a small earthen courtyard, the interior gathered around a central counter with a brass dripper made for the space. Step through the gate and the outside world drops away.

The sitting opens with a welcome tea called Seed — made from the coffee plant's flowers, leaves and fruit before processing — then moves through filter coffees brewed to order, one cup at a time, from a rotating selection of single origins. The framework is the one a serious sake house or wine bar applies to its subject: a specific geography, season and method, and quiet time to notice the difference.

stops.title: Blue Bottle Studio Seoul | 블루보틀 삼청 한옥
stops.caption: Approach the old wooden gate on Samcheong-ro; step through into the earthen courtyard.
stops.transcriptText:
Six seats at the bar counter, ninety minutes per sitting, reservation required. That is the entire format, and the constraint is the point.

The hanok you are approaching on Samcheong-ro, in the lanes between Gyeongbokgung Palace and the Bukchon hanok village, was designed in collaboration with the Korean architect Yang Tae-oh, who integrated Blue Bottle's design philosophy with the hanok's traditional structure: the main gate opening onto a small earthen courtyard, the tiled roof maintained, the interior reshaped around a central brewing counter with a brass dripper crafted specifically for the space. You enter through an old wooden gate; the outside world drops away fairly quickly.

The experience begins with a welcome tea called Seed — made from the flowers, leaves, and fruit of the coffee plant before processing — and proceeds through a series of filter coffees brewed to order, one cup at a time, using a rotating selection of single-origin beans. The approach treats coffee with the same framework that a serious sake house or wine bar might apply to its subject: a specific geography, a specific season, a specific method, and enough quiet time to notice the difference.

Whether that framework is worth the advance booking and the reservation fee depends on how seriously you take coffee. If you do take it seriously, this is one of the more considered settings in which to do so, and the Samcheong neighbourhood outside the gate is a reasonable reason to be in this part of Seoul regardless.

tours.title: Bukchon Hanok Village | 북촌 한옥마을
tours.shortDescription: People live here — a Joseon-era residential quarter between two palaces, genuinely old and still inhabited, where the famous rooftop alley rewards a quiet climb.
tours.longDescription:
People live here — the thing most easily forgotten about Bukchon, and the thing most worth holding onto. The neighbourhood between Gyeongbokgung to the west and Changdeokgung to the east takes its name from its position, and has been continuously inhabited since the Joseon period. The houses are genuinely old, most built between the late fourteenth and early twentieth centuries, and many still occupied by people who have lived in them for decades. This is not a reconstruction but a residential area that happened to survive.

The most photographed spot is the steep alley of Bukchon-ro 11-gil, where the lane curves between tiled rooftops stepping down toward the city. The view holds — but the quieter lanes further north have another quality entirely. Residents have formally asked visitors to lower their voices and keep out of private properties; following that is the whole of good behaviour here.

stops.title: Bukchon Hanok Village | 북촌 한옥마을
stops.caption: Climb the steep alley of Bukchon-ro 11-gil and look down the curve of tiled rooftops toward the city.
stops.transcriptText:
People live here. That is the thing most easily forgotten about Bukchon, and the thing most worth holding onto as you walk through it.

The neighbourhood between Gyeongbokgung Palace to the west and Changdeokgung to the east takes its name from its position — "buk" means north, "chon" means village — and has been continuously inhabited since the Joseon period. The houses you are walking past are genuinely old, most of them built between the late fourteenth and early twentieth centuries, and many are occupied by people who have lived in them for decades. Bukchon is not a reconstruction or a preservation zone in the museum sense: it is a residential area that happens to have survived.

The most photographed spot is on the steep alley of Bukchon-ro 11-gil, where the lane curves between a row of tiled rooftops stepping down toward the city below — the image that has appeared in countless travel guides and social media feeds. It is worth the climb, and the view does hold. But the quieter lanes further north, away from the main approach routes, have a different quality — residents going about their business, courtyard gardens visible through half-open gates, the sound of the neighbourhood more audible than the footsteps of visitors.

There are signs in several places asking for quiet, and they mean it: the residents have formally requested that visitors lower voices and refrain from entering private properties. Following this straightforwardly is the whole of what good behaviour here requires.

The National Folk Museum of Korea is at the north gate of Gyeongbokgung, a short walk downhill from the village's western edge, and its collection of everyday Joseon-period objects gives useful context for the architecture you've just been walking through.

tours.title: Centre Pompidou Hanwha | 퐁피두센터 한화
tours.shortDescription: Jean-Michel Wilmotte's glowing 'box of light' at the foot of Yeouido's 63 Building — the Pompidou's collection in Seoul while Paris renovates for five years.
tours.longDescription:
When the Centre Pompidou in Paris closed in 2025 for a five-year renovation, its legendary collection needed a purpose-built home — and for the next several years, that home is Yeouido. The institution opened on June 4, 2026, exactly a hundred and forty years after France and Korea established diplomatic relations. French architect Jean-Michel Wilmotte transformed a former aquarium annex at the base of the 63 Building into what he calls a box of light: a translucent glass envelope four storeys high that glows across the waterfront after dark, its curves evoking traditional Korean roof tiles.

Inside, two galleries of some fifteen hundred square metres each pair major works from the Pompidou — Cubism, Chagall, Kandinsky, Matisse, Surrealism, Brâncuși — with contemporary Korean and Asian artists, in what curators frame as a reciprocal conversation rather than a one-way introduction. The four-year partnership sits beneath the gold-glass 63 Building, once briefly Korea's tallest.

stops.title: Centre Pompidou Hanwha | 퐁피두센터 한화
stops.caption: Stand on the Yeouido waterfront and take in Wilmotte's low glass box against the gold tower above.
stops.transcriptText:
The Centre Pompidou in Paris closed its doors in 2025 for a five-year renovation. Which means that for the next several years, if you want to see the Pompidou's legendary collection of modern and contemporary art in a purpose-built Centre Pompidou space, you come to Yeouido.

The institution occupying the renovated base of the 63 Building on the Han River opened on June 4, 2026 — exactly one hundred and forty years after France and Korea established diplomatic relations, a date both parties were clearly pleased with. The building, designed by the French architect Jean-Michel Wilmotte, transforms a former aquarium annex into what he calls a "box of light": a translucent glass envelope four storeys high that absorbs natural daylight during the day and glows across the Yeouido waterfront after dark, with curved lines on the exterior deliberately evoking the silhouette of traditional Korean roof tiles.

Inside, two gallery spaces of approximately fifteen hundred square metres each present major exhibitions drawn from the Pompidou's collection alongside original work by contemporary Korean and Asian artists — not as a one-way introduction to Western modern art, but, in the curators' stated intention, as a reciprocal conversation. The partnership runs for four years, with a programme that moves through Cubism, Chagall, Kandinsky, Matisse, Surrealism, and Constantin Brâncuși alongside Korean artists whose work intersects with each period.

The 63 Building's upper floors — gold-glass-clad, briefly the tallest building in Korea when it opened for the 1988 Seoul Olympics — are visible directly above the museum. The contrast between the tower and Wilmotte's low horizontal addition tells you something about the four decades that separate them.

tours.title: Cheonggyecheon | 청계천
tours.shortDescription: The stream found under a demolished six-lane highway — a mayor overruled every warning, and Seoul got a 5.8km cooled corridor threading twenty-two bridges to the Han.
tours.longDescription:
In 2003, a six-lane elevated highway carrying a hundred and sixty-nine thousand vehicles a day through downtown Seoul was demolished. Traffic engineers had promised gridlock, business owners predicted ruin, opponents called it vanity. The mayor proceeded anyway, and this stream is what was found underneath. The Cheonggyecheon had been Seoul's main drainage waterway since the Joseon period, covered with concrete in 1958 and decked as a highway in 1976.

The restoration took twenty-seven months and roughly two hundred and eighty million dollars, and when it opened in October 2005 it became almost at once one of the city's most visited spaces. The water is pumped from the Han — natural flow is seasonal and insufficient — and the 5.8-kilometre corridor passes under twenty-two bridges before reaching the river. Summer temperatures run three to five degrees cooler streamside, and plants, fish and birds have returned to water that concrete had emptied.

stops.title: Cheonggyecheon | 청계천
stops.caption: Stand beside the stream and follow the water pumped from the Han as it heads downstream past the bridges.
stops.transcriptText:
In 2003, a six-lane elevated highway carrying a hundred and sixty-nine thousand vehicles a day through the heart of downtown Seoul was demolished. The mayor who ordered it done had been told by traffic engineers that the result would be gridlock, by business owners that it would destroy their livelihoods, and by political opponents that it was an act of vanity. He proceeded anyway, and the stream you are standing beside is what was found underneath.

The Cheonggyecheon had been Seoul's main drainage waterway since the Joseon period, covered over with concrete in 1958 as the city industrialised rapidly after the Korean War and converted into a highway deck in 1976. By 2003 the structure was deteriorating, the area around it was in decline, and the city faced a choice between expensive repairs and something more radical. The restoration project took twenty-seven months and cost approximately two hundred and eighty million dollars, and when the stream opened to the public in October 2005 it had become, almost immediately, one of the most visited spaces in the city.

The water flowing past you is pumped from the Han River — the stream's natural flow is seasonal and insufficient — and the five-point-eight-kilometre corridor passes under twenty-two bridges before reaching the Han. Temperature measurements have confirmed reductions of three to five degrees Celsius along the streamside compared to adjacent streets during summer. Species of plant, fish, and bird have colonised the restored waterway that were absent from the concrete before it.

Walking the full length of the stream from Cheonggye Plaza to the Han River takes about two hours at an unhurried pace and gives you a cross-section of Seoul's districts that no other linear route in the city quite replicates.

tours.title: Dongdaemun Design Plaza (DDP) | 동대문디자인플라자
tours.shortDescription: Zaha Hadid's silver "metonymic landscape" — 45,000 aluminium panels, not one straight line, floating above 600 years of unearthed Seoul.
tours.longDescription:
Zaha Hadid called it a "metonymic landscape" — a building that flows like terrain rather than sitting on it, its curves suggesting water, or the slow deformation of ground over geological time. Forty-five thousand aluminium panels clad the surface, no two the same shape, and nowhere a single straight line. It is the world's largest three-dimensional atypical structure — meaning the largest building with no right angles — and Seoul promptly nicknamed it the alien spaceship, which Hadid took in her stride.

The site was Dongdaemun Stadium, a relic of the Japanese colonial era, demolished to make way. Excavation turned up Joseon-era walls and irrigation channels, now preserved in the History Park at the base. The silver surface floats above six centuries of the city rather than erasing them.

stops.title: Dongdaemun Design Plaza (DDP) | 동대문디자인플라자
stops.caption: Face the eastern side toward the LED Rose Garden — 25,000 illuminated roses, free and lit from sunset.
stops.transcriptText:
Not a single straight line. On the building in front of you, at its exterior, with its forty-five thousand aluminium panels — not one of them the same shape or curvature as any other — there is not a single straight line anywhere on its surface.

Zaha Hadid designed the Dongdaemun Design Plaza as what she called a "metonymic landscape" — a building that flows like a landscape rather than sitting on one, whose curves suggest the movement of water or the gradual deformation of terrain over geological time. It is the world's largest three-dimensional atypical structure, which is to say the world's largest building with no right angles, achieved through computer modelling techniques that had never been applied to a public building in Korea before. It was also almost immediately nicknamed the "alien spaceship that landed in Seoul," which Hadid took with some equanimity.

The site was chosen deliberately: this was the location of Dongdaemun Stadium, built during the Japanese colonial period, which was demolished to make way for the DDP. During excavation the remains of Joseon-era city walls, irrigation channels, and other archaeological structures were discovered, and these are now preserved and displayed in the History Park running around the building's base — so the DDP sits on six hundred years of Seoul's own history, which the curved silver surface floats above rather than replaces.

The LED Rose Garden — twenty-five thousand illuminated roses that come on at sunset — wraps the eastern side of the complex and is free and open twenty-four hours.

The Dongdaemun fashion district directly around the building operates its wholesale markets through the night. If you come back at midnight, the DDP is at its most persuasively alien, and the surrounding market streets are at full volume.

tours.title: Dorasan Station | 도라산역
tours.shortDescription: "Not the last station from the South, but the first toward the North" — a spotless, silent terminus 650m from the DMZ, waiting for a train to Pyongyang.
tours.longDescription:
A platform sign insists: not the last station from the South, but the first toward the North. Dorasan sits six hundred and fifty metres from the DMZ's southern edge — last stop on the South Korean network, and, in aspiration, first on a line to Pyongyang two hundred and five kilometres away, then onward to the Trans-Siberian and eventually Europe. The Gyeongui line ran that far when it was built between 1902 and 1906. The Korean War cut it in half.

Inaugurated in April 2002 under Kim Dae-jung's Sunshine Policy, with George W. Bush in attendance, its customs halls and passport counters have never seen regular service. Freight ran briefly to Kaesong between 2007 and 2014. Since then, nothing.

stops.title: Dorasan Station | 도라산역
stops.caption: Read the platform sign, then step inside to the clock counting the hours since the peninsula was divided.
stops.transcriptText:
A sign on the platform here reads: "This is not the last station from the South, but the first station toward the North."

Dorasan Station sits six hundred and fifty metres from the southern boundary of the Korean Demilitarized Zone, which makes it the last station on the South Korean rail network, and — as the sign insists on reminding you — potentially the first on a route to Pyongyang, two hundred and five kilometres north, and beyond that to the Trans-Siberian Railway and eventually to Europe. The Gyeongui line, which connects Seoul to this platform, originally ran through to Pyongyang and Sinuiju on the Chinese border when it was built between 1902 and 1906. The Korean War cut it in half. The tracks north of here have been severed for seven decades.

The station was inaugurated in April 2002 during the presidency of Kim Dae-jung, as part of his Sunshine Policy of engagement with North Korea, in a ceremony attended by both Kim and US President George W. Bush. The customs and immigration facilities built alongside it — the warehouses, the inspection bays, the passport counters — have never been used for regular service. Freight trains ran briefly between here and the Kaesong Industrial Complex across the border between 2007 and 2014. Since then, the tracks north of the platform have carried nothing.

The station is modern, clean, and very quiet. The souvenir shop sells stamps for Pyongyang, which you can have applied to your passport as a symbol of a journey that cannot yet be made.

Inside, a clock counts the hours since the Korean peninsula was formally divided. Whatever the number is when you arrive, it has not stopped.

tours.title: Ewha Campus Center (ECC) | 이화캠퍼스 복합단지
tours.shortDescription: Dominique Perrault's answer to a building brief — no building. A 25m glass cleft carved into the hillside, classrooms buried beneath a roof of grass and pear trees.
tours.longDescription:
The building you're looking for is the one you can't see. Dominique Perrault's Ewha Campus Center, opened in April 2008, answered a crowded brief — library, theatre, classrooms, sports halls for twenty-two thousand students — by refusing to build upward at all. He cut a twenty-five-metre valley straight into the hillside, arranged everything underground along its length, and roofed it with grass and pear trees, preserving the campus green.

The two glass walls flanking the descent carry deep vertical fins: solid from an angle, suddenly transparent as you move, drawing daylight to the floors below. At the valley's base, the grand staircase doubles as an open-air amphitheatre. The name Ewha means "pear blossom" — hence the trees overhead.

stops.title: Ewha Campus Center (ECC) | 이화캠퍼스 복합단지
stops.caption: Stand at the main entrance and look down the axis — the granite ramp dropping into the Campus Valley ahead.
stops.transcriptText:
The building you're looking for is the one you cannot see.

Stand at the main entrance of Ewha Womans University and look ahead along the axis of the campus. The ground itself opens — a twenty-five-metre-wide cleft cut straight into the hillside, its walls lined with glass and steel, the floor dropping away in front of you as a long granite ramp descends toward an open staircase two hundred and fifty metres ahead. This is the Campus Valley, and the building is on either side of you, mostly underground.

The Ewha Campus Center was designed by French architect Dominique Perrault and opened in April 2008. The brief was straightforward enough — the university of twenty-two thousand students needed classrooms, a library, a theatre, sports facilities, and administrative offices — but the site was complicated: a sloping hillside at the heart of one of Seoul's oldest and most prestigious campuses, surrounded by Collegiate Gothic buildings from the 1930s. Perrault's answer was to remove the need for a building altogether. He cut the valley into the hillside, arranged the programme underground along its length, and covered the roof with grass and pear trees, so that the campus's green space was preserved and even extended.

The two glass walls that flank you as you walk down hold deep vertical fins that make them appear solid from an angle, then suddenly transparent as you shift your position — and natural light falls through them to the inhabited floors below. At the base of the valley, the grand staircase doubles as an open-air amphitheatre.

The entire building was designed around the pear blossom: Ewha, the university's name, means "pear blossom" in Sino-Korean — a name given by the Joseon emperor in 1887. The trees planted on the roof are pear trees. It is a detail that is either poetic or decorative, depending on your disposition, but the building itself earns the patience required to find it.

tours.title: Futura Seoul | 푸투라 서울
tours.shortDescription: A modernist name in a 500-year-old hanok village — WGNB's 2024 gallery of soaring windows and open sky, opened with Refik Anadol's largest Asian show.
tours.longDescription:
The name is a deliberate provocation. Futura — Paul Renner's 1927 typeface, a byword for modernism, and simply the Latin for "future" — attached to an art institution in Bukchon Hanok Village, among five-hundred-year-old aristocratic houses, each exhibition billed as a verse in a sequence called "A Hundred Poems."

Designed by Baek Jong-hwan of Seoul studio WGNB, the building opened on Bukchon-ro in September 2024: three storeys, ceilings ten point eight metres high, a twenty-four-metre window pulling the tiled rooflines inside, a courtyard open to the sky. The opening show came from Refik Anadol, fresh from crowds at MoMA — his largest in Asia, no accident. Bukchon's layered past, the argument runs, is precisely the right place from which to ask about the future.

stops.title: Futura Seoul | 푸투라 서울
stops.caption: From the rooftop garden, look east across the hanok rooflines toward the mountains.
stops.transcriptText:
There's a curious thing about the name. Futura — as in the typeface designed by Paul Renner in 1927, the sans-serif geometry that became one of the defining fonts of twentieth-century modernism. It is also, simply, the Latin word for "future." An art institution in the middle of Bukchon Hanok Village, a neighbourhood of five-hundred-year-old aristocratic houses, naming itself for a modernist typeface and calling each exhibition a verse in an ongoing sequence titled "A Hundred Poems." The tension is entirely deliberate.

The building on Bukchon-ro in Gahoe-dong opened in September 2024, designed by Baek Jong-hwan of the Seoul studio WGNB. Three storeys, with the main exhibition spaces on the ground and first floors — the ceilings ten point eight metres high, a twenty-four-metre window on the upper level drawing the tiled rooflines of Bukchon into the interior, a courtyard open to the sky. The rooftop garden gives unobstructed views east across the hanok village toward the mountains.

The opening exhibition was by Refik Anadol, the Turkish-American media artist whose machine-intelligence works had drawn large crowds at MoMA in New York the previous year. The show was his largest in Asia — not a coincidental choice of venue. Futura Seoul's stated position is that Bukchon's layered history — Joseon aristocracy, Japanese colonial preservation, contemporary cultural tourism — makes it the right place from which to ask questions about the future, precisely because it carries so much of the past.

The building received the Seoul Architecture Award shortly after opening, with the jury citing particularly the way light moves through the space at different hours. Come in the afternoon if you can, when the courtyard skylight shifts the gallery into a different register entirely.

tours.title: Graphic | 그래픽
tours.shortDescription: A windowless ivory-ceramic stack on an Itaewon slope, reading like a giant weathered book — and, fittingly, a specialist shop for graphic novels.
tours.longDescription:
The building on Hoenamu-ro looks less like a bookshop than an archaeological find — tiered, windowless, clad in textured ivory ceramic that reads from the pavement as a stack of pale, worn pages from some enormous old book. Whether the architects intended that depends on whom you ask, but the building does hold books.

Graphic, by OONN Metaworks and U.LAB and completed in 2021, is a specialist shop for graphic novels, comics, and illustrated works. The windowless shell is partly practical — prints need shelter from sunlight — but the effect exceeds its purpose: the building withholds itself from the street, then opens inside into a surprise, gallery-like and lit from above. Around it, this stretch of Itaewon has been quietly colonised by design studios and independent shops.

stops.title: Graphic | 그래픽
stops.caption: Take in the tiered ceramic façade from the pavement below before stepping inside.
stops.transcriptText:
The building on Hoenamu-ro in Itaewon does not look like a bookshop. It looks, if anything, like an archaeological object — tiered, windowless, its surface covered in textured ivory-coloured ceramic that reads from the pavement as a stack of pale, worn pages from a very old and very large book. Whether that reading was the architects' intention or a happy coincidence depends on who you ask, though the building does in fact contain books.

Graphic is a specialist bookshop for graphic novels, comics, and illustrated works, designed by OONN Metaworks and U.LAB and completed in 2021. The decision to make the exterior windowless was partly practical — graphic novels and prints need protection from direct sunlight — but it produces an effect that is considerably more interesting than a simple UV precaution. The building withholds itself from the street, and the interior, when you enter, is a surprise: gallery-like, generously lit from above, the shelves carrying a curated selection rather than the comprehensive sweep of a conventional bookshop.
