The Itaewon slope around the building is worth some attention itself. This stretch of Hoenamu-ro runs through one of the more architecturally varied streets in Seoul, where narrow residential lanes cut up the hillside between post-war buildings, former military housing, and the occasional small institution. The area has been slowly colonised by design studios and independent shops over the past decade, and Graphic's ceramic exterior has become an unlikely anchor for that shift.

The Leeum Museum of Art is a ten-minute walk east along the hillside — the two make a reasonable pairing for an afternoon in this part of the city.

tours.title: Gwangjang Market | 광장시장
tours.shortDescription: Seoul's oldest market, trading since 1905 — bindaetteok crisping on the griddle, makgeolli in the bowl, and silk lanes running above it all.
tours.longDescription:
Seoul's oldest market has traded on this spot since 1905 — older than the city's liberation from colonial rule, older than almost everything around it. The name means "wide open square," and the covered arcade, Victorian in the spirit of its ironwork, has fed and clothed this quarter for over a century.

The smell reaches you first: bindaetteok on the griddle, the crisp-edged mung bean pancake that is Gwangjang's signature, eaten standing with a bowl of makgeolli alongside. Some stalls have run in the same families for three generations, and with a recipe this simple the bean paste and the heat decide everything. Above and around the food hall runs the market's other trade — silk, hanbok fabrics, pojagi patchwork — a vertical slice of Korean textile history supplying tailors across the city.

stops.title: Gwangjang Market | 광장시장
stops.caption: Head into the main food alley toward the griddles; the quieter back aisles reward a wander east.
stops.transcriptText:
Seoul's oldest market has been trading continuously on this site since 1905, which makes it twenty years older than the city's liberation from Japanese colonial rule and considerably older than most of what surrounds it. The name means "wide open square," and the covered arcade you are walking through — its ironwork Victorian in spirit, its stalls in close continuous rows — has been feeding, clothing, and supplying this part of the city for over a century.

The first thing that reaches you is the smell: bindaetteok on the griddle, the flat mung bean pancake that is Gwangjang's most famous food, crisp-edged and dense, eaten standing at the stall with makgeolli poured into a large bowl alongside. The vendors here have been making it the same way for decades — some of the stalls run by the same families for three generations — and the technique is not complicated, which means the quality of the bean paste and the heat of the griddle are what determine everything.

The market is known equally for its silk and traditional textile trade, which occupies the upper floors and the lanes around the main food hall. Hanbok fabrics, pojagi patchwork cloth, and vintage clothing sit alongside the modern wholesale stalls — a vertical slice of Korean textile history compressed into a few blocks. The silk section in particular has supplied tailors and hanbok makers across Seoul for generations.

At lunchtime the main food alley is busy enough to require patience, but the back aisles are quieter and often equally good. The marinade-braised beef on rice at the smaller stalls near the east entrance is the less-photographed reason to explore further.

tours.title: Gyeongbokgung Palace | 경복궁
tours.shortDescription: "May the king be greatly blessed by heaven" — Joseon's 1395 seat, burned, ruined, rebuilt, demolished, and rebuilt again, still only 40% restored.
tours.longDescription:
It is 1395. The Joseon dynasty is three years old, and its new capital needs a palace to declare its authority. The name means "may the king be greatly blessed by heaven" — a fair hope for a dynasty that would last five hundred and eighteen years. The Gwanghwamun Gate sits on an axis laid out by the court geomancer, running straight north through the Geunjeongjeon throne hall to Bugaksan mountain.

The palace was burned in the Japanese invasions of 1592, left a ruin for two and a half centuries, then rebuilt from the 1860s under the regent Heungseong Daewongun. The colonial government demolished some ninety percent of it again between 1910 and 1945, planting its headquarters across the sacred axis. That building fell in 1995. Reconstruction continues — around forty percent now restored.

stops.title: Gyeongbokgung Palace | 경복궁
stops.caption: Stand before Gwanghwamun Gate and follow the axis north through the palace toward Bugaksan.
stops.transcriptText:
It's 1395. The Joseon dynasty is three years old, and the new capital of Hanyang — what is now Seoul — needs a palace to establish its authority. The name chosen for it means "may the king be greatly blessed by heaven." A reasonable aspiration for a dynasty that would go on to last five hundred and eighteen years.

The Gwanghwamun Gate behind you is the main southern entrance to Gyeongbokgung, and the axis it sits on — straight north from this point through the palace's ceremonial hall to the mountain of Bugaksan — was laid out by the court geomancer according to the principles of p'ungsu, Korea's equivalent of feng shui. Behind the gate, the Geunjeongjeon throne hall stands at the northern end of a vast stone courtyard, raised on two tiers of carved stone, its double-eaved roof carrying ceramic animal figurines on each ridge-line — the number of animals indicating the building's rank in the palace hierarchy.

The palace was burned to the ground during the Japanese invasions of 1592, left as a ruin for two and a half centuries, then painstakingly rebuilt from the 1860s onward under the regent Heungseong Daewongun. The Japanese colonial government then demolished roughly ninety percent of it again between 1910 and 1945 to build the colonial headquarters on the axis line, deliberately blocking the ceremonial view. That building was itself demolished in 1995. The reconstruction continues: around forty percent of the original buildings have now been restored.

The National Palace Museum of Korea sits within the palace grounds to the southeast, and the National Folk Museum is just inside the Hyangwonjeong pavilion area to the northeast. Both are free with palace admission and worth the time — the folk museum in particular gives the social context that the palace architecture doesn't.

tours.title: HAUS NOWHERE SEOUL | 하우스 노웨어 서울
tours.shortDescription: Gentle Monster's four-storey Seongsu world — eyewear as afterthought, retail as art institution, in Seoul's former-industrial answer to Shoreditch.
tours.longDescription:
Gentle Monster does not run a conventional shop. For a decade the eyewear brand has built immersive environments — each location a fresh artist commission, a different conceptual world, the glasses almost incidental to being in the room. The Seongsu space, known as HAUS NOWHERE, pushes that logic toward the permanence of an institution: a name that places itself deliberately outside geography, in a neighbourhood being rapidly remade.

Seongsu has become Seoul's Shoreditch — leather workshops and small manufacturing units taken first by cafés and design studios, then by flagships chasing the industrial look without the industry. A full four-storey building given over to something between installation and shop fits the trajectory exactly. The ground-floor commission changes; the spatial drama — ceiling heights, the transitions between floors — stays.

stops.title: HAUS NOWHERE SEOUL | 하우스 노웨어 서울
stops.caption: Enter from the industrial street and let the ground-floor installation set the register.
stops.transcriptText:
Gentle Monster doesn't run a conventional shop. The South Korean eyewear brand has spent the past decade building immersive environments that use its retail spaces as exhibition venues — each location a different artist commission, a different conceptual world, the eyewear itself almost incidental to the experience of being in the building.

The Seongsu space, in the former industrial district across the Han River from Gangnam, extends that logic into something closer to a permanent institution. The building you're entering is known as HAUS NOWHERE — a name that positions it deliberately outside the logic of place, even while being very specifically located in one of Seoul's most rapidly transforming neighbourhoods.

Seongsu has been Seoul's Shoreditch for the past decade: former leather workshops and small manufacturing units colonised first by independent cafés and design studios, then by flagship stores for brands that wanted the industrial aesthetic without the actual industry. Gentle Monster's choice of location here is consistent with that trajectory, and the building's scale — a full four-storey structure dedicated to an experience that is simultaneously art installation and commercial space — pushes it further into the territory of the cultural institution.

What's on the ground floor changes with each commission, but the permanent spatial quality of the building — its ceiling heights, the transition between floors, the relationship between interior and the industrial street outside — is the consistent thing. The installations have included animatronic sculptures, large-scale narrative environments, and works made in collaboration with artists who don't usually work in retail contexts.

The Leeum Museum of Art and SONGEUN Arts and Cultural Foundation are both nearby in this part of the city, making the area worth a longer afternoon.

tours.title: Juun.J Dosan Flagship Store | 준지 도산 플래그십 스토어
tours.shortDescription: The Seoul flagship of a Korean menswear label that argues quiet rigour beats noise — clothes displayed like works in a gallery.
tours.longDescription:
Jung Wook-jun designs under the label Juun.J, and spent several years at Givenchy in Paris before returning to Seoul to build a fashion house on the proposition that quiet rigour is more interesting than noise. This Dosan Park flagship is where he made that argument in brick and concrete.

On Apgujeong's Dosan-daero, surrounded by boutiques that have defined the area since the 1990s, the building sets itself apart by restraint: modest facade, minimal signage, interior given over to space rather than product.

Jung's menswear is known for elongated proportions and deconstructed tailoring — coats that read as architecture worn on the body. Juun.J joined Paris Fashion Week's official schedule in 2007, among the earliest Korean menswear labels to do so.

stops.title: Juun.J Dosan Flagship Store | 준지 도산 플래그십 스토어
stops.caption: You're on Dosan-daero in Apgujeong, facing the flagship — note how modest the facade is against its showier neighbours.
stops.transcriptText:
Jung Wook-jun, who designs under the label Juun.J, spent several years working at Givenchy in Paris before returning to Seoul to build a Korean fashion house on the proposition that quiet rigour is more interesting than noise. The Dosan Park flagship is the building he made to hold that proposition.

The structure occupies a corner on Apgujeong's Dosan-daero — an address that carries its own set of associations in Korean fashion culture, surrounded by the boutiques and restaurants that have defined the area since the 1990s. What distinguishes the Juun.J building from its neighbours is its restraint: the facade is modest, the signage minimal, the interior given over to space rather than product density.

Jung's menswear is known for a particular manipulation of suiting — elongated proportions, deconstructed tailoring, coats that read as architecture worn on the body — and the shop organises itself around that sensibility. The clothes occupy the space as objects in an exhibition rather than stock on a rail, and the industrial-inflected concrete and steel of the interior gives the garments the kind of neutral backdrop that lets the construction of each piece be the point.

Juun.J showed in Paris Fashion Week's official schedule from 2007, making it one of the earliest Korean menswear labels to establish a sustained presence in the European show calendar. The Dosan flagship is the Seoul-side argument for why that presence makes sense: a building that thinks about clothes the way a gallery thinks about works on paper.

The Dosan Park itself is a short walk north — a useful and quiet green space in a neighbourhood not especially given to quiet.

tours.title: Kukje Gallery K3 | 국제갤러리 K3
tours.shortDescription: A stainless-steel chain-mesh box by SO-IL — present but not quite legible — housing a gallery that has shown Bourgeois, Nauman and Lee Ufan.
tours.longDescription:
Kukje Gallery opened here in Samcheong-dong in 1982, when the Seoul scene was mostly concerned with Korean painting traditions. Its name means "international gallery" — in 1982, either an aspiration or a provocation, depending on who was looking. Four decades on, it runs one of the most recognised programmes in East Asia.

K3, the newest of three adjacent buildings, was completed in 2012 by the New York firm SO-IL with local architects. It's wrapped in a stainless-steel chain mesh that shifts from opaque to transparent with the light — present, but not quite legible from the street. Inside, a single double-height gallery runs through under a changing skylight.

The roster spans Louise Bourgeois, Bill Viola and Bruce Nauman alongside Kimsooja, Koo Jeong-a and Lee Ufan.

stops.title: Kukje Gallery K3 | 국제갤러리 K3
stops.caption: You're standing before K3, the third and newest building — watch its steel mesh shift as you move past it.
stops.transcriptText:
Kukje Gallery opened in 1982 in this Samcheong-dong neighbourhood when the Seoul gallery scene was primarily concerned with Korean painting traditions, and has spent the intervening four decades building one of the most internationally recognised programmes in East Asia. The name means "international gallery," which in 1982 was either an aspiration or a provocation, depending on who was looking.

The K3 building you're in front of — the third of Kukje's three adjacent structures in this block — is the newest addition to the complex, completed in 2012 and designed by SO-IL, the New York architectural firm, in collaboration with local architects. The exterior is wrapped in a stainless-steel chain mesh that shifts from opaque to transparent depending on the angle and the light, giving the building a quality of being present but not quite legible from the street. Inside, a single large gallery space runs through the building at double height, with a skylight that changes the quality of the room throughout the day.

Kukje represents a roster that includes Louise Bourgeois, Haim Steinbach, Bill Viola, and Bruce Nauman alongside major Korean artists including Kimsooja, Koo Jeong-a, and Lee Ufan — a position that has placed it at the intersection of Korean and international contemporary practice for decades. The gallery was also among the first to bring institutional-grade international exhibitions to Seoul on a consistent basis, which shaped the expectations of a generation of Korean collectors and curators.

The K1 and K2 buildings are immediately adjacent, often running simultaneous exhibitions, and the Samcheong-dong gallery district extends north along the street for several more blocks — Gallery Hyundai, PKM Gallery, and the MMCA Seoul are all within easy walking distance.

tours.title: Leeum Museum of Art | 리움미술관
tours.shortDescription: Three architects, three buildings, one museum — Botta, Nouvel and Koolhaas each arguing what art requires, holding a thousand years of Korean culture.
tours.longDescription:
Three architects, three buildings, one museum — and the argument is in the architecture as much as the collection. Operated by the Samsung Foundation of Culture in Hannam-dong, the Leeum opened in 2004 after a competition with no real parallel anywhere.

Museum 1, for traditional Korean art, is Mario Botta's, in dark ceramic tile; Museum 2, for contemporary work, is Jean Nouvel's, in stainless steel and glass; and Rem Koolhaas designed the education centre connecting them. Each makes a different spatial argument about what its contents need.

Museum 1 holds thirty-six national treasures — Goryeo celadon, gilt-bronze Buddhas, Joseon calligraphy. Museum 2 gathers Nam June Paik, Joseph Beuys and Francis Bacon. Between them, a sculpture garden with Anish Kapoor and Serra looks out over the Han River.

stops.title: Leeum Museum of Art | 리움미술관
stops.caption: You're at the entrance on the Hannam hillside — take in all three buildings before heading inside.
stops.transcriptText:
Three architects, three buildings, one museum — and the argument is in the architecture as much as in what it contains.

The Leeum Museum of Art in Hannam-dong is operated by the Samsung Foundation of Culture and holds one of the most significant art collections in Korea, spanning a thousand years of Korean cultural production alongside major international contemporary work. It opened in 2004 after a competition that resulted in an arrangement that has no real parallel anywhere: Museum 1, dedicated to traditional Korean art, designed by the Swiss architect Mario Botta in dark ceramic tile; Museum 2, dedicated to contemporary art, designed by the French architect Jean Nouvel in stainless steel and glass; and the Samsung Child Education and Culture Centre connecting them, designed by the Dutch architect Rem Koolhaas. Each building makes a different spatial argument about what its contents require, and each is worth treating as architecture in its own right before attending to what's inside.

The traditional collection in Museum 1 includes thirty-six national treasures — celadon ceramics from the Goryeo period, Buddhist gilt bronze sculptures, Joseon-dynasty calligraphy — displayed in a sequence that Botta designed to move from compressed, intimate spaces into increasingly open ones as the historical chronology progresses. Museum 2's collection includes works by Nam June Paik, Joseph Beuys, and Francis Bacon alongside major Korean contemporary artists, in a building whose reflective surfaces and shifting light produce a different quality of attention than the terracotta solidity of the building next door.

The sculpture garden between the buildings holds works by Anish Kapoor and Serra, among others, and connects to the top of the Hannam hillside with views over the Han River. Entry to the permanent collection is free on the first Wednesday of each month.

tours.title: Mimesis Art Museum | 미메시스 아트 뮤지엄
tours.shortDescription: A study in white by Álvaro Siza — two curved concrete volumes catching the light — set forty-five minutes north of Seoul in Paju Book City.
tours.longDescription:
This museum is not in Seoul. Paju Book City, where it sits, is a planned publishing district roughly forty-five minutes north — a deliberate removal from the city that suits the building rather well.

The Mimesis Art Museum is Álvaro Siza's, the Portuguese architect who had earlier built Seoul's Anyang Pavilion, and it opened in 2009. His design is a study in white: two curved concrete volumes, smooth and continuous, arranged around a courtyard, their surfaces carrying light rather than deflecting it. The building seems to grow from its site rather than sit on it.

The name comes from Plato's mimesis — art as imitation. Operated by the publisher Openbooks, the collection leans to contemporary art and a particular commitment to artists' books, connecting the museum to the district around it.

stops.title: Mimesis Art Museum | 미메시스 아트 뮤지엄
stops.caption: You're in Paju Book City before Siza's white curved volumes — notice how they follow the land rather than sit on it.
stops.transcriptText:
This museum is not in Seoul. Paju Book City, where it sits, is a planned publishing and cultural district roughly forty-five minutes north of central Seoul by road — a deliberate removal from the city that turns out to suit the building rather well.

The Mimesis Art Museum was designed by Álvaro Siza, the Portuguese architect who had also built the Anyang Pavilion in Seoul a few years earlier, and it opened in 2009. Siza's design here is a study in the architecture of white: two curved concrete volumes, smooth and continuous, arranged around an internal courtyard, their surfaces carrying the quality of light rather than deflecting it. The building appears to grow from its site rather than sit on it, its horizontal orientation following the gentle contours of the Paju landscape.

The name comes from Plato's concept of mimesis — art as imitation, or representation. The museum is operated by Openbooks, one of Korea's major publishers, and the collection centres on contemporary art alongside a particular commitment to artists' books and print culture, which connects the museum to the publishing district around it. The gallery spaces are generous and naturally lit through skylights that Siza positioned to avoid direct solar exposure on the works.

Paju Book City itself is worth exploring if you make the journey: an entire planned district designed in the early 2000s around the book trade, with publishing houses, paper warehouses, and cultural institutions designed by a roster of Korean architects including Kim Jong-soung and Seung H-Sang. The scale and ambition of the project — a town built around publishing — is unusual by any measure.

tours.title: Myeongdong Night Market | 명동야시장
tours.shortDescription: By evening, carts and stalls fill Myeongdong's shopping strip — tteokbokki and tornado potatoes competing with the perfume counters behind them.
tours.longDescription:
In daylight the street through Myeongdong looks like a very busy commercial district. In the evening the pavement vendors arrive, set up their carts, and it becomes something else: a food market running down the middle of Seoul's most internationally minded shopping district, where tteokbokki and tornado potatoes compete cheerfully with the department-store perfume counters behind them.

Hours and stalls vary by season and permit cycle, but the character has held for years. The vendors sell skewered meat, fishcake broth, deep-fried things on sticks, steamed egg, hotteok filled with brown sugar and nuts. What sets Myeongdong apart is the density and the audience — a very high share of international visitors, so the vendors are practised at queues and at pointing when language fails.

Above the eastern end, Myeongdong Cathedral, Gothic brick from 1898, offers a quiet counterpoint.

stops.title: Myeongdong Night Market | 명동야시장
stops.caption: You're on Myeongdong's pedestrian strip as the stalls open — the middle section near Lotte has the densest selection.
stops.transcriptText:
The street that runs through the centre of Myeongdong looks, in daylight, like a very busy commercial district. In the evening, the pavement vendors arrive, set up their carts and stalls, and the street becomes something else: a food market that runs down the middle of Seoul's most densely international shopping district, where the smell of tteokbokki and tornado potatoes competes cheerfully with the perfume counters of the department stores behind it.

The Myeongdong Night Market operates most evenings along this pedestrian strip — the exact hours and stalls vary by season and by permit cycle, but the general character has been consistent for years. The vendors here sell Korean street food in the register that has become familiar globally through food media: skewered meat, fishcake broth, deep-fried items on sticks, steamed egg, hotteok pancakes filled with brown sugar and nuts. What distinguishes the Myeongdong version from markets in other parts of the city is the density and the audience — the district draws a very high proportion of international visitors, which means the vendors are accustomed to managing queues efficiently and to pointing at things when language fails.

The buildings on both sides of the street are mostly fashion retail, cosmetics, and convenience chains, with a few older department stores that have survived several decades of redevelopment. Myeongdong Cathedral — one of the oldest Catholic churches in Korea, built in Gothic brick in 1898 — sits on the hill above the eastern end of the street and provides a useful counterpoint to the commercial intensity below it.

For the street food, the middle section near the Lotte Department Store tends to have the most concentrated selection and the least crowded pavement.

tours.title: National Museum of Modern and Contemporary Art (MMCA) Seoul | 국립현대미술관 서울
tours.shortDescription: A national contemporary-art museum built on the former compound of the intelligence apparatus that helped enforce military rule — beside Gyeongbokgung.
tours.longDescription:
The MMCA opened this Seoul branch in 2013 on a site that carries more history than most: the former compound of the Defence Security Command, institutional home of the surveillance apparatus that helped enforce military rule from the 1960s to the 1990s.

Designed by Min Hyun-jun beside Gyeongbokgung Palace, the complex layers new brick and concrete gallery wings with a traditional Joseon-era structure already on the site — the tiled roof and contemporary galleries coexisting without pretending the relationship is seamless. The outdoor sculpture areas between them are among the most spacious in the city.

One of four national branches, the Seoul site focuses on large-scale commissions; its multi-storey Project Gallery hosts the kind of site-specific work most commercial galleries cannot hold. Entry to the sculpture garden is free daily.

stops.title: National Museum of Modern and Contemporary Art (MMCA) Seoul | 국립현대미술관 서울
stops.caption: You're entering the complex beside Gyeongbokgung — note the old tiled-roof building among the gallery wings.
stops.transcriptText:
The National Museum of Modern and Contemporary Art opened this Seoul branch in 2013 on a site that carries rather more history than most museum sites can claim: the former compound of the Defence Security Command, which in its various iterations served as the institutional home of the intelligence and surveillance apparatus that helped enforce military rule from the 1960s until the 1990s.

The complex you're entering, at the edge of the Samcheong-dong neighbourhood and directly adjacent to Gyeongbokgung Palace, was designed by Min Hyun-jun and incorporates both a series of new brick and concrete gallery buildings and a traditional Joseon-era structure that was already on the site. The result is an unusual layering: the tiled-roof building and the contemporary gallery wings coexist without pretending the relationship is seamless, and the outdoor sculpture areas between them are among the most spacious and pleasant in the city.

The MMCA Seoul is one of four national branches — the main campus in Gwacheon holds the permanent collection, while the Seoul branch focuses on large-scale contemporary commissions and rotating exhibitions. The multi-storey Project Gallery at the centre of the complex is designed for the kind of large-scale site-specific work that most of Seoul's commercial galleries cannot accommodate; it has hosted installations by Korean and international artists that have defined what ambitious contemporary practice can look like in this city.

Entry is free to the sculpture garden, which is open daily and accessible even when the galleries are closed. The path along the eastern wall connects to the back entrance of Gyeongbokgung, and the neighbourhood immediately north is the beginning of the Samcheong-dong gallery district.

tours.title: Noryangjin Fisheries Wholesale Market | 노량진수산시장
tours.shortDescription: The auction floor peaks at four in the morning — pick a live crab downstairs, carry it up, and a kitchen cooks whatever you've chosen.
tours.longDescription:
The market opens at three in the morning; the auction floor peaks around four. By six the wholesale deals are done and the buyers have loaded their vans. You're probably here well after all that — which is fine, because the retail floor runs through the day, in one of the largest, most varied fish markets in Korea.

The wholesale hall across the footbridge handles the auction; visitors spend their time in the newer retail building, moving between tanks, choosing live fish or shellfish, then carrying them upstairs to a restaurant that cooks whatever you've picked. The selection spans Korea's three coasts and import — abalone, king crab, octopus, clam, sea cucumber, eel.

The market has sat here beside the railway and the Han River since the 1970s. Practical advice: agree a price before cooking, and clarify the method.

stops.title: Noryangjin Fisheries Wholesale Market | 노량진수산시장
stops.caption: You're in Noryangjin's retail hall — the footbridge to the wholesale building is the best vantage on its scale.
stops.transcriptText:
The market opens at three in the morning. The peak trading hour, when the auction floor is at its most frenetic, is around four. By six, the major wholesale transactions are done, the restaurant buyers have loaded their vans, and the retail section settles into a more manageable pace. You are probably here considerably after all of this — which is fine, because the retail market and restaurant floor run through the day, and what you find is still one of the largest and most varied fish markets in Korea.

The wholesale structure across the footbridge handles the main auction and distribution operation; the newer retail building is where visitors typically spend their time, moving between the tanks and displays on the lower floors, selecting live fish or shellfish, then taking them upstairs to one of the restaurants that will cook whatever you've chosen. The selection spans what is available from Korea's three coasts and from import: live abalone and king crab, octopus, clam, sea cucumber, eel — alongside the cut fish and dried goods that form the other half of the business.

The footbridge connecting the old and new market buildings is one of the better vantage points from which to understand the scale of the operation. From it, the Han River is visible to the north, and the rail tracks of the Gyeongbu Line run below — the market has been on this site, beside the railway and the river, since the 1970s.

The most practical piece of advice: point at what you want, agree a price before cooking, and clarify the cooking method unless you have strong feelings about it, because the kitchens upstairs have their own preferred approach.

tours.title: POINTTWOFIVE.SECOND Seongsu Haus | 포인트투파이브세컨드 성수 하우스
tours.shortDescription: Named for 0.25 seconds — the instant a form registers before thought — a Seongsu concept space asking what design says before language arrives.
tours.longDescription:
The name refers to time: zero-point-two-five seconds, the interval certain optical studies identify as the moment of first visual recognition — the instant a form or colour registers as something before it becomes a concept. POINTTWOFIVE is a creative studio built entirely around that threshold, asking what design communicates before language gets involved.

This Seongsu location is the flagship — part showroom, part gallery, part experimental retail. It occupies one of the converted industrial units that define the neighbourhood's look: high ceilings, raw structure, the previous life of the space deliberately retained.

Since around 2018, Seongsu has drawn design-forward brands wanting a creative community over conventional retail. The tension with its industrial past is still readable on the street — a shoe workshop beside a coffee bar beside a gallery beside a depot.

The neighbourhood's identity has been shaped by the tension between its industrial history — leather goods manufacturing, light industry — and the wave of studios and cultural spaces that arrived from around 2018 onward. That tension is still readable in the street: a traditional shoe workshop beside a specialty coffee bar beside a gallery beside a logistics depot.

POINTTWOFIVE.SECOND sits within that context deliberately, and the space tends to reward attention paid to how it has been put together rather than simply what it contains. The Seongsu café strip along Achasan-ro is worth exploring on the way out.

tours.title: Photo SeMA — Photography Seoul Museum of Art | 서울시립 사진미술관
tours.shortDescription: Seoul's first public museum devoted entirely to photography — darkrooms and all — tucked in a residential northeast district that few tourists bother to reach.
tours.longDescription:
Opened in 2023 in Jungnang, a northeastern district better known for residential life than culture, Photo SeMA is Seoul's first public museum given over entirely to photography. As a branch of the Seoul Museum of Art, its mandate goes beyond exhibiting: it collects, researches and contextualises the medium as a discipline in its own right. Housed in a refurbished facility, it pairs galleries with real production infrastructure — darkrooms, digital processing, educational labs.

The permanent collection leans toward twentieth-century Korean work, including documentary images of the Korean War, industrialisation and the 1980s democracy movement. Getting here takes some commitment, which means visitors tend to arrive on purpose rather than in passing — and the atmosphere is the better for it.

stops.title: Photo SeMA — Photography Seoul Museum of Art | 서울시립 사진미술관
stops.caption: You're in Jungnang, northeast of the centre — step inside the refurbished complex where galleries meet working darkrooms.
stops.transcriptText:
Seoul's first public museum dedicated entirely to photography opened in 2023 in Jungnang, a northeastern district of the city more associated with residential life than cultural institutions — which is partly the point.

Photo SeMA, the Photography Seoul Museum of Art, was established as a branch of the Seoul Museum of Art with a specific mandate: not simply to exhibit photography, but to collect, research, and contextualise it as a distinct artistic discipline with its own history, techniques, and discourse. The building, a refurbished former facility in the Jungnang Creative Economy Innovation Centre complex, gives the institution an unusual combination of gallery space and production infrastructure — darkrooms, digital processing facilities, and educational labs are part of the site rather than afterthoughts.

The permanent collection focuses particularly on Korean photography from the twentieth century onward, including documentary photography from periods — the Korean War, the industrialisation era, the democracy movement of the 1980s — that are extensively documented in image but rarely exhibited with the curatorial care they deserve. The temporary exhibitions have moved between Korean and international photographers, with a particular emphasis on work that uses photography to engage with social and historical questions rather than purely aesthetic ones.

The neighbourhood itself is worth a note: Jungnang sits northeast of the city centre and is considerably less visited than the cultural clusters in Jongno or Yongsan. Getting here takes some commitment, which means the museum tends to attract visitors who have made the journey specifically, rather than those passing through. That changes the atmosphere inside, and for the better.

tours.title: SONGEUN Art and Cultural Foundation | 송은
tours.shortDescription: A Herzog & de Meuron building on Apgujeong-ro — concrete grid, deep-set windows, a surface that reads differently with every shift of the light.
tours.longDescription:
The building on Apgujeong-ro is by Herzog & de Meuron — the Swiss firm behind Tate Modern and the Elbphilharmonie — and was completed in 2021. Modest by their standards, it still makes its mass and surface the primary argument: a concrete grid with deep-set windows and irregular louvers that reads differently depending on the light and your angle of approach.

Inside, the SONGEUN Arts and Cultural Foundation supports Korean contemporary artists through exhibitions, residencies and an annual prize now among the most significant in the country. Established by the Hyundai Development Company as a non-profit, it keeps a free project space at ground level. The building negotiates the transition between commercial Apgujeong and the quieter streets behind — present and absorbed into its context at once.

stops.title: SONGEUN Art and Cultural Foundation | 송은
stops.caption: Stand on Apgujeong-ro before the ST building and watch the concrete grid and louvers catch the light.
stops.transcriptText:
The building on Apgujeong-ro is by Herzog & de Meuron, the Swiss firm responsible for Tate Modern in London and the Elbphilharmonie in Hamburg, and it was completed in 2021. It is, by the standards of their larger commissions, relatively modest in scale — but the decision it makes about how to occupy its corner plot in Apgujeong is consistent with the firm's wider practice: using the building's mass and surface as the primary argument rather than the programme it contains.

The SONGEUN Arts and Cultural Foundation, which operates the building, was established by the Hyundai Development Company as a non-profit institution dedicated to supporting Korean contemporary artists — through exhibitions, residencies, and an annual prize that has become one of the most significant in the Korean art ecosystem. The gallery spaces occupy multiple floors of the ST building, with a project space on the ground level that functions as an accessible public gallery without admission charge.

Herzog & de Meuron's exterior — a concrete grid with deep-set windows and an irregular pattern of louvers — produces a surface that reads differently depending on the light and the angle of approach. The building negotiates the transition between the commercial density of Apgujeong's main street and the residential scale of the streets behind it, which gives it the quality of being simultaneously present and absorbed into its context.

The collection and exhibitions focus primarily on Korean artists at various career stages, with a particular interest in work that engages with the social and political dimensions of contemporary Korean life. The foundation's annual artist prize nominations are published in autumn and worth tracking if you're following the Korean art scene closely.

tours.title: Seo-Seoul Museum of Art | 서울시립 서서울미술관
tours.shortDescription: A decommissioned colonial-era water purification plant reborn as an art museum — circular concrete tanks turned into galleries you'll find nowhere else.
tours.longDescription:
The western branch of Seoul's municipal art system opened in Yangcheon in 2022, built within and around a decommissioned water purification facility from the Japanese colonial period. The concrete filtration tanks and pump houses were kept and folded into the exhibition architecture — "seo" meaning west, set at the opposite end of the city from the main SeMA building in Jung-gu.

The circular tanks are the star: curved concrete walls and light falling through openings above create gallery conditions unavailable anywhere else, and the curation responds to that specificity. Yangcheon is a residential district with no prior art pedigree, which is rather the point — SeMA has been seeding branches in underserved parts of the city. The result serves a neighbourhood rather than drawing crowds across town, and that changes what happens inside.

stops.title: Seo-Seoul Museum of Art | 서울시립 서서울미술관
stops.caption: Step into the old water purification plant in Yangcheon and find the circular concrete tanks turned into galleries.
stops.transcriptText:
The western branch of Seoul's municipal art system opened here in Yangcheon in 2022, in a building that carries the traces of its previous life quite deliberately. The Seo Seoul Museum of Art — "seo" meaning west, positioned at the opposite end of the city from the main SeMA building in Jung-gu — was built within and around a decommissioned water purification facility from the Japanese colonial period, with the concrete filtration tanks and pump houses retained and incorporated into the exhibition architecture.

The circular tanks in particular have become the museum's most recognisable spatial feature: their curved concrete walls and the quality of light that falls through the openings above them create gallery conditions that are specific to this building and unavailable anywhere else. The museum's curation has consistently engaged with that specificity, commissioning works and selecting exhibitions that respond to the industrial and hydraulic history of the site.

Yangcheon is a southwestern residential district with no particular association with Seoul's art infrastructure, which is itself part of the institution's rationale: the Seoul Museum of Art has been expanding its branch network into parts of the city that are underserved by cultural institutions, and Seo Seoul sits alongside the Buk Seoul Museum of Art and Photo SeMA as evidence of that policy. The result is a museum that serves a neighbourhood rather than drawing visitors from across the city — which changes the character of what happens inside.

The water purification park surrounding the building is publicly accessible and connects to the Anyangcheon stream path — a rewarding piece of urban green infrastructure, worth following north along the water for thirty minutes if you have the time.

tours.title: Seochon Café FORET | 포레 카페
tours.shortDescription: French for forest — and it earns the name before you sit down: a hanok in Seochon opened up and filled with green, light filtered soft through the leaves.
tours.longDescription:
Café FORET takes its name from the French for forest, and the interior earns it before you've sat down: dense with plants, the afternoon light filtered through green in a way you'll find almost nowhere else in Seochon. The hanok-inflected building — courtyard, low eaves, wooden detailing — has been opened up and planted so that architecture and greenery become the whole point rather than an accessory.

Seochon, west of Gyeongbokgung, is among Seoul's most carefully preserved historic districts, its lanes largely unchanged since the Joseon period. It carries a literary streak — the poet Yi Sang and the painter Lee Sang-beom both lived here. FORET sits within that context without overplaying it: a café first, and a pleasant one, keeping its forest character where others trade for cool minimalism.

tours.title: Seodaemun Prison History Hall | 서대문형무소역사관
tours.shortDescription: Built by the colonial government in 1908, run until 1987 — a prison whose eighty years hold the whole arc of modern Korean suffering, now a memorial.
tours.longDescription:
Built in 1908 by the Japanese colonial government and operating until 1987, this prison spans the entire arc of modern Korean suffering: the suppression of the independence movement, the execution of resistance fighters, the military dictatorship that followed liberation. The brick walls, guard towers and several cell blocks before you are original. Redesigned as a museum in 1998, the site now draws around a million visitors a year, many of them school groups.

At the rear stands the Gongdeok-dong execution building, where independence leaders including Yu Gwan-sun — who led resistance in 1919 and died here at seventeen — were held and killed. The memorial around it is the emotional centre, treated quietly, without dramatisation, resisting the easy consolations of commemoration.

The nearly eighty years of that operation encompass the entire arc of modern Korean suffering: the suppression of the independence movement, the imprisonment and execution of resistance fighters, the military dictatorship period that followed liberation.

The brick walls and guard towers in front of you are original, as are several of the cell blocks within. The complex was redesigned as a history museum in 1998, and it now receives around a million visitors a year, many of them school groups for whom this is a mandatory part of learning the twentieth century.

The memorial space around this building is the emotional centre of the site, and it is treated accordingly: quietly, without dramatisation, with the names and faces of those who died here presented in a manner that resists the easy consolations of commemoration.

The history the prison represents is contested in some of its details — the precise scope of the resistance movement, the role of collaboration, the legacy of the subsequent Korean governments who used the same building — and the museum engages with some of that complexity. The Seodaemun Independence Park immediately surrounding the site extends the historical context, with the Independence Gate reconstructed nearby.

tours.title: Seosomun Shrine History Museum | 서소문성지 역사박물관
tours.shortDescription: From 1801 to 1866, forty-four Korean Catholic martyrs died at this execution ground — now a museum that deliberately descends underground to hold the memory.
tours.longDescription:
Between 1801 and 1866, the execution ground outside the Seosomun gate was where forty-four Korean Catholic martyrs were put to death. The site became one of the most significant in Korean Catholic history — partly because some victims had received the faith through books smuggled from China, before any foreign missionary had set foot in Korea.

The museum, opened in 2019 beneath Cheongpa Park, was built underground, its sloping concrete ramp descending below the level of the surrounding city — a deliberate argument about memory and surface. The collection traces Catholicism in Korea from that unusual bookish beginning, through persecution, to a Church now among Asia's largest. The martyrs were canonised by Pope John Paul II in 1984, and Pope Francis visited in 2014. The concrete descends into naturally lit rooms built for contemplation.

The museum you are entering was built underground, beneath Cheongpa Park, and opened in 2019. What happened here was covered over by an ordinary urban park for most of the twentieth century. The building insists on going down.

The collection traces the history of Catholicism in Korea from its unusual beginning — a faith adopted intellectually from texts, without a missionary, by Joseon scholars investigating Western learning — through the periods of persecution that followed, the eventual legalisation of Christianity, and the contemporary Korean Church, which is one of the largest and most internationally significant in Asia. The martyrs commemorated here were canonised by Pope John Paul II in 1984, and Pope Francis visited the site in 2014.

The underground architecture — concrete, naturally lit, the ceiling height varying as the rooms descend — creates a quality of attention that the subject requires. The Holiest Space at the deepest level is designed for contemplation rather than exhibition.

tours.title: Seoul Botanic Park | 서울식물원
tours.shortDescription: One hundred and four hectares on a decommissioned airport site — its centrepiece a hundred-metre glasshouse holding twelve climate zones under suspended glass.
tours.longDescription:
Seoul Botanic Park opened in May 2019 on a former airport site in Gangseo — one hundred and four hectares that served as Gimpo's domestic terminal from the 1970s until decommissioning in 2009. That scale is what makes it unusual: most urban botanic gardens are squeezed into whatever land a city will surrender; this one had an entire aviation zone to work with.

The centrepiece is an umbrella-shaped glasshouse about a hundred metres across, its glass roof suspended from a central column and holding twelve climate zones — from the Mediterranean and Central America to the Canary Islands, South Africa, Australia and the subtropical Pacific. Mature trees predating the park were transplanted inside. Beyond it lie a wildflower meadow, Hangang wetlands, a community garden and a children's zone — a genuine botanic collection, not an ornamental park with a few exotics.

The outdoor park sections include a wildflower meadow, wetland areas along the Hangang riverside, a community garden, and a children's zone that has become one of the most popular family destinations in western Seoul. The scale of the planted areas reflects the ambition of the project: this is a genuine botanic collection, not an ornamental park with a few exotic specimens.

The Magok area around the park has been developing rapidly as a new business and residential district — the park functions as the neighbourhood's central green space as that development continues.

tours.title: Shinsegae Media Facade | 신세계 미디어 파사드
tours.shortDescription: Korea's oldest department store, its 1930s neoclassical stone facade turned after dark into a continuous animated screen — heritage stone as canvas.
tours.longDescription:
The building on the corner of Myeongdong is Korea's oldest department store: Shinsegae, founded in 1930 as the Seoul branch of Mitsukoshi. The original 1930s structure survives, its neoclassical stone facade largely intact behind the retail within. What happens to that facade after dark is another matter.

The Shinsegae Media Facade turns the south and west walls into a digital projection screen, animating the neoclassical stonework into a continuous moving surface. Running in various forms since 2014, it is a rare case of heritage architecture serving as a canvas for media art — the ornament becomes part of the composition rather than an obstacle. Shows run seasonally, typically early evening and again around nine, lasting five to eight minutes. Amid Myeongdong's commercial saturation, it distinguishes itself by architectural rather than advertising logic.

tours.title: Starfield Library | 별마당 도서관
tours.shortDescription: A public library inside a Gangnam shopping mall, open until midnight — thirteen-metre shelves, fifty thousand real books, and the argument that retail and reading can share a room.
tours.longDescription:
At the centre of COEX Mall, Seoul's vast underground shopping complex, the Starfield Library makes a surprising claim: that a thirteen-metre bookshelf holding around fifty thousand volumes can be genuine cultural infrastructure rather than an elaborate visual amenity.

Opened in 2017, the shelves are the building. Two enormous curved walls of books rise the full height of the atrium, reached by ladder and internal staircase, with an open reading area between them. The collection is real — catalogued and available to read, not decorative — and visitors arrive both to read and to photograph.

Placing a library at the main circulation hub, where the greatest foot traffic passes, is an argument that books and retail aren't competing for the same attention. Whether it holds is something you can decide from a reading chair, with the shops moving past on all sides.

tours.title: THE HERITAGE — Former Head Office of Korea First Bank | 구 제일은행 본점
tours.shortDescription: A 1935 bank that outlived ninety years of demolition on its Myeongdong corner — colonial-era stone, now exhibition halls, and a heritage listing that came only recently.
tours.longDescription:
The former head office of Korea First Bank has stood on this Myeongdong corner since 1935, and that it still stands at all — in a neighbourhood demolished and rebuilt several times over — is a small piece of urban good fortune.

It's a modest example of colonial-era banking architecture: stone-clad, symmetrical, neoclassical, finished with the solidity that banks commissioned to signal permanence. Founded in 1929, the bank kept its headquarters here until it was absorbed into later financial structures. The recent renovation that earned it the name THE HERITAGE converted the banking halls into exhibition, retail and cultural spaces while keeping the original fabric — the high ceilings, carved stone, and the quality of light in the main hall.

Nearby stands the 1930s Shinsegae Department Store and a wider survival of colonial-period commercial architecture, a layer of Seoul largely erased elsewhere.

tours.title: Tamburins Seongsu | 탬버린즈 성수

The Seongsu location occupies one of the converted industrial units that define the neighbourhood, its manufacturing past kept in the structure while the interior is rebuilt as carefully proportioned rooms. What sets it apart is curatorial density: product is never isolated from its context, and that context is assembled with a serious gallery's attention to material, light and proportion. The brand's collaborations with Korean and international artists tend to land here as limited editions and installations.

Seongsu's identity as a creative hub is built partly by spaces like this, among specialty coffee, design studios and independent labels holding a consistently high standard.

tours.title: The Shrine of Our Lady of the Rosary of Namyang | 남양 성모 성지
tours.shortDescription: A hillside Catholic shrine ninety kilometres south of Seoul — sacred since the early nineteenth century, crowned by a 1991 Minor Basilica and a much-photographed bronze Pietà.
tours.longDescription:
This one asks for commitment. Namyang Marian Shrine sits in the hills above Hwaseong, roughly ninety kilometres south of Seoul — around ninety minutes by bus or car, a journey rather than a detour.

Korean Catholics have held this hillside sacred since the early nineteenth century, when the region's first communities faced periodic persecution under the Joseon government. Namyang was a significant early Catholic settlement, and martyrs of the persecutions of 1801 and 1866 have connections to this landscape. The current complex took shape across the twentieth century: a large outdoor plaza, a basilica, the bronze Pietà that has become its most photographed element, and devotional paths through the hills. The main basilica, completed in 1991, holds the title of Minor Basilica.

Pilgrims come year-round, with substantial crowds on Marian feast days. The low hills and Chungcheong farmland reward the trip in their own right.

Hwaseong Fortress, the late Joseon-period defensive wall that is a UNESCO World Heritage Site, is in the nearby city of Suwon and can reasonably be combined with the Namyang visit.

tours.title: WOOYOUNGMI Itaewon Flagship | 우영미 이태원 플래그십

WOOYOUNGMI has shown in Paris since 2002, establishing an export market and critical reputation before the wider interest in Korean fashion arrived — recognised internationally, yet undiluted in its Seoul roots.

Usadan-ro climbs from Itaewon through steep, architecturally varied lanes; the dense restaurant strip of Bogwang-dong lies immediately east.

tours.title: Won-Buddhism Wonnam Temple | 원불교 원남교당
tours.shortDescription: Not a sect of Buddhism but a Korean movement founded in 1916 — no gilt statues, no dramatic rooflines, just a black circle on white and a quiet room for meditation.
tours.longDescription:
Won Buddhism is not a sect of Buddhism in the conventional sense. It was founded in 1916 by Pak Chungbin — known by his religious title Sotaesan — to adapt Buddhist thought to modern life: the industrial economy, the decline of agrarian community, and what he diagnosed as the spiritual poverty of material progress. Distinctly Korean in origin, it has roughly one million practitioners worldwide, most in Korea.

The Wonnam Temple in Jongno is a contemporary building on a corner site north of Changgyeonggung Palace. Won Buddhist temples look deliberately unlike traditional ones: no gilt statues, no dramatic rooflines, none of the usual apparatus. The ritual focus is the Irwonsang, a black circle on white representing the undifferentiated oneness the tradition holds as ultimate reality. The spaces are calm and understated, made for meditation and study.

Visitors are generally welcome outside scheduled ceremonies; the location includes a library and study centre.

The movement is distinctly Korean in origin and character, and it has roughly one million practitioners worldwide, the majority in Korea.

The Wonnam Temple in Jongno is one of the Seoul branches of the Won Buddhist institution — a contemporary building occupying a corner site in the neighbourhood north of Changgyeonggung Palace, in an area where several Buddhist and Christian institutions have existed in proximity for many decades.

The neighbourhood around the temple, between Changgyeonggung and Jongmyo, holds several of Seoul's most significant historical institutions within easy walking distance.

tours.title: Yongma Land | 용마랜드
tours.shortDescription: An amusement park that closed in 1999 and never came down — carousel, coaster and bumper cars rusting on a Seoul mountainside, built for noise and movement and now holding neither.
tours.longDescription:

Yongma Land, in northeastern Seoul's Jungnang district, shut after twenty-two years, and the owner never finished dismantling the equipment — carousel, roller coaster, gondola lift and bumper cars all in place, rusting on an open mountainside colonised by weeds and moss.

The site isn't officially open. It works in a legal grey area: the owner periodically permits access for a fee, usually by pre-arranged visit, and it has become one of Seoul's more frequented photography locations for its mix of intact equipment and advanced decay. The structural steel tolerates decades of weather, so the rides deteriorate while staying visually intact — and increasingly interesting to look at.

What Yongma Land offers is a kind of accidental authenticity. Nothing was preserved on purpose. It simply stopped, and the stopping is what's visible.

Yongma Land in northeastern Seoul's Jungnang district shut down after twenty-two years of operation, and the owner has never completed the dismantling of the equipment — the carousel, the roller coaster, the gondola lift and the bumper cars are all still in place, rusting in an open mountainside site that has gradually been colonised by weeds and moss and the particular atmosphere of places that were built for noise and movement and now hold neither.

The site is not officially open to the public. It operates in a legal grey area: the owner periodically permits access for a fee, typically through pre-arranged visits, and it has become one of Seoul's more frequented photography locations precisely because of the combination of intact equipment and advanced decay. The rides have not been run since closure but have not collapsed — the structural steel of amusement park rides is built to tolerate decades of weather, and these are proceeding through their deterioration at a pace that keeps them visually intact while becoming increasingly interesting to look at.

What Yongma Land offers that more formally preserved ruins cannot is a kind of accidental authenticity: this is not a site that was preserved because anyone decided it was worth preserving. It simply stopped, and the stopping is what's visible.

The Jungnang Creative Economy Innovation Centre is nearby, as is the Photo SeMA photography museum — the northeastern corner of Seoul rewards the effort of getting there with a concentration of the city's less-visited but genuinely interesting institutions.

tours.title: Yoonseul — Manridong Reflecting Seoul | 윤슬 - 서울을 비추는 만리동
tours.shortDescription: Yoonseul — the Korean word for light shimmering on water — is a reflecting pool near Seoul Station that makes an unremarkable streetscape the subject of the art below.
tours.longDescription:
Yoonseul is a Korean word for the way a surface of water catches and reflects light — the shimmer of a still pool, the illumination at the boundary between water and air. It's an apt name for what this installation does, and for where it does it.

Yoonseul sits in the Manridong area of Jung-gu, a working district finding a new identity as the area around Seoul Station develops — the kind of public art a city commissions to signal change before knowing what that change will bring. A reflective pool and sculptural elements engage the surroundings through reflection, making the unremarkable streetscape above the subject of the artwork below.

It connects toward the elevated Seoullo 7017 skygarden, a five-hundred-metre planted walkway running west from Seoul Station. Yoonseul is most effective when reflection is maximised: still air, calm water, and the flat light of overcast days or the oblique light of early morning and late afternoon.

stops.title: Yoonseul — Manridong Reflecting Seoul | 윤슬 - 서울을 비추는 만리동
stops.caption: Look down into the reflecting pool and watch the ordinary streetscape above resolve into the subject of the work below.
stops.transcriptText:
The name Yoonseul is a Korean word for the way a surface of water catches and reflects light — the shimmer of a still pool, the particular quality of illumination that happens at the boundary between water and air. It is an appropriate name for what this installation does, and for where it does it.

Yoonseul sits in the Manridong area of Jung-gu, in a neighbourhood that has been undergoing gradual transformation as the area around Seoul Station develops — less a fashionable destination than a working district finding a new identity through the kind of public art interventions that cities commission when they want to signal change without yet knowing what that change will produce. The installation consists of a reflective pool and sculptural elements designed to engage with the surrounding urban environment through reflection, making the unremarkable streetscape above it the subject of the artwork below.

The coordinates place it in an area that connects the neighbourhood around Manri-dong with the elevated Seoullo 7017 skygarden — the former elevated highway converted into a linear garden that runs west from Seoul Station. The skygarden itself is worth the approach: a five-hundred-metre-long planted walkway elevated above the street, open daily, with views of the station and the surrounding districts that are available nowhere else in this part of the city.

Yoonseul is most effective in conditions where reflection is maximised — still air, calm water, and either the flat light of overcast days or the oblique light of early morning and late afternoon. The installation responds to Seoul's weather rather than working against it.

tours.title: Anyang Art Park | 안양예술공원
tours.shortDescription: A two-kilometre valley walk through Korea's only public art triennial, from Álvaro Siza's white concrete hall up to MVRDV's spiral peak tower.
tours.longDescription:
A six-stop walk up a forested valley twenty kilometres south of Seoul, tied by a single idea: what happens when a satellite city takes its own name — utopia — seriously. Since 2005 the Anyang Public Art Project has scattered more than sixty permanent works through these hills, and this route strings six of the best along the stream.

You begin at Álvaro Siza's near-white concrete pavilion, where the space is said to sing, then head upstream to a house built from plastic beer crates that glows with filtered colour inside. Jeppe Hein's mirror labyrinth multiplies you into a crowd; Vito Acconci's tunnel floats a horizontal line through the canopy; NEXT Architects wrap three trees inside a mirrored ring.

It ends at MVRDV's spiral observatory, a structure that extends the mountain upward until the whole of Anyang reveals itself in layers. Roughly two kilometres with some climb, free and open at all hours — an easy, curious afternoon.

stops.title: Anyang Art Park — Introduction | 안양예술공원 — 소개
stops.caption: Start at the Anyang Pavilion at the park entrance; pick up a free collection map before you set off.
stops.transcriptText:
The name Anyang comes from a Buddhist temple built here during the Goryeo Dynasty — the word itself means utopia, a place where the mind and body are renewed. It is, by any measure, an ambitious name for a satellite city of six hundred thousand people twenty kilometres south of Seoul. But Anyang has been taking its own name seriously for two decades now, and the park you're about to walk through is the evidence.

The Anyang Public Art Project — APAP — began transforming this valley in 2005, commissioning international architects and artists to build permanent works in and around what had previously been an unremarkable recreation park. It runs every three years, making it Korea's only public art triennial, and each edition has added to a collection that now totals more than sixty works scattered through the forested hills along the Anyang stream. The whole thing is free to enter and open at all hours — which is either the most generous or the most quietly radical thing about it, depending on your view.

This walk follows the valley path from the Siza Pavilion at the park entrance up through the forest to the MVRDV observation tower at the far end of the ridge — roughly two kilometres with some climb, and a sequence of six very different things to encounter along the way.

Pick up a map from the Anyang Pavilion at the start of the walk if you'd like to locate the full collection — there are considerably more than six works here, and a few of them reward wandering off the main path to find.

stops.title: Anyang Pavilion (Álvaro Siza Hall) | 안양파빌리온 (알바로 시자 홀)
stops.caption: Stand before the gently curved white concrete building at the entrance, then step inside to hear it.
stops.transcriptText:
The brief was almost insultingly modest. A multipurpose hall, a small police office, and some public toilets for visitors to the park — that was the commission Álvaro Siza received in February 2005, delivered with the urgency that, according to his collaborator Carlos Castanheira, characterises everything in Korea.

The gently curved concrete building in front of you is what Siza made of that brief. The shell is near-white exposed concrete — fine enough to carry the quality of light rather than simply reflecting it — and the plan is a flowing series of curves in which concave and convex surfaces move against each other as you walk through the space. Castanheira described stepping inside the completed building in 2006 during the monsoon rains and finding that "the space sings," which is the kind of thing that sounds extravagant in print and makes complete sense the moment you stand inside it.

Siza was born in Porto in 1933 and became one of the most significant architects of the late twentieth century through a practice defined by precision, material economy, and a particular sensitivity to light entering curved interior surfaces. This was his first building in Korea, and it led directly to his next: the Mimesis Art Museum in Paju, completed in 2009 with the same team, and one of the finest small buildings in the country.

The pavilion now serves as the headquarters of the Anyang Public Art Project and the starting point for tours of the park. Free maps of the full collection are available inside.

From here, the path leads into the valley. The Crate House is a short walk upstream — a building made, rather improbably, from plastic beer crates, and best understood from the inside.

stops.title: Anyang Crate House | 안양 크레이트 하우스 (박스 하우스)
stops.caption: Walk a short way upstream to the stacked plastic-crate house, and go in to see the coloured light.
stops.transcriptText:
Multicoloured plastic beer crates, stacked into a building. That is the material and the method, and it is, once you've seen it, entirely logical.

The structure ahead — its full title is Anyang Crate House: Dedicated to the Lost — was made by the German artist duo Wolfgang Winter and Berthold Hörbelt, who have used plastic crates as their primary building material in public works across Europe and now here. The crates come in the standardised format common to German beer distribution, which makes them modular, interlocking, and almost infinitely stackable — a readymade construction system that the artists have been exploiting with considerable intelligence since the 1990s.

From the outside, the building changes character depending on the angle and the light: the colours shift, the pattern of the crates produces a different rhythm from each side, and the scale surprises. Walk inside, and the logic of the work becomes clear — daylight enters through the gaps between every crate, so the interior is filled with a mosaic of coloured light filtered through red, yellow, blue, and green plastic, a grid of small glowing rectangles across floor, walls, and ceiling. The structural principle and the aesthetic effect are inseparable.

The dedication — to the Lost — is one of those titles that refuses to explain itself, which is perhaps the point. Whether the lost are people, things, or something more abstract is left, deliberately, to whoever is standing inside the coloured light.

Continue upstream along the valley path. The Mirror Labyrinth is further into the forest — a work made from polished aluminium columns that turns your reflection into a crowd.

stops.title: Dimensional Mirror Labyrinth | 거울 미로
stops.caption: Find the 115 polished aluminium columns in three rings; walk the outer path before stepping inside.
stops.transcriptText:
One hundred and fifteen polished aluminium columns, arranged in three concentric circles, set into the ground so they rise to roughly eye level — and the whole thing reflects everything around it, including you.

The Dimensional Mirror Labyrinth was made by the Danish artist Jeppe Hein, who was born in Copenhagen in 1974 and works consistently with reflective surfaces, kinetic elements, and installations that reposition the viewer as part of the work rather than an observer of it. Walk into the outer ring and the columns return an image of the forest and sky; move toward the centre and your own reflection multiplies in each successive column, so that by the time you reach the inner circle you are surrounded by versions of yourself, slightly distorted, retreating in every direction.

The work carries a specific local resonance that its title only hints at. Anyang takes its name from a Buddhist temple associated with the concept of heaven — a place where the soul arrives after death and finds renewal. The mirror labyrinth references the Christian tradition of the labyrinth as a pilgrimage path, walked in circles as a form of meditative practice on the way to a sacred centre. Both traditions, different in form, are present in the name and the history of this city, and Hein's work sits quietly at the intersection.

Walk the outer path first before going in. The columns are more interesting from a distance than photographs suggest — the reflection of the tree canopy across all one hundred and fifteen surfaces simultaneously, on a clear day, is rather something.

Continue up the hill toward the trees. The Acconci building is suspended in the forest above the path.

stops.title: Linear Building Up in the Trees | 숲속의 멀티홀
stops.caption: Look up through the trees above the path for the raised tunnel, then climb to enter it.
stops.transcriptText:
The structure visible through the trees above the path is not a walkway, exactly, and not a building, exactly — which is, for Vito Acconci, very much the point.

Acconci Studio's Linear Building Up in the Trees is an elevated tunnel, a long tube raised above the forest floor on supports that keeps it among the canopy rather than on the ground. From below, it reads as a horizontal line through the vertical forest — a counter-gesture to the trees, asserting its own geometry against theirs without dominating them. Walk up to it and you can enter the tunnel and move through the trees at a height that lets you read the forest differently than you would from the path below.

Vito Acconci (1940–2017) began his career as a poet, shifted into performance art in the late 1960s — work that used his own body as both subject and medium — and spent the last decades of his career through Acconci Studio making architectural and public interventions that consistently blurred the line between building, furniture, and sculpture. The question his studio returned to consistently was: what is a building for, and how little of what we conventionally expect from one does it actually need?

The tunnel emerging onto an open platform, with its grid-like floor that lets you see the ground through it, extends that question here — a room with no walls, a roof without cover, a building that is more suggestion than enclosure.

The Secret Forest Pavilion is further up the slope, where NEXT Architects have enclosed part of the forest inside itself.

stops.title: Secret Forest Pavilion | 비밀의 숲
stops.caption: Circle the mirrored ring pavilion first, then enter to meet the three trees enclosed inside.
stops.transcriptText:
Three trees stand inside this pavilion. They were here before the pavilion was — the pavilion was built around them.

The Secret Forest is the most recently completed work on this walk, delivered in December 2023 as part of the seventh Anyang Public Art Project. It was designed by the Dutch firm NEXT Architects, and its logic is one of the more quietly elegant ideas in the park: a circular structure, mirrored on the exterior, that encloses three trees from the surrounding forest and separates them — temporarily, perceptually — from the forest they belong to.

Walk the circular path around the outside first. The mirrored exterior reflects the forest back at itself, so the pavilion appears to disappear into its surroundings while simultaneously enclosing something that those surroundings cannot see. Then enter. Inside, the three trees stand in a space that makes them available for the kind of focused attention that the forest as a whole rarely provides — each one distinct, its bark and branches and the particular angle of its growth legible in a way that a tree among thousands seldom is. Coming back out, the trees re-enter the forest and become anonymous again.

NEXT Architects described the routing through the pavilion as a "transitional zone" — a narrow passage that guides you gradually from open forest to enclosed secret, and back again at a different pace. The word "secret" in the title is well chosen: the forest has no secrets from itself, but the pavilion creates one, briefly, for the person walking through it.

The MVRDV tower is the final stop on this walk — a short climb further up the ridge, and worth every step.

stops.title: Anyang Peak Observatory | 안양전망대
stops.caption: Head up the ridge to the spiral tower; climb slowly as Anyang opens on every side.
stops.transcriptText:
MVRDV's description of this project was that they wanted to "supercharge the hill" — to take the natural elevation that was already here and push it until it became an event rather than a feature. The spiral path wrapping the hillside and continuing up into the tower is the result: a walk that begins on the mountain's own slope and becomes, seamlessly, a structure that extends the mountain upward beyond where it naturally ends.

The tower is ahead and above you — its spiral path ascending from ground level, turning around and around the central void, climbing until the views open in every direction across Anyang and the surrounding mountains: Gwanak to the north, Samseong immediately behind you, the city filling the valley below. The internal space at the base can hold exhibitions or performances; visitors looking down from the top can see it as a kind of stage. MVRDV built this in 2005 as one of the founding commissions of the Anyang Public Art Project — which makes it nearly twenty years old — and the decision it represents still holds up: the best thing you can do with a beautiful natural site is take it seriously, rather than simply building something decorative beside it.

The climb takes about ten to fifteen minutes at a relaxed pace. Go up slowly if you can — the city reveals itself in layers as you gain height, and each turn of the spiral gives a different frame to the same landscape.

This is where the walk ends. The park's full collection continues back down the valley, and several works are best found by wandering rather than following a fixed route. The Anyang stream beside the main path is worth following on the way back.

tours.title: Les Jardins de Médongaule | 메덩골정원
tours.shortDescription: One anonymous man spent thirteen years building a new Korean garden east of Seoul: a two-kilometre loop from a commoners' laundry stream to a garden named for Plato's ideal.
tours.longDescription:
One person spent thirteen years on this. He sold the company he'd built, bought land in a valley ninety minutes east of Seoul, and set about making the first genuinely new Korean garden in a hundred years. He remains anonymous by his own instruction, so the garden speaks for him. Médongaule is the valley's old name, for a place where a modest morning glory once bloomed between the mountains.

The walk is a two-kilometre loop with gentle climbs, and it falls into two halves. The Korean Garden comes first: dry-stone walls and terraced crops in the Commoners' Hometown, a stream built by hand to recreate a village laundry site, then Jaeyedang and the scholars' world of the seonbi — Seung H-Sang's Confucian academy, his Tower of Solitary Pleasure, his inward little hermitage.

West and north, the Contemporary Garden answers that tradition in other hands: a French father-and-son labyrinth, Pezo von Ellrichshausen's green-concrete REST, Ensamble Studio's earth-grown Indomitable Spirit, and Idea, named for Plato's perfect form.

The broad arc runs from the ordinary lives of Korean commoners to the Platonic ideal — from a stream recreating a laundry site to a garden named for the forms behind all forms. It opened in 2025; whether thirteen years were well spent, the valley quietly keeps asking.

stops.title: Les Jardins de Médongaule — Introduction | 메덩골정원 — 소개
stops.caption: Begin just inside the entrance to the Korean section, at the Commoners' Hometown Garden.
stops.transcriptText:
One person spent thirteen years building this. He sold the company he'd built over the previous decade, bought land in a valley ninety minutes east of Seoul, and set about creating what he called the first genuinely new Korean garden in a hundred years. He remains anonymous — his instruction, not ours — so the garden speaks for him.

Médongaule is the old Korean name for this valley: a place where me-kkot, the short-hairy morning glory, once bloomed in the folds between the mountains. The name carries both a location and an image — a valley not of grandeur, but of the kind of modest beauty that ordinary things can produce in the right conditions. That is, quietly, the whole argument of the garden.

The walk covers around two kilometres in a loose circuit, with some gentle climbs. It divides naturally into two halves: a Korean Garden section, which you'll enter first, and a Contemporary Garden section further west and north. The Korean section is organised around three ideas — the lives of ordinary people, the spirit of scholars, and the deeper Korean traditions of Confucianism, Buddhism, and Shamanism. The Contemporary section is where international architects and landscape designers have responded to that tradition, in their own materials and registers.

The garden opened to the public in September 2025, though planning and construction had been underway since 2012. It took this long because it was done this carefully.

Begin at the Commoners' Hometown Garden, just inside the entry to the Korean section.

stops.title: The Commoners' Hometown Garden | 백성의 고향 정원
stops.caption: Stand before the dry-stone walls and terraced plots, planted with cotton, rice and eggplant rather than flowers.
stops.transcriptText:
The stone walls dividing the terraced fields here are not decorative.
