The museum on the grounds shows off the haul, including a glowing amber wall built from hundreds of dire wolf skulls, and the saber-toothed Smilodon, the official state fossil of California. Outside, the Lake Pit steams gently behind its fence, watched over by a famously heart-wrenching sculpture of a mammoth family — one parent trapped in the black water, the others watching from shore. And here's the detail that gets people: the excavation never ended. Scientists are still out here working active digs, pulling new specimens from the ground on ordinary weekdays while traffic idles past on Wilshire.

Watch the pavement as you wander the park. The asphalt still breaks through the grass in slow black puddles, utterly indifferent to the city on top of it. It was here first, and it intends to stay.

tours.title: Academy Museum of Motion Pictures
tours.shortDescription: Renzo Piano's museum of the movies, capped by a floating glass sphere.
tours.longDescription: The Academy's 2021 film museum joins the restored 1939 May Company building to a Renzo Piano concrete-and-glass sphere holding a 1,000-seat theater. Inside: the story of cinema, from Dorothy's ruby slippers to the craft behind the screen.

stops.title: Academy Museum of Motion Pictures
stops.caption: Look up at the glass sphere bridging to the old streamline-moderne building.
stops.transcriptText:
You should be at Wilshire Boulevard and Fairfax Avenue, looking at a golden cylinder rising at the corner — a curved wall of gold mosaic tile catching the sun — attached to a long, clean building of pale limestone. This is the Academy Museum of Motion Pictures, and the building came first: the May Company department store, built in 1939, the grandest piece of Streamline Moderne left in Los Angeles. Its architect, Albert C. Martin, also designed City Hall — the man got around. That gold corner holds more than three hundred fifty thousand tiles, and when restoration required replacements, they came from the original mosaic workshop in Venice, Italy.

Walk around to the north side, or just look past the building, and you'll see the addition: a giant concrete-and-glass sphere, lifted off the ground on piers, connected to the old store by glass bridges. Renzo Piano designed it to hold a thousand-seat theater, with a glass-domed terrace on top that looks straight out at the Hollywood Sign — the museum aiming its best view at the industry's oldest advertisement.

Inside, the collection runs deep — millions of objects going back to the beginning of the movies, from costumes and screenplays to props, including a certain full-sized mechanical shark suspended over the escalators, the only one of its kind to survive its famous 1975 film.

Here's what's worth chewing on. The industry that manufactures permanence for everyone else — that decides which faces and stories get preserved — waited nearly a hundred years to preserve itself, and when it did, it moved into a building designed for selling dresses and dinnerware. A department store from 1939, the same year often called the movies' greatest: the future as imagined then, holding the past as curated now. The gold corner was built to stop traffic on Wilshire. It still does — it just sells something different.

tours.title: Petersen Automotive Museum
tours.shortDescription: A car museum wrapped in 100 tons of ribboning stainless steel.
tours.longDescription: Behind a facade of red aluminum and swooping steel ribbons, the Petersen tells the story of the automobile and LA's love affair with it — four floors of rare cars, hot rods and film vehicles on the Miracle Mile.

stops.title: Petersen Automotive Museum
stops.caption: Trace the silver steel ribbons wrapping the red building on Wilshire.
stops.transcriptText:
You should be at Wilshire and Fairfax, on the corner opposite the Academy Museum's gold cylinder, looking at a building wrapped in ribbons — long bands of brushed stainless steel streaming around a body of hot-rod red, as if someone froze the airflow over a car and made it architecture. This is the Petersen Automotive Museum, and in Los Angeles, a museum about the car is not a niche institution. It's a museum about the landlord.

The bones underneath are older than the ribbons. Inside that red shell is a department store from 1962, designed by Welton Becket — the same firm behind the Capitol Records tower — and when magazine publisher Robert Petersen went looking for a museum home in the 1990s, he picked it precisely because it was nearly windowless: a big sealed box where sunlight couldn't fade the paint on anything. The museum opened in 1994 looking like what it was, a converted store. Then in 2015 came the wrapper: about a hundred tons of steel in more than three hundred custom sections, each one different, streaming around the box.

Critics were split — one famously called it happily tasteless — and the public voted with their cameras. Both sides have a point, which is very Los Angeles: this has always been a city where hot dog stands looked like hot dogs and buildings advertised themselves, and the Petersen simply does it at freeway scale.

Inside, the collection makes the argument the outside promises: race cars, concept cars from the era when the future had fins, machines built for the movies, and the story of how one invention laid out this entire city — the boulevards, the sprawl, the drive-ins, the parking lots. Los Angeles didn't adopt the car; they grew up together.

So stand on this corner and take in the pairing: across the street, the movies in a gold cylinder; here, the automobile in silver ribbons. The two machines that built Los Angeles, facing each other at one intersection, each wearing its Sunday best. If you only have time for the outside, circle the block once. The building is the first exhibit.

tours.title: Original Farmers Market & The Grove
tours.shortDescription: A 1934 open-air market with a clock tower, beside its modern twin, The Grove.
tours.longDescription: The Original Farmers Market has gathered under its landmark clock tower since 1934 — produce stalls, counters and old-LA character — now linked by trolley to The Grove, the 2002 outdoor shopping piazza next door.

stops.title: Original Farmers Market & The Grove
stops.caption: Meet under the white clock tower where the market stalls begin.
stops.transcriptText:
You should be at the corner of Third Street and Fairfax Avenue, under or near the white clock tower — the landmark of the Original Farmers Market since 1948. The market itself is older. In July 1934, with the Depression grinding on, a dozen farmers paid fifty cents a day to park their trucks on the Gilmore family's idle oil land and sell produce straight off the tailgates. The stopgap stuck: within months the trucks had become permanent stalls, and the stalls never closed. This market has fed the city every single day since — through the war, the freeways, and every reinvention Los Angeles has thrown at itself.

Step inside and notice the shape of the place. The aisles are low, narrow, and slightly crooked, because nobody ever master-planned any of this — it grew the way real villages grow, one stall at a time, by appetite. More than a hundred vendors now, selling gumbo, doughnuts, hot corned beef, and produce, some of them run by the same families for generations. The story goes that the market's first restaurant began when a shopkeeper's wife named Blanche Magee saw hungry farmers at their trucks and simply started filling a picnic hamper.

Now look next door. The Grove, opened in 2002, is an outdoor mall designed with enormous care to feel like a small-town square — a trolley, a dancing fountain, music in the air. Which gives this corner something rare: an actual accidental village and a meticulous imitation of one, side by side, sharing a trolley line. You can debate which is the real Los Angeles, but this city has always sold the invented version and the genuine article from adjacent storefronts.

Pick an aisle and order something you've never tried. A place this improvised has outlasted almost everything planned around it — which, in this town, is its own kind of monument.

tours.title: Griffith Observatory
tours.shortDescription: The city's free Art Deco balcony to the stars, on Mount Hollywood.
tours.longDescription: Griffith J. Griffith willed the city an observatory that would be free forever; it opened in 1935, a white Art Deco temple over the basin with the Hollywood Sign across the canyon and telescopes open to all. The best view in LA, no ticket.

stops.title: Griffith Observatory
stops.caption: Step onto the terrace with the basin below and the Hollywood Sign opposite.
stops.transcriptText:
Griffith Observatory is the best balcony in Los Angeles — a white art deco temple on the south slope of Mount Hollywood, with the whole basin spread below, the Hollywood Sign across the canyon, and, on a clear day, the Pacific glittering at the far edge. It is also, and has been since 1935, completely free — and thereby hangs the story.

Griffith J. Griffith was a Welsh-born businessman who made a fortune in mining and Southern California real estate, and in 1896 he gave the city just over three thousand acres of hillside — Griffith Park, still one of the largest urban parks in North America. Later he offered money for a great public observatory on the peak, convinced that looking through a telescope could enlarge a person; he had done it himself and called the experience life-changing. The city said no. Griffith by then was a scandal — he had shot his wife, a crime for which he served prison time — and Los Angeles refused to take his money while he lived. So he left it in his will, and sixteen years after his death the observatory opened on his terms: admission free, forever, for everyone.

Those terms built something genuinely rare — a serious public science institution that functions like a park. Inside you'll find a Foucault pendulum patiently proving the earth rotates, a Tesla coil that snaps to life on schedule, and a planetarium under the great center dome. Up on the roof, the twelve-inch Zeiss refracting telescope opens to the public on clear evenings, and the observatory claims more people have looked through it than any other telescope in history. The line is long, it moves slowly, and it is entirely worth it — the queue for the eyepiece is the whole point, exactly as the donor ordered.

A word about timing: sunset draws half the city up here, and parking becomes a contact sport. Come late morning for the quiet version, or embrace the crowds and watch the basin light up grid by grid as the sky goes orange. Perspective improves people, Griffith believed. The jury may still be out on that one, but the view argues his side every single night.

tours.title: Greek Theatre
tours.shortDescription: A beloved open-air amphitheatre folded into Griffith Park's greenery.
tours.longDescription: Opened in 1930, the 5,900-seat Greek Theatre stages summer concerts under the stars amid Griffith Park's oaks and trails — one of the largest urban parks in North America, Griffith J. Griffith's great gift to the city.

stops.title: Greek Theatre
stops.caption: Look down into the tree-ringed bowl of the open-air Greek stage.
stops.transcriptText:
Los Angeles has a reputation for paving things, so it's worth pausing on what it didn't pave.

You should be near the Greek Theatre, on Vermont Canyon Road where Los Feliz runs out and the hills take over — the amphitheater's white colonnade on one side of you, and on the other, chaparral climbing into what looks, honestly, like wilderness. That's because it is.

Griffith Park covers more than four thousand acres — nearly five times the size of Central Park — and unlike Central Park, most of it was never landscaped. It's genuinely rugged: canyons, coyotes, trails where you can lose sight of the city while standing in the middle of it. It exists because a mining millionaire named Griffith J. Griffith gave the land away in 1896, declaring that public parks were a safety valve for great cities. His own story turned dark afterward — a crime, a prison term — and Los Angeles argued for years about whether to keep taking his money. It did, and his will paid for two things: the Observatory on the ridge above you, and the theater beside you.

The Greek opened in 1930, set into this canyon because the acoustics were already here — the hillside does work an architect would charge millions for. It seats nearly six thousand people, spent World War Two as army barracks, and now fills a season of concerts every year from spring to fall. Angelenos will tell you, with some heat, that a show here beats the Hollywood Bowl.

But the best story in this park walked in on four feet. In 2012, a trail camera caught something that shouldn't have been possible: a mountain lion, living in Griffith Park. He had crossed two of the busiest freeways in America to get here, and he stayed a decade — eight square miles, the smallest territory ever recorded for his species, with millions of people around the edges. They called him P-22, and a photograph of him prowling below the Hollywood Sign made him the most famous cat in the country. He died in 2022, and the city genuinely mourned him; his story helped get a wildlife crossing built over a freeway, so the next lion wouldn't need his luck.

That's the thing to carry up the trail: this isn't a park in a city. It's a piece of wild California the city grew around — and never quite tamed.

tours.title: Santa Monica Pier
tours.shortDescription: The 1909 pier where Route 66 meets the Pacific — and a solar Ferris wheel spins.
tours.longDescription: Santa Monica's wooden pier has drawn crowds since 1909, its Pacific Park carrying the world's only solar-powered Ferris wheel out over the surf. The end of Route 66, an arcade, an aquarium and an unbeatable sunset.

stops.title: Santa Monica Pier
stops.caption: Walk out under the neon arch toward the Ferris wheel over the water.
stops.transcriptText:
The Santa Monica Pier is the last of the great Pacific pleasure piers, the symbolic end of Route 66, and quite possibly the most beloved structure in Southern California — and it began, in 1909, as a utility project. The city built the original concrete pier largely to carry a sewer line out past the breakers. That is the least romantic origin of any adored landmark in America, and the pier has spent over a century living it down in style.

The fun arrived in 1916, when amusement-park builder Charles Looff added a pleasure pier alongside, anchored by the Hippodrome — the fairy-tale carousel building near the entrance, now a National Historic Landmark. Inside spins a carousel of hand-carved horses that has been delighting riders, and moonlighting in the movies, for the better part of a century. Beyond it the pier unrolls the full classic menu: arcade, aquarium, fishermen at the rails, street performers, and the little amusement park whose Ferris wheel — said to be the world's first solar-powered one — has become the postcard of this entire coastline, especially lit up after dark.

The pier very nearly didn't make it. In the early 1970s the city council voted to tear it down, and the residents of Santa Monica staged a revolt, packing meetings until the plan died. A decade later, brutal winter storms chewed off a third of the structure, and the town rebuilt it. This pier exists today purely on affection, twice proven.

And then there's the sign — Route 66, End of the Trail. Full honesty: the highway's official terminus was about a mile inland, where the road had to junction with the coast highway, and this particular famous sign only went up in 2009. But nobody ever drove twenty-four hundred miles from Chicago to finish at an intersection. The pier is where the continent runs out — where generations of arrivals walked to the rail and looked at the Pacific because there was no more west left to want. It's the honest end of the American road, whatever the paperwork says.

Stay for sunset if you possibly can. Everyone claps. Nobody's embarrassed. It's that kind of place.

tours.title: Third Street Promenade
tours.shortDescription: Santa Monica's car-free shopping street of buskers and dinosaur topiaries.
tours.longDescription: Three walkable blocks near the beach, the Promenade mixes street performers, shops and its signature ivy dinosaur fountains into one of LA's most-strolled open-air scenes, steps from the pier.

stops.title: Third Street Promenade
stops.caption: Stroll the car-free blocks past the topiary-dinosaur fountains.
stops.transcriptText:
Here's a piece of history hiding under your feet: this street is one of the oldest pedestrian malls in America — and one of the only ones that ever worked.

You should be standing on Third Street between Wilshire and Broadway, three blocks closed to cars, storefronts on both sides, and — down the middle of the street — a row of enormous topiary dinosaurs spouting water from their mouths. We'll get to the dinosaurs.

Start with the experiment. In the 1960s, American downtowns were losing everything to the suburbs, and roughly two hundred cities tried the same desperate fix: close a shopping street to cars and hope people came back. Santa Monica closed this one in 1965, one of the first in the country. Almost every mall like it eventually failed — and for a while, this one did too. By the 1980s it was struggling: dark storefronts, thin crowds, the same slow fade playing out on pedestrian malls everywhere.

Then Santa Monica did the strange thing. Instead of giving the street back to cars, it doubled down — a full redesign, reopened in 1989, built around restaurants, movie theaters, and street performers rather than shops alone, so the street had a reason to stay alive after dark. It worked spectacularly. For decades this was the proof, cited by planners all over the country, that a street built for feet could beat the shopping mall at its own game.

The dinosaurs arrived with that redesign — six of them, ivy-covered fountains by the French artists Les Lalanne — and they've outlasted nearly every store that was open when they were planted. Which is the honest part of the story: retail comes and goes hard on this street. Right now it's mostly going — you'll see empty windows between the open ones — and the city is responding the way it did last time, by betting on the street itself: looser rules, more restaurants, more events, even a zone where you can carry a drink outdoors as you walk, the first of its kind in Southern California.

So read this street as a running argument, sixty years long, about whether a car city can hold onto a place built for walking. The argument has been won, lost, and won again — and the dinosaurs, who have watched all of it, don't look worried.

tours.title: Venice Beach Boardwalk
tours.shortDescription: LA's carnival of the counterculture — skaters, muscle, murals and hustle.
tours.longDescription: Abbot Kinney's 1905 seaside 'Venice of America' became a boardwalk like nowhere else: street performers, the skate plaza, Muscle Beach, Windward's arcaded colonnades and a running gallery of murals along the Pacific.

stops.title: Venice Beach Boardwalk
stops.caption: Enter under the VENICE archway and let the boardwalk carnival unfold.
stops.transcriptText:
Everything you're looking at is what's left of a utopia that failed in the most Los Angeles way possible: it became famous instead.

You should be on Ocean Front Walk, the wide boardwalk running between the beach and the storefronts — murals, vendors, skaters, and somewhere within earshot, at least one person performing something. To find the origin of it all, look for Windward Avenue, where a row of columned arcades meets the walk. Those Venetian colonnades are more than a hundred years old, and they're the last standing piece of the original dream.

The dreamer was Abbot Kinney, who had made a fortune in tobacco and decided this stretch of salt marsh should become the Venice of America — a real one, with canals dredged where the marsh had been, gondolas and gondoliers brought over from Italy, and a program of lectures and orchestras meant to seed a cultural renaissance on the Pacific. It opened on July 4, 1905, and tens of thousands came on the first day.

They came, they rode the gondolas — and then they made it plain they'd rather have fun. The lecture halls emptied while the amusement pier filled, and Kinney, whatever he privately thought, was too good a businessman to argue. Venice pivoted into the Coney Island of the Pacific: roller coasters, sideshows, dance halls, a miniature railroad threading through it all. The renaissance never arrived. The crowds never left.

Kinney died in 1920, Los Angeles absorbed Venice in the mid-twenties, and most of his canals were paved into streets in 1929. What survived the respectable decades that followed wasn't the culture — it was the carnival. Beat poets took the cheap bungalows, bodybuilders claimed a patch of sand just down the walk, skateboarding got reinvented in this neighborhood's empty pools, and today's boardwalk economy of performers, artists, and vendors runs on the same fuel Kinney's midway did: hold a crowd, then pass the hat.

So the utopia failed — but look around, because something stranger succeeded. Kinney wanted a place unlike anywhere else in America. A century on, whatever else has changed, nobody has ever accused Venice of being like anywhere else.

tours.title: Venice Canals
tours.shortDescription: The 1905 dream that survived — quiet canals, arched footbridges, gliding ducks.
tours.longDescription: A few blocks off the boardwalk, the last of Abbot Kinney's hand-dug 1905 canals endure as a hidden neighborhood of walkways, white footbridges and waterfront cottages — the calm counterpoint to Venice's roar.

stops.title: Venice Canals
stops.caption: Cross a white footbridge over the still canal between the cottages.
stops.transcriptText:
One block from one of the loudest places in Los Angeles, everything goes quiet — and the quiet is an accident.

You should be in the Venice Canal Historic District, a few blocks inland from the boardwalk, standing on or near one of the white arched footbridges. Six narrow canals, low houses with little docks, ducks working the banks, kayaks tied up like parked cars. It reads as a miniature of Venice, Italy, and it is — but not in the way most visitors assume.

Here's the twist: these are not the famous canals. When Abbot Kinney opened his Venice of America in 1905, his showpiece canals — the ones with the imported gondoliers — were dug a few blocks north of here, around what's now Windward Avenue. This set came just afterward: a second tract, dug next door to ride his success, joined to the original network by the Grand Canal. The annex, in other words. The sideshow.

Then the car happened. Venice was absorbed into Los Angeles in the mid-twenties, the canals were declared obsolete, and in 1929 Kinney's originals were drained and paved into ordinary streets. If you've ever stood in the traffic circle where Windward meets Pacific, you've stood in what used to be the lagoon at the heart of the whole dream. And the reason these six survived is almost comically unromantic: this tract didn't have enough residents to pay the assessments that funded the paving. Too poor to become roads — so they stayed water.

They spent decades in genteel decay after that, sidewalks crumbling, the houses cheap and bohemian, until the early 1990s, when the city finally drained and rebuilt them — new walls, new walkways, the arched bridges restored. The district now sits on the National Register of Historic Places, which is its own quiet irony: the afterthought became the protected landmark, while the main event lies under asphalt, with street signs for a headstone.

So walk it slowly. This is the last place where you can feel what Kinney actually meant — a neighborhood built to move at the speed of water, in the city that chose the freeway. It survived by being overlooked, which may be the most Venice thing about it.

tours.title: Muscle Beach
tours.shortDescription: The original 1934 outdoor gym that launched America's fitness craze.
tours.longDescription: Beside Santa Monica Pier, the original Muscle Beach drew acrobats and gymnasts from the 1930s and seeded the bodybuilding culture that made LA the capital of fitness — the rings and bars still swinging at golden hour.

stops.title: Muscle Beach
stops.caption: Watch the acrobats on the rings with the pier behind them.
stops.transcriptText:
You should be on the beach just south of the Santa Monica Pier, where rings, ropes, and bars rise out of the sand. This is the original Muscle Beach, and it began in 1934 as a Depression relief project: the Works Progress Administration installed exercise equipment here to put people to work and give the public something wholesome to do. What grew instead was a phenomenon. Acrobats, gymnasts, wrestlers, Hollywood stunt performers, and bodybuilders made this stretch of beach their open-air stage, stacking human pyramids and pressing barbells while weekend crowds packed the sand to watch. Fitness in America had mostly been a private, faintly eccentric pursuit; here it became a spectacle, a community, and eventually an industry.

The roll call from this sand is remarkable. Jack LaLanne trained here decades before television made him the country's coach. Joe Gold worked out here long before the first Gold's Gym opened. And Pudgy Stockton — a five-foot-one secretary turned barbell star — became the face of women's strength at a time when much of the country insisted lifting was unladylike. Then, in 1959, Santa Monica abruptly shut the whole thing down and bulldozed the platform. The lifters simply migrated two miles south along the sand to a modest city weight pen in Venice — which inherited the crowds, the champions, and eventually the name: it was officially dedicated as Muscle Beach Venice in 1987, the added word a nod of respect to this spot, the original.

Santa Monica came around in the end, restoring and rededicating this beach as the birthplace of the American fitness boom. The equipment is still free, and on most afternoons somebody is on the rings, working on something difficult in full public view — which was always the whole idea.

tours.title: Abbot Kinney Boulevard
tours.shortDescription: Venice's mile of boutiques, murals and 'coolest block in America' cred.
tours.longDescription: Named for Venice's founder, Abbot Kinney Boulevard trades the boardwalk's chaos for indie boutiques, muralled walls, chef-driven restaurants and First-Friday crowds — the polished edge of Venice cool.

stops.title: Abbot Kinney Boulevard
stops.caption: Walk the boulevard's boutiques and muraled walls at an easy pace.
stops.transcriptText:
You're on Abbot Kinney Boulevard, a mile-long diagonal through Venice, named for the tobacco millionaire who founded the neighborhood in 1905 as his "Venice of America." The name is recent, though. For most of the twentieth century this was West Washington Boulevard — auto shops, storefront churches, cheap commercial space — and that cheapness was the making of it. When Venice was at its lowest, artists took over the empty storefronts and garages for studios; the street developed a genuine, unplanned bohemian ecosystem; and around 1990 the neighborhood renamed it after its founder, less as marketing than as a memorial.

The marketing came anyway. Locals half-jokingly date the turn to the arrival of a frozen-yogurt chain in 2007; the tech campuses of Silicon Beach landed nearby around the same era; and in 2012, GQ pronounced this the coolest block in America — a compliment from which no street fully recovers. Rents climbed, the galleries and repair shops gave way to fashion flagships, and the very word that made the boulevard famous became the engine that priced out many of the people who had made it cool in the first place.

Walk it with that double vision and it's a richer street. The murals are real, and so are the brand strategies behind some of them. There are still working artists here, and there are shops selling the idea of the artist's life at a considerable markup. Whether this street is Venice's revival or its replacement is argued at every table on the block — and both sides are describing the same mile.

Kinney named his city for a place he loved and built an imitation of it. A century later, the street with his name sells an imitation of old Venice, California. He'd at least recognize the business model.

tours.title: California Science Center & Endeavour
tours.shortDescription: A real space shuttle you can stand beneath — free, in Exposition Park.
tours.longDescription: The California Science Center's free halls run from kelp tanks to space, crowned by Endeavour — a flown space shuttle displayed up close (soon to stand vertical, stack-and-all). Hands-on science in historic Exposition Park.

stops.title: California Science Center & Endeavour
stops.caption: Stand beneath Endeavour's heat-tiled belly in the display pavilion.
stops.transcriptText:
There is a real spaceship in this building, standing on its tail as if it might leave.

You should be in Exposition Park, facing the California Science Center — and the tall pavilion rising beside it is the Samuel Oschin Air and Space Center, a twenty-story hall built for one purpose: to hold the Space Shuttle Endeavour upright, in launch position, the way a shuttle stood on the pad in the final hours before it flew.

Endeavour is not a replica. It went to space twenty-five times between 1992 and 2011, helped assemble the International Space Station, and was the last space shuttle ever built. When NASA retired the fleet, museums across the country competed for the orbiters, and Los Angeles won this one — then had to get it home. In October 2012, Endeavour was towed from the airport through miles of city streets at walking pace, past gas stations and front lawns, while crowds packed the sidewalks to watch a spacecraft inch through traffic. It may be the only parade in history where the float had been to orbit.

Inside, the shuttle stands mated to two real solid rocket boosters and the last flight-qualified external fuel tank in existence, which makes this the only place in the world to see a complete, authentic space shuttle system — and the only shuttle anywhere displayed as if ready to launch. They did it in the only order that worked: the stack went up first, in 2024, and the building was finished around it. You can circle beneath the engines and look straight up the full height of the thing. And in keeping with the Science Center's founding bargain, admission is free — this is a public museum, funded so that any kid in Los Angeles can stand under a spaceship.

Here's why it lands the way it does. This is a city that manufactures spectacle professionally — sets, effects, illusion by the studio-load. Endeavour is the opposite kind of object. Every scorch mark on those black tiles is real, earned twenty-five times over in the heat of reentry. In the capital of make-believe, the most astonishing thing on display is the one nobody invented.

tours.title: Natural History Museum of LA County
tours.shortDescription: Dueling dinosaurs, a rose garden and 1913 Beaux-Arts grandeur.
tours.longDescription: LA County's Natural History Museum, open since 1913 beneath its domed Beaux-Arts rotunda, stages a T. rex-versus-Triceratops face-off, halls of gems and dioramas, and a rose garden out front — the West's largest natural-history collection.

stops.title: Natural History Museum of LA County
stops.caption: Enter under the 1913 dome to the dueling-dinosaurs hall.
stops.transcriptText:
People love to say Los Angeles has no history. The city's answer is this building, which holds around thirty-five million pieces of it.

You should be at the north end of Exposition Park, facing the Natural History Museum — the grand brick-and-marble building whose domed rotunda rises behind the rose garden. It opened in 1913, which makes it one of the oldest museum buildings in the city, and the age matters more than it sounds.

Consider what Los Angeles was in 1913: no film industry to speak of, no freeways, and until November of that very year — when the aqueduct opened — no reliable water. The city built itself a serious museum before it built almost everything it's now famous for. That was the point. The boosters selling Los Angeles to the world needed proof it was a real city and not a land scheme with good weather, and a domed marble museum is exactly the kind of proof they meant.

It even hedged its bets on the name, opening as the Museum of History, Science and Art — three museums in one, because nobody yet knew what the young city would need. Art eventually moved out and got its own institutions; history and science stayed, which is why this is still the place where Los Angeles keeps its dinosaurs and its own civic memory under one roof.

The dinosaurs are the headliners — the hall includes a growth series of Tyrannosaurus rex, from baby to adult, which is a rarer sight than a single skeleton — and the collections behind the galleries run to some thirty-five million specimens, the largest natural history museum in the western United States. Two details worth carrying out with you: its collection of marine mammal remains is the second largest anywhere, behind only the Smithsonian — and a good number of the Ice Age fossils here came out of the ground a few miles north, at the tar pits on Wilshire. This is one of the only museums on earth that excavates mammoths from the middle of its own city.

So take the old line about LA having no history and hold it up against the rotunda. The city has plenty. It just keeps most of it in drawers.

tours.title: Los Angeles Memorial Coliseum
tours.shortDescription: The only stadium to host the Olympics three times — 1932, 1984, 2028.
tours.longDescription: Opened in 1923 and dedicated to WWI veterans, the Coliseum's peristyle arch and torch have crowned two Olympic Games and will crown a third in 2028 — plus a Super Bowl, a World Series and decades of USC football. Living civic history in Exposition Park.

stops.title: Los Angeles Memorial Coliseum
stops.caption: Face the peristyle arch and its Olympic torch at the stadium's open end.
stops.transcriptText:
This stadium was promised to the world before it existed — which might be the most Los Angeles fact in the entire park.

You should be at the east end of the Coliseum, facing the peristyle: the great arched colonnade with the memorial arch at its center and the Olympic torch rising above it. That torch is the through-line for everything you're about to hear.

The Coliseum went up between 1921 and 1923 as a memorial to the Angelenos who served in the First World War, designed by John and Donald Parkinson — the same father-and-son firm behind City Hall and Union Station, which is why so much of this city's civic architecture feels like one family's handwriting. And here's the audacious part: in April 1923, weeks before construction had even finished, the Olympic committee awarded Los Angeles the 1932 Games. The city had bid for the Olympics with a stadium that did not yet exist. That is boosterism at full volume — sell the dream first, pour the concrete after — and this time, the dream was delivered with nine years to spare.

The 1932 Games repaid the gamble. Held in the depths of the Depression, in a stadium expanded past a hundred and one thousand seats, they invented traditions the Olympics still uses: the first Olympic Village, the first three-tier medal podium. Every athlete who has ever stood a step above silver is standing on an idea from Exposition Park.

The century since reads like the country's scrapbook — the first Super Bowl was played here, a World Series was won here, a presidential nomination was accepted under that peristyle — and the Olympics came back in 1984. When the Games return in 2028, this becomes the first stadium in history to host the Summer Olympics three times: 1932, 1984, 2028. No venue anywhere has a longer Olympic memory.

There's a quiet irony in that. Los Angeles gets accused, fairly, of tearing down everything it builds — yet the city has kept this one working for over a century, renewing it from the inside without losing the bones. Stand at the peristyle and you're looking at the rarest thing in LA: a promise the city made a hundred years ago, and kept.

tours.title: The Huntington
tours.shortDescription: A railroad baron's library, art collection and 120 acres of gardens.
tours.longDescription: Henry Huntington's San Marino estate opened its gates to the public: a research library with a Gutenberg Bible, British and American art including 'The Blue Boy', and a dozen botanical gardens — Chinese, Japanese, desert — across 120 acres.

stops.title: The Huntington
stops.caption: Approach the Beaux-Arts gallery, then wander into the Chinese garden.
stops.transcriptText:
Los Angeles sprawls the way it does largely because of one man — and this is where he went to get away from it.

You should be inside the grounds of The Huntington in San Marino, somewhere with the gardens spreading around you and the white Beaux-Arts mansion on its rise. Two hundred acres of library, art, and botanical garden, all of it one estate, all of it one man's idea of how to spend a railroad fortune.

The man was Henry Huntington, nephew of one of the barons who built the transcontinental railroad — but Henry's empire was local. His Pacific Electric streetcars, the famous Red Cars, ran to every corner of the basin, and here was the trick: he bought the land first, laid the tracks to it, then sold the subdivisions. Whole swaths of greater Los Angeles exist because Henry Huntington's trolleys made them sellable. He built the sprawl, sold it — and then retired to this hilltop and spent the rest of his life assembling its opposite.

What he assembled is astonishing. In the mansion hangs Gainsborough's Blue Boy, which Huntington bought in 1921 for what was reported as the highest price ever paid for a painting — facing Pinkie across the room, a pairing so famous the two are practically a couple. The library he built ranks among the great research collections on earth; its vaults hold millions of rare books and manuscripts, including a Gutenberg Bible printed on vellum. And the gardens run to some hundred and thirty acres in more than a dozen styles — a desert garden with one of the largest collections of mature cacti anywhere, a Japanese garden, and a classical Chinese garden among the largest of its kind outside China.

There's a good detail in the family arrangement, too: Henry married Arabella, his late uncle's widow and one of the richest women in America — reuniting two halves of the same railroad fortune under one roof.

But hold onto the first fact, because it's the real one. Henry Huntington made his money moving people quickly — and his monument is a place engineered entirely for slowness. Books, paintings, gardens: everything here asks you to stop. The man who taught Los Angeles to spread out spent his last years teaching it to sit still.

tours.title: Gamble House
tours.shortDescription: The 1908 masterpiece of American Craftsman design, in teak and shadow.
tours.longDescription: Greene & Greene's 1908 Gamble House is the high temple of the American Arts-and-Crafts movement — hand-joined teak, broad sheltering eaves and art-glass doors, every detail bespoke. A Pasadena landmark open for tours.

stops.title: Gamble House
stops.caption: Take in the low, wide Craftsman elevation and its deep eaves.
stops.transcriptText:
This is what happened when soap money decided the most luxurious thing on earth was a piece of wood, joined perfectly.

You should be on Westmoreland Place, a quiet private lane just off Orange Grove in Pasadena, facing the Gamble House — a long, low, deep-eaved house of dark shingles and timber, sitting on its rise like it grew there. It was built in 1908 as a winter home for David and Mary Gamble, of the Procter and Gamble fortune, back when Pasadena was where wealthy Midwesterners came to escape the cold.

Here's what makes it radical. In 1908, American money announced itself in marble — columns, gilt, imported ballrooms. The Gambles hired two brothers, Charles and Henry Greene, who believed the opposite: that craft itself was the luxury. So the house shows you its construction. The joinery is exposed and celebrated, the pegs and straps polished like jewelry, the teak and mahogany rubbed until the wood glows from within. Look at the front doors and you'll see the signature piece — a spreading oak tree rendered in stained glass across all three panels, so the entrance itself is a landscape.

And the Greenes designed everything. Not just the house: the furniture, the light fixtures, the rugs, the fireplace tools. Two Swedish-born craftsmen, the Hall brothers, built it all by hand. The family clearly understood what they had, because they kept it, unchanged, until 1966 — and then gave it to the city and a university rather than sell. As the story goes, a prospective buyer mused about painting all that woodwork white, and the family quietly took the house off the market. Whether or not it happened exactly that way, the result is real: almost nothing here has changed in over a century, down to the chairs.

One more layer: the second floor has open-air sleeping porches, because the whole point of a Pasadena winter house was the air itself. This is architecture designed around a climate — the most Californian idea in the building.

Movie fans may recognize it as the home of a certain eccentric inventor in a beloved 1985 time-travel film. Fitting, in a way. Walk up the drive and you really have gone back — to the last moment when the height of American luxury was something made slowly, by hand.

tours.title: Old Pasadena
tours.shortDescription: A saved Victorian-and-Deco shopping district of brick and old signage.
tours.longDescription: Once slated for demolition, Old Pasadena's Colorado Boulevard core was rescued into a lively 22-block district of restored Beaux-Arts and Victorian storefronts, alley bars and the route of the Rose Parade.

stops.title: Old Pasadena
stops.caption: Start at the Colorado Boulevard corner beneath the ornate old facades.
stops.transcriptText:
Every old building on this street was supposed to be gone by now.

You should be near Colorado Boulevard and Fair Oaks Avenue, the heart of Old Pasadena — about twenty blocks of brick and stone storefronts from the late 1800s and early 1900s, with restaurants and shops behind the old façades and narrow alleys threading between them. It looks inevitable, the way well-loved places always do. It was nearly demolished.

This was Pasadena's original downtown, built in the boom after the railroad arrived in the 1880s, back when the city was a winter resort for wealthy Easterners. Then the twentieth century did to it what it did to old main streets everywhere: business drifted away, the buildings emptied, and by the 1960s and 70s the vacancy rate had climbed toward seventy percent. The district had become the kind of skid row that city planners solved, in that era, with a wrecking ball — and plans circulated to level much of it for redevelopment.

What happened instead was a fight, and the preservationists won it. The city passed one of California's earliest historic preservation ordinances in 1975, a citizens' group formed to defend the buildings, and through the 1980s the unglamorous work got done — seismic retrofits, restored façades, new tenants coaxed into old rooms. The gamble was that history itself could be the draw. It paid off so completely that Old Pasadena is now cited nationally as the model: proof that a left-for-dead main street can be revived rather than replaced. Notice the alleys as you walk — reclaimed as lanes of doorways and patios, they're the district's best trick, an entire second street system hiding behind the first.

Two through-lines cross here, both older than the buildings. The Rose Parade has rolled down this stretch of Colorado every New Year's since the 1890s. And for decades, Route 66 ran right along it — this street was the triumphant last leg into the promised land.

So here's the reframe: this is the rarest kind of Los Angeles landmark — not a thing that was built, but a thing that was kept. In a region that solves problems with demolition, Old Pasadena is what stubbornness looks like, a century on, with the lights back on.

tours.title: The Getty Center
tours.shortDescription: Richard Meier's travertine acropolis of art, riding a hilltop tram.
tours.longDescription: Reached by cable tram above the 405, the Getty Center is Richard Meier's 1997 campus of cleft-travertine pavilions, a European painting collection, Robert Irwin's Central Garden and a sweeping view of LA — all free.

stops.title: The Getty Center
stops.caption: Ride the tram up to the travertine plaza and its grand staircase.
stops.transcriptText:
You take a driverless tram to get here, which is the first clue that someone thought very hard about the experience of arriving.

You should be at the top of the hill in Brentwood, on the arrival plaza of the Getty Center, with the white stone campus spreading around you and — on a clear day — the whole city laid out below, from downtown to the ocean. Six pavilions of galleries, gardens, and terraces, opened in 1997, designed by Richard Meier, and paid for by the strangest problem in the museum world: too much money.

When the oil billionaire J. Paul Getty died in 1976, he left his fortune to his small museum trust — which by law had to spend a share of it, every year, forever. The result was an institution that became one of the wealthiest in art, could outbid nearly anyone, and eventually built itself this billion-dollar acropolis. In the galleries hangs the collection that spending spree assembled, including Van Gogh's Irises. And in keeping with the founder's terms, admission is free — you pay to park, but the art costs nothing.

Now touch the walls. The campus is clad in travertine, a warm Italian stone quarried near Rome, and the panels were split along their natural grain rather than sawn smooth — so look closely and you'll find fossilized leaves and branches pressed into the surface. The building's skin is full of fifty-thousand-year-old gardens. The living garden below the plaza is its counterpoint: the Central Garden, designed not by a landscape architect but by the artist Robert Irwin, who conceived it as a sculpture you walk through, and it changes with the seasons like any artwork made of plants must.

The hilltop site is also a fortress, quietly. Stone skin, sealed air systems, its own water reserve, cleared brush — the Getty was engineered to defend its collection from wildfire, and in January 2025, when fire moved through these hills with terrible cost to the city, the design held and the art sheltered safely in place.

Museums usually borrow grandeur from the past. This one built its own hill town from scratch — then let everyone in for free. Take the view; it's included.

tours.title: Rodeo Drive
tours.shortDescription: Beverly Hills' three blocks of luxury — and the cobbled Via Rodeo lane.
tours.longDescription: Rodeo Drive is shorthand for wealth: flagship boutiques, the green-domed corner landmark and the stepped, cobblestone Via Rodeo built to look centuries older than it is. Window-shopping as spectacle.

stops.title: Rodeo Drive
stops.caption: Start at the green-domed corner and head for the cobbled Via Rodeo steps.
stops.transcriptText:
These three blocks are a performance, and everyone here — the stores, the cars, the window-shoppers — is in on it.

You should be on Rodeo Drive, somewhere in the three famous blocks between Wilshire and Santa Monica Boulevard: flagship boutiques behind spotless glass, palm trees in formation, and a steady traffic of people photographing storefronts the way people elsewhere photograph cathedrals. Which is the point. Rodeo doesn't just sell luxury goods; it sells the *idea* of Los Angeles wealth, and the idea outsells the goods.

It wasn't born this way. Into the 1960s this was an ordinary shopping street in a well-off suburb — hardware, groceries, a bowling alley in the neighborhood mix. The transformation began when a handful of merchants, most famously a boutique owner named Fred Hayman, started treating retail as theater: champagne for customers, valets, celebrity clienteles cultivated like gardens. The luxury houses of Europe followed, and by the 1980s the street had become shorthand, worldwide, for a particular gilded fantasy of California — a fantasy the movies were happy to amplify, most famously in a certain 1990 romantic comedy built around a shopping spree here.

The street's honest masterpiece is at the Wilshire end: Via Rodeo, a curving, cobbled European lane that climbs past storefronts to a little piazza. It looks centuries old. It was built in 1990 — a brand-new antique street, a stage set you can walk on, and the most candid thing Rodeo ever did, because it admits the whole enterprise is scenery. And for an architectural footnote, look for the odd little zigzag building at number 332: Anderton Court, a late work by Frank Lloyd Wright, holding its corner among the marble flagships like an eccentric relative at a formal dinner.

Here's the way to enjoy it: don't ask whether it's authentic. Nothing in Los Angeles answers that question well, and Rodeo least of all — it's a street performing wealth the way the city's main industry performs stories, professionally and in public. Admission to the show is free, the light is always good, and nobody checks whether you can afford the merchandise. Window-shopping was invented for exactly this.

tours.title: Beachfront: Santa Monica to Venice
tours.shortDescription: Three miles of famous coast — pier, muscle, boardwalk, canals — almost none doing its original job.
tours.longDescription: From the 1909 Santa Monica Pier down through the original Muscle Beach, the Venice boardwalk carnival and the quiet 1905 canals to Abbot Kinney Boulevard — a walk through LA's reinvented seaside, where a sewer pier became a pleasure palace and a real-estate stunt became a beloved neighborhood.

stops.title: Beachfront Walk — Introduction
stops.caption: Start on the Santa Monica Pier; the coast runs three miles south to Venice from here.
stops.transcriptText:
This walk is three miles of the most famous coastline in the world — and almost nothing on it is doing what it was built to do.

That's the thread. The pier ahead of you was built to carry a sewer pipe. The gym down the sand was a Depression make-work project. Venice itself was built as a high-minded cultural resort, and the street that closes this walk spent most of its life as a strip of repair shops. Every one of them became famous for something its builders never planned — which, on this particular stretch of coast, turns out to be the local specialty.

The route runs south from the Santa Monica Pier along the beachfront path to Venice — past the original Muscle Beach, down the boardwalk, then a couple of blocks inland to the Venice Canals and Abbot Kinney Boulevard. It's flat the whole way, on a continuous paved path shared with bikes and skaters, and you can walk it in about an hour of moving time or rent a bike and ride it. Fair warning: on a sunny weekend the path is a river of people, so give yourself the afternoon. There's no rail line along the sand — if you drove, you'll want to loop back or catch a ride from the far end.

One more thing before you start. Keep an eye out for the name Kinney as you go. You'll meet him properly at the end of the walk, but the truth is you'll be inside his imagination for most of it.

Start at the pier.

stops.title: Santa Monica Pier
stops.caption: Walk the 1909 pier deck past the carousel toward the solar Ferris wheel.
stops.transcriptText:
Walk out onto the deck, past the carousel building, until you can feel the boards flex a little under your feet. You're standing on the first concrete pier on the West Coast, opened in 1909 — and it was built, gloriously, to carry a sewer pipe. The city needed to run treated waste out past the surf, engineers needed a structure to hold the pipe, and Santa Monica decided that if it was building a pier anyway, the public might as well be allowed to stroll on it. The pipe is long gone. The strolling stuck.

A century of pleasure got grafted onto that piece of plumbing. The carousel you passed spins inside a 1920s hippodrome building, one of the oldest structures out here. The Ferris wheel at Pacific Park runs on solar power — it makes its own light for the postcard. And somewhere near the deck you'll find the marker for Route 66, because this pier is the symbolic end of the Mother Road: two thousand-plus miles from Chicago, finishing in the Pacific air.

Here's what makes this pier matter, though. It isn't that it's the best of its kind — it's that it's the last. A hundred years ago this coastline was crowded with pleasure piers, each gaudier than the next, stacked with ballrooms and roller coasters, and one by one they burned or fell or were torn down. This is the survivor. When you stand here, you're standing on an entire extinct species of American fun, down to its final specimen — still open every single day.

When you've had your fill of the view, head back to the sand and turn south on the beachfront path. Within a few hundred yards you'll see rings and bars rising out of the beach on your right. That's the original Muscle Beach — and yes, original is doing real work in that sentence.

stops.title: Muscle Beach
stops.caption: Just south of the pier, the rings and bars where the fitness craze began.
stops.transcriptText:
Those rings and bars in the sand, just south of the pier — that patch of beach invented the American gym.

In 1934, in the middle of the Depression, the Works Progress Administration installed exercise equipment here as a public works project: bars, rings, a platform, free to anyone. What the government got for its money was a spectacle nobody ordered. Gymnasts, acrobats, circus performers, Hollywood stunt people, and a new species entirely — the bodybuilder — turned this stretch of sand into an open-air theater of the human body, with crowds packing in on weekends to watch. The regulars here became the founding fathers and mothers of the entire fitness industry: Jack LaLanne, decades before television made him America's trainer; Joe Gold, before there was a Gold's Gym; and Pudgy Stockton, the barbell-pressing star who proved to a skeptical country that strength belonged to women too.

Then it ended. Santa Monica shut Muscle Beach down in 1959 and bulldozed the platform, and the lifters did the only sensible thing — they picked up and moved down the beach to Venice, along the same path you're walking today, where the city of Los Angeles had a modest weight pen waiting. The fitness boom didn't die; it just changed addresses. You'll pass its second home later on this walk.

Santa Monica eventually thought better of the whole affair, and rededicated this spot as the original Muscle Beach — rings, ropes, and bars restored, still free, still busy with acrobats most afternoons. Watch for a minute if someone's flying. Then keep south on the path. The next stretch is a long, easy one, and it ends at the loudest quarter mile in Los Angeles: the Venice Beach Boardwalk.

stops.title: Venice Beach Boardwalk
stops.caption: Join the boardwalk carnival of skaters, performers and muralled walls.
stops.transcriptText:
You'll know you've arrived by ear before anything else — drums, boom boxes, sales pitches, somebody's electric guitar. This is Ocean Front Walk, the Venice Beach Boardwalk, and it is the single strangest outcome of a business plan in the history of Los Angeles.

Because here's what this was supposed to be. In 1905, a tobacco millionaire named Abbot Kinney opened "Venice of America" on this marshland — canals, imported gondoliers, arcaded buildings, an amusement pier — conceived as a cultural resort where Americans would come for lectures, concerts, and moral improvement by the sea. The public skipped the lectures and stampeded to the roller coasters, and Kinney, to his credit, took the hint and gave them a carnival — the Coney Island of the Pacific. He died in 1920; his grand pier burned weeks later; the canals were mostly paved; and by the 1950s his dream city had decayed into what the papers called the slum by the sea. Which is exactly when it got interesting — cheap rent by the ocean pulled in the poets, the artists, the misfits, and the boardwalk grew into what surrounds you now: an unbroken line of street performers, vendors, muralists, fortune tellers, and one of the most famous skate plazas on earth.

As you walk it, look for the outdoor weight pen with the concrete barbell on its roof — Muscle Beach Venice, where the Santa Monica lifters landed after 1959, and where bodybuilding grew from beach curiosity into an industry.

Kinney built a stage for high culture and got the greatest low-culture promenade in America instead — and if his record is any guide, he'd have counted the crowd and called it a win. When you reach Windward Avenue, turn inland, cross the main road, and follow the signs a few short blocks to the water you can hear nothing from: the Venice Canals.

stops.title: Venice Canals
stops.caption: Slip off the boardwalk into the quiet grid of canals and footbridges.
stops.transcriptText:
Stop on one of the little arched footbridges and listen. Two blocks from the loudest promenade in Los Angeles, you can hear ducks.

These are the Venice Canals — the surviving handful of Abbot Kinney's waterways, dug in 1905 when this whole district was laced with them and gondoliers poled visitors past brand-new cottages. They were the heart of the sales pitch, the thing that made "Venice of America" more than a name. And they lost. The car arrived, residents wanted streets instead of water, and in the paving campaigns that followed Venice's annexation by Los Angeles in the mid-twenties, most of the canal network disappeared under asphalt. Traffic drives over Kinney's grand canals today without knowing they're there. This small grid south of the main road survived largely because it wasn't worth the cost of filling — the losing remnant of a bet against the automobile, in the city where the automobile won everything.

Then the strangest reversal on this whole walk: losing turned out to be the smartest thing the canals ever did. Left as a backwater, they slid into decades of neglect — and were finally restored in the early 1990s, sidewalks rebuilt, water clean, bridges repaired. Now the quietest real estate in Venice is the part that progress skipped, and the houses along these walkways are some of the most coveted on the Westside. No cars can reach the front doors. That's the amenity.

Take one slow loop — over a bridge, along a walkway, back over the next bridge. Then head inland a few blocks to the diagonal street full of people carrying shopping bags and expensive coffee. It's named for the man who dug these canals, and it's the final stop: Abbot Kinney Boulevard.

stops.title: Abbot Kinney Boulevard
stops.caption: Finish inland on Venice's boulevard of boutiques and murals.
stops.transcriptText:
The last stop on this walk is a street that sells one product, and the product is the idea of cool.

Abbot Kinney Boulevard runs about a mile on the diagonal, lined with boutiques, galleries, and restaurants you've read about — and for most of its life it was nothing of the kind. This was West Washington Boulevard, a scruffy strip of repair shops, storefront churches, and cheap studio space, which is precisely why artists moved in when Venice was still the slum by the sea. Around 1990, locals had it renamed for the neighborhood's founder, and then the strip did the most Venice thing imaginable: it got discovered. Tech money arrived one street over, the boutiques followed, and in 2012, GQ crowned it the coolest block in America — after which, longtime tenants will tell you, the rents did what rents do. Some people here will say the street was saved; others, that it was bought. Both can point at the same storefronts to make their case, and that argument — who gets to keep a place once the world falls in love with it — is the most honest thing on the boulevard.

So end the walk with the man himself. Abbot Kinney spent his fortune building a dream city that failed at nearly everything it planned — the culture flopped, the pier burned, the canals were paved — and succeeded, wildly, at everything it never intended. The carnival boardwalk. The body-builders. The artists in the cheap studios. And now a street that trades on his name, selling the one thing his Venice actually produced: the feeling that life could be lived differently, closer to the water.

A sewer pipe became a postcard, a relief project became an industry, a failed resort became a way of life. That's the invented seaside — invented, mostly, by accident. Go find a coffee on Abbot Kinney's street. You've walked his whole imagination, end to end.

tours.title: Downtown LA: Bunker Hill to the Pueblo
tours.shortDescription: Bunker Hill down to the 1781 pueblo — Gehry steel to a 1917 market and an 1893 iron atrium.
tours.longDescription: A downhill walk through Downtown's layers: Gehry's Disney Hall and The Broad on Bunker Hill, the little Angels Flight funicular, the neon Grand Central Market, the Bradbury Building's sunlit iron atrium, ending at El Pueblo and Olvera Street where Los Angeles began in 1781.

stops.title: Downtown LA Walk — Introduction
stops.caption: Begin on Bunker Hill at Grand Avenue, then descend toward the old pueblo.
stops.transcriptText:
Everyone will tell you Los Angeles is not a walking city, and mostly they're right — the places worth seeing sit ten or twenty miles apart with a freeway in between. This walk is the exception. Seven stops, about a mile and a half, one hill, and you never need your car once.

Here's the trick of it: the walk runs backward. You'll start at the top of Bunker Hill among the newest architecture in the city — stainless steel from 2003, a honeycomb veil from 2015 — and every block you cover, the clock unwinds. A funicular from 1901. A food hall from 1917. A skylit Victorian office building from 1893. And at the bottom of it all, the plaza where the city was founded in 1781, when Los Angeles was forty-four settlers and a river.

Most cities make you work for this — the layers scattered, the origins paved over. Downtown Los Angeles stacked everything on one slope, oldest ground at the bottom, newest money at the top, and then built a tiny railway so you don't even have to walk down the steepest part.

The route: south along the crest of the hill, then down its face by rail, then north through the old commercial district to the plaza. Flat where it matters, with ninety-six feet of drop handled for a dollar fifty. Start at the corner of First Street and Grand Avenue, in front of the building that looks like it's setting sail — Walt Disney Concert Hall.

stops.title: Walt Disney Concert Hall
stops.caption: Stand beneath Gehry's steel sails at the top of the hill.
stops.transcriptText:
You're at the top of the hill, and the building in front of you is doing something buildings aren't supposed to do — billowing. Stainless-steel sails, curved and stacked and catching the light, no two panels quite alike. This is Walt Disney Concert Hall, home of the Los Angeles Philharmonic, opened in 2003, designed by Frank Gehry — and it took sixteen years to get here.

The story starts in 1987, when Lillian Disney, Walt's widow, gave the city fifty million dollars for a concert hall in her husband's name. Then came the part LA does best: delays, budget fights, a stalled site. The county built the six-story parking garage first; then the money ran out, and for most of the nineties the garage sat under an empty lot with nothing on top of it. It took a civic rescue campaign in the late nineties to finally get the steel out of the drawings.

Walk toward the entrance and look at the surface as you go. Those curves aren't just for show — inside, the hall is lined in Douglas fir and shaped around the orchestra, and musicians rank it among the finest rooms for sound anywhere in the world. A car city, famous for listening to everything through a windshield, finally built itself a room to hear.

One gift before you move on: there's a public garden hidden up on the roof terrace, free to enter, with a fountain shaped like an enormous rose and covered entirely in broken Delft porcelain — Lillian Disney collected it, and the builders smashed and reset thousands of pieces in her memory.

When you're ready, walk south along Grand Avenue, one block, staying on this side of the street. The building coming up ahead looks like a sheet of white coral pulled taut over a box — that's The Broad, and it's twelve years younger than the steel behind you. The clock has started running backward.

stops.title: The Broad
stops.caption: Next door, the honeycombed 'veil' of the free contemporary-art museum.
stops.transcriptText:
The white honeycomb ahead of you is The Broad — rhymes with road, named for Eli and Edythe Broad, who filled it. The skin is called the veil: two thousand five hundred panels of fiberglass-reinforced concrete, lifted at the corners like a curtain caught mid-raise. Underneath it sits the vault — the concrete core where most of the collection actually lives. The architects, Diller Scofidio and Renfro, put the storage at the heart of the building and then let you look at it; ride the escalator inside and you tunnel straight through the vault on your way up.

Here's the number that matters: zero. That's the admission. Eli Broad made billions building tract homes and selling insurance, spent decades collecting postwar and contemporary art — Warhol, Basquiat, Kusama, more than two thousand works — and then built a museum downtown and made it free, permanently. Whatever you make of billionaires putting their names on things, the line down the block most mornings is real, and it's mostly Angelenos.

You'll notice the construction alongside — the museum is adding a second building, an expansion meant to open before the 2028 Games, with admission staying free. The veil got a vault; now the vault is getting a companion.

And the timing tells you something about this hill. When The Broad opened in 2015, it joined a street that already had a concert hall and a contemporary museum — Grand Avenue as a cultural district was a finished argument. It wasn't always. The next stop was here when none of this existed.

Cross Grand Avenue when you get the chance, and continue south half a block. The low building faced in red sandstone, with copper-green pyramids on its roof, is the Museum of Contemporary Art — MOCA — and it has been holding this corner since 1986, back when Bunker Hill was mostly parking lots.

stops.title: MOCA Grand Avenue
stops.caption: The red-sandstone contemporary museum with its pyramid skylights.
stops.transcriptText:
MOCA Grand Avenue is easy to underestimate — it's low where its neighbors are loud, red sandstone and green pyramids, most of it sunk below the street. The architect was Arata Isozaki, and this was his first American commission, finished in 1986. He buried the galleries deliberately: you descend into them, and the pyramids overhead are skylights, feeding daylight down onto the art.

Inside is one of the country's great collections of postwar art — Rothko, Rauschenberg, Pollock — and like its neighbor across the street, general admission is free. But the thing to understand, standing here, is the date. In 1986, Grand Avenue was not a destination. Bunker Hill's Victorian neighborhood had been razed in the sixties — an entire hilltop of houses cleared for a redevelopment that then took decades to actually arrive — and for years this museum sat among the parking lots and the wind, betting the city would eventually show up around it.

The city did. Disney Hall in 2003, The Broad in 2015, the towers and plazas filling in between. MOCA anchored the hill before the hill was anything, which makes it less the quiet sibling on this street and more the reason the street exists.

Now for the best transition in Los Angeles. Continue past the museum into California Plaza — the broad courtyard among the towers just beyond, with a watercourt at its center. Make for its far edge, where the hill drops away, and you'll find a small station house and two vintage railway cars waiting on a steep track. That's Angels Flight, built in 1901, and it's how we get off Bunker Hill.

stops.title: Angels Flight
stops.caption: Ride or watch the little orange funicular drop down Bunker Hill.
stops.transcriptText:
Two cars, one track, two hundred ninety-eight feet — this is Angels Flight, billed for over a century as the shortest railway in the world. The fare is a dollar fifty; pay at the station or tap a Metro card. The cars are named Sinai and Olivet, they ride the same cable, and they counterweight each other — one goes down because the other comes up. They've been doing this, on and off, since 1901.

The "off" is the story. Angels Flight was built when Bunker Hill was a neighborhood — Victorian mansions gone genteelly to seed as rooming houses — and it hauled residents up from the shops on Hill Street for a penny a ride. When the city leveled the entire hilltop in the sixties, the railway was dismantled and put in a warehouse, where it sat for twenty-seven years before being rebuilt half a block from its original line. It has closed and reopened more than once since; Angelenos treat a running Angels Flight as a small civic victory, because history says it is one.

Board when a car's ready, and as you ride, think about what the ride is. Everything you've seen so far was built after this railway — the concert hall, the veil, the museum. You're descending out of the city's newest layer in its oldest machine.

At the bottom, the doors open onto Hill Street. Directly across from you is a doorway into a long brick market building — that's the back entrance of Grand Central Market, which has been feeding downtown without a break since 1917. Cross carefully and walk straight in; we'll come out the other side, on Broadway.

stops.title: Grand Central Market
stops.caption: Into the neon-lit 1917 food hall at the foot of the hill.
stops.transcriptText:
You're inside a market that has been open, through every version of Los Angeles, since 1917. Neon signs overhead, forty-some vendors, the smell of a dozen cuisines negotiating. The building is older still — the Broadway side went up in 1897 as one of the first fireproofed, steel-reinforced structures in the city — and the market runs straight through the block, Hill Street to Broadway, which is exactly how we're using it.

Take your time in here; nothing about this stop rewards hurrying. But as you wander, read the market as a census. In the twenties there were ninety-odd stalls — greengrocers, fishmongers, delis, butchers — serving the crowds that rode Angels Flight down from the Hill. When downtown emptied out in mid-century, the market carried on, selling produce and chiles and menudo to the neighborhoods that stayed. And when downtown came back over the past couple of decades, the new wave moved in — the egg sandwiches with lines out the door, the natural wine — folding in beside legacy vendors whose families have worked these counters for generations.

That's the reframe worth carrying out the door: people call Grand Central Market a food hall, but food halls are invented all at once, by developers. This one accreted, era by era, like the city outside its doors — and every layer is still serving lunch.

When you've eaten what needs eating, head out the far side onto Broadway. Cross at Third Street, angling left, and look for a modest brick office building on the corner, five stories, giving away absolutely nothing from the sidewalk — which turns out to be the whole point. That's the Bradbury Building, finished in 1893, and it's hiding the most famous interior in Los Angeles.

stops.title: Bradbury Building
stops.caption: Across the street, the sunlit iron-and-oak atrium of 1893.
stops.transcriptText:
Step inside the lobby — the ground floor is open to visitors during business hours, free — and give your eyes a second to adjust.

From the street, the Bradbury Building is a plain brick box. Inside, it's a canyon of light: a five-story atrium under a glass roof, marble stairs, French wrought-iron railings running like lace along every landing, and two open-cage elevators rising and falling in plain view, counterweights and all. It was finished in 1893, and it is, by a comfortable margin, the most filmed interior in Los Angeles — science fiction especially keeps coming back, most famously a certain 1982 vision of this city's future, because nothing else on earth looks quite like this.

How it got built is stranger than the movies. Lewis Bradbury, a mining millionaire, rejected an established architect's design and handed the job to George Wyman — a thirty-two-year-old draftsman in that architect's own office, with no formal training. Legend has it Wyman consulted a ouija-style planchette board and received a message from his dead brother telling him to take the commission — and that is a legend, told for decades and impossible to check. What's documented is his inspiration: a utopian novel of the day that imagined the commercial buildings of the year 2000 as vast halls filled with light. Wyman read a description of the future and built it, in brick and iron, seven years before the century turned.

So the most filmed building in the world's film capital was itself science fiction first — a Victorian's guess at 2000, which the movies later borrowed to imagine 2019.

Back on Broadway, turn right and settle in — this is the long leg, about fifteen minutes north on foot, past the marquees of the old movie palaces, with the white tower of City Hall rising ahead of you. We're leaving the nineteenth century now and walking to 1781: El Pueblo, the plaza where Los Angeles began.

stops.title: El Pueblo & Olvera Street
stops.caption: End at the city's 1781 birthplace and its Mexican market lane.
stops.transcriptText:
Cross into the old plaza — round, tree-shaded, a bandstand at its center, historic buildings ringing it on every side. However you came in, aim for the middle and stop.

You are now standing at the bottom of the walk, in every sense. In September 1781, forty-four settlers — men, women, and children, most of them of African, Indigenous, and mixed heritage, recruited from what is now northern Mexico — established a farming pueblo near this spot, beside a river, close to Yaanga, a village of the Tongva people who had lived on this land for thousands of years. That sentence deserves its weight: the second-largest city in the United States was founded by four dozen people, and the ground you're on is where its whole story starts.

The plaza around you took shape in the 1820s. Facing it stands the Avila Adobe, built in 1818 and the oldest house still standing in the city, and just off it runs Olvera Street — the brick-paved lane of puestos, market stalls, many run by the same families across generations. The marketplace opened in 1930, after a preservation campaign led by Christine Sterling saved this block from demolition, and like a great deal of Los Angeles it's part genuine article, part staged romance — a distinction that stops mattering somewhere around the ninety-year mark.

One more thing to find: above Olvera Street, on an upper wall, the ghost of a mural painted in 1932 by the Mexican artist David Alfaro Siqueiros. Its political message got it whitewashed almost immediately; conservators spent decades recovering what survived. The city censored it, then saved it — both impulses, same wall.

Now turn and look back the way you came. City Hall, and beyond it, up on the hill, the towers and the steel sails where you started. You've walked from 2003 to 1781 — from the newest room in the city to its founding ground — in about a mile and a half. Every city has layers. Los Angeles, of all places, turns out to be the one that lets you walk straight down through them.

That's the walk. Stay in the plaza a while — it's a good place to end at the beginning.

tours.title: Museum Row: The Miracle Mile
tours.shortDescription: Wilshire's row of museums — tar pits, art, movies and cars in five easy blocks.
tours.longDescription: Museum Row on the Miracle Mile, lined up in order: the bubbling La Brea Tar Pits, LACMA and its Urban Light lamps, Renzo Piano's Academy Museum sphere, the steel-wrapped Petersen, and the 1934 Original Farmers Market to finish — from the ice age to the Oscars in one stroll.

stops.title: Museum Row Walk — Introduction
stops.caption: Start at the tar pits on Wilshire; the Miracle Mile museums line up from here.
stops.transcriptText:
Museum Row starts with a hole in the ground — several of them, black and bubbling and older than human memory — and it ends with lunch. In between: the largest art museum in the western United States, a museum for the movies, a museum for the automobile, and one flat stretch of Wilshire Boulevard called the Miracle Mile.

The name was a sales pitch. In the 1920s, a developer named A. W. Ross bought a strip of dusty road west of downtown and bet on a strange new idea: that Angelenos would rather shop from their cars than ride the streetcar downtown. He built the whole boulevard for drivers — parking lots behind the stores, bold storefronts you could read at thirty miles an hour. People called it Ross's Folly, right up until it worked. Then they called it the Miracle Mile.

Here's the thread to hold onto as you walk: everything on this stretch came up out of the ground. The tar that trapped the mammoths, the oil that made the fortunes, even the boulevard itself, which rose out of empty ranch land on one man's bet. Keep that in your pocket — it pays off at the very end, at a stop you'll smell before you see.

The route is simple. We start at the La Brea Tar Pits, walk west along Wilshire past LACMA to the Academy Museum and the Petersen, then turn north up Fairfax to the Original Farmers Market — about a mile and a half, flat the whole way, with a Metro station at Wilshire and Fairfax. Start at the pits. They're the oldest thing in Los Angeles.

stops.title: La Brea Tar Pits
stops.caption: Watch the ice-age asphalt bubble beside the mammoths.
stops.transcriptText:
You'll smell this stop before you see it. Find the Lake Pit — the big fenced pond near the corner of Wilshire and Curson — and watch the surface for a moment. Those slow black bubbles are natural asphalt, seeping up from an oil field deep beneath the park, the same way it has for tens of thousands of years. The life-sized mammoth family at the water's edge, one of them caught in the muck, is a sculpture from the 1960s — but it's an honest reenactment, because that is exactly how it happened here, again and again, for millennia.

The trap worked like this: a few inches of sticky tar under a film of rainwater or fallen leaves was enough to hold a mammoth fast, and everything that came to eat the mammoth — dire wolves, saber-toothed cats — sank right alongside it. Dire wolves are the most common large animal ever pulled from these pits; the collection holds thousands of them. And the pulling hasn't stopped.
