His brother Theo — the art dealer who had funded him, believed in him, and received nearly every canvas and letter — died just six months later. Which meant that the entire estate of an unknown, unsellable painter landed on a twenty-eight-year-old widow with a baby: Theo's wife, Jo van Gogh-Bonger.

She could have sold the lot for very little, and been advised to. Instead she spent the next three decades running the longest, shrewdest campaign in the history of art: lending paintings to exactly the right exhibitions, selling a few strategically to seed museums and collectors, keeping the core intact, and — her masterstroke — editing and publishing the brothers' correspondence, which turned Vincent from a painter into a story the world could not put down. By the time she died, the unknown brother-in-law was on his way to being the most beloved painter alive or dead. Her son gave the collection to a foundation, the state built this museum around it, and the doors opened in 1973.

So when you hear that Van Gogh was unrecognised in his lifetime, remember the second half of the sentence, the half that matters here: recognition was manufactured, patiently, by a woman history nearly left as a footnote. This building is her monument as much as his.

Next door — the building that looks like an elegant brick palazzo wearing an enormous white bathtub — is the Stedelijk, the city's museum of modern art. Thirty seconds' walk. The bathtub is not an insult, by the way. Locals mean it fondly. Mostly.

stops.title: Stedelijk Museum
stops.caption: Reach the Stedelijk, the modern-art museum under its white 'bathtub'.
stops.transcriptText:
You see it, of course. The nineteenth-century building — red brick, gabled, perfectly respectable, opened in 1895 — and docked on top of it, the vast smooth white form that the whole city immediately and permanently named the bathtub. The extension arrived in 2012, the nickname arrived roughly a day later, and the museum has long since surrendered to it.

But the bathtub is only the loudest example of what this institution has always done, which is to get there embarrassingly early. While the Rijksmuseum across the lawn was busy canonising the seventeenth century, the Stedelijk collected the art nobody had agreed on yet — the moderns, the abstractionists, the difficult and the possibly-ridiculous — and in 1938 one of its directors did something quietly radical: he painted the ornate interiors white, top to bottom, creating one of the first of the blank white galleries that every modern art museum on earth now treats as natural law. The white cube, more or less, started here, inside a gabled Dutch palazzo.

That's the neat division of labour on this lawn. One museum keeps the argument the nation already won; this one keeps the arguments still running. A city needs both — a memory and a dare — and Amsterdam, characteristically, put them a hundred metres apart and let them stare at each other.

Now walk to the far south end of the lawn, away from the Rijksmuseum, toward the grand pale building with the golden lyre on its roofline. That's the Concertgebouw — and the lawn you're crossing to reach it has a story of its own. Both are next.

stops.title: Museumplein & the Concertgebouw
stops.caption: Cross the Museumplein lawn to the Concertgebouw, one of the world's finest halls.
stops.transcriptText:
First, the ground you're crossing. Museumplein — the museum square — is really the museum lawn: a long green rectangle that serves as the nation's front garden. This is where the city comes to celebrate its football teams, protest its governments, mourn its losses, and sunbathe between grievances. Most squares in Europe are stone and statuary; Amsterdam's grandest public space is, characteristically, grass you're allowed to sit on.

Now the building closing off the far end, pale and formal with a golden lyre on the roof: the Concertgebouw — literally, the concert building — home to one of the most admired orchestras in the world, in one of the most acoustically perfect halls ever constructed. And here is the part musicians tell each other with a straight face: nobody fully intended that. The architect, by his own family's account, had no particular ear for music, and the science of acoustics barely existed in 1888; yet the hall he produced is still ranked by acousticians among the two or three finest on earth. Even the house's own directors have been known to credit a measure of luck. Some cathedrals are designed; some are conjured.

But the detail worth carrying home is who built it. Not a king, not a ministry — a committee of citizens, who decided their city was embarrassingly short of a proper concert hall and raised the money themselves, by subscription. The Stedelijk behind you began the same way: civic-minded Amsterdammers, passing the hat at the grandest possible scale. Of the temples on this lawn, the state built exactly one. The citizens built the rest — which may be the most seventeenth-century thing about this thoroughly nineteenth-century quarter.

One stop remains, and it's the oldest thing here — the citizens' first gift to themselves. Take the busy street running north beside the Concertgebouw, Van Baerlestraat, and follow it a few hundred metres to the park gates on your left. Vondelpark, to finish.

stops.title: Vondelpark
stops.caption: Finish in the Vondelpark, the city's green back garden.
stops.transcriptText:
Through the gates, and the city fades with impressive speed — winding paths, long ponds, big lazy lawns, herons standing around like retired officials. This is Vondelpark, Amsterdam's green living room, and here's what ties the whole walk together: it's older than everything you've just seen. The park came first.

In 1865 — twenty years before the Rijksmuseum opened its doors — a group of private citizens looked at their booming, treeless city, formed an association, bought this stretch of soggy pasture, and hired landscape designers to conjure an English-style park out of it: hills where there were none, a winding stream, vistas arranged like paintings. It was the citizens'-committee trick you've now seen three times, and this was the original. A few years in, they raised a statue to the poet Joost van den Vondel — the city's Shakespeare, more or less — and the public renamed the park after him before officialdom had much say in the matter.

One last gift, and it's very Amsterdam. The park is sinking. It sits below sea level on soft peat, and parts of it settle year by year — paths are re-laid, trees are hoisted, whole sections have been rebuilt while the joggers detour politely around the works. Even the countryside here is invented ground, and keeping it requires the same quiet, perpetual effort as keeping the canals. Nothing in this city stands still by itself; everything is held up on purpose.

Find some grass and sit down — you've earned it, and sitting on it is what this place is for. It's a fair summary of the whole quarter, in the end. A nation of traders spent its great century accumulating, then spent a later one deciding what to keep: the paintings, the letters, the music — and an afternoon on the grass, held gently above the water, on purpose.

tours.title: The Jordaan
tours.shortDescription: The old workers' quarter — its crowned church, the world's first gay monument, hidden hofjes and the prettiest canal.
tours.longDescription: A two-kilometre wander through the Jordaan, Amsterdam's most characterful neighbourhood. From the towering Westerkerk and the Anne Frank House it passes the pioneering Homomonument, threads the narrow lanes and secret courtyards of the old quarter, and ends at the Noordermarkt and the Brouwersgracht.

stops.title: The Jordaan — Introduction
stops.caption: Start on the Westermarkt beside the Westerkerk, the Jordaan opening out before you.
stops.transcriptText:
The grand canal ring has a shadow twin. When the planners drew the seventeenth-century city — those calm, expensive arcs of merchants' houses — they drew this quarter too, on the cheap side of the Prinsengracht: narrower streets, no imported stone, the lanes following the old farm ditches instead of elegant new curves. This was the Jordaan, the workers' annex — tanners, brewers' men, dockhands, and wave after wave of newcomers with more hope than money. One telling derives the name from the French jardin, garden, though the truth is nobody's quite sure, which suits the place.

This walk is about how the city's poorest streets became its most loved — and about what the quarter remembers. Fair warning: the Jordaan carries some of Amsterdam's heaviest memory and its lightest pleasures within a few hundred metres of each other — a hidden annex and an apple-pie rivalry, a riot memorial and cafés that still sing on weekends. The mix is not an accident. The mix is the Jordaan.

Practical notes: the route is flat and short — about two kilometres, an hour at a stroll. We'll pass the Anne Frank House early on; the walk treats it respectfully from the outside, and if you want to go in, know that tickets are online-only, released weeks ahead, and sell out — that visit needs planning of its own.

Start on Westermarkt, the square at the foot of the tallest church tower in the city. You can't miss it. That's rather the point of it.

stops.title: Westerkerk
stops.caption: Begin at the Westerkerk and the Anne Frank House beneath the crowned tower.
stops.transcriptText:
Look up first. The Westerkerk tower — the Westertoren — is the tallest church tower in Amsterdam, about eighty-five metres of it, and it wears something odd at the top: a great blue imperial crown. That's the crown of Maximilian of Austria, granted to the city's coat of arms centuries ago in thanks for services rendered — a Habsburg emperor's hat, gleaming over a Calvinist church, on the edge of a workers' quarter. Amsterdam collects ironies the way other cities collect statues.

Inside the church, somewhere under the floor, lies Rembrandt. Nobody knows exactly where. He died in 1669, poor, a short walk from here, and was buried in a rented grave — the kind whose contents could be cleared when the rent lapsed. The most famous painter the city ever produced, and the city cannot point to his bones. It can only point to this building and say: somewhere.

Now walk to the canal side of the church, along the Prinsengracht, and stop. A few doors along the far quay stands a narrow dark house, number 263, with a queue that forms in every season. Behind its street face, in a concealed annex at the back, Anne Frank and seven others hid for twenty-five months during the German occupation, until they were discovered and deported in the summer of 1944. Anne died in Bergen-Belsen at fifteen. Her father, Otto, was the only one of the eight to survive; helpers had saved her diary, and he gave it to the world.

She could hear these bells from the hiding place — the same carillon of the Westertoren that will likely ring while you stand here — and she wrote of finding a kind of steadiness in them. The tower has become part of how the world remembers her.

Take a moment here; there's no hurry. Then come back around to the square beside the church. Set into the ground and the canal bank there are three pink granite triangles — easy to walk past, impossible to forget once you understand them. The Homomonument is next.

stops.title: Homomonument
stops.caption: Steps away, the Homomonument — the first memorial of its kind in the world.
stops.transcriptText:
Three triangles of pink granite: one flush with the square, one raised like a low podium, one descending in steps into the canal itself, where the water laps over its point. Together they form the corners of a larger triangle you're standing inside. This is the Homomonument, unveiled in 1987 — the first monument anywhere in the world to the gay men and women persecuted and killed for who they were.

The pink triangle was the badge the Nazi camps forced on gay prisoners; the designer, Karin Daan, took the mark of persecution and laid it into the city's stone in granite, at the foot of the national church tower, in the open, unmissably public — everything the badge's inventors intended homosexuality never to be.

And the triangles point. The one at street level aims toward the Anne Frank House, a few hundred metres away. The one at the canal aims at the National Monument on the Dam, the country's memorial to its war dead. The raised one points toward the former headquarters of the COC, one of the oldest organisations of its kind in the world — persecution, national memory, and the long work of organising, held in one quiet geometry. On the steps by the water, people still leave flowers, often for reasons of their own. Carved into the monument is a line by Jacob Israël de Haan — a Jewish and openly gay Amsterdam writer, decades ahead of his time — speaking of a boundless longing for friendship.

If this walk's city has a famous ledger of tolerance — everything permitted, with conditions — then this monument marks its missing page: the people the old arrangement never protected at all, remembered here first, before anywhere else on earth.

When you're ready, cross the Prinsengracht by the bridge near the church and walk straight into the quarter. The streets narrow at once, and they're named for flowers and trees. The Jordaan itself is next.

stops.title: The Jordaan
stops.caption: Wander into the Jordaan's narrow lanes and hidden hofjes.
stops.transcriptText:
Notice how quickly the scale changed. The canals here are narrower, the houses smaller and less regular, the streets bending where the ring's arcs were serene — because under these lanes run the old drainage ditches of the farmland this quarter was thrown up on, cheaply and fast, while the money went into the grand canals behind you. Wander a few streets at will here — Bloemgracht and Egelantiersgracht are as lovely as any — and keep an eye out for two things in particular.

The first: carved stone tablets set into house fronts — a leaping hare, a sower, a ship, a pair of scissors. These are gevelstenen, gable stones, and they're the quarter's original addressing system. Before house numbers existed, you lived "at the Hare" or "at the Golden Scissors"; the stones named the house, advertised the trade, and told the illiterate city who was who. Hundreds survive, lovingly restored — a directory written in sandstone.

The second: unassuming doors that open into hidden courtyards. These are hofjes — almshouses, built around gardens by wealthy benefactors from the sixteen-hundreds onward, mostly to house elderly women of small means, on the theory that charity should come with a garden. Dozens hide in the Jordaan. Some open their outer door to respectful visitors; if you find one ajar, you may step in — quietly, please, because every hofje is still exactly what it was built to be: somebody's home.

The quarter itself has needed rescuing more than once. By the mid twentieth century it was overcrowded and crumbling, and there were serious plans to raze whole blocks; the residents objected, loudly and long, and won. The reward for their loyalty is that the Jordaan is now some of the most coveted property in the country — which is not entirely a happy ending for the people who loved it first.

Head north through the quarter, keeping roughly parallel to the Prinsengracht, until the streets open onto a square with a church in the middle. That's Noordermarkt, our next stop.

stops.title: Noordermarkt
stops.caption: Reach the Noordermarkt around the Noorderkerk.
stops.transcriptText:
The church in the middle of this square is the Noorderkerk, finished in 1623 by Hendrick de Keyser — the same hand that topped the Mint Tower — and it was something new: a church built specifically for the workers of the Jordaan. Look at its shape. No long nave, no grand processional axis; it's built on a cross plan that's nearly a church-in-the-round, with the pulpit at the centre and every seat more or less equal. The merchants on the ring got their soaring towers. The Jordaan got democracy in brick, which the quarter would probably tell you is the better deal.

The square around it has always been where the quarter gathers, and market mornings still fill it — produce and cheese one day, fabrics and second-hand treasure another — while two celebrated cafés within sight of this spot have spent decades in polite dispute over who bakes the best apple pie in Amsterdam. The only responsible research is to try both.

But this square remembers harder gatherings too. A memorial here marks the Jordaan riots of 1934, when, in the depths of the Depression, cuts to unemployment relief brought the quarter into the streets for days, and several residents were killed. And it was on this square, in February 1941, that crowds gathered in the meetings that launched the February Strike — when Amsterdam's workers laid down their tools in open protest at the persecution of their Jewish neighbours, one of the very few such acts in occupied Europe.

A workers' church, a market, an apple-pie feud, and two monuments to the days this quarter stood up. That's the Jordaan on one square.

The finish line is thirty seconds away. Walk to the north edge of the square, where it meets a canal running crossways — broader, lined with warehouses. That's the Brouwersgracht, and it's the last stop.

stops.title: Brouwersgracht
stops.caption: Finish along the Brouwersgracht, often called the city's prettiest canal.
stops.transcriptText:
Find a spot on one of the bridges and look down the water, either direction. Houseboats moulded to the quays, shutters in oxblood and cream, warehouse gables reflected in the canal, trees leaning companionably over all of it. Readers of a local paper once voted the Brouwersgracht the most beautiful canal in the city, and standing here it's hard to build the case against them.

Which is funny, in the Jordaan's favourite way, because nothing here was built to be beautiful. This is the Brewers' Canal — the working waterfront where the breweries and their warehouses stood, storing grain, spices, whale oil, whatever the ships brought in. The shutters were for hoisting sacks, not for charm. And the brewers themselves needed one commodity above all, the one thing this city of water never actually had: clean water. The canals of Amsterdam were, not to put too fine a point on it, undrinkable — so fresh brewing water was shipped in by barge from the rivers outside town. A city floating on water, importing water. The Jordaan has always appreciated a good joke at the planners' expense.

Today the warehouses are flats that trade for fortunes, their loading doors turned into picture windows — the last word in the story this walk has been telling. The quarter built cheap, for the people the grand plan priced out, is now the view everyone wants.

Stay on the bridge a while. Watch a boat slide under your feet, listen for the Westertoren on the quarter hour, floating over the rooftops from where we started. The prettiest view in Amsterdam, by popular vote — from the quarter the planners built cheap, for the people who made it worth loving. Four hundred years is a long time to wait for the last laugh, but the Jordaan got it.

tours.title: The Jewish Quarter: Memory & Resilience
tours.shortDescription: A short, unhurried walk of remembrance — Rembrandt's house, the candle-lit Esnoga, and the Holocaust memorials.
tours.longDescription: A gentle 1.5-kilometre walk through the old Jewish Quarter, holding both its Golden Age vitality and its deepest wound. From Waterlooplein and the Rembrandt House to the candle-lit Portuguese Synagogue, the Names Monument and the Hollandsche Schouwburg — a neighbourhood that remembers, and endures.

stops.title: The Jewish Quarter: Memory & Resilience — Introduction
stops.caption: Start on Waterlooplein, in the heart of what was for centuries the city's Jewish Quarter.
stops.transcriptText:
Some walks in this city are about buildings, and some are about water. This one is about memory.

For more than four hundred years, the streets east of the centre were the heart of Jewish Amsterdam — Sephardic families from Spain and Portugal first, then Ashkenazi families from central and eastern Europe. Their markets, synagogues and printing houses shaped the sound of this city for centuries. The war took almost all of them. What stands here now is a neighbourhood that holds both truths at once — the presence and the loss — sometimes on opposite sides of the same street.

A few practical notes before you set off. The walk is short, flat and unhurried: five stops, all within a few minutes of each other, ending in a botanical garden. Four of the sites along the way — the Jewish Museum, the Portuguese Synagogue, the Hollandsche Schouwburg and the National Holocaust Museum — share a single ticket, valid for a week. The Holocaust Museum uses timed entry and often books out, so if you want to go inside, reserve ahead. The Names Monument is open air, free, and always there.

This is the quietest walk in the city, and it asks a little more of you than the others do. It gives more back.

We start at Waterlooplein — the square with the flea market, and the house where Rembrandt lived. Head there now.

stops.title: Waterlooplein & the Rembrandt House
stops.caption: Begin at Waterlooplein and the Rembrandt House, in the old Jewish Quarter.
stops.transcriptText:
You should be on Waterlooplein, the wide square with the daily flea market — stalls of vinyl records, army coats, bicycle parts, and the occasional genuine find. At the market's edge, on the street called Jodenbreestraat, stands a tall brick house with red-and-green shutters.

If you've walked this city with me before, you've been meeting Rembrandt in pieces — the anatomy lesson he painted for the surgeons at the Waag, the Night Watch at the Rijksmuseum, an unmarked grave somewhere under the Westerkerk floor. This is where he actually lived. He bought the house in 1639, at the height of his fame, and he bought it here, in the middle of the Jewish quarter, on purpose, many think: his neighbours turn up in his paintings and etchings, and the faces of his biblical scenes were the faces of this street.

It didn't end well, and that's the gift. In 1656 Rembrandt went bankrupt, and the clerks handling the sale walked through the house writing down everything he owned, room by room. That inventory survived — and it's the reason the museum inside could be furnished the way it has been. His misfortune became the floor plan.

Now turn back to the square itself. Waterlooplein was made in 1882, when two canals were filled in, and its market is the descendant of the Jewish market that fed and clothed this quarter for generations. Trading stopped in the war, along with everything else, and started again after — which makes this square the whole walk in miniature: ordinary life, carried on, on ground that remembers.

When you're ready, walk past the Rembrandt House to the broad junction just beyond it, and cross. The vast, plain brick building on the other side, standing on its own island of calm, is the Portuguese Synagogue — our next stop.

stops.title: Portuguese Synagogue
stops.caption: Reach the Portuguese Synagogue, the 1675 Esnoga, still lit by candle.
stops.transcriptText:
The building in front of you is a great, plain box of dark brick, ringed by a low run of small houses hugging its base. It doesn't announce itself. It didn't need to.

When it opened in 1675, this was the largest synagogue in the world — built by a community of refugees. The Sephardic Jews of Amsterdam had fled the Inquisitions of Spain and Portugal, and this city let them in and let them build, though its tolerance, as ever here, came with conditions: most guilds stayed closed to them for generations, so they made their living in trade, in printing, in medicine. Within a century of arriving, they raised this.

Inside, almost nothing has changed since the seventeenth century. The synagogue was never wired for electricity — services are still lit by hundreds of candles in the great brass chandeliers — and the wooden floor is still strewn with fine sand, an old Dutch trick to soften footsteps and drink up the damp. In the low buildings around the courtyard sits Ets Haim, the oldest functioning Jewish library in the world. This is not a preserved monument; it's a working house of prayer, and has been for three and a half centuries.

On the square beside it stands a bronze statue of a dockworker, solid and bare-armed. In February 1941, when the first raids fell on this quarter, Amsterdam's dockworkers called a general strike in protest — one of the very few mass public protests against the persecution of Jews anywhere in occupied Europe. He stands here as its memory.

The building came through the war almost untouched. Most of the people it was built for did not. Candles are still lit here every week.

Walk on now toward Weesperstraat, the wide street a few minutes south. Beside it you'll find low brick walls topped with mirrored steel — the National Holocaust Names Monument.

stops.title: National Holocaust Names Monument
stops.caption: Walk the Names Monument, 102,000 bricks for 102,000 lost lives.
stops.transcriptText:
From the street, the monument reads as a low labyrinth — walls of brick, with polished steel floating above them, catching the sky. Walk in. It works at close range.

Every brick carries a name, a date of birth, and an age. There are one hundred and two thousand of them — the Jewish, Sinti and Roma victims of the Netherlands, murdered in the camps or lost without a grave. Seen from above, the steel shapes spell out four Hebrew letters that read "in memory of." Daniel Libeskind designed it, and it opened in 2021, eighty years after the raids on this quarter began.

A number like one hundred and two thousand is not something a person can really hold, and the monument knows that — so it refuses to try. It gives the number back one brick at a time: a name, a birthday, an age. Some of the ages are in single digits. Families appear together, brick after brick along a single row, and that, more than any figure, is where the scale of it lands.

Find one brick. Read the name, and the age, and stand with it for a moment. That is the entire idea — one person, remembered by name, on a wall built so the number could never go abstract again.

When you're ready, continue to the leafy street called Plantage Middenlaan and follow it. You'll pass the gates of a botanical garden on your way — remember them, because this walk ends there. First, a little further along the same street: the Hollandsche Schouwburg.

stops.title: Hollandsche Schouwburg
stops.caption: Pause at the Hollandsche Schouwburg, a theatre turned place of deportation and memory.
stops.transcriptText:
Plantage Middenlaan is a gentle street — plane trees, tram tracks, café tables — and that gentleness is part of what makes this stop land the way it does. On one side stands the pale facade of a former theatre; directly across from it, a sober brick school building. Between them, this street tells the hardest part of the quarter's story, and its most hopeful, at the same time — which is why we take both sides together.

The theatre first. The Hollandsche Schouwburg opened in 1892 as a popular playhouse. Under the occupation it was made a Jews-only theatre, and from the summer of 1942 it was turned into an assembly point: families were ordered to report here and held in the auditorium — for hours, for days, sometimes longer — before being taken away. Today the facade stands, and behind it a quiet memorial courtyard and a wall carrying family names. It is free to enter, and it is kept deliberately still.

Now the other side of the street. Small children were held separately, in the crèche opposite the theatre, and the woman who ran it, Henriëtte Pimentel, decided not to accept what was happening. With her staff, students from the teacher-training college next door, and resistance workers across the country, she had children smuggled out — passed over the garden wall, carried in bags and baskets, walked out when a passing tram blocked the view from the theatre — and hidden in homes across the Netherlands. Around six hundred children were saved this way.

In 2024, the National Holocaust Museum opened inside that school building — the first museum to tell the whole story of the persecution of the Jews in the Netherlands, housed, deliberately, in the building children escaped through. One street. Both truths.

When you're ready, walk back along Plantage Middenlaan the way you came, to the garden gates you passed earlier. The Hortus Botanicus is the end of this walk.

stops.title: Hortus Botanicus & the Plantage
stops.caption: Finish in the Hortus Botanicus, a breath of green in the leafy Plantage.
stops.transcriptText:
It's deliberate that this walk ends in a garden.

The Hortus Botanicus is one of the oldest botanical gardens in the world. The city founded it in 1638 as the Hortus Medicus — a medicinal herb garden, planted in plague years so the city's doctors and apothecaries would have something reliable to work with. Then the trading ships got hold of it. Dutch vessels brought back plants from every coast they touched, and the medicine garden became a world collection — cycads, palms, a giant water lily, an agave older than most countries. It's a beautiful inheritance, and an honest eye sees where it came from: the same empire that made this city rich carried these plants here, and the garden doesn't pretend otherwise.

One story to take with you. By the most-told version, a coffee plant raised in this garden supplied a cutting presented to the King of France — and from that line descend a great share of the world's coffee plantations. If that's even half true, your morning coffee may trace back to this ground.

The garden nearly didn't make it to the present. In 1987, with its funding gone and closure on the table, it was Amsterdammers — ordinary citizens, organising, donating, volunteering — who saved it. The city that planted it kept it.

The Plantage has always been where this part of town came to breathe — the green edge of the old Jewish quarter, a district of slow walks and shade. After everything this route has asked you to carry, that's why it ends here: at a place that has spent nearly four centuries doing one thing, quietly and stubbornly — keeping things alive.

Go in if you can. Find a bench under something older than you, and stay as long as you like. The garden is good at that.

tours.title: Anan Saigon
tours.shortDescription: Peter Cuong Franklin's Michelin-starred 'Cuisine Mới' turns Saigon street food through world-class technique — inside the century-old Chợ Cũ wet market.
tours.longDescription:
Chef Peter Cuong Franklin was evacuated from Saigon as a boy in 1975, raised by an American family, and worked as a Morgan Stanley banker before Le Cordon Bleu, Alinea and Nahm brought him back to open Anan in 2017. The name — ăn ăn — means simply "eat, eat," and the address, 89 Tôn Thất Đạm, sits in Chợ Cũ, the Old Market that has traded in the heart of District 1 for over a century.

From the street it reads as its neighbourhood; inside it is a Michelin-starred restaurant that placed 48th on Asia's 50 Best in 2024. Franklin calls the approach Cuisine Mới — the essential flavours of Vietnamese street food rebuilt with the techniques of the world's most demanding kitchens: the foie gras spring roll, the wagyu mini bánh mì, the One Bite Pho. Four floors climb from the Anan dining room to the Nhậu Nhậu cocktail bar, Pot au Pho, and a rooftop over the city. Book well ahead; open Tuesday to Sunday from five.

stops.title: Anan Saigon
stops.caption: A Michelin-starred New Vietnamese kitchen hidden inside District 1's oldest wet market, from a chef who left Morgan Stanley for Le Cordon Bleu.
stops.transcriptText:
The story matters here. Peter Cuong Franklin was born near Đà Lạt, evacuated from Saigon as a twelve-year-old during the Fall of the city in 1975, adopted by an American naval family, graduated from Yale, became an investment banker at Morgan Stanley — and then, in 1995, when a childhood friend helped him locate his birth mother, returned to Vietnam and found her running a noodle shop. He abandoned finance, enrolled at Le Cordon Bleu, trained at Alinea in Chicago and Nahm in Bangkok, and came back to open this restaurant in 2017 in the oldest wet market in Saigon's city centre. The name, ăn ăn, means simply "eat, eat."

The building at 89 Tôn Thất Đạm stands in Chợ Cũ — the Old Market — a cluster of wet-market stalls and shophouses that has been trading in the heart of District 1 for more than a century. From the outside, it looks like the neighbourhood it belongs to. From the inside, it is a Michelin-starred restaurant that ranked forty-eighth in Asia's 50 Best in 2024, and the first restaurant in Ho Chi Minh City to earn a place on that list.

Franklin calls his approach Cuisine Mới — New Vietnamese Cuisine. The principle is to take the essential flavours of Vietnamese street food and apply the techniques he learned in some of the world's most demanding professional kitchens. The foie gras spring roll, the wagyu beef mini bánh mì, the One Bite Pho — each dish is Vietnamese in its soul and entirely its own thing in execution.

The building has four floors. The ground floor is the main Anan dining room. The second floor is Nhậu Nhậu, the cocktail bar whose name means "drink, drink." The third floor is Pot au Pho, dedicated to the noodle. The rooftop bar looks back across the city. Book well in advance — open Tuesday through Sunday from five in the evening.

tours.title: Bún Bò Huế Mỡ Nổi Cô Như
tours.shortDescription: A Michelin-listed neighbourhood institution down a District 3 alley, serving the citrus-deep beef noodle soup of Huế — with its signature layer of floating fat.
tours.longDescription:
Down the narrow alley at 274/29 Võ Văn Tần, past an opening that looks more residential than commercial, is a room of stools, steel tables, and a broth simmering since long before lunch. Bún Bò Huế Mỡ Nổi Cô Như is a family-run, Michelin Guide-listed bowl shop that runs on the logic of a neighbourhood institution: minimal decor, maximum focus, one thing done with complete seriousness.

The dish is bún bò Huế — the beef noodle soup of the former imperial capital, distinct from phở in almost every way. Beef bones and lemongrass give the broth a citrus-herbal depth and thick round noodles; the thập cẩm mixed version layers in tender beef and pork. The name holds the key: mỡ nổi means "floating fat," a deliberate surface layer that carries the flavour. Add a spoon of chilli sauce before you start. Open daily 11am–8pm — arrive before the lunch peak or after two.

stops.title: Bún Bò Huế Mỡ Nổi Cô Như
stops.caption: A family bowl shop down a District 3 alley, Michelin-listed for one thing done with total seriousness: the beef noodle soup of Huế.
stops.transcriptText:
Down the narrow alley at 274/29 Võ Văn Tần, past the opening that looks more like a residential entrance than a restaurant, and into a room of stools, stainless steel tables, and a broth that has been simmering since long before lunch.

Bún Bò Huế Mỡ Nổi Cô Như is a family-run bowl shop in District 3 — a Michelin Guide-listed address that operates on the logic of a neighbourhood institution: minimal decor, maximum focus, one thing done with complete seriousness. The dish is bún bò Huế, the beef noodle soup of Huế, the former imperial capital of central Vietnam — a soup that is distinct from phở in almost every meaningful way. The broth is made from beef bones and meat alongside lemongrass, giving it a citrus-herbal depth and a darker, more complex character than the cleaner northern pho. The noodles are thick and round. The toppings in the thập cẩm — the mixed version — include tender beef slices, pork, and the cuts that give the dish its full dimension.

The name contains the key gift detail: mỡ nổi means "floating fat." The broth is served with a visible layer of rendered fat on the surface, which is not an accident or an oversight but a deliberate feature — the fat carries flavour and adds richness, and the restaurant is named in part for its presence. Add a small spoon of chilli sauce from the table before you start: the heat opens the broth's flavour in a way that is difficult to describe but immediately legible once you've tried it.

Open daily eleven in the morning until eight in the evening. Arrive before the lunchtime peak or after two o'clock.

tours.title: Bếp Mẹ Ỉn
tours.shortDescription: A Michelin Bib Gourmand address in a District 1 alley, cooking traditional Vietnamese comfort food — bánh xèo, crab fried rice, slow-cooked pork — the way a family does at home.
tours.longDescription:
The name translates as "Mother's Kitchen," and the yellow walls with blue shutters, made to resemble a Vietnamese village house, carry the same reference: home cooking rather than restaurant ambition, entirely deliberate. Bếp Mẹ Ỉn sits in a small alley off Lê Thánh Tôn in District 1, a short walk from Ben Thanh Market.

Recognised by the Michelin Guide with a Bib Gourmand, it runs through the dishes Vietnamese families eat at home: bánh xèo, the sizzling rice-flour pancake filled with shrimp and pork belly; crab fried rice in a coconut shell; beef skewers; vermicelli with slow-cooked pork. None of it is complicated; all of it is carefully done. Order the bánh xèo if it's new to you — tear a piece, wrap it in a leaf with mint and bean sprouts, dip it in nuoc cham. A second branch on Nguyễn Thái Bình runs the same menu if the original is full.

stops.title: Bếp Mẹ Ỉn
stops.caption: "Mother's Kitchen" — a Bib Gourmand address near Ben Thanh serving the Vietnamese dishes families actually eat at home.
stops.transcriptText:
The name translates as "Mother's Kitchen," and the yellow walls with blue shutters — made to resemble the exterior of a Vietnamese village house — carry the same reference. This is the aesthetic and culinary register of home cooking rather than restaurant ambition, and it is entirely deliberate.

Bếp Mẹ Ỉn sits in a small alley off Lê Thánh Tôn in District 1, a short walk from Ben Thanh Market, and it has become one of the better-regarded addresses in the city for traditional Vietnamese comfort food — recognised by the Michelin Guide with a Bib Gourmand, the designation for restaurants that offer good cooking at reasonable prices. The wooden stools and low tables are modest, the space is small, and the menu runs through the kind of dishes that Vietnamese families eat at home: bánh xèo, the sizzling rice-flour pancake filled with shrimp and pork belly, served in a bamboo basket with herbs and lettuce for wrapping; crab fried rice served in a coconut shell; beef skewers; vermicelli with slow-cooked pork. None of it is complicated; all of it is carefully done.

Bánh xèo is the thing to order here if you haven't had it before. The pancake arrives crackling and golden at the edges, the filling visible through the folds, and you tear a piece, wrap it in a leaf with fresh mint and bean sprouts, and dip it in the nuoc cham alongside. The technique for eating it is half the pleasure, and the staff are entirely accustomed to explaining it.

The second location on Nguyễn Thái Bình Street operates on the same menu and at the same standard if the original is full.

tours.title: Ba Son Bridge | Cầu Ba Son
tours.shortDescription: A 1.88km cable-stayed bridge opened in 2022, named for the 19th-century shipyard on its bank, now framing the rising glass skyline of the Thủ Thiêm financial district.
tours.longDescription:
The Saigon River here is barely four hundred metres wide, but until 2022 crossing from District 1 to Bình Thạnh meant navigating some of the city's most congested roads. The Ba Sơn Bridge now makes it effortless — 1.88 kilometres across the river and its approaches, its two cable-stayed pylons visible from the District 1 promenade well before you reach the span.

The name comes from the Ba Sơn Shipyard that once occupied the riverbank, a site of major industrial activity in French colonial Indochina, now being redeveloped. From the bridge the view takes in what Saigon is becoming: the glass towers of Thủ Thiêm on the eastern bank, the older District 1 skyline to the west, Bitexco upriver, and one of Southeast Asia's most important commercial waterways beneath. Best crossed at early morning or the hour before sunset, when the light on the river shifts.

stops.title: Ba Son Bridge | Cầu Ba Son
stops.caption: A cable-stayed bridge whose pylons frame what Saigon is becoming — the glass towers of Thủ Thiêm rising across a 400-metre bend of the river.
stops.transcriptText:
The bridge connects two banks that were separated for most of Saigon's history by logistics rather than distance. The Saigon River here is barely four hundred metres wide, but the crossing that the Ba Sơn Bridge now makes effortless — District 1 on the western bank to Bình Thạnh on the eastern — was, until 2022, a journey that required navigating some of the most congested road networks in the city.

The bridge stretches one point eight eight kilometres across the river and its approaches, with a cable-stayed main span whose two pylons are visible from the District 1 riverside promenade well before you reach the crossing. The name comes from the Ba Sơn Shipyard that once occupied the riverbank on the District 1 side — a shipyard that dates to the early nineteenth century and was the site of some of the most significant industrial activity in French colonial Indochina. The shipyard is being redeveloped as the Thu Thiem 2 Bridge and Ba Sơn urban district transforms this stretch of the river.

From the bridge itself, the view takes in what Saigon is becoming: the glass towers of the Thủ Thiêm financial district on the eastern bank, still under development; the older District 1 skyline to the west; the Bitexco Financial Tower visible upriver; and the river itself, one of the most important commercial waterways in Southeast Asia, carrying the same freight it always has alongside the pleasure boats and river taxis that have multiplied as the waterfront has opened up.

The best time to be on the bridge is early morning or the hour before sunset, when the light on the river shifts and the city on both sides is briefly more interesting than usual.

tours.title: Ben Thanh Market | Chợ Bến Thành
tours.shortDescription: Saigon's iconic covered market since 1914 — a French-built hall of 3,000 stalls and four cardinal gates that is a genuine working market and a tourist landmark at once.
tours.longDescription:
The clock tower above the south gate has been telling people where they are in Ho Chi Minh City since 1914 — not always accurately, but consistently, which in a city transformed this thoroughly earns respect. The French colonial authority built the hall on the site of an older market dating to the eighteenth century, when this was the commercial heart of Saigon.

Four gates face the cardinal directions over roughly three thousand stalls across thirteen thousand square metres: fresh produce and seafood on the wings, clothing and fabric, cookware, coffee, prepared food, and the tourist goods that have grown as Ben Thanh's fame as a landmark outpaced its fame as a market. Treat it as both at once and move accordingly — prices on non-food items are negotiable, and the negotiation is expected. When the hall closes at six, the night market on the surrounding streets takes over.

stops.title: Ben Thanh Market | Chợ Bến Thành
stops.caption: The clock tower above the south gate has marked the centre of Saigon since 1914 — over a working market of three thousand stalls and four cardinal gates.
stops.transcriptText:
The clock tower above the south gate has been telling people where they are in Ho Chi Minh City since 1914. Not always accurately, by several accounts, but consistently — and in a city that has transformed as thoroughly as this one has over the past century, that kind of consistency earns respect.

The market building in front of you was constructed by the French colonial authority on the site of an older market that had existed in various forms since the eighteenth century, when this area was the commercial heart of Saigon. The current structure, with its four gates facing the four cardinal directions and roughly three thousand stalls inside, covers about thirteen thousand square metres of floor space. What it sells is everything: fresh produce, meat and seafood on the east and west wings, clothing and fabric, cookware, souvenirs, coffee, prepared food, and the particular category of goods aimed at tourists that has expanded considerably as Ben Thanh's reputation as a landmark has outpaced its reputation as a market.

The most honest version of a visit here is to treat it as both things simultaneously — a genuine working market and a tourist site — and to move accordingly. The produce and food sections retain the character of a market that serves the surrounding neighbourhood; the souvenir and clothing sections operate in a different register. The prices are negotiable on most non-food items, and the negotiation is entirely expected.

The night market around the market's exterior perimeter — running along Phan Bội Châu and the surrounding streets — begins as the main market closes at six in the evening, and offers street food and retail in a more relaxed outdoor setting.

tours.title: Binh Tay Market | Chợ Bình Tây
tours.shortDescription: The main wholesale market of Cholon, funded by a Teochew merchant in 1928 and built as one of the finest examples of Chinese-influenced market architecture in Southeast Asia.
tours.longDescription:
The clock tower in the central courtyard was a gift from Quach Dam, a Teochew Chinese businessman who funded the market in 1928 and whose statue stands beneath it. The gift wasn't wholly altruistic — he took the commercial lease of the surrounding properties in return — but the building is one of the finest examples of Chinese-influenced market architecture in Southeast Asia, and the commercial heart of Cholon ever since.

Where Ben Thanh accommodates tourists, Binh Tay works primarily as a wholesale market: bulk spices, preserved foods, dried goods, wholesale fabric, hardware, and the specialised supplies of an active Chinese-Vietnamese trading community. The surrounding lanes extend it outward for blocks — more interesting to walk than to shop, unless you need a hundred kilograms of star anise. The courtyard, with the tower and statue, is the calmest and most atmospheric part. The Hào Sỹ Phường alley is a short walk east.

stops.title: Binh Tay Market | Chợ Bình Tây
stops.caption: The commercial heart of Cholon since 1928 — a merchant's gift wrapped in the finest Chinese-influenced market architecture in Southeast Asia.
stops.transcriptText:
The clock tower at the centre of the courtyard was a gift from the merchant Quach Dam, a Teochew Chinese businessman who funded the construction of this market in 1928 and whose statue stands in the courtyard beneath it. The gift was not entirely altruistic — he was given the commercial lease of the market's surrounding properties in return — but the building that resulted is one of the finest examples of Chinese-influenced market architecture in Southeast Asia, and it has been the commercial heart of Cholon ever since.

Binh Tay is the main wholesale market of Cholon, the predominantly Chinese district that makes up the western part of Ho Chi Minh City, and its character is distinctly different from Ben Thanh in District 1. Where Ben Thanh accommodates a significant tourist trade alongside its local function, Binh Tay operates primarily as a working wholesale market — spices in bulk, preserved foods, dried goods, wholesale fabric, hardware, and the specialised supplies of an active Chinese-Vietnamese commercial community. The surrounding lanes extend the market outward for several blocks in every direction, creating a density of trade that is more interesting to walk through than to shop in, unless you happen to need a hundred kilograms of star anise.

The courtyard at the centre of the building, with the clock tower and the statue of Quach Dam, is the most atmospheric part of the complex and relatively calm compared to the market aisles surrounding it.

The Hào Sỹ Phường alley leading to the temple complex nearby is a short walk east — one of the oldest surviving Chinese community alleyways in Cholon, and worth the detour.

tours.title: Bitexco Financial Tower
tours.shortDescription: Carlos Zapata's 262-metre, lotus-inspired tower of 2010, with a helipad disc jutting from the 52nd floor and the Saigon Skydeck viewpoint on the 49th.
tours.longDescription:
The disc protruding from the 52nd floor is a helipad, and it is the single detail that makes Bitexco identifiable from anywhere in the city — a building that can't quite decide between skyscraper and spacecraft, which was the point. American-Ecuadorian architect Carlos Zapata completed it in 2010 at 68 floors and 262 metres, briefly Vietnam's tallest and still its most distinctive.

Asked to reference Vietnam without cliché, Zapata drew the curved, tapering profile from the lotus blossom, expressed through a glass curtain wall that reflects the sky differently through the day. The helipad cantilevers outward at a deliberate upward angle; the Saigon Skydeck on the 49th floor reaches from the river to the Thu Thiem development and out toward the Mekong Delta horizon. The ground-floor plaza is a useful orientation point for downtown District 1 — Tôn Thất Đạm Street, with Anan Saigon and the Old Market, begins one block west.

stops.title: Bitexco Financial Tower
stops.caption: A lotus-inspired glass tower with a helipad cantilevered from the 52nd floor — the one building on Saigon's skyline you can't mistake for anything else.
stops.transcriptText:
The disc protruding from the tower's face at the fifty-second floor is a helipad, and it is the single detail that makes Bitexco immediately identifiable from anywhere in the city. Most tall buildings look like tall buildings. This one looks like something that cannot quite decide between a skyscraper and a spacecraft, and that ambiguity was entirely the point.

The Bitexco Financial Tower was designed by American-Ecuadorian architect Carlos Zapata and completed in 2010 at sixty-eight floors and two hundred and sixty-two metres — briefly the tallest building in Vietnam, and still the most visually distinctive in Ho Chi Minh City. Zapata was asked to create a form that referenced Vietnam without relying on cliché, and what he produced is a building whose curved, tapering profile was inspired by the lotus blossom — a form that appears across Vietnamese art and architecture — expressed through a glass curtain wall that reflects the sky differently at different times of day.

The helipad cantilevers outward from the fifty-second floor at a deliberate upward angle, giving the building its most distinctive profile feature when seen from street level. The Saigon Skydeck observation level is on the forty-ninth floor, accessible by dedicated high-speed lift from the lobby — the view from it takes in the full extent of the city from the Saigon River to the north, with the Thu Thiem development to the east and the flat urban expanse running in every direction until it meets the Mekong Delta horizon to the south and west.

The ground-floor plaza is a useful orientation point for the District 1 downtown area. Tôn Thất Đạm Street — where Anan Saigon, the Opera House, and the Old Market are located — begins one block west.

tours.title: Buu Long Pagoda | Chùa Bửu Long
tours.shortDescription: A hilltop Buddhist meditation monastery whose Khmer-influenced towers have earned the nickname "Angkor Wat in Saigon," set above the fast-changing eastern reaches of the city.
tours.longDescription:
The photograph most people see first makes the complex look Cambodian — the stepped towers, carved stone, and multi-level hillside arrangement resemble Angkor from the right angle, earning the local nickname "Angkor Wat in Saigon." The resemblance reflects the shared Buddhist heritage of Vietnam and Cambodia rather than imitation, and the carved detail is Vietnamese throughout.

Established in 1942 on a then-forested hillside in the eastern reaches of the city, the complex grew over decades into the Thiên Quang Meditation Monastery: a multi-level temple with ponds, gardens, and towers ascending to a viewpoint at the top. It remains an active monastery — visit respectfully, shoulders and knees covered, shoes off before the main pavilions. The view from the upper level reaches across a district changing rapidly as the city expands east, which makes the visit worth making now.

stops.title: Buu Long Pagoda | Chùa Bửu Long
stops.caption: Stepped stone towers on a wooded hillside that have earned the nickname "Angkor Wat in Saigon" — an active meditation monastery above the city's eastern edge.
stops.transcriptText:
The photograph most people have seen before arriving here makes the complex look Cambodian. The stepped towers, the carved stone decoration, the multi-level hillside arrangement — there is more than a passing resemblance to Angkor in the profile of Bửu Long from the right angle, and this has earned it the local nickname of "Angkor Wat in Saigon." The resemblance is not coincidental, but the story behind it is characteristically Vietnamese in its blending of traditions.

The pagoda was established in 1942 in what was then a forested hillside in the eastern reaches of what is now Thu Đức City. The complex expanded gradually over decades into its current form: a multi-level Buddhist temple and meditation monastery — formally the Thiên Quang Meditation Monastery — set on a hill with ponds, gardens, and a sequence of towers and pavilions ascending to a viewpoint at the top. The Khmer-influenced architectural style reflects the shared Buddhist heritage of Vietnam and Cambodia rather than any specific imitation, and the craftsmanship of the carved detail is Vietnamese throughout.

The site functions as an active monastery as well as a visiting destination — the monks here observe a practice schedule, and the complex is open to visitors who come respectfully. Dress requirements are as you would expect for any Buddhist site: shoulders and knees covered, shoes removed before entering the main pavilions.

The view from the upper level of the complex reaches across the Thu Đức and District 9 area, which is changing rapidly as Ho Chi Minh City's eastern expansion continues. In a few years, this hilltop will be surrounded by development in a way it currently is not — which makes the visit worth making now.

tours.title: Cholon | Chợ Lớn
tours.shortDescription: The largest Chinatown in Southeast Asia — a two-century-old Chinese-Vietnamese district of temples, clan associations and dense wholesale lanes across the city's west.
tours.longDescription:
The name means "Big Market," and Cholon is exactly that: a city within the city, the largest Chinatown in Southeast Asia, predominantly Chinese-Vietnamese since the late eighteenth century, when Teochew and Cantonese communities from Guangdong settled here in numbers large enough to build their own temples, clan associations, markets and streets.

The Binh Tay Market precinct and the lanes of Districts 5 and 6 have worked as a wholesale hub for over two centuries, supplying restaurants, pharmacies and food businesses across the metropolis — dried goods, medicine herbs in bulk, temple supplies, and the niche stock that sustains a community's way of living. Walk rather than ride: the covered five-foot-way arcades, the temple courtyards at the end of alleys, the incense from Quan Am Pagoda. The Hào Sỹ Phường alley, the Thiên Hậu Temple, and the Binh Tay courtyard are the three essential things to find.

stops.title: Cholon | Chợ Lớn
stops.caption: "Big Market" — the largest Chinatown in Southeast Asia, a two-century-old city-within-a-city of temples, clan halls and wholesale lanes.
stops.transcriptText:
The name means "Big Market," and Cholon is exactly what it says: a city within the city, the largest Chinatown in Southeast Asia, occupying the western half of Ho Chi Minh City in the districts that have been predominantly Chinese-Vietnamese since the late eighteenth century when Teochew and Cantonese communities from Guangdong Province settled here in numbers large enough to build their own civic infrastructure — their own temples, their own clan associations, their own markets, their own streets.

The area where you're standing — the Binh Tay Market precinct and the surrounding lanes of Districts 5 and 6 — is the commercial heart of that settlement, and it operates today as it has for over two centuries: as a wholesale and trading hub that supplies restaurants, pharmacies, fabric merchants, and food businesses across the entire metropolitan area. The lanes behind the market contain specialist suppliers for almost every category of Chinese and Vietnamese commercial life: dried goods, traditional medicine herbs in bulk, cooking equipment, temple supplies, confectionery ingredients, and the kind of niche stock that sustains a community's particular way of eating and living.

Walk rather than ride. The human scale of Cholon is its entire quality — the covered five-foot-way arcades of the old shophouses, the temple courtyards that appear at the end of residential alleyways, the smell of incense from the Quan Am Pagoda, the sound of Teochew opera from someone's radio. The density of experience per square metre here is higher than almost anywhere else in the city.

The Hào Sỹ Phường alley, the Thiên Hậu Temple on Nguyễn Trãi Street, and the Binh Tay Market courtyard are the three essential things to find.

tours.title: CieL Dining
tours.shortDescription: A Thảo Điền villa where chef Le Viet Hong — trained at Noma, Sézanne and Disfrutar — earned a Michelin star in seven months, Vietnam's fastest ever.
tours.longDescription:
Seven months is how long CieL took to earn a Michelin star after opening in September 2024 — the fastest in Vietnam's history, and a measure of what chef Le Viet Hong brought back from Copenhagen, Paris and Barcelona. The restaurant occupies a modern villa on a quiet street in Thảo Điền; from outside it reads as a private house, inside a ground-floor counter faces an open kitchen backed by a wall of tropical garden, with Nordic minimalism upstairs.

Le trained at Noma, Sézanne and Disfrutar — three of the most technically demanding restaurants on earth — before returning to cook with the ingredients he grew up eating. The seasonal tasting menu runs ten-plus courses at the intersection of French technique and Vietnamese coastal sourcing: Nha Trang lobster, northwest passion fruit, and the fish maw and custard now most associated with the restaurant. Book the ground-floor counter for the quiet theatre of the kitchen; advance booking essential.

stops.title: CieL Dining
stops.caption: A Michelin star in seven months — the fastest in Vietnam's history — from a Thảo Điền villa where Noma technique meets Vietnamese coastal sourcing.
stops.transcriptText:
Seven months. That is how long it took CieL to earn a Michelin star after opening in September 2024 — the fastest in Vietnam's history, and a fact that gives you some sense of what chef Le Viet Hong brought back with him from Copenhagen, Paris, and Barcelona.

The restaurant occupies the ground and upper floors of a modern villa on a quiet street in Thảo Điền, the residential neighbourhood in Thu Đức City where expats and the Vietnamese creative class have clustered for the past decade. From the outside, it reads as a private house. Inside, the ground floor counter faces an open kitchen backed by floor-to-ceiling windows and a wall of tropical garden — ferns, bamboo, the particular green silence of a well-maintained villa. The upper floor takes a different register entirely: Nordic minimalism, the contrast between Saigon's heat outside and the stillness in here operating as its own kind of statement.

Le trained at Noma in Copenhagen, Sézanne in Tokyo, and Disfrutar in Barcelona — three of the most technically demanding restaurants on earth — before returning to Vietnam to cook with the ingredients he grew up eating. The seasonal tasting menu runs to ten or more courses and lives at the intersection of French technique and Vietnamese coastal sourcing: Nha Trang lobster, northwest passion fruit, the fish maw and custard that has become the dish most associated with the restaurant — an East-meets-West creation of extraordinary subtlety that reads simultaneously as French and Vietnamese and entirely its own.

Book the ground-floor counter seats if they are available. The view into the kitchen is a quiet theatre that enhances everything else. Advance booking is essential.

tours.title: Cu Chi Tunnels – Bến Dược | Địa Đạo Củ Chi - Bến Dược
tours.shortDescription: The Bến Dược site of the 250km Củ Chi tunnel network — a wartime command centre, hospital and living space you can crawl through, paired with a substantial memorial.
tours.longDescription:
The tunnel entrance is smaller than you expect, and the descent is immediately disorienting: a rectangular opening barely large enough for a crouching adult drops into a shaft eighty centimetres wide, the dimensions of the original 1960s tunnels widened only slightly for visitors. Most find it genuinely claustrophobic. That is not incidental.

The Củ Chi network extends 250 kilometres beneath the district north of the city, built during the Vietnam War as an underground command centre, supply route, hospital and living space. The Bến Dược site, less commercialised than nearby Bến Đình, integrates a substantial war memorial that places the tunnels in context — the losses on both sides, the conduct of the war here, the relationship between the underground and the surface above. Even a short crawl produces a physical understanding no reading can replicate. Bến Dược is about 75km from central Ho Chi Minh City — around ninety minutes by road.

stops.title: Cu Chi Tunnels – Bến Dược | Địa Đạo Củ Chi - Bến Dược
stops.caption: A 250-kilometre wartime tunnel network you descend into by crouching — the less-commercial Bến Dược site, paired with a substantial war memorial.
stops.transcriptText:
The tunnel entrance is smaller than you expect, and the descent is immediately disorienting. A rectangular opening barely large enough to accommodate a crouching adult drops into a tunnel roughly eighty centimetres wide and slightly taller — the dimensions of the original wartime shafts, which were designed for the body proportions of Vietnamese fighters in the 1960s and adapted for visitors only in the sense that the most confined sections have been widened slightly to accommodate a broader range of people. Most find it genuinely claustrophobic. That is not incidental.

The Củ Chi tunnel network extends two hundred and fifty kilometres beneath the district north of Ho Chi Minh City, built primarily during the Vietnam War as an underground command centre, supply route, hospital, and living space for the National Liberation Front forces who used the surface above as a base of operations. At the Ben Dược site, rather than the more commercialised Ben Đình site closer to the city, the complex is integrated with a substantial war memorial that places the tunnels in their historical context: the scale of the civilian and military losses on both sides, the conduct of the war in this particular district, and the relationship between the underground network and the landscape above it.

The underground experience — even a short crawl through a section of the original tunnels — produces a physical understanding of what the conditions demanded that no amount of reading can replicate.

Ben Dược is about seventy-five kilometres from central Ho Chi Minh City — around ninety minutes by road, best visited by private vehicle or organised tour rather than public transport. The Hồ Chí Minh City Museum of History gives useful pre-visit context if you haven't already.

tours.title: Hào Sỹ Phường Alley
tours.shortDescription: One of Cholon's most intact Chinese community alleys — a narrow lane of shophouses, clan assembly halls and a living temple, kept alive through continuous use since the 18th century.
tours.longDescription:
The alley entrance on Phùng Hưng Street is easy to miss, which is rather the point — Cholon's Chinese community alleys were built to draw in those who knew to enter and let everyone else walk past. This one has existed in some form since the eighteenth century. Hào Sỹ Phường runs between shophouses into a sequence of assembly halls and a temple complex — the civic and spiritual infrastructure Teochew and Cantonese immigrants built to hold their community life together.

The assembly halls, bang, served as community centres, dispute-resolution bodies, welfare providers and social clubs; each dialect group and home province had its own. The temple at the end is functioning rather than preserved — the incense real, the offerings current. That distinction matters here: preservation is continuous use, not heritage designation. Walk slowly and read the shophouse facades — among the most intact Chinese-Vietnamese urban architecture in the city. Binh Tay Market is a short walk west; the Thiên Hậu Temple north.

stops.title: Hào Sỹ Phường Alley
stops.caption: An eighteenth-century Cholon community alley of shophouses, clan assembly halls and a working temple — preserved through continuous use, not heritage listing.
stops.transcriptText:
The alley entrance on Phùng Hưng Street is easy to miss, which is rather the point — the Chinese community alleyways of Cholon were designed to draw in those who knew to enter them and to let everyone else walk past. This particular one has been here, in some form, since the eighteenth century.

Hào Sỹ Phường is one of Cholon's most significant surviving Chinese community alleys: a long, narrow lane that runs between shophouses into a sequence of assembly halls and a temple complex at its far end, the whole arrangement representing the civic and spiritual infrastructure that Teochew and Cantonese immigrants built in this district to maintain their community life in a new country. The assembly halls — bang — served as the community centres, dispute resolution centres, welfare providers, and social clubs of the Chinese immigrant communities; each major dialect group and each home province had its own.

The temple at the end of the alley is dedicated to a specific deity and maintained by the community that has always maintained it — the incense is real, the offerings are current, and the space is functioning rather than preserved. That distinction matters in Cholon more than in most places: the preservation here is continuous use rather than heritage designation.

Walk slowly and look at the architectural details of the shophouses on either side — the decorative plasterwork, the proportions of the facades, the relationship between private domestic space and the semi-public lane. These are among the most intact examples of Chinese-Vietnamese urban architecture in the city.

Binh Tay Market is a short walk west; the Thiên Hậu Temple on Nguyễn Trãi Street is a short walk north.

tours.title: Hanoia
tours.shortDescription: A refined boutique for Vietnamese lacquerware, a 2,000-year-old craft turned fine art — each piece built from fifteen or more layers by artisans from Bình Dương's lacquer villages.
tours.longDescription:
Vietnamese lacquerware has been produced for over two thousand years, mostly as a practical waterproofing technique rather than an art. The transformation into a fine art form came largely in the 1930s, when the École des Beaux-Arts de l'Indochine began teaching lacquer as a discipline — the tradition that Hanoia, the boutique at 15 Đông Du, represents at its most refined.

The shop is gallery-like, its lighting designed to make the surfaces read as jewels. Each piece passes through fifteen or more layers of resin, applied and polished by artisans from the lacquer villages of Bình Dương Province, where Hanoia was founded in 1997. The result is simultaneously deep and reflective, the colour appearing to come from within — an effect reproductions can't achieve. The range runs from vases, bowls and tea sets to jewellery, combining traditional technique with contemporary design. The Opera House is a three-minute walk north on Đông Du; Anan Saigon one block west.

stops.title: Hanoia
stops.caption: A gallery-like boutique for Vietnamese lacquerware — objects of fifteen layers or more, their colour appearing to come from within.
stops.transcriptText:
Vietnamese lacquerware has been produced for over two thousand years, and for most of that time the technique was a practical one — resin applied to wood or bamboo to protect and waterproof — rather than an artistic medium in its own right. The transformation into a fine art form happened largely in the 1930s, when the École des Beaux-Arts de l'Indochine began teaching lacquer as a discipline, and the tradition that developed from that period is what Hanoia, the boutique at 15 Đông Du, represents at its most refined.

The shop is gallery-like in its presentation — the lighting designed to make the lacquer surfaces read as jewels, the display cases holding objects that justify looking at for several minutes rather than several seconds. Each piece goes through fifteen or more layers of resin, applied and polished in sequence by artisans from the lacquer villages of Binh Duong Province, where Hanoia was founded in 1997. The result is a surface that is simultaneously deep and reflective, the colour appearing to come from within the object rather than from its surface — an effect specific to the medium that reproductions in other materials cannot achieve.

The product range covers household objects — vases, bowls, trays, tea sets — alongside jewellery and accessories, all combining the traditional technique with contemporary design sensibilities shaped partly by the French and European designers the brand has collaborated with since its founding. Prices reflect the quality, and begin where you might expect a serious design object to begin.

The HCMC Opera House is a three-minute walk north on Đông Du; the Anan Saigon restaurant is one block west.

tours.title: Ho Chi Minh City Fine Arts Museum | Bảo tàng Mỹ thuật Thành phố Hồ Chí Minh
tours.shortDescription: A 1929 Chinese-Vietnamese merchant's villa housing Vietnamese art from ancient ceramics to the present — the luminous lacquer paintings upstairs its most compelling holdings.
tours.longDescription:
The building at 97A Phó Đức Chính has been several things: a 1929 villa for a wealthy Chinese-Vietnamese merchant, briefly a hotel, then a space for art after reunification. The yellow stucco, carved details, internal courtyard and tiled corridors are colonial-era originals — a synthesis of European structure and Vietnamese decoration that produced buildings unlike anything in France.

The collection runs from ancient ceramics through the colonial period — when the École des Beaux-Arts de l'Indochine trained Vietnamese artists in European technique as they developed a distinctly Vietnamese modern style — to contemporary work. The lacquer paintings on the upper floors are the most compelling: a medium specific to Vietnam, with a depth conventional oil or watercolour can't replicate. The building's own architecture forms an inadvertent third element, the courtyard light shifting through the day. Closed Mondays; the antiques dealers on Lê Công Kiều, one block north, are worth walking even without buying.

stops.title: Ho Chi Minh City Fine Arts Museum | Bảo tàng Mỹ thuật Thành phố Hồ Chí Minh
stops.caption: A 1929 merchant's villa turned art museum, where the building's colonial architecture forms an inadvertent third element of the exhibition.
stops.transcriptText:
The building at 97A Phó Đức Chính has been several things in its life: constructed in 1929 as a private villa for a wealthy Chinese-Vietnamese merchant, briefly a hotel, then repurposed after reunification as a space for art. The yellow stucco exterior, the carved decorative details, the internal courtyard and tiled corridors are all colonial-era originals, and the building is genuinely beautiful in the specific way that French Indochina architecture often was — a synthesis of European structural forms and Vietnamese decorative sensibility that produced buildings unlike anything in France.

The collection inside covers Vietnamese art from ancient ceramics through the colonial period — when the École des Beaux-Arts de l'Indochine trained a generation of Vietnamese artists in European techniques while those artists were simultaneously developing a distinctly Vietnamese modern style — to contemporary work. The lacquer paintings on the upper floors are among the most compelling things in the collection: a medium specific to Vietnam, with a depth and luminosity that paintings in conventional oil or watercolour cannot replicate, made by artists who worked at the intersection of European modernism and Vietnamese craft tradition.

The ceramics and folk art sections provide historical context for the more recent work, and the building's own architecture forms an inadvertent third element of the exhibition — the quality of light falling through the courtyard changes through the day and affects how the works read.

Entry fees are modest. The museum is closed on Mondays. The antiques and art dealers on Lê Công Kiều Street, one block north, sell work from every period of Vietnamese art history — uneven in quality but worth walking even without buying.

tours.title: Ho Chi Minh City Opera House | Nhà hát Thành phố Hồ Chí Minh
tours.shortDescription: Eugène Ferret's 1897 Beaux-Arts theatre at the top of Đồng Khởi Street — colonial opera house, briefly a wartime parliament, and today the city's main performance venue.
tours.longDescription:
The building at the top of Đồng Khởi Street was completed in 1897 as the Municipal Theatre of Saigon, architect Eugène Ferret working in the Beaux-Arts style France exported to its colonies — the ornate facade, arched entrance, and bas-reliefs signalling cultural seriousness as legibly in Saigon as in Paris.

Its history since is a compressed version of Vietnamese twentieth-century history: opera and concerts under French rule, briefly the Lower House of the Republic of Vietnam's National Assembly during the American War, and since reunification the city's main venue for classical music, ballet, traditional performance and variety. A 1990s restoration returned the exterior close to its original appearance. The building faces the square where Đồng Khởi meets Lê Lợi, with the Caravelle and Sheraton adjacent — and the surrounding streets hold the densest surviving concentration of French colonial commercial architecture in the city. Worth walking slowly before or after.

stops.title: Ho Chi Minh City Opera House | Nhà hát Thành phố Hồ Chí Minh
stops.caption: An 1897 Beaux-Arts theatre whose century of use — colonial opera, a wartime parliament, ballet — is a compressed history of twentieth-century Vietnam.
stops.transcriptText:
The building at the top of Đồng Khởi Street was completed in 1897 as the Municipal Theatre of Saigon, and its architect, Eugène Ferret, designed it in the Beaux-Arts style that France was exporting to its colonial territories at the end of the nineteenth century — the ornate facade, the arched entrance, the bas-reliefs and decorative figures that signal cultural seriousness as legibly in Saigon as in Paris.

The history of the building since completion is a compressed version of Vietnamese twentieth-century history. Under French rule it hosted opera, theatre, and concerts for the colonial administration and their guests. During the American War it served briefly as the Lower House of the Republic of Vietnam's National Assembly. After reunification it returned to its performance function and has been operating as the city's main venue for classical music, ballet, traditional Vietnamese performance, and variety shows ever since. A major restoration in the 1990s returned the exterior to something close to its original appearance.

The building faces the square at the intersection of Đồng Khởi and Lê Lợi, with the Caravelle Hotel and the Sheraton Saigon immediately adjacent — a concentration of colonial and post-war history in a single block. The interior can be visited during performances, which run regularly and are available to book through the venue's website or at the box office on the ground floor.

The area immediately around the Opera House — the section of Đồng Khởi running toward the river, and the side streets connecting it to Lê Lợi — contains the densest concentration of French colonial commercial architecture surviving in Ho Chi Minh City. Worth walking slowly before or after.

tours.title: Ho Thi Ky Flower Market | Chợ hoa Hồ Thị Kỷ
tours.shortDescription: One of the city's largest wholesale flower markets, in a District 10 neighbourhood away from the tourist circuit — most intense from midnight to five, when the buyers arrive.
tours.longDescription:
The market is at its best at two in the morning, which is an inconvenient fact and a completely accurate one. The Hồ Thị Kỷ Flower Market in District 10 is one of the largest wholesale flower markets in Ho Chi Minh City, and like most wholesale markets it runs on its buyers' schedule — the florists, street vendors, temple suppliers and restaurant decorators who need stock before the city wakes.

The peak runs from roughly midnight to five: stacked blooms in every colour, buyers moving with purpose, motorbikes loaded with improbable quantities of chrysanthemums and roses threading into the surrounding lanes. It occupies a long stretch of Hồ Thị Kỷ Street in a predominantly Vietnamese and Chinese-Vietnamese neighbourhood, away from the District 1 circuit — that distance is part of the appeal. A late-afternoon visit gives a quieter, retail version, but the nocturnal one, the street bathed in artificial light, is the one that stays with you.

stops.title: Ho Thi Ky Flower Market | Chợ hoa Hồ Thị Kỷ
stops.caption: At its best at two in the morning — one of the city's largest wholesale flower markets, running at full speed while the rest of Saigon sleeps.
stops.transcriptText:
The market is at its best at two in the morning, which is an inconvenient fact and also a completely accurate one.

The Hồ Thị Kỷ Flower Market in District 10 is one of the largest wholesale flower markets in Ho Chi Minh City, and like most wholesale markets it operates on a schedule that serves its buyers — the florists, the street vendors, the temple suppliers, and the restaurant decorators who need their stock ready before the city wakes — rather than the schedule of anyone visiting for experience. The peak hours run from roughly midnight to five in the morning, when the street is at its most intense: stacked blooms in every available colour, wholesale buyers moving through with purpose, motorbikes loaded with improbable quantities of chrysanthemums and roses threading out into the surrounding lanes.

The flower market occupies a long stretch of Hồ Thị Kỷ Street and the lanes around it in a neighbourhood that is predominantly Vietnamese and Chinese-Vietnamese, away from the tourist circuits of District 1. That distance is part of the appeal — the market exists entirely for the people who use it rather than for anyone's benefit in particular.
