tours.title: Tales by Chapter
tours.shortDescription: Vietnam's first zero-waste, plant-based fine dining restaurant — one seating a night, a Michelin Green Star, and a kitchen that works every stem and trim back onto the table.
tours.longDescription:
Every plate here is built around a rule most restaurants would find impossible: nothing gets thrown away. A quiet townhouse on Nguyễn Thành Ý in Đa Kao gives little away — no large signage, a single door — and there's only one seating a night, so the door won't open until your reservation, generally around seven. This is Vietnam's first zero-waste, plant-based fine dining restaurant, and the two ideas are more connected than they sound.

Most of what lands on the table comes from highland farms around Đà Lạt or the restaurant's own rooftop, and the kitchen uses every part — stems, skins and trims worked back into stocks, garnishes or separate courses. Sit at the open counter and you watch it happen, plate by plate. It opened in early 2025 and already holds a Michelin Green Star, the guide's marker for genuine environmental practice. Fine dining has usually meant abundance; here the luxury runs the other way — precision, restraint, a plate thought through until almost nothing is wasted. Ask what happened to tonight's vegetable trim before you leave.

stops.title: Tales by Chapter
stops.caption: Vietnam's first zero-waste, plant-based fine dining room — one seating a night, where the luxury runs toward restraint rather than abundance.
stops.transcriptText:
Every plate that leaves this kitchen is built around a rule most restaurants would find nearly impossible: nothing gets thrown away.

A quiet townhouse front on Nguyễn Thành Ý Street, in Đa Kao, gives very little away from the pavement — no large signage, a single door, warm light spilling out once evening service starts. That's Tales by Chapter, and there's only one seating a night, so the door won't open until your reservation time, generally around seven.

This is Vietnam's first zero-waste, plant-based fine dining restaurant, and the two ideas are more connected than they might sound. Most of what lands on the table comes from highland farms around Đà Lạt or from produce grown on the restaurant's own rooftop, and the kitchen is built to use every part of it — stems, skins, and trims that would usually end up binned are worked back into stocks, garnishes, or entirely separate courses. Sit at the open counter if you can, and you'll watch exactly how that happens, plate by plate, rather than just being told about it on the menu.

The restaurant opened in early 2025 and has already picked up a Michelin Green Star, the guide's marker for genuine environmental practice rather than a marketing claim layered on afterward. It's a young restaurant carrying a fair bit of expectation, but the format helps: one seating, one kitchen team, full attention on a small number of guests each night rather than turning tables twice.

And that's the more interesting idea sitting at that counter. Fine dining has usually meant abundance — rare ingredients, excess, more than you could finish. Here the luxury runs the other way: precision, restraint, and a plate that's been thought through until almost nothing is wasted.

Ask your server what happened to the trim from tonight's vegetables before you leave — the answer is usually a dish, a stock, or a garnish sitting somewhere else on the same table, if you know to look for it.

tours.title: The Cafe Apartment
tours.shortDescription: A nine-storey 1960s apartment block on Nguyễn Huệ, its cramped flats converted one by one into cafes, boutiques and studios — saved by affordability, not heritage listing.
tours.longDescription:
This is a nine-storey apartment block from the 1960s that never stopped being an apartment block, even after most original residents left. At 42 Nguyễn Huệ on the walking street, a weathered concrete facade rises above the crowd — air-conditioning units and the odd washing line still on the upper floors, cafe signage stacked lower down. The entrance is a plain stairwell easy to miss, an old lift waiting inside.

It went up in the mid-1960s as housing for government staff, military personnel and foreign advisors; after 1975 some flats were reassigned to shipyard workers. For decades it was ordinary apartments, and by the early 2000s visibly neglected. What saved it wasn't heritage protection — around 2015, rising central rents made these cheap, awkward little flats an opportunity, converted one by one into cafes, boutiques and studios. That's the story worth sitting with: it wasn't saved because anyone decided it mattered, but because it was affordable, and affordability worked just as well as a listing. Pick a floor and keep climbing — the view over Nguyễn Huệ improves with every flight.

stops.title: The Cafe Apartment
stops.caption: A 1960s apartment block on the walking street, saved from neglect not by heritage protection but by cheap rent — every awkward little flat now a cafe or studio.
stops.transcriptText:
This is a nine-storey apartment block from the 1960s that never stopped being an apartment block, even after most of the original residents left.

Forty-two Nguyễn Huệ, on the walking street, a weathered concrete facade rises above the crowd, air-conditioning units and the odd washing line still visible on some upper floors, cafe signage stacked one on top of another lower down. That's the Cafe Apartment, and the entrance is a plain stairwell easy to miss between two shopfronts at street level, an old lift waiting just inside if you'd rather not take the stairs.

The building went up in the mid-1960s as housing for government staff, military personnel, and foreign advisors, and after 1975 some of the flats were reassigned to shipyard workers. For decades it functioned exactly as designed: ordinary residential apartments, nothing more. By the early 2000s, though, the building had fallen into visible neglect, a tired concrete block surrounded by a rapidly modernising downtown.

What saved it wasn't heritage protection. Around 2015, rents in central Saigon had climbed high enough that young entrepreneurs started looking at this building's cheap, awkward little apartments as an opportunity rather than a problem, converting them one by one into cafes, boutiques, and small studios rather than knocking on any preservation office's door.

That's really the story worth sitting with here. This building wasn't saved because anyone decided it mattered — it was saved because it was affordable, and affordability turned out to work just as well as a heritage listing.

Pick a floor and just keep climbing rather than stopping at the first cafe you like — the building keeps surprising people all the way to the top, and the view out over Nguyễn Huệ gets better with every flight.

tours.title: The Pink Church | Nhà Thờ Giáo Xứ Tân Định
tours.shortDescription: Tân Định Church, finished in 1876 and painted pink walls-and-all since 1957 — by most measures the city's second-largest church, remembered by nearly everyone for the paint.
tours.longDescription:
This is the only church in Saigon painted the colour of bubblegum, on purpose, since 1957. Two symmetrical towers and a taller central spire rise ahead, every surface — walls, columns, window frames — finished in the same soft pastel pink. This is Tân Định Church, formally Nhà Thờ Giáo Xứ Tân Định, one of the oldest still standing in the city.

Construction finished in December 1876, almost exactly as old as Notre-Dame across town, though much altered since: a 53-metre central tower added in 1929, the structure reinforced again in 1949. Inside the tower hangs a three-metre crucifix above five bells weighing five and a half tonnes. The colour came later — in 1957 a priest, Father Eveillard, had the whole building repainted pink, walls and columns and interior alike, choosing it as a gesture toward the city's underprivileged children, pink standing in Christian symbolism for love and compassion. It's by most measures the second-largest church in the city after Notre-Dame — and almost everyone remembers it for one thing only. Step inside; the pink continues through the whole interior.

stops.title: The Pink Church | Nhà Thờ Giáo Xứ Tân Định
stops.caption: The only church in Saigon painted the colour of bubblegum, on purpose, since 1957 — a priest's gesture toward the city's underprivileged children.
stops.transcriptText:
This is the only church in Saigon painted the colour of bubblegum, on purpose, since 1957.

Two symmetrical towers and a taller central spire rise ahead of you, every surface — walls, columns, window frames — finished in the same soft pastel pink. You're facing Tân Định Church, formally Nhà Thờ Giáo Xứ Tân Định, one of the oldest churches still standing in the city.

Construction finished in December 1876, making it almost exactly as old as Notre-Dame Cathedral across town, though it's had more work done to it since. A central tower, 53 metres tall, was added in 1929, and the whole structure was reinforced again in 1949 after decades of tropical weather had taken their toll. Inside that central tower hangs a three-metre crucifix above five bells weighing five and a half tonnes between them, flanked by two smaller towers with their own lanterns and delicate floral window tracery.

The colour, though, came later still. In 1957, a priest named Father Eveillard had the whole building repainted pink, walls and columns and interior alike, choosing the colour deliberately as a gesture toward the city's underprivileged children — pink, in Christian symbolism, standing for love and compassion rather than grandeur.

Here's the slightly odd result. This is, by most measures, the second-largest church in Ho Chi Minh City after Notre-Dame, with a longer, more eventful construction history than most visitors ever ask about — and almost everyone who comes here remembers it for one thing only: the colour of the paint.

Step inside if the doors are open. The pink continues through the whole interior, pillars and all, and it reads completely differently in low afternoon light than it does from the pavement outside.

tours.title: The Running Bean — Bến Thành
tours.shortDescription: A comfortable corner coffee shop near Ben Thanh Market serving Vietnamese specialty beans and all-day Western brunch — reliable rather than inventive, and better for it.
tours.longDescription:
This is a coffee shop built for the slow version of a Saigon morning, in a city that mostly moves at the fast one. At 5 Nguyễn Trung Trực in Bến Thành ward, a corner spot with big windows and pavement seating under the awning, a short walk from the market — one of several branches of the Running Bean around the city.

The coffee is the more consistent draw: Vietnamese specialty beans brewed with more care than the standard roadside cà phê sữa đá, alongside the usual espresso menu. Brunch runs all day — eggs, avocado toast, pastries, fruit bowls — Western-style rather than local. It's worth being straightforward: not the most inventive brunch in the city, reviews on the food genuinely mixed, but the coffee holds up, the room is comfortable, and the staff attentive even when busy. In a crowded District 1 category, that reliability counts. Not every stop needs to be a revelation — sometimes a neighbourhood just needs somewhere dependable to sit down. Lean toward the coffee.

stops.title: The Running Bean — Bến Thành
stops.caption: A coffee shop built for the slow version of a Saigon morning, in a city that mostly moves at the fast one — dependable, near the market, and honest about it.
stops.transcriptText:
This is a coffee shop built for the slow version of a Saigon morning, in a city that mostly moves at the fast one.

Five Nguyễn Trung Trực Street, in Bến Thành ward, a corner spot with big windows and pavement seating spilling out under the awning — that's the Running Bean, one of several branches scattered around the city, this one a short walk from the market.

The coffee is the more consistent draw: Vietnamese specialty beans, brewed with more care than the standard roadside cà phê sữa đá, alongside the usual espresso-based menu for anyone who'd rather have something familiar. Brunch runs all day, built around the kind of dishes you'd expect from a Western-style cafe anywhere in Southeast Asia — eggs, avocado on toast, pastries, fruit bowls — rather than anything distinctly local.

It's worth being straightforward about what this place is. It isn't the most inventive brunch spot in the city, and reviews on the food side are genuinely mixed, but the coffee holds up consistently, the room is comfortable, and the staff are generally attentive even when it's busy. In a category that's grown crowded across District 1 in the past few years, that reliability counts for more than it might sound like.

And that's really the honest read on a place like this. Not every stop needs to be a revelation — sometimes what a neighbourhood needs is simply somewhere dependable to sit down, and this corner does that job well enough.

If you're choosing between coffee and food, lean toward the coffee — order something simple to eat alongside it, and you'll get the better version of what this place actually does well.

tours.title: Thien Hau Pagoda | Miếu Bà Thiên Hậu - Hội Quán Tuệ Thành
tours.shortDescription: One of the city's oldest temples, built around 1760 by Cantonese merchants for the sea goddess Thiên Hậu — four halls in the 'seal' layout, roof figures shipped from China 250 years ago.
tours.longDescription:
It's 1760, and Cantonese merchants who've fled political upheaval in southern China are building a temple to the one goddess they credit with getting them here alive. On Nguyễn Trãi Street deep in Chợ Lớn, incense thick enough to see from the pavement, a low dark temple is built around open-air courtyards. That's Thiên Hậu Pagoda, also the Tuệ Thành Assembly Hall — one of the oldest temples in the city.

The goddess, Thiên Hậu — Mazu outside Vietnam — is credited across the southern Chinese diaspora with protecting sailors and anyone crossing dangerous water. That mattered enormously to Cantonese immigrants who'd made the sea crossing themselves. Four halls link around courtyards in the "seal" layout, tracing from above a shape close to the character for mouth or nation; the roof ridges still carry ceramic figures brought from China more than two and a half centuries ago. A monument built by people who survived a dangerous crossing, to the goddess of that crossing, at the centre of a neighbourhood their descendants have called home for 250 years. Look for the spiral incense coils that burn for weeks.

stops.title: Thien Hau Pagoda | Miếu Bà Thiên Hậu - Hội Quán Tuệ Thành
stops.caption: A 1760 temple to the sea goddess Mazu, built by Cantonese merchants who'd survived the crossing to Vietnam — its roof ridges still carrying figures brought from China.
stops.transcriptText:
It's 1760, and a group of Cantonese merchants who've fled political upheaval in southern China are building a temple to the one goddess they credit with getting them here alive.

Nguyễn Trãi Street, deep in the Chợ Lớn district, incense smoke thick enough to see from the pavement outside — through the gate is a low, dark temple complex built around a series of open-air courtyards. That's Thiên Hậu Pagoda, also known as the Tuệ Thành Assembly Hall, one of the oldest temples in the whole city.

The goddess it's named for is Thiên Hậu, better known outside Vietnam as Mazu, the sea deity credited across southern China and its diaspora with protecting sailors and, by extension, anyone crossing dangerous water. That mattered enormously to the people who built this place — Cantonese immigrants from Guangzhou who'd made the crossing to Vietnam by sea themselves, fleeing the political turmoil of a collapsing dynasty back home, and who built a temple to the goddess they believed had brought them safely across.

The layout is worth noticing as you move through it. Four separate halls link together around open courtyards in a pattern locals call the "seal" style, tracing, from above, a shape close to the Chinese character for mouth or nation — a deliberate bit of symbolism built into the architecture itself. Look up at the roof ridges, too, for the imported ceramic figures still perched along them, brought over from China more than two and a half centuries ago and remarkably intact.

And that's what's really standing here, underneath the incense and the courtyards. A monument built by people who survived a dangerous crossing, dedicated to the goddess of that same crossing, now sitting at the centre of a neighbourhood their descendants have called home for more than two hundred and fifty years.

Look for the enormous spiral incense coils hanging from the ceiling as you move deeper into the complex — some burn for weeks at a time, each one paid for by a family with a specific wish attached to it.

tours.title: War Remnants Museum | Bảo tàng Chứng tích Chiến tranh
tours.shortDescription: A museum of the Vietnam War from a Vietnamese vantage — decommissioned hardware outside, its human and environmental cost within, and a name softened in 1995 as relations normalised.
tours.longDescription:
This museum has changed its own name once already, and the story behind that change says almost as much as anything inside. A three-storey building set back from Võ Văn Tần Street, decommissioned tanks, artillery and aircraft across the forecourt. It opened in September 1975, months after the war ended, under a far more pointed name — the Exhibition House for US and Puppet Crimes — and kept it for two decades. Then, in 1995, as Vietnam and the United States normalised relations, it quietly dropped "crimes" and "aggression," becoming simply the War Remnants Museum.

Outside, the hardware gives the war's scale in physical terms; inside, the exhibitions turn to its human and environmental cost, including the long-term effects of chemical defoliants, presented plainly through documents and photography. An upper-floor exhibition, Requiem, is dedicated to the war photographers of multiple countries who died covering it. It tells the war from a specific national vantage, the way most war museums tell their own country's version first — useful to know walking in. Give yourself real time on the ground floor before heading up.

stops.title: War Remnants Museum | Bảo tàng Chứng tích Chiến tranh
stops.caption: A museum that has changed its own name once already — from a pointed 1975 title to a plainer one in 1995 — tracking a much larger shift between two countries.
stops.transcriptText:
This museum has changed its own name once already, and the story behind that change says almost as much as anything inside.

A three-storey building set back from Võ Văn Tần Street behind a walled forecourt, decommissioned tanks, artillery, and aircraft arranged across the open ground in front of it — that's the War Remnants Museum, its main entrance straight ahead past the outdoor collection.

It opened in September 1975, only months after the war ended, under a considerably more pointed name: the Exhibition House for US and Puppet Crimes, housed in a building that had previously served the American information service. It kept that name for two decades. Then, in 1995, as Vietnam and the United States normalised diplomatic relations after years of embargo, the museum quietly dropped the words "crimes" and "aggression" from its title, becoming simply the War Remnants Museum — a small, deliberate softening that tracked a much larger shift in the relationship between the two countries.

Outside, the collection of tanks, artillery, and aircraft gives a sense of the war's scale in purely physical terms. Inside, the exhibitions turn to its human and environmental cost, including the long-term effects of chemical defoliants used during the conflict — presented plainly, through documents and photography, rather than dramatised. One upper-floor exhibition, called Requiem, is dedicated specifically to the war photographers, from multiple countries and both sides of the conflict, who lost their lives covering it.

It's worth holding onto one thing standing here. This museum tells the war from a specific, national vantage point, the way most war museums anywhere in the world tell their own country's version first. That doesn't make the exhibits any less worth sitting with — it's simply useful to know, walking in, whose account you're about to spend the next hour inside.

Give yourself real time on the ground floor before heading upstairs — the outdoor hardware is often treated as a photo backdrop, but the placards beside each piece are worth reading properly, and most visitors walk straight past them.

tours.title: YUNKA - Nikkei Cuisine & Cocktails
tours.shortDescription: A maximalist Đồng Khởi restaurant serving Nikkei cuisine — the Japanese-Peruvian fusion — reworked a second time for Saigon, tipping into a club when the DJ takes over at 9:30.
tours.longDescription:
The cuisine on this menu was invented on the other side of the Pacific, born from Japanese migration to Peru over a century ago — and it's just made a second crossing, to Saigon. At 80 Đồng Khởi after dark, a narrow entrance opens onto a lit spiral staircase in orange tile climbing to a second floor glowing red under lantern light, a horseshoe bar at its centre. That's YUNKA.

Nikkei cuisine takes its name from the Japanese word for the diaspora: tens of thousands of Japanese labourers emigrated to Peru from the late 1800s, bringing their techniques into a kitchen of Peruvian ingredients. Chef Pier López reworks that tradition again for a Vietnamese city — start with the ceviche, built on Japanese knife work, then the invention-leaning sushi rolls. The room does much of the storytelling: jungle-green tiles, gold barstools, plum lampshades, more Lima nightclub than Tokyo izakaya. Dinner runs from seven; by half past nine the DJ takes over and the room tips into a club. Stay past nine to watch a restaurant fold into a bar without ever closing its kitchen.

stops.title: YUNKA - Nikkei Cuisine & Cocktails
stops.caption: A cuisine born from Japanese migration to Peru a century ago, now making its second crossing to Saigon — and folding from restaurant into club without closing the kitchen.
stops.transcriptText:
The cuisine on this menu was invented on the other side of the Pacific, born from one wave of Japanese migration to Peru more than a century ago — and it's just made a second crossing, to Saigon.

80 Đồng Khởi Street, after dark — a narrow entrance opens onto a lit spiral staircase in orange tile, climbing toward a second floor glowing red under lantern light, a horseshoe-shaped bar lit up at its centre. That's YUNKA.

Nikkei cuisine gets its name from the Japanese word for the diaspora, and it exists because tens of thousands of Japanese labourers emigrated to Peru from the late 1800s onward, bringing their own techniques into a kitchen built on Peruvian ingredients — chilli, citrus, raw fish prepared Japanese-style rather than the Peruvian way. Chef Pier López runs that same tradition here, reworking it a second time for a Vietnamese city with entirely different produce on hand. Start with the ceviche, built on Japanese knife work rather than the harder Peruvian cure, and move on to the sushi rolls, which lean more toward invention than tradition on either side of the fusion.

The room does a fair amount of the storytelling itself — jungle-green tiles, gold-plated barstools, plum-coloured lampshades, the kind of maximalist design that reads as more Lima nightclub than Tokyo izakaya. It's deliberately unsubtle, and the pace of the evening matches it: dinner service runs from around seven, and by half past nine the DJ takes over and the whole room tips from restaurant into something closer to a club.

And that's really what's interesting about a place like this, more than the sushi itself. This is migration doing exactly what it did in Peru over a century ago — a cuisine remade under pressure from a new set of ingredients and a new city, landing here as its second reinvention rather than its first.

Stay past nine if you can. The whole room changes character within about twenty minutes, and watching a restaurant fold itself into a bar without ever closing its kitchen is most of the fun of staying late.

tours.title: Nhiêu Lộc–Thị Nghè Canal | Kênh Nhiêu Lộc - Thị Nghè
tours.shortDescription: A once-notorious 'black canal' transformed over a decade into a palm-lined promenade — a $370m World Bank cleanup that displaced 50,000 people to make the water walkable again.
tours.longDescription:
Twenty years ago, nobody would have stood this close to this water by choice — locals called it the black canal, and for good reason. Trường Sa and Hoàng Sa streets run along opposite banks, palm-lined and paved, the canal running dead straight between them for several kilometres, footbridges crossing every few hundred metres. For most of the twentieth century this was one of Saigon's most admired waterways; a nineteenth-century poem described it unfurling like a sheet of pale paper. Then the decades after 1975 crowded informal housing to the banks and untreated waste turned it dark and foul.

The turnaround took ten years and a World Bank loan of over 370 million dollars. Between 2002 and 2012 engineers laid nearly nine kilometres of sewer beneath these promenades, and around 50,000 people in stilt houses over the water were relocated for the work. The clean water, joggers and boat tours are the visible result — but they came at the cost of an entire riverside community displaced, most with little say. Locals now call it the Seine of Saigon, only half joking; at dusk, with the streetlights on both banks, it's easy to see why.

stops.title: Nhiêu Lộc–Thị Nghè Canal | Kênh Nhiêu Lộc - Thị Nghè
stops.caption: Twenty years ago nobody would stand this close to the water by choice — the "black canal," now a palm-lined promenade locals half-jokingly call the Seine of Saigon.
stops.transcriptText:
Twenty years ago, nobody would have stood this close to this water by choice. Locals called it the black canal, and for good reason.

You're standing on one of two near-identical promenades that follow the water through the middle of the city, footbridges crossing over every few hundred metres.

For most of the twentieth century, this was one of Saigon's most admired waterways — a nineteenth-century poem described it unfurling through the city like a sheet of pale paper. Then came the decades after 1975, when informal housing crowded right up to the banks and untreated waste poured straight into the water, until the canal turned dark, thick, and famously foul-smelling.

A cleaner Saigon, built on somebody else's displacement.

Locals have taken to calling this stretch the Seine of Saigon, only half joking, and at dusk, when the streetlights come on along both banks at once, it's easy to see why. Walk a kilometre or so toward Điện Biên Phủ Bridge and you'll catch the water at its widest, right where the old boat tours still depart most evenings.

tours.title: the Pi
tours.shortDescription: A Đa Kao cocktail bar named for π, its concept and menu resetting around a new theme every four months — closer to a neighbourhood pub than a cocktail temple, with a back listening room.
tours.longDescription:
The whole bar is organised around a number that never ends: three point one four one five, and onward, forever. At 5 Huỳnh Khương Ninh in Đa Kao, behind a welcoming courtyard, a marble counter and a lit bottle shelf, with a quieter listening room tucked further back. That's the Pi.

The name isn't decorative. Roughly every four months the entire concept resets around a new theme tied to the constant, and the drinks follow wherever it leads — a recent run leaned on sherry, savoury and nutty, a spirit most bars here barely touch. Ask what the current theme is when you sit down, because it changes what's worth ordering. What people mention first, though, is the mood: closer to a proper neighbourhood pub than a cocktail temple — regulars who know the staff, easy conversation, nobody making you feel underdressed for a basic question. It also runs regular guest shifts for female bartenders, a deliberate push in a male-dominated industry. Head to the listening room at the back if the front is busy.

stops.title: the Pi
stops.caption: A bar organised around a number that never ends — the entire concept resetting every four months, closer to a neighbourhood pub than a cocktail temple.
stops.transcriptText:
The whole bar is organised around a number that never ends: three point one four one five, and onward, forever.

Five Huỳnh Khương Ninh Street, in Đa Kao, behind a welcoming little courtyard out front — a marble-topped counter inside, bottles lit up on a shelf behind it, and a smaller, quieter listening room tucked further back for anyone after a bit less noise. That's the Pi.

The name isn't decorative. Roughly every four months, the entire concept resets around a new theme tied back to the mathematical constant, and the drinks programme follows it wherever it leads — a recent run leaned heavily on sherry, a spirit most cocktail bars in this city barely touch, built into drinks that were savoury and nutty rather than sweet. Ask what the current theme is when you sit down, because it genuinely changes what's worth ordering.

What people tend to mention first about this place, though, isn't the concept, it's the mood. This is closer to a proper neighbourhood pub than a cocktail temple — regulars who know the staff by name, easy conversation across the bar, nobody making you feel underdressed for asking a basic question about what's in your glass. The bar also runs regular guest shifts for female bartenders, a small but deliberate push in an industry that's still overwhelmingly run by men.

And that's rather the point of naming a bar after an infinite, never-repeating number. Nothing here is meant to stay fixed for long — not the menu, not the theme, not even who's behind the counter on a given night.

Head to the listening room at the back if the front bar's busy — it's a different pace entirely, and worth asking about even if nobody mentions it to you first.

tours.title: Angkaew Reservoir | อ่างแก้ว มช.
tours.shortDescription: Dug in 1961 to solve a plumbing problem for a brand-new university, Angkaew ended up the prettiest spot on the Chiang Mai University campus.
tours.longDescription:
The lake on the western edge of the Chiang Mai University campus was never designed to be looked at. It went in around 1961, a straightforward piece of Royal Irrigation Department engineering to supply water to a university that was then brand new, and it carried the flat, functional name Huai Kaew Reservoir. One of the founding committee members, Professor Mom Luang Pin Malakul, decided on something gentler — Ang Kaew, roughly "glass basin" — for a place that was quietly turning into the loveliest corner of the campus.

On a clear morning the whole of Doi Suthep flips upside down and floats on the water. The path circling the lake fills each evening with students out running, couples on mats in the grass, and food carts doing steady business in grilled skewers and iced tea. Come at dusk rather than dawn: the crowd thins considerably, and the light off the water in the last half hour before sunset does something the morning light doesn't quite manage.

stops.title: Angkaew Reservoir | อ่างแก้ว มช.
stops.caption: A reservoir built to solve a plumbing problem, now the spot where the whole of Doi Suthep floats upside down on the water each clear morning.
stops.transcriptText:
On a clear morning, the whole of Doi Suthep flips upside down and floats on this water.

The Chiang Mai University campus, western edge, where the road curves around a wide artificial lake — you're standing on the bank of Angkaew Reservoir, water stretching out ahead of you, the mountain rising beyond it on the far side.

This lake wasn't built to be looked at. It went in around 1961, dug as a straightforward piece of engineering to supply water to a university that was, at the time, brand new. The Royal Irrigation Department gave it the flat, functional name Huai Kaew Reservoir, and that might have been the end of it, if one of the university's founding committee members, Professor Mom Luang Pin Malakul, hadn't decided the name should be something gentler — Ang Kaew, roughly "glass basin" — better suited to a place that was quietly turning into the prettiest spot on campus.

These days, the path circling the water fills each evening with students out for a run, couples spread out on mats in the grass, and food carts doing steady business in grilled skewers and iced tea to whoever wanders past.

That's really the story worth knowing here. Nobody designed this reservoir to be scenic. It was built to solve a plumbing problem, and only afterwards did it become the place where thousands of students now come to watch the sun come up, the mountain doubled in the still water, the whole scene a kind of accidental postcard nobody planned for.

Come back at dusk if you can, rather than dawn — the crowd thins out considerably, and the light off the water in the last half hour before sunset does something the morning light doesn't quite manage.

tours.title: Aquila | อาควิลา
tours.shortDescription: Italian technique held fixed, everything else allowed to be local — a Michelin-listed kitchen in Tha Sala where roughly 80 percent of the menu is original.
tours.longDescription:
Aquila means eagle in Italian, and the kitchen behind the name has spent a few years quietly rewriting what Italian food is allowed to taste like in northern Thailand. Chef and owner Phubase Chuprakong opened it on Soi Surapol in Tha Sala in August 2021, in a low building wrapped in greenery with an open kitchen visible through the glass. The idea was never to import Italy wholesale: around 80 percent of the menu is original, built by taking classic Italian technique and applying it to whatever is seasonal and local — Thai vegetables, native herbs, ingredients that would never appear on a menu in Rome.

The truffle gnocchi and the tomahawk steak draw the most attention, and a full vegan menu runs alongside the regular one. Recognition has followed: Michelin listings for several years running, a Thailand Favourite Restaurant nod, and a Green Kitchen award for sourcing. The interesting decision sits behind the menu — most fusion starts from the ingredient and works outward, while this kitchen starts from the technique and lets everything else be unapologetically local. Book ahead, particularly for dinner.

stops.transcriptText:

tours.title: Baan Landai Fine Thai Cuisine | บ้านลันได ฟายน์ไทย ควิซีน
tours.shortDescription: A restored old-city townhouse cooking Lamphun family recipes rather than royal court cuisine — Michelin-listed since 2020.
tours.longDescription:
There is a particular kind of Thai cooking that rarely makes it onto restaurant menus: the food a grandmother in Lamphun might make on an unremarkable Tuesday. That is exactly what this kitchen has built its reputation on. Baan Landai occupies a restored townhouse on Prapokklao Road deep in the old city, behind warm lantern light and a narrow garden frontage that is easy enough to spot once you know the soft glow to look for after dark.

The recipes come from Lamphun, the smaller province just south of Chiang Mai and once the seat of its own ancient kingdom — family recipes rather than the royal court cuisine most upscale Thai restaurants reach for. Ingredients are fresh, seasonal and grown chemical-free by trusted local farms, which shows most clearly in the miang kham, leaf-wrapped bites of ginger, lime, chilli and toasted coconut meant to be eaten in one go. The khao soi is worth ordering, alongside pork ribs braised in red wine — a rare crossover on an otherwise wholly northern menu. Michelin-listed since 2020, with a Thai SELECT distinction for authenticity. Reserve ahead; the dining room is intimate enough that walk-ins are genuinely hit or miss.

tours.title: Blackitch Artisan Kitchen | แบล็คคิช อาร์ทิซาน คิทเช่น
tours.shortDescription: Three tables, nine courses, no fixed cuisine — a self-taught chef cooking whatever the season and his own curiosity suggest that week.
tours.longDescription:
There are three tables in this entire restaurant, and getting one of them usually takes real planning. Blackitch sits on Nimmanhaemin Soi 7 behind an unmarked frontage easy to walk straight past, a kitchen small enough that from your seat you can watch every plate finished by hand.

Chef Phanuphol Bulsuwan, known simply as Chef Black, trained first as a civil engineer rather than a cook. He left that career behind, drawn back toward food by memories of his grandmother running her own restaurant, and taught himself the rest through years of working the kind of hours a formal apprenticeship would have demanded anyway. There is no fixed cuisine — no Italian night, no strictly Thai menu — just nine courses built fresh around whatever the season and the chef's own curiosity happen to suggest that week. One sitting might lean toward foraged northern Thai ingredients, another toward European technique. It is this scale, more than anything, that explains the reputation: with only three tables to fill each night, Blackitch has ended up on international best-of lists precisely because it never tried to grow past the size that made it interesting. Book weeks ahead, and go in without checking the menu.

tours.title: Blue Temple (Wat Rong Suea Ten) | วัดร่องเสือเต้น
tours.shortDescription: A student of the White Temple's creator answered his teacher in the opposite colour — electric cobalt instead of blinding white.
tours.longDescription:
Tigers, according to local legend, once danced on this exact spot, which is where the temple gets its name. Wat Rong Suea Ten rises in electric cobalt blue just outside Chiang Rai, gold-flecked nagas coiling along the roofline and a huge white Buddha seated at its centre. Worth knowing before you plan: this sits roughly three hours north of Chiang Mai by road, so it is a separate day trip rather than an afternoon stop.

An older, ruined temple stood on this ground long before the current building, and the local community began talking about replacing it in 1996. Construction did not start until 2005, and the main hall was not finished until 2016 — eleven years for a single building, largely funded and built through community effort rather than an institutional budget. The designer was a Chiang Rai folk artist named Phuttha Kabkaew, who trained under Chalermchai Kositpipat while working on his teacher's far more famous project a few kilometres away. Kabkaew borrowed the exuberant, almost psychedelic style of Buddhist sculpture but flipped the palette entirely. This was not built to compete with the White Temple so much as to answer it. Take your shoes off and go inside; the interior mural work is more intense still.

tours.title: CINDER AND SMOKE | ซินเดอร์ แอนด์ สโมค
tours.shortDescription: A small-batch perfumery working in old paper, worn leather and smoke rather than the crowd-pleasing florals commercial houses default to.
tours.longDescription:
Nothing in this shop is edible, though a few of the scents are designed to smell close enough to convince you otherwise. Cinder and Smoke is a small shopfront, more perfumery than boutique — glass bottles along open shelving, the low hum of something burning slowly near the counter — easy enough to mistake for a café from the pavement until the smell reaches you first.

This is a home fragrance and perfume studio built entirely around small batches, the kind of operation where a scent might exist in a run of a few dozen bottles rather than a few thousand. Everything is handcrafted on-site with a vintage-inspired sensibility running through the collection: notes leaning toward old paper, worn leather and smoke rather than the bright florals most commercial houses default to. Where a big perfume house builds a scent to sell in duty-free worldwide, a niche studio like this builds one to tell a single, sometimes odd story, and accepts it will not be for everyone. Ask whoever is behind the counter about the story; there usually is one. Ask to try something you would not normally choose — the whole point of a shop this size is that it can afford to be a little strange.

tours.title: Doi Inthanon National Park | อุทยานแห่งชาติดอยอินทนนท์
tours.shortDescription: Thailand's highest point, where a king asked to be buried at the summit so nobody would ever have an excuse to cut the forest down.
tours.longDescription:
The summit platform sits 2,565 metres above sea level, the highest point in Thailand, mist drifting through the trees most mornings even when the rest of the country is baking far below. The peak was known for generations as Doi Luang, the Great Mountain, sacred ground for the Karen and Hmong communities who have lived across these slopes for centuries.

Its modern name comes from King Inthawichayanon, one of the last rulers of an independent Chiang Mai before it was fully absorbed into Siam, who spent the late 1800s pushing back against the logging already stripping northern Thailand's forests. When he died, his remains were brought up here and placed at the summit exactly as he had asked — a ruler turning his own burial into a permanent argument against ever touching these trees again. The mountain became Thailand's first national park in 1954, expanded through the 1970s, and picked up the nickname the Roof of Thailand along the way. Two stupas lower down, dedicated to King Bhumibol and Queen Sirikit, echo the same idea a century later. If the summit is crowded, walk the short boardwalk trail through the cloud forest just below instead — fewer people, permanently damp and hung with moss.

tours.title: GRAPH X | กราฟ เอ็กซ์
tours.shortDescription: After fifteen years of pushing coffee toward novelty, Graph opened a shop built on the opposite instinct: a roaster, a scale, and very good espresso.
tours.longDescription:
For seventeen years this coffee company has been getting steadily more experimental, and this particular shop is where it decided to go back to basics instead. Graph X occupies the Matana Building on Chang Moi Road — a compact, unfussy espresso bar behind glass, no elaborate syrups or coffee cocktails on the counter, just a roaster, a scale and a short list of single-origin beans.

Graph Coffee Co. has operated in Chiang Mai since 2009 and has built a small constellation of shops around the city, each with its own concept: an original café near Sriphoom, a contemporary space by the river, a roastery-driven outpost, a spot inside the Nimman shopping district. The original Graph Cafe became known for playful, elaborate coffee-cocktail drinks — rose water cold brews and the like — built to surprise rather than simply satisfy. Graph X takes the opposite approach. Beans are roasted in-house on German Probat machines, and the drinks list stays close to straightforward espresso, black or with milk, letting the beans carry the interest. Ask what is currently on the single-origin list and where it is from; the roastery rotates stock often enough that the answer changes month to month.

tours.title: Golden Triangle Hang Dong | โกลเด้น ไทรแองเกิ้ล หางดง
tours.shortDescription: A refinishing workshop that outgrew its own purpose — now the region's largest antique and reclaimed-teak operation, spread across two hectares.
tours.longDescription:
Half of what is for sale in this building used to be something else entirely — a door, a boat, a temple beam, repurposed rather than replaced. Golden Triangle occupies a sprawling two-hectare site in Hang Dong, its buildings arranged around courtyards and shaded walkways more like a small village than a shop, and it is Chiang Mai's largest single source of antique furniture under one roof.

The business started small in 1995, as a refinishing workshop for a Chicago-based antiques dealer that happened to share the same name. Over three decades it grew into a sourcing and restoration operation pulling furniture from across the region and beyond — China, Thailand, British colonial Burma, India, Pakistan, even Central Europe — all repaired, refinished and resold from this one site. The workshop side is worth seeking out: rather than only selling what is found, the team builds new furniture from reclaimed teak salvaged from old houses, boats and temple structures too damaged to save whole, joined using the same traditional techniques that built the originals. A newer section houses a gallery dedicated to local artists. The whole operation grew backwards from its original purpose — restoration outgrowing the retail it was meant to support.

tours.title: Ho Kham Luang Royal Pavilion | หอคำหลวง
tours.shortDescription: Raised for an exhibition that ran less than five months, and still standing two decades later at the centre of Royal Park Rajapruek.
tours.longDescription:
This building was raised for an exhibition that ran for less than five months, and it is still standing two decades later. Inside Royal Park Rajapruek, at the top of a long formal approach, a soaring Lanna-style pavilion rises in dark teak and gold, steep multi-tiered roofs stacking upward toward a central spire.

The park was built in 2006 to host the Royal Flora Ratchaphruek International Horticultural Exposition, staged to mark King Bhumibol Adulyadej's sixtieth year on the throne and his eightieth birthday in the same year. Once the exposition closed, rather than dismantle the grounds the way most world's-fair sites eventually are, the city preserved the whole two-hundred-acre park permanently — themed gardens representing more than 30 countries still laid out exactly as they were for visiting delegations. The pavilion itself is built entirely in traditional Lanna style, its ornate woodwork and gold detailing drawing on the architectural language of the old northern kingdoms rather than anything from Bangkok. Inside, exhibitions trace King Bhumibol's development philosophy, and the upper level opens onto a genuinely wide view. Climb to that upper level before exploring the gardens below; getting your bearings from above makes the layout far easier to navigate on foot.

stops.caption: The park takes its name from Thailand's national tree — meaning the whole site is one long tribute built in the shape of a flower.

tours.title: KLĀY cafe | เคลย์ คาเฟ่
tours.shortDescription: Part café, part wine bar, part ceramics studio — the bowl your breakfast arrives on might well be for sale a few feet away.
tours.longDescription:
There is a curious thing about this café: it is not really sure it is a café at all, and that is rather the point. KLĀY sits on Nimmanhaemin Soi 5, one of the quieter side streets branching off Chiang Mai's most fashionable strip, behind a facade built almost entirely from natural materials — timber, raw plaster, earthy tones that feel deliberately unfinished. It moved to this spot in September 2024, and the calm, uncluttered interior is very much intentional: this is as much a wine bar and homeware brand as somewhere to get breakfast.

The menu runs Thai and Western side by side without much fuss — eggs on toast with bacon or ham sits comfortably next to more local plates, and the French toast has developed a small reputation of its own. tours.title: Kalm Village Chiang Mai | คาล์ม วิลเลจ เชียงใหม่
tours.shortDescription: Seven buildings around one courtyard — gallery, museum, library, workshops — and not a single shop pushing you to buy anything.

Seven buildings, one shared courtyard, and not a single shop pushing you to buy anything the moment you walk in. Kalm Village sits on Phra Pok Klao Road, Soi 4, in the Phra Sing area of the old city: a cluster of low buildings set back from the lane around a garden courtyard strung with hammocks and low seating.

Each of the seven buildings holds something different — a studio space, a gallery, a small museum given over to local makers, a handful of shops, and a combined restaurant, café and library arranged around the same central garden. The coffee house in particular is built around an older Thai idea: the traditional coffeehouse as a place where a neighbourhood actually gathers to talk. The design throughout blends modern lines with traditional Thai and Japanese elements, and the library holds a genuinely useful collection on craft, art, and Thai culture and history. Regular workshops in weaving, pottery and wood carving run through the week, most open to visitors with a little advance notice. What sets Kalm apart from the city's other craft complexes is the pace it insists on. Find a hammock and stay a while; the whole design only makes sense once you have slowed down enough to notice it.

tours.title: Khao Soi Maesai | ร้านข้าวซอยแม่สาย
tours.shortDescription: A Bib Gourmand khao soi shop in Santitham that sells out by one o'clock — consistency, not ambition, is the whole reputation.
tours.longDescription:
By one o'clock most afternoons this shop has already sold out and gone quiet, which tells you most of what you need to know before you have even ordered. Duck into the narrow alley off the main road in Santitham and follow the smell of curry broth to a simple open-air shopfront with a handful of tables.

Khao soi is northern Thailand's signature noodle soup: a rich, faintly sweet curry broth over soft egg noodles, topped with a tangle of crispy fried noodles, finished with lime, chopped shallots and pickled mustard greens on the side to cut the richness. Choose chicken or pork; the kitchen moves fast enough that the wait rarely stretches past a few minutes even with a queue. The shop has picked up recognition in the Michelin Guide across multiple years along with a Bib Gourmand award, the guide's marker for excellent food at a modest price. The setting matches entirely — open-air, plastic stools, no pretence. Chiang Mai has no shortage of khao soi shops and most locals have a strong opinion about which does it best. What sets this one apart is not ambition but consistency. Come before noon; this is a shop that runs out, not one that closes on a schedule.

tours.title: La Petita | ลา เปติต้า
tours.shortDescription: A family-run Spanish paella house in a wooden house among the rice fields of Mae Rim, cooking every pan from scratch to order.
tours.longDescription:
Good paella takes patience, and a restaurant that makes you wait for it properly is usually a restaurant worth trusting. La Petita is a Spanish kitchen tucked into a wooden house well outside the centre of town, out in the Mae Rim district north of Chiang Mai proper.

There is no sprawling menu — just paellas and fideuà, the noodle-based cousin of paella, made the traditional way from scratch for each table rather than kept warm in a pan somewhere out of sight. That is precisely why every dish takes around twenty-five minutes to arrive, and why booking a day ahead is genuinely necessary rather than a polite suggestion. The black squid-ink paella is the dish most people come specifically for, its rice stained a deep, glossy black and built around fresh seafood, though the seafood-and-chicken fideuà runs it close for regulars who have worked through most of the short menu. Both are cooked with the kind of attention that only comes from a kitchen with very few dishes to get right rather than dozens. A proper Spanish paella house sitting among rice fields on the edge of Chiang Mai is a slightly unlikely find, and that mismatch is part of the charm.

tours.title: Lung Khajohn Wat Ket | ลุงขจรวัดเกต
tours.shortDescription: A folding table, two steaming pots and two dishes — a Michelin-listed street stall near Wat Ket Karam that's usually gone by mid-morning.
tours.longDescription:
Six in the morning, a folding table, two steaming pots, and a queue that is usually gone before most of the city's cafés have opened. Lung Khajohn Wat Ket is a street stall on Charoen Rajadamnoen Road near Wat Ket Karam temple, on the eastern side of the river from the old city.

There is no seating to speak of and no menu beyond two things, both wrapped in banana leaf and sold by the box: khao kriap pak mo, delicate steamed rice dumplings folded around a savoury filling, and sacoo sai moo, translucent tapioca dumplings stuffed with pork and peanut. Both are made fresh in front of you, the dough rolled thin enough to see through, twenty baht a box for either. What has earned the stall a spot in the Michelin Guide year after year is not ambition but texture — get the timing right and the rice dumpling wrapper comes out soft without turning gluey, thin without tearing, wrapped around a filling generous with garlic and pork. Vendors like this are a genuine institution in Chiang Mai's old neighbourhoods. Get there before mid-morning; the stall runs out rather than closing at a fixed hour, and it does not open at all on Sundays.

tours.title: MAIIAM Contemporary Art Museum | หอศิลป์ใหม่เอี่ยม
tours.shortDescription: A thirty-year private family collection opened to the public in 2016, behind a facade of thousands of mirrored tiles borrowed from Lanna temples.
tours.longDescription:
Read the museum's name forwards or backwards and it comes out exactly the same — a small joke worth knowing before you walk in, because it tells you something about the family who built the place. MAIIAM sits on the edge of San Kamphaeng district outside central Chiang Mai, a private contemporary art museum that opened in July 2016.

It was founded by Jean-Michel Beurdeley, a Paris-born gallerist who moved to Thailand with his wife Patsri Bunnag, together with their son Eric Bunnag Booth. The private collection filling these galleries was built up over some thirty years before the family decided to open it to the public. The name is the palindrome: "Mai," as in Chiang Mai, meaning new, combined with "Iam," a reference to Jao Jom Iam, a royal consort to King Rama the Fifth and a relative of the founding family — new and old folded into a single word. Inside, the focus sits squarely on Thai and Southeast Asian contemporary art engaging with the region's recent social and political history. The building's exterior is covered in thousands of small mirrored tiles, a nod to traditional Lanna temple decoration reworked at the scale of a gallery wall. Check the exhibition schedule before you go.

tours.title: Mae Kampong Village | หมู่บ้านแม่กำปอง
tours.shortDescription: A hillside tea village founded over a century ago, run as resident-led ecotourism since 1990 — around twenty of its 130 houses take overnight guests.
tours.longDescription:
Wooden houses on stilts, a stream running straight through the middle of the settlement, and mist that rarely fully lifts — this is a mountain village that has kept its shape for well over a century. Mae Kampong sits roughly forty-five kilometres east of Chiang Mai city and over a thousand metres up, founded more than a hundred years ago by farming families who moved here from the Doi Saket lowlands after realising the cool, wet climate suited tea.

That original economy — tea, along with coffee and miang, fermented tea leaf chewed rather than brewed — is still visible on the steep hillsides today. The village is compact enough to walk in twenty minutes: timber houses connected by narrow concrete paths, a stream cutting through the centre with small wooden bridges every few dozen metres, and a waterfall a short walk up the hill. Around 130 houses stand here in total, home to some hundred and twenty families. What sets Mae Kampong apart from villages simply preserved for visitors is that it has been consciously run as an ecotourism destination since 1990, and the homestay programme remains genuinely resident-led. If you can manage an overnight stay rather than a quick visit, take it.

tours.title: Mae Ping River Cruise | แม่ปิง ริเวอร์ ครุ้ยส์ เชียงใหม่
tours.shortDescription: Flat-bottomed Thai boats leaving hourly from Wat Chai Mongkol, with a stop at a riverside organic herb farm halfway through.
tours.longDescription:
The Ping River built Chiang Mai long before any road did, and there is still no better way to understand the city's shape than from the water. Flat-bottomed, open-sided Thai-style boats leave roughly on the hour from the pier beside Wat Chai Mongkol. Being open on all sides rather than glassed in, every seat gets more or less the same view, and that view changes character fairly quickly — the first stretch runs past riverside cafés, hotels and houses backing straight onto the water, before the city thins out and the banks turn properly green and quiet.

Around halfway through the roughly two-and-a-half-hour round trip, the boat pulls in at a small riverside farm, where a short walk through an organic herb garden shows many of the plants that end up in the food back in the city — lemongrass, galangal, holy basil, laid out in rows rather than on a plate. Lunch is served here too, and the khao soi tends to get singled out by regulars. It is a slower, more domestic side of Chiang Mai than most itineraries make time for: houses on stilts, fishing lines, children waving from the bank.

stops.caption: The ordinary riverside life that's easy to miss entirely if you never leave the streets of the old city.

tours.title: Mae Wang National Park | อุทยานแห่งชาติแม่วาง
tours.shortDescription: Bamboo rafting, elephant camps and overlooked waterfalls, in a valley where roadside restaurants lower lunch down cliffs on pulleys.
tours.longDescription:
Somewhere below you, a restaurant is lowering someone's lunch down a cable, over a cliff, into the middle of a river. That is genuinely how a fair few of the roadside restaurants along the Mae Wang valley operate, about forty-five minutes south of Chiang Mai city — perched above steep drops to the water, with pulley systems rigging food and drinks down to platforms where people sit and bathe in the shallows. It is a fairly good introduction to how this whole area works: practical, a little improvised, built entirely around the river running through it.

The park's best-known activity is bamboo rafting — long rafts lashed together from whole bamboo poles, poled down a stretch of rapids while the current does most of the work. Elephants are the other major draw, though there is a real range in how camps operate: some still offer riding, while a growing number have shifted toward sanctuary-style visits, meeting rescued elephants and walking alongside them rather than riding. It is worth choosing deliberately rather than booking whichever camp comes up first. Beyond both, the park holds waterfalls and trekking routes largely overlooked by visitors who never walk further than the car park.

tours.title: Magokoro Teahouse | มาโกโคโระ ทีเฮาส์ (มีใจให้มัทฉะ)
tours.shortDescription: Tea sourced direct from an award-winning Japanese farm, with a wagashi service the teahouse claims is the only proper one in the city.
tours.longDescription:
There is a curious thing about good matcha: it has almost nothing in common with the sweet, slightly artificial version most cafés serve under that name, and this is one of the few places in the city set up to show you the difference. Magokoro sits on Sridonchai Road behind a facade that leans firmly into traditional Japanese design, with a small garden attached that you are welcome to wander through rather than rush past.

The tea is sourced directly from an award-winning farm in Japan, and the range goes well beyond matcha alone — gyokuro, sencha, hojicha and genmaicha all feature, each brewed to its own method rather than treated as interchangeable green tea. The signature order is the Magokoro latte, ceremonial-grade matcha whisked into properly frothed milk, though the real draw for anyone serious about tea is the wagashi service: traditional Japanese sweets served alongside in the manner of a formal ceremony, something Magokoro claims to be the only place in Chiang Mai doing properly. The matcha kakigori is worth the visit on its own in the afternoon heat. Go slowly, and let staff talk you through the tea before you drink it.

stops.title: Magokoro Teahouse | มาโกโคโระ ทีเฮาส์ (มีใจให้มัทฉะ)
stops.caption: The tea comes first here, and everything else is built to support it rather than distract from it.

tours.title: Monday Attack | มันเดย์ แอทแทค
tours.shortDescription: A Chang Moi café built entirely around 1980s Americana, where the rotating soft-serve and the cheesecake outrank the coffee.
tours.longDescription:
Somewhere between a New York apartment and a video-store rental shelf circa 1988, this café has landed on a very specific decade and stuck with it. Monday Attack sits in Chang Moi, a district just east of the old city walls that has been quietly filling up with independent cafés and small shops in recent years, and its interior is built entirely around 1980s Americana — bold colour blocking, playful retro graphics, styling that feels lifted straight from an old apartment rather than assembled for the aesthetic alone.

The coffee menu covers the expected range without much fuss, but it is the desserts people actually come back for: a soft-serve ice cream that rotates through inventive flavours, and a cheesecake with enough of a local reputation to be worth ordering entirely separately from any coffee. None of it takes itself especially seriously, which suits the room. It is also properly pet-friendly, in the sense of dogs actually being welcome to sit with you rather than merely tolerated near the door, which says something about the unhurried pace the whole place is built around. Chang Moi rewards a bit of wandering beyond this one stop.

stops.title: Monday Attack | มันเดย์ แอทแทค
stops.caption: A very specific decade, committed to entirely — and a cheesecake worth ordering with no coffee at all.
stops.transcriptText:
Somewhere between a New York apartment and a video-store rental shelf circa 1988, this cafe has landed on a very specific decade and stuck with it.

You're in Chang Moi, a district just east of the old city walls that's been quietly filling up with independent cafés and small shops in recent years, and Monday Attack sits among them with an interior built entirely around 1980s Americana — bold colour blocking, playful retro graphics, the kind of styling that feels lifted straight from an old apartment rather than assembled for the aesthetic alone.

The coffee menu covers the expected range without much fuss, but it's the desserts that people actually come back for — a soft-serve ice cream that rotates through inventive flavours, and a cheesecake that's built up enough of a local reputation to be worth ordering on its own, separate from any coffee at all. None of it takes itself especially seriously, which suits the room.

It's also properly pet-friendly, in the sense of dogs actually being welcome to sit with you rather than merely tolerated near the door, which says something about the relaxed, unhurried pace the whole place is built around — nobody's rushing you out for the next table.

Chang Moi rewards a bit of wandering beyond just this one stop — several similarly independent cafés and small studios have opened along these same streets in the past few years, and most of them are within a five-minute walk from here.

tours.title: Nam Lod Cave (Tham Lod) | ถ้ำน้ำลอด
tours.shortDescription: A kilometre and a half of cave with a river running through it, crossed by bamboo raft and pressure lamp to a chamber of centuries-old coffins.
tours.longDescription:
A river runs straight through the middle of this cave, and for well over a kilometre it is the only way through. Tham Lod, sometimes written Nam Lod, sits in Pang Mapha district of Mae Hong Son province, roughly an hour's drive north of Pai along a winding mountain road. The cave runs for around a kilometre and a half underground, its ceiling in places rising fifty metres overhead, divided into three main chambers with names that do most of the describing themselves: the Column Cave, dominated by huge stalagmite formations; the Doll Cave; and, deepest in, the Coffin Cave.

The way through is by bamboo raft, guided by a local boatman carrying a pressure lamp, poling you through sections of near-total darkness where the lamp becomes the only light on the water. It is an odd, quiet sensation, and it is genuinely the only practical way to reach the final chamber. That chamber is where the cave earns its name — the Coffin Cave holds a scattering of centuries-old wooden coffins, left by a people whose identity remains only partly understood. Visit between November and May if you have any choice in timing.

tours.title: One Nimman | วัน นิมมาน
tours.shortDescription: A market hall modelled on a fifteenth-century French village, in Newar brickwork from Nepal, filtered through northern Thailand's Lanna tradition.
tours.longDescription:
The market hall borrows its shape from a French village built in the thirteen hundreds, and the brickwork borrows from Nepal — a fairly unusual pair of references for a shopping complex in northern Thailand. One Nimman sits on Nimmanhaemin Soi 1, a purpose-built lifestyle and cultural complex arranged around a central clocktower and open marketplace in the manner of a traditional village square.

The wooden-roofed market hall at its centre is modelled specifically on a fifteenth-century hall in Monpazier, in southwest France, while the terracotta brickwork and arched entrances draw on thirteenth-century Newar architecture from Nepal, filtered through the vernacular of northern Thailand's own Lanna building tradition. It sounds unlikely on paper and largely works precisely because none of the references are treated as more important than the others. The name plays on the address: "Nimman" shortened from Nimmanhaemin, and "Soi 1," the side street already known locally for arts and crafts decades before any of the current buildings existed. Inside is a mix of design studios, independent shops, restaurants and galleries, with a night market and live music turning the central plaza into a genuine gathering point. Come back after dark if your first visit is by day.

tours.title: PAÑPURI WELLNESS SUITE | ปัญญ์ปุริ เวลเนส สวีท
tours.shortDescription: A Thai-founded wellness brand building its identity on Lanna craft and local herbal compress work rather than imported spa technique.
tours.longDescription:
Thai spa culture usually leans on imported ideas — Balinese massage, Swedish technique, French skincare. This particular suite has built its whole identity on doing the opposite. PAÑPURI, a Thai-founded fragrance and wellness brand with an international reputation, occupies the first floor of Zone B at One Nimman, a dedicated wellness suite rather than a standard hotel spa attached to somewhere else.

The design draws directly on Lanna craftsmanship — terracotta tones, celadon ceramics, textures worked by hand rather than machine-finished, all built to feel grounded and specifically northern Thai rather than generically Asian. Seven treatment rooms sit behind the entrance, a mix of single and couple rooms covering body, facial and foot treatments. What sets the experience apart is the herbal compress work: bundles of local herbs, sourced from farming communities around Chiang Mai and prepared according to traditional Thai and Lanna medicinal principles, steamed and pressed into the skin in a practice that predates the wellness industry by a considerable margin. The fragrance retail up front and the treatment rooms behind it are telling the same story in two formats. Book the herbal compress specifically rather than a generic massage.

tours.title: Pai Canyon | ปายแคนยอน
tours.shortDescription: A maze of knife-edge red sandstone ridges with thirty-metre drops and no railings anywhere — free to enter, eight kilometres south of Pai.
tours.longDescription:
The path ahead is barely wider than your own shoulders, with a thirty-metre drop on either side, and somehow this is still one of the most relaxed sunset spots in northern Thailand. Pai Canyon, known locally as Kong Lan, sits about eight kilometres south of Pai town along Route 1095.

This is not a canyon in the grander sense of the word. It is a maze of narrow red sandstone ridges, carved out over decades by erosion into a network of knife-edge trails threading between drops of thirty to fifty metres. There is no entrance fee and no real infrastructure beyond a car park and a short staircase up to the first ridge, roughly a five-minute climb from the road. Once up top the trails fork in several directions across the ridgeline, and most visitors gather at the first main viewpoint for sunset, when the sandstone and surrounding valley turn a genuinely striking gold. Head further along the narrower paths and the crowds thin considerably, simply because fewer people are willing to walk the tighter sections. None of the trails have railings, which is precisely why the place still feels wild rather than managed.

tours.title: Patongo Ko Neng | ปาท่องโก๋ โกเหน่ง
tours.shortDescription: Thirty-five years of frying dough near Warorot Market, latterly shaped into dragons, dinosaurs and cartoon characters to order.
tours.longDescription:
Fried dough does not usually need to be photogenic, and yet here is a stall that has spent thirty-five years proving it can be. On Praisanee Road, close to Warorot Market on the eastern edge of the old city, this patongko stall has been frying at the same spot since long before "Instagrammable" was a word anyone used.

Patongko is Thailand's answer to the Chinese fried dough stick — plain, simple, usually eaten dunked in warm soy milk or Ovaltine for breakfast. For decades that is precisely what this stall sold, in the ordinary straight-stick shape found across the country. Somewhere along the way the idea changed: rather than simply twisting the dough into sticks, the owner began shaping it — dragons, dinosaurs, cartoon characters, entire small sculptures dropped into hot oil and pulled out holding their shape. A plain patongko still costs a couple of baht a piece, while the shaped versions, worked and fried to order, run closer to twenty or thirty baht each and draw a small crowd filming the process. Go early if you want to watch the shaping rather than just eat the results.

tours.title: Sacred Heart Cathedral | อาสนวิหารพระหฤทัย
tours.shortDescription: The third church to stand on this site since 1931 — the seat of the Catholic Diocese of Chiang Mai, in a city built around Buddhist temples.
tours.longDescription:
A Catholic cathedral in a city built almost entirely around Buddhist temples tends to stand out simply by being there at all. Sacred Heart is the principal church of the Catholic Diocese of Chiang Mai, and the large brick building here is actually the third structure to serve that role.

The first Sacred Heart church dates to 1931, built as a mission outpost in what was, and largely remains, a predominantly Buddhist region. A larger church followed in 1965, the same year the Diocese of Chiang Mai was formally created, and the building standing now was inaugurated in October 1999 — modern, spacious, and deliberately built to serve a growing congregation rather than simply replace what came before. The cathedral still functions as a genuinely active parish, with daily Mass in Thai and an English service on Sundays that draws a noticeably international congregation of missionaries, expatriates and visiting Catholics. A school and kindergarten sit alongside, both dating to 1932, making the site as much an educational institution as a place of worship. What is worth sitting with here is less the architecture, fairly plain by the standards of the temples nearby, than the continuity.

tours.title: Silver Temple (Wat Sri Suphan) | วัดศรีสุพรรณ (พระอุโบสถเงิน)
tours.shortDescription: An ordination hall clad entirely in worked silver, built in 2004 by the Wualai silversmith community whose families have done this for two centuries.
tours.longDescription:
Every surface here has been worked by hand, by people whose families have been doing exactly this for roughly two hundred years. Wat Sri Suphan on Wualai Road was founded around 1501 during the reign of the Lanna king Phra Muang Kaew, though what draws people today has almost nothing to do with its medieval origins.

The temple sits at the heart of Wualai, a neighbourhood of silversmiths whose ancestors were brought to Chiang Mai roughly two centuries ago by King Kawila, who invited skilled metalworking families from further west to help rebuild the city after a period of decline. That community has never left, and the temple has remained its spiritual centre ever since. The building's most famous form dates only to 2004, when the abbot decided to rebuild the ubosot — the main ordination hall — using the skills of the local silversmith community rather than standard temple construction. The result is clad entirely in silver, aluminium and zinc worked into elaborate relief panels covering everything from the outer walls to the roofline. One practical note: by long-held tradition, women are not permitted inside the ubosot itself, though the surrounding grounds remain open to everyone.

tours.title: Su Tong Pae Bridge | สะพานซูตองเป้
tours.shortDescription: Five hundred metres of hand-built bamboo walkway across the rice paddies, built by villagers and monks so the dawn alms round could cross the wetland.
tours.longDescription:
Its name translates roughly to "successful prayer," and there is a story behind that which has nothing to do with tourism. Su Tong Pae is a bamboo walkway stretching over five hundred metres across rice paddies and wetland, connecting the village of Ban Kung Mai Sak to Wat Tham Pha Daeng on the far side. It was built entirely by hand, a joint effort between the villagers and the small community of monks at the temple, and completed in just over two months — a genuinely communal project rather than something contracted out or built for visitors.

The name comes from the Tai Yai language, and it reflects why the bridge was built in the first place: to give roughly seven monks at Wat Tham Pha Daeng a reliable route across the wetland each morning for tak bat, the traditional alms round, when monks walk out at dawn to receive food offerings from local villagers. That ritual still happens daily, and if you are here early enough you can watch it directly. Beyond the ritual, the walk itself is the draw — bamboo underfoot the whole way, rice fields opening out on either side, water buffalo sometimes grazing below. Aim to arrive around six in the morning.

tours.title: Tha Pai Hot Spring | น้ำพุร้อนท่าปาย
tours.shortDescription: Mineral water emerging at up to a hundred degrees, channelled into a series of forest pools — one hot enough only for boiling eggs.
tours.longDescription:
Somewhere beneath your feet, water is being heated close to boiling point by rock pushed up through ancient fault lines, and it has been doing that for a very long time. Tha Pai Hot Spring sits eight kilometres south of Pai town inside Huai Nam Dang National Park, one of the larger protected wilderness areas in this part of northern Thailand.

The water emerges from underground at somewhere between eighty and a hundred degrees Celsius, mineral-rich with silica, sulphur, calcium and magnesium, and the park has channelled that heat into a series of pools rather than one single spring. Each serves a different purpose, and it is worth knowing which is which before you get in. The hottest zone, close to boiling, is used only for boiling eggs, not bathing. Below that sits an observation pool too hot for anything but looking at. The main bathing pools run around thirty-eight to forty-two degrees, warm enough for a proper soak without discomfort, while the lowest pools cool further still. The minerals are the actual draw for most visitors, long credited locally with easing joint pain and improving circulation. Bring a swimsuit; the walk between pools takes you through forest rather than a single paved area.

tours.title: Tha Phae Gate | ประตูท่าแพ
tours.shortDescription: The eastern gate through Chiang Mai's 1296 walls, where goods from China, Myanmar and Laos once entered — rebuilt in brick in the 1980s.
tours.longDescription:
The name means "raft landing," which tells you something the gate itself no longer can: that a river trade route once ended more or less exactly here. Tha Phae Gate is the eastern entrance through the old city walls of Chiang Mai, a city King Mengrai laid out as a fortified square back in 1296. This gate marked the point where goods arriving from the east — silk, silver, spices carried in from China, Myanmar and Laos — were unloaded and brought into the city, making it historically the busiest of the old gates rather than simply the most photographed one today.

What you are actually looking at is a twentieth-century reconstruction rather than the original structure. An earlier restoration took place in the mid-1960s, and the version standing now was rebuilt between 1985 and 1987 by the Chiang Mai Municipality alongside the Fine Arts Department, using red brick to approximate the look of the old fortifications without claiming to be a precise historical replica. The open square in front has become the city's default gathering point, used for Loy Krathong, Songkran and more or less any public celebration. Come back after dark; the gate is lit at night.

tours.title: The Terracotta Garden at Lamphun | สวนไม้ไทยบ้านพ่อเลี้ยงหมื่น
tours.shortDescription: A walk-through garden of unglazed terracotta sculpture built over more than a decade by one family, drawing on Khmer and Chinese traditions.
tours.longDescription:
Everything you can see was fired in a kiln before it was placed here — statues, columns, entire garden features, all of it clay first. The Terracotta Garden is a privately built site around five kilometres outside Lamphun town, the work of the Maiwan family, who run a terracotta arts company under the name Phor Liang Meun. What began as a workshop for their own craft slowly grew, over more than a decade, into a walk-through garden of terracotta sculpture drawing heavily on Khmer and Chinese artistic traditions rather than the Lanna style more typical of temples in this part of Thailand.

The scale is what tends to surprise first-time visitors: not a handful of decorative pieces scattered around a café garden, but dense rows and courtyards of figures, columns and architectural fragments, all unglazed terracotta in its natural reddish-brown, set against carefully kept greenery that makes the place feel closer to an excavated ruin than a modern private project. That illusion is very much intentional. Because everything was purpose-built rather than inherited from history, the family has been free to lean into an aesthetic of scale and accumulation. There is a café on-site, worth timing your visit around.
