When either club wins something, its supporters converge on their own fountain, and the city divides neatly along a boulevard built for science and learning.

stops.title: Fuente de Neptuno
stops.caption: In the middle of the roundabout, a sea god rides a chariot pulled by horses with fish tails, a trident in one hand and a writhing sea snake in the other.
stops.transcriptText:
In the middle of the roundabout, a sea god rides a chariot pulled by horses with fish tails, a trident in one hand and a writhing sea snake in the other. This is the Fuente de Neptuno, and on certain nights of the year it disappears under a sea of scarves and flares as half of football-mad Madrid climbs in to celebrate.

First, the fountain itself. It's one of three that a king commissioned to dress up this boulevard in the seventeen eighties — Charles the Third, turning a scruffy edge of the city into the grand Paseo del Prado you're standing on. Neptune is carved from white marble, and like a surprising number of great statues, the man who began him didn't live to finish him: the sculptor died partway through, and his pupils completed the god after his death. Look at the detail in the water around the base — small creatures spouting, the surface always moving. It's theatre in stone.

Now the part locals will tell you. This fountain belongs, by long tradition, to one of the city's two great football clubs — Atlético de Madrid — while their rivals, Real Madrid, celebrate at the Cibeles fountain just up the road. Win a trophy, and the players are paraded to the family fountain to wave at the crowd.

Here's the gift, though, and it's a lovely one: it wasn't always this way. Go back far enough and the allegiances were the other way round — the club that owns this fountain today once belonged to the other one. Loyalties that feel carved in marble turned out to be as movable as everything else in a living city.

And the statue has wandered too. Neptune wasn't always here in the centre of the traffic; he was shifted and turned to his current spot at the end of the nineteenth century, when the city rearranged its boulevards.

So whichever colours you wear, or none, the fountain has the same quiet lesson. The trident, the snake, the rearing sea horses — they look eternal. But the god has been moved, finished by other hands, and claimed by changing crowds. Even Neptune, it turns out, has switched sides.

tours.title: Palacio de Cristal
tours.shortDescription: A palace made almost entirely of glass, doubled in a lake — built as a greenhouse, and empty on purpose ever since.
tours.longDescription:
Reached through the trees in the Retiro, the Palacio de Cristal barely looks solid on a bright day — more like a drawing of a building than the thing itself: a great domed centre and two wings of iron and glass, mirrored in a small lake with cypresses leaning over the water.

It was never anyone's home. It went up in 1887 as a giant greenhouse to hold living plants for an exhibition about the Philippines, then a Spanish colony — the idea being to bring a piece of the tropics to Madrid for crowds who would never travel there. That history is worth sitting with. Today it is free to enter and usually holds a single contemporary art installation, which is the best possible use for a building whose real exhibit is the light.

stops.title: Palacio de Cristal
stops.caption: Walk a little way into the Retiro and you reach it through the trees: a palace made almost entirely of glass, mirrored in a small lake, with a few cypresses leaning over the water.
stops.transcriptText:
Walk a little way into the Retiro and you reach it through the trees: a palace made almost entirely of glass, mirrored in a small lake, with a few cypresses leaning over the water. On a bright day it barely looks solid — more like a drawing of a building than the thing itself.

This is the Palacio de Cristal, the Crystal Palace, and the first thing to know is that it was never anyone's home. It was built in 1887 as a giant greenhouse — iron frame, glass walls — to hold living plants. Stand back and look at the proportions: the great domed centre, the wings, the way the whole structure exists to let light pour straight through it.

It was built for an exhibition about the Philippines, then a Spanish colony on the far side of the world. The idea was to bring a piece of the tropics to Madrid — exotic plants and flowers under glass for crowds who would never travel there. It's worth being honest about the rest, briefly: these colonial exhibitions also put people on display, men and women brought from the colony to be looked at by visitors. We find that deeply troubling now, and rightly; at the time, much of Europe treated it as ordinary. The beautiful building and that uncomfortable history come from the same moment.

Today the Crystal Palace does something quietly fitting. It belongs to the Reina Sofía museum and is used for contemporary art — but it's usually nearly empty, holding a single installation, sometimes almost nothing at all. After a history of being crammed with things to gawp at, it has become a space whose finest exhibit is the light itself, moving across the glass through the day.

So step inside if it's open, and notice how little there is to see, and how much. The trees outside throw shifting shadows on the floor; the lake bounces ripples up onto the dome; the whole place breathes with the weather. A building made to show off an empire, now content to show you almost nothing but the afternoon.

tours.title: Plaza de Santa Ana & the Barrio de las Letras
tours.shortDescription: The Quarter of Letters — where Cervantes and Lope de Vega lived streets apart, and their words are set in gold into the pavement.
tours.longDescription:
Look down. Among the paving of these streets are lines of writing set into the stone in gilded letters — fragments of plays and poems laid where their authors walked. This is the Barrio de las Letras, and the writers under your shoes once lived in the houses over your head.

This was the neighbourhood of Spain's Golden Age. Within a few narrow streets lived Cervantes, who gave the world Don Quixote; Lope de Vega, who wrote plays faster than theatres could stage them; and their sharp-tongued rivals Quevedo and Góngora, who feuded in verse the way other men duelled with swords. Plaza de Santa Ana is its living room — terraces on every side, the Teatro Español at one end, and a bronze García Lorca holding a bird.

stops.title: Plaza de Santa Ana & the Barrio de las Letras
stops.caption: Look down at the ground beneath your feet.
stops.transcriptText:
Look down at the ground beneath your feet. Among the paving you'll find lines of writing set into the stone in gilded letters — sentences from old plays and poems, running along the street like a trail. You're in the Barrio de las Letras, the Quarter of Letters, and the writers under your shoes once lived in the houses over your head.

This was the neighbourhood of Spain's Golden Age — the great flowering of Spanish writing in the fifteen and sixteen hundreds. Within these few narrow streets lived the giants all at once: Cervantes, who gave the world Don Quixote; Lope de Vega, who wrote plays faster than theatres could stage them; and their sharp-tongued rivals Quevedo and Góngora, who feuded in verse the way other men duelled with swords. The lines set into the pavement are theirs — fragments of what they wrote, laid where they walked.

Here's the gift, and it's a strange neighbourly fact. Cervantes and Lope de Vega lived almost on top of each other and could not stand one another — and the geography of their afterlives kept the joke going. Lope's house still stands a couple of streets away, kept as it was. And Cervantes, the more famous of the two, lies buried in a convent right here in the quarter, behind a plain wall most visitors pass without a glance. The man whose words are underfoot all over this district rests, quietly, in the middle of it.

Now look at the square itself, Plaza de Santa Ana. One side is held by the Teatro Español, a theatre that has stood on this spot, in one form or another, for centuries — open-air playhouses once filled this ground, where audiences shouted plays down or carried them on their shoulders. The bars around the edges have their own literary ghosts; one was a favourite of Hemingway, decades later, when the writers drinking here had swapped Spanish for English.

So take a slow loop and read the ground as you go. Most cities hang plaques on walls to remember their writers. This one did something better — it pressed their words into the street, so that to cross the neighbourhood at all, you have to walk straight through their sentences.

tours.title: El Rastro
tours.shortDescription: Madrid's great Sunday flea market, tumbling down a hill for three centuries — and named, quite literally, after a trail of blood.
tours.longDescription:
On a Sunday morning you can hear El Rastro before you see it: the low roar of thousands of people haggling downhill. Any other day this is a quiet, steep street and you will have to take the noise on faith.

The street is Ribera de Curtidores, the riverbank of the tanners, and the name is the key to everything. Centuries ago this edge of the city was where animals were slaughtered and their hides turned into leather; the carcasses were dragged downhill from the slaughterhouse to the tanning workshops and left a long stain behind them — un rastro, a trail. The most charming market in Madrid is named after it. These days the only thing being hunted is a bargain, from around nine until mid-afternoon.

stops.title: El Rastro
stops.caption: If it's a Sunday morning, you can probably already hear it — the low roar of thousands of people haggling downhill.
stops.transcriptText:
If it's a Sunday morning, you can probably already hear it — the low roar of thousands of people haggling downhill. If it's any other day, you're standing on a quiet, steep street and you'll have to take the noise on faith. Either way, this is El Rastro, the great open-air market that has tumbled down this hill for the better part of three hundred years.

Start with where you are. The street is called Ribera de Curtidores — the riverbank of the tanners — and that name is the key to everything. Centuries ago this edge of the city was where animals were slaughtered and their hides were turned into leather. The carcasses were dragged downhill from the old slaughterhouse to the tanning workshops, and they left a long stain on the ground as they went. A trail. In Spanish, un rastro. The most charming market in Madrid is named, quite literally, after a trail of blood.

These days the only thing being hunted is a bargain. From around nine in the morning until the middle of the afternoon on Sundays and public holidays, hundreds upon hundreds of stalls unfold down the slope — old vinyl, leather, fans, postcards, brass odds and ends, clothes new and ancient, and a great deal of cheerful junk. The serious collectors arrive at opening to skim the best finds; by late morning it's less about buying and more about the crush and the spectacle.

Here's the local wisdom, and the gift of doing it right. Start at the top, near Plaza de Cascorro, and let gravity carry you down — fighting uphill through that crowd is a beginner's mistake. Keep a hand on your bag; the pickpockets work the tightest spots. And know that the market is only half the ritual. When the stalls pack up, everyone pours into the bars of La Latina just around you for a beer and a plate of something — the tapas crawl that turns a morning's shopping into a whole Sunday.

So don't treat it as shopping. Treat it as the city's weekly habit. The hides and the tanners are long gone, but the trail they left still fills, every Sunday, with people following it down the hill.

tours.title: Malasaña & the Plaza del Dos de Mayo
tours.shortDescription: A stone arch that most people walk past as scenery — the gateway of the barracks where Madrid rose against Napoleon.
tours.longDescription:
In the middle of this square stands a stone archway with two figures beneath it. It is not scenery: it is a survivor, the gateway of the Monteleón artillery barracks that once stood here, and it marks where the neighbourhood earned its name.

On the second of May 1808, with Napoleon's army holding Madrid, the city rose. Here a small group of Spanish soldiers and ordinary townspeople made a stand; the officers Daoíz and Velarde died defending the guns and are the two figures under the arch. The uprising was crushed and the reprisals were brutal — Goya painted both days, and they hang in the Prado a short walk from here. The square that remembers it is now the centre of Malasaña, the city's most contrary and best-loved night-time neighbourhood.

stops.title: Malasaña & the Plaza del Dos de Mayo
stops.caption: In the middle of this square stands a stone archway with two figures beneath it, and almost everyone walking past treats it as scenery.
stops.transcriptText:
In the middle of this square stands a stone archway with two figures beneath it, and almost everyone walking past treats it as scenery. It isn't. That arch is a survivor — the gateway of a military barracks that once stood here — and it marks the spot where this neighbourhood earned its name in blood, twice over, two centuries apart.

Go back to the second of May, 1808. Napoleon's army held Madrid, and on that morning the city rose against them. Here, at the Monteleón artillery barracks, a small group of Spanish soldiers and ordinary townspeople made a stand. Two officers, Daoíz and Velarde, are remembered as its heart; they died defending the guns, and the two figures under the arch honour them. The uprising was crushed, and the reprisals that followed were brutal — you can see both days, the fighting and the executions, in two of Goya's most famous paintings hanging in the Prado, a short walk from here. He painted what this square remembers.

The neighbourhood took its name from one of the day's dead — Manuela Malasaña, a young seamstress killed in the chaos. So the whole district is, in effect, named after a teenager who didn't survive the second of May. That's worth carrying for a moment.

Now look around at what the same streets became. Because the second thing Malasaña is famous for is a rebellion of a completely different kind. In the nineteen eighties, after decades under Franco, this is where Madrid's youth exploded into colour — music, clubs, comics, film, a wave of creative noise called La Movida. The bars and record shops you can see grew out of that. Two uprisings, then: one against an emperor's soldiers, one against grey years of silence.

So the square holds both at once. The arch is genuinely old stone, genuinely scarred history; the streets fanning out from it are loud, painted, and very much alive. Stand here a moment and let the distance close — the same few corners that watched a city fight for its life later watched it learn, very loudly, how to enjoy being free.

tours.title: Chueca & the Mercado de San Antón
tours.shortDescription: The heart of LGBTQ+ Madrid — a neighbourhood guidebooks once warned you off, now the place a whole city comes to celebrate.
tours.longDescription:
Stand in the little square at the centre of Chueca and take the temperature: rainbow flags in the windows, busy terraces, a crowd comfortable in its own skin. This is a recent thing, won rather than given.

A generation ago the neighbourhood was run-down and edgy, the kind of place guidebooks steered you away from. From the 1980s the city's gay community moved in, opened bars and businesses and slowly turned a neglected quarter into one of the most confident corners of Madrid; by the time Pride arrives each summer — among the largest celebrations in the world — these streets are its centre. The Mercado de San Antón is the neighbourhood in miniature: an old food market rebuilt as three stacked floors of produce, tapas and a rooftop terrace.

stops.title: Chueca & the Mercado de San Antón
stops.caption: Stand in the little square at the centre of Chueca and take the temperature of the place.
stops.transcriptText:
Stand in the little square at the centre of Chueca and take the temperature of the place. Rainbow flags in windows, busy terraces, a crowd that looks comfortable in its own skin. This is the heart of LGBTQ+ Madrid — and that's a recent thing, won rather than given.

A generation ago this neighbourhood had a very different reputation: run-down, edgy, the kind of place guidebooks warned you off. From the nineteen eighties on, the city's gay community moved in, opened bars and businesses, and slowly turned a neglected quarter into one of the most confident and sought-after corners of Madrid. By the time the city hosts its enormous Pride celebrations each summer — among the largest in the world — these streets are the centre of it, packed shoulder to shoulder. A neighbourhood that was once somewhere to avoid is now somewhere a whole city comes to celebrate.

The square takes its name, by the way, from a composer — Federico Chueca, who wrote the light, popular Spanish operettas called zarzuelas. There's a nice fit there: a district known for performance and good humour, named after a man who wrote crowd-pleasers.

Now find the market — Mercado de San Antón. From the outside it's a plain modern box, easy to overlook, but it tells the neighbourhood's whole story in three floors. The ground floor still works as a proper food market, the fishmongers and grocers locals actually use. Climb up and it changes: stalls to eat at, then a rooftop terrace with a bar and a view over the rooftops. The old neighbourhood market and the new social one, stacked on top of each other in the same building.

So this is a stop about reinvention, and it's worth saying plainly because it didn't have to happen. Streets get written off; communities get pushed to the margins. Here a marginal neighbourhood and a marginalised community found each other and built something open and warm out of it. Grab a coffee on a terrace, watch the square go by, and notice how thoroughly it feels like it was always meant to be this way. It wasn't. That's the point.

tours.title: Plaza de Colón
tours.shortDescription: A column, the largest flag in Spain and a cluster of raw concrete blocks — three monuments in one square that don't quite agree.
tours.longDescription:
Three things compete for your eye here and they do not agree with each other. The column came first: Christopher Columbus — Cristóbal Colón — raised in the 1880s in white neo-Gothic marble, when Spain looked back on his voyages with uncomplicated pride. In 2009 he was shifted to his present perch in the middle of the traffic.

The flag arrived around 2001, deliberately the largest in the country. And off to one side stand the huge rough concrete blocks of the Jardines del Descubrimiento — the Gardens of Discovery — a monument from the 1970s carved with fragments about the voyages, far more ambivalent in tone than the column it shares a square with. Nearby, a quieter memorial remembers the victims of the 2004 Atocha bombings. It is one of Madrid's great civic stages, and one of its quietest arguments.

stops.title: Plaza de Colón
stops.caption: Three things compete for your eye in this square, and they don't quite agree with each other.
stops.transcriptText:
Three things compete for your eye in this square, and they don't quite agree with each other. A tall stone column with a figure on top. An enormous Spanish flag on a white pole. And, off to one side, a cluster of huge rough concrete blocks. Together they make this one of Madrid's great civic stages — and one of its quietest arguments.

The column first. On top stands Christopher Columbus — Cristóbal Colón, which gives the square its name. It was raised in the eighteen eighties, when Spain looked back on his voyages with uncomplicated pride and built him a monument to match: white marble, neo-Gothic, the explorer gazing out with a Castilian flag in his hand. In 2009 he was shifted to his present perch in the middle of the traffic, so the discoverer of a new world now also directs the flow of cars from north to south.

The flag came much later, going up around the year 2001 — and it's deliberately the largest in the country, fourteen metres by twenty-one, on a fifty-metre mast that turns with the wind so it never tangles. This square has long been the place Madrid comes to wave that flag: for football wins, for national days, for protests of every stripe. A stage built to be filled.

Behind it lie the Gardens of Discovery, and the great concrete blocks within them carry carved inscriptions about the voyages, often read as standing in for Columbus's three ships.

Here's the part worth holding lightly, and even-handedly. The very word carved all over this square — "discovery" — is now contested. For centuries it was simply Spain's proudest story. But fourteen ninety-two was also the beginning of conquest and colonisation for the peoples already living across the Atlantic, and many now prefer to call it an encounter, or worse. Monuments to Columbus have become flashpoints across the world. This one stands serenely above the traffic, from an age that felt no doubt, in a city that now holds several views at once.

So read the square as exactly that: a confident answer from one century, standing in the middle of another century's questions. You don't have to settle it. Just notice that the stone is sure, and the conversation around it no longer is.

tours.title: Plaza de Toros de Las Ventas
tours.shortDescription: The largest bullring in Spain and the most important in the world — and a piece of neo-Mudéjar brickwork worth seeing whatever you think of it.
tours.longDescription:
Whatever you make of what happens inside it, the outside of Las Ventas is one of the finest things of its kind in Madrid. The style is neo-Mudéjar, a Spanish revival of the patterns Muslim craftsmen left across the peninsula — horseshoe arches and woven brickwork, set with glazed ceramic tiles carrying the coats of arms of the Spanish provinces one after another around the ring.

It was finished in 1929, opened with a charity bullfight in 1931, and holds close to twenty-four thousand people in a perfect circle sixty metres across. Spaniards call it the cathedral — the place a bullfighter has to succeed to truly arrive. Bullfighting is genuinely contested in Spain today, banned in some regions and defended as heritage in others, and the argument is worth hearing both sides of. The ring runs tours and a museum year-round.

stops.title: Plaza de Toros de Las Ventas
stops.caption: Before anything else, look at the building — because whatever you think of what happens inside it, the outside is one of the finest things of its kind in Madrid.
stops.transcriptText:
Before anything else, look at the building — because whatever you think of what happens inside it, the outside is one of the finest things of its kind in Madrid. This is Las Ventas, the largest bullring in Spain and, by most reckonings, the most important in the world. And the argument about what it's for is one you should hear both sides of.

Start with the brick. The style is called neo-Mudéjar — a Spanish revival of the patterns Muslim craftsmen left across the peninsula centuries ago, all horseshoe arches and woven brickwork, set with glazed ceramic tiles. Look closely and the tiles carry the coats of arms of the Spanish provinces, one after another around the ring. It was finished in 1929 and opened with a charity bullfight in 1931, and it holds close to twenty-four thousand people in a perfect circle sixty metres across. Spaniards call it the cathedral — the place a bullfighter has to succeed to truly arrive.

And here's the thing to sit with, because Spain itself is sitting with it. To one side, bullfighting is defended as an art form and a piece of intangible heritage, protected by national law, drawing full houses here every day during the San Isidro fair in May and June. To the other, it's increasingly opposed as cruelty: attendance has fallen, some regions have turned away from it, and in 2024 the national government scrapped its official bullfighting prize. The country is genuinely divided, and the building stands right on the fault line — admired and contested in the same breath.

One detail before you go, and it captures the whole strange world of this place. Out front, among the statues of famous matadors, stands a monument to a Scottish scientist: Alexander Fleming, who discovered penicillin. The bullfighters paid for it themselves — because the antibiotic he found saved the lives of countless men wounded in this ring. A figure of a matador raises his cap to the doctor in thanks. Whatever you make of the spectacle, that small bronze salute tells you how seriously, and how literally, this was always a matter of life and death.

tours.title: Estación de Atocha
tours.shortDescription: Spain's busiest station hides two very different rooms — one an indoor tropical jungle, the other built around an absence.
tours.longDescription:
Step into the old station hall first: the great iron-and-glass shed of the 1890s that trains once pulled straight into. The tracks are gone, and in their place is a tropical garden — several thousand plants, palms reaching for the roof, turtles in the ponds, travellers dozing on benches among the ferns. A nineteenth-century cathedral of engineering repurposed as a greenhouse in the middle of a working transport hub, and one of the loveliest accidents in the city.

Then the reason this station carries a weight no other does. On the morning of 11 March 2004, coordinated bombs on commuter trains killed 193 people, most of them here or on the approach. The memorial is a glass cylinder above ground and a quiet blue chamber beneath it, inscribed with messages left by strangers in the days after. Both rooms belong to the same building.

stops.title: Estación de Atocha
stops.caption: Atocha is the busiest railway station in Spain, and it hides two very different rooms — one full of life, the other built around an absence.
stops.transcriptText:
Atocha is the busiest railway station in Spain, and it hides two very different rooms — one full of life, the other built around an absence. Take them in order.

Step into the old station hall first, the grand iron-and-glass shed from the 1890s that trains used to pull straight into. The tracks are gone. In their place is a tropical garden — a warm, humid indoor jungle of several thousand plants, palms reaching towards the glass roof, turtles in the ponds, travellers dozing on benches among the ferns. A nineteenth-century cathedral of engineering, repurposed as a greenhouse, in the middle of a working transport hub. It's one of the loveliest accidents in the city.

Then, nearby, the reason this station carries a weight no other does. On the morning of the eleventh of March, 2004, during the rush hour, bombs were set off on four packed commuter trains heading into Madrid. One hundred and ninety-three people were killed. It remains the deadliest attack of its kind in modern Spanish history, and the city has chosen to remember it not with stone or statues, but with light.

The memorial sits below ground, opened in 2024 on the twentieth anniversary, after the original glass tower that once rose above the station was taken down. You descend into a quiet room with walls of deep cobalt blue — a colour the victims' families chose. The names of the dead are inscribed there, along with fragments of the thousands of messages strangers left at the station in the days after, in many languages. Overhead, set into the ceiling, are one hundred and ninety-three points of light. One for each.

That's the whole character of this place, held in a few minutes' walk. A room where things grow, and a room of light for the people who didn't come home. Madrid doesn't ask you to choose between them. It just asks that, passing through, you notice both.

tours.title: Plaza de la Villa
tours.shortDescription: Three buildings, three centuries, one small square — a timeline you can take in without moving your feet.
tours.longDescription:
Step off Calle Mayor into the small square on the south side and you are standing in one of the oldest corners of Madrid — older than the boulevards around it, older than the capital itself. When Madrid was a modest Castilian town its council met here, and the square took its name when the king granted the town the title of Noble and Loyal: la villa.

Three buildings frame you and each comes from a different century. The Torre de los Lujanes is fifteenth-century brick and stone, the oldest civil building in the city, and by tradition held the French king François I after his capture at Pavia. The Casa de Cisneros is sixteenth-century Plateresque. The Casa de la Villa, seventeenth-century Habsburg baroque with slate spires, served as Madrid's town hall for more than three hundred years. Most people walk straight past the opening. Turn in.

stops.title: Plaza de la Villa
stops.caption: Step off Calle Mayor, into the small square on the south side, about halfway between Puerta del Sol and the Royal Palace.
stops.transcriptText:
Step off Calle Mayor, into the small square on the south side, about halfway between Puerta del Sol and the Royal Palace. Most people walk straight past the opening. Turn in.

You're standing in one of the oldest squares in Madrid — older than the grand boulevards around it, older than the capital itself. Back when Madrid was a small Castilian town, the council met right here, and the square took its name when the king granted the town the title of Noble and Loyal: la villa, the town. This was the centre of it.

Three buildings frame you, and here's what's worth slowing down for — each comes from a different century, and together they read like a timeline you can take in without moving your feet.

Start with the tower on your left, the Torre de los Lujanes. Fifteenth century, brick and stone, the oldest surviving civil building in the whole city. Tradition says a king of France was held prisoner inside it — Francis the First, captured at the Battle of Pavia in 1525 and brought here. There's almost no evidence for it, but the story has clung to these stones for five hundred years, which tells you how good a story it is.

The building in the middle is the Casa de Cisneros — sixteenth century, delicate carved stonework, the Renaissance arriving in a town about to get much bigger. Look for the little covered bridge linking it to its neighbour, slung over the lane below, so the city's officials could cross without touching the street.

And the third, the Casa de la Villa — seventeenth century, heavier, with dark slate spires, built by the same architect who gave Madrid its Plaza Mayor. This was the town hall.

Three buildings, three centuries — and you can watch the whole climb from village to royal capital just by turning your head.

Here's the quiet part. Madrid governed itself from this square for roughly three hundred years; the city hall only moved out in 2007, across town to a grander palace. So you're standing where the capital grew from, now mostly left to the pigeons and the occasional wedding photo. The boulevards moved on. This stayed.

tours.title: Cuesta de Moyano
tours.shortDescription: Thirty grey-blue wooden huts that fold open into bookshops — Europe's largest standing open-air book fair, here since 1925.
tours.longDescription:
The Cuesta de Moyano is a short sloping pedestrian street between the edge of the Retiro and the Atocha end of the Paseo del Prado, lined on one side with a row of low wooden stalls — shuttered like beach huts when closed, folded open into tiny bookshops when not. There are around thirty of them and they have been doing exactly this since 1925.

This is Madrid's permanent open-air book fair, the largest standing gathering of open-air bookshops in Europe and the place to come for what you cannot find elsewhere: out-of-print titles, first editions, old magazines and maps, the contents of someone's emptied library. Many stalls are run by the children and grandchildren of the people who ran them decades ago. The writer Ramón Gómez de la Serna nicknamed it the Feria del libro viejo — and the name stuck.

stops.title: Cuesta de Moyano
stops.caption: You're on the Cuesta de Moyano — a short, sloping pedestrian street running between the edge of the Retiro and the Atocha end of the Paseo del Prado.
stops.transcriptText:
You're on the Cuesta de Moyano — a short, sloping pedestrian street running between the edge of the Retiro and the Atocha end of the Paseo del Prado. One side of it is lined with a row of low wooden stalls, grey-blue, shuttered up like beach huts when they're closed and folded open into tiny bookshops when they're not. There are around thirty of them, and they've been here, doing exactly this, since 1925.

This is Madrid's permanent open-air book fair — the largest standing gathering of open-air bookshops in Europe, and the place to come for the books you can't find anywhere else. Out-of-print titles, first editions, old magazines and maps, the contents of someone's emptied library. Many of the stalls are run by the children and grandchildren of the people who ran them decades ago. The stall design itself was drawn up by a city architect, Luis Bellido, who also built Madrid's old slaughterhouse.

There's a phrase worth carrying away. Early on, the writer Ramón Gómez de la Serna nicknamed the place the Feria del boquerón — the anchovy fair — because a book here cost roughly what an anchovy cost. Cheap reading for anyone who wanted it, which was the entire idea.

The stalls have a quietly heroic history. They stayed open almost without a break through the Civil War. In the censorship of the years that followed, this slope became a discreet network for the books that weren't supposed to circulate — banned titles passing hand to hand between sellers who trusted their customers. A row of cheap second-hand stalls turned out to be one of the harder things in the city to fully control.

At the top of the slope stands a statue of the novelist Pío Baroja; at the bottom, the politician Claudio Moyano, whose education law gave the street its name. And as of early 2026 the fair is formally recognised as part of the region's living cultural heritage — a tidy thing to happen to a place that has spent a hundred years selling people books for the price of an anchovy.

Browse. It's the only way to use it properly — you're meant to leave with something you weren't looking for.

tours.title: La Rosaleda
tours.shortDescription: Four thousand rose bushes in a quiet ellipse at the far end of the Retiro — a gift from one gardener, planted twice.
tours.longDescription:
If you have found your way here you have left the busy heart of the park behind. La Rosaleda is a neat ellipse tucked into the southern end of the Retiro, ringed by clipped hedges, with two stone fountains and a run of iron arches the climbing roses are trained over. The Fallen Angel statue is a short walk away if you want a landmark to fix your bearings by.

Time of year decides what you get: in May and June it runs at full volume — more than four thousand bushes, some five hundred varieties, scent you could find with your eyes shut. Any other month it is a calm, almost empty geometric green. Around 1915 the city's head gardener, Cecilio Rodríguez, set out to give Madrid a rose garden to rival Paris and travelled there himself to choose the first stock. The Civil War destroyed it. He came back afterwards and planted the whole thing again.

stops.title: La Rosaleda
stops.caption: If you've found your way here, you've left the busy heart of the park behind.
stops.transcriptText:
If you've found your way here, you've left the busy heart of the park behind. You're in the Rosaleda — the rose garden — a neat ellipse tucked into the southern end of the Retiro, ringed by clipped hedges, with two stone fountains and a series of iron arches the climbing roses are trained up and over. The statue of the Fallen Angel is a short walk away, if you want a landmark to fix your bearings by.

Time of year decides what you get. Come in May or June and the place is at full volume — more than four thousand rose bushes, something like five hundred varieties, scent you could find with your eyes shut, the arches heavy with bloom. Any other month it's a calm, geometric green space, almost empty, which has its own quiet appeal.

The garden is younger than it looks, and it has a good origin story. Around 1915 the city's head gardener, Cecilio Rodríguez, set out to give Madrid a rose garden to rival the famous ones in Paris. He travelled there himself to select the first roses — and chose the worst possible moment, because the First World War broke out while he was away and he had a hard time getting himself and his plants home. He laid the garden out on a spot with its own buried history: it had held a private greenhouse belonging to the Marquis of Salamanca, and before that a pond that froze hard enough each winter for people to skate on it.

The roses he brought back were lost in the Civil War, which left little of the park untouched. The garden was replanted in 1941 — four thousand bushes again — and carefully restored in the decades since. So what you're looking at is a faithful remake of one man's idea, twice over.

It's an easy place to underrate: a rose garden in the corner of a famous park. But it's one of the most deliberate, least hurried things in the Retiro — built, lost, and rebuilt, simply so the city would have somewhere lovely to stand and breathe. Take your time in it.

tours.title: Jardines de Sabatini
tours.shortDescription: The formal garden on the palace's north flank — clipped, symmetrical, and not designed by the man it's named after.
tours.longDescription:
The Jardines de Sabatini run along the northern side of the Royal Palace: all geometry, with clipped hedges in neat beds, a long rectangular pool, marble statues at intervals and the palace looming behind. It feels far older than it is. Despite the name, Francesco Sabatini did not design the garden — he designed the royal stables that stood on this spot. The stables were cleared and the garden laid out in their place in the 1930s; it opened to the public only in 1978.

Several of the statues lined up here are the same royal figures carved for the palace roofline and never hoisted. Come at the end of the day, when the low sun runs along the palace's north face — and, if you have time, compare it with the wild, unclipped Campo del Moro on the other side of the building.

stops.title: Jardines de Sabatini
stops.caption: You're at the edge of the Jardines de Sabatini, the formal garden along the north side of the Royal Palace — and this stop is really about two gardens, because the palace has a green flank on this side and a very different one around the back, and the contrast between them is the whole point.
stops.transcriptText:
You're at the edge of the Jardines de Sabatini, the formal garden along the north side of the Royal Palace — and this stop is really about two gardens, because the palace has a green flank on this side and a very different one around the back, and the contrast between them is the whole point.

Start with where you are. Sabatini is all geometry: clipped hedges in neat beds, a long rectangular pool, marble statues at intervals, the palace looming behind. It feels older than it is. Despite the Italian name — Francesco Sabatini, Charles the Third's architect — Sabatini didn't design this garden; he designed the royal stables that used to stand on this spot. The stables were cleared and the garden laid out in their place in the 1930s, and it opened to the public only in 1978. The statues lined up here are an odd detail: several were originally carved for the roofline of the palace itself, and never made it up there.

Now picture the other side. Around the back of the palace, dropping toward the river, is the Campo del Moro — the Field of the Moor. It's everything Sabatini isn't: not geometric but romantic, a wooded landscape of winding paths, big old trees, two fine fountains and, wandering loose among them, peacocks. Its name reaches back to 1109, when a Muslim army camped on this slope to besiege the fortress that then stood where the palace is now.

So the crown gave itself two kinds of green: a formal parade-ground of a garden out front, to be seen from the palace windows, and a wild romantic park behind, to disappear into. One is for show; the other for escape.

Both are free, both are quiet by Madrid standards, and Sabatini in particular is one of the best places in the centre to watch the sun set behind the palace. Pick the mood you're in — order or wilderness — and the palace will give you either one.

tours.title: Madrid de los Austrias
tours.shortDescription: A short, dense loop through Habsburg old Madrid — the town that was told, almost overnight, to become the capital of a world empire.
tours.longDescription:
Madrid did not grow into a capital slowly, the way most great cities did. In 1561 Philip II pointed at a middling town of perhaps thirty thousand people, with no river port and no Roman past, and decided the court would live there from now on. The town had to become a capital in a hurry, and the bones of that scramble are still all around you.

That is what makes this walk short and dense: everything the Habsburgs built sits within a few hundred metres of itself. Roughly 1.1 flat kilometres from the exact centre of Spain, through the great enclosed plaza where the city performed itself and a glowing iron-and-glass market, to the quiet civic square where the council met — and out at the vast stone palace and cathedral that replaced the fortress it all began with.

stops.title: Madrid de los Austrias — Introduction
stops.caption: This is the oldest part of Madrid — the part locals call Madrid de los Austrias, Madrid of the Austrias, after the Habsburg dynasty that turned a modest Castilian town into the capital of a world empire.
stops.transcriptText:
This is the oldest part of Madrid — the part locals call Madrid de los Austrias, Madrid of the Austrias, after the Habsburg dynasty that turned a modest Castilian town into the capital of a world empire.

Here's the thing to hold onto as you walk. Madrid didn't grow into a capital slowly, over centuries, the way most great cities did. It was made one, almost overnight. In 1561, King Philip the Second pointed at a middling town of perhaps thirty thousand people, with no river port and no Roman past, and decided the court would live here from now on. The town had to become a capital in a hurry — and the bones of that scramble are still all around you.

That's what makes this walk short and dense. Everything the Habsburgs built sits within a few hundred metres of itself: the central point of the whole country, the great enclosed plaza where the city performed itself, the quiet civic heart, and at the far end, the hilltop where the royal castle stood until it burned. We'll end where the dynasty did — on the ashes of the Habsburg Alcázar, looking at the palace the next family built on top of it.

It's a flat, tight loop, fifteen minutes of walking if you never stopped, though you will. Five stops, heading west across the old town.

We start at the exact centre. Make your way to Puerta del Sol.

stops.title: Puerta del Sol (Kilometre Zero)
stops.caption: You're standing in Puerta del Sol, and more precisely, you're standing at the centre of Spain.
stops.transcriptText:
You're standing in Puerta del Sol, and more precisely, you're standing at the centre of Spain. Find the curved building on the south side, the one with the clock tower and the weathervane — that's the old post office, the Casa de Correos, now the seat of the regional government. On the ground in front of it, set into the paving, there's a small stone slab marked Kilómetro Cero. Every numbered road in the country is measured from that exact point, so when a Spaniard says a town is four hundred kilometres from Madrid, this slab is what they're counting from.

This is the centre of the centre, and it has been the city's gathering place for as long as the city has mattered. Crowds come here for everything — protests, celebrations, football wins — and on the last night of the year the whole country watches this square on television to eat twelve grapes with the twelve strokes of that clock, one grape a stroke, for luck. They've done it since 1962.

Before you move on, find the statue at the top of the square: a bear, reaching up into a strawberry tree. It's the emblem of Madrid, lifted straight off the city's coat of arms, and people have agreed to meet "at the bear" for generations.

So this is where the capital begins, literally — kilometre zero of the country Philip the Second chose to govern from here. From this point the Habsburgs built outward, so we'll walk the way the city grew: west, into the heart of their Madrid. Leave the square near the bear and make for Plaza Mayor.

stops.title: Plaza Mayor
stops.caption: Come through one of the archways into Plaza Mayor, and stop as soon as the square opens out around you.
stops.transcriptText:
Come through one of the archways into Plaza Mayor, and stop as soon as the square opens out around you. Notice that it's completely enclosed — nine arched entrances, and otherwise an unbroken wall of buildings four storeys high, wrapping the whole space. That's the key to the place. This isn't a square that simply happened over time; it's a room without a roof, designed all at once.

Philip the Third commissioned it, the architect Juan Gómez de Mora laid it out, and it was finished in 1619. Look up: two hundred and thirty-seven balconies face inward. They face inward because the whole plaza was built as a stage, with the city as the audience. From those balconies Madrid watched everything that mattered — royal proclamations, the crowning of kings, markets, bullfights, plays. The grandest building, on the north side with the painted façade and two towers, is the Casa de la Panadería, the old bakery, and its central balcony was the royal box, where the king and queen sat above it all.

It wasn't only pageantry. During the Inquisition this square was also where the Church staged its public trials and sentences, in front of those same crowds. It's part of the history of the place, and worth knowing as you stand in it.

But mostly what this square was built to do was gather people and impress them — to make a not-very-old capital feel permanent and grand. Stand in the middle, turn once, and you can feel it still working.

The man on the horse in the centre is Philip the Third, the king who ordered all of it. When you're ready, leave by the southwest corner and head down the short slope — we're going to the market hall just outside the old walls, the Mercado de San Miguel.

stops.title: Mercado de San Miguel
stops.caption: Just outside the southwest corner of Plaza Mayor, you'll find a market hall made of iron and glass — the Mercado de San Miguel.
stops.transcriptText:
Just outside the southwest corner of Plaza Mayor, you'll find a market hall made of iron and glass — the Mercado de San Miguel. Walk up to it.

For most of Madrid's history this was an ordinary neighbourhood food market, one of dozens, the place you came for fish and vegetables. The building in front of you went up in 1916, an elegant cage of cast iron and glass in the style of the great covered markets of that age — and it's the last survivor of its kind in the city, the others long since pulled down.

By the early two-thousands it was nearly derelict. Then, in 2009, instead of knocking it down, the city did something cleverer: it reopened the market as a place to eat rather than to shop. Today the old iron stalls sell oysters and croquettes and small glasses of wine, and you graze your way around the room. It's frankly a tourist scene now, busy and not cheap — but the building itself is the real thing, and the easiest way to picture what every Madrid market once looked like is to stand under this roof and look up at the ironwork.

Have something if you like, or just pass through. When you come out, we leave the crowds behind — a short way west along Calle Mayor the noise drops, and we reach the quietest and oldest square on this walk: Plaza de la Villa.

stops.title: Plaza de la Villa
stops.caption: Here, off the north side of Calle Mayor, is Plaza de la Villa — and the contrast with the market you just left is the whole point.
stops.transcriptText:
Here, off the north side of Calle Mayor, is Plaza de la Villa — and the contrast with the market you just left is the whole point. It's small, quiet, paved in stone, easy to walk straight past. It is also one of the oldest squares in Madrid, and for roughly three hundred years it was the city's civic heart: this is where Madrid governed itself.

Three buildings frame you, each from a different century, and together they tell the story of a town becoming a capital. On your left, the brick tower — the Torre de los Lujanes — is fifteenth century, the oldest surviving civil building in the city, from back when Madrid was nobody's capital at all. The building in the middle, with the fine carved stonework, is sixteenth century: the Renaissance arriving as the town began to swell. And the heavier one with the dark slate spires is the old town hall, seventeenth century, built by Juan Gómez de Mora — the same architect who gave you Plaza Mayor a few minutes ago.

So you've now met Gómez de Mora twice on one short walk, which tells you how small the circle of Habsburg Madrid really was: a handful of squares, a handful of builders, one compact town carrying an empire.

The city ran itself from here until 2007, when the government finally moved across town. Then this square went quiet — which is how you find it now.

From here, Calle Mayor runs the last stretch west, gently downhill, to where the whole walk has been heading: the royal palace, and the cathedral facing it. Follow it down to the open courtyard, the Plaza de la Armería.

stops.title: Palacio Real & the Almudena
stops.caption: You've arrived at the Plaza de la Armería, the broad courtyard with the palace on one side and the cathedral on the other.
stops.transcriptText:
You've arrived at the Plaza de la Armería, the broad courtyard with the palace on one side and the cathedral on the other. Stand where you can see both. This is where the walk has been heading, and it's where Habsburg Madrid ends — on the exact spot where it began.

Because there was a castle here long before this palace. The Habsburgs ran their empire from a sprawling old fortress on this hilltop, the Alcázar — the building Philip the Second moved into when he made Madrid the capital. It stood for centuries. Then, on Christmas Eve in 1734, it caught fire and burned for four days. So much was lost that silver melted in the heat; one of the things carried out in time, reportedly thrown from a window to save it, was Velázquez's Las Meninas — which is why you can still see it in the Prado today.

By then the Habsburgs were gone, and a new dynasty, the Bourbons, held the throne. They built what you're looking at now: an enormous stone palace, deliberately fireproof, with no wood in its structure. It has more than three thousand rooms and is the largest royal palace in Western Europe. The king still works here and receives heads of state here — but he doesn't live here; the family long ago moved to somewhere smaller and more private. The palace is kept for the state, and for you to walk through.

Now turn to the cathedral, the Almudena. Notice that it doesn't try to tower over the palace — its dome sits low, and its front echoes the palace's own pale stonework. That was on purpose: when it was finally finished, the designers held it back deliberately so it wouldn't outshine the king's house across the square. And "finished" is a generous word — Madrid argued about, began, and abandoned this cathedral for more than a hundred years, only consecrating it in 1993. A capital made overnight in 1561 took until almost the twenty-first century to give itself a cathedral.

That's the whole story of this walk, standing in one courtyard: the austere Habsburg town that was handed an empire, and the grand Bourbon city that rebuilt on its ashes. Two dynasties, one hilltop. Stay a while — it's a good place to watch the light move across the stone, and you've earned the view.

tours.title: Paseo del Arte: the Golden Triangle
tours.shortDescription: One boulevard, three of the great art museums on earth — and eight hundred years of painting between them.
tours.longDescription:
The Paseo del Prado is a wide, tree-lined boulevard running north to south through the centre of Madrid, and the stretch of it you walk here is known as the golden triangle of art: the Prado, the Thyssen-Bornemisza and the Reina Sofía, three collections within a few minutes of each other that between them cover roughly eight hundred years of painting.

The boulevard is the point as much as the museums are. In the 1700s Charles III — the king Madrid still half-jokingly calls its best mayor — set out to turn this avenue into a promenade of science and learning, lined with fountains, a botanical garden and what is now the Prado. It worked so well that in 2021 the whole axis was named a World Heritage Site under the title 'the Landscape of Light'. Flat, about 1.3 kilometres, downhill all the way.

stops.title: Paseo del Arte: the Golden Triangle — Introduction
stops.caption: You're about to walk one street, and on it, three of the great art museums on earth.
stops.transcriptText:
You're about to walk one street, and on it, three of the great art museums on earth. This is the Paseo del Prado, a wide, tree-lined boulevard running north to south through the centre of Madrid, and the stretch you'll walk is known as the golden triangle of art: the Prado, the Thyssen-Bornemisza, and the Reina Sofía — three collections within a few minutes of each other that between them cover roughly eight hundred years of painting.

The boulevard itself is the point as much as the museums. In the seventeen-hundreds, King Charles the Third — the king Madrid still half-jokingly calls its best mayor — set out to turn this avenue into a promenade of science and learning, lined with fountains, a botanical garden, and what is now the Prado. It worked so well that in 2021 the whole axis, boulevard and park together, was named a World Heritage Site, under the lovely title "the Landscape of Light."

A word of honesty before we start. You cannot do all three of these museums in one day and still enjoy them. Treat this walk as the thread that strings them together: do the fountains and the buildings now, and pick one museum to go inside, or come back another day. It's flat, it's straight, and it's about twenty minutes end to end without stopping.

We'll go north to south. Start at the grand fountain at the top of the boulevard, the one everyone photographs: the Fuente de Cibeles.

stops.title: Fuente de Cibeles
stops.caption: Stand back far enough to take in the whole fountain.
stops.transcriptText:
Stand back far enough to take in the whole fountain. At the centre, a serene woman rides a chariot pulled by two lions: she's Cybele, a goddess the Romans tied to the earth and to cities, and she has been the unofficial symbol of Madrid since the seventeen-eighties, when Charles the Third's architects set her here.

Now look past her at the building behind — the white one that looks like a wedding cake crossed with a cathedral. People assume it's a palace. It isn't. It was built, only a little over a century ago, as the city's main post office: a post office so grand that Madrid eventually decided it was wasted on stamps and moved the city government in instead. Today it's the town hall, and you can ride up to a viewing terrace inside for one of the best high views in the centre.

Here's a small thing worth knowing while you're standing here. This fountain is where one of the city's two great football clubs comes to celebrate its titles, the players climbing up to wrap the goddess in a scarf. Which club, and which fountain, we'll come to at the next stop — because the other half of that story is waiting just down the boulevard.

Walk south, down the Paseo del Prado, to the second fountain: Neptune, the Fuente de Neptuno.

stops.title: Fuente de Neptuno
stops.caption: This is Neptune — Neptuno — Roman god of the sea, carved in white marble, riding a chariot drawn by horses with fishtails, trident in hand.
stops.transcriptText:
This is Neptune — Neptuno — Roman god of the sea, carved in white marble, riding a chariot drawn by horses with fishtails, trident in hand. He belongs to the same scheme as Cibeles up the road: Charles the Third's architects dressed the whole boulevard with fountains like these in the seventeen-eighties, a matched set of gods to make a promenade feel like a stage.

And here's the football story I promised. Cibeles, behind you, is where Real Madrid celebrates. Neptune, in front of you, is where Atlético de Madrid celebrates — the city's other great club, traditionally the underdog. So the two fountains have become the two clubs' shrines, a few hundred metres apart on the same street. The detail people love is that it didn't start this way round: the allegiances were once reversed, the clubs effectively swapping fountains over the years, which is the kind of thing Madrid finds very funny and outsiders find baffling.

Mostly, though, Neptune is your signpost. You're standing at the hinge of the golden triangle now — within a two-minute walk of here are two of the three great museums, facing each other across the boulevard.

Look across and slightly uphill to the long, columned building on the far side. That's the Prado, the heart of the whole walk. Cross over to it.

stops.title: Museo del Prado
stops.caption: Here it is: the Museo del Prado, the heart of the golden triangle and one of the greatest collections of paintings anywhere.
stops.transcriptText:
Here it is: the Museo del Prado, the heart of the golden triangle and one of the greatest collections of paintings anywhere. It opened in 1819 — and here's a surprise: the building wasn't designed as a museum at all. The architect Juan de Villanueva drew it up as a hall of natural history, a home for fossils and specimens. Art only moved in later. So the Prado is, at bottom, a science building that became a temple of painting.

What truly sets it apart is what it is at heart: not a survey of world art, but the private collection of the Spanish crown, opened to the public. For three centuries the kings of Spain bought what they liked — and they had remarkable taste and very deep pockets. So you don't get a little of everything here; you get the best of what Spanish and court painters did, in extraordinary depth.

Three things to hunt for if you go in. Velázquez's Las Meninas, the painting other painters travel here just to stand in front of — a portrait that quietly puts you, the viewer, in the king's place. Goya's "black paintings," the nightmares he painted straight onto the walls of his own house in old age. And from far earlier, Bosch's Garden of Earthly Delights, a five-hundred-year-old triptych so strange it still looks like it was finished yesterday.

That's the Prado: not the world's attic, but one family's eye, across three centuries. When you've had your fill — or made your peace with coming back — cross back over the boulevard to the lower, quieter building opposite: the Thyssen-Bornemisza.

stops.title: Museo Thyssen-Bornemisza
stops.caption: This lower, pinkish building is the Thyssen-Bornemisza, and it's the museum that makes the triangle work.
stops.transcriptText:
This lower, pinkish building is the Thyssen-Bornemisza, and it's the museum that makes the triangle work. Here's why. The Prado, as you just saw, is the crown's taste — deep, but with gaps, because kings bought what kings liked. The Reina Sofía, where we'll finish, is mostly modern. In between sits everything else, and that everything is what this collection is.

It was assembled not by a country but by a family — two generations of Thyssen-Bornemiszas, industrialists, who spent the twentieth century buying privately on a scale that normally only nations manage. The result fills in exactly what the Prado skips: early Italian gold-ground panels, Dutch interiors, the Impressionists, German Expressionism, even American painting and Pop art. Walk it from the top floor down and you walk straight through the history of Western painting, in order, almost without a gap.

The gift detail is how it got here. For decades this was one of the great private collections in the world, kept in Switzerland. In 1993 the Spanish state bought it outright — a coup that completed Madrid's triangle in a single stroke, and is still talked about as one of the great museum deals of the century.

So: the crown's eye behind you, a family's eye here, and one more to go — the modern one. From the front of the Thyssen, carry on south down the boulevard a few hundred metres, to a curious brick building that seems to float just above the ground: CaixaForum.

stops.title: CaixaForum
stops.caption: Stop in front of CaixaForum and give yourself a moment to work out what's odd about it, because something is.
stops.transcriptText:
Stop in front of CaixaForum and give yourself a moment to work out what's odd about it, because something is. The heavy brick building appears to hover — its whole ground floor has been carved away, so the mass of it rests on shadow, with no visible base. That's deliberate. The Swiss architects Herzog and de Meuron — the same pair who turned a London power station into the Tate Modern — took an old electricity station that stood here, stripped it back to its brick shell, lifted it onto a hidden support, and crowned it with a jagged top of rusted steel.

Now turn to the wall on its left and look at the green. That entire flank of the neighbouring building is alive: a vertical garden, four storeys of living plants growing straight up the wall with no soil at all, fed through a kind of felt skin. It was designed by the botanist Patrick Blanc, it was the first of its kind in Spain when it opened, and it has been quietly growing there, changing colour with the seasons, ever since.

Entry to the square, and often the building, is free — which makes this the easy, generous note on the walk, the bit you can stumble into without a ticket.

It's also the boulevard making a point. The same street that began with Charles the Third's eighteenth-century fountains now floats a brick box on shadow and grows a garden up a wall. The art turned modern; so did the architecture.

One museum left, and it's the heaviest of them all. Keep going south to the far end of the boulevard, toward Atocha station, to the Reina Sofía.

stops.title: Museo Reina Sofía
stops.caption: You've reached the end of the boulevard and the end of the walk: the Reina Sofía, Madrid's museum of modern art.
stops.transcriptText:
You've reached the end of the boulevard and the end of the walk: the Reina Sofía, Madrid's museum of modern art. People come here for one painting, and you should too. Inside hangs Picasso's Guernica.

It's enormous — nearly eight metres of black, white, and grey: a screaming horse, a fallen fighter, a woman with her head thrown back, and a bare bulb like an eye burning over it all. Picasso painted it in 1937, in Paris, in a matter of weeks, after German and Italian warplanes — fighting for Franco — flattened the Basque town of Guernica in a single afternoon. It was one of the first times the world had seen a town erased from the air, and Picasso turned that horror into perhaps the most powerful anti-war painting ever made.

Then comes the part that makes standing here matter. Picasso refused to let Guernica come to Spain while Franco ruled: it would only come home, he said, when the country was free again. So for over forty years it lived in exile, mostly at the Museum of Modern Art in New York. Franco died in 1975; democracy returned; and in 1981 the painting finally crossed the Atlantic, arriving for good at the Reina Sofía in the early nineteen-nineties. The painting that came home.

And it still isn't finished arguing. Even now there's a quiet, unresolved tug-of-war over where it truly belongs — whether it should ever travel to the Basque town whose name it carries, where the bombing happened and where it has never once been shown. The museum says the canvas is too old and fragile to move. Others say that's a convenient reason to keep a national treasure in the capital. You don't have to settle it; you only have to know, standing in front of it, that this is a painting people still fight over because it still means something.

That's the whole boulevard, end to end: the crown's collection, a family's collection, a power station reborn, and finally one painting that crossed an ocean to come home and still won't sit quietly. Take your time in here. Of everything on this walk, this is the room to be unhurried in.

tours.title: El Retiro: The Garden Handed to Everyone
tours.shortDescription: From a king's triumphal gate to a public book market — a royal indulgence handed over, piece by piece, until it belonged to everyone.
tours.longDescription:
For most of its life this park was not yours. The Buen Retiro began in the 1630s as a private pleasure ground for Philip IV — a second palace on the edge of the city, with a lake dug for staged naval battles and gardens kept for a court that did not share them. The public got in on sufferance, on the right days, dressed correctly. Only in 1868, after a revolution pushed out a queen, were the gates thrown open for good.

That is the thread of this walk. About 1.8 easy, flat kilometres: a king's gate stranded in the traffic, a lake where anyone can now rent a boat beneath a monument built for a monarch, a glass palace raised for an empire and now free to wander, a rose garden one gardener built as a gift to the city, and a row of book stalls at the bottom of the hill.

stops.title: El Retiro: The Garden Handed to Everyone — Introduction
stops.caption: For most of its life, this park was not yours.
stops.transcriptText:
For most of its life, this park was not yours.

The Buen Retiro began in the sixteen-thirties as a private pleasure ground for Philip the Fourth — a second palace on the edge of the city, with a lake dug for staged naval battles and gardens kept for a court that did not share them. The public got in on sufferance, on the right days, dressed correctly. It was only in 1868, after a revolution pushed out a queen, that the gates were thrown open for good and the royal garden became the city's.

That's the thread of this walk: a private royal indulgence, handed over piece by piece until it belonged to everyone. We'll start at a king's triumphal gate stranded in the traffic, walk down to a lake where anyone can now rent a boat beneath a monument built for a king, step inside a glass palace raised for an empire and now free to wander, pass a rose garden one gardener built as a gift to the city, and finish just outside the railings at a row of book stalls where, for a century, a book cost about the same as an anchovy.

It's an easy walk — flat park paths most of the way, shade in summer, a gentle slope down to the books at the end. Start at the northern corner, at the Puerta de Alcalá. We'll head into the park from there.

stops.title: Puerta de Alcalá
stops.caption: You're at the Plaza de la Independencia, and the gate marooned in the middle of the roundabout is the Puerta de Alcalá.
stops.transcriptText:
You're at the Plaza de la Independencia, and the gate marooned in the middle of the roundabout is the Puerta de Alcalá. Find a spot on one of the corners where you can take in the whole thing — five openings, pale granite, lions and trophies along the top, traffic streaming around it on every side.

Charles the Third put it here in 1778. He had come from ruling Naples to ruling Spain, he thought Madrid was a shabby capital for a great empire, and he set about fixing that — fountains, boulevards, this gate. It marked the eastern edge of the city, the road in from Alcalá de Henares, and it was built to impress whoever arrived: a triumphal arch with no battle behind it, just the confidence of a king who wanted the entrance to his city to look like Rome.

Now look at the two main faces. They aren't the same — different arrangements of columns and carving on each side, because the design was argued over and the architect, Sabatini, more or less built both versions at once. Most people walk past without ever noticing they're looking at two facades on one gate.

What's changed is everything around it. The city long ago swallowed the edge this gate marked; the threshold of Madrid now stands on an island in a roundabout, circled by cars, belonging to no one and everyone. A grand royal gesture, quietly demoted to a traffic landmark — which is a fitting way to begin, because the whole garden ahead went the same way.

From here, cross into the park and walk down toward the water. We're heading for the lake, and the king on horseback who watches over it.

stops.title: The Estanque & Alfonso XII
stops.caption: You should be standing at the edge of the big rectangular lake — the Estanque — with a great curved colonnade rising on the far side and a king cast in bronze on horseback at its centre.
stops.transcriptText:
You should be standing at the edge of the big rectangular lake — the Estanque — with a great curved colonnade rising on the far side and a king cast in bronze on horseback at its centre. That's Alfonso the Twelfth, and the monument is deliberately enormous: a half circle of stone columns wrapped around the water like an open arm, paid for by public subscription after he died young.

Here's the thing to hold in your head while you look at it. This lake was dug for a king's amusement — Philip the Fourth had it made in the sixteen-thirties for staged naval battles and floating concerts, a private toy on a scale most cities couldn't have managed. For two centuries it stayed essentially royal. Then, in 1868, the crown lost the park for good and it passed to the city.

So look at what's on the water now. Boats — dozens of them, anyone can rent one by the half hour, couples pulling badly on the oars, children trailing their hands in the green water, all of it directly beneath a monument the size of a cathedral front built to glorify a dead king. Nobody planned that contrast, and nobody could have designed it better: imperial grandeur as the backdrop for a cheap afternoon on a boat.

That's the whole park in one view — the grand gesture and the ordinary pleasure sharing the same frame, the second having quietly inherited the first.

When you've taken it in, keep walking south, deeper into the park along the tree-lined paths. There's a building ahead made almost entirely of glass, and it's worth seeing up close — the Palacio de Cristal.

stops.title: Palacio de Cristal
stops.caption: In front of you is a pavilion made of glass and iron, sitting at the edge of a small pond that doubles it in reflection.
stops.transcriptText:
In front of you is a pavilion made of glass and iron, sitting at the edge of a small pond that doubles it in reflection. The Palacio de Cristal — the Crystal Palace — a great greenhouse of a building, light pouring straight through it, ducks on the pond, turtles if you're lucky.

It was built in 1887, and it's worth knowing what for. That year Madrid held an exhibition devoted to the Philippines, then a Spanish colony, and this glass house was raised to display what had been brought over from the islands — including, in a practice common to such exhibitions of the time, people. That part of its history is real and it isn't comfortable; the building is beautiful, and it was made to put a colony on show. Both things are true, and worth holding together rather than choosing between.

What it is now is something else entirely. The glass house belongs to the Reina Sofía museum, and it's used for contemporary art — large installations that change through the year, the kind of work that needs a flood of natural light and a lot of empty air around it. There's no ticket. You step in off a park path, into whatever an artist has filled it with this season, and walk out again.

A pavilion built to exhibit an empire, now a bright empty room anyone can enter for nothing — the same democratic turn the whole park keeps taking.

When you're ready, head south and west, toward the quieter side of the park. There's a garden ahead that one man spent years getting right — the Rosaleda, the rose garden.

stops.title: La Rosaleda
stops.caption: This is the Rosaleda, the rose garden — an ellipse of beds and clipped hedges with two fountains and a run of metal arches that the climbing roses are trained up and over.
stops.transcriptText:
This is the Rosaleda, the rose garden — an ellipse of beds and clipped hedges with two fountains and a run of metal arches that the climbing roses are trained up and over. If you've come in May or June you've timed it perfectly; the rest of the year it's a quiet, pretty corner you'll have largely to yourself.

It exists because of one man. Around 1915 the city's head gardener, Cecilio Rodríguez, decided Madrid should have a proper rose garden to rival the famous ones in Paris, and he went to Paris himself to choose the first roses. His timing was terrible — the First World War broke out while he was away, and he had a genuinely hard journey getting himself and his roses back to Spain. He planted them here anyway, on a spot that had held a private greenhouse and, before that, a pond people skated on in winter.

Then the garden was destroyed — the Civil War tore through the park and the roses with it. It was replanted in 1941, more than four thousand bushes, hundreds of varieties, and that's essentially what you're standing in now: a thing built once as a gift to the city, lost, and deliberately made again.

It's a small idea with a lot behind it — that ordinary people should have somewhere beautiful to walk for nothing, and that it's worth a gardener crossing a continent in wartime to get it right.

From here it's a short, gentle walk down toward the southwest corner of the park and out through the gates. Just beyond them, on a sloping street, is the last stop — the book stalls of the Cuesta de Moyano.

stops.title: Cuesta de Moyano
stops.caption: You've come out of the park, and you're standing at the top of a short sloping street lined on one side with a row of low wooden stalls — grey-blue, shuttered like little cabins, each one a second-hand bookshop.
stops.transcriptText:
You've come out of the park, and you're standing at the top of a short sloping street lined on one side with a row of low wooden stalls — grey-blue, shuttered like little cabins, each one a second-hand bookshop. This is the Cuesta de Moyano, and it has been exactly this, in more or less this spot, since 1925.

Around thirty stalls, open every day, many of them run for generations by the same families. They sell old books, out-of-print books, first editions, faded magazines, maps — the things you can't easily find anywhere else. There's a statue of the writer Pío Baroja near the top of the slope, and the politician it's named for, Claudio Moyano, at the bottom; he passed the law that first put schools across Spain.

Here's the detail to take away. In its early years a writer nicknamed this the Feria del boquerón — the anchovy fair — because a book here cost about what an anchovy cost. That was the whole point: reading made cheap enough for anyone. Through the Civil War the stalls barely closed, and in the censored years that followed, this slope quietly became a place to find the books you weren't supposed to read.

It's still here, still cheap, still open in the rain — and as of early 2026 it's formally protected, recognised as part of the city's living heritage.

Which is a fitting place to end. We started at a king's gate and a king's lake, walked through a palace built to show off an empire, and we finish on a public slope where the city's idea of a luxury is a row of cheap books anyone can stop and buy. The garden was handed to everyone; so, in its own way, was this. Stay a while. Browse something you didn't come for.

tours.title: Royal Madrid: The Ring of Green
tours.shortDescription: A circuit of the palace and the landscaped ground wrapped around it — ending at a 2,000-year-old Egyptian temple, for the sunset.
tours.longDescription:
A palace is only the hard centre of a monarchy; the soft part is the green it keeps around it. This walk circles the seat of the Spanish crown but spends most of its time in the gardens and squares wrapped around it — a formal garden to the north, a wild one to the west, a sculpted square to the east: a ring of green insulating the crown from the city.

About 1.4 kilometres, easy, with a gentle uphill final leg. It starts at the palace forecourt, takes in the cathedral that had to be built without upstaging it, rounds the eastern side to the opera house and its line of demoted stone kings, and passes through the Sabatini gardens before finishing on the far edge at something the crown never built and could never have imagined.

stops.title: Royal Madrid: The Ring of Green — Introduction
stops.caption: A palace is only the hard centre of a monarchy.
stops.transcriptText:
A palace is only the hard centre of a monarchy. The soft part is the green it keeps around it.

This short walk circles the seat of the Spanish crown — the Royal Palace — but it spends most of its time in the gardens and squares wrapped around it. That's the idea worth carrying: the monarchy didn't just build itself a vast stone house, it surrounded that house on every side with landscaped ground — a formal garden to the north, a wild one to the west, a sculpted square to the east — a ring of green insulating the crown from the city. We're going to walk that ring, and finish on its far edge at something the crown never built and could never have imagined: a genuine ancient Egyptian temple, two thousand years old, set up on a hilltop to watch the sun go down.

So: we start at the palace, take in the cathedral that had to be built without upstaging it, round the eastern side to the opera house and its square of statue-kings, climb to the formal gardens on the north flank, and walk on up to the temple for sunset.

It's tightly clustered and easy — everything but the final stretch is within a few minutes' stroll, and the last leg is a gentle rise. Begin in the great paved forecourt on the south side of the palace, the Plaza de la Armería, where you can see the full front of the building.

stops.title: Palacio Real (Plaza de la Armería)
stops.caption: You're in the Plaza de la Armería, the wide paved court on the south side, with the full front of the Royal Palace rising ahead of you — pale stone, rows of columns, the whole thing balanced and severe and very large.
stops.transcriptText:
You're in the Plaza de la Armería, the wide paved court on the south side, with the full front of the Royal Palace rising ahead of you — pale stone, rows of columns, the whole thing balanced and severe and very large. By floor area it's the biggest royal palace in Western Europe, thousands of rooms behind that façade.
