The hunting medallions were carved for Hadrian; the figures along the top are captives from Trajan's wars; the attic panels honoured Marcus Aurelius — and the faces of those earlier emperors were recut into Constantine's. A brand-new ruler from the military frontier, wrapping himself in an anthology of better centuries. Scholars still argue whether that was propaganda or simply the best sculpture available. In Rome, it could comfortably be both.

And then the inscription. It credits the victory to "the inspiration of the divinity" — and it never says which divinity. This was the moment Constantine was turning toward Christianity while most of Rome still held to the old gods, and the Senate, needing to please everyone, chose a phrase each side could read its own way. An empire changing its religion, hedging its bets in marble.

The arch survived the Middle Ages the Roman way — by being useful: a powerful family absorbed it into their fortress, and the fortress kept it standing.

Before you go, look once more at the faces in the medallions and panels, and remember whose heads they used to be. Nothing here is quite what it says it is — which may be the most Roman thing about it.

tours.title: Ancient Rome
tours.shortDescription: A kilometre and a half, and roughly a thousand years.
tours.longDescription: From the largest building the Romans ever raised to the hill where their city was born — by way of a triumphal arch, the Forum, and a column carved like a comic strip. The route makes one argument over and over: Rome doesn't preserve its past so much as reuse it, relabel it, and keep it in service. Flat until a gentle climb at the end; give it an hour and a half at a stroll.

stops.title: Introduction
stops.caption: This walk covers about a kilometre and a half, and roughly a thousand years.
stops.transcriptText:
This walk covers about a kilometre and a half, and roughly a thousand years. It begins at the largest building the Romans ever put up and ends on the hill where their city was born — and along the way, it makes one argument over and over: Rome doesn't preserve its past so much as reuse it, relabel it, and keep it in service.

The route is simple. From the Colosseum you'll round its flank to a marble arch, then walk the long straight boulevard called Via dei Fori Imperiali, with the Roman Forum opening up beside you, to a column carved like a comic strip — and finish with a climb up a ramped staircase to the top of the Capitoline Hill. The ground is flat until that final climb, and the climb is gentle. One honest note: the boulevard still carries buses and taxis along part of its length, so use the crossings; the pavements on both sides are wide, and the walking is easy.

Give it an hour and a half at a stroll, longer if the Forum railings catch you — they usually do.

Start on the north side of the Colosseum, the side facing the Metro station, far enough back that you can see the full curve of the wall. That's where we begin: with the building every stadium on earth is still quietly copying.

stops.title: The Colosseum
stops.caption: You should be on the north side of the Colosseum, the flat open stretch between the amphitheatre and the Metro station, looking at the great outer wall where it still rises to its full height.
stops.transcriptText:
You should be on the north side of the Colosseum, the flat open stretch between the amphitheatre and the Metro station, looking at the great outer wall where it still rises to its full height.

Look above the ground-level arches. Carved over each one, if you find the right stretch of wall, is a Roman numeral — XXIII, XXIV, XXV, still legible after nineteen centuries. Those are gate numbers. The building had eighty entrances, seventy-six of them numbered, and your ticket — a shard of pottery or bone — told you which gate, which staircase, which level. Some fifty thousand people could find their seats in minutes and empty out even faster, through passages the architects called vomitoria, which meant exactly what it sounds like: the building disgorging its crowd.

That's the thing to hold onto here, because everyone talks about what the Colosseum staged and almost no one talks about how it worked. This was crowd engineering, solved in the first century — the numbered gates, the ticketing that matched them, the one-way circulation — and it worked so well that when the modern world started building stadiums again, it didn't improve on the system. It copied it. The arena you last watched football in is running Roman software.

And it was fast. The whole thing went up in less than a decade, opened in 80 AD, and stayed in business for the better part of four hundred years — longer than most countries have existed.

Before you move on, look at the wall one more time and find a numbered arch for yourself. It's a small thing, a gate number carved in travertine — and somehow more transporting than the whole silhouette.

Now walk to your right, keeping the Colosseum on your left, and round its flank. In a couple of minutes a three-bayed marble arch appears on the open ground just beyond — the Arch of Constantine. That's our next stop.

stops.title: The Arch of Constantine
stops.caption: The arch in front of you is the largest Roman triumphal arch still standing — twenty-one metres of marble, three bays, raised by the Senate in 315 to celebrate the emperor Constantine's victory over his rival at the Milvian Bridge.
stops.transcriptText:
The arch in front of you is the largest Roman triumphal arch still standing — twenty-one metres of marble, three bays, raised by the Senate in 315 to celebrate the emperor Constantine's victory over his rival at the Milvian Bridge. Stand back far enough to take in the whole face of it.

Here's what the Senate didn't advertise: most of what you're looking at is second-hand. The round hunting medallions were carved for Hadrian, two hundred years earlier. The statues of captive Dacians along the top were lifted from a monument to Trajan. The big rectangular panels up on the attic came from a monument to Marcus Aurelius. And on nearly all of them, the sculptors did one small, remarkable thing — they recut the emperor's face. Look closely at the figures and you're watching Hadrian and Marcus Aurelius wear Constantine's head.

Only the thin horizontal frieze above the smaller arches was carved new, and you can see the difference: the older panels are deep, muscular, alive; the new band is flatter, stiffer, more like a diagram. Historians have argued for centuries about why — whether the great workshops had declined, or whether a new emperor from the frontier was deliberately dressing himself in the wardrobe of the good emperors everyone still trusted. Both can be true at once. Either way, this is the boldest piece of recycling in a city built on it: legitimacy, cut and pasted.

One more thing this arch has seen. In 1960, the Olympic marathon finished right here, under floodlights — and an Ethiopian runner named Abebe Bikila crossed the line barefoot, the first Black African to win Olympic gold — in the capital of the country whose armies had occupied his own only a generation before.

When you're ready, put the arch at your back and walk toward the wide boulevard that runs away from the Colosseum in a dead straight line. That's Via dei Fori Imperiali — and the next stretch of this walk happens along it, with the Roman Forum opening up on your left.

stops.title: The Roman Forum
stops.caption: You're walking now, up the long straight boulevard with the Colosseum shrinking behind you.
stops.transcriptText:
You're walking now, up the long straight boulevard with the Colosseum shrinking behind you. Keep to the left-hand side, and take this one slowly — the railings along here are the best free view in Rome.

Below you on the left, the Roman Forum unrolls: the three great vaults of the Basilica of Maxentius, the Arch of Titus up the slope, and beyond them the columns and broken floors of what was, for centuries, the centre of the known world. You saw it — or will see it — from the terrace on the Capitoline; from down here at the railing it's less a panorama and more a neighbour, close enough to read.

Now, the street you're standing on. It looks eternal. It's not even a hundred years old. In 1932, Mussolini carved this boulevard through the middle of the ancient city so his parades could run from his balcony to the Colosseum in one straight line — flattening a hill, erasing a whole packed neighbourhood, and burying parts of four imperial forums under the asphalt you're walking on. Romans have never stopped arguing about it, and the argument has finally turned into action: the city is now, piece by piece, handing the road back to walkers. You're strolling down the middle of an open question.

While you walk, look down as well as around. The iron drain covers underfoot are stamped SPQR — the Senate and People of Rome, the same four letters the legions carried. The republic fell about two thousand years ago. The plumbing didn't get the memo.

Up ahead, where the boulevard opens out toward Piazza Venezia, a single white column rises across the street on your right, a spiral of carvings winding up it like a ribbon. That's Trajan's Column — cross at the crossing, walk to the railing nearest it, and I'll meet you there.

stops.title: Trajan's Column
stops.caption: You're at the railing now, looking at the column — and behind it, climbing the hillside in a curve of brick, a honeycomb of arched openings stacked three storeys high.
stops.transcriptText:
You're at the railing now, looking at the column — and behind it, climbing the hillside in a curve of brick, a honeycomb of arched openings stacked three storeys high.

The column marks the centre of what was once the grandest of all the imperial forums, built by Trajan in the early hundreds with the loot of his wars. The spiral ribbon of carving that winds to the top tells the story of those wars in more than a hundred and fifty scenes — but you had, or will have, a longer look at that on its own. What this walk wants you to see is the brick curve behind it.

That's Trajan's Markets: a multi-level complex of shops, offices and halls, terraced into the hill, often called — with a wink and an asterisk — the world's first shopping centre. Whatever you call it, it's nineteen hundred years old and structurally sound enough that you can still walk its corridors today. The emperor built his forum for glory; his architect quietly built the thing next door for errands. Guess which one stayed in one piece.

Now for the finale. Face away from the column, cross back over the boulevard, and walk toward the enormous white marble monument ahead — you can't miss it; it's the size of a hillside. Skirt around its left flank, and just behind it you'll find a long, gently ramped staircase rising between two stone lions. That ramp is called the cordonata, and at the top of it is Piazza del Campidoglio — the summit of the Capitoline Hill, and the end of our walk.

stops.title: The Campidoglio
stops.caption: Take the cordonata slowly — it was designed to be climbed slowly, a ramp rather than a staircase, wide enough for a procession.
stops.transcriptText:
Take the cordonata slowly — it was designed to be climbed slowly, a ramp rather than a staircase, wide enough for a procession. At the top, between the two colossal marble horsemen, step into the piazza and stop.

You're standing on the summit of the Capitoline Hill, in a square designed by Michelangelo, on the spot where Rome kept its most important temple for a thousand years. And here's the thing worth knowing at the end of this walk rather than the beginning: you've just retraced, more or less, the last stretch of a Roman triumph. When a victorious general paraded into the city, the route ran past where the Colosseum now stands, through the Forum along the Sacred Way, and ended up here — on this hill, at the temple of Jupiter, where the parade stopped and the sacrifice was made. Emperors walked the mile you just walked, in the other direction of history.

Now cross the piazza, keeping the trapezoid of Michelangelo's paving underfoot, and find the gap to the left of the palace at the back — a narrow lane called Via del Campidoglio. Thirty seconds down it, the city falls away.

There it is: the Roman Forum, from above this time, and beyond it, at the far end of everything, the Colosseum where you started. The whole walk, in one frame.

A kilometre and a half, and look what it held — a stadium the modern world still copies, an arch built from older arches, a dictator's road being handed back to walkers, a shopping centre nineteen centuries old, and a hilltop where the parades ended. None of it preserved under glass; all of it reused, relabelled, still in service. That's been the argument of this walk, and it's the one thing about Rome worth carrying home: this city doesn't keep its past. It keeps using it.

tours.title: The Baroque Heart
tours.shortDescription: The century Rome spent turning itself into a show.
tours.longDescription: The empire was ancient history and the banking fortunes had moved north, so the popes commissioned the one thing Rome could still do better than anywhere on earth: spectacle. This walk links five of the showpieces — Piazza del Popolo, the Spanish Steps, the Trevi Fountain, the Pantheon and Piazza Navona. A bit over two kilometres, flat nearly the whole way, and busy: treat the crowds as part of the design.

stops.title: Introduction
stops.caption: Rome spent the seventeenth century turning itself into a show.
stops.transcriptText:
Rome spent the seventeenth century turning itself into a show. The empire was ancient history, the banking fortunes had moved north, and the popes who ran this city understood that what Rome could still do better than anywhere on earth was spectacle — so they hired the best architects alive, pointed them at the medieval tangle, and commissioned wonder: fountains the size of palaces, staircases that pour downhill like water, squares built less for traffic than for applause.

This walk links five of those showpieces. We start at Piazza del Popolo, climb through Piazza di Spagna and the Spanish Steps, squeeze through the lanes to the Trevi Fountain, cross to the Pantheon, and finish in Piazza Navona. It's a bit over two kilometres, flat almost the whole way, on cobbles and busy shopping streets — and these are some of the most visited places in Europe, so treat the crowds as part of the scenery. Early morning and evening are gentler, but the route works at any hour.

One thing to listen for as we go: very little on this walk is quite what it claims to be. A Spanish square that turns out to be French. A fountain that's really the wall of a palace. A temple signed by the wrong man. Baroque Rome was theatre, and theatre runs on illusion — and the trick is that knowing how it's done makes it better, not worse.

Head for Piazza del Popolo, and make for the obelisk at its centre.

stops.title: Piazza del Popolo
stops.caption: Stand near the obelisk and face away from the city gate, so the two domed churches are ahead of you across the square.
stops.transcriptText:
Stand near the obelisk and face away from the city gate, so the two domed churches are ahead of you across the square. Between them and beside them, three straight streets run off into the city.

That view is the whole reason this piazza exists.

The gate behind you is the Porta del Popolo, where the main road from the north — the old Via Flaminia — entered Rome, which meant that for centuries almost everyone who reached the city overland arrived exactly here: pilgrims, merchants, ambassadors, painters, and eventually the Grand Tourists with their sketchbooks. Rome had one front door, and this was it.

Now look at the three streets. The one on the far left leads toward the Spanish Steps. The one on the right runs down toward the river. And the one in the middle, Via del Corso, drives straight as a ruler for a kilometre and a half into the heart of the city. Together they're known as the Trident, and they turn this square into something much cleverer than a grand entrance — they make it a sorting machine. Rome received you in one magnificent oval room, gave you a moment to be impressed, and then dispatched you down the correct corridor for wherever you were going. We remember the Baroque city for its drama, but underneath the marble it was crowd management: the popes were handling the largest visitor flows in Europe centuries before anyone invented the term, and they did it with architecture instead of barriers.

The obelisk you're standing beside, for the record, is Egyptian — carved for a pharaoh, shipped here by an emperor, and older than the city around it.

Take the left-hand street of the Trident, Via del Babuino. It's about ten minutes of straight, well-dressed walking, and it delivers you to the foot of the Spanish Steps.

stops.title: The Spanish Steps
stops.caption: Via del Babuino ends and the space opens out — this is Piazza di Spagna, and the staircase rising in tiers to your left, up to the church with the two bell towers, is the one you know from a thousand photographs.
stops.transcriptText:
Via del Babuino ends and the space opens out — this is Piazza di Spagna, and the staircase rising in tiers to your left, up to the church with the two bell towers, is the one you know from a thousand photographs. Work your way toward the sinking-boat fountain at its foot and find somewhere to stand.

Start with the name. The Spanish Steps are, in fact, French. The square is named for Spain — the Spanish embassy to the pope has stood here for some four hundred years — but the staircase was paid for with French money, left in the will of a French diplomat, and it climbs to a French church: Trinità dei Monti, up there behind the obelisk. And for decades the French wanted more. The plan was to crown this hillside with a statue of the King of France on horseback, gazing down over the city — and the popes, who had no intention of hosting a foreign monarch above their own rooftops, kept refusing. The staircase, finished in the 1720s, was the eventual compromise: all the sweep and grandeur of a royal monument, with nobody on top. What reads as pure romance is really one of the most elegant diplomatic settlements in Europe — two rival powers, one slope, and the whole argument resolved in travertine.

Notice, too, how the thing behaves. It splits, curves, gathers itself at terraces and spills on again — a staircase designed less for climbing than for lingering. Which makes the modern rule a quiet irony: to protect the stone, sitting on the steps is now banned, so the world's most famous place to sit is standing room only.

The next showpiece hides in the alleys about ten minutes south of here: the Trevi Fountain. Take your time through the shopping streets — it will announce itself.

stops.title: The Trevi Fountain
stops.caption: You hear it before you see it. Somewhere in these last narrow streets the sound begins — a low, steady roar underneath the crowd noise — and it thickens with every corner until you take one final turn and the whole end of the street is water, rock and marble.
stops.transcriptText:
You hear it before you see it. Somewhere in these last narrow streets the sound begins — a low, steady roar underneath the crowd noise — and it thickens with every corner until you take one final turn and the whole end of the street is water, rock and marble.

Stop wherever you first get a clear look, and consider what you're actually looking at. The Trevi is not a fountain standing in a square. It's the front wall of a palace — Palazzo Poli — seized top to bottom and turned into a cliff: sculpted boulders spilling forward into the basin, a screen of columns rising the full height of the building, and striding out of the centre of it all, the sea god Oceanus, his chariot hauled through the spray by winged horses. The fountain doesn't stand in front of the architecture; it is the architecture, nearly as tall as the palace whose face it borrowed.

And the little square was never enlarged to give it room — which, by accident or by design, is the secret of the whole performance. There is no long view of the Trevi, no gradual approach. It's always too big for the space it's in, always arriving all at once, a colossus kept in too small a room. The Baroque understood something every theatre director knows: surprise isn't about the object. It's about the framing.

These days, a small ticket gets you down the steps to the water's edge in daytime hours; the view from street level, where you're standing, costs nothing at any hour.

When you manage to pull yourself away, the next stop is the Pantheon — ten minutes or so west through the lanes. Watch for a grey wall of ancient brick rising over the rooftops as you get close.

stops.title: The Pantheon
stops.caption: Nineteen hundred years, give or take, and nobody has ever built a bigger dome out of plain, unreinforced concrete.
stops.transcriptText:
Nineteen hundred years, give or take, and nobody has ever built a bigger dome out of plain, unreinforced concrete. Not the Renaissance, not the industrial age, not us. The record holder is in front of you, behind a porch of granite columns — wearing a name that isn't its builder's.

Walk up to where you can read the bronze letters across the front. M. AGRIPPA, they begin — Marcus Agrippa, son of Lucius, three times consul, made this. It's the most famous inscription in Rome, and it isn't true — or rather, it's out of date by about a hundred and fifty years. Agrippa did build a temple on this spot, but it burned. What you're looking at is a complete rebuild from the early second century, under the emperor Hadrian — new porch, new rotunda, new dome, the whole miracle — and when it was finished, Hadrian put the old name back on the front.

He did this all over Rome: rebuilt other men's monuments and kept their names on them. It's worth pausing on, because Hadrian did not lack ego. He seems to have grasped something subtler — that in this city, authority came from continuity, and a name two centuries old carried more weight than a fresh one ever could. It's the same instinct you meet everywhere in Rome, where nothing old is discarded and everything gets kept in service; here, what was reused was the signature itself. The most influential building in the history of western architecture, copied by domes from Florence to Washington, is signed by the wrong man — on purpose.

There's a ticket to go inside these days; the porch and the square are free. If you do go in, look at nothing until you've looked up.

Our last stop is the easiest walk of the day: Piazza Navona, five minutes west. Head that way and let the lanes funnel you in.

stops.title: Piazza Navona
stops.caption: It's a Saturday in August, sometime in the 1700s, and the square you're about to enter is underwater.
stops.transcriptText:
It's a Saturday in August, sometime in the 1700s, and the square you're about to enter is underwater. The fountain drains have been stopped, the piazza has flooded from end to end, and the carriages of the Roman nobility are wheeling slowly through the shallows while half the city leans out of windows to watch, cheer, and be seen.

Come into the square and find a spot near the great fountain at its centre.

For more than two centuries — from 1652 until 1866 — that was the August ritual here: on summer weekends, Piazza Navona became a lake, part cooling-off, part carnival, part rolling display of who mattered in Rome. And it tells you what this square was built to be. The long oval you're standing in follows the footprint of an ancient Roman stadium buried beneath your feet, and when the Pamphilj family produced a pope in the 1640s, they rebuilt the whole space as their personal showcase — palace, church and fountains — then threw it open as the city's grandest room. The centrepiece is the Fountain of the Four Rivers, Bernini's marble mountain, four colossal figures for the four continents then known, with an obelisk balanced improbably over the hollow grotto between them; the church rising behind it, Sant'Agnese, wears a facade by Borromini. And around them, the square carries on much as it always has — painters, buskers, café tables, Romans cutting through — the cast changes daily, but the run is permanent.

This is where the walk ends, and it's the right place to end it. Everything we've passed today was built to persuade: a sorting machine dressed as a piazza, a treaty dressed as a staircase, a palace wall dressed as the sea, a signature borrowed for the ages. Illusion, all of it — and none of it any less true. So stay a while. Find a coffee at the edge of the oval, watch the water, and enjoy being exactly what this square has always wanted: an audience.

tours.title: The Ghetto and Trastevere
tours.shortDescription: Rome exists because of its river — and hides it completely.
tours.longDescription: You can spend a whole day in the centre without seeing the Tiber once. That vanishing act was deliberate, and this walk undoes it: south from Largo Argentina into the old Jewish Ghetto, across the oldest bridge in the city, onto the island in midstream, ashore in Trastevere, and up to the Janiculum to look down on all of it. Two and a half kilometres, flat until the climb at the end.

stops.title: Introduction
stops.caption: Rome exists because of its river — and you can spend an entire day in the centre of the city without seeing it once.
stops.transcriptText:
Rome exists because of its river — and you can spend an entire day in the centre of the city without seeing it once. That vanishing act is real, it was deliberate, and this walk is about undoing it.

We're going to the water. From Largo di Torre Argentina we head south into the old Jewish Ghetto, cross the Tiber on the oldest bridge in the city, pause on the island in midstream, come ashore in Trastevere — the neighbourhood whose whole name means "across the river" — and finish on the Janiculum terrace, looking down on everything we've just walked. Along the way, keep an eye out for the massive stone walls that hold the river in its channel. They're the reason you never see the Tiber until you're standing on top of it, and by the end of the walk you'll know their story too.

Practical notes: it's about two and a half kilometres, flat and easy until the very end — the last stretch climbs the Janiculum hill, a stiff fifteen to twenty minutes uphill, and there's no shame in taking a taxi up from Trastevere instead. The route crosses two bridges; the second carries a little traffic, so keep to the side. Otherwise it's lanes, squares and riverbank all the way.

Start at Largo di Torre Argentina, and make for the railing overlooking the ruins.

stops.title: Largo di Torre Argentina
stops.caption: Come to the railing and look down. The temples at the bottom of that pit stand on the ground level of the Roman republic — several metres below your shoes.
stops.transcriptText:
Come to the railing and look down. The temples at the bottom of that pit stand on the ground level of the Roman republic — several metres below your shoes. The oldest of them was already ancient when the empire began; the four of them together are among the oldest things you can see anywhere in this city, and to see them, you look down. Always down.

It's worth asking why. Part of the answer is ordinary: cities rise on their own rubble, and Rome has been rebuilding on top of itself for longer than almost anywhere. But here there's another culprit, and it's the one this walk is about. You're standing in the ancient flood plain of the Tiber, and for two thousand years, every time the river rose — which was often — it left behind a layer of silt and debris when it fell. Flood by flood, century by century, the river quietly raised the street. The Rome of the republic didn't sink. The city grew up over it, on ground the Tiber helped deliver.

So this sunken square makes a fitting first stop: we're setting off to find a river you can already see the fingerprints of, several metres deep, right here in the middle of town. The temples, for the record, are so old that nobody has ever settled which gods most of them belonged to — they're lettered A to D, like exhibits — and they only came back to light in the demolitions of the 1920s, when a modern square was cut through and the republic turned up underneath.

Now let's go find the culprit. Walk south, away from the tram stops, and in a few minutes the lanes will bring you to Via del Portico d'Ottavia — the main street of the old Jewish Ghetto.

stops.title: The Jewish Ghetto
stops.caption: For more than three centuries, the people of this street were locked in at night.
stops.transcriptText:
For more than three centuries, the people of this street were locked in at night.

Walk Via del Portico d'Ottavia slowly, toward the river. In 1555, a papal decree confined Rome's Jewish community — one of the oldest communities of any kind in Europe, present in this city since before the Caesars — to a few walled hectares right here, with gates that closed at dusk. And the ground chosen for the ghetto was not neutral ground. This was the lowest land in Rome, hard against the Tiber, and in the centuries before the flood walls the river came calling almost every winter — into the streets, into the lower rooms of the crowded houses, sometimes storeys deep. The walls kept people in; nothing kept the water out. Poverty was policy here, and the river was part of the sentence.

The gates and walls finally came down in the 1880s — the same decade, as it happens, that the city began raising the great embankments that would end the floods for good. One set of walls fell as the other rose.

One thing more, and it asks for a quieter voice. The community that lives on this street has prayed in this city for more than two thousand years, and it endured its darkest morning in October 1943, when the occupying German forces came here for its people. It is still here. Carry that fact gently as you look around you now — because what you're walking through today is not a memorial but a living neighbourhood, loud with restaurant tables, bakeries and kids on bikes, and its persistence is the point.

At the end of the street, by the synagogue, turn toward the river. The small stone bridge ahead of you is the oldest in Rome, and it's ours: we cross here, to the island.

stops.title: Tiber Island
stops.caption: Sixty-two years before the birth of Christ, a Roman official named Lucius Fabricius built this bridge — and carved his name into it, more than once, so that nobody would ever forget who was responsible.
stops.transcriptText:
Sixty-two years before the birth of Christ, a Roman official named Lucius Fabricius built this bridge — and carved his name into it, more than once, so that nobody would ever forget who was responsible. Two thousand years of feet have crossed it since, and yours are next.

Walk it slowly. Halfway across, stop at the parapet and look at the river — your first proper sight of it all day. The island splits the Tiber into two narrow channels, and that, more than anything else, is why there's a city here at all. A wide river is a wall; a river split by an island is a doorway. Long before Rome had a name, the trade paths of central Italy — salt from the coast, herds and goods from the hills — funnelled toward this one easy crossing, and the settlement that controlled it never looked back. Emperors, forums, basilicas: all of it downstream, historically speaking, of the simple fact that this is where you could get across.

Two details before you move on. On the upstream face of the bridge's central pier there's a small arched opening — a flood vent, cut by builders who knew this river's temper and built for it, which is no small part of why the bridge is still here. And the weathered stone heads on the parapet — faces worn almost to nothing — have been watching crossings since antiquity.

On the island itself, most of what you see today is a working hospital; the little piazza by the church is a good place to stand a moment with water on both sides of you. Then take the second bridge, Ponte Cestio — rebuilt in the 1880s when the flood walls went in, so mind the occasional car — and come ashore in Trastevere. The piazza we want, Santa Maria in Trastevere, is a few minutes into the lanes.

stops.title: Trastevere
stops.caption: Trastevere means, literally, "across the Tiber" — and the name has always been less an address than an attitude.
stops.transcriptText:
Trastevere means, literally, "across the Tiber" — and the name has always been less an address than an attitude.

Come into the piazza and find a spot near the fountain, which has been marked on maps of this city since the 1400s. In ancient times this bank was the workers' side of the river — sailors, dockers, millers, migrants from every port the empire traded with — and it has kept a stubborn sense of itself ever since: its own accent, its own swagger, its own conviction that the real Rome lives over here, and that everything across the water is merely the city. The locals even have a word for it. Every July, this neighbourhood throws itself a festival called the Festa de' Noantri — the feast of "we others" — which is about as clear as an identity gets: one week a year, officially, Trastevere celebrates not being the rest of Rome.

And the festival's centrepiece belongs to this walk. Its patroness is a statue of the Madonna known as the Fiumarola — "of the river" — because, as the story goes, fishermen found her floating at the Tiber's mouth after a storm, some five centuries back, and brought her home to Trastevere. Take the legend as a legend, but notice what it says: even the neighbourhood's miracle came out of the water. On this side of Rome, the river was never scenery. It was the employer, the road, and occasionally the deliverer of small wonders.

The church on the piazza, Santa Maria in Trastevere, is one of the oldest in the city, and its golden facade mosaics are the square's evening entertainment — they catch fire when the light goes low. It's been said that if Trastevere were a town on its own hill somewhere, this would be its cathedral square, and standing here, that's exactly how it feels.

Now for the climb. Take Via della Paglia out of the piazza and follow the signs uphill toward the Gianicolo — fifteen to twenty minutes of switchbacks, or a quick taxi — and meet me at the terrace on top.

stops.title: The Janiculum Terrace
stops.caption: However you got up here — on foot, by taxi, breathing hard or not — take a moment at the balustrade before you look at anything in particular.
stops.transcriptText:
However you got up here — on foot, by taxi, breathing hard or not — take a moment at the balustrade before you look at anything in particular. This is the widest view in Rome: the whole city laid out below you, dome by dome, hill by hill, all the way to the mountains on a clear day.

Now try something. Find the river.

Go ahead — you've just spent the afternoon walking to it, along it and across it, so you know roughly where it runs. And yet from up here the Tiber is nearly invisible: no glint of water, just a winding line of plane trees threading through the rooftops. A city built by a river has managed to hide it — and that was a choice. In December 1870, weeks after Rome became the capital of a newly united Italy, the Tiber rose into one of the worst floods anyone could remember, drowning the streets of the young capital metres deep. The new state answered with the biggest public works project the city had seen since antiquity: the muraglioni, the great embankment walls, kilometres of them, high and sheer. They worked. The floods that had tormented Rome for twenty-five centuries — that raised the streets at Largo Argentina, that ran through the lower rooms of the Ghetto — simply stopped.

But the cure had a cost. The walls that saved the city also severed it from the water: the ports, the boatmen, the floating mills, the whole riverside world that Trastevere lived off — gone within a generation, and the river sank out of Rome's daily sight, down between its stone banks. Nobody misses the floods. Some Romans, to this day, miss the river.

So stay a while, up here where you can see both truths at once — the safe, dry, magnificent city, and the thin green line it owes everything to and no longer looks at. If it's coming up on noon, don't let the cannon below the terrace startle you; it fires once a day, on schedule. Otherwise there's nothing you need to do but watch the light move across Rome — and keep the river company a little longer. Today, you're one of the few who did.

tours.title: The Vatican and the Borgo
tours.shortDescription: A walk that runs between two tombs.
tours.longDescription: At one end, the drum-shaped fortress built eighteen centuries ago as the emperor Hadrian's mausoleum. At the other, the largest church on earth, raised over what tradition holds to be the grave of a Galilean fisherman. Between them: a bridge lined with marble angels, a castle, and a single straight street that pilgrims have finished their journeys along for centuries. About a kilometre and a quarter, flat throughout.

stops.title: Introduction
stops.caption: This walk runs between two tombs. At one end stands the drum-shaped fortress across the river — built eighteen centuries ago as the mausoleum of the emperor Hadrian.
stops.transcriptText:
This walk runs between two tombs.

At one end stands the drum-shaped fortress across the river — built eighteen centuries ago as the mausoleum of the emperor Hadrian. At the other, out of sight for now, rises the largest church on earth by most measures, raised over what tradition holds to be the grave of a Galilean fisherman. Between the two: a bridge, a castle, and a single straight street. Rome has been walking this line for most of its history, and pilgrims by the million have finished their journeys along it.

You should be standing at the southern end of Ponte Sant'Angelo, on the city side of the Tiber, with the bridge and its white marble angels stretching away toward the round castle on the far bank. The full route is only about a kilometre and a quarter, flat the whole way — and since the traffic in front of the castle was sent underground, you can now walk it end to end without crossing a single road.

This is a walk about faith and fear, and about what each of them builds: an emperor's tomb turned fortress, a hidden corridor for popes in flight, a grand avenue for arrivals — and at the end of it all, an embrace.

Walk out onto the bridge, and stop when you reach the middle.

stops.title: Ponte Sant'Angelo
stops.caption: Look down the line of angels. Ten of them, five to a side, each caught mid-gesture on the parapet — and each carrying something: a crown of thorns, a handful of nails, a lance, a sponge raised on a reed.
stops.transcriptText:
Look down the line of angels.

Ten of them, five to a side, each caught mid-gesture on the parapet — and each carrying something: a crown of thorns, a handful of nails, a lance, a sponge raised on a reed. These are the instruments of the Passion, the objects of the crucifixion story, and Gian Lorenzo Bernini designed the series in the late 1660s so that crossing this bridge became a kind of procession. Pilgrims bound for St. Peter's walked the story, object by object, on the last stretch of their journey — the bridge doesn't just deliver you to the basilica, it prepares you for it.

The bridge itself is far older than its angels. Hadrian built it as the approach to his own mausoleum — the round fortress ahead of you — and the three arches beneath the middle of the span are still the Roman originals. For most of the centuries since, this was the main crossing for anyone bound for St. Peter's: the last bridge of a thousand pilgrim roads.

The bridgehead behind you, where you stepped onto the span, was for centuries one of the city's places of public execution. The name Rome remembers most is Beatrice Cenci — a young noblewoman put to death here in 1599, condemned with her family for the killing of her violent father, after a trial the whole city argued over. The verdict has never stopped being argued, and her story has been carried ever since in paintings, plays and Roman legend.

An emperor's approach road, a gallery of Baroque devotion, a place of punishment — this bridge has carried nearly every mood the city has ever had. Cross the rest of it now, and come off onto the wide open square in front of the fortress. Castel Sant'Angelo, up close, is next.

stops.title: Castel Sant'Angelo
stops.caption: No building in Rome has changed jobs more often than the one in front of you.
stops.transcriptText:
No building in Rome has changed jobs more often than the one in front of you.

You should be off the bridge now, standing on the broad square before the castle entrance, the river at your back. This building began as a tomb: the mausoleum of the emperor Hadrian, a marble-clad drum crowned in its first life with cypress trees and a bronze chariot. Then the city's emergencies got hold of it. It was walled into Rome's defences and became a fortress; then a prison, a barracks, a treasury, and a papal residence with frescoed apartments sitting almost directly above the cells — and finally the museum it is today. Eighteen centuries of Roman history, stacked inside a single round building.

Now look to the right of the castle. A stretch of old wall runs away toward the Vatican, higher than the rooftops in places. Inside it is a corridor — the Passetto — a protected passage linking the Vatican palaces to this fortress, and it existed for exactly the reason you'd guess. In 1527, when an imperial army sacked Rome, Pope Clement the Seventh fled down its full length and held out behind these walls until the worst had passed. This castle is what faith kept in reserve: the place the papacy went when prayer needed ramparts.

Along the gardens on the castle's far side you may notice fencing and site hoarding — a new metro station is being built there, a project measured in years rather than months.

One more thing, about the ground you're standing on. This square, Piazza Pia, is newer than it looks: until 2024 it was a traffic junction moving thousands of cars an hour, and the walk you're taking today was cut in two by it. The cars now pass through a tunnel beneath your feet. So cross the square the way pilgrims always meant to — on foot, without stopping — and turn onto the long straight street ahead. Via della Conciliazione.

stops.title: Via della Conciliazione
stops.caption: The name of this street means "reconciliation" — and the street itself is the youngest thing on this walk.
stops.transcriptText:
The name of this street means "reconciliation" — and the street itself is the youngest thing on this walk.

Stand at its eastern end, the castle at your back. Ahead of you, framed dead centre above the rooflines, is the dome of St. Peter's, and you'll have it in view the whole way down.

In 1929, Italy and the papacy signed the Lateran Pacts, ending a standoff that had lasted since Italian troops took the city from the popes six decades earlier. This street commemorates that peace — but it was built by demolition. Until the 1930s, the space you're looking down was filled by the spina di Borgo, a wedge of medieval streets and houses running from here toward the basilica. The regime levelled it in 1936 and 1937 to cut a ceremonial approach it judged worthy of a capital newly reconciled with its church, and the paving wasn't finished until 1950.

Rome gained a vista and lost a neighbourhood, and which mattered more is an argument the city has never quite finished.

As you walk, look at the buildings flanking the street. A few of the palaces are centuries older than the road they now stand on — Renaissance survivors of the old Borgo, some left on their original ground, at least one taken down stone by stone and rebuilt to fit the new alignment. The avenue looks all of a piece; it isn't. Pieces of the old quarter are hiding in plain sight along it.

Walk toward the dome. The street runs about five hundred metres, flat the whole way, and when the buildings finally stop and the space opens wide around you, you've arrived. St. Peter's Square is next — and last.

stops.title: St Peter's Square
stops.caption: Let the street release you into the square, and stop just inside it.
stops.transcriptText:
Let the street release you into the square, and stop just inside it.

Ahead is the facade of the basilica, the dome rising behind it; sweeping out to either side of you, two curved colonnades, four columns deep, carrying a parade of stone saints along their roofline. Depending on the day, barriers may channel the space — go as far toward the middle as they allow, and then turn slowly, all the way around.

Bernini, who built the colonnades in the mid-seventeenth century, described them himself as arms — reaching out from the church to gather people in. Stand still and you can feel the idea working. The great buildings of Rome tend to confront you; this one surrounds you. The square is less a forecourt than an embrace, scaled for crowds of hundreds of thousands and somehow not unkind to a crowd of one.

At the centre stands an Egyptian obelisk that has been on this spot since the 1580s. And beneath it all — under the high altar, deep below the dome — lies what tradition holds to be the grave of Peter: a Galilean fisherman, executed in Rome in the first century, whose tomb this entire church was built to crown.

Which closes the circle of this walk. You began at an emperor's tomb, and you've ended at a fisherman's. Hadrian's monument had to become a fortress to survive; Peter's became the largest church on earth, its arms open to whoever walks up the street.

Stay inside the colonnade a while. Pilgrims have been finishing journeys on this spot for something like two thousand years, most of them on foot, many of them along the exact line you walked today. However you arrived, and whatever you came for, the square holds room for you too.

tours.title: The Aventine and Testaccio
tours.shortDescription: What Rome built for itself, rather than for show.
tours.longDescription: A racetrack for its days off, a hilltop for its quiet, and at the end a working neighbourhood with a hill made entirely by hand out of broken amphorae. No triumphal arches on this route and no domes until one appears through a keyhole. Two and a half kilometres: flat along the Circus Maximus, one steady ten-minute climb up the Aventine, then gently downhill into Testaccio. Bring an appetite.

stops.title: Introduction
stops.caption: Every other walk in this city shows you what emperors and popes built for show.
stops.transcriptText:
Every other walk in this city shows you what emperors and popes built for show. This one shows you what Rome built for itself.

A racetrack for its days off. A hilltop for its quiet. And at the end, a neighbourhood that fed the whole operation — with a hill made entirely by working hands. No triumphal arches on this route, no domes until one appears through a keyhole. Just the ordinary city, which in Rome is never ordinary for long.

You should be standing near the Circo Massimo metro station, at the southeastern end of a long green valley stretching away in front of you. That valley is the Circus Maximus, and it's our first stop. The full route runs about two and a half kilometres: flat along the valley, then one steady climb of about ten minutes up the Aventine Hill, and gently downhill the rest of the way into Testaccio. Wear comfortable shoes and bring an appetite — the finish line has some of the best food in Rome.

Walk along the edge of the valley until you have a clear view down its whole length, and stop there. The Circus Maximus first.

stops.title: The Circus Maximus
stops.caption: For centuries, this was where Rome came to scream. It looks like a long grassy valley now — more than half a kilometre of it, with a raised ridge running down the middle and slopes rising on either side.
stops.transcriptText:
For centuries, this was where Rome came to scream.

It looks like a long grassy valley now — more than half a kilometre of it, with a raised ridge running down the middle and slopes rising on either side. Read it as a racetrack, because that's what it was: the ridge marks the spina, the central barrier the chariots thundered around, and the slopes held tier upon tier of seating. On race days, a crowd far larger than the Colosseum ever held packed into this valley to watch teams of four horses take the turns at full gallop.

And they didn't just watch — they belonged. Every racegoer followed one of four factions, known by their colours: the Blues, the Greens, the Reds and the Whites. People were born into a colour, married within it, rioted for it. Emperors were known to favour one team and to sulk when it lost. Star drivers, many of them born enslaved, earned fortunes that scandalized Rome's poets. If modern sport has an ancestor — the merchandise, the transfers, the heartbreak — it was invented in this valley.

The marble and the seating went the way most Roman marble went, into other buildings, and the valley returned to what it had always been underneath: a space in the middle of a city. Depending on the season, you may find a stage and banks of temporary seating filling one end — the valley hosts opera and concerts on summer nights, so don't be surprised to share it with a crew building something.

Now for the quiet after the roar. With the valley on your left, find the road that climbs the hill behind you — the Aventine — and take your time on the way up. In about ten minutes you'll come to a walled garden full of orange trees. That's our next stop: the Giardino degli Aranci.

stops.title: The Orange Garden
stops.caption: Breathe in as you come through the gate. Depending on the month, the air in here carries bitter orange — blossom in spring, fruit in winter — and either way it's the Aventine's calling card.
stops.transcriptText:
Breathe in as you come through the gate. Depending on the month, the air in here carries bitter orange — blossom in spring, fruit in winter — and either way it's the Aventine's calling card.

You're in the Giardino degli Aranci, the Garden of the Oranges, a walled square of green laid out inside the remains of a medieval fortress — the walls around you belonged to the Savelli family, who held this hilltop when holding hilltops was how power worked. The orange trees have their own story: the first of them, so the story goes, was planted by Saint Dominic himself, from a cutting he carried from Spain eight centuries ago. A descendant of that tree is still tended in the monastery next door. Take the legend as a legend — but the monks take it seriously.

Walk to the terrace at the far end when you're ready. The whole city opens up below you in one sweep, from the river bending at your feet to the domes stacked up on the horizon.

Here's the thing worth knowing about this hill while you look. The Aventine was, for most of ancient history, the outsiders' hill. It stood beyond the pomerium — Rome's oldest sacred boundary — so it collected everyone and everything the official city kept at arm's length: traders, foreign cults, and the plebeians, the common citizens, who by tradition staged their great political walkouts up here when the powerful pushed too far. The hill of the people with the best view in Rome. It took the modern city a few thousand years to catch on, and now the outsiders' hill is the quietest, most coveted address in the centre.

When you've had your fill of the view, come back through the trees and out the gate, and turn right along the quiet street — Via di Santa Sabina. Three minutes of flat walking brings you to a small piazza with decorated walls, and a green door with a crowd in front of it. That's the Keyhole.

stops.title: The Knights of Malta Keyhole
stops.caption: At the far corner of this quiet piazza, a small crowd gathers at a green door, taking turns to press one eye against it.
stops.transcriptText:
At the far corner of this quiet piazza, a small crowd gathers at a green door, taking turns to press one eye against it.

Join them. It's free, it moves quickly, and what's on the other side is worth the wait: through the keyhole, a long tunnel of clipped hedges runs away from you, and floating at the end of it, perfectly framed, is the dome of St. Peter's — kilometres away and seemingly close enough to touch.

The door belongs to the priory of the Knights of Malta, an order of knights founded during the Crusades and still going, and the square you're standing in was designed for them in the eighteenth century by Piranesi — an architect better known for drawing buildings than building them. He decorated these walls with trophies and emblems and built the whole piazza around an old idea of the Aventine as a sacred ship, ready to sail: the hedges beyond the door read as rigging, the hilltop as a deck.

Whether anyone planned the view through the keyhole is another matter. The tidy story says it was composed deliberately, hedge by hedge; the honest answer is that nobody knows who first lined it up, or when. Take the tidy story as a story. The dome doesn't mind either way.

When you've had your turn, take the street that drops downhill from the piazza and keep descending toward the river flats. Ten minutes or so brings you down into a grid of ordinary streets that smells faintly of coffee and frying. That's Testaccio — the last stop, and the reason you saved your appetite.

stops.title: Testaccio
stops.caption: The hill rising at the edge of this neighbourhood was made entirely by hand — and nobody who made it ever thought of it as a monument.
stops.transcriptText:
The hill rising at the edge of this neighbourhood was made entirely by hand — and nobody who made it ever thought of it as a monument.

Make your way toward it through the grid of streets, or start at the covered market if you're hungry; either works, and the neighbourhood is small enough that you can't really go wrong. Testaccio sits on the flats where ancient Rome kept its river port — the Emporium — and behind the docks stood warehouse after warehouse, holding the grain and wine and olive oil that fed a city of a million people. The oil arrived in big clay jars, and here's the catch: an oil jar can't be reused. The residue turns rancid. So for around three centuries, the dockworkers broke the empties and stacked the pieces — neatly, in terraces, dusted with lime — until the pile of broken jars was a hill more than thirty metres high. Monte Testaccio: the paperwork of an empire, filed in clay.

The neighbourhood around it has been Rome's working stomach ever since it was built for labourers' families in the late nineteenth century, and it never really stopped cooking. In the covered market — mornings are its best hours — you can eat as well as anywhere in the city while standing up. And beneath the market floor, excavations have uncovered one of those ancient warehouses itself, broken jars still in place, the whole story of this quarter sitting a few metres under the fruit stalls.

So here's where this walk has been heading. Uphill, emperors and popes built for eternity and mostly got it. Down here, working Rome just got on with the job — racing, unloading, breaking empties — and its leavings piled into the only hill in Rome that ordinary people made. It might be the most honest monument in the city.

Stay for lunch. Order whatever the person next to you is having. This neighbourhood has been feeding Rome for two thousand years, and it's very good at it.

tours.title: Piazza del Quirinale
tours.shortDescription: Same palace, three different countries — popes, then kings, then presidents.
tours.longDescription: For four and a half centuries whoever ran Rome has lived on this hill. The fountain at the centre is the city in miniature: two Roman copies of Greek horse-tamers that once stood at the Baths of Constantine, a granite basin that spent centuries as a cattle trough in the Forum, and an obelisk taken from the door of the Mausoleum of Augustus — a bath ornament, a trough and a dead emperor's doorpost, reassembled into one of the most elegant compositions in Rome.

stops.title: Piazza del Quirinale
stops.caption: For four and a half centuries, whoever ran Rome has lived on this hill — first the popes, then the kings, now the presidents.
stops.transcriptText:
For four and a half centuries, whoever ran Rome has lived on this hill — first the popes, then the kings, now the presidents. Same palace, three different countries.

This is Piazza del Quirinale, the flat, open summit of the highest of Rome's hills. You should be in a wide, quiet square: a long, austere palace on one side, uniformed guards at its door, and at the centre a fountain crowned by an obelisk and two colossal marble men holding rearing horses. Behind you, past the balustrade, the rooftops run all the way to the dome of St Peter's.

So. The fountain group first — because almost nothing in it was made for this square. The two giants are Castor and Pollux, the horse-taming twins, Roman copies of Greek originals that once stood at the Baths of Constantine nearby. The granite basin at their feet spent centuries down in the Roman Forum as a watering trough for cattle, back when the Forum was pasture. And the obelisk between them once stood at the door of the Mausoleum of Augustus — it's the one from the tomb, raised here in 1786. A bath ornament, a cattle trough and a dead emperor's doorpost, reassembled into one of the most elegant compositions in Rome: this city furnishes its present entirely from its past, and here the habit is the whole monument.

The palace began in the 1570s as a papal summer retreat — high ground, cooler air — and grew into one of the largest palaces in Europe. When Italy united, the kings moved in; when Italy voted the monarchy out, the presidents did. In the afternoons the guard changes at the gate, and you're welcome to watch.

One more thing. Walk a few minutes along Via del Quirinale, beside the palace, and you'll settle the rivalry from Piazza Barberini yourself: on this street, Bernini and Borromini each built a small church. Bernini's Sant'Andrea is a warm oval of rose marble he considered his most perfect work; Borromini's San Carlino, just up the road, is a rippling, restless miracle small enough to fit inside a single pier of St Peter's. Two geniuses, one street, no truce.

Popes, kings, presidents — the tenants keep changing, and the twins keep holding their horses. On this hill, that passes for constancy.

tours.title: Monti
tours.shortDescription: Julius Caesar grew up a few streets from here — in the noisy part of town.
tours.longDescription: This was the Suburra, the densest and loudest quarter of ancient Rome, downhill from the Forum in every sense; the young Caesar lived in it. Today Monti is the city's oldest living room — Rione number one, the first on Rome's ancient list of districts — with a Giacomo della Porta fountain from the 1580s still serving as the village well, and half the neighbourhood on its steps most evenings. Nothing to book, nothing to wait for.

stops.title: Monti
stops.caption: Julius Caesar grew up a few streets from here — not in a palace, but in a crowded, noisy, slightly disreputable neighbourhood called the Suburra.
stops.transcriptText:
Julius Caesar grew up a few streets from here — not in a palace, but in a crowded, noisy, slightly disreputable neighbourhood called the Suburra. You're standing in what became of it.

This is Monti, and your anchor is Piazza della Madonna dei Monti: a small, easy square with a stone fountain at its centre, café tables at the edges, ivy down the walls, and — most evenings — half the neighbourhood sitting on the fountain steps with a drink. There's nothing to book here, nothing to wait for. That's rather the point.

The fountain came first. It was set up in the 1580s by Giacomo della Porta, the same hand behind half the fountains in central Rome, and it has served ever since as the village well of a district that has always behaved like a village. Around you runs Rione Monti — number one, the first on Rome's ancient list of districts, named for the hills it climbs.

In antiquity this was the Suburra: the densest, loudest quarter of the ancient city, packed with tenement blocks, taverns and washing lines, downhill from the Forum in every sense. Emperors were carried past it; ordinary Rome actually lived in it — and so, famously, did the young Caesar, in a modest family house, long before anyone imagined a month would carry his name. When the empire fell and the aqueducts were cut, the crowds followed the water down to the river, and for centuries Monti dozed — vineyards, convents, quiet lanes — a country town hiding inside the city walls.

The lanes woke up again. Artisans and their workshops lined these street fronts through the last century; lately the workshops have been turning into wine bars, vintage shops and boutiques, and Romans argue — here as everywhere — about what that trade has gained and lost. The streets themselves haven't moved: Via del Boschetto, Via Urbana and Via dei Serpenti still run where the ancient ones did.

Every other stop on this route shows you what Rome built to be admired. Monti shows you where Rome went home in the evening — twenty-one centuries of it, from Caesar's neighbours to the people sharing the fountain steps beside you. Take a seat. You're in the oldest living room in the city.

tours.title: Santa Maria Maggiore
tours.shortDescription: Every August, white petals fall from the ceiling onto whoever is standing below.
tours.longDescription: Legend says the Virgin marked this hilltop with snow on an August night in the fourth century; the church keeps the story with petals rather than insisting it be true. What is documented is stranger — a basilica consecrated in 434 that, alone among Rome's great churches, has never been torn down and rebuilt. The nave mosaics are the originals, some fifteen hundred years old, and Pope Francis chose to be buried here beneath a slab carrying one word.

stops.title: Santa Maria Maggiore
stops.caption: Every year on the fifth of August, white flower petals fall from the ceiling of this church — thousands of them, drifting down through the nave onto whoever happens to be standing underneath.
stops.transcriptText:
Every year on the fifth of August, white flower petals fall from the ceiling of this church — thousands of them, drifting down through the nave onto whoever happens to be standing underneath. Rome has been keeping that appointment, in one form or another, for centuries.

You should be standing in Piazza di Santa Maria Maggiore, facing the broad eighteenth-century facade with its loggia above the doors. Rising behind it, the tallest bell tower in Rome. And in front of you, a single marble column carrying a bronze Virgin and Child.

Begin with the column. It wasn't made for this square. It stood for more than a thousand years in the ruins of a vast Roman basilica down by the Forum — the only column of that building left upright — until a pope had it hauled up the hill in 1614 and gave it a new job. In this city, even the monuments are second-hand.

Now, the legend. The story goes that one August night in the fourth century, the Virgin appeared to a pope in a dream and promised to mark the site of her church with snow — and the next morning, in the heat of a Roman summer, this hilltop was white. It is a legend, and the church treats it as one; the petals are the city's way of keeping the story without insisting it be true.

What's documented is almost stranger. Behind that facade stands a church consecrated in the year 434 — and unlike every other great basilica in Rome, it has never been torn down and rebuilt. The mosaics along the nave are the originals, some fifteen hundred years old, and the columns beneath them were lifted from older Roman buildings back when the western empire was still breathing. It calls itself the first church in Rome dedicated to Mary — a title Santa Maria in Trastevere also claims, across the river, and after fifteen centuries neither side has blinked.

In 2025, Pope Francis chose to be buried here — the first pope in more than a century to rest outside the Vatican — beneath a plain marble slab carrying one word: Franciscus.

Rome's other churches changed costume with every era that passed through them. This one let the eras pass, and simply stayed — which is the quiet astonishment of the place: not that it's grand, but that underneath everything, it is still the same room.

tours.title: San Giovanni in Laterano
tours.shortDescription: The cathedral of Rome is not St Peter's. It's this church, and it says so.
tours.longDescription: The inscription calls it the mother and head of all the churches of the city and of the world — and it has the seniority to mean it. Consecrated in 324, barely a decade after Constantine legalised the faith, it is by most reckonings the oldest church in the West, and the popes lived here for a thousand years before the Vatican. Its bronze doors were taken from the Roman Senate house; across the street, pilgrims still climb twenty-eight marble steps on their knees.

stops.title: San Giovanni in Laterano
stops.caption: The cathedral of Rome is not St. Peter's. It's this church — and the inscription on its front says so plainly: the mother and head of all the churches of the city and of the world.
stops.transcriptText:
The cathedral of Rome is not St. Peter's. It's this church — and the inscription on its front says so plainly: the mother and head of all the churches of the city and of the world.

You should be standing in the piazza in front of San Giovanni in Laterano, facing the great east facade. Along the roofline, fifteen colossal statues — Christ at the centre, seven metres tall, saints to either side — look out over the rooftops. To one side of the basilica rises the tallest obelisk in Rome. And in the plain building across the street behind you is a staircase people climb only on their knees.

Take the roofline first. That facade went up in 1735, but it's the newest thing here by a wide margin. The church behind it was consecrated in 324, barely a decade after Constantine legalised the faith — which makes this, by most reckonings, the oldest church in the West. For a thousand years the popes lived here, not at the Vatican; when the first Jubilee in history was proclaimed in the year 1300, this is where the pilgrims came. And the great bronze doors at the centre of the porch were taken from the Roman Senate house down in the Forum — Roman senators walked through them centuries before any pope did.

The obelisk is older than all of it: cut in Egypt some three and a half thousand years ago, shipped over in the fourth century to decorate the racetrack at the Circus Maximus, then dug out of the mud and set up here in 1588. Thirty-two metres of granite — by most accounts the tallest of its kind still standing anywhere.

Finally, the staircase across the street. Twenty-eight marble steps — by tradition, the stairs of Pilate's palace in Jerusalem, the ones climbed on the day of the trial. Pilgrims ascend them only on their knees, one step at a time, and have for centuries; the marble is sheathed in wood because devotion was slowly wearing it away. Whatever you make of where the steps began, what happens on them is real, and it is quietly moving to watch.

St. Peter's is where the world looks. But every new pope still comes here to take possession of this church — because before he is anything else, he is the bishop of Rome, and this has been his cathedral for seventeen centuries.

tours.title: Trajan's Column
tours.shortDescription: A war memorial with no dead soldiers on it.
tours.longDescription: A hundred and fifty-five carved scenes spiral up the shaft, more than two and a half thousand figures, the emperor appearing fifty-eight times — and in the entire frieze not one Roman lies dead. The legions build bridges, cut roads and harvest crops; the fighting is almost a sideline. It is the empire exactly as the empire wished to be seen. It is also a tomb, and — because the Dacians left so little of themselves behind — the main place their faces survive, carved by the power that destroyed them.

stops.title: Trajan's Column
stops.caption: This is a war memorial with no dead soldiers on it. Two hundred metres of carved storytelling spiral up the shaft in front of you — a hundred and fifty-five scenes, more than two and a half thousand figures, the emperor Trajan appearing fifty-eight times — and in the entire frieze, not one Roman lies dead.
stops.transcriptText:
This is a war memorial with no dead soldiers on it. Two hundred metres of carved storytelling spiral up the shaft in front of you — a hundred and fifty-five scenes, more than two and a half thousand figures, the emperor Trajan appearing fifty-eight times — and in the entire frieze, not one Roman lies dead. The legions build bridges, cut roads, harvest crops, hold ceremonies; the fighting is almost a sideline. It is the empire exactly as the empire wished to be seen.

You should be at the edge of Trajan's Forum, just off Via dei Fori Imperiali at the Piazza Venezia end, looking at the great marble column that stands between two domed churches. It went up in the year 113 to celebrate Trajan's conquest of Dacia — roughly modern Romania — and it's built from about twenty colossal drums of Carrara marble, stacked with a spiral staircase already carved inside them. The frieze winds around the shaft twenty-three times, and it was designed to be read: the band grows wider toward the top, so the figures hold their size against the distance.

Two details worth carrying away. First, the column is a tomb — Trajan's ashes were placed in a chamber in the base, making him one of the very few Romans buried inside the sacred boundary of his own city. Second, the inscription over the door records something remarkable: the column stands as tall as the hillside that was cleared away to build this forum. It's a monument that doubles as a measuring stick for a piece of landscape that no longer exists. As for the figure on top, that was Trajan once — a pope swapped him for Saint Peter in the fifteen eighties, and Peter has kept the best view in Rome ever since.

And here is the strange power of the thing: it's propaganda, and it became the historical record anyway. The Dacians left almost nothing of themselves behind, so this victory column — carved by the power that destroyed their kingdom — is one of the main places their faces survive. Romanians still come here to study their ancestors on their conqueror's monument.

Get close to the base and follow the first turn of the spiral with your eyes. In the opening scenes, the army is crossing the Danube on a bridge of boats — the whole story begins with men walking over water.

tours.title: Porta San Sebastiano
tours.shortDescription: Rome didn't have walls when it was strong.
tours.longDescription: For its first great centuries the city sprawled undefended, because the empire itself was the wall. Then in the 270s, with invaders reaching Italy, Aurelian threw nineteen kilometres of brick around Rome in a frantic hurry. These walls are not a symbol of Roman power — they are the moment Rome admitted it was mortal. Porta San Sebastiano is the grandest gate left in that circuit, and it kept collecting history for seventeen centuries: a medieval battle carving, hooks that held garlands for Charles V, and a Fascist official's apartment in its towers.

stops.title: Porta San Sebastiano
stops.caption: Rome didn't have walls when it was strong. That's the detail that reframes everything you're looking at.
stops.transcriptText:
Rome didn't have walls when it was strong. That's the detail that reframes everything you're looking at. For its first great centuries the city sprawled undefended, because the empire itself was the wall — the frontier was a thousand kilometres away in every direction. Then, in the 270s AD, with invaders suddenly reaching Italy, the emperor Aurelian threw nineteen kilometres of brick around the city in a frantic hurry. These walls aren't a symbol of Roman power. They're the moment Rome admitted it was mortal.

You're at Porta San Sebastiano, and it is the grandest surviving gate in that whole circuit — two massive marble-based towers flanking a single arch, still doing duty as a city gate with traffic passing underneath. It was born as the Porta Appia, because the road running through it is the Via Appia — the queen of roads, the empire's first great highway, heading out through this arch toward the tombs, the catacombs and, eventually, the sea.

Now, the gate itself, because it kept collecting history for seventeen centuries. Step close to the archway: scratched into the stone inside is a small medieval figure of the archangel Michael slaying a dragon, carved to commemorate a battle fought at this gate in 1327, when Romans beat back an invading army — an inscription beside it names the day. In 1536, the gate was dressed up as a triumphal arch for the entry of Emperor Charles V; the decorations are long gone, but the iron hooks that held the garlands are still up there under the cornice. And in the 1940s, the Fascist regime converted the towers into a private apartment for one of its own officials — the regime moved in, the city, in time, absorbed it, and today the gate houses a small free museum of the walls themselves.

Walk through the arch and out the other side, and you're standing on the first metres of the Appia Antica — the road south, running straight as an argument, two thousand three hundred years old. The wall was built out of fear. The road was built out of confidence. This gate is where the two ideas pass through each other.

tours.title: Testaccio
tours.shortDescription: The hill in front of you is a fake — and every piece of it is a broken jar.
tours.longDescription: Monte Testaccio is thirty-five metres of man-made mountain: by the standard estimate the remains of some fifty-three million olive-oil amphorae, smashed, carried up and laid in tidy terraced rows by ancient Rome's dockworkers for about three hundred years. It is the ancient world's largest landfill and one of its most eloquent monuments — a hill raised to the Roman appetite. The neighbourhood at its feet has never stopped feeding people.

stops.title: Testaccio
stops.caption: The hill in front of you is a fake. Thirty-five metres high, a kilometre around, covered in scrub and grass — and every cubic metre of it is man-made.
stops.transcriptText:
The hill in front of you is a fake. Thirty-five metres high, a kilometre around, covered in scrub and grass — and every cubic metre of it is man-made. Monte Testaccio is a mountain of broken pottery: by the standard estimate, the remains of some fifty-three million olive-oil jars, stacked here, piece by piece, by ancient Rome's sanitation department.

Stand anywhere along the streets that ring the hill — Via Zabaglia or Via Galvani work well — and look at the fenced green slope. Then let the numbers do their work. This district was the Emporium, ancient Rome's river port, where the food supply for a million people came ashore. Olive oil arrived in huge clay amphorae that couldn't be reused — the oil soaked in and went rancid — so the empire's dockworkers smashed them, carried the pieces up, laid them in tidy terraced rows, and dusted the layers with lime to keep the smell down. For about three hundred years. The result is the ancient world's largest landfill, and one of its most eloquent monuments: not a temple to the gods, but a hill raised to the Roman appetite.

The neighbourhood at its feet has never stopped feeding people. Testaccio was built up in the late 1800s as a working-class quarter around the city's slaughterhouse, and out of that slaughterhouse came Rome's boldest cooking — the quinto quarto, the "fifth quarter", the cuts the workers took home as part of their pay and turned into dishes Romans now queue for. The slaughterhouse itself closed in the 1970s and has been reborn as an arts and university complex; the covered market a couple of blocks away is one of the best places in the city to eat like a Roman on a budget. Even the hill still works: cellars and clubs are burrowed into its base, keeping wine cool against two-thousand-year-old potsherds.

Every city is built on its own past. Testaccio just makes it literal — a hill you can walk around in twenty minutes, made entirely of lunch.

tours.title: Notre-Dame Basilica and Place d'Armes
tours.shortDescription: Faith on one side of the square, money on the other, staring each other down since 1847.
tours.longDescription: Place d'Armes holds Montreal's whole argument in one cobbled circle: the Gothic front of Notre-Dame Basilica on one side, the Roman portico of the Bank of Montreal directly opposite, and Maisonneuve, who founded the city in 1642, on a pedestal between them. The basilica was built in 1829 by James O'Donnell, an Irish-born Protestant from New York who converted at the end of his life and lies in the crypt — the only person who does. Inside, Victor Bourgeau's midnight-blue vault is scattered with thousands of gold stars. For a century the church was winning the argument; then, in a single generation, Quebec became one of the most secular societies in North America.

stops.title: Notre-Dame Basilica and Place d'Armes
stops.caption: Stand in the centre of Place d'Armes and turn a slow circle.
stops.transcriptText:
Stand in the centre of Place d'Armes and turn a slow circle. Almost everything this city has ever cared about is looking back at you.

You should be in the cobbled square at the heart of Old Montreal. On the south side, two flat-topped stone towers rise over a grand Gothic front — that's Notre-Dame Basilica. Directly opposite, a domed building with a Roman temple portico: the head office of the Bank of Montreal, built in 1847. And in the centre of the square, a bronze founder on a pedestal — Paul de Chomedey de Maisonneuve, who started all of this in 1642.

Begin with the basilica. It went up in 1829, and the architect was a surprise: James O'Donnell, an Irish-born Protestant working out of New York, hired by Catholic Montreal to build the largest church on the continent at the time. The commission changed him. He converted to Catholicism at the end of his life, and he's buried in the crypt beneath the church — the only person who is. The two towers have names, Perseverance and Temperance, and the western one carries the Gros Bourdon, one of the largest bells in North America. When it rings, you feel it in the pavement.

Inside — and it's worth the ticket — the vault is deep midnight blue, scattered with thousands of gold stars, the whole interior carved and gilded like the inside of a jewel box. Most of that is the later work of Victor Bourgeau, and it's the reason people gasp at the door.

Now turn around. Faith on one side of the square, money on the other, staring at each other since 1847 — and for a century, the church was winning. It ran the schools, the hospitals, the rhythm of the week. Then, in a single generation starting in the 1960s, Quebec became one of the most secular societies in North America. The pews emptied, but the building endures — as a monument, a concert hall, an evening light show.
