In 2011, a tram descending a steep street lost its brakes and derailed, killing six people and injuring dozens more; the whole network was shut down for years afterwards while every mechanism on every tram was rebuilt and tested.

Passenger service resumed gradually from 2015, and the network has kept expanding since — branches to Paula Mattos and Dois Irmãos are running regular daily schedules again, and work is underway to reconnect the tram with the Corcovado train line for the first time in about fifty years.

What's worth knowing, climbing aboard, is that this isn't really a museum piece kept running for nostalgia. It's Santa Teresa's actual public transport, still carrying residents up and down the hill the way it has for well over a century, tourists simply along for the same ride.

Take the open-sided car if you get the choice, and don't rush the crossing over the aqueduct — the arches below, Lapa's rooftops, and the hill climbing away behind you are worth the slow pace this old system has never really given up.

tours.title: Boteco Belmonte
tours.shortDescription: A corner on Ipanema beachfront where the ritual of cold chope and a shared plate counts as civic life.
tours.longDescription: Tables spill out under awnings on both sides of the building where Avenida Vieira Souto meets Rua Teixeira de Melo, directly across from Ipanema beach. This branch belongs to a chain that began in 1952 on Praia do Flamengo as a no-frills spot for beachgoers and off-duty workers wanting draught beer and something salty; a former waiter, Antônio Rodrigues, bought the business in 2002 and grew it across the city. Order the bolinho de bacalhau, fried to order, the dish that built the reputation alongside the beer — then look for the empada aberta, an open-topped savoury pie regulars treat as the real signature. What Belmonte represents more than any single dish is the culture of the boteco itself. The original Flamengo branch was declared cultural heritage in 2023.

stops.title: Boteco Belmonte
stops.caption: Across the road, Ipanema beach is doing what it always does — filling up with football, paddleball and the occasional coconut vendor — and this corner has been where people come to watch it with a cold beer in hand for years.
stops.transcriptText:
Across the road, Ipanema beach is doing what it always does — filling up with football, paddleball and the occasional coconut vendor — and this corner has been where people come to watch it with a cold beer in hand for years.

Avenida Vieira Souto, right where it meets Rua Teixeira de Melo: that's the corner you want, with Belmonte's tables spilling out under awnings on both sides of the building. This branch belongs to a chain that started life in 1952 on Praia do Flamengo, a no-frills spot for beachgoers and off-duty workers wanting draught beer and something salty to go with it. A former waiter named Antônio Rodrigues bought the business in 2002 and grew it into the string of branches across the city that includes this one.

Order the bolinho de bacalhau first — salt cod croquettes, fried to order, the dish that built the chain's reputation alongside the beer itself. Then look for the empada aberta on the menu, an open-topped savoury pie rather than the usual sealed pastry, which regulars treat as Belmonte's real signature.

What Belmonte represents, more than any single dish, is the culture of the boteco itself: standing-room bars where the ritual of ice-cold chope and a shared plate of petiscos after work or a swim counts as something close to civic life in Rio. The original Flamengo branch was declared official cultural heritage of the city in 2023, and this Ipanema outpost carries the same idea onto one of the most photographed beachfronts in the world.

If you follow Rua Teixeira de Melo back away from the beach, it runs straight into the heart of Ipanema's shopping streets — worth the walk once the chope's finished.

tours.title: Igreja da Candelária
tours.shortDescription: The dome took twenty years longer to build than the whole church beneath it.
tours.longDescription: Construction began in 1775, a single nave opened in 1811 for Dom João VI, and the church was not really finished until the dome went up between 1856 and 1877, using limestone shipped from Lisbon — for years afterwards the tallest structure in the city. Italian-style marble, German stained glass and Art Nouveau pulpits were added in layers over the following decades, so what stands here is several different centuries of Rio stacked on one shared foundation. The facade faces the bay quite deliberately: this was the first thing ships would have seen arriving in colonial Rio. It is also a site of modern tragedy. On the night of 23 July 1993, gunmen opened fire on a group of homeless children sleeping on these steps, killing eight, most still teenagers. The case became a turning point in Brazil's child-protection laws; a small memorial cross stands here today.

stops.title: Igreja da Candelária
stops.caption: Look at the dome first, because it took twenty years longer to build than the rest of the church beneath it.
stops.transcriptText:
Look at the dome first, because it took twenty years longer to build than the rest of the church beneath it.

Step back into the square facing Candelária, in Centro, and you're looking at a building that took over a century to complete — construction began in 1775, a single nave opened in 1811 for Dom João the Sixth, and the whole church wasn't really finished until the dome went up between 1856 and 1877, using limestone shipped over from Lisbon. For years afterwards, that dome was the tallest structure anywhere in the city. Inside, Italian-style marble, German stained glass and Art Nouveau pulpits were added in layers over the following decades, so the church you're standing in front of is really several different centuries of Rio stacked on top of one shared foundation.

The facade faces the bay quite deliberately: this was the first thing ships would have seen arriving in colonial Rio, a church built to greet the city's visitors before almost anything else did.

It's also, more soberly, a site of modern tragedy. On the night of the 23rd of July 1993, gunmen opened fire on a group of homeless children sleeping on these steps, killing eight of them, most still teenagers. The case drew international attention to violence against Brazil's street children and became a turning point in the country's child-protection laws — a small memorial cross, renovated in 2023, stands here today in their memory.

From Candelária, the old commercial streets of Centro spread out towards the Paço Imperial and Praça XV — worth continuing that way on foot, carrying both the church's history and what happened on its steps with you.

tours.title: Casa das Canoas
tours.shortDescription: The house where Juscelino Kubitschek asked Oscar Niemeyer to help him build Brasília.
tours.longDescription: A free-form concrete canopy floating over glass walls in São Conrado — Casa das Canoas is the house Oscar Niemeyer designed for himself and built between 1951 and 1953. Rather than clear the site, he built around what was already there: a large granite boulder sits inside the composition, with the swimming pool curving around it and the roof sweeping past, so the rock reads as the centre of the house rather than an obstacle to it. Niemeyer described the idea as designing with complete freedom, adapting to the land's contours without altering them, working in curves rather than straight lines. Roberto Burle Marx laid out the garden. The house is not only a beautiful object but an argument — that modernism need not mean rigid European boxes. It was protected as a national heritage site in 2007, Niemeyer's hundredth year.

stops.title: Casa das Canoas
stops.caption: Brasília was born, in a sense, right where you're standing — this is the house where Juscelino Kubitschek asked Oscar Niemeyer to help him build Brazil's new capital.
stops.transcriptText:
Brasília was born, in a sense, right where you're standing — this is the house where Juscelino Kubitschek asked Oscar Niemeyer to help him build Brazil's new capital.

This free-form concrete canopy in front of you, floating over glass walls in São Conrado, is Casa das Canoas, the house Niemeyer designed for himself and built between 1951 and 1953. Rather than clearing the site, he built around what was already there — a large granite boulder sits inside the composition, with the swimming pool curving around it and the roof sweeping past it, so the rock reads as the actual centre of the house rather than an obstacle to it.

Niemeyer described the idea himself: designing with complete freedom, adapting to the land's contours without altering them, working in curves rather than straight lines. The garden around the house was laid out by Roberto Burle Marx, who'd already worked with Niemeyer on earlier projects and would go on shaping landscapes across Brazil for decades.

Here's what's easy to miss about a house this photogenic: it isn't just a beautiful object, it's an argument. Niemeyer built it partly to prove that modernism didn't have to mean rigid European boxes — that concrete could bend, and a house could grow out of a hillside rather than sit on top of it. The building was formally protected as a national heritage site in 2007, Niemeyer's hundredth year.

The house is currently closed to visitors for maintenance work, so this is very much an outside-the-gate stop for now — worth checking the Fundação Oscar Niemeyer's own channels before you plan a return visit once it reopens.

tours.title: Casa Roberto Marinho
tours.shortDescription: A Cosme Velho house that quietly hosted more of Brazil's cultural history than most museums manage to collect.
tours.longDescription: Built between 1939 and 1943 as the home of Roberto Marinho — the businessman who turned his father's newspaper into Grupo Globo, Brazil's largest media empire — this neocolonial house was deliberately modelled on a historic Pernambuco manor rather than the European styles fashionable among Rio's elite. Roberto Burle Marx laid out the garden early in his career, blending the grounds into the Atlantic Forest at the property's edge. For some sixty years the house worked as an informal cultural and diplomatic salon, hosting Tom Jobim and Dorival Caymmi and welcoming visiting dignitaries. Marinho's own legacy is not simple — his empire's relationship with Brazil's military governments remains genuinely debated — and the house does not try to settle that argument. Since 2014 it has held around 1,400 works of Brazilian Modernism, including Tarsila do Amaral, Portinari and Di Cavalcanti.

stops.title: Casa Roberto Marinho
stops.caption: There's a house in Cosme Velho that quietly hosted more of Brazil's cultural history than most museums manage to collect.
stops.transcriptText:
There's a house in Cosme Velho that quietly hosted more of Brazil's cultural history than most museums manage to collect.

That neocolonial building in front of you, deliberately modelled on a historic Pernambuco manor house rather than the European styles fashionable among Rio's elite at the time, was built between 1939 and 1943 as the home of Roberto Marinho, the businessman who built Grupo Globo into Brazil's largest media empire after taking over his father's newspaper at twenty years old. The garden around it was laid out by Roberto Burle Marx, early in his career, blending the grounds into the Atlantic Forest at the edge of the property.

For roughly sixty years, this house worked as an informal cultural and diplomatic salon — hosting musicians like Tom Jobim and Dorival Caymmi, welcoming visiting dignitaries, and quietly becoming one of the places where Brazil's cultural and political classes actually met. It's worth knowing, standing here, that Marinho's own legacy is not simple: his media empire's relationship with Brazil's military governments in the 1960s and 1970s remains genuinely debated in Brazil today, and this house doesn't try to settle that argument — it simply preserves the collection and the setting.

Since 2014, the building has operated as the Instituto Casa Roberto Marinho, holding around 1,400 works focused on Brazilian Modernism, by artists including Tarsila do Amaral, Cândido Portinari and Di Cavalcanti, displayed through rooms that still feel more like a house than a gallery.

The institute is a short walk from the Corcovado train station, so it pairs naturally with a morning heading up to Christ the Redeemer — worth building into the same outing rather than a separate trip.

tours.title: Catedral Metropolitana
tours.shortDescription: A cone rising seventy-five metres, built to a set of instructions no Gothic cathedral ever received.
tours.longDescription: The foundation stone was laid in 1964 on the feast day of Rio's patron saint, and the Catedral Metropolitana rose across the 1960s and 70s to the design of Edgar de Oliveira da Fonseca, replacing Rio's older Baroque cathedral as seat of the Archdiocese. The shape is usually traced to Mayan step-pyramids rather than the Gothic or Baroque templates most cathedrals borrow, and it follows a very different brief: Vatican reforms of the time called for congregations to sit equally close to the altar on every side, which a cone manages far more naturally than a long nave. Four stained-glass windows run the full sixty-four metres from floor to ceiling, colouring the interior with shifting light rather than individual saints and scenes. It holds 5,000 seated and up to 20,000 standing. Pope Francis said Mass here in 2013 for World Youth Day.

stops.title: Catedral Metropolitana
stops.caption: It's 1964, and on the feast day of Rio's patron saint, the foundation stone is laid for a cathedral that will look nothing like any cathedral built before it in this city.
stops.transcriptText:
It's 1964, and on the feast day of Rio's patron saint, the foundation stone is laid for a cathedral that will look nothing like any cathedral built before it in this city.

Centro, on the site where São Sebastião is honoured: that's where the Catedral Metropolitana stands, a cone rising seventy-five metres, designed by the architect Edgar de Oliveira da Fonseca and built across the 1960s and 70s, replacing Rio's older Baroque cathedral as the seat of the Archdiocese. The shape is usually traced to Mayan step-pyramids rather than the Gothic or Baroque templates most cathedrals borrow from, and it follows a very different set of instructions too — recent Vatican reforms at the time called for congregations to sit equally close to the altar on every side, which a cone does far more naturally than a long nave ever could.

Step inside and look straight up. Four enormous stained-glass windows run the full sixty-four metres from floor to ceiling, colouring the whole interior with shifting light rather than the individual saints and scenes a traditional cathedral window would show. The building holds 5,000 people seated, and up to 20,000 standing, for a scale Rio's older churches were never built to manage.

Pope Francis held Mass here in 2013, during his first overseas trip as pontiff, for World Youth Day — a fitting stop, given the building's own guiding brief decades earlier was simplicity and closeness between clergy and congregation.

The cathedral sits close enough to Arcos da Lapa and the Selarón Steps to fold naturally into the same walk — worth continuing down through Lapa afterwards while the light through those windows is still fresh in mind.

tours.title: Centro Cultural Banco do Brasil
tours.shortDescription: A hundred years before anyone hung a painting here, this rotunda was full of traders shouting over government bonds.
tours.longDescription: The building was begun in 1880 by the architect Francisco Joaquim Béthencourt da Silva and opened in 1906 as headquarters of Rio's Commercial Association, its domed rotunda serving as the city's public bonds exchange. Banco do Brasil bought and remodelled it in the 1920s and ran its own headquarters from here until 1960 — the layered history is still legible, neoclassical columns below, Art Nouveau and Art Deco touches worked in around the dome above. After decades of quiet the bank reopened it in 1989 as a cultural centre, deliberately keeping the historic shell intact while turning the interior into exhibition space. It has become an anchor of Rio's cultural calendar since, hosting major international touring exhibitions alongside theatre, cinema and music, all free to attend.

stops.title: Centro Cultural Banco do Brasil
stops.caption: A hundred years before anyone hung a painting here, this rotunda was full of traders shouting over government bonds.
stops.transcriptText:
A hundred years before anyone hung a painting here, this rotunda was full of traders shouting over government bonds.

Walk in under the dome, because that's the room that explains the whole building. Centro Cultural Banco do Brasil occupies a structure begun in 1880 by the architect Francisco Joaquim Béthencourt da Silva, first opened in 1906 as the headquarters of Rio's Commercial Association, with this same domed rotunda serving as the city's public bonds exchange. Banco do Brasil bought and remodelled the building in the 1920s, running its own headquarters from here until 1960 — you can still read the layered history in the details: neoclassical columns underneath, Art Nouveau and Art Deco touches worked in around the dome above.

The building sat quietly for decades after that before Banco do Brasil reopened it in 1989 as a cultural centre, deliberately keeping the historic shell intact while turning the interior into exhibition space. It's become one of the anchors of Rio's cultural calendar since, regularly hosting major international touring exhibitions, alongside a full programme of theatre, cinema and music, all free to attend.

What makes the building worth lingering in isn't just any single show, though — it's the way the space itself keeps doing double duty, a nineteenth-century financial institution repurposed, floor by floor, into one of the city's busiest public galleries, without ever quite erasing what it used to be.

From the rotunda, Rio's old commercial district spreads out in every direction — the Paço Imperial and the Praça XV waterfront are both a short walk away, worth combining with a visit here if Centro's colonial core is on your route.

tours.title: Christ the Redeemer
tours.shortDescription: On the hidden underside of thousands of its tiles, someone wrote a name or a wish that nobody will ever read.
tours.longDescription: Christ the Redeemer stands 709 metres up on Corcovado peak in Tijuca National Park, a reinforced concrete figure clad in soapstone, built between 1922 and 1931. The French sculptor Paul Landowski designed the face and hands in his Paris studio and shipped them over in pieces; the Brazilian engineer Heitor da Silva Costa oversaw the project, with the French engineer Albert Caquot solving how a concrete figure this size could withstand the wind at the summit. The statue is 30 metres tall with arms spanning 28, on a pedestal adding another 8, visible on a clear day from almost anywhere in the city. In 2007 it was voted one of the New Seven Wonders of the World. Local parish women glued its soapstone tiles onto mesh sheets during construction, and many wrote names and wishes on the hidden underside before they were sealed into place.

stops.title: Christ the Redeemer
stops.caption: Every soapstone tile covering this statue was glued on by hand, and on the back of thousands of them, before they ever went up, someone wrote a name, a wish, or a prayer that no one will ever read again.
stops.transcriptText:
Every soapstone tile covering this statue was glued on by hand, and on the back of thousands of them, before they ever went up, someone wrote a name, a wish, or a prayer that no one will ever read again.

Corcovado peak, 709 metres up in Tijuca National Park: that's where Christ the Redeemer stands, a reinforced concrete figure clad in soapstone, built between 1922 and 1931. The French sculptor Paul Landowski designed the face and hands in his Paris studio and shipped them over in pieces; the Brazilian engineer Heitor da Silva Costa oversaw the whole project, with the French engineer Albert Caquot solving the structural problem of how a concrete figure this size could actually stand up to the wind and weather at the summit.

The statue alone stands 30 metres tall, arms spanning 28 metres, on a pedestal that adds another 8 — visible, on a clear day, from almost anywhere in the city below. In 2007 it was voted one of the New Seven Wonders of the World, alongside the Great Wall of China and Machu Picchu.

Here's the detail most visitors never hear: local parish women glued those soapstone tiles onto mesh sheets during construction, and it became a habit for many of them to write names and wishes on the hidden underside before it was sealed into place. The statue everyone photographs from outside is, underneath its skin, carrying thousands of private messages nobody will ever recover.

If you've come up by train, the return route down through Cosme Velho passes close to Casa das Canoas and Corcovado's other viewpoints — worth building a longer walk around the mountain if the weather's holding.

tours.title: Cidade das Artes
tours.shortDescription: Mocked for years as a monument to waste, it is now one of the most serious music venues in Latin America.
tours.longDescription: Designed by the French architect Christian de Portzamparc and raised on a plaza some ten metres above the crossing of two motorways in Barra da Tijuca, Cidade das Artes reads as two long concrete planes — floor and roof — holding several halls between them. It was announced in 2002 as Cidade da Música, budgeted at around eighty million reais and due to open within two years. It didn't. Costs spiralled towards half a billion, a city council inquiry was opened into the overruns, and the press nicknamed the half-built shell an elefante branco. It finally opened, incomplete, in 2008, and was not properly finished and renamed until 2013. The main hall seats close to 1,800 and is billed as the largest purpose-built concert hall of its kind in South America, home to the Brazilian Symphony Orchestra — the scandal and the achievement both true of the same walls.

stops.title: Cidade das Artes
stops.caption: That vast concrete roof floating above two horizontal slabs took a decade longer to finish than anyone promised, and it very nearly never opened at all.
stops.transcriptText:
That vast concrete roof floating above two horizontal slabs took a decade longer to finish than anyone promised, and it very nearly never opened at all.

Barra da Tijuca, at the crossing of two motorways, raised plaza about ten metres up: that's where you're standing, in front of Cidade das Artes, designed by the French architect Christian de Portzamparc. The whole building reads as two long concrete planes, floor and roof, holding several halls between them like a very expensive sandwich.

Start with the name, because it used to be a different one. This was announced in 2002 as Cidade da Música, budgeted at around eighty million reais and due to open within two years. It didn't. Costs spiralled towards half a billion reais, a city council inquiry was opened to investigate the overruns, and the press nicknamed the half-built shell an "elefante branco" — a white elephant. It finally opened, incomplete, in 2008, and wasn't properly finished and renamed Cidade das Artes until 2013.

Now it does exactly what it was built for. The main hall seats close to 1,800 people and is billed as the largest purpose-built concert hall of its kind in South America, home to the Brazilian Symphony Orchestra, alongside three theatres and a dozen rehearsal rooms tucked into the slabs around it.

And that's rather the pivot worth holding onto: a building mocked for years as a monument to waste has quietly become one of the most serious music venues in Latin America — the scandal and the achievement both true of the same walls.

Walk up onto the raised plaza before you leave. From up there, the whole strange, oversized structure makes a lot more sense than it does from the road.

tours.title: Escadaria Selarón
tours.shortDescription: 2,000 tiles from over 60 countries, covering 215 steps one artist spent two decades turning into his life's work.
tours.longDescription: On the steep staircase joining Santa Teresa to Lapa, the Chilean-born painter and ceramist Jorge Selarón began tiling the steps in 1990, at first with leftover construction materials because that was what he had to hand. As his reputation grew, visitors from around the world sent or brought tiles of their own, and he worked them in alongside roughly 300 he hand-painted himself, most repeating a single motif: a pregnant African woman. He was famously vague about when the work would be finished, reportedly saying only that it would be done the day he died. The city made him an honorary resident in 2005. Selarón died in January 2013, found on the steps he had spent his life covering; the exact circumstances were never fully resolved and remain an open question. The tiling is still maintained, and still occasionally added to, in his memory.

stops.title: Escadaria Selarón
stops.caption: 2,000 tiles, donated from over 60 countries, cover 215 steps that one artist spent more than two decades turning into his life's work.
stops.transcriptText:
2,000 tiles, donated from over 60 countries, cover 215 steps that one artist spent more than two decades turning into his life's work.

Between Santa Teresa and Lapa, on the steep staircase connecting the two neighbourhoods, you'll find the Escadaria Selarón, started in 1990 by Jorge Selarón, a Chilean-born painter and ceramist who'd settled in a house right beside these steps and simply began tiling them, at first using leftover construction materials because that's what he had to hand. As his reputation grew, visitors from around the world started sending or bringing tiles of their own, and Selarón worked them into the design alongside roughly 300 tiles he hand-painted himself, most repeating a single motif: a pregnant African woman.

He was famously vague about when the project would ever be finished, reportedly saying only that it would be done the day he died. In 2005, the city made him an honorary resident in recognition of the work, and the steps became part of Rio's pitch for the 2016 Olympics not long after.

Selarón died in January 2013, found on the steps he'd spent his life covering; the exact circumstances were never fully resolved, and it remains a genuinely open question rather than a settled story. The tiling continues in his memory today, still maintained, still occasionally added to.

The steps sit almost exactly between the Santa Teresa tram route above and the bars of Lapa below — worth treating this stop as the hinge connecting the two neighbourhoods, rather than a destination on its own.

tours.title: Fábrica Bhering
tours.shortDescription: A bankrupt chocolate factory in the old port, now humming with roughly 80 working artists.
tours.longDescription: The iron skeleton of this six-storey building on Rua Orestes in Santo Cristo was bought secondhand and shipped over from a bankrupt chocolate factory in Hamburg before it even opened here in 1930. The Bhering brand itself dated to 1880, founded by a German immigrant who once supplied Brazil's imperial family, and the company made chocolate, coffee and sweets here until it went bankrupt in the 1990s. Artists began moving in around 2005, drawn by the light through the old skylights and rents nobody else wanted. It nearly ended in 2012, when a developer bought the building at auction and moved to evict everyone — until the mayor stepped in with a heritage listing and an expropriation order. What is here now is a working creative economy rather than a museum piece: potters, furniture makers, photographers, booksellers and a small brewery, sharing floors with a century of chocolate machinery left standing as decoration.

stops.title: Fábrica Bhering
stops.caption: Rio's old port district is quiet on most days, warehouses and cobbled streets, and then you reach this six-storey building humming with roughly 80 working artists behind its windows.
stops.transcriptText:
Rio's old port district is quiet on most days, warehouses and cobbled streets, and then you reach this six-storey building humming with roughly 80 working artists behind its windows.

Rua Orestes, in Santo Cristo, right at the edge of the port zone: that's where Fábrica Bhering stands, a building whose iron skeleton was bought secondhand and shipped over from a bankrupt chocolate factory in Hamburg before it even opened here in 1930. The Bhering chocolate brand itself dated back to 1880, founded by a German immigrant who once supplied Brazil's imperial family, and the company kept making chocolate, coffee and sweets here until it went bankrupt in the 1990s and the building sat empty.

Artists started moving in around 2005, drawn by the light pouring through the old skylights and rents nobody else wanted, in a pattern that had already played out in old factories in Berlin and London. It nearly ended in 2012, when a developer bought the building at auction and moved to evict everyone — until the mayor stepped in with a heritage listing and an expropriation order that secured the artists' place for good.

What's here today is a working creative economy rather than a museum piece: potters, furniture makers, photographers, booksellers and a small brewery, all sharing floors with a century of chocolate-making machinery left standing as decoration. Climb to the rooftop terrace, nicknamed "o Pombal," and the view runs clear across Centro to Niterói on the far side of the bay.

Come back on the first Saturday of the month, when the building opens every studio at once for its Circuito Interno — art, music and food running through all six floors simultaneously, the closest thing to seeing the whole factory as one place rather than 80 separate ones.

tours.title: Feira do Lavradio
tours.shortDescription: A monthly antiques fair on a street laid out in 1771 — three decades on, it runs every single week.
tours.longDescription: In the mid-1990s a handful of antique dealers and bar owners on Rua do Lavradio, a street laid out in 1771, decided to turn their block into a market one Saturday a month. Organised by the Associação Polo Novo Rio Antigo, it expanded to weekly Saturdays a few years ago to spread the crowds, and hundreds of stallholders now fill the street with furniture, vintage clothing, records, jewellery and bric-a-brac that resists any tidier description. Music runs through the whole thing rather than sitting off to one side — samba and choro musicians play as you browse, and a root-samba circle gathers most Saturday afternoons at nearby Praça Lima Barreto, drawing dancers as much as shoppers. What makes the street worth returning to is how an eighteenth-century address built for Rio's colonial elite has been repurposed, almost entirely by the people who work there.

stops.title: Feira do Lavradio

stops.transcriptText:
It's the mid-1990s, and a handful of antique dealers and bar owners on one of Rio's oldest streets decide to turn their block into a market one Saturday a month — three decades later, that market runs every single week.

What makes Rua do Lavradio worth returning to isn't really any single stall, though — it's the way an eighteenth-century street built for Rio's colonial elite has been repurposed, gradually and almost entirely by the people who work there, into one of the city's most reliable weekly gathering points.

Look past the furniture and jewellery for the food stalls that have joined more recently — small vendors selling everything from West African dishes to craft beer now line the edges of the market, worth grazing your way through between the antique stalls.

tours.title: Gonza
tours.shortDescription: A Buenos Aires neighbourhood tavern, filtered through carioca ingredients, inside a pink century-old mansion.
tours.longDescription: Gonza occupies a century-old mansion the neighbourhood calls "the pink corner", on Rua Pacheco Leão facing the Botanical Garden. The name comes from the chef, Gonzalo Vidal, an Argentine cook with over two decades in Rio kitchens, who built the place as a bodegón portenho — a Buenos Aires neighbourhood tavern — filtered through carioca ingredients and habits rather than imported wholesale. The milanesa is what regulars order first, but the charcuterie says most about the kitchen's ambitions: cured meats and sausages made in house, pastrami and salami included, alongside a proper steak tartare and a bife de chorizo. The dining room stays intimate and low-lit, built for a long dinner rather than a quick one. It arrived backed by serious money and serious credentials both, and early signs suggest the bet is paying off.

stops.title: Gonza

That pink building on the corner isn't a bakery or a boutique — the colour is just the calling card for one of Jardim Botânico's newest kitchens.

Rua Pacheco Leão, at the corner with Rua Estela, facing the Botanical Garden itself: that's where Gonza sits, inside a century-old mansion the neighbourhood has nicknamed "the pink corner." The name comes directly from the chef, Gonzalo Vidal, an Argentine cook with over two decades in Rio kitchens, who built the place as a bodegón portenho — a Buenos Aires neighbourhood tavern — filtered through carioca ingredients and habits rather than imported wholesale.

The Botanical Garden's back gate sits almost directly across the street, so it's worth timing a visit here around a walk through the gardens themselves — dinner at the pink corner makes a natural close to an afternoon spent among the trees opposite.

tours.title: Grado
tours.shortDescription: A serious Italian kitchen in a 1940s house — the reason turns out to be memory rather than strategy.
tours.longDescription: Grado opened in 2017 in a weathered 1940s house on Rua Visconde de Carandaí in Jardim Botânico, run by the chef Nello Garaventa, whose family roots trace to Liguria, alongside his wife Lara Atamian, who manages the room. The menu draws directly on Garaventa's childhood memories of his grandparents' cooking: handmade pasta is the clear centre of it, dishes like cacio e pepe agnolotti or a double ravioli filled with artichoke and fontina, made without the theatrical plating a lot of contemporary Italian places reach for. A wood-fired oven sits at the centre of the kitchen, used for both bread and mains — a whole roasted beetroot with goat's cheese among them, simple ingredients treated with real technique. The house still carries family artefacts and a small garden, split between an open kitchen downstairs and a quieter dining room above.

stops.title: Grado
stops.caption: Why would a serious Italian kitchen set up in a 1940s house in Jardim Botânico rather than anywhere flashier?
stops.transcriptText:
Why would a serious Italian kitchen set up in a 1940s house in Jardim Botânico rather than anywhere flashier? The answer, once you're inside, turns out to be memory rather than strategy.

This weathered house on Rua Visconde de Carandaí is Grado, opened in 2017 by the chef Nello Garaventa, whose family roots trace back to Liguria in Italy, running the kitchen alongside his wife, Lara Atamian, who manages the room. The menu draws directly on Garaventa's childhood memories of his grandparents' cooking there — handmade pasta is the clear centre of it, dishes like cacio e pepe agnolotti or a double ravioli filled with artichoke and fontina, made without any of the theatrical plating a lot of contemporary Italian places reach for instead.

At the centre of the kitchen itself sits a wood-fired oven, used for both bread and mains — a whole roasted beetroot with goat's cheese is one of the dishes it turns out, simple ingredients treated with real technique rather than dressed up to look complicated. The house still carries family artefacts and a small garden, split between an open kitchen downstairs and a more intimate dining room upstairs.

Grado has picked up real attention in Rio's food press and appears in the Michelin guide's own editorial coverage of the city, recognition that's arrived without the restaurant needing to chase it with spectacle.

Come at dusk if you can, when the garden light softens and the smell of the wood-fired oven reaches the street before you've even opened the door — this is a house built for a slow evening, not a quick one.

tours.title: Guimas
tours.shortDescription: Open since 1981, and the Filé Boursin has never once come off the menu, no matter who has asked.
tours.longDescription: A corner bistro in Baixo Gávea with a black-and-white checkerboard floor and small tables laid with paper cloths rather than linen. Two couples opened it in 1981 — Ricardo and Priscila Guimarães, and Chico and Tintim Mascarenhas — folding their surnames into the name over the door. Chico Mascarenhas trained as a photographer in Portugal before trading the camera for a kitchen, which is why the menu leans on Portuguese comfort food, bacalhau fritters and hearty stews, bound with French sauces and a proper butter-and-pâté couvert. The Filé Boursin came about when a customer asked for "meat with cheese"; the steak the kitchen improvised that night has stayed on the menu ever since, protected, as the family puts it, by something close to decree. Ask for a crayon with the tablecloth — the best diner doodles get framed and hung.

tours.title: Hotel Nacional
tours.shortDescription: Thirty-four storeys of concrete drum — and Niemeyer originally wanted fifty-five.
tours.longDescription: A perfect concrete cylinder rising above gardens by Roberto Burle Marx on the ocean side of the road in São Conrado, Hotel Nacional was designed by Oscar Niemeyer and built between 1968 and 1972. In its first years it was the place to be seen in Rio: a theatre inside hosted Liza Minnelli, B.B. King and James Brown, five restaurants ran at once, and it was a regular stop for the Rio Film Festival through the 1980s. Then the crowd moved on. It closed in 1995 and sat empty and stripped for over a decade — fittings gone, even the lifts pulled out, the convention hall taken over by squatters and, at one point, bats. The city listed it in 1998, though protection alone did not stop the decline. A new owner bought it in 2009 and a careful restoration brought back original details; it reopened in 2017 and has operated independently since.

tours.title: Jobi
tours.shortDescription: Open since 1956, and half in jest it is said to have married off and split up more couples than the local registry office.
tours.longDescription: In 1956 a Portuguese immigrant family opened a bar on the ground floor of a Leblon apartment block called Jobi, and took the building's name for it — a detail the family only fully traced while researching their own history for this year's seventieth anniversary. It is tempting to hear an echo of Antônio Carlos Jobim in the name, but no record ties the two together. Order the bolinho de bacalhau and a chope poured slowly enough to matter; regulars rate both among the best in Rio, and the family has protected the recipe and the pour through three generations since Sr. Adelino bought the business outright in 1960. Behind the bar is a mural by Nilton Bravo, who spent the 1960s decorating bars across the city. Jobi became more than a boteco during the dictatorship years, when artists, musicians and writers used rooms like this one to talk. Listed as cultural heritage in 2011.

It's 1956, and a Portuguese immigrant family that had already tried running a bar in a quieter part of the city opens a new one on the ground floor of a Leblon apartment block called Jobi.

That block still stands behind the counter you're facing, on Avenida Ataulfo de Paiva, and the bar took its name directly from the building's own — a detail the family only fully traced while researching their own history for this year's seventieth anniversary. It's tempting to hear an echo of the composer Antônio Carlos Jobim in that name, but no record ties the two together; it appears to be coincidence, however convenient a coincidence it sounds.

Order the bolinho de bacalhau and a chope, poured slowly enough to matter — regulars rate this among the best versions of both in Rio, and the family has protected the recipe and the pour through three generations of ownership since Sr. Adelino bought the business outright in 1960. The bar was declared official cultural heritage of the city in 2011, and it's now run by the third generation of the same family — a dentist, a doctor and a lawyer among the cousins who've kept it exactly as informal as it always was.

Ask a regular how long they've been coming, and don't be surprised if the answer runs to decades — Jobi has a reputation, only half in jest, for having married off and split up more couples than the local registry office.

tours.title: Libô
tours.shortDescription: The name comes from an Afro-Brazilian ritual: pouring out a sip in honour of a saint before anyone else tastes it.
tours.longDescription: Libô is the wine bar tucked inside Reduto, a cultural centre in a century-old townhouse on Rua Conde de Irajá in Botafogo, founded by the actor Marco Nanini and the producer Fernando Libonati. It opened in October 2024, run by the chef Roberta Ciasca — who also cooks next door at the vegetarian restaurant Brota — alongside the sommelier Maíra Freire, whose work at Lasai earned her recognition from the Michelin guide. Start with the shrimp rice, tossed in a green-tomato vinaigrette with a touch of pimenta-de-cheiro. Around it, a lean menu of cured meats and Brazilian artisanal cheeses is built to sit alongside wine rather than compete with it. The list is the real point: around thirty labels, mostly organic, biodynamic or natural, chalked on a board that changes as bottles run out. Libonati's own surname sits inside the name, too.

tours.title: MAC Niterói
tours.shortDescription: From certain angles it looks less like a museum than something that simply landed on the cliff.
tours.longDescription: A saucer-shaped structure balanced on a single slender column rising from a shallow reflecting pool, set on a promontory above Boa Viagem beach with nothing visible holding it up. MAC Niterói was designed by Oscar Niemeyer with his longtime structural engineer Bruno Contarini and completed in 1996; Niemeyer described wanting the form to grow out of the site "like a flower" rather than sit on it the way a conventional building would. A red-carpeted ramp, roughly a hundred metres of it, spirals around the base into a hexagonal gallery with no interior columns at all, its windows angled at forty degrees to frame Sugarloaf and the Rio skyline across the bay as if the view were part of the collection. That collection is substantial in its own right: over 1,200 works from the João Sattamini holding, one of the largest collections of Brazilian contemporary art anywhere.

tours.title: Madame Olympe
tours.shortDescription: Madame Olympe was Claude Troisgros's mother — a Michelin star arrived within the restaurant's first year.
tours.longDescription: Opened in 2025 on Rua Conde de Bernadotte in Leblon by Claude Troisgros, working alongside Jéssica Trindade, his collaborator of nearly two decades. The name is family history: Madame Olympe was Troisgros's mother, and it echoes an earlier restaurant the family ran for seventeen years before the pandemic closed it. The room is soft and contemporary, rice-paper lamps hung to look like clouds overhead, a deliberate contrast to the precision coming out of the kitchen. The food applies proper French technique, especially in the bread and sauces, to Brazilian ingredients, with touches leaning towards Japanese gastronomy; an eight-course tasting menu is the main event, with a shorter four-course option alongside it. That combination earned a star in the Michelin Guide Brazil within its first year, and a place on Condé Nast Traveler's international hot list soon after.

tours.title: MAM Rio
tours.shortDescription: Brazil's first major work of exposed concrete — and a building that once burned with much of the country's modern art inside.
tours.longDescription: Designed by Affonso Eduardo Reidy with construction beginning in 1954 and completed in stages through the 1960s, the Museu de Arte Moderna is held off the ground on trapezoidal concrete legs, Brazil's first major work of exposed-concrete architecture. Roberto Burle Marx laid out the gardens, and went on to landscape the surrounding Flamengo Park a few years later. On the night of 8 July 1978 fire tore through the galleries, destroying a huge share of the collection — Picasso, Miró, Dalí, Matisse and Magritte among them, alongside most of Brazil's own modernist holdings and a library of roughly 9,000 books. Start at street level, under the raised gallery block. If you've got time, step inside and look for the Cinemateca screenings — MAM's film archive survived the fire behind its own concrete walls, and the museum still runs free screenings from it most weeks, a quieter way into the same collection this building nearly lost.

tours.title: MAR — Museu de Arte do Rio
tours.shortDescription: An ornate palace and a plain old bus station, joined under one wave-shaped concrete roof.
tours.longDescription: On Praça Mauá, an ornate early-twentieth-century palace stands shoulder to shoulder with a plain modernist block that used to be Rio's central bus station. That pairing is MAR, the Museu de Arte do Rio, opened in 2013 to a design by Bernardes plus Jacobsen. What unifies the two mismatched buildings is a single undulating concrete canopy overhead, a wave-shaped roof that ties palace to terminal and turns the whole thing into one continuous museum. The collection is broader than the "contemporary art" label a lot of new museums reach for — over 20,000 items spanning historical and contemporary Brazilian art and visual culture together, alongside a dedicated education wing built into the old terminal side. The roof is not only holding the buildings together visually: climb up and it opens into a working rooftop terrace looking out over the bay towards Museu do Amanhã.

From here, it's an easy walk along the waterfront to Museu do Amanhã itself, and then on towards the old warehouses of Gamboa — worth treating this stretch of Praça Mauá as one connected museum route rather than a single stop.

tours.title: Maracanã
tours.shortDescription: There is a wound in Brazilian football over seventy years old, and this stadium is where it happened.
tours.longDescription: The Estádio Jornalista Mário Filho — universally the Maracanã — was built in 1950 for that year's World Cup and named for the sports journalist who championed it into existence. On 16 July 1950 a crowd officially recorded at just under 200,000, still the largest ever to watch a football match, packed in expecting Brazil to win the final. Uruguay won it instead, two goals to one, in a defeat still known as the Maracanaço and still discussed the way other countries discuss wars. Renovation for the 2014 World Cup and 2016 Olympics cut capacity to 78,838 in a single continuous bowl. After the Olympics the stadium was largely abandoned for a stretch — power cut off, seats torn up, even a bronze bust of Mário Filho stolen. It is in regular use again under a long-term concession held by Flamengo and Fluminense.

You're outside the Estádio Jornalista Mário Filho, better known simply as the Maracanã, built in 1950 for that year's World Cup and named after the sports journalist who championed it into existence, Mário Filho. The wider Maracanã complex includes an athletics stadium and swimming arena next door, both worth a look if you're curious how the whole 1950 sporting complex was originally laid out around this one giant bowl.

tours.title: Museu do Amanhã
tours.shortDescription: This museum owns almost nothing — its curator says the collection isn't objects, it's possibilities.
tours.longDescription: Designed by the Spanish architect Santiago Calatrava and opened in 2015 as the anchor of the Porto Maravilha waterfront redevelopment, the Museu do Amanhã juts out on Pier Mauá into Guanabara Bay, wings of white structure spread overhead and a reflecting pool wrapping the building so it seems to float. Those wing-like roof panels are not purely decorative — they carry solar cells that pivot through the day, tracking the sun, so the silhouette genuinely changes while you watch. Inside, the museum organises itself around five themes rather than a fixed collection: Cosmos, Earth, Anthropocene, Tomorrow and Us, covering climate change, population growth and the future of the species, updated as the questions shift. The one artefact it permanently holds is a churinga, a sacred object from Aboriginal Australia — a reminder that human meaning-making long predates any future on display.

The Museu do Amanhã sits right along the same waterfront as MAR, a short walk further round the harbour — worth pairing the two if Porto Maravilha's cluster of new museums is on your list for the day.

tours.title: Museu Nacional
tours.shortDescription: Twenty million objects, one electrical fault, and a single night in September 2018.
tours.longDescription: In 1808 the Portuguese royal family, having fled Napoleon across the Atlantic, moved into a palace on this spot. The Paço de São Cristóvão served as royal and then imperial residence until 1889 and became home to the Museu Nacional in 1892 — though the museum is older still, founded by royal decree in 1818, Brazil's first museum and arguably its first scientific institution altogether. Before September 2018 its collection ran to roughly 20 million objects: fossils, meteorites, mummies, remains stretching back thousands of years. On the second of that month an electrical fault sparked a fire that destroyed the vast majority of it. The Bendegó meteorite, five tonnes of iron and nickel, survived essentially intact and now sits at the centre of the reopened galleries; Luzia, one of the oldest human skulls found in the Americas, was pulled from the wreckage in fragments and is still being pieced together.

tours.title: Oseille
tours.shortDescription: Sixteen stools around an open kitchen, where the chef is as likely to take a song request as a food question.
tours.longDescription: The counter just inside the door on Rua Joana Angélica is the entire dining room at Oseille, a tasting-menu restaurant that opened in 2024 and picked up a Michelin star roughly a year later. The chef is Thomas Troisgros, part of a dynasty that has shaped Rio's fine dining for decades: his father Claude is a well-known face of French cooking in Brazil, and his grandfather Pierre helped invent nouvelle cuisine in France. The tasting menu runs five courses or seven and tends to move somewhere unexpected — oysters in tucupi, a scallop paired with coffee kombucha, a dessert built to look and taste like a mushroom. Oseille means sorrel, the herb at the centre of the salmon dish Pierre Troisgros created in 1963. What sets the room apart is that nobody asks you to be quiet: Thomas runs his own playlist through service and takes requests from the counter.

The kitchen's closed Mondays and Tuesdays, and seats are limited to sixteen a night, so it's worth booking ahead — then asking for a song once you're through the door.

tours.title: Palácio Gustavo Capanema
tours.shortDescription: Its adjustable sun-shades are widely credited as the first of their kind anywhere in the world.
tours.longDescription: Designed from 1935 by a team led by the young Lúcio Costa — working with Carlos Leão, Affonso Eduardo Reidy and an even younger Oscar Niemeyer, then still an intern in Costa's office, with Le Corbusier brought in from France as consultant — the Palácio Gustavo Capanema went up across the late 1930s and into 1945 as the Ministry of Education and Health. The tower is raised on stilts with the whole ground floor left open as public space beneath it. On the north face, the adjustable brise-soleil are widely credited as the first of their kind anywhere, a simple idea copied by architects everywhere since. Cândido Portinari painted the blue-and-white tiled murals at street level; Roberto Burle Marx planted a tropical roof garden of native species meant to be seen from the office windows above. It reopened to the public in 2025 after years of restoration.

stops.title: Palácio Gustavo Capanema
stops.caption: Rio's Centro is full of colonial churches and nineteenth-century facades, and then, in the middle of all that, this building looks like it dropped in from several decades later.
stops.transcriptText:
Rio's Centro is full of colonial churches and nineteenth-century facades, and then, in the middle of all that, this building looks like it dropped in from several decades later.

Stand back and look up at the tower raised on its stilts, the whole ground floor left open as public space beneath it — that's the Gustavo Capanema Palace, designed from 1935 by a team led by the young Brazilian architect Lúcio Costa, working alongside Carlos Leão, Affonso Eduardo Reidy and an even younger Oscar Niemeyer, then still an intern in Costa's office, with Le Corbusier brought in from France as a consultant. It went up across the late 1930s and into 1945, built as the Ministry of Education and Health.

Look at the north-facing glass wall first. Those adjustable sun-shades, the brise-soleil, are widely credited as the first of their kind anywhere in the world — a simple idea, movable panels controlling heat and glare, that architects everywhere have copied since. Then find the blue-and-white tiled murals at street level, painted by Cândido Portinari, and picture the rooftop above you: a tropical garden designed by Roberto Burle Marx, planted with native Brazilian species and meant to be seen from the office windows looking down, a small piece of Brazil planted on top of European-style modernism.

The building has had to be defended more than once. In 2016, artists occupied it in protest at threats to abolish the Ministry of Culture, and in 2021 public pressure forced the government to withdraw it from a list of properties up for sale.

After years of restoration, the palace reopened to the public in 2025, with free guided visits by appointment — worth booking ahead through the culture ministry's website, then walking the short distance up to Cinelândia afterwards, where Rio's early-twentieth-century architecture picks up the story this building interrupted.

tours.title: Ilha de Paquetá
tours.shortDescription: There is a curious rule about this island — no cars, anywhere, not even for the police.
tours.longDescription: The ferry from Praça XV takes about an hour across Guanabara Bay, and the absence of engines is the first thing you notice stepping off. Paquetá has been car-free for decades; you get around on foot, by bicycle, or in one of the small electric charrete carts that replaced the island's horse-drawn carriages after animal-welfare concerns ended that tradition in 2016. Even the police patrol by bicycle. The quiet was not always this complete: Dom João VI kept a summer residence here after the Portuguese court fled to Rio, and by 1838, with regular ferries established, the island had become a fashionable retreat for Rio's elite, who built grand villas along the shoreline. Some still stand, weathered rather than restored. Around 3,500 people live here year-round today, on streets where broken paving sits alongside genuine civic pride.

There's more island beyond wherever you've landed, and it's worth exploring on foot or by bike rather than staying near the ferry dock — the old villas and the quieter beaches further round the shore are where Paquetá's slower pace really settles in.

tours.title: Parque das Ruínas
tours.shortDescription: The architects decided not to rebuild the palace — they consolidated the ruin exactly as it stood.
tours.longDescription: Roofless and open to the sky, this is the shell of the Palacete Murtinho Nobre, built around the turn of the twentieth century and later home to Laurinda Santos Lobo, an heiress known in her day as "the marshal of elegance". Through the 1920s she turned the house into Rio's most important salon, hosting Villa-Lobos, Tarsila do Amaral and, on at least one occasion, Isadora Duncan — a genuine gathering point for Brazilian Modernism. After Laurinda's death in 1946 the mansion was left to a homeopathic institute that never took possession, and it sat open to looters for decades; by the time the state stepped in to protect the remains in 1993 there was no building left to restore, only walls. So the architects consolidated the ruin as it stood, threading modern steel walkways and glass through old stone and brick, leaving fragments of original tilework under glass domes. The city renamed it for the journalist Glória Maria in 2023.

stops.title: Parque das Ruínas

Climb up to the highest walkway before you go. From there, Sugarloaf, the Arcos da Lapa and the rooftops of Centro all line up in one view — the same skyline Laurinda's guests would have known, seen now through the gaps in her own collapsed house.

tours.title: Parque Lage
tours.shortDescription: That courtyard pool sits at the exact spot where the best-known hiking trail to Christ the Redeemer begins.
tours.longDescription: At the foot of Corcovado in Jardim Botânico, Parque Lage's eclectic palacete was remodelled in the 1920s for the industrialist Henrique Lage and his wife, the opera singer Gabriela Besanzoni, by the Italian architect Mario Vodret. The grounds are older still, laid out as a romantic landscape garden around 1840, but the building everyone photographs — courtyard, swimming pool, geometric gardens — is a product of that 1920s remodel, built around an opera career and an industrial fortune. Since 1975 the mansion has housed the Escola de Artes Visuais, a working art school founded by the artist Rubens Gerchman, so rooms that once hosted private recitals now hold studios and exhibitions instead. Recent restoration has been uncovering historic paintings hidden under decades of plain white paint, so parts of the building are literally revealing more of themselves as the work runs.

Look for the courtyard café before you set off up the Corcovado trail, if that's the plan — it's the last proper stop for a coffee before the climb to Christ the Redeemer gets serious.

tours.title: Pedregulho Housing Complex
tours.shortDescription: 272 homes, seven storeys, and not a single lift shaft.
tours.longDescription: Cut into São Cristóvão hill on the Benfica border, the Pedregulho Housing Complex was designed by Affonso Eduardo Reidy and built between 1946 and 1951. Reidy did not fight the hillside — he let the building trace it, so the seven-storey slab bends and rises with the contour of the land and almost every flat was given a view towards Guanabara Bay. There are no lifts: Reidy ran a single elevated walkway straight into the third floor, with duplex flats stacked above and below that entry level, solving vertical access for 272 homes without a shaft. The complex was never meant to stand alone, either — it included a school, gymnasium, health centre and public swimming pool, because Reidy believed housing for Rio's working class deserved the same civic ambition as anyone else's. Cândido Portinari set an enormous tiled mural on the gymnasium's street wall. It won first prize at the first São Paulo Biennial.

stops.title: Pedregulho Housing Complex
stops.caption: Follow the curve of that long white building along the hillside, and you're looking at one of the boldest ideas in twentieth-century housing.

Reidy didn't fight the hillside — he let the building trace it, so the slab bends and rises with the contour of the land, and almost every flat inside was given a view towards Guanabara Bay.

On the gymnasium's street-facing wall, the painter Cândido Portinari set an enormous tiled mural — still there, still intact.

When Pedregulho was finished, it won first prize at the first São Paulo Biennial, and years later Le Corbusier himself came to see it. But admiration didn't protect it. The city eventually listed the complex as protected heritage in 2011, and one block has since been carefully restored.

It's worth walking the length of the curve before you move on — from one end to the other, the building never once goes straight, which is rather the whole point.

tours.title: Praia Vermelha
tours.shortDescription: The reddish tint in the sand isn't dye or pollution — it's garnet crystal, mixed in naturally.
tours.longDescription: Red Beach sits tucked between two hills, Morro da Urca and Morro da Babilônia, with calmer and more sheltered water than the open ocean beaches further along the coast. The reddish tint in the sand is garnet crystal mixed naturally into the grains, most visible when the light turns warm towards evening. Behind the beach, the cable car station marks the start of the Sugarloaf ride, which has carried passengers from this exact spot since 1912. Urca itself has stayed quieter and more residential than its famous neighbours partly because so much of it belongs to the military — a naval school, a war college and the old Fortaleza de São João guarding the bay entrance all still function. That presence is not merely decorative history: in 1904 the military school that stood on this beach became the flashpoint for an attempted coup, when opposition to a mandatory smallpox vaccination law spilled into open revolt.

stops.title: Praia Vermelha

Most visitors walk straight past Praia Vermelha on their way to the cable car, sand barely registering underfoot — it rewards the few extra minutes it takes to actually stop and look down at what you're standing on.

tours.title: Prainha
tours.shortDescription: Fifty kilometres from Copacabana, the coastline still looks like it did before Rio became Rio.
tours.longDescription: A small horseshoe cove roughly 700 metres across in the far west of the city near Recreio dos Bandeirantes, with hillsides still covered in genuine Atlantic Forest rather than apartment blocks. The whole area is protected as the Prainha Municipal Natural Park, 147 hectares of coast and forest linking this beach to neighbouring Grumari, home to wildlife you will not find near Copacabana — oncillas, crab-eating foxes, marmosets, and birds of prey working the thermals above the cliffs. The waves are the other reason people make the drive: Prainha mixes beach break and reef break in a way serious surfers rate among the best in Rio, good enough to have hosted the Layback Pro Prainha, a World Surf League qualifying event, since 2022. It is protected deliberately rather than by accident, right down to its Blue Flag certification for sustainable coastal management.

stops.title: Prainha

Most visitors turn back towards the city once the light starts fading — staying to watch the sun drop behind the headland, forest silhouetted on both sides, is the version of this beach that's easy to miss if you're on a schedule.

tours.title: Real Gabinete Português de Leitura
tours.shortDescription: Forty-three Portuguese immigrants founded a reading society in 1837. Nothing about that suggests this building.
tours.longDescription: The building came decades after the society: Emperor Pedro II laid its cornerstone in 1880 and Princess Isabel opened it in 1887, in the Neo-Manueline style, a Portuguese Gothic revival modelled directly on Lisbon's Jerónimos Monastery. The stone facade was carved in Lisbon and shipped across the Atlantic before construction here even began, and four statues watch over the entrance: Pedro Álvares Cabral, Luís de Camões, Henry the Navigator and Vasco da Gama. Inside, an iron-and-glass skylight — said to be the first structure of its kind built in Brazil — drops light through a crystal chandelier onto floor-to-ceiling carved wooden bookcases. The collection is the real substance behind the spectacle: around 350,000 volumes, including a 1572 first edition of Camões's Os Lusíadas, and since 1935 a copy of every book published in Portugal.

tours.title: Sambódromo
tours.shortDescription: Carnival's grandest stage has 115 classrooms tucked directly under the seating.
tours.longDescription: Formally the Passarela Professor Darcy Ribeiro, the Sambódromo was designed by Oscar Niemeyer and built in just four months in 1984, commissioned by governor Leonel Brizola and the anthropologist Darcy Ribeiro not long after Brazil's military dictatorship ended. The runway stretches roughly 700 metres between permanent grandstands and finishes at the Praça da Apoteose, marked by a soaring three-legged concrete arch. During Carnival the Grupo Especial samba schools parade along this exact tarmac, each taking seventy to eighty minutes to cross, judged across nine categories, with ninety thousand people in the stands. The rest of the year it hosts open school rehearsals from December and major concerts — the Rolling Stones, David Bowie, Coldplay and Radiohead have all played here. Underneath the seating, a working primary school occupies the structure every school day.

tours.title: SO_Lo
tours.shortDescription: SO_LO isn't Portuguese for anything. It's shorthand: sustainable, organic, local.
tours.longDescription: A kiosk on the Lagoa shoreline, tables close enough to the water to catch the breeze off it, joggers passing two abreast along the path — one branch of a small Rio chain built entirely around sourcing from local growers without much fuss. Sister branches have opened across the city, including a recent one in Copacabana where the architects stripped a 1930s Art Deco building back to its original bones rather than covering them up. Start with the ricotta toast or the avocado bowl, piled with granola and caramelised pumpkin seeds, both on the menu since the first branch opened in Ipanema; the beet hummus with shiitake toast is worth ordering too. This kind of café was rare in Rio a decade ago, when brunch culture in the city still mostly meant imported ideas served in imported ways. SO_Lo's bet was that "local" could be the whole pitch rather than a garnish.

tours.title: Sugarloaf Mountain
tours.shortDescription: When this cable car opened in 1912, it was only the third of its kind anywhere on Earth.
tours.longDescription: The granite peak rising 396 metres above the bay was named by early Portuguese settlers for its resemblance to the moulded cones refined sugar was once shipped in. The cable car up it, the Bondinho, opened in 1912, engineered by Augusto Ferreira Ramos, and climbs in two stages — first to Morro da Urca, then on to the summit — a genuinely ambitious piece of engineering built only a few years after the very first cable cars appeared in Europe. It has not always gone smoothly: in 1951 a cable snapped mid-journey and left 22 passengers stranded high above the rocks for about ten hours before rescuers reached them, though nobody was killed. The cars have been rebuilt and expanded since. It is now among the most visited attractions in Rio, close to a million and a half people a year, with views reaching across Guanabara Bay to Christ the Redeemer.

Praia Vermelha, where the first cable car stage begins, is worth a slow walk before or after the ride — the little red-sand beach at the base of this whole engineering story is easy to skip past on the way to the queue.

tours.title: Teatro Popular Oscar Niemeyer
tours.shortDescription: A 454-seat auditorium whose back wall opens onto a plaza holding twenty thousand.
tours.longDescription: Across the bay from Rio proper, on the Niterói waterfront, this theatre opened in 2007 to mark Oscar Niemeyer's hundredth birthday and was renamed in his honour after his death in 2012 — the first building of what became the Caminho Niemeyer, a whole trail of the architect's late work strung along this shoreline. A curved concrete roof springs from the end walls and a spiral ramp carries visitors up into the foyer, where one whole wall is glass, looking straight across the water to Rio's skyline. On the opposite side, yellow azulejos carry Niemeyer's own allegorical designs rather than a decorator's pattern. The auditorium holds a modest 454 seats, but the rear stage wall opens outward onto a plaza that can hold up to 20,000 for open-air shows. The word in the name is the point: nearly all its programming runs free.

On the Niterói side of Guanabara Bay, at the start of that trail, you'll find this theatre, opened in 2007 to mark Niemeyer's hundredth birthday and renamed in his honour after his death in 2012. A curved concrete roof springs from the end walls and a spiral ramp carries visitors up into the foyer, where one whole wall is glass, looking straight out across the water towards Rio's skyline.

Walk round to the opposite side and you'll find the other wall: yellow tiled azulejos, painted with Niemeyer's own allegorical designs rather than a decorator's pattern. Inside, the auditorium holds a modest 454 seats, but the rear stage wall opens outward onto a plaza that can hold up to 20,000 people for open-air shows — a small room and a huge one, built into the same building.

What makes this theatre worth the ferry crossing is the word in its name: popular. It wasn't built as a prestige venue for Rio's wealthier crowd — nearly all of its programming runs free, and it was conceived, alongside the wider Caminho Niemeyer project, as public architecture genuinely meant for everyone who happened to live nearby.

Look for the skaters. The plaza in front of the theatre has become one of Niterói's best-known spots for skating and rollerblading — a very unplanned, very fitting way for people to actually use one of Niemeyer's curves.

tours.title: The Maze Rio
tours.shortDescription: A British sculptor who once built props for Kubrick bought a half-ruined hillside house and filled it with art.
tours.longDescription: In 1981 Bob Nadkarni bought a half-ruined house at Rua Tavares Bastos 414, inside the Tavares Bastos community, and spent four decades building it out room by room into part guesthouse, part gallery, part jazz room. Nadkarni died in 2023 and the place now carries on under his wife Malu, who grew up in this same community, along with the rest of the family. The view does the introducing: Guanabara Bay opens out below the terrace with Christ the Redeemer visible across the rooftops on a clear day, a vantage point that has drawn DownBeat magazine to name The Maze a top jazz venue seven years running. Every wall and stairwell carries something Nadkarni collected, painted or built, so the house reads less like a venue with decoration than one very large occupied sculpture. It employs around twenty people locally and has funded a ballet school and a football school.

stops.transcriptText:

Walk through and the view does the introducing for you: Guanabara Bay opens out below the terrace, with Christ the Redeemer visible across the rooftops on a clear day, a vantage point that's drawn DownBeat magazine to name The Maze a top jazz venue seven years running, and pulled in guests ranging from footballers to a Hollywood film crew shooting scenes for The Incredible Hulk.
