It employs around twenty people from the community, has funded a local ballet school and a football school, and its presence is credited with drawing a permanent police post to a hillside that spent years without one.

It's open Wednesday to Sunday afternoons with no booking required, and live jazz nights run periodically — worth checking the venue's own page before you climb up, so you catch one.

tours.title: Theatro Municipal
tours.shortDescription: Underneath the opera house sits a basement hall decorated in Assyrian, Babylonian and Persian style.
tours.longDescription: The ornate facade is the result of a design competition in 1903 that ended in a tie, with the two winning entries — one by the French architect Albert Guilbert, one submitted under a pseudonym by Francisco de Oliveira Passos — combined into the building constructed from 1905. It was modelled directly on the Paris Opéra: 1,180 wooden piles were sunk into groundwater to support it, and the whole thing went up in four and a half years, opening in 1909. Inside, sculpture by Henrique Bernardelli and paintings by Eliseu Visconti decorate a hall now seating over 2,000, home to the Municipal Symphonic Orchestra and Rio's resident ballet company, having hosted Toscanini, Stravinsky and Sarah Bernhardt over the decades. Underneath sits the Salão Assyrio, opened alongside the theatre in 1909 as a restaurant and later a jazz-age nightspot where Pixinguinha's group once played.

stops.title: Theatro Municipal
stops.caption: Cinelândia fills up most evenings with people heading to the cinema or a drink nearby, and in the middle of all that stands a building doing something rather grander: staging opera and ballet in a house modelled directly on the Paris Opéra.
stops.transcriptText:
Cinelândia fills up most evenings with people heading to the cinema or a drink nearby, and in the middle of all that stands a building doing something rather grander: staging opera and ballet in a house modelled directly on the Paris Opéra.

This is the Theatro Municipal, its ornate facade the result of a design competition in 1903 that ended in a tie, with the two winning entries — one by the French architect Albert Guilbert, one submitted under a pseudonym by Francisco de Oliveira Passos — combined into the building constructed from 1905. 1,180 wooden piles were sunk into groundwater to support it, and the whole thing went up in just four and a half years, opening in 1909.

Inside, sculpture by Henrique Bernardelli and paintings by Eliseu Visconti decorate a hall that now seats over 2,000 for performances by the Municipal Symphonic Orchestra and Rio's resident ballet company, hosting names over the decades that include Toscanini, Stravinsky and Sarah Bernhardt.

Underneath all of it sits a stranger secret: the Salão Assyrio, a basement hall decorated in Assyrian, Babylonian and Persian style, opened alongside the theatre in 1909 as a restaurant and later a jazz-age nightspot where Pixinguinha's group once played. It doesn't serve food anymore, but the room survives intact, visible only on the theatre's guided tours.

Book one of those tours if the timing works — the Salão Assyrio isn't visible from the main auditorium, and it's the one part of this building most people walk straight past without ever knowing it's underneath their feet.

tours.title: Vista Chinesa
tours.shortDescription: Most viewpoints in Rio celebrate a success. This one marks an experiment that came to nothing.
tours.longDescription: The pagoda roughly 380 metres up in the Tijuca forest was built in 1903 under the mayor Pereira Passos, designed by the architect Luis Rey. Look closely at the columns before deciding what they are made of: they read as bamboo but are solid reinforced concrete, cast and finished to imitate poles that were never actually used. The pavilion honours a stranger piece of history than its shape suggests. Around 1811 King Dom João VI brought several hundred Chinese tea growers to Rio, hoping to establish tea as a crop on this hillside for the Royal Botanical Garden below. Thousands of plants went in and three harvests a year came out, and then the scheme quietly failed as a commercial venture — the workers were eventually put to building roads instead. On a clear day six landmarks are visible from this one spot, from Christ the Redeemer to the beaches of Ipanema and Leblon.

stops.title: Vista Chinesa
stops.caption: Six landmarks are visible from this one spot, on a clear day: Christ the Redeemer, Sugarloaf, Guanabara Bay, the Rodrigo de Freitas lagoon, the twin peaks of Dois Irmãos, and the beaches of Ipanema and Leblon laid out below.
stops.transcriptText:
Six landmarks are visible from this one spot, on a clear day: Christ the Redeemer, Sugarloaf, Guanabara Bay, the Rodrigo de Freitas lagoon, the twin peaks of Dois Irmãos, and the beaches of Ipanema and Leblon laid out below.

The pagoda in front of you, roughly 380 metres up in the Tijuca forest, is Vista Chinesa, built in 1903 under the mayor Pereira Passos and designed by the architect Luis Rey. Look closely at the columns before you decide what they're made of — they read as bamboo, but they're solid reinforced concrete, cast and finished to imitate poles that were never actually used.

The pavilion honours a stranger piece of history than its shape suggests. Around 1811, King Dom João the Sixth brought several hundred Chinese tea growers to Rio, hoping to establish tea as a crop on this very hillside for the Royal Botanical Garden below. Thousands of tea plants went in, three harvests a year came out, and then the whole scheme quietly failed as a commercial venture — the workers were eventually put to building roads instead. Vista Chinesa is, in effect, a monument to an agricultural experiment that never worked.

And that's rather what makes it worth the climb: most viewpoints in Rio celebrate a success, a monument, a conquest of some kind. This one marks an ambition that came to nothing, and got a beautiful folly built on the strength of the attempt anyway.

It's a quiet, wooded spot, so it rewards visiting in good daylight with other people around rather than alone at the edges of the day — after which there's little to do but stand at the rail and let the view do the work.

tours.title: A Casa do Porco
tours.shortDescription: The butcher's counter in the window is most of tomorrow's menu.
tours.longDescription: On the corner of Rua Araújo and General Jardim in República, A Casa do Porco has become one of the hardest tables in Brazil to get without planning ahead. Jefferson Rueda trained as a butcher long before he ran a kitchen, and it shows: the restaurant raises its own pigs, grows much of its own veg, and puts the meat counter in the window facing the street. He opened it in October 2015 with Janaína Rueda of Bar Dona Onça, folding bar, restaurant and small grocery into one address. The signature Porco San Zé — a whole roasted pig — is built from exactly that butchery knowledge, and the place landed twenty-fourth on Latin America's 50 Best, the strongest debut of its year. Weekday afternoons, three until half six, are the quiet window.

stops.title: A Casa do Porco
stops.caption: Look through the window at the butcher's counter. That's not decoration — that's most of tomorrow's menu, on display.
stops.transcriptText:
Look through the window at the butcher's counter. That's not decoration — that's most of tomorrow's menu, on display.

The corner of Rua Araújo and General Jardim, in República — once a fairly unremarkable corner, now one of the hardest tables in Brazil to get without planning ahead.

Chef Jefferson Rueda, previously at Attimo, opened the place on the 12th of October 2015 with Janaína Rueda, of Bar Dona Onça. Before he was a chef, Rueda trained as a butcher, and it shows: the restaurant raises its own pigs and grows most of its own vegetables. The format mixes bar, restaurant, and small grocery in one address, windows open onto the street and the meat counter, with takeaway items like the pork sandwich for anyone not staying to sit down.

The signature dish is Porco San Zé, a whole roasted pig, built from exactly the kind of butchery knowledge Rueda picked up long before he ever ran a kitchen. The restaurant landed at twenty-fourth on the Latin America's 50 Best list, the best debut placement of that year, and was named the city's best bar by VejaSP.

Here's the thing about that open butcher's counter facing the street. It's about as honest as a restaurant's advertising gets — you can watch exactly what's about to become dinner, no menu language required.

Weekday afternoons, three until half six, are the quiet window. Go then if you want a table without the wait the rest of the week has firmly earned.

tours.title: Casa Teo
tours.shortDescription: A shop for furniture most people only ever see photographed in design books.
tours.longDescription: In Jardins, Casa Teo is the retail floor to Galeria Teo next door, and the pairing tells you most of what you need before you step inside. The focus is modern Brazilian furniture — the design language that came out of mid-century São Paulo, the same restless confidence that gave the city its boldest architecture. Heavy wood, cane and leather, forms built for a climate rather than copied from somewhere colder. Casa Teo sells it; Galeria Teo curates it, treating individual pieces less like stock and more like objects a museum would put behind rope. For decades this material was better collected outside Brazil than inside it; somewhere between a shop and a gallery, that balance has been shifting back.

stops.title: Casa Teo
stops.caption: The building behind the glass here isn't a restaurant or a bar.
stops.transcriptText:
The building behind the glass here isn't a restaurant or a bar. It's a shop for furniture most people only ever see photographed in design books.

In the Jardins district, open weekdays from nine until six and a shorter run on Saturdays until two — this is Casa Teo, the retail floor to Galeria Teo next door, and the pairing tells you most of what you need to know before you've even stepped inside.

The focus is modern Brazilian furniture — the design language that came out of mid-century São Paulo, the same period and the same restless confidence that gave this city its boldest architecture. Think heavy wood, cane, leather, forms built for a climate and a way of living rather than copied from somewhere colder. Casa Teo sells it; Galeria Teo, next door, curates it, treating individual pieces less like stock and more like the objects a museum would put behind rope. Between the two, the operation has built a genuinely large following online — tens of thousands of people who follow the gallery's finds without ever setting foot in Jardins, which tells you the appetite for this material runs well past whoever can casually wander in on a weekday afternoon.

That's the quiet correction a shop like this makes. For decades, São Paulo's mid-century furniture was better known and better collected outside Brazil than inside it — specialists and dealers abroad paying closer attention than the city that actually produced the work. Somewhere between a shop and a gallery, that balance has been shifting back.

Ask what's currently on the gallery floor before you go — the selection rotates, and there's usually one piece in there worth building the rest of your Saturday around.

tours.title: Casa de Vidro
tours.shortDescription: In 1951 an Italian-born architect became a Brazilian citizen, and finished her first house the same year.
tours.longDescription: At Rua General Almério de Moura 200 in Morumbi stands the first house built in what is now Jardim Morumbi, and Lina Bo Bardi built it for herself. It rests on slender pilotis planted into the slope like aerial roots, so the structure floats above the terrain rather than cutting into it, and glass walls run the length of the main living space, dissolving the line between house and Atlantic Forest. Bo Bardi worked with the Italian engineer Pier Luigi Nervi in 1950 to get the structure right, later with Túlio Stucchi to refine it. Every idea she would spend four decades developing is already here, worked out for herself before she built for anyone else. Protected as state heritage in 1987, it has housed the Instituto Lina Bo e P.M. Bardi since 1995.

stops.title: Casa de Vidro
stops.caption: In 1951, an Italian-born architect became a Brazilian citizen, and finished building her first house in the same year.
stops.transcriptText:
In 1951, an Italian-born architect became a Brazilian citizen, and finished building her first house in the same year.

Rua General Almério de Moura, number 200, in the Morumbi district — this was the first house built in what's now called Jardim Morumbi, and Lina Bo Bardi built it for herself.

Look at how it sits on the land. The house rests on slender pilotis, planted into the slope like aerial roots, so the whole structure appears to float above the terrain rather than cut into it. Glass walls run the length of the main living space, dissolving the line between the house and the Atlantic Forest surrounding it. Bo Bardi worked with the Italian engineer Pier Luigi Nervi in 1950 to get that structure right, and later with Túlio Stucchi to fine-tune it further.

Have a think about what a first house tells you. Every idea Bo Bardi would spend the next four decades developing — lightness, structure as something almost alive, architecture that refuses to dominate its site — is already present here, worked out for herself before she ever built for anyone else.

The house was protected as state heritage in 1987, and since 1995 it's served as the headquarters of the Instituto Lina Bo e P.M. Bardi, holding part of the art collection she and her husband built over their lives together.

Look for where the glass meets the forest at the edges of the living room — that's the detail the rest of her career kept returning to, in one form or another.

tours.title: Centro Cultural Fiesp
tours.shortDescription: Wrapped floor to roof in what looks unmistakably like a giant cheese grater.
tours.longDescription: Officially the Centro Cultural Fiesp Ruth Cardoso, this building runs along Avenida Paulista at number 1313, its perforated aluminium sunscreen wrapping the entire facade — the detail that earned it the nickname. It came out of a 1969 competition won by Roberto Cerqueira César and Luiz Roberto de Carvalho Franco of Rino Levi Arquitetos Associados. The theatre inside traces back to Sesi's Teatro Popular, founded in the 1960s and moved here in 1977, and since 2008 the centre has carried the name of the anthropologist and former First Lady Ruth Cardoso. Behind the metal skin: free theatre, exhibitions and cinema for more than two hundred thousand visitors a year — bankrolled, on the most expensive pavement in the country, by an industrial lobby group rather than a ministry of culture.

stops.title: Centro Cultural Fiesp
stops.caption: Look at the front of this building. It's wrapped, floor to roof, in what looks unmistakably like a giant cheese grater.
stops.transcriptText:
Look at the front of this building. It's wrapped, floor to roof, in what looks unmistakably like a giant cheese grater.

The building in front of you runs along Avenida Paulista at number 1313 — its perforated aluminium sunscreen wrapping the entire facade, which is exactly the detail that earned it the nickname. Officially, it's the Centro Cultural Fiesp Ruth Cardoso, and you'll want to be standing back far enough on the pavement to take in the whole sweep of metal at once.

The building itself dates to a 1969 architecture competition, won by Roberto Cerqueira César and Luiz Roberto de Carvalho Franco of Rino Levi Arquitetos Associados, who gave São Paulo's industrial federation a headquarters bold enough to hold its own on this avenue. The theatre inside traces back further still — to Sesi's Teatro Popular, founded in the 1960s and moved to this address in 1977. And since 2008, the whole centre has carried the name of Ruth Cardoso, the anthropologist and former First Lady, who died that year.

What's easy to miss, walking past, is what actually happens behind that metal skin. Free theatre, exhibitions, cinema — more than two hundred thousand visitors a year, by the centre's own count, none of them paying for the privilege.

And here's the thing worth sitting with, on the most expensive stretch of pavement in the country: the organisation bankrolling all this free culture is an industrial lobby group, not a ministry of culture or a private foundation with an artist's name on the door. Make of that what you like — it's not a controversial fact, just an interesting one to have in your pocket as you look up at the building that's paying for it.

If museums are more your pace, MASP is only a few minutes further down Paulista — an easy add-on either before or after, depending which way you're walking.

tours.title: Centro Cultural São Paulo
tours.shortDescription: This building exists, in part, because a shopping centre fell through.
tours.longDescription: The complex along Rua Vergueiro drops about ten metres to Avenida 23 de Maio on its far side and is built into that slope rather than sitting on top of it. In the 1970s metro construction freed the land, and the city's original Projeto Vergueiro was considerably grander than what got built — office towers, hotels, a shopping centre, all wrapped around a public library. A change of administration in 1975 cancelled the lot except the library, the one idea worth keeping. Eurico Prado Lopes and Luiz Telles won the competition to build around that seed, and what opened in 1982 deliberately avoids anything like a corridor: multiple entrances, no single obvious route, more a set of internal streets than a building. Inside, the Discoteca Oneyda Alvarenga music archive, first imagined by Mário de Andrade in 1935; on the roof, a suspended garden.

stops.title: Centro Cultural São Paulo
stops.caption: This building exists, in part, because a shopping centre fell through.
stops.transcriptText:
This building exists, in part, because a shopping centre fell through.

The complex running along Rua Vergueiro drops about ten metres down to Avenida 23 de Maio on its far side, and it's built into that slope rather than sitting on top of it — a fair stretch of what you're facing is actually below street level, once you're round on the Paulista side.

Back in the 1970s, this land was freed up by metro construction, and the city's original plan for it, called Projeto Vergueiro, was considerably grander than what got built: office towers, hotels, a shopping centre, all wrapped around a public library. By 1975, a change of administration cancelled the lot — everything except the library, which survived as the one idea worth keeping. Architects Eurico Prado Lopes and Luiz Telles won the competition to build around that seed, and what opened in 1982 deliberately avoids anything like a normal corridor. There are multiple entrances, no single obvious route through — you're meant to wander it more like a set of internal streets than a building.

Two things worth finding once you're inside. The Discoteca Oneyda Alvarenga, a music archive first dreamed up in 1935 by the writer Mário de Andrade, has lived here since the centre opened — vinyl, 78s, sheet music, decades of recorded sound. And up on the roof, a suspended garden: a working community plot, a lawn for lying about reading, and a clean view back across to the towers on Avenida Paulista.

A cancelled shopping centre, by accident, produced one of the most generous free cultural buildings in the city. Head up to the garden before or after you look around inside — the view alone is worth the climb.

tours.title: Cidade Matarazzo
tours.shortDescription: A maternity hospital built for the city's poorest arrivals is now one of its most expensive hotels.
tours.longDescription: Two hundred metres off Avenida Paulista, this complex began in 1904 as the Hospital Umberto I, built by the Società Italiana di Beneficenza for Italian immigrants and their families. The industrialist Francesco Matarazzo funded it and in 1943 added the Maternidade Condessa Filomena Matarazzo, built for the birth of his own daughter and for years considered the best maternity hospital in South America. The hospital closed in 1993 and sat empty until the French entrepreneur Alexandre Allard began redeveloping the site. The 1943 maternity building now houses part of the Rosewood São Paulo, opened January 2022; beside it stands the entirely new Torre Mata Atlântica by Jean Nouvel, fifteen-metre trees built into its terraces and interiors by Philippe Starck. Same walls in places, an almost total swap in who gets to be inside them.

stops.title: Cidade Matarazzo
stops.caption: This was a maternity hospital built for the poorest arrivals in the city.
stops.transcriptText:
This was a maternity hospital built for the poorest arrivals in the city. It's now one of the most expensive hotels in it.

The complex spreading out in front of you, two hundred metres off Avenida Paulista, began in 1904 as the Hospital Umberto I, built by the Società Italiana di Beneficenza for Italian immigrants and their families.

Industrialist and philanthropist Francesco Matarazzo funded the hospital, and in 1943 added the Maternidade Condessa Filomena Matarazzo, built specifically for the birth of his own daughter — for years considered the best maternity hospital in South America. The hospital complex closed in 1993 and sat empty for years, until French entrepreneur Alexandre Allard began redeveloping the whole site.

Have a look at what's standing here now. The 1943 maternity building has been restored to house part of the new Rosewood São Paulo hotel, which opened in January 2022. Alongside it stands an entirely new structure, the Torre Mata Atlântica, designed by Jean Nouvel, with fifteen-metre trees built directly into its terraces, interiors throughout by Philippe Starck.

Here's the reversal worth sitting with. The building that once looked after the city's poorest new mothers now houses guests paying some of the highest room rates in Brazil — same walls in places, an almost total swap in who gets to be inside them.

The restored chapel and gardens are generally open to wander even if you're not a hotel guest — worth a slow walk through before you judge the place purely on the price of a room.

tours.title: Cinemateca Brasileira
tours.shortDescription: This building spent forty years slaughtering cattle before it started saving films.
tours.longDescription: At Largo Senador Raul Cardoso in Vila Clementino stands the old Matadouro Municipal, São Paulo's municipal slaughterhouse, designed by the German architect Alberto Kuhlmann and opened in 1887. Trains pulled straight into these yards to load meat for the whole city until it closed in 1927. The site sat unused for decades before the city handed it to the Cinemateca Brasileira in 1988, and the brick sheds have since been converted into film laboratories, climate-controlled vaults, a library, screening rooms and a public garden, protected as heritage since 1985. Something near forty thousand films and reels are held here, tracing Brazilian film and television back to 1897. In seventy-odd years the archive has been through five fires — the worst in 2016, caused by spontaneous combustion in poor storage, destroying around two hundred and seventy films outright.

stops.title: Cinemateca Brasileira
stops.caption: This building spent forty years slaughtering cattle before it started saving films.
stops.transcriptText:
This building spent forty years slaughtering cattle before it started saving films.

Largo Senador Raul Cardoso, Vila Clementino — the brick complex in front of you is the old Matadouro Municipal, São Paulo's municipal slaughterhouse, designed by the German architect Alberto Kuhlmann and opened in 1887. Trains once pulled straight into these yards to load meat bound for the whole city. That went on until 1927, when the slaughterhouse closed for good.

It sat unused for decades before the city handed the site to the Cinemateca Brasileira in 1988. Since then, the old brick sheds have been converted, gradually, into film laboratories, climate-controlled vaults, a library, screening rooms, and a public garden — all inside a complex that's been protected as heritage since 1985. What's stored here now is enormous: something in the region of forty thousand films and reels, tracing Brazilian film and television all the way back to 1897.

Have a think about what that actually means to look after. In its seventy-odd years as a film archive, the Cinemateca has been through five fires — the worst in 2016, caused by spontaneous combustion in poorly climate-controlled storage. Around two hundred and seventy films were destroyed outright that day, with damage to copies of over four hundred more; more than a thousand reels gone in total.

Here's the uncomfortable part of the story. Old nitrate film doesn't just sit quietly waiting to be watched — it's chemically unstable, prone to combusting on its own given the wrong conditions. So an archive built to protect Brazil's film memory is, in a real sense, in a permanent race against the exact material it exists to save.

The public garden stays open even on days the archive itself doesn't — worth a slow walk through what used to be loading yards for a very different kind of cargo.

tours.title: Edifício Copan
tours.shortDescription: Roughly five thousand people live inside this one building.
tours.longDescription: The wave-shaped Edifício Copan is an S-curve of concrete rising a hundred and fifteen metres over thirty-two floors, unmistakable in any São Paulo skyline photograph. Oscar Niemeyer designed it, and construction ran from 1952 to 1966 — long enough that the building outlasted the company behind it, the Companhia Pan-Americana de Hotéis, whose name survives only in the building's own since the hotel plan never happened. What went up instead is the largest reinforced concrete residential structure in Brazil and the largest residential complex in Latin America: around eleven hundred and sixty apartments, twenty-two lifts, over a hundred staff and seventy-two shops on the ground floor. More residents than a genuine town, all cycling through the same lobby. The curve was not decoration — it let the building follow the site rather than fight it, catching light and air differently on every floor.

stops.title: Edifício Copan
stops.caption: Roughly five thousand people live inside this one building — more than live in over a fifth of all Brazilian municipalities.
stops.transcriptText:
Roughly five thousand people live inside this one building — more than live in over a fifth of all Brazilian municipalities.

The wave-shaped tower in front of you is the Edifício Copan, an S-curve of concrete rising a hundred and fifteen metres over thirty-two floors, unmistakable against pretty much any São Paulo skyline photo you've ever seen.

Oscar Niemeyer designed it, and construction ran from 1952 to 1966 — long enough that the building outlasted the original company behind it, the Companhia Pan-Americana de Hotéis, whose name survives only in the building's own, since the hotel plan never actually happened. What went up instead is the largest reinforced concrete residential structure in Brazil, and the largest residential complex in Latin America: around eleven hundred and sixty apartments, twenty-two lifts, over a hundred staff, and seventy-two shops built into the ground floor.

Have a think about the scale of that for a moment. This single curved wall of concrete holds more residents than a genuine town, all cycling through the same lobby, the same lifts, the same corner shops, day after day.

Niemeyer's curve wasn't just decoration. It let the building bend to follow the site rather than fight it, catching light and air differently on every floor as the facade rolls through its long S.

Walk the full length of the building at street level if you can — the curve reads completely differently close up than it does from any photograph taken at a distance.

tours.title: Dōmo
tours.shortDescription: A needle drops on a record behind the bar, and nobody's talking over it.
tours.longDescription: In Vila Buarque, Dōmo keeps a deliberately low profile — no real frontage, entry mostly by reservation, walk-ins welcome if there is room at the counter, Tuesday to Saturday from seven. The concept borrows from Japan's jazz kissa culture: a kissaten is simply a small café, and a jazz kissa is one built entirely around close, quiet attention to music played on vinyl rather than treated as background. Dōmo keeps a working collection of around four hundred records, with a different DJ or selector each night choosing from that shelf rather than a laptop. The cocktail list leans the same way — sake, ume, techniques borrowed from sherry-based classics — and the Asian-inspired food is built to sit alongside the drinks and the sound rather than compete. A very specific, quite reverent Japanese idea dropped into a city whose nightlife mostly runs loud.

stops.title: Dōmo
stops.caption: It's evening in Vila Buarque, a needle drops on a record somewhere behind the bar, and nobody's talking over it.
stops.transcriptText:
It's evening in Vila Buarque, a needle drops on a record somewhere behind the bar, and nobody's talking over it.

The bar in front of you keeps a deliberately low profile — no big frontage to speak of, entry mostly by reservation, walk-ins welcome if there's room at the counter. It's open Tuesday to Saturday, from seven in the evening, and you'll know you've got the right address if the door gives away almost nothing about what's inside.

The whole concept borrows from Japan's jazz kissa culture — kissa, short for kissaten, simply means a small café, and a jazz kissa is one built entirely around close, quiet attention to music played on vinyl, rather than treating it as background noise. Dōmo keeps a working collection of around four hundred records for that purpose, with a different DJ or selector on the decks each night, choosing from that shelf rather than a laptop. The cocktail list leans the same direction, drawing on Japanese ingredients and references: sake, ume, techniques borrowed from sherry-based classics, like a Bamboo built from sherry, vermouth, sake, ume, and lavender. The food menu, Asian-inspired throughout, is built to sit alongside the drinks and the sound rather than compete with either one.

Here's the thing worth noticing about a room like this. It's a very specific, quite reverent Japanese idea — build the room around the record, not the other way round — dropped into a city whose nightlife mostly runs loud. And it's found an audience: enough people in São Paulo are apparently happy to sit quietly and actually listen that a bar built on that one rule has become genuinely hard to get into.

Go on a weeknight if you can manage it — that's when the selector's playing to a handful of people rather than a full room, and the whole idea makes the most sense.

tours.title: Fábrica de Dengo
tours.shortDescription: Every bar made here started life as a problem someone was trying to fix.
tours.longDescription: The four-storey, timber-clad Fábrica de Dengo in Pinheiros gives roughly fifteen hundred square metres over entirely to watching chocolate get made, floor by floor. The company traces back to Guilherme Leal, co-founder of Natura, who saw first-hand how witches'-broom disease was devastating cacao farms in southern Bahia. In 2017 he and Estevan Sartoreli founded Dengo with a specific aim: use every bar sold to support the growers keeping Brazilian cacao alive. All of it is one hundred per cent Brazilian cacao, bought directly from small and mid-sized producers on fair-trade terms, tied explicitly to conserving the Atlantic Forest it grows in. A restored 1940s chocolate-making machine sits at the centre of the factory floor still doing real work, and you can follow the process from raw cacao almond to finished bar.

tours.title: Estádio do Morumbi
tours.shortDescription: Construction began in 1952. The ground didn't fully open until 1970.
tours.longDescription: Officially the Estádio Cícero Pompeu de Toledo, though almost everyone calls it the Morumbi — or, since a chocolate brand bought the naming rights, MorumBIS. A great grey bowl of raw concrete by João Batista Vilanova Artigas, a modernist who did not believe in decoration for its own sake. It opened in stages: a partial match against Sporting Clube de Portugal in October 1960, the rest not finished until a decade later. In its prime, standing terraces pushed capacity toward 140,000; modern seating and safety rules bring that to around 72,000 today, still one of the largest in the country. Cícero Pompeu de Toledo was the club president who forced the project through against real resistance, and the stadium bore his name from 1956 until 2023, when Mondelez Brasil bought the rights. Eighteen years of stubbornness to build; just over a year for a chocolate bar's name to land on top.

tours.title: Feira da Praça Benedito Calixto
tours.shortDescription: Six days a week this is just a square. One day a week it's the city's attic.
tours.longDescription: Praça Benedito Calixto in Pinheiros, Saturdays, roughly nine until seven, stalls set edge to edge across the whole square. The square has been a fixture here far longer than the fair, but only around 1987 did traders start gathering regularly and the habit stick. It has grown to some three hundred exhibitors on a good Saturday — furniture, vinyl, stamps, coins, jewellery, whatever counts as somebody's inherited treasure or somebody else's inherited clutter, sorted out on folding tables in the open air. Some stalls turn over completely week to week; others belong to traders who have held the same patch of pavement for years, and it shows in how they arrange things. A proper food court runs alongside, and most Saturdays around half past two a live chorinho set turns one corner into something closer to a dance floor.

Come for the music if you can time it — half past two, roughly — and work the stalls either side of that set, when the square's at its fullest and its loudest.

tours.title: Galeria Leme
tours.shortDescription: Its opening show in this building was about having just been forced to move.
tours.longDescription: In Vila Leopoldina, a couple of streets from where Galeria Leme originally stood. That first building, completed in 2004 and designed by Paulo Mendes da Rocha with the young practice Metro Arquitetos, was demolished at the end of 2011 after a developer bought the site for an office tower. Rather than disappear, the gallery negotiated a new plot nearby and rebuilt — the same raw concrete volume, reconstructed almost as it was, down to proportions a returning visitor would recognise without being told. Alongside it stands an annex by Metro's own Martin Corullon, the two buildings joined by a concrete bridge over an open courtyard. The opening show, Transposição, invited twelve artists to respond to the move itself — the eviction, the demolition, the rebuild. Most galleries keep the business of running a gallery out of view of the art; this one made it the subject.

tours.title: Hirá Izakaya
tours.shortDescription: In Japan these would be two separate nights out, in two separate rooms.
tours.longDescription: Rua Fradique Coutinho 1240 in Vila Madalena is the flagship, though a second address has since opened in Jardins: a room built around a long bar with the kitchen in plain view, bowls and small plates moving fast between them. Daniel and Valéria Hirata opened it in 2015 with an idea simple to describe and harder to pull off — fold a ramen shop and an izakaya, a Japanese drinking den, into one address. The word izakaya is itself a clue, breaking down roughly as a place to stay and drink. The ramen runs from shoyu and miso through tan tan, tsukemen and hiyashi chuka, alongside sake, shochu and proper cocktails. In Japan you go to the ramen-ya to eat quickly and leave, and to the izakaya to settle in for hours. Hirá refuses to choose, which is a fairly São Paulo way of solving the problem.

If Vila Madalena's on the busy side tonight, the newer branch on Rua Bela Cintra in Jardins runs the same idea in a rather different neighbourhood — worth trying if you want to compare the two rooms.

tours.title: Instituto Moreira Salles — IMS Paulista
tours.shortDescription: Nine floors, every one double-height — a museum stacked vertically.
tours.longDescription: The glass tower rising from Avenida Paulista is IMS Paulista, opened in September 2017, its translucent facade acting as a second skin rather than a simple window wall. The architects, Andrade Morettin, won the city's top architecture prize the year it opened. On the elevated ground floor they recovered the old Portuguese mosaic paving pattern that once ran the length of Avenida Paulista's pavements and laid it inside the building rather than out on the street. The main gathering space, Praça IMS, sits on the fifth floor, reached by escalator straight from the entrance — a public square suspended above the avenue. Inside is one of Latin America's most significant photographic archives, holding material connected to Henri Cartier-Bresson and generations of Brazilian photographers. The building quietly reuses braking energy from its own lifts and harvests rainwater, dressed as architecture rather than announced as a feature.

tours.title: Jacó
tours.shortDescription: There's no sign on the door. You're simply meant to know you've found it.
tours.longDescription: Rua Fidalga 357, on the seam where Vila Madalena meets Pinheiros: a low 1970s house with its windows thrown wide onto the pavement and an open kitchen visible from the street. No plaque, no awning. Behind that kitchen is Iago Jacomussi, who opened the place in 2024 at twenty-six, having trained at Le Cordon Bleu and worked through Evvai and Maní in São Paulo, Tangará Jean-Georges, Belcanto in Lisbon and Jordnær outside Copenhagen. Within about a year the Michelin Guide had named him Young Chef of the Year and given the restaurant a Bib Gourmand. The menu is short and built for sharing: raw fish of the day under a cool cushion of avocado cream, pork with corn cooked down until it is almost custard. Brazilian ingredients handled with French discipline and the odd Asian accent, nothing on the plate trying to prove a point.

Brazilian ingredients, handled with French discipline and the odd Asian accent picked up along the way — nothing on the plate is trying to prove a point, which is rather the point.

Stay with that thought a moment. Then, if you're not in a hurry, walk on a little further into Vila Madalena — this stretch of streets has quietly become one of the better places in São Paulo to eat well without ever needing a reservation.

tours.title: Japan House São Paulo
tours.shortDescription: The wood on the front is over seventy years old, and none of it grew in Brazil.
tours.longDescription: A building on Avenida Paulista with two entirely different faces: one sheathed in dark timber, the other in pierced concrete blocks. Kengo Kuma, working with FGMF Arquitetos, built the timber facade from hinoki — Japanese cypress more than seventy years old, shipped from Japan and assembled by five specialist joiners using traditional interlocking techniques, no nails, across thirty-six metres of width and eleven of height, more than six tonnes of wood. The idea came to Kuma after visiting the Japanese Pavilion in Ibirapuera Park, built from hinoki with the same joinery decades earlier. The other face is cobogós, a form that had its moment in Brazilian modernism in the 1930s — a home-grown answer beside an imported one, both filtering harsh sun and street noise by completely different routes. Since opening in April 2017 it has passed four million visitors.

Walk around to see both faces properly before you go in. Most visitors only ever notice the one they happened to arrive from.

tours.title: KOTORI
tours.shortDescription: A Brazilian take on a Japanese take on Western food.
tours.longDescription: Rua Cônego Eugênio Leite 639 in Pinheiros: a compact, quietly lit dining room, no big signage, just the address and on busier evenings a small queue. The cuisine draws on yōshoku, a century-old Japanese tradition of reworking Western dishes to suit Japanese taste and ingredients. Chef Thiago Bañares runs that idea through a second filter, folding in Brazilian ingredients most yōshoku cooks in Tokyo would never have reached for, on one fixed menu that changes with what is available. Eryngii mushrooms arrive with a chicken broth sharpened by tucupi, a fermented extract from wild manioc very much of the Amazon rather than of Japan. Fish comes matured and grilled. Dessert is rabanada de shokupan — Japan's soft milk bread treated like French toast. It has picked up a place on Latin America's 50 Best and a Michelin Bib Gourmand.

Booking ahead is worth it, given the single nightly menu — and if you've a few minutes spare either side of dinner, the rest of Cônego Eugênio Leite has quietly become one of Pinheiros's better strips for newer kitchens.

tours.title: Memorial da América Latina
tours.shortDescription: At its centre stands a concrete hand, seven metres tall, bleeding onto a continent.
tours.longDescription: In Barra Funda, on a site running to nearly eighty-five thousand square metres: seven buildings across two plazas linked by a footbridge over Avenida Auro Soares de Moura Andrade. Oscar Niemeyer designed the architecture, but the cultural programme came from the anthropologist Darcy Ribeiro, a committed advocate of Latin American political and cultural integration, and it opened on 18 March 1989 with exactly that ambition — a shared civic space for a whole continent rather than one country. Dominating the Praça Cívica is A Mão, Niemeyer's open concrete hand, with a low-relief map of Latin America painted into its palm in red, a deliberate reference to blood and to the region's shared and often violent history. A monument to continental solidarity, built by one country, centred on an image of collective wounding rather than simple celebration.

tours.title: Mendes Wood DM
tours.shortDescription: Its name is built entirely out of its founders' surnames.
tours.longDescription: On Rua da Consolação, in the three-thousand block, look for a house rather than a storefront — no glass wall, no logo you would notice walking past, just a door into what was once somebody's home. Felipe Dmab, Matthew Wood and Pedro Mendes founded the gallery here in 2010, building a programme around artists who had often worked outside the mainstream story of Brazilian art: Afro-Brazilian artists, self-taught figures, conceptualists, twentieth-century modernists who never quite got their due. The house gives that programme room to breathe — several rooms of varying scale rather than one uniform gallery floor, so a monographic show can unfold room to room instead of arriving all at once. From this one house the gallery has expanded to Brussels, Paris and New York, which runs against the usual traffic pattern, where international names open a São Paulo outpost rather than the other way round.

tours.title: Mendes Wood DM — Casa Iramaia
tours.shortDescription: It doesn't look like a gallery from the street. It looks like a house, because it is one.

This is Mendes Wood DM's second São Paulo address, sister to the flagship house on Rua da Consolação across town. Where that space runs a public-facing program on a busy street, Casa Iramaia does something quieter — several small domestic rooms instead of one open gallery floor, used for projects that need walls closer together, corners, a sense of scale that a converted house gives you and a white cube doesn't. Artists and curators in residence have used exactly that intimacy before, treating the rooms as something closer to a studio than a showroom.

Have a think about what that difference actually does to the art. A single large room tends to flatten everything into one experience, walked past at roughly the same pace. A house forces a different rhythm — you go from room to room, and each one can hold its own separate idea without competing with the last.

Same gallery, opposite instinct: the flagship wants footfall, this one wants a visitor willing to slow down and move through it like a house rather than a hall. Check both spaces' current program before you go — one trip across town can turn into two genuinely different shows under the same name.

tours.title: Mercado Municipal de Campinas
tours.shortDescription: A warehouse built to move sugar out became the room where the city did its thinking.
tours.longDescription: On Rua Doutor Quirino in Campinas, this market hall keeps a rhythm barely changed since it opened on 12 April 1908: stallholders in well before the doors, trade in full swing by mid-morning. The Moorish-style arches and ironwork are the giveaway that it was not designed as an ordinary warehouse — though for two decades that is exactly what it was. Engineered by Ramos de Azevedo, behind a fair share of São Paulo state's grandest public buildings of the period, it was built for the Nogueira family as a private depot for sugar bound by rail for the port of Santos. Only in 1925 did it pass into municipal hands. Between the 1930s and the 1960s this hall was where the city's intellectuals, artists, journalists and politicians actually met — not in a lecture theatre but among the stalls. Heritage-listed in 1982, again in 1995, and restored the following year.

tours.title: Mercado Municipal de Pinheiros
tours.shortDescription: A deed condition from 1909 says this land can only ever sell food to the public.
tours.longDescription: Rua Pedro Cristi 89 in Pinheiros: a two-storey building of around four thousand square metres, parking beneath for fifty cars, more than fifty stalls trading across both floors. The market opened on 10 August 1910, originally sited near Largo da Batata under the name Mercado dos Caipiras — traders in from the countryside selling straight to the city. Its founder Pedro Christe also built the parish of Nossa Senhora do Monte Serrat nearby, and it is his name, slightly altered, on the street sign outside. When construction of Avenida Brigadeiro Faria Lima came for the original site in the early 1970s, the market did not close: in March 1971 it moved wholesale to this building, honouring that century-old deed condition by relocating rather than disappearing. tours.title: Misci
tours.shortDescription: The name is short for miscigenação — the mixing that built Brazil.
tours.longDescription: Rua Mateus Grou 597 in Pinheiros reads more like a design studio than a boutique, clothes, accessories and furniture sharing one floor rather than sitting in separate departments. Airon Martin founded Misci in 2018, having grown up in Sinop, a frontier town in Mato Grosso, raised largely by his mother, his grandmother and his aunts. He moved to São Paulo at twenty-one to study design and kept drawing dresses on the side while building a career in furniture, the two habits eventually merging into one label. Nothing here separates a chair from a jacket conceptually; both come out of the same idea, that mixture itself — of ethnicities, regions, materials — is the most honest description of Brazilian design there is. The studio develops a good deal of its own raw material, with sustainability built into the process rather than bolted on.

tours.title: Monica Pondé
tours.shortDescription: She trained as an architect before she ever touched a piece of silver.
tours.longDescription: Rua Oscar Freire 1148 in Jardins, with a facade closer to a small gallery than a shop. Monica Pondé began in architecture in Rio de Janeiro, working with concrete, structure and the hard geometry of buildings, and somewhere along the way that training changed scale — from buildings down to objects small enough to wear. She has talked about the pull between the hardness of poured concrete and the organic, tangled relief of the forest surrounding Rio, and her jewellery is built on that same argument between the geometric and the organic, worn on a wrist instead of standing on a corner. The silver is not polished to a shine but sandblasted, then worked over by hand with a goldsmith's hammer until it carries a matte, slightly worn texture. Some pieces go further, woven from leather and buriti palm straw using a macramé technique borrowed from Indigenous Brazilian basketry.

tours.title: Museu Catavento
tours.shortDescription: Thirteen years to build, in a city that then had about a hundred thousand people.
tours.longDescription: The Palácio das Indústrias, home to Museu Catavento, is an eclectic brick-and-metal building designed by Domiziano Rossi with Ramos de Azevedo and Ricardo Severo, built between 1911 and 1924. Details worked into the brickwork and the peaks of the roofline reference production directly — bulls, tools — while others, like the dogs and the loopholes cut into the walls, seem to be there simply because the architects wanted them there. The metal structure holding the roof up was imported, a considerable statement for São Paulo at the time. It was not built for science: it opened on 29 April 1924 to host agricultural, industrial and commercial exhibitions, part of a wider plan to revive the low-lying Várzea do Carmo district. Since then it has held the state Legislative Assembly from 1947 to 1968 and City Hall from 1991 to 2004, before the Catavento science museum arrived in 2009.

tours.title: MASP — Museu de Arte de São Paulo
tours.shortDescription: Look underneath the building before you look inside it.
tours.longDescription: The vão livre — the free span — is a plaza roughly seventy metres across running clean underneath the museum's red concrete beams. Lina Bo Bardi designed it as public space first and museum second, usable by the city whether or not anyone ever goes inside. The museum began in 1947, founded by Pietro Maria Bardi at the invitation of the media magnate Assis Chateaubriand, and moved into this building on Avenida Paulista on 7 November 1968. Bo Bardi's design uses raw concrete and glass without decorative finish, favouring lightness and suspension over the usual weight of a museum. Upstairs the paintings hang not on walls but on freestanding glass easels, visible from both sides, floating in the room — a direct challenge to the European way of displaying a collection, made by an architect trained inside that tradition. The collection is the most significant of European art in the Southern Hemisphere, now past eight thousand works.

tours.title: MAC USP
tours.shortDescription: Niemeyer built it as an agriculture palace. It became the traffic department. Now it's an art museum.
tours.longDescription: On the edge of Ibirapuera Park, eight floors of Niemeyer's original 1954 structure, in continuous use since it opened and never for the same thing twice. From 1959 to 2008 this was Detran, São Paulo's vehicle licensing authority. It sat empty for years until the Museu de Arte Contemporânea moved in on 28 January 2012. The museum itself was born out of somebody else's crisis: when the old Museu de Arte Moderna de São Paulo ran into management trouble in the early 1960s, its entire collection transferred to the University of São Paulo in 1963, forming MAC. That founding collection came largely from donations by Yolanda Penteado and Ciccillo Matarazzo, plus prize-winning works from the São Paulo Bienal up to 1961. It has since grown past ten thousand pieces — Picasso and Modigliani alongside Tarsila do Amaral, Anita Malfatti and Lygia Clark.

tours.title: Nelita
tours.shortDescription: The pasta is rolled fresh every day, by a kitchen with not one man in it.
tours.longDescription: Rua Ferreira de Araújo 330, on the Pinheiros side of the neighbourhood line: a house with a wide glass frontage and very little fuss about it, more a well-loved neighbourhood spot than a temple to fine dining, though it has since been ranked among the best restaurants on the continent. The chef is Tássia Magalhães and the restaurant is named after her mother, Nelita. She leads an all-female kitchen team, and her cooking runs on what she calls the Italian DNA of her training, reworked with Brazilian ingredients and a lighter, more local hand — twelfth place on Latin America's 50 Best, and named the city's best restaurant in Folha de São Paulo's 2023 reader survey. There is an eleven-course tasting served only at the kitchen counter, a six-course menu, and an à la carte list. Watch for the pasta and the house-made butter, details most modern kitchens have long since outsourced.

tours.title: Nubank Parque
tours.shortDescription: Just under half a million fans voted on the name of this arena.
tours.longDescription: The stadium in Barra Funda is the home ground of Palmeiras, holding roughly 43,700 for football and up to 55,000 for concerts. None of it started as a football ground: in 1902 the Companhia Antarctica Paulista — the brewery — bought this land to give its own staff somewhere to play sport. Palestra Itália, the club later renamed Palmeiras, began using the pitch in 1917 and bought it outright in 1920, and by 1933 it had grown into the largest, most modern stadium in the country. It closed in 2010, was rebuilt from the ground up over four years and reopened in 2014 as Allianz Parque. Behind the north goal sits a surviving grandstand from the original Parque Antárctica, deliberately preserved — one of the only physical links to what stood here before. In 2026 the name changed again, this time by public vote, with just under half a million people taking part.

tours.title: Orelhão
tours.shortDescription: A phone booth that changed how an entire country made calls.
tours.longDescription: Stand on the pavement facing MASP and look for the small egg-shaped orange or blue shell standing on its own across the street — the object everyone in Brazil calls an orelhão, or big ear. The architect Chu Ming Silveira designed it in the early 1970s while working for São Paulo's telephone company. She built two versions: a smaller indoor one nicknamed the orelhinha, and this one, the Chu Two, made of fibreglass and shaped deliberately like an egg, a form chosen for its acoustic properties to cut street noise around the caller. Orange for one telecoms operator, blue for another, depending where in the country you stood. The first went up in Rio de Janeiro on 20 January 1972; São Paulo got one five days later. In 1982 MASP itself published a book on Brazilian design history formally crediting Silveira's authorship — rare recognition for an object so common it had become invisible.

tours.title: Pinacoteca de São Paulo
tours.shortDescription: The main entrance used to face the wrong way — toward a busy road.
tours.longDescription: The Pinacoteca occupies a building Ramos de Azevedo designed in 1896 to house the Liceu de Artes e Ofícios, a trade school. Over the decades it also sheltered the Military Police, a music conservatory and a drama school, alongside the art collection that eventually took the whole place over. In 1998 Paulo Mendes da Rocha, working with Eduardo Colonelli and Weliton Ricoy Torres, took on a full restoration and effectively reversed the building's circulation — moving the main entrance away from the traffic on Avenida Tiradentes around to the calmer Praça da Luz. Inside, they cut a long covered gallery through the old brick shell and threaded contemporary steel-and-glass walkways through it, leaving the original masonry exposed rather than disguised. That renovation became an international reference point for reworking a historic building without erasing its age — new structure clearly visible, old structure clearly original, neither pretending to be the other.

tours.title: Residências Vilanova Artigas
tours.shortDescription: In 1949 an architect built himself a house that argued with nearly every convention.
tours.longDescription: On a thousand-square-metre plot in Campo Belo, in the southern reaches of the city, two structures share the grounds: a small house from 1942 known simply as the casinha, and behind it the larger, bolder house Vilanova Artigas built for his own family in 1949. The casinha is modest, almost tentative, built while Artigas was still finding his footing. The 1949 house is not — rational lines, exposed geometry, a confidence drawing on Frank Lloyd Wright and Le Corbusier without copying either, filtered into what would become the São Paulo school of architecture. He was already thinking in the language he would later use on a much bigger stage, years before it had a name. The living room did real political work too: Artigas was a member of the Communist Party and it hosted the party's discussions, and in 1960 meetings tied to the Brazilian student movement — part of why the house is heritage-protected.

In 1949, an architect built himself a house that argued with just about every convention of what a house was supposed to look like.

You're on the grounds in Campo Belo, in the southern reaches of the city. Two structures share this thousand-square-metre plot: a small house from 1942, known simply as the casinha, and, standing behind it, the larger and considerably bolder house Vilanova Artigas built for his own family in 1949.

Look at the difference between the two. The casinha is modest, almost tentative, built when Artigas was still finding his footing. The 1949 house is not — rational lines, exposed geometry, a confidence that draws on Frank Lloyd Wright and Le Corbusier without copying either, filtered into something that would go on to define what's now called the São Paulo school of architecture. Artigas was, by this point, already thinking in the language he'd later use on a much bigger stage, years before that language got its name.

Here's what's worth knowing about that living room specifically. It wasn't just a family space. Artigas was a member of the Communist Party, and this room hosted its discussions; later, in 1960, it held meetings tied to the Brazilian student movement. A house built for one family ended up doing real political work, which is part of why it's since been protected as a heritage site — not only for the architecture, but for what happened inside it.

The same architect designed the Morumbi stadium, a concrete bowl built to hold seventy thousand people. Here, at roughly the same time in his career, he was working at the opposite scale entirely — worth holding both buildings in your head at once as you look at this one.

tours.title: SESC 24 de Maio
tours.shortDescription: This was a department store. SESC climbed inside it and rebuilt from within.
tours.longDescription: Rising over Praça Dom José Gaspar near the Theatro Municipal, fourteen storeys still wearing the bones of the Mesbla department store that traded here through the 1970s, its original steel skeleton visible if you know to look. Paulo Mendes da Rocha, working with MMBB Arquitetos, took fifteen years over the project — design from 2002 to 2008, construction from 2012 to 2017 — reusing the existing structure rather than starting from a cleared site. Inside that reused frame they fitted a theatre, a library, exhibition space, a restaurant and a sports block carrying a swimming pool all the way to the roof. Walk through and you can still feel the department store in the proportions: wide open floors, long sightlines, the same generosity of space that once sold furniture now hosting a queue for the pool. Same steel frame, opposite economics, and nothing you are required to buy on the way through.

stops.title: SESC 24 de Maio
stops.caption: This was a department store. SESC didn't tear it down — they climbed inside it and rebuilt from within.
stops.transcriptText:
This was a department store. SESC didn't tear it down — they climbed inside it and rebuilt from within.

Find the tower rising over Praça Dom José Gaspar, near the Theatro Municipal — fourteen storeys, still wearing the bones of the Mesbla department store that traded here through the 1970s, its original steel skeleton visible if you know to look for it under everything added since.

Architect Paulo Mendes da Rocha, working with MMBB Arquitetos, took fifteen years over the project altogether — design work from 2002 to 2008, construction from 2012 to 2017 — reusing the existing structure rather than starting from a cleared site. Inside that reused frame, they fitted a theatre, a library, exhibition space, a restaurant, and a sports block that carries a swimming pool all the way up to the roof. Walk through and you can still feel the department store's old bones in the proportions — wide open floors, long sightlines, the same generosity of space that used to sell furniture now hosting a queue for the pool instead.

What's worth noticing is the swap in what the building's actually for. A department store existed to sell things to people who could afford them. This one exists, largely free or nearly so, for anyone who walks in — same steel frame, opposite economics entirely, and no requirement to buy anything on your way through the doors.

Go up to the pool deck if you can, even just to look. A rooftop swimming pool suspended over the middle of downtown São Paulo isn't something this city hands you twice.

tours.title: SESC Pompéia
tours.shortDescription: Three concrete towers, and every one is a different shape on purpose.
tours.longDescription: The old Mauser Brothers drum factory in Pompéia was converted from 1976 into a leisure and culture centre after SESC's directors invited Lina Bo Bardi to take on the site. She kept the original factory sheds largely as they were once she discovered their structure had been built by François Hennebique, one of the true pioneers of reinforced concrete — worth preserving on its own account, not just for sentiment. Alongside them she raised three new towers: one punched through with irregular, cave-like openings, another scattered with plain square windows at random, and a third, a seventy-metre cylindrical water tower wrapped in a fine concrete lattice. Eight prestressed concrete walkways, each spanning twenty-five metres, link them in mid-air. None of the three towers match because Bo Bardi wanted the building to look assembled rather than designed all at once. Finished by 1986 and now protected as national heritage by IPHAN.

stops.title: SESC Pompéia
stops.caption: This complex has three concrete towers, and every one of them is a different shape on purpose.
stops.transcriptText:
This complex has three concrete towers, and every one of them is a different shape on purpose.

You're facing the old Mauser Brothers drum factory, in the Pompéia district — converted, starting in 1976, into a leisure and culture centre after SESC's directors invited Lina Bo Bardi to take on the site.

Bo Bardi kept the original factory sheds largely as they were, once she discovered their structure had been built by François Hennebique, one of the true pioneers of reinforced concrete in the early twentieth century — worth preserving on its own account, not just for sentiment. Alongside those sheds, she raised three new towers: one punched through with irregular, cave-like openings, another scattered with plain square windows at random, and a third, a seventy-metre cylindrical water tower wrapped in a fine concrete lattice. Eight prestressed concrete walkways, each spanning twenty-five metres, link the towers together in mid-air.

Have a think about why none of the three towers match. Bo Bardi wanted the building to look assembled rather than designed all at once — closer to something that had simply accumulated over time, the way a real factory complex actually would.

The first phase opened in 1982; the whole project was finished by 1986, and it's since been protected as national heritage by IPHAN.

Walk underneath the walkways rather than just past them — from directly below, you get the clearest sense of how much weight Bo Bardi was willing to hang in open air.

tours.title: Sala São Paulo
tours.shortDescription: A train station's whole job is noise and movement. This one's job now is neither.
tours.longDescription: Estação Júlio Prestes opened in 1938 as the grand terminus of the old Sorocabana railway; these days its ticket halls are a concert hall. The conversion, led by the architect Nelson Dupré with the American acoustics firm Artec, took eighteen months and opened as the São Paulo State Symphony's home on 9 July 1999. The hall seats close to one thousand five hundred across twenty-two boxes, arranged so almost nobody is genuinely far from the stage — a choice carried over from the building's old role moving large crowds quickly and without confusion. The standout engineering is overhead: fifteen steel panels clad in wood that rise or fall to physically retune the room, known as the acoustic clouds. It won an international award of honour from the American theatre technology body USITT in 2000 and is regularly ranked among the best-sounding concert halls anywhere.

stops.title: Sala São Paulo
stops.caption: A train station's whole job is noise and movement. This one's job now is neither.
stops.transcriptText:
A train station's whole job is noise and movement. This one's job now is neither.

The building in front of you is Estação Júlio Prestes, opened in 1938 as the grand terminus of the old Sorocabana railway. These days, its ticket halls are a concert hall.

The conversion, led by architect Nelson Dupré with the American acoustics firm Artec, took eighteen months, and opened as the São Paulo State Symphony's new home on the 9th of July 1999. The hall seats close to one thousand five hundred people across twenty-two boxes, arranged so that almost nobody in the room is genuinely far from the stage, a deliberate choice carried over from the building's old role as a place designed to move large crowds through quickly and without confusion.

Have a look up at the ceiling once you're inside. The standout piece of engineering is up there — fifteen steel panels, clad in wood, that can rise or fall to physically retune the room's acoustics, known as the acoustic clouds. It worked: Sala São Paulo picked up an international award of honour from the American theatre technology body USITT in the year 2000, and it's regularly ranked among the best-sounding concert halls anywhere in the world.

Here's what's rather satisfying about that. A building designed to move as many people through as fast as possible turned out to have acoustics flexible enough to be recalibrated into somewhere built for the opposite — absolute stillness, and close listening.

If you've time before a concert, walk the platform side of the building — you can still read the old station in the bones of the place, underneath everything that's been added since.

tours.title: Teatro Cultura Artística
tours.shortDescription: On 17 August 2008 this theatre burned down to almost nothing.
tours.longDescription: The building on Rua Nestor Pestana kept its facade through that fire; everything behind it today is new, rebuilt from the ground up. The facade dates to 1950, when the Sociedade de Cultura Artística — a group that had been dreaming of a theatre of its own since 1919 — finally got its building, designed by Rino Levi with Roberto Cerqueira César. Considered the most advanced theatre in the country at the time thanks to innovations in acoustics and sightlines, it opened with Heitor Villa-Lobos and Camargo Guarnieri each conducting the São Paulo State Symphony on consecutive nights. Across the front runs Alegoria das Artes, painted by Di Cavalcanti and the largest single work he ever made. When the fire tore through the auditoriums, a double wall built into the 1950 facade kept the mural and the foyers largely intact — a structural decision made seventy years earlier, quietly doing its job. The theatre reopened on 3 August 2024.

stops.title: Teatro Cultura Artística
stops.caption: On the 17th of August 2008, this theatre burned down to almost nothing.
stops.transcriptText:
On the 17th of August 2008, this theatre burned down to almost nothing.

The building in front of you, on Rua Nestor Pestana, kept its facade through that fire. Everything you'd find behind it today is new, rebuilt from the ground up — but what you're looking at from the street is the original.

That facade dates to 1950, when the Sociedade de Cultura Artística — a group that had been dreaming of a theatre of its own since 1919 — finally got its building, designed by architect Rino Levi with Roberto Cerqueira César. Considered the most advanced theatre in the country at the time, thanks largely to innovations in acoustics and sightlines, it opened to real fanfare: two of Brazil's leading composers, Heitor Villa-Lobos and Camargo Guarnieri, each conducted the São Paulo State Symphony Orchestra on consecutive opening nights.

Have a look at the mural running across the front of the building. It's called Alegoria das Artes, painted by Di Cavalcanti, and it's the largest single work he ever made. When the fire tore through the auditoriums in 2008, a double wall built into the original 1950 facade kept the mural, along with the ground and first-floor foyers, largely intact — a structural decision made seventy years earlier, quietly doing its job during the one moment it actually mattered.

Everything else took sixteen years to put right. The theatre reopened on the 3rd of August 2024, with two entirely new performance halls designed by architect Paulo Bruna, built behind the facade that survived.

Before you go in, take a proper look at that mural — it's the one piece of 1950 in this building that never actually stopped doing its job, fire or no fire.

tours.title: Teatro Oficina
tours.shortDescription: A fifty-metre runway down the middle, and nowhere comfortable to watch from a distance.
tours.longDescription: On Rua Jaceguai in Bela Vista the building does not announce itself much from the street; the transformation is all inside. Law students from USP founded the company here in 1958 under the director José Celso Martinez Corrêa, known to most of Brazil simply as Zé Celso. In 1967 Oficina staged Oswald de Andrade's O Rei da Vela, a production widely credited with rewriting the rules of Brazilian performance by breaking down the usual distance between actor and audience. That instinct eventually reshaped the building itself: from the late 1980s through 1994 Lina Bo Bardi worked with the architect Edson Elito to rebuild the theatre entirely — a central footbridge stage a metre and a half wide and fifty metres long, with seating for up to three hundred and fifty in galleries across four levels around it. Bo Bardi added a waterfall feeding a still reflecting pool inside the building.

stops.title: Teatro Oficina
stops.caption: This is a theatre with a fifty-metre runway down the middle, and no comfortable place to sit and just watch from a distance.
stops.transcriptText:
This is a theatre with a fifty-metre runway down the middle, and no comfortable place to sit and just watch from a distance.

Rua Jaceguai, Bela Vista — the building doesn't announce itself much from the street; the transformation is all on the inside, and you'll want to be prepared for that before you go through the door.

Law students from USP founded the company here in 1958, under director José Celso Martinez Corrêa, known to most of Brazil simply as Zé Celso. In 1967, Oficina staged Oswald de Andrade's O Rei da Vela — a production widely credited with rewriting the rules of Brazilian performance, breaking down the usual distance between actor and audience.

That instinct eventually reshaped the building itself. From the late 1980s through 1994, Lina Bo Bardi worked with architect Edson Elito to rebuild the theatre entirely: a central footbridge stage, a metre and a half wide and fifty metres long, with seating for up to three hundred and fifty arranged in galleries across four levels around it. Bo Bardi added a waterfall too, feeding a still reflecting pool inside the building — water, inside a theatre, doing exactly what it does outdoors.

Here's what's worth sitting with. Most theatres put the audience at a fixed distance from the stage. This one puts everyone practically inside the performance, wrapped around a runway rather than facing a proscenium.

If you get the chance to see something here, don't pick a seat too early — half the point of the room is how differently the same production reads depending on where around that footbridge you end up.

tours.title: Theatro Municipal de São Paulo
tours.shortDescription: Its entire job was to convince Europe that São Paulo belonged in its company.
tours.longDescription: Construction began on 26 June 1903. The theatre was built by Ramos de Azevedo's technical office from Cláudio Rossi's design, modelled directly on the Paris Opera — you are meant to notice the resemblance, right down to the sweeping staircase and the gilded detail inside. It opened on 12 September 1911 with Ambroise Thomas's opera Hamlet, at exactly the moment São Paulo's coffee wealth was funding a citywide push toward European sophistication. The opening became a genuinely modern event in its own right: something like twenty thousand people crowded the surrounding streets to see it, causing one of the city's first proper traffic jams, in a city that barely had motor traffic worth jamming. A building constructed to project orderly European grandeur ended up producing, on its very first evening, a distinctly modern piece of urban chaos.

stops.title: Theatro Municipal de São Paulo
stops.caption: Construction began on the 26th of June 1903. The building's entire job was to convince Europe that São Paulo belonged in its company.
stops.transcriptText:
Construction began on the 26th of June 1903. The building's entire job was to convince Europe that São Paulo belonged in its company.

The theatre in front of you was built by Ramos de Azevedo's technical office, from Cláudio Rossi's design, modelled directly on the Paris Opera — you're meant to notice the resemblance, not miss it, right down to the sweeping staircase and the gilded detail inside.

It opened on the 12th of September 1911, with a performance of Ambroise Thomas's opera Hamlet, at exactly the moment São Paulo's coffee wealth was funding a citywide push toward European sophistication. The opening itself became a genuinely modern event in its own right — something like twenty thousand people crowded the surrounding streets to see it, causing one of the city's first proper traffic jams, in a city that barely had motor traffic worth jamming yet.

Here's the irony sitting right there on opening night. A building constructed to project orderly European grandeur onto a fast-growing city ended up producing, on its very first evening, a distinctly modern piece of urban chaos — the size of the crowd it drew undercutting the calm it was built to project, a hint of the restless city São Paulo was already becoming.

Look up at the facade before you go in. It's easy to walk straight past the detail while focused on getting through the doors, but the building rewards a minute spent just looking at it from the square.

tours.title: VERNIZ
tours.shortDescription: There's no shopfront window to browse on your way past. You ring ahead.
tours.longDescription: A warehouse space in Barra Funda running to several hundred square metres behind a fairly plain exterior, keeping office hours Monday to Friday and opening Saturdays only by prior arrangement. Three collectors and designers curate what is inside: Fábio Matheiski, Paulo Bega and Luciano Tartália. What they have built is part showroom, part archive — genuine pieces of Brazilian modern furniture from across several decades, arranged alongside the trio's own new designs and other art and design objects that fit neatly into neither category. Nothing is labelled quite like a museum piece, but nothing feels like ordinary stock either; pieces sit close together, a chair from one decade beside a cabinet from another, so the room does some of the curating for you by proximity. The clientele is shopkeepers, architects and decorators sourcing for specific projects, which is precisely why the appointment system exists.

stops.title: VERNIZ
stops.caption: There's no shopfront window here to browse on your way past.
stops.transcriptText:
There's no shopfront window here to browse on your way past. You ring ahead.

The warehouse space in front of you, in Barra Funda, runs to several hundred square metres behind a fairly plain exterior. It keeps office hours, Monday to Friday, roughly eleven until six, and opens on Saturdays only by prior arrangement — worth knowing before you turn up expecting to just walk in.

Three collectors and designers curate what's inside: Fábio Matheiski, Paulo Bega, and Luciano Tartália. What they've built is part showroom, part archive — genuine pieces of Brazilian modern furniture from across several decades, arranged alongside the trio's own new designs and other art and design objects that don't fit neatly into either category. Nothing is labelled like a museum piece, exactly, but nothing feels like ordinary stock either. Pieces sit close together, a chair from one decade next to a cabinet from another, so the room ends up doing a bit of the curating for you just by proximity.

Have a think about who actually walks through that door. This isn't built for casual browsing — the clientele tends to be shopkeepers, architects, and decorators, people sourcing specific pieces for specific projects, which is precisely why the appointment system exists in the first place.

And here's the thing worth noticing about that model. Most shops want footfall — anyone, any time, browsing turned into buying. VERNIZ assumes the opposite: that you already roughly know what you're after, and the job of the space is just to put the right piece in front of you.

Call ahead if you want to see the floor properly, and once you're in, ask what's arrived most recently — the mix changes often enough that no two visits look quite the same.

tours.title: Varal Bar
tours.shortDescription: It started in the backyard of a clothing shop. It's since grown into a house of its own.
tours.longDescription: Rua Artur de Azevedo 636 in Pinheiros: a 1940s house, unassuming from the street, giving very little away about what is inside. There is no sign worth mentioning — you are meant to already know, or to have been sent by someone who does. Once the bar outgrew that original backyard it took over this house entirely, and now runs across a handful of distinct spaces: a tunnel lined with broken tile shards near the entrance, a main lounge dense with sofas, armchairs and a hexagonal bar counter, and beyond that an open-air garden with pebbled ground and beach chairs scattered under the plants. The kitchen is run by Hyssa Abrahim Filho, one of the bar's own partners, cooking a home-style menu built around whole ingredients and very little waste. Behind the bar, Ricardo Ribeiro and Thiago dos Santos run a largely original, cachaça-driven cocktail list.

stops.title: Varal Bar
stops.caption: Varal started small — in the backyard of a clothing shop a few streets from here.
stops.transcriptText:
Varal started small — in the backyard of a clothing shop a few streets from here. It's since grown into a house of its own.
