stops.caption: You've been able to see it since you turned the corner: a gilded dome floating above Oranienburger Strasse, flanked by two smaller ones, catching whatever light the day has to offer.
stops.transcriptText:
You've been able to see it since you turned the corner: a gilded dome floating above Oranienburger Strasse, flanked by two smaller ones, catching whatever light the day has to offer. Walk toward it. This is the Neue Synagoge, and being seen was always the point.

When it opened in 1866, this was the largest synagogue in the country, and nothing about it apologised. The congregation chose a Moorish style — banded brickwork, arched windows, that extraordinary dome — architecture with no intention of blending into a Prussian streetscape. Bismarck attended the opening. Berlin's Jewish community was prosperous, confident and at home here, and it built accordingly: not a discreet prayer house tucked into a courtyard, but a landmark on a main street.

The best place to take it in is from across the street. And it's worth knowing what you're looking at: the building was attacked in the pogrom of November 1938, gutted by wartime bombing, and the ruined main hall behind was cleared away in the 1950s. The front and the dome are a rebuilding, begun in the last years of the GDR and finished in 1995. Today the building holds a museum, a working prayer room and the community's archives. You may also notice the barriers and the police post out front. Synagogues in Germany are guarded, and this walk promised to tell you plainly.

End on what the builders wanted you to feel. The quarter you've just walked keeps every register of its history within a few hundred metres — the polished courtyards, the rough one, the quiet street, the brass squares underfoot — and it saves its gold for this. On a clear evening the dome is still the brightest thing in the Scheunenviertel: a building made to be seen, wrecked for being seen, and then, patiently, made to be seen again.

The walk ends here. Stay across the street a moment longer, and give the dome the long look it was built for.

tours.title: The River Border
tours.shortDescription: For most of its course through Berlin the Wall was a line drawn across land. Here it was water.
tours.longDescription: At Schlesisches Tor, in the thick of Kreuzberg, the city simply ended a few streets away during the division — and where elsewhere a double row of cobblestones traces the Wall's route, here the cobblestones give way to the Spree and the river did that work. Three stops and about two kilometres, flat the whole way, saving the show for the end: the Oberbaumbrücke, a Victorian railway bridge dressed as a medieval gate and repaired after the war with its seam left honest; the East Side Gallery, the longest surviving stretch of the Berlin Wall, painted end to end in the spring after the fall; and a riverbank park where the border strip is now a lawn. One honest note — the stretch along the gallery is narrow and can be crowded near the bridge.

stops.title: Schlesisches Tor
stops.caption: For most of its course through Berlin, the Wall was a line drawn across land.
stops.transcriptText:
For most of its course through Berlin, the Wall was a line drawn across land. On this walk, it was water.

You should be at Schlesisches Tor, under the elevated tracks of the U1, in the thick of Kreuzberg — kebab shops, late-night bars, the railway rumbling overhead on its brick arches. During the division this was a corner of West Berlin pressed so hard against the border that the city simply ended a few streets away. Elsewhere, a double row of cobblestones traces where the Wall once ran; here the river did that work, and the cobblestones give way to the Spree.

This walk is about two kilometres, flat the whole way, and it saves its show for the end: first a bridge that looks like it escaped from a fairy tale, then the longest surviving stretch of the Berlin Wall — painted end to end — and finally a riverbank where the border strip is now a lawn. One honest note: the stretch along the gallery is narrow and can be crowded, especially near the bridge. Take your time anyway.

Walk down Oberbaumstrasse toward the river — you'll see twin brick towers rising ahead. That's the Oberbaumbrücke, and it's where we cross.

stops.title: Oberbaumbrücke
stops.caption: Stop mid-bridge if the crowds allow, between the two brick towers.
stops.transcriptText:
Stop mid-bridge if the crowds allow, between the two brick towers. You are standing on the best-loved bridge in Berlin, and on one of its better jokes: the Oberbaumbrücke looks medieval — turrets, arcades, crenellations — and it is younger than the telephone. It went up in 1896, romantic dress-up for what was really modern infrastructure: the upper deck was built to carry the city's first elevated railway across the Spree, and the U1 still rattles over your head today. And the name is older still: the Oberbaum was the wooden boom that once closed the river here at night, back when this was the city's toll gate on the water.

Now look down at the water, because the water is the point. The border between East and West ran down the middle of this river. The bridge touched both worlds — Friedrichshain on the far bank was East, Kreuzberg behind you was West — and for most of the division it carried no traffic at all. For years it served as a crossing where West Berliners with the right paperwork could walk into the East, one at a time, and back again before the day ended.

Here's the detail worth keeping. After reunification, the two districts that had faced each other across this border were merged into a single borough: Friedrichshain-Kreuzberg, one name, one hyphen. Berliners still joke about the arranged marriage, but look at the geography — the borough's two halves face each other across the river, stitched together by a few bridges, and this is the grandest of them by a mile. The bridge isn't just in the hyphenated borough. The bridge is the hyphen.

Cross to the Friedrichshain side and turn left along Mühlenstrasse, keeping the river on your left. The long run of concrete ahead, covered in paint and people photographing it, is the East Side Gallery — the next stop, and the last stretch of this walk.

stops.title: East Side Gallery
stops.caption: The East Side Gallery runs from the bridge behind you almost to Ostbahnhof — more than a kilometre of Berlin Wall, painted end to end.
stops.transcriptText:
The East Side Gallery runs from the bridge behind you almost to Ostbahnhof — more than a kilometre of Berlin Wall, painted end to end. And here's the friendly advice this walk owes you: do not try to see all of it. There are more than a hundred works. Treat it like any great gallery — walk the full length, but let three or four pieces actually stop you.

First, though, understand what the canvas is. These are the real segments — prefabricated concrete, roughly three and a half metres tall, standing exactly where the border installations sealed off the eastern bank. The border itself was the middle of the river; the Wall stood here to keep everyone away from the water. Through the decades of division, this concrete was blank, and no one could stand where you're standing now. Then, in 1990, with the border open but the Wall still on its feet, artists from all over the world were invited to paint it — and the most forbidding surface in the city became, within months, its most photographed.

So walk, and read as you go. Some works are jokes, some are grief, some are hope painted very fast in a year when anything seemed possible. You'll pass the famous kiss — you'll know it when you see it, and so does everyone else, so the crowd will find it for you. The paintings have been restored and argued over in the years since; the concrete weathers, and the city keeps deciding how much to intervene. That argument is ongoing, and it isn't ours today. Yours is simpler: keep walking.

About halfway along, watch for the openings cut through the Wall. Pick one and step through it — the river side is the last stop, and it's the quiet ending this loud kilometre has been hiding.

stops.title: East Side Park
stops.caption: Step through, and the volume drops. You're on the riverbank now — a strip of grass and trees between the back of the Wall and the Spree, with swans idling and the towers of the Oberbaumbrücke downstream.
stops.transcriptText:
Step through, and the volume drops. You're on the riverbank now — a strip of grass and trees between the back of the Wall and the Spree, with swans idling and the towers of the Oberbaumbrücke downstream. Officially this is East Side Park. Unofficially it's one of the most quietly astonishing places in Berlin, because everything pleasant about it is standing in what used to be the border strip.

Look at the back of the Wall first — this side is mostly bare, grey, patched. Then look at the ground you're on. During the division, this riverbank was sealed territory: cleared, patrolled, off-limits, a city turned away from its own water. The houses that once stood along the bank were demolished to make room for the border installations. No one strolled here, because no one could. Today it's picnic blankets and evening beers, and the traffic on the water is tour boats.

This is where the walk has been heading all along, so give it a minute. Berlin's real achievement isn't that it removed its border — most of it is simply gone, and elsewhere in the city you'd never know. Its achievement is what it did with the pieces it kept: a bridge reopened and made the emblem of a joined-up borough, a wall handed over to painters, a forbidden riverbank handed back to anyone with a free afternoon. Nothing here pretends the division didn't happen. It just refuses to let the division have the last word.

The walk ends here — and so, if you've been following this city's story from the Gate onward, does a much longer one. Find a spot on the grass, face the river, and wait for the U1 to cross the bridge on its way between the two halves of one city. It's a small sight. It took a century to arrange.

tours.title: Aït Benhaddou | آيت بن حدّو
tours.shortDescription: Africa's most-filmed hillside is a thousand-year-old village built entirely of earth.
tours.longDescription: The ksar of Aït Benhaddou climbs its hillside above the Ounila river in tiers of red pisé — earth, straw and lime rammed into moulds and baked by the sun, with no wooden frame and no fired brick, standing for the better part of a thousand years. Crenellated corner towers cap each cluster of houses, carrying the geometric patterns found on kasbahs across Morocco's south. More than eighty films and television series have shot here — more than at any other single location in Africa: Lawrence of Arabia opened with these walls, Ridley Scott turned them into Gladiator's Zucchabar, and Game of Thrones cast them as Yunkai. UNESCO listed the ksar in 1987, though most families long ago moved across the river; a handful still hold on among the towers, and their washing lines strung between fortified turrets are the most honest detail in the scene.

stops.title: Aït Benhaddou | آيت بن حدّو
stops.caption: More than eighty films and television series have been shot on the hillside in front of you — more than at any other single location in Africa.
stops.transcriptText:
More than eighty films and television series have been shot on the hillside in front of you — more than at any other single location in Africa.

Across the Ounila river, the ksar of Aït Benhaddou climbs the hillside in tiers of red pisé, packed earth built up in layers and left to bake in the sun. Corner towers cap each cluster of houses, crenellated like a fortress, and the walls carry the same geometric patterns you'll find on kasbahs right across the south. A line of palm trees marks the riverbank ahead of you, and behind the ksar, the ochre foothills of the High Atlas roll away toward the mountains proper.

Have a look at how it's built first. Pisé has no wooden frame and no fired brick — just earth, straw and lime, rammed into wooden moulds and stacked course by course — and it has kept these walls standing for the better part of a thousand years, with each generation patching and rebuilding as the winter rains wear the towers down.

Ridley Scott shot Gladiator here, turning the ksar into the slave city of Zucchabar; the Game of Thrones crew came back across two seasons and cast it as Yunkai, one of the slave cities of Slaver's Bay; and decades before either, Lawrence of Arabia opened with these same walls on screen. Few places on the continent have stood in for so many different centuries and countries at once.

And here's the thing worth sitting with: almost nobody actually lives inside the ksar any more. Most families moved across the river to the newer village decades ago, once running water and electricity made the old earthen houses hard to justify, and what remains inside the walls today is maintained largely for visitors and film crews rather than daily life. Aït Benhaddou earned its UNESCO listing in 1987 not as a living village exactly, but as proof of how that village once worked.

A handful of families still hold on inside the walls, running small shops and guest rooms among the towers, and their washing lines strung between fortified turrets are, if anything, the most honest detail in the whole scene.

tours.title: Almoravid Koubba | قبة المرابطين
tours.shortDescription: The only Almoravid building left standing in Morocco — and the root of everything built after it.
tours.longDescription: Sunken several metres below street level beside the Ben Youssef Mosque, this small domed pavilion is the only Almoravid building still standing anywhere in Morocco. Ali ibn Yusuf built it around 1125 as an ablutions pavilion, and the city simply rose around it — nine centuries of rebuilding stacked layer on layer until it vanished beneath an unremarkable outbuilding, where excavators found it again in 1952. Inside, the ribbed dome is carved with interlocking arches radiating like a stone starburst, ringed by pine cones, palm fronds and acanthus leaves that historians treat as the starting point for almost every Moroccan decorative style that followed. The horseshoe arch on its western face is the earliest dated example in the country; every riad doorway in the medina descends from it, however roundabout the route.

stops.title: Almoravid Koubba | قبة المرابطين
stops.caption: The dome in front of you is the only Almoravid building left standing anywhere in Morocco.
stops.transcriptText:
The dome in front of you is the only Almoravid building left standing anywhere in Morocco.

The Almoravid Koubba sits several metres below the level of the street, in a sunken excavation just off the Ben Youssef Mosque. The gap isn't an accident of design — the ground around it has simply risen through nine centuries of rebuilding, layer stacked on layer, the way it has right across the old city. Look down from the railing and you'll see a single small stone structure, roughly cube-shaped, topped with a ribbed dome pierced by star-shaped windows, with rubble and foundation walls scattered around it — the remains of later buildings that were cleared away to reveal it.

Have a look at the dome first. It's carved on the inside with a pattern of interlocking arches that radiate out from the centre like a stone starburst, and around the base runs a band of motifs — pine cones, palm fronds, acanthus leaves — that architectural historians treat as the starting point for almost every decorative style that followed in Morocco.

It was built around 1125 by the Almoravid ruler Ali ibn Yusuf as an ablutions pavilion attached to the mosque next door, and it disappeared for centuries under later rebuilding, before excavators finally uncovered it in 1952, buried beneath an outbuilding nobody had thought twice about.

What's worth knowing, standing here, is that this small, slightly awkward building sitting in its pit is effectively the root of Moroccan architecture: the arches, the star windows and the carved foliage all reappear later, larger and grander, in the Almohad and Marinid buildings across the city, but they start here first.

Look for the horseshoe arch on its western face before you move on. It's the earliest dated example of the shape in the country, and every riad doorway in the medina behind you descends from it, however roundabout the route.

tours.title: Bacha Coffee | مقهى الباشا
tours.shortDescription: Churchill, Chaplin and Roosevelt all took coffee in these rooms — and the house pours on as if the century never turned.
tours.longDescription: Bacha Coffee occupies the ground-floor reception rooms of Dar el Bacha — the House of the Pasha — a palace built in the early 1900s for Thami El Glaoui, the Pasha of Marrakech. From 1910 the coffee house drew the era's power brokers, and the guest list reads like a rollcall of the century: Winston Churchill, Charlie Chaplin and Franklin Roosevelt all took coffee within these walls. After the Second World War the palace closed and sat shut for more than sixty years, reopening as a museum in 2017; two years later, at the invitation of King Mohammed the Sixth, the coffee house was revived inside it. The revival is a deliberate period piece — staff in gold-trimmed 1910 uniforms and fez caps, over a hundred single-origin coffees poured tableside from silver pots, and a queue that runs the length of the palm courtyard by mid-morning.

stops.title: Bacha Coffee | مقهى الباشا
stops.caption: Beyond the marble entrance hall, past a courtyard lined with palms and studded with zellij tilework, sits a coffee house dressed as if the twentieth century had never quite finished with it.
stops.transcriptText:
Beyond the marble entrance hall, past a courtyard lined with palms and studded with zellij tilework, sits a coffee house dressed as if the twentieth century had never quite finished with it.

Bacha Coffee occupies the ground floor of Dar el Bacha — the House of the Pasha — a grand palace built in the early 1900s for Thami El Glaoui, the regional governor known as the Pasha of Marrakech. You're standing in what were once his reception rooms: carved cedar ceilings overhead, marble underfoot, and a covered courtyard garden with soaring palms just beyond the counter.

The coffee house itself dates to 1910, when the palace became a meeting place for the era's power brokers, and the guest list over the following decades reads like a rollcall of the century: Winston Churchill, Charlie Chaplin and Franklin Roosevelt all took coffee within these walls.

After the Second World War, the palace shut its doors, and for more than sixty years it sat closed to the public. It reopened as a museum in 2017, and two years later, at the invitation of King Mohammed the Sixth, the coffee house was revived inside it — the same address, the same trade, picking up more or less where it left off.

And here's the thing that makes it worth the visit rather than just the coffee: the whole production is a period piece. Staff dress in gold-trimmed uniforms and fez caps modelled on 1910, the menu runs to well over a hundred single-origin coffees poured tableside from silver pots, and the entire ritual is staged, deliberately, as though Marrakech's belle époque had simply been paused rather than ended.

The queue tends to run the length of the courtyard by mid-morning, which tells you the revival worked rather better than anyone expected.

tours.title: Bahia Palace | قصر الباهية
tours.shortDescription: Two grand viziers spent forty years building 'the brilliant one' — and rivals ransacked it within days of the second one's death.
tours.longDescription: Bahia Palace covers roughly eight hectares of courtyards, gardens and private apartments, built in two waves: begun in the 1860s by Si Moussa, grand vizier to Sultan Moulay Hassan the First, then dramatically expanded by his son Bou Ahmed, who kept enlarging it until his death in 1900. Bou Ahmed named it Bahia — 'the brilliant one' — after his favourite wife, and built a private apartment for each of his four wives and twenty-four concubines, the painted cedar ceilings growing more elaborate with the status of each room. The Grand Courtyard is paved in white and green marble, some imported from Italy. None of it lasted: within days of Bou Ahmed's death the palace was ransacked by rivals and his fortune seized by the sultan's court. In the small riad garden, orange trees and jasmine still grow in the pattern his gardeners planted, quietly outlasting everyone who fought over the place.

stops.title: Bahia Palace | قصر الباهية
stops.caption: Count the courtyards as you go — Bahia Palace has more than you'll be able to hold in your head by the time you reach the end.
stops.transcriptText:
Count the courtyards as you go — Bahia Palace has more than you'll be able to hold in your head by the time you reach the end.

Step through the horseshoe arch into the Grand Courtyard, its floor paved entirely in white and green marble, some of it imported from Italy. Cypress trees stand in each corner, and the surrounding gallery is carried on slender columns topped with carved stucco.

The palace as a whole covers roughly eight hectares of courtyards, gardens and private apartments, and it was built in two waves: first by Si Moussa, grand vizier to Sultan Moulay Hassan the First, starting in the 1860s, and then dramatically expanded by his son, Bou Ahmed, who succeeded him as grand vizier and kept enlarging the place until his death in 1900.

Bou Ahmed named it Bahia — "the brilliant one" — after his favourite wife, and had a private apartment built for each of his four wives and twenty-four concubines, each one slightly different in its tilework and its light, as if the household's private rivalries were built directly into the floor plan. Look up as you move between the rooms: the painted cedar ceilings change pattern from space to space, and the more elaborate the paintwork overhead, the more status the room once carried.

And here's the twist worth knowing: none of it lasted. Within days of Bou Ahmed's death, the palace was ransacked by rivals, his household turned out, and his fortune seized by the sultan's court. The most lavish private residence built in Marrakech in a century stood empty and picked over almost as soon as it was finished.

From the small riad garden at the palace's western end, orange trees and jasmine still grow in more or less the pattern Bou Ahmed's gardeners planted, quietly outlasting every single person who once fought over the place.

tours.title: Baromètre
tours.shortDescription: An unmarked door in Guéliz, a staircase down, and one of the top ten bars in the Middle East and North Africa.
tours.longDescription: Behind an unmarked door inside the Résidence Al Houda on Rue Moulay Ali, a staircase leads down to a basement that was one of the first rooms in Marrakech built entirely around mixology. Apothecary jars, brass fittings and low light give Baromètre the feel of a spice shop crossed with an alchemist's laboratory — the name borrowed from the antique barometers and apothecary scales dotted around the room — and the bartenders work through their ingredients at the counter rather than out of sight. The kitchen alongside runs a short, considered menu: duck leg confit, a risotto built around clams and mhamssa, the small hand-rolled Moroccan pasta. The city's drinking culture traditionally lived in hotel bars and riad terraces; Baromètre treated cocktails as a craft worth an entire evening, and in 2023 the Tales of the Cocktail Spirited Awards named it among the top ten bars in the Middle East and North Africa.

stops.title: Baromètre
stops.caption: There's a curious thing about the ground floor here — it gives nothing away at all.

tours.title: Dar Si Said Museum | متحف دار السي سعيد
tours.shortDescription: A vizier's brother built the palace; since 1930 it has held the everyday craft of the Moroccan south.
tours.longDescription: Dar Si Said was commissioned in the mid-1800s by Si Said ibn Moussa, brother to the powerful grand vizier Bou Ahmed, and shares Bahia Palace's taste for scale and craftsmanship on a smaller, more intimate footing — carved cedar eaves, geometric zellij floors, and stucco cut so finely it reads as lace. In 1930, French administrators cataloguing Morocco's craft traditions chose this palace to hold the collection, and that has been its job ever since. The woodwork gallery upstairs keeps carved cedar panels and painted ceilings lifted from Marrakech palaces that didn't survive, alongside doors and chests inlaid with bone and silver; Berber jewellery, hand-knotted carpets and ceramics are shown here precisely because they were made to be used — worn, sat on, eaten from — rather than admired behind glass. An Andalusian courtyard garden and a roof terrace, where the geometry reads as one continuous pattern, close the visit.

stops.title: Dar Si Said Museum | متحف دار السي سعيد
stops.caption: It's 1930. French administrators are cataloguing Morocco's craft traditions, and they choose this exact palace to hold the collection.
stops.transcriptText:

Inside the palace of Dar Si Said, the entrance courtyard alone does most of the persuading: carved cedar eaves overhead, a floor of geometric zellij tile, and doorways framed in stucco cut so finely it looks more like lace than plaster.

The building was commissioned in the mid-1800s by Si Said ibn Moussa, brother to the powerful grand vizier Bou Ahmed, and it shares the same taste for scale and craftsmanship you'll find at Bahia Palace nearby, if on a smaller and — some say — more intimate footing.

Have a look at the woodwork gallery upstairs first. Carved cedar panels and painted ceilings, some lifted from other Marrakech palaces that didn't survive, sit alongside doors and chests inlaid with bone and silver from craftsmen working right across the south of Morocco. Beyond it, a small courtyard garden laid out in the Andalusian style — citrus trees, a central fountain, beds sunk slightly below the surrounding paths — offers a quieter counterpoint to all that carved detail indoors.

And here's the thing about the collection itself: it isn't really about any single dazzling object. Berber silver jewellery, hand-knotted carpets, ceramics and carved wood are displayed here specifically because they were made to be used — worn, sat on, eaten from — rather than admired behind glass, and the museum's whole point, since it opened in 1930, has been treating everyday craftsmanship as seriously as royal architecture.

Take the stairs up to the roof terrace before you leave. From there, the courtyard's geometry reads as one continuous pattern, rather than the sum of its parts.

tours.title: El Badi Palace | قصر البديع
tours.shortDescription: 'The Incomparable' had 360 rooms, Italian marble and Sudanese gold — a century later another sultan stripped it to the bone.
tours.longDescription: Sultan Ahmad al-Mansur commissioned El Badi — 'the Incomparable', one of the ninety-nine names of God — in 1578, paid for with the war reparations Portugal handed over after its catastrophic defeat at the Battle of the Three Kings. Twenty-five years in the building, it ran to some 360 rooms dressed in Italian marble, gold carried up from Sudan and onyx shipped from India. Barely a century later, Sultan Moulay Ismail stripped it almost bare, hauling marble, cedar and gold off to his new capital at Meknes; what stands today is the skeleton — vast pisé walls around four sunken orange-grove gardens and a huge reflecting pool. One treasure came back: the Koutoubia Minbar, the pulpit inlaid with ivory and silver by Córdoba craftsmen in 1137, sits in a pavilion off the main court. Storks nest along the wall-tops in their dozens, and their clattering bills are most days the loudest sound on the site.

stops.title: El Badi Palace | قصر البديع
stops.caption: The ninety-nine names of God include "the Incomparable" — and that's the name the Saadian sultans gave to the palace whose ruins surround you.
stops.transcriptText:
The ninety-nine names of God include "the Incomparable" — and that's the name the Saadian sultans gave to the palace whose ruins surround you.

Walk to the edge of the sunken garden and look across: what's left standing is a vast rectangular enclosure of pisé walls, punctuated by four sunken orange-grove gardens and a huge reflecting pool at the centre, all of it scaled for a building that once had 360 rooms.

Sultan Ahmad al-Mansur commissioned El Badi in 1578, paid for with the war reparations Portugal handed over after its catastrophic defeat at the Battle of the Three Kings, and it took roughly twenty-five years to finish: Italian marble for the floors, gold leaf carried up from Sudan, onyx shipped in from India — the full inventory of what an early modern superpower could afford.

None of that survives. Barely a century after it was finished, Sultan Moulay Ismail had the palace stripped almost bare — marble, cedar, gold, all of it hauled off to build his new capital at Meknes — and what you're looking at now is essentially the building's skeleton, the plaster and stone left behind because they weren't worth moving.

One genuine treasure did make its way back, though. In a pavilion off the main courtyard sits the Koutoubia Minbar, the carved wooden pulpit made for the Koutoubia Mosque across town, inlaid with ivory and silver by craftsmen in Córdoba in 1137 and eight years in the making — centuries older than El Badi itself, and one of the finest surviving pieces of woodwork anywhere in the Islamic world.

And here's what makes the ruin worth the visit rather than just a curiosity: it's a monument to a specific kind of confidence, the sort that assumes an empire's wealth will always be there to be spent, and it stands today as evidence of exactly how quickly that assumption can be proven wrong.

Storks nest along the tops of the walls in their dozens, and their clattering bills are, most days, the loudest sound anywhere on the site.

tours.title: El Fenn Boutique
tours.shortDescription: Vanessa Branson signed for one crumbling riad and got five — the shop by the courtyard is the whole hotel's eye, distilled.
tours.longDescription: El Fenn means 'the art' in Arabic — and 'the hip thing' in local slang, which tells you most of what you need to know. Vanessa Branson, art collector and sister of Richard Branson, bought what she thought was one crumbling house in 2002 with her business partner Howell James, discovering on signing that it came with four adjoining buildings attached; the boutique hotel that opened in 2004 was five houses knitted into one. The ground-floor boutique, put together by the actress and long-time Marrakech resident Marisa Berenson, lays out Moroccan-made textiles, ceramics, jewellery and leather babouches from workshops the hotel works with directly, priced to reflect the maker rather than the location. Branson founded the Marrakech Biennale and ran it from El Fenn for six editions, and the rotating exhibitions still treat the building as a gallery that happens to rent rooms — half the pieces on display aren't for sale at all, and working out which is which is part of the fun.

tours.title: Jajjah by Hassan Hajjaj
tours.shortDescription: The 'Andy Warhol of Marrakech' built a warehouse where his photographs, tea tins and tagines all hang in one frame.
tours.longDescription: In Sidi Ghanem, Marrakech's industrial design quarter, a converted warehouse fitted out in emerald tiles, yellow walls, bronze chandeliers and cabinets built from repurposed tea tins and oil cans holds Jajjah — the name is owner Hassan Hajjaj's own, simply reversed. The Moroccan-British artist, often nicknamed the Andy Warhol of Marrakech for turning consumer packaging and street style into pop portraiture, runs the space as three things at once: a gallery rotating shows by young Moroccan photographers he champions personally, a boutique of tea blends, clothing and objects of his own design, and a restaurant where an all-female kitchen cooks tagines and couscous the traditional way in a room that looks nothing like tradition. His portraits — models in printed djellabas framed by grids of tin cans — hang throughout, so sitting down to eat, you're inside one of his photographs rather than just looking at one.

stops.caption: Every surface in this room is doing something — colour, pattern, or both — and none of it is accidental.

The gallery walls change with each new show, but the tin-can light fittings overhead stay exactly where they are, season after season.

tours.title: Jardin Majorelle | حديقة ماجوريل
tours.shortDescription: A painter spent a lifetime building this garden and patented its blue — Yves Saint Laurent saved it from the bulldozers.
tours.longDescription: The French painter Jacques Majorelle came to Marrakech to recover from illness, bought this plot in 1923, and spent decades filling it: cactus gardens, bamboo groves, lily ponds, a Cubist villa by the architect Paul Sinoir in 1931, and — by the time he opened the gates to the public in 1947 — more than a hundred and thirty-five plant species from as far afield as Mexico and Madagascar. The saturated ultramarine covering nearly every hard surface is his own invention, mixed in 1937 and patented under his name; it's still called Majorelle Blue. A costly divorce forced him to sell in the 1950s, and the garden had fallen into ruin and was slated for a housing development when Yves Saint Laurent and Pierre Bergé stepped in to buy and restore it, nearly doubling the collection to some three hundred species. A memorial to Saint Laurent stands in the rose garden, where his ashes were scattered in 2008.

stops.title: Jardin Majorelle | حديقة ماجوريل
stops.caption: Cobalt walls, bamboo forty feet overhead, and somewhere beneath it all, several hundred species of plant gathered from five continents.
stops.transcriptText:
Cobalt walls, bamboo forty feet overhead, and somewhere beneath it all, several hundred species of plant gathered from five continents.

Jardin Majorelle sits behind these electric-blue walls exactly as its painter-owner left them: narrow paths threading through cactus gardens, bamboo groves and lily ponds, with the villa's cobalt trim reappearing at every turn — planters, window frames, the pergola over your head.

The garden began in 1923, when the French painter Jacques Majorelle, who'd come to Marrakech six years earlier to recover from illness, bought this plot and started planting. In 1931 he added a Cubist villa designed by the architect Paul Sinoir, and by the time he opened the garden to the public in 1947, he'd gathered more than a hundred and thirty-five plant species from as far afield as Mexico and Madagascar.

Have a look at the shade of blue covering nearly every hard surface. Majorelle mixed it himself in 1937, a saturated ultramarine unlike anything used in local building at the time, and he liked it enough to patent it under his own name — it's still called Majorelle Blue today, and you won't find it used quite this way anywhere else in the city.

And here's the twist: Majorelle didn't get to enjoy his own garden for long. A costly divorce in the 1950s forced him to sell it, and by the following decade it had fallen into ruin and was slated for a housing development. Yves Saint Laurent and his partner Pierre Bergé, who'd visited years earlier, stepped in to buy and restore it, eventually nearly doubling the plant collection to some three hundred species.

A memorial to Saint Laurent stands in the rose garden, where his ashes were scattered after his death in 2008 — a quieter corner than the blue walls, but the one the garden's second owner chose for himself.

tours.title: Jemaa el-Fna | جامع الفنا
tours.shortDescription: UNESCO's first-ever listing to protect what happens in a place rather than what's built on it.
tours.longDescription: Marrakech's great square dates to the eleventh century and the Almoravid dynasty that first laid out the city, and nobody agrees on what the name means — 'the mosque at the end of the world', 'the assembly of the dead', or simply the courtyard of a mosque that no longer exists. Orange-juice carts line up through the day; by early evening dozens of numbered food stalls appear from nowhere, and storytellers, musicians and henna artists work the crowd as they have for centuries. In 2001 UNESCO proclaimed the square a Masterpiece of the Oral and Intangible Heritage of Humanity — the first time it had protected a place for what happens in it rather than what's built on it, a campaign pushed through partly by the writer Juan Goytisolo, who fought off a glass tower on the square's edge. Nothing here is roped off: the performers are the heritage, and the square stays what it is only for as long as people keep showing up.

stops.title: Jemaa el-Fna | جامع الفنا
stops.caption: You probably think you already know this square from a hundred postcards.
stops.transcriptText:
You probably think you already know this square from a hundred postcards. Give it another few minutes before you decide.

Stand anywhere near the centre of Jemaa el-Fna and turn slowly: the Koutoubia's minaret anchors the skyline to the southwest, orange-juice carts line up in neat rows through the day, and by early evening, dozens of numbered food stalls will have appeared from nowhere to fill the open ground around you.

Nobody agrees on what the name actually means. Jemaa can mean "mosque" or "assembly"; fna can mean "courtyard," or more darkly, "death" — so depending on who you ask, you're standing in "the mosque at the end of the world," "the assembly of the dead," referencing public executions once held here, or simply an open square in front of a mosque that no longer exists. The square itself dates back to the eleventh century, to the Almoravid dynasty that first laid out Marrakech.

In 2001, UNESCO proclaimed the square a Masterpiece of the Oral and Intangible Heritage of Humanity, later folded into its wider Intangible Cultural Heritage list in 2008 — the first time the organisation had ever protected a place for what happens in it rather than what's built on it. The campaign was pushed through partly by the writer Juan Goytisolo, a longtime Marrakech resident who fought off a plan to put a glass tower on the square's edge.

And that's the interesting bit: Jemaa el-Fna isn't preserved the way a monument is preserved. Nothing here is roped off. The storytellers, musicians and henna artists working the crowd right now are themselves the heritage, which means the square only stays what it is for as long as people keep showing up to perform in it.

By nightfall the smoke from the food stalls will drift up past the minaret, and the whole square will sound completely different from how it sounds right now.

tours.title: Kabana Rooftop | كابانا مطعم و مشروبات
tours.shortDescription: Sunset over the medina, the Koutoubia on the rail, and a menu that refuses to pick one continent.
tours.longDescription: A short walk from Jemaa el-Fna, Kabana's terrace sits high enough above the medina that the view runs clean across the flat rooftops to the Koutoubia's minaret and, on a clear evening, out to the silhouette of the Atlas Mountains. The kitchen, run by the Spanish chef Luisma, doesn't pin itself to one cuisine — sushi rolls next to ceviche, shareable plates crossing Mediterranean, Latin American and Asian references — and the cocktail list runs just as wide. The space steps down over several levels dressed in tile, greenery and lantern light, so no seat sits far from the rail, and come evening it turns into something closer to a club, with DJ sets and rotating live jazz, salsa and electro timed to pick up as the light fades. Rooftops like this have made the skyline above the square a destination in its own right; the seats with the clearest line to the Koutoubia go first, every single evening.

The kitchen is run by the Spanish chef Luisma, and the menu doesn't try to pin itself to one cuisine: sushi rolls sit next to ceviche, shareable plates cross Mediterranean, Latin American and Asian references without much concern for tradition, and the cocktail list runs just as wide.

What's worth knowing is that Kabana is part of a fairly recent shift in how this part of the medina works. Rooftops like this one have turned the skyline above Jemaa el-Fna into as much of a destination as the square itself, and the view you get for the price of a cocktail here would once have belonged only to whoever owned the building.

Book ahead if you want a table on the rail — the seats with the clearest line to the Koutoubia go first, every single evening.

tours.title: Koutoubia | جامع الكتبية
tours.shortDescription: The tower every minaret in Marrakech is measured against — and the template for Seville's Giralda.
tours.longDescription: The Koutoubia's pink sandstone minaret rises in a single square shaft above the gardens at its base, banded into five stages that narrow as they climb, each face carved with a different geometric pattern. The Almohad caliph Abd al-Mu'min laid the foundations in 1147; his grandson Yaqub al-Mansur finished the tower before the century was out. The name comes from the Arabic for bookseller — more than a hundred manuscript merchants once traded in its shadow. This tower became the template: its proportions were copied almost exactly for the Giralda in Seville and the unfinished Hassan Tower in Rabat, setting the visual standard for Almohad architecture across two continents. At the top, three gilded copper spheres are said to have been paid for by a sultan's wife who melted down her jewellery in penance for breaking a fast — and Marrakech still allows nothing taller anywhere in the city, so wherever you go, the Koutoubia stays on the skyline.

stops.title: Koutoubia | جامع الكتبية
stops.caption: This is the Koutoubia — the building every other minaret in Marrakech is measured against, and the reason nothing else in the city is allowed to rise above it.
stops.transcriptText:

You should be standing in the gardens at the mosque's base, where the pink sandstone tower rises in a single square shaft above the trees, banded into five stages that narrow slightly as they climb, each face carved with a different geometric pattern.

Construction began in 1147, when the Almohad caliph Abd al-Mu'min laid the foundations, and the tower itself was finished decades later under his grandson, Yaqub al-Mansur, sometime before the century was out.

The name Koutoubia comes from the Arabic word for bookseller. More than a hundred manuscript and book merchants once traded from stalls in the tower's shadow, and the name stuck to the whole mosque long after the booksellers moved on.

Marrakech still keeps nothing taller than this tower anywhere in the city, so wherever you go from here, the Koutoubia stays on the skyline behind you.

tours.title: La Grande Table Marocaine
tours.shortDescription: Hélène Darroze's kitchen sends scouts across Morocco every year to bring courtly recipes back from the brink.
tours.longDescription: Inside the Royal Mansour, La Grande Table Marocaine is arranged as a series of intimate dining rooms dressed in the hotel's signature handcrafted plasterwork, zellij and carved cedar — the work of hundreds of Moroccan craftsmen in traditional guild trades. Since opening in 2008 the restaurant has kept one founding habit alive: sending the team across Morocco every year to track down historic courtly recipes and home cooking that might otherwise disappear, writing them down, testing them, and putting them back into circulation. The kitchen has been run since early 2024 by the French chef Hélène Darroze alongside executive chef Karim Ben Baba, and the menu moves in the traditional order — sh'hiwates first, then pigeon pastilla dusted with sugar and cinnamon, once reserved for sultans, then a Berber tagine of chestnuts and Atlas black truffle, sometimes a méchoui of slow-roasted lamb shoulder. Less nostalgia cooking than an act of preservation you can order.

From here, the rest of the Royal Mansour unfolds outward in the same handcrafted detail — gardens, riads, courtyards — all built by the same craftsmen who worked this room.

tours.title: Le Jardin Secret | الحديقة السرية
tours.shortDescription: Two gardens, a chamberlain's private paradise, and a four-hundred-year-old water channel still running underneath.
tours.longDescription: Behind blank walls in the Mouassine district run two gardens off a shared entrance: an Exotic Garden dense with plants from South Africa, Madagascar, Australia and Latin America, and an Islamic Garden laid out in the strict geometric quarters of a sixteenth-century Saadian design, its citrus rows still following the original irrigation channels. The site goes back to the late 1500s under Sultan Moulay Abdallah, but what stands today is largely the work of Muhammad Loukrissi, chamberlain to a later sultan, who bought the ruined plot in 1912 and spent until his death in 1934 filling it with pavilions, a tower and these gardens. The estate then splintered among more than a hundred and thirty heirs and sat neglected until an eight-year restoration reopened it in 2016. Underneath, the team found a khettara — an underground channel that once carried Atlas mountain water into the city — cleared it, and reconnected it, so the water in the Islamic Garden follows the same route it did four hundred years ago.

Mouassine district, behind walls that give away nothing from the street. The site itself goes back to the Saadian dynasty, laid out in the late 1500s under Sultan Moulay Abdallah, though that original palace was gone within a century. What you're standing in today is largely the work of Muhammad Loukrissi, chamberlain to a later sultan, who bought the ruined plot in 1912 and spent until his death in 1934 filling it with pavilions, a tower, and these two gardens.

After Loukrissi's death, the estate splintered among more than a hundred and thirty heirs and sat neglected for decades, until two Marrakech restaurateurs bought it, negotiated the inheritance, and began an eight-year restoration that reopened the gardens to the public in 2016.

And here's the detail that makes the restoration more than cosmetic: buried under the site was a khettara, an underground channel that once carried water from the Atlas Mountains into the city's palace gardens. The restoration team found it, cleared it, and reconnected it to a well on site, so the water running through the Islamic Garden today follows the same route it did four hundred years ago.

Climb the tower at the garden's edge before you leave. From the top, the whole medina spreads out in flat rooftops, with the Koutoubia's minaret marking the skyline beyond.

tours.title: Le MAP — Monde des Arts de la Parure
tours.shortDescription: Seven thousand pieces of adornment from fifty countries — including full ceremonial jewellery made for horses.
tours.longDescription: Le MAP — the Monde des Arts de la Parure, the world of the arts of adornment — descends from one private obsession: the Swiss collectors Marlène and Paolo Gallone spent decades gathering more than seven thousand pieces of jewellery, ceremonial dress and adornment from over fifty countries, and when the museum opened in 2022, about three thousand went on permanent display. The building climbs three levels of terracotta brick and cedar beam, deliberately echoing the Ben Youssef madrasa across the medina, up to a rooftop garden facing the Atlas. Inside, heavy Berber silver and amber sit near goldwork from sub-Saharan Africa and ceremonial costume from across Asia, with textiles hung beside the exact jewellery they were worn with — and cases of full ceremonial saddles and headdresses made for horses rather than people. The argument throughout: how people decorate themselves is as serious a form of craft and identity as any painting, and deserves the same kind of museum.

tours.title: L'mida | مطعم الميدة
tours.shortDescription: Berber gnocchi is the manifesto: Moroccan technique, set loose on whatever the season delivers.
tours.longDescription: In a traditional Marrakchi house just off the medina's lanes — white marble tables, mustard-and-green banquettes, rattan chairs — chef Narjisse Benkabbou cooks under what the restaurant calls a Modern Nomad philosophy: dishes built on Moroccan technique and flavour, but free to borrow wherever the ingredient list leads. The signature Berber gnocchi, Italian potato dumplings folded into distinctly Moroccan spicing, says most of it in a single dish. The menu is served family style and changes with the seasons; the lamb tagine, slow-cooked the way it has been for generations and updated only in the plating, is the dish regulars ask for by name no matter what else has moved on. Moroccan restaurants aimed at visitors tend to freeze the cuisine at its most traditional, all brass trays and set menus — L'mida treats tradition as raw material for something that keeps moving, a much harder trick to pull off convincingly.

tours.title: MACAAL
tours.shortDescription: One family spent forty years collecting African art before the market caught up — then built a museum and opened it to the city.
tours.longDescription: Out past the golf courses and villas of Al Maaden, MACAAL's galleries wrap around open courtyards and a sculpture garden, holding one of the most serious contemporary African art collections anywhere on the continent — more than two thousand five hundred works by roughly three hundred artists. It grew from one family's private collecting: Alami Lazraq and his son Othman spent forty years buying work by African artists, largely before the international market caught up, and set up a foundation in 2016 to make the collection public. MACAAL opened in 2018 as the first museum in Marrakech dedicated entirely to contemporary art, representing artists from all fifty-four African countries across painting, sculpture, photography, textiles, video and installation. The 2023 earthquake closed it for nearly two years; when it reopened in 2025, the collection went on permanent view rather than returning to occasional shows — contemporary African art treated as a fixture, not a rotating guest.

tours.title: Madrasah Ben Youssef | مدرسة ابن يوسف
tours.shortDescription: Nine hundred students once lived in the cells above North Africa's largest Islamic college.
tours.longDescription: The Madrasah Ben Youssef centres on a rectangular courtyard with a long reflecting pool, the walls rising in tier after tier of carved stucco, zellij tile and cedar lattice — with rows of small student cells stacked above the arcades. Founded in the mid-1300s by the Marinid sultan Abu Inan Faris and named for the Almoravid ruler Ali ibn Yusuf, it became the largest Islamic college in North Africa, drawing as many as nine hundred students at a time to study theology, law and the sciences. What stands today is mostly a Saadian rebuild: Sultan Abdallah al-Ghalib reconstructed and expanded the complex in the 1560s, finishing the courtyard essentially as it survives. The calligraphy running through the carved cedar eaves spells out Quranic verses worked so finely they read as pure pattern. And the plain cells upstairs are the point — this was built as housing for real students doing real coursework, and the view down into the courtyard from a student's window is a different building entirely.

tours.title: Marrakech Museum | متحف مراكش الاثري
tours.shortDescription: A defence minister's palace, seized while he was away collecting a medal from Queen Victoria — later the city's first girls' school.
tours.longDescription: Dar Mnebhi was built at the end of the 1800s for Mehdi Mnebhi, defence minister under Sultan Moulay Abdelaziz, and its history turned sharply while he was abroad: travelling to receive a medal from Queen Victoria, he returned to find his palace seized by the regional governor Pasha Glaoui, part of the manoeuvring that eventually opened Morocco to European colonisation. After independence the state took the building over and turned it, in 1965, into Marrakech's first school for girls — decades before the Omar Benjelloun Foundation restored it and reopened it in 1997 as the Marrakech Museum. Behind an unassuming door, a grand Andalusian courtyard opens up — central fountain, patterned tile climbing every wall — hung with rotating shows of modern Moroccan painting alongside a permanent collection of Moroccan Jewish, Berber and Arab art and craft. tours.title: MCC Gallery
tours.shortDescription: Morocco's first gallery dedicated to contemporary photography outgrew the medina — and became an institutional anchor.
tours.longDescription: MCC Gallery began in 2018 inside the medina as Dar El Bacha Gallery — the first space in Morocco dedicated specifically to contemporary photography — founded by Fatima-Zohra Bennani Bennis. The roster runs through some of the most closely watched names in Moroccan contemporary art — Amine El Gotaibi, Houda Kabbaj, Malika Sqalli, Mustapha Azeroual and Hamza Kadiri among them — artists MCC has carried to the AKAA fair in Paris and 1-54 in London. Marrakech's gallery scene traditionally leaned toward decorative work aimed at visitors; MCC bet on serious practice and the international fair circuit instead, and the gamble made it one of the city's institutional anchors.

tours.title: Menara Gardens | حدائق المنارة
tours.shortDescription: Almohad soldiers trained for the crossing to Spain in this pool — the olive grove around it is still a working farm.
tours.longDescription: The Almohad caliph Abd al-Mu'min laid Menara out in 1147, right after taking the city, and by 1157 had the great rectangular pool dug and the surrounding land planted as a working orchard. It wasn't a pleasure garden at first but infrastructure: an agricultural test bed for irrigating a semi-arid city, with the pool doubling as somewhere to train soldiers to swim for the Mediterranean crossing to Andalusia. The Saadian sultan Ahmad al-Mansur expanded the olive groves and irrigation centuries later, and under the Alaouites the green-roofed pavilion of the postcard view was built and rebuilt as a royal retreat, Sultan Sidi Muhammad ibn Abdallah adding the belvedere so his court could take the air above the water. The olive trees stretching away in every direction are still a working grove, harvested every year — one of the few gardens in the city that has never stopped being a farm. Locals come out at sunset, when the pavilion's reflection settles flat and the High Atlas turns pink behind it.

tours.title: Nomad Marrakech | نوماد مراكش
tours.shortDescription: A 1960s carpet shop turned vertical — four floors up from the spice square to a rooftop the owners call a cultural observatory.

It opened in 2014 with a simple premise: take a landmark piece of the souk's architecture and build up rather than sideways, ending in what the owners describe as a cultural observatory over the medina. Nomad helped kick off the whole wave of rooftop dining above the souk, but it opened before that wave existed. Come the hour before sunset, the call to prayer rolls out from the Koutoubia and the spice square below goes quiet for a few minutes at once.

tours.title: Yves Saint Laurent Museum | متحف إيف سان لوران

Studio KO — the architects Olivier Marty and Karl Fournier — designed the whole four-thousand-square-metre building around Saint Laurent's own visual language: they spent time in his archive before drawing a single wall, and the curves running against straight lines throughout the building are a direct response to what they found there. The same pair went on to design several other Marrakech landmarks in the years that followed, but this building is generally regarded as the one that made their name internationally.

Inside, the materials keep the same logic going: soft-coloured granite, glazed brick, zellige tile and oak, all treated as couture-grade materials rather than standard museum finishes, right down to laurel branches worked into some of the interior detailing.

And here's what's worth knowing about the timing: this museum opened on exactly the same day in 2017 as its counterpart in Paris, at the former Saint Laurent fashion house on Avenue Marceau — a deliberate decision to treat Marrakech not as a secondary outpost but as an equal half of how his legacy gets told.

Jardin Majorelle sits directly next door, and the two sites share more than a wall — Saint Laurent found the garden first, decades before anyone thought to build a museum beside it.

tours.title: Abasto de Buenos Aires
tours.shortDescription: The glass-vaulted market that fed the city, in the neighbourhood Carlos Gardel made his own.
tours.longDescription: The vast iron-and-glass building over Corrientes and Agüero went up in the early 1930s to designs by the Slovenian architect Viktor Sulčič — who would go on to design La Bombonera — on a market site dating back to 1888. At 44,000 square metres it was the city's largest metal-structure market, with its own ice factory and refrigeration plant, and the first public building in Buenos Aires connected directly to both the underground and the railway; for half a century it was among the busiest markets in Latin America. It closed in 1984 and reopened in 1998 as a shopping centre with the glass vaults and monumental arches intact. The neighbourhood's deeper identity lives a few streets away: the house at Jean Jaurès 735 that Carlos Gardel bought for his mother in 1927 is a museum now, and Balvanera still trades as the Barrio de Gardel.

stops.title: Abasto de Buenos Aires
stops.caption: This shopping centre used to feed the entire city. For nearly a century, this exact site — or the buildings that stood here before it — was Buenos Aires' central fruit and vegetable market.
stops.transcriptText:
This shopping centre used to feed the entire city. For nearly a century, this exact site — or the buildings that stood here before it — was Buenos Aires' central fruit and vegetable market.

You're at Corrientes and Agüero, in Balvanera, and the vast glass-vaulted building rising above the avenue, all iron arches and skylights, is the old Mercado de Abasto. The market on this site dates back to 1888, but the building you're looking at now went up in the early 1930s, designed by the Slovenian architect Viktor Sulčič, who'd go on to design La Bombonera, the stadium across the river in La Boca.

At 44,000 square metres, it was the largest metal-structure market in the city, with its own ice factory and refrigeration plant, and it was the first public building in Buenos Aires connected directly to both the underground and the railway, so produce could move in and out without ever touching the street. For half a century this was one of the busiest markets in Latin America. It closed in 1984, sat empty for over a decade, and reopened in 1998 as a shopping centre, with the renovation keeping the original glass vaults and monumental arches largely intact.

But the market isn't really why this neighbourhood carries its own nickname, Barrio de Gardel. A few streets from here, at Jean Jaurès 735, the tango singer Carlos Gardel bought a house for his mother in 1927 and lived there himself until shortly before his international touring years began. That house is a museum now, and the whole neighbourhood still trades on the association — tango murals, a Gardel-themed metro stop, restaurants that mention him on the menu.

And that's the layered thing about this building: underneath the shopping centre is a market that once organised the entire city's food supply, and around it is a neighbourhood whose real identity was built by the most famous voice in tango, who simply happened to live a few doors down. Two very different kinds of legacy, sharing the same postcode.

The Museo Casa Carlos Gardel is a short walk from here and worth the detour if you've time — it's less about tango as spectacle and more about what Buenos Aires actually looked like when Gardel was just a man living with his mother on a quiet street.

tours.title: Alo's Bistro
tours.shortDescription: A tasting menu in a leafy suburb, built around whoever turned up that week with something worth cooking.
tours.longDescription: Alejandro Féraud's dining room hides behind a modest doorway on a residential street in Boulogne, on the northern edge of San Isidro — barely a dozen tables, the kitchen close enough to touch. The menu isn't fixed so much as reported: it follows the season and the small growers and fishermen who supply it, course by course, with a wine pairing built dish by dish around what the kitchen is actually doing that night. The duck and the hand-cut pasta get mentioned by name afterwards; the pastry kitchen's chocolate, hazelnut and cinnamon work closes it out. In a city that runs on the parrilla and the pasta joint, a European-register tasting menu half an hour from the centre is a deliberate kind of stubbornness — and it's paid off.

stops.title: Alo's Bistro
stops.caption: There's a curious thing about this corner of San Isidro: barely a mile from the polo grounds and the yacht club, and the table everyone's talking about doesn't have a river view at all.
stops.transcriptText:
There's a curious thing about this corner of San Isidro: barely a mile from the polo grounds and the yacht club, and the table everyone's talking about doesn't have a river view at all. It has a kitchen doing exactly what it wants, and nothing else to prove.

You'll find it at Blanco Encalada 2120, in Boulogne, on the northern edge of San Isidro proper. Look for a modest, low-lit doorway on a residential street — nothing announces itself from the outside, which is rather the point. Inside, the dining room is small and close, barely a dozen tables, the kind of place built for a kitchen you can practically reach out and touch.

That kitchen belongs to chef Alejandro Féraud, and the thing to know before you sit down is that the menu here isn't fixed so much as reported. It follows the season and, more specifically, whoever turned up that week with something worth cooking — a small grower outside the city, a fisherman working the coast. Order the tasting menu if you can; it's built entirely around that logic, course by course, and it comes with a wine pairing worth asking for specifically.

Two dishes tend to get mentioned by name afterwards. One is the duck, cooked until the meat gives without resistance, paired against something sharper to cut the richness. The other is the pasta — hand-cut, made in-house, the kind of dish that looks simple and takes a great deal of quiet skill to get right. And when dessert arrives, it's the work of pastry chef Camila, most often built around chocolate, hazelnut, and cinnamon, which is the sort of combination that sounds ordinary until you taste what she's done with it.

What's worth knowing here is this: Buenos Aires runs, broadly, on two grammars — the parrilla and the pasta joint, both rooted in what the city has always had plenty of. Alo's runs on something closer to a European tasting menu, in a leafy suburb a good half hour from the centre, built around what a farm or a fishing boat happened to bring in that week. It's a deliberate kind of stubbornness, and it's paid off.

Ask whoever's at the door about the wine pairing, if you haven't already booked it — it's built dish by dish around exactly what's coming out of that kitchen tonight, and it's the fastest way to understand what Féraud is actually doing here.

tours.title: Banco de Londres y América del Sur
tours.shortDescription: Clorindo Testa's brutalist landmark — a bank that wanted the street to walk straight through it.
tours.longDescription: A 1959 invitation-only competition for a new head office at Reconquista and Bartolomé Mitre was won by a young architect named Clorindo Testa, working alongside the firm SEPRA, and what went up between 1960 and 1966 is closer to sculpture than to a conventional bank: roughly 3,000 square metres across three basement levels and six floors, rising 26 metres, almost entirely in raw, unclad reinforced concrete — béton brut, the material that gives brutalism its name. Testa and his collaborators refused a formal lobby with a hard line between outside and in; they wanted the ground floor to feel like a covered plaza, an extension of the street, the whole banking hall visible through the deep concrete openings from the pavement. Where the city's grand financial buildings borrowed marble columns and European classicism to look trustworthy, this one argued the opposite, in concrete: transparency, not grandeur, is what a bank should look like.

stops.title: Banco de Londres y América del Sur
stops.caption: This building's architects didn't want it to feel like a bank at all.
stops.transcriptText:
This building's architects didn't want it to feel like a bank at all. They wanted the street itself to walk straight through it.

The Banco de Londres stands at the corner of Reconquista and Bartolomé Mitre, a raw concrete mass of deep, irregular openings, utterly unlike the classical columns and marble facades of the older banks around it.

In 1959, an invitation-only competition was held for a new head office on this site, and it was won by a young architect named Clorindo Testa, working alongside the firm SEPRA. Construction ran from 1960 to 1966, and what they built was something closer to a sculpture than a conventional bank: roughly 3,000 square metres across three basement levels and six floors above ground, rising 26 metres, almost entirely in raw, unclad reinforced concrete — béton brut, the French term that gives brutalism its name.

The idea behind the design was specific and, for a bank, genuinely unusual. Testa and his collaborators didn't want a formal lobby with a hard line between outside and inside; they wanted the ground floor to feel like an extension of the street itself, an open, continuous space they described as a covered plaza, with the whole banking hall visible through those deep concrete openings from the pavement.

What's worth noticing here: in a city where the grand financial buildings mostly borrowed marble columns and European classicism to look trustworthy, this one deliberately did the opposite. Exposed structure, raw material, nothing dressed up or hidden — an argument, built in concrete, that transparency, not grandeur, was what a bank should actually look like.

If it's open, step inside and look up rather than around. The different floor levels stagger and overlap in ways that are completely invisible from the pavement, and that layered structure is really the whole point of the design.

tours.title: Bencich Building
tours.shortDescription: Two identical domes for two brothers who wouldn't share one — on the corner of the five domes.
tours.longDescription: At Roque Sáenz Peña 615 on Diagonal Norte, the construction magnates Miguel and Massimiliano Bencich commissioned the French-trained architect Eduardo Le Monnier — in Buenos Aires since 1896 — to design their office building, completed in 1927 with two matching towers, each crowned with its own dome, joined at the top by a shared terrace. The story goes that rather than build a single dome one brother might claim over the other, the Bencichs simply had Le Monnier design two, identical, side by side. The corner where Diagonal Norte meets Corrientes and Florida is known locally as the corner of the five domes; Le Monnier designed three of them, including the former Banco Argentino Uruguayo facing the cathedral, and the Bencich brothers account for the pair. Sibling stubbornness, solved by doubling the architecture, shaped one of downtown's most photographed rooflines.

stops.title: Bencich Building
stops.caption: There's a curious reason this corner has two identical domes instead of one, and it has nothing to do with architecture.
stops.transcriptText:
There's a curious reason this corner has two identical domes instead of one, and it has nothing to do with architecture.

At Roque Sáenz Peña 615, on the Diagonal Norte, two matching five-storey towers rise side by side, each crowned with its own dome, joined at the top by a shared terrace running between them.

The building belonged to two brothers, Miguel and Massimiliano Bencich, construction magnates who commissioned the French-trained architect Eduardo Le Monnier — who'd arrived in Buenos Aires in 1896 and built most of his career here — to design their new office building, completed in 1927. And rather than build a single dome that one brother might claim credit for over the other, the story goes that the Bencichs simply had Le Monnier design two, identical, side by side, so neither brother's name would sit more prominently than the other's.

This corner, where Diagonal Norte meets Corrientes and Florida, is known locally as the corner of the five domes, and Le Monnier was responsible for three of them, including the former Banco Argentino Uruguayo building a short walk from here, facing the cathedral. The Bencich brothers, between the two of them, account for the other pair.

What's worth knowing, standing here, is that a small family rivalry, solved by simply doubling the architecture rather than resolving the argument, ended up shaping one of the most photographed rooflines in downtown Buenos Aires — proof that sibling stubbornness occasionally produces something worth looking at.

See if you can spot all five domes from this one corner before you move on — most people notice one or two and walk off without realising there are three more within sight.

tours.title: Bis Bistró
tours.shortDescription: Gonzalo Aramburu's everyday sibling — chef-driven cooking without the nine-course commitment.
tours.longDescription: Down a covered passage of small shops off Vicente López in Recoleta, Bis Bistró is the relaxed counterpart to Aramburu, the fine-dining flagship around the corner: same kitchen discipline, considerably lower ceremony. Globe lamps and mirrored walls make a room that could have been lifted straight from 1950 — built to feel unserious, on purpose, around food that very much isn't. The menu is classic bistro with a contemporary edit: a potato omelette lifted with capers and anchovies, a rack of Patagonian lamb, a pavlova built on whatever the season actually produced, and weekday set lunches that undercut the name upstairs. It fills the gap Buenos Aires dining left open between the tasting-menu temple and the neighbourhood bodegón.

stops.title: Bis Bistró
stops.caption: Down a narrow, covered passage lined with small shops — somewhere between a Parisian arcade and a Buenos Aires galería — sits a dining room fitted out with globe lamps and mirrored walls that could have been lifted straight from 1950.
stops.transcriptText:
Down a narrow, covered passage lined with small shops — somewhere between a Parisian arcade and a Buenos Aires galería — sits a dining room fitted out with globe lamps and mirrored walls that could have been lifted straight from 1950.

That passage is on Vicente López 1661, in Recoleta. Duck in past the shopfronts, and Bis Bistró is set back a little from the street, glass-fronted, with a small bar just inside the door and a kitchen you can watch working through more glass at the back.

The chef behind it is Gonzalo Aramburu, and the useful thing to know is that Bis is the relaxed, everyday sibling of his fine-dining flagship, Aramburu, which sits just around the corner. Same kitchen discipline, considerably lower ceremony. The menu leans classic bistro with a contemporary edit: a potato omelette lifted with capers and anchovies, a rack of Patagonian lamb, and a pavlova built around whatever fruit the season has actually produced, along with weekday lunchtime set menus that make the whole thing considerably more affordable than the name upstairs might suggest.

Here's the interesting bit, if you ask me. Buenos Aires fine dining tends to split cleanly in two — the tasting-menu temples on one side, the neighbourhood bodegón on the other, with not much built deliberately in between. Bis is Aramburu's answer to that gap: chef-driven food, properly sourced and properly cooked, without asking for a nine-course commitment or a three-hour evening. The 1950s styling isn't nostalgia for its own sake — it's a room built to feel unserious, on purpose, around food that very much isn't.

Once you've eaten, don't rush straight back out to the street. The passage itself is worth a slow walk — small independent shops on both sides, the kind of covered gallery that Buenos Aires does rather well and that most visitors walk past without ever noticing leads anywhere.

tours.title: Buenos Aires Metropolitan Cathedral
tours.shortDescription: A cathedral modelled on a French parliament, guarding the tomb of the man who freed half a continent.
tours.longDescription: The twelve-column neoclassical portico facing Plaza de Mayo dates to 1822, when the French architect Próspero Catelin, working with Pierre Benoit, modelled the front of Buenos Aires' cathedral on the Palais Bourbon in Paris — a French parliament building, not a church, as the template for an Argentine cathedral standing on a site where a church has stood since the city's founding. Since 1880 it has held the tomb of José de San Martín, the general who led the armies that freed Argentina, Chile and Peru from Spanish rule: built by the French sculptor Carrier-Belleuse, flanked by three female figures for the three nations, and guarded around the clock by Granaderos in dress uniform, with the changing of the guard on the hour. The odd choice of model fits — this building has always been as much civic monument as church, never more so than since it became the place where the country keeps its most important soldier.

stops.title: Buenos Aires Metropolitan Cathedral
stops.caption: This is Buenos Aires' cathedral, though from the outside, with its rows of columns and triangular pediment, you'd be forgiven for mistaking it for a government building or a bank.
stops.transcriptText:
This is Buenos Aires' cathedral, though from the outside, with its rows of columns and triangular pediment, you'd be forgiven for mistaking it for a government building or a bank.

The cathedral sits on the northern side of Plaza de Mayo, its neoclassical portico of twelve columns facing the square directly. A church has stood on this exact site since the city's founding, but the facade you're looking at now dates only to 1822, when the French architect Próspero Catelin, working with Pierre Benoit, designed it in deliberate imitation of the Palais Bourbon in Paris — a French parliament building, not a cathedral, as the model for an Argentine one.

Inside, the building carries a weight that has little to do with religion. Since 1880, this has been the resting place of José de San Martín, the general who led the armies that freed Argentina, Chile, and Peru from Spanish rule. His tomb, built by the French sculptor Carrier-Belleuse, is flanked by three female figures representing those three nations, and it's guarded around the clock by an honour guard of Granaderos in dress uniform. Nearby lie the remains of two of his generals, Las Heras and Tomás Guido, along with the tomb of Argentina's Unknown Soldier of Independence.

Here's what's worth knowing standing here: the facade's odd choice of a French parliament building as a model actually fits the cathedral rather well, because this building has always functioned as much as a civic monument as a religious one — and never more so than since it became the place where the country keeps its most important soldier.

Time your visit, if you can, around the changing of the Granaderos guard at San Martín's tomb — it happens on the hour, and it's one of the few ceremonial military rituals in the city still performed exactly as it was a century ago.

tours.title: Café Tortoni
tours.shortDescription: Brass, marble, and a century and a half of the city's most interesting people walking through one door.
tours.longDescription: Founded in 1858 by a French immigrant named Touan, after a café on the Boulevard des Italiens where the Parisian elite gathered to argue and be seen, Tortoni moved to Avenida de Mayo 825 in 1880 and got its brass-and-marble façade in 1898, designed by Alejandro Christophersen. In the basement, the standing gathering called La Peña ran from 1926 to 1943, pulling in Alfonsina Storni, Arthur Rubinstein, Roberto Arlt and Benito Quinquela Martín; add the decades either side and the guest list runs Carlos Gardel, Federico García Lorca, Albert Einstein, Juan Manuel Fangio — and Jorge Luis Borges, repeatedly, at the window table where his life-size wax figure now sits with a coffee in front of it. The basement still runs as a stage most nights, jazz and tango by turns, and there's a back room with a library, dominoes and a billiards table nobody seems in a hurry to give up. The real achievement was never the marble: Buenos Aires kept sending its most interesting people through this door for over a century and a half, and the café simply kept the room open.

stops.title: Café Tortoni
stops.caption: Sit down, and you might find yourself sharing a table with Jorge Luis Borges — or rather, a life-size wax figure of him, cup of coffee in front of him, at the table he actually used to occupy.
stops.transcriptText:
Sit down, and you might find yourself sharing a table with Jorge Luis Borges — or rather, a life-size wax figure of him, cup of coffee in front of him, at the table he actually used to occupy. Which tells you most of what you need to know about Café Tortoni before we've properly started.

Avenida de Mayo, number 825, on the northern side of the street. The entrance is unmistakable: brass fittings, marble, dark wood panelling under a canopy, with Tortoni picked out in gold lettering above the door.

The café opened in 1858, founded by a French immigrant named Touan, who named it after a café of the same name on the Boulevard des Italiens in Paris — the kind of place, in nineteenth-century Paris, where the city's cultural elite gathered to argue and be seen. Tortoni started a few doors along, moved to this spot in 1880, and got the façade you're looking at now in 1898, designed by the architect Alejandro Christophersen.

Downstairs, in the basement, a group called La Peña ran from 1926 until 1943, a standing gathering that pulled in poets, painters, and musicians for informal readings and performances. The guest list from those years alone would fill a shelf of biographies: the poet Alfonsina Storni, the pianist Arthur Rubinstein, the writer Roberto Arlt, the painter Benito Quinquela Martín. Add in the decades either side, and you're talking Carlos Gardel, Federico García Lorca, Albert Einstein, the racing driver Juan Manuel Fangio, and, repeatedly, over many years, Borges himself, working at that table by the window.

And here's the thing: Tortoni's real achievement was never the marble or the brass. It's that Buenos Aires kept sending its most interesting people through this door for more than a century and a half, and the café simply kept the room open and the coffee coming.

The basement still runs as a stage most nights, jazz and tango by turns, and there's a room at the back with a library, dominoes, and a billiards table nobody seems in a hurry to give up — worth pushing further in than the front room, if you've got the time.

tours.title: Caminito
tours.shortDescription: A rubbish tip a painter turned into one of the ten most photographed streets on earth.
