tours.longDescription: The 110-metre street of corrugated-iron walls in blue, yellow, red and green exists because the painter Benito Quinquela Martín, who grew up in this dockside neighbourhood, decided a patch of wasteland beside a disused railway spur deserved to look like something. He recruited his neighbours, painted the house fronts in the leftover ship paint dockworkers had always used — whatever colour was left in the tin, straight onto the metal — and in 1959 Caminito opened as an open-air street museum, the whole block treated as a single work of art. The colours lean toward Boca Juniors' blue and yellow, which is no accident, and Quinquela went on to fund a school-museum, a theatre, a dental hospital and a kindergarten within a few streets. Not a theme-park recreation of La Boca — a real street, made of the same materials as the neighbourhood around it.

stops.title: Caminito
stops.caption: This 110-metre street is one of the ten most photographed spots on earth, according to Google Maps' own numbers.
stops.transcriptText:
This 110-metre street is one of the ten most photographed spots on earth, according to Google Maps' own numbers. Forty years before it existed as anything worth photographing, this same stretch of ground was a rubbish tip beside a disused railway spur.

You're standing at the mouth of Caminito, in La Boca, with corrugated iron walls in blue, yellow, red and green rising on both sides, wooden balconies overhead, and sculptures of tango dancers and neighbourhood characters set into doorways and on rooftops along the way.

The street exists because of one man: the painter Benito Quinquela Martín, who grew up in this dockside neighbourhood and, by his own account, decided one day to turn a patch of wasteland into what he called a cheerful street. He recruited his neighbours, painted the corrugated-iron house fronts in the leftover ship paint that dockworkers here had always used — whatever colour was left in the tin, straight onto the metal — and in 1959, Caminito opened as an open-air street museum, the whole block treated as a single work of art.

The colours you're looking at lean heavily toward blue and yellow, which is not an accident: those are the colours of Boca Juniors, the football club this neighbourhood raised and still claims as its own. Quinquela didn't stop at paint. He used his own money and standing to fund a school-museum for local children, a theatre, a dental hospital, and a kindergarten, all within a few streets of where you're standing — a working-class neighbourhood that gave the city one of its most recognisable images, largely because one of its own decided the place deserved to look like something.

Here's what's worth holding onto: Caminito isn't a recreation or a theme-park version of La Boca. It's a real street that a real painter turned into public art, using the same materials — corrugated sheet metal, leftover paint — that built the rest of the neighbourhood around it.

Fundación Proa, one of the city's best contemporary art spaces, sits just a few steps from here on Pedro de Mendoza — worth the short walk if you'd like to see what La Boca's art scene looks like now, a century after Quinquela first picked up a paintbrush.

tours.title: Casa Cavia
tours.shortDescription: A 1920 mansion where a restaurant, a bookshop, a florist and a perfumery share one roof.
tours.longDescription: Alejandro Christophersen drew this Palermo Chico mansion in 1920 as a gift to his own wife, facing a plaza laid out by Carlos Thays. A century later the London studio KallosTurin restored it without freezing it: original proportions and cornices kept, contemporary work layered in, the rooms arranged around a central courtyard so you move through them the way you'd move through someone's home. Inside are chef Pablo Massey's restaurant La Cocina, a bookshop and small publishing house, a florist and a perfumery — a grand old house that avoided both fates that usually claim them, neither museum with the clock stopped nor gutted offices, just a building that kept being useful in several directions at once.

stops.title: Casa Cavia
stops.caption: It's 1920, and an architect named Alejandro Christophersen — Norwegian by blood, Spanish by birth, and one of the defining figures of Buenos Aires' golden age — is drawing up a mansion in Palermo Chico as a personal gift.
stops.transcriptText:
It's 1920, and an architect named Alejandro Christophersen — Norwegian by blood, Spanish by birth, and one of the defining figures of Buenos Aires' golden age — is drawing up a mansion in Palermo Chico as a personal gift. Not for a client. For his own wife.

Casa Cavia stands on Cavia street in Palermo Chico, facing the trees of a small plaza laid out at the turn of the last century by the landscape architect Carlos Thays. Look for pale stone, tall shuttered windows, and an iron gate — the kind of grand private house this neighbourhood was once full of, and now mostly isn't.

For decades the house passed quietly between owners, until a London-based architecture studio, KallosTurin, was brought in to restore it without freezing it. They kept the original room proportions, the cornices, the sense of scale a 1920s mansion was built to have, and then layered contemporary work in on top rather than around it. The different parts of the house are arranged around a central courtyard, so you move between them the way you'd move through rooms in someone's home, because that's essentially what this still is.

And what fills those rooms is the interesting part. There's a restaurant, La Cocina, led by chef Pablo Massey — trained under Francis Mallmann, one of Argentina's best-known culinary figures. But there's also a bookshop and small publishing house, a florist, and a perfumery, all operating out of the same building, under the same roof, as though a private house had simply decided to keep being useful in several directions at once.

Here's what makes Casa Cavia worth the detour: most grand old houses in this city end up one of two ways — turned into a museum that stops the clock, or gutted for offices until nothing original survives. This one does neither. It keeps Christophersen's bones and fills them with the kind of contemporary Argentine work — food, ideas, scent, flowers — that a house this old was never built to expect.

Most people book the restaurant and stop there. Don't. Walk the rest of the house before or after your table — the bookshop and the perfumery are only a few steps from La Cocina, and they're as much a part of what Casa Cavia is as anything on the menu.

tours.title: Casa Rosada
tours.shortDescription: Two buildings fused under one arch, painted a pink nobody can entirely explain.
tours.longDescription: Until 1894 this was two separate buildings standing side by side — the presidential offices and the Palacio de Correos, the Post Office — until the Italian architect Francesco Tamburini, the same man responsible for Teatro Colón, was brought in to fuse them into one, his solution a single grand arch straddling the join at what is now the Balcarce 50 entrance. He had already added the balcony above it in 1886: the spot from which Eva Perón and generations of presidents since have addressed the crowds in Plaza de Mayo. The building was first painted pink under President Domingo Sarmiento in the early 1870s, and the most repeated explanation — legend rather than settled fact — is reconciliation between the red of the Federalists and the white of the Unitarians, whose civil wars had torn the century apart. The construction history backs the story better than any paint chemistry could: a seat of government literally assembled by fusing two structures into a single façade.

stops.title: Casa Rosada
stops.caption: The presidential palace in front of you is pink for a reason nobody can entirely agree on.
stops.transcriptText:
The presidential palace in front of you is pink for a reason nobody can entirely agree on.

Casa Rosada faces Plaza de Mayo from its eastern side, a long pink facade crowned by a central arch and, above it, the balcony where presidents have addressed the crowds below for more than a century.

Until 1894, this was actually two separate buildings standing side by side: the presidential offices on one side, and the Post Office, the Palacio de Correos, on the other. The Italian architect Francesco Tamburini — the same man responsible for Teatro Colón — was brought in to fuse the two into one, and his solution was a single grand arch straddling the join, at what's now the main entrance on Balcarce 50. He added the balcony above it two years earlier, in 1886, a small addition that would eventually become one of the most recognisable spots in Argentine political life.

As for the colour, the building was first painted pink under President Domingo Sarmiento in the early 1870s, and the most repeated explanation — treat it as legend rather than settled fact — is that pink was chosen to symbolise reconciliation between the Federalists and the Unitarians, the red and white factions whose civil wars had torn the country apart for much of the nineteenth century.

Whatever the real reason for the colour turns out to be, the building's actual construction history backs up that reconciliation story better than any account of paint chemistry could: a seat of government literally assembled by fusing two separate structures into a single facade.

Check ahead for the free weekend guided tours of the interior — they're the only way to see the balcony from the inside, the exact spot from which Eva Perón and generations of presidents since have spoken to the square below.

tours.title: Confitería del Molino
tours.shortDescription: The Art Nouveau confitería politicians used as a third chamber of Congress — restored, and open again for tours.
tours.longDescription: Francesco Gianotti's domed, stained-glass corner at Rivadavia and Callao went up between 1914 and 1917, its windmill-blade motifs remembering the steam flour mill that once stood nearby, and it reopened deliberately on the 9th of July 1916 — the centenary of Argentine independence. Directly across from Congress, it earned the nickname Tercera Cámara, the Third Chamber, where Alfredo Palacios and Lisandro de la Torre kept arguing over coffee and cognac, and Juan and Eva Perón, Roberto Arlt and Libertad Lamarque all sat. In 1927 Carlos Gardel asked the pastry chef Cayetano Brenna to invent a dessert for his friend the jockey Irineo Leguisamo — the Postre Leguisamo outlived the win it celebrated by decades. Closed in 1997 and expropriated by Congress itself in 2018 for restoration, its interior now opens for the free Experiencia Molino guided tours.

stops.title: Confitería del Molino
stops.caption: There's a dessert that still appears on old Buenos Aires menus named after a jockey, and the story of how it got that name starts at the building you're standing in front of now.
stops.transcriptText:
There's a dessert that still appears on old Buenos Aires menus named after a jockey, and the story of how it got that name starts at the building you're standing in front of now.

Rivadavia and Callao, directly across from the Congress building — the domed, ornate corner with the stained-glass windows and the windmill-blade motifs worked into the façade is the Confitería del Molino. The name means "the mill," a nod to an old steam flour mill that once stood nearby, on what's now Plaza Lorea, long before this building existed.

The current structure went up between 1914 and 1917, designed by the Italian architect Francesco Gianotti in a lavish, anti-academic Art Nouveau style, and it reopened on the 9th of July, 1916, timed deliberately to Argentina's centenary of independence. Marble, bronze, stained glass, and imported Italian furniture went into a building meant to make Buenos Aires feel, for a moment, like it belonged next to Paris.

Because it sat directly across from Congress, the confitería quickly earned a nickname: the Tercera Cámara, the Third Chamber, an unofficial extension of the legislature where politicians crossed the street to keep arguing over coffee and cognac. Alfredo Palacios and Lisandro de la Torre sat at these tables, and so did Juan and Eva Perón, and so did writers and performers like Roberto Arlt and Libertad Lamarque. And Carlos Gardel came often enough that, in 1927, he asked the pastry chef, Cayetano Brenna, to invent a dessert in honour of his friend, the jockey Irineo Leguisamo, after Leguisamo rode a horse called Lunático to victory. The result, the Postre Leguisamo, outlived the racing win it celebrated by decades.

The building survived a fire in 1930, then closed for good in 1997, sat empty for years, and was eventually expropriated by law and taken over by Congress itself in 2018 for a full restoration.

It doesn't function as a working café yet, but free guided tours — the Experiencia Molino — let you walk through the restored interior on request; well worth booking if the dome and the stained glass alone don't already have you sold.

tours.title: Congreso de la Nación Argentina
tours.shortDescription: A dome built to be seen from thirteen blocks away, by an architect who never saw it finished.
tours.longDescription: Víctor Meano won the 1895 international competition for Argentina's Congress with a classical, academic plan whose real achievement is the 80-metre dome: its height and placement were calculated so it would read clearly from Plaza de Mayo, all the way down Avenida de Mayo, tying the legislature to the historic heart of the city in a single sightline. Meano never saw it finished — in June 1904 he was shot dead in his own home by a dismissed butler, leaving the country's most important unfinished building without the one person who understood the whole plan. Congress moved in anyway in 1906, legislators working amid ongoing construction, and the distinctive blue-green copper roof wasn't completed until nearly four years after the official opening.

stops.title: Congreso de la Nación Argentina
stops.caption: The dome above you is 80 metres tall, and its architect built it deliberately large enough to be seen whole from Plaza de Mayo, thirteen blocks away.
stops.transcriptText:
The dome above you is 80 metres tall, and its architect built it deliberately large enough to be seen whole from Plaza de Mayo, thirteen blocks away. He never lived to see it finished.

The Palacio del Congreso stands at the western end of Avenida de Mayo, and its main entrance — the wide stone steps and columned portico — is directly ahead of you now, the green-tinged copper dome rising behind it.

The building came out of an international design competition held in 1895, won by the Italian architect Víctor Meano, who also designed the Teatro Colón nearby. Meano's plan for Congress leaned on classical, academic architecture, but his real achievement was the dome: he calculated its height and placement specifically so that it would still read clearly from Plaza de Mayo, all the way down Avenida de Mayo, tying the legislative building to the historic heart of the city with a single sightline.

Meano didn't see any of it finished. In June 1904, he was shot dead in his own home by a former butler he'd recently dismissed, after finding the man with his wife — a sudden, ugly end that had nothing to do with architecture and everything to do with it, since it left the country's most important unfinished building without the one person who understood the whole plan. Congress moved into the building anyway in 1906, legislators working amid ongoing construction, and the dome's distinctive blue-green copper roof wasn't actually completed until nearly four years after the official opening.

The interesting bit is this: the dome you're looking at is as much a message as a piece of architecture, engineered to make sure Argentina's legislature could always be seen from the plaza where its independence was first declared. The building outlived the man who designed that message by well over a century.

Walk the full thirteen blocks down Avenida de Mayo toward Plaza de Mayo if you've got the time — Meano built the dome to be visible the whole way, and it's worth testing that claim for yourself.

tours.title: Diego Iluminado
tours.shortDescription: Maradona in raw welded iron at the mouth of Caminito — the original, in the neighbourhood that made him.
tours.longDescription: Mounted against the wall behind the San Martín monument at the entrance to Caminito, Alejandro Marmo's Diego Iluminado renders Maradona in scrap and discarded metal, arms raised — unveiled in August 2021, timed to the 151st anniversary of La Boca itself, the neighbourhood where he was born and where his career effectively began. Marmo works almost exclusively in scrap, often building pieces with the communities around them; he also made the giant Eva Perón portraits on Avenida 9 de Julio, and he is the only Argentine artist with work held inside the Vatican Museums. Versions of this tribute stand in La Plata and at two other clubs, but this is the original — and the material is the argument: a working-class hero, built from precisely the kind of metal his neighbourhood always had lying around.

stops.title: Diego Iluminado
stops.caption: Diego Maradona has been rendered in iron more than once around this country, but this is the original — welded, not cast, into the wall behind the monument to General San Martín, at the mouth of Caminito.
stops.transcriptText:
Diego Maradona has been rendered in iron more than once around this country, but this is the original — welded, not cast, into the wall behind the monument to General San Martín, at the mouth of Caminito.

Stand facing the entrance to Caminito, in La Boca, with the statue of San Martín in front of you. Look up and just behind it, mounted against the wall, for the figure of Maradona in raw iron, arms raised.

The sculpture is the work of Alejandro Marmo, born in Buenos Aires in 1971, an artist who works almost exclusively in scrap and discarded metal rather than bronze or marble, and who often builds these pieces with the help of the communities around them rather than alone in a studio. This particular work, titled Diego Iluminado, was unveiled in August 2021, timed to the 151st anniversary of the La Boca neighbourhood itself — the place where Maradona was born and where his career effectively began.

Marmo has described Maradona in terms closer to myth than biography, something like a gladiator built for a different, more modern kind of arena. It's not the only piece of his you'll find watching over Argentine football — versions of the same tribute stand outside the stadium in La Plata and at two other clubs around the country. But this is the original, at the mouth of Caminito, in the neighbourhood that made him.

Marmo is also the sculptor behind the large figure of Eva Perón on Avenida 9 de Julio, and the only Argentine artist with work held inside the Vatican Museums — which makes it worth noting that the same hands chose iron and scrap for La Boca, and something closer to permanence for the capital's grandest avenue. The material is the argument: a working-class hero from a working-class neighbourhood, built from precisely the kind of metal that neighbourhood has always had lying around.

Caminito itself is worth the full walk from here — the corrugated iron and bright paint on the houses further down the street come from the same working-class, dockside material logic as the sculpture behind you, if you know to look for it.

tours.title: El Ateneo Grand Splendid
tours.shortDescription: A 1919 tango theatre turned bookshop — stage, boxes, curtain and painted dome all still in place.
tours.longDescription: The Grand Splendid opened on Avenida Santa Fe in 1919 as a lavish theatre by the architects Peró and Torres Armengol, genuinely ahead of its time — four tiers of boxes, five hundred velvet seats, air conditioning, heating and a retractable roof — and became one of the city's great tango stages, hosting Carlos Gardel himself before a later life as a cinema. The Italian artist Nazareno Orlandi painted the twenty-metre ceiling the year it opened: The Calling of the Arts Toward Peace, an allegory finished just as the First World War was ending. In 2000 the Yenny–El Ateneo chain converted it into a bookshop and kept every theatrical bone: the stage is now a café, the boxes are reading nooks, the heavy velvet curtain still hangs, and a piano still plays from what used to be the stage. It works precisely because nothing was stripped out — you're reading in a room built for spectacle, which is arguably still exactly what it's doing.

stops.title: El Ateneo Grand Splendid
stops.caption: Look up at the ceiling before you look at a single book. That painted dome above the shelves used to belong to a theatre, not a bookshop.
stops.transcriptText:
Look up at the ceiling before you look at a single book. That painted dome above the shelves used to belong to a theatre, not a bookshop.

On Avenida Santa Fe, in Recoleta, a grand theatre facade opens onto rows of bookshelves arranged where seats and a stage used to be. This is El Ateneo Grand Splendid.

It opened in 1919 as a lavish theatre, designed by the architects Peró and Torres Armengol, with features that were genuinely ahead of their time: four tiers of box seating, five hundred velvet seats, air conditioning, heating, and a retractable roof. It quickly became one of the city's great tango stages, hosting performances by Carlos Gardel himself, before a later life as a cinema.

That ceiling is the original, painted the same year the theatre opened by the Italian artist Nazareno Orlandi — twenty metres across, titled roughly The Calling of the Arts Toward Peace, an allegory rather than any specific scene, finished just as the First World War was finally ending.

In 2000, the building was converted into a bookshop by the Yenny–El Ateneo chain, and the conversion kept almost everything theatrical intact: the old stage is now a café, the boxes have become quiet reading nooks, and the heavy velvet curtain is still there, framing the shelves rather than a performance.

Here's the thing: it works as a bookshop precisely because none of the theatre's bones were stripped out to make room for it. You're reading in a room built for spectacle, which — with a mural overhead and a piano still playing from what used to be the stage — is arguably still exactly what this room is doing.

Climb to the upper boxes before you leave, even if you're not buying anything. That's the best angle on Orlandi's ceiling, and almost nobody on the ground floor ever thinks to look up that far.

tours.title: Encuentro Nativo
tours.shortDescription: Grilled meats and live tango in the 1867 conventillo where the song 'Caminito' was written.
tours.longDescription: At Magallanes 854, just off the painted houses of Caminito, an 1867 brick-and-corrugated-iron conventillo — one of the tenement buildings this whole neighbourhood grew out of — carries the name Encuentro Nativo. Before it was a restaurant it was a despensa, a neighbourhood grocery run by Juan de Dios Filiberto, and somewhere inside these walls Filiberto and the poet Gabino Coria Peñaloza wrote 'Caminito', the tango that gave the street outside its name and its whole painted, photographed identity. The restaurant leans into all of it — grilled meats, empanadas, homemade stews, live tango most evenings — the kind of thing that would feel like a tourist trap anywhere else, but here has the odd advantage of being true to the address. Through a side door, the Caminito Vinero wine cellar occupies an old artist's studio, the paintings still on the walls around a hundred-plus boutique Argentine labels; upstairs, improbably, a football shirt museum takes Boca Juniors as seriously as relics.

stops.title: Encuentro Nativo
stops.caption: The song "Caminito" was written by two men working out of a corner grocery on this very spot, and that's rather more interesting than anything on the menu at Encuentro Nativo.
stops.transcriptText:
The song "Caminito" was written by two men working out of a corner grocery on this very spot, and that's rather more interesting than anything on the menu at Encuentro Nativo.

Magallanes 854, just off the painted houses of Caminito itself, in La Boca. Behind you, the crowds and the tango dancers posing for photographs. In front of you, a conventillo — one of the tenement buildings this whole neighbourhood grew out of, brick and corrugated iron, dating to 1867 — with the name Encuentro Nativo written across the front.

Have a look at the building itself first. Before it was a restaurant, this was a despensa, a neighbourhood grocery and general store, run by a man named Juan de Dios Filiberto. In the early 1900s, Filiberto and the poet Gabino Coria Peñaloza sat somewhere inside these walls and wrote "Caminito" — the tango that gave the street outside its name, and its whole painted, photographed, thoroughly reproduced identity. Every visitor who's ever posed for a photo on that street owes the idea to this building.

Inside, the restaurant leans into all of that: grilled meats, empanadas, homemade stews, and live tango danced most evenings — the kind of thing that could feel like a tourist trap anywhere else, but here has the slightly odd advantage of being true to the address.

Through a side door, there's a wine cellar called Caminito Vinero, tucked into what used to be an artist's studio — the paintings are still on the walls, more than a hundred boutique Argentine labels stacked around them, tastings running most weeks.

And upstairs, improbably, a football shirt museum. La Boca is Boca Juniors' neighbourhood before it's anything else, and the shirts on these walls take that seriously — old kits, old names, the kind of reverence usually reserved for religious relics.

And here's the thing: nobody sat down and designed Encuentro Nativo as a restaurant-slash-vinoteca-slash-football museum. It's simply what happens when a building this old, in a neighbourhood this specific, keeps being asked to hold one more thing.

Before you head back out to Caminito, put your head round the door of the wine cellar even if you're not staying for a glass — the old atelier paintings are worth the detour on their own.

tours.title: Escultura Atlas de Recoleta
tours.shortDescription: The oldest tree in Buenos Aires, held up by a titan welded from 3,000 pieces of scrapped cars.
tours.longDescription: Beside the café La Biela at the edge of the Recoleta gardens, the great rubber fig known as the Gomero — its trunk more than ten metres round, its branches reaching thirty metres out across the plaza — is the oldest tree in Buenos Aires, and keeping its limbs from snapping under their own weight is a genuine, ongoing engineering problem. For years the heaviest branch sat on plain wooden props, until 2014, when the Uruguayan artist Joaquín Arbiza replaced the support with a sculpture: more than 3,000 pieces of automobile scrap from cars of the 1950s and 60s, collected and welded over twelve months into a kneeling titan roughly 1.85 metres tall and 250 kilograms, shoulders braced under the branch. The tree needed propping up — and rather than solve that quietly with steel poles nobody looks at twice, the city let the propping become the point.

stops.title: Escultura Atlas de Recoleta
stops.caption: Look closely at the grey figure holding up that branch above you.
stops.transcriptText:
Look closely at the grey figure holding up that branch above you. It isn't bronze. It's spark plugs, gearboxes, and pieces of fifty-year-old car chassis, welded together one by one.

Beside the café La Biela, at the edge of the Recoleta gardens, a giant rubber fig tree — the Gomero — spreads its canopy overhead, its trunk more than ten metres round at the base and its branches reaching thirty metres out across the plaza. At the base of its heaviest branch kneels a metal figure, shoulders braced, holding the whole weight up.

That figure is called Atlas, and it's the work of the Uruguayan artist Joaquín Arbiza. For years, this branch — like several others on the tree — had simply been propped up with plain wooden supports, doing the job but adding nothing to the scene. Arbiza's solution, unveiled in 2014, was to replace the support with a sculpture: more than 3,000 pieces of automobile scrap from cars built in the 1950s and 60s, collected, assembled, and welded over twelve months into a titan roughly 1.85 metres tall and weighing about 250 kilograms.

Here's the detail worth carrying with you: this is the oldest tree in Buenos Aires, old enough that keeping its branches from snapping under their own weight is a genuine, ongoing engineering problem — and rather than solve that problem quietly, with steel poles nobody looks at twice, the city let an artist turn the fix itself into the attraction. The tree needed propping up. The propping became the point.

Walk the full circumference of the Gomero before you leave — several of its other branches still lean on much plainer supports, and seeing those makes it obvious just how deliberate a choice Atlas really was.

tours.title: Estación de La Plata
tours.shortDescription: A dome and English ironwork set down on the pampa, to prove a planned city could be willed into being.
tours.longDescription: La Plata was drawn up from nothing in the 1880s — a brand-new provincial capital plotted onto open pampa on a strict grid crossed by diagonals — and the station that opened at Avenida 1 and Diagonal 80 in 1906 was the argument made in stone. The American Louis Newbery Thomas and the Englishman Paul Bell Chambers mixed Classical detailing with Art Nouveau flourishes over English-style iron arches, the platform roof manufactured by Handyside and Company; it replaced the city's first station, which still stands a few blocks away. In January 1997 it was dressed up as a Nazi-era station for the opening scene of Seven Years in Tibet, and Brad Pitt's visit caused something close to a citywide stir. Restored, and re-electrified in 2017 after a two-year gap, it remains the head station for the line into the capital.

stops.title: Estación de La Plata
stops.caption: It's the 1st of October, 1906, and La Plata — a planned provincial capital not yet thirty years old — finally gets a train station to match the wide boulevards laid out around it.
stops.transcriptText:
It's the 1st of October, 1906, and La Plata — a planned provincial capital not yet thirty years old — finally gets a train station to match the wide boulevards laid out around it.

That station stands at Avenida 1 and Diagonal 80, in the centre of the city, and its main entrance faces you here: a broad stone façade rising to a great dome, with the platforms and their metal roof stretching out behind it.

The building was designed by two foreign architects, the American Louis Newbery Thomas and the Englishman Paul Bell Chambers, and it mixes Classical detailing with Art Nouveau flourishes over a structure of English-style iron arches — the platform roof itself was manufactured by the English firm Handyside and Company. It replaced La Plata's first station, a smaller building known as 19 de Noviembre, which still stands a few blocks away under a different name.

The station's strangest moment of fame came in January 1997, when it was dressed up as a Nazi-era station, red flags and all, for the opening scene of the film Seven Years in Tibet. Brad Pitt's visit to shoot that scene reportedly caused something close to a citywide stir, which is a fairly unusual thing to happen to a working commuter station.

And here's what's worth holding onto standing here: La Plata itself was drawn up from nothing in the 1880s, a brand-new provincial capital plotted onto open pampa on a strict grid crossed by diagonals, built to prove that a modern European-style city could simply be willed into being. This station was the argument made in stone — a dome and ironwork straight out of a much older European capital, set down on land that had been empty a few years before. It's still making that argument. After a renovation restored the façades and dome, and after a two-year gap, electric commuter trains started running again in 2017, and this remains the head station for the line into the capital and for the local university train.

Before you head to the platforms, it's worth finding the original nineteenth-century station a few streets away, now known as Pasaje Dardo Rocha — the two buildings, old and newer, tell the story of this planned city's first decades better than either one manages alone.

tours.title: Florería Atlántico
tours.shortDescription: A working flower shop with one of the world's best bars behind the refrigerator door.
tours.longDescription: At street level on Arroyo in Retiro, this is a florist that sells wine, books and cut flowers by the stem. At the back, a heavy steel door built to resemble a walk-in refrigerator opens onto a staircase down to the bar Renato 'Tato' Giovannoni and Julián Díaz opened in 2013. The room below is dressed for the neighbourhood's own history — Retiro sat close to the docks where hundreds of thousands of European immigrants first stepped onto Argentine soil — and the cocktails are built from the ingredients those arrivals actually brought with them. By 2016 it had climbed into the top three of the World's 50 Best Bars, the highest-ranked bar in South America that year. The shop upstairs isn't a wink at the tourists: a respectable trade at street level with something else happening underneath is exactly how this port neighbourhood always worked.

stops.title: Florería Atlántico
stops.caption: This is a flower shop. Officially, at least — officially, it sells wine, books, and cut flowers by the stem, same as it has since the day it opened.
stops.transcriptText:
This is a flower shop. Officially, at least — officially, it sells wine, books, and cut flowers by the stem, same as it has since the day it opened.

You'll find it at Arroyo 872, in Retiro. Push past the buckets of flowers and the shelves of wine near the entrance, and look toward the back of the shop for a heavy steel door built to resemble a walk-in refrigerator. That door isn't decorative.

Open it, and there's a staircase leading down into a basement bar — Florería Atlántico, opened in 2013 by the bartender Renato Giovannoni, known locally as Tato, together with Julián Díaz. The two of them built the whole concept around Retiro's own history: this neighbourhood sat close to the docks where hundreds of thousands of European immigrants first stepped onto Argentine soil, and the room below the flower shop is dressed to match, all warm low light and decoration that leans hard into that early twentieth-century, portside, just-arrived feeling.

The cocktails follow the same logic, built around the ingredients those waves of immigrants actually brought with them — Spanish, Italian, and beyond — rather than treating Buenos Aires as a blank cocktail-bar canvas. It worked well enough that by 2016, Florería Atlántico had climbed into the top three of the World's 50 Best Bars list, the highest-ranked bar anywhere in South America that year.

What's worth knowing, standing here, is that the flower shop upstairs isn't a wink at the tourists, a gimmick bolted onto a speakeasy. It's the whole idea, staged properly — a respectable, visible trade at street level, with something else entirely happening underneath, which is rather exactly how a lot of this port neighbourhood's real history actually worked a century ago.

Take the stairs back up slowly when you're done, and have a proper look at what's actually for sale in the shop — the flowers and the wine are real stock, not props, and it's worth remembering that upstairs and downstairs are meant to be the same story.

tours.title: Fundación Proa
tours.shortDescription: A nineteenth-century townhouse with glass wings, treating La Boca as the audience rather than the backdrop.
tours.longDescription: Beside Caminito on Pedro de Mendoza, Proa is a nineteenth-century Italian townhouse with sheets of glass grafted onto either side — a building having a conversation with itself before you've walked in. It started in 1996 with a modest programme of exhibitions and reopened in its current form in November 2008, the historic façade kept intact between contemporary glass wings whose panels double as rear-projection screens, so the building itself can join an exhibition and stay visible from the street after closing. Contemporary art institutions are not native to this working-class dockside neighbourhood, and Proa's answer to that tension is transparency in the most literal sense: an interior meant to be seen from the pavement, and a rooftop terrace with one of the better views of the Riachuelo and the old port anywhere in the city.

stops.title: Fundación Proa
stops.caption: A nineteenth-century Italian townhouse, with two sheets of glass grafted onto either side of it — that's the building in front of you, and it's a fairly accurate description of what's inside as well.
stops.transcriptText:
A nineteenth-century Italian townhouse, with two sheets of glass grafted onto either side of it — that's the building in front of you, and it's a fairly accurate description of what's inside as well.

Fundación Proa stands on Pedro de Mendoza, right beside Caminito, in La Boca. Its restored historic front sits in the centre, and on both sides, contemporary glass façades rise up against it, deliberately modern against the old brick and render — a building having a conversation with itself before you've even walked in.

Proa started in 1996, in that original nineteenth-century house, with a modest programme of exhibitions and workshops. In November 2008, it reopened in something close to its current form, after a major renovation that kept the historic façade intact and added the glass wings on either side. Those glass panels aren't just for light — they're built to double as rear-projection screens, so the building itself can become part of an exhibition, visible from the street even after the doors are closed.

The location matters more than it might first appear. La Boca is a working-class, dockside neighbourhood, famous for Caminito's painted houses and for Boca Juniors, and not, historically, a natural home for contemporary art institutions. Proa's answer to that tension is transparency in the most literal sense: glass walls facing the street, an interior meant to be visible rather than walled off, a building that treats the neighbourhood outside as part of the audience rather than something to be screened out.

And here's the thing: Proa doesn't try to look like it belongs in this neighbourhood by pretending to be older or humbler than it is. It sits here as something visibly new, built out of the same directness La Boca has always had, just aimed at contemporary art instead of dockwork.

The rooftop terrace has one of the better views of the Riachuelo and the old port from anywhere in the city — worth the climb even on a day when nothing in the galleries below is calling to you.

tours.title: Galerías Pacífico
tours.shortDescription: A shopping centre with a national monument for a ceiling — 450 square metres, painted by five artists at once.
tours.longDescription: The 1889 building at Florida and Córdoba was intended as a Buenos Aires branch of the French department store Au Bon Marché, spent decades housing the National Museum of Fine Arts instead, and took its lasting name from the Ferrocarril Buenos Aires al Pacífico, the railway company that later occupied it. The dome came alive in 1946, when five of the country's leading painters — Antonio Berni, Lino Enea Spilimbergo, Demetrio Urruchúa, Manuel Colmeiro and Juan Carlos Castagnino — agreed to share it, dividing 450 square metres of curved ceiling and working side by side for a year, lying on scaffolding, on a single vision of family and everyday life. It became a shopping centre in 1990 and was then declared a national historic monument: one of very few malls anywhere protected not for the shops but for the ceiling above them.

stops.title: Galerías Pacífico
stops.caption: Step inside at the corner of Florida and Córdoba, and before you look at a single shop window, look up.
stops.transcriptText:
Step inside at the corner of Florida and Córdoba, and before you look at a single shop window, look up.

The central dome above you is covered edge to edge in mural paintings, and Galerías Pacífico is, officially, a shopping centre — one that happens to have a piece of major twentieth-century Argentine art for a ceiling.

The building itself dates to 1889, originally intended as a Buenos Aires branch of the French department store Au Bon Marché. That never happened; instead the building spent decades as home to the National Museum of Fine Arts, until 1940. Its current name comes from a later tenant, the Ferrocarril Buenos Aires al Pacífico, the railway company that eventually occupied the space and left its name on the building even after the trains were long gone.

The murals came in 1946, and the story behind them is unusual on its own: five of the country's leading painters — Antonio Berni, Lino Enea Spilimbergo, Demetrio Urruchúa, Manuel Colmeiro, and Juan Carlos Castagnino — agreed to share the same dome, dividing up 450 square metres of curved ceiling between them and working side by side rather than each claiming a separate wall. They'd planned to finish in two months. It took a year, lying on scaffolding, sketching in charcoal before laying down paint, building a single coherent vision of family and everyday life out of five distinct hands.

The building became a shopping centre in 1990, and it's since been declared a national historic monument — which is worth sitting with for a second. This is one of very few shopping malls anywhere with that legal status, protected not for the shops inside it but for the ceiling above them, painted by five artists who never intended their most collaborative work to end up over a food court.

Find a bench, or just stand still in the centre of the atrium, and give the dome the two or three minutes it actually takes to look at properly — almost everyone below is looking at storefronts instead, and the ceiling rewards the ones who don't.

tours.title: Los Galgos
tours.shortDescription: Four lives on one corner — family home, Singer showroom, pharmacy, and ninety years of bar.
tours.longDescription: The 1879 building at Callao and Lavalle began as the Lezama family's residence, housed the Singer sewing-machine company's offices and then a pharmacy, and in 1930 was taken over by an Asturian immigrant who opened a grocery, pantry and bar all at once, named after his racing greyhounds. President Arturo Frondizi drank here; so did Luca Prodan and the tango poet Enrique Santos Discépolo, decades apart; in 2018 a future president made it the meeting place for the policy circle he named Grupo Callao, after the avenue outside. Closed in 2015, it was brought back by Julián Díaz and the designer Flor Capella — restored rather than reinvented — and it now leads the revival of Argentina's old vermouth culture from the same tiled floor.

stops.title: Los Galgos
stops.caption: A family home first, then a sewing-machine showroom, then a pharmacy — and for most of the last ninety years, a bar.
stops.transcriptText:
A family home first, then a sewing-machine showroom, then a pharmacy — and for most of the last ninety years, a bar. This corner has had four lives, and you're standing in front of the fourth.

The corner of Avenida Callao and Lavalle holds the building you're after. Look for the old tiled floor and a long wooden bar visible through the windows from the street, and you're in the right place.

The building itself goes back to 1879, when it was built as the residence of the Lezama family, who lived there for more than thirty years. After that it housed the commercial offices of the Singer sewing-machine company, then a pharmacy, which closed toward the end of the 1920s. In 1930, an Asturian immigrant with a passion for greyhound racing took the space over and opened it as a grocery, a pantry, and a bar all at once, naming the whole thing after his dogs: Los Galgos, the greyhounds.

The guest list since then reads like a strange cross-section of the city. President Arturo Frondizi sat at these tables, and so did the musician Luca Prodan and the tango writer Enrique Santos Discépolo, decades apart from one another. More recently, in 2018, a future president chose Los Galgos as the meeting place for his policy circle, known informally as Grupo Callao, named for the very avenue outside.

The bar closed in 2015 and could easily have stayed closed. Instead the gastronomic figure Julián Díaz and designer Flor Capella — the pair behind another well-loved bar nearby, number 878 — took it on and brought it back, restoring rather than reinventing it.

And that continuity is really the point. A bar this ordinary-looking doesn't survive nearly a century through nostalgia alone — it survives because a president, a punk musician, a tango poet, and a policy circle all kept choosing, independently, across nine decades, to sit at the same tables.

Order the vermouth if it's on the list. Los Galgos has led something of a revival of Argentina's old vermouth culture in recent years, and it's the drink that makes the most sense in a room this old.

tours.title: Mercado de San Telmo
tours.shortDescription: An 1897 iron market hall where food and antiques share one roof — and neither has pushed the other out.
tours.longDescription: Juan A. Buschiazzo's market opened in February 1897, built to feed the wave of European immigrants settling San Telmo, and it fills a full block entered from Bolívar, Defensa, Estados Unidos or Carlos Calvo. From the street it presents an Italianate face — round arches, shopfronts opening straight onto the pavement — and inside it switches languages entirely: an open cast-iron frame closely modelled on the great nineteenth-century market halls of Paris, chosen because iron let in light and air the way solid stone never could. It grew with the neighbourhood, expanding toward Defensa in 1900 and Estados Unidos in 1922. Unlike the city's other old markets, closed outright or hollowed into shopping centres, San Telmo's kept its butchers, cheesemongers and fruit stalls while slowly also becoming the antiques market the neighbourhood is famous for — two economies under one iron roof, the seam between building phases still visible in the ironwork.

stops.title: Mercado de San Telmo
stops.caption: Look up at the roof before you look at anything for sale beneath it — cast iron ribs, glass panels, and a century of light falling through them exactly the way the architect intended.
stops.transcriptText:
Look up at the roof before you look at anything for sale beneath it — cast iron ribs, glass panels, and a century of light falling through them exactly the way the architect intended.

The market fills a full block in San Telmo, entered from Bolívar, Defensa, Estados Unidos, or Carlos Calvo, and inside, stalls run beneath a soaring iron-and-glass structure that feels closer to a train shed than a grocery hall.

It opened in February 1897, designed by the architect Juan A. Buschiazzo, built specifically to feed the wave of European immigrants who were settling in San Telmo at the time. From the street, the market presents an Italianate face — round arches, individual shopfronts opening straight onto the pavement — but step inside and the structure switches languages entirely: an open cast-iron frame, closely modelled on the great nineteenth-century market halls of Paris, chosen specifically because iron let in light and air in a way solid stone walls never could.

The market grew as the neighbourhood did. A first expansion in 1900 opened it toward Defensa; a second, in 1922, extended it toward Estados Unidos, gradually filling the whole block you're standing in front of now.

Here's what's worth noticing: unlike so many of the city's old markets, which either closed outright or got hollowed out into shopping centres, San Telmo's kept doing more or less what it always did — butchers, cheesemongers, fruit stalls — while slowly also becoming the antiques market this neighbourhood is famous for today. Two different economies, food and bric-a-brac, sharing one iron roof without ever quite pushing the other out.

Walk to where the original 1897 core meets the later additions — the join is visible if you know where to look, a small seam in the ironwork marking twenty-five years of the market simply growing to keep up with its neighbourhood.

tours.title: Mural de Evita
tours.shortDescription: Two nine-storey Evitas in steel — the gentle face toward the working suburbs, the defiant one toward the north.
tours.longDescription: On the old Ministry of Public Works tower over Avenida 9 de Julio, Alejandro Marmo's two steel portraits of Eva Perón — each 31 by 24 metres, 14 tonnes of steel plate between them, mounted around a hundred metres up and unveiled in 2011 — are deliberately not identical. Eva de los Humildes, based on the cover of La Razón de mi Vida, faces south toward Avellaneda and the working-class suburbs; the north face, drawn from her combative speech of the 22nd of August 1951, microphone at her mouth, looks toward the wealthier neighbourhoods — a placement written into the government decree that approved the murals. Worked into the north portrait's hair are the digits 2025, for 20:25, the official time her death was announced. Switched off for years by one government to save electricity, secretly rewired and relit by utility workers on election nights, then formally reconnected — the lights themselves have become part of the politics.

stops.title: Mural de Evita
stops.caption: Twenty past eight in the evening, the 26th of July 1952 — the official time of Eva Perón's death — is hidden, in numbers, inside the hair of the woman looking down at you from this wall.
stops.transcriptText:
Twenty past eight in the evening, the 26th of July 1952 — the official time of Eva Perón's death — is hidden, in numbers, inside the hair of the woman looking down at you from this wall.

The building rising above Avenida 9 de Julio is the old Ministry of Public Works, and mounted across two of its facades are two enormous steel portraits of the same woman: Eva Perón.

Each portrait measures 31 metres by 24, mounted around a hundred metres up, cut from steel plate with a combined weight of 14 tonnes. They're the work of the sculptor Alejandro Marmo, unveiled in 2011, and they're deliberately not identical. The south-facing portrait, called Eva de los Humildes, is based on the cover photograph from her book La Razón de mi Vida — softer, warmer, looking out toward Avellaneda and the working-class suburbs on that side of the city. The north-facing portrait, simply called Eva, is drawn from a photograph of her famous speech on the 22nd of August 1951, microphone at her mouth, hair pulled tight — combative, unmistakably a woman mid-address — and it looks out toward the wealthier northern neighbourhoods instead.

That's not a coincidence. The placement was written into the government decree that approved the murals: the gentler face toward the working suburbs, the defiant face toward the traditionally aristocratic side of town. And worked into the lines of that north-facing hairstyle, easy to miss unless you know to look, are the digits 2025 — a reference to 20:25, the time her death was officially announced.

The murals have had their own political afterlife: switched off for years under one government to save on electricity, secretly rewired and relit by utility workers to mark election nights and anniversaries, then formally reconnected by a later administration. Whichever way you read that back-and-forth, it says something about how alive this image has stayed, seventy-odd years after the woman in it died.

Come back after dark. Lit or unlit has itself been a political statement at different points in the last decade, so whatever state you find the murals in when you visit is, in its own way, part of the story.

tours.title: Museo Nacional del Cabildo
tours.shortDescription: Five arches remain of eleven — the cut-down building where Argentina began.
tours.longDescription: The long, low, whitewashed Cabildo on Plaza de Mayo hosted the open town-council meeting of the 22nd of May 1810 and, three days later, the formation of the First Junta — the opening act of Argentina's independence movement, and the reason the 25th of May is still a national holiday. The building then paid for the city that followed: three arches came down in the 1880s to widen Avenida de Mayo and three more in 1931 for a new diagonal, leaving five of the original eleven, and the tower had already been demolished for structural problems before Mario Buschiazzo's 1940 restoration returned what was left to its colonial-era appearance. What stands today is less than half the original façade — and still the building where the country effectively began.

stops.title: Museo Nacional del Cabildo
stops.caption: Count the arches in front of you. There are five. There used to be eleven.
stops.transcriptText:
Count the arches in front of you. There are five. There used to be eleven.

The Cabildo sits on the western side of Plaza de Mayo — a long, low, whitewashed building with arched galleries and a single bell tower, dwarfed by the Casa Rosada across the square and the cathedral beside it. Construction began in 1725, and the tower wasn't finished until 1764; by the time of the events that made this building famous, in 1810, it still wasn't entirely complete.

Those events are the reason the Cabildo matters more than its modest size suggests. On the 22nd of May, 1810, an open town-council meeting was held inside to debate whether the viceroy, Baltasar Hidalgo de Cisneros, should keep his post. Three days later, on the 25th, a new government — the First Junta — was formed here, the opening act of Argentina's independence movement, which is why the 25th of May is still a national holiday and this modest building carries the weight it does.

What happened to the arches is its own story. In the 1880s, three were demolished on the northern side to widen Avenida de Mayo. In 1931, three more came down on the southern side to cut through a new diagonal avenue. Of the original eleven arches, only five survived, and the tower had already come down separately due to structural problems. In 1940, the architect Mario Buschiazzo restored what remained, rebuilding the tower and returning the building, as closely as records allowed, to its colonial-era appearance.

And that's really the thing worth sitting with: this is a mutilated building, cut down twice by the same kind of civic ambition — wider avenues, grander boulevards — that it once helped make possible by hosting the government that eventually built modern Buenos Aires. What you're looking at is less than half of the original façade, and it's still the building where the country effectively began.

Step inside when you can — the museum holds paintings and objects from the May Revolution itself, and it's the only way to get a sense of how much larger this building was ever meant to be.

tours.title: MALBA
tours.shortDescription: One collector's argument, made in glass and limestone: Latin American art belongs in Latin America.
tours.longDescription: The Museo de Arte Latinoamericano de Buenos Aires opened on Figueroa Alcorta in September 2001 to house the collection Eduardo Costantini had assembled since 1990 and donated outright to found the museum — 228 works by 80 Latin American artists on opening day, around 400 now, spanning the whole region. It was the first building in Buenos Aires constructed specifically to hold art rather than adapted from something else, and the 1998 competition that produced it drew 450 entries from 45 countries; the winners — Gastón Atelman, Martín Fourcade and Alfredo Tapia — were young Argentines barely out of architecture school. Their building favours openness over grandeur, broad glass and white walls flooding the galleries with natural light, extended in 2015 by the Spanish studio estudioHerreros without disturbing the original logic.

stops.title: MALBA
stops.caption: 450 architects from 45 countries entered a competition to design this building.
stops.transcriptText:
450 architects from 45 countries entered a competition to design this building. Three young Argentines, barely out of architecture school, won it.

You're on Figueroa Alcorta, in Palermo, in front of a low, white, glass-walled building set back from the avenue behind lawns and trees — this is MALBA, the Museo de Arte Latinoamericano de Buenos Aires.

The museum opened in September 2001, built to house a private collection assembled since 1990 by the businessman Eduardo Costantini, who donated it to found the museum outright: 228 works by 80 Latin American artists on opening day, since grown to somewhere around 400 pieces spanning the whole region, not just Argentina. It was, at the time, the first building in Buenos Aires constructed specifically to house artwork rather than adapted from something else.

That competition in 1998 is worth pausing on. Gastón Atelman, Martín Fourcade, and Alfredo Tapia were young, largely unproven architects when their design beat proposals from established firms across 45 countries, and what they built favours openness over grandeur: broad glass surfaces, white walls, natural light flooding spaces meant to hold art rather than announce a monument. In 2015, the Spanish studio estudioHerreros added an expansion clad in Spanish limestone and green glass, without disturbing the original building's basic logic.

What's worth knowing, standing here, is that MALBA exists because one collector decided Latin American art deserved a purpose-built home in the region itself, rather than continuing to circulate mainly through museums in Europe and the United States. That's a specific kind of argument, made in glass and limestone rather than words — that this art belongs here, seen in the light it was made under.

If you're short on time, the permanent collection on the upper level is the one to prioritise — it's arranged more or less chronologically, and walking it in order is the fastest way to see exactly what Costantini set out to build.

tours.title: Museo de Arte de Tigre
tours.shortDescription: A riverside casino for the elite, handed back to everybody as an art museum.
tours.longDescription: The white neoclassical palace facing the Río Luján was the Tigre Club, founded in 1909 by a group of businessmen including the financier Ernesto Tornquist and opened to members in 1912 as one of the great social hubs of the Buenos Aires elite — tennis, golf, regattas, and from 1927 a European-style casino, fitted out with Carrara marble staircases, Slavonian oak floors, wrought iron and gilded bronze. The club eventually closed, the building sat underused for decades, and the municipality expropriated it in 1974; it was declared a national historic site in 1979, restoration began in 1998, and the Museo de Arte de Tigre opened in 2006. The collection concentrates on nineteenth- and twentieth-century Argentine painting, much of it depicting the Tigre Delta itself — the same stretch of river visible from these windows, painted by Juan León Pallière, Carlos Barberis and others who came here and painted what they saw.

stops.title: Museo de Arte de Tigre
stops.caption: A hundred years before this building held paintings, it held roulette wheels.
stops.transcriptText:
A hundred years before this building held paintings, it held roulette wheels.

On the bank of the Río Luján, in Tigre, a white neoclassical palace with wide verandas and elaborate ironwork faces the water. This was once the Tigre Club, and it's now the Museo de Arte de Tigre.

The club was founded in 1909 by a group of businessmen, including the financier Ernesto Tornquist, as a place for tennis, golf, rowing regattas, and games, opening to members in 1912 as one of the great social hubs for Buenos Aires' elite. A European-style casino was added in 1927, and the building was fitted out accordingly: staircases in Carrara marble, floors in Slavonian oak, wrought-iron gates, gilded bronze detailing throughout — built, from the very start, to impress.

The club eventually closed, the building sat underused for decades, and in 1974 the municipality of Tigre stepped in and expropriated it. It was declared a national historic site in 1979, restoration began in 1998, and the Museo de Arte de Tigre finally opened its doors in 2006. Today the collection focuses on nineteenth and twentieth-century Argentine painting, much of it chosen specifically because it depicts the Tigre Delta itself — the same stretch of river visible from these windows, painted by artists like the Frenchman Juan León Pallière and the Italian Carlos Barberis, who came here and painted what they saw.

Here's the interesting bit: the building's whole trajectory, from private casino for Buenos Aires' wealthiest families to a publicly owned art museum anyone can walk into, tracks a pattern this city has repeated more than once — exclusive recreation spaces eventually handed back, in one form or another, to everybody.

After the galleries, walk down to the water's edge behind the building. Several of the paintings inside were made from roughly that exact vantage point, and it's worth comparing the view to the canvas before you leave.

tours.title: Nápoles
tours.shortDescription: Fresh pasta served among seventy classic cars, in the Anchorena family's old carriage depot.
tours.longDescription: Behind an unassuming façade on Avenida Caseros, on the border of San Telmo and Barracas, the building opens into some 2,000 square metres of brick vaults and iron columns, ceilings six metres high — the nineteenth-century carriage depot of the Anchorena family, among the wealthiest and most politically connected in Argentine history. The antiques dealer Gabriel del Campo filled it with a lifetime's collection — roughly seventy classic cars, fifty motorcycles, sculpture and paintings arranged around the tables rather than tucked behind glass — and opened a restaurant in the middle of it. The food is straightforward Italian home cooking, fresh pasta made daily, which is the right register for a room this loud with objects; the Rolling Stones have passed through, which says less about the pasta and more about how few places let you eat dinner inside somebody's private museum.

stops.title: Nápoles
stops.caption: This restaurant used to store carriages for one of Argentina's wealthiest families.
stops.transcriptText:
This restaurant used to store carriages for one of Argentina's wealthiest families. Now it stores roughly seventy classic cars, fifty motorcycles, and, somewhere among all of it, a kitchen.

You'll find it at Avenida Caseros 449, right on the border between San Telmo and Barracas. Behind an unassuming façade, the building opens into something like 2,000 square metres of space, brick vaults and old iron columns overhead, ceilings six metres high from floor to arch.

In the nineteenth century, this was the carriage depot for the Anchorena family, among the wealthiest and most politically connected families in the country's history. Later it became a warehouse for antiques and collectible cars, and eventually it landed in the hands of Gabriel del Campo, an antiques dealer who had spent a lifetime collecting exactly the kind of objects a space this size could actually hold. Rather than open a shop, he opened a restaurant and let the collection take over the whole building — 1950s Italian race cars, motorcycles, sculpture, paintings, all arranged around the tables rather than tucked away behind glass.

The food itself is straightforward Italian home cooking — fresh pasta made daily, pizza from the same tradition — which is exactly the right register for a room this loud with objects. Anything more elaborate on the plate would be competing with seventy classic cars for attention, and losing.

Over the years, Nápoles has quietly become something of a stop for visiting celebrities passing through Buenos Aires — members of the Rolling Stones among them — which says less about the pasta, probably, and rather more about how few places in this city let you eat dinner inside somebody's actual private museum.

Walk the room before you sit down, if the staff will let you, rather than just looking at what's parked near your own table. The collection runs the length of the building, and the pieces tucked into the far corners are just as much a part of Del Campo's life's work as the cars everyone stops to photograph near the door.

tours.title: The Obelisk
tours.shortDescription: Built in 31 days, voted for demolition three years later — now the emotional centre of the city.
tours.longDescription: Alberto Prebisch's 67.5-metre white concrete obelisk went up in just 31 days in 1936, marking the 400th anniversary of the city's first founding, on the site of the Church of San Nicolás de Bari — the tower from which the Argentine flag was first raised in Buenos Aires, in 1812, a history kept in the inscriptions at the base. Inside, a spiral staircase of 206 steps climbs to the top, though the monument is not generally open to visitors. In 1938 panels began falling off, apparently shaken loose by the subway running underneath, and the city council voted twenty-three to three to demolish the whole thing — critics called it an eyesore with a funeral-monument look. It survived to become the place where championships are celebrated and elections watched: nearly voted out of existence by the same city that came to love it.

stops.title: The Obelisk
stops.caption: Buenos Aires' most famous monument took 31 days to build, and three years later the city council voted to tear it down.
stops.transcriptText:
Buenos Aires' most famous monument took 31 days to build, and three years later the city council voted to tear it down.

You're standing in Plaza de la República, where Avenida 9 de Julio meets Corrientes — the white concrete obelisk rising above you, 67.5 metres of it, unmistakable from almost anywhere in the centre of the city.

The architect Alberto Prebisch, who also designed the Gran Rex theatre nearby, built it in 1936 to mark the 400th anniversary of the city's first founding. The site wasn't chosen at random: the Church of San Nicolás de Bari once stood here, and it was from that church's tower that the Argentine flag was raised for the first time in Buenos Aires, on the 23rd of August, 1812. The church came down to make way for the monument, and the flag's history stayed behind, recorded in the inscriptions at its base.

Inside, a single door opens onto a spiral staircase of 206 steps and seven landings, climbing all the way to the top — though almost nobody gets to use it; the obelisk isn't generally open to visitors.

For a monument this loved today, its early years were rough. In 1938, panels covering the structure began falling off, apparently shaken loose by vibrations from the subway running underneath, and the scare that followed pushed the city council to vote, twenty-three to three, to demolish the whole thing in 1939 — for safety, for aesthetics, and because critics called it, among other things, an eyesore with a funeral-monument look about it.

It survived anyway, and the interesting bit is this: the monument porteños now treat as the emotional centre of the city — where championships get celebrated and elections get watched — spent its first years being nearly voted out of existence by the same people who'd eventually come to love it.

Look for the small plaques at the base commemorating the flag-raising — most people walk straight past them on their way to a photo of the obelisk itself, but they're the actual reason this exact spot was chosen.

tours.title: Palacio Barolo
tours.shortDescription: A hundred metres of Divine Comedy, built as a mausoleum for Dante — whose ashes never came.
tours.longDescription: Luis Barolo, a Piedmontese textile magnate convinced that war would eventually destroy Europe and everything in it, hired the Milanese architect Mario Palanti to build a safe resting place for Dante Alighieri's remains on Avenida de Mayo. Palanti coded the whole structure to the Divine Comedy: 100 metres tall for the poem's hundred cantos, 22 floors echoing its verse structure, the building divided into hell, purgatory and heaven rising floor by floor toward the lighthouse at the top, and a crypt in the basement marked by a bronze Ascension, waiting for ashes Italy never agreed to release. The crypt has sat empty since 1923. What's left, a century on, is an elaborate monument to an object that never arrived — a building that took its own symbolism completely seriously, and still keeps its promise.

stops.title: Palacio Barolo
stops.caption: You may already know the roof of this building as a bar. Before you go up, it's worth understanding exactly what you'd be climbing.
stops.transcriptText:
You may already know the roof of this building as a bar. Before you go up, it's worth understanding exactly what you'd be climbing.

Palacio Barolo rises on Avenida de Mayo, impossible to miss: a tapering brick-and-terracotta tower topped by a small lighthouse, considerably taller than anything else on the block, its silhouette closer to a cathedral spire than an office building.

The man who commissioned it, Luis Barolo, was a wealthy Piedmontese textile magnate with a specific fear: that the First World War, or another one like it, would eventually destroy Europe and everything in it. Barolo wanted to build a mausoleum safe on the other side of the Atlantic for the remains of Dante Alighieri, and he hired the Milanese architect Mario Palanti to design a building around that single, strange ambition.

Palanti built the whole structure as a coded tribute to Dante's Divine Comedy: 100 metres tall for the poem's hundred cantos, 22 floors echoing its verse structure, the building itself divided into hell, purgatory, and heaven, rising floor by floor toward that lighthouse at the top. Down in the basement, he designed a central crypt, marked by a bronze sculpture called the Ascension, meant to hold Dante's ashes once Italy agreed to release them.

Italy never agreed. The crypt has sat empty since the building opened in 1923, a mausoleum with no body in it, in a building whose own patron was rumoured, in the way these things get rumoured, to have Masonic sympathies that only deepened the sense that every number and proportion here meant something more.

What you're left with, more than a century later, is an elaborate monument built around an object that never arrived — a building that took its own symbolism completely seriously and still, in its own way, keeps the promise it made, whether or not Dante ever gets here.

If your ticket only takes you as far as the bar, sixteen floors up, consider paying for the full climb. The lighthouse at the very top — the part of the building Palanti called paradise — is a separate ascent, and it's the only way to see the whole allegory through to its end.

tours.title: Puente de la Mujer
tours.shortDescription: Calatrava's two dancers mid-tango — and the only bridge in Buenos Aires that turns.
tours.longDescription: Santiago Calatrava's first project anywhere in Latin America spans Dique 3 in Puerto Madero: 170 metres of steel and concrete built as an image, the leaning white mast a man, the curved walkway a woman, the two frozen mid-tango over the water. It was commissioned and paid for privately by the businessman Alberto González as a gift to the city and a tribute to his wife and daughters, and opened in December 2001; the middle of its three spans hangs from cables and rotates a full ninety degrees on its own axis to let boats through the dock. The bridge also gave its clearest image to a neighbourhood-wide idea — since 1995 Puerto Madero's streets have deliberately carried the names of notable women, a correction to a city where only a small fraction of streets do.

stops.title: Puente de la Mujer
stops.caption: The bridge in front of you is built to resemble two dancers mid-tango, and it's the only bridge in Buenos Aires that actually turns.
stops.transcriptText:
The bridge in front of you is built to resemble two dancers mid-tango, and it's the only bridge in Buenos Aires that actually turns.

Look at the white mast leaning off to one side, and the long curved walkway beneath it, spanning the water of Dique 3 in Puerto Madero. That's Puente de la Mujer — the Women's Bridge — 170 metres of steel and concrete connecting the eastern and western banks of the old dock.

The Spanish architect Santiago Calatrava designed it, his first project anywhere in Latin America, and the whole structure is meant as an image rather than just a crossing: the white mast represents a man, the curved walkway a woman, the two of them frozen mid-tango over the water. It was commissioned and paid for privately by the businessman Alberto González, as a gift to the city and, by his own account, a tribute to his wife and daughters, and it opened in December 2001.

Here's the detail that makes the bridge worth more than a photograph: the middle of its three spans is a moving structure, hung from cables off that leaning mast, and it rotates a full ninety degrees on its own axis to let boats pass through the dock — a bridge built to dance, quite literally, whenever a vessel needs to get by.

And there's a wider story the bridge fits into. Since 1995, the streets of Puerto Madero have deliberately been named after notable women — Juana Manso, Alicia Moreau de Justo, Encarnación Ezcurra, Macacha Güemes — a direct response to the fact that, across the more than two thousand streets of Buenos Aires, only a small fraction carry women's names at all. This neighbourhood was built, street by street, to correct that. The bridge simply gave the whole idea its clearest image.

Come back after dark if you can. The bridge is lit at night, and the water in Dique 3 turns it into a near-perfect mirror image of itself — worth the return trip on its own.

tours.title: Roux
tours.shortDescription: Basque training, Argentine product — the corner bistro that stepped sideways from the parrilla.
tours.longDescription: Martín Rebaudino trained in Spain's Basque Country under Berasategui, Arzak and Subijana, then came home and opened Roux on a Palermo corner in 2013, mid-way through one of Argentina's periodic stretches of economic uncertainty. The room is glassed in on two sides with small terraces spilling onto the pavement — in a city where most good kitchens face inward — and the cooking moves through French, Spanish and Argentine registers without settling into any one of them: strong seafood, careful risottos, red meat treated with more restraint than any parrilla would allow. A Michelin Plate and a standing place on South America's best-tables rankings say the bet placed in a difficult year paid off.

stops.title: Roux
stops.caption: Look at the corner itself first. Small terraces spill onto the pavement on both sides of the building, in a city where most of the good kitchens face inward and keep the street at arm's length.
stops.transcriptText:
Look at the corner itself first. Small terraces spill onto the pavement on both sides of the building, in a city where most of the good kitchens face inward and keep the street at arm's length.

That corner, at Peña in Palermo, is Roux. Step inside and the dining room is glassed in on two sides, so the street stays visible from nearly every seat, and the room itself is intimate and rather classically dressed — tables set close together, the kind of interior that feels a good deal older than the eleven or so years the restaurant has actually been open.

The chef is Martín Rebaudino, and his training tells you most of what you need to know before the food arrives. He worked in Spain's Basque Country under Martín Berasategui, Juan Mari Arzak, and Pedro Subijana — three of the defining names in modern Spanish cooking — and brought that grammar home rather than simply copying it. The menu at Roux moves through French, Spanish, and Argentine influences without settling fully into any one of them: strong seafood, careful risottos, and red meat treated with more restraint than the average parrilla would ever allow.

Rebaudino opened Roux in 2013, in the middle of one of Argentina's periodic stretches of economic uncertainty, betting that this city had room for a restaurant speaking about Argentine product in a more international register rather than through the usual steakhouse script. It's held a Michelin Plate since, and it turns up year after year on rankings of South America's best tables — which is rather a long run for a bet placed in a difficult year.

And that's really the thing worth noticing here: Roux doesn't reject the parrilla tradition so much as step quietly sideways from it, arguing that Argentine beef and Argentine fish can hold their own in a conversation that includes San Sebastián as easily as it includes Buenos Aires.

If you've time before or after your table, Palermo's back streets around Peña reward a slow walk — this corner of the neighbourhood is full of exactly the kind of small, considered restaurants that Roux helped make fashionable again.

tours.title: Recoleta Cemetery — Duarte Family Mausoleum
tours.shortDescription: The most visited grave in the cemetery holds a body that spent sixteen years missing.
tours.longDescription: Along one of Recoleta Cemetery's main paths, the Duarte family vault is plainer than most of what surrounds it, and it is where Eva Perón is buried. Embalmed after her death in 1952 so completely she was said to look almost alive, she lay in public view for three years until the 1955 coup, when the military decided the body itself was dangerous and had it taken away: smuggled abroad, buried in Italy under the false name María Maggi de Magistris with the Vatican quietly involved, reunited with the exiled Juan Perón in Madrid, and only brought home in 1976 — to a tomb built several metres down and reinforced like a bank vault, specifically so nobody could take her again. After sixteen years of theft and hiding, the safest resting place turned out to be an ordinary-looking family plot, reinforced from below rather than decorated from above.

stops.title: Recoleta Cemetery — Duarte Family Mausoleum
stops.caption: The most visited grave in this entire cemetery belongs to a woman whose body spent sixteen years missing, hidden under a false name on another continent.
stops.transcriptText:
The most visited grave in this entire cemetery belongs to a woman whose body spent sixteen years missing, hidden under a false name on another continent.

You're in Recoleta Cemetery, among marble avenues and stone angels — the Duarte family mausoleum is a modest, dark plot along one of the cemetery's main paths, plainer than most of what surrounds it, and easy to miss if it weren't for the small crowd usually gathered in front of it. This is where Eva Perón is buried.

Eva Perón died of cancer in 1952, and her body was embalmed by the Spanish doctor Pedro Ara so completely that it was said to look almost alive. For three years it lay on public display, becoming a kind of shrine for her supporters, until a coup in 1955 removed the government that had built its authority partly around her memory.
