The new military authorities decided the body itself was dangerous — a rallying point waiting to happen — and had it quietly taken away.

What followed reads like something invented rather than lived. The embalmed body was smuggled out of the country and eventually turned up in Italy, buried in a cemetery under a false name, María Maggi de Magistris, with the Vatican quietly involved in the arrangements. It stayed there for years before being reunited with Juan Perón, exiled in Madrid. Only after another change of government, in 1976, was she finally brought home and placed here, in the Duarte family vault, in a tomb built several metres down and reinforced like a bank vault, specifically so nobody could take her again.

What matters, standing here, is the plainness itself: after a body has been stolen, hidden, and fought over for sixteen years, the safest resting place turns out to be an ordinary-looking family plot, reinforced from below rather than decorated from above.

Recoleta Cemetery holds thousands of other vaults and mausoleums beyond this one path, spanning nearly two centuries of the city's history — the walk beyond the crowds rewards a slow amble, mausoleum after mausoleum telling its own version of who Buenos Aires chose to remember.

tours.title: Salón 1923
tours.shortDescription: The rooftop bar Palacio Barolo's architect drew a century ago and never lived to build.
tours.longDescription: Sixteen floors up Palacio Barolo, on the terrace beneath the building's dome and lighthouse beacon, Salón 1923 is the last unbuilt chapter of Mario Palanti's Divine Comedy tower — finished roughly ninety-six years after it was first drawn. A rooftop terrace was part of Palanti and Luis Barolo's original plan for the building, and it simply never happened in either of their lifetimes; the bar only opened in 2019, dressed to evoke the years either side of the building's 1923 debut, with staff in period dress and a cocktail list that plays along with the Dante theme, one drink built around the poet's love for Beatrice. Most rooftop bars are simply the newest flat surface above a hotel. This one is the part of the building its own architect designated as paradise.

stops.title: Salón 1923
stops.caption: Sixteen floors up, on the roof of a building modelled on Dante's own vision of the afterlife, sits a bar its original architect dreamed up but never lived to build.
stops.transcriptText:
Sixteen floors up, on the roof of a building modelled on Dante's own vision of the afterlife, sits a bar its original architect dreamed up but never lived to build.

Take the lift to the sixteenth floor of Palacio Barolo, on Avenida de Mayo, and step out onto the rooftop terrace. The building's dome and lighthouse beacon rise just above you, and Salón 1923 opens out around you in every direction, tables scattered across the terrace under strings of light.

The building itself was designed by the Italian architect Mario Palanti, commissioned by the businessman Luis Barolo, and the whole structure is built as an architectural retelling of Dante's Divine Comedy — a hundred metres tall, divided into sections read as hell, purgatory, and paradise, with the lighthouse beacon at the very top standing in for heaven itself. Palacio Barolo opened in 1923, which is where this rooftop bar gets its name.

Here's the detail worth knowing: a rooftop terrace was part of Palanti and Barolo's original plan for the building, nearly a hundred years ago, and it simply never happened in either of their lifetimes. Salón 1923 didn't open until 2019, decorated to evoke the years either side of the building's original 1920s debut — staff in period dress, carefully chosen music, and a cocktail list that plays along with the Dante theme, including one built around the poet's love for Beatrice.

Most rooftop bars in this city are simply the newest flat surface built above a hotel. This one is different — it's the last unbuilt chapter of a century-old architectural fantasy, finished roughly ninety-six years after it was first drawn, which means that, technically, you're now standing in the part of the building its own architect designated as paradise.

If you've come during the day, it's worth booking the guided climb through the rest of Palacio Barolo before dark — the allegory only really makes sense once you've walked hell and purgatory downstairs first, before finishing up here.

tours.title: Teatro Colón
tours.shortDescription: Twenty years, three architects — two dead before opening night — and one of the best-sounding rooms on earth.
tours.longDescription: Construction began in 1889 and the project outlived nearly everyone involved: the Italian architect Francesco Tamburini designed the original plan and died in 1891; Víctor Meano — who later designed Argentina's Congress — took over and was murdered in 1904; it fell to the Belgian Jules Dormal to finish the job and give the building its French elegance. The theatre finally opened on the 25th of May 1908 with Verdi's Aida. What makes the Colón genuinely remarkable is the sound: the horseshoe-shaped hall and its seven tiers of boxes are regularly ranked among the finest acoustic spaces of any opera house on the planet, a combination of shape, materials and luck that acousticians still study without ever agreeing which ingredient matters most. Proof that a masterpiece doesn't require one unbroken vision — just enough people willing to pick up exactly where the last one was forced to stop.

stops.title: Teatro Colón
stops.caption: Twenty years, three architects — two of whom died before the curtain ever went up — and one opera house that's still ranked among the best-sounding rooms in the world.
stops.transcriptText:
Twenty years, three architects — two of whom died before the curtain ever went up — and one opera house that's still ranked among the best-sounding rooms in the world.

Teatro Colón occupies its own block near Plaza Lavalle, a grand stone theatre with a colonnaded entrance and a scale that makes clear, before you've even stepped inside, that this was never meant to be an ordinary building.

Construction began in 1889, and the project outlived nearly everyone involved with it. The Italian architect Francesco Tamburini designed the original plan and died in 1891, years before it was finished. The work passed to Víctor Meano — the same architect who later designed Argentina's Congress building — who introduced changes of his own and was murdered in 1904, again long before completion. It finally fell to the Belgian architect Jules Dormal to finish the job, and Dormal gave the building much of the French elegance it's known for today. The theatre opened on the 25th of May, 1908, with a performance of Verdi's Aida.

What makes the Colón genuinely remarkable, beyond the drama of its construction, is its acoustics. The horseshoe-shaped hall and its seven tiers of boxes are regularly ranked among the finest acoustic spaces of any opera house on the planet — a combination of shape, materials, and a fair amount of luck that architects and acousticians still study today, without ever fully agreeing on exactly which ingredient matters most.

And that's really the thing worth sitting with: a building this acclaimed for how it sounds was designed, redesigned, and finished by three architects who never worked together, two of whom didn't live to hear a single note played inside it. It's proof that a masterpiece doesn't require one unbroken vision — just enough people willing to pick up exactly where the last one was forced to stop.

If you've the time, book the guided tour rather than just a performance ticket — it's the only way into the underground workshops and rehearsal spaces most opera houses keep entirely out of view.

tours.title: Universidad de Buenos Aires
tours.shortDescription: Three stops, one accidental theme: grand plans that didn't finish the way anyone expected.
tours.longDescription: One square kilometre of the University of Buenos Aires' Recoleta campus, and three architectural ambitions that each swerved. First, on Las Heras, the building students call the Engineering Cathedral — a neo-Gothic pile designed for the Faculty of Law, whose 120-metre central tower was never built and whose architect, Arturo Prins, died without ever being paid. Then the correction: the Law Faculty's vast, deliberately plain Doric temple on Figueroa Alcorta, begun in 1942 on a site shifted two hundred and fifty metres because the city's old drinking-water filtration beds were in the way. And right beside it, Eduardo Catalano's Floralis Genérica, a twenty-metre steel flower engineered to open every morning and close every dusk — which hasn't moved in years. None of the three projects were planned together, but walked in one afternoon they make a pattern: ambitious engineering that doesn't quite land on schedule turns out to be a local tradition. Just over a kilometre on foot, and rather endearing about it.

stops.title: Universidad de Buenos Aires — an introduction
stops.caption: Three buildings, one accidental theme: ambitious plans that didn't quite finish the way anyone expected.
stops.transcriptText:
Three buildings, one accidental theme: ambitious plans that didn't quite finish the way anyone expected. That's this walk, in a nutshell, and it happens entirely inside one square kilometre of the University of Buenos Aires' campus in Recoleta.

You'll cover three stops on foot, none more than a few minutes' walk from the last. First, on Avenida Las Heras, a nineteenth-century-looking cathedral that was never meant to be a church, and never meant to belong to the Faculty of Engineering either — it was designed for lawyers, half a century before anyone studying inside it built a bridge. From there, a short walk brings you to the building the Law Faculty actually settled into: a vast, deliberately plain Doric temple on Figueroa Alcorta, built as a direct correction to everything that went wrong the first time around. And right beside it, in the plaza out front, a twenty-metre steel flower that was engineered to open and close every single day — and hasn't moved in years.

None of these three projects were planned together. They were built decades apart, by different architects, for different reasons. But walk between them in one afternoon and a pattern starts to show itself: grand engineering promises, made in good faith, that ran into money, politics, or plain bad luck, and never quite delivered on schedule. It's not a criticism of the university — if anything, it's rather endearing. Ambition that doesn't always land where it was aimed is a very human thing to build a campus out of.

Start wherever suits you, but the walk works best in the order laid out here — begin on Las Heras, and let the story build as you go.

stops.title: Facultad de Ingeniería — Sede Las Heras
stops.caption: People walking past this building often cross themselves, assuming it's a church.
stops.transcriptText:
People walking past this building often cross themselves, assuming it's a church. It isn't — and the mix-up says something the Faculty of Law would probably rather forget.

Avenida Las Heras 2214, in Recoleta. The pointed arches, ribbed spires, and stone carving in front of you belong to a building students have nicknamed the Engineering Cathedral, even though it was never built to hold a single engineer.

This was meant to be the new home of the Faculty of Law. The engineer Arturo Prins won the design competition in 1909 with a fairly restrained proposal, only for the Law Faculty's council to reject it outright and demand something in the neo-Gothic style instead, on the grounds that it suited the dignity of the discipline better. Prins argued, reasonably, that building a Gothic cathedral in the twentieth century was an odd and expensive choice for a modern country. Nobody listened. He entered a second competition, won again, this time with the design in front of you, and the cornerstone went in in 1912.

The ambition was enormous. The plans called for a central tower a hundred and twenty metres tall, with a clock and bell that would have made it the largest civic bell tower anywhere in Latin America, flanked by two smaller towers fifty metres each. None of them were ever built. Funding crawled for decades, picking up briefly around the end of the First World War, enough to finish classrooms and offices. The first three floors opened in 1925, and law students studied inside an unfinished cathedral for the next thirteen years.

By 1938, the state gave up on completing it and began planning a different building altogether, in a very different style, a short distance away. Prins died the following year, having never been paid for the design. His family's lawsuit against the government dragged on for twenty-two years, and by the time it was finally settled, inflation had reduced the payout to barely the cost of a family lunch.

And here's the thing: the Faculty of Engineering inherited this building in 1948, and never bothered changing the decoration. Look closely at the stonework and stained glass around you — scales of justice, stacks of law books, carved for a profession that hasn't studied here in decades.

Look up at the roofline where the great central tower was supposed to stand — there's nothing there but sky, which is rather the point.

stops.title: Facultad de Derecho
stops.caption: A mile from here, an unfinished Gothic cathedral was quietly abandoned in 1938.
stops.transcriptText:
A mile from here, an unfinished Gothic cathedral was quietly abandoned in 1938. This building is the Law Faculty's answer to that failure, and it couldn't look more different.

Avenida Figueroa Alcorta, in Recoleta. The long, colossal facade in front of you — a row of plain Doric columns running the length of the building, with no ornament beyond their own scale — is the Facultad de Derecho of the University of Buenos Aires.

After decades spent watching their previous building sit half-built on Las Heras, with its towers never raised and its budget forever running short, the Law Faculty tried again. The architects Arturo Ochoa, Ismael Chiappori, and Pedro Mario Vinent won a new competition with a design about as far from neo-Gothic as architecture allows: a strict, Greek-classical temple, all columns and mass, deliberately free of the fussier decoration that had helped sink the last attempt. Construction began in March 1942, and the building was formally inaugurated on the 21st of September, 1949, with President Juan Perón in attendance, though work on the interiors carried on for another decade after that.

Here's a detail worth having in your head as you look at the building: the site wasn't the original choice. City planners had to shift the location roughly two hundred and fifty metres from where they'd first intended, because that original patch of ground was occupied by the old drinking-water filtration beds of the national sanitation utility — the system that once purified the city's water supply. You're standing where Buenos Aires used to clean its drinking water, on a building now dedicated to the rather less exact business of interpreting the law.

And here's the thing: after one architectural gamble collapsed into an unfinished, wildly overambitious ruin, the Faculty's second attempt went in the opposite direction entirely, choosing a style so plain and so classically legible that nobody could accuse it of pretending to be anything other than a monument to its own seriousness.

If you can get inside, the Salón de Actos is worth the detour — the scale of the columns outside carries straight through to the interior halls, without ever losing that same, deliberate lack of decoration.

stops.title: Floralis Genérica
stops.caption: This flower is meant to close every evening and open again each morning, and for the past several years it has done neither.
stops.transcriptText:
This flower is meant to close every evening and open again each morning, and for the past several years it has done neither.

In the Plaza de las Naciones Unidas, right beside the Law Faculty, the enormous steel flower rising twenty metres above the grass, six curved petals around a central stem, is the Floralis Genérica.

It's the work of the Argentine architect Eduardo Catalano, who taught for years at MIT and donated the piece to the city himself. It was unveiled on the 13th of April, 2002, built from stainless steel and aluminium and weighing around eighteen tonnes, with the Argentine aircraft manufacturer Lockheed Martin's local division contributing to the engineering. The name is deliberate: not a rose, not a tulip, but a generic flower, standing in for every flower at once.

What made it genuinely remarkable when it opened wasn't the size, but the movement. A hydraulic system, triggered by photoelectric cells reading the daylight, opened the petals each morning and closed them again at dusk, echoing the way real flowers respond to light — the first sculpture of its kind anywhere, engineering doing a very convincing impression of biology.

That mechanism hasn't run properly in years. A couple of the petals were damaged badly enough that in 2024 they were carefully removed and taken offsite for repair, with help from the original manufacturer, who still had the assembly plans. The underlying hydraulics are reportedly still sound underneath it all, waiting for the petals to go back on.

And here's the thing, standing in this particular stretch of the city: a flower engineered specifically to move has spent years standing still, in a neighbourhood that also gave up on a Gothic cathedral tower and once had to move an entire building site because of old water filters. Ambitious engineering that doesn't quite finish on schedule turns out to be something of a local tradition round here.

Have a look at the joints where the petals meet the stem — you can still see the mechanism built to make this thing move, quietly waiting to be switched back on.

tours.title: Parque Tres de Febrero
tours.shortDescription: One confiscated estate, a hundred and fifty years of additions — the park porteños call the Bosques de Palermo.
tours.longDescription: Everything on this walk sits on land confiscated from the governor Juan Manuel de Rosas after his defeat at the Battle of Caseros in 1852, turned into a park by the landscape architect Carlos Thays, and added to ever since by whoever turned up with the money, the ambition or the political will to leave a mark. Seven stops and an introduction: the monument the Spanish community spent seventeen years building after a ship carrying its statues sank off Brazil; the Victorian-era zoo remade as the Ecoparque after an orangutan named Sandra was recognised by a court as a non-human person; the garden the Japanese community built from nothing in fifty days; Enrique Jan's planetarium built entirely from equilateral triangles; fourteen thousand rose bushes planted on old swampland in seven months; an art museum living in what used to be Rosas' own dairy; and a regatta lake that began life as flood control. Around five kilometres, flat the whole way, in whatever order suits your route through the park.

stops.title: Parque Tres de Febrero — an introduction
stops.caption: Everything on this walk sits on land that used to belong to one man, and none of it looks anything like what he had in mind.
stops.transcriptText:
Everything on this walk sits on land that used to belong to one man, and none of it looks anything like what he had in mind.

This is Parque Tres de Febrero — most porteños just call it the Bosques de Palermo — and the land was confiscated from the governor Juan Manuel de Rosas after his defeat at the Battle of Caseros in 1852. The landscape architect Carlos Thays turned it into a proper park not long after, and ever since, it's worked less like a single unified space and more like a patchwork, added to by whoever turned up with the money, the ambition, or the political will to leave a mark.

Over seven stops, you'll see just how many different hands that turned out to be. A monument the Spanish community spent seventeen years building, a converted zoo that changed its entire purpose after one orangutan's court case, a garden the Japanese community built in fifty days, a planetarium shaped out of triangles, a rose garden planted on old swampland, a museum living inside what used to be Rosas' own dairy, and a lake that was originally built to stop a flood.

None of it was planned as a single project. It's been added to, piece by piece, for more than a hundred and fifty years, by Spanish immigrants, Japanese immigrants, city engineers, animal-rights lawyers, and one landscape architect's protégé, each working on their own patch of the same confiscated estate.

Walk it in whatever order suits your route through the park — each stop stands on its own, but taken together, they tell you more about who's actually shaped this city than any single monument could.

stops.title: Monumento de los Españoles
stops.caption: In the early hours of the 5th of March, 1916, a ship carrying twelve marble and bronze statues bound for this monument struck a reef off the coast of Brazil and sank in six minutes.
stops.transcriptText:
In the early hours of the 5th of March, 1916, a ship carrying twelve marble and bronze statues bound for this monument struck a reef off the coast of Brazil and sank in six minutes.

At the junction of Avenida del Libertador and Avenida Sarmiento, the towering white monument in front of you — twenty-four and a half metres of marble and bronze, topped by a single robed figure — is the Monumento a la Carta Magna y a las Cuatro Regiones Argentinas, known to almost everyone simply as the Monumento de los Españoles.

The Spanish community living in Argentina commissioned it as a gift, timed for the centenary of the May Revolution in 1910 — a gesture of friendship and thanks to the country that had taken so many of them in. The Spanish sculptor Agustín Querol designed it: a figure representing the Republic at the summit, and four bronze groups at the base representing the great regions of Argentina — the River Plate, the Chaco, the Pampas, and the Andes.

It should have taken a few years. It took seventeen. Querol died before the work was finished, and his successors had to carry on from his sketches. Then, in 1916, the ship carrying a dozen of the finished marble and bronze pieces across the Atlantic — the Príncipe de Asturias — struck a reef and went down within minutes, with a great many lives lost along with the cargo. Replacement pieces had to be recast from scratch, and even those got held up at customs. The monument finally opened in 1927, seventeen years after its cornerstone was laid, wearing replicas of the works the sea had taken.

And here's the thing: the original statues didn't stay lost. They were salvaged from the wreck in 1991 and are now on permanent display in Rio de Janeiro, which means fragments of this exact monument have spent decades standing in two countries at once, largely unaware of each other.

Walk a slow circuit around the base if you have the time — each of the four regional groups is worth a proper look on its own, and most visitors only ever see the one facing the road.

stops.title: Ecoparque
stops.caption: In 2014, an orangutan living behind you was recognised by an Argentine court as a non-human person.
stops.transcriptText:
In 2014, an orangutan living behind you was recognised by an Argentine court as a non-human person. That ruling is, in a real sense, part of why this place looks nothing like it used to.

Facing Plaza Italia, the gated grounds behind the ornate old entrance arches are the Ecoparque — for well over a century, this was the Buenos Aires Zoo.

The zoo opened in 1888, built on the classic nineteenth-century model: rows of cages, animals from around the world, displayed for a public that had rarely seen them any other way. It ran largely unchanged for well over a hundred years. One of its residents was Sandra, an orangutan born at Rostock Zoo in Germany in 1986 and living here from 1994 onward. In December 2014, animal-rights lawyers filed a habeas corpus petition on her behalf, and a federal court ruled — for the first time anywhere in the world — that a great ape could be considered a non-human subject of rights, not simply property to be displayed. It took another five years to arrange, but in 2019, Sandra was finally relocated to a sanctuary in Florida built specifically for orangutans and chimpanzees, where she lives today.

Sandra's case landed right in the middle of a much larger reckoning already underway about what this place should be. In 2016, the city government announced the zoo would close and reopen as the Ecoparque, focused on native species, habitat conservation, and the fight against illegal wildlife trafficking rather than display for its own sake. Since then, more than nine hundred animals have been relocated to homes better suited to them, over two thousand have been released back into the wild within Argentina, and thousands more rescued from traffickers have passed through here on their way somewhere safer.

And here's the thing: you're walking through the physical bones of a Victorian-style zoo — the same ornate gates, the same century-old enclosures — repurposed, slowly, around an entirely different idea of what the place is for.

Look out for the older heritage buildings tucked among the newer conservation areas — several of the original nineteenth-century structures are still standing, now doing very different work than the one they were built for.

stops.title: Jardín Japonés
stops.caption: A single royal visit, fifty days, and a community that had never attempted anything on this scale — that's the origin story behind the gate in front of you.
stops.transcriptText:
A single royal visit, fifty days, and a community that had never attempted anything on this scale — that's the origin story behind the gate in front of you.

In Parque Tres de Febrero, the vermilion torii gate marking the entrance is the way into the Jardín Japonés, the Japanese Garden.

Buenos Aires' Japanese community built this from nothing in 1967, raising the funds and constructing the whole garden in just fifty days, to mark the first visit to Argentina by a member of Japan's Imperial Family: the then Crown Prince Akihito and Crown Princess Michiko. It opened on the 17th of May that year, donated to the city through the Japanese Embassy. Ten years later, in 1977, the landscape engineer Yasuo Inomata redesigned much of it along the lines of a proper zen garden, and since 1989 it's been run by a cultural foundation rather than the city directly.

Take your time with the bridges as you walk through — they're not just crossings. The most photographed is the Taikobashi, a curved, lacquered wooden bridge; there's also the God's Bridge, said to represent the road to paradise, and the Zig Zag Bridge, which turns sharply from side to side for a reason that has nothing to do with the water beneath it. In traditional Japanese garden design, evil spirits were believed to travel only in straight lines — so a zig-zag bridge was, quite literally, a piece of engineering built to stop bad luck from following you across.

Keep an eye out, too, for the koi in the ponds — some have lived here for decades — and for the Bonsai Island, where several trees have been trained and shaped for more than fifty years.

If the timing works, the chashitsu tea house sometimes hosts a proper Japanese tea ceremony — worth checking before you go, since it's one of the few places in the city where you can sit still inside the thing you've just been walking around.

stops.title: Planetario Galileo Galilei
stops.caption: This building is made almost entirely out of one shape, repeated: the equilateral triangle, worked from foundations to dome, which is a stranger way to build a planetarium than it sounds.
stops.transcriptText:
This building is made almost entirely out of one shape, repeated: the equilateral triangle, worked from foundations to dome, which is a stranger way to build a planetarium than it sounds.

Inside Parque Tres de Febrero, the silver, dome-topped structure rising out of the surrounding trees, looking rather more like something that landed than something that was built, is the Planetario Galileo Galilei.

The idea started in 1958, pushed by a city councillor, José Luis Pena, and the city's culture secretary, Aldo Armando Cocca, who wanted Buenos Aires to have a proper planetarium of its own. Construction began in 1962 under the architect Enrique Jan, and the building opened on the 20th of December, 1966, though the first public show didn't run until the following June. The city had formally settled on the name Galileo Galilei by decree back in 1963, well before the building was finished.

What makes the structure genuinely unusual is the geometry. According to Jan himself, this is one of the only buildings anywhere in the world designed and built entirely from a single module: the equilateral triangle, repeated at every scale, from the structural framing right up to the dome that gives the building its shape. It wasn't decoration laid over a conventional structure — the triangle is the structure.

That silhouette has earned the building a nickname that's stuck for generations: locals have been calling it the flying saucer since it opened, which is a fairly good joke for a building whose entire purpose is teaching people what's actually up there.

Catch a show inside if the schedule allows — the dome itself, curved from those same repeating triangles, is worth looking at from underneath even before the stars come on.

stops.title: El Rosedal
stops.caption: Nearly fifteen thousand rose bushes went into the ground here in under seven months, which is either remarkable efficiency or a very determined mayor, depending on how you look at it.
stops.transcriptText:
Nearly fifteen thousand rose bushes went into the ground here in under seven months, which is either remarkable efficiency or a very determined mayor, depending on how you look at it.

Inside Parque Tres de Febrero, the formal garden in front of you — curved paths, a small Greek-style temple, and a footbridge arranged around beds of roses — is El Rosedal.

This ground has a history that has nothing to do with flowers. It used to be known as the Bañado de Palermo, a low-lying wetland that was part of the estate of Juan Manuel de Rosas until his defeat at the Battle of Caseros in 1852, after which the land was confiscated and eventually handed to the landscape architect Carlos Thays to design as Parque Tres de Febrero. Decades later, the city's mayor, Joaquín Anchorena, pushed for a dedicated rose garden within it.

The man who actually built it was Benito Carrasco, an agronomist who'd studied under Thays and taken over as the city's director of Parks and Promenades when Thays retired from the post in 1913, after twenty-two years in the job. Carrasco completed the Rosedal, along with its Hellenic-style footbridge, a small temple, and a pergola, between May and November of 1914 — planting fourteen thousand, six hundred and fifty rose bushes across nearly twelve hundred varieties in the process. It opened to the public on the 24th of November, 1914.

And here's the thing worth sitting with: this is old swampland, ground that used to flood on a fairly regular basis, now covered in one of the more demanding, delicate plants anyone grows on purpose. Somebody looked at a drained wetland and decided roses were the obvious next step.

The little Greek temple by the lake is worth finding on your way through — mornings are the best time to catch the roses at their most fragrant, before the heat of the day settles in.

stops.title: Museo Sívori
stops.caption: The building housing this art museum used to be a dairy — Juan Manuel de Rosas' dairy, to be exact — and only later a smart café, long before anyone thought to hang paintings on its walls.
stops.transcriptText:
The building housing this art museum used to be a dairy — Juan Manuel de Rosas' dairy, to be exact — and only later a smart café, long before anyone thought to hang paintings on its walls.

Inside Parque Tres de Febrero, the heritage building in front of you, low and colonial in feel, set apart from the park's more formal architecture, is the Museo de Artes Plásticas Eduardo Sívori.

The building itself predates the museum by decades. It began as the tambo — the dairy — on the country estate belonging to Juan Manuel de Rosas, before that land was confiscated and turned into the park you're standing in. Once the park existed, the old dairy was converted into a fashionable confectionery called El Hostal del Ciervo, a café rather than a gallery.

The museum had a rather more restless journey of its own. It was founded in 1938 as the Municipal Museum of Fine Arts, Applied Arts, and Comparative Arts, and renamed in 1946 in honour of the painter Eduardo Sívori, one of the more significant figures in Argentine art of his generation. For decades after that, it moved from address to address — evicted from the city council chambers, relocated to Avenida del Libertador, then to Paraguay Street, then squeezed for a stretch inside the Teatro General San Martín — before it finally found a permanent home in 1995, in this building, the old dairy turned café turned gallery.

And here's the thing: the museum and the building it now occupies share almost exactly the same story. Both spent most of their existence being repurposed for whatever the city needed that decade, until they landed, more or less by accident, on each other.

The collection rotates fairly often, so it's worth checking what's on before you go in — with roughly four thousand pieces of Argentine art in the archive, there's rarely a repeat if you visit a second time.

stops.title: Lago de Regatas
stops.caption: This lake was never really a lake. It began as an engineered solution to a creek that kept flooding the neighbourhood — dressed up so convincingly that most people rowing across it today have no idea they're sitting on top of infrastructure.
stops.transcriptText:
This lake was never really a lake. It began as an engineered solution to a creek that kept flooding the neighbourhood — dressed up so convincingly that most people rowing across it today have no idea they're sitting on top of infrastructure.

At the southern end of Parque Tres de Febrero, the largest stretch of open water in the park, ringed by rowing clubs and footpaths, is the Lago de Regatas.

It was built between 1906 and 1913, part of the landscape architect Carlos Thays' broader design for the whole park, with a job to do that had very little to do with scenery at first: containing the Maldonado creek, a waterway that had a habit of flooding this part of the city whenever the rains came. The solution was to dig and shape an artificial lake roughly ninety-two thousand square metres across and up to six metres deep, fed by piping running directly from the Río de la Plata rather than left to fill on its own.

The sporting side of things followed almost immediately. Rowing events and open-air festivals have been running along these banks since 1912, and the lake still does exactly that job today — rowing, kayaking, canoeing, and rented boats drifting across water that was originally commissioned to solve a drainage problem, not host a regatta.

And here's the thing: for well over a century, the people using this lake for sport have mostly had no reason to think about why it's actually here. A piece of civil engineering, built to keep a flooding creek under control, has spent generations quietly moonlighting as one of the nicer places in Buenos Aires to spend a Sunday afternoon.

If you fancy getting out on the water yourself, boat rental stands run along the near bank most weekends — worth doing at least once, if only to see the rowing clubs training up close.

tours.title: Cloud Gate (The Bean)
tours.shortDescription: A hundred and ten tons of polished steel with no front, no back, and you in it.
tours.longDescription: Anish Kapoor's Cloud Gate — sixty-six feet long, thirty-three feet high, around a hundred and ten tons — is built from a hundred and sixty-eight stainless steel plates welded together and then ground and polished until every seam vanished. Kapoor said he had been thinking about liquid mercury. It wasn't finished when Millennium Park opened: the plates were assembled inside a tent on this plaza, unveiled in 2004 with the welds still showing, then covered again for two more years of grinding before the dedication in 2006. What separates it from every other monument in the city is that it has no front — no facade, no correct angle, no way to look at it without also looking at yourself, the crowd, and the skyline over your shoulder. Underneath, the concave chamber called the omphalos folds the reflections into each other. The sculpture is a device for looking at a crowd, standing on ground that spent a century as a railyard and a parking lot.

Chicago argued for decades over what to put on this spot, which spent most of a century as a railyard and then a parking lot. What it ended up with is a mirror that does nothing at all unless people are standing in front of it.

Go ahead. Take the photo. You'll be in it, and so will several strangers, and that is the piece working precisely as designed.

tours.title: The Chicago Riverwalk at DuSable Bridge
tours.shortDescription: Two road decks, four stone towers, and a river that has run the wrong way since 1900.
tours.longDescription: The green water under the DuSable Bridge moves west — inland, away from Lake Michigan — because in 1900 Chicago reversed its own river. The city drank from the lake and emptied its sewage into the river that fed it, and the result was typhoid, repeatedly; engineers dug a canal southwest and dropped the river's level until it gave up and flowed backward toward the Mississippi. St. Louis sued. The bridge above opened in 1920, the first double-deck, double-leaf bascule of its kind, each leaf around three thousand four hundred tons and balanced so precisely that two modest motors can raise it. The four corner towers carry 1920s reliefs of the city's founding — including one that renders the removal of the Potawatomi, formalized by the 1833 Treaty of Chicago, as an adventure story, which it was not. The north end sits near the homestead of Jean Baptiste Point DuSable, the city's first permanent settler from outside the Native nations; the bridge took his name in 2010. The southwest tower opens as a small museum in the warm months.

stops.title: The Chicago Riverwalk at DuSable Bridge
stops.caption: In 1900, Chicago decided its river was running the wrong way, and changed it.
stops.transcriptText:
In 1900, Chicago decided its river was running the wrong way, and changed it.

You're on the DuSable Bridge, where Michigan Avenue crosses the Chicago River, or on the Riverwalk just below it. Two road decks, four stone towers at the corners, green water underneath moving west, inland, away from the lake.

Face the water.

That direction is the engineering. Chicago drank from Lake Michigan and emptied its sewage into this river, and this river ran into the lake. The result was typhoid, repeatedly. Rather than move the city or the lake, engineers dug a canal southwest and dropped the river's level until it gave up and flowed backward — away from Lake Michigan, down toward the Illinois River and eventually the Mississippi. St. Louis sued. The earth-moving methods worked out on that canal were later carried to Panama.

Now the bridge. It opened in 1920, the first of its kind: two decks, two leaves, each leaf weighing about three thousand four hundred tons and balanced so precisely that two modest motors can raise it. In the twenties it opened thousands of times a year for shipping. Now it opens a few dozen.

The four corner towers carry stone reliefs of scenes from the city's founding. One of them, on the northeast, celebrates the recovery from the fire. The one on the southwest depicts fighting at Fort Dearborn, which stood at this bridge's south end — carved in the nineteen twenties by sculptors who treated the removal of the Potawatomi from this land as an adventure story. It wasn't. The Treaty of Chicago of 1833 moved them west, and the ground you're standing on is the result.

The north end sits near the homestead of Jean Baptiste Point DuSable, a Black trader who was this place's first permanent settler from outside the Native nations. The bridge took his name in 2010, ninety years after it opened.

That southwest tower is a small museum in the warm months — five floors up from the gear room, if it's open when you pass.

A city that answers a public health crisis by reversing a river is a city that has decided geography is negotiable. Everything Chicago has done since follows from that.

tours.title: The Art Institute
tours.shortDescription: The lions arrived a year late, and the names on the pediment were carved before they were earned.
tours.longDescription: The limestone front on Michigan Avenue went up for the 1893 World's Columbian Exposition — the only fair structure built outside Jackson Park — and hosted the fair's lectures and congresses before the museum moved in at the end of the year. Edward Kemeys's bronze lions, more than two tons each, were installed in May 1894, a full year after the building opened; he described the north one as on the prowl and the south one as standing in defiance, and once you know that you can't unsee it. They have no names, and Chicago dresses them instead — wreaths in December, helmets when a team makes a run. The story that they were cast from World's Fair sculptures is a good one that doesn't survive checking. Behind the facade, commuter trains still run in a trench the museum has been extended over more than once — the Renzo Piano Modern Wing is the latest chapter. And the pediment's carved roll of great artists went up when the museum owned work by almost none of them: ambition first, collection afterward. The names never had to move.

Which isn't embarrassing. It's the most revealing thing on this facade: carve the ambition into the stone first, then go and earn it. They did earn it. The names never had to move.

tours.title: Willis Tower
tours.shortDescription: Nine square tubes bundled into one black tower that the whole city still calls Sears.
tours.longDescription: It isn't one tower — it's nine, bundled like a fistful of square straws, each about seventy-five feet across and tied into one block at the ground. Two stop at the fiftieth floor, two at the sixty-sixth, three around the ninetieth, and the last two carry on alone to the roof at fourteen hundred and fifty feet. That staircase silhouette isn't styling; it's tubes ending. The idea belonged to Fazlur Rahman Khan, a structural engineer born in Dhaka who spent his career at Skidmore, Owings and Merrill in Chicago: bundling the tubes let the building brace against the wind as one thick object rather than one tall thin one, which meant less steel, which meant more height for less money. Sears commissioned it, filled it, then left for the suburbs in the nineties; a London insurance broker bought the naming rights in 2009, and the city declined to update its vocabulary. It stood as the tallest building in the world for roughly twenty-five years, and Chicago is unusually relaxed about having lost the record — this is a place that invented the tall building and mostly just kept going.

tours.title: The Historic Water Tower
tours.shortDescription: There was never a tank up there — and it was not the only building to survive the fire.
tours.longDescription: The yellow limestone castle at Michigan and Chicago Avenues was built in 1869 to house a standpipe: a hundred and thirty-eight feet of iron pipe whose only job was to absorb the surges off the pumps across the street so the water mains wouldn't hammer themselves apart. The pipe came out in 1911; the spiral staircase that wrapped it is still inside. The famous story is slightly wrong in both directions. It was not the only building to survive the Great Fire of 1871 — several came through — but it was the only public building left standing inside the burned district, which is why people walked toward it afterward to work out where their houses had been. And the pumping station across the avenue, the building that actually mattered, failed on the night: its roof collapsed onto the pumps and took the city's water pressure with it. Oscar Wilde came through in 1882 and called the tower a castellated monstrosity with pepper boxes stuck all over it. Chicago kept it anyway. The pumping station is still pumping.

tours.title: The Wrigley Building & Tribune Tower
tours.shortDescription: A gum company dressed as a wedding cake, arguing across the avenue with a newspaper dressed as a cathedral.
tours.longDescription: William Wrigley Jr. built his glowing white tower between 1920 and 1924, when there were no major office buildings north of the river at all — the bridge wasn't even finished when they broke ground. Its terra cotta skin runs in graded shades of white, palest at the top, and it has been floodlit since it opened: a building designed, quite deliberately, to be an advertisement. Across Michigan Avenue, the Tribune ran an international competition for its headquarters in 1922 and more than two hundred entries came in; Howells and Hood won with the Gothic crown of stone buttresses you see today, while Eliel Saarinen's second-place entry — a clean stepped shaft with no historical costume — went on to shape American skyscrapers far more than the design that beat it. Embedded at eye level in the Tribune's base are around a hundred and fifty labeled fragments mailed home by correspondents: the Great Wall, the Parthenon, Westminster Abbey, the Taj Mahal, the Berlin Wall. The newspaper moved out in 2018 and the tower is apartments now. The stones stayed exactly where they were.

tours.title: Buckingham Fountain
tours.shortDescription: A portrait of Lake Michigan in pink marble, twice the size of the Versailles fountain it copies.
tours.longDescription: The fountain is a scale model of the lake sitting half a mile behind it: the pink marble basin is Lake Michigan, the stacked tiers are the water it holds, and the four groups of bronze sea horses — by the French sculptor Marcel Loyau — stand for the four states that touch it. Kate Buckingham paid for it in 1927, put her brother Clarence's name on it, and then left money for its upkeep so the city would never get to argue about maintaining it. The design came from Edward Bennett, co-author with Daniel Burnham of the 1909 Plan of Chicago, and he did not pick the spot casually: in that plan, roughly this point is the center of Chicago. Most of the plan never got built; the fountain marking the middle of it did. When it's running, the center jet reaches around a hundred and fifty feet, with a major display every hour for twenty minutes — and if the basin is dry, that's the calendar, not a failure, because this is a fountain in a city with real winters. The model was at Versailles; this one is about twice the size, which tells you most of what you need to know about the civic mood of the nineteen twenties.

tours.title: Marina City
tours.shortDescription: A janitors’ union financed the tallest apartment buildings in the world — corncobs with the parking on show.
tours.longDescription: The bottom nineteen floors of each round tower are an open spiral parking ramp, and nobody tried to hide it. Above the cars, the apartments start: each one a wedge radiating from the concrete core, opening onto a curved balcony — which is what gives the towers their scalloped edge and their nickname. Sixty-five floors, just under six hundred feet, and when they were finished in the mid-sixties they were both the tallest apartment buildings and the tallest reinforced-concrete structures anywhere. The part worth carrying away is who paid: a union of building janitors and elevator operators, talked out of building themselves a headquarters by the architect Bertrand Goldberg, who argued that if downtown emptied out at five o'clock the high-rises their members worked in would go dark and the jobs would go with them. Build apartments instead; keep people downtown. Goldberg had trained under Mies van der Rohe and then spent his career arguing with him — curves instead of boxes, concrete instead of steel. Look up at the balconies: chairs, plants, someone's laundry. People still live there. That was the whole idea.

tours.title: The Rookery
tours.shortDescription: Two carved rooks above the door remember the crow-filled temporary city hall this building replaced.
tours.longDescription: After the fire of 1871, the city put up a temporary city hall on this corner around an old water tank that had survived. Crows and pigeons moved into the walls, and Chicagoans started calling the place the rookery — partly for the birds, partly for the politicians underneath them. The owners of the grand replacement wanted a dignified name; the old one stuck, and John Root carved a rook into each side of the LaSalle Street arch so nobody could quietly forget why. Root and Daniel Burnham finished the building in 1888, and at its opening it was called the largest office building in the country. It sits on a floating foundation — iron rails laid in a crisscross grid and set in concrete, spreading the load across ground too soft for a normal footing, because Chicago is built on mud. The reason to step inside is the light court: a two-story room under glass that Frank Lloyd Wright remodeled in 1905, wrapping Root's ironwork in white marble with fine gold geometry — the only interior he ever did in downtown Chicago. The lobby is open to the public on weekdays and Saturday mornings; the Adams Street door is the one to use.

tours.title: Jay Pritzker Pavilion
tours.shortDescription: Legally a sculpture, acoustically a concert hall, and the lawn you sit on is a roof.
tours.longDescription: Frank Gehry's bandshell — a burst of curling stainless steel ribbons around a stage opening about a hundred and twenty feet high — opened in July 2004, and people have read the shape as sails, flames, a dropped ribbon, an exploded can. Gehry has been reliably unhelpful about settling it. The part worth understanding is the trellis: the lattice of steel pipes arching over the Great Lawn, some spans running more than four hundred feet, carries dozens of speakers positioned directly above the audience, so sound arrives on the grass at the same instant and volume as it reaches the front row. It is an attempt to build the acoustics of an indoor hall outdoors, with no walls. The lawn itself is a roof — three stories of parking sit under the grass, and the whole park is a deck over a working railyard. And officially, the pavilion is not a building at all: Grant Park has been legally protected against buildings since a notation on an 1836 map, so the city classified a hundred-and-twenty-foot bandshell as a work of art. Free concerts have run in this park since 1931, when the city started them during the Depression and never stopped.

If something's playing while you're here, don't go hunting for a seat. Sit down where you're standing. The lawn is the point.

tours.title: Navy Pier
tours.shortDescription: Half a mile out into the lake, where paddle-wheel aircraft carriers once trained eighteen thousand pilots.
tours.longDescription: The pier runs about three thousand feet east into Lake Michigan — when it opened in 1916 it stood on roughly twenty thousand wooden piles — and the far end is one of the few places you can stand off the coast of Chicago and read the city as a single object. It was built as freight infrastructure: the 1909 lakefront plan called for multiple piers and exactly one got built, a working cargo dock with a public promenade over the top. Then the wars took it. In 1942 the Navy needed to qualify carrier pilots and had no carriers to spare, so it bought two Great Lakes excursion steamers — side-wheel paddle boats with staterooms and a dance floor — cut everything off above the waterline and bolted flight decks on top. The Wolverine and the Sable docked here and steamed out every morning to launch and recover warplanes; around eighteen thousand pilots qualified over the lake, including a young naval aviator named George H. W. Bush. Everything built along the pier since — the Centennial Wheel, the ballroom, the theaters — faces back toward the city. The water is the reason any of it is here.

Then the wars took it.

In 1942 the Navy came back, and what it did with the lake is hard to believe standing next to it. It needed to qualify carrier pilots and had no carriers to spare, so it bought two Great Lakes excursion steamers — side-wheel paddle boats with staterooms and a dance floor — cut everything off above the waterline and bolted flight decks on top. The Wolverine and the Sable, docked right here. Every morning they steamed a mile out and spent the day launching and recovering warplanes, pilots flying with their cockpits open in case they went into the water. Around eighteen thousand qualified out there, including a young naval aviator named George H. W. Bush. Drivers on Lake Shore Drive pulled over to watch.

The Navy chose Lake Michigan because it was big enough to behave like an ocean and quiet enough to be a classroom. That is what this pier is actually for. Everything built along it — the wheel, the shops, the theater — faces back toward the city. The water behind you is the reason any of it is here.

So give it a minute before you walk back. Weather comes off that lake and decides what kind of day Chicago is having, and the end of the pier is the closest you get to asking it directly.

tours.title: The Michigan Avenue Streetwall
tours.shortDescription: One of the great streets of America has only one wall — a sentence from 1836 keeps it that way.
tours.longDescription: Every other great commercial street in the country has two walls of buildings. Michigan Avenue has one: a continuous cliff of facades on the west — different decades, wildly different intentions, all holding one straight line at the sidewalk — and on the east nothing but park and then the lake. That isn't taste; it's law. In 1836, canal commissioners selling lots wrote a note on their map that the ground east of the avenue was to remain public, forever open, clear and free of any buildings or other obstructions whatever. It was a sales pitch — the lots fetched more with a guaranteed view — and it became one of the most consequential sentences ever written about an American city. It held because somebody made it hold: starting in 1890, Aaron Montgomery Ward, who ran a mail-order empire from this street, sued the city again and again to keep structures out of Grant Park, winning four times at the Illinois Supreme Court and blocking a museum, a library, an armory and a circus. The ground itself is an invention too — the avenue was the shoreline, and everything east of it is fill. The view is not a design achievement. It is a legal one.

stops.title: The Michigan Avenue Streetwall

Worth knowing that the ground under your feet isn't original either. Michigan Avenue was the shoreline. Everything east of it is made land, filled in over decades with whatever the city had to hand, a great deal of it rubble. Chicago moved the lake in order to build the park that the law says can't be built on.

The promise held because somebody made it hold. His name is on almost none of it. The park you're standing in belongs to somebody else entirely.

tours.title: The Chicago Cultural Center
tours.shortDescription: England’s condolence library became the People’s Palace, under the largest Tiffany dome anywhere.
tours.longDescription: After the fire of 1871 burned something like two million books out of Chicago, a London collection organized by Thomas Hughes — the author of Tom Brown's School Days — sent roughly eight thousand volumes across the Atlantic, with donations from Queen Victoria, Disraeli, Tennyson, Darwin and John Stuart Mill. Chicago had no public library to put them in, so it started one, in a round iron water tank that had survived the fire. Twenty-five years later the city built this gray classical block to hold it. Up the mosaic staircase from the Washington Street lobby, Preston Bradley Hall carries a dome about thirty-eight feet across holding roughly thirty thousand pieces of glass — Tiffany work, restored in 2008, generally called the largest Tiffany dome anywhere. The Randolph Street half of the building was built for the Grand Army of the Republic, the Union veterans of the Civil War, who kept a hall and memorial room here: two institutions, one roof. When the library moved out in the nineteen seventies the city could have sold the building. It kept it open and free instead — admission has never cost anything — and Chicagoans have called it the People's Palace ever since.

stops.title: The Chicago Cultural Center

tours.title: Daley Plaza & the Picasso
tours.shortDescription: Picasso never titled it, never explained it, never saw it — and Chicago kept it anyway.
tours.longDescription: Fifty feet tall, a hundred and sixty-two tons of steel, and nobody has ever been able to say what it is. Picasso was asked for a sculpture in 1963, sent a model, turned down the hundred-thousand-dollar fee, and described the work as a gift to the people of Chicago — a city he never visited, in a country he never set foot in. It was fabricated at the steel works in Gary, Indiana, and unveiled in August 1967 in front of a very large and largely unimpressed crowd; guesses have run from a woman to a bird to an Egyptian god, and Picasso later suggested it had something to do with his Afghan hound. That is as settled as it gets. Behind it stands the tower it was made for: the Daley Center, mostly courtrooms, six hundred and forty-eight feet tall with only thirty-one floors because courtrooms need the height, designed by Jacques Brownson, who studied under Mies van der Rohe. Both tower and sculpture are Cor-Ten steel, engineered to rust into their own protective skin — the color is the finish. Watch the base for a minute: the lower slope is worn smooth, because for almost sixty years Chicago kids have used the most argued-about artwork in the city as a slide.

tours.title: The Monadnock Building
tours.shortDescription: Six feet of brick at the base — the last building that walls were ever asked to hold up.
tours.longDescription: The north half of the Monadnock, finished by Burnham and Root in 1891, has no frame inside it. The brick is the structure: about six feet thick at the base, tapering to roughly eighteen inches by the sixteenth floor, the wall doing all the work the way walls had done it for six thousand years. It is generally called the tallest load-bearing masonry office building ever built, and that is less a boast than a ceiling — any taller and the ground floor would have been all wall and no room. The Boston investors insisted on no ornament at all, which frustrated John Root until it didn't; what he came back with is closer to an Egyptian pylon than a Victorian office block, and Louis Sullivan called it a cliff of brickwork. Root died that January, forty-one, with the building still going up. Then walk south along the block: two years later the southern half arrived — Holabird and Roche, same color, same profile, and behind the face a steel skeleton carrying everything. On one block, in two years, the wall stopped holding buildings up. Every tall building since sits on the south side of that line. The doorways step down below the sidewalk because it has been settling into the mud since the day it opened.

tours.title: LaSalle Canyon & the Board of Trade
tours.shortDescription: A faceless goddess of grain closes the canyon where the first skyscraper is said to have stood.
tours.longDescription: Look south down LaSalle and the street ends in a single Art Deco tower: the Chicago Board of Trade, 1930, six hundred and five feet and the tallest building in Chicago until 1965. On its very top stands Ceres, Roman goddess of grain — thirty-one feet of aluminum with no face. The usual story is that the sculptor assumed nothing taller would ever rise nearby; what John Storrs actually said was simpler, that from the street she would read as a silhouette, so he suggested the features rather than carving them. Under her, grain and livestock futures were traded by shouting, in tiered pits, by people in colored jackets — a market in wheat that didn't exist yet, grown on land most of the traders had never seen. At the canyon's other end, on the northeast corner of LaSalle and Adams, stood the Home Insurance Building of 1885, widely called the first skyscraper — historians have argued the point for a hundred years — and demolished in 1931 for the taller building standing there now. The street that invented, or nearly invented, the office tower is now quietly converting several of them into apartments: a canyon built for money, turning into somewhere people sleep.

Now turn around and look north to the corner of LaSalle and Adams. tours.title: Merchandise Mart
tours.shortDescription: The largest building in the world for thirteen years, with its own postal code until 2008.
tours.longDescription: Marshall Field's company put up the Mart in 1930 as a wholesale market on a simple theory: instead of buyers traveling to a hundred scattered showrooms, build one roof and make the whole trade come to you. Roughly four million square feet of floor, two full city blocks along the river, big enough to hold the world record for size until the Pentagon opened in 1943 and to keep its own postal code until 2008. It is built over a railyard with the city's freight tunnels running underneath, so goods arrived below the floor and went straight up — a piece of infrastructure wearing a limestone Art Deco facade. The Kennedy family bought it in 1945 and held it for decades; Joseph Kennedy lined the riverfront with bronze busts of American merchants, Marshall Field and Aaron Montgomery Ward among them. For most of its life the building was badge-only, buyers only. That has loosened — the lower floors open on weekdays now, and the riverfront below is public space. After dark, in season, the river face becomes the screen for Art on the Mart: dozens of projectors throwing contemporary artwork across two and a half acres of stone, billed as the largest permanent digital art projection anywhere.

Marshall Field's company put it up in 1930 as a wholesale market — the idea being that instead of buyers traveling around to a hundred scattered showrooms, you build one roof and make the whole trade come to you. The Kennedy family bought it in 1945 and held it for decades. Joseph Kennedy lined the riverfront with bronze busts of American merchants on tall pedestals — Marshall Field among them, and Aaron Montgomery Ward, who is a complicated figure to memorialize outside a building this large.

Which is a strange second act. The biggest building on earth spent its first life as a machine for moving furniture, and spends its evenings now being famous for its surface.

tours.title: North Avenue Beach
tours.shortDescription: A concrete ocean liner that has never sailed, moored on a shoreline the city manufactured.
tours.longDescription: The blue-and-white steamer at the water's edge — portholes, stacked decks, a bridge and a mast — is a building, made of concrete, and it is not going anywhere. The original beach house was a Works Progress Administration job finished in 1940, designed by Park District architect Emanuel Buchsbaum in the Art Moderne style; when the wooden frame rotted out after sixty years, the city rebuilt it slightly larger in concrete, doing the same work the first one did — lifeguards, showers, chair rentals, somewhere to buy something fried. The sand is an invention too: the same Depression-era program pushed something over eight hundred thousand square feet of new shoreline into the lake. South along the path stands the Chess Pavilion of 1957 — twenty boards set into concrete tiers, a five-foot limestone king and queen at either end, sculpture by Boris Gilbertson, paid for by Laurens Hammond of the Hammond organ, who liked to play chess at this beach and thought there ought to be a proper place to do it around the clock. Everywhere else Chicago is making an argument; here it parked a ship that cannot sail on a coastline it built, and the skyline's whole job is to be the view behind somebody's volleyball game.

stops.title: North Avenue Beach
stops.caption: The ship in front of you has never been anywhere. Come down onto the sand south of the beach house, so you are looking back at it with the lake on your left and downtown off to your right.

The sand is an invention too. This beach came out of the same Depression-era program: something over eight hundred thousand square feet of new shoreline pushed into the lake, running north from here to Fullerton.

Now look south along the path, past the volleyball nets, for a low concrete wing hanging over a row of stone tables. That is the Chess Pavilion, from 1957. Twenty boards set into concrete on three tiers, a five-foot limestone king and queen standing at either end, bishops and knights carved into the walls — sculpture by Boris Gilbertson, architecture by Maurice Webster, paid for by Laurens Hammond, the man behind the Hammond organ, who liked to play chess at this beach and thought there ought to be a proper place to do it around the clock.

Which is the thing about this stretch. Everywhere else, Chicago is making an argument — about height, about money, about permanence, about who got there first. Stay a while if you have it. The lake runs colder than it looks well into the summer, and the wind off it will tell you what kind of day you are actually having.

tours.title: Old Town & St Michael’s
tours.shortDescription: The church that burned to its walls, in the neighborhood that marched for the right to rebuild in wood.
tours.longDescription: St. Michael's was finished in 1869 by a German parish on land given by the brewer Michael Diversey, and its tower made it the tallest building in Chicago. Two years later the fire came north: the parishioners packed what they could into an oxcart, and by morning the roof, the interior and the bells were gone — but the walls stood, and the new church went up inside them, rededicated almost two years to the day. The houses around it tell the half of the story downtown doesn't. In January 1872, with parts of the city still smoldering, thousands of German and Irish North Siders marched on City Hall against a proposed ban on wooden buildings — brick cost more than these families had, so a ban meant selling the lot and leaving. They carried signs reading “Leave a home for the laborer,” and they won; the ban only passed city-wide after a second fire in 1874. The small wooden houses of Old Town sit inside that two-and-a-half-year window. Downtown answered the fire with steel and height. This is the same refusal from underneath — a neighborhood rebuilding itself in pine because that was what it could afford.

stops.caption: It is January of 1872, and the ground under this neighborhood is still warm.

Stand at the corner of Cleveland Avenue and Eugenie Street with the church on your side — red brick, a steeple running up past everything around it. This is St. Michael's. Back off far enough to take in the whole front at once.

Start with the walls.

When it went up, its tower made it the tallest building in Chicago. Two years later the fire came north. The priests and parishioners packed what they could into an oxcart and left, and it took the roof, the interior, every parish building. What stood the next morning was the walls — the tower gone, the bells melted together in the wreckage.

Rebuilding began inside the week; the new church went up inside the old walls and was rededicated in October of 1873, almost two years to the day.

Now look past the church at the houses. Small, wooden, close together.

There is a reason for that, and it is the half of the story downtown does not tell. In January of 1872, with parts of Chicago still smoldering, thousands of German and Irish North Siders marched on City Hall to fight a proposed ban on building in wood. Both sides had a case: the city had just burned down, and brick cost more than these families had, so a ban meant selling the lot at a loss and leaving. They carried signs reading "Leave a home for the laborer." They won. The code that passed weeks later changed almost nothing, and wood kept going up until the summer of 1874, when a second bad fire pushed the ban through city-wide.

Which means the wooden houses around you sit inside a window about two and a half years wide.

Downtown gives you the version where Chicago answers the fire with steel and height and nerve. This is the same refusal from underneath — a neighborhood that had just watched everything it owned burn, marching for the right to rebuild it out of pine.

One last thing, if you have the legs. Five blocks north on Hudson Avenue a small wooden cottage came through the fire standing, saved by a policeman named Bellinger who tore up the sidewalk out front and soaked the place down as it went past. The cider he supposedly used is a legend — his widow said so herself, forty years on, and it stuck anyway. The cottage is credited to William Boyington, who also built the Water Tower: one architect, two survivors, one limestone and one boards.

tours.title: Museum Campus
tours.shortDescription: Three century-old institutions became one campus when the city moved a highway out from between them.
tours.longDescription: From the point beside the Adler Planetarium, three buildings line up along the harbor. The Field Museum opened here in 1921 after a quarter century in a leftover world's fair building down in Jackson Park. The Shedd Aquarium followed in 1930 — to fill it, twenty insulated railroad tank cars ran eight round trips to Key West hauling back a million gallons of ocean water, because nobody had tried a serious saltwater aquarium a thousand miles inland. And the twelve-sided Adler opened the same year as the first planetarium in the Western Hemisphere, paid for by the Sears executive Max Adler, who had seen one in Munich and decided Chicago should have the next. The odd part is what never got built: for seventy years these three sat on the same stretch of lakefront and were not one place, because eight lanes of Lake Shore Drive ran between them. In 1998 the city shifted the northbound lanes a few hundred feet west and laid park over the old roadbed, and three institutions became a campus without a single new structure. Chicago's instinct is to add; this is the rare case of the city improving a place by taking something out of it. The view from the point is the angle the postcards use.

stops.transcriptText:
Three of the buildings around you are about a century old. The place they are standing in is not yet thirty.

Work your way out to the point beside the Adler Planetarium — the low round one at the far end of the drive — and stand where the walkway curves and the harbor opens up. Lake at your back, city in front of you, the boats of Monroe Harbor filling the water in between.

Pick out the three.

Furthest north, the long white one with the row of columns is the Field Museum, opened in 1921. It did not start here. For its first quarter century the collection lived down in Jackson Park inside a leftover building from the 1893 world's fair, and this Greek temple is the permanent home it eventually built for itself.

South of that, the white marble box with the wave shapes running along its roofline is the Shedd Aquarium, 1930, by Graham, Anderson, Probst and White — the same firm behind the Wrigley Building and the Merchandise Mart. To fill it, twenty insulated railroad tank cars ran eight round trips down to Key West and hauled back a million gallons of ocean water, because nobody had tried a serious saltwater aquarium a thousand miles inland before.

And the twelve-sided one you are standing beside opened that same year: the first planetarium in the Western Hemisphere, paid for by a Sears executive named Max Adler, who had seen one in Munich and decided Chicago should have the next. It opened on his birthday.

The odd part is what was never built. For seventy years those three buildings sat on the same piece of lakefront and were not one place, because eight lanes of Lake Shore Drive ran between them. In 1998 the city shifted the northbound lanes a few hundred feet west and laid park over the old roadbed, and three institutions became a campus without a single new structure going up.

Chicago's instinct, nearly everywhere else you have stood on this trip, is to add — another floor, another tower, another wing. This is the rare case of the city improving a place by taking something out of it.

Give the skyline a minute from here before you go in. This is the angle the postcards use, and the reason you can stand still and look at it is that somebody moved a highway.

tours.title: Chinatown & Ping Tom
tours.shortDescription: A city hall designed from a library book, and a park the neighborhood went out and bought for itself.
tours.longDescription: The Pui Tak Center on Wentworth — two pagoda-topped towers, open balconies, green and gold dragons in glazed terra cotta — was built in 1928 as the On Leong Merchants Association Building and has been known here for a century as Chinatown's city hall. Christian Michaelsen and Sigurd Rognstad, sons of Norwegian immigrants, got the commission because the exclusion laws had ensured no architect of Chinese descent was licensed to practice in Illinois; they tracked down a German scholar's book on Chinese architecture and worked from the plates, and the terra cotta was fired by an Illinois pottery better known for garden vases. The neighborhood took to it immediately. The gate up the street is younger — 1975, four hand-painted characters reading roughly “the world is for all” — and Chinatown has since expanded past its own front door. By the river, Ping Tom Memorial Park sits on a dead rail yard that a businessman from the neighborhood assembled a private firm to buy, after the Dan Ryan Expressway took both of Chinatown's parks in 1962. Twice, the same shape: something this neighborhood wanted, wasn't handed, and arranged for itself — once with a library book, once with a land purchase. It is one of the few Chinatowns in the country still gaining people.

stops.title: Chinatown & Ping Tom
stops.caption: Two Norwegian-American architects who had never set foot in China designed the building that has stood for Chinatown for almost a hundred years.
stops.transcriptText:
Two Norwegian-American architects who had never set foot in China designed the building that has stood for Chinatown for almost a hundred years.

You should be on Wentworth Avenue a block or so south of Cermak, the tiled gate behind you. Ahead on your left, at twenty-two sixteen, a three-story building faced entirely in glazed terra cotta: two pagoda-topped towers, open balconies across the upper floors, green and gold dragons worked into the tile. That's the Pui Tak Center, built in 1928 as the On Leong Merchants Association Building, and known here for a century as Chinatown's city hall.

Christian Michaelsen and Sigurd Rognstad, sons of Norwegian immigrants, got the commission because no architect of Chinese descent was licensed to practice in Illinois — the exclusion laws had closed that door along with most others. So they took the job, tracked down a German scholar's book on Chinese architecture, and worked from the plates. The terra cotta was fired by an Illinois pottery better known for garden vases. A Chicago meeting hall in a skin copied from photographs, and the neighborhood took to it immediately.

The gate is younger — 1975, four characters hand-painted onto the tile that translate roughly as "the world is for all." When it went up it marked the actual edge of the neighborhood; it doesn't now. Chinatown kept expanding and left its own front door somewhere in the middle.

A few blocks northwest, where the streets run out at the river, there's a park with a red pagoda. Chinatown had two parks until 1962, when the Dan Ryan Expressway took both, and for nearly thirty years afterward it had almost none. Ping Tom, a businessman from here, assembled a private firm and bought a dead rail yard along the water. The park carries his name because he died four years before it opened.

Two moments, forty years apart, the same shape to both: something this neighborhood wanted, wasn't handed, and went and arranged for itself — once with a library book, once with a land purchase. Probably part of why this is one of the few Chinatowns in the country still gaining people rather than losing them. Stay a minute and look at the tile. Copied from a book by two men from Norway, fired in an Illinois kiln, and it has been the face of this place longer than almost anyone on this street has been alive.

tours.title: Pilsen & 18th Street
tours.shortDescription: Czech cornices above, Mexican murals below — one street painted by two migrations.
tours.longDescription: Eighteenth Street runs west about two miles, and for most of it the buildings are a century older than the paint on them. Up high: brick, carved limestone, cornices in what Chicago calls Bohemian Baroque — Old World ornament executed in Illinois brick by Czechs who arrived after the fire of 1871, in a neighborhood that took its name from a restaurant called At the City of Plzeň. At Eighteenth and Allport stands Thalia Hall, 1892, built by the saloonkeeper John Dusek so his neighbors could have theater in their own language, its hall modeled on the opera house in Prague — closed in the 1960s, untouched for fifty years, a working music venue again now. Lower down, on side walls and under viaducts: paint. Mexican families began arriving in the fifties and sixties, many displaced when the University of Illinois built its campus, and the murals started in the late sixties. At the Eighteenth Street station, the schoolteacher Francisco Mendoza spent years painting the platforms with his students; when part of it was mistakenly painted over in 2019, a Pilsen muralist approved by his family put it back. Repainting is the normal life cycle of a mural here — whatever you're standing in front of is the current version, and the wall will outlast it.

stops.title: Pilsen & 18th Street
stops.caption: Eighteenth Street runs west about two miles, and for most of it the buildings are a century older than the paint on them.
stops.transcriptText:
Eighteenth Street runs west about two miles, and for most of it the buildings are a century older than the paint on them.

You should be on Eighteenth somewhere between Halsted and Ashland, storefronts on both sides. Above the ground floor: brick, carved limestone over the windows, cornices with scrolls and steps and small pediments. Lower down — side walls, gaps between buildings, under the viaducts — paint. Almost everything up high is Czech. Almost everything painted is Mexican.

So.

The name came from a restaurant. Czechs arrived in numbers after the fire of 1871, when the factories were hiring, and one of them opened a place called At the City of Plzeň, after the Bohemian city he had left. Those cornices are what Chicago calls Bohemian Baroque — Old World ornament executed in Illinois brick, by people building themselves a version of somewhere else.
