At Eighteenth and Allport, heavy stone, an arched entrance, a carved face peering out of the foliage above the door. Thalia Hall, 1892, put up by a saloonkeeper named John Dusek who wanted his neighbors to have theater in their own language; the hall inside was modeled on the opera house in Prague. Closed in the 1960s, untouched for fifty years, a working music venue again now.

Mexican families began arriving in the fifties and sixties, many pushed out of the Near West Side when the University of Illinois built its campus there. The murals started in the late sixties. At the Eighteenth Street station, a schoolteacher named Francisco Mendoza spent years painting the platforms and stairwells with his students. In 2019 a crew removing graffiti painted over part of the work; after the neighborhood objected, the transit authority brought in a Pilsen muralist, Roberto Valadez, approved by Mendoza's family, and he put it back.

Repainting is the normal life cycle of a mural here, not the exception. In 2018 the city proposed protecting the district by law — the buildings, and, in a first for Chicago, the murals too. Preservationists called it the only real defense against demolition; residents said it would cost them more than they could carry. In 2020 the council committee voted it down, unanimously. So the paint survives the way it always has: somebody redoes it. Whatever you're standing in front of is the current version; the wall will outlast it. Give it a minute anyway. The people who painted it knew that too.

tours.title: Robie House
tours.shortDescription: No front door on the front: Wright’s horizontal masterpiece began as one man’s privacy problem.
tours.longDescription: Frank Lloyd Wright drew it in 1908 and finished it in 1910, and the eaves are the entire argument: everything pulled sideways, nothing rising, the roof reaching about twenty feet past its own support — which in 1910 read less as elegant than as impossible, on a street of tall narrow houses that all did the opposite. Frederick Robie was twenty-eight, an engineer who made bicycle and motorcycle parts, and his requirements were specific: fireproof, no boxed-off rooms, a garage, and — his words — no conglomeration of doo-dads. He also wanted to look out at the neighborhood without the neighborhood looking back in, and that requirement is why the house is shaped this way: the living floor raised a level, the glass run high, the eaves cutting every sightline from the street, the entrance folded around the side behind a wall. The horizontal line architects copied for fifty years began as a privacy problem, solved exactly. Robie lived here about a year before the family business failed. A seminary later used it as a dormitory and twice announced demolition, in 1941 and 1957; Wright turned up to fight for it both times — the only building he ever did that for. The interior is restored to 1910 and guided tours run most days, but the sidewalk is where the argument happens.

stops.title: Robie House
stops.caption: There is no front door on the front of this house. You should be at the corner of Woodlawn Avenue and Fifty-Eighth Street, the long side of the house running away from you down Woodlawn.
stops.transcriptText:
There is no front door on the front of this house.

You should be at the corner of Woodlawn Avenue and Fifty-Eighth Street, the long side of the house running away from you down Woodlawn. Brick in narrow courses, limestone sills carrying the whole length, and a roof that pushes out past the wall about twenty feet with nothing underneath holding it up. Bands of art glass instead of separate windows. What you won't find, from anywhere on this sidewalk, is a way in.

Start with the roofline.

Frank Lloyd Wright drew this in 1908 and it was finished in 1910, and the eaves are the entire argument. Everything is pulled sideways, nothing rises, and the roof reaches twenty feet past its own support — which in 1910 read less as elegant than as impossible, on a street of tall narrow houses that all did the opposite.

Frederick Robie was twenty-eight, an engineer who made bicycle and motorcycle parts. His requirements were specific: fireproof, no boxed-off rooms, a garage, a playroom for the children, and — his words — no conglomeration of doo-dads. He also wanted to be able to look out at the neighborhood without the neighborhood looking back in.

The last requirement is why the house is shaped the way it is. The living floor sits raised a level, the glass runs high, the eaves cut every sightline from the street, and the entrance is folded around the side behind a wall. The horizontal line that architects copied for the next fifty years began as one man's privacy problem, solved exactly.

Robie lived here about a year. His father died, the business went with him, and he sold. By 1926 a theological seminary owned it and was using it as a dormitory, and twice — in 1941, then again in 1957 — announced plans to pull it down. Wright turned up to fight for it both times. It is the only one of his buildings he ever did that for.

The interior has since been taken back to its 1910 condition, and guided tours run most days in small groups, booked ahead. The sidewalk, though, is where the argument actually happens; this thing was built to be seen from exactly where you're standing. Walk the length of it down Woodlawn. You'll get everything Wright wanted you to have and nothing Robie didn't.

tours.title: Griffin Museum of Science and Industry
tours.shortDescription: The last building of the White City stands because a lender demanded a guarantee in writing.
tours.longDescription: In 1893 the World's Columbian Exposition raised some two hundred buildings in Jackson Park, nearly all of them shells of staff — plaster of Paris, hemp fiber and glue troweled over wood — painted white and never intended to see a second winter. This one was the exception, for one unsentimental reason: as the fair's Palace of Fine Arts it would hold borrowed masterworks, and the museums lending them refused to send anything into a plaster shed. So Charles Atwood put steel and brick underneath and plastered over it to match the neighbors. The fair was designed to be thrown away, and the only piece left standing where it was built is the piece somebody demanded a guarantee on. It housed the Field Museum until 1920, then sat empty and came apart — Louis Sullivan argued it should be cleared — until Julius Rosenwald, who ran Sears, took the park commissioners to Germany to show them what a science museum could be, put up several million dollars, and had the crumbling plaster recut in limestone. The museum opened in 1933; Rosenwald insisted his name stay off it. Every column and figure on the front is a nineteen-thirties replacement, but the bones behind them are the last of the White City.

stops.title: Griffin Museum of Science and Industry
stops.caption: It's 1893, and everything around you is white, enormous, and temporary.
stops.transcriptText:
It's 1893, and everything around you is white, enormous, and temporary.

You should be on the north side of the building, out on the lawn, looking up at the long front — a rank of columns, a dome over the center, carved figures along the roofline, all of it pale stone. Behind you, Jackson Park: lagoons, a wooded island, the lake through the trees. Frederick Law Olmsted laid that ground out. This is the Griffin Museum of Science and Industry now, and it is the last building of the World's Columbian Exposition still standing where it was built.

Now.

Twenty-two years after the Great Chicago Fire, the city put on the fair here — roughly two hundred buildings, most of them shaped by Daniel Burnham's office, all of them painted white, which is where the nickname came from. The White City. The walls were a material called staff: plaster of Paris, hemp fiber and glue, troweled over wood and steel. Fast to raise, cheap to demolish, and not intended to see a second winter.

This building was the exception, for one reason. As the Palace of Fine Arts it was going to hold borrowed masterworks, and the museums lending them refused to send anything into a plaster shed. So Charles Atwood put a steel-and-brick structure underneath, then plastered over it to match the neighbors.

The fair was designed to be thrown away. The only piece of it left is the piece nobody was willing to gamble on — and it stands not because anyone judged it the finest building on the grounds, but because a lender in another city wanted a guarantee in writing.

It housed the Field Museum until 1920, then sat empty and came apart. Louis Sullivan, among others, argued it should be cleared. Julius Rosenwald, who ran Sears, disagreed; he took the park commissioners to Germany to show them what a science museum could be, put up several million dollars, and had the crumbling plaster recut in limestone. The museum opened in 1933. He insisted his name stay off it.

Every column and every figure up there is a replacement, carved in the nineteen-thirties. But the bones behind them — the steel and brick that only exist because somebody demanded a guarantee — are the last of the White City, and they have been holding this front up for well over a century.

tours.title: Obama Presidential Center
tours.shortDescription: A 225-foot tower with a speech cut clean through its stone, open since June 2026.
tours.longDescription: The tower at the edge of Jackson Park — stone-clad, square, wider at the top than at the bottom — opened in June 2026, eleven years after it was announced. Tod Williams and Billie Tsien designed it: two hundred twenty-five feet, eight floors, the museum stacked upward so the campus could stay mostly open ground, with a forum, an athletic building and a branch of the Chicago Public Library pressed low into Michael Van Valkenburgh's twenty acres of landscape around John Lewis Plaza. The surface is the part worth standing still for. Text from the speech Obama gave at Selma in 2015 is carved into the stone with the letters cut clean through, so daylight enters the galleries as words, and near the top a room frames the South Side through the sentences. The eleven-year gap holds federal review and litigation — this is a public park on the National Register, and the siting was argued in court for years while neighbors pressed for guarantees on housing costs. Presidential libraries usually go up at a polite distance from ordinary life; this one went into the park at the end of the Midway, a few streets from where the family lived, with no perimeter and the lawn running up to the building.

stops.title: Obama Presidential Center
stops.caption: This is the Obama Presidential Center. It opened in June of 2026, eleven years after it was announced.
stops.transcriptText:
This is the Obama Presidential Center. It opened in June of 2026, eleven years after it was announced.

You should be at the western edge of Jackson Park, near where the Midway runs out, with the tower ahead of you: stone-clad, square, and wider at the top than at the bottom. Around its base, low buildings pressed down into the landscape — a forum, an athletic building, a branch of the Chicago Public Library — and between them, John Lewis Plaza. The Griffin Museum is a few blocks north of here.

Tod Williams and Billie Tsien designed the tower. Two hundred twenty-five feet, eight floors, the museum stacked upward so the campus could stay mostly open ground rather than mostly building. Michael Van Valkenburgh laid out the landscape across roughly twenty acres. Gardens, lawn, a play area, walking ground.

The surface of the tower is the part worth standing still for. Text from a speech Obama gave at Selma in 2015 is carved into the stone, and the letters are cut clean through, so daylight enters the galleries as words. Near the top there's a room where the South Side is framed through the sentences.

Eleven years. Announced in 2015, supposed to open in 2021, ground broken instead that year — and what sits in the gap is federal review and litigation, because this is a public park on the National Register of Historic Places. Preservationists argued that parkland is not a site to be given away, whoever the recipient. Others in the neighborhood argued the South Side had waited long enough for investment of this size, and pressed instead for guarantees on housing costs. The courts allowed construction. The arguments have not entirely stopped, and standing here you are standing in the middle of them.

Presidential libraries usually go up on a donated parcel or a university campus, at a polite distance from ordinary life. This one went into the park at the end of the Midway, a few streets from where the family lived. Whatever you make of that, it is the more difficult choice, and it is legible from where you're standing: no plaza of separation, no perimeter, the lawn simply running up to the building. Give the lettering a minute. The light moves through it all day, so the wall you're looking at is not the wall that was here this morning.

tours.title: The Riverwalk
tours.shortDescription: A mile and a quarter along the south bank, where every stop is a decision about water.
tours.longDescription: Lake Street to the lakefront along the south bank of the main branch, passing underneath every bridge instead of climbing back to the street — which is the whole trick of the Riverwalk. One idea holds the five stops together: everything here is a decision about water — which way it goes, how high it sits, what gets built on top of it, who may cross it and when. None of it is natural. The walk starts at the fork where the city began, looks across at Wolf Point and the Merchandise Mart, pauses at the Eastland site for the one quiet remembrance this catalog gives it, reads Marina City's corncob towers from the water they were designed around, passes under the DuSable Bridge among the counterweights and trunnions that swing three-thousand-ton leaves, and ends where the Chicago Harbor Lock lets the lake in — the gate that keeps a river running inland, away from the lake, because that is what was decided in 1900 and it is still being enforced this morning.

stops.title: The Lake Street stairway
stops.caption: A mile and a quarter, a staircase at every bridge, and a river that has been running the wrong way on purpose since 1900.
stops.transcriptText:
A mile and a quarter, a staircase at every bridge, and a river that has been running the wrong way on purpose since 1900.

You're at the top of the Lake Street stairway, at the west end of the Chicago Riverwalk. Below you the path runs east along the south bank of the river, all the way to Lake Michigan. It's free, it's open from early morning until late, and it passes underneath every bridge instead of making you climb back up to the street, which is the whole trick of the thing.

The honest version: getting down and getting out is stairs — Franklin, Wells, LaSalle, Clark, State, Wabash, Michigan. Between fall and spring most of the boats and the food and the noise go away. Twenty minutes if you march it. We're going to take considerably longer.

One idea holds this walk together. Every stop on it is a decision about water: which way it goes, how high it sits, what gets built on top of it, who is allowed to cross it and when. None of that is natural. All of it was decided by somebody, usually in an argument, and most of those decisions are still being enforced this morning.

We start at the fork where the city began and finish at the gate where the lake is let in.

Go down the stairs, put the river on your left, and walk east until a long limestone building fills the far bank. First stop: Wolf Point and the Merchandise Mart.

stops.title: Wolf Point & the Merchandise Mart
stops.caption: Two ocean basins nearly touch about six miles southwest of here, and that near-miss is the only reason there's a city on this spot.
stops.transcriptText:
Two ocean basins nearly touch about six miles southwest of here, and that near-miss is the only reason there's a city on this spot.

Look across the water and slightly left, where the river splits into three. The blunt point of land in the middle, with glass towers standing on it now, is Wolf Point — site of Chicago's first hotel, and of the first bridges anyone threw across this river.

Why here? Because of the gap. Southwest of the city, past a marsh the early settlers called Mud Lake, the land rises a few feet and then everything changes its mind: water on one side drains east toward the Atlantic, water on the other runs south to the Gulf of Mexico. The rise was so slight that in a wet season the two systems joined and you could paddle straight through, and in a dry one you got out and carried the canoe about a mile and a half. That route had been in use for centuries before the first Europeans were shown it in 1673.

Now look right, at the limestone.

The Merchandise Mart, 1930, by Graham, Anderson, Probst and White — four million square feet, and the largest building in the world when it opened. Marshall Field's built it to pull thirteen scattered wholesale warehouses under one roof, and the company president who pushed hardest for it was also chairman of the Chicago Plan Commission, so the man who wanted the riverfront to look better was chairing the body in charge of making it look better.

A portage is a place you pass through. Less than a century after a canal replaced the carrying, the largest building on earth was parked where people used to hurry past.

Keep going east, under Wells and under LaSalle, to the marker set in near the corner of LaSalle and Wacker: the Eastland.

stops.title: The Eastland
stops.caption: You should be on the wide stone steps between the LaSalle Street bridge and the Clark Street bridge, water in front of you.
stops.transcriptText:
You should be on the wide stone steps between the LaSalle Street bridge and the Clark Street bridge, water in front of you. The marker is set in the ground up at the corner of LaSalle and Wacker.

On a Saturday morning in July 1915, the excursion steamer Eastland was tied up at the dock along this stretch, loading more than two thousand people. Factory workers and their families from the Western Electric plant out in Cicero, going across the lake for the annual company picnic.

The ship never left the dock. It rolled onto its side while still tied up, a short distance from the wall you're standing on. It remains the worst maritime disaster in the history of the Great Lakes.

For most of the century afterward, almost nothing here said so. The first memorial went up in 1990 and was stolen. The plaque that replaced it is what's at the corner now, and that single marker is still the whole of it.

What there is instead is the anniversary. Every July twenty-fourth, descendants come down to this stretch of the Riverwalk. There's a moment of silence. Someone leans over the railing and drops flowers into the water. It's a small thing, kept up by the families, and it has happened every year for longer than most of the people who come to it have been alive.

Stay as long as you like. When you're ready, keep east, under Clark and under Dearborn, until two round concrete towers stand up on the far bank: Marina City.

stops.title: Marina City
stops.caption: It's 1959, and the janitors' union of Chicago has hired an architect to design them an office building.
stops.transcriptText:
It's 1959, and the janitors' union of Chicago has hired an architect to design them an office building.

The two round towers on the far bank are what he talked them into instead. Bertrand Goldberg's argument to the union's president, William McFetridge, ran roughly like this: your members are moving out to the suburbs, and when the last of them goes, downtown empties at six o'clock every evening and stays empty. Don't build yourselves an office. Build your people somewhere to live.

So the building service employees — janitors, elevator operators — put up most of the thirty-six million dollars, and by 1964 there were two towers here holding nine hundred apartments, with a swimming pool underneath them, a bowling alley, an ice rink, a gym, shops, restaurants, parking spiraling up inside each tower, and a harbor. Boat slips, in the river, at the base of the building. The complex is named after the parking.

When they were finished they were the tallest residential buildings in the world, and the tallest concrete ones of any kind.

Consider what this river was in 1964. Working water: freight, sewage, industry, smell. Buildings turned their backs on it and put their front doors on the street, because nobody with a choice faced the river.

Goldberg put nine hundred front doors on it, and a boat harbor, half a century before the city laid the path you're standing on. The first people housed on this river were the people who cleaned the offices across it.

Look up once more before you go: every one of those balconies is a half-circle, and there are hundreds of them. Then keep east, under State and under Wabash, to the bridge with four stone towers at its corners — DuSable Bridge.

stops.title: DuSable Bridge
stops.caption: Each half of the bridge over your head weighs three thousand four hundred tons, and it is lifted by a pair of motors with about as much power as a small car engine.
stops.transcriptText:
Each half of the bridge over your head weighs three thousand four hundred tons, and it is lifted by a pair of motors with about as much power as a small car engine.

The trick is counterweights. Bascule is French for seesaw, and that's the mechanism exactly: the roadway is a lever, a block of concrete and steel sits on the short end, and the whole assembly pivots on a shaft called a trunnion. Balance it finely enough and a hundred and eight horsepower is plenty. The motors were kept that small deliberately — electricity was expensive in 1920.

It opened in May 1920: the first bridge anywhere built as a double-leaf, double-deck bascule, with two roadways stacked one above the other. Before it existed, Michigan Avenue simply stopped at the river, and the street on the far side went by a different name: Pine.

The stone tower on this bank is a museum — five floors of one bridgehouse, with the gear room at the bottom, where you can stand next to the gears that do the lifting. Open most days in season.

In the 1920s this bridge went up more than three thousand times a year. Boats had the right of way and the traffic sat and waited for them. It now lifts about forty times a year, spring and fall, mostly for sailboats heading out to the lake and coming back.

The river used to interrupt the street. Now the street tolerates the river a few dozen times a season, on a schedule the river doesn't set.

Keep east. The path runs out from under Michigan Avenue, opens up, and ends where the river does — at the Lake Shore Drive bridge and the lock.

stops.title: The Chicago Harbor Lock
stops.caption: Which way is the water going? You're at the east end of the Riverwalk, under the Lake Shore Drive bridge.
stops.transcriptText:
Which way is the water going?

You're at the east end of the Riverwalk, under the Lake Shore Drive bridge. Look east, past the bridge, toward open water. Set across the mouth of the river there is a low concrete structure with gates in it. You can see it from here; you can't walk out to it.

The Chicago Harbor Lock — six hundred feet long, eighty feet wide, finished in 1938, and the reason everything behind you works.

The river surface sits somewhere between one and four feet below the level of the lake. Left alone, Lake Michigan would simply pour in. In effect, that's the arrangement: since 1900 this river has run away from the lake, west and inland, because the city dug a canal twenty-eight miles southwest on a downhill grade and let gravity carry the sewage toward the Mississippi instead of toward the water it drank. The lock manages the rest — how much lake water is let in, and how boats get between two surfaces at different heights. It cycles more than ten thousand times in a boating season, ten to fifteen minutes at a time, boats riding up and down inside it like an elevator.

The reversal is not something that happened. It's something being done, right now, by people on shift.

And it isn't absolute. Dozens of times since the mid-1980s, after enormous rain, the gates have been opened to let the river run out into the lake the original way for a few hours, because the alternative is water in basements. The old direction is still there, waiting.

A mile and a quarter behind you, you started at a fork where two ocean basins nearly touch, and where people carried boats over the gap between them. You're standing at the gap now. Somebody put a gate on it.

Stay a while if the boats are moving. The lock is slow on purpose, and nobody has ever worked out how to hurry water. And the whole time you're watching it, the river at your back is running inland, away from the lake, because that is what was decided.

tours.title: The Loop — Where the Skyscraper Was Born
tours.shortDescription: Five stops, about four blocks: how the skyscraper learned to stand up, 1885 to 1893.
tours.longDescription: Between 1885 and 1893, inside four blocks of the financial district, a handful of architects and the landlords who paid them worked out how to hold a tall building up — not how to decorate one. One question runs through all five stops, and it is simpler than it sounds: what holds it up — walls, a frame, or very nearly nothing. The walk starts at the corner where the Home Insurance Building of 1885, widely called the first skyscraper, stood until 1931; steps into the Rookery, floating on iron rails over Chicago mud with Frank Lloyd Wright's white-and-gold light court inside; looks down the LaSalle canyon to the Board of Trade and the faceless aluminum Ceres on its roof; crosses Federal Plaza, where Mies van der Rohe's black steel grid made structure into the whole style; and ends at the Monadnock, where inside a single building the wall stops holding anything up and the frame takes over. Twenty minutes if nobody stops you. Everything works from the sidewalk.

stops.title: LaSalle & Adams
stops.caption: Between 1885 and 1893, inside the four blocks you're about to walk, a handful of architects and the landlords who paid them worked out how to hold a tall building up.
stops.transcriptText:
Between 1885 and 1893, inside the four blocks you're about to walk, a handful of architects and the landlords who paid them worked out how to hold a tall building up. Not how to decorate one. How to keep it standing.

You should be at the corner of LaSalle and Adams — stone on all four corners, not much sky, the middle of the financial district. This is the shortest walk in the set: five stops, about four blocks, all of it sidewalk, twenty minutes if nobody stops you.

Two of the five stops have interiors worth the detour, and both are conditional. One is a working office building that lets the public into its lobby on weekdays and Saturday mornings. The other is a federal complex with security at the door. Everything on this walk works from the outside, so treat the interiors as a bonus rather than a plan.

One question runs through all five stops, and it's simpler than it sounds: what holds it up. Walls, or a frame, or very nearly nothing. The answer changes as you walk, and at the last stop you'll watch it change inside a single building.

The tiered limestone tower on the northeast corner is where we start.

stops.title: 135 S LaSalle — the Home Insurance site
stops.caption: The building that got Chicago called the birthplace of the skyscraper isn't here.
stops.transcriptText:
The building that got Chicago called the birthplace of the skyscraper isn't here. It came down in 1931, forty-six years old, and nobody made much of a fuss.

Look for the plaque first — it's set into the wall of the tiered limestone tower on this corner. It marks the Home Insurance Building: ten stories, finished in 1885, William Le Baron Jenney. It's widely called the first skyscraper, and historians have argued the point for a hundred years and haven't stopped, mostly over how much of Jenney's iron and steel frame was really doing the work.

What nobody argues is what the frame was for. Ask why anyone wanted one and the answer people reach for is height, and height is the least of it. A masonry building carries itself on its outside walls, so the higher you go the thicker those walls get at the bottom — and thick walls eat the two things a landlord is actually selling. They eat floor space, room by room, on every floor. And they shrink the windows, which mattered enormously in a decade when the alternative to daylight was gas. A frame let an owner build up without paying for it in rentable square feet and light.

There were other reasons, and the honest version keeps all of them: the soft ground under the Loop, the passenger elevator, a building code that let Chicago go thinner than eastern cities could. Nobody serious gives one cause.

The forty-four-story tower standing here now opened in 1934 and is a good building in its own right. But the thing that happened on this corner left nothing behind.

The proof outlived the evidence.

Cross Adams and look for the arch. Next stop is the Rookery.

stops.title: The Rookery
stops.caption: This is the Rookery. Twelve stories, 1888, Burnham and Root, and generally called the oldest high-rise still standing in Chicago.
stops.transcriptText:
This is the Rookery. Twelve stories, 1888, Burnham and Root, and generally called the oldest high-rise still standing in Chicago.

Right. The thing to know about it is that its owners hedged.

Two brothers from Boston, Peter and Shepherd Brooks, had been buying Chicago property since the 1860s, and they kept a man here to do their thinking on the ground — Owen Aldis, a lawyer out of Vermont who managed their buildings and talked them into taller ones. Louis Sullivan later named Aldis as one of two men responsible for the modern office building, which is an odd thing to say about a property manager and probably fair.

Three years after Jenney's frame went up two blocks north, the Brooks brothers put up this. Heavy masonry on the outside, carrying its own weight, the way buildings had always done it. And inside, out of sight, an iron and steel frame carrying the floors and the light court, independent of those walls. Two structural systems in one building, because the new one worked and nobody was ready to bet a whole building on it yet.

You can see the hedge from where you're standing. The outside is arches, rough stone and heavy horizontal banding — a building that wants to look like it could stop a cannonball. If the lobby's open, weekdays and Saturday mornings through the Adams Street door, go in, because the middle of this building is the exact opposite: a glass-roofed court, white marble, thin ironwork, all of it light. Frank Lloyd Wright was brought in to rework that court in 1905 and covered Root's dark iron over in marble.

Fortress on the outside, greenhouse in the middle. Same building, two answers, and its owners were hedging their bet in both directions at once.

Now walk south down LaSalle. The next stop is the street itself.

stops.title: The LaSalle canyon
stops.caption: Look south down LaSalle and notice that the street ends. Not bends — ends, in a building, squarely, the way a corridor ends in a wall.
stops.transcriptText:
Look south down LaSalle and notice that the street ends. Not bends — ends, in a building, squarely, the way a corridor ends in a wall.

Follow the street south and watch it close in on you. LaSalle is one of the few streets in the Loop that behaves like a room. The buildings come right out to the sidewalk on both sides and go straight up, thirty and forty floors of continuous stone and glass with no setbacks and no gaps between them, and the effect is less a street than a trench with sky for a ceiling.

This is what the frame bought, eventually. Once walls stopped carrying the load, nothing stopped an owner from filling the lot out to the property line and building until the money ran out. LaSalle is what a street looks like when every owner on it makes that same decision, one after another, for eighty years.

The building that closes the corridor is the Board of Trade — 1930, six hundred and five feet, the tallest thing in Chicago for the next thirty-five years — and it sits at the foot of the street, plugging it. The aluminum figure on the roof is Ceres, Roman goddess of grain, thirty-one feet tall, and she has no face.

One more thing this street did, and it matters four blocks from here. An earlier Board of Trade stood on the same spot from the 1880s, and it turned LaSalle into the money end of downtown and pulled the land prices up after it. Expensive ground here sent a Boston family with Chicago holdings out looking for cheap ground somewhere else — southeast, at the edge of things, on a block nobody else wanted.

Turn left on Jackson. Next stop is Federal Plaza.

stops.title: Federal Plaza
stops.caption: Flat gray granite, three black buildings, and one enormous red thing that looks like it wandered in off a different block.
stops.transcriptText:
Flat gray granite, three black buildings, and one enormous red thing that looks like it wandered in off a different block.

Mies van der Rohe designed the plaza and everything standing on it except the red thing. He took the commission in 1959, he died in 1969, and the last of it was finished in 1974, so he never saw it whole. Three buildings: the courthouse across Dearborn, the tall office block on this side, and the single-story post office parked in the middle of all that open space like a paperweight.

Worth noticing at your feet: the granite pavers are one size on one grid, and they run from out here straight in through the doors without a break — same stone inside as out, the only difference a polish. The red thing is a Calder, fifty-three feet, unveiled the year the complex was finished, and it is the only curve on the block.

Now look at the vertical black lines running the full height of the towers, evenly spaced, edge to edge, floor to roof. Those are I-beams, steel, standing a few inches proud of the glass. And in the towers Mies built to this pattern, they aren't holding anything up.

American fire codes required a building's structural steel to be buried in concrete or plaster, out of sight. Mies wanted the frame visible, because to him the frame was the building's one honest fact. So he buried the real steel where the code insisted and bolted more steel to the outside in a perfect rhythm, whether or not a column stood behind it.

Eighty-nine years after Jenney, the frame has stopped being a solution to a problem and become the thing the building is about. Not hidden, not decorated. Advertised.

Cross Jackson. The last stop is the Monadnock, and it takes all of this back.

stops.title: The Monadnock
stops.caption: The wall beside you leans. Stand close to the brick at the base on the Dearborn side and sight straight up the surface: it curves gently away from you before it straightens.
stops.transcriptText:
The wall beside you leans. Stand close to the brick at the base on the Dearborn side and sight straight up the surface: it curves gently away from you before it straightens. The wall is thicker at your knee than at your shoulder, and it's doing that because it has to.

So. This is the Monadnock, and it's two buildings pretending to be one.

The north half, nearest Jackson, went up in 1891 — Burnham and Root, for the same Boston brothers and the same man on the ground who put up the Rookery three years earlier. Peter Brooks wanted no ornament of any kind, and Root, who had covered the Rookery in ironwork and curls, gave him sixteen stories of brick with nothing whatsoever on it. That wall carries the entire building: six feet thick at the bottom, tapering to about eighteen inches at the top floor. Root called it his Jumbo, and he died while it was going up, forty-one years old.

Two years later the brothers bought the lot to the south and ran the building on to Van Buren. Different firm, same brick, same profile, same window rhythm — and behind that brick, a steel frame. On the south half the walls hold up nothing but themselves.

Walk the length of it and find the seam, about halfway along: a slight shift in the brickwork and in the window bays. On one side of that line the wall is the structure. On the other side it's a curtain. Two years apart, one address, one continuous face of brick laid over the top of the whole argument.

Everything on this walk sits somewhere on that line. Jenney's frame proved it could be done, the Rookery hedged, LaSalle spent a century cashing it in, and Mies bolted the answer to the outside of a federal building so nobody could miss it.

Stay a minute and look at the north half. Six feet of brick at the bottom holding up sixteen floors, and the technique was finished the day it opened. They built it out here anyway, on a block the trade thought was a mistake — and it's still an office building.

tours.title: The Lakefront — Millennium Park to Museum Campus
tours.shortDescription: A mile and a half where none of the ground is ground — a railyard roof, then a filled-in lake.
tours.longDescription: Some of this walk crosses a roof over a working railyard; most of the rest is lake that got filled in, a shoreline pushed out a piece at a time over seventy years. Five stops run north to south from Millennium Park to Museum Campus, flat the whole way, and one question carries through: what was allowed to stand here, and what wasn't. Cloud Gate opens it on a plaza over the trains; the Pritzker Pavilion follows, a hundred-and-twenty-foot bandshell that is legally a sculpture because Grant Park has been protected against buildings since a note on an 1836 map; the Art Institute stop is really about Aaron Montgomery Ward, who spent twenty years and four trips to the Illinois Supreme Court keeping everything else out — the empty part is the achievement; Buckingham Fountain marks the point the Plan of Chicago called the center of the city; and the walk ends at Museum Campus, where in 1998 the city moved eight lanes of Lake Shore Drive so three century-old institutions could finally stand in one park. The last stretch is a long open run with nothing between you and the water. That, too, was decided.

stops.title: None of the ground is ground
stops.caption: None of the ground on this walk is ground. Some of it is a roof over a railyard.
stops.transcriptText:
None of the ground on this walk is ground.

Some of it is a roof over a railyard. Most of the rest is lake that got filled in, a shoreline pushed out into the water a piece at a time over about seventy years. The park you're standing in is younger than the buildings across the street from it, and the museums at the far end are sitting on land that did not exist when the men who paid for them were born.

You should be at the north end of Millennium Park, on Michigan Avenue, with the park dropping away east of you toward the lake. Five stops, running north to south, about a mile and a half end to end. Flat the whole way, all of it park path or sidewalk, and no highway to cross if you stay west of the drive.

Two honest notes. It takes longer than the distance suggests, because the last stretch south of the fountain is a long open run with nothing between you and the water. And the park is a working venue: the concert lawn is open for events rather than for wandering, the trellis over it has been under repair, and one thing or another is usually fenced. Nothing on this walk depends on getting into anything.

One question carries through all five stops: what was allowed to stand here, and what wasn't. The answer is stranger than you'd guess, and it's the reason the last stop is a mile from the first.

The sculpture on the plaza behind you is where we start.

stops.title: Cloud Gate, Grainger Plaza
stops.caption: Look down. Not at the sculpture — at the pavers you're standing on.
stops.transcriptText:
Look down. Not at the sculpture — at the pavers you're standing on.

Under them is a waterproofing membrane, and under that, two multi-level parking garages and a working commuter rail line. Trains run in and out of a station beneath this plaza all day. Millennium Park is a garden on a lid, generally called the largest rooftop garden in the world, and every tree in it is planted in soil that stops a few feet down.

For a century and a half the strip you're on belonged to a railroad. In 1852 the city handed the lakefront edge to the Illinois Central in exchange for the railroad building a breakwater to stop the lake from eating Michigan Avenue — a trade that put tracks and yards between downtown and the water and kept them there for four generations. The park opened in 2004. What you're walking on is the roof somebody finally built over that bargain.

Now the sculpture. Cloud Gate is sixty-six feet long and thirty-three feet high, seamless stainless steel, and Anish Kapoor's team spent years grinding the welds out of it so the surface would read as one continuous skin. There isn't a joint on it you can find with your eye.

Stay a moment and think about what's under your feet rather than what's in front of them. Twenty-five acres of lawn, trees, plazas and one very heavy sculpture, all of it laid over a rail yard the city spent a hundred and fifty years apologizing for. The park didn't replace the trains. It covered them, and they're still running.

Walk south along the promenade toward the shell-shaped bandstand. The next stop is the Pritzker Pavilion.

stops.title: Jay Pritzker Pavilion
stops.caption: If there's a rehearsal on, you're hearing this stop before you look at it, and that's the right order.
stops.transcriptText:
If there's a rehearsal on, you're hearing this stop before you look at it, and that's the right order.

You should be somewhere along the south or west edge of the great lawn, with the stainless steel bandshell ahead of you — the one that looks like a ribbon caught mid-unwrap — and a grid of steel pipes arching over the grass above your head. The lawn itself is open for events rather than for lounging, and the trellis has been under repair, so take the view from the edge and don't count on getting onto the grass.

Look up at the pipes first, because they are the part people mistake for decoration. That trellis is a mounting frame. Speakers are hung across it, out over the audience, so that a crowd sitting on open grass a hundred yards from the stage hears something closer to what a concert hall would give them. Outdoors, sound falls apart with distance and wanders off in the wind. The usual fix is to make it louder. The fix here was to stop sending it from the front and start dropping it from overhead.

So the interesting half of this building is the half that isn't a building. The bandshell is the photograph; the trellis is the machine. Frank Gehry designed both, and while the steel ribbons get all the attention, the thing doing the actual work is the ironwork overhead that nobody points a camera at.

Notice how far out the trellis reaches. It doesn't stop at the edge of the stage or the edge of the seating — it keeps going, out over open grass, past where any wall would be. This building's real dimensions are the distance the sound has to travel, which is a strange way to size a building and the only way this one was ever going to work.

Head south out of the park and cross Monroe. Next stop is the east face of the Art Institute.

stops.title: The Art Institute & Mr. Ward
stops.caption: It's 1892, and the most unpopular man in Chicago decides not to sue.
stops.transcriptText:
It's 1892, and the most unpopular man in Chicago decides not to sue.

You should be on the park side of the Art Institute, south of Millennium Park, with the museum's east flank in front of you and the footbridge running over Monroe toward it. From here you can see the two things this whole walk turns on at the same time: a large museum, and a large amount of empty park.

The empty part is the achievement. Aaron Montgomery Ward spent twenty years and four trips to the Illinois Supreme Court keeping buildings out of this park, and he was loathed for it — a rich man in the newspapers, blocking things ordinary people wanted, at his own expense. The park around you is the result. The argument was settled over a century ago and doesn't need relitigating here.

What's worth standing here for is the exception.

Ward filed his first complaint in 1890. Two years later, when construction started on the Art Institute, he said nothing. No injunction, no protest, and by most accounts only grudging assent — and it happened because the World's Columbian Exposition needed a hall for its lectures nearer downtown than Jackson Park, and the Art Institute needed a permanent home, so one building was made to solve both problems and the museum moved in after the fair went home.

He wasn't perfectly consistent, either. A few years later he agreed to a temporary post office in the park, at a moment when his own mail-order company was the largest single customer the U.S. Postal Service had.

And because nobody ever challenged it, this is the one building here that has been allowed to grow. It has expanded again and again for a hundred and thirty years, right where a court would later rule that nothing could be built at all. One decision not to file a piece of paper, and the museum in front of you is the only structure in Chicago's front yard that gets to keep getting bigger.

Keep going south through the park. You'll see the fountain before you reach it.

stops.title: Buckingham Fountain
stops.caption: Wide, low, pink granite, four basins stacked like a wedding cake, and behind it nothing but lake.
stops.transcriptText:
Wide, low, pink granite, four basins stacked like a wedding cake, and behind it nothing but lake.

Stand on the west side, looking east, so the water is beyond it. Notice what the fountain doesn't do: it doesn't rise up in front of the view. It spreads sideways instead, and the whole composition sits low enough that from here you can see straight over it to the water, and none of that is accidental. Edward Bennett designed it as the centerpiece of a park where a building was not permitted and a view was the entire point, and he solved the problem by making the monument out of the one material that can be enormous without blocking anything.

When it runs, the center jet goes a hundred and fifty feet straight up — which is the whole trick of the thing. It takes up as much room as a tower for twenty minutes an hour, and then puts every bit of it back.

It runs spring through fall and it's dry the rest of the year, which is worth knowing before you plan around it.

Kate Buckingham gave it to the city in 1927 in memory of her brother Clarence, who had been a trustee of the museum you just walked past. So the two things standing in this park — the one building that got permission and the one monument nobody had to give permission for — are connected by one family.

And she did something most donors don't. Along with the fountain she left an endowment to pay for keeping it running, in perpetuity, on the reasonable assumption that a city which accepts a gift like this will eventually be tempted to stop maintaining it. Almost a century on, it still runs.

Now the long stretch. Keep south past Roosevelt — the next stop is Museum Campus, and the walk gets exposed from here.

stops.title: Museum Campus
stops.caption: This is Museum Campus, and it's here because a court said it couldn't be somewhere else.
stops.transcriptText:
This is Museum Campus, and it's here because a court said it couldn't be somewhere else.

You should be on the plaza between the museums, with the columned limestone building to the west, the stadium beyond it, the aquarium ahead and the planetarium out on the point past that. Take a slow look around before any of the buildings. All of this is lake. Every square foot you can see from here was water inside living memory of the men who paid for these institutions — filled a stretch at a time under agreements with the city and the Army engineers, pushed out from the old shoreline until the ground was large enough to put something on.

Now the part that connects to everything behind you.

Marshall Field's estate wanted its natural history museum in Grant Park, at the center of it, and the city agreed. Montgomery Ward sued. He lost in the Chicago courts, appealed, and in October 1909 the Illinois Supreme Court overturned the judgment and held that nothing could be built on that park at all. The museum had nowhere to go — so it waited in a leftover fair building out in Jackson Park for a couple of decades while this ground was still being made, and finally opened here in 1921.

The aquarium followed. The planetarium followed. The stadium followed. A whole cultural district assembled a mile south of where it was supposed to be, on land that didn't exist when the argument started.

So: a garden on a roof, a bandshell sized by sound, one museum that slipped through, and a whole campus of buildings that didn't — standing on made ground, because a park two-thirds of a mile north was held empty and stayed that way.

Stay out here a while if the lake lets you. It usually doesn't, or not for long, and there's nothing between this plaza and the water to slow the wind down — which is its own kind of argument for why somebody once thought it was worth going to court to keep the view.

tours.title: The Magnificent Mile — DuSable Bridge to the Water Tower
tours.shortDescription: Half a mile in four stops, ending deliberately at the one thing nobody thought up first.
tours.longDescription: In 1917 the city renamed a narrow street called Pine — three years before there was any way onto it from Michigan Avenue, because the bridge didn't exist yet. The name arrived first, and the street was rebuilt until the name was defensible: widened, cleared, bridged, then renamed a second time in 1947 by the real estate man Arthur Rubloff, who supplied the phrase Magnificent Mile as a marketing line for thirteen tired blocks. Everything on this half mile was labeled before it was finished. The walk crosses the DuSable Bridge where Burnham and Bennett's Plan of Chicago pushed the avenue over the river, stands between the Wrigley Building and Tribune Tower — the pair that came afterward to justify the label — sights up the avenue at Ontario Street where the second naming took hold, with the John Hancock's black taper crossing the view far up the street, and ends early, and deliberately, at the old stone Water Tower: the one thing on the avenue that nobody thought up first, standing since 1869 in the middle of a street that was invented around it.

stops.title: A street called Pine
stops.caption: In 1917, the city renamed a narrow street called Pine. It became North Michigan Avenue three years before there was any way to get onto it from Michigan Avenue.
stops.transcriptText:
In 1917, the city renamed a narrow street called Pine.

It became North Michigan Avenue three years before there was any way to get onto it from Michigan Avenue. The bridge wasn't built. The street it had just been named after stopped dead at the river, a block and a half short.

The name came first. The street was made to fit the name afterward — widened, cleared, bridged, and then renamed a second time by a real estate man who thought it needed better branding. Everything you're about to look at was labeled before it was finished.

Almost everything.

This walk goes half a mile north, from the river to an old stone water tower, in four stops. It's flat, it's entirely on sidewalk, and there are no stairs and no admission of any kind. It is also one of the busiest half miles in the city, so if you're doing this between about noon and six you'll be sharing it. Nothing about the walk depends on the crowd being thin — the things worth looking at are all above eye level or across the street.

The avenue keeps going north after we stop, another several blocks to Oak Street. We're going to end early, and deliberately, at the one thing on this street that nobody thought up first.

Start at the south end of the bridge, with the water in front of you.

stops.title: The Bridge
stops.caption: Michigan Avenue used to end here. Not narrow, not bend — end.
stops.transcriptText:
Michigan Avenue used to end here. Not narrow, not bend — end.

South of you it's a boulevard. North of you, before 1920, there was no version of this street at all: Pine Street was a modest thing of workshops and rooming houses, and if you wanted to reach it you walked a block west to Rush Street and took your turn on a swing bridge with everybody else, which in practice meant standing there a while.

Point yourself north, across the water.

The thing that changed it was a book. Daniel Burnham and Edward Bennett's Plan of Chicago, published in 1909, proposed connecting Michigan Avenue to Pine Street with a bridge, then widening Pine to match. The concept was approved around 1913, the street was renamed in 1917, and construction started the following spring. It opened in May of 1920.

Bennett designed the bridge himself, which is unusual — the man who co-wrote the proposal got to build the one piece of it everything else depended on. He modeled it on the Pont Alexandre the Third, over the Seine. You can see the argument he was making: two decks, stone-faced towers at all four corners, a river crossing dressed as a civic monument rather than a piece of traffic equipment.

Widening the street on the far side cost something. Buildings that stood in the way had their fronts sliced off to the new curb line; others were simply removed.

Most streets accumulate. They start as a track to somewhere and thicken over a century. This one was issued — proposed on paper, approved by committee, and then constructed underneath its own name.

The first thing built on it is directly across the river, and it's white. Cross the bridge and stop in the plaza at the far end.

stops.title: Wrigley and Tribune
stops.caption: Put your back to the bridge. Two towers are holding the gate of the street, one on each side.
stops.transcriptText:
Put your back to the bridge.

Two towers are holding the gate of the street, one on each side. To your left, on the west, the pale one with the clock tower. To your right, on the east, the darker one with the crown of stone spines at the top.

Take the pale one first.

The Wrigley Building went up starting in 1920, and the thing to hold onto is what wasn't around it. No major office buildings stood north of the river. The bridge was unfinished when the work began. A chewing gum company bought land on a street that had been renamed but not yet built, and put a tower on it.

The architects were Graham, Anderson, Probst and White — the firm that inherited Daniel Burnham's practice after he died. So the office that produced the plan for this street also produced the first building on it. And they gave it white terra cotta, graded in shades that get palest toward the top so the tower seems to lift, and floodlights that have washed the front of it since the day it opened. Nobody was lighting office buildings all night in 1920. It was an advertisement, and it worked.

The Tribune Tower followed in 1925, across the road, from an international design competition the paper ran for its own headquarters.

Neither of these became a landmark. Both were built as one, on purpose, by two companies whose actual business was getting your attention — a newspaper and a gum manufacturer — for a street that as yet had nothing on it worth stopping for. The avenue's opening statement is two very large pieces of advertising, and the earlier one is named after gum.

Keep walking north. Stop when you reach Ontario Street.

stops.title: The Second Naming
stops.caption: The street got named a second time in 1947, and this time by a man who was selling it.
stops.transcriptText:
The street got named a second time in 1947, and this time by a man who was selling it.

Arthur Rubloff was a real estate developer who ran the business association for this stretch of the avenue, and after the war he launched a campaign to rebuild it. He is widely credited with supplying the phrase that came with the campaign: the Magnificent Mile. It was a marketing line for roughly thirteen blocks that were, at the time, a mixed and somewhat tired commercial district.

Sight up the avenue.

What you're looking at is mostly the result of that campaign and the twenty years after it — the postwar boom that filled in the gaps between the twenties buildings, moved the city's shopping weight north off State Street, and finished with the black tower and its crossed steel braces you can see far up the street.

One career runs the whole length of it. Alfred Shaw came to Chicago in the twenties to work at the firm you just looked at, Graham, Anderson, Probst and White, where he had a hand in the Civic Opera House and the Merchandise Mart. From 1937 he ran a series of his own partnerships, which turned out to be among the busiest practices in the city, and they built up here too. One man, one avenue, from the Beaux-Arts version to the plate-glass one.

The pattern holds. The name arrives, and then the street is rebuilt until the name is defensible. It happened in 1917 with an ordinance, and it happened in 1947 with a slogan, and both times the buildings came afterward to justify the label.

Two more blocks north, on the west side, there's a stone building that didn't get a name that way. Walk up to it.

stops.title: The Water Tower
stops.caption: It's called the Water Tower because it is a water tower. After four blocks of names that arrived before their buildings, that's worth saying plainly.
stops.transcriptText:
It's called the Water Tower because it is a water tower.

After four blocks of names that arrived before their buildings, that's worth saying plainly. This one is a description. The stone shell you're standing under was built in 1869 to house a standpipe — a tall vertical pipe that smoothed out the surges from the pumps across the street, so the water reaching taps didn't arrive in shoves. The castle detailing is decoration wrapped around a piece of plumbing.

Read the shape of it: everything narrow and vertical, because the thing inside was narrow and vertical.

By 1906 it was useless. The pumping system had moved on and no longer needed a standpipe, which left a small ornamental stone building sitting on what was about to become the most valuable retail frontage in the city. It was proposed for demolition three times — in 1906, again in 1918, and again in 1948.

The 1918 one is the one that matters. Michigan Avenue was being widened, the tower stood in the path of the work, and the obvious answer was to take it down. The proposal produced enough public anger that the city changed the road instead, and laid the avenue out to keep the building where it was.

Hold both halves of that. This is a city that has demolished and rebuilt and copied itself relentlessly, and the one object it refused to move is a disused pipe housing. And keeping it was never the same as leaving it alone — the restoration in the early sixties replaced much of the deteriorated stone with new limestone, so a good deal of what you're looking at is a careful reproduction of what was here.

Across the road, the pumping station is still doing its job, still sending water north. And the shopping complex opposite took its name from this building rather than the other way round.

Stay in the plaza a minute if you have one. It's the only spot on this avenue where the street had to make room, instead of the other way around.

tours.title: Pilsen — Eighteenth Street, East to West
tours.shortDescription: A little over a mile west on 18th Street: everything arrived from somewhere else and changed on the way.
tours.longDescription: There is a city in western Bohemia that Czechs call Plzeň, and Chicago took the name secondhand, from a restaurant a homesick man opened on this street in the 1870s. Nothing on the street arrived intact. Over a little more than a mile, the walk passes a settlement house that became Casa Aztlan, its front painted with figures from a mural first titled Hay Cultura en Nuestra Comunidad; Thalia Hall, an opera house built in 1892 out of one saloonkeeper's memory of Prague, facing the green spire of St. Procopius; the Eighteenth Street station, where the schoolteacher Francisco Mendoza and his students spent years rendering an Aztec calendar stone in house paint on an elevated platform — repainted since, which is how murals live here; and the National Museum of Mexican Art, whose stated frame is art without borders. Czechs and Poles built the street after the fire; Mexican families remade it after the fifties; the through-line is that everything came from somewhere else and changed on the way — and the changing is the subject.

stops.title: Eighteenth & Halsted
stops.caption: There is a city in western Bohemia, four thousand miles east of this corner, that Czechs call Plzen and Germans call Pilsen.
stops.transcriptText:
There is a city in western Bohemia, four thousand miles east of this corner, that Czechs call Plzen and Germans call Pilsen.

Chicago took the German version, and took it secondhand. Sometime in the 1870s a Bohemian man opened a restaurant on this street and named it, in Czech, At the City of Plzen — a nostalgic name, the kind you give a place when you are not going home. Neighbors started calling the whole district by the restaurant's name, and the post office made it permanent by christening its local branch Pilsen Station.

Nothing on this street arrived intact. Over the next mile you'll pass a Catholic church that was bought used and dragged here, an opera house built out of somebody's memory of Prague, an Aztec calendar stone rendered in house paint on an elevated platform, and a museum whose stated frame is art without borders. All of it came from somewhere else, and all of it changed on the way. The changing is the part worth walking for.

You want the corner of Eighteenth and Halsted, facing west. From here the street runs straight, and every stop sits on it or within a block of it — a little over a mile, flat the whole way, four stops.

Walk west to Racine. Stop at the corner and look south; the brick building with the figures painted across its front is a few doors along.

stops.title: Casa Aztlan
stops.caption: The mural on this building had a title. Hay Cultura en Nuestra Comunidad.
stops.transcriptText:
The mural on this building had a title. Hay Cultura en Nuestra Comunidad. There Is Culture in Our Community.

You should be at Eighteenth and Racine, looking south down Racine at the three-story brick building a few doors along — the one carrying painted figures across its front.

It opened in 1905 as Howell Neighborhood House, a settlement house for the Czechs and Poles and Italians packed into these blocks: English classes, a clinic, somewhere to leave your children. By 1970 the families here were largely Mexican, many of them displaced from the Near West Side by an expressway and a university campus. The settlement house took a new name that year: Casa Aztlan. Aztlan is the northern homeland the Mexica described migrating out of, centuries earlier — so a community center on Racine Avenue took the name of a place out of a migration account.

Ray Patlan painted the interior in 1970, while he was still an art student, and the front between 1971 and 1973, working with about forty neighborhood teenagers on a city youth-jobs program. Patlan was born in Chicago; his parents came from Guanajuato. The faces they put up here — Cuauhtemoc, Benito Juarez, Frida Kahlo — belonged to people who had never set foot in Illinois, and in one case had been dead four hundred years. None of the painters had seen any of them either; they were working from pictures of pictures.

Nothing on this wall originated on this wall. The iconography came north, the name came out of a migration story, the building came out of a Protestant settlement movement, and a Chicago-born art student put the three together on one facade. Faithful reproduction was never the assignment.

The center closed in 2013 and the building holds apartments now. The front was painted over in 2017 and repainted later that year by Patlan and the muralist Roberto Valadez. Patlan died in 2024.

Walk west — barely a block, and Eighteenth crosses Allport. Stop where you can see the limestone building on the corner and the church facing it.

stops.title: Thalia Hall & Saint Procopius
stops.caption: The first Catholic church on this corner was not built on this corner.
stops.transcriptText:
The first Catholic church on this corner was not built on this corner.

You're at Eighteenth and Allport. The heavy limestone building with the corner turret and the storefronts underneath is Thalia Hall. The church is across Eighteenth Street: Saint Procopius.

In the summer of 1875 a committee of Czech residents bought three lots here for thirty-six hundred dollars. A Methodist congregation at Nineteenth and Halsted wanted to put up something in brick and offered its old frame church for two thousand dollars. The committee bought it, had the whole building moved four blocks west and a block over to this corner, using the upper floor for worship and the lower for a school. First Mass, Easter Sunday, 1876. The brick church came in the 1880s, and Czech Benedictines took the parish soon after.

Thalia Hall went up in 1892 for John Dusek, who kept a saloon. Faber and Pagels designed it, and by most accounts they modeled the theater inside on the Old Opera House in Prague. The name comes from Thalia, the Greek muse of comedy. The shops at street level and the flats above them were not an afterthought — halls like this were built with rent attached, because the rent is what kept the theater lit. In 1895 a Shakespearean actor from Prague staged Romeo and Juliet in that room, in Czech.

Not everyone here was in the church. Czech freethinkers in Chicago had organized their own congregation in 1870 — it held weddings and namings, ran schools, and set up gymnastic clubs, the sokols, two of which stood within a few blocks of here. The Benedictine press at Saint Procopius argued with them in print for years. Both sides had crossed the same ocean out of the same country.

What came over on those ships was not only people and not only money. It was a floor plan, a Greek muse, a quarrel about God, and a church that somebody else had finished with.

Keep west on Eighteenth about five blocks, to Paulina and the elevated station.

stops.title: Eighteenth Street station
stops.caption: Go as far as the foot of the station stairs and look up. You're at Eighteenth and Paulina.
stops.transcriptText:
Go as far as the foot of the station stairs and look up.

You're at Eighteenth and Paulina. From the sidewalk you can see the mosaic beside the entrance and the paint climbing the stairwell; the platform walls carry more of it, past the turnstiles.

Trains have stopped here since 1896, and the station was rebuilt in the 1990s. When the work was finished, Francisco Mendoza painted the place — stairwells, corridors, platform walls — with students, through a city youth arts program and a transit-authority scheme that let artists adopt a station. The museum at the far end of this walk helped put it together. Mendoza grew up in South Chicago and taught art in schools around here for more than twenty-five years. He died in 2012.

On the platform he and his students painted the Aztec sun stone, and the moon stone beside it. The original sun stone is basalt, carved in Tenochtitlan five centuries ago, nearly twelve feet across, and it sits today in a museum in Mexico City with a rope around it. This one is house paint on steel panel, at about the height of your shoulder, on a platform where people are watching the arrival board.

The stone never moved. The image did — and on the way it lost the basalt, lost the scale, lost the temple, and picked up a handrail. Nobody here was attempting a monument. They were putting something on a wall that the students painting it would recognize on the way to school, which is a different job, done well.

Cross Eighteenth, go one block west and one block south, into Harrison Park. The long building with the ball fields around it is the last stop.

stops.title: National Museum of Mexican Art
stops.caption: This is a national museum of one country, standing in a different one.
stops.transcriptText:
This is a national museum of one country, standing in a different one.

You're in Harrison Park, in front of the National Museum of Mexican Art: the long low building with the park wrapped around it and the ball fields alongside.

It started in 1982 with a group of Chicago public school teachers and Carlos Tortolero, who ran it for decades. It opened here in 1987 and grew into what you're looking at. It holds one of the largest collections of Mexican art in the United States — more than twenty thousand objects, ancient Mexico through the present. The museum describes what it does in two words worth carrying out of here: sin fronteras. Without borders.

The wall painting on this street has a government behind it, historically. After the revolution, Mexico's education ministry under Jose Vasconcelos put painters onto public buildings through the 1920s to teach a largely unlettered country its own history — a state program with a minister and a budget. That form traveled north. The ministry did not come with it. On Eighteenth Street it turned into art students, summer job programs, teachers with classes of teenagers, and whatever wall was flat and visible.

Every stop on this walk arrived from elsewhere and was altered by the trip. A name off a restaurant sign. A church another congregation was done with. An opera house from memory. A carved stone in house paint. A national art form that showed up without the nation attached. You can measure any of it against its original, and the gap will tell you nothing worth knowing. The distance traveled is the subject.

A museum on this street calling itself borderless isn't a slogan; it's a flat description of the last hundred and fifty years here.

Find a bench. Most afternoons this park is loud in the good way — ball games, radios, somebody's birthday under the trees. Everything you looked at today got here the hard way, none of it arrived unchanged, and none of it is any less itself for that.

tours.title: Above Board
tours.shortDescription: Sixteen seats above a Collingwood pub, and not a single bottle in sight — that's the whole idea.
tours.longDescription: Hayden Lambert's sixteen-seat room above Smith Street hides every bottle on purpose: the spirits are decanted into unmarked crystal and locked into drawers behind the counter, so nobody orders by label or pays extra because a bottle looks expensive. One shared walnut table, no standing, a menu held to around twenty-five drinks known by heart — and the international recognition started arriving soon after the 2016 opening. Most cocktail bars are built to be read, their shelves working like an advertisement; Above Board strips the signalling away and leaves only what actually lands in the glass. From the street you'd never know it was up here, which is exactly how the name works: literally above a board downstairs, and scrupulously above board once you're in.

stops.title: Above Board
stops.caption: There isn't a single bottle on display anywhere in this room, and that's entirely deliberate.
stops.transcriptText:
There isn't a single bottle on display anywhere in this room, and that's entirely deliberate.

Head up the stairwell just off Smith Street, through the door beside Beermash, and you'll come out on the first floor above what locals still call Chopper Lane. Inside, it's compact and quietly lit: one shared table in American walnut rather than rows of bar stools, and room for exactly sixteen people at a time. There's no standing permitted, so once you've found a seat, you're staying a while.

Look at the room itself before you look at a drink. There's no back-bar glowing under spotlights, no wall of labels to read while you wait, because the bartender behind all of this, Hayden Lambert, built the place around hiding them. Every spirit gets decanted into unmarked crystal bottles and locked away in a bank of drawers behind the counter, so nobody's ordering off a brand they recognise, or paying more because a bottle happens to look expensive.

The name plays on that idea twice over: literally above a board, up here on the first floor over the pub downstairs, and scrupulously above board in how the drinks get made. The menu follows the same logic — rather than the enormous cocktail lists you'll find elsewhere in the city, Above Board keeps to around twenty-five drinks, split between house signatures and quietly updated classics, known by heart rather than by recipe card.

And here's the thing: most cocktail bars are built to be read, with the shelves working like a kind of advertisement that tells you what you're paying for before you've tasted a thing. Above Board strips all of that signalling away on purpose, which leaves only what actually lands in the glass, and the conversation happening around that one long table, to judge the place by.

It picked up a small stack of international recognition not long after opening in 2016, and standing inside, that's easy to believe — though from the street, you'd walk straight past without knowing any of it was up here.

If you come back another night with a friend, the door's easy to miss on purpose: unmarked, tucked beside Beermash's signage, up a narrow stairwell that looks like it leads nowhere in particular.

tours.title: Byrdi
tours.shortDescription: A World's-50-Best bar that treats the Victorian bush the way other bars treat a spirits cabinet.
tours.longDescription: Luke Whearty and Aki Nishikura's corner of Melbourne Central builds its drinks almost entirely from the landscape of Victoria — wattleseed, pepperberry, blackcurrant wood oil — fermented, smoked, spun through a centrifuge, and sometimes set in motion months before you sit down. 'Now and Then' runs Tasmanian wasabi against green apple, fig leaf and nasturtium; 'Fallen Fruit' holds distilled Carolina Reaper and lacto-fermented pineapple in tight, deliberate balance. Within a year of opening in 2019 it had landed on the World's 50 Best Bars list, and the sourcing is the point: while most ambitious bars still look to London or New York for their raw materials, Byrdi built an entire programme from what actually grows in this state. The list turns over completely with the seasons — whatever you drink tonight won't be there when the year turns.

stops.title: Byrdi
stops.caption: Byrdi's drink list changes with the seasons, and part of what lands in your glass tonight might have been set in motion months ago.
stops.transcriptText:
Byrdi's drink list changes with the seasons, and part of what lands in your glass tonight might have been set in motion months ago.

Inside Melbourne Central, where La Trobe Street meets Elizabeth Street, Byrdi sits tucked into a corner of the ground floor: low light, a long bar, and a kitchen sending out small plates that arrive faintly charred from the grill. Luke Whearty and Aki Nishikura opened it in 2019, and within a year it had already landed on the World's 50 Best Bars list — a rare feat for a venue that young.

Start with what's actually in the glass. Byrdi builds its cocktails almost entirely from the landscape of Victoria: wattleseed, pepperberry, blackcurrant wood oil, and other native ingredients most bar menus in the world wouldn't think to reach for. Nothing here gets treated simply — components arrive fermented, smoked, reconstituted, occasionally spun through a centrifuge, and some of that work began weeks or even months before you sat down.

Two drinks tend to get talked about most. "Now and Then" mixes Tasmanian wasabi with green apple, fig leaf and nasturtium, while "Fallen Fruit" pairs distilled Carolina Reaper pepper with lacto-fermented pineapple, island bitters and salted Davidson's plum — heat and sweetness held in a tight, deliberate balance rather than left to fight each other.

What's worth knowing, sitting here, is that Byrdi didn't look to London or New York for its raw materials the way most cocktail bars still do. It looked at what actually grows in this state and built an entire bar programme around treating the Victorian bush as seriously as anyone else treats a spirits cabinet.

The food follows the same instinct — most of it cooked over fire, arriving smoky by design rather than by accident.

The list turns over completely with the seasons, so whatever you're drinking tonight almost certainly won't be on the menu by the time the year turns — worth remembering if something here catches you off guard enough to want it again.

tours.title: Caretaker's Cottage
tours.shortDescription: A 1914 bluestone cottage behind a church, now one of the World's 50 Best Bars — walk-ins only.
tours.longDescription: The cottage on Little Lonsdale Street was built to house exactly one person — the caretaker of Wesley Church next door — and the Fancy Free trio who opened a bar inside it in 2022 kept everything the caretaker would recognise: the original wallpaper, the narrow staircase, former bedrooms folded into a room that seats about fifty at a squeeze. Because it was built for one occupant rather than a crowd, everything still feels domestic — Tasmanian oak behind the bar, vinyl on the decks. The martini arrives properly freezer-cold, built on a gin commissioned specifically for the room, and the boilermaker — a shot and a beer, paired with real precision — is what plenty of regulars call Australia's definitive version. In 2025 the World's 50 Best judges ranked this quiet little service building nineteenth anywhere on earth. No bookings; the queue forms along Little Lonsdale Street, and it's usually worth it.

stops.title: Caretaker's Cottage
stops.caption: The building in front of you was built to house exactly one person: the caretaker of the church next door.
stops.transcriptText:
The building in front of you was built to house exactly one person: the caretaker of the church next door.

That bluestone cottage on Little Lonsdale Street, tucked in behind Wesley Church, has stood since 1914 — long before anyone thought to put a bar inside it. Rob, Matt and Ryan, the trio behind the bar group Fancy Free, opened it here in 2022, and they kept almost everything the caretaker would have recognised: the original wallpaper, the narrow staircase, even a couple of former bedrooms, now folded into a room that seats around fifty people at a squeeze.

The scale is really the whole point. Because the cottage was built for one occupant rather than a crowd, everything inside still feels domestic rather than designed — Tasmanian oak behind the bar, vinyl on the decks, and a warmth that owes more to somebody's front room than to any cocktail bar you'd expect to find behind a church.

Two things anchor the reputation. The martini arrives properly freezer-cold, built on a custom-commissioned gin made specifically for the room, and it's become the drink most people mention first when they talk about this place afterward.
