Alongside it sits what plenty of regulars will call Australia's definitive boilermaker: a shot and a beer, paired with the kind of precision that turns a simple order into something worth ordering twice.

This cottage was built to be quietly functional, a service building nobody was meant to notice, and it's ended up as one of the most talked-about small rooms in the country: in 2025, the World's 50 Best Bars judges ranked it nineteenth anywhere on earth.

There's no booking system here, walk-ins only.

If the room's already full when you arrive, the queue tends to form quietly along Little Lonsdale Street — and it's usually worth the wait.

tours.title: Carlton Gardens
tours.shortDescription: Twenty-six plane trees lined up on purpose, all pointing at the dome Melbourne built to impress the world.
tours.longDescription: William Sangster and Joseph Reed laid these gardens out so that every visitor's eye would travel down a single avenue of plane trees to the Royal Exhibition Building's dome — an 1880 announcement that a gold-rush city considered itself ready for the world stage. Josef Hochgurtel's fountain, carved for the exhibition, dresses the idea of trade between nations in Victorian flora and exuberance. The building behind it hosted the first sitting of Australia's Commonwealth Parliament in 1901, served as an emergency influenza hospital in 1919, and staged Olympic weightlifting, wrestling and basketball in 1956 — and unlike almost every other world's-fair hall on earth, it never came down. UNESCO listed building and gardens together in 2004: one of the few places anywhere still doing the job it was built for. The quieter northern half holds a second garden, and the Melbourne Museum beyond it.

stops.title: Carlton Gardens
stops.caption: It's 1880, and Melbourne wants to prove something to the rest of the world.
stops.transcriptText:
It's 1880, and Melbourne wants to prove something to the rest of the world.

Carlton Gardens: stand where the long plane-tree avenue meets the fountain at its northern end, facing the dome of the Royal Exhibition Building, and you're standing exactly where the whole layout was designed to point. William Sangster and Joseph Reed planned it that way on purpose, lining twenty-six plane trees up in a single avenue so that every visitor's eye would travel straight down them toward the building at the far end.

Have a look at the fountain first. It was carved by Josef Hochgurtel for the 1880 exhibition, and it represents trade between nations, dressed up in Victorian-era flora and fauna — the kind of confident, slightly over-the-top gesture you'd expect from a city trying to announce its arrival on the world stage.

Behind it, the Royal Exhibition Building has done a lot more than sit still and look grand. It hosted the very first sitting of the Commonwealth Parliament of Australia in 1901, became an emergency influenza hospital during the 1919 pandemic, and even staged Olympic weightlifting, wrestling and basketball when the Games came to Melbourne in 1956.

The interesting bit is this: almost every other building raised for a nineteenth-century world's fair was meant to be temporary, and most of them came down within a few years of the exhibitions that built them. This one didn't. It's still standing, still hosting exhibitions the way it always has, which is part of why UNESCO listed the building and these gardens together as a World Heritage site in 2004 — one of the few places on earth still doing the job it was built for.

The gardens run on well past this fountain in both directions.

If you've got the time, the quieter northern half holds a second garden and the Melbourne Museum beyond it — worth the extra walk, especially once the avenue behind you starts filling up with tour groups.

tours.title: Carnation Canteen
tours.shortDescription: Twenty seats, a pink marble bar, and a menu that reinvents itself every single week.
tours.longDescription: Behind a peeling, barely-signed shopfront on Gore Street in Fitzroy, chef Audrey Shaw runs one of the neighbourhood's hardest bookings: twenty seats total, fresh flowers against a slab of pink marble, warm lamplight, and a menu rewritten weekly around whatever produce is actually worth cooking. Shaw's pedigree — London's River Cafe, Tedesca Osteria — sits quietly behind every plate without the room ever announcing it, and the wine list is curated to follow the kitchen rather than perform on its own. A dozen dishes that change every week is a far harder trick than a long static list: nowhere to hide a weak plate, nothing to fall back on when a season moves on. Book a few days out, not a few hours — and come back in a month, when the menu will have moved on completely.

stops.title: Carnation Canteen
stops.caption: On a quiet backstreet in Fitzroy, behind a shopfront easy to miss entirely, twenty seats and a slab of pink marble make up one of the neighbourhood's most talked-about bookings.
stops.transcriptText:
On a quiet backstreet in Fitzroy, behind a shopfront easy to miss entirely, twenty seats and a slab of pink marble make up one of the neighbourhood's most talked-about bookings.

Find Gore Street and look for the narrow frontage with the layered, slightly cracking paint — that's Carnation Canteen, and there's rarely much of a sign announcing it. Inside, the room leans modern rustic French bistro: fresh flowers set against that pink marble bar, warm lamplight, and just twenty seats total, which means every table in the place is, in some sense, the good one. With a room this small, the tables tend to book out well ahead of the weekend, so most regulars have learned to plan a few days rather than a few hours in advance.

The kitchen is where the real story sits. Chef Audrey Shaw curates a menu that changes weekly according to whatever produce is actually worth cooking that week, and she's brought serious pedigree to a genuinely small room — time spent at London's River Cafe and at Tedesca Osteria sits behind every plate that comes out of this kitchen, even though nothing about the space itself tries to announce that.

A menu this size, changing this often, is a much harder trick than a long, static one. There's nowhere to hide a weak dish on a list of a dozen items, and nothing to fall back on once a season's produce moves on, which means the room is essentially reinventing itself every week, quietly, without ever making a show of it. The wine list gets the same care, curated to sit alongside whatever's coming out of the kitchen rather than existing as its own separate performance.

Come back in a month and the menu will have moved on completely.

That's rather the appeal of a kitchen that refuses to print the same thing twice — worth treating this less as a restaurant you've visited once and more as one you keep circling back to.

tours.title: Chin Chin
tours.shortDescription: No bookings, communal tables, ten thousand guests a week — the restaurant that democratised dinner in Melbourne.
tours.longDescription: When restaurateur Chris Lucas walked into this Flinders Lane building with chefs Andrew Gimber and Ben Cooper in 2011, it was a defunct nightclub that had lost its liquor licence, buried under disco balls and velour carpet. Underneath was, in Lucas's words, simply a beautiful building — and the modern Thai hawker-style room they opened in it has never taken a booking. Everyone queues, everyone sits at communal tables, and a food critic waits like a family passing through on a Tuesday. A custom sound system runs upbeat playlists at genuine volume, rotating artwork covers the walls, and the room reads as a party even at half capacity. Feeding more than ten thousand guests a week, Chin Chin is by some measures the most successful restaurant Australia has produced — and most of the venues its success spawned still run on the same no-reservations rule.

stops.title: Chin Chin
stops.caption: Look at the room around you: the exposed brick, the high ceilings, the artwork crowding almost every wall.
stops.transcriptText:
Look at the room around you: the exposed brick, the high ceilings, the artwork crowding almost every wall. None of it was visible the day this building was found.

You're on Flinders Lane, at the door where the queue tends to gather, and that's the same entrance chefs Andrew Gimber and Ben Cooper walked through with restaurateur Chris Lucas back in 2011. At the time, the building was a defunct nightclub that had lost its liquor licence, buried under disco balls, velour carpet and boarded-up windows — and underneath all of it, the three of them found what Lucas later called simply a beautiful building.

Start with how the place actually runs. Chin Chin doesn't take bookings, and it never has: everyone queues, everyone sits at communal tables, and nobody gets treated as more important than anyone else in the room, whether that's a food critic or a family passing through on a Tuesday. It's a small, deliberate act of democratising what going out for dinner in this city used to feel like.

Then there's the atmosphere holding it all together: a custom sound system running upbeat playlists at genuine volume, and rotating artwork from both established and emerging artists covering the walls, which is part of why the room reads more like a party than a restaurant, even at half capacity.

This modern Thai hawker-style menu now feeds more than ten thousand guests a week, by some measures making Chin Chin the most successful restaurant Australia has produced, and its success gave Chris Lucas the platform to open half a dozen more rooms across two cities.

Most of them still don't take bookings.

If the queue tonight looks too long, Lucas's other venues are scattered within a few minutes' walk in almost every direction, and most of them run on exactly the same no-reservations rule.

tours.title: CIBI
tours.shortDescription: A Japanese breakfast, a Sori Yanagi kettle, and a Collingwood warehouse that ended up opening a branch in Tokyo.
tours.longDescription: Meg and Zenta Tanaka named their converted Keele Street garment factory after the Japanese word for a small child — curious, still playing, not yet weighed down by grown-up rules — and split its eight hundred square metres between a café built around traditional Japanese breakfast and a design shop where Hakusan porcelain, Sori Yanagi homewares, Tendo Mokko furniture and Noguchi's paper Akari lights sit on the shelves with no more ceremony than the coffee cups next door. They opened the original, much smaller CIBI on this same street in 2008 and outgrew it entirely. The direction of travel is the real story: most Japanese cafés in Melbourne import a culture that flows one way, but in 2017 the Tanakas opened a second CIBI back in Tokyo — Melbourne, for once, exporting rather than borrowing.

stops.title: CIBI
stops.caption: There's a nice bit of wordplay folded into this shop's name, if you know where to look for it.
stops.transcriptText:
There's a nice bit of wordplay folded into this shop's name, if you know where to look for it.

Inside a converted warehouse on Keele Street in Collingwood — once a garment factory, now flooded with daylight through its high industrial windows — CIBI splits cleanly into two halves under one roof: a design shop on one side, a café built around Japanese breakfast on the other. Meg and Zenta Tanaka opened the original, much smaller version on this same street back in 2008, and outgrew that first site so thoroughly that they eventually moved the whole operation into this larger, eight-hundred-square-metre space.

The name itself comes from the Japanese word for a small child: someone curious, still playing, not yet weighed down by grown-up rules, which the Tanakas have said is exactly the spirit they wanted the whole space to carry.

On the retail side, look for Hakusan porcelain, homewares by the designer Sori Yanagi, furniture from Tendo Mokko, and Noguchi's paper Akari lights sitting among the shelves — genuinely significant pieces of Japanese design, sold with no more ceremony than the coffee cups next door. On the café side, the traditional Japanese breakfast anchors everything: a coffee bar, sake, oden, and workshops that shift with the seasons.

CIBI's success ran in a direction you don't usually see. Most Japanese cafés and design shops in Melbourne are importing a culture that flows one way, but CIBI grew so established in this warehouse that in 2017, the Tanakas opened a second CIBI back in Tokyo — Melbourne, for once, exporting rather than borrowing.

The retail side turns over often enough to reward a second visit.

Zenta and Meg also run a smaller sister space nearby called Mina-no-ie, worth finding if the mood's still Japanese by the time you finish your coffee.

tours.title: Four Pillars Gin Distillery
tours.shortDescription: Three friends who'd never distilled a drop taught themselves gin — and were named the world's best producer three times.
tours.longDescription: Matt Jones, Stuart Gregor and Cameron Mackenzie bought a German copper still in 2013 with no distilling experience between them, set up in a former Healesville timber yard on the edge of the Yarra Valley, and opened to the public in 2015. The still — Wilma, named after the head distiller's late mother — works behind portholes alongside the botanicals and a solera of ageing barrels, with the bottling line usually running in view. The flagship Rare Dry Gin was built to give Australian gin its own character rather than copy London; the Bloody Shiraz — cool-climate Yarra Valley shiraz grapes steeped in it for eight weeks, no added sugar — is the one people talk about afterwards, deep ruby until soda flushes it iridescent pink. Named international gin producer of the year three times since opening: precision over volume, from a standing start. Tours run most weekday afternoons, ten guests at a time.

stops.title: Four Pillars Gin Distillery
stops.caption: Three friends bought a copper still from Germany in 2013, and not one of them had ever distilled a drop of gin before.
stops.transcriptText:
Three friends bought a copper still from Germany in 2013, and not one of them had ever distilled a drop of gin before.

Healesville, on the edge of the Yarra Valley, in what used to be a timber yard: that's where Matt Jones, Stuart Gregor and Cameron Mackenzie set up shop, and Four Pillars has stayed on this same site since opening its doors to the public in 2015. Sensing a gin boom on the way, the three of them decided to teach themselves the craft from scratch rather than wait for someone else to do it properly.

Look for the portholes along one wall — that's the still itself, nicknamed Wilma after the late mother of the head distiller, and behind it sit the botanicals and a solera of ageing barrels, working their way down toward the bottling line you can usually see running most days.

The flagship is the Rare Dry Gin, built specifically to give Australian gin its own character rather than copy anything London was already doing. But the drink most people end up talking about afterward is the Bloody Shiraz: cool-climate Yarra Valley shiraz grapes steeped in that Rare Dry Gin for eight weeks with no added sugar, turning a deep ruby that flushes iridescent pink the moment soda hits the glass.

The founders' stated goal was to help people drink better, not more, and it's paid off well beyond Healesville — Four Pillars has been named international gin producer of the year three times since it opened, proof that starting from zero experience isn't necessarily a disadvantage, provided the ambition is precision rather than volume.

Guided tours run most weekday afternoons, past the stills and down to the bottling line, limited to just ten guests at a time.

If the timing doesn't suit, ask about the Maker's Session instead — a few hours building and bottling a gin of your own to take home.

tours.title: France-Soir
tours.shortDescription: The same blue neon, the same brasserie, the same owner since 1986 — and a 4,500-bin cellar built bottle by bottle.
tours.longDescription: Jean-Paul Prunetti has run the room at 11 Toorak Road more or less unchanged for four decades. He opened it in 1986 with Yvon Vogel, a former professional rugby player who toured Australia, liked Melbourne enough to stay, and simply found a shop for lease; Vogel went home to France for good in 1988, and Prunetti — in hospitality since he was fourteen — has run it alone ever since, refusing every offer to expand or franchise. The service keeps a classic Parisian brasserie rhythm, unhurried and precise, and the wine list runs to roughly four and a half thousand bins, one of the largest attached to any single restaurant in Melbourne — the kind of list you build over decades, bottle by bottle, as a room slowly earns the trust to hold them. Springsteen and Jagger have both eaten here in passing. Go on a weeknight; the list gets the attention it deserves.

stops.title: France-Soir
stops.caption: You'll spot France-Soir from down the block by its blue neon sign, glowing over Toorak Road the way it has since 1986.
stops.transcriptText:
You'll spot France-Soir from down the block by its blue neon sign, glowing over Toorak Road the way it has since 1986.

Look for that sign at number eleven, and you're standing outside a restaurant that's barely changed its address, its menu, or its owner in forty years. Jean-Paul Prunetti opened it with Yvon Vogel, a former professional rugby player who'd been touring Australia, liked Melbourne enough to stay, and simply found a shop for lease on this stretch of road rather than heading home. Their partnership lasted only until 1988, when Vogel returned to France for good, and Prunetti — in hospitality since he was fourteen years old — has run the place alone ever since, refusing every offer to expand or franchise it elsewhere.

Inside, the service still follows the rhythm of a classic Parisian brasserie: unhurried, precise, and built around a wine list that runs to roughly four thousand five hundred bins, one of the largest attached to any single restaurant in Melbourne. It's the kind of list you build over decades rather than order in for an opening night, bottle by bottle, as the room itself slowly earns the trust to hold onto them. That combination of food, wine and old-world service has quietly drawn in some unlikely regulars over the years, including Bruce Springsteen and Mick Jagger, both of whom have eaten here while passing through the city.

Restaurants up and down this strip have opened, reinvented themselves and closed again many times over across four decades, but Prunetti never chased any of those trends. He kept the same bistro doing the same thing, and outlasted almost everyone who tried something newer.

The blue sign still glows every night, exactly where it's always been.

Weeknights tend to be quieter here than weekends, and that's genuinely the better time to visit — the wine list gets the attention it deserves, and so does the room.

tours.title: Gimlet at Cavendish House
tours.shortDescription: Andrew McConnell's grand Art Deco dining room, named — deliberately — after the humblest drink on the list.
tours.longDescription: Cavendish House has stood at the corner of Russell Street and Flinders Lane since the 1920s, heritage-listed Art Deco in a Chicago style that was rare for Melbourne, and when Andrew McConnell moved Gimlet into its ground floor in 2020 the Sydney design firm Acme leaned into that history rather than covering it up: chequerboard tiles, deep leather booths, a long curved marble bar, ornate light fixtures hanging above head height. Naming a room this grand after gin-and-cordial is a small, deliberate joke about not taking the grandeur too seriously, and the house martini follows the same instinct — orange-bergamot bitters, drinking looser and rounder than the sharp classic. The roast chicken with vadouvan sauce and fried curry leaves is the dish people name first; the coal-grilled T-bone and half a southern rock lobster round out the signatures. Look up at the lights before you sit down — most of the room's personality sits above eye level.

stops.title: Gimlet at Cavendish House
stops.caption: The black-and-white tiled floor under your feet is doing a lot of the talking before a single dish arrives.
stops.transcriptText:
The black-and-white tiled floor under your feet is doing a lot of the talking before a single dish arrives.

Cavendish House, at the corner of Russell Street and Flinders Lane, has stood since the 1920s, and Andrew McConnell moved his restaurant Gimlet into its ground floor in 2020 — chequerboard tiles, deep leather booths and all. The building itself is heritage-listed, Art Deco, built in a Chicago style that wasn't common in Melbourne at the time, and the Sydney design firm Acme leaned into that history rather than covering it up: a long, curved marble bar, ornate hanging light fixtures, and a room that channels the glamour of an early twentieth-century European bistro without pretending to actually be one.

Gimlet takes its name from one of the simplest cocktails on any bar list, just gin and cordial, and naming a genuinely grand dining room after it is a small, deliberate joke about not taking the grandeur too seriously. The house martini follows the same instinct — built with orange-bergamot bitters, it drinks with the looser, rounder feel of a negroni rather than the sharp, classic version most people expect.

On the food side, the roast chicken has become the dish people mention first, finished with vadouvan sauce and fried curry leaves, while the T-bone comes grilled over coals with fries and house-made condiments, and half a southern rock lobster shows up often enough to count as a genuine signature rather than a special.

This room is dressed up properly, marble and brass and all, but it borrowed its name from the humblest drink behind the bar: grandeur, deliberately, without any stuffiness attached to it.

Before you sit down, look up at the light fixtures over the bar.

Most of this room's personality sits above head height, and it's easy to miss on the way to a table if you're not looking for it.

tours.title: Heide Museum of Modern Art
tours.shortDescription: The farmhouse where Sidney Nolan painted the Ned Kelly series at the dining table — now fifteen acres of museum.
tours.longDescription: John and Sunday Reed bought this Bulleen property on a bend of the Birrarung, the Yarra River, in 1934 and opened their home to a circle of painters that included Sidney Nolan, Joy Hester, Albert Tucker and Arthur Boyd. At the dining table of the farmhouse now called Heide I, between 1946 and 1947, Nolan painted most of his twenty-seven-painting Ned Kelly series amid the books, arguments and general noise of the household. Heide II, commissioned from architect David McGlashan as 'a gallery to be lived in', took the profession's Building of the Year award in 1968 with no real line drawn between home and exhibition space. When Heide finally opened to the public in November 1981, the first exhibition was the Kelly paintings, hung in the same dining room where they were made. Most museums house art made somewhere else entirely; this one brought the art home. The sculpture park runs the full fifteen acres down toward the river, with the Reeds' kitchen garden still planted at the northern end.

stops.title: Heide Museum of Modern Art
stops.caption: It's 1946, and a circle of friends gathered round a dining table are about to become one of the most influential groups in Australian art.
stops.transcriptText:
It's 1946, and a circle of friends gathered round a dining table are about to become one of the most influential groups in Australian art.

Bulleen, on a bend of the Birrarung, the Yarra River: the modest farmhouse now known as Heide I sits at the heart of fifteen acres of parkland, sculpture and heritage kitchen garden, and it was here that John and Sunday Reed, who bought the property in 1934, opened their home to a circle of painters that included Sidney Nolan, Joy Hester, Albert Tucker and Arthur Boyd.

Have a look at the dining room first, if you can. It was at that table, between 1946 and 1947, that Sidney Nolan painted most of his twenty-seven-painting Ned Kelly series, working while surrounded by books, arguments and the general noise of the household, rather than in any studio built for the purpose.

Then there's Heide II, the second house the Reeds commissioned once their first arts venture, the Museum of Modern Art of Australia, had run its course. Architect David McGlashan designed it as, in his words, a gallery to be lived in, and it won Building of the Year from the profession's own institute in 1968 — a home and an exhibition space with no real line drawn between the two.

When Heide finally opened to the public in November 1981, the very first exhibition was Nolan's Ned Kelly paintings, hung in the same dining room where he'd painted them thirty-five years earlier. Most museums are built to house art that was made somewhere else entirely. This one brought the art home.

The sculpture park continues well beyond both houses, scattered across the full fifteen acres down toward the river.

Give yourself time to walk all of it — the kitchen garden at the northern end, planted in the same beds the Reeds once tended themselves, is easy to miss if you only came for the paintings.

tours.title: HER
tours.shortDescription: Five floors of one venue, each deliberately unlike the last, stacked inside a century-old CBD building.
tours.longDescription: The HQ Group — the team behind Arbory Bar and Arbory Afloat — gutted 270 Lonsdale Street entirely and reopened it in 2022 as a single venue that changes character floor by floor: Italian marble and orange velvet at the ground-floor bar, a stairwell lit specifically for the job by the French lighting designer Hervé Descottes, a dedicated music room and separate dining rooms mid-climb, and a Tamsin Johnson-designed rooftop on level five serving barbecue-driven Thai food with natural wine under art nouveau fixtures. A hundred-year-old shell asked to hold five rooms that deliberately refuse to agree with each other is a strange trick, and HER pulls it off precisely by not trying to reconcile them. Start at the ground-floor bar and work your way up — the mood gets looser and louder as you climb, and the rooftop is at its best just as the sun drops behind the skyline.

stops.title: HER
stops.caption: This is HER: five floors of it, stacked on top of a Melbourne CBD building that's been standing for roughly a century.
stops.transcriptText:
This is HER: five floors of it, stacked on top of a Melbourne CBD building that's been standing for roughly a century.

Two hundred and seventy Lonsdale Street: the HQ Group, the team behind Arbory Bar and Arbory Afloat, gutted this building entirely and reopened it in 2022 as a single venue that changes completely depending on which floor you're standing on. The ground floor runs as a bar with Italian marble underfoot, orange velvet banquettes and skirted stools borrowed from a Parisian sensibility, while the stairwell connecting every level was lit specifically for the job by the French lighting designer Hervé Descottes.

Keep climbing and the mood shifts each time. Somewhere in the middle sits a dedicated music room, and a handful of separate dining spaces besides, each fitted out with its own colour palette and its own reason for existing, so that moving up through the building feels less like changing floors and more like changing venues entirely. By the time you reach the rooftop on level five, the whole thing opens into an open-air room designed by Tamsin Johnson, dressed in art nouveau fixtures and old-world glamour, serving barbecue-driven Thai food alongside natural wine and fruit-forward cocktails.

A hundred-year-old shell is being asked to hold five entirely different rooms at once, each deliberately unlike the last, rather than one consistent theme repeated floor by floor. It's a strange trick to pull off inside a heritage building, and HER pulls it off simply by not trying to make the floors agree with each other.

The rooftop is at its best right as the sun starts to drop behind the skyline.

If you've got the stamina for all five floors, start at the ground floor bar and work your way up — the mood gets looser, and louder, the higher you climb, and the rooftop rewards the patience it takes to get there.

tours.title: Lune Croissanterie Fitzroy
tours.shortDescription: A former Formula One aerodynamicist applies materials science to butter and flour, in a glass cube inside a warehouse.
tours.longDescription: Kate Reid designed airflow for the Williams Formula One team before she ever laminated a croissant, and Lune runs on the same rigour: the kitchen is a climate-controlled glass cube by Studio Esteta, dropped into a crumbling brick Fitzroy shell, with ceiling lights splayed in long lines deliberately modelled on the Millennium Falcon's jump to hyperdrive. She opened a tiny Elwood shop in 2012, then moved here in 2015 with her brother Cam and café operator Nathan Toleman, and in 2016 the New York Times called her croissants some of the finest anywhere in the world. RMIT — the university where she trained as an aerospace engineer — later awarded her an honorary doctorate for the work, which is not a sentence many pastries have earned. Everything in the room is concrete, down to the stools. The queue moves faster than it looks; the better flavours rarely survive past midday.

stops.title: Lune Croissanterie Fitzroy
stops.caption: The woman who runs this kitchen used to design the aerodynamics of Formula One cars.
stops.transcriptText:
The woman who runs this kitchen used to design the aerodynamics of Formula One cars.

The glass box in the middle of this converted Fitzroy warehouse is the kitchen itself: a climate-controlled cube, designed by the local firm Studio Esteta, that sits inside a crumbling brick shell like something dropped in from outside. Kate Reid trained as an aerospace engineer, worked as an aerodynamicist for the Williams Formula One team in her early twenties, then walked away from it and opened a tiny Elwood shop making croissants in 2012, before moving into this much larger space in 2015 with her brother Cam and the café operator Nathan Toleman.

Look up while you're inside, and you'll notice the ceiling lights run in long splayed lines — deliberately modelled on the blur of stars when the Millennium Falcon jumps to hyperdrive, which gives the whole room the feel of a space station rather than a bakery.

The engineering habit never really left her. Lamination, temperature, timing — the entire discipline of croissant-making is essentially a materials-science problem, and Reid approaches it with the same rigour she once applied to airflow over a race car, which is part of why the New York Times called her croissants some of the finest anywhere in the world back in 2016. RMIT, the same university where she trained as an aerospace engineer, later awarded her an honorary doctorate for the work, which is an unusual thing for a croissant to earn anyone.

Everything in the room is made of concrete: the counters, the islands, even the stools.

If the queue looks long, it usually moves faster than it looks — worth staying for, since the better flavours rarely last past midday, and the cabinet empties out well before closing most days.

tours.title: Matilda 159 Domain
tours.shortDescription: Scott Pickett's most personal restaurant — named after his daughter — runs entirely on fire.
tours.longDescription: There's no gas burner in Matilda's open kitchen: everything that reaches the table at 159 Domain Road has crossed live coals or open flame — wood-roasted kohlrabi, smoked saltbush lamb rump, barramundi, wagyu, a bone-in rib-eye charred outside and pink through the middle, and a Pink Lady apple tarte tatin finished with smoked yoghurt ice cream. The room plays along: rough-edged timber tables, leather banquettes, glass cabinets packed with botanicals, and the kitchen essentially on display rather than hidden behind a wall. The choice worth noticing is that Pickett put the project carrying his own daughter's name inside someone else's hotel — the ground floor of United Places — rather than a standalone building of his own, and let the fire do the talking. Special-occasion territory, at around a hundred to a hundred and twenty dollars a head; Domain Road runs quiet, and it's a pleasant street to walk while you wait.

stops.title: Matilda 159 Domain
stops.caption: Look toward the open kitchen at the back of the room, and you'll notice there's no gas burner in sight — only fire.
stops.transcriptText:
Look toward the open kitchen at the back of the room, and you'll notice there's no gas burner in sight — only fire.

You're on Domain Road in South Yarra, on the ground floor of the United Places hotel, inside a restaurant chef Scott Pickett named after his own daughter. Even the number in the name is really just the street address, one five nine, folded into the restaurant's own title rather than left on a sign outside. Everything that reaches the table has passed across live coals or open flame at some point: wood-roasted kohlrabi, smoked saltbush lamb rump, bush lamb, barramundi and wagyu, and a rib-eye bone-in charred outside and pink through the middle, finished off with a Pink Lady apple tarte tatin glazed in caramelised toffee and topped with smoked yoghurt ice cream.

The room itself plays along with the theme — rough-edged wooden tables, leather banquettes, and glass cabinets packed with botanicals, all built around a kitchen that's essentially on display rather than hidden behind a wall.

The choice worth noticing is putting Pickett's most personal project, the one carrying his own daughter's name, inside someone else's hotel rather than a standalone building of his own. Most chefs save the eponymous project for somewhere entirely theirs; Pickett folded his into someone else's address instead, and let the fire do the talking rather than the room.

Watch the kitchen for a minute before you sit down.

Domain Road runs quiet compared with the main strips nearby, so if you're early for your table, it's a pleasant enough street to walk while you wait, and worth knowing that a meal here tends to run somewhere around a hundred to a hundred and twenty dollars a head — squarely special-occasion territory rather than a casual Tuesday.

tours.title: Melbourne Museum
tours.shortDescription: A living rainforest behind one glass door, seventeen dinosaurs behind another, and Phar Lap standing in between.
tours.longDescription: Museums Victoria's flagship sits in Carlton Gardens next to the Royal Exhibition Building, on the same World Heritage site, holding natural science, cultural history and the state's First Peoples' stories across seven galleries and an IMAX cinema. The Forest Gallery is a genuine cool-temperate rainforest under glass — fifty-five metres long, over a hundred plant species, its own mist and birdsong rising thirty-five metres to the roof. Dinosaur Walk marches a twenty-metre Mamenchisaurus over sixteen other specimens, and the taxidermied Phar Lap stands exactly as he did the day he died — though his famously oversized heart is in Canberra, several hundred kilometres away. Bunjilaka, the museum's Aboriginal Cultural Centre, was built in direct collaboration with the Kulin Nation to tell Victoria's First Peoples' stories on their own terms — worth setting aside real time for, rather than squeezing in on the way to the dinosaurs. It's easy to lose half a day here without reaching the gift shop.

stops.title: Melbourne Museum
stops.caption: Behind one set of glass doors in this building, there's an actual rainforest growing.
stops.transcriptText:
Behind one set of glass doors in this building, there's an actual rainforest growing. Behind another, seventeen dinosaurs are marching through a gallery.

Inside this building, in Carlton Gardens, next door to the Royal Exhibition Building on the same World Heritage site, Melbourne Museum holds the flagship collection of Museums Victoria — natural science, cultural history and the state's own First Peoples' stories, spread across seven separate galleries and its own IMAX cinema, all under one roof.

Start with the Forest Gallery. It's a genuine cool-temperate rainforest under glass, twenty-seven metres wide and fifty-five long, home to over a hundred plant species and around twenty different vertebrates, complete with its own mist and birdsong rising toward a roof thirty-five metres up at its tallest point.

Then there's Dinosaur Walk, where a Mamenchisaurus stretching twenty metres from nose to tail towers over sixteen other specimens, and the taxidermied body of the racehorse Phar Lap, standing exactly as he did the day he died — though his heart, famously oversized, isn't here at all. It's on display in a museum in Canberra, several hundred kilometres away.

The Bunjilaka Aboriginal Cultural Centre sits within the same building, built in direct collaboration with the Kulin Nation to tell Victoria's First Peoples' stories in their own terms, which makes this one building doing an unusual amount at once: living ecosystem, celebrated legend, and living culture, all under a single roof.

The giant squid in the Marine Life gallery is twelve metres long, pulled from eight hundred metres down off Tasmania's coast.

Bunjilaka is worth setting aside real time for rather than squeezing in on the way to the dinosaurs — it rewards a slower visit than most of the museum around it, and it's easy to lose half a day here without ever reaching the gift shop.

tours.title: Minamishima
tours.shortDescription: Twelve seats, one chef, fish flown in from Toyosu — the counter widely called Australia's finest sushi.
tours.longDescription: Koichi Minamishima spent two years simply washing rice at a restaurant in Nagoya before anyone let him near the sushi master, then fifteen years running the kitchen at Kenzan in the CBD, before opening this Richmond room under his own name in 2014. The hinoki wood counter seats exactly twelve, and he works its full length himself, plating each piece of nigiri and passing it across without much ceremony. Seatings run as a full omakase of around fifteen courses, or a shorter menu ending in ten courses of nigiri, built from local seafood alongside fish flown in directly from Tokyo's Toyosu market; a private room behind follows the precise geometry of a traditional tatami room. The scarcity is the whole philosophy — twelve seats, one chef, one continuous line of attention, and not a single seat ever added to make it easier. Bookings open weeks ahead and disappear almost as fast; put a date in the diary rather than chancing a walk-in.

stops.title: Minamishima
stops.caption: There's a rule at this counter that most restaurants would find commercially reckless: only twelve seats, ever.
stops.transcriptText:
There's a rule at this counter that most restaurants would find commercially reckless: only twelve seats, ever.

The hinoki wood counter running through this Richmond dining room seats exactly that many, and chef Koichi Minamishima works the whole length of it himself, plating each piece of nigiri and passing it across without much ceremony. Before any of this, he spent two years simply washing rice at a restaurant in Nagoya before anyone let him near the sushi master, then another fifteen years running the kitchen at one of the CBD's most respected Japanese restaurants, Kenzan, before finally opening this place under his own name in 2014.

The room strips everything back to what matters: dark, moody lighting that puts the spotlight on the chefs rather than the diners, fine timber with a near-perfect grain, and a private dining room built on the precise geometry of a traditional tatami room.

Every seating is either a full omakase of around fifteen courses, or a shorter menu of shared dishes followed by ten courses of individual nigiri, built from local seafood alongside fish flown in directly from Tokyo's Toyosu Fish Market. Diners choose between that counter, watching every cut made an arm's length away, or the smaller private dining room set aside for larger groups, where the square, tatami-derived geometry does most of the talking instead. The scarcity is really the whole philosophy — twelve seats, one chef, one continuous line of attention, rather than a room built to turn tables quickly.

Bookings open weeks ahead and disappear almost as fast.

If you can't get a seat this trip, it's worth putting a date in the diary for next time rather than trying to walk in — this is not a room that takes chances on passing trade, and Minamishima himself has never seemed inclined to add a single extra seat to make it easier.

tours.title: MPavilion
tours.shortDescription: Tadao Ando's first Australian building — a floating concrete disc that was meant to come down, and didn't.
tours.longDescription: Every MPavilion commissioned for Queen Victoria Gardens since 2014 was designed as a season-long architecture pavilion — OMA, Amanda Levete, Studio Mumbai and Glenn Murcutt among the authors — hosting a full programme of free talks, performances and workshops before being dismantled and the site handed back. MPavilion 10, commissioned by the Naomi Milgrom Foundation and opened in November 2023, is the Pritzker Prize-winning Tadao Ando's first built work in Australia: a concrete disc fourteen and a half metres wide resting on a single central column, two seventeen-metre walls with horizontal openings framing the park and the skyline like deliberate photographs, half the plan paved and half given to a still reflecting pool — pure geometry, borrowed from the logic of a traditional Japanese walled garden. It was meant to follow its nine predecessors out; public support kept it standing, and its stay now runs through 2030. Few Ando buildings exist south of the equator — walk the full loop of the walls.

stops.title: MPavilion
stops.caption: Every pavilion built in this park since 2014 was designed to come down again within a year or two.
stops.transcriptText:
Every pavilion built in this park since 2014 was designed to come down again within a year or two. This one wasn't supposed to be the exception, and then it became one anyway.

Queen Victoria Gardens, beneath a concrete disc fourteen and a half metres wide, resting on a single central column: that's MPavilion 10, the first Australian project by the Pritzker Prize-winning architect Tadao Ando, commissioned by the Naomi Milgrom Foundation and opened in November 2023.

Look at the two long concrete walls first, each seventeen metres, with horizontal openings cut through them that frame the park and the city skyline like a pair of deliberate photographs. Ando calls the whole approach pure geometry: a circle and a square working together, with the space between them half paved and half given over to a still reflecting pool, borrowing directly from the logic of a traditional Japanese walled garden.

Nine pavilions came and went here before this one — designs by OMA, Amanda Levete, Studio Mumbai and Australia's own Glenn Murcutt among them, with a single year skipped during the pandemic — each one a season-long architecture commission, hosting a full programme of free talks, performances, workshops and installations before it was dismantled and the site handed back. This one was meant to follow the same pattern. Instead, public support for keeping it standing was strong enough that its stay has now been extended all the way through to 2030.

Walk the full loop around the walls before you leave.

The gardens themselves run right down to the lake beyond the pavilion, and that stretch is worth the extra ten minutes if the weather's on your side, especially given how few of Ando's buildings exist anywhere south of the equator.

tours.title: Napier Quarter
tours.shortDescription: A two-dollar espresso at the counter by day, a small-producers wine bar by night — same room, same tables.
tours.longDescription: Daniel Lewis and Simon Benjamin — cousins-in-law who each live close enough to walk here in under a minute — have run this Fitzroy corner since 2016 on a double identity: an unfussy espresso bar by day, with a strict no-alt-milk, no-takeaway policy and a standing-at-the-counter price it has more or less refused to move off two dollars, becoming a wine bar over the same twenty-odd seats at night without changing staff or moving a table. The anchovy toast — thick house mayonnaise and salsa verde under a scatter of anchovies, boiled egg on rye — is credited with starting a citywide obsession; beyond it the kitchen follows what's genuinely in season, yellow peaches with honey one month, ricotta with native pepperberry and persimmon the next. Venues that run two identities usually feel like two businesses sharing a lease; Napier Quarter simply lets the light change outside. Ask for a wine recommendation — the list moves faster than the printed version.

stops.title: Napier Quarter
stops.caption: Find the espresso bar at the front of the room, and order standing at the counter — it'll cost you two dollars, a price this place has more or less refused to move on.
stops.transcriptText:
Find the espresso bar at the front of the room, and order standing at the counter — it'll cost you two dollars, a price this place has more or less refused to move on.

That's Napier Quarter, on a residential backstreet in Fitzroy, run since 2016 by Daniel Lewis and Simon Benjamin, cousins-in-law who each live close enough to walk here in under a minute. By day it runs as an unfussy espresso bar with a strict no-alt-milk, no-takeaway policy; by evening, the same twenty-odd seats quietly become a wine bar built around small producers, without ever changing staff or moving a single table.

The dish most people mention first is the anchovy toast: thick house mayonnaise and salsa verde under a scatter of anchovies, finished with a sliced boiled egg on rye, and it's credited with starting something of a citywide obsession when it first appeared on the menu. Beyond that, the kitchen leans hard into whatever's genuinely in season — yellow peaches dressed simply with honey one month, ricotta lifted with native pepperberry and persimmon the next — rather than running a fixed menu year-round.

And here's the appeal: most venues that try to run two identities end up feeling like two separate businesses sharing a lease, but Napier Quarter simply lets the light change outside while the room keeps doing what it always does, just with wine glasses instead of coffee cups.

The wine list leans hard into small, lesser-known producers rather than anything you'd recognise from a bottle shop shelf.

Ask whoever's behind the bar for a recommendation rather than reading the list top to bottom — it changes often enough that the printed version is already a little out of date.

tours.title: National Gallery of Victoria
tours.shortDescription: Australia's oldest art museum, inside Roy Grounds' bluestone fortress — under the world's largest stained-glass ceiling.
tours.longDescription: The National Gallery of Victoria was founded in 1861, which makes it Australia's oldest public art museum and older than Federation itself; Roy Grounds' 1968 building on St Kilda Road — bluestone walls, deep moats, bold and deliberately blunt geometry — is really just the fourth or fifth home for the collection. Visitors arrive through the Waterwall, a continuous sheet of water running down glass at the entrance, and in the Great Hall overhead Leonard French's stained-glass ceiling — four years in the making, sixty point nine metres long — remains the largest work of its kind anywhere in the world, held up by its own forest of slim columns. None of it was decoration added later: Grounds built the sculpture, the ceiling and even the Featherston furniture into the plan from the beginning, so the building and its collection were never really two separate things. Lie down on a Great Hall bench if the room isn't busy — it's the only way to take in the whole ceiling at once.

stops.title: National Gallery of Victoria
stops.caption: The ceiling above the Great Hall is so heavy with glass and steel that it needed its own forest of slim columns just to keep it from sagging under its own weight.
stops.transcriptText:
The ceiling above the Great Hall is so heavy with glass and steel that it needed its own forest of slim columns just to keep it from sagging under its own weight.

The Great Hall sits dead centre of the National Gallery of Victoria on St Kilda Road, a building designed by Roy Grounds and opened in 1968, all bluestone walls, deep moats and bold, deliberately blunt geometry. The gallery itself is far older than its building — founded in 1861, it's Australia's oldest public art museum, which means this striking modernist shell is really just the fourth or fifth home for a collection that predates Federation. Overhead, Leonard French's stained-glass ceiling took him and his team four years to build, running sixty point nine metres long and thirteen point seven metres high, and it remains the largest work of its kind anywhere in the world.

Outside, the Waterwall along St Kilda Road does something similarly simple and effective: a continuous sheet of water running down glass at the entrance, so visitors walk straight through it on their way inside, arriving slightly changed before they've seen a single painting.

None of this was decoration added after the fact. Grounds built the sculpture, the ceiling and even the furniture into the plan from the very beginning — Norma Redpath's coat of arms above the entrance, furniture designed specifically for the space by Grant and Mary Featherston, French's glass overhead — so the building and its collection were never really two separate things to begin with, more one long, continuous artwork that visitors happen to walk through.

Lie down on one of the benches in the Great Hall if the room isn't too busy.

It's the only way to take in the whole ceiling at once, and most visitors walk straight underneath without ever trying it.

tours.title: Pellegrini's Espresso Bar
tours.shortDescription: The 1954 espresso bar that taught Melbourne coffee — same curved counter, same red vinyl, seventy years on.
tours.longDescription: Leo and Vildo Pellegrini had spent years pouring coffee at Florentino's down the street before opening their own room on Bourke Street in 1954, running one of the first genuine Italian espresso machines in the city — very likely the first inside the CBD, though a handful of Lygon Street cafés still contest the wider title. The room expanded once, in 1958, and has barely needed to change since: red vinyl stools along a long curved counter, mirrored walls, a chequerboard floor, and a short menu of pasta dishes served to a clientele that shifted over the decades from Italian migrants to theatre crowds, writers and tourists working from guidebooks. The National Trust formally listed it in 2014 — really just a certificate for something regulars had decided long before. Order a spaghetti if there's room at the counter, not just a coffee; it's the longest-serving dish and the best evidence of why this room never needed to reinvent itself.

stops.title: Pellegrini's Espresso Bar
stops.caption: Two Italian brothers who'd spent years pouring coffee at a restaurant down the street opened their own room on Bourke Street in 1954, and this city's coffee habit changed not long after.
stops.transcriptText:
Two Italian brothers who'd spent years pouring coffee at a restaurant down the street opened their own room on Bourke Street in 1954, and this city's coffee habit changed not long after.

Take a stool at the counter on Bourke Street if you can find one — red vinyl, set along a long curved bar that's barely moved since the room was built, with mirrored walls and a chequerboard floor doing the rest of the talking. Leo and Vildo Pellegrini had worked at Florentino's nearby before striking out on their own, and Pellegrini's became one of the first places in the city to run a genuine Italian espresso machine, helping kick-start Melbourne's coffee culture in the process. Whether it was truly the very first, ahead of a handful of cafés on Lygon Street doing much the same thing at roughly the same time, is still argued over by historians, though it was very likely the first inside the CBD itself.

The room expanded once, in 1958, and has barely needed to change since: the same narrow counter, the same handful of pasta dishes, and a clientele that shifted over the decades from Italian migrants to theatre crowds, writers, and eventually tourists working from a guidebook.

The debate over who really had the first machine matters far less than what's actually still running here — the same counter, doing the same job, more than seventy years on. In 2014 the National Trust formally listed the place, which is really just a certificate for something regulars had already decided long before.

Order a spaghetti if there's room at the counter, not just a coffee.

It's the dish that's been on the menu the longest, and it's usually the best evidence of why this room never needed to reinvent itself.

tours.title: Piccolina Gelateria
tours.shortDescription: Third-generation gelato in Hardware Lane, made from scratch on site — down to baking the brownies.
tours.longDescription: Sandra Foti learned gelato first from her father, who'd been making his own at home for years, then left a career in graphic design, went to Italy to sharpen the craft properly, and opened her first shop in Hawthorn in 2015. In the Hardware Lane store every batch is still made from scratch on site — no pre-made bases, no shortcuts, down to baking the brownies for the brownie gelato — with a core range of classics (salted caramel, passionfruit, honeycomb, a well-regarded dairy-free pistachio) beside a blackboard of seasonal Victorian produce that regulars check the way other people check the weather. Scaling up usually costs a gelateria its method — most that grow past one shop start buying bases in — but Piccolina kept the from-scratch rule as the stores multiplied, which is presumably part of why Nigella Lawson is said to stop in whenever she's in Melbourne. Ask what's on the blackboard before ordering from the regular menu.

stops.title: Piccolina Gelateria
stops.caption: There's a family recipe behind this counter, and it's barely changed in three generations.
stops.transcriptText:
There's a family recipe behind this counter, and it's barely changed in three generations.

Inside 43 Hardware Lane, one of the narrowest laneways in the CBD, Sandra Foti sells gelato made from a technique she learned first from her father, who'd been making his own at home for years before she ever thought to turn it into a business. She left a career in graphic design, went to Italy to sharpen the craft properly, and came home to open her first shop in Hawthorn in 2015.

Every batch is still made from scratch on site — no pre-made bases, no shortcuts — right down to baking her own brownies for the brownie gelato rather than buying them in. The core range leans toward the familiar, salted caramel, passionfruit, honeycomb, alongside a genuinely well-regarded pistachio made without dairy, but the flavours lean just as heavily on local, seasonal Victorian produce, and the blackboard changes often enough that regulars check it the way other people check the weather.

Not much got lost in scaling up here. A lot of gelato businesses that grow past one shop start relying on bases made somewhere else entirely, but Piccolina kept the same from-scratch method even as more stores opened, which is presumably part of why it's built a following well beyond the neighbourhood — Nigella Lawson is said to make a point of stopping in whenever she's in Melbourne, a detail regulars bring up almost as often as the flavours themselves.

Ask what's on the blackboard before ordering from the regular menu.

The rotating flavours are usually where the more interesting combinations turn up, and they don't last long once they're gone — worth checking even if you already know exactly which classic flavour you came in for.

tours.title: Pidapipó Laboratorio Fitzroy
tours.shortDescription: A gelato laboratory in a former bank, with beehives and a micro-garden on the roof feeding the counter below.
tours.longDescription: Lisa Valmorbida trained at Italy's Carpigiani Gelato University before starting Pidapipó as a pop-up in 2013, and the Laboratorio — inside a former 1960s bank at the northern end of Brunswick Street — is the fourth store she runs with her brother Jamie, and by far the most ambitious. The menu is held to eight flavours, deliberately far smaller than the other shops, built around local fruit growers and specialty seasonal ingredients so each flavour gets real attention rather than being one of forty in the same cabinet. The roof carries a working micro-garden of lemon myrtle, figs and wild strawberries, plus custom beehives installed by the urban beekeeping outfit Honey Fingers, whose honey ends up back in the gelato downstairs. A fourth store could easily have been another scoop shop; the siblings built something closer to a research kitchen stacked on a bank vault instead. Ask which flavour uses the rooftop honey that week — it changes with the bees' own schedule.

stops.title: Pidapipó Laboratorio Fitzroy
stops.caption: This building used to guard people's money. Now it guards gelato.
stops.transcriptText:
This building used to guard people's money. Now it guards gelato.

The Laboratorio sits inside a former 1960s bank on the northern end of Brunswick Street, the fourth and by far the most ambitious store from siblings Lisa and Jamie Valmorbida, who started Pidapipó as a pop-up back in 2013. Lisa trained at the Carpigiani Gelato University in Italy before bringing the technique home, and this flagship location is built specifically to be a working laboratory rather than just another counter — an eight-flavour menu, deliberately kept far smaller than any of the other three stores, built entirely around local fruit growers and specialty seasonal ingredients so that each flavour gets real attention rather than being one of forty crowding the same cabinet.

Look up, if you get the chance, toward the roof. There's a working micro-garden up there growing lemon myrtle, figs and wild strawberries, and a set of custom beehives installed by the urban beekeeping outfit Honey Fingers, producing actual honey that ends up back in the gelato downstairs. None of this was strictly necessary for a fourth store — Pidapipó could easily have opened another straightforward scoop shop and called it a day — but the siblings chose to build something closer to a genuine research kitchen instead.

Most gelato shops buy their specialty ingredients in. This one grows a meaningful share of them on its own roof, which turns the whole building into something closer to a working farm stacked on top of a bank vault than a typical dessert shop.

Ask which flavour uses the rooftop honey that week.

It changes with the season and the bees' own schedule, so the honey flavour on any given visit is genuinely one-of-a-kind, and it may well be different again the next time you come back to the same counter.

tours.title: Reine & La Rue
tours.shortDescription: Dinner on the floor of Melbourne's original Stock Exchange, under stained glass built for money rather than appetite.
tours.longDescription: William Pitt's 1891 Stock Exchange — lavish Free Gothic behind the old ANZ banking chamber at the corner of Queen and Collins — spent its first life moving money: stained glass throwing colour across a mosaic marble floor, towering pillars framing men shouting share prices. The Nomad Group's Al and Rebecca Yazbek spent more than two years working with Heritage Victoria and a pair of specialist architecture firms, negotiating what could be touched and what absolutely couldn't, before opening Reine & La Rue in August 2023 with the grandeur inherited rather than invented. The menu leans French — a baguette with cultured butter, wood-roasted leeks with hazelnut, zucchini flowers stuffed with duck, an eye fillet in café de Paris sauce — and flexes from a glass of Champagne at the bar to a whole table of shared plates under the glass. Look up before you look at the menu; the room fills, and the noise rises to meet the ceiling.

stops.title: Reine & La Rue
stops.caption: Before anyone ordered a baguette in this room, people were trading shares in it.
stops.transcriptText:
Before anyone ordered a baguette in this room, people were trading shares in it.

Behind the old ANZ banking chamber, on the corner of Queen and Collins, Reine and La Rue occupies the heritage-listed shell of Melbourne's original Stock Exchange, a building designed by William Pitt and finished in 1891 in a lavish Free Gothic style. Stained glass windows still throw colour across a mosaic marble floor, and the pillars that once framed men shouting share prices now frame up to a hundred and fifty people eating dinner instead.

It took the Nomad Group's Al and Rebecca Yazbek more than two years to get here, working alongside Heritage Victoria and a pair of specialist architecture firms to restore the space without smoothing away its history — an approach that opened to the public in August 2023, after months of negotiating what could be touched and what absolutely couldn't.

The menu leans French: a baguette served simply with cultured butter, wood-roasted leeks with hazelnut, zucchini flowers stuffed with duck, an eye fillet finished in café de Paris sauce. It's built to flex around however you want the night to go — a glass of Champagne and a snack at the bar, a full three courses tucked into a booth, or a whole table's worth of shared plates under that stained glass.

What's worth knowing, standing in the middle of all this, is that almost nothing here was built for eating. The mosaic floor, the marble, the towering pillars — every bit of the room's grandeur was designed to move money, not appetite, and the restaurant simply inherited it rather than inventing anything new.

Look up before you look at the menu.

The stained glass runs the full height of the room, and it's easiest to appreciate before the tables fill and the noise rises to match the ceiling.

tours.title: Royal Botanic Gardens Victoria — Melbourne Gardens
tours.shortDescription: The gardens where 'picturesque' beat 'scientific' — and the winner's framework still shapes every path.
tours.longDescription: Melbourne set this land aside south of the Yarra in March 1846 and gave it first to Ferdinand von Mueller, a serious botanist more interested in cataloguing species than arranging them beautifully. Public pressure eventually pushed him out, and from 1873 William Guilfoyle spent thirty-six years remaking the landscape as a picturesque English park crossed with a subtropical fantasy — bold foliage, sweeping lawns, sightlines engineered to surprise, plant collections chosen as much for drama as for science. Very little you walk through today escaped his hand: the ornamental lake and the great central lawn trace straight back to his opening years as director. The tension between the two men is the whole story of the place — a working scientific institution versus somewhere lovely for a Sunday afternoon — and the public won comprehensively. Guilfoyle's plantings are labelled throughout if you want the science under the scenery, and von Mueller's herbarium survives too, tucked away from the main paths.

stops.title: Royal Botanic Gardens Victoria — Melbourne Gardens
stops.caption: In 1873, Melbourne's botanic gardens got a new director for one specific reason: the previous one wasn't picturesque enough.
stops.transcriptText:
In 1873, Melbourne's botanic gardens got a new director for one specific reason: the previous one wasn't picturesque enough.

South of the Yarra, on land set aside for the gardens back in March 1846, the Melbourne Gardens spent their first decades under Ferdinand von Mueller, a serious botanist more interested in cataloguing species than arranging them beautifully. Public pressure eventually pushed him out, and William Guilfoyle took over in 1873 with an entirely different brief: make it beautiful, not just correct.

Guilfoyle spent the next thirty-six years reshaping the landscape into something closer to a picturesque English park crossed with a subtropical fantasy — bold foliage, sweeping lawns, sightlines engineered to surprise, and plant collections chosen as much for drama as for science. Very little of what you're walking through today wasn't touched by his hand at some point between 1873 and 1909.

The tension between those two directors is really the whole story of this place. Von Mueller wanted a working scientific institution, filled with specimens organised for study, while the public wanted somewhere lovely to walk on a Sunday afternoon, and in the end the public won, comprehensively enough that Guilfoyle's framework still shapes every path and lawn more than a century after he stopped working here. Even the ornamental lake and the sweeping central lawn, the parts most visitors photograph first, trace straight back to decisions Guilfoyle made in his opening years as director.

Somewhere between the ornamental lake and the tree fern gully, both instincts are still quietly at work.

Guilfoyle's plantings are labelled throughout the gardens if you want to hunt down the science underneath the scenery — worth doing, even if it's the scenery that pulled you in first, and von Mueller's original herbarium collection still exists too, just tucked away from the main paths where the crowds rarely wander.

tours.title: Royal Exhibition Building
tours.shortDescription: The world's-fair hall that refused to be temporary — and hosted a nation's first parliament for good measure.
tours.longDescription: Joseph Reed modelled the dome directly on Florence Cathedral, wrapped the rest in a French Beaux-Arts cross borrowed from half a dozen European traditions at once, and the whole structure went up in eighteen months for the Melbourne International Exhibition of 1880 — a young gold-rush colony arguing it belonged in the same conversation as London, Paris and Vienna. On the twenty-fifth of May 1901, the Great Hall under that dome hosted the opening of the first federal parliament of Australia: a brand-new nation choosing a Victorian exhibition hall, rather than anywhere purpose-built, to mark the moment. Almost every other building raised for a nineteenth-century world's fair was temporary and came down within a few years; this one never did, and it still hosts exhibitions the way it always has — a large part of why UNESCO listed it together with Carlton Gardens in 2004. Step well back at some point: the proportions only make sense from a distance, and the gardens were designed around exactly that long view.

stops.title: Royal Exhibition Building
stops.caption: This building went up in just eighteen months, and it's been standing for well over a century since.
stops.transcriptText:
This building went up in just eighteen months, and it's been standing for well over a century since.

Stand back far enough to take in the whole dome at once, and you're looking at architect Joseph Reed's answer to Florence Cathedral — he modelled the octagonal roof and dome on it directly, then wrapped the rest of the building in a French Beaux-Arts cross shape borrowed from half a dozen different European traditions at once. Governor George Bowen laid the foundation stone in February 1879, and the whole structure was finished in time for the Melbourne International Exhibition the following year.

The dome isn't just decoration sitting on top of a warehouse. It crowns a genuine Great Hall, built from brick, timber, steel and slate, and the building as a whole was Reed's attempt to convince the rest of the world that a young gold-rush colony belonged in the same conversation as London, Paris and Vienna, all of whom had already staged their own international exhibitions by then. Reed borrowed freely from Byzantine, Romanesque and Italian Renaissance sources at once, rather than committing to any single tradition, which is part of why the building still reads as slightly unplaceable today.

It clearly worked well enough, because on the twenty-fifth of May 1901, this same Great Hall hosted the opening of the first federal parliament of Australia — a brand-new nation choosing a Victorian exhibition hall, rather than anywhere purpose-built, to mark the moment officially.

Walk the full width of the building at some point, not just underneath the dome.

The proportions only really make sense from a distance, and most visitors never step back far enough to see the whole thing in one go — the surrounding gardens, laid out at the same time as the building, were designed with exactly that long view in mind.

tours.title: Shot Tower Museum
tours.shortDescription: A nine-storey Victorian shot factory, swallowed whole by a shopping centre under a glass cone.
tours.longDescription: Coop's Shot Tower has stood on this spot since 1889, dropping molten lead through a sieve from height to form pellets — up to twenty-five million an hour at full output. It was the tallest structure in Melbourne's CBD until the mid-1940s and kept producing shot commercially until 1961, when tightening firearms regulations finally killed the demand. Saved from the wrecking ball in 1973, it was then absorbed rather than restored: in 1991 Melbourne Central was built around it, with the Japanese architect Kisho Kurokawa's eighty-four-metre conical glass roof — twenty storeys of glazing — enclosing the whole tower above shopfronts that have nothing to do with Victorian industry. The free museum on the tower's second floor keeps the numbers: three hundred and twenty-seven steps, six tonnes of shot a week at peak, and the sheer strangeness of a heritage building surviving because a shopping mall built itself around it rather than through it. Find the seam where the old brickwork meets the modern glass; that join is the whole story.

stops.title: Shot Tower Museum
stops.caption: Look straight up through the glass, and you'll see a nine-storey brick tower that has no business being inside a shopping centre — and yet here it is.
stops.transcriptText:
Look straight up through the glass, and you'll see a nine-storey brick tower that has no business being inside a shopping centre — and yet here it is.

Coop's Shot Tower has stood on this spot since 1889, originally built to manufacture lead shot: molten metal dropped from height through a sieve, cooling into pellets on the way down, at a rate of up to twenty-five million pellets an hour when the tower was at full output. It was the tallest structure in Melbourne's CBD until the mid-1940s, and it kept producing shot commercially right up until 1961, when tightening firearms regulations finally killed the demand.

Rather than demolish an obsolete factory in the middle of the city, planners saved it from the wrecking ball in 1973 and, in 1991, built an entire shopping centre around it — enclosing the whole tower beneath an eighty-four-metre conical glass roof designed by the Japanese architect Kisho Kurokawa, twenty storeys of glazing rising above shop fronts that have absolutely nothing to do with lead shot or Victorian industry.

The museum on the tower's second floor, free to enter, tells the rest of the story: the three hundred and twenty-seven steps to the top, the six tonnes of shot produced weekly at its peak, and the sheer strangeness of a Victorian industrial relic surviving because a shopping mall was willing to build itself around it rather than through it. It's a genuinely unusual piece of adaptive reuse — most heritage buildings get restored and reopened; very few get quietly absorbed into the middle of a food court.

Look for the join where the old brickwork meets the modern glass overhead.

It's easy to miss while you're shopping, but that seam is really the whole story of the building above you.

tours.title: Shrine of Remembrance
tours.shortDescription: Victoria's memorial to the First World War, engineered so that once a year, light falls on a single word.
tours.longDescription: The Shrine of Remembrance opened on Armistice Day — the eleventh of November 1934 — before a crowd of three hundred thousand, as Victoria's memorial to the hundred and fourteen thousand men and women of the state who served in the First World War. Architects Phillip Hudson and James Wardrop, both veterans themselves, won the 1922 design competition with a building that borrows the Parthenon's Doric columns for its porticoes and the stepped pyramid roofline of the Mausoleum at Halicarnassus. In the Sanctuary, an aperture in the ceiling is calibrated so that at eleven in the morning on the eleventh of November, a narrow ray of sun crosses the Stone of Remembrance and settles precisely on the word LOVE — the exact hour the Armistice took effect in 1918 — with a quieter daily echo falling at eleven each morning year-round. Outside, the Eternal Flame lit by Queen Elizabeth II in 1954 extends the Shrine's remembrance to the conflicts that came after. The balcony above the Sanctuary looks back over the forecourt and out to the city.

stops.title: Shrine of Remembrance
stops.caption: Once a year, for a matter of seconds, a beam of sunlight finds one specific word carved into the stone in front of you.
stops.transcriptText:
Once a year, for a matter of seconds, a beam of sunlight finds one specific word carved into the stone in front of you.

The Stone of Remembrance sits at the heart of the Shrine's Sanctuary, and the Shrine itself was built as Victoria's memorial to the hundred and fourteen thousand men and women who served in the First World War, opened and dedicated on Armistice Day, the eleventh of November 1934, before a crowd of three hundred thousand people. The design came from a public competition held in 1922, drawing eighty-three entries, won by architects Phillip Hudson and James Wardrop, both veterans themselves, whose winning design borrowed the Doric columns of the Parthenon for the north and south porticoes and the stepped pyramid roofline from ancient reconstructions of the Mausoleum at Halicarnassus.

An aperture in the ceiling above the Stone lets a narrow ray of light through, and at eleven in the morning, on the eleventh day of November, that beam settles precisely on the word LOVE — timed to mark the exact hour the Armistice took effect in 1918.

The same beam falls at eleven each morning, year-round, as a quieter daily echo of that one calibrated moment.

Outside, in the forecourt added after the Second World War, the Eternal Flame has burned continuously since Queen Elizabeth the Second lit it in February 1954, extending the Shrine's purpose to commemorate the conflicts that came after the one it was first built for.

Take a moment in the Sanctuary before you move on.

The balcony above offers a view back down over the forecourt and out toward the city — worth the climb, particularly on a clear afternoon.

tours.title: Siglo
tours.shortDescription: An unmarked door beside The European, a run of chesterfields, and a rooftop built for cigars and slow drinks.
tours.longDescription: The door has never had a sign: slip through it beside The European, past a run of worn leather chesterfields, and the stairs bring you out on the roof of the Melbourne Supper Club — a room dressed more like a French bistro than a rooftop bar, white tablecloths and wicker chairs arranged for conversation rather than showing off, with Parliament House and St Patrick's Cathedral both visible from the edge. The real draw sits in a cabinet behind the bar: a proper humidor stocked with Cohiba, Partagás, Upmann and Punch, beside a list built for slow drinking — the Maker's old fashioned gets mentioned most, though the Fijian Old Spice has its own following among regulars who settle in for the evening. Most Melbourne rooftops chase the same formula of big views, loud music and a queue; Siglo trades all of it for something closer to a private members' room in the open air, which is why so many regulars found it by accident, wandering upstairs on a whim. Ask for a seat near the edge, facing the spire.

stops.title: Siglo
stops.caption: There's an unmarked door beside one of Bourke Street's best-known restaurants, and it leads somewhere else entirely.
stops.transcriptText:
There's an unmarked door beside one of Bourke Street's best-known restaurants, and it leads somewhere else entirely.

Slip through it next to The European, past a run of worn leather chesterfields, and the stairs bring you out on the roof of the Melbourne Supper Club — a room dressed more like a French bistro than a rooftop bar, with white tablecloths, wicker chairs and wooden garden furniture arranged more for conversation than for showing off the view, even with Parliament House and St Patrick's Cathedral both visible from the edge.

The real draw sits in a cabinet behind the bar: a proper humidor stocked with Cuban cigars, Cohiba, Partagas, Upmann and Punch among them, alongside a drinks list built for slow drinking rather than quick rounds. The old fashioned made with Maker's bourbon gets mentioned most often, though the Fijian Old Spice has its own following among regulars who come specifically for the cigars and settle in for the evening rather than moving on to somewhere else.

Most Melbourne rooftops chase the same formula — big views, loud music, a queue at the door. Siglo does almost none of that on purpose, trading the spectacle for something closer to a private members' room that happens to sit in the open air, which is presumably why the door downstairs was never given a sign, and why so many regulars discovered it entirely by accident, wandering upstairs from the restaurant below on a whim.

Ask for a seat near the edge if the weather's cooperating.

The view toward St Patrick's spire is better from there than anywhere else on the roof, and it's rarely the seat people think to request first.

tours.title: State Library Victoria
tours.shortDescription: The reading room whose concrete dome was, for a moment in 1913, the largest ever poured on earth.
tours.longDescription: The La Trobe Reading Room — six storeys of galleries stacked beneath a single octagonal dome — was designed by Norman Peebles to rival the great reading rooms of the British Museum and the Library of Congress, and opened in November 1913 with room for thirty-two thousand books and three hundred and twenty readers. Its reinforced-concrete shell was, briefly, the largest anywhere on the planet. Leaks forced the library to sheet the skylights in copper in 1959, and the room spent four decades under artificial light until a major restoration reopened the glass in July 2003 — a renovation precise enough to order its new linoleum from the same Scottish company that supplied the original ninety years earlier, simply because nobody wanted to be the ones who got it wrong. Stand at the exact centre of the floor and look straight up: the dome only reads as one shape from directly underneath, and most visitors walk the perimeter without ever finding the spot.

stops.title: State Library Victoria
stops.caption: When this dome went up in 1913, its concrete shell was the largest ever poured anywhere in the world.
stops.transcriptText:
When this dome went up in 1913, its concrete shell was the largest ever poured anywhere in the world.
