Lower ground floor, Paramount House, eighty Commonwealth Street, Surry Hills, is where you want to be — down a narrow stair that still feels a bit like sneaking into somewhere you shouldn't.

This little theatrette has never really stopped being a room for insiders. Through the middle of the twentieth century it hosted trade screenings for exhibitors and studio executives, then critics with famously sharp tongues, then — during the Second World War — servicemen and women brought in to watch newsreels from the front. It kept that use right through to the 1970s, quietly running its own small cinema inside a working film company's offices.

Have a think about that lineage while you're standing here, because it's the whole reason this space still exists. When the building was refurbished in 2013, rather than gut the old theatrette for something else, the new owners kept the format and simply reopened it — fifty-six seats and standing room for another seventy, with a forty-two-seat bar built alongside it.

Paramount House itself is heritage-listed, and the rest of the building — the old film vaults, the former offices — has since become a boutique hotel, so the cinema now shares its home with overnight guests rather than film executives.

What's worth carrying with you is this: eighty years ago, this room existed so a small, invited audience could see something before the wider public did. It still does exactly that — just with a ticket instead of an invitation.

Stay for a drink upstairs at the bar before or after a screening — the building's Art Deco bones are easiest to spot from up there, in the original lift doors and the stairwell detailing that survived every renovation since 1940.

tours.title: Luna Park Sydney
tours.shortDescription: Nine decades of grinning at the harbour — a pleasure park built to catch the Bridge's crowds.
tours.longDescription: Eight different faces have grinned over Luna Park's entrance since 1935 — rebuilt and replaced in 1938, 1939, 1946, 1950, 1973, 1982 and finally 1994, each version reflecting whatever technology and taste the decade allowed, all modelled on Old King Cole and all keeping essentially the same expression. The park borrows its name and format from Coney Island's original of 1903, by way of Melbourne in 1912, and its timing was no accident: it opened in 1935 at Milsons Point to catch the crowds who had come from all over the country to see the newly completed Harbour Bridge. Past the thirty-foot face, the Midway runs down toward Coney Island, the historic fun-house zone, flanked by descendants of the original 1930s Big Dipper, Ghost Train and Rotor. A pleasure park riding the coattails of Sydney's biggest construction story — for nine decades and counting.

stops.title: Luna Park Sydney
stops.caption: Eight different faces have grinned over this entrance since 1935.
stops.transcriptText:
Eight different faces have grinned over this entrance since 1935. The one above you now has only been there since 1994.

Look up at the archway before you walk through it — a giant laughing face, roughly thirty feet wide, built into the front of the park with the name lit up above its head.

That face is modelled on Old King Cole, and it's been rebuilt, redesigned, and replaced more times than most visitors would guess — 1935, 1938, 1939, 1946, 1950, 1973, 1982, and the current one in 1994, each version reflecting whatever technology and taste the decade allowed. This one's polyurethane, sturdier than anything that came before it, though it's kept the same essential expression the whole way through.

The park itself borrows its name and format from Coney Island in New York, where the original Luna Park opened in 1903. The idea crossed the Pacific to Melbourne in 1912, and finally reached Sydney in 1935 — timed, rather cannily, to open right as the Harbour Bridge was completed, catching the crowds who'd come from all over the country to see it.

Past the face, the Midway runs straight down toward Coney Island, the park's historic fun-house zone, flanked by rides that trace almost a century of amusement design — descendants of the original Big Dipper, Ghost Train, and Rotor that opened here in the 1930s.

Here's what's worth registering, looking up at the bridge from inside the park. Luna Park didn't just happen to open near an engineering marvel. It was built specifically to catch its shadow — a pleasure park riding on the coattails of Sydney's biggest construction story, and it's been doing exactly that for nine decades.

Walk to the harbourside edge of the park in the evening if you can — the view back across to the Opera House and the bridge, framed by fairground lights, is one most visitors never think to look for.

tours.title: Mona Vale Rockpool
tours.shortDescription: A pool on a sand spit with water on more sides than you'd expect — walk out at low tide.
tours.longDescription: At low tide you can walk straight out to Mona Vale rockpool across the sand; at high tide the same walk means wading, sometimes waist-deep. The pool sits at the tip of a narrow sand spit between the main beach and Bongin Bongin Bay — not tucked into a headland like most of Sydney's sea pools, but carved from a low rock shelf sitting proud of the open beach, almost alone out on the sand. There are two pools: a thirty-metre main pool and a gentler children's pool alongside. Both were cut during the 1930s under a Depression unemployment relief scheme — men put to work turning exposed rock into something the whole community could use. Much of Sydney's coastal swimming culture was built exactly this way: not as grand civic gesture, but as work found for men who badly needed it, using whatever rock the coastline offered.

That position is what makes this pool unusual. Most ocean pools shelter behind rock walls or cliffs; this one was carved instead from a low natural rock shelf sitting proud of the beach, which is why the walk out to it changes so much with the tide. There are two pools here — a larger one, thirty metres end to end, and a smaller, gentler pool alongside it for children and less confident swimmers.

Both were cut during the 1930s, funded through an unemployment relief scheme in the depths of the Depression — men put to work turning a stretch of exposed rock shelf into something the whole community could use. It's free to swim in today, and kept clean partly by council crews, partly by the ocean itself simply washing through it.

What's worth sitting with, standing on this spit of sand, is how much of Sydney's coastal swimming culture was built this way. Not as a grand civic gesture, but as work found for men who badly needed it, using whatever rock the coastline happened to offer — in this case, an unusually exposed shelf that nobody would have chosen if the point had only been convenience.

Time your visit around the tide if you can — arriving an hour either side of low water gets you the easiest walk out, and the clearest sense of just how isolated this little pool really is.

tours.title: Museum of Contemporary Art Australia
tours.shortDescription: Contemporary art that waited forty-eight years for an address, in an Art Deco block on the Quay.
tours.longDescription: The MCA took forty-eight years to open after the money for it was already sitting in a bank account. The expatriate artist J. W. Power left funds and his own work to the University of Sydney in 1943 specifically to establish a museum of contemporary art, and the collection spent decades travelling and sitting in storage while nobody quite knew where to put it. It finally found a home in 1991 in Walter Liberty Vernon's solid Art Deco block on Circular Quay West — built for the Maritime Services Board and finished in 1952, a building that spent four decades managing Sydney's working port rather than showing art, on a site close to where the First Fleet is thought to have made its earliest landing. The 2010–2012 rebuild wrapped a deliberately transparent glass wing around the sandstone-coloured original. An idea funded in 1943 didn't get an address to match its ambition until 2012.

That forty-eight-year gap starts in 1943, when the expatriate Australian artist J. W. Power left money and a body of his own work to the University of Sydney, specifically to establish a museum of contemporary art. Nobody quite knew where to put it. The collection spent decades travelling between exhibitions and sitting in storage across two university buildings, waiting for an actual home.

It finally found one in 1991, when this building came free — originally built for the Maritime Services Board, the authority that once ran Sydney's working port. Designed by Walter Liberty Vernon and finished in 1952, it's a solid, handsome slab of Art Deco that spent its first four decades managing shipping rather than showing art. The site itself sits close to where the First Fleet is thought to have made its earliest landing in the harbour.

The museum opened here properly in November 1991, then underwent a major rebuild between 2010 and 2012 — the glass wing you can see wrapped around part of the original block, deliberately transparent so you can still glimpse the old sandstone through it as you walk past.

Here's what's worth carrying away from that long, slow timeline. An idea funded in 1943 didn't get a permanent building until 1991, and didn't get one that properly suited it until 2012. Contemporary art in this country had to wait the better part of seventy years for an address to match its ambition.

If you're short on time, at least walk the harbourside terrace outside — free to enter, and one of the better places in the city to watch the ferries come and go while you decide whether to go in.

tours.title: North Curl Curl Rockpool
tours.shortDescription: A headland pool the ocean destroyed once already — rebuilt, and holding its ground since 1957.
tours.longDescription: At the far end of the North Curl Curl headland, cut off from the beach at high tide, sits a twenty-five-metre pool that has already been rebuilt once after the ocean simply took it away. A natural rock pool existed here as early as the 1900s; the proper version began in 1937 under a Depression-era Unemployment Relief Fund, workers deepening the basin and walling out the sea. Heavy seas destroyed it in 1947, and it took a full decade before the 1957 rebuild picked up where the relief workers had left off. Since 1962 a winter swimming group called the Cool Cats has met here on cold Sunday mornings, using this exposed pool precisely when most people wouldn't dream of it. A pool in ongoing negotiation with the ocean that built it — deepened, walled, wrecked and rebuilt, never really finished, just holding its ground for now.

Neither, in the end, did the pool. Heavy seas destroyed it in 1947, and it took a full decade before it was rebuilt in 1957, essentially starting the project over from where the Depression-era workers had left off.

Since 1962, a winter swimming group calling themselves the Cool Cats has met here on cold Sunday mornings, carrying on a tradition of using this exposed pool precisely when most people wouldn't dream of it.

Time your walk out here around low tide for the easiest crossing, and stay for a swim if the Cool Cats happen to be in — regulars are generally happy to explain exactly why anyone would choose to swim here in winter.

tours.title: Paddington Reservoir Gardens
tours.shortDescription: A reservoir, then a petrol station, then the roof fell in — now a sunken garden wearing all three.
tours.longDescription: For decades this garden was a car park, and before that it held drinking water for half of Sydney. Edward Bell's reservoir of 1864–66 pumped water up from the Botany Swamps as part of the city's third water supply system, holding roughly two million gallons at a time until a newer reservoir at Centennial Park made it redundant in 1899. Then the story turns properly strange: through the twentieth century the site became a service station, then storage, still selling petrol until 1990 — the year its worn-through roof finally caved in. Rather than patch it up, the City of Sydney spent the 2000s turning it into something new, reopening in 2009 with the original brick, timber and iron deliberately kept and worked around, framing a sunken garden of subtropical planting below street level. Most heritage gardens erase their industrial past; this one left every layer visible.

stops.title: Paddington Reservoir Gardens

stops.transcriptText:

Corner of Oxford Street and Oatley Road, Paddington, is where you want to be — a sunken garden set below street level, framed by the original brick and iron of a nineteenth-century reservoir wall still standing on three sides.

Start with what this actually was. By 1899, a newer reservoir at Centennial Park had made this one redundant, and what followed is where the story turns properly strange. Through the twentieth century the site became a service station, then storage and workshop space, still functioning as a petrol stop until 1990 — the year its roof, unmaintained and worn through, finally caved in.

That collapse is, in a roundabout way, the reason you're standing in a garden today. Rather than patch the site back up, the City of Sydney spent the 2000s turning it into something new — reopening in 2009 with the original brick, timber, and iron fixtures deliberately kept and worked around, rather than replaced, sitting alongside a sunken garden of subtropical planting.

Here's what's worth carrying away, walking through it. Most heritage gardens try to erase their industrial past. This one didn't — you're standing inside a reservoir, a collapsed service station roof, and a contemporary garden all at once, each layer left visible rather than smoothed over.

Walk down into the lower, sunken section if you haven't already — that's where the old reservoir floor is still exposed underfoot, the clearest single spot to feel exactly how far below street level this whole site sits.

tours.title: Pellegrino 2000
tours.shortDescription: Roman trattoria cooking and a thousand-bottle cellar behind an unglamorous Surry Hills corner.
tours.longDescription: Six weeks is roughly the wait for a weekend dinner booking at Pellegrino 2000 — a restaurant with no view, no rooftop, and its best room in the basement. On the corner of Campbell and Foster Streets, in the address that used to house Bar H, Dan Pepperell, Mikey Clift and Andy Tyson — the team behind Bistrot 916 — cook from the trattorias of Rome and Florence rather than anything more polished: a handful of dishes done properly, led by the prawn ravioli in brown butter and sage that most reviewers can't stop mentioning. Downstairs, hidden under the street-level dining room, is a proper wine cellar — bottle-lined walls, white tablecloths, candlelight, something close to a thousand bottles. The whole place relies on remarkably little spectacle: just an already well-regarded team cooking food people will wait over a month for.

If you can't get a table, the neighbourhood around Campbell and Foster is worth a wander regardless — several of the same crew's other openings sit within a few minutes' walk, if you fancy tracking down where else they've been busy.

tours.title: Queen Victoria Building
tours.shortDescription: Twenty-one copper domes that survived the 1960s wrecking ball by public argument.
tours.longDescription: An entire city block of Romanesque arches and copper domes on George Street, easy to mistake for a cathedral — but built between 1893 and 1898, to a design by the Scottish-born architect George McRae, as a produce and general marketplace timed to mark Queen Victoria's Diamond Jubilee. The scale was the point: a whole block given to a single ornate civic building, twenty-one copper domes along the roofline, stained glass and light-filled atriums, at a time when Sydney wanted its public architecture to say something. That grandeur nearly didn't survive. By the early 1960s, the market use long gone and the building in decay, demolition was seriously on the table — until the Friends of the Queen Victoria Building organised public opposition and stopped it. Restored and reopened as retail space late in the twentieth century, it stands today because enough people argued, loudly, that it shouldn't come down. Look for the two great animated hanging clocks inside, each performing on the hour.

stops.title: Queen Victoria Building
stops.caption: Twenty-one copper domes, one hundred and ninety metres of sandstone, and at least one serious attempt in the 1960s to knock the whole thing down.
stops.transcriptText:
Twenty-one copper domes, one hundred and ninety metres of sandstone, and at least one serious attempt in the 1960s to knock the whole thing down.

George Street, between Market and Druitt — that's your stretch, an entire city block of Romanesque arches and copper domes, easy enough to mistake for a cathedral if you're only glancing at it from across the road.

It wasn't built as a cathedral, or even as shops in the beginning. Constructed between 1893 and 1898 to a design by the Scottish-born architect George McRae, it opened as a produce and general marketplace, timed to mark Queen Victoria's Diamond Jubilee the year before. The scale was the point — an entire block given over to a single, ornate civic building, at a time when Sydney wanted its public architecture to say something.

Have a look at the roofline while you're here. Twenty-one copper domes run the length of it, sitting over a Romanesque Revival facade that hasn't really been matched anywhere else in the city — stained glass, light-filled atriums, and decoration that owes more to European civic buildings than to anything strictly Australian.

That grandeur nearly didn't survive. By the early 1960s, the market use long gone and the building fallen into decay, demolition was seriously on the table — until a group calling themselves the Friends of the Queen Victoria Building organised public opposition and stopped it. The building was eventually restored and reopened as retail space in the late twentieth century, which is what you're walking through now.

What's worth sitting with is this: nothing about this building's survival was automatic. It stood empty and unloved for long enough that pulling it down looked like the sensible option, and it's still standing today because enough people argued, loudly, that it shouldn't be.

Look for the two large hanging clocks inside — the Royal Clock and the Great Australian Clock — each one animated on the hour, and easy to miss if you're moving through the building rather than stopping to look up.

tours.title: Studio GARDNER
tours.shortDescription: Collectible vintage from Europe and Japan beside handmade contemporary work — never the same room twice.
tours.longDescription: Half the stock at Studio GARDNER has already had one life somewhere else entirely — a chair from Japan, a lamp from Europe — before it ever landed in this light-filled showroom on Bayswater Road, Rushcutters Bay. Opened in 2023, it runs on a specific idea: collectible vintage pieces, personally sourced across Europe and Japan, shown in the same room as contemporary work by local and international artists and makers. Nothing is mass-produced, and even the freshly made pieces are built by hand, one at a time; each object is chosen for what it can tell you about timeless design and quiet craftsmanship. A vintage shop has fixed stock and a gallery has a fixed collection — this is deliberately neither, rotating with each season's finds, with no guarantee the piece you like today will still be there next month.

Sixty-five Bayswater Road, Rushcutters Bay, is the address — a light-filled showroom on a fairly quiet stretch of road, easy enough to walk past unless you already know to look for it.

tours.title: Sydney Harbour Bridge
tours.shortDescription: Six million hand-driven rivets in a single steel arch — nine years to close five hundred metres.
tours.longDescription: The single steel curve of the arch is what holds the whole structure up — the deck, the pylons, the traffic are all hanging from it. The idea is older than you'd think: the colonial architect Francis Greenway suggested a harbour crossing as far back as 1815, but it was John Bradfield's 1912 design concept that eventually got built, with construction beginning in 1923. The English firm Dorman Long fabricated every truss, girder and panel in workshops on the northern shore — including six million rivets, each one heated and hand-driven by workers balanced high above the harbour. The two halves of the arch grew out from opposite shores on cables and met in the middle in 1930, a moment that took real nerve to trust; the bridge opened on the nineteenth of March 1932, after just over nine years of work, at a human cost the narration doesn't let you forget.

stops.title: Sydney Harbour Bridge
stops.caption: Stand anywhere along the foreshore with a clear line to the bridge, and look at the arch itself — that single steel curve is what actually holds the whole structure up.
stops.transcriptText:
Six million rivets, sixteen men who never made it to opening day, and one bridge that took nine years to close a five-hundred-metre gap over water.

Stand anywhere along the foreshore with a clear line to the bridge, and look at the arch itself — that single steel curve is what actually holds the whole structure up. Everything else, the deck, the pylons, the traffic — is just hanging from it.

The idea is older than you'd think. As far back as 1815, the colonial architect Francis Greenway suggested a harbour crossing to Governor Macquarie, though nothing came of it for the best part of a century. It wasn't until 1912 that the engineer John Bradfield put forward the design concept that eventually got built, and construction itself only began in 1923, when workers turned the first sod on the southern side.

The English firm Dorman Long and Company won the contract and set up their own steel-fabrication workshops on the northern shore, producing every truss, girder, and panel the bridge needed — including six million rivets, each one heated and hand-driven into place by workers balanced high above the harbour.

The two halves of the arch grew out from opposite shores, supported by cables, and finally met in the middle in 1930 — a moment that must have taken real nerve to trust, given how much steel was hanging in the air with nothing but engineering holding it there. The bridge opened properly on the nineteenth of March, 1932, after just over nine years of work.

What's worth carrying with you, standing here, is what that construction cost. Sixteen men died building this bridge — a detail easy to lose against the numbers of rivets and tonnes of steel, but worth remembering every time you watch someone stroll across it without a second thought.

If you've got a few hours, the climb to the very top of the arch is worth it for the view alone — though even from down here, the pedestrian walkway on the eastern side gets you close enough to hear the rivets creak as trains cross underneath.

tours.title: Sydney Opera House
tours.shortDescription: A million Swedish tiles on shells their architect never saw finished.
tours.longDescription: In 1966 the architect who designed this building resigned and left the country — without ever seeing it finished. Jørn Utzon, a Dane, won the international competition of 1956 with a concept so unconventional that opinion split immediately: white sails catching the light over the harbour, or an engineering headache dressed up as architecture. Both readings turned out to be correct. The shells are clad in more than a million ceramic tiles shipped from Sweden, set in matte and gloss chevrons that catch the light differently depending on where you stand. Construction began in 1959 and ran into exactly the trouble critics predicted — delays, spiralling costs, shell engineering that took years to solve — and in 1966, after a prolonged dispute with the New South Wales Government over money, Utzon resigned and returned to Denmark. The building opened without him in October 1973; only in 1999, working from Denmark, was he brought back to redesign one interior space, now the Utzon Room. The man who imagined it never once stood here to see the finished result.

stops.title: Sydney Opera House
stops.caption: It's 1966, and the architect who designed this building has just resigned and left the country — without ever seeing it finished.
