This is the Rhodes Memorial, designed by the architect Herbert Baker and unveiled in 1912, a decade after the death of Cecil John Rhodes, the man it honours.

Rhodes made an immense fortune from diamond and gold mining, became prime minister of the Cape Colony, and pursued a vision of British imperial expansion across Southern Africa that dispossessed and subjugated the people who already lived on the land he claimed. That legacy is genuinely contested in South Africa today — memorialised here in solid granite, and challenged, loudly and often, by movements like Rhodes Must Fall, which argue that a monument like this has no place celebrating a figure so bound up with colonial exploitation.

Baker built the memorial to resemble the ancient Greek temple at Segesta, using Cape granite quarried from the base of Table Mountain itself, which means the stone honouring Rhodes came from the same mountain his memorial now looks out over.

Below the steps, and easy to miss if you arrive from the wrong side, stands a large bronze statue of a horse and rider straining forward — a piece called Physical Energy, by the English sculptor George Frederic Watts, cast specifically as a tribute to the restless, expansionist drive that defined Rhodes's career. It's arguably a more honest monument than the temple above it: forward motion with no stated destination.

Whatever you make of the man, the view from the top is worth the climb on its own terms: Devil's Peak behind you, the northern suburbs and Table Bay spread out below. Stand there a moment and decide for yourself what a monument like this is actually for.

tours.title: Rosetta Roastery Cafe
tours.shortDescription: Years spent roasting coffee nobody outside the trade ever tasted, before a single cup was sold here.
tours.longDescription: A rustic, unfussy shopfront on Bree Street, which is a little surprising once you know the reputation behind it. Rosetta began as a wholesale roastery supplying other cafés and restaurants for years before opening a counter of its own, so the people running it had already mastered the craft quietly, long before anyone outside the industry knew the name. That wholesale-first approach let them build something unusual for South Africa at the time: a direct-trade supply chain sourcing rare single-origin beans that had simply not been available in the country. The roastery evaluates well over a hundred and fifty coffees a year, chasing specific describable flavours rather than a generic idea of quality — which is why the menu changes with the seasons of growing regions on the other side of the world rather than with the seasons here. The beans now ship internationally, a rare export success for a South African coffee brand.

Ask whoever's on the counter what's brewing as a single-origin filter that day rather than defaulting to the espresso menu — it changes constantly, and it's usually the more interesting cup in the building.

tours.title: Southern Guild Cape Town
tours.shortDescription: Almost nothing here is simply furniture, even when it looks exactly like a chair.
tours.longDescription: Trevyn and Julian McGowan founded Southern Guild in 2008, having returned to South Africa from London five years earlier specifically to build a platform for the country's designers and makers. The gallery had no permanent home until 2014 and moved into Silo 5 in the V&A Waterfront's Silo District in 2017, alongside the museum next door — together turning this stretch of harbour into one of the most serious contemporary art and design addresses on the continent. What Southern Guild pioneered, and is still best known for, is collectable design: one-off or very limited pieces by African artists and designers that function as furniture or objects but are collected and priced as art. The results have entered the Metropolitan Museum of Art, the Centre Pompidou and the Vitra Design Museum. Look for Andile Dyalvane's large ceramic vessels, drawing on Xhosa scarification patterns and family firing techniques, and Porky Hefer's woven, nest-like seating.

Take your time with the pieces that look most functional. A stool or a cabinet here often carries the same conceptual weight as anything hanging on a gallery wall — it's just built to be sat on too, occasionally, if the artist allows it.

tours.title: Table Mountain Aerial Cableway
tours.shortDescription: Sixty-five people, one rotating floor, and a full spin of the view before you reach the top.
tours.longDescription: Engineers proposed a rack railway up Table Mountain as far back as 1870, an idea that stalled when war broke out and was never revived in that form. It took a Norwegian engineer, Trygve Strømsø, to make it work: his cableway opened on the fourth of October 1929 and has been upgraded three times since, most dramatically in 1997, when the current cars arrived with rotating floors running on a double cable that keeps them stable in the wind this mountain is famous for. The ride takes four to five minutes, during which the floor turns a full circle so nobody is stuck facing the wrong window — one of only three cableways anywhere built to do that. More than twenty-seven million people have been carried to the summit since it opened. Wind can shut the whole operation without warning, which is why checking the live status before committing to the queue is generally worth the minute.

If the queue's long, it's usually moving faster than it looks — cars run every few minutes on a clear day. And once you're up top, walk past the main viewing platforms; the quieter paths further along the summit plateau tend to empty out fast.

tours.title: The Company's Garden
tours.shortDescription: In 1652 the vegetables planted here were the entire reason Cape Town existed at all.
tours.longDescription: This green space at the heart of the city began as a vegetable garden, planted by the Dutch East India Company to resupply ships passing the Cape on the long route to and from the East Indies. The need had been proven a few years earlier when a Dutch ship wrecked nearby and its survivors, waiting months for rescue, reported back how useful a proper refreshment station would be. Jan van Riebeeck arrived in 1652 to establish exactly that, and a master gardener named Hendrik Boom sowed the first seeds on the twenty-ninth of April that year — peas, beans, radishes, spinach, cabbage and wheat, grown purely to keep passing crews from scurvy. Simon van der Stel, governor from 1679, redesigned it with formal canals and water furrows, and the shift from feeding ships to simply being beautiful has continued since. At one corner stands the Iziko Slave Lodge, built to house people enslaved by the very company that planted the garden.

The garden you're walking through now is a good deal grander than that first vegetable patch. The garden's edges do some of that storytelling on their own: the Iziko Slave Lodge sits at one corner, originally built to house enslaved people owned by the very company that planted this garden — a reminder of who did the work behind the produce.

Look for the fragments of the old boundary wall as you walk, if you know roughly where to find them — this garden used to be considerably larger, and cutting it down to its current size is really the story of Cape Town growing up around it.

tours.title: The Gin Bar
tours.shortDescription: Every gin and tonic on the menu is billed as a cure for something. The room used to be a morgue.
tours.longDescription: The way in is through the Honest Chocolate Café on Wale Street, past the chocolate counter and out into a small hidden courtyard — deliberately unmarked, this being Cape Town's original speakeasy-style bar, tucked into what remains of a heritage building whose considerably grimmer former use supplies the theme. Gin has a medicinal backstory that fits neatly: juniper, the botanical that defines the spirit, was used for centuries against everything from digestive trouble to the plague, long before anyone drank it for pleasure. The bar takes that literally. More than a hundred and forty gins sit on the shelves, over seventy of them South African, in a country that has had something of a craft gin boom — driven largely by producers infusing their spirit with fynbos botanicals unique to this part of the world, so a South African gin here tastes distinctly of somewhere rather than nowhere in particular.

Ask the bartender to build you something rather than picking blind off the list — with this many options, a good bartender's recommendation, matched to whatever you actually feel like drinking, will save you several rounds of trial and error.

tours.title: Two Oceans Aquarium
tours.shortDescription: Cold water on one side, warmer on the other, and rather more species in the difference than you'd expect.
tours.longDescription: Opened on the thirteenth of November 1995 through a partnership between the V&A Waterfront developers and a marine research organisation that wanted Cape Town to have a serious conservation and education facility rather than a tourist tank. The name refers to the cold Atlantic on the city's western side and the noticeably warmer Indian Ocean current further along the coast — two very different marine environments that both shape what lives in these waters. Over three thousand animals across some three hundred species are housed here as a result, representing both rather than picking one. It is not only fish: the aquarium keeps a colony of African penguins, the same endangered species found at Boulders Beach down the peninsula, specifically so visitors who cannot make it out to Simon's Town still see them up close. Daily feeding shows are posted at the entrance.

tours.title: Zeitz Museum of Contemporary Art Africa (Zeitz MOCAA)
tours.shortDescription: Fifty-seven metres, forty-two concrete tubes, and for most of the twentieth century sub-Saharan Africa's tallest building. It was a grain silo.
tours.longDescription: Completed in 1924, this silo spent decades doing unglamorous, essential work — grading and holding maize shipped in from across the country, a working node in South Africa's export economy rather than a landmark. Decommissioned in 2001, it stood empty beside the harbour for years, too solid to demolish cheaply and too strange a shape to obviously reuse. The architect Thomas Heatherwick solved that by subtraction rather than addition: instead of building something new around the silo, his studio carved directly into it, cutting an atrium through dozens of the original tubes in the shape of a single grain of corn, magnified enormously, and leaving the surrounding cylinders largely intact to hold gallery floors instead of grain. The result opened in 2017 as the largest museum anywhere dedicated to contemporary art from this continent and its diaspora, spread across nine floors, plus a rooftop sculpture terrace and a hotel at the top.

tours.title: Arc de Triomf
tours.shortDescription: A triumphal arch in red brick that commemorates nothing more violent than a trade fair.
tours.longDescription: Josep Vilaseca's arch went up in 1888 as the gateway to the Universal Exposition, and almost everything about it is a deliberate departure from the form. It is deep red brick rather than pale stone, Neo-Mudéjar rather than Roman, borrowing horseshoe arches and geometric brickwork from Moorish Iberia and pairing them with sculpture that is entirely Catalan. Josep Reynés' frieze on the near face shows a crowd welcoming visitors — Barcelona Welcomes the Nations — while Josep Llimona's Recompense on the far side shows the exposition handing out its prizes: arrival on one side, reward on the other. Look higher for small stone bats, the emblem of Jaume I long since adopted by the city, and for the coats of arms of Spain's forty-nine provinces as they stood in 1888, with Barcelona's own in the keystone. Paris and Rome built arches for armies coming home. Barcelona had no war to celebrate, so it built a monument to itself.

stops.title: Arc de Triomf

You're on Passeig de Lluís Companys, at the northern end, where the promenade opens wide and the arch spans it from side to side, brick pillars rising to a single wide vault. Ahead of you, the promenade runs straight down toward Ciutadella Park; behind you, the city continues toward the Eixample. The arch sits squarely across your path — there's no way into the park without walking underneath it.

Start with the brickwork. Architect Josep Vilaseca chose a Neo-Mudéjar style, borrowing the horseshoe arches and geometric brick patterns of Moorish Iberia and pairing them with sculpture that's entirely Catalan, an odd combination that reads as neither foreign nor formal, just festive.

Now look at the frieze above the arch on this side: a crowd of figures welcoming visitors, carved by Josep Reynés and titled, simply, Barcelona Welcomes the Nations. Round on the far side sits its opposite number, Josep Llimona's Recompense, showing the exposition handing out its prizes — arrival on one face, reward on the other.

Higher still, carved into the pillars, look for small stone bats, the emblem of King Jaume the First and long since adopted by the city itself, and running along the underside of the arch, a row of coats of arms, one for each of Spain's forty-nine provinces as they stood in 1888. Barcelona's own crest sits dead centre, in the keystone position — a fair hint at who was hosting the party.

And that's really the point of the whole structure. Most triumphal arches — the ones in Paris, in Rome — commemorate a military victory, an army coming home. This one commemorates nothing more violent than a trade fair: a city showing off its bridges, its industry, its own confidence, to the rest of the world. Barcelona didn't have a war to celebrate in 1888, so it built a monument to itself instead.

Walk under the arch and keep going. The promenade leads straight into Ciutadella Park, past the ornate Cascada fountain the same exposition left behind, and if you're here in late October, the arch opens its roof for the day during Barcelona's Open House festival — a climb of around a hundred and twenty steps for a clear line of sight to the Sagrada Família.

tours.title: Bar Colòmbia (Ca l'Albert)
tours.shortDescription: Opened in 1913 by a man named Albert. There has been an Albert behind the counter ever since.
tours.longDescription: A plain corner bar in Sant Andreu with wooden chairs, marble-topped tables and walls that have accumulated rather than curated a century of neighbourhood photographs. It opened in 1913, and when the founding Albert and his wife died young not long after the Civil War it passed to his brother and mother, staying inside the same family through every decade since — run for some fifty years by Albert Miró and now passing to his daughter Anna. Ca l'Albert simply means Albert's place, and for over a hundred years there has always been one. The record collection announces itself before the menu does: more than two hundred jazz vinyls kept behind the bar and played through the day in no particular order. The connection runs deeper than the turntable, too — the singer and trumpeter Andrea Motis grew up in the flat directly above and helped organise sessions on the pavement below. Most bars this old survive on nostalgia; this one survives on continuity.

stops.title: Bar Colòmbia (Ca l'Albert)
stops.caption: It's 1913, and a young man named Albert and his wife open a bar on this corner.
stops.transcriptText:
It's 1913, and a young man named Albert and his wife open a bar on this corner. A century and change later, it's still known as Ca l'Albert, and there's still an Albert behind the counter.

Rambla de Fabra i Puig, number one, right where it meets Carrer Gran de Sant Andreu — a plain corner bar with wooden chairs, marble-topped tables, and walls crowded with old photographs and neighbourhood memorabilia that have accumulated, rather than been curated, over eleven decades.

Well, start with the name. When the founding Albert and his wife died young, not long after the Spanish Civil War, the bar passed to his brother and mother, and it's stayed inside the same family ever since — run for around fifty years by Albert Miró, and now, as one generation gives way to the next, passing to his daughter Anna. "Ca l'Albert" simply means "Albert's place," and for over a hundred years, remarkably, there's always been one running it.

You'll notice the record collection before you notice the menu. Albert kept more than two hundred jazz vinyls behind the bar, played through the day in no particular order, and the connection to music runs deeper than the turntable: singer and trumpeter Andrea Motis grew up in the flat directly above the bar and helped organise small jazz sessions out on the street below.

Then there's the food, which is real but secondary to all of that. The sandwiches are the thing to order — particularly the suflé, sobrasada and melted cheese pressed together — alongside a classic tortilla de patatas and a bowl of Russian salad, the kind of menu that hasn't needed reinventing in a hundred years because nobody's asked it to.

Here's what's worth knowing, standing at this counter: most neighbourhood bars this old survive on nostalgia alone. This one survives on continuity instead — a family name behind the till, and a turntable that's been running since long before anyone thought to call it a "vibe."

If you're here midweek, don't be surprised to hear jazz drifting out onto the pavement rather than piped-in radio — and if the timing's right, an informal street session outside is exactly the kind of thing this corner was built for.

tours.title: Basílica de Santa Maria del Mar
tours.shortDescription: Most Gothic cathedrals were paid for by kings. This one was carried uphill by dockworkers.
tours.longDescription: Between 1329 and 1383 the bastaixos — the guild of dockworkers who unloaded ships in the old port — carried every block of foundation stone from the royal quarry on Montjuïc to this site on foot, unpaid, as an act of devotion to their own parish church. They are still here, cut into the side door facing Passeig del Born: small barefoot figures bent double under their sacks. Because the building went up in one unbroken stretch of barely fifty years, remarkably fast for the period, it has none of the mismatched styles of a cathedral built across centuries. Every column matches and every arch repeats the same unfussy formula, three aisles of almost equal height on slender octagonal columns spaced further apart than in almost any other Gothic church. The bareness inside is not original: in 1936 the interior burned for eleven days, destroying centuries of Baroque altarpieces added long after the builders finished. What survives is, in its way, closer to what the bastaixos actually built.

stops.title: Basílica de Santa Maria del Mar
stops.caption: Most Gothic cathedrals were paid for by kings or bishops. This one was carried on the backs of dockworkers, stone by stone, from a quarry across town.
stops.transcriptText:
Most Gothic cathedrals were paid for by kings or bishops. This one was carried on the backs of dockworkers, stone by stone, from a quarry across town.

Stand facing the main façade, on Plaça de Santa Maria, with the twin octagonal towers rising above the rose window and the carved main doorway directly ahead. Push inside and the space opens out at once — three aisles of almost equal height, held up on slender octagonal columns spaced further apart than in almost any other Gothic church you'll have stood in.

Look first at the side door facing Passeig del Born, where small stone figures show barefoot men bent double under sacks — the bastaixos, the guild of dockworkers who unloaded ships in the old port. Between 1329, when construction began, and 1383, when the last stone went up, they carried every block of foundation stone from the royal quarry on Montjuïc to this site on foot, unpaid, as an act of devotion to their own parish church.

Because the building went up in one unbroken stretch — barely fifty years, remarkably fast for the period — it has none of the mismatched styles you find in cathedrals built across centuries. Every column matches, and every arch repeats the same, unfussy formula.

Then notice how little decoration survives inside: no gilded altarpieces, no side chapels stacked with paintings, just stone, glass, and space. That isn't how it always looked. In 1936, at the outbreak of the Spanish Civil War, the interior burned for eleven days, destroying centuries of Baroque altarpieces and furnishings added long after the original builders finished — a genuine loss, and one still remembered as such. And yet what's left standing is, in its way, closer to what the bastaixos actually built: bare stone and tall glass, with nothing between you and the architecture itself.

Before you go, if the roof terrace is open, take it — recently restored, over thirty metres up, and one of the few Gothic rooftops in Barcelona you're actually allowed to walk across. And if the name rings a bell for reasons you can't quite place, it's probably the novel: Ildefonso Falcones set his bestselling Cathedral of the Sea here, following the same bastaixos who hauled the stone you just walked past.

tours.title: Bunkers del Carmel
tours.shortDescription: An anti-aircraft battery, then a shantytown, now the best free view in Barcelona.
tours.longDescription: In 1938, with Barcelona being bombed from the air, the city's defence authority picked the highest hilltop for miles and poured four concrete gun emplacements straight into the bedrock within weeks. Four Vickers cannons tracked Italian and Nationalist bombers coming in over the coast until Republican forces disabled the battery themselves during a retreat in January 1939, days before the city fell. What came after matters as much: families with nowhere else to live moved into the abandoned platforms and built around them, and the shantytown that grew here had its own name — Los Cañones, the cannons. By the 1970s it held around a hundred and ten huts and six hundred residents, organised enough to form a residents' association in 1972 to get water and electricity connected. Every layer here erased the one before it. An Iberian settlement excavated at the summit in 1932 predates the guns by two thousand years; the guns gave way to the shantytown within a decade; and the shantytown, which lasted into the 1990s, predates the sunset crowd.

stops.title: Bunkers del Carmel
stops.caption: It's 1938, and Barcelona is being bombed from the air. The city's defence authority picks this hilltop, the highest point for miles around, and pours four concrete gun emplacements straight into the bedrock within weeks.
stops.transcriptText:
It's 1938, and Barcelona is being bombed from the air. The city's defence authority picks this hilltop, the highest point for miles around, and pours four concrete gun emplacements straight into the bedrock within weeks.

The hilltop in front of you, Turó de la Rovira, is still scattered with those low concrete platforms and walls, roughly circular, sunk directly into the rock. Walk the perimeter and the whole city opens out below — the sea to the south, Tibidabo's hill to the north-west, and directly ahead, unmistakable even from this distance, the towers of the Sagrada Família.

Start with the guns themselves, or rather, where they used to stand. Four Vickers cannons were mounted here from 1938, tracking Italian and Nationalist bombers as they came in over the coast, until Republican forces disabled the battery themselves during a retreat in January 1939, days before the city fell.

Then there's what came after, because the story doesn't end with the war. Families with nowhere else to live moved into the abandoned gun platforms and built around them, and the shantytown that grew here even had its own name: Los Cañones, the cannons. By the 1970s it held around a hundred and ten huts and six hundred residents, tight enough that they formed a residents' association in 1972 just to get running water and electricity connected.

Here's what's worth sitting with, up here: this hill has been fought over, lived on, and abandoned in almost every decade of the last century, and each layer erased the one before it. An Iberian settlement excavated at the summit in 1932 predates the guns by more than two thousand years; the guns gave way to the shanty town within a single decade; and the shanty town, which lasted into the 1990s, predates the sunset crowd you're probably standing among right now.

Stay for the light to change if you can — most people come for exactly this view and leave the moment the sun's down. Walk the platforms properly before you go, too; some still carry the low concrete ridges of the old gun mounts, easy to miss if you're only looking outward at the skyline.

tours.title: Cafè de l'Arquitecte
tours.shortDescription: Barcelona's most prolific architect built this house for himself. Now you can have lunch in it.
tours.longDescription: Enric Sagnier put his name on an enormous share of Barcelona's built fabric between 1882 and his death in 1931 — the Palau de Justícia, the Temple del Sagrat Cor still rising over the city from Tibidabo, entire blocks of the Eixample — and yet ask a visitor to name a Barcelona architect and you will hear Gaudí, or Domènech i Montaner, or Puig i Cadafalch long before you hear him. Casa Dolors Vidal de Sagnier is the exception: a five-storey townhouse on Rambla de Catalunya he built in 1892 as his own family home and studio, named for his wife. The ground floor now belongs entirely to this café and restaurant, where a fireplace anchors the room and black-and-white photographs hang around it — a man in a high collar, sketches of buildings, drafting tools behind glass. Chef Jorge Aranda cooks on Catalan produce rather than nostalgia; the open-faced tortilla with butifarra and Mahón cheese is what regulars order first. Sagnier spent five decades designing buildings for other people. It is this one that carries his name on the door.

stops.title: Cafè de l'Arquitecte
stops.caption: He's often called Barcelona's most prolific architect, and also its least famous — and the building around you is the one he designed purely for himself.
stops.transcriptText:
He's often called Barcelona's most prolific architect, and also its least famous — and the building around you is the one he designed purely for himself.

Casa Dolors Vidal de Sagnier is the house you're standing inside, a five-storey townhouse on Rambla de Catalunya that architect Enric Sagnier built in 1892 as his own family home and studio, naming it for his wife. The ground floor, all gothic-tinged stonework and bay windows outside, now belongs entirely to this café, bar, and restaurant. Find the fireplace at the centre of the room, and the black-and-white photographs hung around it — a man in a high collar, sketches of buildings, drafting tools kept behind glass. That's Sagnier, looking back at you from his own front room.

Start with the scale of the man's career. Between 1882 and his death in 1931, Sagnier put his name on an enormous share of Barcelona's built fabric — the Palau de Justícia, the vast Temple del Sagrat Cor still rising over the city from Tibidabo, entire blocks of the Eixample around you — and yet ask most visitors to name a Barcelona architect and you'll hear Gaudí, or Domènech i Montaner, or Puig i Cadafalch, long before you hear his.

Then look at what's actually on the plate. Chef Jorge Aranda, formerly of the restaurant Gresca, runs a kitchen built on Catalan produce rather than nostalgia — the open-faced tortilla with butifarra sausage and Mahón cheese is the dish regulars order first, alongside oysters and a changing rice course sent over from the hotel's sister kitchen.

And here's the pivot worth sitting with, fork in hand: Sagnier spent five decades designing buildings for other people — banks, churches, other families' mansions — and it's this one, his own, that finally carries his name on the door.

Finish your coffee and take Rambla de Catalunya on foot in either direction; Sagnier's fingerprints are on more of this street, and this city, than almost any other architect's, even if you have to look twice to notice them.

tours.title: Can Culleretes
tours.shortDescription: Barcelona's oldest restaurant, open since 1786, and still selling 300 plates of cannelloni a week.
tours.longDescription: In 1786 a woman who had just left convent life began selling her homemade mató, a soft goat's cheese, through a window near her old convent, and did it well enough to open a proper dining room around the corner. That dining room is this one, considerably enlarged in the two hundred and thirty-eight years since, its walls lined with faded murals, Portuguese-style tiles and decades of signed photographs. The name means little spoons, and the most-told story is that this was among the first Barcelona dining rooms to hand diners metal spoons rather than wooden ones, which had a habit of splintering — a small enough innovation to become the whole restaurant's name. The canelons, stuffed with veal and pork under a nutmeg-scented béchamel, only joined the menu in the 1950s and now sell around three hundred portions a week; the escudella still appears every Christmas. Plenty of self-proclaimed oldest restaurants coast on the history and let the kitchen slide. Selling out the signature dish three hundred plates a week is the harder trick.

stops.title: Can Culleretes
stops.caption: It's 1786, and a woman who's just left convent life is selling her own goat's cheese from a ten-seat dining room on this street.
stops.transcriptText:
It's 1786, and a woman who's just left convent life is selling her own goat's cheese from a ten-seat dining room on this street. Two hundred and thirty-eight years later, the dining room's a great deal bigger, but the cheese is still on the menu.

Carrer Quintana, a narrow lane in the Gothic Quarter a few steps off the Rambla — you'll know Can Culleretes by the dark wooden front and the queue that tends to form before it's even open. Inside, faded murals and Portuguese-style tiles line walls hung with decades of signed photographs, a dining room that reads like a scrapbook of everyone who's eaten here since.

Start with how it began. In 1786, that same woman started selling her homemade mató, a soft goat's cheese, through a window near her old convent, and did it well enough that she opened a proper dining room around the corner soon after. That dining room is the one you're standing in, considerably enlarged over the centuries since.

The name is where local stories diverge a little. Culleretes means "little spoons," and the most-told version is that this was among the first Barcelona dining rooms to hand diners metal spoons instead of wooden ones, which had a habit of splintering — a small enough innovation to eventually become the whole restaurant's name.

Then there's what's actually on the table. The canelons — Catalan-style cannelloni stuffed with veal and pork under a nutmeg-scented béchamel — only joined the menu in the 1950s and now sell somewhere around three hundred portions a week; escudella, a hearty broth with snail-shaped pasta called galets, still shows up every Christmas, much as it always has.

And that's the real point, standing here. Barcelona's oldest continuously running restaurant, and the second-oldest in Spain, isn't surviving on the claim alone — plenty of self-proclaimed "oldest" restaurants coast on the history and let the kitchen slide. This one still sells out its signature dish three hundred plates a week, which is the harder trick.

Take a table if there's one free, and order the canelons without overthinking it — it's what two hundred and thirty-eight years of regulars have already decided for you. If you're curious where the story started, the mató, drizzled with honey, is still on the dessert menu too.

tours.title: Casa Amatller
tours.shortDescription: A stepped Amsterdam gable on Passeig de Gràcia, with a chocolate maker's private joke by the door.
tours.longDescription: Between 1898 and 1900 Josep Puig i Cadafalch took a plain building from 1875 and rebuilt its front almost entirely, fusing Catalan Gothic detail with Flemish gables and hand-painted ceramic tile. The result is the near end of the Illa de la Discòrdia, the Block of Discord, and its stepped castle-like roofline is about the last thing you would expect on a street this Mediterranean. The client was Antoni Amatller, whose fortune came from chocolate but whose real enthusiasms ran to photography and travel, and the building says so directly: look for the small sculpted rat clutching a camera tucked into the stonework near the entrance. Inside, Amatller's dining room, salon and bedroom survive furnished much as they were in 1900 — kept that way by his daughter Teresa until around 1960 and preserved deliberately since — making this a genuine time capsule rather than a recreation. Everyone comes to this block for Gaudí's building a few doors along. This is arguably the more honest of the three: one family's actual rooms, largely undisturbed.

stops.title: Casa Amatller
stops.caption: Look up at the gable first — a stepped, castle-like roofline copied more or less directly from Amsterdam, about the last thing you'd expect to find on a street this Mediterranean.
stops.transcriptText:
Look up at the gable first — a stepped, castle-like roofline copied more or less directly from Amsterdam, about the last thing you'd expect to find on a street this Mediterranean.

Passeig de Gràcia, number forty-one: part of a row of three famously mismatched buildings known as the Illa de la Discòrdia, the Block of Discord. Casa Amatller sits at the near end, its cream-and-pink facade and stepped gable a deliberate jolt after the neighbours on either side. Between 1898 and 1900, architect Josep Puig i Cadafalch took a plain building from 1875 and rebuilt its front almost entirely, fusing Catalan Gothic detail with Flemish gables and hand-painted ceramic tile.

The client was Antoni Amatller, whose fortune came from chocolate but whose real enthusiasms ran to photography and travel — and the building tells you so directly. Find the small sculpted rat clutching a camera, tucked into the stonework near the entrance: a chocolate manufacturer's private joke, carved into his own front door.

Step inside, if the museum's open, and the joke gives way to something quieter. Amatller's dining room, salon, and bedroom survive furnished much as they were in 1900, kept that way first by his daughter Teresa until roughly 1960, then preserved deliberately ever since — a genuine time capsule rather than a recreation. The stair court above them is lit through a stained-glass ceiling that turns the whole space faintly underwater in the afternoon.

Here's what's worth noticing, standing between these three houses: everyone comes to this block for Gaudí's building a few doors along, and understandably so. But Casa Amatller is arguably the more honest experience of the three — not a theatrical set piece built for crowds, but one family's actual rooms, largely undisturbed for well over a century.

Once you've looked up at the gable, look sideways too — the whole Illa de la Discòrdia is walkable in a couple of minutes, Casa Batlló on one side and Casa Lleó Morera on the other, three architects arguing with each other in stone along a single block of pavement.

tours.title: Casa Batlló
tours.shortDescription: The scaled roof is a dragon's back, and the tower at the end is Saint George's lance.
tours.longDescription: Textile industrialist Josep Batlló bought an ordinary 1877 apartment block in 1903 and asked Gaudí to knock it down. Gaudí talked him out of it and reworked the existing structure instead, which is part of why the building still feels inhabited rather than staged. The front ripples in pale stone across the lower floors under a mosaic of blue, green and gold climbing above it, and the roof arches up in coloured scales to a single cross-topped tower — a dragon's back, with Saint George's lance driven into it, Catalonia's patron saint retold as a roofline over one of the city's busiest avenues. At street level the balconies are wrought-iron carnival masks set beneath columns modelled loosely on thigh bones, which is why locals called this the Casa dels Ossos, the House of Bones, long before it had a politer name. Inside, the central light well is tiled in graduated blues, darkest at the top, so daylight arrives at roughly the same brightness on every floor. A million people a year walk through for the spectacle. The roofline reads differently once you know what it is.

stops.title: Casa Batlló
stops.caption: The roof is covered in what looks unmistakably like scales, and that's not an accident of imagination — it's a dragon, and you're looking at its spine.
stops.transcriptText:
The roof is covered in what looks unmistakably like scales, and that's not an accident of imagination — it's a dragon, and you're looking at its spine.

Stand back on the wide pavement of Passeig de Gràcia if you can, with the whole rippling front of Casa Batlló in view: pale stone curving across the lower floors, a mosaic of blue, green, and gold fragments climbing above it, and that scaled roof arching up to a single cross-topped tower at one end. Gaudí didn't build this from scratch, either — textile industrialist Josep Batlló bought an ordinary 1877 apartment block in 1903 and asked Gaudí to knock it down. Gaudí talked him out of it, and reworked the existing structure instead, which is part of why the building still feels inhabited rather than staged.

Now the roof, properly. The arched ridge and coloured scales read as a dragon's back, and the tower at one end, topped with a cross, becomes Saint George's lance driven into it — Catalonia's patron saint, slaying the dragon, retold as a roofline over one of the city's busiest avenues.

Come down to the main floor and look at the balconies: wrought-iron railings shaped like carnival masks, set beneath columns modelled loosely on thigh bones. Locals have called this front the Casa dels Ossos, the House of Bones, for exactly that reason, long before it had a more polite name.

Inside, if you go in, the theme keeps going. A central light well is tiled in graduated shades of blue, darkest at the top and palest lower down, so daylight arrives at roughly the same brightness on every floor; ceilings and railings ripple like water, whirlpools worked into the plaster and the banisters both. Between the ocean overhead and the dragon on the roof, the whole house reads as one continuous story, floor to ridge.

A million or so people walk through Casa Batlló every year, most of them for the spectacle alone. Stand outside a little longer before joining them, though — the roofline reads differently once you know it's Catalonia's own patron saint, built at full scale, over a family's front room. And if you'd like the same argument made twice, Casa Amatller's stepped Dutch gable is only a few doors down, quietly disagreeing with this one across the same stretch of pavement.

tours.title: Casa Bonay
tours.shortDescription: A family has owned this Eixample block since the nineteenth century. They still own it.
tours.longDescription: Casa Bonay sits on the corner of Gran Via and Carrer de Bailèn, built originally as the Bonay family's own home and later an artists' workspace, its balconies and stone detailing largely as they were. When the Brooklyn studio Studio Tack redesigned the interior in 2016 they kept the original marble bathtubs, the mosaic floors and the solariums that pull daylight down through the upper storeys — a soft minimalism, as they called it, that leaves the old bones visible rather than stripping them out. What fills the building is deliberately local: coffee from Satan's Coffee Corner, juice from Mother, a library curated with Blackie Books, and a rooftop that keeps a working orchard and herb garden rather than just a bar. Founder Inés Miró-Sans, who cut her teeth at Ace Hotel in New York, built it around partnerships with Barcelona makers rather than an imported house style. There is a real tension in that — the format itself, curated local partnerships and design pedigree and all, is an international hospitality formula — and the building does not pretend otherwise.

stops.title: Casa Bonay
stops.caption: The name isn't a design flourish. Bonay is the family that's owned this building since the nineteenth century, and they still own it now.
stops.transcriptText:
The name isn't a design flourish. Bonay is the family that's owned this building since the nineteenth century, and they still own it now.

Gran Via de les Corts Catalanes, at the corner with Carrer de Bailèn, in the Eixample Dreta: a nineteenth-century block built originally as the Bonay family's own home and, later, an artists' workspace, its balconies and stone detailing kept largely as they were. Step through the entrance and the ground floor opens into Bodega Bonay, the hotel's tapas bar, with the rest of the building's public rooms — café, cocktail bar, library, rooftop — layered above and around it.

Start with what survived the renovation. When the Brooklyn-based Studio Tack redesigned the interior in 2016, they kept the building's original marble bathtubs, its mosaic floors, and the solariums that pull daylight down through the upper storeys — a "soft minimalism," as the designers called it, that leaves the old bones visible rather than stripping them out.

Then look at how deliberately local the rest of it is built. Coffee comes from Satan's Coffee Corner, juice from Mother, the library's curated with Blackie Books, and the rooftop keeps a working orchard and herb garden instead of just a bar — founder Inés Miró-Sans, who cut her teeth at Ace Hotel in New York, built the place around partnerships with Barcelona makers rather than an imported house style.

Here's the interesting tension, standing in a hundred-and-fifty-year-old family building dressed as a hotel: Casa Bonay sells itself on authenticity, on being unmistakably of this city, and mostly earns that claim — even though the format itself, curated local partnerships, design pedigree and all, is an international hospitality formula. Both things are true at once, and the building doesn't pretend otherwise.

Take the lift or the stairs up to the rooftop if you can; the orchard's small, but it's real, and the view over the Eixample's grid of balconies is worth the extra floors on the way up.

tours.title: Casa Calvet
tours.shortDescription: The only Gaudí building the city ever gave a prize to, and the one that looks least like a Gaudí.
tours.longDescription: Built between 1898 and 1900 on a narrow street a few blocks off Passeig de Gràcia, Casa Calvet is symmetrical, restrained and almost polite: baroque-leaning stonework, a pair of curved gables, an ornate bay window rather than anything that ripples or bulges. The detail is where Gaudí hid the client. The columns flanking the door are carved as stacked bobbins of thread, a nod to Pere Màrtir Calvet's textile business on the ground floor; small mushroom-shaped reliefs poke out above the bay window because Calvet was a keen amateur mycologist; three carved heads look down from higher up — his patron saint, Peter Martyr, with two saints connected to the family's hometown — and a large stone letter C sits above the door as plainly as a monogram. When Barcelona's city council handed out its very first prize for the year's best building, this was the Gaudí that won it. Not the melting facade of Casa Batlló a few streets over, not the stone quarry of Casa Milà. The establishment liked the Gaudí who behaved himself.

stops.title: Casa Calvet
stops.caption: This is the only building of Gaudí's that ever won an official prize from the city, and it's also the one that looks the least like a Gaudí.
stops.transcriptText:
This is the only building of Gaudí's that ever won an official prize from the city, and it's also the one that looks the least like a Gaudí.

Carrer de Casp, number forty-eight, a narrow street a few blocks off Passeig de Gràcia — nothing about the block announces itself the way his later buildings do. The facade, built between 1898 and 1900, is symmetrical, restrained, almost polite by comparison: baroque-leaning stonework, a pair of curved gables, and an ornate bay window rather than anything that ripples or bulges.

Look at the entrance first. The columns flanking the door are carved to resemble stacked bobbins of thread, a direct nod to client Pere Màrtir Calvet's textile business, which occupied the ground floor when the building went up. Above the central bay window, small mushroom-shaped reliefs poke out of the stonework — Calvet, it turns out, was a keen amateur mycologist, and Gaudí worked the hobby straight into the facade.

Higher up, three carved heads look down over the street: Calvet's own patron saint, Peter Martyr, alongside two saints connected to the family's hometown. Between them, two carved globes carry the date 1899, and a large stone letter C, for Calvet, sits above the door as plainly as a monogram.

Here's the part worth pausing on. When Barcelona's city council handed out its very first prize for the year's best building, this restrained, symmetrical Gaudí was the one that won it — not the melting facade of Casa Batlló a few streets over, not the stone quarry curves of Casa Milà that came a few years later. The establishment liked the Gaudí who behaved himself, and it's his wilder, later buildings the world remembers instead.

Have a look through the ground floor if it's open — a restaurant and a chocolate shop now share the space where Calvet's offices once stood, and the chocolate shop still keeps one of Gaudí's original domed ceilings on view above the counter, worth ten minutes if you've got a sweet tooth to justify it.

tours.title: Casa Costa
tours.shortDescription: Four different names since the 1940s, and the same family through every one of them.
tours.longDescription: A two-storey building at the foot of Barceloneta beach, with a terrace out on the sand and a dining room upstairs looking straight out over the Mediterranean. The Costa family opened the original Casa Costa here in the 1940s, running it alongside a spot called Lo Deporto through the following two decades; by the 1980s the business had become La Pinxa, and by the 2000s, rebuilt in a newer building, it was Pinxo Playa. Barceloneta was built as a fishing and dockworkers' quarter, and this corner has spent eighty years renaming itself to match whatever the neighbourhood needed. The name changed four times. The family never did.

Start with the name itself, because it's done a lot of travelling. The Costa family opened the original Casa Costa here in the 1940s, running it alongside a spot called Lo Deporto through the following two decades; by the 1980s the business had become La Pinxa, and by the 2000s, rebuilt in a newer building, it was Pinxo Playa. tours.title: Casa Elizalde
tours.shortDescription: The family here built Spain's first cars, then its fighter-plane engines. Now anyone can walk in.
tours.longDescription: A four-storey Eixample townhouse designed by Emili Sala Cortés in 1888, its stone facade restrained by Modernista standards — no dragons, no bones, just careful classical detailing around the windows and a grand double doorway at street level. The name belongs to industrialists in the most literal sense: Arturo Elizalde Rouvier founded one of Spain's pioneering automobile companies here in 1914, building and racing cars through the following decade before the firm pivoted entirely to aircraft engines in 1925 — engines that powered Spanish military aircraft until nationalisation in 1951. His son Miguel trained as an aeronautical engineer and later ran the business. The turn in the story is what the building does now. Rather than becoming a paid museum behind a ticket desk, the way several grander Eixample mansions have, Casa Elizalde was handed over entirely to public use as a civic and cultural centre — exhibitions, workshops and evening classes open to anyone who signs up. A few streets away, Casa Amatller and Casa Batlló charge admission to see how one wealthy family lived. This one went the other way.

stops.title: Casa Elizalde
stops.caption: The family that once lived here helped build Spain's first cars, and later, its first fighter-plane engines.
stops.transcriptText:
The family that once lived here helped build Spain's first cars, and later, its first fighter-plane engines. Today, anyone can walk in and take a life-drawing class.

Casa Elizalde, the building in front of you at Carrer de València three-oh-two, is a four-storey Eixample townhouse designed by architect Emili Sala Cortés in 1888 — its stone facade fairly restrained by Modernista standards, no dragons, no bones, just careful classical detailing around the windows and a grand double doorway at street level.

Start with the family whose name it carries. The Elizaldes weren't just wealthy; they were industrialists in the most literal sense. Arturo Elizalde Rouvier founded one of Spain's pioneering automobile companies here in 1914, building cars and racing them competitively through the following decade, before the firm pivoted entirely to aircraft engines in 1925 — engines that powered Spanish military aircraft until the company was nationalised in 1951. His son, Miguel Elizalde Biada, trained as an aeronautical engineer and later ran the business himself.

Then look at what the building actually does now, because that's the real turn in the story. Rather than becoming a paid museum behind a ticket desk, the way several of the grander Eixample mansions have, Casa Elizalde was handed over entirely to public use: it now runs as a genuine civic and cultural centre, hosting exhibitions, workshops, and evening classes open to anyone who signs up, no industrialist's fortune required.

Here's what's worth noting, standing at the entrance: a few streets from here, Casa Amatller and Casa Batlló charge admission to see how one wealthy family used to live. This building went the other way entirely — the same scale of house, the same industrial-dynasty history, handed instead to whoever in the neighbourhood wants to use it.

Check the noticeboard just inside the entrance before you leave; the programme changes constantly, and it's not unusual to find a photography exhibition or a pottery class running in rooms that once belonged to a family building aircraft engines for the air force.

tours.title: Casa Gomis – La Ricarda
tours.shortDescription: Under a dictatorship that banned the avant-garde, this living room was where you could still hear it.
tours.longDescription: A low, flat house among pine trees on a strip of land between the sea and Barcelona's airport: a grid of shallow brick vaults on slender columns, walls of glass, the floor lifted just over two metres above the sandy ground. Antoni Bonet i Castellana, who had trained under Le Corbusier and Josep Lluís Sert, was commissioned in 1949 by Ricardo Gomis and Inés Bertrand and spent until 1963 building it module by module on an eight-point-eight-metre grid that treats covered rooms and open courtyards by exactly the same rules — even the floor tiles were chosen individually. Gomis turned the main living room into an informal concert hall, its acoustics good enough to become a genuine gathering point for Catalonia's suppressed avant-garde through the 1960s, drawing musicians and artists connected to ADLAN and Club 49 through his friendship with Joan Prats, who moved in Miró's circle. The airport that was small and far away when the house went up crept to within four hundred metres of it. In January 2025 Spain's Ministry of Culture bought the house outright, to be run as a museum under the MNAC.

stops.title: Casa Gomis – La Ricarda
stops.caption: For fifteen years under a dictatorship that banned most avant-garde art, this living room was one of the only rooms in Catalonia where it was still legal to hear it.
stops.transcriptText:
For fifteen years under a dictatorship that banned most avant-garde art, this living room was one of the only rooms in Catalonia where it was still legal to hear it.

You're standing among pine trees on a strip of land between the sea and Barcelona's airport, in El Prat de Llobregat, looking at a low, flat house that barely rises above the treeline — a grid of shallow brick vaults on slender columns, walls of glass, its floor lifted just over two metres above the sandy ground beneath it.

Start with the building itself. Architect Antoni Bonet i Castellana, who'd trained under Le Corbusier and Josep Lluís Sert, was commissioned in 1949 by Ricardo Gomis and Inés Bertrand and spent until 1963 building it, module by module, on an eight-point-eight-metre grid that treats covered rooms and open courtyards by exactly the same rules. Even the floor tiles were chosen individually, to a design this precise.

Then there's what happened inside it. Gomis turned the main living room into an informal concert hall, its acoustics good enough that it became a genuine gathering point for Catalonia's suppressed avant-garde through the 1960s — musicians and artists connected to the groups ADLAN and Club 49, brought here in part through Gomis's friendship with Joan Prats, who moved in Joan Miró's circle. Under a regime that shut most of that culture down elsewhere, this house quietly kept it alive.

And here's the pivot worth knowing before you leave. The airport that was "small and far away" when the house went up crept close enough that a runway now sits four hundred metres from the property, threatening it for decades — until, in January 2025, Spain's Ministry of Culture bought the house outright for the family, to be run from now on as a museum under the National Art Museum of Catalonia.

The Gomis Bertrand family kept every original piece of furniture, every colour, every fitting in place for over fifty years before handing it over, so what you're looking at is essentially unchanged. Check current visiting arrangements before you come — the transition to public museum status is still under way, and access has been limited while it happens.

tours.title: Casa Lleó Morera
tours.shortDescription: Its carved figures were pickaxed off the pavement in 1943. Some ended up in Dalí's museum.
tours.longDescription: Around 1902 Francesca Morera hired Lluís Domènech i Montaner to remodel an older house on the corner of Passeig de Gràcia and Consell de Cent, naming the result after her son Albert Lleó i Morera, who died two years into the project. Eusebi Arnau carved feminine figures onto pink marble columns, Lluís Bru and Mario Maragliano filled the gaps with mosaic, and mulberry motifs run throughout — morera is Catalan for mulberry tree, a quiet pun on the family name. It is the third building of the Illa de la Discòrdia and the easiest to walk past, because its ground floor now looks like any other luxury storefront. That is not an accident. In 1943, when the ground floor was refitted for a Loewe store, workers destroyed the original sculpted flower boxes and their figures on the pavement with picks; several recovered heads were sold on and ended up in Salvador Dalí's museum in Figueres, worked into his collection as found objects. Of the three houses on this block, this is the one that was actually vandalised — not by war or neglect, but by a retailer chasing a fresher shopfront.

stops.title: Casa Lleó Morera
stops.caption: Some of this building's original decoration didn't just disappear — it was pickaxed off the pavement in 1943 and later turned up two hundred kilometres away, inside a museum built by Salvador Dalí.
stops.transcriptText:
Some of this building's original decoration didn't just disappear — it was pickaxed off the pavement in 1943 and later turned up two hundred kilometres away, inside a museum built by Salvador Dalí.

Passeig de Gràcia, number thirty-five, on the corner with Consell de Cent: the third building of the Illa de la Discòrdia, and the easiest of the three to walk straight past, since its ground floor now looks like any other luxury storefront. Look up rather than at street level, and the Modernista building reasserts itself — carved figures, floral ironwork, ceramic detail climbing the facade in tiers.

Start with how it came to be. Around 1902, Francesca Morera hired architect Lluís Domènech i Montaner to remodel an older house on this corner, and named the result after her son, Albert Lleó i Morera, who died just two years into the project. Sculptor Eusebi Arnau carved feminine figures onto pink marble columns across the facade, mosaic artists Lluís Bru and Mario Maragliano filled the gaps between them, and mulberry-tree motifs run throughout — morera means "mulberry tree" in Catalan, a quiet pun on the family's own name.

Then comes the part most guidebooks skip. In 1943, when the ground floor was refitted for a Loewe store, workers destroyed the original sculpted flower boxes and their feminine figures directly on the pavement, with picks. Several of the recovered heads didn't go to a skip, though — they were sold on and ended up in Salvador Dalí's own museum in Figueres, worked into his surrealist collection as found objects, a hundred and thirty kilometres from the building they were carved for.

Here's the thing worth sitting with, at the corner of this block: of the three houses making up the Illa de la Discòrdia, this is the one that actually got vandalised, and not by war or neglect, but by a fashion retailer chasing a fresher shopfront. Restoration work across the 1980s and into 2012 brought back much of what could be recovered — though Loewe, notably, still occupies the ground floor today.

Look up one more time before you move on, toward the upper balconies where Arnau's carving survives untouched, and you'll have completed the whole disagreement — Amatller's Dutch gable, Batlló's dragon roof, and this one's quieter, more damaged beauty, three architects and three arguments along one short block.

tours.title: Casa Vicens
tours.shortDescription: Gaudí's very first house, tiled with the marigolds he found growing on the empty building site.
tours.longDescription: Gaudí's first major commission, designed in 1883 for a currency broker named Manel Vicens as a family summer retreat, on what was then a quiet street in the separate town of Gràcia. The facade is a riot of green-and-white ceramic tile over a rough stone base, three sides enclosed toward the street and the fourth opening onto a garden; nothing built in Barcelona at the time looked remotely like it. The tiles have the neatest origin story in his whole career: visiting the empty plot to take measurements, Gaudí found it covered in small yellow marigolds, and rather than clear the site and forget them he had the flower pattern worked directly into the ceramic covering the entire house — the actual weeds of the building site, fired into permanent decoration. The entrance gate, woven by Lorenzo Matamala into overlapping iron palm fronds, echoes a real palm that grew on the property before construction. Everything critics later praised in his wilder buildings is already fully formed here, at the first attempt, aged thirty.

stops.title: Casa Vicens
stops.caption: Every ceramic tile and twisting iron gate that later made Gaudí famous starts here, on a quiet street in Gràcia, with a stockbroker's summer house.
stops.transcriptText:
Every ceramic tile and twisting iron gate that later made Gaudí famous starts here, on a quiet street in Gràcia, with a stockbroker's summer house.

Casa Vicens, the building in front of you, was Gaudí's first major commission, designed in 1883 for a currency broker named Manel Vicens as a family summer retreat. The facade is a riot of green-and-white ceramic tile set over a rough stone base, three sides enclosed toward the street and the fourth opening onto a garden — nothing else built in Barcelona at the time looked remotely like it.

Start with the tiles themselves, because the story behind them is almost too neat. When Gaudí visited the empty plot to take measurements, he found it covered in small yellow marigolds, and rather than clear the site and forget them, he had the flower pattern worked directly into the ceramic tiles covering the whole house — the actual weeds of the building site, fired into permanent decoration.

Then look at the entrance gate, woven from iron into overlapping palm fronds by sculptor Lorenzo Matamala, echoing the real palm tree that once grew on the property before construction began. Between the tiles and the gate, the whole house reads as a portrait of the specific patch of ground it's built on, rather than a style imported from somewhere else.

Here's what's worth noticing, standing outside this one: everything critics later praised in Gaudí's wilder buildings — ornament pulled directly from nature, obsessive attention to a single site, colour used structurally rather than decoratively — is already fully formed here, at his very first attempt, aged thirty. Casa Batlló and the Sagrada Família didn't invent that instinct. This house did.

Step inside if the museum's open; the garden survives too, considerably smaller than Vicens's original plot but still shaded by exactly the kind of greenery that gave the whole facade its pattern in the first place.

tours.title: Cascada del Parc de la Ciutadella
tours.shortDescription: Before Gaudí designed a single building, he was hired here to do the plumbing.
tours.longDescription: Josep Fontserè designed this monumental fountain loosely on Rome's Trevi and finished it for the 1888 Universal Exposition, after an earlier and much-criticised version was reworked. A great curved double staircase climbs toward a gilded chariot at the top, water falling in sheets down the centre and pooling among carved rock below. At the summit Aurora, Roman goddess of dawn, rides a chariot drawn by four horses representing freedom and light; winged griffins guard the front, and water nymphs and fauns are scattered through the rockwork — a full cast of classical mythology in stone and concrete. From certain angles the curved staircases either side read unmistakably as a crab's claws, an effect nobody planned and everybody eventually mentions. The detail worth pausing on is invisible. Fontserè did not design this alone: a very young Antoni Gaudí, still an architecture student, was brought on for his skill with calculation and worked out the hydraulics and the hidden water tank behind the whole ornamental facade. It was plumbing rather than art, and it was his first paid job in the profession that made him famous.

stops.title: Cascada del Parc de la Ciutadella
stops.caption: Before Gaudí designed a single building, he was hired here to do the plumbing.
stops.transcriptText:
Before Gaudí designed a single building, he was hired here to do the plumbing.

Stand at the base of the fountain, facing the great curved staircase that climbs toward a gilded chariot at the top, water falling in sheets down the centre and pooling below among carved rock and greenery. Architect Josep Fontserè designed the whole structure, loosely modelled on Rome's Trevi Fountain, and finished it in time for the 1888 Universal Exposition after an earlier, criticised version was reworked.

Start with the sculpture crowding the upper terrace. At the very top, Aurora, the Roman goddess of dawn, rides a chariot pulled by four horses representing freedom and light; lower down, winged griffins guard the front, and water nymphs and fauns are scattered through the rockwork below — a full cast of classical mythology, poured in concrete and stone rather than painted.

Then there's the part almost nobody notices first: from certain angles, the curved double staircase either side of the cascade looks unmistakably like a crab's claws, an effect nobody planned and everybody eventually mentions.

Now the detail worth pausing on. Fontserè didn't design this alone — a very young Antoni Gaudí, still an architecture student, was brought on for his skill with calculation, and worked out the hydraulics and the water tank hidden behind the whole ornamental facade. It was invisible work, plumbing rather than art, and it was also his first paid job in the profession that made him famous.

Here's the thing worth sitting with, looking up at Aurora's chariot: everyone photographs the mythology on display here, and almost nobody realises the real historical curiosity is buried out of sight, in the tank and pipework holding the whole performance up.

If engineering interests you more than the sculpture, the Dipòsit de les Aigües is a short walk from here, across the park — another Fontserè project where the young Gaudí did the calculations, and this time you can actually walk inside what he built.

tours.title: Cheriff
tours.shortDescription: Named for a Murcian fishmonger who liked Westerns enough to dress as a sheriff for work.
tours.longDescription: A modest corner restaurant on Carrer de Ginebra in Barceloneta, tables spilling onto the narrow street, the kind of place that looks like it has been here since before the neighbourhood had tourists — because it has. Pedro Ruipérez opened a small fishmonger's on this spot in the late 1950s and was known locally for dressing up like an American film sheriff, sombrero and gun belt and all, a habit cheerful enough that neighbours started calling him Cheriff. The name stuck to the restaurant that grew out of his shop. What justified the reputation was the rice: paella and seafood sourced daily from boats docking at the nearby Moll de la Planxeta, recipes kept close within the family rather than written down. Pedro's son Simón eventually opened Lobito next door, while his daughter María de los Ángeles — Nini to regulars — took over the kitchen here and ran it for decades. When she retired in 2016 the Iborra group bought Cheriff outright and a 2019 renovation by Mesura modernised the dining room. That is usually the moment character gets sanded off. It does not appear to have happened here.

stops.title: Cheriff
stops.caption: The man this restaurant is named after wasn't from Texas, or anywhere near a ranch — he was a fishmonger from Murcia who liked Westerns a bit too much.
stops.transcriptText:
The man this restaurant is named after wasn't from Texas, or anywhere near a ranch — he was a fishmonger from Murcia who liked Westerns a bit too much.

Carrer de Ginebra, in the heart of Barceloneta, Barcelona's old fishing quarter: a modest corner restaurant, tables spilling onto the narrow street, the kind of place that looks like it's been here since before the neighbourhood had tourists at all. It has.

Start with the name. Pedro Ruipérez, who opened a small fishmonger's on this spot in the late 1950s, was known locally for dressing up like an American film sheriff — sombrero, gun belt, the full costume — a habit cheerful enough that neighbours started calling him Cheriff, and the name stuck to the restaurant that grew out of his shop.

Then there's what actually justified the reputation: the rice. Cheriff built its name on paella and seafood sourced daily from boats docking at the nearby Moll de la Planxeta, with recipes kept close within the family rather than written down for anyone to copy. Pedro's son Simón eventually opened his own place next door, Restaurante Lobito, while his daughter María de los Ángeles — known to regulars simply as Nini — took over the kitchen at Cheriff and ran it for decades.

When Nini retired in 2016, the Iborra Restaurants group bought Cheriff outright, and a 2019 renovation by Mesura Architecture Studio modernised the dining room. Here's the thing worth noting, given how these stories usually go: a restaurant group buying out a beloved family kitchen is exactly the moment character often gets sanded off in favour of something more generic. That doesn't appear to have happened here — the name, the sourcing, the neighbourhood grounding, all survived the sale intact.

Order the paella and don't rush it; Cheriff plates rice the traditional way, cooked to order rather than pre-made. And if you're curious about the family that started it all, Pedro's son's restaurant, Lobito, is just next door — same bloodline, different kitchen.

tours.title: Cocina Hermanos Torres
tours.shortDescription: Twin brothers split up on purpose in 1986 so they could learn different things, then reunited here.
tours.longDescription: An eight-hundred-square-metre converted industrial building with no wall between the dining room and the kitchen — one continuous black room, tables set in white, and five kitchen stations arranged in plain view rather than hidden behind a service door: pastry, research and development, the chefs' own office, a cold section and the main line. Javier and Sergio Torres grew up watching their grandmother Catalina cook for Barcelona's high society and talked their way into culinary school at fourteen. In 1986 they made an unusual decision for identical twins and split up deliberately, training separately across Spain and France — Alain Ducasse, the Basque Akelarre, Le Jardin des Sens — with a long-term plan to reunite once each had learned something different. When they opened here in 2018 the Office of Architecture in Barcelona built the space and Pete Sans lit it, around a single claim: that the kitchen is not a backstage element to a dining room, it is the dining room. The Michelin Guide agreed enough to award a third star in 2022, alongside a green star for sustainability.

stops.title: Cocina Hermanos Torres
stops.caption: There's no wall between the dining room and the kitchen here — just one continuous black room, and that's entirely deliberate.
stops.transcriptText:
There's no wall between the dining room and the kitchen here — just one continuous black room, and that's entirely deliberate.

You're inside an eight-hundred-square-metre converted industrial building, tables set in white against a black backdrop, and five separate kitchen stations arranged in plain view around the room rather than hidden behind a service door: pastry, research and development, the chefs' own office, a cold section, and the main line.

Start with the two men running it. Twins Javier and Sergio Torres grew up watching their grandmother Catalina cook for Barcelona's high society, and talked their way into culinary school at fourteen. In 1986 they made an unusual decision for identical twins: they split up on purpose, training separately at kitchens across Spain and France — Alain Ducasse's, the Basque Akelarre, Le Jardin des Sens among them — with a long-term plan to reunite once they'd each learned something different.

Then look at what that reunion eventually produced.
