tours.shortDescription: Named after a utopian novel, built on the rubble of a cement factory, and meant to be one of five.
tours.longDescription: Walden 7 rises as a deep red-brick tower in a dense cluster of interlocking blocks, its facade broken by rounded window openings arranged with no obvious repeating pattern, giving it a heavier, more fortress-like presence than a typical apartment block. The name nods to B. F. Skinner's novel Walden Two, itself named for Thoreau's Walden — a lineage running from nineteenth-century self-reliance through mid-century behaviourist utopianism to a very real, very dense apartment building outside Barcelona. Ricardo Bofill's studio built it between 1972 and 1974 on a site formerly occupied by a cement factory, which explains both the industrial-scale ambition and the raw brick. Inside are four hundred and forty-six apartments, each assembled from modular units of around thirty square metres into everything from studios to four-module family flats, arranged around a vertical labyrinth of interior courtyards rather than conventional corridors, deliberately designed to avoid the monotony of a uniform housing block. Rooftop pools, shared meeting rooms and ground-floor shops were all in the original plan. It was meant to be one of five nearly identical towers. Only this one was built.

stops.title: Walden 7
stops.caption: This entire housing complex takes its name from a utopian novel, and it was built on the rubble of an actual cement factory.
stops.transcriptText:
This entire housing complex takes its name from a utopian novel, and it was built on the rubble of an actual cement factory.

Walden 7 rises as a deep red-brick tower in a dense cluster of interlocking blocks, its facade broken by rounded window openings arranged with no obvious repeating pattern, giving the whole structure a heavier, more fortress-like presence than a typical apartment block.

Start with that name, because the chain of reference runs further back than you'd expect. It nods to B. F. Skinner's novel "Walden Two," itself named after Henry David Thoreau's "Walden" — a lineage running from nineteenth-century self-reliance, through mid-century behaviourist utopianism, to a very real, very dense apartment building outside Barcelona. Architect Ricardo Bofill's studio built it between 1972 and 1974, on a site formerly occupied by a cement factory, which explains both the industrial-scale ambition and the raw, unfinished-looking brick.

Then look at how it's actually organised inside. Four hundred and forty-six individual apartments, each built from modular units of around thirty square metres, combine into everything from studios to four-module family flats, arranged around a vertical labyrinth of interior courtyards rather than conventional corridors — deliberately designed, according to the architects, to avoid the monotony of a standard uniform housing block. Rooftop swimming pools, shared meeting rooms and ground-floor shops were all part of the original plan, treating the building less as housing and more as a self-contained small society.

Here's what's worth knowing, standing at the base of a building named after a utopian experiment: Walden 7 was originally meant to be one of five nearly identical towers forming a larger complex, and only this one was ever actually built — proof that even architecture this ambitious runs into the same budgets and politics as everything else.

Take the tram to the stop actually named "Walden" if you're arriving from central Barcelona — it's a small, quietly amusing detail that the building's fame earned it its own transit stop.

tours.title: Xavier Corberó
tours.shortDescription: One sculptor spent almost fifty years on a single artwork you can walk through and get lost inside.
tours.longDescription: Espai Corberó spreads out as a rambling, brick-toned compound of towers, staircases and courtyards in Esplugues de Llobregat, its outer walls giving little indication of the nine interconnected buildings and roughly three hundred archways behind them. Xavier Corberó was a Catalan artist known internationally for monumental public sculpture, prominent enough to be chosen to design the medals for the 1992 Barcelona Olympics, and in 1967 he bought an old farmhouse here called Can Cargol and began quietly turning the entire property into an extension of his own practice. Over the following decades nine interconnected buildings, twelve courtyards and hundreds of archways grew up around the original farmhouse, drawing visibly on Italian Futurism and Surrealism; an underground space that once served as a garage now hosts concerts, and a subterranean residence uses staggered floor levels to scatter daylight in ways that shift through the day. He filled it with a genuine cabinet of curiosities — chairs by Gaudí among the collected objects — and used it as a residence for younger artists passing through. Most sculptors make pieces you look at from a fixed distance. Corberó built one you move through.

stops.title: Xavier Corberó
stops.caption: One sculptor spent almost fifty years building a single artwork you can actually walk through, sleep in, and get lost inside.
stops.transcriptText:
One sculptor spent almost fifty years building a single artwork you can actually walk through, sleep in, and get lost inside.

Espai Corberó spreads out as a rambling, brick-toned compound of towers, staircases and courtyards in Esplugues de Llobregat, its outer walls giving little indication of the nine interconnected buildings and roughly three hundred archways hidden behind them.

Start with the sculptor himself. Xavier Corberó was a Catalan artist known internationally for monumental public sculpture, prominent enough to be chosen to design the medals for the 1992 Barcelona Olympics, and in 1967 he bought an old farmhouse here called Can Cargol and began quietly turning the entire property into an extension of his own artistic practice.

Then look at what that extension became over the following decades. Nine interconnected buildings, twelve courtyards and hundreds of archways grew up around the original farmhouse, drawing visibly on Italian Futurism and Surrealism, an underground space that once served as a garage now hosts concerts, and a subterranean residence uses staggered floor levels to scatter daylight in ways that shift constantly through the day. Corberó filled the complex with a genuine cabinet of curiosities — chairs by Gaudí among the collected objects — and used it not just as his own workshop but as a residence for younger artists passing through.

Here's what's worth knowing, standing outside a house that took roughly half a century to finish: most sculptors make individual pieces you look at from a fixed distance. Corberó built one continuous piece you're meant to move through, and the building itself, rather than any single object inside it, is arguably his most complete work.

Book ahead through the Esplugues de Llobregat council's culture department rather than turning up unannounced — the complex is a private house museum, open by appointment only, and walk-in visits aren't possible.

tours.title: Dreta de l'Eixample
tours.shortDescription: Seven stops through the block where three architects spent a decade arguing with each other in stone.
tours.longDescription: A walk through the Dreta de l'Eixample in seven stops, beginning on the Illa de la Discòrdia — the Block of Discord — where three houses went up within a few years of each other and spent the early nineteen-hundreds quietly competing. It starts at Casa Lleó Morera, whose prize-winning sculpture was taken to with picks in 1943 and whose salvaged fragments ended up in Salvador Dalí's museum; then Casa Amatller, where a chocolate fortune paid for a piece of Amsterdam to appear unannounced in Barcelona; then Casa Batlló, where Gaudí answered both neighbours with a dragon. From there it turns the corner onto Carrer d'Aragó for Museu Tàpies, an earlier and utterly different building by the same architect who began the walk, before heading up to Rambla de Catalunya and Hotel Casa Sagnier — the one house on the route an architect built for himself. La Pedrera is where the competition finally runs out of neighbours to outdo, and Casa Elizalde, lived in quietly for a century while the rest of the street showed off, is where the whole argument runs out of steam. About 1.4 kilometres, all of it flat.

stops.title: Casa Lleó Morera
stops.caption: In 1943, workers took picks to a set of prize-winning modernist sculptures on this very facade, and some of the salvaged fragments ended up, of all places, in Salvador Dalí's own museum.
stops.transcriptText:
In 1943, workers took picks to a set of prize-winning modernist sculptures on this very facade, and some of the salvaged fragments ended up, of all places, in Salvador Dalí's own museum.

Passeig de Gràcia, number thirty-five: a corner building crowded with carved stone and mosaic, its upper floors busy with sculpture in a way its ground floor, oddly, no longer is. This is Casa Lleó Morera, and it's the first of three houses on this one short block that spent the early nineteen-hundreds quietly competing with each other.

Start with what made it special. Architect Lluís Domènech i Montaner redesigned the building between 1902 and 1905 for the widow Francesca Morera, and after her death it took the name of her son, Albert Lleó i Morera. Sculptor Eusebi Arnau carved four pairs of women into the upper facade, each holding an object representing a new technology of the age — a phonograph, an electric lamp, a telephone, a camera — while mosaic artists Lluís Bru and Mario Maragliano filled in the colour. In 1906, Barcelona's city council gave the building its own annual prize for the year's best new architecture — officially, at the time, this was the winner of the block.

Then look at what's missing lower down. In 1943, the leather goods firm Loewe took over the ground floor and had the original modernist windows and sculpted planters smashed out with picks to make way for a shopfront — an act of vandalism, by any modern definition, that stripped away Arnau's street-level work entirely. Some of the rescued carved heads later surfaced in Dalí's museum in Figueres, of all unlikely destinations.

Here's what's worth knowing before you look at its neighbours: this building technically won the argument this block is famous for, and almost nobody visiting today knows that.

Turn slightly to your right — Casa Amatller stands immediately next door, and the competition properly starts there.

stops.title: Casa Amatller
stops.caption: A chocolate fortune paid for a piece of Amsterdam to appear, entirely unannounced, in the middle of Barcelona.
stops.transcriptText:
A chocolate fortune paid for a piece of Amsterdam to appear, entirely unannounced, in the middle of Barcelona.

Next door to Casa Lleó Morera stands a narrower building topped with a stepped, triangular gable that looks lifted straight from a Dutch canal house, its facade covered in patterned ceramic tile and carved stone rather than the flowing curves you'll find further along this block.

Start with who paid for it. Antoni Amatller, whose family chocolate factory was turning out more than ten thousand kilograms of chocolate a day by the turn of the century, hired architect Josep Puig i Cadafalch to rebuild an older house here between 1898 and 1900. Puig i Cadafalch reached north for his inspiration rather than looking to Barcelona's own tradition, giving Amatller a facade with sculpted figures representing painting, music, architecture and sculpture, and staircase details that quietly nod to the cocoa trade that paid for the whole project.

Then look for the door knocker, because it's easy to walk straight past. Cast in the shape of a dragon, it references Sant Jordi — Saint George — Catalonia's patron saint and the same legend you're about to see handled very differently one door further along. Amatller himself was a keen amateur photographer, and part of what's now displayed inside comes from his own collection, alongside the family's original furniture, kept largely as he left it.

Here's what's worth knowing, standing between two very different visions of prestige: three wealthy families commissioned three separate architects on this one block, each apparently determined that their house would be the one people talked about, and the results still don't agree with each other in the slightest.

Keep walking the same few steps along the block — Casa Batlló is next, and it takes that same dragon legend somewhere considerably stranger.

stops.title: Casa Batlló
stops.caption: The roofline in front of you is generally read as a sleeping dragon, and the balconies beneath it are generally read as bones — which tells you everything about how far this block's rivalry eventually went.
stops.transcriptText:
The roofline in front of you is generally read as a sleeping dragon, and the balconies beneath it are generally read as bones — which tells you everything about how far this block's rivalry eventually went.

Casa Batlló fills the third and final plot on this stretch of Passeig de Gràcia, its facade a shifting mosaic of blue, green and gold ceramic fragments beneath a roof that arches and scales like something alive rather than built.

Start with why it looks nothing like the perfectly ordinary building that stood here before. Textile industrialist Josep Batlló owned a respectable but unremarkable house on this plot, built back in 1877, and by 1904, with two striking new neighbours already going up beside him, he hired Antoni Gaudí to transform it completely rather than start again from nothing. Gaudí gutted most of the interior, replaced straight structural columns with organic, bone-like supports, and covered the whole facade in trencadís — broken ceramic tile — assembled into a surface that seems to shimmer instead of sitting still.

Then look at the roof itself, because the reading almost everyone reaches for is Saint George and the dragon: the scaled ridge as the dragon's back, the small tower and cross as the lance that finally kills it, the skull-like balcony shapes as its earlier victims. Gaudí himself never confirmed that interpretation in writing, though it's stuck regardless, and Barcelona settled on its own blunter nickname for the building — the House of Bones.

Here's what's worth knowing, standing at the end of the block that gave this whole area its nickname: Casa Lleó Morera technically won the official architecture prize the year it was finished, but it's this house, the last of the three, that ended up owning the popular imagination almost completely.

Head up Carrer d'Aragó instead of continuing along Passeig de Gràcia — a short walk brings you to Museu Tàpies, where the same architect behind the first house on this block built something else entirely.

stops.title: Museu Tàpies
stops.caption: The same architect who designed the first house on this tour also built this one, and yet the two buildings barely look related.
stops.transcriptText:
The same architect who designed the first house on this tour also built this one, and yet the two buildings barely look related.

Carrer d'Aragó carries a red-brick facade with rounded arched windows, distinctly industrial in rhythm compared with the ornate stone and mosaic you've just left behind on Passeig de Gràcia, the whole thing topped by an odd tangle of aluminium wire with a chair jutting out of its centre.

Start with the commission that came before Casa Lleó Morera made him famous for houses. Lluís Domènech i Montaner designed this building between 1880 and 1882 as the headquarters of Editorial Montaner i Simon, a publishing firm, working here in brick, iron and glass rather than the carved stone and sculpture he'd later bring to Passeig de Gràcia — proof that the same architect could sound completely different depending on who was paying and what they were paying for, decades apart in the same career.

Then look at what sits on the roof, because it arrived over a century later. When the building reopened in 1990 as the Fundació Antoni Tàpies, the artist installed "Núvol i Cadira" — Cloud and Chair — directly onto the roofline, using his own recurring symbol of a chair to give the low industrial building a presence it couldn't otherwise claim against its taller neighbours.

Here's what's worth knowing, standing between a Victorian print works and a piece of contemporary sculpture: this whole neighbourhood keeps doing the same thing, over and over, in different centuries — buildings put up to declare something about the person or institution behind them, whether that's a chocolate fortune, a publishing house, or one artist's late-career signature.

Cut back toward Rambla de Catalunya rather than retracing your steps — Hotel Casa Sagnier sits a short walk from here, and it's a different architect's turn to build himself a statement.

stops.title: Hotel Casa Sagnier
stops.caption: Most of the buildings on this walk were designed by one architect for someone else entirely.
stops.transcriptText:
Most of the buildings on this walk were designed by one architect for someone else entirely. This one, the architect built for himself.

Rambla de Catalunya holds a five-storey stone facade with deep bay windows and gothic-tinged carving climbing toward the roofline, altogether quieter than the showpieces you've just left behind, though no less deliberate.

Start with who actually lived here. Enric Sagnier, one of the busiest architects working in Barcelona at the turn of the century, built this as his own house and studio in 1892, naming it Casa Dolors Vidal de Sagnier for his wife — a rare chance, for an architect who spent his career designing statement buildings for other wealthy families, to design one entirely on his own terms, answerable to nobody's taste but his own.

Then look at what happened to it more recently, because the story doesn't end with Sagnier. The building opened as a fifty-one-room hotel in 2008, a fairly conventional conversion of a grand family home into bedrooms, before undergoing a second, more considered restoration in 2021 that seems to have been less about adding polish and more about making the building feel specifically like itself again, rather than a generic five-star shell with old stonework out front for atmosphere.

Here's what's worth knowing, standing outside a house its own architect got to design without a client looking over his shoulder: everywhere else on this walk, the buildings tell you what someone wanted people to think of them. This one just tells you what Sagnier, left alone, actually built.

Head back toward Passeig de Gràcia and continue north — La Pedrera is only a few minutes further on, and it closes out this walk with the most extreme version of everything you've seen so far.

stops.title: La Pedrera — Casa Milà
stops.caption: Everything you've seen on this walk so far was one family or one architect trying to outdo their neighbours.
stops.transcriptText:
Everything you've seen on this walk so far was one family or one architect trying to outdo their neighbours. This building is what happens when that competition simply runs out of neighbours to outdo.

Six storeys of pale limestone bend around this corner of Passeig de Gràcia in unbroken waves, no straight line anywhere across the whole facade, with wrought-iron balconies twisted into shapes that look grown out of the stone instead of bolted onto it.

Start with the reception it actually got, because the whole street turned against it at first. Antoni Gaudí built this for Pere Milà and Roser Segimon between 1906 and 1912, and Barcelona's residents, distinctly unimpressed, nicknamed it "La Pedrera" — the quarry — a jab at how rough and unfinished the stone looked beside its tidier neighbours. Homeowners further along the avenue reportedly stopped greeting Milà socially, worried his building would drag property values down across the whole street.

Then look at what made it genuinely radical, not just strange to look at. The stone facade carries no structural load at all, so every floor inside was freed from fixed interior walls, and on the roof, chimneys shaped like helmeted sentries stand guard over the skylights in what the poet Pere Gimferrer later called "the garden of warriors." UNESCO recognised the building as a World Heritage Site in 1984, eight decades after Barcelona first laughed at it.

Here's what's worth knowing, standing at the last and strangest house on this entire walk: three families started this rivalry a few streets back, each trying to impress the others with sculpture and stonework and carved facades. Gaudí, handed the same basic brief roughly a decade later, simply threw out the rulebook those earlier houses were still playing by.

If you've got twenty minutes left, Casa Elizalde on Carrer de València is worth the detour — the same neighbourhood's grandest houses eventually led somewhere considerably more ordinary, and rather lovely for it.

stops.title: Casa Elizalde
stops.caption: After six houses built to be looked at, here's one that spent a century quietly being lived in instead.
stops.transcriptText:
After six houses built to be looked at, here's one that spent a century quietly being lived in instead.

Carrer de València holds a handsome but comparatively restrained townhouse, its facade giving little hint that this is where the walk's whole competitive streak finally runs out of steam.

Start with the family who actually lived here. The Elizalde family owned this house from 1865 until 1964, treating it as an ordinary private residence for essentially a century, through the exact decades when their near neighbours a few streets over were locked in increasingly elaborate architectural one-upmanship. No dragons, no chocolate-funded gables, no prize-winning sculpture, no picks taken to the facade — just a family home, occupied and largely unremarked upon while the rest of the neighbourhood competed for attention.

Then look at what happened once the family finally sold up in 1964. Barcelona's city council acquired the building in 1981 and opened it to the public, first with exhibitions, then with lectures, and eventually with the packed cultural programme it runs today — more than two hundred courses, workshops, concerts, theatre, poetry readings and film screenings, aimed as much at children as adults, and mostly free or close to it.

Here's what's worth knowing, standing at the end of a walk that started with two women carved in stone holding a telephone and a phonograph: every other stop on this route was built to declare something about the person who paid for it. This one simply became everyone's, which is arguably the more interesting ending.

Step through to the inner courtyard if the centre's open when you visit — it's free to wander, considerably quieter than anywhere else on this walk, and a genuinely good place to sit down after several hours on your feet.

tours.title: The Monumental Rosary of Montserrat
tours.shortDescription: Five stops down the mountain path where Catalonia's great architects each carved a mystery into the rock.
tours.longDescription: A walk down the Camí de la Santa Cova in five stops, following the path pilgrims carved by hand into the side of Montserrat two centuries before Barcelona's Modernista architects ever set foot on the mountain. It begins at the monastery, turning away from the basilica's main doors toward the plain stone gateway at the eastern edge of the complex, then passes the upper station of the Santa Cova funicular — two hundred and sixty-two metres of track dropping nearly a hundred and twenty metres in under three minutes. Below that the Monumental Rosary begins: fifteen sculptural groups set into niches along the descent, commissioned from the leading Catalan artists and architects of the age. The third stop holds the one religious sculpture Antoni Gaudí saw finished, blessed and opened to the public in his own lifetime, and it is not in Barcelona at all. Four more mysteries follow in quick succession, each paid for by a different confraternity, none of them coordinating with the others, and yet read in order the sequence holds together as one story. The path ends at the Santa Cova itself, a chapel built directly into the mountainside. About one kilometre, downhill.

stops.title: Monestir de Montserrat
stops.caption: Two centuries before Barcelona's Modernista architects ever set foot on this mountain, pilgrims were already carving a path down its side by hand.
stops.transcriptText:
Two centuries before Barcelona's Modernista architects ever set foot on this mountain, pilgrims were already carving a path down its side by hand.

Turn away from the basilica's main doors and head toward the eastern edge of the monastery complex, past the shops and the queue for the funicular, where a plain stone gateway marks the start of a route most day visitors never notice.

Start with what's underfoot before any of the sculptures come into view. The path itself, known as the Camí de la Santa Cova, was cut into the mountainside between 1691 and 1704 under the patronage of Gertrudis de Camporrell, a noblewoman who funded the route so pilgrims could walk down to the cave where Montserrat's story began, on foot rather than by any easier means. For close to two hundred years, that's all it was: a track cut into rock, with nothing to look at but the mountain itself.

Then, between 1896 and 1916, that changed completely. Confraternities, wealthy families, and Catholic associations from across Catalonia began paying, one station at a time, for sculpted scenes to mark the walk, and the roster of architects and sculptors who took on those commissions reads like a who's who of Barcelona's Modernista scene: Antoni Gaudí among them, alongside Josep Puig i Cadafalch, Enric Sagnier, and a long list of others who spent their working lives designing rival mansions along Passeig de Gràcia.

And here's the thing: up here, none of them got a whole building to call their own. Each architect was handed a single station in a sequence that only makes sense walked start to finish, funded by two dozen different patrons who never coordinated with one another at all — a genuinely strange way for Barcelona's most competitive generation of architects to end up working, almost without meaning to, on the very same project.

A few minutes' walk from here, past the gateway, brings you to the upper station of the Santa Cova funicular — worth a look even if you're planning to walk the whole way down.

stops.title: Santa Cova Funicular
stops.caption: Two hundred and sixty-two metres of track drop you nearly a hundred and twenty metres down this mountainside in under three minutes, on a gradient steep enough to make the walking path look almost gentle by comparison.
stops.transcriptText:
Two hundred and sixty-two metres of track drop you nearly a hundred and twenty metres down this mountainside in under three minutes, on a gradient steep enough to make the walking path look almost gentle by comparison.

The upper station sits a short walk from the monastery's main square, a squat building of glass and steel that looks almost incidental beside the basilica behind it, easy enough to miss if you're not specifically looking for it.

Start with why it's here at all. The funicular opened in 1929, built specifically to carry pilgrims and visitors down to Santa Cova without forcing them to manage the older walking path's full descent, and it's stayed in more or less continuous use since, aside from a stretch after severe flood damage in 2000, which shut the line until a renovation reopened it the following year.

Then there's the mechanism itself, which is the genuinely clever part. The line runs on a single track with one passing loop, and two carriages share it: only one carries passengers at a time, while the other simply rides along as a counterweight, rising as its partner descends and dropping as its partner climbs. Each car holds up to ninety people, and the whole journey lasts about two and a half minutes.

Worth sitting with, for the two and a half minutes the ride takes: pilgrims have been finding ways down this exact stretch of mountain for over three centuries, on foot the entire time until this line opened, so the choice between riding and walking is really a choice about how much of that older effort you still want to feel in your legs.

However you make the descent, look for the walking path again once you're past the lower station. The first of the sculptures, cut directly into the rock, is only a few minutes further down, and it's unlike anything else on this mountain.

stops.title: I Misteri de Glòria — La Resurrecció de Crist
stops.caption: Antoni Gaudí has exactly one religious sculpture that was finished, blessed, and opened to the public in his own lifetime, and it isn't in Barcelona at all.
stops.transcriptText:
Antoni Gaudí has exactly one religious sculpture that was finished, blessed, and opened to the public in his own lifetime, and it isn't in Barcelona at all.

Cut into the rock a little further down the path, a shallow cave frames a scene unlike anything else on this walk: a carved sepulchre set back into the stone, figures gathered around it, and a wrought iron gate marking the threshold.

Start with the commission. The Lliga Espiritual, a Catholic devotional association, hired Gaudí in December 1903 to design this scene: the Resurrection, the moment Christ's tomb is found empty. Rather than simply mount a statue against the rock face, Gaudí had the cave itself dug further back into the mountainside, so the sepulchre would sit inside real stone instead of a sculpted approximation of it — the kind of literal-minded solution that runs through nearly everything he built.

Then look at what happened next, because it isn't the tidy story you might expect. Gaudí fell out with his collaborators over exactly where the figure of the risen Christ should stand, and in 1907 he withdrew from the project entirely, handing the remaining work to sculptor Josep Llimona, who carried it through to completion. The whole ensemble — Llimona's Christ and angel, the Three Marys by Dionís Renart, a wrought iron gate by architect Jeroni Martorell — was finally blessed in 1916.

The interesting bit is this: a hundred and ten years later, Gaudí's most famous project, the Sagrada Família, is still not finished. This modest mountainside scene is one of the very few things he designed that he actually got to see completed, and even that only happened because he was willing to walk away and let someone else finish it in their own way rather than his.

A few steps further along the path, four more niches follow in quick succession, each one telling the next chapter of the same story Gaudí began here.

stops.title: II to V Misteri de Glòria
stops.caption: Four separate confraternities paid for four separate sculptures along this short stretch of path, and none of them coordinated with one another at all — yet walked in order, the sequence reads as one continuous story.
stops.transcriptText:
Four separate confraternities paid for four separate sculptures along this short stretch of path, and none of them coordinated with one another at all — yet walked in order, the sequence reads as one continuous story.

Four more niches follow in quick succession here, cut into the rock at intervals close enough that you can see the next one before you've finished looking at the last.

Start with the third of these scenes, the Pentecost, designed in 1904 by architect Joan Martorell with sculptor Josep Maria Barnadas and mosaicist Mario Maragliano. Two stone columns frame a mosaic of the Holy Spirit descending, topped by a seven-branched candlestick carrying a Latin inscription that translates, roughly, to sacred sevenfold — worth knowing, because this same Martorell is the architect who, a few years earlier, had recommended a promising young colleague named Antoni Gaudí to take over an entirely different unfinished church back in Barcelona.

A little further on sits the Ascension, carved from two blocks of Carrara marble by sculptor Josep Reynés to a design by architect Bonaventura Bassegoda, its relief work bordered by bronze symbols of the four evangelists — a noticeably different material and register from its neighbours, since each of these scenes was funded, designed, and carved entirely independently of the rest.

The row finishes with the Assumption, sculpted by Venanci Vallmitjana for the Daughters of Mary association in 1900, Mary rising toward heaven with two musical angels at her feet, and then the Coronation beyond it, closing the cycle with Mary crowned in glory, the last of the fifteen mysteries carved into this mountainside.

Which says something worth pausing on: not one of these four scenes was planned as part of a matching set, and between different architects, different sculptors, different materials and even different decades, they still read in sequence as a single piece of storytelling — proof, maybe, that this kind of accidental collaboration works precisely because nobody was trying to make it look uniform.

The path continues a short distance further, past the last of these niches, to the chapel the whole route has been leading toward.

stops.title: Santa Cova de Montserrat
stops.caption: The chapel in front of you was restored, in part, by the same architect who started Barcelona's most famous unfinished building, and then handed it to somebody else entirely.
stops.transcriptText:
The chapel in front of you was restored, in part, by the same architect who started Barcelona's most famous unfinished building, and then handed it to somebody else entirely.

The path ends here, at a chapel built directly into the mountainside, its dome only becoming visible once you're almost at the door, the rock itself forming part of the back wall.

Start with why anyone built anything here at all. Tradition holds that in the year 880, shepherds on this mountainside saw a light and heard music coming from this exact spot, and inside the cave they found a statue of the Virgin, the same figure now enthroned in the basilica above. A proper chapel went up around the cave between 1696 and 1705, funded once again by Gertrudis de Camporrell, the same noblewoman whose money cut the path you've just walked down.

Then look at who restored it. After Peninsular War damage in 1811 and 1812, architect Francisco de Paula del Villar carried out repairs here between 1857 and 1859 — the same Villar who designed the apse of the basilica above, and under whom a young, still largely unknown Antoni Gaudí did some of his earliest professional work, right here on this mountain. Villar went on to begin an entirely different, far more famous church back in Barcelona in 1882, before stepping back from it in 1883 after a dispute with Joan Martorell, the architect advising the project's founder — the same Martorell behind the Pentecost scene you passed a few minutes ago. It was Martorell who recommended Gaudí as his replacement.

Here's what's worth knowing, having walked a path that started with Gaudí's own Resurrection scene: this whole mountainside, in a roundabout way, maps the handoffs that produced Barcelona's most famous building. Villar trained Gaudí here, Martorell promoted him there, and Gaudí himself, a few hundred metres back, walked away from his own finished work and let somebody else complete it — the same pattern, repeating itself across three separate architects, on one mountain, decades apart.

Step inside if the chapel's open — it's small, quiet, and considerably less crowded than the basilica above. When you're ready to head back, the funicular from stop two will carry you back up to the monastery, or you can simply walk the path in reverse and meet all five of these scenes again from the other direction.

tours.title: Caffè del Lupo
tours.shortDescription: A Portello café that runs on two clocks — office lunches by day, a sharing-plates bar by night.
tours.longDescription: Chef Luca Ferrara opened this Via Francesco Albani address in 1997, and it has been leading a double life ever since. Through the working week it is a straightforward daytime canteen for the office crowd on this northwest-edge street, serving a lunch menu built around whatever was genuinely good that morning rather than a fixed printed card. Then, Wednesday to Saturday evenings, the same room and the same kitchen turn into a tapas-style bar of comfort food and small plates meant for sharing — no change of furniture, no change of address, just a different set of regulars filling the tables. The frontage gives none of this away, which is rather the point.

stops.title: Caffè del Lupo
stops.caption: By day, this is a canteen for the office workers on this street.
stops.transcriptText:
By day, this is a canteen for the office workers on this street. By evening, without moving a single table, it turns into something else entirely.

Via Francesco Albani, in the Portello district on Milan's northwest edge: a plain café frontage that gives very little away about what happens here once the sun goes down.

Chef Luca Ferrara opened the place back in 1997, and for years it's run on two entirely different clocks. Through the working week it's a proper daytime café, serving a healthy, changing lunch menu built around whatever's genuinely fresh that morning rather than a fixed printed card, to the local office crowd on tight breaks. Then, Wednesday through Saturday evenings, the same room and the same kitchen become a tapas-style bar built around comfort food and small plates meant for sharing. The regulars who show up for lunch are rarely the same people filling the tables on a Friday night, and the room adjusts its whole personality to match — quieter and quicker at midday, slower and more sociable after dark. On top of that, Ferrara also takes on private chef bookings, building custom menus and wine pairings for people celebrating something at home rather than out — essentially the same skill set that runs the café by day, just relocated to somebody's dining room.

Most restaurants pick one identity and defend it fiercely. This one runs two, on the same equipment, depending purely on the hour — a small, quiet act of reinvention that happens here every single day, without any fuss made about it.

Nothing about the shopfront tells you which version of the place you've walked into. You generally just have to check the time.

Portello itself takes its shape from the old Alfa Romeo factory that once stood on this ground, redeveloped over the last couple of decades into the flats and parkland now surrounding you — worth a walk if industrial Milan's second life interests you.

tours.title: Sidewalk Kitchens
tours.shortDescription: Five independent kitchens around one courtyard, and you eat whatever you like at the same table.
tours.longDescription: On Via Bonvesin de la Riva, a little south of Porta Venezia, an open courtyard is lined with separate kitchen counters and filled down the middle with shared tables — closer to a food market than a restaurant. The format is deliberately loose: order from whichever of the independent kitchens appeals, usually alongside a café and a natural-wine counter, and eat it all together rather than committing to one menu for the evening. The line-up rotates, with pop-ups moving through beside the regulars, so what is actually cooking depends on the week you turn up. It is a way of eating that suits a group who can never agree.

stops.title: Sidewalk Kitchens
stops.caption: Nobody here has just one kitchen. This address has five, all under the same roof, all doing something different.
stops.transcriptText:
Nobody here has just one kitchen. This address has five, all under the same roof, all doing something different.

Via Bonvesin de la Riva, a little south of Porta Venezia — an open courtyard lined with separate kitchen counters, more food market than restaurant, with shared tables filling the middle.

Notice how deliberately loose the format is. The idea is straightforward: order from whichever of the independent kitchens takes your fancy — there's usually a café and a natural-wine counter running alongside them — and eat it all together at the same table, rather than picking one restaurant and committing to it for the evening. The line-up of vendors rotates fairly regularly, with pop-ups moving through alongside the regulars — a gastro-trattoria called CreDa took over one of the counters for a run earlier this year — so what's actually cooking on any given visit isn't fixed the way a normal restaurant's menu would be. It runs breakfast through to dinner and aperitivo, too, which is unusual for a format like this — most street-food collectives pick a lane, lunch or evening, rather than trying to cover the whole day — and the natural-wine counter running alongside the kitchens means you can build a proper meal here without ever sitting down at what most people would call a restaurant table. The whole format borrows its logic from a market rather than a restaurant — you're free to mix a plate from one counter with a glass from another and call that dinner, which most conventional kitchens would find a bit chaotic to allow.

Which is really street food with an address attached: all the informality of eating off a cart, staged instead as something closer to a proper institution, wine list and all.

Five kitchens, one roof, and a menu that's different every time you ask what's good today.

Check what's actually cooking before you commit to a table — the rotating line-up means the best reason to come back next month might be a kitchen that isn't even here yet.

tours.title: Triennale di Milano
tours.shortDescription: For its first decade this exhibition was not even held in Milan — it ran in Monza.
tours.longDescription: Giovanni Muzio built the Palazzo dell'Arte on Viale Alemagna between 1931 and 1933, purpose-made for an exhibition that had outgrown its old home: the Monza Biennale of Decorative Arts moved to Milan, switched from a two-year cycle to a three-year one, and gained international standing all in the year the doors opened. The first show alone carried murals by Giorgio de Chirico and Mario Sironi, and handed a gold medal to a young Finnish architect named Alvar Aalto. The building is faced in clinker and sits deliberately at the end of a monumental sightline that runs from the Arco della Pace through Castello Sforzesco to here — a piece of civic staging as considered as anything shown inside it.

stops.title: Triennale di Milano
stops.caption: For its first ten years, this exhibition wasn't even held in Milan — it ran in Monza, twice a decade, until it outgrew the format entirely.
stops.transcriptText:
For its first ten years, this exhibition wasn't even held in Milan — it ran in Monza, twice a decade, until it outgrew the format entirely.

Viale Alemagna, on the edge of Parco Sempione — a broad, deliberately classical-looking building in warm ochre brick, closing off the same monumental sightline that runs from the Arco della Pace, through Castello Sforzesco, to here.

Start with how it landed on this exact spot. The architect Giovanni Muzio built it between 1931 and 1933, purpose-made for what had been the Monza Biennale of Decorative Arts — moving to Milan, switching from a two-year cycle to a three-year one, and gaining international recognition, all in the same year the doors opened. The opening exhibition alone included murals by Giorgio de Chirico and Mario Sironi, and a gold medal went to a young Finnish architect named Alvar Aalto. The building itself is faced in clinker, a fired material chosen deliberately to echo Lombardy's traditional brickwork without copying it outright — old materials, reworked in a distinctly 1930s idiom. Today the ground floor holds the Museo del Design Italiano, permanent since 2019 and substantially reworked for the institution's centenary in 2023: three hundred objects out of a collection of sixteen hundred, a Vespa and a Lambretta among them, tracing a hundred years of Italian design in one long curved gallery.

The interesting bit is this: the building and the Compasso d'Oro design prize were both born out of the very same 1950s moment — sibling institutions from the same design boom that have since gone their separate ways: the prize's own collection now lives in its own museum across town, while this building kept the exhibition itself.

A hundred years of Italian design, and it all still runs through a building that started out as a temporary loan from Monza.

Step into the garden behind the building if the weather allows — de Chirico's Mysterious Baths sculpture and a small puppet theatre by the Mendini family sit permanently among the trees, a five-minute detour most visitors on their way to the castle never make.

tours.title: Velasca Tower
tours.shortDescription: The top third is wider than the bottom, propped out on concrete struts, and it has been that way on purpose since 1958.
tours.longDescription: BBPR built the Torre Velasca between 1957 and 1958 with the engineer Arturo Danusso, and the mushroom-shaped top was never decoration: it bought extra residential floor space above street level, in direct homage to the way medieval Lombard towers were propped out on wooden and stone beams. At a hundred and six metres it broke sharply with the clean rationalist architecture Milan had been building for decades, and one of its architects, Ernesto Nathan Rogers, defended it at the time as an attempt to sum up the whole character of the city in a single building. The same practice later designed the Nazi-deportation memorial at the Monumental Cemetery, with one of their founding partners among those who never came back.

stops.title: Velasca Tower
stops.caption: Look up. The top third of this building is wider than the bottom, and it's been that way on purpose since 1958.
stops.transcriptText:
Look up. The top third of this building is wider than the bottom, and it's been that way on purpose since 1958.

You're on Piazza Velasca, just southeast of the Duomo, above Missori metro station — the tower's upper floors overhang the street below, visibly propped out on diagonal concrete struts.

Start with the firm behind it. BBPR — the same practice that later designed the understated Nazi-deportation memorial at the Monumental Cemetery, with one of their own founding partners among those who never came back from the camps — built the tower between nineteen fifty-seven and 1958, working with the engineer Arturo Danusso. The mushroom-shaped top wasn't decoration: it let them add extra residential floor space above street level, in direct homage to the way medieval Lombard towers were traditionally propped out on wooden or stone beams. At a hundred and six metres and twenty-six storeys, it was accused, when it opened, of vandalising Milan's skyline — a rupture with the clean rationalist architecture the city had been building for decades. One of the architects, Ernesto Nathan Rogers, defended it at the time as an attempt to sum up the whole character of the city in a single silhouette, which did little to calm the critics down. Opinion has shifted since: the tower gained protected landmark status in 2011, and a restoration completed in 2025 added a restaurant on the eighteenth floor with a panoramic view over the exact skyline it was once accused of ruining.

Which is rather a satisfying turn: a building once condemned for breaking with the city around it is now protected because of it, and sells that same disputed view for the price of dinner.

Once vandalism, now a landmark, now also a dinner reservation — the tower hasn't changed. Milan's opinion of it has, twice over.

The piazza at its base was repaved as part of the same restoration, olive trees and all — worth standing directly underneath the cantilever and looking straight up, which is the one angle photographs of this building never quite capture.

tours.title: ADI Design Museum
tours.shortDescription: It kept the city's lights on for decades before it started keeping its trophies.
tours.longDescription: The Compasso d'Oro has been running since 1954, which makes it one of the oldest design prizes anywhere, and it is not awarded for paintings or sculpture — it goes to manufactured things that got their job right: a coffee maker, a typewriter, a scooter headlamp, a chair. It began as a department-store initiative dreamed up by Aldo Borletti at La Rinascente to push Italian manufacturers toward better design. The collection now lives on Piazza Compasso d'Oro in a former electrical substation, reworked in 2021 by Ico Migliore and Mara Servetto, who kept the old brick shell and wrapped a new atrium around it — industrial function given a second life as design, which is more or less the museum's whole argument in one building.

stops.title: ADI Design Museum
stops.caption: This building didn't always keep trophies. For decades, it generated electricity.
stops.transcriptText:
This building didn't always keep trophies. For decades, it generated electricity.

Piazza Compasso d'Oro, in Milan's Porta Volta district: a long, glass-fronted structure that was once a power substation, reworked in 2021 by the architects Ico Migliore and Mara Servetto, who kept the old brick shell and wrapped a new atrium around it. The building itself already tells you something about what's inside — industrial function, given a second life as design.

Start with what the museum actually collects. Since 1954, the Compasso d'Oro has been one of the oldest design prizes anywhere, and it isn't handed out for paintings or sculpture — it goes to ordinary manufactured things that got their job right: a coffee maker, a typewriter, a scooter headlamp, a chair. It started life as a department-store initiative, dreamed up by Aldo Borletti at La Rinascente to push Italian manufacturers toward better design, and only in 1962 did this museum's own parent body, the Associazione per il Disegno Industriale, take full control of the prize. More than three hundred and fifty of the winning objects sit in the collection here, a kind of trophy case for the idea that a well-designed teapot deserves the same attention as a well-painted canvas.

And here's the thing worth knowing. In 2004, Italy's Ministry of Culture classified this collection as being of exceptional historical and artistic interest — the same legal category used to protect a Renaissance fresco. A stapler, officially, on the level of a masterpiece. Last year, the publisher Treccani spent a thousand pages and over two thousand photographs cataloguing every winner from 1954 through 2022, which gives you some sense of how seriously this small museum takes objects most people throw away without a second thought.

That's really the whole argument of the place: design isn't decoration bolted onto a product afterwards, it's the product, and Milan has been quietly insisting on that for seventy years.

Before you head off, look across the piazza — the brick-and-steel complex bordering the museum is the Fabbrica del Vapore, a former steam-tram factory reworked by the architects Herzog and de Meuron into studios and exhibition space. Worth the extra ten minutes if design's caught your interest today.

tours.title: Altriménti
tours.shortDescription: Altrimenti means otherwise, or if not — the word you reach for when the obvious option will not quite do.
tours.longDescription: There is a joke folded into the name of this Brera bar, and it turns out to describe the drinks list exactly: cocktails built on second thoughts and detours, presented as the result of research rather than an aperitivo list poured on autopilot. Behind a quiet, lounge-style frontage on Via Castelfidardo, a short walk off the main gallery streets, the room runs to low light, close-set tables and a counter positioned so you can watch the drinks actually being made. The kitchen works the same logic in reverse — Japanese-Italian dishes designed around the wine rather than wine chosen to match a plate.

stops.title: Altriménti
stops.caption: There's a small joke folded into this bar's name. Altrimenti is Italian for otherwise, or if not — the kind of word you reach for when the obvious option won't quite do, and it turns out to be exactly the right name for a cocktail list built on second thoughts and detours.
stops.transcriptText:
There's a small joke folded into this bar's name. Altrimenti is Italian for otherwise, or if not — the kind of word you reach for when the obvious option won't quite do, and it turns out to be exactly the right name for a cocktail list built on second thoughts and detours.

Via Castelfidardo runs through Brera, one of Milan's oldest artistic quarters, and behind a quiet, lounge-style frontage a short walk off the main gallery streets, you'll find low light, close-set tables, and a bar counter positioned so you can watch the drinks actually get made rather than just arrive.

Notice how the place describes its own cocktails: the result of careful research, balancing fine ingredients against newer technique, rather than a standard aperitivo list poured on autopilot. The food follows the same logic in reverse. Instead of picking wine to match a plate, the kitchen designs Japanese-Italian dishes specifically to sit alongside particular drinks, which flips the usual order of an Italian aperitivo almost entirely.

Which says something about Brera itself, standing on this street: the Accademia di Brera was founded here in seventeen seventy-six, on the orders of the Empress Maria Theresa of Austria, and its picture gallery and fine-art school have anchored this quarter for close to two hundred and fifty years, with painters once living cheaply in the studios round the corner. The neighbourhood didn't stop taking craft seriously when the art students grew up and moved on — it just found a new medium. A cocktail built with the same fussy attention as a canvas, in a district that's always rewarded people who take small things seriously.

That's Brera's trick, really: it never announces itself as precious, it just quietly assumes you'll notice the care.

If you've time before or after a drink, the Pinacoteca di Brera is a few minutes' walk north — one of Italy's great picture galleries, sitting almost directly above the aperitivo crowd without most of them ever going in.

tours.title: Alzaia Naviglio Grande
tours.shortDescription: The towpath where men and mules once hauled the Duomo's marble upstream by rope.
tours.longDescription: Alzaia simply means towpath, and that is precisely what you are standing on: the strip of ground along the canal's southern bank running out from the Darsena basin, past long rows of former boatmen's housing now given over to bars, galleries and antique shops. What moved along this water was the making of the city — building stone, coal, wine, meat, fish and timber heading in; salt, linen, wheat and rice heading back out toward Lake Maggiore. On the 24th of October 1387 Duke Gian Galeazzo Visconti signed an entire marble quarry at Candoglia over to the cathedral's builders, and for more than five centuries the Duomo arrived here by barge.

stops.title: Alzaia Naviglio Grande
stops.caption: It's 1270, and a barge loaded with marble is inching along this canal toward a cathedral that won't be finished for another five centuries.
stops.transcriptText:
It's 1270, and a barge loaded with marble is inching along this canal toward a cathedral that won't be finished for another five centuries.

The Alzaia Naviglio Grande is the towpath running along the canal's southern bank, out from the Darsena basin past long rows of former boatmen's housing, now mostly bars, galleries, and antique shops. Alzaia itself just means towpath — the strip of ground where men and mules once hauled loaded barges upstream by rope, which is precisely what you're standing on.

Consider what actually moved along this water: building material for the Duomo, coal, wine, meat, fish, timber heading in, and salt, linen, wheat, and rice heading back out toward Lake Maggiore and beyond. On the 24th of October, 1387, Duke Gian Galeazzo Visconti signed over an entire marble quarry at Candoglia, up near Lake Maggiore, to the cathedral's builders, and for more than five centuries afterward, that pale, pink-streaked stone travelled down exactly this route — river, lake, and this canal — into a small basin near the building site. The system only stopped in 1920, when lorries finally took over. This canal is generally reckoned Europe's oldest still-navigable one, dug from a defensive moat in the 1170s and reaching all the way into the city by 1270.

Leonardo da Vinci worked here too, maintaining the locks and channels that kept the water level workable, and was paid, in part, with a water right of his own — a legal claim to an irrigation outlet, the Renaissance version of stock options. That system of engineering he refined is still doing its job: the network fed by this canal irrigates around fifty thousand hectares of farmland to this day, and a passenger service ran along it from 1645 right up to 1913.

Which is really the point of standing here: this stretch of water built the Duomo, stone by stone, long before it ever poured a single aperitivo. The working canal came first, and the leisure came later — you're currently enjoying the second act.

A narrow lane just off the towpath, the Vicolo dei Lavandai, still has the stone troughs where the neighbourhood's washerwomen once did the laundry — worth the two-minute detour if you want to see the canal's working life up close.

tours.title: Antonia
tours.shortDescription: A Habsburg government headquarters, a Radetzky command post, and now somewhere to buy a cashmere jumper.
tours.longDescription: Palazzo Cagnola went up on Via Cusani between 1822 and 1825 for the Milanese nobleman Giuseppe Cagnola, designed by Pietro Pestagalli — nine bays across, fluted pilasters, Bramante-style capitals. It did not stay a private house for long. The building became the seat of the Austrian administration in Milan, the actual headquarters of Habsburg government in the city, and during the Five Days of Milan in 1848 Field Marshal Radetzky based himself here before retreating under pressure to Castello Sforzesco just up the road. The ground floor is now entirely given over to a fashion boutique, which is a considerable demotion for a room where an empire was once run.

stops.title: Antonia
stops.caption: This is Palazzo Cagnola, and buying a cashmere jumper here is not remotely what the building was built for.
stops.transcriptText:
This is Palazzo Cagnola, and buying a cashmere jumper here is not remotely what the building was built for.

You'll find it on Via Cusani, a short walk from Castello Sforzesco: a neoclassical palazzo with nine bays across its facade and fluted pilasters topped with Bramante-style capitals, its ground floor now given over entirely to a fashion boutique called Antonia.

Look at the layers underneath the clothing racks. The palazzo went up between 1822 and 1825, commissioned by the Milanese nobleman Giuseppe Cagnola and designed by the architect Pietro Pestagalli, and it didn't stay a private house for long: it became the seat of the Austrian administration in Milan, the actual headquarters of Habsburg government in the city. In 1848, during the uprising known as the Five Days of Milan, Field Marshal Radetzky based himself here, before retreating under pressure to Castello Sforzesco just up the road. Later in the century the building held a private art collection instead, assembled by Guido Cagnola, before it eventually moved on to a villa outside the city.

Two centuries on, the building is still doing the same job under a different name: deciding what matters enough to keep inside it. First an empire's paperwork, then one family's art, and now a curated mix of established fashion houses and newer, less obvious names, since the label Antonia opened its doors in 1999 and has since grown as far as Shanghai and Macao. A second Antonia opened in 2022 inside Portrait Milano, a former sixteenth-century seminary a few streets from here — two very different historic buildings, both repurposed for the same idea of carefully curated fashion.

Power moved out of this building generations ago. What's replaced it is smaller, and rather less bloody, but the instinct to curate carefully hasn't changed at all.

Castello Sforzesco is only a few minutes' walk from here — the fortress Radetzky retreated to in 1848, and worth the short detour if this palazzo's history has caught your attention.

tours.title: Arco della Pace
tours.shortDescription: A monument to a war that had already been lost by the time anyone finished building it.
tours.longDescription: Napoleon commissioned the arch in 1807 as part of a grand plan for this stretch of the city, and Luigi Cagnola built it as an Arch of Victory meant to celebrate French conquest. History did not cooperate. By the time it was completed the campaign it honoured was over and the empire behind it gone, so the monument was rededicated — to peace instead. At the top a bronze chariot is driven by a figure representing Peace, flanked by winged Victories; around the base sit four women standing for the rivers of this region, the Adige, the Po, the Ticino and the Tagliamento. Stand at the western edge of Parco Sempione and it frames the whole of Corso Sempione, once the road to Paris.

stops.title: Arco della Pace
stops.caption: Stand at the western edge of Parco Sempione and this arch frames the whole of Corso Sempione stretching away in front of you — a monument built to celebrate a war that had already been lost by the time anyone actually finished it.
stops.transcriptText:
Stand at the western edge of Parco Sempione and this arch frames the whole of Corso Sempione stretching away in front of you — a monument built to celebrate a war that had already been lost by the time anyone actually finished it.

Turn to face outward, away from the park, down the wide straight road that continues toward what was once the road to Paris. Castello Sforzesco and the gardens sit directly behind you, the arch rising ahead.

Begin at the top of the arch: a bronze chariot, driven by a figure representing Peace, flanked by winged Victories, and around the base, four seated women representing rivers of this region — the Adige, the Po, the Ticino, and the Tagliamento. Napoleon commissioned the whole thing in 1807, part of a grand plan for this stretch of the city, and the architect Luigi Cagnola built it as an Arch of Victory, meant to celebrate French conquest. Cagnola's arch was meant to be the grand gateway of a much larger scheme, the Foro Bonaparte, imagined as a vast forum ringing the castle behind you — most of it was never built, and this arch is one of the few pieces that actually got finished. Then, in 1814, Napoleon abdicated with the arch only half-built, and the project simply stopped, half of Milan's grandest monument left standing here unfinished for over a decade.

What's worth knowing is what happened next. The Austrians took over the city, and rather than tear the half-built arch down, they renamed it — Arco della Pace, the Arch of Peace, after the Congress of Vienna that had just settled Europe's borders. Construction resumed in 1826, and the arch was finally inaugurated in 1838, dedicated now to an Austrian emperor instead of a French one. Two decades later, when the Austrians left too, the city rededicated it again — this time to a unified Italy.

The stone itself never moved an inch through any of that. Only the label kept changing, depending on who was currently in charge of writing it.

Walk back through Parco Sempione toward Castello Sforzesco, and you're tracing the same short stretch of ground that's carried Napoleonic troops, Austrian garrisons, and now, considerably more peacefully, an evening stroll.

tours.title: Bar Basso
tours.shortDescription: Every Negroni Sbagliato in the world exists because somebody here reached for the wrong bottle in 1972.
tours.longDescription: Giuseppe Basso opened the bar in 1933 elsewhere in the city, moving to this Lima district corner after the war. In 1967 a Venetian barman named Mirko Stocchetto took it over with Renato Haussmann, arriving with a résumé that ran through Harry's Bar in Venice and the Hotel de la Poste in Cortina d'Ampezzo. Five years later somebody behind the counter reached for sparkling wine instead of gin, and the sbagliato — the mistaken one — became a drink served in every city on earth. The room has barely changed: bright dining-room lighting, waiters in white jackets, a very long bar, and none of the dim theatrics that a bar with this story could easily have leaned into.

stops.title: Bar Basso
stops.caption: Every Negroni Sbagliato served anywhere in the world exists because, one evening in 1972, somebody behind this counter reached for the wrong bottle.
stops.transcriptText:
Every Negroni Sbagliato served anywhere in the world exists because, one evening in 1972, somebody behind this counter reached for the wrong bottle.

Milan's Lima district, a plain corner address: bright dining-room lighting and a look that's stayed largely the same across decades of business — no dim mood lighting, no speakeasy theatrics, just tables, waiters in white jackets, and a very long bar.

It's worth knowing how long this place has actually been running. Giuseppe Basso opened it back in 1933, in a different part of the city, before the bar relocated here after the war. In 1967, a Venetian barman named Mirko Stocchetto took it over with his business partner Renato Haussmann, bringing with him a résumé that included Harry's Bar in Venice and the Hotel de la Poste in Cortina d'Ampezzo — the Alpine resort where Italy's postwar jet set spent its winters — where he'd once poured drinks for the Agnelli family, Elizabeth Taylor, and Richard Burton. Five years later, mixing a classic Negroni, Mirko found the gin had been moved and grabbed sparkling wine instead — the drink he served that night, sbagliato, meaning mistaken, became one of Italy's most exported cocktails, later trademarked by his son Maurizio to protect the name.

The other detail worth knowing sits in your hand if you order one: the tall glass, thirty centimetres of it, was designed by Mirko himself, back when Milan simply didn't have proper glassware for the drinks he wanted to serve. That glass, the bicchierone, now belongs to the permanent design collection at the Triennale.

A cocktail bar that accidentally produced both a world-famous drink and a museum object, from a single mistake behind the counter — not bad, for an accident.

The Triennale di Milano, over in Parco Sempione near Castello Sforzesco, holds that original glass in its design collection, if you'd like to see the object itself rather than just drink from a copy of it.

tours.title: Baratie
tours.shortDescription: Exposed concrete and a crowd on the pavement, giving away nothing about what arrives on the plate.
tours.longDescription: On Via Stendhal in the Solari district, southwest of the centre, the front of the place is industrial and the cooking behind it is considerably more ambitious. Co-founder and chef Andrea Cicu works to a simple philosophy — good raw ingredients, real technique, served as small shareable plates rather than formal courses. Spago, a prawn pasta finished with butter, chilli and garlic, sits on the same menu as aubergine cooked Sassari-style so the skin stays properly crisp, and suckling pig plated with yellow courgette. The room is built around a busy aperitivo counter that turns, table by table, into a proper dinner service as the evening goes on.

stops.title: Baratie
stops.caption: Exposed concrete, a crowd spilling out onto the pavement, tables jammed close together — nothing about the front of this place gives away what's about to arrive on the plate.
stops.transcriptText:
Exposed concrete, a crowd spilling out onto the pavement, tables jammed close together — nothing about the front of this place gives away what's about to arrive on the plate.

Via Stendhal, in the Solari district southwest of the centre: industrial on the outside and considerably more ambitious on the inside, the room built around a busy aperitivo counter that gradually turns, table by table, into a proper dinner service.

The kitchen tells the real story here. Co-founder and chef Andrea Cicu runs the food with a fairly simple philosophy: good raw ingredients, handled with real technique, then served as small shareable plates rather than formal courses. Spago — a prawn pasta finished with butter, chilli, and garlic — sits on the same menu as aubergine cooked Sassari-style, a Sardinian technique that leaves the skin properly crisp, and suckling pig plated alongside yellow courgette. None of it particularly needs explaining once it's in front of you, and a glass and a shared plate can turn into a full dinner without anyone deciding that in advance — the bill, typically somewhere between twenty-five and sixty euros a head, reflects that flexibility rather than a fixed tasting menu.

It's part of a wider shift in this city, if you're used to a Milanese aperitivo meaning a plate of crisps and a spritz: bars that start the evening pouring drinks and quietly end it running one of the better kitchens in the neighbourhood, without ever changing the unpretentious shopfront out front. Solari itself has quietly become one of Milan's more interesting streets to eat on over the last decade, without ever really being marketed as one.

Nothing here dresses itself up, and nothing on the menu is trying to impress you on looks alone. It just gets better the longer you stay.

The Navigli canal district is a short walk south from here, if you fancy carrying on the evening — this whole stretch of southwest Milan tends to reward wandering rather than planning.

tours.title: Basilica di Santa Maria delle Grazie
tours.shortDescription: An Allied bomb took the roof off the room next door in 1943, and the wall holding the Last Supper was still standing when the dust cleared.
tours.longDescription: Construction began in 1463 under Guiniforte Solari and the church was consecrated in 1482 — a fairly conventional Gothic brick building, until Ludovico Sforza decided in 1492 that his family needed something grander attached to it. He brought in Donato Bramante to rework the east end in the new Renaissance style, and a few years later commissioned Leonardo to paint the refectory wall. That refectory is now entered separately from the church and booked well in advance: visitors go in forty at a time, for exactly fifteen minutes, before the next group is let through. The basilica itself faces the piazza in red brick and terracotta, and the survival of the painting through 1943 remains the most improbable thing about it.

stops.title: Basilica di Santa Maria delle Grazie
stops.caption: It's 1943, and an Allied bomb has just taken the roof off the room next door — somehow, the wall carrying the painting inside is still standing when the dust clears.
stops.transcriptText:
It's 1943, and an Allied bomb has just taken the roof off the room next door — somehow, the wall carrying the painting inside is still standing when the dust clears.

The basilica of Santa Maria delle Grazie faces the piazza in red brick and terracotta, and its most famous room, the refectory holding Leonardo's Last Supper, is tucked around the side, entered separately from the church and booked, these days, well in advance — visitors go in forty at a time, for exactly fifteen minutes, before the next group is let through the door.

The building itself came first. Construction began in 1463 under the architect Guiniforte Solari, the monastery was finished by 1469, and the church was consecrated in 1482 — a fairly conventional Gothic brick building, until Ludovico Sforza, Duke of Milan, decided in 1492 that his family needed something grander attached to it. He brought in Donato Bramante to rework the east end in the new Renaissance style, and a few years later commissioned a mural for the monks' dining hall from an artist he already employed at court: Leonardo da Vinci, who painted the Last Supper on the refectory's north wall between 1495 and 1498.

What's genuinely remarkable, standing here nearly five hundred and thirty years later, is how close all of it came to being lost. When the bomb hit in 1943, it destroyed the refectory's roof and brought down the south wall entirely — the north wall, carrying Leonardo's painting, happened to be the one still standing when the smoke cleared. In 1980, UNESCO added the church and the painting together to its World Heritage list — one of the relatively few times a single artwork, rather than just the building around it, earned that kind of protection.

Two of the era's sharpest minds working on the same building, for the same duke, and one wartime accident nearly took the whole thing with it.

Sant'Ambrogio, generally reckoned Milan's oldest basilica, sits a short tram ride from here, if church history from an even earlier century has caught your interest today.

tours.title: Basilica of Sant'Ambrogio
tours.shortDescription: Ambrose is buried directly beneath the altar of the church he consecrated with his own hands in 387.
tours.longDescription: A broad quadrangular atrium stands between the street and the church doors — a walled courtyard you cross before you arrive, and part of the building for most of its long life. A Benedictine monastery has been attached since 784, when Archbishop Pietro established a community to look after it. The older story is down in the crypt, where the remains of Ambrose rest alongside two early martyrs, Gervasius and Protasius, where they have rested for over sixteen centuries. Above ground, an archbishop named Angilbert the Second commissioned a golden altar in the ninth century specifically to enclose those relics, worked in gold and silver, and it still stands behind the high altar today.

stops.title: Basilica of Sant'Ambrogio
stops.caption: The saint this basilica is named for is buried directly beneath the altar, in the very church he consecrated with his own hands, in the year 387.
stops.transcriptText:
The saint this basilica is named for is buried directly beneath the altar, in the very church he consecrated with his own hands, in the year 387.

A broad quadrangular atrium stands between the street and the actual church doors — a walled courtyard you cross first, a threshold that's been part of the building for most of its long life.

A Benedictine monastery had been attached to the church since 784, when the Archbishop Pietro first established a community here to look after it. Down in the crypt is where the older story starts: the remains of Ambrose himself, alongside two other early martyrs, Gervasius and Protasius, resting where they've rested for over sixteen centuries. Above ground, an archbishop named Angilbert the Second commissioned a golden altar in the ninth century specifically to enclose those relics, worked in gold and silver and still standing behind the high altar today. Underneath the pulpit sits something older still — a carved Roman sarcophagus from the fourth century, traditionally linked to the general Stilicho, predating the church itself by decades.

This building has never really belonged to one single era. It was entirely rebuilt in the Romanesque style around the turn of the twelfth century, and even the two communities who ran it — the resident monks and a separate body of canons — spent years disputing who actually controlled which part of it, especially after the emperor Frederick Barbarossa laid siege to Milan in 1162 and the canons fled while the monks stayed behind to protect the church. The dispute dragged on for decades before it was finally settled in 1201, by which point the basilica had already been serving Milan for the better part of eight centuries.

Almost sixteen hundred years on, and the man this place was built for has never actually left it.

Look for the two bell towers before you go — one noticeably older and plainer than the other, added roughly three centuries apart, and each one telling you something different about who was in charge of building it at the time.

tours.title: Bosco Verticale
tours.shortDescription: Nine hundred trees are growing right now, rooted in pots bolted to balconies a hundred metres above the street.
tours.longDescription: Stefano Boeri and his studio completed the two towers in 2014, one eighty metres tall and the other a hundred and twelve. The numbers are the easiest way in: four hundred and eighty large and medium trees, three hundred smaller ones, eleven thousand perennials and ground-cover plants and five thousand shrubs, spread across the balconies of both buildings. Laid flat on open ground that much vegetation would cover close to two hectares of woodland — all of it currently growing sideways off a residential tower instead. What matters more than the count is the work it does: filtering air, shading glass, damping noise, and standing as a deliberate act of defiance against everything else going up around it. The model has since been copied well beyond Milan.

stops.title: Bosco Verticale
stops.caption: Nine hundred trees are growing right now on two apartment towers in front of you, rooted in pots bolted to concrete balconies more than a hundred metres above the street.
stops.transcriptText:
Nine hundred trees are growing right now on two apartment towers in front of you, rooted in pots bolted to concrete balconies more than a hundred metres above the street.

The two towers here, one eighty metres tall and the other a hundred and twelve, make up the Bosco Verticale — vertical forest, in English — completed in 2014 by the architect Stefano Boeri and his studio.

The scale is the first thing worth grasping: four hundred and eighty large and medium trees, another three hundred smaller ones, eleven thousand perennials and ground-cover plants, and five thousand shrubs, spread across both buildings' balconies. Laid flat on open ground, that much vegetation would cover something close to two hectares of actual woodland — all of it currently growing sideways off a residential tower instead.

What matters more than the number is what all that greenery actually does. The trees filter dust and pollution out of the air, offer some shade in summer and let winter light through once their leaves drop, and give birds and insects a genuine foothold in a very dense part of the city. It stands inside Porta Nuova, the business district rebuilt almost entirely over the last fifteen years, within sight of the Unicredit tower's spire — for a while, among the tallest buildings in Italy — which makes the greenery here look even more like a deliberate act of defiance against everything else going up around it. Since it opened, the model's been copied — Boeri's studio has gone on to build variations on the same idea in cities well beyond Milan.

Most towers this size settle for maximising glass and floor space and call the job finished. This one deliberately gave a large chunk of its structure over to something that needs watering.

The wider Porta Nuova district around you was almost entirely rebuilt in the years either side of these towers going up — worth a wander if you want to see how far the rest of the neighbourhood ran with the same ambition.

tours.title: Bulgari Hotel Milano
tours.shortDescription: A jeweller's first hotel anywhere in the world, hidden down a private street behind its own walled garden.
