tours.longDescription: Bulgari had never run a hotel until this one opened its gates in 2004, on a private street screened by a garden of its own — you see very little of the building until you are through the gate, a deliberately quiet threshold a few streets from the busiest shopping in Milan. Antonio Citterio designed it and furnished the interiors from his own Flexform and Maxalto ranges rather than reaching for anything off the shelf: black marble quarried in Zimbabwe, stone from Vicenza and Afyon, teak and oak throughout, cream linen on the walls. The building underneath began life in the 1950s and was folded quietly into the new design rather than knocked down.

stops.title: Bulgari Hotel Milano
stops.caption: Bulgari had never run a hotel anywhere in the world until this one opened its gates in 2004.
stops.transcriptText:
Bulgari had never run a hotel anywhere in the world until this one opened its gates in 2004.

Down a private street off the main road, screened by its own walled garden, is where you'll find the Bulgari Hotel — you won't see much of the building itself until you're actually through the gate, a deliberately quiet threshold just streets away from some of the busiest shopping in Milan.

The materials do a lot of the talking here. The hotel was designed by the architect Antonio Citterio, who furnished the interiors with pieces from his own Flexform and Maxalto ranges rather than reaching for anything off the shelf: black marble quarried in Zimbabwe, stone brought from Vicenza and Afyon, teak and oak throughout, cream linen on the walls. The building underneath all of it started life in the 1950s, folded quietly into the new design rather than knocked down and replaced. Inside, beyond the rooms themselves, there's a spa built partly below ground and a swimming pool that opens onto the garden — the kind of amenities usually associated with a resort, tucked instead into the middle of a European fashion capital.

Bulgari itself started a very long way from hotel-keeping. Sotirio Bulgari, a twenty-seven-year-old Greek silversmith, opened his first shop in Rome in 1884, selling handmade silver ornaments and curiosities to residents and travellers alike. It took the company a hundred and twenty years to decide that the same instinct for craft and material could be applied to an entire building rather than just a piece of jewellery — and it got the idea right enough on the first attempt that Bulgari now runs hotels on several continents.

None of that ambition shows from the street. The garden and the gate see to that, deliberately.

The Quadrilatero della Moda, Milan's fashion quarter of Via Montenapoleone and its neighbouring streets, starts just a short walk from here, if you'd like to see where the rest of this city's luxury business happens rather more visibly.

tours.title: Camparino in Galleria
tours.shortDescription: The drink that gave Milan its evening ritual was invented by the family who built the room.
tours.longDescription: Gaspare Campari opened his first café nearby in 1867; in 1915 his son Davide opened this grander companion on the corner where the Galleria meets Piazza del Duomo, commissioning genuine Art Nouveau work rather than simple decoration. Its windows face the cathedral on one side and the glass-vaulted arcade on the other. That arcade cost its architect his life — Giuseppe Mengoni fell from the scaffolding on the entrance arch days before the official opening and never saw the finished building. The bitter red aperitivo that made the family's name is still poured here, in the room the family built to show it off.

stops.title: Camparino in Galleria
stops.caption: The bitter red drink that gave this entire city an evening ritual was invented by the very family who built the room you're standing in.
stops.transcriptText:
The bitter red drink that gave this entire city an evening ritual was invented by the very family who built the room you're standing in.

You're at the northern corner of Piazza del Duomo, exactly where the Galleria Vittorio Emanuele meets the square, and Camparino occupies the ground floor here, its windows facing the cathedral on one side and the glass-vaulted arcade on the other. That arcade itself, designed by the architect Giuseppe Mengoni and built through the 1870s, cost Mengoni his life — he fell from the scaffolding on its entrance arch just days before the official opening, and never saw the finished building.

The craftsmanship is worth pausing on. Gaspare Campari opened his original café nearby in 1867, and in 1915, his son Davide opened this grander companion venue as the bar's new showcase, commissioning genuine Art Nouveau work rather than simple decoration: cabinetwork by Eugenio Quarti, wrought ironwork by Alessandro Mazzucotelli, and a mosaic by the painter Angelo d'Andrea, all still in place around you. The war reached this room too — bombing in 1943 damaged the bar badly, and afterward a family of tailors from Puglia, the Mianis, took over its management and ran it for decades, expanding it in the 1990s into the former state library next door before finally stepping back from it in 2018. These days the bar is regularly ranked among the best in the world, which would probably not have surprised either Campari, father or son — both understood, well before most of their competitors, that atmosphere was half of what they were actually selling.

The whole ritual of the Italian aperitivo says something bigger, standing here: that bitter drink at golden hour, now poured across the world, was effectively manufactured and marketed from this exact corner, and the room built to sell it just happened to end up one of the most beautiful bars in the country.

Step back outside and the Duomo is directly in front of you — worth turning round for, before you carry on into the Galleria itself.

tours.title: Castello Sforzesco
tours.shortDescription: Torn down by an angry mob, and rebuilt almost immediately by the next man in charge.
tours.longDescription: Galeazzo the Second Visconti began the original fortress in 1358 — four walls of a hundred and eighty metres each with a square tower at every corner, finished a decade later. When Visconti rule collapsed in 1447 the short-lived Ambrosian Republic pulled the castle down as a symbol of the family it despised, only for Francesco Sforza to seize power and rebuild it at once, adding the central Torre del Filarete you now face from the main facade. His son Ludovico il Moro later brought Leonardo da Vinci in to decorate its rooms. Seventy metres up, flanked by two thick round towers and a long crenellated wall, it is a building that has effectively started over more than once and shows it.

stops.title: Castello Sforzesco
stops.caption: This fortress has been torn down by an angry mob once already, and rebuilt anyway by the next man in charge.
stops.transcriptText:
This fortress has been torn down by an angry mob once already, and rebuilt anyway by the next man in charge.

You should be standing in front of the main facade, facing the tall brick tower directly ahead — the Torre del Filarete, seventy metres up, flanked by two thick round towers and a long crenellated wall running off in both directions.

This building has effectively started over more than once. Galeazzo the Second Visconti began the original fortress in 1358, four walls of a hundred and eighty metres each with a square tower at every corner, finished a decade later. When Visconti rule collapsed in 1447, the short-lived Ambrosian Republic tore the castle down as a symbol of the family it despised, only for Francesco Sforza to seize power and rebuild it almost immediately, adding the central tower you're looking at now. His son, Ludovico known as il Moro, later brought Leonardo da Vinci in to fresco one of the towers, the Sala delle Asse, with an intricate ceiling of interlacing branches that still survives inside.

By the nineteenth century the castle had degraded into little more than an army barracks, scheduled at one point for demolition, before the architect Luca Beltrami stepped in during the 1890s and rebuilt it as a public institution instead, opening it to the city in 1900. Today its museums span an unusually wide range for one building — archaeology, furniture, musical instruments, ancient Egyptian and prehistoric collections — but the single object most people come for is the Rondanini Pietà, Michelangelo's final sculpture, left unfinished when he died in 1564, still bearing chisel marks from work he never got to finish.

Torn down once, rebuilt twice, nearly lost a third time — and what's inside it now is another genius's work that was never actually completed either.

Field Marshal Radetzky retreated to this very fortress in 1848, from Palazzo Cagnola a few streets away, now home to the boutique Antonia — and Parco Sempione, with the Arco della Pace at its far end, opens up directly behind the castle from here.

tours.title: Colonne di San Lorenzo
tours.shortDescription: Sixteen genuinely Roman columns, dragged here from somewhere else when Milan was still an imperial city.
tours.longDescription: They were salvaged from a second-century temple or bathhouse elsewhere in the city and reassembled here in the fourth century to front what was then a new basilica — recycled masonry, already old by the time anyone set it down again. Look closely and the mismatch shows: this was never purpose-built as a colonnade, and the columns stand over seven metres tall in front of the Basilica of San Lorenzo, with an open piazza running out ahead of them. It is also, most evenings, where a fair portion of Milan sits on the steps with a drink in hand — a Roman ruin doing duty as the city's front porch.

stops.title: Colonne di San Lorenzo
stops.caption: These sixteen columns are properly, genuinely Roman — salvaged from a second-century temple or bathhouse somewhere else in the city, and dragged to this exact spot when Milan was still an important outpost of an empire that was already starting to come apart.
stops.transcriptText:
These sixteen columns are properly, genuinely Roman — salvaged from a second-century temple or bathhouse somewhere else in the city, and dragged to this exact spot when Milan was still an important outpost of an empire that was already starting to come apart.

The colonnade runs along Corso di Porta Ticinese, directly in front of the Basilica of San Lorenzo, with an open piazza stretching out in front of the columns — on most evenings, you'll find a fair portion of Milan sitting on the steps here with a drink in hand.

Notice, first, how mismatched the columns look up close: this wasn't purpose-built as a colonnade, it's recycled Roman masonry, over seven metres tall, reassembled here sometime in the fourth century to front what was then a new basilica, using stone that was already old by the time anyone laid it down again. Count them properly and there's a small surprise: sixteen at ground level, and a seventeenth, miniature and topped with a cross, perched above the arch — local legend says the Devil himself put it there, and nobody's ever bothered correcting the story. The columns nearly didn't survive the sixteenth century either — the Spanish governor Ferrante Gonzaga was pressed to clear them for Philip the Second's ceremonial entry into the city, and declined. And the open square you're standing in is newer than it looks: this whole area stayed dense with housing right up until 1935, and wartime bombing cleared even more of it, leaving the columns standing in far more open space than they ever had in antiquity.

The interesting bit is this: almost none of Roman Milan survived above ground — most of it got quarried, piece by piece, into later churches and walls, the way builders across this city recycled stone for centuries. These columns survived by staying useful: first as a temple, then a colonnade, then a backdrop, and now, most evenings, a very popular place to sit down.

Two thousand years of repurposing, and the columns still haven't been asked to do anything more strenuous than hold up the sky and a fair number of Milanese elbows.

Basilicas Park runs behind the church itself, a quieter green stretch if the piazza's too crowded — worth the walk round if you fancy seeing the columns from the other side.

tours.title: Duomo di Milano
tours.shortDescription: A decision taken in 1386 that would not be finished for nearly six hundred years.
tours.longDescription: Duke Gian Galeazzo Visconti insisted on marble rather than the brick Milan usually built with, and in October 1387 founded the Veneranda Fabbrica specifically to manage the project, recruiting master masons from France and Germany as well as Italy. The marble, pale and faintly pink, came from a quarry near Lake Maggiore and travelled the last stretch by canal. For a century nobody could agree how to finish the tower over the crossing; in the 1480s and 1490s the era's master builders were invited to submit solutions, Leonardo among them, though another design won. The Madonnina went up in 1774 and gave the city a rule that has held for two and a half centuries: nothing should stand taller than her. Thirty-four hundred statues, a hundred and thirty-five spires, and the last bronze door was not hung until 1965.

stops.title: Duomo di Milano
stops.caption: It's 1386, and the Duke of Milan has just made a decision that won't actually be finished for nearly six hundred years.
stops.transcriptText:
It's 1386, and the Duke of Milan has just made a decision that won't actually be finished for nearly six hundred years.

You're facing the west front of the Duomo across the piazza: three enormous bronze doors at street level, a forest of pale marble spires rising above them, and, right at the top of the tallest one, a small gold figure you'd need binoculars to make out properly from down here — the Madonnina.

Start with why this building took so long. Duke Gian Galeazzo Visconti insisted on marble instead of the brick Milan usually built with, and founded an organisation, the Veneranda Fabbrica, in October of 1387 specifically to manage the project — recruiting master masons from France and Germany as well as Italy, which made the site, for a while, one of the most genuinely European building projects anywhere on the continent. The marble itself, pale and faintly pink, came from a quarry near Lake Maggiore and travelled the last stretch into the city by canal, the same waterway that still runs through the Navigli district today.

For a century, nobody could agree how to finish the tower over the crossing, the tiburium, and in the 1480s and 1490s, several of the era's master builders were invited to submit their own solution — Leonardo da Vinci among them, though in the end a different design altogether was chosen. The Madonnina went up in 1774, gilded copper, on the tip of the tallest spire, and gave Milan an unofficial rule that's held for two and a half centuries since: nothing in the city should stand taller than her. When the Pirelli Tower went up taller than the Duomo in the 1960s, the builders solved the problem by mounting a small Madonnina of their own on its roof, keeping the letter of the tradition intact even as they broke it.

Thirty-four hundred statues, another seven hundred figures worked into the stonework, a hundred and thirty-five spires, and the last bronze door wasn't hung until 1965 — which makes this cathedral, in a very real sense, still barely finished.

The roof terraces are open to visitors and let you walk out among the spires at close range, at eye level with details nobody at street level ever sees properly — worth the climb, and the ticket, if you've the time today.

tours.title: ERIS
tours.shortDescription: Café, wine bar or furniture showroom — the honest answer is all three, depending on the hour.
tours.longDescription: The identity crisis is deliberate. ERIS opened in June 2025 on the corner of Via Bartolomeo Eustachi and Via Stoppani, just off the main Porta Venezia streets, laid out less like a café than a modular showroom: the tables you sit at are arranged among furniture and objects that are also genuinely for sale. The name is a joke about scale once you know it — Eris is a dwarf planet out past Pluto, and the room is barely thirty-five square metres, a whole compact universe packed into one corner site. The coffee comes from Nudo, the specialty roaster founded by Nicolò Zorloni, pulled single-origin only, no blends.

stops.title: ERIS
stops.caption: There's a small identity crisis built into this place on purpose: is it a café, a wine bar, or a furniture showroom?
stops.transcriptText:
There's a small identity crisis built into this place on purpose: is it a café, a wine bar, or a furniture showroom? The honest answer is all three, depending on the hour and what you're looking at.

You'll find ERIS at the corner of Via Bartolomeo Eustachi and Via Stoppani, just off the main Porta Venezia streets — opened in June 2025, and laid out less like a conventional café and more like a modular showroom, with the tables you're sitting at arranged among furniture and objects that are also, genuinely, for sale.

The name is a small joke about scale, once you know it: Eris is also a dwarf planet out past Pluto, and this room is barely thirty-five square metres — a whole compact universe packed into one corner site.

Notice what's actually running the kitchen. The coffee comes from Nudo, the specialty roaster founded by Nicolò Zorloni, pulled single-origin only, no blends, through a Slayer machine, and best known alongside a cinnamon roll that's become something of a local fixture. Food runs on a rotating menu of savoury bread pairings rather than a conventional kitchen line, made by the same team behind Rome's Retrobottega, one of that city's more talked-about modern restaurants, brought north to cook for this single Milanese room. A natural wine list of around seventy labels, curated together with Retrobottega's own people, runs alongside both, chosen with the same slightly restless curiosity as everything else on the premises.

Which says something about where Milan's food and design scenes have landed lately: the old boundaries between a café, a bar, and a shop have mostly stopped mattering, and a space like this one exists precisely because nobody insisted it pick a single identity and stick to it.

Half the fun here is not quite knowing whether you'll leave with a coffee, a bottle, or a chair.

Porta Venezia's wider café and aperitivo scene runs for several streets in every direction from here — better wandered than mapped out in advance.

tours.title: Fioraio Bianchi Caffè
tours.shortDescription: Half the room is a florist, and the flowers are the business the café grew out of.
tours.longDescription: The story runs in the opposite direction from the one you would expect. Raimondo Bianchi opened this Via Montebello address in Brera as a flower shop around four decades ago, and the café arrived roughly a decade later, growing up inside the florist rather than the other way round. Both still share the same floor — buckets of stems out front, café tables threaded in among them — and the shopfront functions as a working flower shop first. The food is Italian with a faintly Parisian bistro air, leaning on tradition without being stuck in it, and the menu turns with the seasons much as the buckets outside do.

stops.title: Fioraio Bianchi Caffè
stops.caption: Half of this room is a florist, and the flowers aren't decoration — they're the actual business the café grew out of.
stops.transcriptText:
Half of this room is a florist, and the flowers aren't decoration — they're the actual business the café grew out of.

On Via Montebello, in Brera, the shopfront still functions as a working flower shop first and a café second: buckets of stems out front, café tables threaded in among them, Fioraio Bianchi Caffè's two businesses genuinely sharing the same floor.

The story runs in the opposite direction from what you'd expect. Raimondo Bianchi opened this as a florist around four decades ago, and the café side only arrived roughly a decade later, growing up inside the flower shop rather than the other way round — a slightly Parisian-feeling bistro serving Italian food that leans on tradition without being stuck in it, a menu that changes with the seasons the same way the buckets out front do. On any given week that might mean a carnaroli risotto with quail, hand-made Tuscan cenci pastries paired with cod, or a tuna tartare sharpened with citrus, alongside a Mont Blanc for pudding if the season's right for it. The business has since expanded into private dinners and events, but the floral laboratory, and Bianchi's own eye for arranging it, stays the anchor of the whole place.

Which is really the charm of it: most café-and-florist combinations treat the flowers as set dressing for the food. Here it's the food that got added, decades in, to a flower shop that didn't especially need the help. The working laboratorio floreale still sits at the front of the room rather than tucked away out of sight, so the same hands assembling a table centrepiece for tonight's private dinner are visible from your seat, cutting stems between orders — the flower shop was never asked to make way for the restaurant it grew into, and it clearly hasn't.

You'll leave smelling faintly of something you didn't order, which is rather the point.

Brera's gallery streets fan out in every direction from here — the Pinacoteca is a short walk north, if today's wandering has a few more minutes left in it.

tours.title: Fondazione Luigi Rovati
tours.shortDescription: Objects twenty-seven centuries apart, deliberately placed side by side rather than kept in separate rooms.
tours.longDescription: The palazzo on Corso Venezia had a lavish 1960s makeover by the decorator Filippo Perego, in the gilded, colour-saturated taste then fashionable among Milan's bourgeoisie, and much of that survives upstairs. Below it the architect Mario Cucinella dug an entirely new level more than forty-five feet down, stabilising the old foundations with piling and lining the new rooms in pietraforte, a dark stone worked into curving vaulted chambers that owe more to Etruscan tombs than to any modern gallery. The collection is arranged so the oldest and newest pieces sit together on purpose — the argument being that twenty-seven centuries is not as long a gap as a museum floor plan usually implies.

stops.title: Fondazione Luigi Rovati
stops.caption: The oldest object in this museum is about twenty-seven centuries old.
stops.transcriptText:
The oldest object in this museum is about twenty-seven centuries old. The newest was made within living memory, and the whole building is arranged so the two of them sit side by side, deliberately, rather than kept in separate rooms.

A Corso Venezia palazzo houses the museum, its ground floor still recognisably a grand nineteenth-century Milanese townhouse, before a staircase takes you down into something else entirely underground.

Start with the building's own layered history. The palazzo got a lavish makeover in the 1960s by the decorator Filippo Perego, in the bold, gilded, colour-saturated taste fashionable among Milan's bourgeoisie at the time, and much of that survives on the upper floors. Below it, the architect Mario Cucinella dug an entirely new level more than forty-five feet down, stabilising the old foundations with piling and lining the new rooms in pietraforte, a dark stone hauled up from Florence, to create a space that's kept deliberately dim and cave-like. That's where the museum's real argument gets made: around two hundred and fifty objects, Etruscan bronzes and vessels set beside twentieth-century work by artists like Lucio Fontana and Luigi Ontani, arranged by theme rather than by century. The single piece most visitors remember afterwards is the Cernuschi Warrior, a votive Etruscan bronze figure staged, deliberately, in its own case as something close to the museum's unofficial symbol. The garden at the back opens onto the Giardini Pubblici Indro Montanelli next door, so the underground galleries you've just walked through end, unexpectedly, at daylight and trees.

Which is really the point of digging downward instead of building up: walking through this museum means physically descending toward antiquity, so the mixing of eras isn't just a curatorial trick on the wall labels, it's built into the floor plan itself. The whole thing exists because of one man, Luigi Rovati, a physician who built the pharmaceutical company Rottapharm. He died in 2019, and the museum opened three years later, in 2022, carrying his name.

Most museums ask you to walk forward through time. This one asks you to walk down into it instead.

Corso Venezia itself is lined with nineteenth-century palazzi for several blocks in both directions, if you fancy seeing what this one looked like before it grew a basement.

tours.title: Fondazione Prada
tours.shortDescription: A century-old distillery, seven original buildings kept, and one of them clad floor to roof in real gold.
tours.longDescription: Rather than demolish the industrial complex at Largo Isarco, Rem Koolhaas and OMA kept seven of its original buildings and added three new ones — a cinema, a gallery and a tower — when the foundation opened in 2015. The gold building, nicknamed the Haunted House, is genuinely clad in twenty-four-karat gold leaf on every surface except the windows; Koolhaas has described the decision as almost an afterthought and pointed out that gold leaf is cheaper than most people assume. Nowhere on the site does old architecture sit quietly beside new — the two were built to blur into each other. Bar Luce, designed by Wes Anderson, is open to anyone, ticket or not.

stops.title: Fondazione Prada
stops.caption: This whole complex used to distil spirits. These days it exhibits art, and one of the buildings on site is wrapped, floor to roof, in real gold.
stops.transcriptText:
This whole complex used to distil spirits. These days it exhibits art, and one of the buildings on site is wrapped, floor to roof, in real gold.

Largo Isarco, south of the centre, is where a former distillery now houses Fondazione Prada — a cluster of low brick warehouses and silos, with one particular building, gold from top to bottom, more or less impossible to miss among the rest.

Consider what actually happened here. The site is a century-old industrial complex, and rather than demolish it, the architect Rem Koolhaas and his studio, OMA, kept seven of the original buildings and added three new ones — a cinema, a gallery, and a tower — when the foundation opened in 2015. The gold building, nicknamed the Haunted House, is genuinely clad in twenty-four-karat gold leaf, every surface except the windows. Koolhaas has described the decision as almost an afterthought, and pointed out that gold leaf actually worked out cheaper than the marble or paint he'd first considered, with the added benefit that reflected gold light spills into the whole courtyard around it.

The bar on site, Bar Luce, was designed by the film director Wes Anderson, styled after 1950s and 60s Italian pop culture and the neorealist cinema of the period — and its arched ceiling is a deliberate miniature echo of the vaulted glass roof over the Galleria Vittorio Emanuele in the city centre, shrunk down to café scale. A second building, the sixty-metre Torre, opened three years after the rest of the site and holds six floors of the permanent collection, works spanning the 1960s to today by artists including Carsten Höller, Jeff Koons, and Damien Hirst, with a panoramic lift running through the middle of it. At the top, a restaurant looks out over the whole city from a triangular terrace, furnished in deliberate homage to the original Four Seasons dining room in New York.

A gold-clad former factory next to a converted grain silo next to a tiny cinema-scaled version of Milan's grandest arcade: nowhere on this site does old architecture sit quietly next to new. Koolhaas built them to blur into each other instead.

Bar Luce is open to anyone, not just ticket-holders, and worth a coffee even if you've no time for the exhibitions today — ask for a seat under the arched ceiling and see if the Galleria echo lands.

tours.title: Fortela Store Milano
tours.shortDescription: A century-old upholstery workshop where nobody painted over the ceiling frescoes when the clothes moved in.
tours.longDescription: Fortela's Milan store fills three hundred square metres in the Liberty district near Porta Venezia, and a good deal of the room is not for sale. Alessandro Squarzi started as a shop assistant in 1992, spent years as a sought-after menswear consultant, and founded the label in 2015; Alessia Giacobino joined five years later to lead the women's side. Together they have built it around Italian-made clothing and design objects in natural fibres — wool, cotton, linen, hemp, cashmere — drawn from the pair's own travels. Squarzi is a serious collector of vintage fabric, which turns up directly in the signature pieces, and the original frescoes overhead were left exactly where they were.

stops.title: Fortela Store Milano
stops.caption: This was an upholstery workshop a century ago, and the ceiling frescoes are original — nobody painted over them when the clothes moved in.
stops.transcriptText:
This was an upholstery workshop a century ago, and the ceiling frescoes are original — nobody painted over them when the clothes moved in.

In the Liberty district near Porta Venezia, Fortela's Milan store fills a three-hundred-square-metre space that still carries plenty of traces of its working past, alongside everything the brand has added since.

Notice how much of the room isn't actually for sale. Alessandro Squarzi started out as a shop assistant back in 1992, then spent years as a sought-after menswear consultant before founding Fortela in 2015; Alessia Giacobino joined five years later to lead the women's side, and together they've built a label around Italian-made clothing and design objects in natural fibres — wool, cotton, linen, hemp, cashmere — inspired by the pair's own travels. Squarzi is also known as a serious collector of vintage fabric, which shows up directly in signature pieces like the Bruce duffle coat, the Pences trouser, and cycle jackets cut from Japanese selvedge denim. This particular shop, their third and newest, opened in June 2025 during Men's Fashion Week, restored to keep the original frescoes, herringbone Wengé flooring, Portoro marble, and burnished brass fittings intact rather than stripped out. Vintage furniture and nineteen-seventies objects, picked up on those same travels, sit among the clothing rails, and there's a customer bar with a fireplace lounge built in, clearly meant for lingering rather than a quick transaction.

Which is really the trick of a shop like this: it's built to feel like somebody's well-travelled living room rather than a retail floor, so the clothes end up almost secondary to the sense that you've been invited somewhere private. It helps that everything on the rails is made in Italy rather than sourced abroad and rebranded, which keeps that living-room feeling honest — nothing here is standing in for something it isn't.

Nothing here is trying to move you through quickly. The fireplace alone tells you that.

Porta Venezia's wider Liberty-style architecture, ornate ironwork and floral facades from the same turn-of-the-century period as this building, rewards a slow walk in any direction from here.

tours.title: Galleria Vittorio Emanuele II
tours.shortDescription: Put your heel on the bull and spin three times — clockwise, or legend says you get the opposite of luck.
tours.longDescription: Nobody knows where the tradition started, but generations of visitors have worn a visible dip into the mosaic floor of the central octagon doing exactly what you would expect, and the wear has forced repeated restoration. The bull is Turin's heraldic emblem, one of four Italian cities set into the floor where the two glass-vaulted arcades cross. Giuseppe Mengoni designed the arcade between 1865 and 1877, four glass-and-iron vaults meeting under a central dome, built to declare a newly unified country rather than merely a prosperous city. Mengoni fell from the scaffolding on the entrance arch days before the opening and never saw it finished.

stops.title: Galleria Vittorio Emanuele II
stops.caption: Put your right heel on the bull's groin and spin three times, clockwise.
stops.transcriptText:
Put your right heel on the bull's groin and spin three times, clockwise. Get the direction wrong, and legend has it you get the opposite of luck.

You're standing in the central octagon of the Galleria, where its two glass-vaulted arcades cross — look down, and the mosaic floor beneath you shows the coats of arms of four Italian cities, one of them a bull, rearing up on its hind legs.

Start with the ritual, since you've probably already seen someone doing it. Nobody actually knows where the tradition started, but generations of visitors have worn a visible dip into the mosaic doing exactly what you'd expect: heel down, three turns, hope for luck. The wear got bad enough that the floor's needed repeated restoration over the years, purely from the sheer volume of tourists queuing to grind their heel into a nineteenth-century artwork. The bull itself is Turin's heraldic symbol, one of four city crests laid into the octagon floor alongside Milan's own, Rome's, and Florence's — a small, permanent reminder that this arcade was always meant to represent the whole newly unified country, not just this city.

Above you, the engineering is doing more work than it lets on. Giuseppe Mengoni designed the arcade between 1865 and 1877, four glass-and-iron vaults meeting under a central dome, the tie-rods actually holding it up hidden inside the walls so the ironwork above reads as pure, weightless decoration — which is presumably why Milanese have called it il salotto di Milano, the city's drawing room, for as long as anyone can remember.

And here's the thing worth knowing, standing at the exact centre of it: this building is also home to Italy's oldest bookshop. Libreria Bocca, tucked into a fifty-square-metre unit just off this octagon, has been trading books since 1775, run by the same family for generations. A shopping arcade built to show off the new nation's ambitions, still doing exactly that job a century and a half later, just with a slightly wobblier floor.

Most people spin on the bull and move straight on to the shopfronts. Very few notice they've just walked past the oldest bookshop in the country to get there.

Libreria Bocca is worth finding properly before you leave the Galleria — ask any shopkeeper nearby to point you to it, and take a proper look at what's on the shelves rather than just the doorway.

tours.title: Gelateria Umberto 1934 Milano
tours.shortDescription: A twenty-seven-year-old from near Naples opened here in 1934, in a city that did not yet know what proper gelato tasted like.
tours.longDescription: Umberto learned the craft in Naples before moving north and opening this corner shop on Piazza Cinque Giornate, building a reputation on ingredients that cut no corners: real lemons in the lemon, a proper egg custard base for the crema, nothing shipped in pre-mixed. It closed only briefly during the war, reopened, and has run continuously since 1945 — the same Art Deco-era counter and weathered wooden booths still doing the work, with wicker tables set out on the pavement for anyone who would rather sit. In more than ninety years of business it has never needed to reinvent itself, which in this city counts as a position.

stops.title: Gelateria Umberto 1934 Milano
stops.caption: It's 1934, and a twenty-seven-year-old from Pozzuoli, near Naples, has just opened a gelato shop in a city that doesn't yet fully know what proper gelato tastes like.
stops.transcriptText:
It's 1934, and a twenty-seven-year-old from Pozzuoli, near Naples, has just opened a gelato shop in a city that doesn't yet fully know what proper gelato tastes like.

Gelateria Umberto sits on Piazza Cinque Giornate, a straightforward corner shopfront that hasn't needed to reinvent itself in over ninety years of business.

Start with the man himself. Umberto learned the craft in Naples before moving north and opening this shop in 1934, building a reputation on ingredients that weren't cutting any corners: real lemons in the lemon flavour, a proper egg custard base for the crema, nothing shipped in pre-mixed. The shop closed only briefly during the war, then reopened and has run continuously since 1945, the same Art Deco-era counter and weathered wooden booths still doing the work, with wicker tables set out on the pavement for anyone who'd rather sit outside. It's changed hands twice since Umberto's day — first to his daughter Cesira and son-in-law Elio, then to grandson Stefano — and each generation has kept the same policy: a short, seasonal flavour list, made in small batches, with no exceptions made for convenience. These days it's particularly known for its affogato al caffè, a scoop of that same gelato drowned in hot espresso at the table, and for a rotating pair of specialties — a deep, dark crema caramellata and, in warmer months, a pink grapefruit sorbet sharp enough to cut through the heat.

Which is a slightly unusual way to run a food business for ninety years: most places expand their menu as they grow more established. This one has mostly done the opposite, narrowing and refining rather than adding, on the theory that fewer things done properly beat a long list done adequately.

Three generations in, and the flavour list is still short enough to read in one breath.

The piazza itself is named for the Five Days of Milan, the 1848 uprising against Austrian rule — take a look at the monument in the square before you settle down with your gelato.

tours.title: Giacomo Bistrot
tours.shortDescription: A dining room designed by the heir to one of the most theatrical interior stylists of his generation.
tours.longDescription: Roberto Peregalli trained under Renzo Mongiardino and later carried his work forward — and Mongiardino himself laid down this room's antique French bistro look decades before Peregalli inherited it. The name runs back further still: Giacomo Bulleri, a Tuscan who started as a dishwasher in Turin in 1936, opened the original Trattoria da Giacomo on Via Donizetti in 1958 and moved the whole operation to this Via Sottocorno corner in 1989. The street is calm and residential, a short walk from the main shopping district, and the dim, richly layered room gives no hint that it belongs to a group of eleven restaurants.

stops.title: Giacomo Bistrot
stops.caption: The room you're sitting in was designed by Roberto Peregalli, the decorator who trained under, and later carried forward, Renzo Mongiardino — one of the most theatrical, richly layered interior stylists of his generation, and the man who first set this whole look decades before Peregalli inherited it.
stops.transcriptText:
The room you're sitting in was designed by Roberto Peregalli, the decorator who trained under, and later carried forward, Renzo Mongiardino — one of the most theatrical, richly layered interior stylists of his generation, and the man who first set this whole look decades before Peregalli inherited it.

Via Sottocorno, a relatively calm residential street a short walk from the main shopping district, is where you'll find Giacomo Bistrot on the corner, its dim, richly decorated dining room not looking remotely like it belongs to a group of eleven restaurants.

Consider how far back the name actually runs. Giacomo Bulleri, a Tuscan who started as a dishwasher in Turin in 1936, opened the original Trattoria da Giacomo on Via Donizetti in 1958, then relocated the whole operation to this Sottocorno address in 1989, which is when Mongiardino laid down the antique French bistrot tables, the folding screen, the salvaged paintings — the design language Peregalli later extended rather than replaced. The kitchen leans Tuscan and Milanese at its core, a saffron risotto and a cotoletta alla Milanese anchoring a menu that also runs to oysters, champagne, and foie gras in a properly French-bistrot register. That cultural following the room built around 2015, the kind people specifically arranged evenings around, quietly faded by 2017. A family of investors bought in as partners in 2019, then took full ownership in 2023, and rather than modernise the place into something more generic, they built outward from it instead — the group now runs eleven locations across Milan, Florence, and the Tuscan coast, with roughly two hundred staff, while insisting the original design language stays the template for every new room they open.

Which is a fairly unusual growth strategy: most hospitality groups scale by simplifying, stripping out whatever's expensive or particular about the original. This one scaled by protecting the one thing that nearly closed it down.

You're sitting, essentially, in the room the whole company was built to preserve rather than replace.

Via Sottocorno itself stays noticeably quieter than the shopping streets just north of here — worth a slow walk if you want to see this end of the fashion district without the crowds.

tours.title: Langosteria Montenapoleone
tours.shortDescription: Three floors up inside a former bank, now a fashion house, decorated throughout with hot-air balloons.
tours.longDescription: Palazzo Fendi is a nineteen-thirties Rationalist building by the Milanese architect Emilio Lancia, and Langosteria occupies its top three floors, reached by lift from the boutique below in the middle of the Quadrilatero della Moda. Fendi's own architecture department handled the interiors: Venetian blinds, travertine and walnut, brass fittings, Murano glass, and that recurring balloon motif, all meant to suggest slow romantic travel rather than a fashion-house restaurant. The kitchen has humbler roots than the address implies — the original Langosteria began as a small seafood restaurant, and the cooking here still runs on the quality of what arrives that morning rather than on elaboration.

stops.title: Langosteria Montenapoleone
stops.caption: Three floors up, inside a nineteen-thirties building that used to be a bank and is now a fashion house, and the decorative theme running through the dining room is, oddly, hot-air balloons.
stops.transcriptText:
Three floors up, inside a nineteen-thirties building that used to be a bank and is now a fashion house, and the decorative theme running through the dining room is, oddly, hot-air balloons.

Langosteria Montenapoleone occupies the top three floors of Palazzo Fendi, right in the middle of the Quadrilatero della Moda, reached by lift from the boutique on the ground floor below.

Notice the building before you notice the menu. Palazzo Fendi is a nineteen-thirties Rationalist building designed by the Milanese architect Emilio Lancia, recently converted, and Fendi's own architecture department handled the interiors up here: Venetian blinds, travertine and walnut surfaces, brass fittings, Murano-glass lighting, and that recurring hot-air-balloon motif, all meant to suggest slow, romantic travel rather than a fashion-house restaurant. The kitchen itself has humbler roots. Enrico Buonocore, then thirty-one, opened the original address on Via Savona, a scruffier industrial street on the other side of the city, in 2007, built entirely around very good seafood treated simply — lobster above everything else, alongside dishes like charcoal-grilled black grouper and Galician turbot. What began as that one room has since spread into a bistrot, a café, outposts on the Ligurian coast and in Paris, and now this Montenapoleone address, all still answering, in one way or another, to the original kitchen on Via Savona.

Which says something about how this brand's grown: the same appetite for a properly cooked piece of fish that started on an industrial side street now operates three floors above one of the most expensive shopping streets in Europe, considerably better dressed but not actually different in substance. There's a London opening reportedly on the way too, alongside a return to Sardinia — which would put a kitchen that began on a scruffy industrial street on nodding terms with two of Europe's more expensive postcodes at once.

The lobster hasn't changed. Only the view from the table has.

Via Montenapoleone and the rest of the Quadrilatero stretch out below you in every direction — step back down to street level and walk it properly before or after the meal.

tours.title: Libreria Bocca
tours.shortDescription: Two hundred and fifty years of bookselling, in a building where the rents are among the highest in Europe.
tours.longDescription: The Bocca brothers came from Turin and opened the shop in 1775. It stayed in Bocca hands until 1951 before passing eventually to Giacomo Lodetti, who had spent years distributing books nationally and took it over outright in 1979 — old enough, by either reckoning of the handover, to be generally recognised as Italy's oldest still-operating bookshop. Under Lodetti the stock turned hard toward rare books and artists' editions. What survives is a fifty-square-metre unit tucked into the Galleria's arcade, easy to miss among the flagship fashion stores unless you already know it is there, which is the more remarkable half of the story.

stops.title: Libreria Bocca
stops.caption: This shop has been trading books from the same family name, on and off, for two hundred and fifty years — inside a building where retail rents now rank among the highest in Europe.
stops.transcriptText:
This shop has been trading books from the same family name, on and off, for two hundred and fifty years — inside a building where retail rents now rank among the highest in Europe.

Look for a fifty-square-metre unit tucked into the Galleria's arcade — easy enough to miss among the flagship fashion stores unless you already know Libreria Bocca is there.

Start with the family behind the name, or rather the two families. The Bocca brothers, originally from Turin, opened the shop in 1775, and it stayed in Bocca hands until 1951, before passing eventually to Giacomo Lodetti, who'd spent years distributing books nationally and took the shop over outright in 1979 — old enough at that point, either way you count the handover, that it's generally recognised as Italy's oldest still-operating bookshop. Under Lodetti the stock pivoted hard toward rare books, artist's editions, and exhibition catalogues, reportedly sparked by customers repeatedly asking for one specific photography catalogue he didn't yet stock; his own catalogue history includes works by Gioberti, Silvio Pellico, Segantini, Nietzsche, and Freud. His children, Giorgio and Monica, have run the shop together since 2010, and Giorgio published a full history of the business in 2023, documenting two and a half centuries of Milanese bookselling in one volume.

Here's the thing worth knowing, standing in front of a shop this size: rents in this arcade are now among the highest anywhere in Europe, driven up by the luxury fashion houses that fill most of the other units. A fifty-square-metre bookshop, run for two and a half centuries by one family and its successors, is a genuine holdout in that economy, not a quaint leftover nobody's bothered to modernise.

This shop has outlasted an empire, a kingdom, and a republic, each of which in turn governed the building around it. The rent pressure from the fashion house next door is, comparatively, a minor threat.

Step inside properly rather than just glancing through the window — the first editions and the artwork on the walls reward a slower look than most Galleria shopfronts ask for.

tours.title: Locanda Perbellini Bistrot Milano
tours.shortDescription: The two Michelin stars on the door were earned two hundred kilometres away, in Verona.
tours.longDescription: Giancarlo Perbellini runs his two-starred flagship down in Verona and opened this Milan address in 2018 as something deliberately looser: cicchetti and tapas-style small plates built for grazing and easy sharing rather than a formal tasting menu. The room seats thirty-eight, finished in copper, slate and wenge wood by the architect Silvia Bettini, with a frosted glass wall keeping Via della Moscova at a polite distance and an open counter for anyone who wants to watch the kitchen work. It occupies a Brera-Moscova corner that housed a different restaurant altogether before this one moved in.

stops.title: Locanda Perbellini Bistrot Milano
stops.caption: The chef whose name is on the door has two Michelin stars — earned two hundred kilometres away, in Verona, not here.
stops.transcriptText:
The chef whose name is on the door has two Michelin stars — earned two hundred kilometres away, in Verona, not here.

Locanda Perbellini Bistrot occupies a corner on Via della Moscova, in the Brera-Moscova district, in a space that used to house a different restaurant altogether before this one moved in.

Notice how deliberately relaxed the format is, given the name attached to it. Giancarlo Perbellini runs his two-starred flagship restaurant down in Verona, and opened this Milan address back in 2018 as something looser: cicchetti and tapas-style small plates, built for grazing and easy sharing rather than a formal tasting menu, in a thirty-eight-seat room finished in copper, slate, and wenge wood by the architect Silvia Bettini, with a frosted glass wall keeping the street outside at a polite distance and an open counter facing the kitchen for anyone who wants to watch the antipasti and desserts being finished. Day-to-day, the kitchen is entrusted to a younger chef, Michael Pozzi, who trained under Federico Zonta at a well-regarded restaurant in Verona before taking this one on himself. A handful of dishes travel up from Verona directly — the millefoglie, one of Perbellini's best-known desserts, chief among them — alongside a risi e bisi served two ways, hot and cold in the same bowl, and a wine list that mixes natural and conventional bottles without much ceremony, priced by the glass and served without a sommelier hovering over the choice.

Which is really the interesting bit about a place like this: it's a two-Michelin-star chef deliberately lending his technique and his name to the most informal end of the business, the aperitivo-adjacent bistrot format that doesn't usually get that level of kitchen behind it. Most fine-dining chefs open a second flagship. This one opened somewhere you could drop in on a Tuesday without booking weeks ahead.

The stars are in Verona. The technique, rather usefully, travelled to Milan without them.

Via della Moscova and the surrounding Brera streets are dense with similar small kitchens — worth continuing the crawl if tonight doesn't need to end at one table.

tours.title: Maison Senato
tours.shortDescription: Six front doors, six completely different apartments, and no sign at street level saying you can stay here.
tours.longDescription: Via Senato sits a few streets back from Via Montenapoleone and Via della Spiga and gives nothing away — there is no lobby in the conventional sense and no room design repeated six times over. Each of the six residences has its own layout, its own furnishings and its own marble bathroom, built more like a private flat than a hotel suite. Five run to somewhere between a hundred and fifty and a hundred and seventy square metres apiece, each with a twenty-square-metre balcony of its own; the sixth is a two-floor penthouse with a hundred-and-forty-five-square-metre terrace and a private pool. What has been deliberately left out is most of what a hotel usually is.

stops.title: Maison Senato
stops.caption: There are only six front doors in this entire building, and each one opens onto a completely different apartment.
stops.transcriptText:
There are only six front doors in this entire building, and each one opens onto a completely different apartment.

Via Senato, a few streets back from Via Montenapoleone and Via della Spiga, gives nothing away at street level — no sign marks Maison Senato out as somewhere you could actually stay the night.

Consider what's been deliberately left out here. There's no lobby in the conventional sense, no uniform room design repeated six times over — each of the six residences has its own layout, its own furnishings, its own marble bathroom, built more like a private flat than a hotel suite. Five of them run somewhere around a hundred and fifty to a hundred and seventy square metres apiece, each with its own twenty-square-metre balcony, and the sixth is a two-floor penthouse with a hundred-and-forty-five-square-metre terrace and a private pool of its own. The whole address opened in April 2025, restored inside a historic palazzo by the studio Locatelli Partners under what they call an inhabitable-artwork concept, and it's owned not by a hotel chain but by Diomede, part of the Del Bono family's pharmaceutical group, Mediolanum Farmaceutici — a private fortune, in other words, quietly bankrolling somewhere to stay rather than something to sell. What you do get is the service you'd expect from a proper hotel anyway: round-the-clock concierge, a small spa, a private courtyard tucked behind the facade, just without any of the scale or signage that usually comes with it.

Which is really the boutique-hotel idea taken to its logical end point: rather than build a small hotel, build no hotel at all, just six genuinely private apartments with a concierge attached, for people who'd rather not be easy to find on a map.

You could walk past this building a dozen times and never clock that anyone's staying inside it.

Via della Spiga and Via Montenapoleone are both a short walk from here, if the city's most expensive shop windows are part of today's plan.

tours.title: Mandarin Oriental
tours.shortDescription: Four eighteenth-century buildings knocked together around one courtyard, with a swimming pool hidden underneath.
tours.longDescription: Via Andegari is quiet and a few minutes from La Scala, and the facade gives almost nothing away about the scale of what is arranged behind it. Four separate eighteenth-century structures were restored and joined around a single open courtyard when the hotel opened in 2015, and the interior designers Antonio Citterio and Patricia Viel made a deliberate choice not to blend the two eras quietly together — an oriental-inflected contemporary aesthetic, nodding to the brand's Hong Kong origins, sits directly inside the historic shell. Contrast rather than imitation, which is the harder of the two to bring off.

stops.title: Mandarin Oriental
stops.caption: Four separate eighteenth-century buildings, knocked together around one shared courtyard, and from the street you'd never guess there's a swimming pool tucked somewhere underneath all of it.
stops.transcriptText:
Four separate eighteenth-century buildings, knocked together around one shared courtyard, and from the street you'd never guess there's a swimming pool tucked somewhere underneath all of it.

Via Andegari is a quiet street just a few minutes from La Scala, and the Mandarin Oriental's facade here gives almost nothing away about the scale of what's arranged behind it.

Start with the basic trick of the building. Four separate eighteenth-century structures were restored and joined around a single open courtyard when the hotel opened in 2015, and the interior designers, Antonio Citterio and Patricia Viel, made a deliberate choice not to blend the two eras quietly together. Instead, an oriental-inflected, distinctly contemporary aesthetic — a nod to the brand's origins in Hong Kong — sits directly inside the historic shell, contrast rather than imitation. The courtyard itself, recently reworked as what the hotel calls the Mandarin Garden, is built around a cocktail menu tracing the stages of Around the World in Eighty Days, with fans of Licuala Grandis palm running through as a recurring botanical motif. Behind it, the hotel holds seventy-three rooms and thirty-one suites, a spa with its own pool below ground, the two-Michelin-starred Seta restaurant under chef Antonio Guida, and a bar that's become a fixture for people who aren't actually staying the night.

Which is really the more interesting decision than it first sounds: most hotels dropped into historic European buildings try to soften a foreign design language until it barely shows. This one leans into the friction instead, letting two very different traditions sit inside the same four walls without pretending to agree. It's the same instinct that runs through the food: at Seta, chef Antonio Guida sets his kitchen out in full view of the dining room, cooking closer to Mediterranean and Asian influences than strict Milanese tradition, which is really the same friction as the building itself, just plated rather than built.

Nothing about the eighteenth-century facade prepares you for what's arranged behind it.

La Scala is a two-minute walk from the door — take the short detour even if opera's not on tonight, just to see the square the hotel is quietly hiding behind.

tours.title: Massimo Alba
tours.shortDescription: A logo small enough that you might not notice it is there at all.
tours.longDescription: Massimo Alba spent years as creative director at Malo and Agnona, and worked with Ballantyne too, building a reputation dressing other people's labels in sharp formal tailoring before launching his own line in 2006 in New York. The branding stayed deliberately quiet — a small lowercase logo, easy to miss — and the clothes went in the opposite direction from his earlier work, stripping the stiffness out of classic tailored pieces in favour of something looser. The Milan showroom doubles as the brand's headquarters: a run of interconnected rooms split between the men's and women's collections rather than a single conventional shopfront.

stops.title: Massimo Alba
stops.caption: The logo on these clothes is deliberately small enough that you might not clock it's there at all.
stops.transcriptText:
The logo on these clothes is deliberately small enough that you might not clock it's there at all.

Massimo Alba's Milan showroom doubles as the brand's headquarters, a run of interconnected rooms split between the men's and women's collections rather than a single conventional shopfront.

Consider the route the designer took to get here. Massimo Alba spent years as creative director at Malo and Agnona, and worked with Ballantyne too, building a reputation dressing other people's labels in sharp, formal tailoring, before launching his own eponymous line in 2006 in New York. The branding stayed deliberately quiet — a small lowercase logo, easy to miss — and the clothes themselves went in the opposite direction from his earlier work: stripping the stiffness and severity out of classic tailored pieces, jackets and coats included, aiming for what the brand calls a decontracté aesthetic, built around a recurring signature fabric the label calls baby corduroy. The quiet approach hasn't kept the clothes off the radar entirely — Daniel Craig wore Massimo Alba as James Bond in No Time to Die, corduroy trousers and a long corduroy duster among them, reportedly pieces the actor already owned and wore personally before the production settled on the label. Recent capsule collaborations with Valextra and the eyewear house Garrett Leight California have kept that quiet visibility ticking along without the brand ever raising its own volume. The label has stayed small on purpose too, with only five monobrand boutiques anywhere in Italy, in Milan, Rome, Courmayeur, Sestri Levante, and Forte dei Marmi — each a place with its own specific character rather than the usual international flagship-city rollout.

Which says something about the designer's own instincts: having spent a career making other people's clothes formal and precise, he built his own label around undoing exactly that, one small, specific address at a time.

Even the shop itself refuses to shout about what's inside it.

Ask to see through to the far rooms if you've only browsed the front of the showroom — the interconnected layout rewards wandering further back than most visitors bother to go.

tours.title: Abbazia di Mirasole
tours.shortDescription: In 1344 the forty-four brothers here were running a textile business — and supplying timber to a cathedral just starting to go up.
tours.longDescription: The abbey began in the twelfth and early thirteenth centuries as a rural estate of the Umiliati, a religious order that combined prayer with serious manual labour, mostly wool and textile production, and was formally recognised by Pope Innocent the Third in 1201. By 1344 the community numbered forty-four and ran a genuine agricultural economy — including a contract to supply timber to the Duomo, eight miles north and barely begun. What survives is a walled cluster of brick cloisters and a church standing in open farmland south of Milan, in fields that still surround it much as they did eight centuries ago.

stops.title: Abbazia di Mirasole
stops.caption: It's 1344, and forty-four monks and lay brothers here are running what amounts to a small textile business — among their contracts, a deal to supply timber to a cathedral that's just started going up in the city, eight miles north of here.
stops.transcriptText:
It's 1344, and forty-four monks and lay brothers here are running what amounts to a small textile business — among their contracts, a deal to supply timber to a cathedral that's just started going up in the city, eight miles north of here.

Abbazia di Mirasole sits well outside the centre, in open farmland south of Milan, a walled cluster of brick cloisters and a church rising out of fields that still surround it much as they did eight centuries ago.

Consider what kind of monastery this actually was. It began, in the twelfth and early thirteenth centuries, as a rural estate of the Umiliati, a religious order that combined prayer with serious manual labour, mostly wool and textile production, and was formally recognised by Pope Innocent the Third in 1201. By 1344 the community numbered forty-four, running a genuine agricultural economy that included that timber contract for the Duomo's builders — this abbey helped construct the cathedral you may already have visited today, or will later. The good years didn't last. Plague-era decline pushed the abbey toward leasing out its land, it became a commenda, a benefice held without any real active governance, in 1482, and the Umiliati order itself was dissolved outright in 1571, after one of its members was implicated in a failed attempt on the life of Archbishop Charles Borromeo.

What followed was five centuries of the building being handed to whoever needed it most: a Swiss college from 1582, then Napoleon's administration, which transferred it to Milan's main hospital in 1797. Today it's run by that same hospital's foundation, with the complex itself managed since 2016 by a charity supporting homeless and vulnerable people. Walk through what survives and you'll find the abbey church, dedicated to Santa Maria Assunta, still holding a pair of fourteenth-century terracotta reliefs either side of its rose window, and a frescoed vault above the altar showing the four Evangelists; beyond it, the cloister, the old refectory, and the chapter room are all open to wander through, arranged exactly as the Umiliati left them.

An abbey that helped build one of the world's most famous cathedrals has spent the centuries since being quietly repurposed for whoever in the city needed it next.

The farmland around the abbey is part of the Parco Agricolo Sud Milano, open for walking well beyond the abbey walls — worth the wander if today's already taken you as far as the Duomo it once helped supply.

tours.title: Cimitero Monumentale
tours.shortDescription: A cemetery with its own hall of fame, and Italy's most famous novelist at the exact centre of it.
tours.longDescription: It opened in 1866 to gather Milan's scattered burial grounds onto one site, designed by Carlo Maciachini, with the Famedio built as a neo-medieval hall of marble and stone at the entrance to hold the tombs of the city's most distinguished citizens. Alessandro Manzoni was given the central position; the dancer Carla Fracci only recently became the first woman granted a place inside. Walk further in and the range of styles gets genuinely wide, from full-scale replicas of classical temples to the stark BBPR memorial to Milan's Nazi-deportation victims. It is a cemetery that has been used, continuously and rather competitively, as a place to make an argument about who mattered.

stops.title: Cimitero Monumentale
stops.caption: This cemetery has its own hall of fame, and the most famous writer in Italian history is buried at the exact centre of it.
stops.transcriptText:
This cemetery has its own hall of fame, and the most famous writer in Italian history is buried at the exact centre of it.

The Famedio, the grand marble hall just inside the main gate, is the obvious place to start — behind it, row after row of increasingly elaborate family tombs stretch out across the grounds beyond.

Begin with the cemetery itself. It opened in 1866, designed by the architect Carlo Maciachini to gather Milan's various scattered burial grounds into one site, with the Famedio built as a neo-medieval hall of marble and stone at the entrance, holding the tombs of the city's most distinguished citizens — the novelist Alessandro Manzoni given the central position, and the dancer Carla Fracci only recently becoming the first woman granted a place inside it. Walk further into the grounds and the range of styles gets genuinely wide: full-scale replicas of Greek temples, an obelisk copied from Trajan's Column in Rome, and tombs designed by some of the era's most significant names, the sculptor Adolfo Wildt and the architect Gio Ponti among them, each commissioned by one of Milan's great industrial families competing, one last time, in stone. In 1876, the cemetery's crematorium became the first in the Western world.

There's a quieter section worth knowing about too, further into the grounds: a memorial to the roughly eight hundred Milanese citizens deported to Nazi concentration camps during the war, designed by the rationalist architecture group known as BBPR — one of whose own founding partners died in Mauthausen. It's a plain, dignified structure, deliberately restrained against the elaborate tombs surrounding it.

What you're walking through, really, is a century and a half of Italian sculpture and architecture, commissioned not by a museum but by families who wanted the same ambition in death that they'd had in life — right alongside a memorial to people who were given no monument at all until long after the war ended.

A map at the entrance marks the notable graves individually, the conductor Arturo Toscanini among them — pick one up before you set off, since the grounds are larger, and easier to get pleasantly lost in, than they first look.

tours.title: Morelli Ristorante
tours.shortDescription: The chef spent his early years cooking on American ocean liners before he ever ran a kitchen of his own.
tours.longDescription: Giancarlo Morelli grew up on a farm in the countryside near Bergamo, trained young under Bernard Loiseau and Alain Ducasse in France, and at twenty-four became director of Italy's first golf club before circling back to cooking properly. His flagship, Pomiroeu, sits an hour outside Milan in Seregno, opened in 1993 and awarded a Michelin star in 2009 — this Isola address is a separate, newer venture rather than a satellite of it. It occupies part of the ground floor of the Hotel VIU Milan on Via Aristotile Fioravanti, with a cocktail bar, Bulk, sharing the address next door.

stops.title: Morelli Ristorante
stops.caption: The chef here spent his early years cooking on American ocean liners, long before he ever opened a restaurant of his own.
stops.transcriptText:
The chef here spent his early years cooking on American ocean liners, long before he ever opened a restaurant of his own.

On Via Aristotile Fioravanti, in the Isola district, part of the ground floor of Hotel VIU Milan holds Morelli Ristorante, with a separate cocktail bar, Bulk, sharing the same address next door.

Start with the chef's own route here. Giancarlo Morelli grew up on a farm in the countryside near Bergamo, trained young under Bernard Loiseau and Alain Ducasse in France, and at twenty-four became director of Italy's first golf club before circling back to cooking properly. His actual flagship restaurant, Pomiroeu, sits an hour outside Milan in Seregno, opened in 1993 and awarded a Michelin star in 2009 — this Isola address is a newer, separate venture rather than a satellite of that original kitchen. The kitchen here runs its own register too: a mantecato rice with Robiola cheese and a saffron-whipped hen consommé, a barbecued artichoke, baccalà finished under a potato foam, and a chef's table facing straight into the kitchen for anyone who books ahead. The format splits deliberately in two: Morelli Ristorante for that more considered cooking, and Bulk next door for a looser mixology-and-food register, same chef, two different registers of the same appetite.

Which fits a career that's always run two tracks at once, sport administration and serious cooking, a countryside upbringing and international kitchens — Morelli also runs a restaurant on Sardinia's Costa Smeralda these days, and sits on industry boards pushing more sustainable cooking practices across Italy. He's talked about that early stretch on the ocean liners as the thing that actually taught him to cook under pressure, in a kitchen the size of a cupboard, for a dining room that never stopped moving — training that shows up now in how calmly this particular kitchen runs two very different menus out of one small space.

Not every chef's biography includes both a golf club and an ocean liner. This one apparently needed both to arrive here.

The Monumental Cemetery is a short walk from here if today's itinerary includes it — an unusual but genuine pairing, a serious dinner and one of Europe's most elaborate cemeteries, a few minutes apart in the same quiet corner of the Isola district.

tours.title: Nilufar Depot
tours.shortDescription: Thirty years of quiet stockpiling behind an unmarked facade, opened to the public only in 2015.
tours.longDescription: Nina Yashar opened her first gallery, Nilufar, on Via della Spiga in 1979 at twenty-one, having grown up around her family's Persian carpet trade — an eye for objects that clearly runs back generations. For decades she collected design pieces faster than any single shop could show them, and this converted warehouse on Viale Lancetti exists specifically to let that overflow finally breathe. The architect Massimiliano Locatelli arranged it as a soaring central atrium ringed by three storeys of black-metal balconies, closer to a small opera house than a storage depot, and almost nobody was let inside for thirty years before the doors opened.

stops.title: Nilufar Depot
stops.caption: For thirty years, almost nobody was let inside. What Nina Yashar had been quietly stockpiling behind these walls only opened to the public in 2015.
stops.transcriptText:
For thirty years, almost nobody was let inside. What Nina Yashar had been quietly stockpiling behind these walls only opened to the public in 2015.

A converted warehouse on Viale Lancetti, just north of Porta Garibaldi station, holds Nilufar Depot behind an unmarked industrial facade — inside, a soaring central atrium ringed by three storeys of black-metal balconies, closer to a small opera house than a storage depot.

Start with the collector herself. Yashar opened her first gallery, Nilufar, on Via della Spiga in 1979, aged twenty-one, having grown up around her family's Persian carpet trade — an eye for objects that clearly runs back generations. For decades she kept collecting design pieces faster than any single shop could show them, and this depot exists specifically to let thirty years of that overflow finally breathe. The architect Massimiliano Locatelli designed the atrium deliberately in homage to Teatro alla Scala, and it shows: balcony after balcony of furniture and lighting, stacked rather than shelved, so the whole fifteen-hundred-square-metre space reads more like a set than a shop floor. Around three thousand pieces live here at any one time, twentieth-century names like Franco Albini and Charlotte Perriand set beside work commissioned specifically for this space by contemporary designers — Lindsey Adelman, Michael Anastassiades, and India Mahdavi among them. Look, too, for the six-metre brass curtain by the artist Leonor Antunes, hung through the centre of the atrium like a piece of stage scenery that never quite gets struck.

And here's the thing that makes the Depot different from a conventional gallery: this was never built to sell quickly. It was built to finally show what one collector's eye had been quietly gathering for three decades, all at once, in a single room built to take the weight of it.

Thirty years of collecting, staged in one atrium — most galleries would call that an exhibition. Yashar just calls it storage that finally got a proper room.

The original Nilufar gallery, tucked into a much smaller space on Via della Spiga in the Quadrilatero, is worth the contrast — the same eye for objects, compressed into a fraction of the room.

tours.title: Officina Antiquaria
tours.shortDescription: Everything here is for sale, and almost nothing has been resold without first being taken apart.
tours.longDescription: Officina Antiquaria opened on Via Maroncelli in Isola in 1993 and has run less like a shop than a hospital for furniture ever since: a restoration atelier on site has been repairing, reupholstering and re-lacquering pieces for more than thirty years, quietly outlasting most of the antique dealers who started out alongside it. The stock sorts roughly into three moods — the rational, disciplined elegance of the nineteen-forties, the softer optimism of the fifties, and the sharper experiments that followed. Behind a plain shopfront it is as much a working atelier as a gallery, which is why the pieces here tend to have been understood before they were priced.

stops.title: Officina Antiquaria
stops.caption: Everything in this shop is technically for sale, and almost nothing here has ever been resold without first being taken apart.
stops.transcriptText:
Everything in this shop is technically for sale, and almost nothing here has ever been resold without first being taken apart.

On Via Maroncelli, in the Isola district just north of Porta Garibaldi, a plain shopfront hides a working restoration atelier as much as a gallery — furniture and objects from three very different decades of Italian design, all genuinely in dialogue with each other.

Start with the workshop rather than the showroom. Officina Antiquaria opened in 1993, and from the start it ran less like a shop and more like a hospital for furniture: a restoration atelier on site has been repairing, reupholstering, and re-lacquering pieces for more than thirty years, quietly outlasting most of the antique dealers who started out alongside it. The stock sorts itself, roughly, into three moods: the rational, disciplined elegance of the nineteen-forties, the softer organic curves of the fifties, and the bolder, brasher experiments of the sixties and seventies — named and unnamed designers side by side, since not every good chair needs a famous signature attached to it. Nothing on the floor is displayed as untouchable; pieces move between the workshop bench and the showroom regularly, so what you're looking at on any given visit might have been reupholstered the week before.

Which is really the difference between this place and a museum: nothing here is roped off. Everything's been repaired at least once, and everything is, in principle, still meant to be sat on. It helps to know what Isola actually was before it became known for this sort of shop: for most of the twentieth century, this was a working-class railway district, hemmed in on most sides by tracks, and better known for factories than for furniture. Officina Antiquaria opened here decades before the design crowd properly arrived, when a restoration workshop on this street would have looked like the odd one out rather than part of a trend.

A thirty-year-old restoration bench, tucked behind a shopfront most people walk straight past — not much about it announces itself.

Isola's wider design district runs for several streets around here — keep heading north if today's wandering has room for more workshops than showrooms.

tours.title: Palazzo Citterio
tours.shortDescription: Fifty years is a long time to wait for a museum to open. This one finally did, in December 2024.
tours.longDescription: The state bought the palazzo on Via Brera in 1972, under the Pinacoteca's then-director Franco Russoli, who wanted a dedicated home for twentieth-century art alongside Brera's older collection. The British architect James Stirling drew up ambitious plans in the 1980s that were never built, and his death left them unfinished. A first completed attempt, finished in 2018 at a cost of over twenty million euros, ran straight into serious damp problems. What finally opened is an eighteenth-century palazzo whose grand entrance now runs straight through to the gallery next door, the two buildings working as one continuous museum campus.

stops.title: Palazzo Citterio
stops.caption: Fifty years is a long time to wait for a museum to open its doors.
stops.transcriptText:
Fifty years is a long time to wait for a museum to open its doors. Palazzo Citterio finally did, in December 2024.

Via Brera, numbers twelve to fourteen, right next to the Pinacoteca — an eighteenth-century palazzo whose grand entrance now opens straight through to the historic gallery next door, the two buildings effectively one continuous museum campus.

Consider how long this actually took. The state bought the palazzo back in 1972, under the Pinacoteca's then-director Franco Russoli, who wanted a dedicated home for twentieth-century art alongside Brera's older collection. The British architect James Stirling drew up ambitious plans in the 1980s that were never built; his death left them unfinished, and the building waited for a further renovation. A first attempt, finished in 2018 at a cost of over twenty million euros, ran straight into serious damp problems and had to be redone almost from scratch — which is a fair part of why the final opening slipped a further six years, this time under the architect Mario Cucinella. What's inside now is largely the Jesi and Vitali family collections, donated decades ago and finally given proper walls: Picasso's Head of a Bull from 1942, an early Morandi still life, Boccioni's Riot in the Gallery, and studies by Modigliani and Braque, among more than two hundred works in total.

What's worth remembering, walking through, is that most of what's on these walls has been sitting in storage for longer than this building's been open — the delay isn't backstory here, it's basically the whole story.
