Booking here takes planning, often months out, so if a table isn't available, the Frantzén Group runs several easier brasseries elsewhere in the city under the Astoria name, built for the version of an evening that doesn't need months of notice.

tours.title: Gasklockorna (the Gasholders)
tours.shortDescription: Five vast drums once held the city's gas in Hjorthagen; one is becoming a hotel.
tours.longDescription: The skyline at Hjorthagen, on the edge of Norra Djurgårdsstaden, is dominated by a cluster of enormous cylinders — some still ringed in dark red brick, others stripped to bare steel frames. These are the Gasklockorna, the gasholders of the old Värtaverket gasworks, which operated from 1893 until 2011. At its peak the site held five holders of different sizes built at different times, each a vast expandable drum storing gas for the city's streetlights and kitchen stoves. The two oldest, from 1893 and 1900, were designed by the architect Ferdinand Boberg, who gave them red brick façades with rounded arched windows and decorative bands of brown and yellow brick — heritage-protected industrial buildings that were never meant to be looked at this closely.

stops.title: Gasklockorna (the Gasholders)
stops.caption: Five enormous drums once stored this city's gas, and one of them is about to become a hotel.
stops.transcriptText:
Five enormous drums once stored this city's gas, and one of them is about to become a hotel.

You're in Hjorthagen, on the edge of Norra Djurgårdsstaden, where the skyline is dominated by a cluster of vast cylindrical structures — some still ringed in dark red brick, others stripped down to bare steel frames. These are the Gasklockorna, the gasholders of Stockholm's old Värtaverket gasworks.

The gasworks operated from 1893 until 2011, and at its peak stood five gasholders of different sizes, built at different times, each one a vast expandable drum that stored gas for the city's streetlights and kitchen stoves. The two oldest, dating from 1893 and 1900, were designed by the architect Ferdinand Boberg, who gave them red brick façades with rounded arched windows and decorative bands of brown and yellow brick — heritage-protected industrial buildings that were never meant to be looked at this closely.

Each holder is being given a different second life. One is becoming a hotel; another, a cultural venue; a third keeps only its bare steel skeleton, repurposed as a shell for events; a fifth has already become office space. The fourth, built in 1932 and the tallest of the five at ninety metres, didn't survive in its original form at all — architects Herzog and de Meuron replaced it with a residential tower built to the exact same height and fifty-metre diameter, its apartments arranged in a wedge-shaped "finger plan" for better light, and its façade built from glass brick in muted colours that echo Boberg's original masonry a short walk away.

It's one of the more literal examples of a city recycling itself: the same drums that once held the gas lighting Stockholm's streets are being hollowed out to hold, in one form or another, the people who'll live and work here next. Around twelve thousand new homes are planned for the district as a whole, and the tower alone accounts for over three hundred of them.

Walk the perimeter rather than settling on just one holder to look at. From certain angles you can see brick, bare steel, and glass tower standing side by side — three different decades of the same site's future, stacked into a single view.

tours.title: Hammarbybacken Ski Slope
tours.shortDescription: A ninety-three-metre ski hill on the edge of Södermalm, built entirely out of the city's rubbish.
tours.longDescription: Nothing underfoot here is natural. Hammarbybacken rises on the southern edge of Södermalm, in the district that also gave its name to Hammarby IF, one of Stockholm's best-supported football clubs — though the slope is a much younger addition than the club, a hill built from construction waste and landfill rather than shaped by any glacier or fault. Through the 1980s it grew as debris was piled onto what had begun as a rubbish tip, reaching eighty-seven and a half metres; a second round of deposits in the late 2000s pushed the summit to its present ninety-three and a half. It is a modest operation by ski-resort standards — four runs, operated by Skistar — better suited to beginners and to locals getting a first taste of skiing than to anyone chasing a black diamond.

stops.title: Hammarbybacken Ski Slope
stops.caption: This entire hill is made of Stockholm's own rubbish. Look at what's underfoot, skis or no skis — none of it is natural.
stops.transcriptText:
This entire hill is made of Stockholm's own rubbish.

Look at what's underfoot, skis or no skis — none of it is natural. Hammarbybacken rises on the southern edge of Södermalm, in the district that also gave its name to Hammarby IF, one of Stockholm's best-supported football clubs, though the slope itself is a considerably younger addition than the club is: a hill built entirely from construction waste and landfill rather than shaped by any glacier or fault line.

What you get in exchange for the modest scale is the view on the way down. Instead of pine forest and granite peaks, the skyline of Stockholm rises to meet you — hotels and apartment blocks standing in for mountains, glimpsed between turns rather than admired from a chairlift. The hill doesn't fully quiet down once the snow machines stop either; when the season ends, skiers switch to grass, taking the same runs at a rougher, drier pace rather than waiting out the summer for the next snowfall.

There's something quietly fitting about that. A hill built from what the city threw away has become one of the better places to look at the city itself, and the fact that most people skiing down it grew up a few kilometres from where they're standing gives it a different relationship to ski culture than any resort built purely for tourists.

Come at dusk if skiing isn't the plan for the day. The same slope makes for one of Södermalm's better short walks, and the view holds even without snow underfoot.

tours.title: Hosoi
tours.shortDescription: A listening bar in the old meatpacking district where the sound system comes before the menu.
tours.longDescription: Hosoi keeps to a single low-lit room on Styckmästargatan, a few streets from Bar Montan in the same stretch of Slakthusområdet, with a sound system built to headline standard and a bar running along one side. Call it a listening bar with a kitchen attached, or a restaurant that happens to book real acts — it runs all three roles at once: live music and DJ sets most nights, a cocktail and wine list built around unconventional bottles, and a sharing menu that folds Japanese technique into Swedish and local ingredients rather than importing a whole cuisine wholesale. The idea borrows from Japan's own listening-bar tradition, where a serious sound system, not conversation, is the reason people turn up at all.

stops.title: Hosoi
stops.caption: The music comes before the menu here, and that's not a slogan, it's the running order.
stops.transcriptText:
The music comes before the menu here, and that's not a slogan, it's the running order.

Hosoi keeps to a single, low-lit room on Styckmästargatan, a few streets from Bar Montan in the same stretch of Slakthusområdet, with a sound system built to headline standard and a bar running along one side.

Call it a listening bar with a kitchen attached, or a restaurant that happens to book real acts — Hosoi runs all three roles at once: live music and DJ sets most nights, a cocktail and wine list built around unconventional bottles, and a sharing menu that folds Japanese technique into Swedish and local ingredients rather than importing a whole cuisine wholesale. The venue's own line for itself is blunt about the order of priorities: share, bottle, food, bill — four words that put the social experience ahead of any individual dish or drink. Music genuinely comes first here, not as branding but as the reason the room was designed the way it was, built around the sound system rather than fitted with one afterward, and the booking calendar leans toward acts who'll treat the room as a proper venue rather than background noise for a dinner service.

Which makes Hosoi a useful contrast to its neighbour down the street. Bar Montan restores an old industrial building and lets the food carry the room, while Hosoi builds its identity from scratch around sound, treating the meal as something that happens alongside the music rather than the other way round.

If you started the evening at Bar Montan, this is where it's worth ending it. Walk the short distance over once the kitchens elsewhere have wound down, and let the night run later than dinner usually does.

tours.title: Konserthuset Stockholm
tours.shortDescription: Ten blue columns on Hötorget, and a single entrance built so no audience could be sorted by class.
tours.longDescription: On the north side of Hötorget a façade painted a deep unmistakable blue rises behind a row of tall columns, giving the whole building the look of a temple set down in a city square. Ivar Tengbom won the competition to design it while still a young professor of architecture and built it between 1923 and 1926 in a neoclassicism drawing directly on ancient Athens — the cradle, as he saw it, of democracy itself. That idea was not merely decorative: Tengbom gave the hall a single entrance for every visitor, rich or otherwise, at a time when many concert halls still sorted their audiences by class before anyone had taken a seat. Carl Milles' Orpheus group stands on the steps outside.

stops.title: Konserthuset Stockholm
stops.caption: Ten blue columns, and every one of them is holding up a story about ancient Athens.
stops.transcriptText:
Ten blue columns, and every one of them is holding up a story about ancient Athens.

On the north side of Hötorget, a façade painted a deep, unmistakable blue rises behind a row of tall columns, giving the whole building the look of a temple set down in the middle of a city square. This is Konserthuset.

Ivar Tengbom won the competition to design it while still a young professor of architecture, and built it between 1923 and 1926 in a neoclassical style drawing directly on ancient Athens — the cradle, as he saw it, of democracy itself. That idea wasn't just decorative: Tengbom designed a single entrance for every visitor, rich or otherwise, at a time when many concert halls still sorted audiences by class before they'd even taken their seats.

Out in front, the bronze figures rising from the fountain are the work of Carl Milles, installed in 1936 and known as the Orpheus group — the mythical musician reaching skyward, surrounded by figures said to represent all of humanity drawn toward music. It's easy to walk past without registering what it's doing there, but it was placed to greet exactly the people about to walk into the hall behind it.

Since the year it opened, this has also been the permanent home of the Nobel Prize award ceremony, held here every tenth of December. The Nobel Foundation once planned its own dedicated building for the purpose; that building was never built, and Konserthuset simply absorbed the role instead.

So the blue temple on Hötorget ended up doing double duty: home to the Royal Stockholm Philharmonic for well over two hundred concerts a year, and, one night annually, the room where science and literature's biggest prizes get handed out under the same roof Tengbom built for democratic music-going.

Cross the square and look back at the façade from a distance before you go inside. The ten columns read very differently once you're not standing directly beneath them, and the blue holds its colour even on Stockholm's greyest days.

tours.title: Kouthoofd Familie Winkel
tours.shortDescription: A deliberately unfindable shop on Stora Nygatan, run by Teenage Engineering's head of design.
tours.longDescription: Stora Nygatan, a few steps from Stortorget in the heart of the old town, hides Kouthoofd Familie Winkel behind a frontage so quiet it is easy to walk straight past without noticing it is open. It belongs to Jesper Kouthoofd, founder and head of design at Teenage Engineering, the Stockholm company behind some of the more distinctive synthesizers and audio gear in recent design history. He built the place with almost no online presence and no interest in being easy to find — a rare thing for a venue sitting in the most photographed square mile in Stockholm, and rarer still for someone whose day job is built almost entirely on being noticed.

stops.title: Kouthoofd Familie Winkel
stops.caption: There's no sign outside worth photographing, and that's rather the point.
stops.transcriptText:
There's no sign outside worth photographing, and that's rather the point.

Stora Nygatan, a few steps from Stortorget in the heart of Gamla Stan, hides Kouthoofd Familie Winkel behind a frontage so quiet it's easy to walk straight past without noticing it's open.

It belongs to Jesper Kouthoofd, founder and head of design at Teenage Engineering, the Stockholm company behind some of the more distinctive synthesizers and audio gear in recent design history. He built this place with almost no online presence and no interest in being easy to find, a rare thing for a venue sitting in the most-photographed square mile in Stockholm, and rarer still for someone whose day job is built almost entirely on being noticed.

Inside, vinyl runs the room in two directions at once: records play through the speakers, and more records line the walls as part of the décor itself, so the music and the furnishing are, in effect, the same collection doing double duty. The menu stays modest on purpose, snacks and small plates alongside a carefully chosen wine list, built to support a few hours of sitting and listening rather than a full evening's dining.

The street itself has been doing this kind of quiet cultural work for centuries. Stora Nygatan was laid out around 1630, rebuilt in the wake of the great fire of 1625, and Carl Michael Bellman, Stockholm's best-loved songwriter, kept two different addresses along it during the 1780s — a coincidence worth knowing if you've already stood above Mariaberget and heard his story from that end of Södermalm.

A designer known for building things other people are meant to notice decided, instead, that Stockholm's Old Town needed one more quiet room built around good wine and better music — the whole idea behind Kouthoofd, really, rather than another venue competing for visibility in a neighbourhood that already has plenty of that.

Stortorget itself is only a two-minute walk if you haven't already crossed it — Gamla Stan's oldest square, and the noise of it makes the quiet inside Kouthoofd feel a good deal more deliberate on the way back.

tours.title: Mariaberget
tours.shortDescription: Monteliusvägen runs four hundred metres along a cliff, and hands you the whole city at once.
tours.longDescription: Monteliusvägen, the footpath along the cliff edge on Mariaberget, delivers one of Södermalm's best views in a single sweep — Lake Mälaren below, the spires of Gamla stan across the water, and the City Hall further along the shoreline, all without moving your feet. The stone houses just behind you date from the 1700s and survived when much of the surrounding hillside did not; a restoration in the 1970s kept them standing rather than clearing them for something newer, and Stockholm's city museum has singled the cluster out as one of the more architecturally significant survivals of its kind. The path itself runs barely four hundred metres end to end with no room for cars, which is a large part of why the view stays this uninterrupted.

stops.title: Mariaberget
stops.caption: The songwriter who practically invented the Stockholm ballad grew up on this hill, in a house that no longer stands.
stops.transcriptText:
The songwriter who practically invented the Stockholm ballad grew up on this hill, in a house that no longer stands.

Monteliusvägen, the footpath running along the cliff edge here, delivers one of Södermalm's best views in a single sweep: Lake Mälaren below, the spires of Gamla Stan across the water, and Stockholm City Hall further along the shoreline, all without moving your feet.

The buildings just behind you, stone houses dating from the 1700s, survived when much of the surrounding hillside didn't; a restoration in the 1970s kept them standing rather than clearing them for something newer, and Stockholm's own city museum has singled the cluster out as one of the more architecturally significant survivals of its kind in the city. Monteliusvägen itself runs barely four hundred metres end to end, a narrow footpath with no room for cars, which is a large part of why the view stays this uninterrupted even at the busiest times of year.

This particular stretch of hillside also produced Sweden's best-loved songwriter. Carl Michael Bellman was born in 1740 in the Stora Daurerska house, one of the finest houses then standing on this part of Södermalm, and spent his final years dogged by debt so persistent it eventually landed him in a debtors' cell for a genuinely small sum — a rough end for a man whose songs about Stockholm's taverns and back streets are still sung today.

There's a particular kind of irony in that: the man who wrote Stockholm's most affectionate songs about drinking and poverty ended up living out both, on the very hill now known for one of the city's most sought-after views.

Follow Monteliusvägen east rather than turning back, and it drops you down toward the Old Town within about fifteen minutes, past Stora Nygatan, where Bellman kept two later addresses of his own — the same slope he would have walked, minus the debt collectors.

tours.title: Ministry of Enterprise (Näringsdepartementet)
tours.shortDescription: A ministry that has been renamed so often its current title is only two years old.
tours.longDescription: An office building on Herkulesgatan, a short walk from Sergels torg, houses the ministry behind nothing more dramatic than a discreet sign and the Swedish state's three-crown emblem beside the door. The office traces back to 1969, when it was established as the Ministry of Industry to steer Sweden's industrial and business policy, and it has been renamed repeatedly since as successive governments reorganised its remit: Industry, Employment and Communications; then Enterprise and Innovation; and, after a merger with the Ministry of the Environment on the first of January 2023, the Ministry of Climate and Enterprise. It is one of ten ministries making up Sweden's Government Offices, all sharing a single civil service — part of why so many of these buildings look this interchangeable from outside.

stops.title: Ministry of Enterprise (Näringsdepartementet)
stops.caption: This ministry has changed its name more times than most people change their minds.
stops.transcriptText:
This ministry has changed its name more times than most people change their minds.

An office building on Herkulesgatan, a short walk from Sergels torg, houses the ministry behind nothing more dramatic than a discreet sign and the Swedish state's three-crown emblem beside the door.

The office traces back to 1969, when it was established as the Ministry of Industry, responsible for steering Sweden's industrial and business policy. Since then it's been renamed several times as successive governments reorganised its remit: Industry, Employment and Communications; then Enterprise and Innovation; and, since a merger with the Ministry of the Environment on the first of January, 2023, its current title, the Ministry of Climate and Enterprise.

That most recent merger tells its own story about priorities. A single ministry now handles everything from business regulation and innovation policy to climate targets, energy and the natural environment, portfolios that in an earlier era would have sat in entirely separate departments, occasionally working against each other rather than together. It's one of ten ministries that together make up Sweden's Government Offices, all sharing a single civil service and administrative structure rather than each running its own separate operation, which is part of why so many of these buildings look this interchangeable from the outside.

Whether folding environment and enterprise into one ministry produces better policy than keeping them apart is, reasonably, still argued over — supporters point to fewer contradictions between economic and climate goals, while critics worry one agenda quietly outweighs the other inside a single office. Either way, the building itself gives nothing away: Swedish government ministries tend toward the unshowy, function over statement, and this one is no exception.

Sergels torg, with its sunken plaza and glass obelisk, is a few minutes' walk from here if you'd like a louder contrast. Plenty of Stockholm's civic architecture makes its case in glass and light rather than in the quiet office block standing in front of you now.

tours.title: Moderna Museet
tours.shortDescription: Rafael Moneo's museum on Skeppsholmen, where in 1966 visitors walked inside a reclining woman.
tours.longDescription: The low russet-and-white building on Skeppsholmen, its roofline punctuated by rows of angled lanterns, stands right beside the older drill hall that ArkDes now occupies. This is Rafael Moneo's design for Moderna Museet, opened in 1998 under the same commission that had him extend the older hall next door. The museum itself is considerably older than its building: it opened on the ninth of May 1958 inside that very drill hall, after decades of argument about giving twentieth-century art a home separate from the crowded Nationalmuseum across the water. Its most famous single moment came in 1966, when it built a reclining figure some thirty metres long that visitors entered on foot.

stops.title: Moderna Museet
stops.caption: In 1966, this museum built a reclining woman some thirty metres long, and visitors walked inside her through the space between her legs.
stops.transcriptText:
In 1966, this museum built a reclining woman some thirty metres long, and visitors walked inside her through the space between her legs.

Find the low, russet-and-white building on Skeppsholmen with a roofline punctuated by rows of angled lanterns, standing right beside the older Drill Hall that ArkDes now occupies. This is Rafael Moneo's design for Moderna Museet, opened in 1998 — the same commission under which Moneo extended the older hall next door.

Moderna Museet itself is older than this building: it opened on the ninth of May, 1958, inside that very Drill Hall next door, after decades of debate about giving twentieth-century art a home separate from the crowded Nationalmuseum across the water.

Pontus Hultén took over as director in 1960 and turned the museum into something genuinely international for its size. Picasso's Guernica hung here in 1956, even before the museum formally opened, and by 1966 Hultén was letting Niki de Saint Phalle, Jean Tinguely and Per Olof Ultvedt build "Hon" — that reclining figure some thirty metres long, entered through an opening between her legs. Warhol, Rauschenberg and Oldenburg all showed here during the same run of years.

By the 1990s the collection had outgrown the old hall entirely, and a competition drew two hundred and eleven entries before Moneo's design, code-named Telemachos, was chosen. The building opened on the twelfth of February, 1998, inaugurated by the King and Queen, and gave the collection permanent, purpose-built galleries for the first time in its history.

Which means the museum you're about to walk into, and the museum that first made Stockholm's name in contemporary art, are technically two different buildings sharing one collection — the Drill Hall gave Hultén's generation room to be genuinely wild in, and Moneo's building has spent the years since trying to give that same wildness somewhere permanent to live.

Once you're done here, it's worth crossing to the older Drill Hall next door, now home to ArkDes. The two buildings were designed as a pair, and Moneo's daylight solution is easiest to appreciate by seeing it applied to both a brand-new museum and a nineteenth-century one, in the same afternoon.

tours.title: National Museum (Nationalmuseum)
tours.shortDescription: A palace built for a collection, with vaults kept light by sixty thousand hollow clay jars.
tours.longDescription: The museum commands Blasieholmen, a spit of land between two arms of water, its long stone facade facing Skeppsholmen across the channel — a nineteenth-century palace built specifically to give Sweden's art collection a permanent address. The German architect Friedrich August Stüler took charge of the design in 1847, drawing on his experience at Berlin's Neues Museum, and the building took some twenty years to finish, opening to the public on the fifteenth of June 1866. Inside, the engineering is quietly inventive for its time: the upper vaults were built using nearly sixty thousand hollow clay jars, a way of keeping a very heavy ceiling surprisingly light, and the windows, shipped from Germany, were among the largest panes of glass then installed in any Swedish building.

stops.title: National Museum (Nationalmuseum)
stops.caption: Three hundred and forty-nine ceiling roses decorate the rooms inside, and no two floors use quite the same pattern.
stops.transcriptText:
Three hundred and forty-nine ceiling roses decorate the rooms inside, and no two floors use quite the same pattern.

The museum commands Blasieholmen, a spit of land between two arms of water, its long stone facade facing Skeppsholmen across the channel — a nineteenth-century palace built specifically to give Sweden's art collection a permanent address.

The German architect Friedrich August Stüler took charge of the design in 1847, drawing on his experience at Berlin's Neues Museum, and the building took some twenty years to finish, finally opening to the public on the fifteenth of June, 1866. Inside, the engineering is quietly inventive for its time: the upper vaults were built using nearly sixty thousand hollow clay jars, a way of keeping a very heavy ceiling surprisingly light, and the windows, shipped in from Germany, were some of the largest panes of glass installed in a Swedish building up to that point.

It wasn't originally meant to be only an art museum. The building was designed as a three-floor home for the nation's whole cultural inheritance — antiquities, royal collections, even the Royal Library — though the library never moved in, and over the following century most of those other collections found separate homes of their own, leaving Nationalmuseum with what it holds today: painting, sculpture, and design, spanning six hundred years.

Look for The Water Sprite, painted by Ernst Josephson in 1882: a green-haired, half-human figure crouched on a rock in dark water, drawn from Nordic folklore about spirits that lure travellers toward the shore. It's one of the paintings visitors describe standing in front of the longest, less because of its size than because of how uncomfortable it manages to make a quiet gallery feel.

The whole building is a bit of a paradox, in the end: a palace built for absolutely everything Sweden wanted to remember about itself now holds only a fraction of that ambition, whittled down over a century and a half into one very good art museum.

Step back outside and look along the waterfront to your right, and you'll spot the Strand Hotel, now the Radisson Collection, close enough that its guests have been waking up to this exact facade for well over a century.

tours.title: Nordic Museum (Nordiska museet)
tours.shortDescription: A Danish-castle silhouette on Djurgården, built as a palace for ordinary people's memories.
tours.longDescription: The museum rises on Djurgården as a long red sandstone building bristling with towers, battlements and spires that borrow more from a Danish Renaissance castle than from anything native to Stockholm. Isak Gustaf Clason took over the design in 1890 after the previous architect Magnus Isaeus died partway through, and drew on Kronborg and Frederiksborg, two of Denmark's grandest castles — hence the battlements and the eighty-one-metre tower rising over a facade a hundred and fifty-three metres long. Ground was broken in 1888 and the museum did not fully open until the eighth of June 1907. Its founder Artur Hazelius, who wanted a palace for the people's memories rather than for kings, did not live to see it.

stops.caption: Artur Hazelius wanted to build a palace for the people's memories, and then he died before it opened.
stops.transcriptText:
Artur Hazelius wanted to build a palace for the people's memories, and then he died before it opened.

The museum rises on Djurgården, a long red sandstone building bristling with towers, battlements and spires that borrow more from a Danish Renaissance castle than from anything native to Stockholm.

Isak Gustaf Clason took over the design in 1890, after the previous architect, Magnus Isaeus, died partway through the project, and drew his inspiration from Kronborg and Fredriksborg, two of Denmark's grandest castles — hence the battlements and the eighty-one-metre tower rising over a facade a hundred and fifty-three metres long. Ground was broken in 1888; the museum didn't fully open to the public until the eighth of June, 1907.

Inside the entrance, the Great Hall runs the length of a cathedral nave and is dominated by a single carved figure: Gustav Vasa, Sweden's sixteenth-century founding king, carved from oak by the sculptor Carl Milles and finished in 1925. Several metres tall, painted and gilded, he sits enthroned at the far end of the hall, watching everyone who walks in.

Hazelius never saw any of it finished. He'd spent decades collecting the everyday objects of Swedish rural life — clothes, tools, entire farmhouses, which he later reassembled just across the water at Skansen — convinced that industrialisation was erasing a way of life worth preserving in something more permanent than memory, and he died in 1901, six years before the museum he'd spent his life building finally opened its doors.

The building itself is really an argument he never got to finish making out loud: that a country's ordinary, unglamorous past deserved a monument just as grand as any king's, built the same way, with towers and a great hall and a scale that dares you to take folk culture less than seriously.

Skansen, the open-air museum Hazelius built to go with this one, sits a short walk from here on the same stretch of Djurgården — the farmhouses and windmills he rescued, set back outdoors among trees, rather than carved in oak under a roof.

tours.title: Observatorium
tours.shortDescription: Not a scientific observatory but a piece of art shaped like one, standing on piles in the water.
tours.longDescription: Walk out along the pier at Södra Hammarbyhamnen and the walkway gives way to a low wooden structure standing on piles in the water — timber decking, a few simple geometric openings, nothing that announces itself as art until you are standing inside it. Gunilla Bandolin, a professor of landscape architecture, built it in 2003 and called it Observatorium not because it tracks stars but because its geometry is arranged specifically to let you follow the sun's path across the sky over the course of a day, from a spot suspended between water and open air. It is free, unstaffed and almost entirely unsignposted, which is a large part of its character.

stops.title: Observatorium
stops.caption: This isn't a scientific observatory. It's a piece of art shaped like one.
stops.transcriptText:
This isn't a scientific observatory. It's a piece of art shaped like one.

Walk out along the pier at Södra Hammarbyhamnen and the walkway gives way to a low wooden structure standing on piles in the water — timber decking, a few simple geometric openings, nothing that announces itself as art until you're standing inside it.

Bandolin built it as what she called a social and functional sculpture — art that only really finishes itself once people are using it, eating lunch on it, letting their kids run across the decking, rather than standing back to admire it from a respectful distance.

That's a fairly quiet rebellion against how most public art gets treated: fenced off, labelled, photographed rather than touched. Observatorium only works if you actually go and sit in it, which most passers-by in this waterfront neighbourhood do without a second thought, because nothing about the place tells them not to. It helps that the neighbourhood itself was built on the same instinct: Hammarby Sjöstad was a working industrial harbour until the 1990s, redeveloped since as a model for sustainable urban living, with district heating, waste and water systems designed to work together rather than in isolation — a district that, like the sculpture at its edge, was built to be used rather than admired from outside.

Come close to sunset if you can manage the timing. That's when the whole point of the name becomes obvious, the light moving low and flat across the water exactly where Bandolin built the platform to catch it.

tours.title: Parliament House (Riksdagshuset)
tours.shortDescription: An entire island rebuilt from scratch to house parliament and the national bank under one roof.
tours.longDescription: The building spreads across most of Helgeandsholmen, a Neoclassical facade with a grander Baroque Revival centrepiece marking the main entrance — altogether more restrained than the palace visible just across the water, as if the architect had deliberately chosen not to compete with royalty on its own doorstep. Aron Johansson won the commission by competition in 1889, and what he built between 1897 and 1905 was originally two separate semicircular chambers under one roof: one for the Riksdag, the other for Sveriges Riksbank. It was an unusual pairing of lawmaking and currency that made sense only because both institutions needed grand ceremonial space and neither could justify a whole island alone. That arrangement lasted until 1971, when Sweden moved to a single chamber.

stops.title: Parliament House (Riksdagshuset)
stops.caption: Between 1897 and 1905, an entire small island in the middle of Stockholm was rebuilt from scratch to give parliament and the national bank a single shared home.
stops.transcriptText:
Between 1897 and 1905, an entire small island in the middle of Stockholm was rebuilt from scratch to give parliament and the national bank a single shared home.

The building spreads across most of Helgeandsholmen in front of you, a Neoclassical facade with a grander, Baroque Revival centrepiece marking the main entrance, altogether more restrained than the palace visible just across the water, as if the architect deliberately chose not to compete with royalty on its own doorstep.

The architect Aron Johansson won the commission through a design competition in 1889, and what he built was originally two separate semicircular chambers under one roof: one for the Riksdag, Sweden's parliament, and the other for Sveriges Riksbank, the national bank, an unusual pairing of lawmaking and currency that made sense only because both institutions needed grand, ceremonial space and neither could justify an entire island to itself. That arrangement lasted until 1971, when Sweden abandoned its two-chamber parliament for a single chamber and the Riksbank finally moved out to its own building elsewhere in the city, freeing up its old semicircular hall to be rebuilt as parliament's new Assembly Hall, with the sitting parliament relocating temporarily to Kulturhuset while the work went on. The building today also hosts the annual ceremony for the Right Livelihood Award, sometimes described as an alternative Nobel Prize, one more reminder that Helgeandsholmen has rarely been used for just one purpose at a time.

What's easy to miss, given how solid and permanent the building looks today, is that it's already been substantially rearranged once, an entire half of it repurposed rather than demolished when the political arrangement it was built around simply stopped making sense, the sort of quiet institutional flexibility that rarely shows up in a building's public face. Democracies, it turns out, renovate rather than rebuild whenever they possibly can.

Sankt Jacobs kyrka is a short walk north from here, and its own tower tells a similarly patched-together story, rebuilt from scratch after a fire nearly two centuries before parliament even moved in.

tours.title: Radisson Collection (Strand Hotel)
tours.shortDescription: Opened by the king in February 1912 as the host hotel for that summer's Olympic Games.
tours.longDescription: The hotel faces the water at Nybrokajen, a long pale facade a short walk from Nationalmuseum — close enough that the two buildings have effectively been sharing a view of each other for over a century. Gustaf V inaugurated the Strand Hotel on the twenty-fourth of February 1912, timed deliberately so that it could serve as the host hotel for that summer's Olympic Games: the first Olympics ever to be filmed, and the moment Sweden briefly sat at the centre of the world's attention. The building has changed hands and names since, but the position has not, and the steamers still moor along the quay directly outside.

stops.title: Radisson Collection (Strand Hotel)
stops.caption: It's February 1912, and King Gustaf the Fifth has just cut the ribbon on Stockholm's Olympic hotel.
stops.transcriptText:
It's February 1912, and King Gustaf the Fifth has just cut the ribbon on Stockholm's Olympic hotel.

The hotel faces the water at Nybrokajen, a long pale facade a short walk from Nationalmuseum, close enough that the two buildings have effectively been sharing a view of each other for over a century.

King Gustaf the Fifth inaugurated the Strand Hotel on the twenty-fourth of February, 1912, timed deliberately to serve as the host hotel for that summer's Olympic Games — the first Olympics ever to be filmed, and the first where Sweden itself briefly sat at the centre of the world's attention.

The ground underneath is older news than the hotel: this stretch of shoreline is where the warship Vasa was built in the 1620s, the doomed vessel that famously capsized and sank on her maiden voyage, only to be raised from Stockholm's harbour floor over three centuries later and put on permanent display a short walk from here.

Guests over the decades have included Frank Sinatra, Audrey Hepburn, and Greta Garbo, who filmed a silent picture here in 1921, and in 2017 the whole building went through a careful restoration by the Swedish architecture firm Wingårdhs, who introduced a custom colour, Strand Grey, running through the oak, walnut, leather and stone of the renewed interiors.

There's a nice symmetry in a hotel built to host the world for one Olympic summer still being, over a century later, the kind of place people travel specifically to stay in — the audience changed, but the basic idea of putting Stockholm's best foot forward for visitors never really went anywhere.

Nationalmuseum is close enough to see from several of the rooms facing the water, worth crossing over if you haven't already, if only to look back at the hotel from the other side of the channel.

tours.title: Rolfs Hav
tours.shortDescription: A seafood counter buried in crushed ice, with no meat anywhere on the menu — not even a garnish.
tours.longDescription: Rolfs Hav sits on Drottninggatan, though the room worth heading for is the Sea Bar at its centre: a long counter buried in crushed ice, chefs and waiters working it from behind, seafood laid out like a catch just landed. Johan Jureskog and Klas Ljungquist opened it in September 2023 as the sister project to their long-established Rolfs Kök a short distance away, and built its entire identity around the sea — no meat anywhere on the menu, not even as a garnish. The tasting menu, called Storskär after an island out in the archipelago, is an entirely seafood-focused sequence, the kind of ambitious menu you would normally expect to have a beef course tucked in somewhere for balance, and simply does not.

stops.title: Rolfs Hav
stops.caption: There's no menu at the bar here, just crushed ice, cold bottles, and whatever the chefs pull out next.
stops.transcriptText:
There's no menu at the bar here, just crushed ice, cold bottles, and whatever the chefs pull out next.

You'll find Rolfs Hav on Drottninggatan, though the room worth heading for is the Sea Bar at its centre: a long counter buried in crushed ice, chefs and waiters working it from behind, seafood laid out like a catch just landed.

Run by Johan Jureskog and Klas Ljungquist, the restaurant opened in September 2023 as the sister project to their existing Rolfs Kök, an established Stockholm kitchen a short distance away, and builds its entire identity around the sea — no meat anywhere on the menu, not even as a garnish. Their tasting menu, called Storskär after an island out in the archipelago, is an entirely seafood-focused sequence of courses, the kind of ambitious tasting menu you'd normally expect to have a beef course tucked in somewhere for balance, and simply doesn't.

The Sea Bar itself runs on a first come, first served basis: no reservation, just a seat at the counter and chefs working directly across the ice from you, plating and pouring with nothing between you and the process. It's a deliberately different register from the formal tasting room elsewhere in the building — the same serious cooking, served with considerably less ceremony.

It says something about where Stockholm's fine dining has been heading lately: fewer white tablecloths, more counters, the same level of technique aimed at a room that would rather watch the work happen than have it explained course by course.

If a table isn't free, Savant Bar is a short walk from here and keeps a similarly unfussy attitude toward serious drinking, should you want to keep the evening going without another booking to plan around.

tours.title: Rönnells Antikvariat
tours.shortDescription: Over a hundred thousand second-hand books, in what is left of a much larger empire.
tours.longDescription: Behind an unassuming storefront on Birger Jarlsgatan the shop opens up far bigger than the frontage suggests: room after room of shelving climbing toward a cool light-filled atrium at the centre. Gösta Rönnell founded it in 1929, and for most of the twentieth century it was considerably larger than what survives — several branches scattered across Stockholm plus a mail-order operation substantial enough to reach collectors who never set foot in the city. Nearly a century on, only this single storefront remains in person, though the business still ships books out through an online catalogue to customers who will never see the atrium at all.

stops.title: Rönnells Antikvariat
stops.caption: Over one hundred thousand books live here, and the shop used to be several times this size.
stops.transcriptText:
Over one hundred thousand books live here, and the shop used to be several times this size.

Behind an unassuming storefront on Birger Jarlsgatan, the shop opens up far bigger than the frontage suggests: room after room of shelving climbing toward a cool, light-filled atrium at the centre.

Gösta Rönnell founded the shop in 1929, and for most of the twentieth century it was considerably larger than what you're looking at now — several branches scattered across Stockholm, plus a mail order operation substantial enough to reach collectors who never set foot in the city. Nearly a century on, only this single storefront remains in person, though the business still ships books out through an online catalogue to customers who never see the atrium at all.

Inside, the stock runs past one hundred thousand books, organised with more care than the words "secondhand bookshop" usually promise: early editions of Astrid Lindgren sit near nineteenth century travel guides, an entire section is given over to art and design, and shelves of foreign language titles wait for anyone hunting a specific book they couldn't find at home.

There's a particular kind of luck in a shop like this surviving at all: rents in this part of Stockholm have pushed out plenty of businesses that needed less floor space and made less obvious money per square metre than a hundred thousand secondhand books do. Rönnells has managed it by simply being good enough at the one thing it does that people keep coming back for exactly that.

If browsing here has put you in the mood for more, Stockholms stadsbibliotek, Gunnar Asplund's round reading room, is a short walk north — a rather different way of organising the same basic love of books.

tours.title: Saint James's Church (Sankt Jacobs kyrka)
tours.shortDescription: Sixty years in the building, and three centuries of architectural fashion stacked on top of each other.
tours.longDescription: Look up from beside Kungsträdgården and the church wears three different centuries at once: a red facade climbing into a copper-green dome, late Gothic windows sitting comfortably alongside Renaissance detailing and, higher still, an unmistakably Baroque tower. Johan III set the current building in motion in the 1580s intending something grand enough to match the European architecture he admired, but funding and changing taste stretched the work across more than six decades, so that by the time Queen Kristina consecrated it in 1643 the building had absorbed whatever style happened to be fashionable in whichever decade the masons were working. It is an accidental architectural timeline poured into one set of walls rather than a deliberate design.

stops.title: Saint James's Church (Sankt Jacobs kyrka)
stops.caption: This church took over sixty years to build, and it shows: three different architectural fashions are stacked into the same building, one on top of the other.
stops.transcriptText:
This church took over sixty years to build, and it shows: three different architectural fashions are stacked into the same building, one on top of the other.

Look up from beside Kungsträdgården and the church wears three different centuries at once, a red facade climbing into a copper-green dome, late Gothic windows sitting comfortably alongside Renaissance detailing and, higher still, an unmistakably Baroque tower.

King Johan the Third set the current building in motion in the 1580s, intending something grand enough to match the European architecture he admired, but funding and changing tastes stretched the work across more than six decades, so that by the time Queen Kristina finally consecrated it in 1643, the building had absorbed whatever style happened to be fashionable in whichever decade the masons were working, an accidental architectural timeline poured into a single set of walls rather than a deliberate design choice. A fire in 1723 took the original tower down entirely, and its replacement was designed by the architect Göran Josuae Adelcrantz, whose son Carl Fredrik would go on, a generation later, to design both the Court Theatre and the Chinese Pavilion out at Drottningholm — a family business, in effect, spanning some of Stockholm's grandest royal and religious commissions across two generations. Inside, elaborately carved stone portals by Heinrich Blume and Markus Hebel frame the entrances, and the whole building is dedicated to Saint James the Greater, the patron saint of travellers and pilgrims.

There's a certain logic in that dedication landing on a building that never quite settled into one architectural period itself: a church for people always passing through, built, as it turned out, by a whole succession of different hands passing the job along in turn, none of whom lived to see the whole thing finished under a single unified plan.

Kungsträdgården is right next door if you'd like somewhere to sit afterwards, Stockholm's oldest public park and usually busy enough that you'll have company while you take the church back in from a distance.

tours.title: Savant Bar
tours.shortDescription: Ten or more natural wines open at any moment, bought straight from the growers.
tours.longDescription: Savant Bar keeps to a compact room — no reservations taken except for the chef's table tucked at the back, a counter built for drinking rather than dining formally, and a kitchen visible enough to watch the plates go out. The list runs on natural wine sourced by working directly with growers rather than through the usual distributor chain: more than ten wines by the glass at any one time, rotating constantly, backed by a longer bottle list for anyone who wants to commit further than a single pour. The result is that no two visits pour quite the same thing, which is either the appeal or the problem depending on how you feel about being surprised.

stops.title: Savant Bar
stops.caption: Ten or more wines are open and pourable here at any given moment, and none of them will taste quite like the last bottle you had.
stops.transcriptText:
Ten or more wines are open and pourable here at any given moment, and none of them will taste quite like the last bottle you had.

Savant Bar keeps to a compact room, no reservations taken except for the chef's table tucked at the back, with a counter built for drinking rather than dining formally and a kitchen visible enough to watch the plates go out.

The list runs on natural wine, sourced by working directly with growers rather than through the usual distributor chain — more than ten wines by the glass at any one time, rotating constantly, backed by a longer bottle list for anyone who wants to commit further than a single pour.

The people behind Savant Bar run their own natural wine import business too, called Vin Vivant, supplying restaurants and private customers since 2020, and each year they put on Natural Mystics, generally reckoned to be Sweden's leading natural wine festival — the sixth edition is due in 2027, which gives some sense of how quickly the whole scene has grown around a bar this size.

Food follows the same logic as the wine: seasonal, mostly Swedish vegetables, built for sharing or eating solo at the counter, served in a room built from recycled materials rather than anything shipped in new — sustainability less as a marketing line here than as the actual operating principle.

It says something about how far natural wine has travelled from its scrappy, slightly suspicious reputation a decade ago that a bar built entirely around it can now run its own import business and headline its own festival, rather than scraping by on whatever a distributor happened to bring in that month.

Rolfs Hav is close enough to make an easy pairing if you haven't eaten yet — seafood first, then wine here afterward, in whichever order suits the evening better.

tours.title: Stockholm City Hall (Stadshuset)
tours.shortDescription: Eight million dark red bricks, three gold crowns, and a Blue Hall that was never painted blue.
tours.longDescription: Stadshuset anchors the tip of Kungsholmen, eight million dark red bricks stacked into towers and arcades along the waterfront, with a single square tower topped by three gold crowns rising above the rest. Ragnar Östberg designed the whole complex and spent twelve years seeing it built, finishing in 1923 in a style now generally filed under Swedish National Romanticism — his own attempt to build something that felt distinctly Swedish rather than borrowed wholesale from Italian or French precedent, at a time when a great deal of European civic architecture was doing exactly that borrowing. He was also, a few years later, the architect of the studio built for his close friend the sculptor Carl Eldh on the other side of the city.

stops.title: Stockholm City Hall (Stadshuset)
stops.caption: The Blue Hall inside has never once been painted blue. Stadshuset anchors the tip of Kungsholmen, eight million dark red bricks stacked into towers and arcades along the waterfront, with a single square tower topped by three gold crowns rising above the rest.
stops.transcriptText:
The Blue Hall inside has never once been painted blue.

Stadshuset anchors the tip of Kungsholmen, eight million dark red bricks stacked into towers and arcades along the waterfront, with a single square tower topped by three gold crowns rising above the rest.

Ragnar Östberg designed the whole complex and spent twelve years seeing it built, finishing in 1923 in a style now generally filed under Swedish National Romanticism — his own attempt to build something that felt distinctly Swedish rather than borrowed wholesale from Italian or French precedent, at a time when a lot of European civic architecture was doing exactly that borrowing. He was also the architect, a few years later, behind the studio he built for his close friend, the sculptor Carl Eldh, on the other side of the city: a much smaller, much quieter building, but recognisably the work of the same hand.

Inside, the Golden Hall is the one room every visitor remembers: over eighteen million tiles of gold mosaic covering every wall, arranged into scenes from Swedish history and myth, mixing Byzantine, Islamic and Renaissance influences into something that belongs to none of them specifically.

The Blue Hall, confusingly, was never painted blue at all — Östberg planned to, then changed his mind partway through construction once he saw how the bare red brick actually looked under light, and left it exactly as it was. The tower above both halls climbs a hundred and six metres, and the climb up is rewarded with one of the better views in the city: Gamla Stan laid out across the water in one direction, Skinnarviksberget's granite summit in the other.

There's something rather fitting about that: the single most photographed formal room in the country, host every December to the Nobel Prize banquet, sits right next door to a hall that's been quietly wrong about its own name for a hundred years, and nobody's ever felt the need to fix it.

Skinnarviksberget, the granite hilltop across the water in Södermalm, offers the clearest view back at this whole building from a distance — cross over and see Stadshuset the way most photographs of it are actually taken, from across the water rather than underneath it.

tours.title: Stockholm Public Library (Stockholms stadsbibliotek)
tours.shortDescription: Every book in the main room shelved on one continuous curve, with no straight wall in sight.
tours.longDescription: Sveavägen delivers you to the library's rotunda from a distance — a plain cylindrical drum rising above a low rectangular base, painted the same warm red the city keeps returning to for its public buildings. Gunnar Asplund designed it between 1924 and 1928, drawing on a much older reference: the Rotonde de la Villette, an eighteenth-century French customs building by Claude-Nicolas Ledoux, stripped here of its ornament and rebuilt as pure abstract geometry. Readers climb a grand staircase to reach the rotunda itself, arriving at the top of the building rather than the bottom, in what Asplund clearly intended as a small ceremony before you have even opened a book.

stops.title: Stockholm Public Library (Stockholms stadsbibliotek)
stops.caption: Every book in the main room is shelved on a single continuous curve, and there isn't a straight wall in sight.
stops.transcriptText:
Every book in the main room is shelved on a single continuous curve, and there isn't a straight wall in sight.

Sveavägen delivers you to the library's rotunda from a distance, a plain cylindrical drum rising above a low rectangular base, painted the same warm red brick Stockholm keeps returning to for its public buildings.

Gunnar Asplund designed it between 1924 and 1928, drawing on a much older reference: the Rotonde de la Villette, an eighteenth century French customs building by Claude Nicolas Ledoux, stripped here of its ornament and rebuilt as pure, abstract geometry. Readers climb a grand staircase to reach the rotunda itself, arriving at the top of the building rather than the bottom, in what Asplund clearly intended as a small ceremony before you even open a book.

Inside the rotunda, the shelves run in one unbroken curve around the entire circumference, lit from above by a ring of high clerestory windows rather than anything at eye level, so every reader ends up positioned the same distance from the centre of the room — a deliberately levelling piece of design, nobody granted a better seat than anyone else.

Asplund's own description of what he was after was almost stubbornly plain: simplicity in form, simplicity in the whole conception. That restraint is exactly what made the building matter afterward — architects across Scandinavia, Alvar Aalto among them, spent the following decades working out what they'd learned from a library that refused to decorate its way toward importance. Asplund carried the same instinct into his other major project, Skogskyrkogården, the woodland cemetery he designed on the city's southern edge, which UNESCO added to its World Heritage list in 1994 for much the same reason: restraint, treated as a genuine architectural achievement rather than a lack of ambition.

Rönnells Antikvariat, Stockholm's biggest secondhand bookshop, is a short walk south on Birger Jarlsgatan — a fittingly different way of holding a hundred thousand books, if the rotunda's single curved shelf has left you wanting to see the more chaotic version.

tours.title: Stockholm Stadshotell
tours.shortDescription: Built in the 1870s as a home for widows, reportedly to rebuke a king for his infidelities.
tours.longDescription: The building stands three storeys tall on a quiet stretch of Södermalm, its facade still carrying the gilded tympanum that commemorates King Oscar I — the king whose behaviour, the story goes, prompted Queen Josefina to pay for a home for upper-class widows here in the 1870s as a pointed rebuke. The current owners chose to keep that detail rather than smooth it over. After the widows moved on the building passed through a therapist school and a brief stint under the Department of Transportation before standing empty for sixteen years, and it is that empty stretch that makes the present transformation feel less like a renovation than a rescue: five founders, led by creative director Fredrik Carlström, reopened it as Stockholm's first stadshotell — a Swedish tradition of smaller civic gathering houses that the capital had somehow never had.

stops.title: Stockholm Stadshotell
stops.caption: It's the 1870s, and Queen Josefina has just paid for a home for upper-class widows — reportedly as a pointed rebuke to her husband, King Oscar the First, and his infidelities.
stops.transcriptText:
It's the 1870s, and Queen Josefina has just paid for a home for upper-class widows — reportedly as a pointed rebuke to her husband, King Oscar the First, and his infidelities.

The building stands three storeys tall on this quiet stretch of Södermalm, its facade still carrying the gilded tympanum that once commemorated the king whose behaviour supposedly prompted the whole project in the first place, a detail the current owners chose to keep rather than smooth over.

After the widows moved on, the building passed through a therapist school and a brief stint under the Department of Transportation, before standing empty for sixteen years, and it's that empty stretch that makes the current transformation feel less like a renovation and more like a rescue: five founders, led by creative director Fredrik Carlström, reopened it as Stockholm's first stadshotell, a Swedish tradition of smaller civic gathering houses that the capital had somehow never actually had one of. Inside, the restoration leans hard into craft rather than polish — a hand-cut intarsia elevator by the Swedish artist Klara Knutsson, pew-inspired bistro seating carved by hand, rattan furniture from a ninety-year-old workshop called Larsson Korgmakare, and textiles from the long-running mill Insjöns Väveri, alongside furnishings sourced from Svenskt Tenn.

The dining room, Matsalen, occupies what was once a chapel, a hundred and fifty years old, and the choice to serve dinner under a consecrated ceiling rather than disguise it says something about how the whole project was approached: less about erasing the building's past lives than about setting a table inside all of them at once. The corridors carry that same instinct further still, lined with a hundred and eighty photographs by the Stockholm photographer Gunnar Smoliansky, chosen to document the city rather than decorate the walls around it.

If Matsalen's booked out or you fancy something looser, Tripletta is a walk away on Åsögatan — the third restaurant to occupy that particular address, run by the same owner each time, which is its own small story about a neighbourhood remembering a spot rather than a menu.

tours.title: Sundbyberg Water Tower
tours.shortDescription: Twenty-seven metres of brick that held the town's water for eighty years, then sat empty for decades.
tours.longDescription: The tower stands at the centre of Tornparken, a cross-banded brick cylinder in the National Romantic style with a decorative terrace ringing the top, where a five-storey drum of concrete and brick once carried four hundred cubic metres of drinking water for the whole town — an early example of poured concrete construction dressed up to look considerably older than the technology inside it. The architect was Ivar Tengbom, better known now as founder of the firm that still bears his name, and he finished it in 1912. It drew water pumped in from Brunkebergsåsen at Ulriksdal until Sundbyberg switched to a larger supply from Lake Mälaren in 1926 and the tower's job simply stopped. It sat unused for decades until residents voted in a 2005 referendum to bring it back rather than let it decay.

stops.title: Sundbyberg Water Tower
stops.caption: Twenty-seven metres of Helsingborg brick rise above the park in front of you, and for eighty years it did nothing more glamorous than hold water.
stops.transcriptText:
Twenty-seven metres of Helsingborg brick rise above the park in front of you, and for eighty years it did nothing more glamorous than hold water.

You'll find the tower at the centre of Tornparken, a cross-banded brick cylinder in the National Romantic style, with a decorative terrace ringing the top where a five-storey drum of concrete and brick once carried four hundred cubic metres of drinking water for the whole town, an early example of poured concrete construction dressed up to look considerably older than the technology inside it.

The architect was Ivar Tengbom, better known today as the founder of the firm that still bears his name, and he finished the tower in 1912, drawing water pumped in from Brunkebergsåsen out at Ulriksdal until Sundbyberg switched to a larger supply from Lake Mälaren in 1926 and the tower's actual job simply stopped. It sat unused for decades after that, heritage-listed but empty, until residents voted in a 2005 local referendum to bring it back into use rather than let it quietly decay, and a careful restoration completed in 2009 preserved the original wooden staircases and even matched the new entrance door to the historic design, right down to using linseed-oil paint of the kind the original builders would have recognised. The tower is formally protected under Sweden's strictest heritage classification now, which means every change made to it, inside or out, has to answer to that original 1912 design first.

What's worth sitting with here is that a water tower is about as unglamorous a piece of infrastructure as a town can have, purely functional, built to be forgotten about the moment it worked, and yet Sundbyberg fought to keep this one standing decades after it had any function left to serve. That's not nostalgia so much as a town deciding its own skyline was worth the upkeep.

Climb up if the café's open — the top terrace gives you the clearest view of Sundbyberg's rooftops in any direction, precisely the vantage the tower was never actually built to offer its own town.

tours.title: Svenskt Tenn
tours.shortDescription: The shop that disproves everything people assume about Swedish design being pale and spare.
tours.longDescription: Strandvägen runs along the water at this point, and the shop has held this corner of it since 1927, its interiors originally laid out by the functionalist architect Uno Åhrén before the whole place gradually warmed into something considerably less austere. Estrid Ericson founded the business in 1924 as a pewter workshop — an art teacher's attempt to make good modern design affordable — and won the Grand Prix at the Paris exhibition the very next year. But the shop most people recognise took shape only after January 1934, when the Austrian architect Josef Frank arrived in Stockholm fleeing persecution at home and began a collaboration with Ericson that produced roughly three thousand sketches and two hundred and fifty textile patterns before his death in 1967 — dense, botanical, and nothing like pale.

stops.title: Svenskt Tenn
stops.caption: Ask most people what Swedish design looks like and they'll describe something pale, spare, and quiet.
stops.transcriptText:
Ask most people what Swedish design looks like and they'll describe something pale, spare, and quiet. Step inside here and none of that applies.

Strandvägen runs along the water at this point, and the shop occupies a corner of it that Svenskt Tenn has held since 1927, its interiors originally laid out by the functionalist architect Uno Åhrén before the whole place gradually warmed up into something considerably less austere.

Estrid Ericson founded the business in 1924 as a pewter workshop, an art teacher's attempt to make good modern design affordable, and won the Grand Prix at the Paris exhibition the very next year, but the shop most people recognise today only really took shape after January 1934, when the Austrian architect Josef Frank arrived in Stockholm, fleeing persecution at home, and began a collaboration with Ericson that produced roughly three thousand sketches and two hundred and fifty textile patterns before his death in 1967 — dense, botanical prints in colours that have nothing to do with Scandinavian restraint whatsoever. Since 1975 the business has belonged to the Kjell and Märta Beijer Foundation, which means it answers to no shareholders chasing quarterly growth, and it still works with twenty-five Swedish workshops to produce furniture and textiles that are, even now, more than eighty per cent original Frank and Ericson designs rather than reissues chasing trends. For the company's centenary in 2024, the archive yielded one more: a new Frank-designed Jubilee pattern, printed on fabric, mapping out the streets of the Stockholm he'd once fled to.

And here's the thing worth sitting with: the pattern most tourists now associate with "Swedish design" the world over was drawn by a refugee from Vienna who spent his career deliberately working against the minimalism his adopted country would later become famous for.

Nybroplan is barely a couple of minutes' walk from here, and the Royal Dramatic Theatre's Art Nouveau facade facing it makes a rather good next stop if colour and pattern have put you in the mood for more.

tours.title: The Royal Dramatic Theatre (Dramaten)
tours.shortDescription: An Art Nouveau facade worked on by Carl Milles, Carl Larsson and a painting prince at once.
tours.longDescription: A pale stone facade dense with sculpture and ornament faces directly onto Nybroplan with the water just beyond the square. The architect Fredrik Lilljekvist completed it in February 1908, replacing an older theatre at Kungsträdgården that had served Stockholm since 1788 and had simply worn out, and he brought in genuine collaborators rather than mere decorators: the sculptor Carl Milles contributed work to the exterior, the painter Carl Larsson worked on the interior, and Prince Eugen, the so-called Painter Prince, added his own contribution to the design. The theatre opened with a production of Strindberg's Mäster Olof, and has been the country's principal stage ever since.

stops.title: The Royal Dramatic Theatre (Dramaten)
stops.caption: Look at the facade in front of you and you're looking at a small committee of Sweden's best-known artists, all working on the same building at once.
stops.transcriptText:
Look at the facade in front of you and you're looking at a small committee of Sweden's best-known artists, all working on the same building at once.

Look for a pale stone facade dense with sculpture and ornament, in the Art Nouveau style, facing directly onto Nybroplan with the water just beyond the square.

The architect Fredrik Lilljekvist completed the building in February 1908, replacing an older theatre at Kungsträdgården that had been serving Stockholm since 1788 and had simply worn out, and he brought in genuine collaborators rather than mere decorators: the sculptor Carl Milles contributed work to the exterior, the painter Carl Larsson worked on the interior, and Prince Eugen, the so-called Painter Prince, added his own contribution to the design as well. The theatre opened with a production of Strindberg's "Mäster Olof," and in the decades since it has run through a run of directors that reads like a history of Swedish stagecraft on its own, including Ingmar Bergman, who led the theatre through the mid-1960s, while its attached training academy has produced actors who went on to Hollywood, Greta Garbo and Ingrid Bergman among them. The theatre now runs five separate stages under one roof and stages something in the region of a thousand performances a year, which makes the building considerably busier today than its ornate, slightly hushed facade tends to let on.

What's easy to overlook, given how familiar the name has become, is that this facade wasn't handed to one visionary architect and left at that: it's a genuinely collaborative civic monument, sculptor and painter and prince all contributing to a single public building, in a way that feels distinctly Swedish rather than the work of one signature name.

Villa Dagmar sits just round the corner on Nybrogatan, on the exact spot where the author and royal physician Axel Munthe once lived — worth the two-minute walk if only to see what became of his old address.

tours.title: Tripletta
tours.shortDescription: Italian for a hat trick — the same man's third consecutive restaurant at this exact address.
tours.longDescription: Åsögatan on Södermalm is an ordinary run of shopfronts, and partway along them an understated frontage marks Tripletta: a cosy dining room with a bar tucked along one side and walk-ins welcomed as readily as reservations. The restaurateur Robert "Boban" Rudinski named it Tripletta, Italian for a hat trick, because it is his third consecutive restaurant at this exact spot — a run of ownership rather than a run of identical menus. The current concept leans into Italian cooking pulled from across the country, with particular influence from the south and, further still, from North Africa: pasta made in house, charcuterie boards, and seasonal plates that change with whatever is good that week instead of sticking to a fixed card.

stops.title: Tripletta
stops.caption: There's a small superstition running through this address: whatever restaurant opens here, it's always run by the same man.
stops.transcriptText:
There's a small superstition running through this address: whatever restaurant opens here, it's always run by the same man.

Åsögatan, Södermalm: an ordinary run of shopfronts, and partway along them an understated frontage marks Tripletta, a cosy dining room with a bar tucked along one side and walk-ins welcomed as readily as reservations.

The restaurateur Robert "Boban" Rudinski named the place Tripletta, Italian for a hat trick, because it's his third consecutive restaurant at this exact spot, a run of ownership, not a run of identical menus, and the current concept leans into Italian cooking pulled from across the country, with particular influence from the south and, further still, from North Africa — pasta made in house, charcuterie boards, and seasonal plates that change with whatever's good that week instead of sticking to a fixed card. The wine list runs the same way, built to be picked through rather than skimmed, and the bar keeps its own separate rhythm for anyone who's only after a glass and a plate to share. The dining room itself favours warmth over formality, graphic design on the walls doing more of the talking than white tablecloths would, and that combination of serious food and a genuinely relaxed room has earned it some of the strongest word-of-mouth reviews of any newer opening in this part of Södermalm, the kind of place regulars now recommend before they've even finished their own plate.

There's something worth noticing in a single address hosting three different restaurants from one owner rather than three different owners cycling through: the neighbourhood, it turns out, remembers a spot and trusts whoever's running it, which is a fairly rare kind of loyalty for a restaurant scene that usually rewards the newest concept over the most familiar face.

Nytorget, the square a few streets over, is worth the short detour afterwards — benches, a bit of green, and on a warm evening roughly half of Södermalm seems to end up there.

tours.title: Vasa Museum
tours.shortDescription: A warship that sailed for twenty minutes, and taught us more by failing than it ever could have by floating.
tours.longDescription: Gustavus Adolphus commissioned the Vasa as one of the most heavily armed warships of its era, built between 1626 and 1628. On the tenth of August 1628 it set out on its maiden voyage, sailed about one thousand three hundred metres, heeled over in a gust and sank in some thirty-two metres of water. The cause, established only centuries later, was a hull built dangerously top-heavy — oversized deck beams, excessive headroom, and a construction crew working to two different measurement standards. The wreck lay forgotten until 1956, when the amateur archaeologist Anders Franzén located it with a homemade coring probe; after more than thirteen hundred dives the hull broke the surface again in April 1961, remarkably close to intact. What the disaster preserved is the point: some five hundred carved and painted sculptures, a three-metre lion figurehead, sixty-four guns, six of the original ten sails, and the only complete whipstaff steering mechanism to survive from any ship of this age anywhere.

stops.title: Vasa Museum
stops.caption: The warship Vasa sailed for roughly twenty minutes before it sank, and it's precisely because it failed that fast that we now know more about seventeenth-century shipbuilding than almost anywhere else on earth.
stops.transcriptText:
The warship Vasa sailed for roughly twenty minutes before it sank, and it's precisely because it failed that fast that we now know more about seventeenth-century shipbuilding than almost anywhere else on earth.

Stand back far enough from the entrance and you'll notice the museum building itself is shaped like the hull it protects, a dark timber-clad silhouette rising above Djurgården with the actual ship visible through the windows once you're inside.

King Gustavus Adolphus commissioned the Vasa as one of the most heavily armed warships of its era, built between 1626 and 1628, and on the tenth of August 1628 it set out on its maiden voyage, sailed about one thousand three hundred metres, heeled over in a gust of wind, and sank in around thirty-two metres of water with roughly thirty people aboard lost. The cause, established only centuries later, was a hull built dangerously top-heavy — oversized deck beams, excessive headroom, and a construction crew mixing two different measurement standards that left the ship structurally uneven from one side to the other before it ever left the dock. The wreck lay forgotten until 1956, when the amateur archaeologist Anders Franzén located it using a homemade coring probe, and after more than thirteen hundred individual dives to prepare the hull, the Vasa broke the surface again on the twenty-fourth of April 1961, after three hundred and thirty-three years underwater, remarkably close to intact. She sat in a temporary shed on the harbourside for nearly thirty years while conservators soaked the timber in polyethylene glycol, a treatment that ran for seventeen years straight, before the ship finally moved into this purpose-built museum in 1990, and more than forty-five million visitors have filed past the hull since.

What makes the ship worth the visit isn't really the disaster, it's what the disaster preserved: nearly five hundred carved and painted sculptures in Renaissance style, a three-metre lion figurehead carved from several separate pieces of oak, sixty-four guns including forty-eight twenty-four-pounders cast with a precision unusual for the period, six of the original ten sails, and the only complete whipstaff steering mechanism to survive from any ship of this age anywhere, a genuinely unmatched snapshot of naval life that a successful voyage would simply never have left behind.

The Nordic Museum's turreted red sandstone building is close enough to see from the car park here, a short walk further along Djurgården, and its own founder, Artur Hazelius, would have approved of a museum built entirely around one perfectly preserved object.

tours.title: Victoriahuset
tours.shortDescription: A cast-iron dome built purely so the world's largest water lily could survive a Swedish winter.
tours.longDescription: The Bergius Botanic Garden opens onto Frescati and the shore of Brunnsviken, and at its edge a cast-iron and glass dome catches the light — Victorian in style, and noticeably more delicate-looking than anything else around it. The botanist Veit Wittrock secured approval from the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences in 1899 to build a dedicated home for tropical water plants, and Victoriahuset was the result: an artificial slice of Amazonian climate assembled entirely from cast iron and curved glass, heated for decades by coal fires that had to run continuously through the coldest months just to keep the water warm enough for its star resident. That resident is the Victoria water lily, whose pads grow broad enough to support a small child.

stops.title: Victoriahuset
stops.caption: Under this glass dome grows the largest water lily species in the world, and the whole building exists purely because one botanist refused to let it die of a Swedish winter.
stops.transcriptText:
Under this glass dome grows the largest water lily species in the world, and the whole building exists purely because one botanist refused to let it die of a Swedish winter.

Behind you, the Bergius Botanic Garden opens onto Frescati and the shore of Brunnsviken; ahead, a cast-iron and glass dome catches the light — Victorian in style, and noticeably more delicate-looking than anything else in the garden around it.

The botanist Veit Wittrock secured approval from the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences in 1899 to build a dedicated home for tropical water plants, and Victoriahuset was the result, an artificial slice of Amazonian climate assembled entirely from cast iron and curved glass, heated for decades by coal fires that had to run continuously through the coldest Stockholm months just to keep the water warm enough for its star resident to survive.
