That resident is the Victoria water lily, whose pads can grow broad enough to support a small child's weight, and the building was designed specifically around its needs rather than adapted afterwards, which makes it something closer to a life-support system than a conventional greenhouse. Restoration work through the 1980s and into the early 2000s has kept the structure standing despite its long-running vulnerability to the very humidity it was built to contain, and it's now protected as a national monument, one of Europe's rarer surviving examples of this particular style of glasshouse. It only opens to visitors from the first of May to the end of September, closed through the winter months the coal fires once had to fight so hard against.

What's worth pausing on is the sheer single-mindedness of it: an entire building, engineered down to its heating system, constructed around the needs of one plant species that most visitors had never heard of before walking in, decades before anyone worried much about biodiversity as a concept in its own right.

The wider Bergius garden rewards a slower walk afterwards, especially the path down toward Brunnsviken, where the lake gives you the best angle back at the dome from outside.

tours.title: Villa Dagmar
tours.shortDescription: Built on the address where Axel Munthe once kept his Stockholm door, and named for a real woman's taste.
tours.longDescription: Nybrogatan 25–27 was the address where Axel Munthe — the physician and author who once treated Queen Victoria and wrote one of the best-selling memoirs of his era — kept his Stockholm residence, and the current building carries that layered history into a considerably more contemporary interior. The name comes from Dagmar Bergsten, a member of the family behind the Diplomat Collection, the fourth- and fifth-generation hospitality business that opened the hotel. Rather than inventing a generic backstory, the designers built the place around her actual taste: a modern, well-travelled woman drawn to figures like Hilma af Klint and Peggy Guggenheim, whose real family home in Båstad was an eclectic gathering place through the 1920s and '30s that borrowed its Mediterranean warmth from Villa d'Este and Villa San Michele on Capri.

stops.title: Villa Dagmar
stops.caption: Before this was a hotel, it was the front door of Axel Munthe, the physician and author who once treated Queen Victoria and wrote one of the best-selling memoirs of his era.
stops.transcriptText:
Before this was a hotel, it was the front door of Axel Munthe, the physician and author who once treated Queen Victoria and wrote one of the best-selling memoirs of his era.

You're on Nybrogatan, at numbers twenty-five to twenty-seven, the same address where Munthe kept his Stockholm residence, and the current building carries that layered history into a considerably more contemporary interior.

The name comes from Dagmar Bergsten, a member of the family behind the Diplomat Collection, the fourth and fifth-generation hospitality business that opened the hotel, and rather than inventing a generic backstory, the designers built the whole place around her actual taste: a modern, well-travelled woman inspired by figures like Hilma af Klint and Peggy Guggenheim, whose real family home in Båstad, an eclectic gathering place through the 1920s and '30s, borrowed its Mediterranean warmth from Villa d'Este and Villa San Michele on Capri. The same family still runs several other hotels around the city, but this is the only one named for a specific person rather than a place or a period. Furniture, art, and colour throughout Villa Dagmar the hotel trace back to details from that actual villa rather than a mood board assembled for the brief, which gives the place a specificity that most newly built luxury hotels simply don't bother with, right down to the warm Mediterranean palette running through rooms otherwise built to look thoroughly Stockholm.

And that's really the pivot worth noticing: most hotel concepts are invented from scratch by a design team chasing a trend, while this one was built as a fairly faithful portrait of one particular woman's real house and her real friendships, down to the art on the walls.

Nationalmuseum is a ten-minute walk south from here along Nybrogatan and down toward the water, and its collection of six centuries of Swedish and European art makes a natural next stop if today's theme has been one person's taste shaping a whole building.

tours.title: Woodland Cemetery (Skogskyrkogården)
tours.shortDescription: Two thirty-year-old architects won a competition here by refusing to level the ground flat.
tours.longDescription: A wide gravel path runs out from the main entrance with a large granite cross standing off to one side and the pine forest that gives the cemetery its name stretching beyond it in every direction; the noise of the city drops away almost immediately. In the autumn of 1914 Stockholm ran a design competition for an extension to its southern cemetery, and the winning entry — submitted by two thirty-year-old architects named Gunnar Asplund and Sigurd Lewerentz under the title "Tallum" — rejected the tidy formal parkland most European cemeteries favoured at the time in favour of something rooted in older Nordic burial tradition, working with the site's slopes and gravel pits rather than levelling them flat. Asplund's Woodland Chapel opened first, in 1920. The result is now a UNESCO World Heritage Site and has shaped cemetery design worldwide.

stops.title: Woodland Cemetery (Skogskyrkogården)
stops.caption: Walk through the low stone entrance and the noise of the city drops away almost immediately, replaced by pine trees and a single sloping lawn that most visitors say they weren't expecting.
stops.transcriptText:
Walk through the low stone entrance and the noise of the city drops away almost immediately, replaced by pine trees and a single sloping lawn that most visitors say they weren't expecting.

A wide gravel path runs out from the main entrance here, with a large granite cross standing off to one side and the pine forest that gives the cemetery its name stretching out beyond it in every direction.

In the autumn of 1914, Stockholm ran a design competition for an extension to its southern cemetery, and the winning entry, submitted by two thirty-year-old architects named Gunnar Asplund and Sigurd Lewerentz under the title "Tallum," rejected the tidy formal parkland style most European cemeteries favoured at the time in favour of something rooted in older Nordic burial tradition, working with the site's slopes and gravel pits rather than levelling them flat. Asplund's Woodland Chapel opened first, in 1920, a small and deliberately modest timber-roofed building tucked among the pines, followed by Lewerentz's Chapel of Resurrection in 1925, and the pair spent the following two decades adding to the site until Asplund completed the monumental Woodland Crematorium in 1940, the final major work of his career, only months before his death that October. UNESCO added the whole cemetery to its World Heritage list in 1994, citing it as one of the twentieth century's clearest demonstrations of architecture built to work with a landscape rather than against it, an approach that's gone on to shape cemetery design well beyond Sweden's borders. Lewerentz returned decades later still, in the 1960s, to design the Remembrance Garden, and a new crematorium by the architect Johan Celsing joined the site as recently as 2015, proof the place has never entirely stopped growing.

It's worth remembering, walking through, that this was never conceived as a place purely for mourning: it was designed, competition brief and all, as one continuous architectural statement about how a city holds both life and death within the same patch of ground.

Look for the Woodland Chapel itself, small and easy to walk straight past among the larger buildings — Asplund is buried in the cemetery he spent half his career designing, which feels like the right way for an architect to have the last word.

tours.title: Yasuragi Spa Hotel
tours.shortDescription: A Japanese bathhouse on the archipelago shore, with every room turned to face the water.
tours.longDescription: Hasseludden juts out into the archipelago here, and the hotel's low timber buildings follow the shoreline rather than rising above it — a deliberately quiet silhouette against the water and the pines behind, the whole site angled so that every wing stays within sight of Höggarnsfjärden rather than tucked behind the next building along. Yasuragi opened in 1997 around a single idea borrowed wholesale from Japan: the bathhouse, communal and ritualised, built for cleansing and stillness instead of treatments and appointments. That Japanese bath has remained the foundation of the place ever since, expanded repeatedly but never replaced by everything built up around it, and in 2017 the entire bath complex was rebuilt from the ground up specifically to move closer to authentic bathhouse tradition.

stops.title: Yasuragi Spa Hotel
stops.caption: Out here the water is called Höggarnsfjärden, and every one of the hotel's rooms has been built to face it.
stops.transcriptText:
Out here the water is called Höggarnsfjärden, and every one of the hotel's rooms has been built to face it.

Hasseludden juts out into the archipelago at this point, and the hotel's low timber buildings follow the shoreline rather than rising above it, a deliberately quiet silhouette against the water and the pine trees behind it, the whole site angled to keep every wing within sight of Höggarnsfjärden rather than tucked behind the next building along.

Yasuragi opened in 1997 around a single idea borrowed wholesale from Japan: the bathhouse, communal and ritualised, built for cleansing and stillness instead of treatments and appointments, and that Japanese bath has remained the actual foundation of the place ever since, expanded again and again but never replaced by everything built up around it. In 2017 the entire bath complex was rebuilt from the ground up specifically to move closer to authentic Japanese bathhouse tradition, a renovation overseen with architecture from Yoji Kasajima that deliberately lets the Nordic landscape outside show through the Japanese design inside, and the hotel's hundred and ninety-one rooms all still face the same fjord view regardless of which side of the building they're on. Three restaurants on site work from modern Japanese cooking rather than a watered-down hotel-buffet version of it, and guests move through the day in the robe-like yukata provided at check-in, a small ritual carried over wholesale, not softened for a Nordic audience.

The interesting bit is how deliberately hybrid the place is: it's not attempting to recreate Japan wholesale on a Swedish shoreline, and it's not diluting the bathhouse tradition into a generic Nordic spa either, it's holding both traditions at once, which is a harder trick than either extreme.

If you can manage it, get out to the outdoor pools right at dusk — the light off Höggarnsfjärden at that hour is the one part of the experience no renovation could ever really improve on.

tours.title: Östermalms Saluhall (Östermalm Food Hall)
tours.shortDescription: Seventeen traders under one red brick roof, and more than one will pour champagne with the oysters.
tours.longDescription: Östermalmstorg holds the hall, a red brick building with tall arched windows that has anchored this corner of Östermalm since 1888 — inside, the smell of smoked fish and fresh bread reaches the door before you do. Oscar II inaugurated it in 1888, the work of two architects splitting the job cleanly in two: Kasper Salin designed the cast iron frame and roof holding the whole structure up, while Isak Gustaf Clason, who would go on a few years later to design the much larger Nordiska museet across town, gave it the brick facade, borrowing the look of medieval brick market buildings from northern Germany. The hall is now listed, which made its most recent chapter a delicate operation: between 2016 and 2020 it was restored while the traders decanted to a temporary hall on the square outside.

stops.title: Östermalms Saluhall (Östermalm Food Hall)
stops.caption: Seventeen traders work under one red brick roof, and more than one of them will pour you champagne to go with your oysters.
stops.transcriptText:
Seventeen traders work under one red brick roof, and more than one of them will pour you champagne to go with your oysters.

Östermalmstorg holds the hall, a red brick building with tall arched windows that has anchored this corner of Östermalm since 1888 — inside, the smell of smoked fish and fresh bread reaches the door before you do.

King Oscar the Second inaugurated the hall in 1888, the work of two architects splitting the job cleanly in two: Kasper Salin designed the cast iron frame and roof holding the whole structure up, while Isak Gustaf Clason, who would go on a few years later to design the much larger Nordiska museet across town, gave it the brick facade, borrowing the look of medieval brick market buildings from northern Germany. The hall is now a listed building, which made its most recent chapter a genuinely delicate operation: between 2016 and 2020, every trader moved out into a temporary pavilion across the square while the original structure was completely gutted and rebuilt from the inside, then reopened looking, deliberately, almost exactly as it had before.

What's inside now is less a market than a very good excuse to eat standing up: seventeen specialist traders, several with their own small bar built into the counter, selling everything from fresh herring and smoked salmon to game meats you won't find in an ordinary supermarket, and a fair number of stalls where you can simply order a plate and a glass and eat right there, elbow to elbow with strangers doing the same thing.

Most cities with a market hall this old have let it drift toward tourist theatre, all photo opportunities and overpriced souvenirs. Östermalmshallen has mostly avoided that, because the people buying lunch here on any given Tuesday are still, largely, locals doing their actual shopping — the atmosphere just happens to be considerably fancier than the job strictly requires.

Find a counter with stools rather than a table, order whatever the trader recommends without asking too many questions, and you'll get roughly the same lunch Stockholmers have been having in this exact spot for well over a century.

tours.title: Bedrock Caverns: The Subway Art Itinerary
tours.shortDescription: Six stations along what is often called the world's longest art gallery, from the end of the line to a hanging dodecahedron.
tours.longDescription: Stockholm's metro is routinely described as the world's longest art gallery, and well over ninety of its hundred-odd stations carry some form of art — most of it added station by station since the 1950s rather than planned as one grand scheme. This itinerary takes six of them in sequence, and it is a ride rather than a walk: it begins at Akalla, the raw ochre cave that was the literal dead end of the Blue Line for decades, and works back toward the centre. Solna centrum's ceiling burns red above a dying spruce forest running unbroken for the better part of a kilometre. Rådhuset is tinted salmon pink and decorated to look like archaeology someone buried and forgot. T-Centralen is the blue-and-white vine ceiling that is very likely the most photographed room in Sweden's transport network. Stadion arcs a rainbow across a deep blue vault, and Tekniska högskolan hangs a twelve-sided solid above the platform to represent an element that officially does not exist.

stops.title: Akalla
stops.caption: It's the fifth of June, 1977, and this raw ochre cave is about to open as the new end of the line.
stops.transcriptText:
It's the fifth of June, 1977, and this raw ochre cave is about to open as the new end of the line.

You're standing at the platform's northern end, where the rock overhead hasn't been smoothed or tiled so much as left the colour it came out of the ground: a warm, dusty ochre, blasted rather than built, with the drill marks from construction still visible if you look closely at the walls.

Set into that rock are ceramic pictures by the artist Birgit Ståhl-Nyberg, made the same year the station opened, and they're worth spending a minute with: ordinary scenes of daily life, leisure and work, rendered not as a grand civic statement but as something closer to a neighbourhood scrapbook, optimistic in exactly the unguarded way the mid-1970s tended to be about new housing estates and new transport lines reaching the edge of the city. Akalla was built, quite literally, at the edge — this was the actual end of the Blue Line for decades, the last stop before the tunnel simply ran out, and it's only now, with a new extension toward Barkarby under construction and its tunnel completed in early 2025, that Akalla is finally becoming a station people pass through rather than a station people turn around in.

There's something fitting about starting a tour of what's often called the world's longest art gallery at its literal dead end: no grand entrance hall, no famous vault, just raw rock and pictures of ordinary people going about ordinary days, exactly the kind of art you'd expect from a station built for a new estate rather than a landmark. Well over ninety of the network's hundred-odd stations carry some form of art or decoration by now, most of it added station by station since the 1950s rather than planned as one grand scheme from the start, and Akalla is as good a place as any to see that approach in its plainest, least self-conscious form.

From here, ride the blue line toward the city centre — Solna centrum is a handful of stops down the line, and the contrast, once you're standing under its ceiling, could hardly be greater.

stops.title: Solna centrum
stops.caption: The ceiling above you is painted like a sky on fire, and the forest running along the walls underneath it is already dying.
stops.transcriptText:
The ceiling above you is painted like a sky on fire, and the forest running along the walls underneath it is already dying.

The platform curves gently here, cut straight into the bedrock and painted a deep, saturated red from end to end, with a green spruce forest silhouette running along the lower walls for close to a kilometre in either direction — one continuous, unbroken tree line rather than a repeated pattern.

The artists Anders Åberg and Karl-Olov Björk originally planned something considerably calmer, but found the bare red-and-green scheme too sparse once they saw it in place, so they began improvising directly onto the rock, cutting small peep-show openings into the painted forest that reveal individual scenes when you stop and look through them. Those scenes tell the story of some of the most furiously debated issues of 1970s Sweden: environmental destruction, deforestation, and the slow emptying-out of the Swedish countryside as people moved to cities exactly like the one this train line was built to serve. The whole platform holds twenty-two separate painted locations in total, and in 2016 the BBC named Solna centrum's ceiling one of the ten most beautiful in the world, a strange kind of fame for a piece of public art that was, at its core, a protest. None of it was commissioned as protest art in any formal sense — Åberg and Björk were simply given a bare rock ceiling and told to fill it, and filled it with whatever was on the news that year instead.

And that's really the thing worth sitting with here: this is a working transit platform doubling as a piece of 1970s political theatre, thousands of commuters walking beneath a burning sky and a dying forest every single day, most of them almost certainly not reading it as the argument it was originally painted to be. The forest itself never gets a happy ending painted back in, either — the artists left the loss standing, rather than resolving it into something more comfortable for people just trying to catch a train.

Stay on the blue line heading toward the city centre — Rådhuset is a couple of stops further on, and its rock face changes colour entirely once you arrive.

stops.title: Rådhuset
stops.caption: Everything decorating this platform is designed to look like rubbish someone buried a thousand years ago and forgot about.
stops.transcriptText:
Everything decorating this platform is designed to look like rubbish someone buried a thousand years ago and forgot about.

Look around at the rock face itself, tinted a warm salmon pink rather than the ochre or red you'll have seen at the last couple of stops, a colour the artist Sigvard Olsson chose deliberately, modelled, he said, on the pink rock of North Africa's Atlas Mountains and reimagined as something that might plausibly turn up beneath Stockholm instead.

Olsson finished the station in 1975 and named it, like the courthouse standing directly above it on Kungsholmen, for the word rådhuset, meaning town hall, and he built the entire decorative scheme around a single idea: that everyday objects sink slowly into soft earth over centuries and eventually resurface somewhere unexpected. Scattered across seven locations along the platform, you'll find birchwood, an old gate, a pair of galoshes, even a chimney, all rendered as though they'd been excavated mid-dig, fragments of Kungsholmen's own buried history caught in the act of resurfacing. It's a quietly clever choice of imagery for a station sitting directly beneath a courthouse — a building whose entire purpose upstairs is digging up evidence and turning over what's been buried, whether that's a legal case or, down here, somebody's old boots. Olsson himself trained across several disciplines before settling into this kind of work, as a painter, playwright and stage designer as much as a visual artist, and that theatrical instinct is arguably why the objects here feel staged rather than simply displayed, each one caught mid-emergence rather than laid out flat for inspection.

What's worth noticing is how differently "archaeology" reads depending on which floor you're standing on: upstairs it means facts, testimony, judgment; down here, in Olsson's version, it just means objects that got lost and came back, no verdict required.

T-Centralen is the very next stop on the blue line — no need to change platforms, just one stop and you're standing in the busiest, most photographed room in the entire network.

stops.title: T-Centralen
stops.caption: You are standing in what's very likely the single most photographed room in Sweden's entire transport network.
stops.transcriptText:
You are standing in what's very likely the single most photographed room in Sweden's entire transport network.

Blue Line platforms run beneath a vaulted rock ceiling here, painted entirely blue and white in a rolling pattern of vines and leaves that follows the natural curve of the stone rather than sitting flat against it, the paint tracing every bump and dip the bedrock happened to leave behind when it was blasted out.

The artist behind it, Per Olof Ultvedt, completed the work in 1975 as part of the Blue Line's twenty-five-and-a-half-kilometre opening stretch between Kungsträdgården and Akalla, and he came to the job from an unusual direction: Ultvedt was best known for kinetic, mechanical sculpture, and had spent the previous decade as part of the team behind "Hon — en katedral," a giant walk-in sculpture of a reclining woman that briefly filled an entire hall of Stockholm's Moderna Museet in 1966. That background shows here in the way the vines seem to move rather than simply decorate, flowing across the rock like something built to run rather than something painted to sit still, an oddly organic gesture for a station whose entire job is shuttling several hundred thousand people through a hole in the ground every single day. Look closely near the escalators and you'll find small silhouetted figures worked into the pattern too, tucked in among the leaves rather than announced, exactly the sort of detail a sculptor used to building things you walk around, rather than simply look at, would think to leave behind.

And that's the pivot worth holding onto as you stand here: T-Centralen is simultaneously the calmest, most contemplative artwork on this itinerary and the system's single busiest pinch point, proof that a genuinely great piece of public art doesn't need a quiet room to work in.

Transfer here to the red line, direction Mörby centrum — Stadion is two stops out, and you'll know you've arrived the moment the ceiling changes colour above you.

stops.title: Stadion
stops.caption: Above you, a rainbow runs the length of the ceiling, painted onto a sky so deeply blue it could almost pass for the real thing.
stops.transcriptText:
Above you, a rainbow runs the length of the ceiling, painted onto a sky so deeply blue it could almost pass for the real thing.

The vault overhead is an intense, saturated blue from wall to wall, and directly ahead of you the rainbow itself arcs from one side of the platform to the other in bright, distinct bands of colour, the single largest gesture on this whole itinerary and very possibly the most photographed.

The artists Enno Hallek and Åke Pallarp completed it in 1973, the same year the station opened as part of the extension carrying the line out to Tekniska högskolan, and their idea was straightforwardly poetic: a rainbow, painted directly onto an underground ceiling, to suggest that daylight and open sky are never really as far away as a train platform two storeys underground might make them feel. Stadion sits directly beneath the Olympic Stadium built for the 1912 Summer Games, and the station leans into that history too, displaying the original 1912 Games poster alongside smaller sporting references scattered along the platform — bandy shields, the colours of the local football club Djurgården — a whole scrapbook of what's actually happened on the pitch above your head for well over a century. In the decades since it was painted, the rainbow has also taken on a second life the artists likely never planned for: it's become one of the city's best-known unofficial backdrops for Stockholm Pride, a meaning layered on top of the original rather than built into it, but no less real for that. Both Hallek and Pallarp came to the commission as painters first, which is part of why the whole vault reads more like a canvas stretched overhead than a piece of architecture, colour doing the entire job that carved stone or mosaic tends to do elsewhere on this itinerary.

One more stop on the red line, same direction, brings you to Tekniska högskolan — the final platform on this itinerary, and arguably the strangest one.

stops.title: Tekniska högskolan
stops.caption: There's a twelve-sided solid hanging from the ceiling here, suspended above the platform to represent an element that, officially, doesn't exist.
stops.transcriptText:
There's a twelve-sided solid hanging from the ceiling here, suspended above the platform to represent an element that, officially, doesn't exist.

This station's ceiling and walls follow the natural bedrock rather than a poured, uniform tunnel, one of the earliest of Stockholm's genuine "cave stations," and the design won Sweden's Kasper Salin architecture prize the same year it opened, in 1973, an unusual honour for a piece of public transport infrastructure.

The artist Lennart Mörk built the whole scheme around the university sitting directly overhead, the Royal Institute of Technology, known locally as KTH, and rather than reaching for circuit boards or test tubes, he reached backward instead: Newton's apple appears rendered on the rock, the wings of Icarus stretch across another section, and quotations drawn from the long history of science run along the walls in among them. The centrepiece is that suspended dodecahedron overhead, a twelve-faced solid taken from the five Platonic shapes the ancient Greeks believed underpinned the physical world, and in that old classical system it stood specifically for aether — the fifth element, the invisible substance once thought to fill the space between everything else, later disproved and quietly dropped from physics altogether. The other four Platonic solids, standing in for earth, water, air and fire, are worked into the station too, scattered across the walls and floor rather than gathered in one obvious spot, so the full set only really reveals itself if you walk the platform end to end.

And here's the thing to end the itinerary on: a station built for one of Europe's leading technical universities, and asked to represent science, chose classical philosophy and a discredited element over anything resembling modern engineering — reaching into the history of being wrong about the universe rather than the history of getting it right.

The KTH campus itself is right outside the entrance if you'd like to keep the theme going above ground — but before you go, look along the walls for the actual Newton quotation carved into the rock, easy to miss under that hanging dodecahedron.

tours.title: Gamla stan
tours.shortDescription: Four stops through the old town, from a palace with 1,430 rooms to a shop full of worlds nobody lived in.
tours.longDescription: A short walk of a few hundred metres through the oldest part of Stockholm, running downhill from the Royal Palace to Västerlånggatan. It starts at Kungliga slottet, a long pale Baroque block of some one thousand four hundred and thirty rooms, only around six hundred and sixty of which have a window. It stops at Storkyrkan, the cathedral, for a carved knight spearing a dragon whose horns are made from real elk antlers. It crosses Stortorget, the old market square lined with tall gabled merchant houses, framed at one end by the Stock Exchange where the Swedish Academy still meets to choose the Nobel Prize in Literature — and marked, for a few days in November 1520, by events that gave the square its darker name. It ends deliberately lighter, at a bookshop on Västerlånggatan devoted entirely to worlds nobody actually lived in.

stops.title: The Royal Palace (Kungliga slottet)
stops.caption: One thousand four hundred and thirty rooms, and only around six hundred and sixty of them actually have a window.
stops.transcriptText:
One thousand four hundred and thirty rooms, and only around six hundred and sixty of them actually have a window.

The palace spreads out in front of you as a long, pale Baroque block, three storeys of brick and sandstone arranged around a central courtyard, considerably more restrained on the outside than a building this large usually bothers to be.

A fire destroyed the medieval castle that stood here, Tre Kronor, on the seventh of May 1697, and the architect Nicodemus Tessin the Younger began designing its replacement that same year, only for the costly Great Northern War to halt construction in 1709. Work resumed in 1727, continued under Carl Hårleman after Tessin died the following year, and the royal family finally moved in on the seventh of December 1754 — though the interiors kept absorbing money and craftsmanship for another two decades, and the palace wasn't formally declared complete until 1771, seventy-four years after the fire that started it all. A facade restoration is underway right now, addressing sandstone quarried on Gotland that's been quietly weathering for three centuries, and it isn't expected to finish until 2050.

What's easy to assume, standing here, is that this is where the King actually lives — and it isn't. Carl the Sixteenth Gustaf and Queen Silvia live at Drottningholm, out on the water; this building is where the monarchy works, housing offices for the King and the Royal Court alongside four separate museums, among them the Royal Armoury with its collection of coronation carriages and ceremonial dress, and around eight hundred thousand visitors a year, closer to a very grand government building than anyone's actual home. The changing of the guard still happens here daily regardless, a piece of genuine, functioning ceremony rather than a re-enactment staged purely for visitors.

Storkyrkan stands just a short walk from here, and inside it you'll find one of the strangest, most political pieces of religious art anywhere in Sweden — a dragon with real antlers.

stops.title: Storkyrkan
stops.caption: There's a dragon inside this cathedral, and its horns are made from real elk antlers.
stops.transcriptText:
There's a dragon inside this cathedral, and its horns are made from real elk antlers.

The brick exterior gives very little away, a plain medieval facade that could belong to almost any northern European church, but once you're through the doors, look for the large carved group standing to one side: a knight on horseback, spearing a dragon coiled beneath him.

The sculpture dates to around 1490 and arrived in Stockholm the year before, traditionally credited to the German master craftsman Bernt Notke of Lübeck, though no surviving document actually confirms his hand on it. It's carved largely from oak, but built up with genuine elk antlers for the dragon's horns, metal for the horse's saddle and bridle, leather strips standing in for armour, and gemstones set into the gilding, a mix of materials well beyond what plain woodcarving alone could achieve. The scene depicts Saint George, dressed pointedly in Swedish blue and yellow, and it commemorates a real battle rather than only a legend: the Swedish regent Sten Sture's victory over the Danish King Christian the First at Brunkeberg in 1471, with Sture himself said to have prayed to Saint George beforehand. Sture was briefly buried inside the sculpture after his death, and it doubled as a reliquary too, with small compartments built in to hold relics associated with the saint, his own water-lily coat of arms carved into the base as a final, unmistakable signature. The cathedral around it is still a working church rather than a museum piece in its own right, and it's hosted royal weddings and coronations for centuries, including as recently as this current king's own wedding in 1976.

And that's really the thing worth knowing before you leave: this isn't devotional art in any simple sense, it's fifteenth-century political messaging carved in oak, Sweden cast as the besieged town, Denmark cast as the dragon, and Saint George doing exactly what Sture's own propaganda needed a national hero to do.

Step outside and you're standing a few metres from Stortorget, the square where the other side of that same rivalry between Sweden and Denmark would end far less symbolically, less than fifty years later.

stops.title: Stortorget
stops.caption: The square in front of you, lined with narrow, brightly painted merchant houses, looks like one of the gentlest corners of the old town — and for a few days in November 1520, it was the opposite of that.
stops.transcriptText:
The square in front of you, lined with narrow, brightly painted merchant houses, looks like one of the gentlest corners of the old town — and for a few days in November 1520, it was the opposite of that.

You're standing in Stortorget, Stockholm's old market square, framed on every side by those tall gabled facades, with the cathedral you've just left rising just behind you and the Stock Exchange building at the far end, the same building where the Swedish Academy still meets each year to choose the winner of the Nobel Prize in Literature.

In September 1520, the Danish king Christian the Second conquered Stockholm and was crowned King of Sweden, and during the coronation festivities Archbishop Gustav Trolle accused a group of Swedish noblemen, loyal to the deposed regent Sten Sture the Younger, of heresy. Close to a hundred people, bishops, councillors and noblemen among them, were publicly executed in this square over the days that followed, a purge broad and indiscriminate enough that even a man reported to have simply wept at what he was witnessing was put to death alongside them. Christian the Second's reputation in Sweden never recovered from what happened here, and decades later Gustav Vasa, who would go on to lead Sweden's revolt against Danish rule, used vivid propaganda images of the massacre to help rally support for the war that followed.

That war ended the Kalmar Union entirely and put Gustav Vasa on the throne as Sweden's first modern king in 1523, which makes this ordinary, picturesque square, whatever you make of the history debated around Christian's later reputation, something close to the site where modern Sweden actually began. None of that history announces itself today: on an ordinary afternoon the square is simply full of café tables and tourists photographing the coloured facades, the old market function long since replaced by something considerably gentler.

Walk down Västerlånggatan from here, and after several centuries of kings, cathedrals and executions, the next stop offers something considerably lighter.

stops.title: The Science Fiction Bookstore
stops.caption: After six centuries of kings, dragons and executions, here's something considerably lighter: a shop devoted entirely to worlds nobody actually lived in.
stops.transcriptText:
After six centuries of kings, dragons and executions, here's something considerably lighter: a shop devoted entirely to worlds nobody actually lived in.

Västerlånggatan carries you here along one of Gamla Stan's oldest medieval streets, and the shopfront sits among centuries-old stone buildings, giving no real hint from outside of just how much is packed into the shelves within.

The shop opened in 1978, which makes it very nearly as old a fixture of this street as some of its neighbours are, in its own considerably younger way, and it's grown well beyond its original brief: alongside the science fiction, fantasy and horror titles, you'll find board games, tabletop role-playing games, comics, manga, collectible card games, and enough plush toys and film merchandise to fill several rooms. The staff have built a genuine reputation for actually knowing the material rather than simply stocking it, reading the books, watching the films, and playing the games they sell, which means a specific, slightly obscure recommendation is usually just a question away rather than a guess. The shop also hosts regular author signings and events, keeping it a working part of Stockholm's genre fiction scene rather than a static shrine to it, and nearly half a century in business now makes it something of a landmark in its own right, however deliberately unserious the subject matter is compared with everything else on this walk.

There's a nice symmetry in ending a walk through so much verified, occasionally brutal history at a shop built entirely around the opposite instinct, imagined futures and invented worlds, sitting on one of the most genuinely old streets you'll have walked all day.

Västerlånggatan keeps going in both directions from here, lined with more shops, cafés and courtyards than any single afternoon can really cover, so let whatever's caught your eye on the way decide where you wander next.

tours.title: Drottningholm
tours.shortDescription: The royal island in three parts: the palace, an eighteenth-century theatre that still works, and a pavilion built as a surprise.
tours.longDescription: A walk of roughly a kilometre through the grounds of the royal residence on Lovön, taking the island in three parts. The palace came after the one before it burned to the ground in 1661, and faces a formal forecourt in pale stone and steep dark roofs with the kind of strict symmetry only French-trained taste produced. The Court Theatre gives away nothing from outside — a plain low country-manor exterior with no columns and no dome, exactly as its architect intended — while behind that facade the original eighteenth-century stage machinery still changes an entire scene in about six seconds. The walk ends well back from the formal gardens at Kina slott, the golden-yellow Chinese Pavilion built as a birthday surprise for a queen, and handed over by a seven-year-old boy dressed as a mandarin carrying a golden key.

stops.title: Drottningholm Palace
stops.caption: It's 1661, and the palace that used to stand on this island has just burned to the ground.
stops.transcriptText:
It's 1661, and the palace that used to stand on this island has just burned to the ground.

The current building faces you across a formal forecourt, pale stone and steep dark roofs arranged with the kind of strict symmetry that only French-trained taste could produce, a facade built to be looked at from a distance before it's ever walked through.

Queen Dowager Hedwig Eleonora bought the estate the same year the old palace burned, and brought in the architect Nicodemus Tessin the Elder to rebuild it from nothing, work that began the following year and stretched on for two decades. Tessin died in 1681 with the exteriors largely finished but the interiors still unresolved, and it was his son, Nicodemus Tessin the Younger, who inherited the commission and spent years afterward completing the rooms inside, a genuinely two-generation project rather than one architect's single vision. UNESCO, when it added Drottningholm to the World Heritage list in 1991, called it the finest surviving example of a northern European royal residence built in direct imitation of Versailles, and the palace earns that comparison twice over in its gardens: a strict Baroque parterre laid out under Hedwig Eleonora at the end of the seventeenth century on one side, and a looser, deliberately wandering English landscape garden that Gustav the Third commissioned generations later on the other, two completely different ideas about nature sitting side by side on the same estate.

What's easy to miss, given how museum-like the grounds can feel, is that Drottningholm isn't a preserved relic in the way most palaces this old are: King Carl the Sixteenth Gustaf and Queen Silvia have lived in the southern wing since 1981, which makes this one of the very few royal residences in Europe where the family upstairs and the paying visitors downstairs are, quite literally, under the same roof.

The Court Theatre stands just a few minutes' walk from here, plain enough from the outside that you could easily mistake it for a stable block — which is rather the point, once you're inside.

stops.title: Drottningholm Court Theatre (Drottningholms Slottsteater)
stops.caption: Six seconds. That's how long the original eighteenth-century machinery backstage here still takes to change an entire scene, start to finish.
stops.transcriptText:
Six seconds. That's how long the original eighteenth-century machinery backstage here still takes to change an entire scene, start to finish.

From the outside, the building gives away nothing at all — a plain, low, country-manor exterior with no columns, no dome, no hint that an opera house is sitting behind that unremarkable facade, which is exactly how its architect wanted it.

A German master builder named Georg Greggenhofer completed the first theatre here in 1754, only for it to burn down eight years later, and Queen Lovisa Ulrika commissioned the architect Carl Fredrik Adelcrantz to rebuild it, work that began in 1764. Adelcrantz gave the interior an illusion of wealth the crown's actual budget couldn't quite stretch to: trompe l'oeil painting, papier-mâché, and stucco, designed by Adrien Masreliez to mimic marble and gilding that was never really there. What survives backstage matters even more than the decoration: a chariot-and-pole system, wave machines, thunder effects, and flying apparatus for the kind of last-minute divine rescues eighteenth-century opera loved, much of it possibly designed by the Italian engineer Donato Stopani, and still operational today, exactly as installed. After King Gustav the Third's assassination in 1792 the theatre simply stopped being used and became a storeroom, gathering dust for over a century until the theatre historian Agne Beijer rediscovered it in 1921 and found the stucco and original wallpaper essentially untouched underneath the clutter.

And that's really the pivot worth sitting with: this theatre survived intact precisely because nobody bothered renovating it for a hundred and thirty years — neglect turned out to be the best preservation strategy anyone could have planned. Today the Drottningholm Theatre Museum runs a summer opera festival on that same stage, favouring Haydn, Handel, Gluck and Mozart performed on period instruments, so the machinery Beijer found gathering dust is now back in nightly use rather than sitting behind a rope as a museum piece.

Adelcrantz was working on a second commission for Lovisa Ulrika at almost exactly the same time: walk through the gardens toward the Chinese Pavilion, a genuine hidden gem tucked well off the main path, and you'll find his other Drottningholm building waiting at the far end.

stops.title: The Chinese Pavilion (Kina slott)
stops.caption: Here's what most day-trippers to Drottningholm miss entirely: a seven-year-old boy, dressed as a Chinese mandarin, once handed a golden key to a queen who genuinely believed she'd stepped into a fairy tale.
stops.transcriptText:
Here's what most day-trippers to Drottningholm miss entirely: a seven-year-old boy, dressed as a Chinese mandarin, once handed a golden key to a queen who genuinely believed she'd stepped into a fairy tale.

The path through the park brings you to a low golden-yellow building set well back from the main palace, deliberately tucked out of sight of the formal gardens, exactly the kind of secluded pleasure pavilion an eighteenth-century monarch would build for a surprise rather than a state occasion.

King Adolf Fredrik commissioned the very first version of this building as a birthday gift for Queen Lovisa Ulrika, unveiled on the twenty-fourth of July, 1753, with their young son, the future King Gustav the Third, presenting her with the key while costumed as a Chinese official. Lovisa Ulrika wrote to her mother afterwards that she'd been astonished to find herself suddenly inside a fairy tale, delighted that the king had built her an entire Chinese castle in secret. That first pavilion, though, was a prefabricated wooden structure assembled using log-cabin techniques, and it rotted through within a decade in Sweden's damp climate, forcing a full replacement in stone between 1763 and 1769, designed by Carl Fredrik Adelcrantz, the same architect responsible for the Court Theatre nearby. Inside, the interior designer Jean Eric Rehn filled the rooms with Swedish Rococo furniture built to look Chinese alongside genuine imported lacquer, silk, and porcelain, and the Yellow Room in particular still carries lacquered panels depicting the trading posts of Canton, tangible evidence of a China most Swedes at the time knew only through objects like these.

One nearby building, the aptly named Confidence, took the fantasy of total privacy even further, with a dining table on a lift mechanism that could be lowered to the kitchen below and raised again fully laid, so royal guests could eat an entire meal without a single servant ever entering the room.

Wander the wider gardens back toward the harbour when you're ready to leave — the walk retraces almost the entire arc of this tour, from formal French symmetry to English wilderness to this last, most private fantasy of all.

places.name: Centraal Station
places.description: Pierre Cuypers' 1889 terminus stands on three artificial islands and some 8,600 wooden piles, its turreted red brick deliberately echoing the Rijksmuseum he had just finished. Putting it here walled the old city off from the water it was built on.

places.name: Dam Square
places.description: The medieval dam across the Amstel stood here, and the city that grew up behind it took the structure's name. The Royal Palace on the western side went up in the 1660s as a town hall, on some thirteen thousand piles driven into the marsh.

places.name: Rijksmuseum
places.description: Cuypers' 1885 palace holds eight hundred years of Dutch art, and its plan makes one argument: the Gallery of Honour narrows and rises until it delivers you to The Night Watch and nothing else.

places.name: Waterlooplein
places.description: A flea market has traded on this square since the nineteenth century, in what was the heart of Amsterdam's Jewish Quarter. Rembrandt's house stands a minute away — the one he bought at the height of his fame and lost to his creditors.

places.name: Westerkerk
places.description: Hendrick de Keyser's church was finished in 1631, and its tower is still the tallest in Amsterdam, crowned with the blue imperial crown of Maximilian. Rembrandt was buried somewhere inside it, poor, in a grave nobody marked.

places.name: Brandenburg Gate
places.description: Built in 1791 as a gate of peace, and marched through, sealed off and claimed by everyone who has held the city since. Pariser Platz around it sat inside the border strip for twenty-eight years, reachable from neither side.

places.name: Hackesche Höfe
places.description: One handsome facade on Rosenthaler Strasse, and behind it eight courtyards chained together the full depth of the block. The first is August Endell's showpiece — glazed brick in blue, cream and gold patterned all the way to the rooflines.

places.name: Oberbaumbrücke
places.description: The two towers mid-span guard nothing and never did: when Berlin ran its elevated railway across the Spree in 1896 it dressed the crossing in brick Gothic, battlements and all. For twenty-eight years afterwards the water beneath was the border.

places.name: Potsdamer Platz
places.description: Busy enough in the 1920s to need one of continental Europe's first traffic lights, put up here in a five-sided tower in 1924. The war flattened it and the Wall kept it empty; everything standing now arrived after 1990.

places.name: Al Shindagha
places.description: Where the creek meets the open sea, on the oldest ground in Dubai's story — the quarter the ruling family settled, and where the ruler still lived in a coral-stone house until 1958. More than twenty of those houses have been restored, wind towers and all.

places.name: The Marina Walk
places.description: None of this water is natural. In the early 2000s engineers cut a channel some three and a half kilometres through open desert and let the Gulf in to fill it; the towers arrived afterwards, ring by ring.

places.name: The Textile Souk
places.description: A straight shaded street under a restored timber arcade, running back from the abra station on the Bur Dubai bank. Silk, cotton and pashmina by the bolt, in a market laid out so strangers from opposite ends of the sea could reach a price.

places.name: Walt Disney Concert Hall
places.description: Gehry's 2003 hall wraps a world-class auditorium in sails of brushed stainless steel that throw the downtown light around. Inside it turns warm — a Douglas-fir room, and an organ whose splayed silver ranks earned it the nickname the french fries.

places.name: Dorchester Square
places.description: The Sun Life Building rises behind the square in granite tiers, and when its last phase was finished in 1931 it was the largest building by floor space in the British Empire. In 1940 its vault took Britain's gold reserves for safekeeping, and nobody on the square was told.

places.name: Notre-Dame Basilica
places.description: Place d'Armes sets the Gothic front of the basilica against the Roman portico of the Bank of Montreal directly opposite, with Maisonneuve, who founded the city in 1642, on a pedestal between them. Faith on one side and money on the other, since 1847.

places.name: Square Saint-Louis
places.description: Named for the Saint-Louis brothers, the businessmen who developed the blocks around it — a real estate play from the start. Rows of 1880s greystones dressed with turrets and gingerbread face a leafy rectangle of park, painted in colours no Victorian would recognise.

places.name: Largo di Torre Argentina
places.description: Four temples of the Roman Republic sit several metres below the modern street, in a hole the twentieth century opened by accident. Nobody ever settled which gods most of them served, so they are still known by letters.

places.name: Piazza del Popolo
places.description: For centuries this was Rome's front door: travellers from the north came through the gate on the far side, and this was the first thing the city showed them — arranged entirely with that in mind. The obelisk at the centre was carved for Ramses II three thousand years ago.

places.name: The Circus Maximus
places.description: The largest venue for live entertainment ever built, and today an open field in a valley. A hundred and fifty thousand people filled the banks on either side; the grass you walk on was tiers of stone and timber.

places.name: The Colosseum
places.description: Nearly fifty metres of travertine still stands on the north side, pocked with thousands of square holes. They are the sockets of some three hundred tonnes of iron clamps, mined out by a medieval city that needed the metal more than the monument.

places.name: Art Gallery of Ontario
places.description: A 180-metre curve of Douglas fir and glass along Dundas West, wrapped around the Grange, the 1817 house the gallery grew out of. Gehry was born a few blocks away and played in the park behind it; this was his first building in Canada.

places.name: CN Tower
places.description: Five hundred and fifty-three metres of self-climbing concrete balanced on a Y-shaped footing with no guy-wires, put up in 1976 to fix the city's television reception. It held the world height record for thirty-two years.

places.name: Royal Ontario Museum
places.description: Canada's largest museum has an argument welded to its corner at Bloor and Avenue Road: carved stone from 1914 meeting Daniel Libeskind's glass Crystal from 2007, five interlocking volumes with almost no right angles. The seam where they meet is the most honest thing on the block.

places.name: Union Station
places.description: Twenty-two columns run longer than a city block along Front Street, finished in 1927 just as the automobile arrived to make railway cathedrals obsolete. Inside, the Great Hall lifts a barrel vault some twenty-six metres over Tennessee marble.

places.name: American Museum of Natural History
places.description: One city block on the Upper West Side, with four public faces that were never meant to agree. J. Cleaveland Cady's rough pink Milford granite on 77th Street was the front door for thirty-six years; the Beaux-Arts arch on Central Park West replaced it as a state memorial to Theodore Roosevelt, whose equestrian statue came down in January 2022 and left the pedestal empty. On 81st Street a glass cube holds the Hayden Planetarium's aluminium sphere, and on Columbus Avenue Jeanne Gang's Gilder Center opened in 2023 with almost no straight lines in it. Most visitors only ever see the inside.

places.name: Green-Wood Cemetery
places.description: Four hundred and seventy-eight acres of landscaped hills, ponds and mausoleums, laid out in 1838 on the highest natural ground in Brooklyn — before New York had public parks at all. By the 1850s half a million people came each year, second only to Niagara Falls, and the crowds were part of what convinced the city it needed a Central Park; Frederick Law Olmsted walked these paths before he drew that one. Richard Upjohn's Gothic Revival brownstone gate still opens onto it from Fifth Avenue. Six hundred thousand people are buried here, among them Leonard Bernstein, Jean-Michel Basquiat, Samuel Morse, Louis Comfort Tiffany and Boss Tweed. The cemetery is still active, and increasingly a public space again.

places.name: Oedo Antique Market
places.description: Twice a month the long outdoor plaza of the Tokyo International Forum fills with two hundred and fifty licensed dealers, beneath the elliptical glass hall Rafael Viñoly finished in 1996. The market opened in September 2003 for the four-hundredth anniversary of the Edo shogunate, with a deliberate brief — not a flea market but a professional fair whose dealers could account for what they sold. Around fifteen thousand people come to each edition, which makes it the largest outdoor antique market in Japan: Edo-period lacquerware three tables from Victorian clocks, ukiyo-e sharing a run with European jewellery, in the plaza of a working convention centre.

linkPins.longDescription: 🦑The American Museum of Natural History’s Sperm Whale and Giant Squid Diorama is one of the Museum’s most captivating dioramas. The darkness of this diorama is deliberate—to approximate the pitch-black conditions of the deep ocean where no sunlight penetrates. And, unlike other dioramas in the Museum, this one has no glass. Why? Reflections created a mirror effect against the scene’s dark interior, leading visitors to think the diorama was empty. #museum #nyc #stem #marinebiology #animals

linkPins.title: Poché - Studio Gang | episode 2 of 3 Completed in May 202…
linkPins.longDescription: Poché - Studio Gang | episode 2 of 3 Completed in May 2023, Studio Gang’s Richard Gilder Center for Science, Education, and Innovation is a 230,000-square-foot addition to New York’s American Museum of Natural History. Studio Gang approached the building as an act of architectural grafting: rather than creating an isolated object, the addition stitches together a museum campus that had accumulated over 150 years. It creates 33 connections to 10 existing buildings, replacing dead ends with continuous circulation. The design is conceived as a geological landscape shaped by wind, water, erosion, and flow. Its five-story Griffin Atrium forms the heart of the building, resembling a canyon whose irregular walls, bridges, stairs, and openings encourage exploration. The architecture was conceived from the inside out, with circulation and visual connections determining the building’s form. Its most significant innovation is structural. The canyon-like walls are load-bearing shotcrete, sprayed directly onto digitally modeled and custom-bent rebar without conventional formwork. This allowed Studio Gang and engineers Arup to achieve the non-repetitive curves economically while reducing construction waste. The technique was particularly appropriate to the museum because shotcrete was originally developed by museum naturalist Carl Akeley. Extensive mock-ups and digital modeling were required to resolve the complex geometry and construction process. Externally, the building uses Milford pink granite, echoing the museum’s historic Central Park West entrance, while its masonry courses reference Manhattan schist. This gives the contemporary addition a material relationship to its historic neighbors. The major challenge was therefore not simply creating an expressive form, but integrating structure, circulation, historic fabric, construction technology, and landscape into one coherent intervention. The result is a building where the architecture itself becomes part of the museum’s lesson about natural processes, scientific discovery, and exploration. ~poché: the space between #nycarchitecture #museumofnaturalhistory #studiogang #visitnyc

linkPins.title: At Quinta da Regaleira, nothing is accidental. Especially…
linkPins.longDescription: At Quinta da Regaleira, nothing is accidental. Especially the number nine. 🌀 ⠀ It appears in the architecture. In the descent. In the geometry of the space. Not loudly — subtly. The kind of detail most visitors walk straight past. The Initiation Well has nine platforms. Many connect this to Dante's nine circles of the Inferno. But in esoteric traditions, nine carries a deeper meaning: completion. The end of a cycle before something new begins. ⠀ Then there's another layer. Some interpretations suggest the well was designed for rituals involving eight participants surrounding one central figure. Eight witnesses. One initiate. Eight directions around a single axis. Eight plus one. Nine again. ⠀ At the bottom of the well, you don't find emptiness. You find a compass symbol set into the stone, marked with a cross. A point of orientation. If eight stand around and one stands at the centre, that centre becomes the axis — the point of transformation. The descent was never about going down. It was about alignment. And emergence into something new. ⠀ Olá, it's Peppe — Quinta da Regaleira is part of my private Sintra-Cascais tour: 🔗 www.portugaljourneyswithpeppe.com/sintra-cascais Because these are not just tours, they are Portugal Journeys with Peppe. linkPins.title: Did you know that perched at 763 meters in the Vosges, th…
linkPins.longDescription: Did you know that perched at 763 meters in the Vosges, there's a monastery that's been standing since 690 AD? Here's the story behind it. In 690 AD, a woman named Odile was born blind into the Alsatian nobility. Her father ordered her killed at birth. She survived, was raised in secret by nuns, and at her baptism she received her sight. She went on to found this monastery on top of the Vosges mountains, opened it to the poor and the sick, and never left. She died there in 720 AD. Her remains are still inside. Thirteen centuries later, the stained glass still catches the light. The corridors are cool and quiet. The courtyards, chapels and stone terraces feel frozen in time. And the views from the ramparts stretch over the Rhine Valley all the way to the German border — on a clear day, four countries. But the monastery is only part of it. Behind the gates, a forest path winds through a Via Crucis of stone chapels. And tucked against the outer walls, Merovingian tombs carved directly into the rock — older than the monastery itself, dating back to the 5th and 6th centuries. One thing to know: the road up can have snow and ice well into late March. Always check the forecast — winter tires are not optional on that mountain pass. Mont Sainte-Odile in the Vosges is the kind of place that carries weight. History, silence, and views most people don't even know exist. Save this for your next France trip. #montsainteodile #Alsace #hiddengem #francetravel #europehiddengems
